units.la: SYNOPSIS THEOLOGIÆ, ET SPECIATIM Oeconomiæ Fœderum Dei. LIBER V. De Messia, ejusque persona & statu. LOCUS TRIGESIMUS PRIMUS DE TESTAMENTO NOVO. CAPUT I. De natura Testamenti Novi.
units.tr: SYNOPSIS OF THEOLOGY, AND ESPECIALLY OF THE DISPENSATIONS OF GOD'S COVENANTS. BOOK V. On the Messiah, his person and his state. LOCUS THIRTY-FIRST: ON THE NEW TESTAMENT. CHAPTER I. On the nature of the New Testament.

units.la: I. ATque hactenus Ecclesiæ infantiam & adolescentiam, tardosque ejus auctus & incrementa vidimus, utque illa diu circa matrem suam luctata, ac Cananæae finibus conclusa fuerit; in quâ, difficili ministerio exercita, terrenæ istius hæreditatis pignus tractare, & templi umbris ac figuris sese oblectare, ac veluti per cancellos ejus, Salvatorem suum de longinquo tantum prospicere necesse habuit. Nunc vero clarior & il-lu-
units.tr: I. So far we have seen the infancy and adolescence of the Church, and its slow growth and increase: how it struggled for a long time around its mother and was confined within the borders of Canaan. Exercised in a difficult ministry, it had to handle the pledge of that earthly inheritance and take its delight in the shadows and figures of the temple, and, as if through its lattice, to look out only from afar upon its Saviour.

units.la: A lustrior rerum facies aperitur; &, fatis scse paulatim explicantibus, quicquid illa in occulto hastenus struxerant, in apertum producitur; & salutis humanæ opus dignissimo maximeque decoro Deo modo absolvitur. Estque hoc Ecclesiæ tempus longè beatissimum; quo illi Servatorem suum coram intueri ac amplecti, cunctaque quæ hactenus obscura ac velata fuerant, in puro liquidoque die pervidere datum fuit; postquam per adventum Messiæ discussæ nebulæ, remotæ umbræ, & quicquid ex veteri nocte reliquum erat, inducta luce & serenitate deletum est.
units.tr: Now, however, a clearer and brighter face of things is revealed. As the fates gradually unfold themselves, whatever the Church had hitherto built in secret is brought out into the open, and the work of human salvation is at last completed in a manner most worthy and most becoming to God. This is by far the most blessed time of the Church, in which it has been granted to see its Saviour face to face and embrace him, and to behold clearly in the pure and bright day all that had hitherto been obscure and veiled. Since the coming of the Messiah, the clouds have been scattered, the shadows removed, and whatever remained of the old night has been destroyed by the light and serenity that have been brought in.

units.la: II. Cujus gratiæ tempora tractaturi, omnemque ejus ordinem ac ambitum breviter perlustraturi, quædam in ipso limine 1. de Novi Testamenti naturâ; 2. bonis; 3. ejus initio primisque auspiciis prælibabimus.
units.tr: II. Intending to treat of the times of this grace and to survey briefly its whole order and scope, we shall first premise some matters at the very threshold: 1. concerning the nature of the New Testament; 2. concerning its goods; 3. concerning its beginning and first auspices.

units.la: III. Diversa dari Ecclesiæ tempora Apostolus manifesto innuit, cum Eph. 1: 10. τὴς οἰκονομίας τῶ πληρώματος χαίρων meminit. Fuit enim tempus præcedens τὴν ἀρεθεσίαν, statutum tempus, Hab. 2: 3. quod tempus severitatis, ac jugi, & cærimoniarum erat: ac tempus quod illud consecutum est, quod Scriptura appellat sæculum & mundum futurum, Hebr. 1: 6. & 2: 5. tempus videl. libertatis & gratiæ, ac beatum Nov. Test. sæculum.
units.tr: III. The apostle clearly indicates that there were different times of the Church, when he mentions "the dispensation of the fullness of the times" [οἰκονομίας τοῦ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν] (Eph. 1:10). For there was a preceding time, "the appointed time" [τὴν ἀρεθεσίαν] (Hab. 2:3), which was a time of severity, of yoke and of ceremonies; and there was the time that followed it, which Scripture calls "the age and the world to come" (Heb. 1:6; 2:5), namely the time of liberty and grace, the blessed age of the New Testament.

units.la: IV. Juxta quæ tempora diversa quoque Ecclesiæ fata fuere, ac diversum ejus regimen & œconomia. Ad prius tempus pertinet spes & expectatio Messiæ. Unde fideles ejus ætatis προφήτες dicuntur, qui ante speraverant, Eph. 1: 12. conf. Act. 26: 6, 7. Et nunc de ste promissionis, a Deo factâ ad patres, sto judicandus; ad quam duodecim tribus nostra sperant pervenire. Ad secundum, fides & gaudium de Christo revelato. Antequam autem venisset fides, sub lege custodiebamur conclusi in fidem, quæ futurum erat ut revelaretur. Gal. 3: 23. Quæ est œconomia Nov. T. de quâ nunc agendum.
units.tr: IV. According to these times, the fortunes of the Church also differed, and so did its government and economy. To the first time belongs the hope and expectation of the Messiah. Hence the faithful of that age are called prophets [προφῆται], "who had hoped beforehand" (Eph. 1:12; cf. Acts 26:6, 7): "And now I stand judged for the hope of the promise made by God to the fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain." To the second belongs faith and joy in the revealed Christ. "But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up to the faith which was to be revealed" (Gal. 3:23). This is the economy of the New Testament, of which we are now to speak.

units.la: V. Dicit autem Novum T. eam consilii Dei partem, quâ, exhibito tandem, ultimis temporibus Christo, interveniente ejus morte, perfectiora ac spiritualia bona Ecclesiæ largiri statuit, justitiam ac libertatem plenam, una cum mundi hæreditate, in hac vita; ac post illam, cœlestis Cananæ possessionem, intemeratam, nulloque terrestri pignore ac jugo vel latam. Duplex enim erat Dei propositum de hæreditate Ecclesiæ danda; aut duæ potius ejusdem propositi partes; prout Deus eam vel in typo, & sub umbris figurisque ostentare, interimque Ecclesiam suam exercere; vel nudam perfectamque
units.tr: V. The New Testament names that part of God's counsel by which he decided, once Christ had at last been manifested in the final times and his death had intervened, to bestow the more perfect and spiritual goods upon the Church: justice and full liberty, together with an inheritance of the world in this life, and after it the possession of the heavenly Canaan, unspoiled and not burdened by any earthly pledge or yoke. For there was a twofold purpose of God in giving the inheritance to the Church, or rather two parts of the same purpose: whether God chose to display it in a type and under shadows and figures, meanwhile exercising his Church; or to set it forth bare and perfect.

units.la: Quam Scriptura respiciens, duplex me moral tempus:
units.tr: Scripture, looking to this, marks out a twofold time:

units.la: ac proinde duplicem œconomiam.
units.tr: and therefore a twofold economy.

units.la: Quarum posterior pertinet ad TESTAMENTUM NOVUM, quod describitur. que exhibere decreverat. Ut latius tomo priore, lib. iv. c. i. explicatum dedimus.
units.tr: The latter of these belongs to the NEW TESTAMENT, which is described, and which he had decided to set forth, as we explained at more length in the earlier volume, book 4, chapter 1.

units.la: VI.Novum appellatur, cum temporis, tum praesertim successionis ratione; quod Veteri Test. antiquato, in locum ejus successerit. In eo, quod dixit Novum, antiquavit primum. Quod autem antiquatur & senescit, prope abolitionem est. Hebr. 8: 13. Post quod ulteriori innovationi ac tertio Testamento, locus nullus est, cum illud morte testatoris obsignatum & immutabile redditum sit: nisi ipsum Dei foedus inane, & decreta consiliaque ejus fluxa ac vana, & mortem denique Christi irritam ac nullo pretio statuas.
units.tr: VI. It is called New, both by reason of time and especially by reason of succession, because it has come in the place of the Old Testament, which has been made obsolete. "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away." (Heb. 8:13). After this there is no place for a further renewal or a third testament, since it has been sealed by the death of the testator and rendered unchangeable, unless you would make the covenant of God empty, his decrees and counsels fluid and vain, and finally the death of Christ void and of no worth.

units.la: VII. Promittitur hoc Testamentum Jer. 31: 31. Ecce dies veniunt, ait Jehovah; & pangam cum domo Israel, & cum domo Juda foedus Novum. Quod foedus cum immutabile sit, & a morte testatoris pendeat, Apostolus, Lxx. imitatus, recte per διαθήκη Testamentum, vertit.
units.tr: VII. This testament is promised in Jeremiah 31:31: "Behold, the days come, saith Jehovah, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah." Since this covenant is unchangeable and depends on the death of the testator, the apostle, imitating the Seventy, rightly translates it by διαθήκη, testament.

units.la: VIII. Ut autem Veteris Testam. haereditas victimarum sanguine firmata est; ita coelestis haec haereditas Christi quoque testatoris morte obsignata ac ratificata fuit. Etiam tu, o Zion, pro sanguine Test. tui, dimisi vinctos tuos e fovea, in qua non est aqua. Zach. 9: 11. Ubi enim Testamentum est, mortem necesse est contingere Testatoris. Hebr. 9: 16, 17. Ut Christus vi Testamenti hujus mortuus sit, tum ut sponsor ac mediator illius, tum etiam ut Testamenti illius auctor ac testator. Et ego Testamento dispono vobis regnum, ut Pater Testamento disposuit mihi. Luc. 22: 29. Unde testamenti utriusque discrimen elucescit: cum in priore sacerdotium modo typicum, & vilis pecudum cruor conspiceretur; hic autem ipse testamenti conditor, ejusdem mediator, ipseque sacerdos & victima factus, ac conversus in pretium Deus est. Quo solo sanguine Deus placari poterat. Qui — per se ipsum purgatione facta peccatorum nostrorum, consedit ad dexteram magnitudinis in alto. Hebr. 1: 3. Ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam per sanguinem proprium acquisivit. Act. 20: 28.
units.tr: VIII. As the inheritance of the Old Testament was confirmed by the blood of victims, so this heavenly inheritance was also sealed and ratified by the death of Christ the testator. "As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water" (Zech. 9:11). "For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator" (Heb. 9:16, 17). Christ died by virtue of this testament, both as its surety and mediator and also as its author and testator. "And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me" (Luke 22:29). Hence the difference between the two testaments shines forth: in the former, only a typical priesthood and the blood of base cattle were seen; but in this one, the very founder of the testament, its mediator, himself made priest and victim, and God turned into the price. By this blood alone could God be appeased: "who, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Heb. 1:3). "To feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20:28).

units.la: IX. Ut autem in omni testamento, praeter testatoris consilium, testamenti conditionumque ejus promulgatio, ac promissae haereditatis oblatio locum habet: ita quoque testamenti hujus spectanda est, tum νομοθεσία, seu legislatio; quae per legem seu mandatum fidei peragitur, quo scripti a Deo haeredes bona testamenti hujus desiderare, & ampliecti, tantamque salutem non negligere jubentur: tum promissio, non rerum terrestrium, ut olim, sed spiritualium ac coelestium stium, omnisque istius hæreditatis, illis, qui salutis suæ cura ducuntur, atque illa accipere dignantur, sacta. quæ promissio exstat Jer. 31: 31, 32. Hebr. 8. 7. Ex qua testamenti προσθήκη, atque adjunctis promissis, illud veluti in Fœdus & pactum commutatur, mutuâ stipulatione ac restipulatione firmatum ac immutabile redditum. Cum nec Deus frustra salutem promittere, nec homo in vanum illi promissioni confidere, seque ipsi salvandum dedere possit.
units.tr: IX. As in every testament, apart from the testator's counsel, there is the promulgation of the testament and its conditions and the offer of the promised inheritance, so in this testament we must consider both: (1) the νομοθεσία, or legislation, which is carried out through the law or command of faith, by which the heirs, written down by God, are bidden to desire and embrace the goods of this testament and not to neglect so great a salvation; and (2) the promise, not of earthly things, as formerly, but of spiritual and heavenly goods, and of the whole of that inheritance, made to those who are concerned for their salvation and deign to accept it. This promise stands in Jeremiah 31:31, 32 and Hebrews 8:7ff. From this there is also a προσθήκη, an addition, and by the addition of promises the testament is changed into a covenant and pact, confirmed by mutual stipulation and counter-stipulation and rendered unchangeable. For God cannot promise salvation in vain, nor can man trust that promise in vain or surrender himself to be saved by it.

units.la: X. Non tangimus autem hac vice Socinianorum ulcera, quæ jam sæpe nudavimus; quorum theologemata de fœdere ac testamento Dei nihil sani, quodve Deo homineve dignum sit, sapiunt; & merum pus ac venenum sunt. Ex quo fonte universa ipsorum religio corrupta est. Illis enim Testamentum Vetus est fœdus operum legale, nulla vitæ æternæ promissione adjutum; unde ejus in homine ad Deum convertendo imbecillitas: Testamentum autem Novum est idem fœdus, seu lex operum, nova dignitate, ac præceptorum sanctimonia veterem legem longè exluperans, à Christo lata, & cœlestibus promissis firmata, ipsoque sponsore (talem enim solum sponsorem agnoscunt, qui divinæ voluntatis interpres & internuntius, fusoque sanguine ejus sponsor sit) roborata; quo cœlesti præmio hominem efficacius duci, atque ita legem, alioqui pro captu ipsorum nimis sublimem, in cordibus ipsorum inscribi autumant. Quo pacto, ut alia omittam, omne Testamentum Dei; omneque ejus consilium de gratiâ faciendâ, quod Scriptura tam sæpe memorat, inane reddunt ac prorsus negant. Cum toto cœlo fœdus tale ac Testamentum discrepent.
units.tr: X. For the present we do not touch the sores of the Socinians, which we have often laid bare; their theses concerning the covenant and testament of God savour of nothing sound, nor of anything worthy of God or man, and they are pure pus and poison. From this source their whole religion has been corrupted. For to them the Old Testament is the legal covenant of works, aided by no promise of eternal life; hence its weakness in converting man to God. The New Testament, however, is the same covenant or law of works, given by Christ with a new dignity and with a sanctity of precepts far surpassing the old law, and confirmed by heavenly promises, and strengthened by its sponsor himself (for they acknowledge only such a sponsor as is the interpreter and messenger of the divine will, and who is surety by shedding his blood). By this heavenly reward, they hold, man is more effectively led, and so the law, otherwise too sublime for their capacity, is written on their hearts. By this method, to omit other things, they make the whole testament of God, and his whole counsel of bestowing grace, which Scripture so often mentions, empty and utterly deny it. For such a covenant and testament differ from it as far as heaven from earth.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De bonis Novi Testamenti.
units.tr: Of the Benefits of the New Testament.

units.la: I. Æquuntur secundo loco bona & prærogativæ Novi Test. præ veteri, œconomiam illius comitantia, jamque ex parte supra, ubi de Veteris Novique Test. discrimine, à nobis narrata. Sunt autem ea valde insignia, tum justificationem, tum sanctificationem, tum denique consolationem nostram spectantia; partimque ad fidelium inter-num, partim ad externum Ecclesiæ statum pertinentia; atque hisce septem potissimum absolvuntur.
units.tr: I. In the second place, the benefits and prerogatives of the New Testament over the Old, which accompany its economy, are to be weighed. We have already described some of them in part above, where we discussed the difference between the Old and New Testaments. They are very notable, bearing on our justification, our sanctification and finally our consolation. Some pertain to the internal state of believers, others to the external state of the Church. They are chiefly comprised in these seven.

units.la: II. Primum H. Primum est, perfecta cunctisque numeris absoluta justitia, quam Messias sanguine suo paravit, Dan. 9: 24. cum pro humano genere victima factus peccatum totius terrae uno die, Zach. 3: 9. h. e. unico sacrificio, ἅπαξ, Hebr. 9: 28. delevit, ut nihil ex veteri maledictione, ac multiplici illa irae specie, nunc, supersit, quod fidelium spem atque fidem concutere possit. Quae justitia & justificatio per emphasin ac excellentiori modo appellatur, ac nunc primum data est. Ad adducendum justitiam aeternam. Dan. 9: 24. in cognitione sui יצדיק justificabit justus servus meus multos. Esai. 53: 11.
units.tr: II. The first is a justice that is perfect and complete in every respect, which the Messiah obtained by his blood, Dan. 9: 24, when he was made a victim for the human race and, in one day, Zech. 3: 9, that is, by a single sacrifice, once for all [ἅπαξ], Heb. 9: 28, blotted out the sin of the whole earth, so that nothing remains of the old curse and its many forms of wrath that could shake the hope and faith of believers. This justice and justification is called such by emphasis and in a more excellent way, and it has now been given for the first time. To bring in everlasting righteousness, Dan. 9: 24. By his knowledge [יצדיק] my righteous servant shall justify many, Isa. 53: 11.

units.la: III. Consequitur plenam hanc justitiam, atque ex ea ceu sonte promanat peccatorum ἀφέσεις & remissio plenissima, in emphasi ita dicta; sine ulla criminatione, ac peccati tanquam necdum expiati ἀνείδισμῷ & improperio. Quae Novi T. temporibus olim promissa (Nam condonabo pravitatem eorum, et ipsum peccatum eorum non recordabor amplius. Jer. 31: 34. Heb. 8: 12.) ac exhibita est. Ubi autem ἄφεσις remissio horum peccatorum non adhuc oblatio pro peccato est, Hebr. 10: 18. Veteris enim temporis potius erat πάρεσις, & noxarum dissimulatio, ut Apostolus appellat Rom. 3: 25. διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν propter transmissionem peccatorum ante factorum: cum Lex umbras solum ac imagines futurorum bonorum exhibens, cultores suos per se non posset τελειῶσαι. Hebr. 10: 1.
units.tr: III. There follows from this full justice, and flows from it as from a fountain, the forgiveness [ἄφεσις] of sins and the most complete remission, so called by emphasis, without any reproach or insult [ἀνείδισμῷ] of sin as though it were not yet expiated. This was promised in former times to the New Testament and has now been exhibited: For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more, Jer. 31: 34; Heb. 8: 12. But where there is remission of these sins, there is no longer an offering for sin, Heb. 10: 18. For in the earlier time there was rather a passing over [πάρεσις] and a disregard of offences, as the Apostle calls it, Rom. 3: 25: through the forbearance of God, for the remission of sins that are past. The Law, which showed only the shadows and images of the good things to come, could not make perfect [τελειῶσαι] those who came to it, Heb. 10: 1.

units.la: IV. Ac comitatur hanc ἄφεσιν & remissionem conscientiae τελείωσις, consummatio, ejusque jam perpurgatae summa tranquillitas & fiducia: cum, deletis jam peccatis omnibus, nihil queri, nihil pavescere, semper autem gaudere ac laetari possit, in sinu Dei posita, ac sanguine Christi inundata ac lota. Lex – nunquam potest accedentes τελειῶσαι consummare, Hebr. 10: 1. una enim oblatione consummavit in perpetuum qui sanctificantur v. 14. Cum illi sine nobis consummati non fuerint. Hebr. 11: 39, 40.
units.tr: IV. Accompanying this forgiveness [ἄφεσιν] and remission of conscience is perfection [τελείωσις], consummation, and therewith the highest tranquillity and confidence of a conscience now thoroughly cleansed. With all sins now blotted out, it can complain of nothing and fear nothing, but can always rejoice and exult, placed in the bosom of God and bathed and washed in the blood of Christ. The Law can never make those who draw near perfect [τελειῶσαι], Heb. 10: 1. For by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are being sanctified, v. 14. Since they were not made perfect without us, Heb. 11: 39, 40.

units.la: V. Huc pertinet quoque tertium bonum, quod Ecclesiae nunc datus sit Spiritus Christi. Et effundam in domum Davidis Spiritum gratia et supplicationis. Zach. 12: 10. Hoc enim dixit de Spiritu, quem acceperi erant credentes in ipsum. Nondum enim erat Sp. S. quia Jesus nondum glorificatus erat, Joh. 7: 39. Non Spiritus servitutis, ut olim, quando fideles legis tortoris verbera & flagellum quotidie experiebantur, & illiberali isto ministerio occupati, ac serviliter fere habiti, serviles quoque propemodum animas gerebant; sed Spiritus adoptionis, qui blando ductu fideles cum fiducia ad Deum tanquam patrem accedere, ipsumque ingenuo ac liberali cultu propitiare docet. Rom. 8: 15. Gal. 4: 3, 5. Ita & nos, quum essemus infantes, sub elementa mundi eramus in servitutem subjecti — ut eos, qui sub lege erant, emtos liberaret, ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Unde adoptio antonomasticè ac augustiori titulo N. T. tribuitur. Ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Gal. 4: 5. Sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, Rom. 8: 15. Joh. 1: 12.
units.tr: V. To this belongs also the third good: that the Spirit of Christ has now been given to the Church. And I will pour out on the house of David the Spirit of grace and of supplication, Zech. 12: 10. For he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified, John 7: 39. It is not the spirit of bondage, as formerly, when believers daily suffered the blows and scourge of the law's torturer, and, occupied in that illiberal ministry and treated almost as slaves, bore almost servile souls. It is rather the Spirit of adoption, who by a gentle guidance teaches believers to approach God with confidence as a father, and to propitiate him with a free and liberal worship. Rom. 8: 15; Gal. 4: 3, 5. So we also, when we were children, were held in bondage under the elements of the world ... so that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption as sons. Whence adoption is attributed to the New Testament by way of pre-eminence and with a more august title. That we might receive adoption as sons, Gal. 4: 5. But you have received the Spirit of adoption, Rom. 8: 15; John 1: 12.

units.la: VI. A quo spiritu ac divino illius ductu quasi major ac perfectior Ecclesiæ istius quoque oritur sanctitas. Cum ejus sit inscribere legem in corda fidelium, Jer. 31: 33. atque illa veluti scripturam Dei sanctissimis notis perarare: Qui estis epistola Christi, administrata à nobis, scripta non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei vivi, non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carneis, 2 Cor. 3: 3. ut Lex jam non in saxo aut lapide tantum extet, & merè litera sit, sed pretiosioribus tabulis, intimisque cordis nostri fibris insculpta, ipsum nostrum animum vivam loquentemque legem faciat.
units.tr: VI. From this Spirit, and from his divine guidance, there arises also the greater and more perfect holiness of this Church. For it is his task to write the law on the hearts of believers, Jer. 31: 33, and, as it were, to engrave God's writing with the most holy marks: You are a letter of Christ, delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of flesh, the heart, 2 Cor. 3: 3. So the Law no longer stands only on rock or stone and is a mere letter, but, engraved on more precious tablets and on the innermost fibres of our heart, it makes our very mind a living and speaking law.

units.la: VII. Sequitur quintum bonum, quod magis publicum erat, Nominis Dei in Ecclesia, atque hinc in universo mundo, clara notificatio: hoc est, virtutum, quæ nomen atque gloriam ejus absolvunt, Exod. 34: 6, 7. uberior manifestatio; quæ non unquam alibi magis, quam in redemtionis opere patuerunt; ubi Deus omnem suam gloriam nudavit, cunctasque sapientiæ, justitiæ, ac misericordiæ suæ divitias ostendit, ac palam exposuit. Unde Christus, cujus adventu ac morte nomen illud Dei præsertim illustratum est, nomen Dei nobis edidisse ac manifestasse, Joh. 17: 26. Patremque hactenus mortalibus obscurum, lucequē suâ impervium, edisserusse traditur. Joh. 1: 18.
units.tr: VII. There follows the fifth good, which was more public: the clear proclamation of the name of God in the Church and thence in the whole world. That is, a fuller manifestation of those virtues which make up his name and glory, Exod. 34: 6, 7. These were never more clearly displayed anywhere than in the work of redemption, where God laid bare all his glory and showed and openly set forth all the riches of his wisdom, justice and mercy. Hence Christ, by whose coming and death that name of God was especially made illustrious, is said to have made known and manifested the name of God, John 17: 26, and to have set forth the Father, hitherto hidden from mortals and inaccessible to his light, John 1: 18.

units.la: VIII. Sextum bonum, idemque externum & publicum, est pax, non interna solum cum Deo, per Christi sanguinem, per quem omnia pacata; cum in Veteri T. magis obtinerent induciæ, nec tam pax foret, quam pactio: quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad ostensionem justitiæ suæ, propter transmissionem peccatorum ante factorum in tolerantia Dei, Rom. 3: 25. sed potissimum externa, extinctis populorum inimicitiis, nulloque amplius Gentium & Judæorum discrimine, quod mundum hactenus in duas magnas partes, duasque veluti civitates diviserat: Ipse enim pax nostra, qui fecit utrumque unum, & intergerinum parietem solvit, inimicitiam — ad nihilum redegit; ut duos illos crearet in se in unum novum hominem, faciens pacem. Eph. 2: 14, 15. Cum Deus nunc sit omnibus idem: unusque omnium dominus, & una fides, & salus, & Ecclesia sit; gentesque ipsæ post longum repudium in Ecclesiæ sinum rursum receptæ sint: Non enim est distinctio Judæi & Græci; nam idem est dominus omnium, dives in omnes qui nominant ipsum, Rom. 10: 12. Quæ est illa mundi hæreditas, Abraham olim promissa. Rom. 4: 13.
units.tr: VIII. The sixth good, which is likewise external and public, is peace: not only internal peace with God through the blood of Christ, through whom all things are reconciled. In the Old Testament there were rather truces, and it was less a peace than a pact: whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness, because in his forbearance he had passed over the sins previously committed, Rom. 3: 25. But above all it is external peace, with the enmities of peoples put to death and no further distinction between Gentiles and Jews, which had hitherto divided the world into two great parts, as it were two cities: For he himself is our peace, who has made both one and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility ... reducing the enmity to nothing, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace, Eph. 2: 14, 15. Now God is the same for all, one Lord of all, one faith, one salvation, and one Church; and the Gentiles themselves, after a long rejection, have been received again into the bosom of the Church. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, rich towards all who call on him, Rom. 10: 12. This is that inheritance of the world promised of old to Abraham, Rom. 4: 13.

units.la: IX. Sequitur tandem maximum bonum, quodque reliquorum omnium compendium habet, libertas. Quæ omnem illam veterem servitutem, omnemque ejus imaginem ac speciem longissime removens, Ecclesiam, per Christi sanguinem manumissam & vere beram, omni prorsus dominatu, omnibusque dominis, præter Christum solum, liberat, statumque ejus beatissimum reddit. Multiplex enim in Vet. T. erat servitus, saltem quoad statum Ecclesiæ externum, multique domini: cum præter legem, quæ plusquam maritali imperio peccatorem urgebat, ac terrebat, etiam homines, accepta ab ea potestate, tanquam veteris sæculi principes ac dii, in gregem Domini, non sine injuria sæpe, dominarentur; quorum disciplinam Ecclesia perferre, subque ferulâ eorum gemere debebat. Quæ cuncta veteris servitii mala nunc amota, soliumque deastrorum illorum eversum, Lexque ipsa pædagogico throno cedere, ac gratiæ potius subservire jussa est.
units.tr: IX. Finally there follows the greatest good, which contains the sum of all the rest: liberty. Removing far away all that old servitude and every image and form of it, it frees the Church, redeemed by the blood of Christ and truly free, from every domination and every master except Christ alone, and makes her state most blessed. For in the Old Testament there was a manifold servitude, at least as regards the external state of the Church, and many masters. Besides the law, which pressed upon and terrified the sinner with more than marital authority, men too, having received power from it, ruled over the flock of the Lord as princes and gods of the old age, often not without injury. The Church had to endure their discipline and groan under their rod. Now all these evils of the old servitude are removed, the throne of those rulers is overturned, and the Law itself is commanded to yield its pedagogue's throne and rather to serve grace.

units.la: X. Ita ut nunc omnimoda obtineat libertas. 1. Libertas videl. à superbo Legis dominatu, tævisque jussis, quibus peccatorem terrebat, & quotidianis diris exagitabat, ac tantum non enecabat. Nam viro subjecta mulier, viventi viro devincta est per legem: quod si mortuus fuerit vir, liberata est à lege viri. Itaque fratres mei, vos quoque mortificati estis legi in corpore Christi. Nunc autem liberati sumus à Lege &c. Rom. 7: 2, 4, 6. 2. Inde etiam ab ista mundi servitute, ac primis infantilis Ecclesiæ elementis liberati sumus, Gal. 4: 3, 9. Dicit ei Jesus, mulier, crede mihi, quod veniat hora, quum neque in monte hoc, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis patrem. Joh. 4: 21. 3. Libertas ab infinito illo & inexplicabili Cæremoniarum jugo & onere; quod non tam multitudine, quam tristi ac sævo significatu ac usu suo, Ecclesiam premebat. Jugum — quod nec Patres nostri, nec nos potuimus ferre, Act. 15: 10. Conf. Col. 2: 14. Gal. 3: 25. 4. Hinc quoque liberi sumus à timore mortis, cui olim obnoxii degebant fideles, juxta Hebr. 2: 15. Ut liberaret eos, qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti. conf. 10: 28. Infringens quis legem Mosis, sine commiseratione, duobus aut tribus testibus, moritur. Cujus rei exempla in Davide, Hiskia, aliisque sub V.T. videmus. Qui, cum omnes afflictiones, tanquam legis lævientis verbera, servilesque notas, tum præsertim mortem immaturam horrere debebant. Qui terror non parum intendebatur, quod terrenum pignus, ac longævæ vitæ in terra ista promissa à Deo accepissent; quo erepto, ac de manibus excusso, non poterant non lugere, & amarum tanquam ad irati Dei speciem ingemiscere. Cum nunc non uni terræ, tanquam glebæ, adfixi, eam vehementer adeo deamare, & tanquam sacrum aliquid colere, & perpetuo tractare; istique pignori incumbere, & tantum non servire cogamur; ad quodvis calamitatum mortisve impetum stupentes territique; sed universa nobis tellus ex æquo patria & hospita, ac cælum potius civitas nostra sit. Phil. 3: 20. & gloriamur in ipsis afflictionibus, Rom. 5: 3. 5. Cumque externis illis cæremoniis exercendis tunc præsiderent veteris Ecclesiæ principes, ac patres carnis, Hebr. 12: 9. & universa illa pædagogorum cohors; etiam hi, tanquam Ecclesiæ graves, & abolitis cæremoniis inutiles, remoti, & throno suo decedere jussi sunt. Scriptum enim est, perdam sapientiam sapientum – ubi scriba, ubi inquisitor hujus sæculi? 1 Cor. 1: 19. Sapientium vero loquimur in persectis. Sapientiam autem non hujus sæculi, neque principum hujus sæculi abolendorum. cap. 2: 6. Ita ut Ecclesia nunc non hominum, sed solius Dei vivi peculium & cœtus sit, 1 Tim. 3: 15. ac cælorum quoddam regnum; in quo non aliud quam Dei nomen audiri debet; cum hæc nunc publica Ecclesiæ vox sit, Jehovah est judex noster; Jehovah est Legislator noster, Jehovah est Rex noster, is salvat nos, Esai. 33: 22. quo omnem hominum dominatum, omnesque dominos ac legislatores, quacunque specie in plebem Dei grassantes, & fidei legem ferentes, procul abstere jubet. Igitur in regno cœlorum nec angelis subjicimur, Heb. 2: 5. nec œconomis aut tutoribus, Gal. 4: 2. 6. Cui libertati, quo plenior, & ab omni humano nomine absolutior foret, accedit ultimo libertas à subjectione prophetarum, juxta Jer. 31: 34. Hebr. 8: 11. Et non docebunt amplius quisquam proximum suum, & quisquam fratrem suum, dicendo; cognoscite Jehovam: nam omnes ipsi cognoscent me, non minus parvus ipsorum, quam magnus ipsorum, ait Jehovah.
units.tr: X. So now a complete liberty holds sway. 1. Liberty, namely, from the proud dominion of the Law and its harsh commands, by which it terrified the sinner and tormented him with daily curses, and all but put him to death. For the woman who is under a husband is bound by law to her living husband; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband. Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ. But now we are released from the Law, etc. Rom. 7:2, 4, 6. 2. We are also freed from that worldly servitude and from the first elements of the infant Church, Gal. 4:3, 9. Jesus says to her, woman, believe me, the hour comes when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. John 4:21. 3. Liberty from that endless and inexplicable yoke and burden of the ceremonies, which weighed upon the Church not so much by their number as by their grim and cruel meaning and use. A yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear. Acts 15:10. Cf. Col. 2:14. Gal. 3:25. 4. Hence also we are free from the fear of death, to which the faithful of old were subject, according to Heb. 2:15: that he might free those who through the fear of death were subject to bondage all their lives. Cf. Heb. 10:28: Whoever breaks the law of Moses dies without mercy at the word of two or three witnesses. We see examples of this in David, Hezekiah and others under the Old Testament. They had to dread all afflictions, as blows of a law that lashed them and as marks of servitude, and above all an untimely death. This terror was not a little increased because they had received from God an earthly pledge and the promise of a long life in this land; when this was taken away and snatched from their hands, they could not but mourn and groan bitterly, as in the face of an angry God. Now, however, we are not fixed to the earth as to a clod, so as to love it vehemently, honour it as something sacred and handle it continually, clinging to that pledge and almost compelled to serve it, stunned and terrified at every onslaught of calamity or death. Rather, the whole earth is to us alike a fatherland and a place of sojourn, and heaven is more truly our citizenship. Phil. 3:20. And we glory in our afflictions, Rom. 5:3. 5. Since the princes of the old Church and the fathers of the flesh, Heb. 12:9, and that whole band of tutors, presided over the performance of those external ceremonies, these men too, as burdensome to the Church and useless once the ceremonies were abolished, have been removed and ordered to give up their thrones. For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise... where is the scribe, where is the inquirer of this age? 1 Cor. 1:19. We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. Ch. 2:6. So that the Church is now not the property of men, but only of the living God, and a certain assembly, 1 Tim. 3:15, and a kind of heavenly kingdom, in which nothing but the name of God ought to be heard. For this is now the public voice of the Church: Jehovah is our judge; Jehovah is our lawgiver; Jehovah is our king; he will save us, Isa. 33:22. By this he bids far away every dominion of men, and all lords and lawgivers, in whatever form they rage against the people of God and impose laws of faith. Therefore in the kingdom of heaven we are subject neither to angels, Heb. 2:5, nor to stewards or guardians, Gal. 4:2. 6. To this liberty, to make it fuller and more completely free of every human name, is finally added liberty from subjection to prophets, according to Jer. 31:34 and Heb. 8:11: And they shall no more teach each his neighbour, and each his brother, saying, know the Lord; for all of them shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says Jehovah.

units.la: XI. Quo loco duo docentur. 1. Non superfore in Ecclesia amplius cathedram, collegium, aut locum aliquem, qui religionis metropolis & sedes sit; quæque cum auctoritate universam Ecclesiam doceat; atque à quo verba Dei haurire reliqui omnes necesse habeant, quasi ad eam solam ea incorrupta pervenissent. Qualis ex. gr. in Vet. T. fuit Hierosolyma, ubi cathedra Mosis collocata erat, ad quam Christus etiam discipulos suos ablegat Matth. 23:2,3. In cathedra Mosis sedent scriba & Pharisæi; omnia igitur, quæ vobis dixerunt servare, servate & facite. juxta Deut. 17:9,10. Et venies ad sacerdotes Levitas — & indicabunt tibi rem judicii; & facies secundum id, quod indicabunt tibi ex eo loco, quem eliget Jehovah. conf. Mal. 2:7. Nunc enim nulli homini subjecta est Ecclesia, ob cujus nomen ac auctoritatem aliquid credere ac recipere debeat. Et multus glorietur in hominibus. Omnia enim vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas &c. 1 Cor. 3:21. Pretio emti estis, ne fiatis servi hominum. 7:23. Cum unctionem nunc acceperint omnes; nec opus habeant, ut cum auctoritate aliquis eos doceat, 1 Joh. 2:20,27. 2. Neque etiam restare amplius novi & hactenus inaudíti verbi revelationem; qualis expectabatur antea, cum Messias nondum advenisset; cum multa adhuc explicanda, & clavis illa, quæ doctoribus credita erat, Luc. 11:52. reseranda essent; doctrina enim Ecclesiæ nunc publica est, nec manet hominum certorum peculium, ut ex parte sub V. T. contigit. 3. Quibus tertio additur, omnes Deum cognituros, à parvo usque ad magnum. Cui consonat Esai. 54:13. Joh. 6:45. Et omnes filii tui discipuli Jehovæ. Quæ Novi Test. prærogativa est. Sub V. T. enim pauci Deum vere cognoscebant; unde fidelibus de novo semper dici poterat, cognoscite Dominum. Quod nunc expositâ palam salutari doctrina, ac Ecclesia per Spiritum ipsonfi sui, quem aliunde petere cum Pontificiis opus non habet, de omnibus edoctâ, dici necesse non est. Quanquam profectu, ac quotidiana confirmatione in sacra doctrina opus sit. 1 Joh. 2:24,27.
units.tr: XI. Two things are taught here. 1. That there no longer remains in the Church any chair, college or place which is the metropolis and seat of religion, which teaches the whole Church with authority, and from which all others must draw the words of God, as though only there had they arrived uncorrupted. Such, for example, in the Old Testament was Jerusalem, where the chair of Moses was set, to which Christ also sends his disciples, Matt. 23:2, 3: The scribes and Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses; therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do. Compare Deut. 17:9, 10: And you shall come to the Levitical priests... and they shall declare to you the sentence of judgment; and you shall act according to what they declare to you from that place which Jehovah shall choose. Compare Mal. 2:7. For now the Church is subject to no man, on whose name and authority it ought to believe or receive anything. Let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, etc. 1 Cor. 3:21. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. 1 Cor. 7:23. Since all have now received the anointing, and have no need for anyone with authority to teach them, 1 John 2:20, 27. 2. Nor does any revelation of a new and hitherto unheard word remain, such as was expected before, when the Messiah had not yet come, when many things were still to be explained and that key, which had been entrusted to the teachers, Luke 11:52, was yet to be unlocked. For the doctrine of the Church is now public, and it no longer remains the property of certain men, as in part happened under the Old Testament. 3. To these a third is added: all shall know God, from the least to the greatest. Isa. 54:13 and John 6:45 agree with this: And all your sons shall be disciples of Jehovah. This is a prerogative of the New Testament. For under the Old Testament few truly knew God; whence it could always be said anew to the faithful, know the Lord. Now that saving doctrine is set out openly, and the Church, taught about everything by its own Spirit, which it has no need to seek elsewhere, as the Papists would have it, there is no need to say this. Although progress and daily confirmation in sacred doctrine are needed. 1 John 2:24, 27.

units.la: XII. Atque in hisce consistit varia illa Ecclesiæ Novi Test. libertas; quæ & satietatis, Esai. 55:1,2. & quietis, Psal. 95:11. Matth. 11:28. nomine, oppositè ad Vet. T. sitim & lassitudinem, aliisque vocabulis appellatur: quam Pontificii tamen non una in parte violant, & contrario errore ipsi quoque Sociniani. Utrique enim (ut alias Romanæ Ecclesiæ thesis, quibus veterem famem sitimque reducunt, & satiatam sitienti adjungere non verentur; diversaque illas servitutis apud ipsos species modosque omittam) servitutem hominum in Ecclesia retinuerunt. Illi quidem palam & aperta fronte, dum novos legislatores, novas leges, ac cathedram in N. T. rursus erigunt. Hi autem alia via, dum Ecclesiam Christo, mero homini, subjiciunt; quem videl. ad summum in deorum nuncupatorum fastigium collocant; de quibus scriptum est in lege, ego dixi, dii estis, Joh. 10: 34. Quae tamen appellatio sub N. T. cessat; etenim licet sint dicti dii, sive in cælo, sive in terra (ut sunt dii multi, & domini multi) nobis unus Deus est, Pater, ex quo omnia sunt, & nos ad ipsum; & unus Dominus Jesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. 1. Cor. 8: 5, 6. Diis istis mortuis, ac amotis, Psal. 82: 6, 7. ac veteri isto cœlo convoluto, & cum diis suis decedere jusso.
units.tr: XII. In these things consists that varied liberty of the New Testament Church, which is called by names of satiety, Isa. 55:1, 2, and of rest, Ps. 95:11, Matt. 11:28, set against the thirst and weariness of the Old Testament, and by other words. The Papists nevertheless violate it in more than one respect, and the Socinians too by the opposite error. For both (to omit other things, such as the theses of the Roman Church by which they bring back the old hunger and thirst, and do not hesitate to add to the satisfied what is thirsty, and the various forms and modes of servitude among them) have retained the servitude of men in the Church. The former do so openly and with brazen face, while they raise up new lawgivers, new laws, and a chair again in the New Testament. The latter do so by another way, while they subject the Church to Christ as a mere man, whom they place, namely, at the summit of the so-called gods: of whom it is written in the law, I have said, you are gods, John 10:34. Yet this appellation ceases under the New Testament: for though there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. 1 Cor. 8:5, 6. Those gods are dead and removed, Ps. 82:6, 7, and that old heaven is rolled up, and they are ordered to depart with their gods.

units.la: XIII. Atque hæc præcipua illa Novi Test. bona sunt quæ magnam partem angelico isto hymno, in ipsa Euangelii initiatione dicto, absolvuntur: Gloria Deo in excelsis, & in terra pax, in hominibus beneplacitum. Luc. 2: 13. ac divinis Pauli ad Romanos verbis, c. 14: 17. Non est enim regnum Dei esca & potus, sed justitia, & pax, & lætitia, in Spir. S. Unde & loci ad Hebræos, c. 8: 6. sententia patet, ubi Apostolus meliora & potiora promissa Novo Test. præ veteri affirmat; quod de hisce similibusque bonis, quæ in hac vita Ecclesia nova præ veteri possidet, intelligendum est. Ut non necesse sit profano Socinianorum commento accedere, qui essentiale inter utrumque testamentum discrimen asserunt, ac de futuris & cœlestibus bonis Apostoli verba intelligunt; ac si in Vet. T. tantum terrestres promissiones obtinuissent. Quæ sæpius explosa sunt.
units.tr: XIII. These are the chief blessings of the New Testament, which for the most part are summed up in that angelic hymn sung at the very beginning of the Gospel: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men" (Luke 2:13), and in Paul's divine words to the Romans: "For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom. 14:17). Hence also the meaning of the passage in Hebrews 8:6, where the Apostle affirms that the New Testament has better and more excellent promises than the Old. This must be understood of such blessings, and similar ones, which the new Church possesses in this life beyond the old. It is therefore unnecessary to resort to the profane invention of the Socinians, who assert an essential difference between the two covenants and understand the Apostle's words of future and heavenly blessings, as if the Old Testament had only earthly promises. This has often been refuted.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De Novi Testamenti initio.
units.tr: On the beginning of the New Testament.

units.la: I. Onstituenda tandem est Novi Test. veluti Epocha; verumque ejus initium, quo illud inceperit, ac veteris Test. servitus finierit, investigandum est. De quo nonnulla sententiarum est discrepantia, quæ tamen in consensum redigi facile potest.
units.tr: I. The New Testament must finally be fixed as an epoch, and its true beginning, the point at which it started and the bondage of the Old Testament ended, must be investigated. Concerning this there is some disagreement among opinions, which can nevertheless easily be brought into agreement.

units.la: II. Quidam enim à Christi nativitate; alii à publico ejus ministerio; alii denique à morte ejus novi status exordium sumunt.
units.tr: II. For some take the beginning of the new state from the birth of Christ; others from his public ministry; and others finally from his death.

units.la: III. Quæ ita conciliari possunt: ut non unum momentum, sed aliqua latitudo ac spatium isti Ecclesiæ innovationi indulgeatur: &, primo ejus auspicio à Salvatoris adventu capto, Novum Test. per prædicationem ejus promulgatum; morte autem, ubi Veteris Test. vis propriè desiit, plenè ratificatum fuerit. Et dixit ipsis Angelus, ne timeatis: ecce enim annuncio vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo, quod natus sit vobis hodie Salvator &c. Luc.2:10, 11. A diebus Johannis Baptistæ usque huc regnum cælorum βιάζεται vim facit; & vim facientes rapiunt illud. Matth. 11:12, 13. Et propter hoc Testam. N. mediator est, ut, morte obitâ &c. Heb.9:15. Testamentum enim in mortuis firmum est; siquidem nunquam valet, quando vivit testator. v. 17.
units.tr: III. These views can be reconciled in this way: that not one single moment but a certain breadth and span of time be allowed for this renewal of the Church; so that at its first beginning, taken from the Saviour's coming, the New Testament was proclaimed through his preaching, but was fully ratified by his death, when the force of the Old Testament properly ceased. And the angel said to them, Fear not; for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people, for unto you is born this day a Saviour, etc. Luke 2:10, 11. From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force. Matt. 11:12, 13. And for this reason he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, a death having occurred, etc. Heb. 9:15. For a testament is of force after men are dead; otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth. v. 17.

units.la: IV. Distinguì etiam debet vis ipsa Novi T. ab ejus promulgatione. Ac vis quidem Novi Test. in morte ac expiatione Christi sita est; promulgatio autem sæpius, & per partes facta est; præcipuè autem, plenè ac sollemnem in modum in die pentecostis, cum Novi Test. status publicè inauguratus, ac auspicia ejus cœlesti miraculo consecrata sunt.
units.tr: IV. The force itself of the New Testament must also be distinguished from its promulgation. The force of the New Testament lies in the death and expiation of Christ; its promulgation, however, was made often and in parts, but especially fully and solemnly on the day of Pentecost, when the state of the New Testament was publicly inaugurated and its beginnings were consecrated by a heavenly miracle.

units.la: V. Pariterque distinguì necesse est initium Euangelii ab initio Nov. Testamenti. Illud enim mox à nativitate Christi cœpit, cum adventus ejus protinus Euangelisari cœptus est, Luc.2:10, 11. Hoc de jure in morte potius ejus collocandum est. Eo usque enim Veteris T. vis ac rigor adhuc obtinebat; omnisque ejus cultus necessarius erat; ac Judaicæ gentis præ reliquo mundo sanctitas perdurabat; quæ Veteris T. vim ostendebant. Si offeras donum tuum in altari &c. Matth.5:23. Abi, ostende te ipsum sacerdoti, & offer donum, quod jussit Moses ipsis in testimonium, c. 8:4. Ad viam gentium ne eatis, neque ingrediamini urbem Samaritanorum; abeatis vero potius ad oves domus Israelis, quæ perierunt. c. 10: 5, 6. Sub Novo Test. autem contigit illa Euangelii prædicatio, quæ facta est per Apostolos post ascensionem Christi, qua Euangelium εὐαγγελίζων, Hebr. 2:3.
units.tr: V. Likewise, the beginning of the Gospel must be distinguished from the beginning of the New Testament. For the former began immediately from the birth of Christ, when his coming was at once begun to be preached as good news, Luke 2:10, 11. The latter ought rather to be placed, in point of right, at his death. For until then the force and rigour of the Old Testament still prevailed; all its worship was necessary; and the holiness of the Jewish nation above the rest of the world endured, which showed the force of the Old Testament. If you offer your gift at the altar, etc. Matt. 5:23. Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them, ch. 8:4. Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, nor enter a city of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, ch. 10:5, 6. Under the New Testament, however, came that preaching of the Gospel which was made by the Apostles after the ascension of Christ, by which the Gospel was proclaimed [εὐαγγελίζων], Heb. 2:3.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Atque hinc jam antiquationis quoque Veteris T. constitui epocha poterit; quæ duos gradus habet. De jure enim illud in morte Christi abolitum fuit, quâ Novum Test. initiatum ac firmatum est: de facto autem non nisi spatio aliquo, per prædicationem Apostolorum, destructum; tandemque à Deo ipso, everso urbe & templo, quo solo illc Ecclesiæ status nitebatur, funditus eversum est.
units.tr: And from this the abrogation of the Old Testament can also be fixed as an epoch, which has two stages. For it was abolished in point of right by the death of Christ, by which the New Testament was initiated and confirmed; but in point of fact it was destroyed only after some interval, through the preaching of the Apostles; and at last it was utterly overthrown by God himself, when the city and temple, on which alone the state of the Church rested, were overturned.

units.la: VII. Decidi quoque hinc potest quæstio de Johanne Baptista, ad quæ nempe tempora minisferium ejus referendum sit, ac cujus tempus minister fuerit? Si enim de epocha temporis quæratur, indubium est, vigente adhuc Vet. T. ipsum ministerio suo functum: si vero ipsum ejus ministerium consideretur, illud ad N. Test. unicè pertinebat, cujus solius minister fuit; cum adventantis, jamque affulgengentis istius lucis ac diei, nuncius, præco & phosphorus fuerit: Ut perperam Pontificii, aliique, eum Nov. Testam. ministrum negent; atque inde etiam baptismo ejus derogent. Cum ministerium ejus prorsus Euangelicum fuerit. Hic (Johannes) venit in testificationem, ut testaretur de luce, ut omnes crederent per ipsum. Joh. 1: 7. Postridie videt Johannes Jesum venientem ad se, & dicit; ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, v. 29.
units.tr: VII. From this, too, the question about John the Baptist can be settled: namely, to what times his ministry is to be referred, and of which time he was the minister? For if the question concerns the epoch of time, it is beyond doubt that he exercised his ministry while the Old Testament was still in force; but if his ministry itself is considered, it pertained wholly to the New Testament, of which alone he was the minister, since he was the herald, the crier and the morning star of that light and day which was coming and already dawning. So the Papists and others wrongly deny that he was a minister of the New Testament, and on that ground also detract from his baptism, since his ministry was altogether evangelical. He (John) came for a testimony, to bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him. John 1:7. The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world, v. 29.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS SECUNDUS. DE Adventu Messiæ, Jesu Nazareni. CAPUT IV. De prodromo Messiæ, Johanne Baptista.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Forerunner of the Messiah, John the Baptist.

units.la: I. Isce prædelibatis, sequitur consideranda ipsa Novi Test. œconomia, in universo ordine ac ambitu suo. Cujus hæc quatuor primaria erunt capita, 1. de Messia. 2. de Beneficiis Messiæ. 3. de Sacramentis. 4. de Ecclesia.
units.tr: I. Having made these preliminary remarks, we must consider the economy of the New Testament itself in its whole order and compass. Its four principal heads will be: (1) the Messiah; (2) the benefits of the Messiah; (3) the sacraments; (4) the Church.

units.la: II. Messiam quod præcipuum œconomiæ hujus caput est, quo solo omnis iste Ecclesiæ status nititur, considerabimus, 1. quoad adventum. 2. quoad personam, ac 3. status illius.
units.tr: II. The Messiah, which is the chief head of this economy and the sole foundation on which the whole state of the Church rests, we shall consider (1) as to his coming, (2) as to his person, and (3) as to his state.

units.la: III. Adventum Messiæ præcedit ipsius prodromus, Johannes Baptista; cujus cum persona, tum ministerium spectandum est.
units.tr: III. The coming of the Messiah was preceded by his forerunner, John the Baptist; in him both the person and the ministry are to be considered.

units.la: IV. Johannes, à ministerio Baptista dictus, sacerdotali genere fuit; patre Zachariâ, & matre Elizabetha. A quibus, in tanta ætate, non sine miraculo genitus, majoris in Christo miraculi rudimentum fuit; qui virgineo ex utero nulla viri opera progerminaret. Luc. 1: 5,7. Meminit ejus non sine honore Josephus, aliique Hebræi auctores.
units.tr: IV. John, called the Baptist from his ministry, was of priestly stock: his father was Zechariah and his mother Elizabeth. Born of them at so advanced an age, not without a miracle, he was the beginning of a greater miracle in Christ, who was to spring from a virgin's womb without any man's agency. Luke 1:5, 7. Josephus and other Hebrew writers also mention him with honour.

units.la: V. Adventus ministeriumque ejus longè ante prædicta sunt: Ut ex ista etiam phosphori luce ac radiis sol justitiæ agnosceretur. Ac præconem hunc designat Malachias, c. 4: 5. Ecce ego mitto vobis Eliam Prophetam, antequam veniat dies Jehovæ, magnus ille & terribilis. Ac concionantis vocem in deserto audiri facit Jesaias, cap. 40: 3. Vox clamantis exstat in deserto: vacuam facite viam Domini, viam munitam Deo nostro. Quæ oracula ad Johannem applicant Euangelistæ, Matth. 11:14. Et, si vultis ipsum accipere, hic est Elias, qui venturus erat. & Luc. 1:17. Et ipse prægredietur coram facie ejus in spiritu & potentiâ Eliæ, ut reducat corda patrum ad filios, & inobedientes in φρονήσει δικαίων in sensu justorum. Quod Malachias dixit, cor filiorum ad patres ipsorum, id est, ut eadem sentiant ac credant de justitia Dei, quæ patres ipsorum fideles crediderunt. & Matth. 3: 3. Nam hic ille est, de quo dictum est per Esaiam Prophetam, dicentem, vox clamantis in deserto &c.
units.tr: V. His coming and ministry were foretold long beforehand, so that by this light of the morning star the Sun of Righteousness might also be recognised. Malachi designates this herald in chapter 4:5: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the day of the LORD, that great and terrible day." Isaiah makes the voice of a preacher heard in the wilderness, chapter 40:3: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight the way of the LORD, a highway for our God." The Evangelists apply these oracles to John: Matthew 11:14, "And if you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah, who was to come"; and Luke 1:17, "He shall go before his face in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom [φρονήσει] of the just, to the mind of the righteous." What Malachi said, "the heart of the children to their fathers," means that they should think and believe concerning the righteousness of God what their faithful fathers believed. And Matthew 3:3: "For this is he of whom it was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness," etc.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Absolvitur ministerium Johannis hisce tribus: prædicatione resipiscentiæ, quæ ipsi peculiaris erat; baptismo; denique insigni testimonio Christo publice perhibito. Miracula enim ac signa nulla ipse edidit, quanquam aliqua circa nativitatem ejus facta sint: Et multi veniebant ad illum, & dicebant, Johannes quidem signum fecit nullum: omnia autem, quæ dixit Johannes de hoc, vera erant, Joh. 10:41. Ne videlicet putaretur ipse esse Christus & Messias.
units.tr: John's ministry is summed up in these three things: the preaching of repentance, which was peculiar to him; baptism; and finally a striking public testimony borne to Christ. For he performed no miracles or signs, although some were wrought at his birth: "And many came to him and said, John indeed did no sign, but all the things that John said of this man were true," John 10:41. Evidently so that no one would suppose that he himself was Christ and the Messiah.

units.la: VII. 1. Erat resipiscentia prædo. In diebus illis aderat Iohannes Baptista, prædicans in deserto Judæa & dicens: resipiscite, appropinquavit enim regnum cælorum, Matth. 3: 1, 2. Quæ unica ad regnum Christi Præparatio erat. Dum non solum depravatos populi mores severiori disciplina emendaret; sed præsertim falsas istas de justitia sententias, omneque Pharisæorum virus ac venenum ex auditorum pectoribus auferre niteretur. Unde & illorum hypocrisin, & perversum legis studium, tristesque quas vultu portendebant sanctimonias non leviter sæpe perstrinxit & jugulavit. Quam exhortationem ad pœnitentiam singulari vitæ instituto, ac perpetuâ veluti censurâ comprobavit.
units.tr: VII. 1. There was the preaching of repentance. "In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying, Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand," Matthew 3:1, 2. This was the sole preparation for the kingdom of Christ, since he sought not only to correct the depraved morals of the people by a stricter discipline, but especially to remove from the hearts of his hearers those false opinions about righteousness and all the poison and venom of the Pharisees. Hence he often sharply rebuked and struck down their hypocrisy, their perverse zeal for the law, and the gloomy sanctimony they displayed in their countenance. He commended this exhortation to repentance by a singular manner of life and by a constant, as it were, censure.

units.la: VIII. 2. Baptisabat pro more Judæorum, proselytos suos aqua lustrantium. Nec differebat illa lotio, nisi respectu circumstantiarum duntaxat, à Christi aut Apostolorum baptismo: cum & divinam auctoritatem haberet; & ritus, resque significata ac ritu illo obsignata, utrobique eadem forent. Non aliōs enim tingebat, quam qui abjectis vanis ac inanibus illis, quibus hactenus insueverant, Messiæ jamjam venturi fidem profiterentur, inque eum spes suas omnes dirigerent. Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua ad resipiscentiam, qui venit post me — ipse vos baptizabit in Spir. S. & igne. Matth. 3: 11.
units.tr: VIII. 2. He baptized, according to the custom of the Jews, who washed their proselytes with water. That washing differed from the baptism of Christ or the Apostles only in its circumstances; for it had divine authority, and the rite, the things signified and the seal of those things in the rite were the same on both sides. For he baptized only those who, having cast off those vain and empty practices to which they had hitherto been accustomed, professed faith in the Messiah who was now about to come, and directed all their hopes towards him. "I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance; but he who comes after me... he shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire," Matthew 3:11.

units.la: B. 3 Iohannes baptizavit baptismum respiscentia, populo dicens, ut credant in eum, qui post ipsum veniret, id est, in Christum Iesum. Act. 19: 4. Quod & nostri baptismi mysterium est. Unde & ritus ille in Ecclesia conservatus, & à Christo ac Apostolis ejus similiter usurpatus fuit.
units.tr: 3. "John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus," Acts 19:4. This is also the mystery of our baptism. Hence that rite was preserved in the Church and likewise used by Christ and his Apostles.

units.la: IX. Ut inique nimis Pontificii Baptismum Johannis minuant, aquasque ejus (ut Tertullianus olim locutus est) viduas, & infoecundas, nec Spiritu S. foetas, mentiantur: quo majori videlicet virtute Christiani baptismi undam impraegnent; cujus efficaciam superstitiosè, & ultra quam fas est, augent, ut postea videbimus.
units.tr: IX. The Papists unjustly diminish the baptism of John, and falsely assert that his waters (as Tertullian once put it) are "widowed" and barren, not made fruitful by the Holy Spirit; evidently so that they may impregnate the wave of Christian baptism with greater power, whose efficacy they superstitiously magnify beyond what is right, as we shall see later.

units.la: X.3. Denique illustre Christo testimonium praebuit, & praesentem divino elogio ornavit: cum personae dignitatem, tum praesertim munus ipsius magnificis verbis extollens; utpote cui ipse indignus foret qui calceos ministraret, Joh. 1:27. Matth. 3: 11. quique solus foret agnus verus ille & incontaminatus, agnus Dei, tot agnorum balatu & cruore in templo vocatus & postulatus, qui solus peccata mundi ablaturus & expiaturus foret. Cujus testimonii auctoritatem ne quis elevaret, ad istud usque tempus Johanni Christus de facie ignotus erat; dumque forte concionanti praesens adstaret, à Spir. S. monstratus, ac, addito divinitus signo, agnitus & universo coetui ostensus fuit. Et ego nesciebam eum, sed qui misit me ad baptizandum aqua, ille mihi dixit; super quem videris Spiritum S. descendere, & manere super eo, hic est, qui baptizat in Spir. S. Joh. 1:33.
units.tr: X. 3. Finally, he gave a remarkable testimony to Christ and adorned him with a divine eulogy, extolling both the dignity of his person and especially his office with magnificent words: he was one to whom he himself was unworthy "to carry the sandals" (John 1:27; Matthew 3:11), and who alone was that true and undefiled Lamb, "the Lamb of God," called for and demanded by the bleating and blood of so many lambs in the temple, who alone was to take away and expiate "the sins of the world." Lest anyone should weaken the authority of this testimony: up to that time Christ was unknown to John by sight; but when he happened to stand by while John was preaching, he was pointed out by the Holy Spirit, and, with a sign added from God, was recognised and shown to the whole assembly. "And I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit," John 1:33.

units.la: XI. Atque hoc fuit ministerium Johannis, prophetarum omnium maximi, ac evangelisantium primi. Sed ad quid videndum exiistis? prophetam? certe, dico vobis, etiam majorem propheta. Matth. 11:9. Omnes enim prophetae & lex, usque ad Johannem prophetarunt. v. 13. Quo ille expleto, Christo decessit, ac Veteris T. coelum clausit. Ut albescente aurora fieri videmus, cum languentes astrorum ignes ac emorientia sidera cogit lucifer, & coeli statione novissimus exit, ut soli in suo regno integer locus sit. Illum oportet crescere, me vero minui. Joh.3: 30. Quare qui in regno coelorum minimus est, major & beatior Iohanne dicitur. Matth. 11: 11.
units.tr: XI. Such was the ministry of John, the greatest of all the prophets and the first of the evangelists. "But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Surely, I tell you, even more than a prophet," Matthew 11:9. "For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John," v. 13. When he had completed this, he yielded to Christ and closed the heaven of the Old Testament, just as we see happen at the whitening of dawn, when the morning star drives out the fading fires of the stars and the dying constellations, and, last to leave its station in the sky, leaves the sun's kingdom wholly clear. "He must increase, but I must decrease," John 3:30. Therefore he who is "least in the kingdom of heaven is greater and more blessed than John," Matthew 11:11.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De adventu Messiæ.
units.tr: On the coming of the Messiah.

units.la: I. EOhannem præconem ac prodromum excipit Messias ipse: de quo duo impræsens probanda sunt: 1. in genere, Messiam jam advenisse. 2. in specie, Jesum Nazarenum esse verum Messiam.
units.tr: I. The Messiah himself follows John, the herald and forerunner. Two things must be proved here: (1) in general, that the Messiah has already come; (2) in particular, that Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah.

units.la: II. Messias, qui Græce χριστὸς, Latinè unctus, (quæ appellatio bis in Vet. bis in Novo instrum. occurrit, Psal.2:2.Dan. 9: 24.Joh. 1:42. & 4: 25.) advenisse, ex generali argumento patet, à certitudine divinarum prædictionum & promissionum desumto; in quibus Deum falli, vel fallere velle impossibile est. De Messia autem talia oracula extare adeo manifestum est, ut universa prophetarum cohors, facto veluti cinno, ipsi testimonium perhibeat; idque præcipuum illorum munus fuerit; ipsèque unus oraculorum omnium compendium & finis sit. Ut omnem illorum fidem laborare, omnemque eorum intellectum ac explicationem perire, demto ac obscurato hoc religionis capite, necesse sit. Quod ex infelicibus Judæorum conatibus patet, qui, Christum in plerisque prophetiis non videntes, frustra illas tentarunt, & ne unius quidem capitis sinceram explicationem dederunt; cum testimonium Christi sit Spiritus prophetiæ. Apoc. 19: 10. conf. 1 Pet. 1: 10, 11, 12.
units.tr: II. That the Messiah, in Greek christos [χριστὸς], in Latin "anointed" (a title that occurs twice in the Old Testament and twice in the New, Ps. 2:2; Dan. 9:24; John 1:42; 4:25), has come is plain from a general argument drawn from the certainty of God's predictions and promises. It is impossible for God to be deceived or to wish to deceive. That there are such oracles about the Messiah is so manifest that the whole band of prophets, as if with one voice, bears witness to him. This was their chief office, and he is the one point to which all the oracles sum up and aim. Remove or obscure this article of religion, and the faith of all of them must fail and their whole meaning and explanation perish. This is clear from the unhappy efforts of the Jews, who, not seeing Christ in most of the prophecies, tried in vain to explain them, and did not give a sound explanation of even one chapter, since "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy." Rev. 19:10; cf. 1 Pet. 1:10, 11, 12.

units.la: III. Illustriora autem de adventu ejus vaticinia, ac temporis characterem exhibentia, sunt hæc: 1. Jacobi in ipsa morte oraculum, de Messiæ, ante reip. ac Ecclesiæ Judaicæ finem, adventu: Non recedet sceptrum, vel tribus, ex Iuda, & legislator, vel doctor legis, ex medio pedum ejus, donec veniat Siloh, cui erit obedientia populorum. Gen. 49: 10. De quo supra egimus. 2. Haggai disserta prædictio, de ipso venturo, stante templo illo, quod tum struebatur; quodque præsens olim incoleret, ac priori æde longè augustius redderet. Et commovebo omnes gentes, & accedent ad desiderium omnium gentium, & implebo domum hanc gloria, ait Iehovah, Deus exercituum — major fiet gloria domus hujus posterioris quam prioris &c. cap. 2: 7, 9. 3. Cui concinit Malachias prophetarum ultimus, qui illum præ foribus adstantem tantum non inclamat, & ad templum suum invitat, cap. 3: 1.
units.tr: III. The clearest prophecies about his coming, which also show the time, are these: (1) Jacob's oracle at his death, about the coming of the Messiah before the end of the Jewish state and Church: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the tribe, nor a lawgiver or teacher of the law from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, to whom the obedience of the peoples shall be." Gen. 49:10. We have discussed this above. (2) Haggai's clear prediction of his coming while the temple then being built was still standing, a temple he would one day visit and make far more glorious than the former house: "And I will shake all nations, and they shall come to the desire of all nations, and I will fill this house with glory, says Jehovah of hosts ... the glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former" etc. Hag. 2:7, 9. (3) Malachi, the last of the prophets, agrees with this. He almost cries out to the Messiah as already standing at the doors, and invites him to his temple. Mal. 3:1.

units.la: 3:1. Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, ut vacuam faciat viam ante me: & derepente veniet ad templum suum Dominus ille, quem vos quaeritis, & angelus ille foederis, quo vos delectamini; ecce venit, dixit Iehovah, Deus exercituum. Venturus ergo erat stante templo secundo; nondum abolitis pastoribus & principibus. Esa. 49:7. qui tamen mox abolendi erant, Zach. 11:7,8. Non debuit Damascus caput Judaeae fieri, antequam nasceretur Immanuel, Esa. 7:8,14. Et debuit in pace nasci, & omnibus bonis rebus abundante terra. ibid. 7:15,4. Danielis expressa oracula; qui non solum, post regnorum illorum, quorum fata & exitum descripserat, finem, regnum Messiae aeternum inducit; cujus in caetera omnia foret imperium; cum non uno mundi cardine claudendum, sed toto orbe extendendum esset; quod partim eventu ipso probatum, partim adhuc in fatis conclusum est: cap. 2:44. Et in diebus regum illorum eriget Deus coeli regnum, quod in saecula non corrumpetur; & regnum ejus populo alii non relinquetur; comminuet & consumet omnia haec regna, & ipsum stabit in saeculum. Sed & nono capite, altiori ore sonans, digitis omnium veluti ad calculum aptatis, ipsa venturi Messiae tempora digerit & numerat; ac juxta captivitatis, in qua Ecclesia degebat, periodum, septuaginta quoque annorum septimanas ponit; intra quas prophetia omnis finiri ac impleri deberet. Septimanae septuaginta decisae sunt super populo tuo, & super urbe tua sancta, ad coercendum defectionem, & ad consummandum peccata, & ad expiandum pravitatem, & ad adducendum justitiam aeternam, & ad obsignandum visionem & prophetiam, & ad ungendum sanctum sanctorum &c. c. 9:24,25. Quod tempus rursus in tres periodos distinguit. Quarum prima septem hebdomadarum, seu 49. annorum est: quo tempore sancta urbs & templum restauranda forent, quamvis summis in angustiis. Altera sexaginta duas septimanas, sive annos 434. complectitur, secundo urbis ac reipubl. illius statui futuro, in quo eam inventurus esset Messias, destinatos ac dimensos. Tertia unius septimanae est; quae Messiam ostenderet, ac rursus tolleret; inque urbis ac reipubl. istius funere ac excidio aeterni ipsius regni fundamenta collocaret. Et cognosce & animadverte ab exitu sermonis de reducendo, & de aedificandis Hierosolymis, usque ad unctum principem septimanas septem, & septimanas sexaginta duas; quibus denuo aedificabuntur quoad forum & fossam; & in angustia erunt quaedam tempora; & post septimanas illas sexaginta duas exscindetur unctus, & non erit ipsi quicquam; & urbem & sanctum corrumpet populus principis advenae, & finis.
units.tr: 3:1 "Behold, I send my messenger, that he may prepare the way before me; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight. Behold, he comes, says Jehovah of hosts." He was therefore to come while the second temple stood, and before the ministers and princes had been abolished, Isa. 49:7, though they were soon to be abolished, Zech. 11:7, 8. Damascus was not to become the head of Judah before Immanuel was born, Isa. 7:8, 14, and he was to be born in peace, with the land abounding in all good things, ibid. 7:15, 4. Daniel's oracles are express. After the end of those kingdoms whose fates and outcome he had described, he introduces the eternal kingdom of the Messiah, whose rule would extend over all other things, since it was not to be enclosed within one corner of the world but spread over the whole globe. This has been partly proved by the event itself and is partly still decided in the fates. Dan. 2:44: "And in the days of those kings God will set up a kingdom of heaven, which shall never be destroyed; and its kingdom shall not be left to another people. It shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever." In chapter nine too, speaking with a loftier voice, he arranges and counts the very times of the coming Messiah, as if the fingers of all were fitted to a reckoning. According to the period of the captivity in which the Church lived, he sets out seventy weeks of years, within which all prophecy should be finished and fulfilled. "Seventy weeks are determined upon your people and upon your holy city, to restrain transgression, to put an end to sins, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy" etc. c. 9:24, 25. He again divides this time into three periods. The first is of seven weeks, or 49 years, in which the holy city and temple were to be restored, though in the greatest distress. The second embraces sixty-two weeks, that is 434 years, marked out and measured for the future state of the city and commonwealth, in which the Messiah was to find it. The third is of a single week. It would show the Messiah and then take him away, and would lay the foundations of his eternal kingdom in the funeral and destruction of that city and commonwealth. "Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem unto the anointed prince shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times. And after sixty-two weeks shall the anointed one be cut off, and shall have nothing; and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be with a flood..." Dan. 9:25, 26.

units.la: Dan. 2:44. ejus erit cum exundatione, & usque ad finem belli decisa sunt desolationes. Corroborabit quidem foedus multis septimana una. Sed in medio septimana ipsius abolebit sacrificium &c. cap. 9: 25, 26, 27. Nec vero de scrupulis Chronologicis hic quæstio est, sed de sæculis integris; cum, ut vel latissimè hæc tempora ordinentur, jam ante quindecim sæcula ea expiraverint. Ut certo certius sit Messiam jam dudum advenisse.
units.tr: Dan. 2:44. "Its end shall be with a flood, and to the end of the war desolations are determined. He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week; but in the midst of the week he shall cause sacrifice to cease" etc. c. 9:25, 26, 27. Nor is the question here one of chronological niceties, but of whole centuries. However widely these periods are arranged, they had already expired fifteen centuries ago, so that it is more certain than certain that the Messiah has long since come.

units.la: IV. Nec leve est argumentum, quod ab ipso populi Judaici statu desumitur. Satis enim constat Messiam ad populum illum, in tribus ac familias suas distinctum; ad terram illam; ad templum denique, in quo quotidiano cultu expectabatur, venire debuisse. Nunc autem Judæi nec populus sunt, cum rempublicam non habeant: nec à gentibus discreti ac separati, ut olim; sed iis partim immisti, partim toto orbe exules ac vagi in asperrima fortuna degunt: nec discretas tribus ac familias habent; cum genealogiis suis dudum caruerint; ut, si vel veniat ipsorum Messias, nulla nota ab ipsis agnosci posset: nec etiam terram suam habent; in qua tamen sola Messiam expectare debebant; quod præcipuum mysticæ illius terræ decus erat: nec denique templum amplius possident; omnisque illé cultus, qui figurando Messiæ solum serviebat, ac adventuri olim pompa & comitatus erat, non viso ipso desiit, & tantum non in mendacium ac ludibrium vertit; illeque, tamdiu expectatus, totque umbris expressus, Rex Ecclesiæ ad locum illum nunquam venit. Quæ omnia certe à misera gente attentius perpitari debebant, ut vel ex sese ipsis suoque statu errorem ac perfidiam suam agnoscerent.
units.tr: IV. The argument drawn from the very state of the Jewish people is no slight one. For it is well established that the Messiah had to come to that people, divided into its tribes and families; to that land; and finally to that temple, in which he was expected under the daily worship. But now the Jews are neither a people, since they have no commonwealth, nor are they separated and set apart from the nations as they once were; rather they are mingled partly with them, and partly, exiled and wandering throughout the whole world, live in the harshest fortune. Nor do they have distinct tribes and families, since they have long lacked their genealogies, so that even if their Messiah came, no mark could be recognised by them. Nor do they have their own land, in which alone they ought to expect the Messiah, and which was the chief glory of that mystical land. Finally, they no longer possess the temple. And all that worship, which served only to foreshadow the Messiah and was the pomp and retinue of the one who was once to come, ceased when he himself was seen, and has almost turned into a lie and a mockery. And he, so long awaited and so often pictured in shadows, the King of the Church, never came to that place. All these things the wretched nation ought to have considered more carefully, so that from their own state they might recognise their error and their unbelief.

units.la: V.
