Quam enim alioquin causam dicent, cur tot sæculis, à Deo neglecti, tam duris fatis exerciti, tam latè sparsi ac exules, universo generi humano adeo sævum ludibrium debeant? præsertim cum tam anxiè Messiam suum expectent, & quotidianis votis ac precibus vocent ac fatigent, nec revera adeo probrosi, vel idolorum cultu aliisve gentium vitiis fœdi sint, ut olim majores ipsorum. Ut certe aliam causam subesse necesse sit, quæ populum hunc, Deo olim perdilectum, miserè adeo errare sinat. Quæ non alia est, quam veri Messiæ flagitiosa rejectio ac cædes, & à vera fide apostasia, in qua ad hodiernum usque diem perseverant. Unde fata ipsis sua perpetim agitanda, pœnæque, quas Moses olim præsago ore cecinit, ad ultimum usque tempus exantlandæ manent.
units.tr: V. For what other cause will they give why, neglected by God for so many centuries, so harshly afflicted by fate, so widely scattered and exiled, they must be the cruel mockery of the whole human race? Especially since they await their Messiah so anxiously, and call upon him and weary him with daily vows and prayers, and are not in truth so disgraced or defiled by idolatry or other vices of the nations as their forefathers once were. Surely there must be some other cause lying hidden, which allows this people, once most dearly loved by God, to err so wretchedly. It is none other than the shameful rejection and slaughter of the true Messiah, and their apostasy from the true faith, in which they persist to this very day. Hence their fates must ever be bewailed and the punishments, which Moses once foretold with prophetic voice, must be endured until the last time.

units.la: VI. Quibus addimus proprias Iudaeorum confessiones. Ex quibus imprimis celebris est domus Eliae traditio, quae mundi tempora in tres periodos distribuit, omnemque ejus aetatem sex annorum millibus concludit, ac postremos bis mille annos Messiae regno tribuit. Estque haec, ut alia ipsorum praeteream, communis apud illos sententia, impletos jam esse omnes terminos, nec aliunde universum negotium, quam a poenitentia bonisque operibus dependere.
units.tr: VI. To these we add the Jews' own confessions. Among them the most famous is the tradition of the house of Elijah, which divides the times of the world into three periods, closes the whole of its age at six thousand years, and assigns the last two thousand years to the kingdom of the Messiah. This is, to pass over their other views, the opinion common among them: that all the appointed limits have now been reached, and that the whole matter depends on nothing else than repentance and good works.

units.la: VII. Non aliud autem crebrius contra haec omnia excipiunt, quam Messiae adventum, utcunque poltulantibus ipsum prophetiis, ac tantum non laborante tot oraculorum fide, propter peccata differri, tum sua, tum praesertim quae majores sui sub utraque domo commiserint. Ad quod respondemus. 1. Agi hic non de hoc vel illo vaticinio obscuriore, sed omnium prophetarum ac prophetiarum fide; quae ad hunc terminum omnes ipsectant, factoque consensu, uno omnes ore, hoc Messiae regnum, sequentemque Ecclesiae mundi statum, canunt. Ut nulla universae prophetiae certitudo ac veritas superfit, si in hoc capite, a quo reliqua omnia dependent, ea non praestetur. Ut levi adeo exceptione transmitti haec non debeant. 2. Nec Deus, si quid boni olim promisit populo, ob peccata illius unquam intermisit; ut ex illustribus ex Aegypto ac Babylone liberationis exemplis patet; quam cum longe ante, additis annorum spatiis ac numeris, praedixerit, non ultra terminum moratus est, sed ipso annorum fine promissa sua praestitit; etsi populus tunc non minus peccatis onustus foret, ac nunc. Fuit vero exactis quadringentis triginta annis, fuit, inquam, eodem ipso die, ut egederentur omnes exercitus Jehovae. Exod. 12:41. conf. Gen. 15:13. Nam sic dixit Jehovah, simulac impleti fuerint Babylone septuaginta anni, visitabo vos, et faciam, ut exstet super vos verbum meum bonum, ut reducamini &c. Jer. 29:10, 11. Ut similiter in palmaria hac promissione, in qua universae gentis bonum situm est, illud fieri, nec ultra 16. saecula ea negligi, ac tanti promissi fides labefactari debuerit. 3. Et an non hoc colore fieri possit, ut magna haec promissio nunquam impleatur, atque universae Ecclesiae, a condito usque mundo, in Messiam fides ac religio frustra sit? Semper enim populus hic non prorsus ab omni scelere liber erit; atque inde si dependeat, semper differri Messiae adventum oportebit. 4. Nec de corporali ac externo aliquo liberatore ac liberatione sermo est, qualem illi expectant, & ob populi peccata cunctari ajunt: sed de spirituali servatore, quo solo fides ac consolatio Ecclesiæ nititur: quique adeo peccatis retardari non potest, ut ad ea averruncanda ac tollenda & populum suum mundumque universum ab ferroribus ac sceleribus convertendum, præcipuè venturus dicatur. Et dabo illis cor unum, & spiritum novum dabo in medio ipsorum &c. Ezech. 11:19,20. Et erit illo die, ait Iehovah Deus, exscindam nomina idolorum ex terra, & non memorabuntur amplius, atque etiam prophetas & spiritum impuritatis faciam transire ex terra, Zach. 13:2. Ut convertat cor patrum ad filios, & cor filiorum ad patres ipsorum Mal. 4: 6. 5. Unde non conditionaliter, si populus omni labe purus, ac Deo dignus foret; sed absolute ille promissus est, tanquam certo venturus, nec ultra terminum tardaturus. Non enim, si incertus ejus adventus fuisset, fides Ecclesiæ tot sæculis in eum ferri potuisset. Quin & præcisum adventus ejus tempus designatum, variisque, ut ante vidimus, characteribus expressum fuit. Quod in conditionali promisso locum non habet. 6. Peccata autem Judæorum quod attinet; hoc unicum revera & summum eorum crimen est, quod tempore suo venientem Salvatorem repudiarunt, & contumeliosè tamquam pseudo-prophetam & magum obtruncarunt; inque eo scelere etiam hodie perseverant, ac quotidianis precibus ac execrationibus nomen ejus disputant & blasphemant. Hinc longa ipsorum captivitas.
units.tr: VII. Against all this they most often object that the coming of the Messiah is deferred on account of sins, both their own and especially those committed by their ancestors under both houses, even though the prophecies demand it and the faith in so many oracles almost depends on it. To this we reply. 1. The question here is not about this or that rather obscure prophecy, but about the faith in all the prophets and prophecies. All of them look to this limit, and by common consent, with one voice, they sing of this kingdom of the Messiah and the state of the Church that follows it. So no certainty or truth of the whole of prophecy remains if this point, on which all the rest depends, is not secured. Therefore these things ought not to be set aside with such a light objection. 2. Nor has God, when he promised some good to his people in the past, ever suspended it on account of their sins. This is clear from the famous examples of deliverance from Egypt and from Babylon. Although he foretold these long beforehand, with added spans and numbers of years, he did not delay beyond the limit, but fulfilled his promises at the very end of the years, even though the people were then no less burdened with sins than they are now. Indeed, when four hundred and thirty years had passed, it was, I say, on that very same day, that all the armies of Jehovah went out. Exod. 12:41; compare Gen. 15:13. For thus said Jehovah: as soon as seventy years are completed at Babylon, I will visit you and fulfil my good word toward you, to bring you back, etc. Jer. 29:10, 11. In the same way, in this chief promise, on which the good of the whole nation rests, that ought to have been fulfilled, and it should not have been neglected beyond sixteen centuries, nor should the faith in so great a promise have been weakened. 3. And could it not come about, by this same reasoning, that this great promise is never fulfilled, and that the faith and religion of the whole Church in the Messiah, from the foundation of the world, is in vain? For this people will never be wholly free from every wickedness; and if the coming depended on that, the coming of the Messiah would always have to be deferred. 4. Nor is the talk about some bodily and external deliverer or deliverance of the kind they expect, and which they say is delayed on account of the people's sins. It is about a spiritual Saviour, on whom alone the faith and comfort of the Church rest, and who cannot be held back by sins, since he is said to come chiefly to avert and remove them, and to convert his people and the whole world from errors and wickedness. And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them, etc. Ezek. 11:19, 20. And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord God, that I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered; and I will also cause the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness to pass out of the land. Zech. 13:2. He shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, Mal. 4:6. 5. Hence he was promised not conditionally, as if the people were to be free of every stain and worthy of God; he was promised absolutely, as one who would certainly come and would not delay beyond the limit. For if his coming had been uncertain, the faith of the Church could not have been directed toward him through so many centuries. Indeed, the exact time of his coming was designated and expressed by various marks, as we saw earlier. This has no place in a conditional promise. 6. As for the sins of the Jews, this is in truth their only and greatest crime: that they rejected the Saviour when he came in his time, and shamefully struck him down as a false prophet and a magician; and in this crime they persist even today, and by their daily prayers and curses they dispute and blaspheme his name. Hence their long captivity.

units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Jesu Nazareno Messia.
units.tr: Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, the Messiah.

units.la: I. Quod tum ex iis, quæ ortum ac nativitatem ejus spectant; denique ex illis tum, quæ ipse inter homines & fecit & docuit; denique ex illis quæ post exitum ejus in mundo consecuta sunt, manifestum fiet.

units.tr: VII. Against all this they most often object that the Messiah's coming is delayed on account of sins, their own and especially those committed by their ancestors under both houses, although the prophecies plainly demand it and the faith of so many oracles almost depends on it. To this we reply. 1. The question here is not about this or that rather obscure prophecy, but about the faith in all the prophets and all the prophecies. All of them look to this end, and by common agreement, with one voice, they sing of this kingdom of the Messiah and the subsequent state of the Church in the world. So if this point, on which all the rest depend, is not secured, no certainty or truth remains in the whole of prophecy. Therefore these matters must not be dismissed with such a slight objection. 2. Nor has God ever suspended a good he once promised to his people because of their sins. This is clear from the famous examples of deliverance from Egypt and Babylon. Although he foretold these long beforehand, with added spans and numbers of years, he did not delay beyond the set term, but fulfilled his promises at the very end of the years, even though the people were then no less burdened with sins than now. Now it was at the end of four hundred and thirty years, yes, on that very day, that all the armies of the LORD went out (Exod. 12:41; cf. Gen. 15:13). For thus said the LORD: when seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you and fulfil my good word to you, to bring you back, and so on (Jer. 29:10–11). So too in this foremost promise, on which the good of the whole nation rests, it ought to have been fulfilled, and it ought not to have been neglected beyond sixteen centuries, nor should faith in so great a promise have been shaken. 3. And is it not possible, on this reasoning, that this great promise is never fulfilled, and that the whole Church's faith and religion in the Messiah has been in vain from the foundation of the world? units.tr: CAPUT VI.

units.la: De Jesu Nazareno Messia.
units.tr: Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, the Messiah.

units.la: I. Eracta disputatione de Messiæ adventu, jam in proclivi est ostendere, non alium eum esse quam Jesum Nazarenum; cum non solum alius nullus aliqua cum specie pro Messia hactenus se se gerere, atque mundo fui fidem facere potuerit; sed vero in Jesum nostrum illa omnia conveniant, quæ de Messia unquam prædicta ac præfigurata fuerunt. Quod tum ex iis, quæ ortum ac nativitatem ejus spectant; tum, quæ ipse inter homines & fecit & docuit; denique ex illis quæ post exitum ejus in mundo consecuta sunt, manifestum fiet.
units.tr: I. Having finished the discussion of the coming of the Messiah, it is now easy to show that he is none other than Jesus of Nazareth. For no one else has so far been able to present himself as the Messiah with any credible appearance or win the world's belief, whereas all the things that were ever foretold and foreshadowed about the Messiah agree in our Jesus. This will become clear from what concerns his origin and birth, from what he did and taught among men, and finally from what followed in the world after his departure.

units.la: II. 1. Ortum ejus quod spectat: natus fuit, quum venisset temporis plenitudo, Gal. 4:4. quum venisset annus assertorum Dei, Esai. 63:4. illo temporis articulo, quo prophetæ Messiam venturum cecinerant; quo- temporis.
units.tr: II. 1. As to his origin: he was born when the fullness of time had come (Gal. 4:4), when the year of God's redeemed had come (Isa. 63:4), at that point of time in which the prophets had foretold that the Messiah would come; that is, at the time.

units.la: {y} Gal. 4:4 quum venisset temporis plenitudo. quoque Ecclesia, post longum desiderium, salvatorem suum singulis momentis expectabat. Cum fatorum stamine detexto, illa jam sese aperire, ac Messiam terris ostendere deberent. De quo tempore modo vidimus.
units.tr: {y} Gal. 4:4, when the fullness of time had come. The Church also, after long longing, was waiting for its Saviour at every moment. When the thread of the fates had been unwound, the Church was now bound to open up and show the Messiah to the earth. We have already seen what time this was.

units.la: III. Natus etiam est illo loco, quem Propheta Michæas Mariæ puerperio, ac Domini nostri cunis, tot sæculis ante designaverat. At tu Bethlehem Ephratah, parvus es, ut sis inter familias Juda: ex te mihi prodibit judex, ut sit dominator in Israële, cujus egressiones sunt ab initio, a diebus sæculi. cap. 5: 1. Ubi natus Jesus nolter, non humano consilio, sed occulta manu ducentibus fatis, ac Christo nascituro diversorium metantibus. Exiit enim edictum a Cæsare Augusto — et ascendit Joseph et Maria in civitatem David, quæ vocatur Bethlehem Luc. 2: 1. Nunc autem frustra ille locus in Judæa quæreretur.
units.tr: III. He was also born in the place which the prophet Micah had designated many centuries before as the birthplace of Mary's childbearing and our Lord's cradle: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient days (Mic. 5:1). Our Jesus was born there, not by human plan but by fates guided by a hidden hand, which arranged lodging for the Christ about to be born: For a decree went out from Caesar Augustus... and Joseph and Mary went up to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem (Luke 2:1). Otherwise that place would have been sought in vain in Judea.

units.la: IV. Natus itidem est è tribu Juda atque è Davidis familia, cui tantus olim hæres destinabatur. Quod adeo ἐξαγγελτον est, ut nec ipsi Judæi refragentur, qui ipsum propinquum regni, h. e. regiæ stirpis ramum appellitant.
units.tr: IV. He was likewise born of the tribe of Judah and of the family of David, to which so great an heir had once been destined. This is so manifest [ἐξαγγελτον] that even the Jews themselves do not deny it, since they call him the close kinsman of the kingdom, that is, a branch of the royal stock.

units.la: V. Tandemque ex intemerato virginis sinu, purissimi instar floris progerminavit, ut Esaiæ oraculum agnoscueremus: Ecce virgo concipit, et parit filium, et vocabit nomen ejus Immanuel, id est, nobiscum Deus. cap. 7: 14. Ubi de Messiæ e virginali utero exortu agi, nec ipsis Judæis olim ignoratum fuit. Recentiores tamen magistri prænobile hoc vaticinium carpere, quam patrum suorum fidem sequi ac Messiæ elogia agnoscere malunt. Hæc enim ipsorum exceptio est; cum regi signum propinquæ liberationis exhibeatur, non de longinquo Messiæ ortu cogitandum; nec de Messiæ matre, ac divino ejus partu, sed de prophetæ uxore; nec adeo de virgine, sed de conjugatâ, sermonem esse: cum illa etiam vocis עלמה acceptio fit. Qui sublestus color est. Nam I. non insolens Deo est, ingentium promissorum commemoratione minorum fidem adstruere; præsertim ubi majora illa sine minorum fide non consistunt. Quæ præsentis loci ratio est. Cum enim Messias è regia Davidis stirpe oriri olim deberet, idque durante illa republica; manifestum est, nec terram illam, cui prolixe adeo Rex Achaz metuebat, in potestatem hostium prorsus concedere, nec domum Davidicam penitus extirpari potuisse. Qui oraculi istius scopus erat. Et revera maxime illo Judaicæ gentis promisso, ac veluti peculio, in rebus dubiis ac asperis confirmari piorum animi non vulgariter poterant. Cum exinde inde sese Deo peculiariter curae esse aestimare satis possent. 2. Contra in prophetae uxorem vaticinii istius pondus non congruit; cum non magnum signum sit, mulierem de viro accipere, & parere. Nec in filium ejus cadunt elogia ista Immanuelis, ac Domini terrae illius; quae altero capite Propheta subnectit. 3. Quod autem de עלמה excipiunt, pariter infirmum est: cum vox illa in Scriptura semper uno illo virginis significatu accipiatur.
units.tr: V. And at last, from the undefiled womb of a virgin, he sprang up like a flower of purest bloom, so that we recognise the oracle of Isaiah: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Immanuel, that is, God with us (Isa. 7:14). That this speaks of the Messiah's coming forth from a virginal womb was not unknown even to the Jews of old. More recent teachers, however, prefer to pick at this most noble prophecy rather than follow the faith of their fathers and acknowledge the praises of the Messiah. Their objection is this: since a sign of near deliverance is given to the king, one should not think of a distant birth of the Messiah; and the talk is not of the Messiah's mother and her divine childbearing, but of the prophet's wife, and not of a virgin at all but of a married woman, since the word almah [עלמה] also has that sense. This is a flimsy pretence. For, first, it is not unusual for God to strengthen faith in lesser things by recalling greater promises, especially where the greater things cannot stand without faith in the lesser. And this is the reasoning of the present passage. For since the Messiah ought in time to arise from the royal line of David, and this while the commonwealth was still standing, it is plain that God neither allowed that land, which King Ahaz feared so greatly, to fall wholly into the power of enemies, nor could the house of David have been utterly rooted out. This was the aim of that oracle. And indeed it was especially by that promise to the Jewish nation, as by a kind of peculium, that the hearts of the pious could be strengthened, in doubtful and hard circumstances, in no ordinary way; since they could reasonably judge from it that they were under God's special care. Second, the weight of this prophecy does not fit the prophet's wife; for it is no great sign that a woman should conceive by a husband and bear a child. Nor do those titles, Immanuel and Lord of that land, which the prophet attaches in the next chapter, fit her son. Third, what they claim about the word almah is equally weak, since that word in Scripture is always taken in its one sense of virgin.

units.la: VI. 2. Sequuntur illa, quae Jesus & fecit, & docuit, & passus est, dum in terris ageret: quae adeo magnifica, adeo Deo digna, Joh. 7: 17, 18, 19: denique Mosi & prophetiis omnibus adeo concinna fuerunt, Joh. 5: 45, 46. ut nullum dubium superfit, quin ille qui talia patravit, totque Messiae notas & characteres gessit, revera Messias fuerit. Impossibile enim est impostorem aliquem eo setempore, quo Messias expectabatur, Ecclesiae fucum facere, ac Messiae imagine ac habitu se ostentare, omniaque quae de ipso praedicta erant implere; nisi prophetarum oracula fortuito, ac ab alienis personis adimpleri posse putemus; omnemque illorum fidem, ac Dei in mundo ac Ecclesia sua providentiam tollamus. De Jesu vero nostri doctrina, miraculis ac morte, passim ex historia Euangel. constat. Vide potissimum Luc. 4: 21, 22. Spiritus Domini super me est. Quia unxit Jehovah me ad Euangelium nuntiandum mansuetis. Misit me ad obligandum confractos corde, ad praedicandum abductis in captivitatem libertatem, & vinctis acutum visum. Conf. Esai. 61: 1. Multi vero ex populo crediderunt in ipsum. Et dicebant; Christus, quum venerit, nunquid plura signa his faciet, quae hic fecit? Joh. 7: 31. De Jesu Nazareno, qui erat vir propheta, potens in opere & sermone coram Deo, & omni populo, Luc. 24: 19. Vid. Matth. 11: 4. 5. conf. Esai. 11: 1. Et exibit virga ex trunco Jesse — & quiescet super ipso spiritus Jehovae, spiritus sapientiae & prudentiae, spiritus consilii & fortitudinis, spiritus cognitionis & timoris Jehovae. Act. 17: 3. Aperiens Scripturas, & clare proponens, quod Christum decuit pati, & resurgere ex mortuis &c. conf: Psal. 22. & 69. Esai. 53. Zach. 9. & 12.
units.tr: VI. 2. Next come the things that Jesus did, taught and suffered while he was living on earth. These were so splendid and so worthy of God (John 7:17-19), and in the end so harmonious with Moses and all the prophets (John 5:45-46), that there remains no doubt that the one who performed such things and bore so many marks and characteristics of the Messiah was truly the Messiah. For it is impossible that some impostor, at the very time when the Messiah was expected, could deceive the Church, present himself in the likeness and dress of the Messiah, and fulfil everything that had been foretold about him, unless we suppose that the oracles of the prophets could be fulfilled by chance and by persons unconnected with them, and unless we abolish all faith in them and in God's providence over the world and his Church. The teaching, miracles and death of our Jesus are everywhere established from the history of the Gospels. See especially Luke 4:21-22: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach the gospel to the meek; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and sight to the blind (compare Isa. 61:1). Many of the people believed in him, and they said: when the Christ comes, will he do more signs than this man has done? (John 7:31). Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people (Luke 24:19). See Matt. 11:4-5; compare Isa. 11:1-3: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse... and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Acts 17:3: Opening the Scriptures and setting forth clearly that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, etc.; compare Ps. 22 and 69, Isa. 53, Zech. 9 and 12.

units.la: VII. 3. Denique eandem rem confirmant illa, quae Jesu nostri praedicationem in mundo consecuta sunt. Non enim ipse solum sublimis in coelum ascendit; deque ista sede etiamnum mundum ac Ecclesiam moderatur; quod clarissimis eventis a Novi Test. incunabulis ad hunc usque diem patuit: sed & in mundo agnitus, publiceque pro Messia acceptus est; gentesque, ut de ipso praedictum erat Psal. 20. & 22. & 117. Esai. 42. & 49. missis idolis, Deo subditæ & ad fidem ejus conversæ sunt. Quod certe maximum Dei in mundo opus à Messia solo expectari poterat. Nec enim mundi conversio falsæ cuidam doctrinæ sine piaculo accepta referri potest.
units.tr: VII. 3. Finally, the same point is confirmed by what has followed in the world from the preaching of our Jesus. For he alone did not ascend on high into heaven and from that seat still govern the world and the Church; this has been plain from the clearest events from the cradle of the New Testament to this very day. He was also recognised in the world and publicly accepted as the Messiah; and the nations, as was foretold of him (Ps. 20, 22 and 117; Isa. 42 and 49), cast away their idols, submitted to God and were converted to his faith. This is certainly the greatest work of God in the world, and it could be expected from the Messiah alone. For the conversion of the world cannot be attributed to some false doctrine without sin.

units.la: VIII. 4. Tandem & Jesu nostro testimonium dant, non Iosephus sci-lum, Antiq. l. 18. c. 4. cujus testimonium falsitatis nondum demonstrationibus convictum est, non magis quam elogium, quod idem scriptor Johanni Baptistæ & Jacobo justo, fratri Domini, perhibet sed; & Judæi reliqui; ipsique Talmudici; quamquam admistis falsis multis & horrendis; per quas tamen blasphemias veritatis radii quidam interlucent. Quale est, quod Mariam meretricio cognomento, Stadam; & Josephum, cui juxta veteres Pantheri nomen, Pandiram indigitant. Narrant præterea ipsum magicas artes in Ægypto didicisse, atque ita mirabilia patrasse: veteri calumnia: Pharisæi autem dixerunt, in principe daemoniorum ejicit daemonia, Matth. 9: 34. conf. 12: 24. Quæ tacita miraculorum ejus consessio est. Ita denique in Talmude regni propinquus fuisse, ac vespera paschatis, propter præstigias & apostasiam (h. e. miracula, quodque Deum Israëlis vocaret Patrem suum) suspensus legitur.
units.tr: VIII. 4. Finally, they also give testimony to our Jesus: not only Josephus, Antiquities book 18, chapter 4, whose testimony has not yet been convicted of falsehood by demonstrations, any more than the commendation which the same writer gives to John the Baptist and to James the Just, the brother of the Lord; but also the remaining Jews, and the Talmudists themselves, although they mix in many false and horrible things, through which blasphemies some rays of truth shine. Such is their story that Mary was nicknamed Stada, a harlot, and that they call Joseph, to whom according to the ancients the name Panthera belonged, Pandira. They further narrate that he learned magical arts in Egypt and so performed wonders; the old slander: But the Pharisees said, he casts out demons by the prince of demons (Matt. 9:34; compare 12:24). This is a tacit admission of his miracles. Thus finally in the Talmud it is read that he was the close kinsman of the kingdom, and that on the eve of the Passover he was hanged for sorcery and apostasy (that is, for his miracles, and because he called the God of Israel his Father).

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Judæorum in hoc capite errores.
units.tr: The errors of the Jews in this chapter.

units.la: I. Atque ita veritas abunde patet, & quem scripsit Moses in lege, & prophetæ, invenimus, Iesum, filium Iosephi à Nazareth, Joh. 1: 46. Contra quem Judæorum natio tamen oculos claudit, atque animum suum ingenti odio obfirmat, & lucis istius radios ac tela tandem omnia in se extinguit: partim perversis de Messia ipso theses ac commentis, quæ eos aberrare faciunt ne verum unquam Messiam inveniant; partim nugacibus quibusdam contra Christum nostrum objectamentis & exceptiunculis; denique & à pseudo-Messiis suis sæpe decepti & ludibrio habiti.
units.tr: I. And so the truth is abundantly clear: we find him of whom Moses wrote in the law and the prophets, Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth (John 1:46). Against him the Jewish nation nevertheless closes its eyes and hardens its mind with immense hatred, and in the end it extinguishes all the rays and darts of that light upon itself. Partly it does so with perverse theories and fictions about the Messiah himself, which lead them astray so that they never find the true Messiah; partly with certain trifling objections and quibbles against our Christ; and finally they have often been deceived by their own false Messiahs and made a laughingstock.

units.la: II. Circa Messiam ipsum; quanquam aliqui ipsum Hiskiæ tempore jam olim venisse; alii pridem natum, & hodieque in mundo agere, sed dissimulato oris habitu, ut agnosci nequeat, testentur; manet tamen hic fidei Judaicæ articulus, expectandum Messiam, adventumque ipsius quotidianis votis ac precibus flagitandum. Quamquam illum, præ pudore, ac ne mundo iterum ludibrium debeant, ad finem ferme mundi, ac rerum omnium consummationem rejiciant.
units.tr: II. Concerning the Messiah himself, some testify that he already came long ago, in the time of Hezekiah; others that he was born long ago and is still living in the world today, but with his appearance disguised so that he cannot be recognised. Yet this remains an article of Jewish faith: the Messiah is to be awaited, and his coming must be sought with daily vows and prayers. Still, from shame, and lest they again become a laughingstock to the world, they put him off almost to the end of the world and the consummation of all things.

units.la: III. Messiam autem suum faciunt duplicem; unum filium Josephi, ex tribu Ephraim, qui in prælio contra Gogum occubiturus sit; alterum Davidis filium, victorem perpetuo & felicem: quod, ad oracula, quæ de utroque Messiæ statu, cum humili, tum glorioso, agunt, evitanda, excogitatum, & Scripturæ, & veterum Judæorum fidei, qui unicum tantum Messiam expectarunt, apertè refragatur.
units.tr: III. They make their Messiah twofold: one, the son of Joseph, of the tribe of Ephraim, who is destined to fall in battle against Gog; the other, the son of David, a victor who is perpetually fortunate. This was devised to avoid the prophecies which speak of both states of the Messiah, the humble and the glorious, and it openly contradicts Scripture and the faith of the ancient Jews, who expected only one Messiah.

units.la: IV. Revera autem nihil magni ac divini ab ipso expectant, cum regem solum terrenum faciant; qui Judæorum gentem, post longum exilium, liberaturus; ipsisque, paulo ante mundi interitum, terram, templum ac sceptrum suum redditurus; ac 40 circiter annos imperaturus sit. Quæ etiam ipsis Messiæ nota ac character est: non doctrina cœlestis, vel miracula: sed felicitas externa, belli gloria, gentis liberatio &c. Ut si quis inter eos vir insignis oriretur, qui ipsos liberare, ac in terram reducere posset; ille procul dubio ab ipsis pro Messia agnoscendus foret. Ita vero Judæi palam religioni ac ipsi suæ convitium fecerunt; ac profano isto de Messia commento omnem sibi ad verum Messiam agnoscendum aditum præcluserunt.
units.tr: IV. In truth they expect nothing great or divine from him, since they make him only an earthly king. He is to free the Jewish nation after a long exile, to restore to them, shortly before the end of the world, their land, temple and sceptre, and to reign for about forty years. This is also the mark and character they give the Messiah: not heavenly teaching or miracles, but external prosperity, military glory, deliverance of the nation, and so on. If some distinguished man arose among them who could free them and lead them back into their land, he would doubtless be acknowledged by them as the Messiah. In this way the Jews have openly insulted their own religion and, by this profane fiction about the Messiah, have closed to themselves every approach to recognising the true Messiah.

units.la: V. Unde non mirum est, cos nec Jesum Nazarenum pro vero Messia agnoscere posse. Cum notas illas, quas in suo Messia quærunt, in ipso non inveniant. Offenduntur enim magnopere humili ejus in terris statu & mortis contumelia, quam à gente ista perpessus est. Cum tamen hæc veri Messiæ potius indicia sint; nec apud priscos Judæos quicquam celebrius sit, quam חבלי משיח dolores Messiæ.
units.tr: V. Hence it is no wonder that they cannot acknowledge Jesus of Nazareth as the true Messiah, since they do not find in him the marks they seek in their Messiah. For they are greatly offended by his humble state on earth and by the shame of the death which he suffered at the hands of this nation. Yet these are rather the signs of the true Messiah, and among the ancient Jews nothing was more widely spoken of than חבלי משיח [chevlei mashiach], the birth pangs of the Messiah.

units.la: VI. Quod enim præterea vatum quorundam sacrorum dicta adferunt, quorum fidem in Christo nostro requirunt: ut cum montis templi elationem supra alios omnes montes; & longa pacis tempora; & ferarum armentorumque concordiam, ipso regnante canunt, Esai. 2. Hag. 2. illa quidem ænigmata & parabolas esse vel cæcus videat; quibus partim doctrinae è Zione prodeuntis celebritas, Ecclesiæ gloria ac latitudo, gentiumque omnium ad sacrum illum montem concursus; partim, rupto per Christi mortem velo intermedio, vocatisque ad Ecclesiam gentibus, & ferociam per mitem Euangelii sermonem ponere jussis, populorum sub Christo rege.
units.tr: VI. As for the passages of certain holy prophets which they bring forward, whose fulfilment they demand in our Christ, such as when they sing of the mountain of the temple raised above all other mountains, of long times of peace, and of the harmony of wild beasts and herds under the reigning Messiah (Isa. 2; Hag. 2), even a blind man can see that these are enigmas and parables. In them is signified partly the renown of the doctrine going forth from Zion, the glory and breadth of the Church, and the gathering of all nations to that holy mountain; partly, with the veil of separation torn by Christ's death and the Gentiles called into the Church and ordered to lay aside their fierceness through the gentle word of the Gospel, the peoples under Christ the King.

units.la: 11. Circa Jesum Nazarenum. rege concordia, & publica mundi pax ac quies, cessante in novâ Ecclesia Judæi ac Ethnici, omniumque omnino hominum, discrimine, augustis verbis denotatur. Quod externum enim rerum statum spectat, Ecclesiam tum nondum laboribus omnibus defunctam fore, sed artuolo veluti freto iterum in altum resorbendam, ac restare ipsi adhuc altera bella, & longa rerum discrimina, antequam regno suo potitura sit, nec prophetæ tacuerunt, nec Christus dissimulavit; An putatis, me venisse ad pacem dandam in terra? non, dico vo- bis, sed potius divisionem. Luc. 12:51. atque ipsi denique Judæi fateнtur; dum Messiam suum variarum gentium victorem faciunt; qui Judæos non sine vulneribus & cæde ad regnatas majoribus terras reductūrus sit. Ut istorum temporum pacem alio modo accipere necesse sit; de pace nempe spirituali & cœlesti, deque gentium populorumque in candem Christi doctrinam consensu & concordia, nullis exclusis, aut extra Ecclesiæ pomeria ablegatis.
units.tr: 11. Concerning Jesus of Nazareth. Under the king the harmony and public peace and quiet of the world, with the distinction between Jew and Gentile, and indeed between all men, ceasing in the new Church, is denoted in lofty words. As for the external state of things, the prophets did not keep silent, nor did Christ conceal, that the Church would not yet be finished with all its labours, but would be plunged again, as it were, into the deep on a fragile raft, and that other wars and long perils would remain before it obtained its kingdom: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division (Luke 12:51). Indeed the Jews themselves confess this, when they make their Messiah the conqueror of various nations, who is to lead the Jews back, not without wounds and slaughter, to the lands once ruled by their forefathers. So the peace of those times must be understood in another way: namely, as a spiritual and heavenly peace, and as the agreement and harmony of nations and peoples in the same doctrine of Christ, with none excluded or banished beyond the boundaries of the Church.

units.la: VII. Atque ex hoc, de vero Messia notisque ejus, errore, Judæi non solum Jesum Nazarenum, ut imparem, istoque fastigio minorem, impie repudiarunt: sed justo Dei judicio obvium quemque, qui sacrum illud nomen præferre ausus erat, acceperunt; & levissimi cujusque impostoris spolium & ludibrium fuerunt. Ut Christi vaticinio Joh. 5:43. ego veni in nomine Patris mei, & non accipitis me. Si alius veniat in nomine proprio, illum accipietis: fides fieret. Quales fuere, tempore Adriani imp. Bar Cochab, filius stellæ, juxta Num. 24:17. Incedet stella ex Jacobo &c. postea Bar Coziba, filius mendacii dictus. Sub Theodosio juniore, pseudo-Moses Cretensis. Maimonidis tempore, in Persia, David al David, præstigiator ac magus. Et superiori sæculo Rabbi Lemlem in Germania. Ne nostræ ætatis dedecora, nuperosque in Asia motus tangam. Quorum nullus discipulos sectamve superstitem reliquit; multo minus mundum à profanis ritibus expiavit, ac triuni cœli ac terræ conditori parere jussit. Quæ solius Jesu Nazareni laus & gloria est. Cujusreditus ac adventus ultimus, adhuc expectandus, & perpetuis precibus festinandus est.
units.tr: VII. From this error about the true Messiah and his marks, the Jews not only impiously rejected Jesus of Nazareth as unequal to them and lower than their rank, but by the just judgment of God they received everyone who dared to bear that sacred name, and they became the prey and mockery of every lightest impostor. So Christ's prophecy was fulfilled: I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him (John 5:43). Such were, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, Bar Cochba, son of the star, in line with Num. 24:17, A star shall come forth from Jacob, etc., who was later called Bar Coziba, son of falsehood. Under Theodosius the Younger there was the pseudo-Moses of Crete. In the time of Maimonides, in Persia, there was David al-David, a charlatan and magician. And in the last century there was Rabbi Lemlem in Germany. I shall not touch on the disgraces of our own age or the recent disturbances in Asia. None of these left a surviving body of disciples or sect; much less did any of them cleanse the world from profane rites or order it to obey the Triune Creator of heaven and earth. This is the praise and glory of Jesus of Nazareth alone, whose return and final coming are still to be awaited and hastened with unceasing prayers.

units.la: VIII. Quæri autem nonnunquam solet, cur Messiæ adventus, de quo jam egimus, tam diu, atque in ista demum, quæ vidimus, mundi tempora dilatus sit? Ad quod respondere licet, istam temporum œconomiam sapientibus de causis Deo placuisse, ut ex universa ejus administratione ac eventu patet. Ita enim umbræ debebant praecedere corpus; & magni adeo operis fundamentum prius jaci; & desiderium ac expectatio ejus excitari; denique peccati vis ac regnum, & omnium quae unquam adhibitae fuerunt expiationum imbecillitas ostentari: ut humani generis miseria magis elucesceret, Christique salvatoris necessitas ac pretium constaret.
units.tr: VIII. It is often asked why the coming of the Messiah, of which we have now spoken, was delayed so long, and was finally put off to the times of the world which we have seen. To this one may answer that this arrangement of the times pleased God for wise reasons, as is clear from his whole administration and its outcome. For the shadows had to go before the body; the foundation of so great a work had to be laid first; the desire and expectation of it had to be stirred up; and finally the power and reign of sin, and the weakness of all the expiations that were ever employed, had to be shown, so that the misery of the human race might stand out more clearly and the necessity and price of Christ the Saviour might be established.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS TERTIUS
units.tr: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS TERTIUS

units.la: DE Christi Persona & Incarnatione. CAPUT VIII. De persona & naturis Christi.
units.tr: CONCERNING the Person and Incarnation of Christ. CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the person and natures of Christ.

units.la: I. ATque ita de Messia, deque adventu ejus constat. Videamus nunc qualis quantusque inter homines apparuerit, & quis visus fuerit. Deus videl. in carne manifestatus.
units.tr: I. And so it is established concerning the Messiah and his coming. Let us now see what sort of man he appeared to be among men, how great he was, and who he was seen to be: namely, God manifested in the flesh.

units.la: 1. Tim. 3: 16. Et sermo caro factus, qui habitavit in nobis, plenus gratia & veritate. Joh. 1: 14. Quam 1. persona considerationem sequentur. 2. ejus status & officia.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 3:16. And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth. John 1:14. The consideration of his person is followed by the consideration of (1) his status and (2) his offices.

units.la: II. Circa personam occurrunt. 1. naturae ejus diversae: 2. earum unio. 3. Unionis illius consummatio ac terminus, in incarnatione.
units.tr: II. Concerning the person three matters present themselves: (1) his natures, which are diverse; (2) their union; and (3) the completion and terminus of that union, in the incarnation.

units.la: III. Natura est, cum assumens, tum assumta.
units.tr: III. A nature is either the assuming or the assumed.

units.la: IV. Natura assumens est divina, non in latitudine sua sumta, sed quatenus in persona filii seu λόγω subsistit. Incaute enim loquuntur Lutherani quidam, cum naturam divinam corporatam dicunt; quod personae proprium est. Estque hic gradus ad veterum Sabellianorum & Patripassianorum errorem; qui, cum de personarum distinctione, ut ante vidimus, non multum laborarent, totam trinitatem incarnatam dixere. Solent autem in scholis haec ita distinguí, quod incarnatio inchoative & effective quidem totius trinitatis sit, terminative autem solius filii.
units.tr: IV. The assuming nature is the divine, taken not in its whole extent but insofar as it subsists in the person of the Son, or the Logos. Some Lutherans speak carelessly when they say that the divine nature was embodied, since that belongs to the person. This is a step toward the error of the ancient Sabellians and Patripassians, who, as we saw earlier, did not much trouble themselves over the distinction of persons and said that the whole Trinity was incarnate. In the schools, however, these matters are usually distinguished in this way: the incarnation is indeed of the whole Trinity inchoatively and efficiently, but terminatively of the Son alone.

units.la: V. Cur autem filius hominem induerit, & non alia trinitatis persona? itemque an non plures personae eandem numero naturam assumere potuerint? quaerere irreligiosum est. Fuitque hoc Scholasticae Theologiae probrum, illa Dei arcana tam parum revereri, D ac ingenio suo tentare, cœlumque ipsum stultitia sua impetere. Quod non simplex scelus & flagitium est. Quanquam à posteriori, cum filium in carne visum Scriptura testatur, ultro tum agnoscimus, Deum non dedecere, filium suum, quem amat, cujus gloriam quærit, & per quem mundum condidit, quique mundi salus & vita est, etiam, ad redimendum ac salvandum eum, in mundum mittere. Atque hic acquiescere debemus.
units.tr: V. But to ask why the Son, and not another person of the Trinity, put on a man, or whether several persons could not have assumed the same nature numerically, is irreligious. It was a reproach to scholastic theology that it showed so little reverence for God's hidden counsels, tested them by its own wit, and assailed heaven itself with its folly. This is no simple crime and disgrace. Yet, from the effect, since Scripture testifies that the Son was seen in the flesh, we readily acknowledge that it did not disgrace God to send into the world his Son whom he loves, whose glory he seeks, through whom he made the world, and who is the salvation and life of the world, even to redeem and save it. Here we ought to rest.

units.la: VI. Extremum alterum est natura humana, vera & integra nostrãque per omnia similis, excepto solo peccato.
units.tr: VI. The other extreme is the human nature, true and complete, and in all things like our own, apart from sin alone.

units.la: VII. Veram carnem induisse tum expressis sacræ Scripturæ testimoniis; tum ex singulis naturæ humanæ partibus, earumque proprietatibus & affectionibus constat. Et sermo caro factus est. Joh. 1: 14. Quia ergo pueri communem habent carnem & sanguinem, & ipse similiter particips factus est eorundem. Hebr. 2: 14. Debuit per omnia fratribus similari, v. 17. Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non possit compati infirmitatibus nostris, sed tentatum per omnia ad similitudinem absque peccato. Hebr. 4: 14. Enim vero morbos nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros bajulavit, Esai. 53: 4. Videte manus meas, & pedes meos, quod ego ipse sum. Contrectate me, & videte; quod spiritus carnem nec ossa habeat, sicut me habere videtis. Luc. 24: 39. Ac speciatim de corpore, corporisque affectionibus, cum essentialibus, quod nimirum illud visibile, palpabile, numerisque ac partibus suis dimensum fuerit; tum accidentalibus ipsisque etiam infirmitatibus corporeis, fame, siti, defatigatione &c. videre licet: Corpus autem aptasti mihi. Hebr. 10: 5. Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum, Matth. 26: 26. Hic enim est sanguis meus &c. v. 28. Os non conteretur ipsi. Ioh 19: 36. Et Jesus profecit sapientia & statura &c. Luc. 2: 52. Non erat eis species, & non decus; & videbimus illum, & non erat spectabilis forma, ut appeteremus illum. Esai. 53: 2. Clamans voce magna dimisit spiritum. Matth. 27: 50. Ac de anima ejusque proprietatibus omnibus; præsertim intellectu, voluntate, affectibus; quin & imperfectionibus non culpabilibus; videri pariter possunt sequentia loca: Supra modum mæsta est anima mea ad mortem usque, Matth. 26: 38. Et Jesus profecit sapientia & statura. Luc. 2: 52. Non vero ut ego volo, sed ut tu vis. Matth. 26: 39. Qui in diebus carnis petitiones & supplicatincs — cum clamore valido & lacrymis offerens, exauditus a metu, didicit obedientiam. Hebr. 5: 7. Iesus igitur, ut vidit eam flentem, & qui venerant cum ea Judaeos flentes, infremuit Spiritu, & commovit seipsum. Ioh. 11:33. Et videns eum longinquo ficum, habentem folia, venit, si forte quid in ea inveniat. Et ad ipsam accedens, nihil invenit. Marc. 11: 13. De illo autem die & hora nullus novit, neque angeli, qui in coelo sunt, neque Filius, nisi Pater. cap. 13. v. 32.
units.tr: VII. That he put on true flesh is established both by the express testimonies of Holy Scripture and from the individual parts of human nature and their properties and affections. And the Word was made flesh. John 1:14. Since therefore the children have flesh and blood in common, he himself likewise partook of the same. Heb. 2:14. He ought in all things to be made like his brothers, v. 17. For we have not a high priest who cannot sympathise with our infirmities, but one who has been tempted in all things in like manner, apart from sin. Heb. 4:14. Surely he bore our sicknesses and carried our sorrows, Isa. 53:4. See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Handle me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have. Luke 24:39. Concerning the body in particular, and its affections, we may see both the essential, namely that it was visible, tangible, and measured by its own number and parts, and the accidental, and even the bodily infirmities, hunger, thirst, weariness, and so on: But a body you have prepared for me. Heb. 10:5. Take, eat; this is my body, Matt. 26:26. For this is my blood, etc., v. 28. Not a bone of him shall be broken. John 19:36. And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, etc., Luke 2:52. He had no form or comeliness; and we shall see him, and he had no attractive appearance, that we should desire him. Isa. 53:2. Crying with a loud voice he gave up the spirit. Matt. 27:50. Concerning the soul and all its properties, especially the understanding, the will, and the affections, and also its blameless imperfections, the following passages may likewise be seen: My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death, Matt. 26:38. And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature. Luke 2:52. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Matt. 26:39. Who in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, and being heard for his godly fear, learned obedience. Heb. 5:7. Jesus therefore, when he saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who had come with her, groaned in the spirit and troubled himself. John 11:33. And seeing from afar a fig tree having leaves, he went to see whether perhaps he might find anything on it. And coming to it, he found nothing. Mark 11:13. But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father. Mark 13:32.

units.la: VIII. Ut rejiciendi hic veniant veterum haereticorum errores, Christi olim naturam humanam impugnarunt. Quam totam eversam ibant Marcionita, Manichaei, caeterique Docetae dicti, qui non verum corpus, sed externam hominis speciem, corporisque phantasma ac spectrum Christo imposuere. Quos non male Tertullianus imaginarios Christianos appellat; atque hoc argumento obruit, Si Christi caro phantastica, tum & omnia quae per carnem gesta sunt. Ex parte eam destruebant ἀφνεῖς dicti, qui animae loco λόγου ac divinitatem constituebant, ut Arius & Apollinaris, quanquam diversa utrunque ratione. Nec abludebat Eutyches, qui confusis naturarum proprietatibus, unicam in Christo naturam restare, nec quicquam magnopere de homine superesse, docuit. Quem errorem, cum aperta fronte fateri non auderent, per posticum revocabant Monothelitae, unicam in Christo voluntatem statuentes. Sicut earum quoque propago fuerunt Agnoetae dicti, quorum princeps Themistius, Diaconus Alexandrinus; ut Apellis, Valentini, aliorumque portenta sileam, qui Christi corpus de sydereum materia, animamque ejus de Dei substantia delibabant; & non ex virgine, sed per virginem, perque naturales ejus egressus in mundum editum docebant. Ita hi omnes ἀμοιοσίαν naturae Christi humanae, eandemque cum nostra originem negabant; & Christo vel non veram, vel aliunde derivatam carnem tribuebant; ac animam vel tollebant prorsus, vel longe ante natum eum praeextitisse, & ex Deo ipso decerptam, errabant.
units.tr: VIII. So that the errors of the ancient heretics may be rejected here, they attacked the human nature of Christ in former times. The Marcionites, the Manichaeans, and the others called Docetae destroyed it entirely. They did not ascribe a true body to Christ but an outward appearance of a man, a phantasm and specter of a body. Tertullian aptly calls them imaginary Christians, and he overwhelms them with this argument: If Christ's flesh was a phantasm, then so also were all the things done through the flesh. The so-called aphnei [ἀφνεῖς] destroyed it in part, since they put the Logos and divinity in place of the soul, as Arius and Apollinaris did, though each in a different way. Eutyches did not differ much from them, teaching that the properties of the natures were confused, that only one nature remained in Christ, and that little of the man was left. Since they did not dare to confess this error openly, the Monothelites brought it back by the back door, positing one will in Christ. Offspring of these errors were also the so-called Agnoetae, whose leader was Themistius, a deacon of Alexandria. I pass over the monsters of Apelles and Valentinus and others, who took the body of Christ from celestial matter and his soul from the substance of God, and taught that he was born not of a virgin but through a virgin, and by natural outflows into the world. So all these men denied the dissimilarity [ἀμοιοσίαν] of Christ's human nature from ours and its common origin with ours; they attributed to Christ either no true flesh or flesh derived from elsewhere, and they either removed his soul altogether or wrongly held that it existed long before his birth and had been plucked from God himself.

units.la: IX. Nostro saeculo (ut Pontificios praeteream, qui humanam Christi naturam nonnihil carpunt, ac veterum haereticorum salivas lambunt; dum Christum viatorem simul & comprehensorem pronunciant, eumque nihil unquam ignorasse, nullisque perturbationibus agitatum, docent: quae non tam extollendae quam minuendae verae ejus humanitati faciunt) eandem sectam tenuere Swenkfeldiani, Weigeliani & Anabaptistae; qui, etsi inter se discordes, in hoc tamen conveniunt, quod carnis dominicae originem aliunde quam ex Maria virgine arcessunt. Nec abludunt Socinian, qui non Adamo Christum ortum, sed e materia immediate diate à Deo creata, virginisque utero immissa, editum affirmant.
units.tr: IX. In our own age (to pass over the Papists, who somewhat belittle the human nature of Christ and lick the spittle of the ancient heretics, while they pronounce Christ both a wayfarer and a comprehender, and teach that he never knew anything nor was disturbed by any perturbations, which things serve to diminish rather than to exalt his true humanity), the Swenkfeldians, the Weigelians, and the Anabaptists held the same sect; although they disagree among themselves, they agree in this, that they derive the origin of the Lord's flesh from somewhere other than from the Virgin Mary. The Socinians do not differ, who affirm that Christ was not born from Adam, but was produced from matter created immediately by God and sent into the womb of the virgin.

units.la: X. Quibus omnibus obstat 1. Scripturarum auctoritas. Quæ Christo non solum veram carnem, nostræ huic similem & ὁμοούσιον, ut jam vidimus; sed eandem nobiscum originem attribuunt: & Christum non solum hominem, sed passim hominis filium, mulieris, Evæ videlicet, quæ ex illo oraculo viventium mater dicta fuit, semen. Gen. 3: 15. Abrahami ac Davidis sobolem & filium, ex visceribus ejus ortum, 2. Sam. 7: 12. quod carnem attinet, Rom. 1: 3. appellant. Ad quos adeo, tanquam ad stirpis auctores, generis quoque ejus series longo progenitorum ordine deducitur Luc. 3. Matth. 1. Ac de Maria ejus matre, utque uterum ferre coeperit, ac divino onere gravida istum filium suum sueto tempore enixa fuerit, ac primogenitum ventris fructum ediderit, aliisque, eodem modo sermo fit, ut de aliis matribus fieri consuevit. Quæ nimis valida sunt, quam ut Christi per virginem transitum, ac divinitatis in corpore ejus hospitantis levem tantummodo moram designent. Quibus 2. Accedit & ratio ex Scripturis petita: quod munus ac officium ejus talem requirerent carnem, quæ nobis non aliena foret. Cum enim generis humani redemtor, ac Goël, atque electorum caput futurus foret; certe nos fratres ipsius atque membra debebamus esse; ut ipse veluti verus Goël, cognatam ac consanguineam sibi carnem servare; electosque homines tanquam proprium corpus, ipsosque artus suos, ac membra, adspicere, tenerrimeque adamare posset. Quod Apostolus urget Eph. 5: 23, 25, 26. Quoniam vir est caput uxoris, ut & Christus est caput Ecclesiæ: & ipse est qui salutem dat corpori. Viri diligite uxores vestras, sicut & Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & semet ipsum exposuit pro ea. & Heb. 2: 11. Nam & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes. Quam ob causam non erubescit eos vocare fratres. Tandem & 3. adversantium sententiarum absurditas & intemperies, quæ miris adeo modis Christi corpus contexunt, ut cœlestis id originis faciant, illas ipsas perimit; ut debellandis illis monstris inhærere necesse non sit.
units.tr: X. Against all these stands, first, the authority of the Scriptures. These attribute to Christ not only true flesh, like ours and homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], as we have already seen, but also the same origin as ours. They call Christ not only man but everywhere the son of man, the seed of the woman, that is, of Eve, who was called the mother of all living from that oracle, Gen. 3:15; the offspring and son of Abraham and David, sprung from his loins, 2 Sam. 7:12; and, as concerning the flesh, Rom. 1:3. To these, as to the authors of his stock, the series of his lineage is also traced through a long line of ancestors, Luke 3 and Matt. 1. Concerning Mary his mother, it is spoken as is customary of other mothers: how she began to bear him in her womb, how she brought forth her son, pregnant with a divine burden, at the usual time, and how she bore the firstborn fruit of her womb. These statements are too strong to designate merely a slight passage of Christ through the virgin, or a brief sojourn of the divinity dwelling in his body. To these is added, second, an argument taken from the Scriptures: his office and function required a flesh of such a kind that it would not be alien to us. For since he was to be the redeemer of the human race, and the Goël, and the head of the elect, we must surely have been his brothers and members, so that he, as the true Goël, might keep flesh akin and related to himself, and might look upon the chosen men as his own body and his own limbs and members, and love them most tenderly. The Apostle presses this in Eph. 5:23, 25, 26: For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church; and he is the one who gives salvation to the body. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her. And Heb. 2:11: For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one. For which cause he is not ashamed to call them brothers. Finally, third, the absurdity and extravagance of the opposing opinions, which weave the body of Christ in such marvellous ways that they make it of heavenly origin, destroys those very opinions; so there is no need to cling to them in order to crush those monsters.

units.la: XI. Sed objiciunt: Christum appellari Dominum de cælo, 1 Cor. 15: 47. & factum in spiritum vivificantem, v. 45. deque cælo descendisse, Joh. 3: 13. & sine patre ac matre fuisse, Hebr. 7: 3. Quæ illi pro acumine suo de solâ ejus naturâ humana intelligunt; cum de toto Christo sermo sit, qui nobilioris naturæ respectu Dominus de cælo fuit; deque cœlo veluti descendit cum sese in carne ostenderet; atque illa carnis cum deitate unione in spiritum vivificantem evasit; denique & sine patre ac matre in terris fuit.
units.tr: XI. But they object that Christ is called the Lord from heaven (1 Cor. 15:47), and made a life-giving spirit (v. 45), and came down from heaven (John 3:13), and was without father or mother (Heb. 7:3). With their keen wit, they understand these things only of his human nature. But the discussion concerns the whole Christ, who, in respect of his nobler nature, is the Lord from heaven; who, when he showed himself in the flesh, came down from heaven, as it were; who, through the union of the flesh with the deity, became a life-giving spirit; and who, finally, was on earth without father or mother.

units.la: XII. Postquam utramque Christi naturam vidimus, sequitur explicanda earum unio: quae non mutatione vel conversione aliqua perasta est, cujus divinitas incapax est; sed assumtione, ac divinae naturae in humana carne manifestatione ac inhabitatione. Non enim sane ut iam angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahami apprehendit. Hebr. 2:16. Sed se ipsum exinanivit, dum formam servi assumsit, quando in similitudine hominis esse incepit, Phil. 2:7. Deus est manifestatus in carne. 1. Tim. 3:16. Et sermo caro factus est: & habitavit in nobis, plenus gratia & veritate. Joh. 1:14. Quae assumtio vulgo personalis dicitur, quod propius considerandum.
units.tr: XII. Having seen both natures of Christ, we must now explain their union. It was not accomplished by any change or conversion, to which his divinity is incapable of being subjected, but by assumption, and by the manifestation and indwelling of the divine nature in human flesh. "For surely he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham" (Heb. 2:16). "But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, when he came to be in the likeness of men" (Phil. 2:7). "God was manifested in the flesh" (1 Tim. 3:16). "And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). This assumption is commonly called personal, which must be considered more closely.

units.la: XIII. Est autem persona natura rationalis, ipsa per sese subsistens, nec alteri cuiam unita. Quae subsistentia non quidem aliquid positivum dicit, aut quidquam subsistantiae superaddit, cum omni subsistantiae per se existenti necessario conveniat; sed illum substantiae modum indicat, quo illa actu per se completa est, nec ad alterius rei compositionem vel constitutionem ordinatur. Accedente enim tali ordinatione, vel divina, vel humana, persona esse definit: quae ordinatio ipsi etiam personae accidere potest.
units.tr: XIII. A person is a rational nature which subsists in itself and is united to no other. This subsistence does not express anything positive or add anything to the substance, since it necessarily belongs to every substance existing in itself. Rather, it indicates that mode of substance by which the substance is actually complete in itself and is not ordered to the composition or constitution of another thing. For when such an ordering, either divine or human, is added, it is defined as a person. This ordering can also happen to the person itself.

units.la: XIV. Communicantur autem duae substantiae atque coalescunt in unam personam, ubi ita conjunguntur, ut actiones & passiones utriusque toti composito communi nomine appellato attribuantur. Per quod nihil quidem positivi illis substantiis superadditur, sed tantum relatio, atque inde denominatio aliqua, per ordinationem, seu divinam, seu humanam.
units.tr: XIV. Two substances are communicated and coalesce into one person when they are so joined that the actions and sufferings of each are attributed to the whole compound, which is called by a common name. Nothing positive is added to those substances by this, but only a relation, and from that some denomination, through an ordering, whether divine or human.

units.la: XV. Atque ita in hoc mysterio, unio personalis nihil aliud est, quam quod persona secunda trinitatis, cum antea non esset conjuncta cum alia natura ad constituendum unum suppositum, nunc per ordinationem propriam ita cum illa conjungatur, ut utriusque actiones & alterius passiones toti composito, communi nomine appellato, attribuantur. Unde ex duabus hisce naturis unum quasi in Christo oritur suppositum, quod vere subsistit, cum illi ulterior ad aliam substantiam ordinatio denegetur.
units.tr: XV. Thus, in this mystery, personal union is nothing other than this: the second person of the Trinity, who previously was not joined with another nature to constitute one supposit, is now, through its own ordering, so joined with that nature that the actions of each and the sufferings of the other are attributed to the whole compound, called by a common name. Hence from these two natures there arises in Christ, as it were, one supposit, which truly subsists, since a further ordering to another substance is denied to it.

units.la: XVI. Humanitas ergo revera persona fuisset, si sola subsistitisset; nunc autem cum a primo ortu ad naturam divinam ordinata fuerit, in λόγῳ subsistit, & cum illo unum suppositum constituit. Ut male concludant Socinian, naturam Christi humanam personam esse, quia est substantia prima intelligens. Quod in ea verum fuisset, uti in omni substantia intelligente, nisi ad divinam naturam condita & ordinata fuisset.
units.tr: XVI. The humanity would therefore truly have been a person had it subsisted alone. But now, since from its first origin it has been ordered to the divine nature, it subsists in the Word [λόγῳ] and constitutes one supposit with it. So the Socinians wrongly conclude that Christ's human nature is a person because it is a first intelligent substance. This would have been true of it, as of every intelligent substance, had it not been created and ordered to the divine nature.

units.la: XVII. Bene autem concludi hinc potest, cum scholasticis, substantiam irrationalem hypostaticè assumi non potuisse. Sed male iidem rursus inferunt, personam humanam à λόγῳ assumptibilem non fuisse, cum illa jam propriam personalitatem habeat. Quid enim illa personalitas aliud dicit, quam quod illa ad aliam personam hactenus ordinata non erat, utcunque eo ordinari posset? quam tamen ordinationem per divinitatis assumtionem acquisivisset, & sic persona esse desiisset. Quod nulla ex parte pugnat.
units.tr: XVII. From this, however, it can rightly be concluded, with the Schoolmen, that an irrational substance could not be assumed hypostatically. But the same men wrongly infer again that a human person could not be assumed by the Word, since it already has its own personality. For what does that personality mean, except that up to now it was not ordered to another person, although it could be so ordered? That ordering it would have acquired through the assumption of the divinity, and so would have ceased to be a person. This clashes with nothing.

units.la: XVIII. Ad dubium: an duæ hæ naturæ duas partes fecerint, ex quibus persona veluti composita sit? Resp. improprie, præsertim de divina natura, ista vocabula usurpari, cum potius principia diversa, divino nexu inter se conjuncta ac unita, dicenda sint. Similia etiam quæ hic adhibent, pleraque incongrua sunt. Appositissimum est, quod de anima humana in corpore hospitante accersitur; ubi duæ substantiæ, in se completæ, ita divina ordinatione conjunguntur, ut exinde actiones utriusque & passiones toti composito communes sint. Quanquam nec hic omnia quadrent.
units.tr: XVIII. To the question whether these two natures made two parts from which the person is, as it were, composed: the answer is that these terms are used improperly, especially of the divine nature. Rather, different principles joined and united with one another by a divine bond ought to be spoken of. The similes which they also employ are mostly unsuitable. The most apt is the one drawn from the human soul dwelling in the body, where two substances, each complete in itself, are joined by divine ordering so that the actions and sufferings of each become common to the whole compound. Yet not even here do all things match.

units.la: XIX. Veritas modusque hujus unionis optime expressus est à concilio Chalcedonensi A. C. 451. ubi coërcendis Nestorii ac Eutychetis erroribus, qui diversis ex partibus personam Christi lacerabant orthodoxi vocabulis quibusdam, ceu repagulis, Christianam fidem sepserunt; dum unionem eam factam ciiverunt, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως, ἀτρέπτως & ἀσυγχύτως.
units.tr: XIX. The truth and manner of this union have been best expressed by the Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451. There, to check the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, who tore the person of Christ apart in different directions, the orthodox fenced the Christian faith with certain words, as with bars, when they declared that union to have been made undividedly, inseparably, unchangeably and unconfusedly [ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀσυγχύτως].

units.la: XX. Nestorii, qui jam in concilio œcumenico Ephesino, A. C. 431. damnatus erat, error ferebatur: quod non naturas solum, sed & personas divideret; quas in Christo duas statuebat, divinam & humanam pro duplici videl. natura. Quod revera, præterquam quod non unum mediatorem faciebat, juxta Paulum 1. Tim. 2: 5. 1. Cor. 8: 6. sed duplicem, divinitatis quoque Christi abnegatio, & tectum Arianismi virus erat; ac mediatorem faciebat nudum hominem, in quo divinitas non alio modo, quam in prophetis ac sanctis olim, præsens erat, ac externa quadam conjunctione, ac κατὰ σωματικῶς, ut loquebantur, inhabitabat: cum tota plenitudo deitatis in ipso habitet corporaliter, Col. 2: 9 Quanquam alii Nestorium excusare malint, nec tanta peccasse autument. Ut ut sit, etsi forte de Nestorio obscurius esset; error tamen quem edunt patres, recte damnatus & Synodi auctoritate confossus fuit.
units.tr: XX. The error of Nestorius, who had already been condemned at the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, A.D. 431, was that he divided not only the natures but also the persons. In Christ he posited two, the divine and the human, on account of the twofold nature. Besides not making one mediator, according to Paul (1 Tim. 2:5; 1 Cor. 8:6), but a twofold one, this was in fact a denial of the divinity of Christ and a veiled poison of Arianism. It made the mediator a bare man, in whom the divinity was present in no other way than in the prophets and saints of old, dwelling by some external conjunction and bodily [κατὰ σωματικῶς], as they put it. Yet "the whole fullness of the deity dwells in him bodily" (Col. 2:9). Some would rather excuse Nestorius and think he did not sin so gravely. However that may be, even if perhaps the matter concerning Nestorius were more obscure, the error which the Fathers set forth was rightly condemned and struck down by the authority of the Synod.

units.la: XXI. Contrarius error fuit Eutychis, Archimandritæ Constantinopolitani: cum quo fecit Dioscorus, patriarcha Alexandrinus: unde sectæ hujus partiarii modo Eutychetæ, modo Dioscoritæ, appellantur. Ille autem, Nestorium oppugnans, in contrarium ferebatur; &, ne duas in Christo personas agnosceret, unam tantum in eo statuebat naturam. Ex eodem autem fonte peccabat, unde Nestorius. Damnatus est in concilio Chalcedonensi A. C. 451.
units.tr: XXI. The contrary error was that of Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople, with whom Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, sided. Hence the adherents of this sect are called now Eutychians, now Dioscorians. He, attacking Nestorius, was carried to the opposite extreme, and, lest he acknowledge two persons in Christ, he posited only one nature in him. But he erred from the same source as Nestorius. He was condemned at the Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451.

units.la: XXII. Quem errorem aliqua ex parte imitantur Lutherani quidam, qui unionem naturarum in naturæ humanæ cum divina exæquatione, vel divinarum proprietatum communicatione, collocare, saltem verbis quibusdam, videntur. Gravius autem errant Anabaptistarum quidam, qui deitatem in humanitatem commutatam volunt; & quanquam Christum Deum & hominem affirmant, duas tamen in eo naturas negant: unam in eo delirantes superesse naturam, & vitam, & essentiam, quæ simul à patre processerit, & ex patribus sit genita; extincta prioris naturæ essentia, ubi altera cœperit. Ita illi omnem unionem hypostaticam abnegant. Gravissimè vero peccant Sociniani, qui universum hoc incarnationis mysterium, omnemque naturarum unionem pro fabula & commento habent.
units.tr: XXII. Some Lutherans imitate this error in some respects, seeming, at least in certain phrases, to place the union of the natures in an equalising of the human nature with the divine, or in a communication of divine properties. Some Anabaptists err more gravely, who want the deity changed into humanity. Although they affirm Christ to be God and man, they deny that there are two natures in him, raving that one nature, life and essence remains in him, which proceeded at once from the Father and was begotten from him. The essence of the former nature, they say, is extinguished when the other begins. Thus they deny every hypostatic union. The Socinians sin most gravely of all, who hold this whole mystery of the incarnation, and every union of natures, to be a fable and invention.

units.la: XXIII. Succedunt nunc unionis hujus effectα, partim in donorum ac gratiæ communicatione, in natura humana; partim in communicatione idiomatum utriusque naturæ, quoad personam.
units.tr: XXIII. Now follow the effects of this union: partly in the communication of gifts and grace to the human nature, and partly in the communication of the properties of each nature as regards the person.

units.la: XXIV. Quæ humanæ naturæ ex ea unione communicata sunt, hæc sunt: 1. Gratia unionis, quæ ea in divinæ naturæ societatem assumta, unum cum ea ὑπόστασιν constituit. Quod non exiguum decus atque χάρισμα est. Quod Deus in carne nostra habitare, illamque ut sibi non alienam adamare, & tanquam proprium corpus divinitate sua implere voluerit. Ut natura nostra hoc pacto proximè infra divinum fastigium collocata sit. 2. Gratia habitualis, donorumque omnium S. Spiritus communicatio, ea perfectione ac modo, quam creata natura capere potest. Non enim ex mensura dat Deus (ipsi, & in ipsorum nobis) Spiritum. Joh. 3:34. Propterea unxit te, ô Deus, Deus tuus oleo alacritatis ultra consortes tuos. Psal. 45:8. conf. Hebr. 1:9. Quo pertinet & gratia, quà Christus peccare nunquam potuit; cum in tanta luce intellectus, ac perfecto voluntatis amore rc re, sanctisque motibus, aberrare prorsus impossibile foret. Unde de se ipso dicit: In noctibus castigant me renes mei. Psal. 16: 7. & ipse appellatur praeco, vel index, qui non mentitur. Hab. 2: 3. & de ipso dicitur: Non est fraus in ore ejus, Esai. 53: 10. sed judicat in justitia, Esai. 11: 4. 3. Gratia potestatis mediatoriae; qua Ecclesiae sponsor, caput & Rex, atque universi mundi judex est. Et potestatem dedit ipsi etiam judicium faciendi, quia filius hominis est. Joh. 5: 27. 4. Quam consequitur gratia adorationis, seu summus honor, & adoratio, quae Christo ϑεανθρώπῳ debetur, Hebr. 1. 6. Non quod proximum & formale adorationis fundamentum sit munus mediatorium; cum illud sit ipsius divinitas: multo minus quod, cum Lutheranis quibusdam, ipsa Christi humanitas, in persona λόγος adoranda sit; quod foret personas discerpere, & ad Socinianos ἀνθρωπολάτρας accedere. Sed quod illa persona, quae mediator est, omnino adoranda sit; ipsumque munus mediatorium divinum honorem quoque includat: cum ad eum, qui isto munere fungitur, preces omnes, atque vota fidelium omnisque Ecclesiae affectus & cultus tendere debeant: & non minus fideli redemptori nostro, quam creatori animas nostras credere possimus ac debeamus.
units.tr: XXIV. The following things were communicated to the human nature from that union. 1. The grace of union, by which that nature, taken into fellowship with the divine nature, constitutes one hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] with it. This is no small honour and gift [χάρισμα]: that God willed to dwell in our flesh, to love it as not alien to himself, and to fill it, as his own body, with his divinity, so that our nature is in this way placed next below the divine summit. 2. The habitual grace, and the communication of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the perfection and mode that a created nature can receive. "For God does not give the Spirit by measure" (John 3:34). "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows" (Ps. 45:8; cf. Heb. 1:9). To this belongs also the grace by which Christ could never sin, since, with such light of understanding and perfect love of the will and holy motions, it was altogether impossible for him to go astray. Hence he says of himself: "My reins instruct me in the nights" (Ps. 16:7). He is called a herald, or witness, who does not lie (Hab. 2:3). And of him it is said: "There is no deceit in his mouth" (Isa. 53:10), but he judges in righteousness (Isa. 11:4). 3. The grace of the mediatorial power, by which he is the sponsor, head and king of the Church, and judge of the whole world. "And he gave him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man" (John 5:27). 4. Following upon this is the grace of adoration, or the highest honour and worship, which is due to Christ the God-man [θεανθρώπῳ] (Heb. 1:6). Not that the proximate and formal ground of adoration is the mediatorial office, since that is his divinity itself. Much less is it, as some Lutherans hold, that the humanity of Christ itself is to be adored in the person of the Word [λόγος]; for that would tear the persons apart and approach the Socinian man-worshippers [ἀνθρωπολάτρας]. Rather, the person who is mediator is altogether to be adored, and the mediatorial office itself includes divine honour as well, since all the prayers and vows of the faithful and all the affection and worship of the whole Church ought to be directed to him who discharges that office. We can and ought to entrust our souls no less to our faithful Redeemer than to our Creator.

units.la: XXV. 5. Accedit tandem, tanquam effectus hujus unionis, quod filius hominis factus sit filius Dei; non adoptivus; ut olim volebant haeretici, adoptionarii dicti, Elipandus & Felix Urgelitanus, in concilio Francofurtensi, sub Carolo M. A. C. 794. damnati; sed verus & proprius: juxta Rom. 8: 32. qui quidem proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum &c. Quod dextre intelligendum est. Non enim stricte secundum humanam naturam, si eam abstracte sumas, ac de formali causa filiationis quaeras, proprius Dei filius appellari potest. Sed proprie haec appellatio ϑεανθρώπῳ est, ac Christo mediatori convenit: proprie quidem quatenus Deus est; sed consequenter etiam quatenus humana carne vestitus est; quae in unitatem personae accepta, ab ipso non aliena, nec tanquam extranea considerari potest; sed ista unione in eundem filiationis honorem & appellationem venit. Ut Deus Christum hominem, non tanquam filium adoptivum (est enim adoptio personae extraneae) sed tanquam proprium consideret, & ametque eademque persona, quae homo est hominisque filius, etiam Deus propriusque Dei filius existat.
units.tr: XXV. 5. Finally, as an effect of this union, the Son of man was made the Son of God. This is not adoptive sonship, as the heretics once held, called Adoptionists, Elipandus and Felix of Urgel, who were condemned at the council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne in A.D. 794. It is true and proper sonship, according to Rom. 8:32: who indeed did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, etc. This must be understood rightly. Strictly speaking, if you take human nature abstractly and ask about the formal cause of sonship, he cannot be called the proper Son of God. But this title belongs properly to the God-man [θεανθρώπῳ] and suits Christ the mediator: properly indeed insofar as he is God, but consequently also insofar as he is clothed in human flesh. That flesh, taken into the unity of the person, is not alien to him and cannot be regarded as foreign to him. By that union it shares in the same honour and title of sonship. So God regards Christ the man not as an adopted son (for adoption concerns a stranger) but as his own, and loves him; and the same person who is man and son of man also exists as God and the proper Son of God.

units.la: XXVI. Alterum hypostaticae unionis effectum est, proprietatum
units.tr: XXVI. The second effect of the hypostatic union is the communication of properties.

units.la: 11. In communicatione idiomatum: tum atque idiomatum utriusque naturæ in eadem persona conspiratio & communicatio. Unde de persona illæ quoque prædicantur: idque vel directius, cum personæ naturæ illius proprietates adscribuntur, à qua ipsa tum appellatur; vel indirectius, cum, à diversa natura denominata, alterius naturæ proprietates gerit. Prior communicatio realis; altera, quæ in prædicatione potissimum consistit, verbalis magisque impropria appellari solet. Quanquam, si fundamentum spectes, unionem personalem, omnis hæc prædicatio realis fit: cum solo loquendi modo verbalis & synecdochica fit, nimirum quoad diversas naturas; unde hæc prædicatio in concreto, non autem in abstracto peragitur.
units.tr: 11. In the communication of idioms: the joining together and communication of the idioms of each nature in the one person.
