Hence those things are also predicated of the person, either more directly, when the properties of that nature from which the person is then named are ascribed to the person, or more indirectly, when, named from one nature, he bears the properties of the other nature. The former communication is real; the latter, which consists chiefly in predication, is usually called verbal and more improper. Yet if you look to the foundation, namely the personal union, all this predication is real. It is verbal and synecdochical only in the mode of speaking, namely with respect to the different natures; whence this predication is carried out in the concrete, not in the abstract.

units.la: XXVII. Corruperunt hanc idiomatum communicationem, ac in realem divinæ naturæ proprietatum communionem sic satis transmutarunt Lutherani quidam. Quam vetustiores unionis personalis formam; recentiores ejus effectum ac consequens dixere; Rintelenses autem nuper paulo aliter explicuerunt. Ipsa autem Augustana confessio commentum hoc ignorat; ac Flaccianorum illud inventum est, in subsidium ubiquitatis suæ advocatum.
units.tr: XXVII. Certain Lutherans have corrupted this communication of idioms and have so far changed it into a real communion of the properties of the divine nature. Older writers called this the form of the personal union; more recent writers called it its effect and consequence; the Rintelen theologians have recently explained it a little differently. But the Augsburg Confession itself is ignorant of this fiction. It was an invention of the Flacians, called in to support their doctrine of ubiquity.

units.la: XXVIII. Verum contra eam proprietatum divinarum transfusionem facit: 1. ipsarum proprietatum naturæ, quæ, si verè proprietates sunt, alii naturæ, utcunque unitæ (cum unio ea salvis rerum naturis & proprietatibus fiat) communicari nequeunt. 2. Ac præsertim summa earum in Deo unio est. Cum enim ab essentia divina non differant, ipsam ejus essentiam simul communicari & transfundi oportet. 3. Et quam rationem dabunt, cur non omnes proprietates, adeoque & ipsam Dei æternitatem, sed quasdam tantum communicatas statuant? cum ipsæ inter se non distinguantur, nec in Deo detur aliud & aliud. 4. Quin, si, vi unionis, de natura divina humana accipiat, cur non eadem ratione humanæ naturæ proprietates in divinam transfundentur; cum unio illa mutua & reciproca sit? 5. Sed non solum naturam divinam, ejusque proprietates, commento isto multipliciter violant adversarii; sed ipsam naturarum unionem in Christo lædunt. Unio enim dicenda non est, ubi unius naturæ propemodum extinctio, atque alterius naturæ proprietatum transmeatio & confusio asseritur. Cum tamen in Christo hæc distincta sint; una videl. persona, unumque agens, duo principia activa, atque hinc fluentes duplices actiones, veteribus ἐνέργειαι dictæ; quæ in unum denique συνθέσεως atque opus rursus coëunt & conveniunt. E Hæc beatificam, qua humana ejus natura nunc in coelis fruitur; nullam autem omniscientiam. Nam scientia ejus naturalis, pro aetatis aetu, incrementa sumsit; tum ex ideis innatis, quae paulatim clariores ac defaecationes ipsi affulgebant, idque longe felicius ac celerius quam ulli hominum; tum ex rerum experientia ac usu, quomodo lectionem, scriptionem, ut reliqua infantum aetas, atque artem quoque fabrilem addidicit. Nonne ipse est faber ille, filius Maria? Marc. 6: 3. Scientia infusa ex divinae gratiae arbitrio ac modo, ac pro diversa lucis istius radiatione ac copia, gradus suos habuit: cum λόγον, veluti domesticum oraculum, in potestate sua non habueret; nec illuminationes ejus accipere posset quotiens liberet; sed, non aliter ac prophetae, licet longe majori gradu, lucis illius temporaac modum expectare cogeretur. Imo qualiscunque illa illuminatio ponatur, eo ipso omniscientiam tollit. Tandem nec scientia ejus in coelis, quanquam humanitatem ejus satiare & profusus beare posset, infinita est, cum longo intervallo infra Dei ipsius scientiam posita sit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Indeed, the following points stand against this transfusion of divine properties. (1) The properties of the nature themselves: if they are truly properties, they cannot be communicated to another nature, however united, since that union takes place with the natures and their properties preserved. (2) Especially their supreme unity in God. For since they do not differ from the divine essence, the essence itself must necessarily be communicated and transfused at the same time. (3) What reason will they give why not all properties, and so God's eternity itself, but only some are communicated? For they are not distinguished from one another, and in God there is not one thing and another. (4) Indeed, if by virtue of the union the human nature receives things from the divine, why by the same reasoning would properties of the human nature not be transfused into the divine, since that union is mutual and reciprocal? (5) But the opponents not only violate the divine nature and its properties in many ways by this fiction; they also harm the union of the natures themselves in Christ. For it should not be called a union where the near extinction of one nature and the passing over and confusion of the properties of the other are asserted. Yet in Christ these things are distinct: one person, and one agent, two active principles, and from these two flowing actions, called energies by the ancients, which in the end come together and meet in one composite work [συνθέσεως]. This knowledge is beatific, by which his human nature now enjoys in heaven, but it is not omniscience. For his natural knowledge grew with the measure of his age: partly from innate ideas, which gradually shone upon him more clearly and were purified, and this far more happily and quickly than in any other human being; partly from experience and practice of things, just as he learned reading, writing, and the other things of childhood, and also the carpenter's craft. Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary? Mark 6:3. His infused knowledge had its degrees according to the decision and manner of divine grace, and according to the varying radiance and abundance of that light. For he did not have the Word [λόγον], as it were a domestic oracle, in his own power, nor could he receive its illuminations whenever he pleased. Rather, no differently from the prophets, though to a far greater degree, he was compelled to wait for the time and manner of that light. Indeed, whatever kind of illumination is posited, by that very fact omniscience is removed. Finally, his knowledge in heaven, though it could satisfy and richly bless his humanity, is not infinite, since it is placed at a great distance below God's own knowledge.

units.la: XXXV. Unde & ignorantia quarundam rerum in Christo fuit, dum in terris ageret.
units.tr: XXXV. Hence there was also some ignorance of certain things in Christ while he lived on earth.

units.la: Non illa quae in vitio poneretur, quaeque ipsum in judicando aberrare faceret; cum extra peccati noxam positus, illum mentis habitum haberet, ut de rebus nisi bene perceptis ac examinatis non judicaret; sed quae simplicis esset nescientiae, extra culpam ac animae labem. Quomodo diem judicii ignorasse dicitur, Marc. 13:32. cum ille in fatis adhuc lateret, nec mortali ulli revelatus esset. Ac de ficu arbore hesit, ac dubitavit, an forte, alieno anni tempore, praecoces fructus haberet, quos praematuro virore & frondibus spondebat. Marc. 11: 13. Unde & scientia ejus incrementi capax fuit. Sicuti Luc. 2: 40. dicitur: Puerulus crescebat & corroborabatur spiritu, implebaturque sapientia, & gratia Dei erat super eum: & com. 52. Jesus vero proficiebat sapientia, & statura apud Deum & homines. Primae enim ejus aetatis auctus ac laeta incrementa isto in loco narrantur, memorato insigni sapientiae ejus in teneris annis rudimento.
units.tr: This was not the kind of ignorance that would count as a fault and make him err in judgement, since he was free from the guilt of sin and so had the habit of mind never to pronounce on matters he had not thoroughly grasped and examined. It was rather a simple not-knowing, which carried no blame and no stain on his soul. Thus he is said not to have known the day of judgement, Mark 13:32, since that day was still hidden in the counsels of God and revealed to no mortal. And he hesitated and wondered about the fig tree, whether perhaps it had early fruit out of season, which its premature greenness and leaves promised, Mark 11:13. Hence his knowledge was also capable of growth, as Luke 2:40 says: The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him; and v. 52: But Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men. For the growth and happy advance of his early age is recounted in that place, together with the notable first sign of his wisdom in his tender years.

units.la: XXXVI. 4. Similiter omniprasentiam, & πανταχοπίαν Christi humanae naturae tribuunt: quam maxime adoptarunt Lutheranorum illi, qui cuderunt formulam concordiae Bergensis; atque eam praecipue ex naturarum unione deduxerunt, quam perperam in exaquatione earum constituunt. Ac miris distinctionum formis ac praestigiis
units.tr: XXXVI. 4. Similarly they attribute omnipresence and pantachopia [πανταχοπία] to the human nature of Christ. This was especially embraced by those Lutherans who drew up the Formula of Concord of Bergen, and they derived it chiefly from the union of the natures, which they wrongly establish in an equalising of the natures. And with wondrous forms of distinction and sleights of hand they defend this opinion, which cannot be reconciled and contradicts itself:

units.la: Omnipra-sentia. stigiis insociabilem ac contradictoriam istam sententiam tuentur: dum Christi corpus non uno modo præsens esse nugantur, videl: circumscriptive, à parte naturæ; & definitive, à parte unionis; localiter, in uno loco; & spiritualiter, in omnibus: rursusque quoad actum naturalem, cui certo tantum in loco esse concedunt; & personalem, cui omnipræsentiam adfingunt; idque vel in actu primo, dum in statu exinanitionis esset; vel in actu secundo, in exaltatione. Quomodo & diversos corporis Christi respectus statuunt, vel secundum natura proprietates, vel gratiam unionis, vel gloriam exaltationis. Quæ omnia pugnantia sunt. Verum tot velamentis opus est, ad insanæ sententiæ dedecus tegendum; istoque ambitu eo tandem veniendum erat, ut natura humana tantum non deificaretur.
units.tr: Omnipresence. They trifle that the body of Christ is present not in one way only, namely circumscriptively, on the side of its nature, and definitively, on the side of the union; locally, in one place, and spiritually, in all places. And again, with respect to natural action, which they grant only in a certain place, and personal action, to which they ascribe omnipresence; and this either in the first act, while he was in the state of humiliation, or in the second act, in his exaltation. In this way too they set up different respects of the body of Christ: either according to the properties of the nature, or the grace of the union, or the glory of the exaltation. All these things are contradictory. But so many veils are needed to cover the disgrace of this mad opinion; and by this circuitous route they had at last to arrive at the point where the human nature is hardly not deified.

units.la: XXXVII. Contra, Christi humanitatem aut omnipræsentem aut multipræsentem esse, nec Scriptura, nec natura patitur.
units.tr: XXXVII. On the other hand, neither Scripture nor nature allows the humanity of Christ to be either omnipresent or multipresent.

units.la: Ut enim Christianæ fidei articulos præterearn, in quos propudiosa ista sententia incurrit; aperta extant Scripturæ testimonia, quæ corpus ejus finitum, nec toto orbe sparsum ac diffusum testantur. Ad istatum enim exinanitionis pertinet, quod est Joh. 6: 14. Quum igitur vidit turba, ibi Jesum non esse. & 11: 15. Lator propter vos (ut credatis) quod non fui ibi. Sed eamus ad ipsum. & 16: 28. Exivi à patre, & veni in mundum: rursus relinquo mundum & proficiscor ad patrem. Atque ad statum exaltationis pertinent loca sequentia: Semper enim pauperes habetis vobiscum; me vero non semper habetis. Matth. 26: 11. Et factum est, cum ipse benediceret illis, distitit ab ipsis, & sublatus est in cœlum. Luc. 24: 51. Nostra autem civitas est in cœlis, unde & Salvatorem expectamus, Dominum Jesum Christum, Phil. 3: 20. Quem oportet cœlum quidem capere &c. Act. 3: 21.
units.tr: To pass over the articles of the Christian faith into which this shameful opinion falls, there stand open the testimonies of Scripture, which attest that his body is finite and not spread and diffused through the whole world. To the state of humiliation belongs what is said in John 6:14: When therefore the crowd saw that Jesus was not there; and 11:15: I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, that you may believe; but let us go to him. And 16:28: I came out from the Father, and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father. And to the state of exaltation belong the following places: For you have the poor with you always, but me you do not have always, Matt. 26:11; And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them and carried up into heaven, Luke 24:51; For our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, Phil. 3:20; Whom the heaven must receive, etc., Acts 3:21.

units.la: XXXVIII. Obstat & ratio, ac corporum natura, quorum loca & spatia multiplicari non possunt, nisi & ipsa multiplicentur, cum spatium reipsa unum sit cum corpore. Atque ita corpus, quod hic, & alio in orbe & in cœlo præsens est, non unum, sed diversum erit ac multiplex. Adeoque unum & non unum. Quod se ipsum perimit. Quas autem mirabiles distinctionum chimæras adferant ad pugnas has tollendas, jam vidimus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Reason and the nature of bodies also stand in the way, since their places and spaces cannot be multiplied unless they themselves are multiplied, because space is really one with the body. And so the body, which is present here and in another world and in heaven, will not be one but diverse and manifold; and so it will be both one and not one, which destroys itself. As for the wondrous chimeras of distinctions which they bring forward to remove these conflicts, we have already seen them.

units.la: XXXIX. Quod autem argutantur, humanam maturam in λόγῳ subsistere; adeoque unionem naturarum lædi, nisi illa una cum λόγῳ omnipræsens statuatur; tum enim λόγον fore extra carnem assumtam; id facile tollitur, mystica illa unione rite explicata. Quæ profecto facta non est juxta locorum spatia; sed, ut vidimus, in divina ordinatione consistit, qua humana natura a divina assumta est, ut in ea habitet, operetur, patiatur, resurgat &c. ita ut quicquid illi accidit, filio Dei non alienum, sed a proprio ejus corpore patratum sit. Unde & actiones passionesque ejus personae ab utraque natura denominatae tribuuntur. Ad hoc autem non pertinet, nec necessarium est, ut humana natura divina idiomata acquirat, ac simul cum ea omnibus in locis praesens sit.
units.tr: XXXIX. As for their quibble that the human nature subsists in the Word [λόγος], and that therefore the union of the natures would be impaired unless that nature were held to be omnipresent along with the Word, since then the Word would be outside the assumed flesh: this is easily removed once that mystical union is rightly explained. That union was certainly not made according to the spaces of places, but, as we have seen, consists in the divine ordering by which the human nature was assumed by the divine, so that it might dwell in it, act in it, suffer, rise again, and so on; so that whatever happened to it was not alien to the Son of God but was done by his own body. Hence the actions and sufferings of that person are also attributed, named from either nature. Moreover, it does not belong to this, nor is it necessary, that the human nature should acquire the divine attributes, and so be present in all places at once.

units.la: XL. Sequitur 5. potestas judiciaria, quam humanae Christi naturae adscribunt. Quae tamen potestas personae in universum competit, atque ex mediatorio munere fluit. Ut divina pariter & humana natura hic suas partes habeant; ut in progressu operis videbimus.
units.tr: XL. There follows 5., the judicial power, which they ascribe to the human nature of Christ. Yet this power belongs in general to the person and flows from his mediatorial office, so that the divine and human natures alike have their parts to play here, as we shall see in the progress of the work.

units.la: XLI. Cui addunt 6. denique vim vivificam, quam ipsius carni tribuunt; juxta Joh. 6:59. qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet, & ego in ipso. Sed valde improprie. Fons enim vitae proprie Deus est. Ac vivificatio est opus mediatorium, toti personae commune; ad quod divina natura principaliter & efficienter, ac humana natura meritorie concurrit.
units.tr: XLI. To these they finally add 6., the life-giving power, which they attribute to his flesh itself, according to John 6:59: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. But this is very improperly said. For the fountain of life is properly God. And quickening is a mediatorial work common to the whole person, to which the divine nature concurs principally and efficiently, and the human nature meritoriously.

units.la: XLII. Atque hi Lutheranorum in gravissimo hoc capite errores sunt; quibus tamen ipsi, quod & alibi eos facere vidimus, pruden-ter obicem ponunt, ne universam Christi personam perimant, ac Eutychianismum pariter & Nestorianismum utrimque damnant; maluntque imperceptibilia & pugnantia loqui, quam istas Christianae fidei apices tangere, ac Salvatoris personam violare, & non-hominem fateri. Ne jam dicamus, sententiam illam apud plurimos eorum magis in loquendi formulis fallacibusque terminorum ambiguitatibus & strophis, quam in rei ipsius abnegatione consistere. Unde de momento quaestionis hujus, alioquin gravissimae, judicari potest.
units.tr: XLII. These are the errors of the Lutherans on this most weighty head. Yet, as we have seen them do elsewhere, they prudently set a barrier against them, so as not to destroy the whole person of Christ, and they condemn both Eutychianism and Nestorianism on either side. They prefer to speak in unintelligible and contradictory terms rather than touch these peaks of the Christian faith, violate the person of the Saviour, and confess a non-man. Not to mention that the opinion of most of them lies more in forms of speech, deceptive ambiguities of terms and turns of phrase, than in an actual denial of the thing itself. From this one can judge the importance of this question, otherwise most grave.

units.la: XLIII. Estque haec etiam unica cum ipsis reconciliationis & totius reconciliationis via & ratio; ut totum videl. Christum, ac naturae utriusque veritatem & proprietates agnoscant; quod pro fundamento statui debet. Modus autem est, ut ad veteris Ecclesiae fidem redeant, parsque utraque intra quatuor Chalcedonensis concilii vocabula maneant, quae naturarum in Christo unionem facta docet ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀχωρίστως, ἀδιαιρέτως & ἀσυγχύτως. Quae si quis teneat, circa personam Christi errare non potest. Solari autem sese debet
units.tr: XLIII. And this is also the only way and method of reconciliation with them and of all reconciliation: that they acknowledge the whole Christ, and the truth and properties of each nature, which must be laid down as the foundation. The manner, however, is that they return to the faith of the ancient Church and that each party keep within the four terms of the Council of Chalcedon, which teaches that the union of the natures in Christ was made unconfusedly [ἀσυγχύτως], unchangeably [ἀτρέπτως], inseparably [ἀχωρίστως], undividedly [ἀδιαιρέτως]. If anyone holds these, he cannot go astray concerning the person of Christ. But the Church ought to console itself

units.la: Ecclesiae; ... Ecclesia, dum non ab extraneis solum, Judaeis, gentibusque, de Servatore suo controversiam sibi moveri, sed ipsos suos filios de eo contendere videt, prophetarum dictis, quae id ejus fatum cecinerunt, Esai. 41, 45, 48, 50, 52, 53. cap. Unde ille in scandalum suturus praedicitur, Esai. VIII: 14, 15. Et plus quam unica vice in mystico illo Salomonis Cantico fideles de sponso suo litem sibi moveri audiunt, idque ab ipsis puellis Hierosolymitanis, rogantibus, quisnam est dilectus tuus &c. quibus sponsa vicissim de Servatoris sui persona, cunctoque decore & ornatu pulcherrimam consessionem edit. vide cap. 5.
units.tr: the Church, when it sees that a dispute about its Saviour is raised against it not only by outsiders, Jews and Gentiles, but that its own sons contend about him. It should take comfort from the sayings of the prophets, who foretold this fate of his: Isa. 41, 45, 48, 50, 52, 53. Hence he is foretold as one who would become a stumbling-block, Isa. 8:14, 15. And more than once in that mystical Song of Solomon the faithful hear that a dispute about their bridegroom is raised against them, and that by the very maidens of Jerusalem, who ask: What is your beloved? etc., to which the bride in turn gives a most beautiful confession of her Saviour's person and of all his grace and adornment. See chapter 5.

units.la: CAPUT IX. De Incarnatione, conceptione & nativitate Christi.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the Incarnation, conception and birth of Christ.

units.la: I. Idimus personam Messiae, naturamque ejus duplicem, & utriusque naturae unionem. Sequitur propius consideranda unionis illius consummatio & perfectio, in incarnatione: quae Christi conceptione & nativitate perfecta est.
units.tr: I. We have considered the person of the Messiah, his twofold nature, and the union of the two natures. There follows a closer consideration of the consummation and perfection of that union, in the incarnation, which was brought to completion by Christ's conception and birth.

units.la: II. Dicitur ea vocabulis, partim scripturariis, partim Ecclesiasticis, incarnatio, ἐνσάρκωσις, ex analogia loci Joh. 1:14. ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο. 1. Tim. 3:16. Deus est manifestatus in carne. Ἐφανερώθη; quod Belgae imitantur. Ἐξαποστολή, Gal. 4:4. Quum vero venit plenitudo temporis, ἐξαπέστειλεν emisit Deus filium suum. Visitatio filii hominis. Psal. 8:5. Quid est homo, quod memor es ipsius, & filius hominis, quod visitas ipsum? Luc. 1:78. Ἐπιφάνεια & Θεοφάνεια. Nunc autem manifestata διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας per apparitionem Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, 2 Tim. 1:10. In quibus nos visitavit ortus ἀνατολὴ (vide Hebr. 7:14.) ex alto, Luc. 1:78. Quod desumtum ex Esa. 40:5.
units.tr: II. The incarnation is called by words partly scriptural and partly ecclesiastical: incarnation, ensarkōsis [ἐνσάρκωσις], by analogy with John 1:14, "The Word became flesh" [ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο]; 1 Tim. 3:16, "God was manifested in the flesh" [Ἐφανερώθη], which the Belgians imitate. Sending forth [Ἐξαποστολή], Gal. 4:4, "But when the fullness of time came, God sent forth [ἐξαπέστειλεν] his Son." The visitation of the Son of man, Ps. 8:5, "What is man, that you are mindful of him, and the son of man, that you visit him?" Luke 1:78. Appearing [Ἐπιφάνεια] and divine appearing [Θεοφάνεια]: "Now made manifest [διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας] by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ," 2 Tim. 1:10. "Whereby the dayspring [ἀνατολὴ] from on high has visited us" (see Heb. 7:14), Luke 1:78, which is taken from Isa. 40:5.

units.la: III. Possibilem esse Dei corporationem aut incarnationem, ac posse summum numen in humano corpore hospitari, seque mortalibus visendum & contrectandum praebere, ac familiariter inter homines agere, & loqui, & operari, & pati; quanquam natura mysterium illud proprio lumine non detegat; tamen ubi aliunde illud accipit, non invita admittit & adsentitur. Potest enim Deus humano corpore uti ut organo ac instrumento per quod operetur, eaque veluti veste ac velo majestatem suam tegere: ut olim nube, tanquam paludamento, indutus, voce humana, quae vox Dei dici poterat, oracula edebat; quod in rubo, in monte Sinai, ac diutissime sīmè in tabernaculo ac templo factum. Quid ni ergo, qui vocem hominis sibi fabricare potuit, etiam oculos, manus, & integrum corpus, animam denique humanam, in quo obedire ac pati queat, sibi formare possit? Certe nihil hic est, quod naturæ rerum adversetur.
units.tr: III. That the corporation or incarnation of God is possible, and that the supreme deity can dwell in a human body and present himself to mortals to be seen and handled, and can deal, speak, act and suffer familiarly among men; although nature does not disclose that mystery by its own light, yet when it receives it from elsewhere, it admits and assents to it without reluctance. For God can use a human body as an organ and instrument through which he works, and can cover his majesty with it as with a garment and a veil, as once he was clothed with a cloud as with a cloak and delivered oracles in a human voice, which could be called the voice of God. This was done in the bush, on Mount Sinai, and for a very long time in the tabernacle and the temple. Why then should he who could fashion for himself a human voice not also be able to form for himself eyes, hands and a whole body, and finally a human soul, in which he might obey and suffer? Certainly there is nothing here that conflicts with the nature of things.

units.la: IV. Necessitatem autem mysterii hujus, & quomodo Salvator noster, ad humanum genus salvandum, Deus pariter & homo esse debuerit; supra, libri secundi cap. xv. parag. 5, 6. vidimus. Quod vero Ostandro, & Pontificiis quibusdam, Socinianis denique, quanquam diverso scopo, placuit, Dei filium etiam extra istam humani generis necessitatem incarnandum fuisse; inquirere curiosum, & asserere temerarium est. Ac satius est in divinis Scripturis acquiescere, quæ non aliam adventus Christi in carne causam & occasionem dicunt, quam humani generis à prisca labe redemtionem & restitutionem. Fidelis est sermo & omni receptione dignus, quod C. J. venerit in mundum, ad peccatores salvandum. 1 Tim. 1:5. Venit enim filius hominis quærere & salvare id quod perditum erat. Luc. 19:10.
units.tr: IV. We have already seen above, in book two, chapter xv, paragraphs 5 and 6, the necessity of this mystery, and how our Saviour, in order to save the human race, had to be both God and man. As for the view that pleased Ostander, certain Papists, and finally the Socinians, though for different purposes, that the Son of God would have been incarnate even apart from this necessity of the human race, to inquire into this is curious, and to assert it is rash. It is better to rest in the divine Scriptures, which name no other cause and occasion of Christ's coming in the flesh than the redemption and restoration of the human race from its ancient fall. "This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners," 1 Tim. 1:15. "For the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost," Luke 19:10.

units.la: V. Futuram denique olim Dei incarnationem prædixit Vetus Test. Ecce virgo concipit, & pariet filium, & vocabit nomen ejus Immanuel. Esai. 7:14. Nam puer natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis. cap. 9:5. Ecce dies veniunt, ait Jehovah, & excitabo Davidi germen justum, quod regnabit Rex, & prosperabitur, & faciet judicium, & justitiam in terra. Jer. 23:5. Ac veritatem ejus ostendit & implevit Novum Test. Ac S. Johannes præsertim pulcherrimis verbis Euangelium suum exorditur: In principio erat sermo, & sermo erat apud Deum, & Deus erat sermo — & sermo caro esse incepit, & habitavit in nobis, plenus gratiâ & veritate. cap. 1:1,14. Quibus verbis ad veterem Dei in tabernaculo inhabitationem alludit, quæ inhabitationis in carne & typus & rudimentum erat. Ad istum enim modum hæc corporatio filii Dei intelligi debet. Unde & Apostolus simili figura manifestationem Dei in carne appellat; in qua visus totiquē mundo'ostensus fuit. 1 Tim. 3:16.
units.tr: V. Finally, the Old Testament foretold that God would one day be incarnate: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel," Isa. 7:14. "For unto us a child is born, and unto us a son is given," Isa. 9:5. "Behold, the days come, says Jehovah, that I will raise up to David a righteous branch, who shall reign as king, and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the land," Jer. 23:5. The New Testament shows and fulfils its truth. Saint John in particular begins his Gospel with most beautiful words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God ... and the Word became flesh [caro esse incepit] and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth," John 1:1, 14. By these words he alludes to God's ancient indwelling in the tabernacle, which was both a type and a rudiment of the indwelling in the flesh. For it is in this manner that this embodiment of the Son of God ought to be understood. Hence the Apostle also calls it, by a similar figure, the manifestation of God in the flesh, in which he was seen and shown to the whole world, 1 Tim. 3:16.

units.la: VI. Peracta autem res ipsa est in tempore duobus veluti gradibus; Christi videl. conceptione, & nativitate.
units.tr: VI. The thing itself was accomplished in time, in two steps as it were: namely Christ's conception and birth.

units.la: VII. In conceptione Christi duplex considerandum principium, ab unâ parte, Spir. S. ; ab altera, Maria virgo. Illud principium activum, hoc passivum fuit.
units.tr: VII. In the conception of Christ two principles are to be considered: on the one hand the Holy Spirit, on the other the virgin Mary. The former was the active principle, the latter the passive.

units.la: VIII. De Spiritu S. est Luc. 1:35. Spiritus S. veniet super te &c. Ubi
units.tr: VIII. Concerning the Holy Spirit there is Luke 1:35, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you," etc. Where

units.la: Primus ad illam gradus fuit Christi CONCEPTIO. de Spiritu S.
units.tr: The first step toward this was the CONCEPTION of Christ by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ubi per Spiritum S. veterum quidam tertiam S. S. Triados personam, cujus informando Christi corpore præcipuæ partes fuerunt, juxta illud, corpus aptasti mihi, Hebr. 10: 5. alii personam divinam filii, divinumque ejus spiritum ac potentiam, quo proprium sibi templum, in quo habitaret, fabricavit, intelligunt: juxta Zach. 6: 12. Ecce vir, GERMEN nomen ejus, & de subter se germinabit, & ipse ædificabit templum Jehova, & Phil. 2: 7. formam servi assumsit, quando in similitudine hominis esse incepit. Quem utrumque sensum Catechesis Heidelbergensis conjungit, dum filium Dei naturam humanam ex carne & sanguine virginis, per Spiritus S. operationem, assumsisse dicit.
units.tr: Here some of the ancients understood by the Holy Spirit the third person of the Holy Trinity, whose chief part was in forming Christ's body, according to "a body you have prepared for me," Heb. 10:5. Others understand the divine person of the Son, and his divine spirit and power, by which he fashioned for himself a proper temple in which to dwell, according to Zech. 6:12, "Behold the man, THE BRANCH is his name, and from beneath him he shall sprout, and he shall build the temple of Jehovah," and Phil. 2:7, "he took the form of a servant, when he came to be in the likeness of man." The Heidelberg Catechism joins both senses, when it says that the Son of God assumed human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: IX. Habuit autem Spiritus S. se efficienter, non materialiter, ut perversè Anabaptistæ nonnulli. Neque ideo tamen Christi pater dicendus est; cum ex ejus substantia humana Christi natura progenita non sit.
units.tr: IX. The Holy Spirit acted efficiently, not materially, as some Anabaptists perversely hold. Nor, however, is he therefore to be called the Father of Christ, since the human nature of Christ was not produced from his substance.

units.la: X. Hæ vero Spiritus partes fuerunt: 1. Semini virginis vim prolificam indidit, beatumque ejus uterum sancto onere constipavit.
units.tr: X. These were the parts of the Spirit: 1. He infused a generative power into the seed of the virgin and filled her blessed womb with a holy burden.

units.la: 2. Ex massâ ista virginea Christi corpus effinxit, & per gradus suos, naturæ porro manibus, ut in aliis hominibus fieri solet, efformavit, ac infuso deinde spiritu animavit. 3. Utque anima Christi ab ipso ortu erat sanctissima, ita quoque corpus ab omni labe defœcavit, sive potius ab omni impuritate præservavit; ut non nisi sanctissimis motibus obtemperaret, dignumque Deo habitaculum esset. 4. Tandem illam, præparatam veluti numini sedem, filio Dei inhabitandam tradidit, ut ab eo gratiâ donisque omnigenis impleretur, ac pro individuo organo & instrumento ei inserviret, nec alium rectorem pateretur. Unde quicquid in corpore isto gestum est, & quicquid illud vel egit, vel passum est, ad filium auctorem refertur. Quæ vera unionis hypostaticæ ratio & perfectio est.
units.tr: 2. From that virginal mass he formed the body of Christ, and fashioned it through its stages, by the hands of nature, as is usually done in other men, and then animated it by infusing a spirit. 3. And just as the soul of Christ was most holy from its very origin, so he also purified the body from all stain, or rather preserved it from all impurity, so that it would obey only the most holy motions and be a habitation worthy of God. 4. Finally, he handed over that dwelling, prepared as it were as a seat for deity, to the Son of God to inhabit, so that it might be filled by him with grace and gifts of every kind, and serve him as an individual organ and instrument, and not suffer any other ruler. Hence whatever was done in that body, and whatever it did or suffered, is referred to the Son as its author. This is the true reason and perfection of the hypostatic union.

units.la: XI. Alterum principium fuit Maria virgo: quæ de suo quidem sanguinem ac genitale semen contulit; sed quod Spiritu demum animante fœcundum redditum fuit. Unde principii potius passivi rationem habuit. Qua tamen ratione mater ejus, ac Christus illius filius verè dicitur, Matth. 2: 11. & 1: 25. Sicut enim pueri communem habent carnem & sanguinem, & ipse similiter particeps factus est eorundem. Hebr. 2: 14.
units.tr: XI. The other principle was the virgin Mary, who indeed contributed blood and generative seed from her own substance, but which was at last made fruitful when animated by the Spirit. Thus she had the character of a passive principle rather. Yet in this sense she is truly called his mother, and Christ her son, Matt. 2:11 and 1:25. "For since the children share in flesh and blood, he too likewise partook of the same," Heb. 2:14.

units.la: XII. Rejicimus autem Scholasticorum nugationem, qui, temporum videlicet moras ac tarda molimina à Spir. S. gratia exclu-den-
units.tr: XII. We reject the nonsense of the Scholastics, who, shutting out from the grace of the Holy Spirit the delays and slow labours of time, [dream that] at the very moment of conception Christ's body was already fully formed.

units.la: Illius bis operationes.
units.tr: His two operations.

units.la: E sanguine virginis Maria.
units.tr: From the blood of the virgin Mary.

units.la: In qua non est eorundem momento, sed soluto tempore per-secta fuit. dentes,ipso conceptionis momento Christi corpus plenissimè conformatum hariolantur. Cum tamen temporis spatia in hoc negotio S. Scriptura expresse numeret, ejusque initium & finem memoret; mense autem sexto &c. Luc. 1: 26. Et factum est, cum ipsi ibi essent, impleti sunt dies, ut ipsa parceret. Luc 2: 6. Nec aliter quam humano more, utque in aliis matribus fieri consuevit, de virginis conceptu ac partu loquatur: Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium &c. Matth. 1: 23. Quin ea quoque in parte Christum humanæ infirmitati similem fuisse dicat: Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similari &c. Hebr. 2: 17. conf. 4: 15. Quo pertinent quoque Hieronymi ad Eustochium verba: Novem mensibus in utero ut nascatur expectat, fastidia sustinet, cruentus egreditur &c.
units.tr: In which the conception was not complete in an instant, but was perfected in the due time. Yet Holy Scripture expressly counts the spans of time in this matter and records its beginning and end: "Now in the sixth month," etc., Luke 1:26; "And it came to pass, while they were there, that the days were accomplished that she should be delivered," Luke 2:6. Scripture speaks of the virgin's conception and delivery just as it does of other mothers, and in the usual human way: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son," etc., Matt. 1:23. Indeed in this respect too it says that Christ was like to human weakness: "Wherefore he ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren," etc., Heb. 2:17; cf. 4:15. To this also belong the words of Jerome to Eustochium: "For nine months he waits in the womb to be born, endures its discomforts, and comes forth bloodied," etc.

units.la: XIII. Nec satis verecunde iidem de ipso conceptionis momento disceptant. Hoc certum est, eam non factam antequam angelus legationem absolvisset: Et vocatum est nomen ejus Jesus, sic vocatum ab angelo, priusquam ipse conciperetur in utero. Luc. 2: 21. conf. 1: 31.
units.tr: XIII. Nor do they discuss the very moment of conception with sufficient modesty. This much is certain: it did not take place until the angel had completed his message. And his name was called Jesus, so called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. Luke 2:21; cf. 1:31.

units.la: XIV. Atque hac conceptione Christi, qua ille nostra de causa adeo sese demisit, ut tanta majestas intra materni uteri angustias delitescere, utque nasceretur novem mensibus expectare, non dedignata est, conjunctâ cum reliqua ipsius obedientiâ, immunda nostra conceptio ac genitura, obtecta & expiata est. Utque spiritu fœcundante illa peracta & absoluta fuit, ita inde novæ quoque vitæ capienda auspicia, deque eo novum hominem renasci ac animari debere, præ-ostensum fuit. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est; quod natum est ex Spiritu, Spiritus est, Joh. 3: 6.
units.tr: XIV. By this conception of Christ, in which for our sake he so humbled himself that such majesty did not disdain to lie hidden within the narrow confines of a mother's womb, and to wait nine months to be born, our unclean conception and birth were covered and cleansed, together with the rest of his obedience. Just as that conception was accomplished and completed by the fruitful Spirit, so it was shown beforehand that new life must begin from it, and that a new man must be born and quickened from it. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; that which is born of the Spirit is spirit, John 3:6.

units.la: XV. Conceptionem excipit nativitas Salvatoris, ex matre virgine. Quæ Davidis regis sanguis (Matth. 1: 1. Indiculus ortus Christi, filii Davidis, filii Abrahami. Rom. 1: 3. Qui extitit ex semine Davidis, secundum carnem.) quo & genus ejus à Luca deducitur; Josepho, ejusdem stipitis longinquo ramo, denupta; quo matris pudori ac filii olim honori consuleretur; sub honesto matrimonii velo divinum illum partum edidit. Desponsata enim Josepho mater ejus ---- inventa est gravida &c. Matth. 1: 18.
units.tr: XV. The conception is followed by the birth of the Saviour from a virgin mother. He was of the blood of King David (Matt. 1:1: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Rom. 1:3: who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh), and his line is traced by Luke as well. He was betrothed to Joseph, a distant branch of the same stock, so that the mother's honour might be protected and, in time, the son's as well. Under the respectable veil of marriage she brought forth that divine child. For when his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found with child, etc. Matt. 1:18.

units.la: XVI. Virgo autem Maria Deum fudit infantem: ut prophetarum oracula cecinerant, Esai. 7: 14. Ecce virgo concipit &c. Jer. 31: 22. Nam creavit Jehovah novum in terra: fœmina circumdat in utero masculum. conf. Apoc. 12: 5. Aliter autem virginitas ejus sese habuit ante partum, aliter in partu, aliter denique post partum. Ante par-
units.tr: XVI. The Virgin Mary, however, bore God as an infant, as the oracles of the prophets had foretold. Isa. 7:14: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc. Jer. 31:22: For the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth: a woman shall compass a man. Cf. Rev. 12:5. Her virginity stood in one state before the birth, in another during the birth, and in yet another after the birth. Before the birth

units.la: Aliter gradus NATIVITAS virginitas Salva illius partum, virginem eam fuisse fide divina credimus: Dixit vero Maria ad angelum: quomodo erit hoc, quoniam virum non cognosco? Luc.1: 34. Et non cognovit eam, donec peperit filium suum primogenitum. Matt. 1:25. Pariterque nec in partu virginitas ejus imminuta est. Post partum autem virgineum florem retinuisse, fide humana ac veteris Ecclesiae consensu constat; nec ad fidem ultra necesse est. Probabile enim est, uterum illum, in quo Servator noster vitae auspicia accepit, atque unde tanquam e templo in mundum hunc egressus est, tanto hospite consecratum ac sanctificatum fuisse.
units.tr: Her virginity stood differently at each stage: before the birth, during the birth, and after it. Before the birth, we believe by divine faith that she was a virgin. But Mary said to the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? Luke 1:34. And he knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son. Matt. 1:25. Likewise her virginity was not diminished in the birth itself. That after the birth she kept the flower of her virginity is established by human faith and by the agreement of the ancient Church, and there is no need to go further in matters of faith. For it is probable that the womb in which our Saviour received the beginnings of life, and from which he came forth into this world as from a temple, was consecrated and sanctified by so great a guest.

units.la: XVII. Ut male olim Helvidius Mariam ἀειπαρθένον negaverit, levissimis fretus argumentis: utpote, quod Christo fratres tribuantur in Euangelio; quod ex more Hebraeorum est, qui omnem cognatum vel affinem sanguinem ita appellant: quod matris primogenitus appelletur; quod apud eosdem commune primi partus, qui integrum adhuc matris uterum resolvit, vocabulum est, sive eum alii consequantur, sive non; conf. Num. 18: 15. Exod. 13: 2. quod denique de virginitate Mariae non ultra testetur Scriptura, quam donec peperisset filium primogenitum, quo futurum tempus excluditur; cum tamen particula donec illud non inferat. conf. Gen. 28:15.
units.tr: XVII. Helvidius long ago wrongly denied that Mary was ever-virgin [ἀειπαρθένον], relying on very weak arguments: namely, that the Gospel ascribes brothers to Christ, which is the Hebrew custom, since they call every blood relation or kinsman by that name; that he is called the firstborn of his mother, which among the same people is the common term for a first birth, which opens the mother's womb whole, whether or not others follow it (cf. Num. 18:15; Exod. 13:2); and finally that Scripture bears witness to no virginity of Mary beyond until she had brought forth her firstborn son, by which the future time is excluded, although the particle until does not imply that (cf. Gen. 28:15).

units.la: 2 Sam. 6:23. Matth. 28:20. Quanquam ab altera parte Pontificii ultra quam fas est tendant, dum votum perpetuae virginitatis a Maria emissum volunt; quod ex verbis ejus ad angelum, Luc. 1:34. quoniam virum non cognosco: frustra excsulpunt.
units.tr: (2 Sam. 6:23; Matt. 28:20.) On the other hand, the Papists go further than is right when they maintain that Mary made a vow of perpetual virginity. They vainly try to carve this out of her words to the angel, Luke 1:34: seeing I know not a man.

units.la: XVIII. Nec partus de virginitate Mariae quicquam delibavit, cum ea congressu solo polluatur. Partus autem miraculosus fuit, qua virgineus; naturalis vero, quia consueto matribus more enixa est.
units.tr: XVIII. Nor did the birth take anything away from Mary's virginity, since she is defiled by intercourse alone. The birth was miraculous in that it preserved her virginity, but natural in that she bore the child in the customary manner of mothers.

units.la: XIX. Fabula enim est, quod Pontificii Mariam clauso utero, ac illaesso foeminali, peperisse ajunt; contra Scripturam, ac rationem, ac veteris quoque Ecclesiae auctoritatem. Diserte enim Scriptura Luc. 2: 6. Factum est, quum illi ibi essent, impleti sunt dies, ut ipsa pareret. & v. 22, 23. Adduxerunt eum Hierosolymas, ad sistendum coram Jehovah (ut scriptum est, quod omnis mas, aperiens vulvam, sanctus Jehova vocabitur.) conf. Ex. 13: 21. Omnem primogenitum, aperientem omnem uterum. Heb. 2: 17. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri &c. Ac rei quoque natura istam dimensionum penetrationem, ac duorum corporum uno in loco moram non fert. Corpus enim a spatio non differt, & ne cogitatione quidem ab eo separari potest. Unde & apud veteres, tantam Majestatem per genitales foeminae transfisse egressu, Ruffinus dixit. XX. Eo-
units.tr: XIX. It is a fable that the Papists say Mary gave birth with her womb closed and her genital parts unharmed, contrary to Scripture, to reason, and to the authority of the ancient Church as well. For Scripture plainly says, Luke 2:6: It came to pass, while they were there, that the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. And vv. 22, 23: They brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written, every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord). Cf. Exod. 13:2: Every firstborn that openeth the womb. Heb. 2:17: Wherefore it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren, etc. The nature of the thing also does not allow such a penetration of dimensions, nor two bodies to occupy one place. For a body does not differ from space, and cannot even in thought be separated from it. Hence also the ancients, Rufinus said that so great a Majesty passed through the genital parts of a woman in going out. XX. Eo-

units.la: XX. Eorundum quoque commentum est, sine dolore Mariam enixam, quod vel nullo, vel falso fundamento asserunt. Non enim Maria, ut volunt, peccato caruit. Unde & peccati poenas, ac primum matrum sortem perferre debuit. Dixit ad foeminam — in dolore paries liberos, Gen. 3: 16. Foemina, quando parit, tristitiam habet, quod venit hora ipsius. Joh. 16: 21.
units.tr: XX. The same people also invent the story that Mary gave birth without pain, which they assert on no foundation or a false one. For Mary, as they claim, was not free from sin. Hence she had to bear the penalty of sin and the common lot of mothers. To the woman he said: in pain you shall bring forth children, Gen. 3:16. A woman, when she is in labour, has sorrow, because her hour is come, John 16:21.

units.la: XXI. Atque ex hac conceptione ac nativitate recte Christus Mariae filius appellatur. Duae enim in Christo filiationes sunt, pro diversarum naturarum respectu. Non tamen duo filii. Hoc enim personae vocabulum est: quae unica tantum est. Ac Maria non solum Θεοτόκος, sed & Χριστοτόκος, recte appellatur: contra ac Nestorium voluisse vidimus.
units.tr: XXI. From this conception and birth Christ is rightly called the son of Mary. There are indeed two sonships in Christ, according to the respect of his different natures. Yet they are not two sons, for that is a term of person, and there is only one person. And Mary is rightly called not only Theotokos but also Christotokos, contrary to what we have seen Nestorius wished.

units.la: XXII. Auctuarii vice quaedam de tempore nativitatis Christi annectemus: quod considerari potest vel generalius, respectu praecipuarum Epocharum, vel specialius, quod ad ipsum diem natalem.
units.tr: XXII. By way of an appendix, we shall add some remarks on the time of Christ's birth. This may be considered either more generally, with respect to the chief epochs, or more specifically, with respect to the birthday itself.

units.la: XXIII. Ac priori respectu occurrit, epocha conditi mundi, ad cujus annos Christi nativitas praecise ordinari non potest: cum hodiernus calculus, quo a Christo nato tempora signamus, fero decimum usurpatus fuerit, auctore Dionysio Exiguo. Unde temporum ratio, praesertim anterioribus saeculis, non parum confusa fuit. Communissimae autem sententiae Christi natalem ponunt, a condito mundo A. 3928. aut 3949. aut 3970. vel 4020. 2. Secunda epocha est Romanorum imperatorum. Constat autem sub Augusto Christum natum; qui cum 44 annos, post victoriam Actiacam, in rei Romanae arbitrio egerit, trigesimo, vel etiam trigesimo primo ejus anno praestantissimi auctores nativitatem Christi deputant. Baptisatus vero est anno Tiberii 15. seu 16. inchoante. 3. Tertia est epocha regni Herodis, quae paulo incertior est: cum de ipsis Herodis annis auctores discrepent, eique vario respectu vel 37 vel 34 annos tribuant, quibus regnum vel acceperit, vel gesserit. Hoc certum est, sub extrema Herodis Christum natum, nec longo admodum tempore illum superfuisse. 4. Denique respectu principum Synedrii magni, sub Hillelis Babylonii praefectura, an. ejus circiter 27, Christus in carne apparuit. Alii tamen aliter calculum hunc ordinant.
units.tr: XXIII. With respect to the former, there is the epoch of the creation of the world, to whose years Christ's birth cannot be assigned precisely, since the present reckoning by which we date from Christ's birth was introduced only in the sixth century, by Dionysius Exiguus. Hence the chronology, especially of earlier centuries, has been not a little confused. The most common opinion places Christ's birth in the year of the world 3928, or 3949, or 3970, or 4020. 2. The second epoch is that of the Roman emperors. It is established that Christ was born under Augustus; and since he lived in the power of the Roman state for 44 years after the victory at Actium, the most distinguished authors assign his birth to the thirtieth, or even the thirty-first, year of that reign. He was baptised in the fifteenth or sixteenth year of Tiberius. 3. The third is the epoch of Herod's reign, which is somewhat less certain, since authorities disagree about the years of Herod himself and, in different respects, ascribe to him either 37 or 34 years, from the time when he either received or held the kingdom. It is certain that Christ was born under the latter part of Herod's reign, and that he did not survive him by very long. 4. Finally, with respect to the principal men of the great Sanhedrin, Christ appeared in the flesh under the presidency of Hillel the Babylonian, in about his 27th year. Others, however, reckon this calculation differently.

units.la: XXIV. Quod specialius anni tempus, ac diem Christi natalem spectat, pariter diversae sunt auctorum sententiae; nec ex Scriptura ille constat; quae tribus illis locis, quae temporum Christi characterem habent (videl. Matth. 2: 1. Jesu vero nato Bethlehemi Judaeae, in diebus diebus regis Herodis. Luc. 2: 1, 2. Et factum est in diebus illis, exivit decretum a Caesare Augusto, ut totus orbis describeretur. Hic census primus actus est, praeside Syriae Cyrenio. & 3: 1. Anno decimo quinto imperii Tiberii Caesaris — factum est verbum Dei ad Iohannem) generalem tantum eorum notam tradere contenta, nihil praecise de die determinat. Inter veteres, orientis Ecclesiae die sexto Ianuarii illum celebrarunt, quem Θεοφάνεια appellabant; quemque cum manifestatione Dei in carne confundebant. Nec felicius Scaliger, ut aliorum sententias praeteream, circa festum Scenopegiae, Septembri mense, illum collocat; quem ex sacerdotum in templo stationibus ac ἐφημερίαις ingeniose subducit, ex Luc. 1: 8. nam & ille calculus multis partibus laborare videtur, nec ubique certus est. Communiori vero praxi hodierna Ecclesia fine anni, die Dec. 25. natalem Christi celebrat. Quae sententia a Romanis ubi Christi fidem acceperint, ex tabulis censualibus, quae Romae asservabantur, hausta, ac Ecclesiae tradita dicitur, indeque in totum porro orbem Christianum dimanasse. Ad quas publicas tabulas vetustissimi Patrum saepe provocarunt. Tertull. lib. 4. contra Marc. Conflat census actos sub Augusto — apud quos genus ejus inquirere potuissent.
units.tr: XXIV. As for the more specific season of the year and the birthday of Christ, the opinions of authors are likewise divided, and Scripture does not settle the matter. In those three passages, which give the marks of Christ's time (namely Matt. 2:1: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of Herod the king; Luke 2:1, 2: And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed. This taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria; and 3:1: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar ... the word of God came unto John), Scripture is content to give only their general marks and determines nothing precisely about the day. Among the ancients, the Church of the East celebrated it on the sixth of January, which they called Theophania [Θεοφάνεια], and which they confused with the manifestation of God in the flesh. Nor did Scaliger, to pass over the opinions of others, fare any better when he placed it around the Feast of Tabernacles, in September, which he ingeniously deduced from the courses of the priests in the temple and their ephemeriae [ἐφημερίαις], from Luke 1:8; for that calculation also seems to labour in many parts and is not everywhere certain. In the more common practice of today, however, the Church celebrates Christ's birthday at the end of the year, on 25 December. It is said that this opinion was drawn from the Roman census registers, which were kept at Rome, and handed on to the Church once the Romans had received the faith of Christ, and from there spread through the whole Christian world. The most ancient Fathers often appealed to these public records. Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion: It is established that the census was taken under Augustus, at which he might have inquired into his family.

units.la: XXV. Atque haec probabiliter de natali Christi haberi possunt. Scriptura, enim, cum alioqui multa levioris momenti tempora tradat, hunc tamen diem data opera silentio involvit: ostendens temporum doctrinam adeo necessariam non esse ad aeternitatem festinantibus; atque hac in parte Novi Test. Ecclesiam cum veteri exaequans, quae cum Salvatorem suum tot per saecula expectaret, tamen non nisi in latitudine aliqua adventantis tempora dimetiri ac mensurare poterat, ut videl. semper in speculla starent fideles. Quanquam mysterio non caret, quod in universa Scriptura nullius unquam hominis praecisum nativitatis tempus annotetur; mortis vero nonnunquam. Qua in re Christus reliquis Adami filiis assimilari voluit.
units.tr: XXV. These things may be held with probability concerning Christ's birthday. For Scripture, although it otherwise records many matters of lesser importance, nevertheless deliberately passes over this day in silence, showing that knowledge of times is not so necessary for those who hasten toward eternity; and in this respect the New Testament Church is made equal to the Old, which, though it awaited its Saviour through so many ages, could yet only measure and reckon the times of his coming within some range, since the faithful were always to stand on watch. Nevertheless, it is not without mystery that in the whole of Scripture the exact time of no man's birth is recorded, though the time of death sometimes is. In this matter Christ willed to be made like the other sons of Adam.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS QUARTUS DE VITA & OFFICIIS CHRISTI.
units.tr: Locus XXXIV: On the Life and Offices of Christ.

units.la: CAPUT X. De vita Christi privata.
units.tr: Chapter X. On the private life of Christ.

units.la: I. PErsonam Christi excipit ejus status, qui duplex est, exinanitionis & exaltationis. At Jehovah volentem enervare ipsum infirmavit; ubi posuit satisfactionis pretium animae ejus, videbit semen quod prolongabit dies, & beneplacitum Jehovae in manu ejus prosperabitur. Esai. 53: 10. Qui quum esset in forma Dei, non raptum duxit esse instar Dei, sed se ipsum exinanivit, dum formam servi assumsit — quemadmodum & Deus ipsum superexaltavit, & in gratia donavit ei nomen quod supra omne nomen est. Phil. 2: 7–10. Perscrutati in quod & quale tempus manifestavit Spiritus Christi, qui in ipsis erat, ante testatus passiones, quae Christo evenirent, & glorias post hasce. 1 Petr. 1: 11. An non oportebat Christum hac pati, & ingloriam suam ingredi? Luc. 24: 26.
units.tr: I. The person of Christ is followed by his state, which is twofold: of humiliation and of exaltation. But it pleased Jehovah to bruise him and put him to grief; when he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, prolong his days, and the pleasure of Jehovah shall prosper in his hand. Isa. 53:10. Who, being in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and, as God also highly exalted him, bestowed on him the name that is above every name. Phil. 2:7–10. Searching what time or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ, who was in them, signified when he testified in advance the sufferings that would come upon Christ and the glories after them. 1 Pet. 1:11. Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Luke 24:26.

units.la: II. Humiliatio Christi tum in vita, tum in morte ejus spectanda est. Alteram κένωσις exinanitionis, alteram ταπείνωσις humiliationis nomine Apostolus Phil. 2. praecipue designat.
units.tr: II. The humiliation of Christ is to be considered both in his life and in his death. The Apostle, in Phil. 2, especially designates the first by the name of emptying [κένωσις] and the second by the name of humiliation [ταπείνωσις].

units.la: III. Non autem simpliciter ad κένωσιν spectat ipsius incarnatio. Non enim divina majestate indignum est, humano corpore vestiri, ac creaturis videndum sese praebere. Ac Christus, postquam jam coelesti gloria fruitur, non tamen humanae carnis exuvias deposuit. Talis autem humanae naturae status divinae ejus gloriae ossiceit, qui non patitur ipsum esse ἴσα Θεῷ, quique servi forma ipsum induit, omnibusque naturae infirmitatibus obnoxium, ac legi tandem ipsi subditum ac execrabilem fecit. Unde etiam humana ejus natura minoribus instructa fuit donis & commodis, ac postea acquisivit. In intellectu ipsius emicuit maxima & purissima scientia, sed quae incrementi fuit capax, Luc. 2: 40 52. Voluntas ejus exornata fuit perfecta sanctitate, quae nullius quidem incrementi fuit capax, sed tamen talis, qualis viatorem decebat: neque potentiae ejus humanae tum datum fuit evitare & depellere infirmitates corporis, quibus subjectus fuit: neque etiam istis corporis dotibus tunc effulsit, quibus post exaltationem condecoratus fuit.
units.tr: III. Yet the incarnation is not simply a matter of the emptying. For it is no disgrace to the divine majesty to be clothed with a human body and to show himself to be seen by creatures. And Christ, although he now enjoys heavenly glory, has not laid aside the garments of human flesh. Yet this state of human nature does not hinder his divine glory: it does not allow him to be equal with God, and it clothed him in the form of a servant, made him subject to all the weaknesses of nature, and at last made him subject to the law and accursed. Hence also his human nature was furnished with smaller gifts and advantages, which he afterwards acquired. In his understanding there shone the greatest and purest knowledge, yet one capable of growth (Luke 2:40–52). His will was adorned with perfect holiness, which was indeed incapable of increase, but was such as befitted one on the way; nor was it granted to his human power then to avoid and drive away the infirmities of the body to which he was subject, nor did he then shine with those bodily endowments with which he was adorned after his exaltation.

units.la: IV. Consideranda autem in hoc statu: 1. vita Christi privata. 2. publica. 3. passio & mors.
units.tr: IV. In this state we must consider: (1) the private life of Christ; (2) his public life; (3) his suffering and death.

units.la: V. Privata Christi vita complectitur infantiam ejus, reliquamque aetatem, usque dum publice munus suum capesseret. Quam paucis Euangelistae tangunt Luc. 2. & Matth. 2.
units.tr: V. The private life of Christ comprises his infancy and the rest of his age until he took up his public office. The Evangelists touch on it briefly in Luke 2 and Matt. 2.

units.la: VI. Pueritiam enim ac incipientis aetatis primordia more aliorum puerorum egit. Ecce virgo concipit, & parit filium, butyrum & lac comedet, donec dignoscat reprobare malum & eligere bonum, Esai. 7: 14, 15. Cum esset puer, ut puer cogitabat, ut puer loquebatur, ut puer ratiocinabatur. 1. Cor. 13: 11. Hoc solo, quod ab illius aetatis peccatis ac erroribus liber, & mature spiritu auctus, aequalibus suis longe praefulserit; & sub sanctissima parentum disciplina occultae instar arboris crescens, tandem, maturantibus fatis, ex ignobili domo tantus derepente prodiit, ac publico oblensus fuit.
units.tr: VI. For he passed his childhood and the first beginnings of his age in the manner of other children. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and he shall eat curds and honey until he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. Isa. 7:14, 15. When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. 1 Cor. 13:11. By this alone, that being free from the sins and errors of that age, and maturing early in spirit, he far surpassed his equals; and growing like a hidden tree under the most holy discipline of his parents, at last, as the fates ripened, he came forth suddenly from an obscure house and was made known to the public.

units.la: VII. Memorabilia illius aetatis haec praecipue erant: nativitatis ejus promulgatio angelorum ministerio facta: circumcisio, ac primi cruoris libatio; itaque in sacramento sacratissimi nominis Jesu impositio: ejusdem, ex primogenitorum lege, in templo oblatio, & pauperum matris sacrificium: magorum adventus, & recens nati regis adoratio, ac auri, myrrhae & thuris honores: insidiae ab Herode infanti paratae, ac cunae tot puerorum caede cruentatae: fuga in Aegyptum, ductore angelo; ac, mortuo tyranno, eodem deducente, reditus; & Nazarethanum denique domicilium, ubi educatus fuit; natumque hinc, errore an improperio populi, Prophetam tenui municipio ortum dedignantis, Nazarenum cognomentum. A qua appellatione, etsi ex vulgi consuetudine vel contumelia orta, tamen Dei consilium non abfuit. Unde nunquam Bethlehemaeum, ubi Christus natus, sed Nazarenum semper eum indigitatum legimus. Quo vocabulo Deus fidelium aures animosque scire volebat, cosque sono illo ad vetus oraculum considerandum advertere, quod Christum non semel netzer illum, ac magnum Davidicae domus incrementum appellat, Zach. 6: 12. Jes. 11: 1. Et exibit virga e trunco Jesse, netzer & surculus ex radicibus ejus fructificabit. Cui geminum Jer. 23: 5. Ecce dies veniunt, ait Jehova, & excitabo David tzemach germen justum. Affinis enim tw netzer erat Nazareth; atque inde Christi Nazareni appellatio.
units.tr: VII. The memorable events of that age were these especially: the announcement of his birth made through the ministry of angels; his circumcision and the first offering of his blood, and so the imposition of the most sacred name of Jesus in the sacrament; his presentation in the temple according to the law concerning firstborn sons, and his mother's offering of the sacrifice of the poor; the arrival of the magi and the worship of the newborn king, and the honours of gold, myrrh and frankincense; the plots prepared against the infant by Herod, and the cradle stained with the slaughter of so many children; the flight into Egypt under the guidance of an angel, and, when the tyrant was dead, the return under the same guidance; and finally his home at Nazareth, where he was brought up. From this came the name "the Nazarene," whether by the error or by the reproach of the people, who scorned a prophet born in a humble town. Though this appellation arose from the custom or insult of the common people, it was not outside God's counsel. Hence we never read that he was designated the Bethlehemite, where Christ was born, but always the Nazarene. By this word God wished the ears and minds of believers to know, and by that sound to turn their attention to the ancient oracle, which calls Christ more than once netzer [נֵצֶר], and the great branch of the house of David: Zech. 6:12; Isa. 11:1. And a shoot shall come forth from the stump of Jesse, and a branch [netzer] shall grow out of his roots. To this corresponds Jer. 23:5. Behold, the days are coming, says Jehovah, when I will raise up for David a righteous branch [tzemach] [צֶמַח]. For Nazareth was akin to netzer, and hence the appellation of Christ the Nazarene.

units.la: VIII. Propius vero paulo considerandum est nomen Jesu, quod ab angelo Gabriele (quem in ministerio hoc, & olim Dan. 9: 21. & nunc Luc. 1: 26. à Deo adhibitum, Hieronymus cunarum Domini custodem, cubiculi Mariae janitorem, ac infantis Jesu gerulum appellat) antequam natus foret, infanti inditum, Servatorem, sive, ut Ecclesia maluit loqui, Salvatorem significat: non Graecâ, ut quidam olim nugati sunt, ab ἰάομαι; sed Hebraeâ origine: non ex יהוה & איש, ut Cabbalisticè Reuchlinus; sed simpliciter à forma ישוע, unde ישוע seu Josua, Num. 13: 17. quod, omisso in capite ה Syrorum more, ac extrema gutturali, ex Graecorum consuetudine; in σ emollita, in Ἰησοῦς transiit: quod non sine occulto scelere Judaei per Jeschu efferre malunt, ad Psal. 109: 13. alludentes.
units.tr: VIII. But the name Jesus must be considered a little more closely. It was given to the infant before he was born by the angel Gabriel (whom God used in this ministry both formerly, Dan. 9:21, and now, Luke 1:26; Jerome calls him "the guardian of the Lord's cradle, the doorkeeper of Mary's chamber, and the carrier of the infant Jesus"). It signifies a Saviour, or, as the Church preferred to say, a Savior. It does not derive from the Greek verb ἰάομαι (to heal), as some foolishly claimed long ago, but has a Hebrew origin: it is not from Jehovah and ish [יהוה] [איש], as Reuchlin fancifully argued by the Cabbalah, but simply from the form ישוע [יְשׁוּעַ], whence Joshua [יְהוֹשֻׁעַ], Num. 13:17. This, with the ה dropped at the end in the manner of the Syrians and the guttural at the end, passed by the Greek custom into Ἰησοῦς, where the σ is softened. The Jews prefer to pronounce it Jeschu, which they do not do without a hidden wickedness, alluding to Ps. 109:13.

units.la: IX. Fuit vero Salvator, non externa ac corporali liberatione, qualis Josua Dux, aut Pontifex ejusdem nominis, Hebr. 4: 8. coll. Act. 7: 45. Zach. 3: 1. sed spirituali ac aeterna: non potentia tantum ac vi, quales illi potissimum erant; sed merito ac lytro: non solum agendo, sed praecipuè patiendo.
units.tr: IX. He was a Saviour, however, not by an external and bodily deliverance, such as Joshua the leader, or the high priest of the same name, brought about (Heb. 4:8, compared with Acts 7:45; Zech. 3:1), but by a spiritual and eternal one: not by power and might alone, which were chiefly what those men had, but by merit and ransom; not only by acting but chiefly by suffering.

units.la: X. Nec satis digne Samosateniani ipsum salvationis ministrum, non vero proprio nomine Salvatorem volunt, qualis ipsis solus Pater est. Nam triplici eum modo salutem nostram peregisse statuunt: 1. annuntiatione, per doctrinam. 2. Confirmatione, per vitam sanctissimam, miracula, mortem denique ac proprii sanguinis testimonium; & tandem, devicta morte, in vitam reditum, quo praesens suoque in exemplo veritatem doctrina suae assereret. 3. Communicatione, ac actuali collatione, qua data à Patre potestate, omnibus in se credentibus vitam confert. Quae cuncta à mero homine praestari possunt, nec Deum, qualem nec illi Christum habent, praesentem postulant.
units.tr: X. The Samosatenians do not rightly enough call him only the minister of salvation and not the Saviour in his own proper sense, which they hold belongs to the Father alone. For they hold that he accomplished our salvation in three ways: (1) by proclamation, through his teaching; (2) by confirmation, through his most holy life, his miracles, and finally his death and the testimony of his own blood; and at last, death having been overcome, by his return to life, by which, present and by his own example, he asserted the truth of his doctrine; (3) by communication, and an actual conferring, by which, having received power from the Father, he bestows life on all who believe in him. All these things can be done by a mere man, and they do not require a God present, such as they do not hold Christ to be.

units.la: XI. Male etiam Episcopius, ac cum sacri istius nominis imminutione, Christum duplici modo Servatorem disserit; partim sine effectu, in iis quibus salutis media offert, qui ea accipere dedignantur; partim cum effectu, in fidelibus actu credentibus & perseverantibus: quomodo non nisi novissimo die, ut Rex, Salvator Ecclesiae dici posset; cum quandiu in mundo degit Ecclesia, omnia adhuc suspensa & incerta sint.
units.tr: XI. Episcopius also speaks badly, and with a diminishing of this sacred name, when he sets out a twofold way in which Christ is Saviour: partly without effect, toward those to whom he offers the means of salvation and who disdain to accept them; partly with effect, toward the faithful who actually believe and persevere. On this view he could be called the Saviour of the Church, as King, only on the last day, since while the Church lives in the world all things are still pending and uncertain.

units.la: XII. Sed de universo nominis hujus valore, ipsoque salvationis negotio, postea plenius. Tangenda nunc verbo superstitio Pontificiorum: qui 1. nomen illud Cabbalisticè, per aspirationem ex nomine Jchova assumtam, aut magico propemodum ritu tribus tantummodo litterulis I.H.S. quarum mediæ crux appicta sit, exprimunt. 2. idque longe sanctius habent quam ipsum nomen Jehova. 3. cumque cordi præcipue inscribendum esset, amuleti instar collo appendunt. 4. ac religioso ritu venerantur.
units.tr: XII. But the full value of this name, and the business of salvation itself, will be treated more fully later. Here I will only touch briefly on the superstition of the Papists, who (1) express that name in a Cabbalistic way, by an aspiration taken from the name Jehovah, or almost by a magical rite, using only three little letters, I.H.S., with a cross placed over the middle one; (2) hold it far more sacred than the very name Jehovah; (3) since it ought especially to be inscribed on the heart, hang it around the neck like an amulet; and (4) venerate it with a religious rite.

units.la: XIII. Quod & Lutherani imitantur ex Phil. 2: 10 Quamobrem & Deus ipsum [superexaltavit, & in gratia donavit ei nomen, quod supra omne nomen est &c. Quos tamen illum cultum nominibus Christi, Dei, Jehovæ, aut adorandæ Triades, quæ tamen non minus sacrosancta sunt, exhibere non videmus. Ut syllabarum veneratio, ac ægri animi error & superstitio sit, istud unum Salvatoris nomen, non autem alia isto ritu prosequi, ac cultum illum magna cum necessitate aliis imponere: quod veteri Ecclesiæ incognitum, nec ab Apostolo præceptum fuit, qui loco isto non de externo nomine, sed de Salvatoris persona, ac mediatoris potestate & honore agit. Quanquam alioquin religiose Dei ac Salvatoris nostri nomina habenda ac usurpanda non inviti fateamur. Et Scriptura cæteroquin discrimen quoque servat, nec promiscue Servatoris nominibus utitur.
units.tr: XIII. This the Lutherans also imitate, citing Phil. 2:10: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name," etc. Yet they do not show that same veneration to the names Christ, God, Jehovah, or the adorable Trinity, which are no less sacred. The veneration of syllables, and the error and superstition of a sick mind, consists in singling out this one name of the Saviour, and not others, for such a rite, and in imposing that worship on others with great insistence. This was unknown to the early Church, and the Apostle did not enjoin it; in that passage he speaks not of an outward name but of the person of the Saviour and the power and honour of the Mediator. Yet we do not deny that the names of God and of our Saviour ought to be held and used with reverence. Scripture, moreover, otherwise observes this distinction and does not use the names of the Saviour indiscriminately.

units.la: XIV. Duodecimo ætatis anno, parata pueritia, egregium suturi muneris specimen ac rudimentum edidit; in sapientum cœtu de lege patris sui, ad stuporem omnium, gravissime differens, Lu. 2.
units.tr: XIV. In his twelfth year, his childhood being past, he gave an outstanding sample and first taste of the office that lay before him: in the assembly of the wise, to the amazement of all, he spoke most weightily about the law of his father, Luke 2.

units.la: XV. Cætera privatus vixit in parentum domo, quæ priscâ sanctitate, quanquam in re tenui, agebat, eoque omni honore ac obsequio percoluit. Ac maturescente ætate fabrilem quoque artem, ut videtur, exercuit: Nonne hic est faber, filius Mariæ? Marc. 6: 3. Quod adeo non dedecori ipsi fuit, ut idem celebrium apud Judæos doctorum, ac præsertim Pharisæorum, institutum fuerit. Unde scitum magistrorum Misnah Aboth. 2: 2. Pulchra est doctrina legis cum via terræ (id est, opificio) nam labor utriusque facit hominem oblivisci pravitatis. Quomodo & Paulus συνεργὸς dicitur, Act. 18: 3.
units.tr: XV. In other respects he lived as a private man in his parents' house, which kept up its ancient holiness, though in a modest way, and he honoured and obeyed them in every respect. And as he came to maturity he also practised, it seems, the craft of a carpenter: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" Mark 6:3. This was so far from being a disgrace to him that the same custom was followed by the famous teachers among the Jews, and especially the Pharisees. Hence the saying of the masters in the Mishnah, Aboth 2:2: "Beautiful is the teaching of the law together with a worldly occupation (that is, a trade), for the labour of both makes a man forget sin." So also Paul is called a fellow-worker, Acts 18:3.

units.la: XVI. Sed nec sibi soli in longo isto otio vixit, sed jam tum altioris curas volvens, ac magna illa, ad quæ paulatim surgebat, meditans, in privatis rebus nostrum tamen negotium egit. In omni enim vita sese pro nobis sanctificavit, & ab ipso ejus initio, legis subjectione, paupertate, continua mortis meditatione, precibus & supplicationibus, denique jugi illa ad munus publicum præparatione, & præstituti temporis expectatione, sese jam tum generis humani vadem ac Servatorem præstitit. conf. Gal. 4: 4. Misit Deus filium sum—subjicientem se legi. Luc. 9: 58. Vulpes lustra habent, & volucres caeli nidos; filius autem hominis non habet ubi inclinet caput. 2 Cor. 8: 9. Cognoscite enim gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod propter vos pauper factus est, quum esset dives, ut vos paupertate ipsius ditesceretis. Hebr. 5: 7. Qui in diebus carnis petitiones & supplicationes, ad eum, qui poterat eum salvum facere ex morte, cum clamore valido, & lacrymis offerens; & exauditus a metu &c.
units.tr: XVI. Yet he did not live for himself alone in that long leisure; even then, turning over higher cares and meditating on those great tasks to which he was gradually rising, he nonetheless carried out our business in his private affairs. For in his whole life he sanctified himself for us, and from the very beginning of it, by submission to the law, by poverty, by constant meditation on death, by prayers and supplications, and finally by that continual preparation for his public office and by waiting for the appointed time, he already then presented himself as the surety and Saviour of mankind. Cf. Gal. 4:4: "God sent his Son... made under the law." Luke 9:58: "Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." 2 Cor. 8:9: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich." Heb. 5:7: "Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared," etc.

units.la: XVII. Eclipsis autem ac tentatio fidei fuit, in illis qui Messiae adventum jam acceperant, ubi ob Herodis insidias exulare jussus, Pharri accola, in Ægypto aliquandiu delituit. Quo tempore priorum desiderium ac expectatio non leviter concutiebatur, cum Messias, qui jam Ecclesiae ostensus erat, non amplius esse videretur. Qua de re propheta agit Jer. 31: 15, 16. & reditum illius ex terra hostium policetur: Vox in Rama auditur, ejulatus, ploratus amari, Rachelis plorantis super filiis suis, quae recusat consolationem admittere super filiis suis; quia ipse non erat. Sic dixit Jehovah: Prohibe vocem tuam a ploratu, & oculos tuos a lacryma. Nam est merces in opera-pretium tuum, ait Jehovah, & revertentur ex terra inimici.
units.tr: XVII. There was also an eclipse and a trial of faith for those who had already received the coming of the Messiah, when, ordered to flee from the plots of Herod, he lay hidden for a while in Egypt as a sojourner in Pharaoh's land. At that time the longing and expectation of those who had waited was shaken not slightly, since the Messiah, who had already been shown to the Church, no longer seemed to be present. The prophet speaks of this in Jer. 31:15, 16, and promises his return from the land of the enemy: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted for her children, because they are not. Thus saith the LORD: Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears; for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD, and they shall come again from the land of the enemy."

units.la: XVIII. Rejicimus autem Pontificiorum apocrypha, de miraculis infantiae Christi, aliaque ejus commatis, quibus quisquiliis plebis Christianae aures contaminare & pascere illi solent: silente non sofum Scriptura, sed & contra insulsas istas fabulas praescribente, Joh. 2: 11. Hoc initium signorum fecit Iesus Cana, oppido Galilaeae. Vera enim miracula doctrinam non praecedere, sed comitari & subsequi amant. Nec παιδικά ac puerilia miracula facere ex majestate Dei est. Ejusdem auctoritatis est Suidae figmentum de Christo Pontifice ante justam aetatem; aliaque id genus naeniae frigidissimae.
units.tr: XVIII. We reject, however, the apocryphal tales of the Papists about the miracles of Christ's infancy, and other such things with which they are wont to fill and feed the ears of the Christian people with these trifles, while Scripture not only keeps silent but, against these silly fables, prescribes otherwise: "This beginning of signs Jesus did at Cana, a town of Galilee," John 2:11. For true miracles do not go before the teaching but accompany and follow it. Nor is it consistent with the majesty of God to work childish and puerile miracles.
