Of the same authority is the fiction of Suidas about Christ as a priest before the proper age, and other such utterly frigid trifles.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De initiatione & unctione Christi.
units.tr: On the initiation and anointing of Christ

units.la: I. Neunte trigesimo aetatis anno, ex Levitarum instituto, Christus in publicum productus, ac munera sua auspicatus est. Et ipse Iesus inceperat quasi triginta annorum esse, Luc. 3: 23. Ubi consideranda 1. ejus initiatio 2. ministerium, ac munera quae gessit. 3. vitae denique publicae conclusio. Ad primum pertinet baptismus, per Johannem ministratus; atque eum consecuta tentatio in deserto.
units.tr: I. In his thirtieth year, according to the custom of the Levites, Christ was brought forward in public and began his offices. And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years old, Luke 3:23. Here we must consider (1) his initiation, (2) the ministry and the offices he performed, and (3) finally the conclusion of his public life. The first concerns the baptism administered by John, and the temptation in the desert that followed it.

units.la: G
units.tr: G

units.la: II. Potissimum initiatio ejus facta est per baptismum ipsius, quem accipere & proprio in corpore consecrare voluit; tum ut illo ritu pro humano genere sese vadem sisteret, omnemque obedientiam legè debitam sponderet; tum ut illud amoris ac gratiæ divinæ pignus ac arrhabonem pro se, ac pro fidelibus omnibus, præciperet & prælibaret; tum ut in ipso remissio peccatorum & ablatio jugi obsignaretur.
units.tr: II. His initiation took place chiefly through his own baptism, which he chose to receive and to consecrate in his own body. He did so partly so that by that rite he might stand surety for the human race and pledge all the obedience the law required; partly so that he might present and foretaste, for himself and for all believers, the pledge and earnest of divine love and grace; and partly so that the forgiveness of sins and their removal might be sealed in him.

units.la: III. Quanquam altius quoque hæc spectarent. Cum enim cœlesti voce pater interveniret, atque hunc filium suum mundo publice ostenderet & traderet; fuit in baptismo simul illius inauguratio ad munera publica. Quorum non levia indicia hic comparent. Rex enim monstrabatur, qui filius ac hæres Dei erat. Et sacerdotem pater admittebat, quem sibi placere, ac cujus sacrificium sese accipere teltabatur: conf. Jef.42:1. ecce servus meus, quem accipit anima mea. Præsupponit autem כפר & piamentum.
units.tr: III. These things also looked further. When the Father intervened with a heavenly voice and publicly showed and handed over this his Son to the world, at the baptism there was at the same time his inauguration to public offices. Not slight indications of these appear here. For a king was shown, the Son and heir of God. And the Father was admitting a priest, whom he testified was pleasing to himself and whose sacrifice he accepted. Compare Isa. 42:1: Behold my servant, whom my soul accepts. Moreover it presupposes [כפר] and atonement.

units.la: Denique propheta erat, qui de cœlo commendabatur, ut sine exceptione audiendus. Atque hæc omnia visibili Spiritus S. descensu confirmabantur, qui leni motu, instar columbæ, in ipsum allabi certo modo visus est.
units.tr: Finally, he was a prophet, who was commended from heaven to be heard without exception. And all these things were confirmed by the visible descent of the Holy Spirit, who was seen to alight upon him in a certain manner, with a gentle motion, like a dove.

units.la: IV. Jordanis aquis ablutus, ac, cœlo teste, non dubius salutis auctor & præco, in deserto abductus est; in secreto illo familiarius Deo suo fruiturus, ac cum inferorum principe pugnaturus; istoque auspicio plenissimè munus suum inchoaturus.
units.tr: IV. Washed in the waters of the Jordan, and, with heaven as witness, a surety and herald of salvation beyond doubt, he was led away into the desert, there to enjoy his God more intimately in that secret place and to fight with the prince of the underworld; and with this as his beginning he would fully launch upon his office.

units.la: V. Atque in solitudine illa non simplici cum diabolo certamine defunctus est. Matth. 4. Nam & in corpore, quod historiæ simplicitas ac verborum emphasis ostendit, abreptus; & in anima complures inferni prædonis insultus tulit. Sed cunctis ejus artibus superior, quanto priori Adamo fortior ac major foret ostendit: istoque pugnæ rudimento bellum, quod sibi ac Ecclesiæ suæ cum diabolo resistabat, imbuit; ac denique felicem faustumque ejus exitum fore ostendit. Præterquam quod & ad obedientiam, quam Deo debebat, pertinuit, omnes Satanæ suggestiones ac fraudes vincere, quo ea omnibus numeris perfecta foret: ac muneris ejus interrerat, cuncta hominum mala degustare, ut proprio exemplo edoctus, miseriis eorum promtius succurrere posset.
units.tr: V. And in that solitude he did not come through with a simple contest with the devil. Matt. 4. For he was carried away both in body, as the plainness of the history and the emphasis of the words show, and in soul he bore many assaults of the infernal robber. But superior to all his arts, he showed how much stronger and greater he was than the first Adam. By this rudiment of combat he imbued the war which he waged against the devil on behalf of himself and his Church, and he showed that its outcome would be happy and fortunate. Besides which, it belonged to the obedience he owed to God to overcome all the suggestions and frauds of Satan, so that this obedience might be perfect in every respect. And it belonged to his office to taste all human evils, so that, taught by his own example, he might be the more ready to succour their miseries.

units.la: VI. Ad hanc initiationem pertinet unctio illa Christi, à qua unctus & Christus, & Hebraicè Messias dicitur: quæ licet ab initio incarnationis ipsius, imo certo respectu, ut videbimus, ante eam locum habuerit, quia tamen in publica illius initiatione munerumque ipsi impositorum administratione praecipuè emicuit, hoc loco eam considerabimus.
units.tr: VI. To this initiation belongs that anointing of Christ, from which he is called anointed and Christ, and in Hebrew Messiah. Although it had its place from the beginning of his incarnation, indeed in a certain respect, as we shall see, even before it, yet because it chiefly shone forth in his public initiation and in the administration of the offices laid upon him, we shall consider it at this point.

units.la: VII. Erat autem unguentorum usus in populo Dei frequens; tum ad honestam vitæ voluptatem, Joh. 11:2. & 12: 3. Psal. 23:5 141: 5. tum in praecipuo aliquo officio mandando usurpatus. Unde metaphora Prov. 8:23. A saeculo unctus sum, à capite, à primis terræ.
units.tr: VII. The use of ointments was frequent among the people of God, both for the honest pleasure of life (John 11:2; 12:3; Ps. 23:5; 141:5) and as something employed in the commissioning of some particular office. Hence the metaphor in Prov. 8:23: From everlasting I was anointed, from the head, from the first of the earth.

units.la: VIII. Ungebantur in adeundo munere non omnes, sed qui celsioris gradus erant; praecipuè terni ordinis homines: 1. Prophetæ, quanquam rarius, & vix illo ritu. Jehu autem filium Nimshi ungito in regem, super Israelem; & Elisam ungito in Prophetam loco tuo. 1 Reg. 19: 16. conf. Psal. 105: 15. 2. Sacerdotes, praesertim Pontifices. 3. Reges. De quorum unctione supra lib. IV. cap. VIII. §. 14, 15.
units.tr: VIII. Not everyone was anointed on entering office, but those of higher rank, chiefly men of three orders: (1) prophets, though more rarely, and hardly with that rite: But anoint Jehu, son of Nimshi, as king over Israel; and anoint Elisha as prophet in your place. 1 Kings 19:16; compare Ps. 105:15. (2) Priests, especially high priests. (3) Kings. On their anointing see above, book IV, chapter VIII, §§ 14, 15.

units.la: IX. Christus autem externo oleo delibutus non est. Non enim typicis istis institutis opus erat, cum non externo ritu, ut aliquis de saeculo Rex, aut veteris templi minister; sed sublimiori ac spirituali modo munera ista impleturus foret. Unde & unctio quoque mystica ac spiritualis fuit: partim quæ in persona ejus ad munus mediatorium designatione; partim in deitatis incarne ejus inhabitatione; partim in donorum ac charismatum collatione constitit.
units.tr: IX. Christ, however, was not anointed with external oil. For he had no need of those typical institutions, since he was to fulfil these offices not with an external rite, like some king of the world or a minister of the old temple, but in a more sublime and spiritual manner. Hence his unction was also mystical and spiritual: it consisted partly in his designation to the mediatorial office in his person, partly in the indwelling of the deity in his incarnate nature, and partly in the bestowal of gifts and charisms.

units.la: X. Ordinatio ejus dupliciter considerari potest: tum prout aeterno Dei consilio isti muneri destinatus fuit: Praecogniti quidem ante jacta mundi fundamenta, manifesti autem facti ultimo temporibus propter vos.
units.tr: X. His ordination can be considered in two ways: first, as he was destined for that office by God's eternal counsel: Foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but made manifest in the last times for your sake.

units.la: 1 Pet. 1: 20. tum prout in tempore ad illud rite administrandum in terram ablegatus ac dimissus (emisit Deus filium suum Gal. 4:4. A me non veni; sed est verus, qui misit me, quem vos nescitis. Joh. 7:28.) inque munus coelesti ritu introductus, Matth. 3. rursusque in coelum receptus est; quae similiter quaedam ejus in Ecclesiae regem quasi inauguratio fuit. Certo igitur cognoscat tota domus Israelis, quod Deus illum Jesum, quem vos cruci affixistis, Dominum & Christum fecit. Act. 2:36.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1:20. Second, as in time he was sent down to earth and dispatched to administer that office duly (God sent forth his Son, Gal. 4:4; I did not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know, John 7:28), and was introduced into the heavenly office with a heavenly rite, Matt. 3, and then was received back into heaven. This likewise was a kind of inauguration of him as King of the Church. Let therefore the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made that Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. Acts 2:36.

units.la: XI. Unctus etiam est, quatenus divinitas in carne ejus inhabitavit, cum potentia dandi Spiritum S. Unde Spiritus Jehova dicitur esse super ipsum; idque quia unxit ipsum Jehova ad Evangelium nuntiandum mansuetis, Esa. 61: 1.
units.tr: XI. He was also anointed, inasmuch as the deity dwelt in his flesh, with the power of giving the Holy Spirit. Hence the Spirit of Jehovah is said to be upon him, and that because Jehovah anointed him to preach the gospel to the meek, Isa. 61:1.

units.la: XII. Charismata denique in naturam ejus humanam effusa sunt magna copia. Propterea unxit te, ô Deus, Deus tuus oleo laetitiae, ultra consortes tuos. Psal. 45:8. Et ex plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Joh. 1: 16. Non enim ex mensura dat Deus Spiritum. c. 3:34. Unde ab ipsa nativitate quiescebat super ipso Spiritus Iehova, hova, spiritus sapientiæ & prudentiæ, spiritus consilii & fortitudinis, spiritus cognitionis & timoris Iehova, Iesai 11:2. ita tamen, ut pro ætate majori postea auctu & incremento ageret: Et Iesus profecit sapientia & statura, & gratia apud Deum & homines, Luc. 2:52. tum præsertim cum publicè pro Servatore ac Messia se gesturus foret: Vidi Spiritum descendentem, tanquam columba, ex cælo, & mansit super eo. Hic est, qui baptizat in Sp. S. Ioh. 1:32,33. Unde unctus est spiritu & virtute. Act. 10:38. Quæ in cœlesti gloria majori cumulo adaucta dubitari non potest: ex qua proinde Sp. S. effudit; ita factus, h.e. demonstratus Christus, Act. 2:33,36.
units.tr: XII. Lastly, the charisms were poured out in great abundance into his human nature. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. Ps. 45:8. And of his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace. John 1:16. For God does not give the Spirit by measure. John 3:34. Hence from his very birth the Spirit of Jehovah rested upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and fear of Jehovah, Isa. 11:2. Yet he was so endowed that, with his later growth in age, it would act with increase: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men, Luke 2:52. This was especially so when he was about to act publicly as Saviour and Messiah: I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him. This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit, John 1:32, 33. Hence he was anointed with the Spirit and power, Acts 10:38. This was increased to a greater measure in heavenly glory, beyond doubt; and from it he therefore poured out the Holy Spirit, thus made, that is, shown to be Christ, Acts 2:33, 36.

units.la: XIII. Atque ex hac unctione Christus suscepto muneri renunciare, humanumque genus semel in fidem acceptum abdicare nunquam potuit. Ut Remonstrantes asserere audent. Cujus sententiæ labem ac periculum lib. 2. cap. 15. §. 16, 17, 18, 19. fusius ostendimus.
units.tr: XIII. From this anointing Christ could never renounce the office he had undertaken, nor abandon the human race once taken into faith, as the Remonstrants dare to assert. We have shown the taint and danger of this opinion more fully at book 2, chapter 15, §§ 16, 17, 18, 19.

units.la: XIV. A Christo appellantur fideles Christiani; qui in nascente Ecclesia Discipuli & Nazareni dicebantur, Act. 9:1. & 24:5. Postea Nazarenorum vocabulo pseudo-prophetis, qui legem cum Evangelio miscebant, relicto, Christiani dicti sunt. Quæ appellatio Antiochiæ primum nata, Act. 11:26. ac deinde porro usurpata fuit, 1 Pet. 4:16. quanquam Apostolorum tempore, ut videtur, rarius, cum suavia illa discipulorum, fratrum, ac fidelium, nomina magis placerent. Atque ad novum istud nomen referunt quidam prophetæ oraculum: Et videbunt gentes justitiam tuam, & omnes reges gloriam tuam; & nominabent nomine novo, quod os Iehova exprimet. Esa. 62:2.
units.tr: XIV. Faithful Christians are called after Christ. In the nascent Church they were called Disciples and Nazarenes, Acts 9:1; 24:5. Later, the name Nazarenes, which had been applied to pseudo-prophets who mixed the law with the gospel, was abandoned, and they were called Christians. This appellation first arose at Antioch, Acts 11:26, and was then used further, 1 Pet. 4:16; though in the time of the apostles it was apparently less common, since those sweeter names of disciples, brothers and believers pleased more. And some prophets refer this new name to an oracle: And the nations shall see your righteousness, and all kings your glory; and they shall name you by a new name, which the mouth of Jehovah shall express. Isa. 62:2.

units.la: XV. Dicuntur autem Christiani, quasi unctionis Christi participes & hæredes; quod non de superstitioso aliquo ritu, aut impuro chrismate, quale vel catechumenorum, vel sacerdotum, vel infirmorum in papatu est; sed de divina Spiritus S. gratia intelligendum est; qua fideles inuncti, & prophetæ, & sacerdotes, & reges sunt. Et vos unctionem habetis à Sancto. 1 Joh. 2:20.
units.tr: XV. The name Christians is given to us as sharers and heirs of the anointing of Christ. This must not be understood of some superstitious rite or impure chrism, such as the chrism of catechumens, priests or the sick among the Papists; it must be understood of the divine grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the faithful are anointed as prophets, priests and kings. And you have an anointing from the Holy One. 1 John 2:20.

units.la: XVI. Iniqui sunt in sacram hanc unctionem apud Pontificios Monachi, è Dominici, Francisci, Antonii &c. familia, qui ab humano nomine censeri malunt, divisque istis impiâ devotione se obstringunt. Quorum dedecus augent Minorita, Franciscum suum, ut ipso Jesu vix minorem, ipsaque ejus stigmata præferentem, Iesum typicum appellantes. Ac majori adhuc fastu Loiolita, qui, Christiano nomine non contenti, Jesuitas ac Jesu socios se jactant: quæ appellatio & schismatica, & ambitiosa, & irreligiosa est. Nam vel solos sese Jesu discipulos, vel sibi solis collatam Jesu Domini gratiam ac salutem, vel denique ejus in divino munere socios sese mentiuntur.
units.tr: XVI. Among the Papists, those are wrong about this sacred anointing who are monks of the families of Dominic, Francis, Anthony and so on, who prefer to be named after a human name and bind themselves by impious devotion to these saints. They add to their disgrace: the Minorites, calling their Francis, as if he were scarcely less than Jesus himself and bearing his stigmata, a typical Jesus. And with even greater arrogance the Loyolites, who are not content with the Christian name but boast of being Jesuits and companions of Jesus. That title is schismatic, ambitious and irreligious. For they falsely claim either to be the only disciples of Jesus, or that the grace and salvation of the Lord Jesus has been granted to them alone, or finally that they are his companions in his divine office.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: De munere Christi prophetico.
units.tr: On the prophetic office of Christ.

units.la: I. Unera, ad quæ Christus unctus est, tria sunt, propheticum, sacerdotale, regium: quæ tum ex nostra necessitate, tum ex salutis conferendæ ordine colliguntur. Nos enim laborabamus profunda rerum divinarum ignorantia, & turpi peccatorum labe ac reatu obstricti, in summa ad Deum redeundi impotentia veluti vincti ac ligati jacebamus. Cui triplici necessitati Christus subvenit, & partim docendo, ut Propheta; partim pro noxis nostris satisfaciendo, ut sacerdos; partim beneficia illa applicando, ut Rex; salutem nostram ordine quodam peregit. Ac singula hæc munera prophetarum vocibus jam ante ipsi attributa videmus. Prophetam excitabo ipsis ex medio fratrum eorum, sicut te; & dabo verba mea (quæ nemo præter me poterit eloqui) in ore ipsius. Deut. 18:18. Juravit Jehova, & non pœnitebit ipsum. Tues sacerdos in saeculum, secundum ordinem Melchizedeki. Psal. 110: 4. Et unxi Regem meum in Zionem, montem sanctum meum. Psal. 2:6.
units.tr: I. There are three offices to which Christ was anointed: prophetic, priestly and kingly. We can gather this both from our need and from the order in which salvation is brought about. For we were labouring under a deep ignorance of divine things, and bound by the foul stain and guilt of sin, and we lay as if bound and fettered, utterly unable to return to God. Christ came to help us in this threefold need. By teaching, as Prophet, by making satisfaction for our offences, as priest, and by applying those benefits, as King, he carried out our salvation in a certain order. We also see that each of these offices was assigned to him in advance by the voices of the prophets. "I will raise them up a prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and I will put my words (which no one but I can speak) in his mouth." Deut. 18:18. "The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." Ps. 110:4. "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." Ps. 2:6.

units.la: II. Licet autem multi olim in populo Dei prophetæ & sacerdotes, ac reges fuerint; vix tamen ullus cuncta ista munera pleno titulo simul complexus fuit: quod solus Christi est. Qui ideo non simplici diademate insignitus legitur, Apoc. 19:12. & prophetis omnibus, sacerdotibus, ac regibus longe celsior ac sublimior extitit. Propheta vel ipso Mose major, Deut. 18:18. Hebr. 3:1-6. inque domo Dei solus audiendus, Matth. 17:5. & 23:8. Sacerdos, supra Aaronis sanctitatem, utpote alterius sacerdotii, Psal. 110. & epist. ad Hebr. Rex denique, qui non terreno in solio, sed in coelo sublimis, divosque, mortalesque turbas, imperio regit unus æquo. Psal. 110: 1. Psal. 89: 28. Etiam ego primogenitum faciam illum, summum regibus terræ. Quod regium munus officiorum ejus colophon & apex est; cui reliqua subordinantur.
units.tr: II. Although in former times there were many prophets, priests and kings among the people of God, scarcely any one of them united all these offices in full measure at once; this belongs to Christ alone. He is therefore read of as wearing not a single diadem, Rev. 19:12, and he stands far higher and more exalted than all the prophets, priests and kings. He is a prophet greater even than Moses, Deut. 18:18; Heb. 3:1-6, and in the house of God he alone is to be heard, Matt. 17:5; 23:8. He is a priest above the holiness of Aaron, being of another priesthood, Ps. 110, and the Epistle to the Hebrews. Lastly, he is King, who rules not from an earthly throne but from heaven on high, and who alone governs by his command, with equal justice, both divine and mortal multitudes. Ps. 110:1; Ps. 89:28. "I will also make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth." This kingly office is the crown and summit of his offices, to which the rest are subordinate.

units.la: III. Primum ordine est sacerdotium Christi; tum ratione sponsionis, tum quia ut Propheta de sacerdotio suo debuit loqui. Ut tamen receptum ordinem sequamur, cum etiam Christus, antequam se.
units.tr: III. The priesthood of Christ comes first in order, both because of the order of the promise and because, as Prophet, he ought to speak of his own priesthood. Yet, to follow the accepted order, let us first set out his prophetic office, since Christ too spoke the words of God before he presented himself in his prophetic office.

units.la: Munus Propheticum se offerret, verba Dei locutus sit, præmittamus officium ejus propheticum. Per hoc de sinu ac concilio veluti Dei in terram missus, mortali ore hactenus indicta edisseruit; ac verba Dei, quæ Deum Deique filium solum proloqui fas erat, locutus est; omneque redemptionis mysterium planissime nudavit ac evulgavit. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Unigenitus filius, qui est in gremio patris, ille edisseruit, Joh. 1:18. Quem enim misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur. c. 3:34.
units.tr: Through this office he was sent, as it were, from the bosom and council of God into the earth, and he set forth in mortal speech what had until then remained unspoken. He spoke the words of God, which only God and the Son of God had the right to declare, and he laid bare and made fully known the whole mystery of redemption. "No one has seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him." John 1:18. "For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God." John 3:34.

units.la: IV. Venturum eum promisit olim Moses, prophetarum omnium maximus, ac sese majorem hoc ipso fassus est, cum ipsi testimonium perhibeat, ut servus domino suo: (Si enim crederetis Mosi, crederetis mihi: de me enim scripsit, Joh. 5:46. Moses quidem fidelis in tota domo ipsius, ut famulus; Christus autem tanquam filius. Hebr. 3:1-6.) atque in Ecclesia retinere quædam adhuc λαλῆσαι non obscure innuat, quæ verba Dei appellat, in emphasi. Deut. 18:18. conf. Hebr. 3:3. quæ non à servo, sicuti Moses erat, sed à filio ac divinæ familiæ hæredes proloquenda erant; qui sub excidii pœna audiendus erat. Deut. 18:18. Erit autem, ut quicunque non auscultaverit verbis meis, quæ loquuntur ex in nomine meo, ego repetam ab illo. conf. Matth. 17:5. Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo benepla-citum habeo: ipsum audite. Quæ profecto augustiora sunt, quam ut in alium quemvis ex prophetarum numero conveniant, quæ Judæorum corruptela est. Sed & reliquorum prophetarum de prophetico Christi munere vaticinia extant. Filii Zion gaudete et lætamini in Jehova, Deo vestro, quia dedit vobis Doctorem illum ad justitiam: qui fecit vobis cadere pluviam primam et serotinam in primo mense. Joel 2:23. Ecce servus meus, quem teneo; dilectus meus, quo acquievit anima mea. Dedi spiritum meum super ipsum, judicium gentibus proferet. Jes. 42:1. Ecce testem nationum dedi ipsum, principem et præceptorem nationum. Jes. 55:4. Spiritus Domini Jehova super me est, quia unxit Jehova me ad Evangelium nuncliandum mansuetis, Jes. 61:1. conf. Luc. 1:76. Hebr. 3:1. Considerate Apostolum et Pontificem aspirationis nostræ Christum Jesum. Unde quoque sub nomine prophetæ cognitus est; concludente vel ipsa turba: Hic est vere propheta, qui venit in mundum. Joh. 6:14.
units.tr: IV. Moses, the greatest of all the prophets, promised long ago that he would come, and by this very testimony Moses confessed that Christ was greater than himself, since he bore witness to him as a servant does to his master: "For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote of me." John 5:46. "Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, but Christ as a son." Heb. 3:1-6. And Moses clearly hints that in the Church there must still be retained certain things which he calls, emphatically, "the words of God" [λαλῆσαι], to be spoken not by a servant, as Moses was, but by the Son and the heirs of the divine household, and whoever did not heed them was to be heard under pain of destruction. Deut. 18:18: "And it shall be that whoever will not listen to my words, which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him." Compare Matt. 17:5: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." These words are certainly too exalted to fit any other of the number of the prophets, which is the corruption of the Jews. Moreover, prophecies of the prophetic office of Christ also survive in the other prophets. "Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given you a teacher for righteousness, who will cause the former and the latter rain to fall in the first month." Joel 2:23. "Behold my servant, whom I uphold; my elect, in whom my soul delights. I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations." Isa. 42:1. "Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a prince and commander to the peoples." Isa. 55:4. "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good tidings to the meek." Isa. 61:1; compare Luke 1:76; Heb. 3:1. "Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Christ Jesus." Hence he was also known under the name of prophet, as the crowd itself concluded: "This is truly the prophet who comes into the world." John 6:14.

units.la: V. Munus autem prophetarum hisce fere absolvebatur partibus: 1. quod populum docerent, ac in fide patrum, & præcipuo illo de Messia articulo, confirmarent. Et loqueris ad illos omnia verba hæc, et non auscultabunt tibi; et vocabis illos, et non respondebunt tibi, Jer. 7:27. 2. quod futura, tum præsentem, tum sequentem Ecclesiam... clesiæ statum spectantia, prædicerent. 3. quod miracula patrarent: Dixit enim Elisa, vir Dei, veniat ad me, & cognoscat quod sit Propheta in Israële. 2 Reg. 5:9. Quæ omnia Christus plenissimè præstitit. Nam & passim in Euangelio docentem audimus; variisque ænigmatis & parabolis, ac apertis quoque verbis novæ Ecclesiæ fatum, ad extremum usque finem, describentem, Matth. 13. & 24. & cuncta denique magnificis operibus ac stupendis miraculis confirmantem videmus.
units.tr: V. The office of the prophets was carried out chiefly in these parts: (1) they taught the people and confirmed them in the faith of the fathers and in that chief article concerning the Messiah. "So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you; you shall call to them, but they will not answer you." Jer. 7:27. (2) They foretold future things concerning the present and the following state of the Church. (3) They performed miracles: "For Elisha the man of God said, Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel." 2 Kings 5:8. Christ fulfilled all of these most fully. For we hear him teaching everywhere in the Gospel, and we see him describing, in various enigmas and parables, and also in plain words, the fate of the new Church right down to the last end, Matt. 13 and 24; and we see him finally confirming all things by magnificent works and astonishing miracles.

units.la: VI. Prophetam vero egit, tum priscis temporibus, sub Vet. T. per Spiritum S. prophetasque ministros: Perscrutantes in quod & quale tempus Spiritus Christi, qui in ipsis erat &c. 1 Pet. 1:11. In quo (spiritu) abiens, spiritibus, qui in custodia sunt, prædicavit. c. 3:18, 19. Unde ejus nomen est הַמְּרֵב is, qui loquitur, Esa. 52:6. sicut & dicit se initio locutum, Joh. 8:25. conf. Esa. 48:15, 16. tum præsertim sub Novo T. cum præsens Ecclesiam suam doceret, non externo affatu solum, sed & interiori via et potentia, qua apud animum pollebat: discedens denique reliquit Ecclesiæ Spiritum suum ducem, & Apostolos doctores, sequentemque eos Euangelizantium turbam. Eph.4. Perverse enim Sociniani Novi Test. ministros ultra Christi in terris prophetiam ascendere, ac perfectiora longe tradere, blasphemant, quæ videl. à Christo, vel regnaturo, vel regnante, acceperint.
units.tr: VI. He carried out the prophetic office both in earlier times, under the Old Testament, through the Holy Spirit and the prophets as his ministers: "searching what, or what manner of time, the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify" etc. 1 Pet. 1:11. "In which (Spirit) he went and preached to the spirits who are in prison." 1 Pet. 3:18, 19. Hence his name is "the one who speaks" [הַמְּדַבֵּר], Isa. 52:6, just as he says that he spoke "from the beginning," John 8:25; compare Isa. 48:15, 16. And he did so especially under the New Testament, when, being present, he taught his Church not only by outward speech but also by inward influence and power, by which he prevailed upon the mind. Finally, departing, he left his Spirit to the Church as its leader, and his Apostles as teachers, and after them the host of evangelists. Eph. 4. For the Socinians blaspheme perversely when they claim that the ministers of the New Testament rose above the prophecy of Christ on earth and delivered things far more perfect, which they supposedly received from Christ either about to reign or already reigning.

units.la: VII. Primum muneris specimen dedit duodecimo ætatis anno, quando templum ingressus, interque doctores assidens, futuro ministerio præluxit, Luc. 2. publice autem illud auspicatus est post baptismum, quo decedenti Johanni veluti succederet, cœptumque ab ipso Euangelium perficeret & consummaret. Postquam vero traditus esset Johannes, venit Jesus in Galilæam, prædicans Euangelium regni Dei. Marc. 1:14. coll. Matth. 4:12–17.
units.tr: VII. He gave the first specimen of his office in his twelfth year, when he entered the temple and, sitting among the teachers, foreshadowed his future ministry. Luke 2. He publicly began that ministry after his baptism, by which he was, as it were, to succeed John, who was departing, and to complete and bring to its end the Gospel which John had begun. "Now after John was put in prison, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God." Mark 1:14; compare Matt. 4:12-17.

units.la: VIII. Ubi notanda Socinianorum fabula: qui ut Christum pro mero homine agnoscunt, qui tam sublimem ac divinam doctrinam, quæ veteri lege longè sanctior ac perfectior fuerit, ex pectoris sui adyto proferre nequiverit; eam ab ipso de cælo, ubi post baptismum sublatus, ac aliquo tempore moratus fuerit, è divino contubernio haustam afferere non dubitant: non solum nulla Scripturæ auctoritate, quæ raptum istum nullibi narrat: sed & nulla necessitate. Cum enim, si quisquam mortalium, Christus Deo plenus, ac cœlesti spiritu inunctus foret; sua de cœlo profecto arcessere, ibique arcana doctrinâ erudiri, necesse non habebat; neque eo ad muneris sui auspicia rite capienda ascendere tenebatur, cum istud non in coelo, sed in terra, sollemniter praestiterit. Ac tandem omnis haec nugatio contra manifestam Scripturam est; quae Christum semel tantum in coeleste sanctuarium ingressum docet, Hebr. 9: 12. & proximis post baptisimumdiebus non in coelo, sed in deserto egisse, & à diabolo tentatum testatur. Matth. 4.
units.tr: VIII. Here the Socinian fable must be noted. They acknowledge Christ as a mere man, and yet they do not hesitate to assert that he could not have brought forth from the inner shrine of his own breast so sublime and divine a teaching, which was far holier and more perfect than the old law; so they say he drew it from the bosom of the divine fellowship, having been taken up into heaven after his baptism and kept there for some time. This is supported not only by no authority of Scripture, which nowhere narrates that rapture, but also by no necessity. For if Christ were, as he was, a man full of God and anointed with heavenly Spirit, he had no need to fetch his teaching from heaven or to be instructed there in hidden doctrine; nor was he bound to ascend there in order to take up his office duly, since he performed that solemnly not in heaven but on earth. And finally, all this trifling is against plain Scripture, which teaches that Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary only once, Heb. 9:12, and testifies that in the days immediately after his baptism he was not in heaven but in the wilderness, where he was tempted by the devil. Matt. 4.

units.la: IX. Obivit ministerium suum Christus deinceps plenissimè & perfectissimè. Nam 1. doctrina, quam tradebat, praeceptis sanctissimis, ac pretiosissimis de salute & vitâ aeternâ promissis, constabat. 2. & modus docendi erat omnibus numeris absolutus; cum divina quadam auctoritate, quae ipsi pro eloquentia erat, polleret; nec humili sermone, qualis eorum est qui de terrâ loquuntur, sed coelesti suada auditorum mentes afficeret; quae, quanquam non multum humani cultus praeferret, simplicitate tamen potens & veneranda erat. Accedebat orationis libertas, summa cum prudentia conjuncta, & perspicuitas, & modo illecebrae, modo aculei & stimuli, nudandae impiorum hypocrisi; quo in genere immensum valebat. Docebat enim ipsos, ut potestatem habens, & non ut scriba. Matt. 7: 29. Novimus quod verus fis, & viam Dei in veritate doceas, & non curat tibi sit de ullo: non enim aspicis personam hominum. c. 22: 16. Responderunt ministri, nunquam ita locutus est homo, ut hic homo. Joh. 7: 46. 3. Denique, cum doctrina Christi potissimum in moribus consisteret, & solam fidem ac respiscentiam doceret, nec ritibus ac caeremoniis magnopere occuparetur, ita ea comparata erat, ut longe lateque à cunctis gentibus adoptari, atque ad ultima mundi tempora perdurare posset.
units.tr: IX. Christ discharged his ministry thereafter most fully and most perfectly. For (1) the doctrine he taught consisted of most holy precepts and most precious promises concerning salvation and eternal life. (2) His manner of teaching was complete in every respect. He carried weight with a certain divine authority, which for him took the place of eloquence. He did not speak in a lowly style, such as belongs to those "who speak of the earth," but moved his hearers' minds with heavenly persuasion, which, though it showed little human polish, was powerful and venerable in its simplicity. To this was added a freedom of speech joined with the greatest prudence, and clarity, and at one time an allurement, at another a goad and sting, for stripping bare the hypocrisy of the wicked; in this respect he was immensely effective. "For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." Matt. 7:29. "Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, neither carest thou for any man: for thou regardest not the person of men." ch. 22:16. "The officers answered, Never man spake like this man." John 7:46. (3) Finally, since the doctrine of Christ consisted chiefly in morals, and taught only faith and repentance, and was not much occupied with rites and ceremonies, it was framed so that it could be adopted far and wide by all nations and endure to the last times of the world.

units.la: X. Unde excellentia Christi supra omnes alios Prophetas apparet; quae potissimum in hisce tribus elucet. 1. quod caeteri aliunde accepto lumine, nec nisi per intervalla corusfcante; hic autem propria gauderet; nec aliunde petere Spiritum necesse haberet, quem in proprio corpore hospitantem habebat. 2. quod illi omnia Dei nomine & auctoritate gererent, hic autem in proprio nomine ad Ecclesiam venerit, tanquam ad propria; erat enim Dei filius, ac familiae istius princeps & haeres. Hebr. 3: 6. Unde locuturus erat ut testis, princeps ac praeceptor, Esa. 55: 4. & ut legem suam, Esa. 42: 4. 3. quod illorum opera exteriori ministerio absolveretur; Christus autem interiori sermone mentem ipsam affari, & victam subjugum suum ducere poterat. Et dixit unus ad alium, nonne cor nostrum erat urens in nobis, quum loqueretur nobiscum in via, & quum aperiret nobis Scripturas? Luc. 24: 32. Omnis igitur, qui audivit a Patre, & didicit, venit ad me. Joh. 6: 45. Quibus adde, caeteros, cum nudi homines solerent, ex terra locutos; Christum autem, de sinu Patris demissum, quae viderat quaeque audiverat mortalibus enarrasse: Qui super ne venit, supra omnes est: qui e terra est, terrenus est, & terrena loquitur: qui e coelo venit, supra omnes est. Et quod vidit & audivit, hoc testatur. Joh. 3: 31, 32. Ut pateat Prophetam hunc simul Deum fuisse. Quis enim hominum novit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est? sic etiam ea, quae sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei. 1. Cor. 2: 11, 16.
units.tr: X. Hence the excellence of Christ above all the other prophets appears, which shines forth chiefly in these three things. (1) The others had their light from elsewhere, and it flashed only at intervals; but he rejoiced in his own light, and had no need to seek the Spirit from elsewhere, since he dwelt in his own body. (2) The others carried out everything in the name and authority of God, but he came to the Church in his own name, as to his own house; for he was the Son of God, and the prince and heir of that family. Heb. 3:6. Hence he was to speak as "witness, prince and teacher," Isa. 55:4, and to publish "his law," Isa. 42:4. (3) The others' work was completed by outward ministry, whereas Christ could address the mind itself by inward speech and lead the conquered will captive. "And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the Scriptures?" Luke 24:32. "Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me." John 6:45. To these add that the others, being mere men, usually spoke from the earth, whereas Christ, sent down from the bosom of the Father, declared to mortals what he had seen and heard: "He that cometh from above is above all: he that is of the earth is earthly, and speaketh of the earth: he that cometh from heaven is above all. And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth." John 3:31, 32. So it is clear that this prophet was at the same time God. "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God." 1 Cor. 2:11, 16.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Atque haec de prophetia Christi. Videndi nunc oppositi errores, quibus ea ab haereticis passim defoedata est. Atque occurrunt hic primo Socinianí, qui, ut justitiam Euangelicam abnegant, eamque in operibus collocant, eo etiam Christi ministerium subservire faciunt. Cum enim vita aeterna, ut ipsos sepius docentes audivimus, ex veteris legis praeceptis sperari non posset; sanctiori quadam lege ac perfectioribus praeceptis opus erat, quibus aeternae beatitudinis praemium annecteretur. Hinc jam Christum novum legislatorem faciunt: cumque prisca lex nec praeceptis, nec promissis perfecta esset, Christum illam partim correxisse, partim variis in partibus sanctitatem ejus intendisse, denique novis ac propriis praeceptis adauxisse docent. Inque eo munus ejus propheticum absolvi tradunt. Quae propius excutienda sunt.
units.tr: So much for the prophecy of Christ. We must now see the opposing errors, by which it has been everywhere defiled by heretics. Here first come the Socinians, who, while they deny evangelical righteousness and place it in works, also make Christ's ministry serve this end. For since, as we have often heard them teach, eternal life could not be hoped for from the precepts of the old law, a holier law and more perfect precepts were needed, to which the reward of eternal blessedness would be attached. Hence they now make Christ a new lawgiver; and since the old law was perfect neither in its precepts nor in its promises, they teach that Christ partly corrected it, partly extended its holiness in various parts, and finally increased it with new and proper precepts. And they maintain that his prophetic office is fulfilled in this. These points must be examined more closely.

units.la: XII. Ac de Christo legislatore, & quo sensu id nomen ferre vel non ferre possit lib. 2. cap. 16. §. 6. vidimus. Sine convitio autem novi & sanctioris legis, novique ac perfectioris foederis (quod pariter operum foedus foret) auctor dici nequit. Quod ita ostendimus:
units.tr: XII. We have already seen about Christ as lawgiver, and in what sense that name may or may not be borne, in book 2, chapter 16, §6. But the author of a "new and holier law," and of a new and more perfect covenant (which would likewise be a covenant of works), cannot be named without insult. We show this as follows.

units.la: XIII. 1. Illud foret divinae legis sanctitatem criminari, ejusque perfectionem abnegare, quam Scriptura tam luculenter testatur. Lex Jehovae est integra, restituens animam. Psal. 19: 8. Omne quod praecipio vobis, hoc observabitis, ut faciatis; neque ad hoc addes, neque ab eo diminues. Deut. 12: 32. Nec enim perfectius ac sanctius quiddam illibato Dei ac proximi amore cogitari potest, quem omnem divina lex jubet, Matth. 22: 37. Unde vitam ex ea sperare juvenis ille in Euangelio ab ipso Christo jubetur. Matth. 19: 17.
units.tr: XIII. (1) It would be to accuse the holiness of the divine law and to deny its perfection, which Scripture so clearly attests. "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul." Ps. 19:8. "Whatsoever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it." Deut. 12:32. For nothing more perfect and holier can be conceived than the undivided love of God and neighbour, which the whole divine law requires. Matt. 22:37. Hence the young man in the Gospel was bidden by Christ himself to hope for life from it. Matt. 19:17.

units.la: XIV. 2. Quin est illud ipsius Dei sanctitatem abnegare. Cujus expressio est in lege. Ut enim Deus sanctitatem & imaginem suam intus
units.tr: XIV. (2) Indeed, it is to deny God's own holiness. Its expression is in the law. For as God expressed his holiness and image inwardly

units.la: Errores prophetiae Christi oppositi. 1. Socinianorum, de novi Christi lege.
units.tr: Errors opposed to the prophecy of Christ. 1. Of the Socinians, concerning a new law of Christ.

units.la: Quod revincitur. intus in cordibus nostris expressit; ita eandem in legis tabulis quoque exaravit. Est autem eadem utrobique sanctitas; tum in Deo ipso, tum in imagine ejus; sive ea in nominum animis, sive in legis tabulis spectetur. Ut legis sanctitate & perfectione negata, ipsa Dei sanctitas & imago blasphemetur.
units.tr: Refuted here: in our hearts, so he likewise engraved the same on the tablets of the law. The holiness is the same in both: in God himself and in his image, whether it is viewed in men's minds or on the tablets of the law. So by denying the holiness and perfection of the law, the very holiness and image of God are blasphemed.

units.la: XV. 3. Sed & hypocriseos Deum arguunt; qui imperfectam sanctitatem olim praescripserit, istoque pacto coli volucrit; vitamque æternam ad istum cultum dederit: ac si pro justitia accipere posset, quod justitia non erat; suiqué communionem eâ viâ largiri, qua tamen ad Deum non itur, sed potius ab eo disceditur.
units.tr: XV. (3) They also charge God with hypocrisy, since he prescribed an imperfect holiness of old, willed to be worshipped in that way, and gave eternal life for that worship; as if he could accept as righteousness what was not righteousness, and grant communion with himself by a way on which one does not go to God but rather departs from him.

units.la: XVI. 4. Denique quod de nova non solum lege, sed & fœdere jactant; quod tamen rursus operum fœdus fit; id eo nitur, quasi Christus novam religionem, patribus inauditam, introduxisset: quod quantopere veterum sanctitati ac religioni injurium; spei ac fidei ipsorum inimicum; reiqué ipsi, ac Veteris Novique Testam. Scripturis adversum, cumque iis aperta fronte pugnans fit, sub Veteris Test. œconomia non uno loco demonstravimus. Est enim Jesus Christus & heri & hodie idem, & in sæcula. Hebr. 13: 8. Sicut nec per adventum Christi religio veterum mutata, aut lex Dei irrita facta fuit. Legem igitur inutilem reddimus per fidem: absit. Imo legem stabilimus. Rom. 3: 31. Præsertim cum ipsi illi legi Christus obedire, atque hoc pacto salutem nostriam peragere debeat. Factus ex muliere, factus legi subjectus. Gal. 4: 4.
units.tr: XVI. (4) Finally, as to their boasting of a new covenant as well as a new law, which nevertheless again becomes a covenant of works: this rests on the idea that Christ had introduced a new religion, unheard of by the fathers. How greatly this injures the holiness and religion of the ancients, and is hostile to their hope and faith, and contrary to the Scriptures of both Testaments, and fights against them with open face, we have shown in more than one place under the economy of the Old Testament. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. Heb. 13:8. Just as the religion of the ancients was not changed by the coming of Christ, nor was the law of God made void. "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law." Rom. 3:31. Especially since Christ himself was bound to obey that very law, and by this means accomplish our salvation. "Made of a woman, made under the law." Gal. 4:4.

units.la: XVII. 5. Accedere tandem posset ipsius Christi consideratio, & Evangelii summa, quæ certe longè alio spectant, quam ad salutem per nova opera quærendam.
units.tr: XVII. (5) Lastly, one may add the consideration of Christ himself and the sum of the Gospel, which certainly look far otherwise than to seeking salvation through new works.

units.la: XVIII. Atque ita patet, pessimè ab adversariis ipsius munus mutari, quod sine legis Mosaicæ criminatione perficere non poterant; quam videl. emendaverit, additoque novo rigore, propriisque præceptis, auxerit. Quæ ipsorum ad singula præcepta additamenta, quæ memorant, percurrere nunc animus non est; cum illa tractatio ad decalogum pertineat. Sufficit sententiæ istius fundamentum, ac præcipuum præsidium, quod in cap. Matth. 5. quæruntur, breviter examinasse. Ad quod hæc annotamus.
units.tr: XVIII. And so it is clear that his office has been very badly altered by the adversaries, since they could not carry it out without accusing the Mosaic law, which they say he amended and, by adding new rigour and his own precepts, increased. I do not intend now to run through the additions they mention to the individual precepts, since that discussion belongs to the Decalogue. It is enough to have briefly examined the foundation of this opinion and its chief support, which is sought in Matt. chapter 5. To this we add the following notes.

units.la: XIX. 1. Versu 17. Christum legem implevisse, non eam corrigendo, vel, sicubi deficeret, perficiendo; sed, tum sermone, eam explicando, (conf. Rom. 15: 19. ab Hierosolyma usque ad Illyricum πεπληρωκέναι annunciationem Christi. Col. 1: 25.) tum opere, omnem ejus
units.tr: XIX. 1. In verse 17 Christ is said to have fulfilled the law, not by correcting it or, where it was lacking, by completing it, but by explaining it in his teaching (cf. Rom. 15:19, from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum he has fully preached [πεπληρωκέναι] the proclamation of Christ; Col. 1:25), and by his work, fulfilling its holiness in every respect, and finally by actually bringing in the body and filling out and completing the shadows and types of the Mosaic laws.

units.la: An legem Dei correctis? iuxta Matth. 5. ¶.17. ejus sanctitatem adimplendo; tum denique reipsa legum Mosaicarum umbras & typos, inducto corpore, spissando & complendo.
units.tr: Is the law of God then corrected? Compare Matth. 5:17. He fulfils its holiness, and in the reality itself he brings in the body and fills out and completes the shadows and types of the Mosaic laws.

units.la: XX. 2. Versu 21, 27, 33, 38, 43. per dicta ac tradita antiquis, non lex ipsa, patribus tradita, aut veterum fides ac religio, vel incorrupta Patrum Catechesis; sed Scribarum traditiones intelliguntur; ut ex iis ipsis, quæ Christus ibi adfert constat, quæ certe in lege non omnia extant. vid. v. 44. Audistis dictum fuisse, diligES proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Erat enim hæc traditionariorum stilorum formula, dictum esse antiquis; ut videri potest Misnah Sanhedr. cap. x. § 2. quo suco errores suos facile venditabant. Ac si quando à Christo vel ipsa Mosis dicta citantur, non illa, sed sublestus sensus, quem Pharisæi iis dabant, corrigitur.
units.tr: XX. 2. In verses 21, 27, 33, 38 and 43 the things said to the ancients are not the law itself, handed down to the fathers, nor the faith and religion of the ancients, or the uncorrupted catechesis of the Fathers, but the traditions of the scribes. This is clear from the very things Christ cites there, which certainly are not all found in the law. See also verse 44: You have heard that it was said, You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy. For it was said to the ancients was the standard formula of the traditionists, as can be seen in the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10 §2, by which they easily peddled their errors. And when the words of Moses themselves are cited by Christ, it is not those words that are corrected, but the shallow sense which the Pharisees gave them.

units.la: XXI. 3. Versu 21. & 22. Audistis quod dictum sit veteribus, non occides; qui autem occiderit, reus est judicii. Ego autem dico: quod quisquis irascitur contra fratrem suum temere, reus est judicii; & quisquis dixerit fratri suo raka, obnoxius est consilio; & omnis, qui dixerit fatue, obnoxius est gehennæ ignis: non sextum præceptum, sed perversa Scribarum glossa castigatur; ac si ille solum, qui proximi sanguine sese polluisset, judicii reus foret. Quod Christus ad fratrum iras ac odia etiam extendit; quæ apud Deum capitalia censeri, ac pro cæde reputari, phrasibus ab humanis judiciis desumtis ostendit. Hoc autem etiam sub Veteri Testam. obtinuit. Maledicta sit ira ipsorum; quia robusta, & excandescentia ipsorum, quia gravis. Gen. 49: 7. Irascimini, & ne peccate. Psal. 4: 5. coll. Eph. 4: 26.
units.tr: XXI. 3. In verses 21 and 22: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, You shall not kill; but whoever kills is liable to judgment. But I say to you, that whoever is angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother, Raca, is liable to the council; and whoever says, You fool, is liable to the fire of hell. It is not the sixth commandment that is rebuked, but a perverse gloss of the scribes, as if only the one who had polluted himself with his neighbour's blood were liable to judgment. Christ extends this to the anger and hatred of brothers, and by phrases taken from human courts he shows that these are reckoned capital offences before God and counted as murder. This also held under the Old Testament: Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was grievous (Gen. 49:7); Be angry, and do not sin (Ps. 4:5; cf. Eph. 4:26).

units.la: XXII. 4. Pariter v. 27, 28. Audistis dictum fuisse veteribus, non mœchaberis. Ego vero dico vobis, quicunque aspicit mulierem, ut eam concupiscat, jam adulteravit eam in corde suo; non augetur præceptum septimum, sed vis ac sanctitas ejus ostenditur; quæ ipsos cordis motus, aspectusque omnes lubricos & adulteros coërcet: sicut & in veteri œconomia illi damnantur: & viderunt filii Dei filias hominis, quod pulchræ illæ essent, Gen. 6: 2. conf. Job. 31: 1. Quod nec prorsus diffiteri Socinus potuit.
units.tr: XXII. 4. Likewise in verses 27 and 28: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. The seventh commandment is not enlarged; rather its force and holiness are shown, which restrains the very movements of the heart and every lustful and adulterous glance. So also in the old economy these are condemned: the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair (Gen. 6:2; cf. Job 31:1). Socinus could not altogether deny this.

units.la: XXIII. 5. Quæ de libello repudii v. 31. Servator addit, illa legem politicam, non moralem, spectant. Nec à Mose licentia illa divortiorum, tanquam labe omni careret, approbata, sed Judæis potius durissimum ipsorum cor non sine probro ingestum ac exprobratum fuit. Cujus manifestum exemplum ac publica accusatio erat, in frequentibus illis uxorum repudiis, quibus maritorum asperitas propalam vulgabatur, ac non leviter traducebatur. Quod non Christus solum, sed inter veteres Prophetas Malachias jam notavit: qui Deum repudiatarum suspiriis veluti fatigatum, aramque ejus non sanguine magis quam lacrymis ac quærimoniis ipsarum plenam, inducit; acriterque contra maritorum iras invehitur, quas injuriam suspiri-duisse vestimento suo licit, ut peccata ipsorum cuivis nota essent, Mal. 2:16. Quibus consonant Christi verba Matth. 19:8. Moses τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν concessit vobis uxores vestras dimittere. sed a principio non ita fuit. Manifestum enim est primævo conjugii instituto, ex qua, veluti certissima lege, leges omnes interpretandæ veniunt, hanc divertendi libidinem directa fronte repugnare; ac lacerare par illud, quod Deus propria manu conjunxit, & initio rerum in Paradiso collocavit.
units.tr: XXIII. 5. As to the bill of divorce in verse 31, the Saviour adds that those words concern the political law, not the moral law. Nor did Moses approve that licence of divorce as though it were free from all stain; rather, the hardness of the Jews' hearts was not without reproach, and was thrown up to them as a disgrace. A clear example of this, and a public accusation, was the frequent repudiation of wives, by which the harshness of husbands was openly made known and not lightly held up to scorn. Not only Christ but also the earlier prophet Malachi noted this. He introduces God as wearied by the sighs of the repudiated wives, and his altar full not so much of blood as of their tears and complaints; and he rails sharply against the anger of husbands, who covers violence with his garment, so that their sins might be known to everyone (Mal. 2:16). Christ's words in Matth. 19:8 agree with this: Moses permitted you, because of your hardness of heart [τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν], to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. For it is plain that the original institution of marriage, from which as from a most certain law all laws are to be interpreted, flatly opposes this lust for divorce, and that it tears apart what God joined with his own hand and placed in Paradise at the beginning of things.

units.la: XXIV. 6. Versu 33. ad tertii præcepti corruptelas Christus pergit, & magistrorum axiomata de votis & juramentis corrigit. Fas enim ipsis non solum per nomen Dei, sed & templum, & aram, ac præsertim dona templi jurare; idque temere sæpe & nulla cogente religione, quin & leviculo, uti putabant, peccato per quædam eorum pejerare. Qui juraverit per templum, nihil est; qui vero juraverit per aurum templi, debet — Et qui juraverit per altare, nihil est, qui vero juraverit per donum, quod est super altare, debet. Matth. 23:16-19. Quam ipsorum hypocrisin Christus castigat, & non solum spuriis istis juramentorum formulis, sed vero omnino jurejurando extra necessitatem abstinere jubet, ne vulgari ac quotidiano usu Dei nomen, quod omnino sanctum haberi debet, evilescat. Non feres nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum. Exod. 20. cui concinit Eccles. 9:2. Qui jurandum metuit. & Jac. 5:12. Fratres mei, ne juretis, neque per cælum, neque per terram, neque aliud ullum juramentum. Ac præsertim Christus hoc ipso loco: Ego vero dico vobis, ne jurate omnino: neque per cælum &c. neque per terram &c. neque per Hierosolymam &c. neque per caput tuum &c. Esto autem sermo vester etiam, etiam; non, non. Quod autem supra hac redundat, à malo est v. 34.
units.tr: XXIV. 6. In verse 33, on the corruptions of the third commandment, Christ goes on to correct the teachers' maxims about vows and oaths. For they thought it lawful to swear not only by the name of God but also by the temple, the altar, and especially the gifts of the temple; and they often did this rashly and without any compelling religious reason, and even, as they thought, committed a trifling sin by perjuring themselves in certain ways. Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound. And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon the altar, he is bound (Matth. 23:16–19). Christ rebukes this hypocrisy of theirs, and orders them to abstain not only from these spurious forms of oath but altogether from swearing without necessity, lest the name of God, which ought to be regarded as wholly holy, be cheapened by common and daily use. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain (Exod. 20). This agrees with Eccles. 9:2, he who fears to swear, and with Jas. 5:12, My brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath. And Christ especially in this very place: But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven etc.; nor by the earth etc.; nor by Jerusalem etc.; nor by your head etc. But let your word be, Yes, yes; No, no. Whatever is more than these is of evil (v. 34).

units.la: XXV. Versu 38. Audistis dictum fuisse, oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente. Ego vero dico vobis, ne obsistite improbo &c. fatetur ipse Socinus non sensum legis, sed perversam ejus glossam carpi: cum ne quidem sub Vet. T. Privatæ vindictæ indulgere licuerit. Quam tamen, sumto e legis verbis, (Exod. 21:24. oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente) colore, vulgo homines exercebant, atque illis peccato suo veluti nubem obducebant. Cum tamen de publicis judiciis lex illa diserte agat. conf. Ex.21:22. Si viri rixati fuerint, & percusserint multando multabitur dabit e sententia judicum. Lev. 24:19. Vir, cum infixerit proximo suo vitium, secundum quod fecit, sic ipsi fiet. Deut. 32:35. Mea est vindicta & retributio. Quod autem nunc ne illa quidem privata in causa implorare Christiano fas putet, magnopere fallitur. Advim enim ac injuriam arcendam tribunalia exposita sunt, ac publice adire ea sine crimine licet; sed absque fremitu & indignantis animi motu, ne condita nobis odia magistratibus imputantes judiciorum sanctitatem livore ac animi tabe praepolluamus: nedum, ut unice nobis propositum sit, legibus ipsis odia nostra armare, fratremque overtere, ac jacenti insuper illudere; quae saeva ἐπιχαιρεκακία est, & olim, & nunc, vetita.
units.tr: XXV. Verse 38: You have heard that it was said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you, do not resist an evil person etc. Socinus himself admits that what is attacked here is not the sense of the law but a perverse gloss upon it, since under the Old Testament private revenge was not permitted even then. Yet people commonly exercised it, taking colour for it from the words of the law (Exod. 21:24, eye for eye, tooth for tooth), and by their sin they drew a cloud over those words. Yet that law speaks plainly of public judgments; compare Exod. 21:22: If men quarrel and strike, he shall be fined, and shall pay according to the sentence of the judges. Lev. 24:19: If a man injures his neighbour, as he has done so shall it be done to him. Deut. 32:35: Vengeance is mine, and recompense. But to think that a Christian may not even in a private matter appeal to the law now is a great mistake. For courts are set up to repel force and wrong, and it is lawful to approach them publicly without sin; yet this must be done without raging and without the stirring of an indignant mind, lest by imputing to the magistrates the hatreds we have stored up within us, we defile the holiness of the courts with envy and the rot of the mind. Still less is it to be our sole aim to arm our hatreds with the laws themselves, to overthrow our brother, and to mock him further when he has fallen; that is savage malicious joy [ἐπιχαιρεκακία], and it was forbidden both then and now.

units.la: XXVI. 8. Sequitur tandem Scribarum circa amorem proximi κατὰ χρως, immitis nimium & implacida, nec ex veri amoris lege. Cum enim peculiaribus de causis devotam Cananaeorum gentem exscindere juberentur, Deut. 7:2. illi credita sibi odia male regentes, quicquid usquam gentium ac populorum extra Judaicum nomen est, tanquam ad Deum nihil pertinens, ilti praecepto includebant, eosque abominari ac palam odisse, pro justo ac sancto habebant. Cujus impietatis surculus est, quod apud Matth. v. 43. occurrit. Audistis dictum fuisse, diliges proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Quae certe a lege charitatis valde aliena erant. Unde Christus veri amoris regulam uberius explicat, ipsosque hostes diligendos esse, maledicentibus benedicendum, oderibus nostris benefaciendum, & precandum pro iis qui animo nos afficiunt, ac persequuntur, monet; addita v. 45. ratione, quae Vetus quoque Testam. spectat: Ut sitis filii Patris illius vestri, qui est in coelis; facit enim ut sol suos exoriatur super malos & bonos, & pluit super justos & injustos. Atque ad alienigenas etiam, ipsosque inimicos nostros, sanctum illud proximi nomen extendendum luculenta pictura ac parabola ostendit, Luc. 10: 30. Quae & legis sententia erat. Quae enim de proximo & fratre Lev. 19:17,18. Non odio prosequeris fratrem tuum in corde tuo, redarguendo redargues proximum tuum, & non feres ejus causa peccatum; non obtrectabis popularis tuo; non stabis contra sanguinem proximi tui; non vindictam sumes, & non observabis iram cum popularibus tuis, & amabis proximum tuum sicut te ipsum. ego Jehovah: ac ipso nono legis praecepto, non respondebis falsum testimonium contra proximum tuum; jubentur, omnibus, bus, ni fallor, hominibus, ipsisque inimicis debemus, quos tam prepinquo nomine conciliare nobis divina lex voluit. Neque haec Novi Testam. solum explicatio est, Rom. 13: 10. Dilectio proximo malum non facit. Impletio itaque legis dilectio: cui concedere tamen adversarii debebant: sed & ipsius legis auctoritatem habet: Cum occurres bovi inimici tui, aut asino ejus errantí, reducendo reduces eum ipsi: cum videbis asinum osoris tui recubantem sub onere suo, an omittis vacare ipsi? vacando vacabis cum eo. Exod. 23: 4, 5. Cui concinit quoque Paroemiastæ dictum cap. 25: 22. Si esurit osor tuus, ciba illum pane: &, si sitit, pota illum aqua. Quod repetitur & confirmatur Rom. 12: 20.
units.tr: XXVI. 8. Finally follows the scribes' teaching about love of neighbour, which is superficially [κατὰ χρως], excessively harsh and implacable, and not according to the law of true love. For when they were ordered for particular reasons to destroy the devoted nations of the Canaanites (Deut. 7:2), they, managing badly the hatreds entrusted to them, included under that command whatever people or nations existed anywhere outside the Jewish name, as if they had nothing to do with God, and they held it right and holy to abhor them and openly to hate them. A shoot of this impiety is what occurs in Matth. 5:43: You have heard that it was said, You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy. These things were certainly quite foreign to the law of charity. Hence Christ more fully explains the rule of true love, and admonishes that enemies themselves are to be loved, that those who curse us are to be blessed, that those who hate us are to be done good to, and that we are to pray for those who are disposed against us and persecute us. He adds in verse 45 a reason that also looks to the Old Testament: That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. And by a vivid picture and parable (Luke 10:30) he shows that the holy name of neighbour is to be extended even to foreigners and to our very enemies. This too was the sense of the law. For what is said of neighbour and brother in Lev. 19:17, 18 is this: You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your neighbour, and not bear sin because of him; you shall not seek revenge, nor bear a grudge against the children of your people; you shall not stand against the blood of your neighbour; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord. And in the ninth precept of the law, You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour, all men, unless I am mistaken, are commanded, and even enemies, whom the divine law wished to win to us by so near a name. Nor is this only the explanation of the New Testament, Rom. 13:10: Love does no harm to a neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. The adversaries ought to have granted this; but it also has the authority of the law itself: When you meet your enemy's ox or his ass going astray, you shall bring it back to him. When you see the ass of one who hates you lying under its burden, will you refrain from helping it? You shall surely help it with him (Exod. 23:4, 5). The proverb of the Preacher in 25:22 agrees with this: If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. This is repeated and confirmed in Rom. 12:20.

units.la: XXVII. Atque hoc quidem pacto Christus Patris sui legem expurgavit; Levitarum fæces, quibus aurum sanctuarii obscuraverant, abradendo, & divina sua lima illud pristino nitori restituendo, denique duos illos omnium officiorum fontes, Dei ac proximi amorem, qui oblimati jacebant, ac hominum incuria lutulenti fluebant, rursus recludendo, salubresque inde aquas derivando. Quæ scribarum ac magistrorum censura ipsi jam olim debebatur, ex Malachiæ vaticinio, cap. 3: 3. Nam ipse quasi ignis conflatoris, & ut smegma fullonum est. Ut sedet conflans & purgans argentum, ita purgabit filios Levi; defecans ens velut aurum & argentum.
units.tr: XXVII. In this way Christ cleansed his Father's law. He scraped off the dregs of the Levites, with which they had darkened the gold of the sanctuary, and by his divine file restored it to its former lustre. Finally, he reopened those two fountains of all duties, the love of God and the love of neighbour, which lay clogged and flowed muddy through human neglect, and he channelled healthy waters from them. This scrutiny was long ago owed to the scribes and teachers themselves, as the prophecy of Malachi, ch. 3:3, foretells: For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap. He will sit refining and purifying silver; he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver.

units.la: An nova præcepta super hæc addiderit?
units.tr: Did he add any new precepts to these?

units.la: XXVIII. Sed legem non solum correctam, ac sanctitatem ejus in singulis præceptis non parum intensam, sed trium præterea præceptorum appendice de novo adauctam statuunt: quæ sunt, de abnegando semet ipso, ferenda cruce, ac Christo imitando: quæ peculiaria Christianæ philosophiæ placita ajunt, iis qui ad ipsam aggregari volebant, in discipulatus rudimentum imposita: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget se ipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Matth. 16: 24. Quod ex perverso adversariorum studio proficit: quo Veteris Novique Testam. non discrimen solum, sed premodum dissidium statuunt; unde totis Scripturis, quæ huc facere posse putant, venantur, ut non sine Veteris T. spoliis ac injuria novum hunc Ecclesiæ statum exornent.
units.tr: XXVIII. But they maintain that the law was not only corrected, and its holiness in each precept not a little intensified, but was also newly enlarged by an appendix of three further precepts: denying oneself, bearing the cross, and imitating Christ. They call these the peculiar tenets of Christian philosophy, imposed as the first rudiments of discipleship on those who wished to be enrolled in it: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. Matt. 16:24. This comes from the perverse zeal of the adversaries, by which they set up between the Old and New Testaments not merely a distinction but almost a discord. Hence they hunt through all the Scriptures that they think can serve this purpose, so as to adorn this new state of the Church not without plundering and wronging the Old Testament.

units.la: XXIX. Quid enim tria hæc, quæ adferunt, præcepta aliud sunt, quam generalia ad excellentissimam virtutem, ac perfectissimam Dei obedientiam monita & hortamenta, quæ jam olim sub præcepto perfectæ Dei dilectionis, ac purissimæ sanctitatis, sicut Deus sanctus est, Deut. 6: 5. Lev. 19: 2. continebantur, & ab Abrahamo, à Mose, aliisque
units.tr: XXIX. For what are these three precepts they adduce, other than general admonitions and exhortations to the most excellent virtue and the most perfect obedience to God? These were long ago contained under the precept of perfect love of God and purest holiness, be holy, as I am holy, Deut. 6:5; Lev. 19:2, and were offered long before by Abraham, by Moses, and

units.la: moralia? aliisque sanctis viris dudum praestita fuerunt? Certe in Mose trinae hujus sanctitatis compendium extat, qui negavit dici filiae Pharaonis filius; elegit vexari cum populo Dei; ac majores divitias duxit improperium Christi; quem calcatis Ægypti deliciis in deserturn usque secutus est. Hebr. 11: 24. Nec levius Abrahami exemplum est, qui patriam cognatosque deserens, Deum praecuntem secutus est; ac novus Cananaeae accola non simplici calamitate isto in ex.lio exercitus fuit. Ac speciatim abnegationem sui sextum, septimum, octavum, nonum, ac praesertim decimum legis praeceptum aperte satis comprehendunt: tolerantiam crucis cunctae Veteris Test. Scripturae, ac praesertim Psalmi suadent: ac imitari Deum, sanctitatemque ejus aemulari vel ipse Moses expresiis verbis jussit: Sitis sancti quia ego sanctus, Lev. 19: 2.
units.tr: by other holy men? Certainly in Moses there is an epitome of this threefold holiness: he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; he chose to suffer with the people of God; and he counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, following him into the desert after trampling underfoot Egypt's delights. Heb. 11:24. Nor is the example of Abraham less clear: he, leaving his country and kindred, followed God going before him, and the new sojourner in Canaan was in that exile no stranger to a not simple calamity. Specifically, the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and above all the tenth commandments of the law plainly enough comprehend self-denial. The whole of Old Testament Scripture, and the Psalms especially, urge endurance of the cross. And Moses himself, in express words, commanded us to imitate God and emulate his holiness: Be holy, because I am holy, Lev. 19:2.

units.la: XXX. Absurdiores adhuc sunt adversarii, cum moralibus hisce praeceptis unicum praeterea caerimoniale de sacra Cena superaddunt. Ita enim amoris Dei pignora ac sigilla in praecepta commutare ipsis libet. Et quasi non vetus quoque Ecclesia illa habuerit? Quin & ipsius legis praeceptum non sit, ubi Deus favoris sui signa exhibet, ea ampleCti, & publico isto ritu eum Deum suum fateri?
units.tr: XXX. The adversaries are even more absurd when they add to these moral precepts one further ceremonial precept concerning the holy Supper. For thus they like to turn the pledges and seals of God's love into precepts. As if the Old Church did not have such things too! Indeed, is it not a precept of the law itself, where God shows signs of his favour, to embrace them and to confess him as their God by this public rite?

units.la: XXXI. Cum Socinianis paria erram Anabaptista & Remonstrantes multi; praesertim primores illorum, Puppius & Espicopius: qui non aliud aeque crepant, quam mandatorum Christi obedientiam, quae immensum in modum supra Mosis praecepta evehunt. Quo in genere copiosi admodum sunt, nec eodem omnes ordine ea digerunt. Quae ambages in Socinianae impietatis summam aliquo modo perveniunt, ac Christum in novum legislatorem, fidem in opera, & justitiam Euangelicam in justitiam legalem commutant; & pro Christi obedientia nostram obedientiam fere substituunt; omnemque prope fidei justitiam, ipsumque Christianae religionis apicem, evertunt ac produnt.
units.tr: XXXI. Many Anabaptists and Remonstrants err in agreement with the Socinians, especially their leaders Poppius and Episcopius. They harp on nothing so much as obedience to the commands of Christ, which they raise immensely above the precepts of Moses. In this genre they are very copious, nor do they all arrange them in the same order. These circumlocutions in some way reach the height of Socinian impiety: they change Christ into a new lawgiver, faith into works, and evangelical righteousness into legal righteousness. They almost substitute our obedience for Christ's obedience, and they overthrow and betray nearly all the righteousness of faith, and the very summit of the Christian religion.

units.la: XXXII. Accedunt tandem & Pontificii, qui, in divinae legis opprobrium, consilia sua Euangelica jactare non desinunt, quae Dei praeceptis sanctiora praedicant. In religiosa autem monachorum suorum disciplina illa potissimum constituunt. Quae ipsorum consilia revera praecepta sunt hominum, Esai. 29: 13. quin imo consilium improbi, ut Scriptura ea merito infamat, Psal. 1: 1. dum religioso praetextu veram resipiscentiam ac fidem in Christum non parum obscurant, ac ad falsam justitiam paulatim deflectunt, & a Christo tandem apostasiam inducunt. Huc enim tandem omnia evadunt, ac speciosis istis verbis & legis sanctitas, & Christi meritum, ac præcipua Novi Test. bona injurioso pede proruuntur. In externa autem monachorum disciplina, quicquid boni ac sancti est, divina lege continetur; quicquid autem ultra illam sese tendit, & malum, & superstitiosum, ac Christo denique inimicum est.
units.tr: XXXII. Finally the Papists also come in, who, to the disgrace of the divine law, never cease to boast of their evangelical counsels, which they proclaim holier than God's precepts. They chiefly locate these in the religious discipline of their monks. Those counsels of theirs are really precepts of men, Isa. 29:13; indeed they are the counsel of the wicked, as Scripture rightly brands them, Ps. 1:1. Under a religious pretext they considerably obscure true repentance and faith in Christ, gradually turn people aside to a false righteousness, and at last lead them into apostasy from Christ. For all things end up here: under those specious words the holiness of the law, the merit of Christ, and the chief goods of the New Testament are trampled underfoot in injury. In the external discipline of the monks, whatever is good and holy is contained in the divine law; whatever goes beyond it, however, is evil, superstitious, and finally hostile to Christ.

units.la: XXXIII. Nec satisfaciunt quæ in causam suam afferunt; nos sub N. T. ad puriorem sanctitatem teneri, nec displicere Deo pietastem, quæ ultra imperata se extendat. Est enim extra omnem controversiam lex perfectissima sanctitatis formula. Et si vel Novi Test. fideles, pro temporum istorum felicitate, atque uberiore divinæ gratiæ copia, supra veterem populum longe eminere deberent; istud tamen ex ejusdem legis jussu ac postulato foret. Illa enim cum sanctitatem omnimodam, toto corde cunctisque ex viribus præstandam, jubeat, illi profecto, qui majorem gratiæ mensuram acceperunt, ad peculiaria quædam charitatis ac dilectionis officia obligari possunt, ad quæ aliorum mediocritas non pertingit. Ut, si quem Deus, non ex vulgo athletam, ad martyrii honorem, & ipsa Christianæ militiæ decora vocet; certe ille, non ex consilio quodam, quod facere majoris quidem meriti, omittere autem peccatum non sit, ut adversarii loquuntur; sed ex ipsa amoris Dei lege ad palmam istam contendere debet. Quo tamen accedere non alii jubentur, quam quibus idem Spiritus audendi auctor est, &c., pari undique rerum forte, depugnaturis eundem veluti campum aperit. Quo sensu si adversarii perpetuam castitatem, & angelicum vitæ candorem, aliaque sublimiora quibusdam, pro donorum ac occasionum occursu, peculiariter servanda urgerent, in rectum sensum exire illa possunt. Verum istud quidem ab iis non agitur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Nor do the things they bring forward in their cause satisfy: that under the New Testament we are bound to a purer holiness, and that piety which extends beyond what is commanded does not displease God. For the law is, beyond all controversy, the most perfect formula of holiness. And even if the believers of the New Testament, given the happiness of those times and the richer abundance of divine grace, ought to stand far above the ancient people, that would nevertheless be by the command and demand of the same law. For since it commands holiness in every respect, to be performed with the whole heart and with all strength, those who have received a greater measure of grace can certainly be obliged to certain peculiar duties of charity and love, to which the mediocrity of others does not reach. So, if God calls someone, not an ordinary athlete, to the honour of martyrdom and the glories of Christian warfare, that person ought to strive for that palm not from some counsel which, as the adversaries say, is of greater merit to perform but whose omission is not sin, but from the very law of love for God. Yet to this are not called others, except those whom the same Spirit is the author of daring, etc., opening the same field to those who will fight in similar circumstances on every side. In this sense, if the adversaries urged perpetual chastity, angelic purity of life, and other more sublime things to be peculiarly observed by some, according to the occurrence of gifts and occasions, those things could be taken in a right sense. But this, indeed, is not what they pursue.

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De miraculis Christi.
units.tr: On the miracles of Christ.

units.la: I. ABD prophetiam Christi pertinent ejus miracula, & vitæ mortisque exemplum; quibus doctrinam suam valide confirmavit.
units.tr: I. To the prophecy of Christ belong his miracles and the example of his life and death, by which he powerfully confirmed his teaching.

units.la: II. Miracula enim, cum vera doctrina conjuncta, non exiguum ad eam commendandam robur habent; suntque veluti divinæ manus signacula, quibus illam sibi curæ esse publicè testatur. Unde in Ecclesiæ exordio ea plerunque adhibita fuere, tum olim sub Vet. T. tum etiam in nova Ecclesia à Christo.
units.tr: II. Miracles, joined to sound doctrine, lend it no small force for commending it. They are, as it were, the signs of God's hand, by which he publicly testifies that the teaching is his concern. For this reason they were commonly employed at the beginning of the Church, both under the Old Testament and later in the new Church from Christ.

units.la: III.
