Verorum autem miraculorum quatuor ponunt conditiones: 1. ut opus aliquod sit stupendum, ac supra naturæ ambitum. 2. ut idem sit publicum ac patens, & luce sua oculos perstringens. 3. ut non longo molimine veluti elaboratum, sed repente ac protinus, ad nutum Dei, productum sit. 4. tandemque non aliqua ex parte imperfectum, ut naturæ manus agnoscas, sed perfectum atque integrum sit. Quæ omnia in Christi operibus locum habuerunt; quæ naturæ vires immensum supergressa, & publica, & perfecta, ac ad solum loquentis jussum repente edita fuerunt. Quod non dubium divinitatis ejus testimonium fuit.
units.tr: III. Those who lay down the conditions of true miracles name four: (1) that the work be astonishing and beyond the range of nature; (2) that it be public and open, dazzling the eyes with its light; (3) that it not be wrought laboriously, as it were, over a long effort, but suddenly and at once, at God's command; (4) and finally that it be not imperfect in any respect, so that you could recognise the hand of nature, but be complete and whole. All of these had their place in the works of Christ, which surpassed the powers of nature by far, were public and perfect, and were performed suddenly at the mere word of the speaker. This was an undoubted testimony to his divinity.

units.la: IV. Quibus accedunt in Christi miraculis quædam singularia, quæ ipsum supra reliquos Prophetas longè evehebant: 1. quod miracula ejus non divinæ omnipotentiæ solum, sed & bonitatis opera erant; ac talia quæ Messiam ipsum faterentur; quæque Deo ipso, si, humani generis misertus, in terras venire, illudque gratiosè visitare vellet, dignissima erant. In quo manifesto à Mosis miraculis differebant. Bis autem, peculiaribus de causis, severitate usus legitur; tum circa Gadarenorum porcos, Matth. 8. tum circa ficum istam mendacem ac sterilem, Matth. 21.2. Quod opera post se relinquerent permanentia, ut in ægrorum sanationibus patet. Longe aliter ac illa erant, quæ Moses coram Pharaone gessit. 3. Quod in omni naturæ parte ea ediderit in cœlo, in terrâ, in mari &c. ea veluti universâ doctrinæ ipsius suffragante. 4. Quod singularis exempli forent, à faculis non exaudita. Joh. 9: 32. 5. Nec ea parcè exhibita, sed frequentia, & numero propemodum infinita; certe multitudine sua omnia retro Mosis ac prophetarum oracula non exæquantia solum, sed superantia. 6. Quod propriâ potestate illa peregerit; quod & publicè fassus est, Matth. 9: 28. Dixit ipsis Jesus, an creditis quod possum hoc facere? dixerunt ipsi, na Domine. Unde & pro arbitro ea patravit, quoties liberet, Domine, si vis, potes me purificare. Matth. 8:2. eorumque patrandorum potestatem aliis quoque fecit: Dedit ipsis (discipulis) potestatem, spiritus impuros ejiciendi: Matth. 10:1. Tandemque illa non vanæ gloriæ, aut commodi studio; sed in Dei solius, ac, quod non vanum deitatis argumentum erat, in suam quoque ipsius gloriam, suæque divinitati testandæ, fecit. Dixit Jesus, hæc infirmitas non est ad mortem, sed propter gloriam Dei, ut glorificetur filius Dei per eam, Joh. 11:4. strem numinis ædem, vilemque jam domum, sed in cœlum ingredi, ibique regnare debuit.
units.tr: IV. To these, in the miracles of Christ, there are added certain singular features which raised him far above the other prophets: (1) his miracles were works not only of divine power but also of goodness, and such as declared him to be the Messiah, and were most worthy of God himself, if he, moved by pity for the human race, wished to come to earth and visit it in grace. In this they plainly differed from the miracles of Moses. Twice, however, for particular reasons, he is recorded as having used severity: once concerning the swine of the Gadarenes, Matt. 8, and once concerning that deceitful and barren fig tree, Matt. 21. (2) His works left behind lasting results, as is plain in the healing of the sick, quite unlike those which Moses performed before Pharaoh. (3) In every part of nature he displayed such works, in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and so on, as if the whole of nature were lending support to his teaching. (4) They were of a kind never heard of from the ages. John 9:32. (5) Nor were they displayed sparingly, but often, and in number almost infinite; certainly by their multitude they not only equalled but surpassed all the oracles of Moses and the prophets. (6) He performed them by his own power, which he also openly confessed: Jesus said to them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord. Matt. 9:28. Hence he worked them at his own will whenever he pleased: Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. Matt. 8:2. He also gave others the power to work them: He gave them (the disciples) power over unclean spirits, to cast them out. Matt. 10:1. Finally, he did these things not for the sake of empty glory or gain, but for the glory of God alone, and, which was no slight proof of his deity, also for his own glory, to attest his divinity. Jesus said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby. John 11:4. He was to enter not the temple of a divine power, now a vile house, but heaven, and there to reign.

units.la: IX. Quod celare nonnunquam miracula sua jusserit, id non mo- destiæ causa fecit, quæ in eo sita non erat, sed peculiaribus de causis 1. Non enim propere nimis, ac saltu veluti in ora famamque hominum venire, sed spatio & mora invalescere debebat; Judæi{que} de Messia quærendi, & miracula sua examinandi tempus largiri volebat. Et dixit ipsi Jesus: vide, nemini dicas: sed abi, ostende te ipsum sacerdoti, & offer donum, quod præcepit Moses. Matth. 8. 4. Unde sparsit quidem radios quosdam, quibus agnosceretur: Si opera non fecisem in ipsis, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent: nunc vero & viderunt, & oderunt, & me & Patrem meum. Joh. 15: 24 nimia autem luce illorum oculos ferire ac offendere noluit. 2. Præsertim, cum sufficerent illa, quæ publicè extabant, quædam intra privatos parietes gesta intempestive nimis efferri vetuit. Matth. 9: 30. coll. Marc. 8: 26. 3. Idonco enim tempore ista in lucem ventura erant. Sicuti maximam eorum partem, non nisi post resurrectionem ejus, ut & alia ad ipsum pertinentia, primum publicata constat. Quod sapienti de causa fiebat, ut ab opere isto omnium maximo, ac publico divini favoris testimonio, reliqua ipsius miracula, ac doctrina universa, pondus ac auctoritatem acciperent. Unde & antea nonnunquam non miracula solum quædam, Matth. 17: 9. sed & sese Messiam esse aperte nimis divulgari vetuit, Matth. 16: 20. Luc. 9: 21. Atque huc spectat signum illud quod flagitantibus Judæis ut omnium maximum pollicitus est; Tunc responderunt quidam ex Scribis ac Pharisæis, dicentes, præceptor, volumus ex te signum videre. Ip- se vero respondens dixit eis: gens mala & adulterina signum requirit, sed signum non dabitur ei nisi signum Jonæ Prophetæ: sicut enim fuit Jonas in ventre ceti tres dies & tres noctes; ita erit filius hominis in corde terræ tres dies & tres noctes. Matth. 12: 38, 39, 40. 4. Magis autem in dignabatur, si à mendaci spiritu ipsi testimonium præberetur, quod non nisi infamandæ ipsius doctrinæ servire poterat, unde os istud impurum sæpe compescuit. Marc. 1: 34. & 3: 12. Matth. 12: 16.
units.tr: IX. That he sometimes ordered his miracles to be kept secret, he did not do for the sake of modesty, which did not lie in this matter, but for particular reasons: (1) For they ought not to come into the mouths and fame of men too hastily, as if by a leap; they had to grow strong through space and delay, and he wished to give the Jews time to inquire about the Messiah and to examine his miracles. And Jesus said unto him, See thou tell no man; but go thy way, shew thyself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded. Matt. 8:4. Hence he indeed scattered certain rays by which he might be recognised, If I had not done among them the works which no other man did, they had not had sin; but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father. John 15:24; yet he did not wish to strike and offend their eyes with too strong a light. (2) Especially since what was publicly in view was sufficient, he forbade certain things done within private walls to be published too untimely. Matt. 9:30, compare Mark 8:26. (3) For those things were to come to light at a fitting time. As is established, the greater part of them were not made public until after his resurrection, as were other matters concerning him. This was done for a wise reason: so that the rest of his miracles and his whole teaching might receive weight and authority from that greatest work, the public testimony of divine favour. Hence also he sometimes forbade not only certain miracles, Matt. 17:9, but also openly making known too widely that he was the Messiah, Matt. 16:20; Luke 9:21. To this refers the sign he promised, the greatest of all, to the Jews who demanded it: Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee. But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas: for as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Matt. 12:38, 39, 40. (4) He disdained more to have testimony given to him by a lying spirit, which could serve only to defame his doctrine; hence he often silenced that unclean mouth. Mark 1:34; 3:12; Matt. 12:16.

units.la: X. Tandem non Christus solum ipse miracula patravit, sed & Apostolos ea virtute induit, qui & post ipsius discessum miraculorum gloria claruerunt, ut isto commeatu doctrina sacra mundo placeret. Unde cum toto orbe sermonem illum spargere deberent, qui à Christo in Judæa solâ prædicatus fuerat, operum magnitudine & copia Christo non inferiores: sed propemodum majores fuerunt. Qui credit in me, opera quae ego facio, & ille faciet, & majora his faciet; quia ego ad patrem proficiscor, Joh. 14:12.
units.tr: X. Finally, Christ not only performed miracles himself, but also endowed the Apostles with that power, and they too, after his departure, shone with the glory of miracles, so that by this means the sacred teaching might please the world. Hence, since they were to spread that message throughout the whole world, which had been preached by Christ in Judea alone, they were not inferior to Christ in the greatness and number of their works, but were almost greater. He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father. John 14:12.

units.la: XI. Quanquam inter Apostolorum & Christi Domini miracula hoc intercesserit: 1. quod illi in nomine Jesu miracula fecerint, nullo proprio honore: Dixit vero Petrus – in nomine Jesu Christi Nazareni, surge & ambula. Act. 3:6. Quid miramini, quasi potentia propria, aut pietate, fecissemus hunc ambulare? v. 12. Christus autem & suam & patris gloriam saepissime testatus ea peregerit: Jesus autem respondit eis, Pater meus usque operatur, & ego operor. Joh. 5:17. Hoc fecit initium signorum Jesus in Cana Galilaeae, & manifestavit gloriam suam. cap. 2:11. 2. Illi, cum facultatem eam aliunde accepissent, eandem aliis tradere nequiverint: Christus autem Apostolis, successoribus suis, eam quoque largitus fueris: Ecce, dovobis potestatem ambulandi super serpentes & scorpiones &c. Luc. 10:19. Infirmos sanate, leprosos purificate, mortuos suscitate, daemones ejicite, gratis accepistis, gratis date. Matth. 10:8. 3. Denique quod nec ipsi Apostoli, quoties ac ubicunque vellent, facultatem eam ad manum haberent, ac non sine precum ambitu eam plerumque a Deo eblandirentur. Quod in Christo aliter sese habuit, cui ad nutum omnis natura praesto erat: Ita enim filius, quos vult, vivificat, Joh. 5:21.
units.tr: XI. Yet between the miracles of the Apostles and those of Christ the Lord there was this difference: (1) The Apostles worked miracles in the name of Jesus, with no honour of their own: Then Peter said, In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk. Acts 3:6. Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? v. 12. Christ, however, very often testified to both his own glory and the Father's while performing them: But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work. John 5:17. This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory. John 2:11. (2) The Apostles, having received that power from elsewhere, could not pass it on to others; Christ, however, also bestowed it on his successors the Apostles: Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, etc. Luke 10:19. Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give. Matt. 10:8. (3) Finally, the Apostles themselves did not have that power at hand whenever and wherever they wished, and they often obtained it from God not without an approach of prayer. With Christ it was otherwise, to whom all nature stood ready at his will: For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will. John 5:21.

units.la: Vindicata illa a Judaeorum calumniis.
units.tr: Vindicated from the Jews' calumnies.

units.la: XII. Quae vero contra miracula Christi objectant Judaei, levia admodum, & ex mero odio ad fulgorem eorum obscurandum quaesita, dignitatem eorum minuere nullo modo valent. Quem enim colorem habet, quod ea daemonis ope, vel magico ministerio perac-ta blasphemant, quae regno ejus adeo adversa fuerunt, ut potentiorem contra Satanae castra bellatorem Servatore nostro mundus habuerit neminem? Ad hoc manifestatus est Filius Dei, ut solvat opera diaboli, 1. Joh. 3:8. quem & invitum regno suo occupatisque corporibus cedere saepe coegit: Et rogarunt ipsum, ne ipsos juberet in abyssum abire, Luc. 8:32. Si Satanas Satanam ejicit, contra se ipsum est divisus. Matth. 12:26. quaeque non falsa vel inani specie oculos praestringerent, ut magorum artes agnoscerent, sed vera & manifesta in genus humanum beneficia erant; qualia aut diabolo, aut magis imputari nulla ratione possunt. Quod autem ipsos Scribarum quoque discipulos daemonas fugasse addunt, Matth. 12:27. id ipsum Christi miracula non destruit, sed confirmat; cum ne illi quidem nisi appellato Christi nomine istam in daemones potestatem exercuerint. Filii vestri per quem ejiciunt daemones! Matth. 12:27. Novimus quendam, qui in nomine tuo ejicit daemones. Luc. 9:49. Multi dicent, in nomine tuo ejecimus daemonia, Matth. 7:22.
units.tr: XII. The objections which the Jews raise against Christ's miracles are very slight, and are sought out of pure hatred in order to obscure their brilliance; they can in no way diminish their dignity. For what plausibility is there in their charge that these works were done by the help of a demon or by magical ministry, when they were so opposed to his kingdom that the world has never had a mightier warrior against Satan's camp than our Saviour? For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil, 1 John 3:8. Often he forced the devil, against his will, to give up his kingdom and the bodies he had seized: And they begged him that he would not command them to go out into the deep, Luke 8:32. If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself, Matt. 12:26. These were not works which dazzled the eyes with a false or empty appearance, so that they could be recognised as the arts of magicians; they were true and manifest benefits to the human race, and such things can by no reasoning be ascribed to the devil or to magicians. As for their claim that even the disciples of the scribes cast out demons, Matt. 12:27, this does not destroy Christ's miracles but confirms them, since even those men did not exercise that power over demons except by calling on the name of Christ. Your sons, by whom do they cast them out? Matt. 12:27. We saw someone who casts out demons in your name, Luke 9:49. Many will say, we have cast out demons in your name, Matt. 7:22.

units.la: XIII. Talia ergo cum undiquaque fuerint miracula Christi, vera & divina, imò & Mosis Prophetarumque miraculis majora, apparet non fuisse illa ad Israëlem tentandum composita, ut pseudo-prophetarum signa, Deut. 13:1,2,3. sed verbis doctrinæque ejus fidem fecisse. Esai. 8:18. Joh. 20:31. Hebr. 2:3,4.
units.tr: XIII. Since, then, the miracles of Christ were in every respect true and divine, indeed greater than the miracles of Moses and the Prophets, it is plain that they were not designed to test Israel, like the signs of false prophets, Deut. 13:1–3, but made faith in his words and teaching, Isa. 8:18; John 20:31; Heb. 2:3–4.

units.la: XIV. Præter miraculaad munus Christi propheticum pertinet quoque vitæ ac mortis ejus exemplum. Æmuli mei sitis, ut & ego Christi. 1. Cor. 11:1. conf. 1. Thess. 1:6. Qui dicit, se in ipso manere, debet, ut ille ambulavit, & ipse sic ambulare, 1. Joh. 2:6. Ad hoc enim vocati estis, quod etiam Christus passus sit pro vobis, relinquens nobis exemplar, ut sequamur vestigia ejus. 1. Pet. 2:21.
units.tr: XIV. Besides the miracles, the example of his life and death also belongs to Christ's prophetic office. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:1; cf. 1 Thess. 1:6. He who says that he abides in him ought himself to walk just as he walked, 1 John 2:6. For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps, 1 Pet. 2:21.

units.la: XV. Vitâ enim sanctissimâ doctrinæ, quam prædicavit, non mediocriter alluxit; nobisque omnibus præluxit, ut eandem vitæ sectam teneremus. Non quidem ubi mortale fastigium supergressus divinam virtutem exerit, vel mediationis opere perfungitur, & salutem nostram apud patrem peragit; quæ supra nostram mediocritatem sunt. Sed ubi eximiâ morum sanctitate nobis præit, utque ipsi eandem quoque semitam tereremus, pressa pedum posuit claris vestigia signis.
units.tr: XV. For by the most holy life he lived, he shed no small light on the doctrine he preached, and he went before us all so that we might hold to the same way of life. Not indeed where, having passed beyond the mortal height, he exerts divine power or performs the work of mediation and secures our salvation with the Father; those things lie above our lowly condition. But where he goes before us in outstanding holiness of conduct, and so that we too might tread the same path, he set down, in his footsteps pressed clearly, the marks for us to follow.

units.la: XVI. Nec parum denique doctrinam suam veluti supremo actu confirmavit morte sua ac martyrio: coram Jesu Christo, qui testatus est coram Pontio Pilato pulchram illam confessionem. 1. Tim. 6:13. à Jesu Christo, teste illo fideli, primogenito ex mortuis. Apoc. 1:5. Ut de resurrectione ac cœlesti ejus gloria taceam: quæ totidem divinæ ejus doctrinæ publica fuerunt testimonia, ac de cœlo edita præconia.
units.tr: XVI. Finally, he confirmed his teaching, as it were by a final act, no little, by his death and martyrdom: before Jesus Christ, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed that good confession, 1 Tim. 6:13. From Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, Rev. 1:5. I say nothing of his resurrection and heavenly glory, which were as many public testimonies to his divine doctrine and proclamations sent down from heaven.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CAPUT XIV.

units.la: De munere Christi sacerdotali.
units.tr: De munere Christi sacerdotali.

units.la: I. Um salutem humano generi non solum promulgari, sed & exhiberi ac præstari oportuerit; post propheticum Christi munus, sequitur sacerdotale, ac denique regium ejus officium.
units.tr: I. Since salvation had to be not only proclaimed to the human race but also actually offered and secured, the priestly office of Christ follows his prophetic office, and finally his kingly office.

units.la: II. Considerandum autem sacerdotale Christi munus dupliciter: 1. in genere quoad naturam & dignitatem ejus muneris. 2. in specie, quoad praecipuas illius functiones.
units.tr: II. Christ's priestly office should be considered in two ways: (1) in general, as to the nature and dignity of the office; (2) in particular, as to its principal functions.

units.la: III. Sacerdos describitur Hebr. 5: 1. talisque Christus, cum sponsor & angelus Jehovae intercessor esset, exhibitus jam olim fuit, Psal. 110: 4. Tu es sacerdos in saeculum, secundum ordinem Melchizedeci. Zach. 6: 13. Et erit sacerdos in throno ejus. Et consilium pacis erit inter utrumque. Dan. 9: 24. Septuaginta hebdomades decisae sunt ad consummandum peccata, & ad expiandum praevaricatem, & ad adducendam justitiam aeternam. Et in Novo T. Hebr. 9: 11. Christus autem quum advenit, sacerdos summus futurorum bonorum &c. & 3: 1. Considerate Apostolum & Pontificem confessionis nostrae Christum Jesum.
units.tr: III. The priest is described in Heb. 5:1. Such a priest, when he was to be the surety and the intercessor with the angel of Jehovah, was already shown long ago: Ps. 110:4, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." Zech. 6:13, "And he shall be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both." Dan. 9:24, "Seventy weeks are determined to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness." And in the New Testament, Heb. 9:11, "But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come," etc.; and 3:1, "Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus."

units.la: IV. Adeptus autem id munus est, ex patris jussu ac vocatione: Sic & Christus non semet ipsum glorificavit, ut fieret Pontifex, sed qui locutus est ad eum: filius es meus tu, ego hodie genui te. Hebr. 5: 5. Cum enim filius foret, ad ipsum merito divinae familiae sacerdotium pertinebat. conf. Num. 3: 12, 13. Ecce ego cepi Levitas pro omni primogenito: nam mihi est omnis primogenitus: sanctificavi mihi omnem primogenitum ex filiis Israelis. & Psal. 89: 28. Etiam ego primogenitum faciam illum, summum regibus terrae. Nec simplici mandato, sed jurisjurandi religione illud ipsi confirmatum legimus; quo propositi Dei de salute hominum immutabilitatem intelligeremus. Et in quantum non sine juramento (nam illi quidem sunt, qui sine juramento sacerdotes exciterunt: hic autem cum juramento, per illum, qui dicit ad eum, juravit Dominus, & non poenitebit illum) in tantum melioris testamenti exitiit sponsor Jesus. Hebr. 7: 20, 21, 22.
units.tr: IV. He obtained this office by the Father's command and call: "So also Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee." Heb. 5:5. For since he was the Son, the priesthood of the divine household belonged to him by right. Compare Num. 3:12, 13: "Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn... for all the firstborn are mine; I sanctified to myself all the firstborn in Israel." And Ps. 89:27: "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth." We read that this was confirmed to him not by a simple command but with the solemnity of an oath, by which we might understand the unchangeableness of God's purpose concerning the salvation of men: "And inasmuch as not without an oath he was made priest (for those priests were made without an oath, but he with an oath by him that said unto him, The Lord sware and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever), by so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament." Heb. 7:20, 21, 22.

units.la: V. Fuit vero sacerdos, non ex Aaronidarum instituto, sed ex Melchizedeci ritu & ordine, Psal. 110: 4. qui Aaronidis sacerdotibus & antiquior & major fuit. Qualis ille nobis Melchizedecus, in Cananaeae partibus, paulo post mundi a diluvio renascentis exordium occurrit, inter cives suos regnum pariter & Pontificatum gerens. Quo in genere, interprete Apostolo, eximius fuit typus Christi, tum in iis, quae de ipso in S. Scriptura narrantur; tum etiam quae praetereuntur, & religiosi silentii supparo involvuntur: in quo supra reliquos typos eminet.
units.tr: V. He was a priest not according to the institution of the sons of Aaron, but according to the rite and order of Melchizedek, Ps. 110:4, who was both older and greater than the priests of Aaron's line. Melchizedek, such as he appears to us in the land of Canaan, shortly after the world was renewed from the flood, held both kingship and priesthood among his own people. In this respect, as the Apostle explains, he was a remarkable type of Christ, both in what is told of him in Holy Scripture and in what is passed over and wrapped in a silence of reverence. In this respect he stands out above the other types.

units.la: VI. Narrantur enim de ipso 1. munus ipsius sacerdotale simul ac regium; cum foret Rex idem hominum, coelique sacerdos. 2. ejus prae ipso Abrahamo dignitas; a quo decimas accepit; cuique solemnem in modum benedixit. 3. Sacerdotii ejus prae Levitico antiquitas. 4. Nec sacrificium ejus prorsus praeteritur, cum decimarum mentio occurrat, de quibus de more sacrificavit. 5. Tacentur autem successores ejus, ipseque solus derepente ea in gente sacerdos prodit. 6. quin & reliqua ejus universa historia reticetur; &c, nulla vitae mortisque mentione, ipse prorsus ἀγενεαλόγητος, & tanquam ex se natus, producitur. Ut non sacerdotium solum Christi ἀπαρχῆς ἀπάτωρ & perpetuum, sed & personae ejus aeternitatem figuratam intelligamus. Quae Paulus latius in epist. ad Hebr. c. 7. exequitur, ubi Melchizedecum hunc ex tenebris illis, quibus eum sacra historia non sine mysterio obtexerat, evolvit; ac sacerdotii ejus dignitatem prae Levitico multis in rebus ostendit; istumque Christi typum per partes explicat ac ostendit.
units.tr: VI. For the following things are told of him: (1) his priestly and at the same time kingly office, since he was both king of men and priest of heaven; (2) his dignity above Abraham himself, from whom he received tithes and whom he blessed in a solemn manner; (3) the antiquity of his priesthood compared with the Levitical; (4) his sacrifice is not wholly passed over, since mention of tithes occurs, from which he offered sacrifice as was customary; (5) his successors are not mentioned, and he alone suddenly appears as priest among that people; (6) indeed, the rest of his whole history is also left unrecorded, and without any mention of his life or death, he is brought forward entirely [ἀγενεαλόγητος], as if born of himself. Thus we understand that the priesthood of Christ is [ἀπαρχῆς ἀπάτωρ], without beginning and without father, and perpetual, and that the eternity of his person is foreshadowed. Paul pursues this more fully in his Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 7, where he unfolds this Melchizedek from those shadows in which sacred history, not without mystery, had wrapped him, and shows in many respects the dignity of his priesthood above the Levitical, and explains and displays this type of Christ part by part.

units.la: VII. Neque solum in Melchizedeco, sed & in hieratico Aaronidarum ordine Christi sacerdotium expressum fuit: ut jam tunc sacerdotem ipsum viguisse sciamus, ac per ministros, & vicarium pecudem sanguinem, id munus peregisse. Quales, sicuti ante adventum ipsius in Ecclesia dari potuerunt, ut venturo viam panderent, ejusque fidelibus de longinquo ostentarent; ita, peracto nunc Christi sacrificio, & vero sanguine libato, nulli amplius ejus vicario vel mystarchae in terris locus; quales sese falso sacrificuli in papatu, cum suo sacrorum rege, jactant. Possidet enim Christus sacrificaturam ἀπαρχῆς ἀπάτωρ, nec ulli mortalium communicandam. Hebr. 7: 24.
units.tr: VII. Christ's priesthood was foreshadowed not only in Melchizedek but also in the hierarchical order of the sons of Aaron, so that we may know that the priesthood itself already flourished then, and that it was carried out through ministers and through the blood of a substitute animal. Such ministers could be appointed in the Church before his coming, to open the way for the one to come and to show his faithful ones his coming from afar. But now that Christ's sacrifice has been completed and his true blood offered, there is no longer any place on earth for his vicar or any mystarch of this kind. Yet the false little sacrificers in the papacy boast of such things, together with their king of sacred rites. For Christ possesses an unchangeable priesthood [ἀπαρχῆς ἀπάτωρ], and it is to be shared with no mortal. Heb. 7:24.

units.la: VIII. Ut autem ad muneris hujus praecipuas functiones pergamus, Muneris ilconstitit illud in sacra ἱερωσύνη Deo placando ac hominibus concilia\-ndo, peccatisque ipsorum digno cruore expiandis, instituta. Et per ipsum omnia reconciliare ad se, pacem faciens per sanguinem crucis ejus, tum quae in coelis, tum quae in terris sunt Col. 1: 20. Quod Deus in Christo mundum sibi reconciliavit, non imputans ipsis lapsus ipsorum. 2. Cor. 5: 19. Ac duabus partibus absolvebatur 1. Sacrificii immolatione, & 2. intercessione: quae & veteris sacerdotii partes erant.
units.tr: VIII. Now let us proceed to the principal functions of this office. This office consisted in the sacred priesthood [ἱερωσύνη], established to propitiate God, to reconcile men to him, and to expiate their sins with worthy blood. "And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven." Col. 1:20. "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." 2 Cor. 5:19. The office was carried out in two parts: (1) the immolation of the sacrifice, and (2) intercession. These were also the parts of the old priesthood.

units.la: IX. Immolatio Christi sui ipsius oblatio erat, ac proprii sanguinis libatio, quem per spiritum aeternum obtulit, immaculatum Deo, purificantem conscientias nostras. Hebr. 9: 14. Ubi Christus simul sacerdos, & victima, & altare fuit.
units.tr: IX. The immolation of Christ was the offering of himself, and the shedding of his own blood, which through the eternal Spirit he offered without spot to God, to purge our conscience. Heb. 9:14. Here Christ was at once priest, victim, and altar.

units.la: X. Sacerdos fuit juxta utramque naturam, cum actus hic in qua ipse fuerit, praecipua tamen divinae naturae dignitate ac usu; qui sacerdos, spiritus ille aeternus est, per quem se ipsum obtulit. Hebr. 9: 14. Non enim in sacerdotii hujus honorem latronum turba, qui ipsum cruci suffixerunt, venire potest. Quicquid enim illis Christus in sacrum suum corpus permiserit, ipse solus animam suam, nulli hominum obnoxiam, posuit, & propria voluntate patri obtulit. Nemo tollit eam à me, sed ego depono eam per me ipsum. Joh. 10: 18.
units.tr: X. He was priest according to both natures, although this act was performed in the nature in which he was, yet chiefly by the dignity and function of the divine nature; for the eternal Spirit is the priest through whom he offered himself. Heb. 9:14. For the crowd of robbers who fastened him to the cross could not come to the honour of this priesthood. Whatever Christ allowed them to do to his sacred body, he alone laid down his soul, which was subject to no man, and offered it to the Father by his own will. "No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself." John 10:18.

units.la: XI. Victima maxime fuit secundum humanam naturam. Oblatio enim corporis Christi appellatur Hebr. 10: 10. 1. Pet. 2: 14. Cui divinitas pretium & valorem contulit. Cum non hominis cujuslibet, sed Dei fuerit ille sanguis, qui fundebatur, Act. 20: 28. Unde unus pro omnibus mori potuit, 2. Cor. 5: 15. eosque unico illo libamine expiare, Hebr. 9: 26. Nam ille Christi θεανθρωπίας amor: illudque amoris martyrium tanti profecto erat, ut humanum genus universum & amplecti & salvare potuerit.
units.tr: XI. The victim was chiefly according to the human nature. For the offering of the body of Christ is so called, Heb. 10:10; 1 Pet. 2:14. To this the divinity gave price and worth, since the blood that was poured out was not that of any man, but of God, Acts 20:28. Hence he could die for all, 2 Cor. 5:15, and expiate them by that single offering, Heb. 9:26. For that was the love of Christ, God-man; and that martyrdom of love was indeed so great that it could both embrace and save the whole human race.

units.la: XII. Altaris autem cum duplex olim usus foret, tum victimarum carnes sustinendi, tum easdem consecrandi; quo praesertim ignis sacer in ara perpetuo excubans faciebat: priori respectu altare hujus sacrificii fuit crux, in quam Christus sursum elatus fuit, 1. Pet. 2: 24. Secundum respectum ipsa ejus divinitas & spiritus aeternus sustinuit, qui victimam hanc consecravit divinisque flammis accendit, Hebr. 9: 14. Qui per spiritum aeternum se ipsum obtulit, immaculatum Deo. Joh. 17: 19. Et pro ipsis ego sanctifico me ipsum. Utque duae olim in templo arae erant, una pro victimis, altera pro oroboribus: ita utramque in Christi sacrificio reperire est. Non enim solum peccata nostra ab eo expiata sunt, ut sanctorum anima requiescere sub altari illo suaviter possint, Apoc. 6: 9. conf. Hebr. 13: 10. sed & preces nostrae, ab ipso sanctificatae & odorae redditae, in altaris illius aurei fumo recta in coelum eunt. Et alius angelus venit, & constitit apud altare, habens thuribulum aureum; & data sunt ei thymiamata multa, ut daret orationibus sanctorum omnium super altare aureum, quod est coram throno. Apoc. 8: 3.
units.tr: XII. The altar had a twofold use in former times: to bear the flesh of the victims, and to consecrate them, which the sacred fire burning perpetually on the altar especially effected. In the first respect, the altar of this sacrifice was the cross, on which Christ was lifted up, 1 Pet. 2:24. In the second respect, his divinity itself and the eternal Spirit sustained it, who consecrated this victim and kindled it with divine flames, Heb. 9:14: "who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God." John 17:19: "And for their sakes I sanctify myself." And just as there were formerly two altars in the temple, one for the victims and the other for incense, so both are to be found in Christ's sacrifice. For not only were our sins expiated by him, so that the souls of the saints may rest sweetly under that altar, Rev. 6:9; cf. Heb. 13:10; but also our prayers, sanctified by him and made fragrant, go straight up to heaven in the smoke of that golden altar. "And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne." Rev. 8:3.

units.la: XIII. Tempus peracti hujus sacrificii idem fuit, quod olim lege definitum erat; inclinante videl. vespera, quando juge mactari moris erat, Num. 28: 4. idque juxta angeli vaticinium apud Danielem, cap. 9. Matth. 27: 46. Circa horam autem nonam clamavit Jesus voce magna.
units.tr: XIII. The time of this sacrifice's completion was the same as the law had once prescribed: toward evening, when the continual sacrifice was customarily slain, Num. 28:4. This also accords with the angel's prophecy in Daniel, ch. 9. Matt. 27:46: "About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice."

units.la: XIV. Altera sacerdotii Christi functioest intercessio. Quae preces sunt non privatae, quales illae quae Matth. 26: 39 occurrunt: & precatus est; Pater mi, si possibile est, transeat à me poculum hoc, sed non ut ego volo, sed ut tu vis: sed publicae, quales & olim, Joh. 17. & maxime nunc in cœlis fundit. Introiit in ipsum cœlum, ut nunc appareat faciei Dei pro nobis Hebr. 9: 24. Et, si quis peccet, παράκλητον advocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum iustum, 1 Joh. 2: 1. Quis est, qui condemnat? Christus is est qui mortuus est, imo qui & suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis, Rom. 8: 34. Quod ex veteris quoque sacerdotii ritu, ubi publicam intercessionem in intimo sanctuario offerri, deinde veluti solio affundi à Pontifice moris erat.
units.tr: XIV. The other function of Christ's priesthood is intercession. These prayers are not private, such as those in Matt. 26:39, "And he prayed, My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will." They are public, such as he offered once in John 17 and now pours out most of all in heaven. "He entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us," Heb. 9:24. And "if anyone sins, we have an advocate [παράκλητον] with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous," 1 John 2:1. "Who is it that condemns? Christ is the one who died, yes, who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us," Rom. 8:34. This also follows the rite of the old priesthood, where it was customary for the High Priest to offer public intercession in the innermost sanctuary and then, as it were, pour it out upon the throne.

units.la: XV. Atque hac ratione παράκλητος seu Advocatus nostfamiliaris dicitur, 1. Joh. 2: 1. quod nomen & Spiritui S. tribuitur, sed diverso sensu. Non enim ille preces proprie pro nobis fundit, ut Christus sacerdos noster, sed suspiria ac tacitas preces nobis insinuat ac dictat, atque interioribus responsis animam nostram mulcet ac solatur. Nam quod oremus, quemadmodum oportet, nescimus: sed ipse Spiritus interpellat pro nobis gemitibus, qui sermone non explicantur. Rom. 8: 26. Emisit Deus Spiritum filii sui in corda nostra, qui clamat, Abba Pater. Gal. 4: 6.
units.tr: XV. For this reason Christ is called [παράκλητος], or Advocate, 1 John 2:1. The name is also given to the Holy Spirit, but in a different sense. For the Spirit does not properly pour out prayers for us as Christ our priest does. Rather he suggests and dictates sighs and silent prayers to us, and soothes and comforts our soul with inner responses. "For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be put into words," Rom. 8:26. "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father," Gal. 4:6.

units.la: XVI. Non autem supplici ritu, in humum prostratus, patrisque genibus minor, hac generis humani advocatione perfungitur, sed gloriosò patrocinio causam nostram in cœlis agit, sanguinemque suum ac exanimatos pro Ecclesia labores, ipsam denique crucem suam testatur, eademque in voluntate, quâ olim in terras venit, nunc etiam in cœlis perseverat, debitumque laboribus suis pretium poscit. Unde ipse sanguis ejus clamare dicitur, Hebr. 12: 24.
units.tr: XVI. Yet he does not perform this advocacy for the human race in a suppliant manner, lying prostrate on the ground and humbler than the Father's knees. He pleads our cause in heaven with glorious patronage. He testifies to his blood, to the labours he endured for the Church, and finally to his cross itself. With the same will by which he once came to earth, he now persists in heaven too, and demands the price owed to his labours. Hence his very "blood is said to cry out," Heb. 12:24.

units.la: XVII. Concurrit enim ad preces has, quæ συμπαθῶς sunt, divina ejus natura & humana. Hæc, intimis visceribus commota, laboranti Ecclesiæ condolere, proqueea patrem rogare, fusumque olim sanguinem ostentare non cessat. Debuit per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret—in eo enim quod passus est ipse, potest iis, qui tentantur, auxiliari. Hebr. 2: 17, 18. Ascendo ad patrem meum, & patrem vestrum, & Deum meum & Deum vestrum. Joh. 20: 17. Quod eo majori efficacia facit, quod ipsa jam in regnum evecta rebus Ecclesiæ majori cum auctoritate præsit. Illa autem non orat, sed exorat, & dignitate sua intercessioni Christi pretium facit.
units.tr: XVII. For his divine and human natures both come together in these prayers, which are [συμπαθῶς] (sympathetic). His human nature, moved in its inmost bowels, does not cease to sympathize with the suffering Church, to ask the Father on its behalf, and to display the blood once poured out. "He had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become merciful... for in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted," Heb. 2:17, 18. "I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God," John 20:17. This makes his intercession all the more effective, because he, now exalted into the kingdom, presides over the affairs of the Church with greater authority. And he does not pray in the sense of asking; he entreats, and by his dignity gives weight to Christ's intercession.

units.la: XVIII. Cumque hæc intercessio <bl>συμπαθῶς</bl> conveniat, & sacerdotalis sit, atque universa Christi merito nitatur, facile patet quam impiè in honoris hujus societatem sancti adscisantur, quos Pontificiorum Ecclesia, non sine delectu, invocare & apprecari, ac Dei
units.tr: XVIII. Since this intercession is [συμπαθῶς], belongs to the priesthood, and rests entirely on the merit of Christ, it is easy to see how impiously the saints are admitted into the fellowship of this honour. The Church of the Papists, not without selection, is accustomed to invoke and entreat them, and

units.la: Pars II. K præpraesertim parentem veluti summo ac praecipuo folio sedentem propitiare consuevit. Quasi aliquem in sanctuario versari sas sit qui Pontifex non sit: vel Christus socia hominum opera indigeat, cum in summis animae laboribus solus torcular calcaverit: vel denique sine servorum adstipulatione impetrari non possit, quod à patre filius postulat. Sed vide de his uberius tomi superioris lib. 2. cap. 14. §. 14.
units.tr: especially to propitiate the Father by seating him, as it were, on the highest and principal throne. As if anyone who is not the High Priest could be permitted into the sanctuary; or as if Christ needed the help of human works, since he alone trod the winepress in the greatest labours of the soul; or finally, as if what the Son asks of the Father could not be obtained without the assistance of servants. But see more fully on these matters in the previous volume, book 2, chapter 14, §14.

units.la: XIX. Sed non ipse solum intercedit Christus, sed & precea sanctorum, sanguine suo tinctas & lustratas, ad Dei thronum perfert; quod quoque ex sacerdotali officio facit, ac juxta veterum sacerdotum ritum. Quomodo & in sacra Apocalypsi à Johanne visus est c. 8:3.
units.tr: XIX. But Christ does not intercede alone. He also carries the prayers of the saints, tinged and cleansed with his blood, to the throne of God. He does this too as part of his priestly office, following the rite of the ancient priests. So it was seen by John in the sacred Apocalypse, Rev. 8:3.

units.la: XX. Ad intercessionem quoque Christi, & sacerdotii ejus in coelis actus, spectat sacrificii ejus applicatio, sanguinisque adspersio, quae per Sp. sanctum peragitur. In sanctificatione Spiritus, ad obedientiam, & adspersionem sanguinis Christi. 1 Pet. 1:2. Sed accessistis ad sanguinem adspersionis, praestantiora loquentem pro Abel. Hebr. 12: 24. Et sacerdotalis denique benedictio, Num. 6:22, 23. quam non moriens solum in cruce, Gal. 3:13, 14. sed vivens praesertim & regnans in coelesti solio nobis impertit: Qui benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali, in coelestibus, in Christo, Eph. 1:3. palamque ac plenissime in extremo mundi actu largietur. Tunc dicet Rex iis, qui ad dextram ipsius erunt: venite benedicti patris mei, haereditarie jure possidete praeparatum a fundatione mundi regnum. Matth. 25:34
units.tr: XX. The application of his sacrifice and the sprinkling of his blood, which is carried out through the Holy Spirit, also belongs to Christ's intercession and to the acts of his priesthood in heaven. "Through the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ," 1 Pet. 1:2. "But you have come to the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better things than the blood of Abel," Heb. 12:24. Finally there is the priestly blessing, Num. 6:22, 23, which he bestows on us not only by dying on the cross, Gal. 3:13, 14, but especially by living and reigning on the heavenly throne: "who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ," Eph. 1:3. He will bestow it openly and most fully in the final act of the world. "Then the King will say to those on his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father, inherit by hereditary right the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world," Matt. 25:34.

units.la: XXI. Has sacerdotalis officii functiones sequuntur fructus ejus & effectus: qui sunt 1. peccata nostra expiare ac delere. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, 1 Joh. 2:2. Per se ipsum purgatione facta peccatorum nostrorum. Hebr. 1:3. peccatores cum Deo reconciliare: Gloriantes in Deo, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum; per quem nunc reconciliationem accepimus, Rom. 5:11. Omnia vero sunt ex Deo, qui nos sibi reconciliavit per Jesum Christum. 2 Cor. 5:18. 3. coelum nobis aperire, templumque istud sanguine suo consecrare: Necesse ergo, figuras quidem eorum, qui in coelis sunt, hisce mundari; ipsa autem coelestia melioribus hostiis propriis ipsis. Hebr. 9:23. 4. Tandemque Ecclesiam suam ista mercede acquirere ac sibi desponsare: Ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo illo proprio sanguine acquisivit. Act. 20:28. Quod ex more veterum. conf. Gen. 29:20, 28. 1. Sam. 18:25. Hos. 3:1,2.
units.tr: XXI. These functions of the priestly office are followed by its fruits and effects, which are: (1) to atone for and blot out our sins: "And he himself is the propitiation for our sins," 1 John 2:2; "when he had by himself made purification of our sins," Heb. 1:3. (2) to reconcile sinners to God: "rejoicing in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation," Rom. 5:11; "All things are of God, who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ," 2 Cor. 5:18. (3) to open heaven to us and to consecrate that temple with his blood: "It was necessary, therefore, that the copies of heavenly things should be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these," Heb. 9:23. (4) and finally to acquire his Church at this price and betroth it to himself: "to feed the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood," Acts 20:28. This follows the custom of the ancients; cf. Gen. 29:20, 28; 1 Sam. 18:25; Hos. 3:1, 2.

units.la: XXII. Sequitur tandem errorum circa sacerdotium Christi ἀντίθεος & ἀναιρέσεις. In sacerdotio Christi agmen ducunt & omnium instar sunt
units.tr: XXII. There follows at last the errors concerning Christ's priesthood, the antitheses [ἀντιθέσεις] and refutations [ἀναιρέσεις]. In the priesthood of Christ they lead the column and serve as the pattern for all the rest.

units.la: Hinc quoque sperat sacrificii Christi applicatio nostra benedictio.
units.tr: To this also belongs the application of Christ's sacrifice to our blessing.

units.la: Sacerdotii Christi fructus & effectus.
units.tr: The fruits and effects of Christ's priesthood.

units.la: Errores socinianorum circa sacerdotium Christi, qui Sociniani. Qui ut Christi satisfactionem negant, eumque sacerdotem revera non credunt: ita, quo testatam ac obviam adeo in Scripturis veritatem evadant, mirum in modum se torquent. Cum enim sacerdotem eum persæpe appellari, cunctasque officii illius partes tribui ipsi videant; quo vim istam effugiant. 1. Sacerdotem quidem vulgo prædicant, sed sacerdotium ejus à regno non distinguunt, saltem Ecclesiæ suæ respectu. 2. Oblationem omnem negant, nisi quod tenui sensu pro se ipso, proprieque infirmitatibus obtulisse eum fingunt. 3. Proprie autem munere sacerdotali in cœlis demum fungi statuunt. 4. Atque illud denique omne in sola intercessione, atque hanc rursus in fiduciario in Ecclesiam regno, ac continua pro ea cura ponunt. Quæ corruptelæ paucis profligandæ sunt.
units.tr: The errors of the Socinians concerning Christ's priesthood. Since they deny Christ's satisfaction, they do not truly believe him to be a priest. In order to escape the truth so plainly attested and present everywhere in the Scriptures, they twist themselves in remarkable ways. For since they see that he is very often called priest, and that all the parts of that office are ascribed to him, they try to escape this force. (1) They indeed preach him commonly as priest, but do not distinguish his priesthood from his kingdom, at least with respect to his Church. (2) They deny every oblation, except that they imagine he offered himself in a thin sense, for himself, properly for his infirmities. (3) They maintain that he properly performs the priestly function only in heaven at last. (4) And finally they place the whole of it in intercession alone, and this again in a kind of fiduciary rule over the Church and a continual care for it. These corruptions must be overthrown briefly.

units.la: XXIII. Ac primo quidem sacerdotium Christi cum regno confundunt: quod quid aliud est quam verum ejus sacerdotium negare, & figurate solum ac improprie sacerdotem fateri. Quod hi homines aperte audent. Quod enim proprie regnum est, impropriè sacerdotium appellant; quia videl. non solum potestate, quod meri regis est, verum etiam benigna voluntate ac amore, ad instar sacerdotis, Ecclesiam suam curet & pascat. Scripturæ autem sacerdotium & regnum Christi distinguunt; cum hoc munus apud homines, illud apud Deum peragat: Omnis enim Pontifex, qui ex hominibus capitur, pro hominibus constituitur, in iis quæ apud Deum agenda sunt, Hebr. 5:
units.tr: XXIII. First of all they confuse Christ's priesthood with his kingdom. This is nothing other than to deny his true priesthood and to acknowledge him as priest only figuratively and improperly. These men openly dare to do this. For what is properly a kingdom they call improperly a priesthood, because he cares for and feeds his Church not only with power, which belongs to a king alone, but also with kindly will and love, like a priest. But Scripture distinguishes the priesthood and kingdom of Christ, since the one works among men and the other before God: "For every High Priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God," Hebr. 5:1.

units.la: 1. Ego inunctus regem meum præfeci Zioni, monti sanctitatis meæ. Psal. 2: 6. illumque non externo nomine, & figura quadam, sed verum sacerdotem describunt, cunctasque ejus muneris partes exequuntur; ac veterum denique sacerdotum turbam ministerio ejus præluisse, ac munus ipsius figurasse docent: qui certe si umbræ fuerint, in Christo veritas & corpus existere debent. Col. 2: 17. Quæ sunt umbra rerum futurarum, at corpus est Christi.
units.tr: 1. I have anointed my king over Zion, my holy mountain. Psal. 2: 6. They describe him not by an outward title and some figure, but as the true priest, and they carry out all the parts of that office. Finally, they teach that the whole crowd of the old priests went before his ministry as a foreshadowing and prefigured his office. If those priests were shadows, the truth and the body must exist in Christ. Col. 2: 17. These are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's.

units.la: XXIV. Sed & secundo oblationem Christi negant, quæ cum sacerdotii præcipua pars ac sequentis eam intercessionis fundamentum sit, hinc sacerdotem quoque eum omnino negare debent. Quod enim in terris, non pro Ecclesia, sed pro se ipso obtulisse ajunt; ut olim Veteris T. sacerdotes, hancque solam ejus oblationem intelligunt; quem colorem, aut quem revera sensum habere potest? Utcunque enim, dum mortali in corpore versaretur, infirmitatibus nostris & aerumnis, non tamen peccatis succinctus erat. Obtulisse autem Christus in Scripturis cum dicitur, non id mortalis corporis fortem, ut ab eo liberemur, sed peccata solummodo spectat. Unde pro se obtulisse dici non potest, cum peccatis caruerit. Verum adversarii oblationem pro peccatis, qui tamen communissimus ejus locutionis sensus est, ignorare volunt; ac ad humanæ vitæ infirmitates, corporisque nostri ærumnas, & mortem denique ipsam, hoc quicquid Christo tribuunt muneris referunt; quæ ille videl. ut sacerdos, aut potius ut rex, sanaverit & abstulerit. Unde & reperierunt, quomodo, cum peccata non haberet, pro se tamen ipso in terris offerre potuerit; ad veterum videl. sacerdotum morem. Quæ insincera sunt, ac tollendo ejus sacerdotio excogitata. Hic enim a veterum sacerdotum instituto Christus paulum diversus fuit, cum iis, utpote peccatoribus, pro se ipsis primo litandum foret, Lev. 4: 3, 4. Quo & Paulus spectat Hebr. 5: 2, 3. Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumitur — Qui equanimis esse possit ignorantibus & errantibus: quoniam & ipse circumdatus est infirmitate; & propter eam debet, quemadmodum pro populo, ita & sua causa offerre pro peccatis. Quæ ubi Christo applicat, misericordem nobis sacerdotem, & infirmitatibus obnoxium, sed absque peccato, contigisse ait, ac infirmatum illarum finem ac usum ostendit: Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum: sed tentatum in omnibus similiter, absque tamen peccato. Hebr. 4: 15. Quamvis filius esset, tamen ex iis, quae passus est, didicit obedientiam. Hebr. 5: 8. Ac pro illis suis infirmitatibus non nisi lacrymas & preces libasse dicit. 7. Qui in diebus carnis sua deprecationibus & supplicationibus oblatis, cum clamore valido & lacrymis &c. Aliter ac Aaronide olim, quibus necesse fuit, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi. Hebr. 7: 27.
units.tr: XXIV. Secondly, they also deny the offering of Christ. Since this is the principal part of the priesthood and the foundation of the intercession that follows, they must on this ground deny that he is a priest at all. For they say that he offered on earth not for the Church but for himself, as the priests of the Old Testament did, and they understand this offering alone as his. What sense, or indeed what plausible meaning, can this have? For while he was in a mortal body, he was surrounded by our infirmities and troubles, yet not by sins. When the Scriptures say that Christ offered, this does not refer to the strength of his mortal body, by which we are freed, but looks to sins alone. Hence it cannot be said that he offered for himself, since he was without sin. Yet the adversaries wish to ignore the offering for sins, which is nevertheless the most common sense of that expression. They refer whatever they attribute to Christ of office to the infirmities of human life, the troubles of our body, and death itself, which he, as priest or rather as king, healed and removed. Hence they have also worked out how, though he had no sins, he could nevertheless offer on earth for himself, namely in the manner of the old priests. These are insincere notions, devised to abolish his priesthood. For here Christ departed somewhat from the institution of the old priests, since they, as sinners, had first to sacrifice for themselves. Lev. 4: 3, 4. To this Paul also refers, Heb. 5: 2, 3: Every high priest is taken from among men... who can have compassion on the ignorant and the erring, since he himself also is compassed with infirmity; and because of it he ought, as for the people, so also for his own sins to offer for sins. When he applies this to Christ, he says that we have a merciful priest, subject to infirmities but without sin, and he shows the end and use of those infirmities: For we have not a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin. Heb. 4: 15. Though he was a son, yet he learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Heb. 5: 8. And for those infirmities of his, he says that he offered only tears and prayers. 7. Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, etc. This is unlike the sons of Aaron of old, who had to offer victims first for their own sins and then for the sins of the people. Heb. 7: 27.

units.la: XXV. Cum autem sacerdotium Christi non in oblatione ejus collocent; nec sanguinis fusionem ad eam pertinuisse existiment, denique non in liberatione a peccatis, per interpositum lytrum ac pretium, sed in liberatione a miseria ac peccatorum poenis per potentiam, quicquid istud muneris est confiteri faciant, hinc & tertio exordium sacerdotii ab ejus ingressu in cœlum demum arcessunt, & mortem ejus, ac quicquid in terra pro humani generis salute egit, ab ea excludunt. Quod commentum 1. non solum ex veteris sacerdotii analogia refutatur, cujus multæ partes peragendæ erant, antequam victimarum sanguis in adytum inferretur: quin & erant victimæ nonnullæ, quarum sanguis nunquam in interiorem thalamum infcinferebatur: quomodo & Christus præcipuos sacerdotii actus in terra peregit; in cœlesti adyto autem non de novo obtulit, sed hostiam in terris oblatam ad patrium limen stitit, ac, peracto officio, in cœlum redux, pro animæ labore mercedem flagitavit. 2. Sed & apertis N. T. Scripturis refragatur, quæ oblationem ejus ab oblationis in cœlo repræsentatione accurate distinguunt: Purificatione peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum facta, sedit ad dextram majestatis illius in locis excelsissimis Hebr. 1:3. Per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium, æternam redemtionem nactus. c. 9:12. Una pro peccatis oblata in perpetuum victima, consedit ad dextram Dei, c. 10: 12. Ac sanguini ejus in terris fuso peccatorum purgationem; sessioni autem ad dextram patris jugem pro Ecclesia tua interpellationem assignant: Et sanguis Jesu Christi Filii ejus, purificat nos ab omni peccato. r. Joh. 1:7. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est, imo vero qui etiam suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Rom. 8. 34. Hebr. 7:25.
units.tr: XXV. But since they do not place the priesthood of Christ in his offering, nor think that the shedding of blood belonged to it, and finally do not place it in deliverance from sins through an interposed ransom and price, but in deliverance from misery and the punishments of sins by power (whatever kind of office this is that they make us confess), therefore thirdly they fetch the beginning of the priesthood only from his entrance into heaven, and exclude from it his death and whatever he did on earth for the salvation of the human race. This fiction (1) is refuted not only by the analogy of the old priesthood, many parts of which had to be performed before the blood of the victims was carried into the sanctuary; indeed there were some victims whose blood was never carried into the inner chamber. In the same way Christ performed the chief acts of his priesthood on earth; in the heavenly sanctuary, however, he did not offer afresh, but presented the victim offered on earth at the Father's threshold, and, the work finished, returned to heaven and demanded his reward for the labour of his soul. (2) It is also contradicted by the plain Scriptures of the New Testament, which carefully distinguish his offering from the representation of that offering in heaven: When he had by himself purged our sins, he sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high. Heb. 1: 3. By his own blood he entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption. Heb. 9: 12. One sacrifice for sins for ever, he sat down on the right hand of God. Heb. 10: 12. They assign the purging of sins to his blood shed on earth, but the perpetual intercession for your Church to his sitting at the Father's right hand: And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. 1 John 1: 7. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Rom. 8: 34. Heb. 7: 25.

units.la: XXVI. Denique quarto ipsum quoque Christi sacerdotium in cœlis, pariterque regnum ejus, corrumpunt.
units.tr: XXVI. Fourthly and finally, they also corrupt Christ's priesthood in heaven, and likewise his kingdom.

units.la: Ne enim Deus esse summus putetur, qui absoluta potestate Ecclesiam regat, sacerdotem potius quam regem appellare malunt. Et sacerdotale illud munus in cura quadam,& precario in Ecclesiam imperio collocant. Unde infirma profecto fides nascitur. Cum Christus, juxta ipsos potestatem nullam nisi precariam alterique obnoxiam habeat. Ac multo satius sit, ipsum Deum recta adire, nec tali sponsore ac interprete niti, qui non solum nostram fidem roborare non posset, sed & in contumeliam ipsius Dei cedat; quasi ipsi soli, sine homine fidejussore, qui pro ipso spondeat, confidere non liceat.
units.tr: For lest God be thought the highest, who rules the Church with absolute power, they prefer to call him priest rather than king. They place that priestly office in a certain care and in a rule over the Church held only by sufferance. Hence indeed a weak faith is born, since Christ, on their view, has no power except a revocable one, dependent on another. It is far better to approach God himself directly and not to rest on such a surety and interpreter, who could not only fail to strengthen our faith but also turns to the insult of God himself, as though it were not lawful to trust in him alone without a human guarantor who vouches for him.

units.la: XXVII. Atque ita plane sacerdotium Christi hi homines tollunt, cum nullam salutis impetrationem, nullam à peccatis liberationem, nullam victimam, nullam denique mediatoriam in cœlis intercessionem agnoscant; quæ cuncta ut non necessaria rejiciunt. Similitudine solum quadam, regnum Christi, ut & illud corrumpant, sacerdotium appellant; quod videl. benevole, & summo in genus humanum amore, illud administret, acceptaque à patre potestate, Ecclesiam à peccatorum pœna, (quæ pœnæ ablatio illis omnis peccatorum expiatio est) liberet: denique in Christo metaphoricam sacerdotis ac Pontificis appellationem solum superesse docent. 4. denique intercessionem ejus in precaria potestate tantum collocant.
units.tr: XXVII. And so these people plainly abolish the priesthood of Christ, since they acknowledge no obtaining of salvation, no liberation from sins, no sacrifice, and finally no mediatorial intercession in heaven, all of which they reject as unnecessary. They call it a priesthood only by a certain likeness, in order to corrupt his kingdom as well: that he administers it kindly and out of supreme love for the human race, and, having received power from the Father, frees the Church from the punishment of sins (and for them this removal of punishment is the whole expiation of sins). Finally, they teach that only a metaphorical appellation of priest and high priest remains in Christ, and they confine his intercession to a merely revocable power.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: De munere Christi regio.
units.tr: On the kingly office of Christ.

units.la: I. Ost sacerdotium Christi de regno ejus agendum: cujus tum natura, tum partes, ac functiones praecipuæ considerandæ.
units.tr: I. After the priesthood of Christ, his kingdom must be treated, and both its nature and its principal parts and functions considered.

units.la: II. Ac principio distinguendum venit regnum ejus mediatorium à regno naturali, quod juxta cum Patre ac Spir. S obtinet. Est enim hic quædam diversitas χίσεων, pari cæteroquin regni utriusque majestate ac honore. Cum illud Christo qua Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος, hoc qua Deo competat; illud speciatim Ecclesiam, hoc autem cunctas creaturas complectatur. Ut male Pontifex, qui se Christi in Ecclesia vicarium facit, hoc colore universa mundi regna subjiciat suo subjecta velit. Cum alii mundi, alii Ecclesiæ fines sint; ac dispar utriusque sit gubernatio.
units.tr: II. First, his mediatorial kingdom must be distinguished from the natural kingdom, which he holds together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. There is indeed a certain difference of administration between them, though the majesty and honour of each kingdom is otherwise equal. The former belongs to Christ as God-man [Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος], the latter to him as God; the former embraces the Church in particular, the latter all creatures. So the Pontiff acts wrongly when he makes himself Christ's vicar in the Church and, under that pretext, wishes all the kingdoms of the world to be subject to himself. For the world and the Church have different boundaries, and their governance is unlike.

units.la: III. Est autem regium Christi munus, ea mediatoris potestas ac auctoritas, qua, Ecclesiæ caput ac Rex constitutus, suprema potestate in cœlo ac terra viget; cunctaque ad Ecclesiam spectantia pleno jure gubernat; eamque & verbo ac interiore spiritus sui potentia regit & perficit, & adversus hostium quorumcunque assultus & potentiam tuetur tandemque victricem, ac corpore animoque perfectam, in cœlo æternum coronabit.
units.tr: III. The kingly office of Christ is that mediatorial power and authority by which he, appointed head of the Church and King, reigns with supreme power in heaven and on earth, governs fully and with full right everything that pertains to the Church, rules and perfects it both by the Word and by the inward power of his Spirit, defends it against the assaults and power of any enemies whatever, and at last will crown it, victorious and perfected in body and soul, in heaven for ever.

units.la: IV. Regem Messiam fore omnia prophetarum oracula canunt: vide Psal. 2. 6. Et ego unxi regem meum in Zionem montem sanctum meum Dan. 2: 44. In diebus regum illorum, eriget Deus cæli regnum, quod in æternum non corrumpetur &c. Luc. 1: 33. Et regnabit in domum Jacobi in æternum, & regni ejus non erit finis. Psal. 89: 28. Primogenitum faciam illum, summum regibus terræ. Esai. 9: 5, 6. Venit principatus in humerum ipsius ad amplificationem principatus, & pacem sine fine super thronum Davidis. Jer. 23: 3. Et excitabo Davidi germen justum, quod regnabit Rex, & prosperabitur. Zach. 9: 9. Gaude admodum, filia Zion; Ecce rex tuus venit tibi &c. Prima autem regni ejus mentio in vaticinio Bileami extare videtur: Incedit stella ex Jacob, & surget sceptrum ex Israële; & defigit angulos Moab, & demolitur omnes filios Seth. Et Israel fortiter aget, & dominabitur aliquis ex Jacobo, & perdet superstitem de urbe. Num. 24: 17, 18, 19. Ac deinde in Hannæ Cantico: Jehova judicabit in finibus terræ, & dabit robur invictum regi suo, & efferet cornu Unctii sui. 1. Sam. 2: 10. Post quæ Davidi regia ista proles promissa est, 2. Sam. 7: 1. Chron. 18. A quo tempore Messias in Ecclesia expectatus fuit, tanquam Rex stirpis Davidicæ: Et servient Jehova Deo suo, & Davidi regi suo, quem excitabo ipsis Jer. 30: 8, 9. Et constituam super ipsas pastorem unum, & pascet eas, servum meum Davidem; — & ego Jehovah ero ipsis in Deum, & servus meus David princeps in medio earum. Ezech. 34: 23, 24. Postea convertentur filii Israel, & quærent Jehovam Deum suum, & Davidem regem suum. Hos. 3: 5:
units.tr: IV. All the oracles of the prophets sing that the Messiah will be King. See Psalm 2:6: And I have anointed my king upon Zion, my holy mountain. Daniel 2:44: In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, etc. Luke 1:33: And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. Psalm 89:28: I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. Isaiah 9:5, 6: The government shall be upon his shoulder, to increase the government, and of peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David. Jeremiah 23:5: And I will raise up to David a righteous branch, a King who shall reign and prosper. Zechariah 9:9: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, etc. The first mention of his kingdom seems to occur in the prophecy of Balaam: A star shall come forth out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth. And Israel shall do valiantly, and one out of Jacob shall have dominion, and shall destroy the remnant of the city. Numbers 24:17, 18, 19. Then in the Song of Hannah: The LORD shall judge the ends of the earth, and he shall give strength to his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed. 1 Samuel 2:10. After this, that royal line was promised to David, 2 Samuel 7:1; 1 Chronicles 18. From that time the Messiah was looked for in the Church as the King of the line of David: They shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them, Jeremiah 30:8, 9. And I will set up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; and I the LORD will be their God, and my servant David a prince among them. Ezekiel 34:23, 24. Afterward shall the children of Israel return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. Hosea 3:5.

units.la: V. Est autem regnum hoc spirituale ac cœleste; non qualia inter homines regna ac principatus videmus, externa vi ac potestate subnixa, ac multum humani splendoris præferentia; sed plane alterius generis. Cum in hominum animis ejus sedes sit, inque cordibus Deum amantibus, ac humana cuncta calcantibus, Christique crucem læto animo sequentibus, consistat. Ad quæ profecto externa vi ac imperio opus non erat. Unde nec Christus regio apparatu in mundum venit; sed, tanquam cœlestis sapientiæ doctor, divinam istam philosophiam tum ipse, tum per discipulos palam tradidit; veteremque humani generis labem sanguine suo eluit; atque eo pacto mundum devicit, inque eo adhuc regnat.
units.tr: V. This kingdom, however, is spiritual and heavenly; it is not like the kingdoms and principalities we see among men, which rest on external force and power and display much human splendour. It is of a wholly different kind, since its seat is in men's minds, and it stands in the hearts of those who love God, who trample on all things human and gladly follow the cross of Christ. For such a kingdom there was truly no need of outward force or command. Hence Christ did not come into the world with royal display; but, as the teacher of heavenly wisdom, he himself, and through his disciples, openly delivered that divine philosophy. He washed away the ancient stain of the human race with his own blood, and in this way conquered the world, and still reigns in it.

units.la: VI. Tantum autem abest, quod externum in eo regnum erexerit, quod sacrorum illud regnum, nomenque humanum, quod in Ecclesia adhuc extabat, abrogaverit; & sacerdotum thronos ac veterum regulorum solium everterit; & ne qua ejus erigendi amplius vel occasio vel necessitas foret, carnalem illum cultum superinducto meliori deleverit; ipsamque tandem regni ejus sedem ac palatium, templum Hierosolymitanum, devastaverit ac exciderit. Denique ne quis in externo nomine amplius gloriaretur, carnalem illum populum repudiavit, & cœlo soloque exulem toto terrarum orbe erasse jussit, novumque gentium populum in Ecclesiæ hæreditatem succedere fecit. Unde Christus recte Joh. 18: 36. Regnum meum non est de hac mundo &c. & Apostolus Rom. 14: 17. Non enim est regnum Dei esca & potus, sed justitia, & pax, & gaudium per Sp. S.
units.tr: VI. Far from having set up an external kingdom, he abolished that sacred kingdom and human dignity which still stood in the Church. He overthrew the thrones of the priests and the seat of the old petty kings, and so that there should be no further occasion or necessity for their restoration, he destroyed that carnal worship by introducing a better one. Finally, he laid waste and levelled to the ground the very seat and palace of his kingdom, the temple at Jerusalem. Lastly, so that no one should boast any longer in an external name, he rejected that carnal people, bade them be exiles from heaven and land throughout the whole orb of the earth, and caused a new people of the nations to succeed to the inheritance of the Church. Hence Christ rightly says, John 18:36: My kingdom is not of this world, etc., and the Apostle, Romans 14:17: For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VII. Unde regni hujus præstantia patet, quod & cœleste prorsus, & divinum, ac denique æternum est. Ascendisti in altum, egisti prædam, accepisti dona in hominibus &c. Psal. 68: 19. Et agnus vincet eos, quia dominus dominorum est, & Rex regum. Apoc. 17: 14. Dixit dominus minus domino meo, sede ad dextram meam. Psal. 110: 1. Talem habemus sacerdotem maximum, qui consedit in dextra throni magnitudinis in caelis, Hebr. 8: 1.
units.tr: VII. From this the excellence of this kingdom is evident: it is wholly heavenly, divine, and finally eternal. You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts among men, etc. Psalm 68:19. And the Lamb shall overcome them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings. Revelation 17:14. The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. Psalm 110:1. We have such a high priest, who is set down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. Hebrews 8:1.

units.la: VIII. Ut Judaeorum stuporem admirari liceat, qui ut Messiam non nisi carnalem regem agnoscunt, instar Davidis vel Salomonis, ita religionis ipsorum hoc nunc praecipuum caput ac compendium est; exorturum aliquem de gente ipsorum regem, qui Judaeos exules, non sine multa hostium caede, in patrias sedes reducturus sit, ubi tamen forte quadraginta annorum regnum sibi polliceri vix audent. Atque haec est spes, ut ipsi appellant, Israelis; ac huc tendit omnis ipsorum religio. Quod profecto indignum est, hoc pro religionis capite, quin & summa, habere, quod terrenus aliquis rex forte oriturus & late imperaturus sit. Quod certe, si vel verum esset, non animam satiare, non hominem beare, neque fides ista iis, qui beata ista tempora non attingunt, prodesse quicquam posset. Non ultra enim insanam istam opinionem vexare attinet, cum id saepius praestitum sit. Ita autem Judaeorum acies in regio isto Messiae fulgore stupet, ut huic praecipua ejus beneficia, ac magnam illam salutem, quam attulit, considerare nec velint, nec possint.
units.tr: VIII. One may marvel at the stupidity of the Jews, who, since they acknowledge the Messiah only as a carnal king, like David or Solomon, have made it now the chief point and summary of their religion that some king will arise from their nation who will bring the exiled Jews back to their ancestral seats, not without great slaughter of their enemies, where they scarcely dare promise themselves a reign even of forty years. This, they call the hope of Israel, and to this their whole religion aims. It is truly unworthy to hold as the head, indeed the sum, of religion that some earthly king may perhaps arise and rule widely. Even if this were true, it could not satisfy the soul, nor make a man blessed, nor could such faith benefit those who do not reach those happy times. For it is no longer worth troubling oneself with that mad opinion, since it has been refuted many times. Yet the eyes of the Jews are so dazzled by the royal splendour of the Messiah that they neither wish nor are able to consider his principal benefits and the great salvation he has brought.

units.la: IX. Sicut autem regnum Messiae spirituale, ita & universale est omnium saeculorum, omniumque terrarum fideles, quin & universae naturae potentiam, ambitu suo complexum. Jesus Christus heri & hodie idem est & in saecula. Hebr. 13: 8. Et huic datus est dominatus, gloriaque & regnum, ut omnes populi, nationes & linguae ei serviant; cujus dominatus est perpetuus, qui non praeteriet &c. Dan. 7: 13, 14. Et omnia subjecit ejus pedibus, eumque constituit caput super omnia Ecclesiae. Eph. 1: 22. Quod Judaei certe de suo illo Messia praestare non possunt, de cujus regno veteres omnes Ecclesiae patres nihil degustarunt; nec Abrahamus, nec David, nec alii veteris Ecclesiae principes, imo ne ullus quidem in hunc usque diem fidelium.
units.tr: IX. But just as the kingdom of the Messiah is spiritual, so it is also universal, embracing the faithful of all ages and all lands, and indeed the power of all nature within its compass. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. Hebrews 13:8. And to him was given dominion, glory, and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, etc. Daniel 7:13, 14. And he put all things under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things to the Church. Ephesians 1:22. The Jews cannot show this of their Messiah, of whose kingdom all the ancient Fathers of the Church tasted nothing; neither Abraham, nor David, nor the other leaders of the ancient Church, indeed not even any of the faithful up to this day.

units.la: X. Similiterque regno huic subduntur omnia, omnesque ei creaturae famulantur: Facis ipsum potestatem habere in opera manuum tuarum; omnia posuisti sub pedes ejus. Psal. 8: 7. coll. Hebr. 2: 8. 1. Cor. 15: 27. Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & terra. Matth. 28: 18. Non quod omnes ad regnum illud proprie pertineant; sed quod sine infinita illa potestate administrari nequeat.
units.tr: Likewise all things are made subject to this kingdom, and all creatures serve him: You have made him to have dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet. Ps. 8:7; cf. Heb. 2:8; 1 Cor. 15:27. All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Matt. 28:18. This does not mean that all things belong to that kingdom in the proper sense, but that it could not be administered without that boundless power.

units.la: XI. Subjecti ac vera hujus regni membra, sunt soli fideles, populus ille voluntarius, Psal. 110. qui non ex Judaeis solum, sed maximam partem ex gentibus constat. In Christo enim inane istud populorum discrimen sublatum est: estque Deus nunc omnibus idem & unus. Gal. 3: 20.
units.tr: XI. The true and proper members of this kingdom, its subjects, are the faithful alone, that willing people of Ps. 110, who consist not only of Jews but for the most part of the Gentiles. For in Christ that empty distinction between peoples has been removed, and God is now one and the same for all. Gal. 3:20.

units.la: XII. Administratio autem ejus hoc modo se habuit. Veteris Testamenti temporibus, cum iidem reipubl. Judaicæ ac Ecclesiæ fines essent, regnabat, etiam quoad externa, eo in populo proprie Deus; ac regimen illius θεοκρατίας quædam erat. Erat enim ibi terrenum ejus solium, omniaque ad principalis domus formam composita; erant & regni ministri, Levitæ ac sacerdotes, qui cærimoniis præsiderent, populoque jugum imponerent; qui cum majori quadam potestate instructi essent, Dei regnantis socii, & dii, ac veteris sæculi principes dicebantur, Psal. 45: 8. Psal. 82. 1. Cor. 8. &c. Unde cum Deus non proxime aut solus Ecclesiam istam cu- ræ videretur, vigente qualicunque isto hominum imperio ac dominatu, nondum plenè ibi erat regnum Dei. Quod demum sub N. T. manifestatum ac promulgatum fuit; ubi omne hominum in Ecclesia regimen sublatum est. Qui rerum status in Scripturis Novi T. Regnum cœlorum persæpe appellatur.
units.tr: XII. Its administration, moreover, has been as follows. In the times of the Old Testament, when the boundaries of the Jewish commonwealth and of the Church were the same, God himself reigned, even in external matters, over that people, and the government was in some sense a theocracy. For there was his earthly throne, and everything was arranged after the pattern of a royal household. There were also ministers of the kingdom, the Levites and priests, who presided over the ceremonies and laid the yoke upon the people.
