Since they were endowed with a certain greater authority, they were called companions of the reigning God, and gods, and princes of the old age: Ps. 45:8; Ps. 82; 1 Cor. 8, etc. Hence, since God did not seem to watch over that Church directly or alone while that kind of human rule and lordship was in force, the kingdom of God was not yet fully present there. This was at last made manifest and proclaimed under the New Testament, where all human government in the Church was abolished. This state of affairs is often called in the Scriptures of the New Testament the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: XIII. Præco regni illius, regisque jam adventantis præambulo suit Johannes Baptista. Lex enim ac prophetæ, ac omnino vetus ille Ecclesiæ status, usque ad Johannem duravit, Matth. 11: 13. cujus adventu fata in melius commutata sunt, ac Dei regnum, non sine motu, explicare sese cœpit. A diebus vero Johannis Baptistæ usque nunc regnum cœlorum vim patitur (vel vim facit) & vim facientes rapiunt illud. Matth. 11: 12.
units.tr: XIII. The herald of that kingdom, the forerunner of the King now approaching, was John the Baptist. For the law and the prophets, and indeed that whole old state of the Church, lasted until John. Matt. 11:13. With his coming the state of affairs was changed for the better, and the kingdom of God began to unfold itself, not without commotion. From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (or, makes violence), and the violent take it by force. Matt. 11:12.

units.la: XIV. Christus ipse, Rex Ecclesiæ, quanquam à nativitate Rex erat, dissimulatâ tamen plerunque majestate in terris egit: nisi quod miraculis & doctrina eam nonnunquam ostenderit. Verum tenuia erant illa initia. Postquam autem è morte revixit, ac in cœlum ascendit, tum demum publicè regem fassus est; atque inde potissimum regni ejus fasti originem sumunt. Hunc Jesum suscitavit Deus — Certo sciat ergo tota domus Israelis, quod Deus hunc fecerit Dominum & Christum &c. Act. 2: 32, 36. Et nunc glorifica me, tu, Pater, apud te, gloria, quam habui, priusquam mundus esset, apud te. Joh. 17: 5. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo, & in terra. Matth. 28: 18.
units.tr: XIV. Christ himself, the King of the Church, although he was King from his birth, nevertheless for the most part acted on earth with his majesty concealed; except that he sometimes displayed it by miracles and by his teaching. But those beginnings were humble. After he had risen from death and ascended into heaven, then at last he openly acknowledged himself King, and from that point the record of his kingdom chiefly takes its origin. This Jesus God raised up... Let all the house of Israel therefore know assuredly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, etc. Acts 2:32, 36. And now, O Father, glorify me with your own self, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. John 17:5. All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Matt. 28:18.

units.la: XV. Regia ejus functio duabus potissimum partibus constat, Ecclesiæ gubernatione & defensione.
units.tr: XV. His royal office consists chiefly of two parts: the government and defence of the Church.

units.la: XVI. Gubernat eam, tum verbi, tum Spiritus efficacia. Scipionem robustum tuum emissurus est Dominus Zione &c. Psal. 110: 2. Scepirum re-
units.tr: XVI. He governs it by the efficacy both of the Word and of the Spirit. The Lord shall send the rod of your strength out of Zion, etc. Ps. 110:2. The sceptre

units.la: Pars II. L stum lum est sceptrum regni tui. Psal. 45: 7. Et ego rogabo patrem, & alium advocatum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in saeculum, Spiritum veritatis, quem mundus accipere non potest. Joh. 14: 16, 17. Vos autem non estis in carne, sed in spiritu: siquidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Rom. 8: 9.
units.tr: of your kingdom is a right sceptre. Ps. 45:7. And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever, even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive. John 14:16, 17. But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Rom. 8:9.

units.la: XVII. Cumque nec hostes, nec certamina ipsi desint, non homines solum ac mundus hic, qui Christum regnantem plerunque dedignantur; sed praesertim intestina vitia, atque homo sibi ipsi parum concors; & daemonum denique vis ac furor, ac multiformes orci pestes; quae tum interno tumultu, tum externa vi ac terrore fideles quotidie infestant; ab omnibus illis tutos ac invictos suos Christus praestat. Ut frustra infernalis lupus ovile Domini circumgemat; cum aeternae pastoris nostri excubiae gregem suum ab ejus rabie defendant; nec ulla unquam ovicula interni raptoris praeda fiat. Simon, Simon, ecce Satanas appetit vos, quos ventilaret sicut triticum: sed ego deprecatus sum pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Luc. 22: 31, 32. Qui virtutis Dei praesidio custodimini per fidem, ad salutem paratam revelari.
units.tr: XVII. Since neither enemies nor conflicts are lacking, not only men and this world, which for the most part disdain Christ's reign, but especially inward vices, and man, who is little at peace with himself; and finally the power and fury of demons and the manifold plagues of hell, which assail the faithful every day both with inward tumult and with outward force and terror, Christ keeps his people safe and unconquered from all of these. So the infernal wolf roars round the Lord's fold in vain, since the eternal watchfulness of our Shepherd defends his flock from his rage, and no little sheep ever becomes the prey of the inward robber. Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not. Luke 22:31, 32. Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed

units.la: 1 Pet. 1: 5. Quis nos separabit a charitate Dei? num afflictio, num angustia, num persecutio, num fames?—imo in his omnibus amplius quam vincimus per eum qui dilexit nos. Nam mihi persuasum est, neque mortem, neque vitam, neque angelos, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque praesentia, neque futura, neque sublimitatem, neque profunditatem, neque ullam rem aliam creaturam posse nos separare a charitate Dei. Rom. 8: 34. &c.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1:5. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine?... Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God. Rom. 8:34, etc.

units.la: XVIII. A gubernatione fluit vocatio, resipiscentia, fides, nova obedientia; itemque dona illa extraordinaria, quae nascentis Ecclesiae originem illustrarunt, nunc autem constituta ea ac firmata, necessaria non sunt. A defensione ejus est fidelium perseverantia, crebrae Ecclesiae liberationes, hostium vel conversio, vel interitus, tandemque peracto certamine fidelium coronatio & glorificatio. Ut satis patet, non alium quam Christum, Deum, Ecclesiae caput ac regem esse posse, cum non alius ab illo munia ista explere possit; Papam autem, vel quicunque Christi vices subire, ac supremam in Christi populum auctoritatem sibi arrogare audet, esse Antichristum. Nam fundamentum aliud nemo potest statuere praeter id quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus, 1 Cor. 3: 11. con. Eph. 2: 20, 21.
units.tr: XVIII. From the government flow calling, repentance, faith and new obedience; and likewise those extraordinary gifts which illuminated the origin of the infant Church, but which are no longer necessary now that it is established and confirmed. From the defence of the Church come the perseverance of the faithful, the frequent deliverances of the Church, the conversion or destruction of its enemies, and at last, when the struggle of the faithful is finished, their crowning and glorification. As is quite plain, the head and king of the Church can be none other than Christ, God, since no other can perform these offices in his place; whereas he who dares to take the place of Christ, and to arrogate to himself supreme authority over Christ's people, the Pope, is Antichrist. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. 1 Cor. 3:11; cf. Eph. 2:20, 21.

units.la: XIX. Adjuncta regni hujus illud ab imperiis terrenis aperte distinguunt. Imperat enim Rex noster in ipsas animas hominum, iisque leges figere, ac poenas statuere potest. Ne timete vobis ab iis, qui
units.tr: XIX. The attributes of this kingdom clearly distinguish it from earthly empires. For our King rules over the very souls of men, and can impose laws upon them and fix penalties. Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul; but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

units.la: Adjuncta regni buqui trucidant corpus, animam autem non possunt trucidare: sed timete potius eum qui potest & animam & corpus perdere in gehenna. Matth. 10: 28. Nec solum externo ministerio virtutum praecepta docere, sed & per Spiritum suum eadem animis potenter insinuare novit: Hoc illud est foedus quod indam legem meam menti eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam eam. Jer. 31: 33. Dispensat praeterea absolutissima potestate vitam & mortem aeternam, ac ultra saeculi hujus cursum dominatu suo pervadit; & inferni carcerem ac coeli gaudia solo nutu, pro singulorum meritis, distribuit. Habeo claves inferorum & mortis. Apoc. 1: 18. Denique regnum ejus aeternum ac incorruptibile est. Temporibus regum iisdem suscitabit Deus caeli regnum, quod in saecula non destruetur. Dan. 2: 44.
units.tr: Matt. 10:28. He knows how to teach the precepts of virtue not only by external ministry, but also through his Spirit to instil the same powerfully into souls: This is the covenant that I will make... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts. Jer. 31:33. Moreover, with absolute power he dispenses life and eternal death, and extends his dominion beyond the course of this age; and by a mere nod he distributes the prison of hell and the joys of heaven, according to the merits of each. I have the keys of hell and of death. Rev. 1:18. Finally, his kingdom is eternal and incorruptible. In the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed. Dan. 2:44.

units.la: XX. Finem enim Christi regnum ignorat. Cum & Deus, & mediator, ac supremum Ecclesiae caput perpetuo mansurus, nec ab isto fastigio unquam descensurus, aut gloria sua carituras sit. Quae enim ex verbis Apostoli, 1. Cor. 15: 24, 25. nectitur difficultas, recto explicatu facile dissolvi potest.
units.tr: XX. Indeed, the kingdom of Christ knows no end, since he, both God and Mediator and the supreme Head of the Church, will remain for ever, and will never come down from that height or be deprived of his glory. As for the difficulty that is drawn from the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 15:24, 25, it can easily be resolved by a correct explanation.

units.la: De regno enim Christi in terris medios inter hostes, deque pugnis ac certaminibus ejus, eo loci Apostolus agit, ac finem eorum praedicit, deque Christi ac Ecclesiae victoriis loquitur. Atque hoc est quod ait, postea finis erit. praesentis enim regni faciem tantum mutandam toto contextu narrat. Ac simili modo Christus regnum Patri tradet, regnum videl. in terris gestum consummatum ac pacatum exhibendo, non in terra amplius, sed in coelo regnaturus. Nisi potius passive per regnum Christi ipsam ejus Ecclesiam, ex terris assertam & victricem, ac post longum exilium coelo redonatam, intelligas. Quod est eam Patri tradere, h. e. triumphantem coelo inducere, ac ante ora Patris sistere, gloriosam, Ecclesiam non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut quicquid talium, sed ut sit sancta & sine vitio, Eph 5: 27. Atque ita etiam filius subjicietur Patri, 1. 28. nempe in corpore suo mystico, ac in Ecclesia illa, cujus princeps & caput est: Ecce ego, & pueri mei, quos dedit mihi Jehova, Jes. 8: 18. coll. Hebr. 2: 13. Qui status praesentis finis regno gloriae initium ac auspicium dabit.
units.tr: Concerning the kingdom of Christ on earth, standing in the midst of enemies, and its battles and conflicts, the Apostle speaks in that place, foretells their end, and tells of the victories of Christ and the Church. This is what he means when he says then the end will come. For throughout the whole context he describes only a change in the form of the present kingdom. In a similar way Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father, presenting the kingdom carried on upon earth as brought to completion and pacified, and reigning no longer on earth but in heaven. Unless perhaps, passively, you understand by the kingdom of Christ the Church itself, asserted and victorious on earth and restored to heaven after a long exile. This is to hand her over to the Father, that is, to bring her into heaven in triumph and to present her before the face of the Father, glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish, Eph. 5:27. And thus also the Son will be subjected to the Father, v. 28, namely in his mystical body and in that Church of which he is the prince and head: Behold, I and the children whom Jehovah has given me, Isa. 8:18, compared with Heb. 2:13. This state will give the beginning and the auspices of the kingdom of glory, once the present end has come.

units.la: XXI. Componendi nunc cum hisce veniunt adversariorum, ac praecipue Socini de regno Christi errores, qui potissimum circa ini- tium, naturam, amplitudinem, ac denique durationem ejus versantur. Quos & alibi (praesertim ubi de filii divinitate) tactos, enu- merare tantum sufficiet. XXII. Ac regem quidem Christum recentem ac modernum tantum
units.tr: XXI. We now come to the errors of the adversaries, and especially of Socinus, concerning the kingdom of Christ, which chiefly concern its beginning, its nature, its extent, and finally its duration. It will be enough merely to list these, which have also been touched on elsewhere (especially where he treats of the divinity of the Son). XXII. And indeed they acknowledge Christ as king only as a recent and modern one

units.la: Ann illius datur finis?
units.tr: Is an end given to his [reign]?

units.la: Sociniano- rum errores circa regni Christi
units.tr: The errors of the Socinians concerning the beginning of Christ's kingdom.

units.la: initium, tantum faciunt, ex quo videl. devicta morte in cœlum ascenderit, ac triumphalia adeptus fuerit, juxta Matth. 28: 19. Data est mihi omnis potestas &c. Joh. 17: 5. Et nunc glorifica me, tu, Pater, apud te, gloria, quam habui, priusquam mundus esset, apud te. 1 Pet. 3: 22. Qui est in dextra Dei, ingressus in cœlum, ipsi subjectis angelis, & potestatibus, & potentiis: diversa regni ejus tempora, vel clariora, vel minus illustria, discernere non valentes. Sub Vet. enim Test. prophetas regnasse nolunt; & si qua regni Messiæ ibi mentio, id de regno tantum aliquo terreno à piis tum intelligi potuisse asserunt.
units.tr: They make his reign begin only from the point when, having overcome death, he ascended into heaven and obtained his triumphal dignity, according to Matt. 28:18, All power is given to me, etc.; John 17:5, And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was; 1 Pet. 3:22, who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him. They are unable to distinguish the different periods of his reign, some more clear and some less illustrious. Under the Old Testament they will not allow that the prophets reigned; and if there is any mention of the reign of the Messiah there, they assert that the pious could then have understood it only of some earthly kingdom.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Naturam deinde regni ejus talem tradunt, ut illud Patri subordinatum, atque ab eo dependens sit; utpote ab eo donatum. Patrem enim in Vet. Test. solum regnasse, in Novo autem Test. Christum socium ac collegam adscivisse, divisumque cum eo imperium possidere; ac, servato sibi reliquo mundo, Ecclesiam potissimum ipsi regnandam tradidisse, docent. Quanquam illud quoad exercitium rursus absolutum & independens faciant. Quæ pugnantia sunt.
units.tr: Next they teach that the nature of his reign is such that it is subordinate to the Father and dependent on him, as given by him. They teach that the Father alone reigned under the Old Testament, but that under the New Testament he took Christ as his partner and colleague and possessed the rule divided with him; and that, keeping the rest of the world for himself, he handed over the Church chiefly to be ruled by him. Yet on the question of its exercise they again make it absolute and independent. These things are contradictory.

units.la: XXIV. De amplitudine regni ejus ita philosophantur: Ecclesia finibus imperium ejus contineri; circa res autem alias non aliter quam in quantum Ecclesiæ usus postulat versari: naturale autem Christi regnum in cœlum ac terram abnegant, solique illud patri creatori ac conservatori tribuunt. Ac Dominum quidem angelorum quoque eum fatentur, sed post exaltationem demum dominum factum. Quando & in diabolos potestatem acceperit, ad eos nunc quidem sceptro suo coërcendos, extremo autem fine abolendos. Et quid de animabus piorum atque impiorum statuant notum est. Ut in angustum exeant quæ alioquin tam magnificè de Christi regno, independente & absoluto, jactant. XXV. Denique, ut Christum regem nuper factum asserunt, ita eundem regem πρόεκαυρον & ἐφήμερον facere non dubitant. Ut enim illum post quatuor annorum millia sub N. T. demum regnare coepisse ajunt, ita die novissimo regnum abdicaturum, ac de rege subjectum ac privatum rursus futurum docent. Cum autem nunc in multis augustiis Ecclesiam regat, ac extremo demum mundi actu, in celebri illo humani generis comitio ac judicio, sese verè regem ac Ecclesiæ vindicem præstiturus sit, hostibus ejus refuscitis publicè damnatis, ac una cum diabolis æternum perire sive annihilari jussis, revera unicum tantum diem plenissime Christum regnaturum ferunt. Quod manifestè verbis angeli repugnat,
units.tr: XXIV. On the extent of his kingdom they reason thus: his rule is confined to the bounds of the Church, and he is concerned with other things only so far as the needs of the Church require. But they deny that Christ's natural kingdom extends over heaven and earth, and they ascribe it solely to the Father, the creator and preserver. They do confess that he is also Lord of the angels, but say that he became Lord only after his exaltation. They ask when he received power over the devils, to restrain them now with his sceptre and at the last to destroy them. And what they decide about the souls of the pious and the impious is well known. So what they boast so magnificently about the reign of Christ, independent and absolute, shrinks into a narrow compass. XXV. Finally, just as they assert that Christ became king only recently, so they do not hesitate to make the same king temporary [πρόεκαυρον] and ephemeral [ἐφήμερον]. For just as they say he began to reign under the New Testament only after four thousand years, so they teach that on the last day he will lay down the kingdom and will again become a subject and a private person. But since he now rules the Church in many straits, and at the last act of the world, in that famous assembly and judgment of the human race, he will show himself truly king and avenger of his Church, with his enemies brought back and publicly condemned and ordered to perish eternally or be annihilated together with the devils, they in fact maintain that Christ will reign fully for one day only. This plainly contradicts the words of the angel,

units.la: Luc. 1:33. Et regnabit in domum Jacobi in saecula, & regni ejus non erit finis.
units.tr: Luke 1:33, And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: De Christi obedientia.
units.tr: On the obedience of Christ.

units.la: I. Ita autem Christi publica laborum, calamitatum ac miseriarum plena fuit. Tunc dicit ei Jesus, vulpes habent foveas, & volucres caeli nidos, filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet, Matth. 8:20. Quanquam ignominia & mendicitas abluerint, quam non pie satis mendicantium familiae in papatu Christo adscribunt.
units.tr: I. Such was the public life of Christ, full of labours, calamities and miseries. Then Jesus said to him, Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head, Matt. 8:20. Although disgrace and beggary have washed away the stain that the families of mendicants in Papistry do not piously enough ascribe to Christ.

units.la: II. Utque ad hominum praecipue calamitates mollis & tener erat, ita intimo earum sensu tactus illacrymasse iis saepenumero legitur: I. ad sepulchrum Lazari, Joh. 11. 2. super Judaicae gentis excidio, quod jam tum praevidebat ac praedicebat, Luc. 19. 3. denique super universo genere humano. Qui in diebus carnis petitiones & supplicationes – cum clamore valido & lacrymis obsulit. Hebr. 5:7.
units.tr: II. Just as he was especially gentle and tender towards human calamities, so we read that he often wept, moved by a deep sense of them: (1) at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11; (2) over the destruction of the Jewish nation, which he already foresaw and foretold, Luke 19; (3) and finally over the whole human race. Who, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, Heb. 5:7.

units.la: III. Eminuit vero in vita ejus obedientia illa perfectissima. Unde Paulus Phil. 2:7. Cum dixisset, cum formam servi accepisset, addit com. 8. quod semet ipsum submiserit, factum obedientem, &c. Sicut & inde per avrotouaciav servus Jehova appellatur, Esai. 42:1, 19.43: 10.49:3, 5.52:13.53:11.
units.tr: III. Moreover, that most perfect obedience stood out in his life. Hence Paul, Phil. 2:7, after saying that he took the form of a servant, adds in verse 8 that he humbled himself and became obedient, etc. For this reason too he is called the servant of Jehovah, by obedience [ὑπακοήν], Isa. 42:1, 19; 43:10; 49:3, 5; 52:13; 53:11.

units.la: IV. Dupliciter autem eam debuit, tum qua homo & creatura, quae Deo subjecta esse necessario debebat, a quo nexu ne nunc quidem in gloria solutus est; tum qua sponsor (licet ordine naturae sponsio praecesserit, ex qua assumtio naturae humanae profluxit) quatenus legi se ultro subjecit, & peragendae salutis nostrae certum obedientiae curriculum implevit. Qui appellantur dies carnis ejus. Heb. 5:7,8. De quo vide lib. 2. cap. 15. §. 8, 9.
units.tr: IV. He owed this obedience in two respects: first as a man and a creature, who was necessarily bound to be subject to God, a bond from which he was not released even now in glory; and secondly as surety (although in the order of nature the suretyship preceded, from which the assumption of human nature flowed), inasmuch as he voluntarily placed himself under the law and fulfilled the sure course of obedience needed to accomplish our salvation. These are called the days of his flesh, Heb. 5:7, 8. On this see book 2, chapter 15, §§ 8, 9.

units.la: V. Cum enim ϑεάνθρωπος foret, ac sine ullo certamine ac mora beatitudine potiri posset, ad illud obedientiae curriculum, legisque postulatum, pro sese quidem non tenebatur; neque hoc pacto sub lege erat. Postquam autem ex sponsione hominem induerat, jamque humano generi in summam miseriam lapso succurrere poterat, amor certe ille immensus, ac charitatis ardor, quo proximum suum, Deique gloriam adamabat & quaerebat, ipsum ad mediatorium munus capessendum, & perfectam illam obedientiam praestandam urgere non cessabat.
units.tr: V. For although he was the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], and could have obtained blessedness without any struggle or delay, he was not bound to that course of obedience and the demand of the law on his own account; nor was he under the law in this way. But after he had put on man by the suretyship, and could now help the human race fallen into the greatest misery, that immense love and burning charity by which he loved and sought his neighbour and the glory of God did not cease to urge him to undertake the mediatorial office and to render that perfect obedience.

units.la: VI. Qui eo major ac admirabilior fuit, quod ex tanto fastigio (Θεάνθρωπ@ quippe jamque filius & hæres omnium, ab ipso assumtæ carnis initio erat) descendere, & gloriam suam humani generis necessitatibus posthabere, jamque parata beatitudine ad tempus carere, atque infimas demque calamitates & crucem ipsam perpeti maluit; ut eam tanquam operæ impensæ præmium & mercedem acquirere, hominemque servare, eorumque caput & ad salutem dux fieri posset.
units.tr: VI. This was all the greater and more admirable because he chose to descend from such a height (for he was already the God-man, the Son and heir of all things, from the very beginning of the assumed flesh), to set his own glory behind the needs of the human race, to forgo for a time the blessedness that was ready for him, and to endure the lowest depths of misery and the cross itself; so that he might acquire it as the reward and wage of the work undertaken, save man, and become their head and leader to salvation.

units.la: VII. Perfectissima autem fuit hæc ejus obedientia, tum sanctitate animæ habituali, tum actuali ejusdem præstatione, & divinæ legis obsequio; denique constanti & ad finem usque currente perseverantia, constans. Hæc enim requirebantur ad διαίωμα legis implendum, quæ justitiam non habitibus solum, sed præcipuè actibus circumscriberat ac definierat.
units.tr: VII. This obedience of his was most perfect, both in the habitual holiness of his soul and in its actual performance, and in obedience to the divine law; and finally in a constant perseverance running to the end. For these were required for fulfilling the requirement of the law [δικαίωμα], which defined righteousness not only by habits but chiefly by acts.

units.la: VIII. Nec dirimenda obedientia ejus activa ac passiva. Utramque enim nostro nomine debuit; tum vitæ tum mortis obedientiam. Ac in passionibus obedientia ejus vel maxime sese exeruit; ac charitas præcipuè emicuit, tum vel maxime circa hominum salutem laborans & operans, tantoque experimento rursus consummata.
units.tr: VIII. His active and passive obedience must not be separated. For he owed both in our name: the obedience of life and the obedience of death. And his obedience showed itself most of all in his sufferings; and his charity shone forth chiefly there, labouring and working most of all for the salvation of men, and was thus again perfected by so great a proof.

units.la: IX. Quam ipsius obedientiam ut perimit Durandi blasphemia, qui Christum peccare ac damnari potuisse non fine flagitio docuit: ita non parum lædunt eam Remonstrantes, dum eundem mandatum munus sine crimine deponere potuisse asserunt. Quæ quantopere Dei fœderi ac testamento, Christi sponsioni, ac denique fidelium spei ac fiduciæ adversentur, lib. 2. cap. 15. §. 16, 17. vidimus.
units.tr: IX. The blasphemy of Durandus, who taught that Christ could have sinned and been damned, and not without disgrace, destroys this obedience; the Remonstrants also do it no little harm while they assert that he could lay down his assigned office without sin. We have seen in book 2, chapter 15, §§ 16, 17, how greatly these views oppose God's covenant and testament, Christ's suretyship, and finally the hope and trust of believers.

units.la: X. Ita ergò non solum officiis omnibus legis naturalis seu dilectionis, cui omnis homo subjectus est, defungi voluit, verum etiam majoris humiliationis & subjectionis servilis testandæ ergo, legibus Dei positivis propter peccatum impositis illudque commemorantibus, se submisit; ut hac ratione se peccata nostra in se suscepisse testatum faceret. Hinc circumcidi se passus est, Luc. 2: 21, (ut in ipso nobis obsignaretur consummata circumcisio, Col. 2: 11.) oblationemque pro se, tanquam immundo, offerri, com. 22, 24. Ita etiam aliis legibus ceremonialibus se subjecit; Paschatis festum celebrando, Luc. 2: 42, 43. & Hierosolymam circa tempora festiva adscendendo; quod passim historia Euangelica testatur. Ipse tamen non obtulit victimas, nec pro ipso illæ unquam nominatim oblatæ leguntur. Civem reipublicæ istius se etiam professus est, ut vel ex didrachmi persolutione patet, Matth. 17:24. & seqq. Nec minus sacramentis N. T. initiatus est: baptizatus, Matth. 3:16. 17. & S. Cœnæ æque, ut videtur, conviva, quam ejus auctor, Matth. 26:29. Ita nimirum omnem justitiam implens. Matth. 3:15. Quin non Deo solum minor est factus. Joh. 1:28 sed & diis reliquis ac Ecclesiæ istius dominis, h. e. angelis reliquisque potestatem habentibus, & veteris populi tutoribus. Ita minor pauxillo per factus est angelis, Hebr. 2:7. subjectus nimirum legi, angelorum ministerio latæ, iisque vindicibus munitæ, Act. 7:55. & servus factus potestatem habentium, Esai. 49:7. Ne jam dicam de obedientiæ ejus colophone, quem superaddit tandem Apostolus Phil. 2:8. Factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Per quam mortem servitus ipsius finita est; de quo suo loco.
units.tr: X. Therefore he wished not only to discharge all the duties of the natural law, or of love, to which every man is subject, but also, to bear witness to a greater humiliation and servile subjection, he submitted himself to the positive laws of God imposed on account of sin, and to those that recall it; so that in this way he might show that he had taken our sins upon himself. Hence he allowed himself to be circumcised, Luke 2:21 (so that in him the perfect circumcision might be sealed to us, Col. 2:11), and an offering was made for him, as for one unclean, in verses 22 and 24. So too he submitted himself to other ceremonial laws: by keeping the feast of the Passover, Luke 2:42, 43, and by going up to Jerusalem at the festival times, as the Gospel history attests everywhere. Yet he did not offer sacrifices himself, and no victims are ever read of as offered for him by name. He also professed himself a citizen of that commonwealth, as is clear even from the payment of the didrachma, Matt. 17:24 ff. Nor was he less initiated into the sacraments of the New Testament: he was baptized, Matt. 3:16, 17, and was equally, as it seems, a guest at the Lord's Supper, though its author, Matt. 26:29. Thus, of course, fulfilling all righteousness, Matt. 3:15. Nor did he become less only than God, John 1:28, but also than the other lords of this Church, that is, the angels and others who held power, and the guardians of the old people. So he was made a little lower than the angels, Heb. 2:7, being of course subject to the law given through the ministry of angels, and guarded by their avengers, Acts 7:55; and made a servant of those who have power, Isa. 49:7. I need not say more of the crown of his obedience, which the Apostle finally adds, Phil. 2:8: becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. By that death his servitude was ended; of which in its own place.

units.la: XI. Quæri hic solet de obedientiæ Christi spatio ac curriculo, quot annos in publico ministerio egerit? Quos certo definire non licet. Probabilissimus vero calculus est, qui a numero paschatum, quorum in historia Christi mentio est, desumitur. Quæ alii quatuor, nonnulli quinque numerant. Quatuor colligunt ex locis, Joh. 2:13, 14. cum purgaret templum; & c. 5:1. cum sanaret paralyticum circa piscinam: coll. cum c. 4:35. Nonne vos dicitis, adhuc quatuor menses sunt, & messis veniet? & c. 6:4, 9, 19. cum turbam miraculose pasceret: denique Σαναέρ ejus pascha occurrit Matth. 21:12. cum rursus purgaret templum. Hisce quatuor autem quidam quintum, ex Luc. 6:1. superadduntt, ubi mentio fit. Cum vero hic ipse numerus non prorsus certus sit, ut in re non omnino liquida, rectius alii sibi statuere videntur, Christum anno 30 incunte ministerium incepisse, Luc. 3:23. ac anno 33. decurrente absolvisse. Ut omne id spatium vitæ publicæ trium annorum ac dimidii sit. Quo alludi putant Luc. 13:7. Ecce tres anos venio, quærens fructum in ficu hac, & non invenio, exscinde eam. Cum vero duo duntaxat Paschata Christi à baptismo ejus exacta adstrui solide possint; rectius statuisse videntur veterum illi, qui multo contractius illud ministerii Christi publici curriculum ponendum esse crediderunt.
units.tr: XI. Here it is usually asked about the span and course of Christ's obedience: how many years did he spend in his public ministry? These cannot be fixed with certainty. The most probable reckoning, however, is taken from the number of Passovers mentioned in the history of Christ. Others count four, and some five. Those who count four gather them from John 2:13, 14, when he cleansed the temple; and ch. 5:1, when he healed the paralytic by the pool; together with ch. 4:35, Do you not say, There are yet four months, and the harvest comes?; and ch. 6:4, 9, 19, when he miraculously fed the crowd; and finally his Passover occurs in Matt. 21:12, when he again cleansed the temple. To these four some add a fifth, from Luke 6:1, where a feast is mentioned. But since this very number is not wholly certain, being a matter not entirely clear, others seem to hold more rightly that Christ began his ministry in the year 30, Luke 3:23, and finished it in the course of the year 33. So that the whole span of his public life is three and a half years. It is thought that Luke 13:7 alludes to this: Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none; cut it down. But since only two Passovers after his baptism can be solidly established, the ancient writers who believed that the course of Christ's public ministry should be placed much more narrowly seem to have judged more rightly.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS QUINTUS DE HUMILIATIONE CHRISTI.
units.tr: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS QUINTUS DE HUMILIATIONE CHRISTI.

units.la: CAPUT XVII. De Christi Passionibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. On the Sufferings of Christ.

units.la: {a}DUplici quasi facie, duplicique gradu, circa hæc probe notando, contemplandum nobis se objicit status humiliationis Christi. Quorum alter gradus dicitur κένωσις seu exinanitio & evacuatio, qui constitit in incarnatione, & forma servi accepta; quem hactenus explicatum dedimus. Restat alter gradus expediendus, ταπείνωσις dicta, quæ exinanitæ jam deitatis, totiusque personæ quædam fuit depressio; quando velut radix è terra, in passionibus & morte sua fuit conculcatus. Fundus hujus distinctionis est ad Phil. 2:7, 8. Semetipsum ἐκένωσε exinanivit, assumens formam servi — & ἐταπείνωσε humiliavit, dum se præstitit obedientem usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis.
units.tr: {a}The state of Christ's humiliation presents itself to us for contemplation in a twofold aspect and at two stages, which we must carefully note. The one stage is called kenosis [κένωσις], that is, emptying and self-abasement, which consisted in the incarnation and in taking the form of a servant; we have explained this above. The other stage remains to be expounded, called tapeinosis [ταπείνωσις], which was a kind of lowering of the already emptied deity and of the whole person; when, like a root out of the earth, he was trampled underfoot in his sufferings and death. The basis of this distinction is Phil. 2:7, 8: he emptied [ἐκένωσε] himself, taking the form of a servant, and he humbled [ἐταπείνωσε] himself, becoming obedient even unto death, the death of the cross.

units.la: {b}II. Passionum nomine veniunt hic omnia ea, quæ Christus, præter naturalem voluntatis suæ propensionem propter peccata nostra tulit. Nam ea demum est passio, quæ invito homini accidit, & naturali corporis constitutioni, indeque ortæ mentis proclivitati contraria est: non tamen hæc tollunt, quin sponte quis patiatur; atque ita Christus, ipse lubens se invitum vicit, atque illam naturæ imbecillitatem, prolixa in homines voluntate superavit; ut zelus domus Dei ipsum, hoc modo etiam devoraverit. Joh. 2:17. Siquidem pro propositio ipsi præmio, sustinuit crucem, Hebr. 12:2. & sic quidem, ut nemo vitam tollat ab ipso, sed ipse ponat eam à se ipso. Joh. 10:19. Ita memoratur labor animæ ejus Esai. 53:11. quo scilicet se ipsam etiam expugnavit, & se ipsam effudit in mortem. com. 12. conf. Joh. 21:18. Quum senueris extendes manus tuas, & alius te cinget, & feret quò non vis. Item Joh. 10:11. Gal. 2:10.
units.tr: {b}II. Under the name of sufferings are included here all those things which Christ endured, apart from his natural inclination of will, on account of our sins. For suffering properly is that which happens to a man against his will and is contrary to the natural constitution of the body and the resulting disposition of the mind. Yet these things do not prevent a person from suffering voluntarily; and so Christ, gladly and of his own accord, overcame his unwillingness and that weakness of nature by his abundant love towards men, so that the zeal of God's house consumed him in this way too (John 2:17). For he endured the cross for the joy set before him (Heb. 12:2), and so indeed that no one takes his life from him, but he lays it down of himself (John 10:18). Thus the travail of his soul is recorded (Isa. 53:11), by which he indeed overcame even his own soul and poured out himself unto death. Cf. comm. 12, and compare John 21:18: "When you are old you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go." Likewise John 10:11; Gal. 2:10.

units.la: III. Strictiori autem significatu, illæ appellantur passiones, quas Christus proximis duabus ante mortem diebus perpessus est. Nihilominus tamen ad eas referuntur, omnes infirmitates, contumeliæ, passiones & dolores, quos ab inde exordio vitæ tulit; quæ ipsi in pœnam irrogata fuisse, vel hinc conficitur, quod nostri causa pauperem factum fuisse docet Paulus 2 Cor. 8:9. ex qua paupertate, simili ratione, de reliquis etiam malis ejus putare debemus. IV. Harum rerum non ignaros fuisse veteres luculenter testatur Petrus 1. Epist. 1:11 1. utpote quibus testificatus fuerit Spiritus, passionem Christi, non unam & singularem, sed παθήματα, numero plura. Sicut inde etiam tam celebres sunt apud Judaeos Messiae dolores, חבלי המשיח. Vide Act. 26:23.
units.tr: III. In a stricter sense, however, those are called sufferings which Christ endured during the last two days before his death. Nevertheless, all the infirmities, reproaches, afflictions and pains which he bore from the beginning of his life are also included, which were inflicted upon him as punishment; this is clear from the fact that Paul teaches that he became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8:9), and from this poverty we ought to think, in a similar way, of his other evils too. IV. That the ancients were not unaware of these things is clearly attested by Peter, 1 Pet. 1:11, since the Spirit had testified to them that the sufferings of Christ were not one single suffering, but were [παθήματα] sufferings, plural in number. Hence the "pangs of the Messiah" [חבלי המשיח] are also so famous among the Jews. See Acts 26:23.

units.la: V. Passionum harum subjectum, pro vario considerandi modo, distinguitur vulgo vel subjectum quod, vel quo. Illud est persona Christi; hoc humana ejus natura. Passa quidem tota est persona, at passa tantum in carne. 1. Pet. 4:1. Hebr. 5:7,8. Quae caro non corpus solum notat, sed & animam; ut utriusque fuerint passiones, aeque iterum vel in genere damni, vel in genere sensus. de quibus consulendi auctores. Corporis vero passiones non ita dicimus, ac si corpus ipsum etiam doleret, aut sentiret, quod menti proprium est; sed dolor corporis ille vocatur, quem anima percipit, ex turbato & male affecto corpore; vel qui, per corpus, tanquam per instrumentum animae sufficitur, aut cujus occasionem per sensus exteriores praebet: quibus omnibus Christus obnoxius fuit. Dolor autem animae est, quem citra laesionem corporis aut occasionem per illud exhibitam proxime in anima sustinuit. De quibus doloribus generalius agit Paulus Hebr. 5:7. Qui in diebus carnis petitiones & supplicationes ad eum, qui poterat eum salvum facere ex morte, cum clamore valido & lacrymis offerens, est exauditus a metu. Specialius autem eos exprimunt Evangelistae, Matth. 26:37,38,39,42,44. Luc. 22:43,44.
units.tr: V. The subject of these sufferings, according to the different ways of considering them, is commonly distinguished as either the subject which or the subject by which. The former is the person of Christ; the latter is his human nature. The whole person indeed suffered, but only in the flesh (1 Pet. 4:1; Heb. 5:7, 8). This flesh denotes not only the body but also the soul; so that there were sufferings of both, again either in the kind of loss or in the kind of sense, on which matters the authors should be consulted. We do not, however, speak of the sufferings of the body as if the body itself grieved or perceived, which is proper to the mind; rather, that is called pain of the body which the soul perceives from a disturbed and ill-affected body, or which is conveyed through the body as an instrument of the soul, or which the outer senses occasion. Christ was subject to all of these. But pain of the soul is that which he endured immediately in the soul, without any injury to the body or occasion given through it. Paul treats of these pains more generally in Heb. 5:7: "who, in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, was heard because of his fear." The Evangelists, however, express them more specifically: Matt. 26:37, 38, 39, 42, 44; Luke 22:43, 44.

units.la: VI. Alienum igitur a veritate statuunt Pontificii, quasi satis fuissent dolores corporis, nec anima Christi pati debuisset: contrarium enim evincunt loca Esai. 53:10. Ubi posuit satisfactionis pretium, subjectum, anima ejus videbit semen. Luc. 22:41,44. Matth. 27:46. Deus mi, Deus mi, cur me deseruisti? vid: 1. Cor. 6:20. Insulse etiam iidem cum Thoma excipiunt, dolores illos tantum fuisse in parte animae inferiori, aut ex sympathia ejus cum corpore: commentitia enim est isthaec animae divisio, cum eadem anima indivisa sentiat atque intelligat. Tum etiam ipse in se ipso, non ex sympathia tantum, maledictionem tanquam sponsor noster substulit Christus, factus pro nobis execratio. Gal. 3:13.
units.tr: VI. The Papists, therefore, wrongly maintain, as if the sufferings of the body had been enough and the soul of Christ ought not to have suffered; for the passages Isa. 53:10 prove the contrary: "When he has made his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed." See also Luke 22:41, 44; Matt. 27:46: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Compare 1 Cor. 6:20. The same men foolishly add, with Thomas, that those pains were only in the lower part of the soul, or arose from its sympathy with the body; for that division of the soul is a fiction, since the one undivided soul both feels and understands. Moreover, Christ himself, as our surety, bore the curse not merely through sympathy but in himself, "made a curse for us" (Gal. 3:13).

units.la: VII. Ingens fuit harum perpessionum cumulus: In eo enim quod divertitas passus est ipse quum tentaretur, potest iis qui tentantur, auxiliari. Hebr. 2:18. Tentatus per omnia ad similitudinem absque peccato. Hebr. 4:15. Tentationes enim ipsi tum ab hominibus, tum a diabolo, tum etiam a Deo Patre suo obvenerunt. Quid ab hominibus sustinuerit
units.tr: VII. The accumulation of these sufferings was great: "For in that he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted" (Heb. 2:18); "tempted in all things like as we are, yet without sin" (Heb. 4:15). For he was assailed by temptations from men, from the devil, and also from God his Father. What he endured from men has been considered in general terms.

units.la: Illarum in genere con-fideratarum notum est. Concertationem cum diabolo tentationesque ejus, juxta primævum oraculum Gen. 3: 15. sibi imminentes ipse indicavit Joh. 14: 30. Venit princeps hujus mundi & in me non habet quicquam. Quo etiam respexisse videtur Luc. 22: 53. Hæc est hora illa vestra & potestas tenebrarum. Denique à Deo se derelictum in cruce pendens conquestus est Matth. 27: 46.
units.tr: The conflict with the devil and his temptations, which were threatened against him according to the primal oracle (Gen. 3:15), he himself pointed out (John 14:30): "The prince of this world comes, and he has nothing in me." He seems also to have had this in mind in Luke 22:53: "This is your hour, and the power of darkness." Finally, hanging on the cross, he complained that he had been forsaken by God (Matt. 27:46).

units.la: VIII. Tenenda hic sunt duo, 1. Passionem hanc Christi, licet poenarum nostrarum vim omnem quoad intensionem quasi exhauserit, non tamen æternitatem earum tulisse: temporis enim infinitatem, infinita personæ dignitas recompensavit; in cujus persona omnigena subjectione tam in vita, quam in morte, qua sese Patri subjecerat, satis luculenter apparuit ira Dei adversus peccatum; atque integer honos independentiæ Deo amplissime restitutus est, quem nostra illi ereptum iverat inobedientia: quare non eadem Christi ac nostri erat ratio, qua æterna nobis poena subeunda erat, quod honorem illum Deo nunquam restituere liceret.
units.tr: VIII. Two points must be held here. 1. Although this suffering of Christ, as far as its intensity goes, seems to have exhausted all the force of our punishments, it did not bear their eternity; for the infinite dignity of the person compensated for the infinity of time. In his person, by his complete subjection both in life and in death, by which he had submitted himself to the Father, the wrath of God against sin appeared quite clearly, and the full honour of independence, which our disobedience had taken away from God, was restored to him most abundantly. Hence Christ's case was not the same as ours, for we had to undergo eternal punishment, because we could never restore that honour to God.

units.la: IX. 2. Nec minori etiam cum jure, omni peccati culpa absolvendus est Christus, in omnibus suis passionibus; nam licet peccatum sæpe peccati poena sit, ipsaque poena peccatum pariat, non tamen ad essentiam poenæ pertinet; sed adjunctum quoddam est in peccatoribus, illis accidens; ideoque illud in Christo usu venire non potuit. Nihil enim erat in illo, quod ingruente quasi poenarum vento turbari posset. Ut nullus omnino blasphemiæ locus fuerit in Christo; qui Deum dilexit vel in media poena, lubensque eam subiit. Joh. 14: 31. Ut cognoscat mundus, quod diligam Patrem, & quemadmodum præcepit mihi Pater, ita faciam. Remotissimus etiam suit ab omni murmure & desperatione: non enim damnatorum, sed damnandorum poenas sustulit: quin nec ipsa hæc mala, proprie ad poenas infernales spectant, quarum auctor est Deus; sed tantum iis accidunt in homine damnato; à Christo vero alienissima fuerunt. Matth. 26: 39. Pater mi, si possibile est, transeat à me poculum hoc; sed non ut ego volo, sed ut tu. Act. 2: 24. Quem Deus resuscitavit, quum solvisset dolores mortis, sicut non erat possibile, ut ipse ab illa teneretur. Joh. 2: 19. Matth. 20: 18, 19.
units.tr: IX. 2. With equal right Christ must be acquitted of all guilt of sin in all his sufferings. For although sin is often the punishment of sin, and punishment itself produces sin, it does not belong to the essence of punishment; rather, it is an accompaniment, an accident in sinners, and therefore it could not occur in Christ. For there was nothing in him which could be disturbed by the storm, as it were, of punishments bearing down upon him. So there was no place at all for blasphemy in Christ, who loved God even in the midst of punishment and gladly underwent it (John 14:31): "That the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do." He was also most remote from all murmuring and despair; for he took away not the punishments of the damned, but of those who were to be damned. Indeed, these evils themselves do not properly pertain to the punishments of hell, whose author is God; they fall only upon the damned man, and they were utterly alien to Christ. Matt. 26:39: "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will." Acts 2:24: "Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it." John 2:19; Matt. 20:18, 19.

units.la: X. Insignis igitur Pontificiorum diabolismus est, nostros, & præcipue Calvinum, hujus tam fœdæ blasphemiæ accusare; ac si Christum desperasse diceret; quo nihil salsius est, cum, objectionem ex adversariorum sententia fingens, Christo tantum desperationis vocem tribuat, id est, qualem homines ferme ex desperatione edere solent; non vero qualis ipsius Christi revera fuit ut ipse hoc propius explicat. Vide eum in Harm. & Instit. l. II. c. 16. §. 12. Nihilo æquius ex ejus verbis conficiunt Christum cruciatus damnati hominis pertulisse; cum solummodo eas tulisse velit, quibus obnoxius fuisset homo damnatus; & speciatim damnationem pro condemnatione intelligat.
units.tr: X. It is therefore a remarkable piece of Papist diabolism to accuse our writers, and Calvin above all, of this foul blasphemy, as if he said that Christ despaired. Nothing is more absurd. In framing an objection from the opponents' view, he attributes to Christ only the voice of despair, that is, the kind men usually utter out of despair, and not what Christ's own state truly was, as he himself explains more closely. See him in the Harmony and the Institutes, book 2, chapter 16, §12. Nothing is more unfair than their inference from his words that Christ suffered the torments of a damned man, since he only wishes him to have borne those to which a damned man would be liable, and he understands "damnation" specifically as "condemnation."

units.la: XI. Atque ita delibavimus quædam quæ huc pertinent, nunc ipsam porro aggrediamur passionem; cujus partes præcipuæ tres sunt. 1. mortis antecedanea. II. mors ipsa. III. mortem consequentia.
units.tr: XI. Having thus touched on some matters relevant here, let us now take up the passion itself, whose principal parts are three: I. the things preceding death; II. death itself; III. the things following death.

units.la: XII. Antecedanea mortis fuerunt vel in horto; vel in ipsa crucifixione, eique adjunctis malis & circumstantiis. In horto fuit 1. ipsa agonia. 2. effectus ejus; tum in sudore sanguineo; tum in vehementissima deprecatione. Est quidem proprie agonia, vitæ mortifque confinium & inter utramque quasi certamen; hic vero notat, certamen Christi cum extremis doloribus & animi angoribus ex tentationibus Satanæ, aliisque causis, mox dicendis, atque inde natum horrorem: tum in genere damni, tum sensus, ut loquuntur: caruit enim gaudio, quippe divinam gratiam, tot doloribus stupefactus, sentire non poterat; lethalis quoque tristitia animum ejus assecit. Math. 26: 37, 38. Incipiebat contristari & angi – valde tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Joh. 12:27. Nunc anima mea turbata est Luc. 22:44. Et constitutus in agone intentius orabat. Erat autem sudor ejus &c.
units.tr: XII. The things preceding death took place either in the garden or in the crucifixion itself, with the evils and circumstances attached to it. In the garden there was 1. the agony itself, and 2. its effects, both the bloody sweat and the most vehement entreaty. Agony properly is the border between life and death, a kind of contest between the two. Here, however, it denotes Christ's struggle with extreme pains and anguish of spirit, arising from Satan's temptations and other causes to be mentioned shortly, and the horror born of these, both as to the nature of the loss and as to what they call sense. For he lacked joy, since, stupefied by so many pains, he could not perceive the divine grace; a deadly sadness also affected his soul. Matt. 26:37, 38. He began to be sorrowful and troubled ... my soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death. John 12:27. Now my soul is troubled. Luke 22:44. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat was ...

units.la: XIII. Hujus quidem horroris causa fuit, non metus naturalis mortis, sic enim infirmior esset Christus multis martyribus; verum tentationes Satanæ. Tu conteres ipsum quoad calcem. Gen. 3:15. quibus procul dubio accesserunt, sensus iræ divinæ, & συμπάθεια cum Ecclesiæ suorumque tentationibus & malis. Quare mors ejus alterius omnino generis fuit, ac mors martyrum, conjuncta quippe cum sensu judicii divini & aculeo peccati. 1. Cor. 15:56. Stimulus autem mortis, peccatum: vis autem peccati lex.
units.tr: XIII. The cause of this horror was indeed not the natural fear of death, for then Christ would be weaker than many martyrs; it was the temptations of Satan. You shall bruise his heel. Gen. 3:15. To these were undoubtedly added the sense of divine wrath and sympathy [sympatheia] with the temptations and evils of the Church and of his own people. Hence his death was of an altogether different kind from the death of the martyrs, being joined with a sense of divine judgment and the sting of sin. 1 Cor. 15:56. The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law.

units.la: XIV. Significatum hoc fuit per calicem illum, qui Christo oblatus fuit; hoc velut emblemate exprimente genus loquendi inter illas gentes de doloribus perferendis frequentatum. Perverse hunc calicem Smalcius refert ad angorem illum animi & corporis antequam caperetur; ac si tantum constitisset in illo metu mortis jam imminentis; pariter ut Episcopius ἀγωνιᾷ illam Christi in horto, compositam arbitratur fuisse ex omne genus doloribus & ærumnis piorum in hac vita, quibus Deus Christum hic proxime & totum delibutum & immersum dedisset; ut misericors esset Pontifex. Heb. 2:17, 2:17, 18. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret et fidelis sacerdos &c. Heb. 4:15. Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non possit compati infirmitatibus nostris, sed tentatum per omnia ad similitudinem, absque peccato. Haec enim eo spectant, ut sensum irae divinae a Christo amoliantur, eamque propter peccata nostra ipsum subiisse negent; quae tamen utramque hic, ut vidimus, fecerunt paginam.
units.tr: XIV. This was signified by that cup which was offered to Christ, the image expressing a way of speaking, common among those nations, about enduring sufferings. Smalcius wrongly refers this cup to that anguish of soul and body before he was taken, as if it consisted only in the fear of death now at hand. Likewise Episcopius thinks that Christ's agony [agōniā] in the garden was made up of every kind of pain and trouble the godly suffer in this life, with which God had immediately and wholly steeped and immersed Christ, so that he might be a merciful high priest. Heb. 2:17, 18. Wherefore it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest ... Heb. 4:15. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. For these views aim to remove from Christ the sense of divine wrath and to deny that he underwent it on account of our sins; yet, as we have seen, they have done both of these on this same page.

units.la: XV. Sequuntur effectus hujus ἀγωνίας; quorum primus est, quod sanguinem sudaverit, Luc. 22:44. qui sudor sanguineus, verus fuit; non enim particula ὡσεὶ hic similitudinis, sed veritatis nota est. Sic Joh. 1:14. Ut unigeniti a Patre. Luc. 24:11 ὡσεὶ λῆρος. Fuit etiam in illo Christi statu naturalis; quemadmodum omnium ejus symptomatum naturales causae et exempla prorsus gemina, in summis angoribus, reddi possunt. Refertur huc a quibusdam locus Gen. 49: 11. Juda lavat in vino indumentum suum et in sanguine uvarum, tegmen suum. Magis autem huc respicitur ab Esaia cap. 63:2. Quare rubrum adest vestimento tuo, et vestes tuae sunt, ut calcantis in torculari. & com. Quis est veniens ex Edom, maculatis vestibus Bozra?
units.tr: XV. Now follow the effects of this agony. The first is that he sweated blood, Luke 22:44. This bloody sweat was real; for the particle ὡσεὶ [hōsei] here marks not likeness but truth, as in John 1:14, as of the only begotten of the Father, and Luke 24:11, ὡσεὶ λῆρος [hōsei lēros]. It was also natural to that state of Christ, just as all his symptoms can be explained by natural causes and by quite parallel examples of extreme anguish. Some refer here Gen. 49:11: He washes his garment in wine, and his covering in the blood of grapes. But Isaiah 63:2 looks more to this: Why is thy apparel red, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat? ... Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?

units.la: XVI. Alter effectus fuit anxia illa deprecatio calicis, ut transiret, si pote. Matt. 26:39. Si possibile est, transeat a me poculum hoc; sed non ut ego volo, sed ut tu. sive hora. Marc. 14:35. Joh. 12:27. Salva me ex hora hac. quas preces tertia vice iterasse legitur Matth. 39:42, 44. Ita ut non absoluta fuerit haec deprecatio, sed ea lege, si Patris voluntati consentanea esset; neque adeo Christus per eam indicavit constantem voluntatem suam, sed potius naturae desiderium, quae mortem non horrere non potest; ut non tam diserta et articulata fuerit Christi vox, quam extortum naturae dolenti suspirium. Quare citra peccatum omnino fuit haec correctio, seu anticipatio; cum Christus etiam ex iis quae passus est, obedientiam didicerit. Hebr. 5:8.
units.tr: XVI. The second effect was that anxious prayer that the cup might pass, if it were possible. Matt. 26:39. If it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt. Or, save me from this hour. Mark 14:35; John 12:27. These prayers are recorded as repeated a third time, Matt. 26:42, 44. So this entreaty was not absolute, but was made on the condition that it agreed with the Father's will. Nor did Christ by it show his settled will, but rather the desire of nature, which cannot but shrink from death; so that Christ's voice was not so much a clear and articulated utterance as a sigh wrung from a suffering nature. Hence this correction, or anticipation, was altogether without sin, since Christ learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Heb. 5:8.

units.la: XVII. Non defuit huic passionis quasi antecoenio modus etiam suus et remissio, qua respirare aliquantum et ad se redire datum est; ut par esset et locus concederetur officiis ab eo praestandis. Fuit autem haec remissio vel interna; vel externa. Interna erat, quando animus ex anxietate maxima paululum relaxatus ad hominum curam et officia iis debita se advertebat. Hebr. 5:9. Et consummatus, factus est omnibus obtemperantibus sibi, causa salutis aeternae. Externa vero ex angeli consolatione ipsi fuit collata, Luc. 22:43. Apparuit vero ipsi angelus e coelo, corroborans ipsum. Unde aqua Christo quasi asperia, et otium datum est, in depressissima hac humiliatione, etiam miracula praestandi; ut ne tunc quidem ulla in parte officiis suis defuerit.
units.tr: XVII. This passion had, as it were before the supper, its own measure and its own remission, by which he was allowed to breathe a little and come to himself, so that there might be time and room for the duties he had to perform. This remission was either inward or outward. It was inward when his spirit, somewhat relaxed from the greatest anxiety, turned its attention to the care of men and the duties owed to them. Heb. 5:9. And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him. The outward consolation was brought to him by an angel, Luke 22:43. And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him. Hence a kind of refreshment was, as it were, sprinkled on Christ, and in this deepest humiliation leisure was also granted for working miracles, so that even then he was not lacking in his duties in any part.

units.la: XVIII. Ex
units.tr: XVIII. From

units.la: XVIII. Ex hoc propylæo quasi, in ipsum passionis adytum deducimur; ubi insolito Judæis supplicio, lurida mortis imago se conspiciendam præbet; ubi medio in monte, stipes erectus cum antenna, & cruciarius adstat, cruci suffigendus; mortis genus atrocissimum, tum vero servile & ignominiosum valde; prædictum tamen de Messia: Cætus malefconcorum me circuierunt, foderunt manus meas & pedes meos. Psal. 22: 17. & 69: 22. Et dederunt in cibo meo (vel refectione mea) venenum, & in siti mea potaverunt me aceto. Esai. 5 3: 8. Excisus est ex terra viventium propter defectionem populi mei. Zach. 12: 10. & 13: 7. Gladie excitare in pastorem meum & in virum proximum meum (vel, qui est instar mei) ait Jehovah Deus exercituum.
units.tr: XVIII. From this vestibule, as it were, we are led into the very sanctuary of the Passion, where an unusual punishment for the Jews presents itself to view, a gloomy image of death. There, on the central hill, stands an upright post with a crossbeam, and a crucifier waits to nail him to the cross. It is the most atrocious kind of death, and a very servile and shameful one. Yet it was foretold of the Messiah: A company of evildoers has encircled me; they have pierced my hands and my feet. Ps. 22:17; 69:22. And they gave me poison for my food (or my refreshment), and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Isa. 53:8. He was cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of my people. Zech. 12:10; 13:7. Awake, O sword, against my shepherd and against the man who is my fellow, says the LORD of hosts.

units.la: XIX. Quam mortem Christus non fortuito adiisse censeri debet cum maledictio legalis necessario hanc illi irrogaret; quippe quæ à Christo erat auferenda; illa vero speciatim incumbebat illi, qui è ligno suspensus erat. Deut. 21: 23. Non enim omnia peccata expiabat, aut omnem maledictionem tollebat Lex: Non delectaris sacrificio, alias autem holocaustum non accipis. Sacrificia Dei sunt spiritus fractus. Psal. 51: 18, 19. Quinimo quosdam ipsos peccata sua, id est, poenam eorum ferre jubebat; maledicens talibus quantum in se erat. Gal. 3: 10. Quotquot enim sub operibus legis sunt, sub maledictione sunt, in cujus maledictionis signum graviores peccatores è ligno suspendebantur. Gal. 3: 13. Maledictus omnis qui pendet è ligno; hanc igitur maledictionem ut tolleret Christus, ipse eam prius subire, & è ligno suspendi debuit. Joh. 3: 14. Quemadmodum Moses extulit serpentem in deserto; ita efferri oportet filium hominis. & cap. 12: 32. Et ego quum elatus fuero ex terra, omnes traham post me. Item cap. 18: 32. Ut sermo Jesu impleretur, significans quali morte moriturus esset. Ut nulla de causa mors hæc Judæis scandalo esse debeat, cum & prædicta fuerit, & necessium etiam, ut mortem hanc oppeteret Messias.
units.tr: XIX. Christ must not be thought to have undergone this death by chance, since the curse of the Law necessarily brought it upon him; for it was his to bear away, and it lay especially upon the one who hung from a tree (Deut. 21:23). The Law did not expiate all sins or remove every curse: You do not delight in sacrifice, otherwise I would give a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. Ps. 51:18, 19. Indeed, the Law even bade some to bear their own sins, that is, their punishment, cursing such persons as far as it lay in its power (Gal. 3:10). For as many as are under the works of the Law are under the curse, and as a sign of this curse the greater sinners were hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13). Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. So in order to remove this curse, Christ himself had first to undergo it and be hanged on a tree (John 3:14). As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up. And in chapter 12:32: And I, when I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself. Likewise in chapter 18:32: that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying what kind of death he would die. Therefore this death ought to be no stumbling block to the Jews, since it was both foretold and necessary that the Messiah should undergo it.

units.la: XX. Raptus fuit Christus ad hoc supplicium ex sententia judicis, postquam se stiterat ejus judicio; quo adumbrata fuit forma judicii divini; sicut eo respicit Apost. Rom. 8: 32. Ut in hac judiciaria morte appareret satisfactio pro peccatis nostris; quæ in morte naturali non fuisset conspicua. Intervenit hic etiam, singulari Dei providentia imperium Romanum; ut ita à toto quasi orbe, quo illi potiebantur, condemnaretur Christus; & quemadmodum imperium illud, partem aliquam fecerat in ejus nativitate, ita non exiguam hic facit in morte.
units.tr: XX. Christ was carried off to this punishment by the sentence of the judge, after he had presented himself to his judgment. In this the form of the divine judgment was foreshadowed, as the Apostle alludes to when he says (Rom. 8:32) that God did not spare his own Son. So that in this judicial death the satisfaction for our sins might appear, which would not have been evident in a natural death. The Roman empire also intervened here by the singular providence of God, so that Christ was condemned by what was almost the whole world, over which that empire held sway. And just as that empire had played some part at his birth, so here in his death it plays no small part.

units.la: XXI. Ad externum hoc & dirissimum supplicii genus, accessit in justissimo.
units.tr: XXI. To this external and most dreadful kind of punishment there was added, in the most just...

units.la: illius supplicii.
units.tr: of that punishment.

units.la: necessitas.
units.tr: necessity.

units.la: tas.
units.tr: -tas.

units.la: veniente judicio.
units.tr: the judgment coming.

units.la: Romanorum. internus dolor acerbissimus, ex iisdem causis ex quibus dolor antea in horto conceptus, animumque ejus afflixit; cujus ingentem paroxysmum ostendebat querela illa desertionis divinæ. Psal. 22: 2. Deus mi, Deus mi, quare deseruisti me? conf. Matth. 27: 46. Quæ facta non naufragio unionis hypostaticæ, sed cohibita, per paulum temporis, virtute divina. Sed paulisper pro angelis minoratum videmus Jesum (qui propter passionem mortis gloria & honore coronatus est) ut gratia Dei pro omni gustaret mortem. Hebr. 2:9. Ad quem ultimum vitæ ejus articulum præcipuè pertinet illud quod de eo refert Paulus Hebr. 5: 7. Quod in diebus carnis petitiones & supplicationes ad eum, qui poterat eum salvum facere ex morte, cum clamore valido & lacrymis obtulerit, & exauditus sit à metu.
units.tr: of the Romans. An exceedingly bitter inner anguish, arising from the same causes from which the grief conceived earlier in the garden arose and afflicted his soul. The cry of divine desertion showed its great paroxysm: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Ps. 22:2; cf. Matt. 27:46. This was not a shipwreck of the hypostatic union, but was restrained, by divine power, for a short time. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. Heb. 2:9. To his final moment of life especially pertains what Paul relates of him (Heb. 5:7): who, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and was heard because of his reverent fear.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XVIII.

units.la: De morte Christi.
units.tr: On the death of Christ.

units.la: I. Vemadmodum salus nostra ex uno Christo dependet, & in illo consummatur, quicquid per orbem terrarum salvum est; ita Christus ipse, in morte sua perficitur; quando non solum consummatum est, quicquid prophetarum vaticinia prædixerant, sed ipse hactenus consummatus fuit Christus; utpote in quam derivarentur omnes ejus passiones, quas nostri gratia subiit; ita ut nisi in hunc tandem finem terminatæ fuissent, vanus fuisset omnis labor anteactus, & tam pertinaci studio exantlatus; Mortem enim gustare pro omnibus debebat, & hac ratione tanquam princeps salutis per passiones consummari, Hebr. 2: 9, 10. Atque hanc ob causam Euangelistarum singuli certatim, historiam hanc mortis diligentissime referunt.
units.tr: I. Just as our salvation depends on Christ alone, and whatever is saved throughout the world is completed in him, so Christ himself is brought to completion in his death. Not only has everything the prophets foretold been fulfilled, but Christ himself has so far been brought to completion, since all his sufferings, which he underwent for our sake, were directed toward this end. Unless they had finally been brought to this end, all the labour he had undergone before, and endured with such persistent zeal, would have been in vain. For he ought to taste death for all, and in this way, as the prince of salvation, he was made perfect through sufferings, Heb. 2:9, 10. For this reason each of the Evangelists, eagerly vying with the others, records this history of the death with the greatest care.

units.la: II. Accuratissima autem hæc quatuor Euangelistarum enarratio, omnimodo docet veram hanc fuisse mortem, non fictam aut simulatam. Naturalis quoque fuit, quatenus per causas naturales fuit adscita; at supernaturalis eadem fuit, quatenus ex absoluta sua potestate, vitam lubens posuit. Joh. 10: 18. Potestatem habeo ponendi eam (vitam) & potestatem habeo recipiendi eam. & Joh. 2: 19. Solvite templum hoc, & in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Quare licet maxime violenta, non tamen eo minus voluntaria fuit.
units.tr: II. The most exact account of the four Evangelists teaches in every way that this death was true, not feigned or pretended. It was also natural, in so far as it was brought about by natural causes; yet at the same time it was supernatural, in so far as by his own absolute power he willingly laid down his life. John 10:18: I have power to lay it (my life) down, and I have power to take it up again. And John 2:19: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Therefore, although it was most violent, it was none the less voluntary.

units.la: III. Subnascitur hic quæstio; num mortis hoc triduo, Christus verus fuerit homo? quod merito negatur à Thoma; licet æquivoce homo dicipossèt, id est, homo mortuus; non autem univoce. Quo vero modo desiit esse homo, eo etiam haetenus desiit esse Θεάνθρωπος: licet caeteroquin laxato vinculo animae & corporis, illaesa manserit utriusque unio cum λόγῳ; & soluta unione naturali, perstitit tamen personalis.
units.tr: III. Here the question arises whether, during these three days of death, Christ was a true man. Thomas rightly denies this, since a dead man may be called a man only equivocally, and not univocally. But in the way in which he ceased to be a man, in that same way he also ceased to be the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος] for that time. Although, otherwise, with the bond of soul and body loosened, the union of each nature with the Word [λόγῳ] remained unharmed, and although the natural union was dissolved, the personal union nonetheless continued.

units.la: IV. Sicut autem immerito nostram sententiam criminantur Lutherani; quasi dicamus merum hominem pro nobis mortuum; cum subjectum quo quidem referamus ad solam naturam humanam; subjectum vero quod ad totam personam Θεανθρώπου, ut divinam naturam non excludamus: ita vicissim e contrario, jure maximo carpendi hic veniunt iidem, qui Deum proprie & sine tropo, atque adeo ipsam divinam naturam pro nobis passam volunt; quin SS. Trinitatis funus, in morte Christi, elatum esse, quidam eorum dicere sustinent. A quibus non abludunt Anabaptistae Flandri, qui Christum mortuum statuunt in natura divina, & nihil in illo vivum mansisse praeter Spiritum, quem Patri tradebat; ipsum autem cadaver filium Dei fuisse. Ex qua quidem sententia aut efficietur plures esse Deos; sin vero; triduo illo mortis Christi, mundum absque Deo fuisse; quod eadem opera qua recitamus, item refellimus.Deum autem illum diserte ait Scriptura. Si enim novissent, non crucifixissent Dominum gloriae. 1 Cor. 2: 8. Deus Ecclesiam proprio sanguine acquisivit. Act. 20: 28.
units.tr: IV. Just as the Lutherans unjustly accuse our view, as though we said that a mere man died for us, since we refer the subject, in one sense, only to the human nature, but in another sense to the whole person of the God-man [Θεανθρώπου], so that we do not exclude the divine nature; so, conversely, those who want God to have suffered for us properly and without a figure, and indeed the divine nature itself, deserve the greatest censure here. Some of them even venture to say that the funeral of the Holy Trinity was carried out in the death of Christ. The Flemish Anabaptists do not differ from them. They hold that Christ died in the divine nature, and that nothing living remained in him except the Spirit, which he handed over to the Father, while the corpse itself was the Son of God. From this opinion it follows either that there are several gods, or else that during those three days of Christ's death the world was without God. By the same argument by which we set this out, we also refute it. Scripture plainly calls him God: For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8. God acquired the Church with his own blood, Acts 20:28.

units.la: V. Veritatem hujus mortis indubitate probavit perfossum hasta latus, & flumen illud sanguinis largiter prorumpens, eumque subsecuta ex eodem vulnere aquae unda. Unus militum lancea ipsius latus pupugit & statim exivit sanguis & aqua. Joh. 19: 34. Cui rei explicandae non illico ad miraculum, tanquam ad sacram anchoram consugere necesse est, cum ex ipsis naturae legibus & solito cursu, ad istam causam, effectus iste consequi debeat. Quid, quod quantum hac in re tribuitur miraculo, tantum a veritate passionis Christi intervertitur; quem enim nos violaveramus naturae ordinem, illum non praeter ordinem restituere oportebat. Effluxerunt autem humores isti, non indistincte, atque promiscue, sed separatim; quod graves illae contestationes, & accurata Johannis observatio satis luculenter docet. Joh. 19: 35. Et qui vidit, testis est, & vera est ipsius testificatio, & ille novit quod vera dicat, ut vos credatis, & 1. Joh. 5: 6. Hic est Jesus Christus, qui venit per aquam & sanguinem, non in aqua solum, sed in aqua & sanguine. At nec lateris hujus transfactio a Prophetis fuit tacita; utpote quam diserte praedixerit Zacharias cap. 12: 10. Et invebuntur me cum (eo), quem transfoderunt, & plangent super illo, ut planctum super unigenito. coll. Apoc. 1: 7. Ecce venit cum nubibus, & videbit eum omnis oculus, etiam qui eum transfixerunt.
units.tr: V. The reality of this death was beyond doubt proved by the side pierced with a spear, and by the stream of blood that burst forth abundantly, followed by a flow of water from the same wound. One of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out, John 19:34. In explaining this fact it is not necessary to flee at once to a miracle, as to a sacred anchor, since this effect ought to follow from this cause by the very laws of nature and its ordinary course. Indeed, the more that is attributed to a miracle in this matter, the more the truth of Christ's passion is undermined. For the order of nature which we had violated had to be restored by him, not outside the order. These fluids flowed out not confusedly and mixed together, but separately, as that solemn testimony and John's careful observation show quite clearly: John 19:35, And he who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he tells the truth, so that you may believe. And 1 John 5:6: This is Jesus Christ, who came by water and blood, not by water only, but by water and blood. Nor was this piercing of the side passed over in silence by the prophets, since Zechariah foretold it plainly, ch. 12:10: And they shall look on me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son. Compare Rev. 1:7: Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him.

units.la: VI. Non enim altiori significatu, aut mysterio caesum est, quod studiose notat Johannes 1. Epist. 5: 6. Christum venisse per aquam & sanguinem. Quippe docuit ille effluxus, in una Christi morte concurrisse & impletum esse, quidquid olim per ingentem illum baptismorum apparatum, largissimam aquarum profusionem; per exundantem sacrificiorum cruorem praefiguratum erat. 1 Joh. 1: 7. Eph: 1: 7. In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius. Rom. 3: 25. Apoc. 1: 5. Qui (Christus) dilexit nos & lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Quibus, in quantum erant sacramenta, cum maxime respondent baptismus & S. Coena. Hebr. 10: 19, 23. Habemus igitur fiduciam ad introitum sanctorum in sanguine Jesu. — accedamus cum vero corde in plenitudine fidei, asperso corda a conscientia mala & ablui corpus aqua munda.
units.tr: VI. Nor was this wounding done with some higher meaning or mystery, which John carefully notes, 1 John 5:6: that Christ came by water and blood. Indeed, that outflow showed that everything which was once prefigured by the great array of baptisms, the abundant pouring out of waters, and the overflowing blood of the sacrifices, came together and was fulfilled in the death of Christ alone: 1 John 1:7; Eph. 1:7: In whom we have redemption through his blood; Rom. 3:25; Rev. 1:5: He (Christ) who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood. Baptism and the Holy Supper correspond most closely to these, insofar as they were sacraments. Heb. 10:19, 22: Therefore we have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus; let us draw near with a true heart, in fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

units.la: VII. Exprimebatur etiam hoc emblemate justificatio nostri, & regeneratio ex aqua & sanguine Christi; id est, ex pura ejus obedientia, quae vim purificandi habet, & merito mortis, simul cum potentia Spiritus. Nisi quis natus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Joh. 3: 5. Denique etiam per hanc transfossionem, singulari Dei providentia praeoccupatum fuit ossifragium; quando enim vibrata manu centurionis hasta, latus hausit apertum, nec ullum vitae signum appareret, superseded solito caeteroquin crurifragio. Joh. 19: 32, 33. Ut viderunt eum mortuum, non confregerunt ipsius ossa &c. in quo retulit Christus typum agni paschalis. Exod. 12: 46. & os non frangetis in eo. atque explevit, vimque dedit verbo illi consolationis Psal. 34: 21. Servat omnia ossa ejus, unum ex illis non frangitur.
units.tr: VII. By this emblem was also expressed our justification and our regeneration from the water and blood of Christ; that is, from his pure obedience, which has the power to cleanse, and from the merit of his death, together with the power of the Spirit. Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, John 3:5. Finally, by this piercing, the breaking of the bones was also prevented by the singular providence of God.
