For when the soldier's spear was thrust with a hand that was raised, and struck his open side, and no sign of life appeared, the usual breaking of the legs was set aside: John 19:32, 33, When they saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs, etc. In this Christ referred to the type of the Passover lamb, Exod. 12:46, and you shall not break a bone of it, and fulfilled it, giving force to that word of consolation, Ps. 34:21, He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.

units.la: VIII. Atque ita omissa supplicii capitalis accurata descriptione; tum quoque personarum, loci, aliarumque rerum circumstantiis, memorabili prae caeteris est tempus, tum quoad periodum annorum, tempestatem, mensem, diem denique atque alia, quae nunc diffusa omnem in partem cogitatione, exequi non est animus. Illud unum obiter adverte, ipsam etiam horam qua Christus mortuus, eandem esse quam olim praedixerat angelus apud Danielem, c. 9: 21. & seqq. Et vir ille Gabriel, advolitans celeritate maxima pertingebat ad me circa tempus doni vespertini, & docebat &c.
units.tr: VIII. Thus, leaving aside a detailed description of the capital punishment, and likewise the circumstances of the persons, the place and other matters, the time is especially memorable above the rest, both as to the period of years, the season, the month, and finally the day, and other things which I do not now intend to pursue at length in every direction. Let me note this one thing in passing: the very hour in which Christ died was the same one that the angel had once foretold to Daniel, ch. 9:21 and following: And that man Gabriel, flying swiftly, came to me about the time of the evening offering, and instructed me, etc.

units.la: IX. Morti huic summa itetit necessitas, illa de causa, quod Christus noster ἐγγυος & mediator & testator erat. Hebr. 9: 15: 16. Et Et propter hoc Teft. Novi mediator est, ut morte obita--promissionem accipiant vocati aterna hereditatis. Ubi enim testamentum est, mortem necesse est contingere testatoris. Quo faciebat typus vaccæ rufæ. Num. 19: 9. Unde in hac morte vis & efficientia divinæ justitiæ demonstrata fuit. Rom. 3: 25. Quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium, per fidem in sanguine ipsius. 2. Cor. 5. 21. Qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut fimus justitia Dei in ipso. Quare etiam non solum corpore, sed & anima pati debuit Christus, ferendo omnes quæ nobis debebantur, pœnas. Esai. 53: 11. A labore anima sua videbit femen & satiabitur. Rom. 6: 23. Matth. 26: 28. Valde tristis est anima mea, usque ad mortem.
units.tr: IX. There was the highest necessity for this death, for this reason, that our Christ was surety [ἔγγυος], mediator and testator. Heb. 9:15, 16: And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance, since death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions. For where there is a will, the death of the one who made it must necessarily occur. The red heifer also pointed to this, Num. 19:9. Hence in this death the power and efficacy of divine justice were displayed: Rom. 3:25, whom God set forth as a propitiation, through faith in his blood; 2 Cor. 5:21, He who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Therefore Christ had to suffer not only in body but also in soul, bearing all the punishments that were owed to us: Isa. 53:11, He shall see the fruit of the labour of his soul and be satisfied; Rom. 6:23; Matt. 26:28; My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Ut eximiis solis vitiosis affectionibus, quæ in nostris pœnis ex peccato accidunt, Christi mors fuerit genere & proportione eadem, cum illa morte, quæ peccatis nostris ex justitia convenit, eosdem omnino gradus, membra & species exhibens; quæque idcirco omnem miseriam & pœnas nobis debitas, exhauft. Unde per fynecdochen mors & passio Christi sæpe notat universam medicationem illi incumbentem, & pro tota ejus satisfactione, tam in vita, quam in morte sumitur. Angelis minoratus est, ut gratia Dei pro omni gustaret mortem. Hebr. 2: 9.
units.tr: So that, leaving aside solely the evil affections that arise from sin in our punishments, Christ's death was of the same kind and proportion as that death which justice assigns to our sins, displaying exactly the same degrees, parts and forms, and therefore exhausting all the misery and punishments owed to us. Hence by synecdoche the death and passion of Christ often denotes the whole mediation undertaken by him, and it is taken for his entire satisfaction, both in life and in death. He was made a little lower than the angels, that by the grace of God he might taste death for every man. Heb. 2:9.

units.la: XI. Ineptiunt igitur Pontificii, cum guttulam sanguinis Christi fufficiffe prædicant; quomodo cum sibi videntur pretium & dignitatem meriti Christi immane quantum extollere; omnem ejus vim eludunt, & solutionem quandam imaginariam faciunt; Deoque crudelitatis notam insignem inurunt, Legique & Euangelio contradicunt. Non enim per particulas adeo conscindi debet aut potest Christi mors, non magis quam lux illa solis, quæ vel tanta requiritur, ut unum illustret hominem, quanta est, cum rebus omnibus lætos afflat honores.
units.tr: XI. The Papists therefore talk nonsense when they preach that a single drop of Christ's blood was sufficient. In doing so, while they seem to exalt the price and dignity of Christ's merit beyond measure, they nullify its whole power and invent a kind of imaginary payment. They also brand God with the mark of cruelty and contradict both the Law and the Gospel. For Christ's death must not, and cannot, be divided into fragments, any more than that light of the sun which, though it is needed in such amount as to illuminate one man, is as great as it is when it breathes its cheerful favour on all things.

units.la: XII. Tandem denique hac morte Christi ademtus est morti ftimulus & aculeus 1 Cor. 15: 55, 56. non solum circumcisa ab omni parte ejus dominatione, sed penitus sublata; ut nullo modo nunc formidolosa fit, qualis olim erat sub servitute legis & metu mortis. Hebr. 2: 14, 15. Ut per mortem aboleret illum, qui mortis habebat poteftatem, hoc est, diabolum; & liberaret eos, qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti. quod Davidis, Ezechiæ, aliorumque exempla evincunt. Reliquos illius effectus nunc mittimus.
units.tr: XII. Finally, by this death of Christ the sting of death has been taken away (1 Cor. 15:55, 56). Its dominion has not merely been cut back on every side but utterly abolished, so that death is now in no way fearful, as it once was under the servitude of the law and the dread of death. Heb. 2:14, 15: That through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their lives. The examples of David, Hezekiah and others prove this. We now pass over the remaining effects of this.

units.la: CAPUT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: De Satisfactione & fructibus mortis Christi.
units.tr: On the Satisfaction and Fruits of Christ's Death.

units.la: I. Uit ipsa mors & passio; restat, ut quænam inde fruges redundarit, & cui bono fuerit, videamus; nisi enim hoc constiterit, vana erit mors, vanus ipse Christus. Fructus autem hic considerari poterit, pro duplici fine; nempe ꝰ, cujus gratia; & ῷ cui persona. Prioris respectu tres sunt fructus primarii, seu fructuum capita, ex quibus alii derivantur: satisfactio nimirum; ex qua profluit nostri cum Deo reconciliatio, & hereditas vitæ æternæ.
units.tr: I. Since the death and passion themselves are established, it remains to see what fruits have flowed from them and to whose benefit they have turned out. For unless this is settled, the death is in vain and Christ himself is in vain. The fruit may be considered here under a twofold aim: namely ꝰ, for whose sake; and ῷ, to whom (as person). With respect to the former, there are three primary fruits, or heads of fruits, from which the others are derived: satisfaction, namely, from which flows our reconciliation with God, and the inheritance of eternal life.

units.la: II. Ipsa satisfactionis vox, quæ forensis est, & alterius sensus, ἀντολέξει in sacris paginis non legitur; at parium & æquivalentium vocum abunde est; ut λύτρωσις, ἀντιλύτρωσις &c. Originem ejus debemus adversariorum importunitati & fallaciæ, quæ illam nobis expresserit.
units.tr: II. The word satisfaction itself, which is forensic and has another sense, [ἀντολέξει], is not read in the sacred pages. But words that are equal and equivalent to it abound, such as redemption [λύτρωσις], ransom [ἀντιλύτρωσις], and so on. We owe its origin to the importunity and trickery of our opponents, who forced it upon us.

units.la: III. Satisfacere est idem quod τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι Marc. 15: 15. tantum facere, quantum postulanti satis est, seu verbis seu factis illud fiat. Quare in ære alieno & re debiti, est exolvere. In causa injuriæ, est illius compensatio & redintegratio. Ita Christus vadem se sistens nostro loco, justitiæ Dei satistecit; restituens illi omnimoda subjectione sua, tam in vita, quam in morte, auctoritatis & independentiæ honorem integrum, quem nos delibaveramus; injuriamque per nos Deo illatam propulsans; nec minus nos debitis tam ingentibus exolvens. Unde Deus per justitiam sanctificatus dicitur, Esai. 5: 16.
units.tr: III. To satisfy is the same as to do what is sufficient [τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι], Mark 15:15: to do as much as is enough for the one who demands, whether this is done by words or by deeds. Hence, in a debt of money and a thing owed, it means to pay in full. In a case of injury, it means to make compensation and restitution for it. So Christ, standing surety in our place, satisfied the justice of God, restoring to him, by his complete subjection both in life and in death, the full honour of his authority and independence, which we had diminished. He also averted the injury done to God through us, and likewise paid our so great debts. Whence God is said to be sanctified through justice, Isa. 5:16.

units.la: IV. In hac satisfactione videbimus. 1. rem ipsam: 2. errorum ἀντιθεσιν. In ipsa re se consideranda offert 1. ejus necessitas. 2. veritas. 3. pretium. 4. Cui id oblatum & persolutum? 5. solutionis ejus modus & jus. 6. meritum pretio conjunctum.
units.tr: IV. In this satisfaction we shall see: 1. the thing itself; 2. the opposing errors. In the thing itself, there present themselves for consideration: 1. its necessity; 2. its truth; 3. its price; 4. to whom it was offered and paid; 5. the mode and right of its payment; 6. the merit joined to the price.

units.la: V. Necessitatem 1. docet justitia Dei, seu constans ac æterna illius voluntas, qua, secundum ordinem immutabilem à se constitutum, cuique suum reddit, adeoque & peccatori, malum facienti, malum rependit, & ab eo sese separat. Ita ut nisi huic ordini satisfiat, Deus peccatori similis esset, & cum illo communionem haberet. Qui tamen negare se ipsum non potest. 2 Tim. 2: 13. Visitat peccata patrum in filios, in tertios & quartos osorum suorum. Exod. 34: 5, 7. & 20: 5. Hæc fecisti & silni, putasti (quod) omnino tui similis exsituras sim: arguamte, aciem dirigam contra oculos tuos. Psal. 50: 21. Rom. 1: 32. & 2: 5. & 3: 25, 26. 2. Thess. 1: 6.
units.tr: V. Necessity is first taught by the justice of God, that is, his constant and eternal will, by which, according to the immutable order he has established, he renders to each his due, and so also repays evil to the sinner who does evil, and separates himself from him. So unless this order is satisfied, God would be like the sinner and would have communion with him. Yet he cannot deny himself, 2 Tim. 2:13. He visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, upon the third and fourth generation of those who hate him, Exod. 34:5, 7; 20:5. "These things you have done and I was silent; you thought I would be altogether like you. I will reprove you and set my line against your eyes," Ps. 50:21. Rom. 1:32; 2:5; 3:25, 26. 2 Thess. 1:6.

units.la: VI. Porro hanc necessitatem demonstrant 11 comminationes quas denunciat Deus. Quo die comederis de ea, moriendo morieris. Gen. 2: 17. Maledictus qui non stare facit verba legis hujus, ut faciat ea. Deut. 27: 26. 111. Eodem pertinent prophetarum vaticinia. Esai. 53: 4, 5. & seq ]. Enimvero morbos nostros ipse tulit & dolores nostros bajulavit &c. aliisque in locis ;t um quoque iv. sacrificia Vet. Test. Quae parabola est in praesens tempus, quo munera & sacrificia offeruntur, quae non possunt quoad conscientiam consummare eum, qui cultum praestat. Hebr. 9: 9.
units.tr: VI. Moreover, this necessity is shown by the threats which God proclaims: "On the day you eat of it, dying you shall die," Gen. 2:17. "Cursed is he who does not establish the words of this law, so as to do them," Deut. 27:26. To the same point belong the prophecies of the prophets, Isa. 53:4, 5 and following: "Surely he has borne our diseases and carried our sorrows," and so on, and in other places. Also the sacrifices of the Old Testament, "which is a parable for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make perfect, as to the conscience, him who performs the worship," Heb. 9:9.

units.la: VII. v. Quin ipsa lex operum idem evincebat, utpote quae sine promissione vitae & comminatione mortis ferri aut juberi non poterat. Lev. 18. Deut. 27. jam vero per carnem imbellis factae est. Rom. 8: 3. atque ita nos per peccatum praemii compotes facere, aut peccatum accusans condemnare nequibat, alii locum praestans. vi. Nec minus ex ipsa Christi passione veritas & necessitas hujus rei conficitur; quippe indignum Deo facinus erat, hominem sanctum, & summo Dei amore dignum, morti tradere, si non cogat, durum telum, necessitas: adde, quod hoc pacto, Deus in morte Christi, non suum erga nos amorem patefecisset, sed summum potius in Christum jus & imperium; imo supervacuam impositionem dolorum super hominem innocentem, & suo, & alterius nomine: praeterquam Paulus docet Rom. 5: 8. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quod quum adhuc peccatores essemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Ex quibus omnibus abunde liquet decentia passionum Christi, & consummationis ejus per illas. Hebr. 2: 10. Decebat enim ipsum—Principem salutis ipsorum per passiones consummare. coll. cap. 5: 7, 89.
units.tr: VII. Indeed, the law of works itself proves the same, since it could not be given or commanded without the promise of life and the threat of death, Lev. 18; Deut. 27. Now, "what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh," Rom. 8:3. Thus it could not make us partakers of the reward through sin, nor condemn sin by accusing it, but only gave place to another. Nor less is the truth and necessity of this matter established from Christ's passion itself. For it would have been an unworthy deed for God to hand over to death a holy man, deserving of the highest love of God, unless necessity compelled it, a hard constraint. Add that in this way God would not have shown his love for us in Christ's death, but rather his supreme right and dominion over Christ; indeed, a superfluous laying of sufferings upon an innocent man, both in his own name and in another's. As Paul teaches, Rom. 5:8: "But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." From all these things it is abundantly clear that Christ's sufferings were fitting, and that he was made perfect through them, Heb. 2:10: "For it was fitting for him... to make the Prince of their salvation perfect through sufferings," compare chap. 5:7, 8, 9.

units.la: VIII. Dissolvunt hanc necessitatem Durandus, aliique scholastici, negando necessariam fuisse satisfactionem; a quibus haeresin suam hausit Socinus. Si enim citra satisfactionem peccata remittere potuerit Deus, solvitur omnis lex, eaque soluta, nil quicquam a Christo praestari opus fuit.
units.tr: VIII. Durandus and other scholastics dissolve this necessity, denying that satisfaction was necessary; from them Socinus drew his heresy. For if God could have remitted sins without satisfaction, all law is dissolved, and once that is dissolved, there was no need for anything to be accomplished by Christ.

units.la: IX. At opponunt nobis, Deum ut partem offensam, quae id potest, imo debet, de jure suo remittere potuisse: verum non solum ut pars offensa, sed praecipue ut judex considerandus venit hic Deus, eum de poenarum irrogatione & remissione agatur; quod judicis est; quum personam Deus hac in re primario gerit, nec unquam dedeponere potest, licet simul sit pars offensa. Quod regerunt, etiam supremum judicem juri suo renunciare posse; verum equidem est, si legem suam violet; at hoc Deo tribuere, impium & blasphemum est. Nec quoque Deus summum & absolutum dominii sui, & crediti jus prosecutus est, sed justitiam suam hic ostendit: ut apparet ex Rom. 3:25,26. Quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad ostensionem justitiae suae — ad hoc ut ipse sit justus.
units.tr: IX. But they object to us that God, as the offended party, who can and indeed ought to remit his own right, could have done so. But God is to be considered here not only as the offended party but chiefly as judge, since the matter concerns the imposition and remission of penalties, which belongs to a judge. In this matter God primarily plays the role of a person and can never lay it aside, even though he is at the same time the offended party. They reply that even a supreme judge can renounce his right. That is true indeed if he violates his own law, but to attribute this to God is impious and blasphemous. Nor has God pursued the supreme and absolute right of his dominion and of his claim, but here he shows his justice, as appears from Rom. 3:25, 26: "Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness... that he himself might be just."

units.la: X. Objiciunt porro; si tanta hinc rerum difficultas importetur, facili negotio, peccatum impediendo, potuisse Deum praevenire omnem hanc satisfactionis necessitatem. Verum enimvero nostrum non est juri vel voluntati divinae intercedere; licuit Deo jus suum exequi, quamvis inde lapsus hominis consequeretur; multo magis quam homini illud licet, etiamsi peccatum proximi extra suam culpam inde consequatur. Peccatum cohibere aut permittere divini fuit arbitrii; at vero jam commissum sine satisfactione a Deo condonari non potest. Denique, quamvis nullum ex peccato commodum vel incommodum patiatur Deus, nullisque gaudii vel tristitiae affectibus ducatur, eadem tamen manet necessitas puniendi.
units.tr: X. They object further: if so great a difficulty is brought in, God could easily have prevented the whole necessity of satisfaction by preventing sin. But it is not for us to interfere with the right or will of God. God was free to exercise his right, even though a fall of man would follow from it, much more than a man is permitted to do so, even if the sin of a neighbour follows from it without his own fault. To restrain sin or to permit it belonged to the divine decision; but once it has been committed, sin cannot be pardoned by God without satisfaction. Finally, although God suffers no gain or loss from sin, and is moved by no affections of joy or sadness, the same necessity of punishing remains.

units.la: XI. Haec vero satisfactionis necessitas ex rigore justitiae, ipsam tamen ponit gratiam; tum qua vocatus & disinctus fuit Christus ad satisfaciendum; tum qua satisfactio illa accepta est nostro nomine, & in nostrum bonum. 1. Joh. 3:16. Rom. 3:24. Qui justificamur gratis ipsius gratia per redemtionem, quae est in Christo Jesu 5:5. Gratia Dei & donatio in gratia, quae est unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos abundavit. Justitia igitur fuit in satisfactione ipsa & in Christo; gratia in modo dispensationis & in nobis.
units.tr: XI. This necessity of satisfaction, however, arises from the rigour of justice, yet it presupposes grace itself: both the grace by which Christ was called and appointed to make satisfaction, and the grace by which that satisfaction was accepted in our name and for our good. 1 John 3:16; Rom. 3:24: "Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus"; 5:5: "The grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded unto many." Justice, therefore, was in the satisfaction itself and in Christ; grace was in the manner of its dispensation and in us.

units.la: XII. 11. Oblata necessitate, veritas hujus satisfactionis sese probandam offert; idque triplici potissimum via ex analogia sacrificiorum. 1. Christo peccata nostra fuisse imputata. 2. ipsum ob ea nostro loco fuisse mortuum. 3. morte hac peccata expiata esse.
units.tr: XII. Having set forth the necessity, the truth of this satisfaction presents itself to be proved, and that chiefly in three ways, from the analogy of the sacrifices: 1. our sins were imputed to Christ; 2. he died in our place on account of them; 3. by this death the sins were expiated.

units.la: XIII. Imputata fuisse Christo peccata nostra, variis modis patet 1. Cum appellatur sponsor noster. In tantum melioris testamenti existit sponsor. Hebr. 7:22. quare illum poenae nostrae vicarium succedere oportet: atque hinc etiam vices nostras in peccato tulit, fatus pro nobis peccatum. Qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut simus justitia Dei in ipso. 2. Cor. 5:21. Attigerunt me pravitates meae, & non possum cernere, numerosiores sunt pilis capitis mei. Psal. 40:13. Christum enim ibi loqui patet ex comm. 7, 8, 9, ideoque peccata nostra portasse dicitur; eodem scilicet modo, quo siebat in victimis. Et id (sacrificium pro peccato) dedit Deus vobis, ut ferretis pravitatem cætus, ad expiandum pro ipsis coram Jehova. Levit. 10: 17. Nam sanguis ille pro anima expiationem facit. ibid. 17: 11. Eodem etiam modo Christo tribuitur; quod morbos nostros ipse tulit & dolores nostros bajulavit. Esai. 53: 4. Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Joh. 1: 29. Qui nostra peccata ipse sursum tulit in corpore suo super crucem. 1. Pet. 2: 24. hinc tam notanter, peccata nostra in ipsum incurrisse, & ab eo exacta fuisse dicuntur. Jehova in eum fecit incurrere pravitatem omnium nostrum. Es. 53: 6.
units.tr: XIII. That our sins were imputed to Christ is clear in various ways. 1. He is called our surety: "By so much Jesus has become the surety of a better covenant," Heb. 7:22. Hence it is necessary that he take the place of our punishment as its substitute; and hence also he bore our place in sin, "made sin for us," as it were: "He who knew no sin was made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him," 2 Cor. 5:21. "My iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more numerous than the hairs of my head," Ps. 40:13. For it is clear that Christ is speaking there, from verses 7, 8, 9, and therefore he is said to have carried our sins, in exactly the same way as happened with the victims. "And God has given it (the sin offering) to you, that you might bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before Jehovah," Lev. 10:17. "For that blood makes atonement for the soul," ibid. 17:11. In the same way it is ascribed to Christ that "he himself bore our diseases and carried our sorrows," Isa. 53:4. "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," John 1:29. "Who himself bore our sins up in his body on the cross," 1 Pet. 2:24. Hence so pointedly our sins are said to have run upon him and been exacted from him: "Jehovah made the iniquity of us all to run upon him," Isa. 53:6.

units.la: XIV. 2. Quando mors ejus dicitur מוסר id est, pœna exemplaris, coërcitio: Paradigma pacis nostræ super ipso erat. Esai. 53: 5. Et ejusdem capitis com. 10. dicitur אשם satisfactio, sicut vox hæc eodem modo de victimis usurpatur. Eadem mors alibi etiam λύτρον vocatur. Venit filius hominis, ut daret animam suam λύτρον, redemptionis pretium pro multis. Matth. 20: 28. & ἀντίλυτρον. Qui dedit se ipsum ἀντίλυτρον redemptionis pretium pro omnibus. 1. Tim. 2: 6. quod dicit vicarium redemptionis pretium: sicut & ad alias res pretiosissimas, aurum & argentum, tanquam sub hoc respectu, ejusdem naturæ, contenditur. Non auro aut argento empti estis—sed pretioso sanguine— Christi. 1. Petr. 1: 18. Pretio empti estis. 1. Cor. 6: 20. Adde quod hac ratione, & vi istius pretii, λύτρωσις & ἀντιλύτρωσις redemtio Christo adscribatur. Mortem subiit ad redemptionem transgressionum, quæ sub priori testamento erant. Heb. 9: 15.
units.tr: XIV. 2. When his death is called מוסר [musar], that is, exemplary punishment or chastisement, the chastisement that brought us peace was laid upon him. Isa. 53: 5. In the same chapter, v. 10, it is called אשם [asham], satisfaction, the word being used in the same way of sacrifices. The same death is elsewhere also called λύτρον [lytron]: The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom [λύτρον], the price of redemption for many. Matt. 20: 28. It is also called ἀντίλυτρον [antilytron]: who gave himself as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], the price of redemption for all. 1 Tim. 2: 6. This word denotes a substitute price, just as the most precious things, gold and silver, are set against it as being of the same nature in this respect: You were not redeemed with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ. 1 Pet. 1: 18. You were bought with a price. 1 Cor. 6: 20. Add that by this reasoning, and by the power of that price, redemption [λύτρωσις, lytrōsis] and ransoming [ἀντιλύτρωσις, antilytrōsis] are ascribed to Christ: He underwent death for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the former testament. Heb. 9: 15.

units.la: XV. Vitilitigant hic adversarii; redemptionem illam notare tantum liberationem impropriam, quæ fit per vim & potentiæ robur, non pretium; sicut olim ex Ægypto Israelem redemisse dicitur Deus: quibus non inficiamur, interdum hoc modo redemptionem sumi; at hic ea tantum notione venire, id vero pernegamus; ubi tum ipse modus redemptionis explicatur; tum λύτρον adjungitur: ut non solum propria fuerit respectu poenarum ex jure domini & potentiæ; verum etiam respectu peccatorum, ex jure judicii & pretii. Quam Ecclesiam Deus proprio sanguine acquisivit. Act. 20: 28.
units.tr: XV. Here our opponents quibble: they say that this redemption signifies only an improper liberation, which is effected by force and the strength of power, not by a price, as God is said to have once redeemed Israel out of Egypt. We do not deny that redemption is sometimes taken in this way, but we deny that it has only this sense here. For in these passages the manner of redemption is itself explained, and ransom [λύτρον] is added. So the redemption was proper not only with respect to punishments, by the right of a lord and of power, but also with respect to sins, by the right of judgment and of price: the Church which God acquired with his own blood. Acts 20: 28.

units.la: XVI. Propter peccata nostra, nostro loco mortuum esse Christum, probatur etiam variis ex locis. 1. Cum dicitur mortuus pro aliis. Tradidi vobis imprimis, quod & accepi, Christum mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas. 1. Cor. 15: 3. Judicantes hoc, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt. 2. Cor. 5: 15. non tantum ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Rom. 5: 8. sed & ἀντὶ ἡμῶν, seu ἀντὶ πολλῶν. Matth. 20: 28. Marc. 10: 45. ἀντὶ enim vel oppositionem, vel substitutionem notat. Atqui cum priori modo nullum hic locum habeat; posteriori ut veniat necessum est; quemadmodum & vidimus 1. Tim. 2: 6. mortem ejus ἀντίλυτρον dici. Non alia ratione ac olim ἀντίψυχοι vocabantur homines seu victimæ, quæ pro alio morti tradebantur; ita & Christus 2. Sam. 19: 2. &c. 1. Cor. 1: 13. An Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis?
units.tr: XVI. That Christ died in our place for our sins is proved also from various passages. First, when he is said to have died for others: I delivered to you first of all what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. 1 Cor. 15: 3. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died. 2 Cor. 5: 14. Not only is it ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν [for us], Rom. 5: 8, but also ἀντὶ ἡμῶν [instead of us], or ἀντὶ πολλῶν [instead of many], Matt. 20: 28; Mark 10: 45. For ἀντί signifies either opposition or substitution. Now since the first sense has no place here, the second must be the one intended, just as we saw in 1 Tim. 2: 6 that his death is called ἀντίλυτρον. This is no different from the way men or victims that were handed over to death in place of another were once called ἀντίψυχοι [substitutes for life]. So Christ is also in that sense: 2 Sam. 19: 2, etc.; 1 Cor. 1: 13: Was Paul crucified for you?

units.la: XVII. 2. Cum significantissimo loquendi genere, pro nobis execratio dicitur factus. Gal. 3: 13. conf. Deut. 21: 23. cui formulæ tantum abest ut satisfaciant adversarii, ut nihil omnino commune cum illa habeat eorum doctrina, quam de Christi munere, ejusque-partibus tradunt. Ubi perhibetur mortuus pro peccatis nostris. Rom. 4: 25. ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν pro peccatis nostris. 1. Cor. 15: 3. Ipse enim unam pro peccatis oblatam habens hostiam, in perpetuum consedit in dextra Dei. Hebr. 10: 12. Gal. 1: 4. & περὶ ἁμαρτίας. Pro peccato condemnavit peccatum in carne. Rom. 8: 3. & 1. Pet. 3: 18.
units.tr: XVII. Second, in the most significant mode of speech, he was made a curse for us. Gal. 3: 13; compare Deut. 21: 23. Our opponents are so far from satisfying this formula that their doctrine, which they hand down concerning the office of Christ and its parts, has nothing at all in common with it. There he is said to have died for our sins, Rom. 4: 25; ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν [for our sins], 1 Cor. 15: 3; For he, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sat down forever at the right hand of God, Heb. 10: 12; Gal. 1: 4; and περὶ ἁμαρτίας [concerning sin]. He condemned sin in the flesh as a sin offering, Rom. 8: 3; and 1 Pet. 3: 18.

units.la: XVIII. Tandem etiam per mortem Christi peccata nostra expiata esse liquet ex loco Rom. 5: 9, 10. Si enim quum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ipsius, multo magis reconciliati salvi erimus in vita ipsius. 2. Cor. 5: 19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans ipsis lapsus ipsorum. 1. Joh. 2: 2. Et ipse Christus expiatio est pro peccatis nostris. Huc pertinet, quod mors hæc sacrificium pro reatu appelletur. Efai. 53: 10. Eph. 5: 2. Christus tradidit se ipsum pro nobis oblationem & sacrificium Deo, odorem fragrantiæ. Hebr. 9. 14. Per spiritum æternum se ipsum obtulit Christus immaculatum Deo. Sacrificium videlicet illud, quod per victimas, Lev. 17: 11. & sacerdotes antiquos, Lev. 10: 17. adumbratum erat. Quæ omnia eam ob causam post peractum Christi sacrificium cum maxime cessant. Una enim oblatione consummavit in perpetuum, qui sanctificantur. Hebr. 10: 12, 14. Cum qua expiatione conjuncta est ἱλασμὸς proprie dicta, seu perfecta peccatorum remissio; sine exactione chirographi aut commemoratione peccati. Hebr. 10: 3, 4, 18. Eodem refer quod Christus dicatur venisse εἰς τὸ ἀνενέγκειν ἁμαρτίας. Hebr. 9: 28. quod non notat solum ablationem peccatorum, sed sublationem eorundem sursum in crucem; ut 1. Pet. 2: 24. Qui ipse nostra peccata sursum tulit in corpore suo super crucem. Quod & contentio primi cum secundo Christi adventu ibidem docet. Ut frustra
units.tr: XVIII. Finally, it is also clear that our sins were expiated through the death of Christ, from Rom. 5: 9, 10: For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. 2 Cor. 5: 19: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. 1 John 2: 2: And he himself is the expiation for our sins. To this belongs the fact that this death is called a sacrifice for guilt: Isa. 53: 10; Eph. 5: 2: Christ gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma. Heb. 9: 14: Through the eternal Spirit Christ offered himself without blemish to God. This is the sacrifice that was foreshadowed by the victims of Lev. 17: 11 and the ancient priests of Lev. 10: 17. All of these things have especially ceased after the sacrifice of Christ was completed for this very reason: For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. Heb. 10: 12, 14. Joined with this expiation is ἱλασμός [propitiation] properly so called, that is, the perfect remission of sins, without the cancelling of a bond or the remembrance of sin. Heb. 10: 3, 4, 18. To the same point refers the statement that Christ came εἰς τὸ ἀνενέγκειν ἁμαρτίας [to bear away sins], Heb. 9: 28, which signifies not only the removal of sins but their lifting up upward onto the cross, as in 1 Pet. 2: 24: Who himself bore our sins upward in his body on the cross. The contrast between the first and second coming of Christ in the same place also teaches this. Thus the opponents are wrong in vain, who wish that to bear sin indicates nothing other than to take it away.

units.la: {y} Morte sua ca- tx- piavit. frustra sint adversarii, qui ferre peccatum, nihil aliud indicare volunt, quam ea auferre.
units.tr: By his death he made atonement. The opponents are vain who wish to bear sin to mean nothing more than to remove it.

units.la: XIX. Iidem haec omnia eludere conantur, purgationem hanc peccatorum per sanguinem Christi in alium sensum detorquendo. Idque 1. quia scilicet effusio illa sanguinis non pretium, sed causa fuerit, per quam Christus accepit potestatem nos purgandi a peccatis, id est, liberandi a poenis eorum. At vero obstat locus diserte Matth. 26: 28. Hoc est sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. tum quoque ipsa illa purgatio per sanguinem, potestatem Christi antecessit. 2. Reponunt, purgare peccata, nihil aliud esse, quam purgationem eorum demonstrare; quatenus Christi sanguis promissiones Dei nobis confirmat, & promissam olim remissionem peccatorum nunc declarat. Verum illud vel minimo e Prophetis licuit, nec sanguine Christi hac in parte opus fuit, cum abunde per miracula praestari petuerit.
units.tr: XIX. The same people try to evade all these things by twisting this purification of sins through the blood of Christ into another sense. And they do this, first, because that effusion of blood was not the price but the cause through which Christ received the power to cleanse us from sins, that is, to free us from their punishments. But the passage Matt. 26: 28 stands in the way plainly: This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins. Moreover, that very purification by blood preceded the power of Christ. Second, they reply that to purge sins is nothing other than to show them to be purged, insofar as the blood of Christ confirms God's promises to us and now declares the remission of sins once promised. But that could have been done even by the least of the prophets, and the blood of Christ was not needed for this purpose, since he had already sufficiently provided it through miracles.

units.la: 3. Pergunt obtundere; ergo purgare peccata ad summum erit, conferre symbolam aliquam ad nostram regenerationem, videlicet argumentum quo persuaderi, & ad eam moveri possimus. At contra facit illud 1. Joh. 1: 7. Sanguis Jesu Christi filii ipsius purificat nos ab omni peccato. Ubi sanctificatio & purgatio peccatorum discernuntur. Vide & 1. Petr. 1: 2. Secundum praecognitionem Patris, in sanctificatione Spiritus, ad obedientiam & conspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi. Conf. Apoc. 1: 5. Atque ipse etiam fatetur Socinus, τὸ καθαρίζειν, quod sanguini Christi tribuitur, rectius liberationem a poena, quam animi emendationem notare.
units.tr: Third, they go on to wear us out: therefore to purge sins will at most be to contribute some token to our regeneration, namely an argument by which we can be persuaded and moved to it. But against this is 1 John 1: 7: The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. Here sanctification and the purging of sins are distinguished. See also 1 Pet. 1: 2: According to the foreknowledge of the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Compare Rev. 1: 5. Indeed Socinus himself admits that τὸ καθαρίζειν [to cleanse], which is ascribed to the blood of Christ, signifies more correctly liberation from punishment than the amendment of the mind.

units.la: XX. III. Sequitur nunc satisfactionis pretium. Pretium proprie est res aut factum aliquod, quod alicui pro alio persolvitur, ut ejus valore redimatur alter; atque eo nomine pretium hac in re venit. Venit filius hominis – ut daret animam suam redemptionis pretium pro multis. Matth. 20: 28. 1. Tim. 2: 6. 1 Pet. 1: 18, 19. Pretium vero illud ad legem Dei relatum; vel illius execrationem respicit, cui satisfactum per execrationem Christi, Gal. 3: 13. vel ejus mandatum & jus seu δικαίωμα, quod impletum est Christi obedientia. Per obedientiam unius justi constituuntur multi. Rom. 5: 19. Quamvis autem ad prius potissimum membrum satisfactio haec referatur; non tamen divellenda est satisfactio mortis ab obedientia vitae; cum alteram ab altera non sejungas, nisi utrique noxam inferas; & exutraque juncta, plena tandem surgit satisfactio; sine illa enim obedientia vitae, nulla nobis conferri potuisset vita. Per unum justitiae meritum
units.tr: XX. III. There follows now the price of satisfaction. A price is properly a thing or some deed that is paid to someone in place of another, so that the other is redeemed by its value; and in this sense the price comes into play here. The Son of Man came … to give his life as the price of redemption for many. Matt. 20: 28; 1 Tim. 2: 6; 1 Pet. 1: 18, 19. That price, moreover, is referred to the law of God, and it looks either to its curse, to which satisfaction was made by the curse borne by Christ, Gal. 3: 13, or to its command and right, or δικαίωμα [righteous requirement], which was fulfilled by the obedience of Christ: through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous. Rom. 5: 19. Although this satisfaction refers chiefly to the first member, nevertheless the satisfaction of death must not be separated from the obedience of life; for you do not separate the one from the other without doing harm to both, and from the two joined together a full satisfaction finally arises. For without that obedience of life no life could have been conferred on us. Through the one righteous act

units.la: III. Pretium. tum (seu causam) in omnes homines, in justificationem vitæ. Rom. 5. 18. conf. com. 19. Qui Christus Iesus, factus est nobis justitia &c. 1 Cor. 1: 30. Honor enim absoluti dominii divini, ut redintegraretur, requirebat utramque hanc obedientiam, licet ultimum complementum huic satisfactioni in passionibus Christi adjectum sit. Decebat ipsum—principem salutis ipsorum per passiones consummare. Heb. 2: 10.
units.tr: III. The price (or cause) for all men, for the justification of life. Rom. 5:18, compare verse 19. Who is Christ Jesus, made unto us righteousness, etc. 1 Cor. 1:30. For the honour of the absolute divine dominion to be restored, it required both of these obediences, although the final completion was added to this satisfaction in the sufferings of Christ. It was fitting that he, the author of their salvation, should be made perfect through sufferings. Heb. 2:10.

units.la: XXI. Inane igitur est, quod causatur Socinus, pretium semper esse aliquid externi & adventitii, ut aurum, argentum, similia; quod cum defit in Christi satisfactione, deesse quoque vult pretium: cum saepe pretium consistat in facto aliquo; non enim in poena aliquid annumeratur, uti fit in re concredita, sed omne debitum persolvitur praestando illud quod praestari debebat. nec alter Christus.
units.tr: XXI. It is therefore empty to allege, as Socinus does, that a price is always something external and adventitious, such as gold, silver, and the like; and because this is lacking in Christ's satisfaction, he wants to deny that there is a price at all. Often a price consists in some action. For nothing is reckoned as a penalty, as happens with a thing entrusted on deposit; rather every debt is paid by rendering what ought to have been rendered. Nor is Christ any different.

units.la: XXII. Pretium hoc sufficiens fuit, & merito contra carum. Tum propter personam persolventem, qui fuit ipse Deus; ex cujus dignitate pretii valor crescit. Tum propter intrinsecam rei oblatæ dignitatem; cum Deus & homo semetipsum obtulerit. Deus Ecclesiam proprio sanguine acquisivit. Act. 20: 28. Tertio etiam propter modum offerendi, qui divinus fuit, in persona divina; à qua, licet passiones in se essent finitæ, moralem tamen respectum infinitatis aliquo modo acceperunt.
units.tr: XXII. This price was sufficient, and rightly so, against them. First, on account of the person who paid it, who was God himself; the value of the price grows from his dignity. Second, on account of the intrinsic dignity of the thing offered, since God and man offered himself. God purchased the Church with his own blood. Acts 20:28. Third, on account of the manner of offering, which was divine, since it was in a divine person; and although his sufferings were in themselves finite, they nonetheless received, in a certain way, a moral regard of infinity from that person.

units.la: XXIII. Unde consequens est, satisfactionem hanc Christi, sufficiisse quoad substantiam; superabundantem vero fuisse quoad circumstantias illas, quæ Christo non conveniebant; æternam videlicet pœnæ durationem, desperationem &c. quæ tamen aliunde, ut jam vidimus, satis superque fuerunt compensatæ. Consequens item erit satisfactionem hanc non fuisse acceptilationem; quæ est commentitia & imaginaria solutio, quæque nihilo secius per victimas & cerimonias legales præstari potuisset, quod negatur Hebr. 9: 9. Quæ sacrificia non possunt quoad conscientiam consummare eum qui cultum præstat. Cum igitur tam operosa, tam cara Christi mors requisita fuerit, facile patet veram hanc & plenam esse solutionem.
units.tr: XXIII. Hence it follows that this satisfaction of Christ was sufficient as to its substance, but more than abundant as to those circumstances which did not belong to Christ: namely, the eternal duration of the punishment, despair, and so on. These, however, were elsewhere, as we have already seen, fully and more than fully compensated. It will also follow that this satisfaction was not an acceptilation, which is a made-up and imaginary release that could nonetheless have been achieved through the legal sacrifices and ceremonies. This is denied in Heb. 9:9: which sacrifices cannot make the worshipper perfect as to the conscience. Since, then, a death so laborious and so costly was required of Christ, it is easy to see that this solution is true and full.

units.la: XXIV. Declinanda igitur hic ab una parte, ridicula Pontificiorum superstitio; qua sanguini Christi ita parcunt, ut putent vel solam gutam ejus sufficiisse, cum in ea nec Deus fuisset ex æquo sanctificatus, nec odium ejus adversus peccatum satis ostensum; quam ad rem tractu temporis opus erat. Ab altera parte cavendum est, ne putemus, plus solutum esse, quam oportuit; cum pretium infinitum tum requiratur, ut infinitorum bonorum compotes fiamus, & æterna mala depellantur; quemadmodum ex luce solis nihil quod demas, superesset, si vel uni duntaxat homini luceat, cum tamen eadem luce mundus universus illustrari, & multo plures perfundi queant.
units.tr: XXIV. Here, therefore, we must avoid, on the one side, the ridiculous superstition of the Papists, who are so sparing of the blood of Christ that they think even a single drop of it sufficed. In that case neither would God have been equally sanctified, nor his hatred of sin sufficiently shown, for which a long span of time was needed. On the other side we must take care that we do not think more was paid than was necessary. For an infinite price is required both so that we may become partakers of infinite goods and so that eternal evils may be driven off. Just as nothing would be lacking from the light of the sun if it shone on only one man, though the same light could illuminate the whole world and bathe far more people.

units.la: XXV. Videndum nunc iv.cui proprie pretium hoc solutum fue- rit. Primo in vestibulo hic se iterum objicit Socinus;
units.tr: XXV. We must now consider to whom this price was properly paid. First, at the very threshold, Socinus again raises an objection:

units.la: cavillando, pretium alicui solvendum esse; verum in morte Christi, nulli cuiquam solutum; quare nec in ea pretium esse. At norunt Jurisconsulti, pœnæ creditorem proprie non dari; non enim judex in ea se, suamque privatam spectat utilitatem, uti supra dictum, sed bonum tantummodo publicum & ordinem rerum; itaque in pœna nulli proprie aliquid solvitur; quamvis impropriè, atque illo etiam modo à Christo factum est. Idque non diabolo, qui carnificis & tortoris tantum vices egit: sed Deo tanquam judici. Unus est legislator, qui potest salvare & perdere. Jac. 4: 12. Ne aliquando adversarius te tradat judici & judex te tradat ministro, & in custodiam conjiciaris. Matth. 5: 25. Patrique spectatim, qui ratione œconomiæ illius divinæ, judicis personam gerit, cui exhibita fuit hæc solutio. Nam quamvis filius quoad essentiam & re ipsa à Patre diversum quid non sit, est tamen diversus ab eo, qua θεανθρωπος & quatenus spectatur in hoc statu.
units.tr: by quibbling that the price must be paid to someone, but in the death of Christ nothing was paid to any person; therefore there was no price in it. But jurists know that properly speaking no creditor is given in punishment. For the judge does not look to himself and his own private advantage in it, as said above, but only to the public good and the order of things. So in punishment nothing is properly paid to anyone, although it was improperly paid by Christ, and in that way as well. Nor was it paid to the devil, who acted only as executioner and torturer, but to God as judge. There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. James 4:12. Lest at any time the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Matt. 5:25. And it was paid to the Father specifically, who, by reason of that divine economy, bears the person of judge, to whom this payment was offered. For although the Son is not in essence and in fact anything different from the Father, he is nonetheless different from him, as [θεάνθρωπος] theanthropos, and insofar as he is regarded in this state.

units.la: XXVI. v. Indaganda sunt modus & jus hujus satisfactionis; quo pacto Christus hanc præstare potuerit; ipse innocens pro nocentibus. Ubi notandum venit, in pœnis humanis capitalibus hunc quidem à Deo positum esse obicem, ne filius patris vicem gerat in subeundis pœnis.
units.tr: XXVI. v. The manner and right of this satisfaction must be investigated: by what means Christ, innocent, could render it on behalf of the guilty. Here it must be noted that in human capital punishments God has set this obstacle, that a son may not take the father's place in undergoing punishment.

units.la: Non occidentur patres pro (in textu est, propter vel cum) filiis, & filii non occidentur pro patribus, quisque ob peccatum suum occidetur. Deut. 24: 16. 2. Reg. 14: 6. Ezech. 18: 20. Anima peccans illa morietur, filius non feret de pravitate patris, nec pater feret de pravitate filii. Non tamen illam sibi Deus fixit metam, quin interdum pro jure suo, propter peccata patrum filios puniat; ut patet ex secundo præcepto decalogi, & 2. Sam. 21. quod ipsa naturæ lex dictat; quin certis in casibus inter gentes publici & legitimi juris est.
units.tr: The fathers shall not be put to death for (in the text it is, on account of or with) the children, nor shall the children be put to death for the fathers; each shall be put to death for his own sin. Deut. 24:16. 2 Kings 14:6. Ezek. 18:20. The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son. Yet God has not set this limit for himself so that he never, on his own right, punishes children for the sins of their fathers. This is clear from the second commandment of the Decalogue and from 2 Sam. 21, and the law of nature itself dictates it. Indeed, in certain cases it is part of the public and lawful right among nations.

units.la: XXVII. At vero præ hisce omnibus æquior causa & majus quoddam jus est Deo puniendi Christum ob peccata nostra; utpote qui non solum arctissimo naturæ & sanguinis nexu, sed etiam prolixo voluntatis consensu, nobiscum sit conjunctus: fidem enim suam
units.tr: XXVII. But, beyond all these, there is a fairer ground and a greater right for God to punish Christ for our sins, since he was joined to us not only by the closest bond of nature and blood, but also by a long-standing consent of will.

units.la: {v} Solutionis modus. suam pro nobis adstrinxit, & spopondit; quod sicut ab humanis legibus non abhorret, ita multo magis absoluto Dei imperio convenit. Atque hoc pacto patet, quomodo Deo non indecorum fuerit,Christum nostro loco punire. Verum nec etiam alienum à Christo fuit, sponsionem hanc suscipere, & fidem suam jubere; quo facit duplex potestas Christo peculiaris. 1. qua licuit ipsi ponere animam. Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo iterum accipiendi eam. Joh. 10: 18. tanquam membrorum suorum Dominus, quod nulli homini competit. 2. qua potuit illam liberare, & forti manu à morte vindicare; ut ibidem ipse ait Christus; quod nec item de ullo homine, pro alio morituro dici potest. Ut undequaque liquet juste omnino Christum, Goelem nostrum, cognatum, itemque vindicem & fidejussorem, pro nobis pati potuisse.
units.tr: {v} The manner of the solution. He bound himself by his own faith on our behalf, and pledged it. As this is not repugnant to human laws, so it agrees much more with the absolute dominion of God. In this way it is clear how it was not unfitting for God to punish Christ in our place. Yet nor was it foreign to Christ to undertake this pledge and to give his own faith: a twofold power peculiar to Christ makes it so. First, by which it was permitted to him to lay down his life: I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. John 10:18. He did so as Lord of his own members, which belongs to no man. Second, by which he was able to free it, and to rescue it from death by a strong hand, as Christ himself says in the same place. This cannot be said of any man who is to die for another. So it is entirely clear that Christ, our redeemer [goel, גֹּאֵל], our kinsman, and likewise our avenger and surety, could justly suffer on our behalf in every respect.

units.la: XXVIII. Subdole hic agit Socinus, dum plena manu largitur, posse Deum affligere creaturam innocentem occasione alienorum peccatorum; non vero punire. At 1. falsum est prius membrum:
units.tr: XXVIII. Socinus acts craftily here when, with a full hand, he grants that God can afflict an innocent creature on account of the sins of others, but not punish. But first, the former clause is false:

units.la: 2. Jam vidimus casus quoque dari, in quibus propter aliena peccata alii puniri possunt. 3. Christus insons, non afflictus est occasione alienorum peccatorum, ut quidem illi contendunt, sed veras dedit poenas à Deo judice ipsi irrogatas.Ut liberi essemus ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis execratio factus est. Gal. 3: 13. Non enim hunc in finem, vel ex ipsa Socini hypothesi, opus fuisset tam acerba Christi morte. Apertius vero contra hanc doctrinam excipit, inauditam esse; & nunquam locum habere hanc surrogationem vadis in poenis corporalibus; at tantum in multis pecuniariis. Nec mirum sane, cum in rebus humanis similis casus nunquam obtigerit: verum nec desunt exempla surrogationum in poenis corporalibus; qualia videre licet Gen. 42: 37. Et dixit Ruben ad patrem suum, dicendo, duos filios meos occides, si non reducam illum ad te 1. Reg. 20: 39–41. Tum quoque peculiaris est Christi ratio, ut §. praeced. ostensum. XXIX. vi. Restat nunc considerandum hujus satisfactionis meritum; nam quae satisfactio fuit respectu Dei, meritum fuit respectu nostri. Per obedientiam unius multi constituentur justi. Rom. 5: 19. & com. 21. Ut quemadmodum regnavit peccatum ad mortem, ita etiam gratia regnaret per justitiam ad vitam aeternam, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum — quod meritum fuit proprie dictum; cum omnes conditiones meriti in eo reperiantur; quin propter infinitam personae dignitatem meritum hoc fuit ex condigno, ut ajunt. Quod quidem meritum à satisfactione reapse non differt; sed pro vario tantum considerandi modo, prout vel ad Deum relatum, satisfactionis respectum habet; vel ad homines, meriti. Quare nullo modo meritum hoc divellendum est; ut vel morti ejus denegetur, in qua maxima meritus est; vel dicatur Christus, in vita nobis vitam meruisse, in morte tantum satisfecisse, cum in ipsa satisfactione meritum positum esse viderimus. Conjungenda ergo potius arctissime obedientia ejus vitæ & mortis, simulque universa humiliatio; exclusa tantum à merito exaltatione humanæ ejus naturæ.
units.tr: Second, we have already seen that there are cases in which others may be punished on account of the sins of others. Third, Christ, though innocent, was not afflicted on account of the sins of others, as they indeed contend, but suffered true punishments inflicted on him by God the judge. That we might be free from the curse of the law, since he became a curse for us. Gal. 3:13. For, even on Socinus's own hypothesis, there would have been no need for so harsh a death of Christ to this end. More openly, however, he objects against this doctrine that it is unheard of, and that such a substitution of a surety never has a place in bodily punishments, only in many monetary ones. Indeed there is no wonder in this, since in human affairs a similar case has never occurred. Yet examples of substitutions in bodily punishments are not lacking; such may be seen in Gen. 42:37: And Reuben said to his father, saying, Slay my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. 1 Kings 20:39–41. Moreover, Christ's case is peculiar, as was shown in the preceding section. XXIX. vi. It remains now to consider the merit of this satisfaction. For what was satisfaction with respect to God was merit with respect to us. By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Rom. 5:19, and verse 21: that as sin reigned unto death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. This was merit properly so called, since all the conditions of merit are found in it. Indeed, on account of the infinite dignity of the person, this merit was, as they say, of condign worth. This merit does not really differ from satisfaction, but only in the different way of considering it: in relation to God it has the aspect of satisfaction, and in relation to men, of merit. Therefore this merit must in no way be separated from it, so that either his death is denied to be meritorious, though it is the most meritorious of all, or it is said that Christ merited life for us in his life but only satisfied in his death, since we have seen that merit is contained in satisfaction itself. Rather, his obedience of life and death, and his whole humiliation together, must be joined most closely; only his exaltation of human nature is excluded from merit.

units.la: XXX. Male igitur Sociniani obducunt; Christum nihil meritum esse; quia nempe creditori tantum satisfecit, in qua solutione debiti, nullus merito locus superest; quod largimur omnino, siquidem proprio creditori, debitum à se contractum solvendo; alia vero jam est ratio, cum alieno satisfecerit. Male iidem meritum Christo respectu sui adscribunt, quod denegant ei respectu nostri, ac si illa invicem pugnarent: quod tantum abest, ut verum sit, ut quicquid sibi meruerit, nobis omne illud meruisse maxime censendus sit; & nihil ferme sibi meruerit, nisi in nostrum bonum. Sibi vero meruisse gloriam illam & beatitudinem in humanitate, docet Paulus Philip. 2:9. Se ipsum exinanivit – quamobrem & Deus ipsum superexaltavit & in gratia donavit ei nomen, quod supra omne nomen est. At de hoc negotio pluribus etiam visum lib. 11. cap. xv. §. x.— xiv.
units.tr: XXX. It is therefore wrong of the Socinians to maintain that Christ merited nothing, because he paid only to his creditor, and in the payment of a debt no room for merit remains. We fully grant this, provided one pays one's own creditor a debt one has contracted oneself. The case is quite different when someone pays on behalf of another. The same men wrongly ascribe merit to Christ with respect to himself while denying it to him with respect to us, as if these were mutually opposed. Far from it being true that whatever he merited for himself he merited for us, we should rather judge that he merited almost nothing for himself except for our good. That he merited for himself that glory and blessedness in his humanity, Paul teaches, Phil. 2:9: "He emptied himself ... wherefore God also highly exalted him and gave him in grace the name which is above every name." On this matter more has been said in book 11, ch. 15, §§10–14.

units.la: XXXI. Ex hac satisfactione sua Christus quoque justificatus est à debito, quod sponsor contraxerat, & à præcepto, quo obligabatur ad præstandam justitiam & omnes gratias N. T. de qua justificatione ejus videre est Psal. 16: 2. 1. Tim. 3: 16. Unde etiam ipsi competit hæreditas, præcipuè gentium, quâ habet nos ut <bl>ἀπόκληρον</bl> & λαὸν περιούσιον sive κληρονομίαν. Tit. 2: 14.
units.tr: XXXI. Through this satisfaction of his, Christ too was justified from the debt which the surety had contracted, and from the precept by which he was bound to render righteousness and all the graces of the New Testament. For this justification of his see Ps. 16:2; 1 Tim. 3:16. Hence there also belongs to him the inheritance, especially of the Gentiles, by which he holds us as those without an inheritance [ἀπόκληρον] and as a peculiar people [λαὸν περιούσιον], or possession [κληρονομίαν], Tit. 2:14.

units.la: XXXII. Atque ita nobis de veritate hujus satisfactionis constat, vidimusque rem ipsam nobis eo modo tradi ex S. Literis; contendamus nunc hanc lucem ad tenebras huic veritati offusas, ut ex utriusque comparatione lux hæc manifestior fiat. Quo in negotio nobis res erit cum Pontificiis, Socinianis, Anabaptistis & Remonstrantibus.
units.tr: XXXII. Thus we are assured of the truth of this satisfaction, and we have seen that the thing itself is delivered to us from Holy Scripture in this way. Let us now contend against the darkness spread over this truth, so that this light may become clearer by comparing the two. In this matter we shall have to deal with the Papists, the Socinians, the Anabaptists and the Remonstrants.

units.la: XXXIII. Ut igitur horum errorum scaturiginem repetamus, unde ad reliquos dimanarunt, initium faciendum erit à Pontificiis: qui 1. satisfactionem Christi temere & scelestè circumciduntur, eamque solum factam volunt pro peccato originali, vel actualibus ante baptismum commissis; pro iis vero quæ post baptismum committuntur, non admittunt, nisi ea lege, ut sint tantum mortalia, & restringatur ad reatum culpæ, pœnamque æternam; cæ tera enim hominibus reliqua faciunt, aliis modis expianda. Verum omnem circumcisionem & coarctationem tollit Paulus Rom. 8: 1. NULLA igitur nunc condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Jesu Christo. 1 Joh. 1: 7. Sanguis Jesu Christi filii ipsius purificat nos ab OMNI peccato.
units.tr: XXXIII. So, to trace the source of these errors from which the rest have flowed, we must begin with the Papists, who (1) rashly and wickedly cut down Christ's satisfaction, and want it made only for original sin or for actual sins committed before baptism. For sins committed after baptism they do not admit it, except on the condition that they are only mortal sins, and it is restricted to the guilt of fault and eternal punishment; the remaining debts they leave men to expiate by other means. But Paul removes all this cutting down and restriction, Rom. 8:1: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." 1 John 1:7: "The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from ALL sin."

units.la: XXXIV. Illud autem hac in re peccant Pontificii. 1. quod satisfactiones illas quæ Canonicæ tantum erant & externæ in foro Ecclesiæ, transtulerint nimis finistre ad satisfactiones veras & inter nas, apud Deum. 2 Diminuunt eandem Christi satisfactionem, & par te suitnon exigua mutilant, quando omnem obedientiæ ejus imputationem tollunt, & præter mortis ejus promeritum aliquod, nihil ad nos pertinere contendunt. 3. Majorem etiam in modum offu scant hanc, suffectio in ejus locum, aut saltem succenturiato alio sacrificio propitiatorio, Missæ nempe; contra Rom. 3: 24, 25. Qui justificantur gratis, ipsius gratia per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Je su, quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem cum sanguine ipsius.
units.tr: XXXIV. But in this matter the Papists go wrong: (1) in that they have transferred those satisfactions which were merely canonical and external, in the forum of the Church, far too crudely to true and inward satisfactions before God. (2) They diminish Christ's satisfaction itself and mutilate no small part of it, when they remove the imputation of his whole obedience and contend that, apart from some merit of his death, nothing pertains to us. (3) They also obscure this to a greater degree, by substituting satisfaction in his place, or at least a further propitiatory sacrifice alongside it, namely the Mass; contrary to Rom. 3:24, 25: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood."
1 John 1:7.

units.la: XXXV. Excipit hos Socinus, qui post Abailardum, statuit, peccata remitti a Deo per acceptilationem, sine vero & proprio pretio mortis Christi: de quo vidimus. 2. negat satisfactionem Scripturæ testimonio probari posse. 3. Subdole tamen fatentur satisfecisse Christum; ita nempe, ut expleverit omnia, quæ ipsi obeunda erant, ut summam illam potestatem adipisceretur; nequaquam vero justitiæ Dei satisfecisse volunt. 4. Largitur etiam illum victimam piacularem fuisse, pro peccatis nostris, id est, secundum ejus gloriam, pignus seu depositum gratiæ divinæ, nobis datæ; non vero quasi poena ab illo esset sublata. 5. Tandem quoque dat nobis, illum expiasse peccata, sed casso hoc & nullo prorsus sensu; scil. illum accepisse potestatem nos ab omni miseria liberandi. Hinc illum, doctrina magis & exemplo, ut alias visum, quam merito salvatorem facit.
units.tr: XXXV. Socinus follows these men. After Abelard, he held that sins are remitted by God through acceptilation, without the true and proper price of Christ's death, as we have seen. (2) He denies that satisfaction can be proved by the testimony of Scripture. (3) Yet craftily they confess that Christ made satisfaction, in the sense that he fulfilled all the things he had to undergo in order to obtain that supreme power; but they will by no means have him to have satisfied the justice of God. (4) He also concedes that Christ was a propitiatory victim for our sins, that is, according to his glory, a pledge or deposit of the divine grace given to us; but not as if punishment had been removed by him. (5) Lastly, he also grants us that Christ expiated sins, but in an empty and wholly meaningless sense, namely that he received the power of freeing us from all misery. Hence he makes Christ a saviour by teaching and example rather than by merit, as seen elsewhere.

units.la: 11. Socinianorum quædam dogmata
units.tr: 11. Some dogmas of the Socinians

units.la: XXXVI. Ultimo denique facile etiam nobis concedit, nostri causa mortuum esse Christum; at non nisi posito hoc obice, ut metonymice, (quæ solita scilicet eorum acies est, in fingendis tropis & schematibus) per mortem nihil aliud intelligatur, quam potestas illa, ipsi in bonum nostrum, morte interveniente, concessa. Atque hinc speciatim tres hosce mortis Christi fines ponunt: 1. ut hoc pacto novum fœdus, illiusque ajdunc-ta promissa divina sanciret. 2. ut homines ad amplectendas fœderis conditiones ad ducc. duceret: per illas autem conditiones intelligunt, tum obedientiam mandatorum Christi, tum spem promissionum divinarum; atque hanc utramque fidei nomine comprehendunt. 3. ut Christus hac ratione misericordiam edoctus, & supremam hanc potestatem adeptus, tanquam Pontifex, isque misericors nobis succurreret, & promissa divina reapse praestaret. Has potissimum ob causas mortuum esse Christum statuunt. Ex quibus liquet, quemadmodum subruto hoc fundamento, & negata satisfactione, cadat simul huic innixa fides vera & salvifica; quam idcirco aliam omnino faciunt; & pro vera fide substituunt obedientiam mandatorum Christi.
units.tr: XXXVI. Finally, they readily concede to us that Christ died for our sake; but only on this condition: that, by a metonymy (their usual cleverness in inventing tropes and figures), nothing else is understood by death than that power granted to him for our good through the intervention of his death. And so they specifically set down three ends of Christ's death: (1) that by this means he might ratify the new covenant and the divine promises attached to it; (2) that he might lead men to embrace the conditions of the covenant, which conditions they understand as both obedience to Christ's commands and hope in the divine promises, and they comprehend both under the name of faith; (3) that Christ, having thus learned mercy and attained this supreme power, might come to our aid as a merciful high priest and actually perform the divine promises. These are the chief reasons for which they hold that Christ died. From this it is clear how, with this foundation undermined and satisfaction denied, the true and saving faith resting upon it falls with it; which is why they make faith something quite different, and substitute obedience to Christ's commands for true faith.

units.la: XXXVII. Quibus omnibus ut sigillatim quicquam reponamus, nihil attinet; accurate interim haec tenebimus, unde singula facile cadunt; 1. Christo sic nihilo plus tribui, quam ipsis martyribus tribuitur à Paulo Col. 1:24. Nunc laetor in meis passionibus pro vobis, & vicissim impleo reliquias afflictionum Christi in carne mea pro corpore ejus; quod est Ecclesia. coll. 2. Tim. 2:10. quod tamen ipse negat Paulus 1.Cor. 1:13. An Christus divisus est? an Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis? aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? 2. Ita dicendum potius esset, Christum pro nobis resurrexisse; quam cruci affixum esse, cum potestatem illam quam ipsi tribuunt, ex resurrectione nactus fuerit: contra ac S. Scriptura, quae salutem cruci ipsius adscribit. Nos autem praedicamus Christum crucifixum. 1 Cor. 1:23.
units.tr: XXXVII. It is unnecessary to answer all these points one by one; meanwhile we shall hold to the following, by which each of them readily falls. (1) Christ is thus given no more than is given to the martyrs themselves by Paul, Col. 1:24: "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for his body, which is the Church"; compare 2 Tim. 2:10. Yet Paul himself denies this in the case of Christ, 1 Cor. 1:13: "Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" (2) It would rather have to be said that Christ rose again for us than that he was fixed to the cross, since they ascribe to him that power which he obtained from the resurrection. This is contrary to Holy Scripture, which ascribes salvation to his cross: "But we preach Christ crucified," 1 Cor. 1:23.

units.la: XXXVIII. 3. Ex hac sententia fructus mortis Christi in nullos redundant, nisi solos fideles N.T. exclusis plane V. Test. fidelibus; cum tamen Scriptura diserte testetur, a Christo, ut fidejussore, etiam pro fidelibus V. Test. redemptionis pretium solutum esse. Et propter hoc Testamenti Novi mediator est; ut morte obita ad redemptionem transgressionum, quae sub priori testamento erant, promissionem accipiant, vocati aeterna haereditatis. Hebr. 9:15. 4. Nunquam refert Scriptura, Christum tantum mortuum esse, ut Prophetam & Martyrem; verum expressissimis loquendi generibus, ut testatorem & testamenti conditorem. Hebr. 9:15,16,17. Gal. 3:17. Testamentum ante ratum factum à Deo in Christum, lex, quae post quadringentos & triginta annos extitit, non facit irritum, ad obolendam premissionem. Act. 20:28.
units.tr: XXXVIII. (3) From this view the fruit of Christ's death flows to none except the faithful of the New Testament alone, the faithful of the Old Testament being plainly excluded. Yet Scripture expressly testifies that the price of redemption was paid by Christ as surety also for the faithful of the Old Testament: "And for this reason he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, a death having taken place for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance," Heb. 9:15. (4) Scripture never speaks of Christ as having died merely as a prophet and martyr, but in the most express terms as testator and maker of the testament, Heb. 9:15, 16, 17; Gal. 3:17: "The testament previously ratified by God in Christ, the law which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul it so as to abolish the promise." Acts 20:28.

units.la: XXXIX. 5. Tum non sine insigni in Deum injuria statuitur, Christum nobis in morte sua solummodo exemplum exhibuisse; eo quippe tollitur 1. omnis demonstratio justitiae Dei in peccatores. 2. quasi Deus ex se non sit fide dignus, & alio egeat, qui fidem pro ipso adstringat; Christum, qui nostro nomine apud Deum sponsorem agit, faciunt pro deo apud nos spondere, qui homo cum sit, divina nobis confirmabit promissa; atque ita simul rerum ordinem invertunt.
units.tr: XXXIX. (5) Then it is laid down, not without a notable injury to God, that Christ in his death showed us only an example. By this one removes (1) every demonstration of the justice of God towards sinners; (2) as if God were not of himself worthy of trust and needed another to bind himself to faith on his behalf. They make Christ, who acts as surety with God in our name, into one who gives surety to us on God's behalf, who, being a man, will confirm the divine promises to us; and thus at the same time they invert the order of things.

units.la: XL. Fines illi particulares, quos morti Christi adsignant, ejusdem omnino commatis sunt. 1. Quid confirmatio illa novi foederis, divinarumque promissionum magis dicit, quam quod etiam martyrum sanguis praestare potuit, qui Euangelium confirmarunt, sine tamen peccatorum remissione? 1. Cor. 1:13. tum quoque tantundem ipsa Christi miracula efficere potuerunt. Ut cognoscatis, quod potestatem habeat filius hominis in terra remittendi peccata &c. Matth. 9: 6, 7, 8. quin & multo magis fecerunt illud Christi resurrectio & gloria; quibus tamen nunquam peccatorum remissio adscribitur; ut peculiare quicquam & quod caeteris commune non est, in morte Christi indicetur.
units.tr: XL. Those particular ends that they assign to the death of Christ are wholly of the same kind. (1) What does that confirmation of the new covenant and of the divine promises say more than what the blood of the martyrs could also accomplish, since they confirmed the Gospel, yet without the remission of sins? 1 Cor. 1:13. Likewise, the miracles of Christ themselves could achieve as much: That you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, etc. Matth. 9:6, 7, 8. Indeed, Christ's resurrection and glory did far more of this, yet the remission of sins is never ascribed to them. Thus something peculiar, which is not common to the rest, is not indicated in the death of Christ.

units.la: XLI. 2. Similiter vanus est ille praetextus finis, de adducendis per Christi mortem hominibus ad ineundas conditiones Novi Test. nam vel ex ipsorum sententia, non adeo illustris apparuit Dei charitas in morte Christi; neque certius, aut praeclarum magis exemplum dedit haec, quam universa ejus vita; neque ira Dei vehementior exarsisse vita est, ut a peccato deterreremur; neque aliquid per illam nobis revera acquisitum est, ut ad virtutem alliceremur; & novis argumentis constringeremur.
units.tr: XLI. (2) Likewise, that pretext of an end is empty, namely that by Christ's death men are brought to enter the conditions of the New Testament. For, even by their own judgment, the love of God did not appear so conspicuously in the death of Christ; nor did this give a more certain or more remarkable example than his whole life; nor has the wrath of God blazed more fiercely in it than in his life, so that we might be deterred from sin; nor has anything really been acquired for us through it, so that we might be drawn to virtue and bound by new arguments.

units.la: XLII. 3. Eadem omnino est ratio tertii illius finis, quo volunt Christum morte interveniente accepisse potestatem nos servandi & a peccatis absolvendi. Nam 1. ipse Socinus fatetur, Christum jam eam potestatem in terra habuisse, quod ex Scriptura saltem vel maxime palam est. Ut cognoscatis quod potestatem habeat filius hominis in terra remittendi peccata. Matth. 9:6. 2. Ita quoque, ut jam vidimus, ad fideles Veteris Test. nullo modo spectasset haec mors, ejusque effectus, cum tamen illi per Christum vitam aeternam adepti sint; quando Christus, ex placito Socini, nondum illa potestate praeditus fuit. 3. nec ipse Socinus dabit hoc, Christum nos liberasse a servitute peccati, sed tantum a miseria & malo ejus; quippe qui nequidem salutem ipsam nobis praestiterit, sed viam duntaxat monstraverit, qua nosmet ipsos ipsi liberemus. At vero liberavit nos Christus per ἀντίλυτρον, quod sane non datur liberandis, sed illi, a quo sunt liberandi, ut per hujus valorem, libertatem & salutem eorum impetret: qui verus est & dignus mortis Christi efsectus, non ii, quos commentus est Socinus. Rom. 3:24. XLIII. Rudiores hisce in rebus sunt, at saepe non meliores Anabaptistae; qui 1. negant Christum in anima sua iram Dei percepisse, aut poenas infernales sensisse: quia scilicet Scriptura totidem verbis illud non dicit: quasi vel corpus sine anima dolore affici posse, nec dolores animae ej is memorentur. 2. Christum etiam stricte loquendo, pro nobis non satisfecisse, sed tantum exemplum praebuisse: scripto videlicet consignatum est, unum pro altero non morituram. Ezech. 18. verum hisce jam supra occurrimus.
units.tr: XLII. (3) The reasoning about that third end is wholly the same, by which they hold that Christ, by his intervening death, received the power to save us and absolve us from sins. For (1) Socinus himself admits that Christ already had that power on earth, which is at least very plainly evident from Scripture: That you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins. Matth. 9:6. (2) Likewise, as we have already seen, this death and its effects would not have had any bearing on the faithful of the Old Testament, yet they obtained eternal life through Christ; since, according to the pleasure of Socinus, Christ was not yet endowed with that power. (3) Nor will Socinus himself grant that Christ freed us from the slavery of sin, but only from its misery and evil; for he did not even give us salvation itself, but merely pointed out the way by which we ourselves might free ourselves. Yet Christ truly set us free through [ἀντίλυτρον], a ransom, which is certainly not given to those to be freed, but to him from whom they are to be freed, so that through its worth he might obtain their liberty and salvation. This is the true and worthy effect of the death of Christ, not those which Socinus has invented. Rom. 3:24. XLIII. The Anabaptists are cruder in these matters, yet often no better; who (1) deny that Christ in his soul bore the wrath of God or felt the pains of hell, because, of course, Scripture does not say this in so many words, as if the body could be affected by pain without the soul, and its anguish of soul were not recorded. (2) They also deny that Christ, strictly speaking, satisfied for us, but only gave an example; for it is written that one shall not die for another. Ezek. 18. But we have already met these points above.

units.la: XLIV. Errant pariter Remonstrantes. 1. Dum quidam eorum statuunt Christum non sustinuisse nostro loco poenas gehennales, sed mortem duntaxat temporariam; eamque plenae satisfactionis vicem a Deo fuisse habitam & acceptam. De quibus jam actum. 2. dum contendunt, huic solum fini Christum mortuum, ut Patri acquireret jus nobiscum redintegrandi foedus, & de remissione peccatorum contrahendi, quacunque vellet conditione. Sed 1. non Patri quicquam acquisivit Christus, cui omnia competebant; at nobis, & quidem reconciliationem actualem, utpote quibus omnia deerant. 2. Posita morte Christi nova conditio justitiae iniri non poterat; nisi haec sola, quae nunc rata est, & testamento Christi unice innititur; neque enim novo pacto legali ullus locus concedi poterat. 3. non ita nobis impetrata fuisset reconciliatio, sed tantum nova conditio & modus constitutus, quo reconciliari possemus, dummodo nobis ipsi ne desimus. 4. nec esset inde, quare magis Christo illud imputaremus, quam nobis ipsis, quippe qui conditionem illam praestiterimus. 5. denique repugnat hoc naturae sponsionis, per quam constat, primarium debitorem ipso actu, ut ajunt, liberari debere; nos vero hic non liberari censemur, nisi accedente demum novo pacto.
units.tr: XLIV. The Remonstrants likewise err. (1) While some of them hold that Christ did not bear the pains of hell in our place, but only a temporary death, and that this was regarded and accepted by God in place of full satisfaction. These matters have already been dealt with. (2) While they contend that Christ died for this end alone: that he might acquire for the Father the right to renew the covenant with us and to contract the remission of sins on whatever condition he wished. But (1) Christ acquired nothing for the Father, to whom all things belonged; but for us he acquired actual reconciliation, since we lacked everything. (2) Once Christ had died, a new condition of righteousness could not be entered upon, except this one, which is now ratified and rests solely on the testament of Christ; for no place could be granted to a new legal covenant. (3) Reconciliation would not have been obtained for us in this way, but only a new condition and a mode established by which we might be reconciled, provided only that we ourselves did not fail. (4) Nor would there be any reason why we should impute it to Christ rather than to ourselves, since we are the ones who had fulfilled that condition. (5) Finally, this contradicts the nature of a surety, by which it is established that the primary debtor must, as they say, be released by the very act; but we here are not considered released unless a new covenant finally intervenes.

units.la: XLV. iii. Dum non absolutam, sed conditionariam reddunt hanc satisfactionem; quae Deo quidem plena sit, sed nobis non efficax, nisi demum, ubi eam prona voluntate acceperimus; caeteroquin ipsam hanc satisfactionem ex Dei voluntate irritam facimus: quomodo non veretur Episcopius profari. Verum obstat hisce; quod 1. morti Christi assignetur, praesens & actualis reconciliatio, tanquam repraesentato jam pretio; quae idcirco ex nulla conditione suspendi potest.
