Et ipse Jesus Christus expiatio est pro peccatis nostris. 1. Joh. 2: 2. Rom. 3: 25. Omnia autem sunt ex Deo, qui reconciliavit nos secum in Jesu Christo. 2. Cor. 5: 18. In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Col. 1: 14. Et Et placuit per ipsum omnia reconciliare ad se, pacem faciens (sive dum pacem fecit) per sanguinem crucis ejus per ipsum. com. 20. Rom. 8: 34. & praecipue 5: 10.
units.tr: XLV. (3) While they make this satisfaction not absolute but conditional, which is indeed full for God, yet not effective for us unless we have at last accepted it with a willing mind; otherwise, by God's will, they make this very satisfaction void. Episcopius does not fear to utter this. But against these things stands the fact that (1) to the death of Christ is ascribed present and actual reconciliation, as if the price were already paid; which therefore cannot be suspended on any condition. And Jesus Christ himself is the propitiation for our sins. 1 John 2:2. Rom. 3:25. But all things are of God, who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ. 2 Cor. 5:18. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. Col. 1:14. And it pleased (the Father) through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace (or, when he made peace) through the blood of his cross, through him. Col. 1:20. Rom. 8:34, and especially 5:10.

units.la: XLVI. 2. Cum conditio haec suspensa haereret ex voluntate hominis, eaque indifferente & ambigua; incertum omnino & ambiguum fuisset, totum hoc opus, quod tum Deo indignum est, quem mutata hominis voluntate, ipsum mutari necesse esset: quique cum aeternum praescīverit, quosdam mortem Christi aspernaturos, nullo tamen consilio, nulloque scopo filium pro iis morti tradidisset: tum Dei rerumque naturae contrarium fuisset; nam cum hominum voluntates Deus flectat, frustra fingitur exspectare, quo tandem evasurus sit earum motus: tum quoque promissis Novi Foederis non convenit. Quod super potioribus promissionibus in legis formulam redactum est. Hebr. 8: 6.
units.tr: XLVI. (2) Since this condition would hang suspended on the will of man, and that will is indifferent and ambiguous, it would be wholly uncertain and doubtful whether this whole work was accomplished, which would be unworthy of God, for he would necessarily have to be changed if the human will were changed. And since he had foreknown from eternity that some would spurn the death of Christ, yet without any plan or aim he would have given up his Son to death for them; this would be contrary to God and to the nature of things. For since God bends human wills, it is vain to imagine that he waits to see where their movements will finally lead. Nor does it agree with the promises of the New Covenant: which has been enacted on better promises. Heb. 8:6.

units.la: XLVII. 3. Denique cum satisfactio sit surrogatio unius pro alio, absonum omnino erit illam ex conditione suspenderi. Hoc judicantes, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt. 2. Cor. 5: 15. Ipse crucia batur propter defectiones nostras, continebatur ob praevaritates nostras. Esai. 53: 5.
units.tr: XLVII. (3) Finally, since satisfaction is the substitution of one for another, it will be utterly absurd to make it depend on a condition. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died. 2 Cor. 5:15. He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities. Isa. 53:5.

units.la: XLVIII. iv. Contradicunt hoc modo; satisfactionem Christi universalem esse pro omnibus, subtratam quippe foederi gratiae universalis, ut pro pereuntibus aeque ac salvandis Christus mortem obierit; nam merito mortis ejus tantum effectum est, ut Deus cum peccatoribus sit reconciliabilis, iisque det gratiam sufficientem ad reconciliationem consequendam, si velint. Huic gemina est aliorum distinctio; qua Christum dicunt mortuum pro omnibus sufficienter, non vero efficaciter. Vide Apolog. pag 94,95.
units.tr: XLVIII. iv. They contradict this in the following way: they say that the satisfaction of Christ is universal, for all, since it is included in the universal covenant of grace, so that Christ died for those who perish just as much as for those who are saved; for by the merit of his death it has only been brought about that God can be reconciled to sinners, and that he gives them sufficient grace to obtain reconciliation, if they will it. Alongside this they make a twofold distinction of others, by which they say that Christ died sufficiently for all, but not effectively. See the Apology, pp. 94, 95.

units.la: XLIX. At i. insolens est & inauditum in S. Scriptura, eodem prorsus modo mortuum esse Christum pro damnandis ac salvandis. vide Matth. 21. Joh. 10. & 17. Eph. 5. 2. Itidem absurdum est, Deum reconciliabilem factum, & peccata posse remitti; cum non semel expressissime peccata dicantur jam reapse condonata. Hoc judicantes, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt.
units.tr: XLIX. But (1) it is strange and unheard of in Holy Scripture that Christ died in exactly the same way for those who are damned and for those who are saved. See Matth. 21; John 10 and 17; Eph. 5. (2) It is likewise absurd that God should be made reconcilable and that sins can be remitted, when sins are not once but most expressly said to have been already truly forgiven. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5: 15. & com. 18. Omnia autem sunt ex Deo, qui reconciliavit nos secum in Jesu Christo. 3. Turpiter hoc modo se ipsos jugulant, cum sufficienter mortuum velint Christum, non vero efficaciter; quae se mutuo tollunt; cum sine efficacia nulla sit sufficientia. 4. Omnia illa quae huc aurigantur, tum ipse satisfactionis modus in Christo; tum omnes loquendi modi, notant semper aliquid quod jam revera fit, non quod possit esse. Ita in Scriptura mori pro alio quo semper significat surrogationem, adeoque actualem satisfactionem; quare vel peccata nostra in Christo punita sunt, quando simul vere remissa esse oportet; sin vero; vanam esse omnem Christi sponsionem necesse est. De quibus amplius cap. seq.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:15, and verse 18. But all things are of God, who has reconciled us to himself in Jesus Christ. (3) In this way they shamefully cut their own throats, since they want Christ to have died sufficiently but not effectively; which cancel each other out, since without efficacy there is no sufficiency. (4) All those things that are dragged in here, both the very mode of satisfaction in Christ and all the modes of speech, always denote something that is really done already, not what might be possible. Thus in Scripture to die for another always signifies substitution, and so actual satisfaction; so either our sins were punished in Christ, when they ought at the same time to be truly remitted; or else every surety of Christ must be vain. More on these matters in the following chapter.

units.la: L. v. Fallunt item, cum ita ordinant decreta Dei; ut Deum prius velint decrevisse filium dare morti; tum eos eligere, quos praevidit in illum creditur os; in quo Lutheranorum vestigia premunt: ut mois Christi praeordinata sit electioni ad vitam aeternam. At nihil absurdius est, quam ut Deus prius media ordinaverit, quam finem; cum satisfactio medium sit ad salutem, ubi videlicet haec duo inter se conferuntur; respectu enim Dei coordinata sunt haec omnia, qui simul destinavit salutem, simulque satisfactionem; adeo ut in decreto Dei mors Christi non praecesserit nostram fidem; quamvis in executione res aliter se habeat.
units.tr: L. v. They also go astray when they so arrange God's decrees that they hold God first decreed to give his Son to death, and then chose those whom he foresaw would believe in him (here they tread in the footsteps of the Lutherans), so that the death of Christ was foreordained to the election to eternal life. But nothing is more absurd than that God should ordain the means before the end, since satisfaction is a means to salvation, when these two are compared with each other. For with respect to God all these things are coordinated: he simultaneously destined salvation and satisfaction, so that in God's decree the death of Christ did not precede our faith, although in execution the matter stands otherwise.

units.la: LI. Post hanc sequitur alter mortis Christi fructus, ex satisfactione fluens, quae est nostri cum Deo reconciliatio.
units.tr: LI. After this follows the other fruit of Christ's death, flowing from satisfaction, which is our reconciliation with God.

units.la: LII. Hac autem reconciliatio, ne in ipso limine impingamus, non est concipienda καταλλαγη, ut fingit Socinus, seu tantum à nostra parte, quae fiat per regenerationem, qua revertimur ad Deum, illique nosmet ipsos supplices objicimus, praetexto loco 2. Cor. 5: 20. Reconciliamini cum Deo. – nam liquet apertissime ex Scriptura, aeque nobis Deum reconciliatum esse, quam nos Deo.
units.tr: LII. This reconciliation, so that we do not stumble at the very threshold, is not to be conceived as reconciliation [καταλλαγή] in the way Socinus imagines, or as something only on our side, effected by regeneration, by which we turn back to God and present ourselves to him as suppliants, citing 2 Cor. 5:20 as a pretext: Be reconciled to God. For it is quite clear from Scripture that God has been reconciled to us just as much as we have to God.

units.la: LIII. Repugnat hisce etiam sinistra Remonstrantium opinio, qui impetratam quidem omnibus reconciliationem, sed non applicatam volunt, ut Deus non nisi credentibus & obedientibus sit reconciliatus; reconciliabilis tamen omnibus. Primum intelligi volunt 2. Cor. 5: 19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans ipsis lapsus: secundum ibidem com. 20. Itaque nomine Christi legatione fungimur, & velut Deo rogante per nos, oramus Christi nomine, reconciliamini Deo. Verum hoc pacto 1. tollitur Testamentum Novi foederis, quod non hypotheticum est, sed absolutum. Ubi enim testamentum est, mortem necesse est contingere testatoris: Testamentum enim in mortuis firmum est. Hebr. 9: 16, 17. Ego at, pono vobis, sicut mihi Pater disposuit regnum. Luc. 22: 29. 2. Cum hypothetica hac reconciliatione, conciliari non possunt loca Eph. 2: 15, 16. Pars. II. P Col. 2: 14. Hebr. 10: 14. Una oblatione consummavit in perpetuum qui sanctificantur & vs. 17. Peccatorum ipsorum & iniquitatum ipsorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: LIII. The unsound opinion of the Remonstrants also conflicts with these. They hold that reconciliation has indeed been obtained for all but has not been applied, so that God is reconciled only to believers and the obedient, yet is reconcilable to all. They wish first to understand 2 Cor. 5:19: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their trespasses to them; and secondly, in the same place, verse 20: So we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us; we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. But in this way, first, the Testament of the New Covenant is abolished, which is not conditional but absolute. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must take place. For a testament is valid only at death. Heb. 9:16, 17. I covenant to you, as my Father has covenanted to me, a kingdom. Luke 22:29. Second, the passages Eph. 2:15, 16, Col. 2:14, and Heb. 10:14 cannot be reconciled with this hypothetical reconciliation. Pars. II. P Col. 2:14. Heb. 10:14. By one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified; and verse 17: Their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more.

units.la: LIV. 3. Non consistit cum ea mors Christi, ut sponsoris nostri, per quam reapse reconciliati sumus. In tantum melioris testamenti extitit sponsor Jesus. Hebr. 7: 22. Hoc judicantes, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt. 2. Cor. 5: 15. Caeteroquin enim, ut supra vidimus, non punita sunt in ipso nostra peccata. 4. Frustra quoque reconciliationem illam priorem universalem faciunt, cum ipsi extra illam amandent fideles Veteris Test. 5. Denique ita fieri potuisset, ut lytrum solvisset, mortemque obiisset Christus, nulli bono; quippe, unde ipse nihil reportasset praemii, nec quisquam alius ex ea vel minimum salutis retulisset: simulque testator fuisset Christus, cum tamen nullum forte habuisset haeredem? quare frustra mori, frustra testari potuisset Christus; quod tamen negat Paulus Gal. 2: 21. Si enim per legem est justitia, ergo Christus frustra mortuus est.
units.tr: LIV. Third, the death of Christ as our surety, by which we are actually reconciled, does not agree with that view. Jesus has become the surety of a better testament. Heb. 7:22. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all died. 2 Cor. 5:15. Otherwise, as we have seen above, our sins were not punished in him. Fourth, they vainly posit that earlier universal reconciliation, since they exclude from it the faithful of the Old Testament. Fifth, it could thus have come about that Christ gave his life as a ransom and died for no good, since he would have gained no reward from it, and no one else would have derived the least salvation from it; and at the same time Christ would have been a testator, though perhaps having no heir at all? Hence Christ could have died in vain and made a testament in vain, which Paul nevertheless denies, Gal. 2:21: For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died in vain.

units.la: LV. Huc etiam vehificantur illi, qui dispartiuntur reconciliationem in absolutam, & in comparatam, seu ex conditione suspensam; ut Christus non prorsus propitiationem & placamentum impetraverit, nisi ea lege, ut ipsa haec reconciliatio per Sp. sanctum & fidem intimaretur. Quae sane indigna fuisset filio Dei ratio, & labori suo tam immani non conveniens, ut beneficium tam care acquisitum, non nisi post novam conditionem aliunde praestandam, daretur. Nullam ergo haec reconciliatio agnoscit legem aut conditionem; sed merus est effectus sponsoris, isque secundum pactum aliquod, ex quo dictum, reconciliationem hanc absolutam in homines per Sp. Sanctum & fidem redundaturam esse; atque ita juxta promissus est Sp. Sanctus & fides, citra omnem incertam conditionem.
units.tr: LV. Those also are carried along who divide reconciliation into an absolute one and one obtained, or suspended on a condition, as if Christ had not wholly obtained propitiation and appeasement except on the condition that this same reconciliation be made known through the Holy Spirit and faith. This would surely have been an unworthy plan for the Son of God, and not in keeping with so immense a labour, that a benefit so dearly bought should be given only after a new condition to be supplied from elsewhere. Therefore this reconciliation acknowledges no law or condition; it is the mere effect of the surety, and that according to some agreement, from which it follows that this absolute reconciliation will flow over to men through the Holy Spirit and faith. And so the Holy Spirit and faith are promised in accordance with it, without any uncertain condition.

units.la: LVI. Interpolans haec Episcopius, realem omnino ait & actualem esse, etiam a parte Dei, hanc reconciliationem; ea tamen lege, ne homo illam negligat; ut nulla quicquam ex parte desit, sed utrinque plena sit & perfecta. Verum liquido contra apparet, Deum non omnibus quantum in se, placatum esse, aut eodem affectu prosequi; quo nihil crebrius & studiosius Scriptura inculcat. Ita 1. sub Veteri Test. ut anteacta Patrum tempora praetereamus, adoptat Israelitas, rejectis gentibus. Nam populus sanctus tu es. Jehovae Deo tuo, te elegit Jehovah, ut sis ipsi in populum peculiarem ex omnibus populis. Deut. 7: 6. Psal. 147: 18, 19. 2. In Novo Test. versis rerum vicibus, Judæis exterminatis, adsciscit gentes. Quod querit Israel, hoc non est consecutus. Electio autem consecuta est, reliqui vero obcaluerunt, quemadmodum scriptum est, dedit illis Deus spiritum compunctionis: oculos, ut non videant, & aures ut non audiant, usque in hodiernum diem. Rom. 11:7,8. 3. nec etiamnum multis hominibus, quinimo populis, modus & via salutis oftensa est, quod tamen fieri oportuisset, si quidem omnibus impetrata salus. 4. Nec absoluta erit illa reconciliatio, quæ ex mutabili hominis voluntate & conditione prorsus incerta, suspensa est. 5. Tum quoque non nisi ad adultos spectabit hæc reconciliatio, alienis ab ea infantibus, utpote quibus hæc conditio offerri non possit.
units.tr: LVI. Episcopius, in qualifying these things, says that this reconciliation is wholly real and actual, even on God's part; yet on the condition that man not neglect it, so that nothing is lacking on any side, but it is full and perfect on both. But it clearly appears to the contrary that God has not been reconciled to all as far as in himself lies, nor does he regard them with the same affection, which Scripture most often and most earnestly impresses upon us. Thus, first, under the Old Testament (to pass over the earlier times of the Fathers), he adopted the Israelites and rejected the Gentiles: For you are a holy people to Jehovah your God; Jehovah has chosen you to be his own special people out of all the peoples. Deut. 7:6. Ps. 147:18, 19. Second, in the New Testament, when the situation was reversed, with the Jews cast off, he took in the Gentiles: What Israel seeks, it has not obtained; but the chosen have obtained it, and the rest were hardened, as it is written: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, down to this very day. Rom. 11:7, 8. Third, even now the way and manner of salvation has not been revealed to many people, indeed to whole nations, which yet ought to have happened if salvation had been obtained for all. Fourth, that reconciliation will not be absolute which is suspended on the changeable will and condition of man, which is wholly uncertain. Fifth, this reconciliation will also apply only to adults, since infants, being strangers to it, cannot be offered this condition.

units.la: LVII. Porro pergit errare Episcopius, circa redemptionem Christi; quam duplicem facit; alteram prævenientem, quæ ad homines movendos conducit ut redimi se patiantur. 2. Cor. 5:18, 20.
units.tr: LVII. Further, Episcopius goes on erring concerning the redemption of Christ, which he makes twofold: one preceding, which serves to move men so that they allow themselves to be redeemed. 2 Cor. 5:18, 20.

units.la: Alteram, qua, persuasi jam homines, & in mutuam gratiam cum Deo reversi, reapse à morte liberantur; quæ redemptio completa illi dicitur, eaque locum habet in iis, qui constanter Christo obedire perseverant; sicut priorem inde incompletam vocat. Sed indigna nimis & perversa hæc est rei tractatio; nam 1. redemptio illa præveniens, nomen suum tueri non potest; cum redemptionis tantum sit oblatio; uti nec altera, quæ ejusdem est applicatio, qua homines vel illam sibi, vel ad illam se applicant. 2. Quod alteram illam completam vocet, non nisi demum post emensum vitæ nostræ stadium, fallit itidem, cum redemptio incompleta nulla detur; & etiam in hac vita certo redimantur omnes, pro quibus Christus mortuus est. Act. 26: 17,18.
units.tr: The other, by which men, now persuaded and returned into mutual grace with God, are actually freed from death; this redemption is called complete by him, and it takes place in those who persevere in constant obedience to Christ; just as he calls the former incomplete. But this handling of the matter is far too unworthy and perverse. For, first, that preceding redemption cannot maintain its own name, since it is only an offering of redemption, just as the other, which is its application, by which men either apply it to themselves or themselves to it, is not redemption either. Second, that he calls the other complete, only after the course of our life has been run through, is likewise a mistake, since no incomplete redemption is given; and even in this life all those for whom Christ died are certainly redeemed. Acts 26:17, 18.

units.la: LVIII. Ex iisdem lacunis hausit idem, cum duplici modo Christum redemptorem vocat: priori, redemptor est sine effectu; quatenus ad salutem consequendam homines adducit, nulla tamen certa cum efficientia: posteriori modo, cum effectu; quatenus post perseveratum sanctitatis studium, plenam salutem eamque ir- recusabilem confert. Quando Christus Salvator noster erit, non ut Sacerdos, sed ut Rex tantum, qui ex mera sua potestate vitam æternam nobis largitur; cum tamen & reapse & certissimo cum effec- tu, tanquam sacerdos, propitiatorio suo sacrificio nos salvet. Una oblatione consummavit in perpetuum, qui sanctificantur. Hebr. 10: 14. & 9: 24. Ipse salvabit populum suum à peccatis ipsorum. Matth. 1:21. LIX. Ultimus denique mortis Christi fructus restat; quo legata est salvandis hæreditas vitæ æternæ. Et ego dispono vobis, sicut Pater vita aterna.
units.tr: 58. The same man drew from the same shallow pits when he calls Christ the Redeemer in two ways. In the first way he is a redeemer without effect, in that he brings men toward obtaining salvation but without any certain efficacy. In the second way he is a redeemer with effect, in that after a sustained pursuit of holiness he confers full salvation, which cannot be revoked. Christ our Saviour will not be a priest in that sense but only a king, who bestows eternal life on us out of his sheer power, whereas in fact and with the most certain effect he saves us as priest, by his propitiatory sacrifice. By one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. Heb. 10:14; 9:24. He will save his people from their sins. Matt. 1:21. 59. Last of all remains the final fruit of Christ's death, by which the inheritance of eternal life is bequeathed to those who are to be saved. And I appoint to you, as my Father appointed to me, eternal life.

units.la: termihi disposuit regnum. Luc. 22: 29, 30. quem etiam intercipiunt, quin plenum ejus effectum negant, Sociniani & Remonstrantes: sed planissime probari potest. 1. Ex testamentaria Christi dispositione, quæ morte ejus confirmata est. Testamentum enim in mortuis firmum est. Heb. 9: 16, 17. 2. Ex mandato Patris, cui cum Christus satisfecerit, omnibus etiam sibi datis vitam æternam acquisivit. Hæc est voluntas Patris qui me misit, ut omne, quod dedit mihi, non perdam ex eo: Hæc vero est voluntas ejus qui me misit, ut omnis qui videt filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Joh. 6: 39, 40. 3. Ex ipso fine mortis Christi, qui is erat, ut vitam æternam nobis reapse conferret. Introduxit in gloriam multos filios. Heb. 2: 10. 4. Ex jurejurando Patris, per quod sancitum & firmatum est Christo regnum sacerdotale. Psal. 110. regnum vero illud absque iis qui tanquam vere salvati, regno illi subjecti erunt, vanum prorsus erit & inane. 5. Ex certissima consolatione, quam solam ex morte Christi, contra damnationem & mortem capere licet. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est. Rom. 8: 34. & 5: 17, 22. Joh. 5: 24. Qui sermonem meum audit & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in judicium non venit, sed transiit ex morte in vitam. 6. Ex sollemni Christi precatione jamjam morituri, eoque efficaciori. Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo, ut ubi ego sum, etiam illi sint mecum. Joh. 17: 24. 7. Secus nulla foret in hac vita, vel adoptionis gratia, vel ejus hæreditas. Rom. 8: 16, 17. Eph 1: 5. Dum definivit nos ad adoptionem filiorum per Jesum Christum. 1. Pet. 1: 3, 4. Regenuit nos ad spem vivam – ad hereditatem incorruptibilem. quin imo ne quidem electio ad gratiam; hæc enim simul sunt & se mutuo ponunt. Eph. 1: 5.
units.tr: appointed to me a kingdom. Luke 22:29, 30. The Socinians and Remonstrants also cut this off and deny its full effect, but it can be proved very plainly. (1) From the testamentary disposition of Christ, which was confirmed by his death. For a testament is firm over the dead. Heb. 9:16, 17. (2) From the command of the Father, to which Christ, having made satisfaction, also acquired eternal life for all those given to him. This is the will of the Father who sent me, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing; and this is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. John 6:39, 40. (3) From the very end of Christ's death, which was that he should really confer eternal life on us. He brought many sons into glory. Heb. 2:10. (4) From the oath of the Father, by which the priestly kingdom was sanctioned and confirmed for Christ. Ps. 110. That kingdom, however, without those who, as truly saved, will be subject to it, would be utterly empty and vain. (5) From the most certain consolation which, alone from the death of Christ, we may take against condemnation and death. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died. Rom. 8:34; 5:17, 22; John 5:24. He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life. (6) From the solemn prayer of Christ, who was about to die, and therefore the more effective. Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me. John 17:24. (7) Otherwise there would be in this life neither the grace of adoption nor its inheritance. Rom. 8:16, 17; Eph. 1:5. He has predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ. 1 Pet. 1:3, 4. He has begotten us again to a living hope ... to an incorruptible inheritance. Indeed, not even election to grace would exist, for these are simultaneous and posit one another. Eph. 1:5.

units.la: LX. Ut huic negotio nullo modo respondeat adversariorum patio hypothetica, qua acquirenda statuitur vita æterna, post nostram demum obedientiam: cum ultro & indubitate illa ex morte Christi fluat; unde tum plena reconciliatio, tum hæreditas indivulse & necessario consequitur. Qui dedit se ipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni adversus legem delicto, & purificaret sibi populum in divitiis suis perpetuo habendum. Tit. 2: 14. 1. Joh. 1: 7.
units.tr: 60. So that this matter may in no way be answered by the hypothetical scheme of our opponents, by which eternal life is held to be acquired only after our obedience, whereas it flows freely and undoubtedly from the death of Christ, and from it both full reconciliation and inheritance follow inseparably and necessarily. He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every lawless deed and purify for himself a people to be kept for his own possession. Titus 2:14. 1 John 1:7.

units.la: CAPUT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: De Objecto mortis Christi, sive pro quibus Christus mortuus sit.
units.tr: Concerning the object of the death of Christ, or for whom Christ died.

units.la: I. Vidimus quem in finem suscep tum sit tantæ molis opus, & quo scopo mortem obiverit Christus; restat nunc considerandus
units.tr: I. We have seen for what end Christ undertook so great a work and with what aim he submitted to death. It remains now to consider

units.la: {•} OBJECTUM mortis Christi, sive pro quibus Christus mortuus sit. finis?, seu pro quibus ingens hoc negotium fuerit confectum. Sicut enim provinciam hanc non subivit Christus temere ex vana gloria, nec incerta de causa, quod ab insania non multum distaret; ita quoque eventus tanto conatui minime defuit, & quem sibi proposuit scopum certissime assecutus est. Qua in re dum versamur, praecipua nobis opera collocanda erit in retundendis adversariorum ictibus, quos veritati intentant.
units.tr: {•} THE OBJECT of the death of Christ, or for whom Christ died, the end?, that is, for whom this great undertaking was accomplished. For just as Christ did not take up this task rashly from vainglory or for no certain cause, which would hardly have differed from madness, so the outcome was by no means lacking to so great an effort, and he most certainly attained the aim he set before himself. In dealing with this matter, our chief labour must be spent on beating back the blows which the adversaries aim at the truth.

units.la: II. Triplex potissimum sententiarum divortium est. 1. Agmen ducunt Socitiani, qui inficias eunt, Christum, ut sponsorem mortuum esse; verum tamen omnium hominum bono: quos supra refutatos dedimus. Secunda sententia est eorum, qui non omnimodo sponsoris vices Christo derogant, at illum mortuum volunt pro omnibus & singulis hominibus, quibus licet reconciliationem promeruerit, nemo tamen, praeter fideles, illius participes fit. Atque haec Remonstrantium est opinio. Ultima sententia est, quae Christum agnoscit vadem, non quidem omnium & singulorum hominum, at vulttamen, redundare ex morte Christi, utilitatem aliquam in omnes; ut pro omnibus & singulis, sufficienter mortuus esse dici possit, quorundam tamen scilicet loco; aliorum vero bono: quam suam faciunt quidam inter Reformatos.
units.tr: II. There are chiefly three divisions of opinion. (1) The Socinians lead the line; they deny that Christ died as surety, but say he died for the good of all men. We have refuted them above. The second opinion belongs to those who do not wholly take away the office of surety from Christ, but want him to have died for all and each of men, so that although he earned reconciliation for them, nobody except believers becomes a partaker of it. This is the opinion of the Remonstrants. The last opinion acknowledges Christ as surety, not indeed of all and each of men, but holds that some benefit flows from Christ's death to all, so that he can be said to have died sufficiently for all and each, yet effectively for some only, and for the good of others. Some among the Reformed hold this view.

units.la: III. Quibus quidem sententiis, quatenus in eandem hanc universalitatem conspirant, opponemus primo Scripturae veritatem; tum argumenta eorum & objectamenta examinabimus. Haec enim sententia, quae antiquorum etiam Pelagianorum fuit, statuentium pro universo genere humano Christum mortuum esse, palam ex S. Scriptura & rei veritate refellitur. Nam 1. cum morte Christi, salvati sint fideles ante Christum; fatentibus illud, ut videtur, quibusdam adversariorum, necessario hinc sequitur, mortuum illum duntaxat esse, pro iis qui jam revera salvati erant; nam pro damnatis mortuum esse, quo colore dici posset? quamvis illud affirmare non vereantur Remonstrantium quidam. Nec meliori etiam cum specie mortuus dicetur pro iis qui peccarunt in Sp. sancto, jam ante mortem Christi. Qui dixerit verbum in spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro. Matth. 12:31,32. coll. Joh. 5:16. Serpentes, progenies viperarum, quando effugietis judicium gehennae? Matth 23:33. Joh. 8:24. ita nec mori potuit pro Juda proditore. Nemo ex iis periit, nisi filius perditionis, ut Scriptura impleretur. Joh 17:12. Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi, & unus ex vobis est diabolus? Joh. 6:70. & 13:11.
units.tr: III. Against these opinions, so far as they agree in this same universality, we shall first set the truth of Scripture; then we shall examine their arguments and objections. For this opinion, which was also held by the ancient Pelagians, who maintained that Christ died for the whole human race, is plainly refuted by holy Scripture and by the truth of the matter. For (1) since believers were saved before Christ through his death, and some of the adversaries seem to admit this, it necessarily follows that he died only for those who were already truly saved. For what pretext could there be for saying he died for the damned? Yet some of the Remonstrants do not hesitate to affirm it. Nor will he be said to have died, with any better show, for those who sinned against the Holy Spirit before Christ's death: Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Matt. 12:31, 32, compared with John 5:16. Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of hell? Matt. 23:33; John 8:24. Thus he could not die for Judas the traitor either. None of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. John 17:12. Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil? John 6:70; and 13:11.

units.la: IV. 2. Nequaquam etiam unquam pro omnibus intercessisse legitur. Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro iis, quos dedisti mihi. Joh. 17: 9. Da peccatum ad peccatum illorum, & non veniant ad justitiam tuam, deleantur ex libro viventium, & cum justis non scribantur. Psal. 69: 28, 29. Jam vero arctissimo & indivulso nexu haec utraque, intercessio nimirum & satisfactio, inter se cohaerent; quinimo hac quodammodo illa major & latior est.
units.tr: IV. (2) Nowhere is it read that he interceded for all. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me. John 17:9. Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not come into your righteousness; let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous. Ps. 69:28, 29. Now these two things, namely intercession and satisfaction, cohere with one another in a very close and inseparable bond; indeed, in a way, intercession is greater and wider than satisfaction.

units.la: V. 3. Si pro omnibus mortuus sit Christus; 1. etiam omnes actu reconciliati erunt. Haec enim mortis ejus vis est & efficientia. Hoc judicantes, quod, si unus pro omnibus mortuus est; ergo illi omnes mortui sunt. 2. Cor 5: 15. 2 Omnium peccata erunt remissa. Hoc est sanguis meus qui pro multis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Matth. 26: 28. 3. Omnibus omnia gratificabitur Pater, & sanctificati erunt omnes. Quomodo non etiam cum eo filio, omnia nobis largietur Deus? Rom. 8: 32. Et pro ipsis ego sanctifico me ipsum, ut & ipsi sint sanctificati in veritate. Joh. 17: 19. quod falsum esse apparet. Quem Spiritum veritatis mundus non potest accipere, quia non vidit eum, neque cognoscit eum. Joh. 14: 17. 4. Omnes erunt amore summo dilecti. Majorem hac dilectionem nemo habet, ut quis animam suam ponat pro amicis suis. Joh. 15: 13. coll. 1. Joh. 3: 16. at contra est. Tum profitebor ipsis, quod nunquam novi vos. Matth. 7: 23. 5. Ita nullus revera posset condemnari. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est &c. Rom. 8: 34. aliter ac habetur Marc. 16: 16. Qui vero non credit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: V. (3) If Christ died for all: (1) then all would actually be reconciled, for this is the power and efficacy of his death. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died. 2 Cor. 5:14. (2) The sins of all would be forgiven. This is my blood which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. Matt. 26:28. (3) The Father would grant all things to all, and all would be sanctified. How will he not also with him freely give us all things? Rom. 8:32. And for their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. John 17:19. Which is plainly false. The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. John 14:17. (4) All would be loved with the highest love. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. John 15:13; compare 1 John 3:16. But the contrary is the case. Then I will declare to them, I never knew you. Matt. 7:23. (5) So in fact no one could be condemned. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, etc. Rom. 8:34. Otherwise than is stated in Mark 16:16: But whoever does not believe will be condemned.

units.la: VI. 6. Omnibus foret acquisita fides. Quem Jesum Christum proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Rom. 3: 25. Fides ex auditu &c. Rom. 10: 17. cujus contrarium evincitur ex Psal 147: 19, 20. Indicat verba sua Jacobo, statuta sua, & judicia sua Israeli; non fecit sic ulli genti, & judicia, quod attinet, non cognoverunt ea. Act. 13: 48. Et crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam aeternam. Act. 16: 6. Prohibiti a Spiritu sancto loqui verbum in Asia. 2. Thess. 3:
units.tr: VI. (6) Faith would have been procured for all. Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. Rom. 3:25. Faith comes from hearing, etc. Rom. 10:17. The contrary of this is proved from Ps. 147:19, 20: He declares his words to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel; he has not dealt so with any nation, and as for his judgments, they have not known them. Acts 13:48: And as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Acts 16:6: They were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. 2 Thess. 3:2: For not all have faith.

units.la: 2. Non enim omnium est fides. 7. Omnes liberati erunt a servitute peccati, & habebunt spiritum regenerationis. Hoc scientes, veterem nostrum hominem una crucifixum esse, ut aboleatur corpus peccati, ut non amplius serviamus peccato. Rom. 6: 6, 2 Cor. 5: 15. Hebr. 2: 14, 15. Jer. 31: 33. quod experientia quotidiana refellit. 8. Nullus erit ex natura filius irae, sed omnes in statu gratiae; diserte contra Eph. 2:
units.tr: VII. (7) All would be freed from slavery to sin and would have the Spirit of regeneration. Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer be enslaved to sin. Rom. 6:6; 2 Cor. 5:15; Heb. 2:14, 15; Jer. 31:33. Daily experience refutes this. (8) No one would be a child of wrath by nature, but all would be in a state of grace; this flatly contradicts Eph. 2:3: We too were by nature children of wrath, as the rest are. 1 Cor. 7:14: Otherwise your children would be unclean. (9) Indeed, all would be partakers of eternal life. For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, since a death has taken place for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who are called may receive the promise of eternal inheritance. Heb. 9:15. Paul denies this: But if children, then heirs also, heirs of God. Rom. 8:17.

units.la: 3. Eramus filii natura irae, ut & reliqui. 1. Cor. 7: 14. Alioqui liberi vestri impuri sunt. 9. Quinimo omnes erunt participes vitae aeternae. Propter hoc Testamenti Novi mediator est, ut, morte obita, ad redemp-tionem, quae sub priori Testamento (erant) transgressionum, promissio-nem accipiant vocati aeternae haereditatis. Hebr. 9: 15. quod negat Pau-lus. Si autem filii, & haeredes summus. Rom. 8: 17.
units.tr: 3. We were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also were. 1 Cor. 7:14. Otherwise your children are unclean. 9. Nay, all shall be partakers of eternal life. For this cause he is the mediator of the New Testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance. Heb. 9:15, which Paul denies: And if children, then heirs. Rom. 8:17.

units.la: VII. 4. Hinc S. Scriptura ut huic errori occurreret, diligenter admodum notat, mortuum esse Christum non pro omnibus hominibus, sed distincte pro iis, qui ex hominibus electi sunt. Et audivi numerum signatorum, centum & quadraginta quatuor chiliades, ex omni tribu filiorum Israel. Apoc. 7: 4. Acquisivit Deus per sanguinem suum Ecclesiam. Act 20: 28. atque idcirco passim pro multis illum mortuum testatur, non sine accurata notione, qua liquido negatur, pro omnibus morte functum. Ef. 53: 11, 12. Matth. 20: 28. & 26: 28. Hoc est sanguis meus--qui pro multis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Hebr. 9: 28. & 2: 10. Ita speciatim mortuus perhibetur pro populo suo. Ipse autem salvabit populum suum a peccatis ipsorum. Matth. 1: 21. Futurum erat ut Iesus moreretur pro gente Joh. 11: 51. Ipse est salvator corporis. Eph. 5: 23. & pro ovibus suis. Joh. 10: 15. Animam meam pono pro ovibus. & com. 28. Ego do vitam aeternam eis, & non peribunt in saeculum.
units.tr: VII. 4. Hence Holy Scripture, to meet this error, very carefully notes that Christ died not for all men, but specifically for those who are chosen from among men. And I heard the number of the sealed: a hundred and forty-four thousand, of all the tribes of the children of Israel. Rev. 7:4. God acquired the Church by his own blood. Acts 20:28. And therefore he everywhere testifies that he died for many, not without a careful distinction by which it is plainly denied that he died for all. Isa. 53:11, 12. Matt. 20:28 and 26:28. This is my blood... which is shed for many, for the remission of sins. Heb. 9:28 and 2:10. Thus he is said to have died specifically for his own people. But he shall save his people from their sins. Matt. 1:21. Jesus was to die for the nation. John 11:51. He himself is the Saviour of the body. Eph. 5:23. And for his sheep. John 10:15. I lay down my life for the sheep. And verse 28: I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish.

units.la: VIII. 5. Denique ex ipsa adversariorum hypothesi destruitur universalis mors Christi. Nam 1. non statuunt mortuum pro infantibus, quos a peccato originali immunes faciunt; quare mediatore non egent. Licet aliter doceamur Matth. 1: 21. 1. Cor. 7: 14. Alioquin liberi vestri impuri sunt. Conf. Act. 2: 39. 2. Mortuum etiam nolunt pro iis qui vixerunt ante N. Test. sine cognitione vitae aeternae; & qui sub Novo Test. vixerunt, sine notitia Evangelii; illi enim aeternae condemnationi non sunt obnoxii. 3. Nec etiam pro reliquo genere humano; cum negent peccatum originale; & ab actuali omnes sibi cavere potuisse, a multis revera cautum esse velint. Unde certo consequitur, maximae hominum parti inutilem fuisse Christi mortem.
units.tr: VIII. 5. Finally, the universal death of Christ is overturned by the opponents' own hypothesis. For (1) they do not hold that Christ died for infants, whom they declare free from original sin, and so they do not think infants need a mediator. Yet we are taught otherwise at Matth. 1:21 and 1 Cor. 7:14: Otherwise your children would be unclean. Compare Acts 2:39. (2) They also deny that Christ died for those who lived before the New Testament without knowledge of eternal life, or for those who lived under the New Testament without knowledge of the Gospel, since they are not liable to eternal condemnation. (3) Nor do they hold that he died for the rest of the human race, since they deny original sin and want all people to have been able to guard against actual sin, and indeed many to have done so. From this it certainly follows that Christ's death was useless to the greatest part of mankind.

units.la: IX. Hisce satis superque deturbavimus hanc universalitatem mortis Christi. Nunc etiam loco suo movenda veniunt, quae speciose huic errori praetendunt argumenta. Qualia sunt. 1. quod passim pro omnibus mortuus dicatur Christus. 2. Cor. 5: 15. Hebr. 2: 9. Ut gratia Dei pro omni gustaret mortem. 1. Tim. 2: 6. qua in re tenendum hoc est, voculam omnis creberrime ita usurpari, ut excludat omnem Ἀγωνίαν distinctionem; non vero exceptionem. Dicit enim Scriptura, omnis, qui credit in eum, non pudefiet; non enim est distinctio Filio Judaei & Graeci— &c. Rom. 10: 11, 12. Gal. 3: 26, 27, 28. Col. 3: 20, 28. Rom. 11: 32. Conclusit Deus omnes (utrosque, Judaeos & gentes) ut omnium misereatur. Ut per hanc vocem quidem innuatur sublatum esse omne discrimen inter Judaeos & gentes; nequaquam tamen efficiatur omnes omnino Judaeos & gentiles, sine ulla exceptione salvandos. 2. Aperte satis respicitur hac voce ad promissionem Abrahamo factam, qua semen seu haereditas ex omnibus gentibus adeunda ipsi promissa & confirmata fuit. Benedicentur in te omnes familiae terrae. Gen. 22: 18. & 12: 3. & 28: 14. Hinc dicitur: haeres mundi. Rom. 4: 13. Gal. 3: 8. ut omnes hic intelligendi sint, non de omnibus universim hominibus, sed de omni semine Abrahamo promisso. In Isaaco vocabitur tibi semen. Gen. 21: 12. Non enim omnes, qui ex Israele, hi Israel. Rom. 9: 6.
units.tr: IX. With these arguments we have overthrown this universality of Christ's death more than enough. Now the arguments that they put forward plausibly in support of this error must also be moved from their place. Such are these. (1) That Christ is said everywhere to have died for all: 2 Cor. 5:15; Heb. 2:9, That by the grace of God he might taste death for every man; 1 Tim. 2:6. In this matter we must hold that the little word all is very often used so as to exclude every distinction, but not to make an exception. For Scripture says: Whoever believes in him, all of them, will not be put to shame; for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, etc. Rom. 10:11, 12; Gal. 3:26–28; Col. 3:11, 28; Rom. 11:32: God has shut up all (both Jews and Gentiles) that he might have mercy on all. By this word it is indeed indicated that all distinction between Jews and Gentiles has been removed, but by no means is it made to follow that absolutely all Jews and Gentiles, without any exception, are to be saved. (2) This word clearly refers to the promise made to Abraham, by which the seed or inheritance to be gathered from all nations was promised and confirmed to him: In you shall all the families of the earth be blessed, Gen. 22:18; 12:3; 28:14. Hence he is called heir of the world, Rom. 4:13; Gal. 3:8. So all here must be understood not of all people universally, but of all the seed promised to Abraham: In Isaac shall your seed be called, Gen. 21:12; For not all who are of Israel are Israel, Rom. 9:6.

units.la: X. Atque hinc facile etiam apparet, quis speciatim sensus sit singulorum locorum in quibus haec vocula occurrit. ut 1. Hebr. 2: 9. Ut gratia Dei pro omni gustaret mortem. & com. 10. Multos filios in gloriam introduxit. 2. Rom. 5: 18. Per unum justitia meritum (seu causam) in omnes homines in justificationem vita. Vide & com. 19. Per obedientiam unius justi constituentur multi. 3. 2 Cor. 5: 15. Hoc judicantes, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus est; ergo omnes mortui sunt. & com. 17. Si quis in Christo, nova est creatura. & com. 18. Omnia sunt ex Deo &c. tum etiam illi omnes sunt illi qui Christo jam vivunt, cum. 15. quales non sunt omnes & singuli. Vide & 1 Cor. 15: 22, 23. Act. 2: 39.
units.tr: X. From this it also readily appears what the particular sense is of the individual passages in which this little word occurs. (1) Heb. 2:9, That by the grace of God he might taste death for every man; and in verse 10, In bringing many sons into glory. (2) Rom. 5:18, Through one man's righteousness (or cause) came justification of life to all men. See also verse 19: Through the obedience of one righteous man many shall be made righteous. (3) 2 Cor. 5:15, Judging this, that if one died for all, then all were dead; and verse 17, If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; and verse 18, All things are of God, etc. Then also those "all" are those who now live to Christ, as in verse 15, and they are not all and each. See also 1 Cor. 15:22, 23 and Acts 2:39.

units.la: XI. Deinde, quod saepe pro mundo Christus mortuus dicatur. Joh. 1: 29. facile illud explicari poterit; nam, ut omissis caeteris mundi significationibus, illas tantum recensemus, quae nostro instituto inserviunt; sumitur interdum pro universitate electorum, saepe pro solis gentilibus; quandoque pro semine illo promissionis, ex gentibus sine discrimine. qua notione hisce in locis commodissime capi poterit.
units.tr: XI. Next, that Christ is often said to have died for the world, John 1:29, can easily be explained. For, leaving aside the other meanings of the word world, we list only those that serve our purpose: sometimes it is taken for the whole body of the elect, often for the Gentiles alone, and sometimes for that seed of promise from the Gentiles without distinction. In this sense it can be most conveniently understood in these passages.

units.la: XII. Sic 2. Cor. 5: 19. Deus erat mundum secum reconcilians in Christo, intelliguntur gentes; non vero omnes universe homines. vide com. 17, 18, 19. Omnia sunt ex Deo, qui nos secum reconciliavit per Jesum Christum &c. Col. 1: 20. Per ipsum omnia reconciliavit ad se. quemadmodum 1. Joh. 2: 2. per peccata totius mundi non intelliguntur omnium hominum, verum electorum ex gentibus, seu potius universi feminis Abrahae, ex Judaeis non solum, sed etiam ex gentibus collecti Vide Joh 11: 52. Non tantum pro gente, sed ut ut filios Dei dispersos congeret in unum. idem indicat quoque dictio tota epistolæ scriptæ ad Hebræos, ut pro nobis sit tantundem ac pro Judæis; pro mundo ac pro gentilibus. Ita & Joh. 3:16. Sic enim dilexit Deus mundum; ut filium suum &c.
units.tr: XII. Thus at 2 Cor. 5:19, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, the Gentiles are understood, not all human beings universally. See verses 17, 18, 19: All things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, etc. Col. 1:20, Through him he reconciled all things to himself. Just so, at 1 John 2:2, by the sins of the whole world are not meant the sins of all men, but of the elect from the Gentiles, or rather of the whole seed of Abraham, gathered not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. See John 11:52: not only for the nation, but that he might also gather into one the scattered children of God. The whole letter written to the Hebrews also shows the same, so that for us means the same as for the Jews, and for the world the same as for the Gentiles. So also John 3:16: For God so loved the world, that he gave his Son, etc.

units.la: XIII. Objiciunt nobis locum 1 Tim. 2: 4. ad quem respondeti potest; non dicitur ϑέλειν sed σωθῆναι, quod quid sit, explicatur mox; nempe ut perveniant ad cognitionem veritatis, id est Euangelii: posito fine rei & consequente, pro antecedente: sicut Marc. 16:16. Abeuntes per totum mundum prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. quare nos ita censere debemus, Deum velle, ut omni homini Euangelium annuncietur, atque idcirco juxta pro omnibus orandum esse. com. 1: 2. Quo facit, quod com. 5, 6. Christus dicatur se dedisse ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων; illud autem non pro omnibus & singulis factum est, sed tantum pro semine promissionis. Similiter 2. 1 Pet. 3:9. Pet. 3:9. Sed Dominus longanimis est in nos, nolens ullos perire, sed omnes venire ad resipiscentiam, sermo tantum est de electis.
units.tr: XIII. They object to us 1 Tim. 2:4, and to this one may reply: it does not say wills [θέλειν] but be saved [σωθῆναι], and what that means is explained immediately: namely that they might come to the knowledge of the truth, that is, of the Gospel. The end is put for the consequence, and the consequence for the antecedent, as at Mark 16:15–16: Going into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature. Therefore we ought to judge that God wills that the Gospel be proclaimed to every man, and for this reason we must pray for all, as in verses 1, 2. To this agrees what is said at verses 5, 6, that Christ gave himself a ransom for all [ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων]; but that was not done for all and each, but only for the seed of promise. Similarly 1 Pet. 3:9: The Lord is patient toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance; the discourse is only about the elect.

units.la: XIV. Parratio est locorum Rom. 14:15, 20. Noli cibo tuo illum perdere, pro quo Christus mortuus est. & 1 Cor. 8:11. non enim in illis agitur de effectu ipso, & eventu quem res sortitur, sed de conatu & molimine, quando nimirum per infirmorum scandalum frater infirmus, quantum in nobis est, perditur, non quidem funditus & internecivo prorsus interitu, aliquatamen ex parte. Similes phrases vide Matth. 5:28. Quicunque aspicit mulierem, ut concupiscat eam, jam adulteravit eam in corde suo. Heb. 6:6.
units.tr: XIV. There is a similar case in Rom. 14:15, 20: Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died; and 1 Cor. 8:11. For these passages do not concern the actual effect and outcome that the thing brings about, but the attempt and effort: namely, when through the stumbling of the weak a weak brother is, as far as lies in us, ruined, not indeed utterly and with complete destruction, but in some part. Compare similar phrases at Matth. 5:28: Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart; and Heb. 6:6.

units.la: XV. Nec tandem etiam aliquid efficitur ex loco 2 Pet. 2:1. ubi falsi doctores abnegare dicuntur Dominum, qui eos redemit. Nam vox illa δεσπότης, distincta à voce κύριος, secundum multos Patri hic tribuitur, ut Luc. 2:29. Nunc dimittis servum tuum δεσπότα, Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace. & ex quorundam sententia 2. Tim. 2:21. Jud. 4. Negantes illum solum δεσπότην, Herum, Deum & τὸν κύριον Dominum Jesum Christum. 2. At demus licet per δεσπότην Filium hic intelligi, aliter tamen consideratur ut δεσπότης, herus; aliter ut κύριος Dominus, qualis est non nisi verorum Ecclesiæ membrorum; at herus etiam est eorum, quos quocunque modo in Ecclesiam visibilem adscisicit. In magna domo non sunt tantum vasa aurea & argentea, sed & lignea & testacea, & alia quidem ad honorem, alia autem non ad honorem. 2 Tim. 2:20. Joh. 8:35. Gal. 4:30. 3. Adde, quod empti dicantur illi non pretio, 1 Cor. 6:20. Empti estis pretio. 1. Pet. 1:19. Redempti estis pretioso sanguine Christi: sed empti tantum, id est, sine pretio; ut operarii & servi mercede & externis bebeneficiis conducti. Vide Matth. 20: 1, 2, 3. Deut. 7: 8. & 9: 26. Et oravi Dominum & dixi: Domine Deus, ne perdas populum tuum & hereditatem tuam, quam redemisti per magnitudinem tuam, quam vel cum eduxisti eam ex Ægypto, per manum fortem...
units.tr: XV. Nor finally is anything gained from 2 Pet. 2:1, where false teachers are said to deny the Lord who bought them. For, according to many, that word despotēs [δεσπότης], distinct from the word kyrios [κύριος], is here ascribed to the Father, as at Luke 2:29, Now you dismiss your servant, Master [δέσποτα], according to your word in peace; and in the opinion of some, at 2 Tim. 2:21 and Jude 4: denying the only Master [δεσπότην], God, and our Lord [κύριον] Jesus Christ. Second, even if we grant that by despotēs the Son is understood here, he is nonetheless considered in one way as despotēs, master of the house, and in another way as kyrios, Lord, which is true only of the genuine members of the Church. But the master of the house is also the master of all whom he admits in any way into the visible Church: In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, and some indeed for honour, others not for honour, 2 Tim. 2:20; John 8:35; Gal. 4:30. Third, add that those men are said to be bought, not with a price: 1 Cor. 6:20, You were bought with a price; 1 Pet. 1:19, You were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ. But they were bought only in the sense of being without price, as labourers and servants are hired for wages and external benefits. See Matth. 20:1, 2, 3; Deut. 7:8; 9:26: And I prayed to the Lord and said: O Lord God, do not destroy your people and your inheritance, which you have redeemed through your greatness, which you brought out of Egypt with a strong hand...

units.la: XVI. Atque ita cum nullum ex S. Scriptura præsidium causæ suæ reportent, ad inanes logos & ratiocinationes recurrunt; clamantes Christum pro omnibus esse mortuum, quod omnes debeant credere, illum pro se esse mortuum; secundum πολυδεύκτον illud; quod unusquisque credere debet, illud est verum. Resp. 1. quoad formam, argumentum hoc paralogismum esse; hoc pacto restituendum: quicunque tenentur credere Christum pro se mortuum esse, sunt ii, pro quibus Christus mortuus est; atqui omnes & singuli tenentur credere &c. 2. Resp. quoad materiam, non omnes & singulos hoc debere credere; nam 1. non omnibus & singulis Euangelium annunciatur. Quomodo autem credent, quem non audierunt? Rom. 10: 14. 2. Tum illi, quibus annunciatur, credere quidem debent, Jesum esse Filium Dei, recepturum omnes resipiscentes & ad se confugientes; non tamen continuo pro se esse mortuum, quinimo impoenitentes contrarium credere jubentur. Ne date sanctum canibus; neque projicite margaritas vestras coram porcis. Matth. 7: 6. & cap. 16: 19. Joh. 20: 23. Non est tibi pars, neque fors in verbo hoc. Act. 8: 21. 2 Cor. 13: 5. 3. Patet ex hisce, juberi omino, ut omnes fide sua in Christum recumbant. Ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat. Joh. 3: 16. per modum & rationem praecepti. Ubi igitur gloriatio? exclusa est: per quam legem? operum? non; sed per legem fidei. Rom. 3: 27. post quae jussa, jubetur demum fides in Christum tanquam pro nobis mortuum. Vide Rom. 6: 3--8.
units.tr: XVI. Since they find no support for their cause in Holy Scripture, they fall back on empty arguments and reasoning, crying out that Christ died for all, so all must believe that he died for them, according to that much-quoted saying [πολυδεύκτον]: "whatever each man ought to believe, that is true." Reply: (1) as to form, this argument is a paralogism, and should be restated thus: whoever is bound to believe that Christ died for him are those for whom Christ died; but all and each are bound to believe, etc. (2) As to matter, I reply that not all and each are bound to believe this. For (a) the gospel is not announced to all and each. But how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? Rom. 10:14. (b) Those to whom it is announced ought indeed to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, who will receive all who repent and flee to him; but they are not at once to believe that he died for them, and indeed the unrepentant are commanded to believe the opposite. Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine. Matt. 7:6; cf. ch. 16:19; John 20:23. You have no part or lot in this word. Acts 8:21; 2 Cor. 13:5. (3) It is plain from these things that everyone is absolutely commanded to rest with his faith in Christ, that whoever believes in him should not perish, John 3:16, by way of precept and command. Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. Rom. 3:27. After these commands, faith in Christ as having died for us is finally enjoined. See Rom. 6:3–8.

units.la: XVII Instant, Deum hoc modo non posse simulationis crimine absolvi, qui tales jubeat credere. Verum non jubet Deus, ut impoenitentes credant, sed ut poeniteant & credant, atque ita vult, generatim nunciari, Christum pro poenitentibus & fidelibus mortuum esse; ut hisce haec consolatio serio nec temere proponatur; reliquis vero monstratur via, quam calcare debeant, ut fructus mortis Christi reciperent, idque sine omni simulatione.
units.tr: XVII. They object that God cannot be absolved of the guilt of pretence if he commands such people to believe. But God does not command the unrepentant to believe; he commands them to repent and believe, and so he wills that it be announced in general that Christ died for the penitent and the faithful, so that this comfort is offered to them seriously and not rashly, while the rest are shown the way they ought to tread in order to receive the fruit of Christ's death, and that without any pretence.

units.la: XVIII. Extricanda nunc restat quaestio; an non Christus, non quidem quoad efficaciam, sed tamen quoad sufficientiam mortuus sit pro omnibus? Hanc autem ut recte ponamus, discernendum accurate est, inter ea quae Remonstrantes sentiunt, & quae a quibusdam ex nostris traduntur.
units.tr: XVIII. It remains now to unravel the question: whether Christ did not die for all, not indeed as to efficacy, but at least as to sufficiency? To put this rightly, we must carefully distinguish between what the Remonstrants hold and what is taught by some of our own people.

units.la: XIX. Re-
units.tr: XIX. Re-

units.la: XIX. Remonstrantes quod attinet, discrimen illi fecerunt inter salutis impetrationem & applicationem: illam dicunt esse factam à Christo, ex consilio Patris, pro omnibus & singulis; hanc relinquunt uniuscujusque arbitrio. Ita olim constituerunt in collatione Hagiensi. 1. Deum morti destinasse filium suum, antequam quemquam destinaret saluti. 2. Redemptionem in se indeterminatam esse, adeoque mortem Christi pertinere ad omnes. 3. Deum non intendisse eam mortem alicui applicare ad salutem, sed scopum suum obtinuisse mortuo Christo; adeo ut ejus morte non legata sit alicui vita aeterna, sed via tantum patefacta Novo Fœderi, in quo per mandata Christi vitam aeternam quilibet adipisci potest.
units.tr: XIX. As for the Remonstrants, they made a distinction between the impetration and the application of salvation. They say that the impetration was made by Christ, by the counsel of the Father, for all and each; but the application they leave to each person's own will. This is how they laid it down long ago at the Hague conference: (1) God destined his Son to death before he destined anyone to salvation. (2) The redemption is indeterminate in itself, and so the death of Christ pertains to everyone. (3) God did not intend to apply that death to anyone for salvation, but attained his purpose by the death of Christ, so that eternal life was not bequeathed to anyone by his death, but only a way was opened under the New Covenant, in which anyone can obtain eternal life through the commandments of Christ.

units.la: 4. Et haec illis est salutis impetratio, dum per mortem Christi effectu est, ut Deus salva sua justitia, peccatorem salvare possit, seu per fidem, seu per opera; ex quo aliud etiam decretum posterius fabricantur.
units.tr: (4) This, for them, is the impetration of salvation, since by the death of Christ it is brought about that God, with his justice preserved, can save the sinner, whether through faith or through works. From this they then devise another, later decree.

units.la: 5. Inde dicunt Christum tam indeterminato & vago modo morti destinatum, nec pro fidelibus, nec pro infidelibus (utrisque qua talibus) mortuum esse, sed pro omnibus; ex quibus postea quidâ fideles, quidam infideles fiunt, ut ea intentione æque pro Pharaone ac Maria sit mortuus. 6. Quicquid autem deinceps fiat in applicatione post præstitam ab homine conditionem requisitam, id, secundum illos, confertur, non sub ratione finis, sed præmii ac mercedis, adeoque potius ad justitiam, quam ad gratiam & charitatem spectat. 7. Quin etiam ex eorum sententia Christus sibi jus acquisivit infideles perdendi. 8. Quidam tamen eorum docent universum genus humanum, actu non solum reconciliatum esse, modo in eo persistant, sed & universalem applicationem docere videntur, statuentes universalem & sufficientem gratiam omnibus & singulis dari. Quam applicationem alii negant, nolentes Christum intendisse in impetratione applicationem reconciliationis, uti dictum est, sed eam tantum velle post impetrationem completam.
units.tr: (5) From this they say that Christ was destined to death in so indeterminate and vague a manner that he died neither for the faithful nor for the unfaithful (each as such), but for all; so that afterwards some become faithful and some unfaithful, and with that intention he died equally for Pharaoh and for Mary. (6) Whatever then happens in the application, after the condition required of man has been performed, is conferred, according to them, not under the aspect of purpose but of reward and wages, and so pertains rather to justice than to grace and charity. (7) Indeed, in their view Christ acquired for himself a right to destroy the unbelievers. (8) Some of them, however, teach that the whole human race is not only actually reconciled, provided they persist in it, but they also seem to teach a universal application, holding that universal and sufficient grace is given to all and each. Others deny this application, not wishing that Christ, in the impetration, intended the application of reconciliation, as has been said, but willing it only after the impetration is complete.

units.la: XX. Circa haec autem notandum est; tum quod supra etiam observavimus, à Christa ito Testamentum factum, absque haeredum institutione, in qua tamen omnis Test. fundamentum & ratio posita est; tum distinctionem hanc impetrationis ab applicatione haustam esse è lacunis Pelagii, quo libero arbitrio litaret; quod tamen discidium res ipsa non patitur. Nam 1. vana est omnis impetratio sine applicatione, nec una mutilari debet, aut latius extendi, quam altera, infausto discidio: utramque enim in mote sua intendit Christus, qui mortuus est, ut salvaret electos; ad quod tam impetratio quam applicatio requirebatur. 2. Tum ab ea excludentur infantes, donec eam reipsa sibi applicent, vel potius illa non egent, quippe qui & peccato originali careant. Imo nec adultis erit necessaria, cum à peccato actuali cavere sibi possint, & in morte æterna, quæ quidem peccati pœna sit, natura non hæreant. 3. Denique universalis illa reconciliatio seu impetratio ne unum quidem hominem amplius salvari facit, quam absolutum illud, quod nostris tribuunt, decretum; unde supervacuum esse abunde constat.
units.tr: XX. On these points, however, it must be noted: first, as we observed above too, a testament was made by Christ without any institution of heirs, although the whole foundation and reason of the testament is laid down in it. Second, this distinction between impetration and application has been drawn from the cisterns of Pelagius, to whom free will was the object of sacrifice; yet the matter itself does not admit this severance. For (1) every impetration without application is vain, and the one should not be maimed or extended more widely than the other by an unhappy separation. Christ, who died that he might save the elect, intended both in his purpose, and for this both impetration and application were required. (2) Then infants would be excluded from it until they apply it to themselves in fact, or rather they have no need of it, since they are free from original sin. Nor will it be necessary even for adults, since they can guard themselves against actual sin, and do not cling to eternal death by nature, which indeed is the punishment of sin. (3) Finally, that universal reconciliation or impetration does not make one more man saved than that absolute decree which they attribute to ours; whence it is abundantly clear that it is superfluous.

units.la: XXI. Porro causam suam non parum produnt, dum reconciliationem hanc universalem per fidem applicari volunt. Fides enim illa, vel erit modus & via, per quam Deus reipsa reconcilietur, & tum causa erit divinæ voluntatis, qua nos salvare velit; quod Deo indecorum; vel duntaxat instrumentum erit applicationis; qua ratione Deus, cum fides hæc ex hominis arbitrio suspensa hæreat, incertus plane erit, quis salutis impetratæ futurus sit particeps. Summum igitur hinc nihil aliud conficitur, quam per impetrationem hanc effectum esse, ut Deus peccatorem salvare possit, modo velit; cum qua possibili redemptione homo æternum perire potest.
units.tr: XXI. Moreover, they betray their cause not a little when they want this universal reconciliation applied through faith. For that faith will either be the mode and way by which God is really reconciled, and then the cause will lie in the divine will by which he wishes to save us, which is unbecoming to God; or it will be merely the instrument of application, and in that case, since this faith hangs suspended on the choice of man, God will plainly be uncertain who will be a partaker of the salvation procured. The sum of the matter, therefore, comes to nothing more than that by this procuring God has been enabled to save the sinner, provided he is willing; with this merely possible redemption man can perish eternally.

units.la: XXII. Facile hinc exístimare datur, quo respectu mors Christi dici possit sufficiens pro omnibus. Ita nempe, ut si intrinsecum illud mortis pretium consideretur, omnino sufficiens sit; hinc tamen non efficitur, Christum pro omnibus sufficienter esse mortuum: quoties enim in Scriptura Christus pro aliquo mortuus dicitur, notatur vera substitutio in locum ejus, pro quo mortuus est. Hoc judicantes, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt.
units.tr: XXII. From this it is easy to judge in what respect the death of Christ can be called sufficient for all. Namely, if that intrinsic worth of his death is considered, it is entirely sufficient; yet it does not follow from this that Christ died sufficiently for all: for whenever in Scripture Christ is said to have died for someone, a true substitution in the place of him for whom he died is indicated. Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5: 15. hoc autem nullo respectu de Christo respectu omnium dici posse, ante docuimus.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:15. We have shown above that this cannot be said of Christ with respect to all.

units.la: XXIII. Huic errori etiam innexi sunt Lutherani, qui, cum eadem distinctione sufficientiæ & efficaciæ, Christum ex sua & Patris intentione, pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse volunt; quod difficilius illi tuentur; cum applicationem mortis Christi non suspendant ex viribus liberi arbitrii, sed ex gratia Dei. Ut ita ex illorum hypothesi fingi nequeat, quomodo salutis impetratio latius patere possit, quam ejus applicatio.
units.tr: XXIII. The Lutherans too are bound up with this error, who, with the same distinction between sufficiency and efficacy, want Christ to have died for all and each by his own intention and that of the Father; this they defend with more difficulty, since they do not make the application of Christ's death depend on the powers of free will, but on the grace of God. So, on their hypothesis, it cannot be imagined how the procuring of salvation could extend more widely than its application.

units.la: XXIV. Aliter paulo concipiunt hæc quidam Reformatorum, quamvis omnes etiam non eodem modo. Nam 1. volunt quidam Christum ita sufficienter pro omnibus esse mortuum, & salutem iis impetrasse, ut applicatio tamen illius pendeat à sola Dei gratia. 2. Alii, cum dicunt Christum sufficienter mortuum esse pro omnibus, tantundem volunt significare ac bono & utilitate omnium. Ita ut Christum non velint mortuum loco omnium (hoc enim electorum tantum est) sed bono, eoque non tanto, ut salutem in eo assequantur, sed communiori, quo, vi hujus mortis, reprobi etiam vocentur, illuminentur, sordes & inquinamenta seculi effugiant &c. Hebr. 6:4,5. unde mors Christi iis manifestatur, cum obligatione eam non negligendi. Verum usui Scripturæ repugnat hæc expositio: nam illa, ubi de morte Christi loquitur, particulam pro, eo semper significatu accipit, ut notet vice ac loco alicujus, nunquam vero, in alicujus bonum ad hanc vitam pertinens. Phrasis vero illa nunquam enervanda est; cum generalis sit hæc regula, non solum locum habens in particula ἀντί, verum & in altera ὑπὲρ; quæ quidem aliquando latius sumitur, ut Col. 1: 24. Vicissim impleo reliquias afflictionum Christi in carne mea ὑπὲρ pro corpore ejus, quod est Ecclesia. cum tamen usurpatur de morte Christi, ex analogia aliorum locorum sumenda est.
units.tr: XXIV. Some of the Reformed think about these matters somewhat differently, though not all of them in the same way. For (1) some hold that Christ has died for all in such a sufficient way, and has so obtained salvation for them, that its application nevertheless depends on the grace of God alone. (2) Others, when they say that Christ has died sufficiently for all, want this to mean no more than that he died for the good and benefit of all. They do not mean that he died in place of all (for that belongs to the elect only), but for a good, and not so great a good that they might attain salvation through it, but a more general one: by the power of this death the reprobate too are called, enlightened, and escape the defilements and pollutions of the world, and so on (Heb. 6:4,5). From this, the death of Christ is made known to them, with an obligation not to neglect it. But this explanation is at odds with the use of Scripture. For Scripture, where it speaks of the death of Christ, always takes the preposition "for" [pro] in the sense of standing in the place and stead of someone, and never in the sense of a benefit pertaining to this life for someone's good. That phrase must never be weakened, since this is the general rule, holding not only for the particle ἀντί [anti] but also for the other, ὑπὲρ [hyper]. This latter is indeed sometimes taken more broadly, as in Col. 1:24: "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the Church" [ὑπὲρ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ]. Yet when it is used of the death of Christ, it must be understood according to the analogy of other passages.

units.la: XXV. Quam tamen utilitatem illi ex morte Christi pro reprobis arcessunt, non negamus quidem talia beneficia communia illis conferri, quamvis ipsi illis abutantur. Abnegantes herum, qui ipsos emit.
units.tr: XXV. Nevertheless, we do not deny that those who draw this benefit from the death of Christ for the reprobate are right that such common benefits are conferred upon them, although they abuse them: "denying the Lord who bought them" (2 Pet. 2:1).

units.la: 2. Pet. 2:1. non tamen hæc illis conceduntur à Deo tanquam redemptore, ut illos servet, at potius, ut in iis demonstret longanimitatem & potentiam suam, & simul duritiem cordis illorum. Deus volens ostendere & notam facere potentiam suam, tulit in multa longanimitate vasa iræ aptata ad interitum, Rom. 9: 22. Esai. 5: 3, 7. multo minus respectu talium beneficiorum & illius utilitatis, Christus pro illis & maxime pro reprobis mortuus dici potest. Nec repetenda sunt illa beneficia, ex amore Dei erga tales, qui sit fructus mortis Christi, sed potius ex providentia Dei, qua eos damnare non vult citra demonstrationem bonitatis suæ tam illustris. Ut hoc respectu Christus nequaquam mortuus pro iis dici debeat: adeoque novis hisce loquendi generibus & formulis in Scriptura non usitatis abstinendum potius est. Tantum de morte Christi.
units.tr: Yet these benefits are not granted to them by God as Redeemer, so that he might preserve them; rather, they are granted so that he might display in them his long-suffering and power, and at the same time the hardness of their hearts: "God, willing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction" (Rom. 9:22; cf. Isa. 5:3, 7). Much less, with respect to such benefits and that advantage, can Christ be said to have died for them, and especially for the reprobate. Nor are those benefits to be traced back to the love of God towards such people, which is the fruit of Christ's death, but rather to the providence of God, by which he does not wish to condemn them without a demonstration of his goodness so illustrious. Thus, in this respect, Christ ought by no means to be said to have died for them; and therefore we ought rather to abstain from these new modes of speaking and formulas, which are not used in Scripture. So much concerning the death of Christ.

units.la: CAPUT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: De Sepultura & descensu Christi ad inferos.
units.tr: On the Burial and Descent of Christ into Hell.

units.la: I. Ultimus exinanitionis Christi gradus, seu complementum ejus, fuit sepultura; non enim decebat Christum gustata morte continuo emergere, sed per aliquantum temporis quasi mor-tis tis vinculis irretitus teneri debebat, ut veritas mortis eo magis elucesceret & patesceret justitia Dei. Cum vero absolvissent omnia, quæ de ipso scripta erant, auferentes à ligno, posuerunt ipsum in sepulcro. Act. 13: 29, conf. Matth. 26: 12. Joh. 12: 7.
units.tr: I. The last step of Christ's humiliation, or its completion, was his burial. For it was not fitting that Christ, having tasted death, should rise up at once. He had to be held for some time, as if caught in the bonds of death, so that the reality of his death would shine out all the more and the justice of God would be made plain. But when they had carried out all that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. Acts 13:29; cf. Matt. 26:12; John 12:7.

units.la: II. Præd ita fuit hæc sepultura. Et quod sepultus est, & quod exitatus est, tertio die, secundum scripturas. 1. Cor. 15: 4. præcipue Esai. 53: 9. Dedit cum improbis sepulturam ejus & cum divite in mortibus ipsius. quibus verbis duo dicuntur 1. sepulcrum ipsius futurum fuisse cum improbis, more facinorosorum. 2. Providentiam tamen divinam effecturam, ut non in illis facinorosorum sepulcris, sed in divitis sepulcro sepeliretur; quod & factum Matth. 27: 59, 60. Joseph (homo dives, Arimathaeensis, com. 57.) cum accepisset corpus, involvit illud syndone pura, & posuit illud in monumento suo novo, quod excideratin petra. Marc. 15: 43. Luc. 23: 50. Joh. 19: 38.
units.tr: II. This burial took place in the following way. That he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. 1 Cor. 15:4; especially Isa. 53:9: And they gave him a grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death. Two things are said in these words: (1) that his tomb would be with the wicked, after the manner of criminals; (2) that nevertheless divine providence would ensure that he was buried not in the tombs of criminals but in the tomb of a rich man. This also happened: Matt. 27:59, 60. Joseph (a rich man of Arimathea, cf. v. 57), when he had received the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and laid it in his own new tomb, which had been hewn out of the rock. Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50; John 19:38.

units.la: III. Ut modum hunc sepulturæ Christi rectius cognoscamus, sciendae est sepulcrorum Judaicorum ratio. Erant autem ea, nimirum nobiliora, hanc ferme in formam, ut primo aream haberent in medio ad ingressum sepulcri; ad utroque autem latere spelunccam, area quatuor cubitis depressiorem, quæ suos iterum habebat loculos, in quibus componebantur cadavera, numero vero octo, interdum etiam tredecim; qualis loculus <bl>כוך</bl> appellabatur: unde ratio universa sepulcri Christi intelligi potest, ut & historiæ Evangelicæ Luc. 14: 3, 12. Marc. 16: 5. Joh. 20: 5, 11.
units.tr: III. To know more accurately the manner of Christ's burial, we must understand the arrangement of Jewish tombs. The more noble ones were generally of this form: there was a court in the middle at the entrance to the tomb, and on each side a cave. The court, which was four cubits lower, had its own niches, in which the corpses were laid, eight in number and sometimes even thirteen. Such a niche was called kokh [כוך]. From this the whole arrangement of Christ's tomb can be understood, as also the gospel history: Luke 14:3, 12; Mark 16:5; John 20:5, 11.

units.la: IV. Speciatim hæc ita fieri voluit divina providentia; 1. ut sepulcrum hoc in petra esset Matth. 27: 60. ne per occultos meatus Christum inde extractum calumniari possent. 2. ut novum esset Luc. 23: 53. Et posuit illud corpus in monumento, in saxo incisio, ubi nondum ullus erat positus. Matth. 27: 60. ne objici posset, Christum aliena virtute inde resurrexisse; ut 2. Reg. 13: 20, 21. 3. ut alienum esset, quo Christus pro aliena salute mortuus & sepultus offenderetur.
units.tr: IV. Divine providence willed that this should happen in particular ways: (1) that this tomb should be in rock, Matt. 27:60, so that they could not accuse him of having been taken out by secret passages. (2) That it should be new, Luke 23:53: And he laid the body in a tomb hewn out of rock, where no one had yet been laid, Matt. 27:60, so that it could not be objected that Christ had risen by another's power; compare 2 Kings 13:20, 21. (3) That it should belong to another, so that Christ, who died and was buried for another's salvation, should be buried in another's tomb.

units.la: V. Præterea ex consuetudine Judæorum, qui variis ritibus fidem suam circa mortuorum resurrectionem testabantur, corpus Christi, puræ syndoni, cum aromatibus, fuit involutum. Matth. 27: 59. Joh. 19: 39, 40. non autem Christi corpus pollinctum etiam fuit, propter temporis brevitatem, instante nempe Sabbato. Et regressæ præparaverunt aromata & unguenta, & Sabbato quidem quieverunt secundum præceptum. Luc. 23: 56.
