units.tr: V. Moreover, following the custom of the Jews, who bore witness to their faith in the resurrection of the dead by various rites, Christ's body was wrapped in clean linen with spices. Matt. 27:59; John 19:39, 40. His body was not anointed in full, however, because of the shortness of time, since the Sabbath was at hand. And they returned and prepared spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment. Luke 23:56.

units.la: VI. Factum vero illud confici potest 1. ut declararetur Christi innocentia. 2. ut probrum crucis honesta sepultura jam propulsaretur. 3. ut notaretur vivificum odorem e sepultura Christi emanaturum. 4. Quod autem pollinctura non fuerit adhibita, contigit, ut ostenderetur, Christum, etiam sine illa, corruptioni non fore obnoxium. Non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Psal. 16: 10. tum quoque ne virtuti illius integritas & incorruptio corporis Christi adscriberetur.
units.tr: VI. This event may be seen to have happened (1) so that Christ's innocence would be declared; (2) so that the disgrace of the cross would be averted by an honourable burial; (3) so that it would be noted that a life-giving fragrance would flow out from the burial of Christ; (4) and the fact that no embalming was applied came about so that it would be shown that Christ, even without it, would not be subject to corruption. You will not let your holy one see corruption. Ps. 16:10. It also happened so that the integrity and incorruptibility of Christ's body would not be ascribed to the power of embalming.

units.la: VII. Ingens praeterea saxum sepulcro Christi fuit advolutum, Judaeorum rogatu. Abeuntes vero munierunt sepulcrum, obsignato lapide cum custodia. Matth. 27: 66. quod factum quibusdam videtur secundum Thren. 3: 53. Manciparunt foveam vitam meam, & conjecerunt lapidem in me. quo pacto simul a ludibrio custoditum fuit Christi cadaver, & obsignata simul resurrectionis veritas. Atque ita contraria adversariorum studia veritatem & justam causam non solum non laedere, sed promovere debent.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, a huge stone was rolled over Christ's tomb at the request of the Jews. So they went and made the tomb secure, sealing the stone and setting a guard. Matt. 27:66. This seems to some to have been foreshadowed in Lam. 3:53: They have cut off my life in a pit and cast stones upon me. By this arrangement Christ's corpse was both guarded against mockery and the truth of the resurrection was sealed at the same time. Thus the hostile efforts of the adversaries ought not only not to harm the truth and the just cause, but to advance them.

units.la: VIII. Sepultura haec hos in fines instituta fuit. 1. ut Scriptura impleretur. Psal. 16: 10. & 22: 16. In pulverem mortis disponis me. Psal. 88: 7. Reputatus sum cum descendentibus in foveam, exuti, ut vir, sine viribus—posuisti me in foveam profundissima, in tenebris, in abyssis. Esai. 53: 9. 2. Ut constaret certissimis argumentis, eum vere mortuum esse. Pilatus, advocato centurione, interrogavit eum—& rem cognoscens &c. Marc. 15: 42, 43. 3. ut expiationem peccati morte sua peractam esse testaretur & confirmaret; ex typo Deut. 21: 23. Nam execratio Dei est suspensus. quo vetabatur ut cadaver suspensi in ligno relinqueretur; nam cum in hoc supplicio per mortem Christi abolenda esset execratio, non debebat, aut ipsum corpus Christi, aut suspensi illius e ligno, in Veteri Test. sub execratione illa noctem transfigere. 4. Ut mortem in ultimo quasi arcis suae angulo & asylo persequens, illam inde deturbaret, & sepulcra nostra sanctificaret. 5. Ut peccata nostra secum sepeliret; cujus rei veritas & certitudo obsignatur nobis in baptismo. Consepulti sumus igitur ipsi per baptismum in mortem. Rom. 6: 4. Col. 2: 12. 6. ut Sabbatum caeteraque legis Mosaicae caerimonias simul etiam ut emeritas & rude donatas tanquam cadaver in sepulcro componeret; quare & Sabbatismum suum in sepulcro peregit.
units.tr: VIII. This burial was instituted for the following ends: (1) so that Scripture would be fulfilled, Ps. 16:10 and 22:16; You lay me in the dust of death, Ps. 88:7; I am counted among those who go down to the pit, I am like a man without strength, cast off among the dead... you have put me in the lowest pit, in dark places, in the depths, Isa. 53:9. (2) So that it would be established by the most certain evidence that he had truly died: Pilate, summoning the centurion, asked him... and learning the fact, etc. Mark 15:42, 43. (3) So that he would bear witness to and confirm that the expiation of sin had been accomplished by his death, in accordance with the type of Deut. 21:23: For he who is hanged is accursed of God. This law forbade that the body of one hanged on a tree be left there; for since in this punishment the curse was to be abolished through the death of Christ, neither his body nor the body of one hanged from the tree was to spend the night under that curse in the Old Testament. (4) So that, pursuing death into its last corner, as it were, its citadel and refuge, he might drive it out from there and sanctify our graves. (5) So that he might bury our sins with himself; the truth and certainty of this is sealed to us in baptism. We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death. Rom. 6:4; Col. 2:12. (6) So that he might lay the Sabbath and the other ceremonies of the Mosaic law in the tomb as well, as though they were dead bodies, now fulfilled and dismissed; hence he also carried out his own Sabbath rest in the tomb.

units.la: IX. Appendix huic articulo adjecta, lustranda hic nobis etiam est; quae hisce verbis concepta; descendit ad inferos; tum historicae, tum dogmaticae disquisitionis est. In antecessum tenendum hic est, quod nunc omittimus, Symbolum Apostolicum male statui compositum ab Apostolis; neque ab initio tot quoque articulorum fuit, ac nunc deprehenditur.
units.tr: IX. An appendix added to this article must also be examined here, which is expressed in these words: he descended into hell. This belongs both to historical and to dogmatic inquiry. Beforehand it must be held here, which we now set aside, that the Apostles' Creed was badly put together by the Apostles; nor did it at the beginning contain as many articles as it is now found to have.

units.la: X. Articulum igitur hunc, qui nobis sub manibus est, quod attinet, ultra patet, ab Apostolis compositum non esse; quo maxime facit, quod nec in Veteris Ecclesiæ Symbolis, usque ad tempora Caroli Magni; nec in ipso hoc Symbolo, quod Apostolicum dicitur, apud Orientales & Romanos etiam comparet. Prima ejus mentio fit in Symbolo Athanasiano, quod tamen Athanasii non est. Ex hisce igitur probabilis, nec haud difficilis est conjectura: cum in Symbolo Niceno habeantur verba, sepultus est; in Athanasiano vero, omissis iis, legatur: descendit ad inferos; sequentibus seculis ad verba Symboli Niceni: sepultus est; ex Symbolo Athanasiano in margine, explicationis gratia, adjecta fuisse verba, descendit ad inferos; quæ deinceps ex margine in ipsum Symbolum recepta, simulque eodem tenore recitata tuerint; quod ex variis MSS. Codicibus ostendi potest.
units.tr: X. As for this article which lies before us, it is clear enough that it was not composed by the Apostles. This is especially shown by the fact that it does not appear in the creeds of the ancient Church up to the time of Charlemagne, nor in the creed itself which is called Apostolic, among the Eastern and Roman churches. Its first mention occurs in the Athanasian Creed, which nevertheless is not Athanasius's. From this a probable and not difficult conjecture follows: since the Nicene Creed has the words was buried, while in the Athanasian, where these are omitted, the phrase he descended into hell is read; in later centuries, the words he descended into hell were added in the margin of the Athanasian Creed, by way of explanation, against the words was buried of the Nicene Creed; and these, afterwards received from the margin into the creed itself, were recited in the same form at the same time. This can be shown from various manuscript codices.

units.la: XI. Hæc ergo cum eorum verborum origo sit, quid auctores per illa intellexerint, cum non fuerint Apostoli, scire non multum refert; laborandum potius est, quis conveniens sensus ex iis erui possit.
units.tr: XI. Since this is the origin of these words, it matters little for us to know what the authors meant by them, since they were not Apostles. Rather, the effort should be to work out what suitable sense can be drawn from them.

units.la: XII. Plurimas equidem interpretationes articulus hic est passus. Aliis cum ad descensum duntaxat virtualem, ut vocant, referentibus; aliis ad realem; iisque rursus quadruplici sententiarum genere distrahuntur. 1. Quidam volunt, descensum hunc solummodo factum secundum divinitatem. 2. Alii, quoad animam solam: idque vel metaphorice sumunt, vel de statu animæ in loco invisibili, vel de acerbissimis ejus doloribus; vel de dormitione, triduo mortis: vel etiam secundum literam: quando volunt, vel animam adscendisse in cœlum, vel descendisse in locum obscurum terræ, sive ille sit limbus Patrum & Purgatorium, sive puerorum & Gehenna simul, sive etiam hæc tantum; varios item fines hujus descensus in hæc loca comminiscentes; intrantes seu involantes, in ea quæ nunquam viderunt. Col. 2: 18. 3. Intercedunt quidam, volentes descensum hunc factum secundum corpus & animam idque iterum vel realiter, ut quidam Lutherani; vel ita, ut anima & corpore apud inferos relictis, divinitate sola in cœlum ascenderit, ut olim hæretici χειλοσλύται. 4. Denique alii soli corpori descensum hunc tribuunt, quando nimirum per triduum in sepulcro fuit detentum; vel de statu corporis intelligunt, quando per triduum istud vita naturali caruit; vel simpliciter de sepultura sumunt, ut in his verbis sit propior explicatio priorum; sicut infernus pro sepulcro ita passim venit. Gen. 42: 38. 1 Reg. 2: 6, 9. Psal. 16: 10.
units.tr: XII. This article has indeed undergone very many interpretations. Some refer it only to a so-called virtual descent, others to a real one; and these are further divided into four kinds of opinion. (1) Some hold that this descent took place only according to the divinity. (2) Others, as to the soul alone; and they take this either metaphorically, of the soul's state in an invisible place or of its most bitter sufferings, or of its sleep during the three days of death; or even literally, when they hold either that the soul ascended into heaven, or that it descended into some dark place of the earth, whether that be the limbo of the Fathers and Purgatory, or the place of children and Gehenna together, or these alone; and they devise various purposes for this descent into these places, entering or intruding into those things which they have never seen. Col. 2:18. (3) Some intervene, holding that this descent took place according to both body and soul, and that either really, as some Lutherans held, or in such a way that, with body and soul left among the dead, only the divinity ascended into heaven, as the Christologically heretical Cerinthians once did. (4) Finally, others attribute this descent to the body alone, namely when it was detained in the tomb for three days; or they understand it of the state of the body, when for those three days it was without natural life; or they take it simply of burial, so that in these words the nearer explanation of the former is found; just as hell is often used for the tomb. Gen. 42:38; 1 Kings 2:6, 9; Ps. 16:10.

units.la: XIII. Sensus ergo horum verborum idoneus statui potest, vel literalis, vel metaphoricus. Literalis notat Christi descensum in sepulcrum, seu triduanam perseverationem status illius sub dominio mortis. Quem Jesum Deus excitavit, solvens dolores mortis, sicut non erat possibile ipsum ab ea teneri. Act. 2: 24. conf. v. 27, 31. quod notatur etiam Eph. 4: 9. ubi explicatur per κατωτερα τῆς γῆς. Confer Matth. 12: 40. Sic filius hominis erit tres dies & tres noctes in corde terrae. Vide & Psal. 69: 16.
units.tr: XIII. So the sense of these words may fairly be taken either as literal or as metaphorical. The literal sense denotes Christ's descent into the grave, or his remaining for three days in that state under the dominion of death: Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. Acts 2:24; compare vv. 27, 31. This is also noted at Eph. 4:9, where it is explained by the lower parts of the earth [κατώτερα τῆς γῆς]. Compare Matt. 12:40: So shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. See also Ps. 69:16.

units.la: XIV. Analogice etiam & metaphorice per haec verba notari possunt cruciatus & dolores Christi, tum in horto, tum in cruce tolerati, per quos improprie in infernum descendit: ita ut externis Christi passionibus in Symbolo subjungantur passiones animae internae; conf. 1 Sam. 2: 6. Psal. 18: 6. 116: 3. 88: 16, 17, 18. ut inepte Pontificii, praetextu horum verborum negent spirituales Christi dolores ab ipso toleratos. Ab altera tamen parte cavendum item ne cum aliis statuamus, Christum post mortem in anima passum esse, quod repugnat verbis Christi: Consummatum est. Joh. 19: 30. verum dolores illos tulit in vita, post ultimam coenam; Matth. 26: 37, 38. Et coepit Christus adfici tristitia & gravissime angi; tunc dixit ipsis, valde tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Luc. 22: 44. & in cruce, Matth. 27: 46. qui etiam improprius in infernum descensus repraesentatus fuit tenebris. Matth. 27: 45. Luc. 23: 44, 45.
units.tr: XIV. The sufferings and pains of Christ, endured both in the garden and on the cross, may also be indicated analogically and metaphorically by these words, and through them he improperly descended into hell. Thus the inward sufferings of the soul are added in the Creed to the outward sufferings of Christ; compare 1 Sam. 2:6, Ps. 18:6, 116:3, 88:16–18. The Papists foolishly use the pretext of these words to deny that Christ endured spiritual anguish. On the other side, however, we must also beware of holding with others that Christ suffered in his soul after death, since this contradicts the words of Christ: It is finished. John 19:30. Rather, he bore those sorrows in his life, after the last supper: Matt. 26:37–38, And Christ began to be sorrowful and very heavy; then he said to them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. Luke 22:44; and on the cross, Matt. 27:46. The improper descent into hell was also represented by the darkness: Matt. 27:45; Luke 23:44–45.

units.la: XV. Male ergo Pontificii & Lutherani caput hoc Symboli de descensu incrustant & detorquent; cum descensionem hanc Christi in infernum localem faciunt; quamvis non eodem sensu omnes; cum alii praeterea hunc descensum poenalem, alii triumphalem efficiant. Verum falsa horum omnium est hypothesis, ac si effecta illius in variis inferni locis quae fingunt, peragi a Christo nequiverint, nisi anima ejus reipsa descenderit; tum quoque concesso licet hoc descensu, non tamen inde limbus vel purgatorium efficietur, sed infernus tantum. Praeterea falsum esse quem huic hypothesi superstruunt errorem, patet Luc. 23: 43. Et dixit ipsi Jesus, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. ut anima quae in Paradiso jam erat, simul in inferno esse non potuerit.
units.tr: XV. The Papists and the Lutherans therefore wrongly twist and distort this article of the Creed concerning the descent, when they make this descent of Christ into hell a local one; though not all of them understand it in the same sense, since some make it a penal descent and others a triumphal one. But the hypothesis common to all of them is false, namely that the effects they imagine in various parts of hell could not have been accomplished by Christ unless his soul had actually descended. Even if this descent were granted, it would not follow from it that a limbo or a purgatory is established, but only hell. Moreover, that the error they build upon this hypothesis is false is evident from Luke 23:43: And Jesus said to him, Today you shall be with me in Paradise. So the soul, which was already in Paradise, could not at the same time have been in hell.

units.la: XVI. Nec quicquam turbat hanc sententiam, vox inferni: il-lorum ratio enim in Scriptura, non locum damnatorum, sed mortuorum, seu sepulcrum notat; quae sola tum Hebraei nominis קבר, tum Graeci
units.tr: XVI. Nor does the word hell disturb this opinion. For in Scripture the usage of that word denotes not the place of the damned but the dead, or the grave; this is the sole meaning both of the Hebrew word קבר and of the Greek

units.la: Pars II. Graeci ἁδης, notio est; nisi forte uno in loco Luc. 16: 23. nec aliud probatur ex locis Num. 16: 30. 1 Sam 2: 6. Matth. 11: 23. ubi infernus pro sepulcro etiam ponitur. Frustra quoque objicitur 1. Pet. 3: 19, 20. In quo Spiritu abiens, iis spiritibus, qui in carcere sunt praedicavit. & c.4:6. Ad hoc enim etiam mortuis evangelizatum est. nam licet carcer ibi inferos significet; non tamen eo profectus fuit Christus per animam separatam, sed in Spiritu, id est, divina inspiratione per Noachum praedicavit spiritibus, qui sunt in carcere; quae iterum non jungenda sunt, ac si praedicaverit iis jam mortuis; sed a se mutuo separanda; dum scilicet in vivis erant. Act. 2: 27. ubi anima Christi in inferno fuisse dicitur, per synecdochen anima sumitur pro cadavere. ut קבר Lev. 21: 1, 11. Num. 19: 11. Luc. 6: 9. Vide & Act. 2: 31. Nihil amplius etiam infert, quod in corde terrae dicatur fuisse Matth. 12: 40. cum illud tantundem sit, ac infra terram descendisse. Vide Ezech. 28: 2. & Eph. 4: 9. de quo supra visum.
units.tr: Part II. ᾅδης [ἅδης], except perhaps in one place, Luke 16:23; nor is anything else proved from the passages Num. 16:30, 1 Sam. 2:6, Matt. 11:23, where hell is also used for the grave. The objection from 1 Pet. 3:19–20 is likewise in vain: In which Spirit he went and preached to the spirits that are in prison, etc. and 4:6: For this cause was the gospel preached also to the dead. For although the prison there signifies the underworld, Christ did not go thither in a separated soul, but in the Spirit, that is, by divine inspiration he preached through Noah to the spirits who are in prison. These things again must not be joined as if he had preached to them when they were already dead, but must be separated from each other, since they were still alive at that time. In Acts 2:27, where the soul of Christ is said to have been in hell, the soul is taken by synecdoche for the corpse, as קבר is used at Lev. 21:1, 11, Num. 19:11, Luke 6:9. See also Acts 2:31. Nor does anything further follow from the statement that he was in the heart of the earth, Matt. 12:40, since that is the same as having descended beneath the earth. See Ezek. 28:2 and Eph. 4:9, which was considered above.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS SEXTUS DE EXALTATIONE CHRISTI
units.tr: LOCUS THIRTY-SIXTH: ON THE EXALTATION OF CHRIST

units.la: Et quae eam consecuta sunt.
units.tr: And the things that followed it.

units.la: CAPUT XXII. De statu Exaltationis & Resurrectione Chri- sti.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. On the State of Exaltation and the Resurrection of Christ.

units.la: JÆ sunt rerum humanarum vices, ut non nisi post depugnatam rite pugnam victoria reportetur, & post depressionem sequatur demum exaltatio. Hasce etiam vices subivit Christus: qui se ad infernum usque abjici passus est, at vicissim etiam in coelos sublatus; & tanquam herba terrae conculcatus, excrevit demum immensum in modum: unde ταπείνωσιν humiliationem & abjectissimum ejus statum mox subsecuta est ὕψωσις exaltatio. Minorem eum fecisti paulisper Angelis, gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum. Hebr. 2: 7. ex Psalmo 8: 6. Esai. 50: 8,9. & 52: 13. Ecce, feliciter aget servus meus, efferetur, & extolletur valde. 1. Petr. 1: 11. Spiritus Christi ante testatus est, passiones in Christum, & post eas, glorias. Luc. 24: 26. Nonne oportuit Christum haec pati & ingredi in gloriam suam? conf. Dan. 9: 25, 26. Zach. 9: 9. 6: 13.
units.tr: There are alternations in human affairs: victory is not won unless the battle has been duly fought, and exaltation follows at last after depression. Christ too underwent these alternations. He allowed himself to be cast down even to the depths of hell, but in turn was also taken up into the heavens; and, trodden down like the grass of the earth, he at last grew immensely. Hence his humiliation [ταπείνωσιν] and most abject state were soon followed by exaltation [ὕψωσις]. "Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels; thou hast crowned him with glory and honour, and hast set him over the works of thy hands." Heb. 2:7, from Psalm 8:6. Isa. 50:8, 9 and 52:13: "Behold, my servant shall deal prudently; he shall be exalted and extolled greatly." 1 Pet. 1:11: "The Spirit of Christ testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow them." Luke 24:26: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and to enter into his glory?" Compare Dan. 9:25, 26; Zech. 9:9; 6:13.

units.la: II. Hanc
units.tr: II. This

units.la: DE STATU EXALTATIONIS & RESURRECTIONE CHRISTI. 131
units.tr: ON THE STATE OF EXALTATION AND THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST. 131

units.la: II. Hanc autem ut explicatius teneamus, sciendum est, eam non consistere in abdicatione humanæ naturæ, ut ea quasi rude donata sit; sed tantum formæ servilis, ejusque commutatione in gloriam cœlestem: quoad humanam igitur naturam recepit illa reapse; quoad divinam egit illa, & gloriam suam æternam tantum manifestavit. Phil. 2: 9. Joh. 17: 5. Et nunc glorifica me tu, Pater, apud te gloria quam habui, prius quam mundus esset, apud te.
units.tr: To hold this more clearly, it must be understood that it does not consist in the laying aside of human nature, as if that nature had been given away as something crude. It consists only in the change of the form of a servant into heavenly glory. So as regards human nature, he truly received it; as regards the divine nature, he acted, and only manifested his eternal glory. Phil. 2: 9. John 17: 5. And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was, with you.

units.la: III. Sicut autem non statim in extremum illum humiliationis statum devolutus; ita quoque paulatim superas evasit ad auras, & non nisi per gradus quosdam in sastigium gloriæ surrexit. Gradus hi potissimum tres sunt. Prima est, resurrectio e mortuis. 1. Cor. 15: 45. Factus est primus homo Adam in animam viventem, ultimus vero Adam in Spiritum vivificantem. Secunda, ascensio in cœlos. Act. 1: 11. Sic veniet, quemadmodum vidistis ipsum abeuntem in cœlum. Tertia, Sessio ad dextram. Phil. 2: 9. Eph. 1: 20. Eum excitavit ex mortuis & collocavit ad dextram suam in supercœlestibus. Hebr. 10: 12.
units.tr: But just as he did not sink at once into that lowest state of humiliation, so too he rose only gradually to the heights, and he did not reach the summit of glory except by certain steps. There are chiefly three of these steps. The first is resurrection from the dead. 1 Cor. 15: 45. The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The second is ascension into the heavens. Acts 1: 11. He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven. The third is sitting at the right hand. Phil. 2: 9. Eph. 1: 20. He raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places. Heb. 10: 12.

units.la: IV. Resurrectio quidem est, qua natura ejus humana, vere ad vitam fuit resuscitata; suo scilicet & improprio modo anima; corpus vero proprie. Partes ejus sunt, tum interna excitatio, facta per resarcitam corporis vivificationem, & animæ cum illo unionem; tum externus e sepulcro exitus in dias luminis auras. Cæterum de hac resurrectione videnda 1. illius veritas. 2. natura & modus. 3. causa efficiens. 4. tempus. 5. rationes & effectus.
units.tr: Resurrection is that by which his human nature was truly restored to life: the soul in its own and improper way, but the body properly. Its parts are the inner quickening, brought about by the restoration of the body to life and the reunion of the soul with it, and the outward exit from the tomb into the light of day. Concerning this resurrection, we are to consider: 1. its truth; 2. its nature and manner; 3. its efficient cause; 4. its time; 5. its reasons and effects.

units.la: V. Certitudo ejus maximi, si quicquam, est momenti; nisi enim hoc constiterit, actum est de nobis & Christo. Si autem Christus non suscitatus est, vanum igitur prædicatio nostrum, vana autem etiam fides vestra; deprehendimur etiam falsi testes Dei, quia testati sumus de Deo quod excitavit Christum. 1 Cor. 15: 12, 14, 15. liquido autem illa patet, cum ex Veteri, tum ex Novo Test. Primo loco occurrunt vaticinia. Quod suscitatus est tertio die, secundum Scripturas. 1. Cor. 15: 4. qualia sunt Psal. 16: 10. Non relinques animam meam in inferno, non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. quem locum de Messia solo intelligendum esse docet Petrus Act. 2: 27, 31. Ita & Esai. 55: 3. eodem pertinere, luculentum Pauli testimonium evincit Act. 13: 34. Nec aliter Esai. 53: 10, 11. Psal. 22. & 40. &c.
units.tr: Its certainty is of the greatest importance, if anything is; for unless this stands, it is all over for us and for Christ. But if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is vain, and your faith is also vain. We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified of God that he raised Christ. 1 Cor. 15: 12, 14, 15. That this is clear, both from the Old and from the New Testament, is evident. In the first place come the prophecies. That he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. 1 Cor. 15: 4. Such are Ps. 16: 10. You will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you suffer your holy one to see corruption. Peter teaches that this passage must be understood of the Messiah alone, Acts 2: 27, 31. So too Isa. 55: 3 pertains to the same point, as Paul's clear testimony proves, Acts 13: 34. Nor otherwise Isa. 53: 10, 11; Ps. 22 and 40, etc.

units.la: VI. Vaticiniis secundo loco succedunt typi, Gen. 2: 2. qualis & illustris admodum est Isaacus, Gen. 22: 12, 13. Hebr. 11: 18, 19. deinde Josephus, Gen. 41: 14. Jonas. Jon. 2: 11. Ezechias, 2 Reg. 20: 5. Ecce ego sanabo te, tertio die ascendes in domum Jehovæ. quorum primus & duo posteriores ipsum etiam resurrectionis tempus præfigurarunt. Partes hic etiam suas habet Simson. Jud. 16: 3. Huc etiam pertinet caro sacrificii eucharistici, quæ ex præscripto legis ante tertium diem comedi debebat. Lev. 7: 16, 17, 18. Huc etiam spectabat manipulus ille Lev. 23. qui in Paschate, postridie Sabbati, offerebatur, & agitabatur eo die, quo Christus surrexit.
units.tr: In the second place, after the prophecies come the types, Gen. 2: 2. Especially illustrious is Isaac, Gen. 22: 12, 13; Heb. 11: 18, 19. Then Joseph, Gen. 41: 14. Jonah, Jon. 2: 11. Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20: 5: Behold, I will heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the house of the LORD. The first of these, and the two latter, even foreshadowed the very time of the resurrection. Samson also has his part here, Judg. 16: 3. To this also belongs the flesh of the eucharistic sacrifice, which by the prescription of the law had to be eaten before the third day, Lev. 7: 16, 17, 18. To this also looked that sheaf in Lev. 23, which was offered at Passover, on the day after the Sabbath, and was waved on the day Christ rose.

units.la: VII. Omnium vero clarissime tota hæc res conficitur ex historia Novi Test. & serie universa narrationis. Nam primo corpus idem fuit, ut ex novo monumento apparet. Luc. 23: 53. Joh. 19: 41. deinde furto ablatum non est; sive illud factum dicatur à discipulis timidissimis; seu à militibus custodiæ illius admotis; quod etiam somnus eorum evertit; seu ab hostibus, qui cadaver illius ostentassent; ut undequaque cadat hæc suspicio. Contra vero vivum fuisse Christum apertissime liquet 1. ex testimonio Angelorum, qui Angeli fuerunt lucis, quales se suo fulgore satis probabant, atque ideo mentiri non poterant. Matth. 28: 6. Non est hic, excitatus est, sicut dixit. Luc. 24: 5, 6. 2. mulierum innocentissimarum, in quas nulla fraudis suspicio cadebat, cum Christum surrexisse ignorarent, quin & dolerent. 3. Petri & Johannis. Joh. 20: 5--8. qui sepulcrum videbant inane; & speciatim sepositum cum linteis sudarium; quod securitatem Christi resurgentis testabatur. 4. Thomæ aliorumque infidelitas maximum & gravissimum resurrectioni præbet argumentum. Joh. 20: 25, 27. 5. Ante omnia faciunt huc tot apparitiones Christi, eæque variis modis factæ, omnes efficacissime resurrectionem probantes. Apparuit quippe variis personis, vicibus, locis, modis, & diuturno sæpe tempore. Gravissimus etiam & locupletissimus hujus rei testis est universa Ecclesia, quando in memoriam resurrectionis Christi diem Dominicum dedicavit. Nec tenue est argumentum in baptismo gentium, post illam resurrectionem institute, Judæorum non credentium judicio &c.
units.tr: Most clearly of all, this whole matter is established from the history of the New Testament and the entire sequence of the narrative. For first, the body was the same, as appears from the new tomb. Luke 23: 53. John 19: 41. Then it was not stolen away, whether this is said to have been done by the very timid disciples, or by the soldiers set to guard it (whose sleep also undid them), or by enemies who had displayed the corpse; so that this suspicion falls apart on every side. On the contrary, that Christ was alive is most openly clear: 1. from the testimony of the angels, who were angels of light, as their brightness sufficiently showed, and who therefore could not lie. Matt. 28: 6. He is not here; he has risen, as he said. Luke 24: 5, 6. 2. From the most innocent women, against whom no suspicion of fraud could fall, since they did not know that Christ had risen and were even grieving. 3. From Peter and John, John 20: 5–8, who saw the tomb empty, and especially the linen cloths lying apart and the napkin, which bore witness to the certainty of the risen Christ. 4. The unbelief of Thomas and others provides the greatest and weightiest argument for the resurrection. John 20: 25, 27. 5. Above all, so many appearances of Christ, made in various ways, all most effectively prove the resurrection. For he appeared to various persons, on various occasions, in various places and modes, and often over a long period of time. The most weighty and abundant witness to this matter is also the whole Church, which dedicated the Lord's Day to the memory of Christ's resurrection. Nor is the argument slight from the baptism of the Gentiles, instituted after that resurrection, in the judgment of the unbelieving Jews, etc.

units.la: VIII. Maximi ergo momenti est hic articulus, & fidei Christianæ compendium. Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & credideris in corde tuo quod Deus eum excitaverit ex mortuis, salvus futurus es. Rom. 10: 9. Ut præfractus sit Judæorum error, quo in hanc veritatem invictam insurgunt. Multum argentum dederunt militibus; dicentes: dicite quod discipuli ipsius, nocte venientes, surripuerunt ipsum &c. Matth. 28: 12.
units.tr: This article is therefore of the greatest importance, and is a summary of the Christian faith. If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Rom. 10: 9. Let the error of the Jews be broken, by which they rise up against this invincible truth: They gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: say that his disciples came by night and stole him away, etc. Matt. 28: 12.

units.la: IX. Considerandam nunc se offert resurrectionis natura & persectio. Per hanc autem animæ dotes eximia accessione fuerunt adauctæ, &æ pro natura scilicet humanæ animæ: summa lux fuit in intelle&tu, ut perceperit & noverit omnia, quæ scire potuit aut debuit humana natura; summa itidem in voluntate fuit sanctitas, gaudium &c. quæ summa caritate ejusque reciproco sensu cum Deo fuit conjuncta. Corpus vel in sepulcro, corruptioni nequaquam fuerat obnoxium; quod factum tum ob brevem in eo moram, tum præcipue omnipotente vi divinæ ejus naturæ, vivificantis illud & ab omni labe præservantis; resurrexit vero gloriosum, & depositο pulvere, in naturam cœlestium corporum transiit. Phil. 3: 21. Act. 13: 34. Rom. 6: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 15: 44, 49. Hebr. 2: 9, 14. Phil. 2: 9. Matth. 26: 29. quod & editæ ejus operationes satis demonstrant.
units.tr: Now the nature and perfection of the resurrection presents itself for consideration. Through it the endowments of the soul were greatly increased, according to the nature of the human soul: there was the highest light in the intellect, so that it perceived and knew all that the human nature could or ought to know; likewise in the will there was the highest holiness, joy, etc., joined to God by the highest love and its reciprocal sense. The body, even in the tomb, was by no means liable to corruption; this came about both because of its brief stay there and, especially, by the omnipotent power of his divine nature, quickening it and preserving it from every stain. It rose glorious and, having laid aside its dust, passed into the nature of the heavenly bodies. Phil. 3: 21. Acts 13: 34. Rom. 6: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 15: 44, 49. Heb. 2: 9, 14. Phil. 2: 9. Matt. 26: 29. His subsequent works sufficiently demonstrate this.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Quod hisce obtendant, Christum edisse & bibisse post resurrectionem; frustra est. Non enim illud fuit humanæ indigentiæ, sed benignitatis prorsus divinæ & liberæ œconomiæ, ad demonstrandam veritatem resurrectionis suæ; ideoque semel tantum factum est, Luc. 24: 41. 43. nam sæpius id contigisse ex Luc. 24: 30. Et sactum est, cum ipse accumberet cum illis, accepto pane benedixit, & fracto dedit ipsis. Joh. 21: 13. Act. 10: 41. cogi non potest. Pariter solvitur, quæ de cicatricibus vulnerum ipsius nectitur difficultas. Primo enim dubitari non immerito potest, an eas semper habuerit. Joh. 20: 24, 25. an vero in illud tempus tantum, pro arbitratu suo & œconomice assumpserit, & deinceps sit assumpturus. Videbit eum omnis oculus, & qui eum transfixerunt. Apoc. 1: 7. Deinde, si vero eas habuerit, œconomicum nihilominus fuit, nec de gloriosso corporis illius statu quicquam demit.
units.tr: Their objection that Christ ate and drank after the resurrection is worthless. That was not a matter of human need but of a wholly divine and free dispensation, meant to demonstrate the truth of his resurrection. So it happened only once, Luke 24:41, 43. That it happened more often cannot be inferred from Luke 24:30, And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. Nor from John 21:13 or Acts 10:41. Likewise the difficulty raised about the scars of his wounds is resolved. First, it may not unreasonably be doubted whether he always had them (John 20:24, 25), or whether he took them on for that time only, at his own pleasure and as the dispensation required, and will take them on again later: Every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him, Rev. 1:7. Second, even if he did have them, they were still a matter of dispensation, and they take nothing from the glorious state of that body.

units.la: XI. Obscurata tamen & obnubilata fuit hæc gloria quantisper in terris egit, quo conversari cum discipulis posset: quod docet analogia loci 2. Cor. 3: 7. Si autem ministerium mortis – in gloria fuit; adeo ut filii Israelis non possent intueri faciem Mosis, propter gloriam faciei ejus, quæ periret; quomodo non magis ministerium Spiritus erit in gloria? Vide Luc. 24: 16. Act. 22: 11. Cum vero non viderem pra, vel a gloria lucis illius, manu deductus – veni Damascum.
units.tr: XI. Nevertheless, this glory was dimmed and clouded for as long as he lived on earth, so that he could converse with his disciples. The analogy of the passage in 2 Corinthians 3:7 teaches this: But if the ministration of death ... was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away: how shall not the ministration of the Spirit be rather glorious? See Luke 24:16 and Acts 22:11: And when I could not see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of them that were with me, I came into Damascus.

units.la: XII. Non ergo amplius secundum carnem cognoscendus est Christus, 2. Cor. 5: 16. id est, quoad infirmitatem & subjectionem sub lege. Mansit tamen corpus illud idem numero & substantia; retinuit etiam essentiam & proprietates essentiales corporis; speciatim quoad locum & dimensionem. Sursum latus est in cœlum. Luc. 24: 51. Matth. 28: 6.
units.tr: XII. Therefore Christ is no longer known after the flesh, 2 Corinthians 5:16, that is, as to his weakness and subjection under the law. Nevertheless that body remained the same in number and substance. It also kept the essence and essential properties of a body, especially as to place and dimension: he was taken up into heaven, Luke 24:51; Matthew 28:6.

units.la: XIII. Inepte igitur Pontificii corpus illud intra angustias hostio-
units.tr: XIII. Therefore the Papists foolishly confine that body within the narrow confines of the host,

units.la: Pontificii ac Lutherani læ cogunt, & sub specie panis contineri volunt, per esse sacramentale, ut vocant; cum esse illud tantopere ab essentia corporis differat, quantopere modus & significatio rei sacramentalis ab ipsa re. Nec melius Lutherani dimensionem ab hoc corpore auferunt, per commentum suum de ubiquitate, seu multiprætsentia & replicatione, quæ sine multiplicatione cogitari nequit. Nec obstat quod ἀφαντος dicatur factus. Luc. 24: 31. quod notat illum ex conspectu eorum subductum esse, sive quod discipulorum oculos perstrinxerit & præpedierit; sive quod celerrime se iis surripuerit: non quod ἀόρατος aut invisibilis sit factus, sed quod iis non amplius sit visus. Ita nec clauso sepulcro resurrexit. ut liquet Matth. 28: 2. Nec per clausas januas se penetravit, Joh. 20. 18. illud enim loquendi genus vel tempus duntaxat significat, vespertinum scilicet, cum clausæ jam essent januæ; non vero modum: sin vero; non tamen clausæ manserunt; ut patet ex analogia loci Act. 5: 19. Angelus Domini noctu aperuit fores carceris. & com. 23. ministri – renuntiarunt, carcerem inventum quidem clausum, cum omni certitudine. conf. c. 12: 10.
units.tr: and the Papists and Lutherans alike force it, and want it contained under the appearance of bread, through what they call a sacramental being. Yet that being differs from the essence of the body as much as the mode and signification of a sacramental thing differ from the thing itself. The Lutherans do no better in stripping this body of its dimension, by their invention of ubiquity, or multipresence and replication, which cannot be conceived without multiplication. Nor does it stand in the way that he is said to have become invisible [ἀφαντος], Luke 24:31. This means that he was withdrawn from their sight, either because he dazzled and blocked the disciples' eyes, or because he very quickly slipped away from them. It does not mean he became unseen [ἀόρατος] or invisible, but that he was no longer seen by them. Likewise he did not rise with the tomb closed, as is clear from Matthew 28:2. Nor did he penetrate through the closed doors, John 20:18. That manner of speaking signifies only the occasion or time, namely evening, when the doors were already shut, and not the manner. And if the doors were shut, they did not remain shut, as the analogy of Acts 5:19 shows: The angel of the Lord by night opened the prison doors, and verse 23: the officers reported that they had found the prison truly shut with all security; compare chapter 12:10.

units.la: XIV. Graviter hic errant etiam Socviniani.
units.tr: XIV. The Socinians also err gravely here.

units.la: XIV. Graviter hic errant etiam Sociniani. Qui primo, Christum ante resurrectionem, tempore mortis, esse desiisse volunt, seu in infernum non existentiæ detrudunt; quod ab horrenda blasphemia non abest. Permansit enim 1. Anima. Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23: 43. & corpus. Non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Psal. 16: 10. 2. Ipse erat vita. Ego sum via & veritas & vita. Joh. 14: 6. & 11: 25. habet potentiam vitæ indissolubilis. Hebr. 7: 16. 1 Cor. 15: 45. 3. Ita Christus bis ἐξ ἀνάστασις emersisset, semel in generatione, iterum in resurrectione. Secundo iidem negant, corpus Christi, statim à resurrectione gloriosum esse factum, sed demum post ascensionem: præter quam supra vidimus.
units.tr: XIV. The Socinians also err gravely here. First, they want Christ to have ceased to exist at the time of death, or they thrust him into a state of non-existence in hell. This is not far from horrible blasphemy. For (1) his soul remained: Today shalt thou be with me in paradise, Luke 23:43; and his body: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell ... neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption, Psalm 16:10. (2) He himself was life: I am the way, the truth, and the life, John 14:6; and 11:25. He has the power of an indissoluble life, Hebrews 7:16; 1 Corinthians 15:45. (3) Thus Christ would have come forth twice out of the resurrection [ἐξ ἀναστάσεως], once in generation and again in resurrection. Second, the same men deny that the body of Christ became glorious immediately upon the resurrection, but only after the ascension, apart from what we have seen above.

units.la: XV. Succedit nunc resurrectionis causa efficiens. Facta quidem illa est virtute Christi propria, Joh. 2: 19. & 10: 18. 1 Cor. 15: 45. Zach. 6: 12. Joh. 5: 26. Act. 1: 3. tribuitur tamen generatim Deo. Hunc Jesum excitavit Deus, cujus nos omnes sumus testes. Act. 2: 32. Patri vero. Quam, præpollentiam virium, operatus est (Pater gloriæ, cum. 17.) in Christo, dum eum excitavit ex mortuis. Eph. 1: 20. Sp. S. Spiritus ejus qui Jesum è mortuis excitavit. Rom. 8: 10. Christus quidem mortificatus est carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu. 1 Pet. 3: 18. Speciali ratione Patri adscribitur, utpote qui in hoc negotio tanquam judex spectatur, qui Filium pro peccatis jam mortuum excitando, absolvit à culpa, qua peccatorum nomine tenebatur, & è carcere de-
units.tr: XV. Next comes the efficient cause of the resurrection. It was indeed effected by the power proper to Christ, John 2:19; 10:18; 1 Corinthians 15:45; Zechariah 6:12; John 5:26; Acts 1:3. Yet it is generally attributed to God: This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses, Acts 2:32. It is attributed to the Father in particular: which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead (the Father of glory, chapter 1:17), Ephesians 1:20. It is attributed to the Holy Spirit: the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead, Romans 8:11. Christ was indeed put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit, 1 Peter 3:18. It is ascribed to the Father in a special way, since in this business he is regarded as judge, who, by raising the Son already dead for our sins, absolved him from the guilt under which he was held on account of sins, and released him from prison,

units.la: ut & Sociniani.
units.tr: as also the Socinians.

units.la: III. Causa efficiens: quae est Christi propria, tum virtus.
units.tr: III. Efficient cause: which is proper to Christ, namely power.

units.la: speciali ratione Patris. demisit. Qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4:25. conf. c. 6:4. & Hebr. 13:20. Caeteroquin virtus haec & operatio toti Trinitati fuit communis. Ut nulla cum specie Sociniani & Anabaptistae Filio hoc denegent, quia nempe Patri tribuitur.
units.tr: in a special way of the Father, and let him go. Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification, Romans 4:25; compare chapter 6:4 and Hebrews 13:20. Otherwise this power and operation was common to the whole Trinity. So the Socinians and Anabaptists, with no appearance of reason, deny this to the Son, namely because it is ascribed to the Father.

units.la: XVI. Recte igitur hinc probatur Christi deitas & divina filiatio. Rom. 1:4. ὁρισθεὶς, nempe Filius Dei ex resurrectione. Longe aliter ac Sociniani, qui illum inde Filium Dei denominatum fingunt, quo detorquent locum Psal. 2:7. Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. coll. Act. 13:32,33. & Hebr. 5:5. Col. 1:18. contra locorum istorum genium.
units.tr: XVI. Hence Christ's deity and divine sonship are rightly proved from Romans 1:4: declared [ὁρισθεὶς], that is, the Son of God by the resurrection. The Socinians, quite differently, imagine that he was named Son of God from this, twisting Psalm 2:7, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee, against the sense of those passages, compare Acts 13:32, 33; Hebrews 5:5; Colossians 1:18.

units.la: XVII. Negligenda circa hoc negotium minime etiam est circumstantia temporis. Fuit autem tertius dies. Et occident ipsum, & tertio die excitabitur. Matth. 17:23. Luc. 24:21. Joh. 2:19. Solvite templum hoc, & tribus diebus excitabo illud. Act. 10:40, Hunc Jesum excitavit Deus tertio die. 1. Cor. 15:4. Tempus hoc Christo plane peculiare fuit; cum nec sub V. nec Novo Test. ullus tertio die excitatus legatur. Vide speciatim Joh. 11:39. Dixit ipsi Martha, Domine, jam olet, quarti enim dies est. Praefiguratum illud fuit in tribus praecipue viris Isaaco, Ezechia, Jona; Patriarcha, Rege, Propheta. Distinctissime vero typum hunc in se ipso exhibuit Jonas. Matth. 12:40. Reliquos typos supra lustravimus. Conf. Hos. 6:2. Vivificabit nos a duobus diebus: die tertio resuscitabit nos, & vivemus coram illo.
units.tr: XVII. The circumstance of time must not be neglected in this matter either. It was the third day: And they shall kill him, and the third day he shall be raised up, Matthew 17:23; Luke 24:21; John 2:19: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up; Acts 10:40: God raised him up the third day; 1 Corinthians 15:4. This time was wholly peculiar to Christ, since no one is read of in the Old or New Testament as raised on the third day. See especially John 11:39: Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days. This was foreshadowed chiefly in three men: Isaac, Hezekiah, and Jonah, a patriarch, a king, and a prophet. Jonah exhibited this type in himself most distinctly, Matthew 12:40. We have examined the other types above. Compare Hosea 6:2: After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.

units.la: XVIII. Ad difficultatem quam hic nectunt de triduo mortis Christi, cum summum per quadraginta tantum horas mortuus fuerit; facilis est responsio: triduum illud recte dici posse, tam proprie & ex nudo literarum sensu; quam ex analogia. Proprie quidem, ut per Synecdochen, sub tribus hisce diebus, eorumque partibus, noctes etiam comprehendantur; quod Judaeis & S. Scripturae frequens est. Vide Gen. 1:5. &c. Unde & numerum hunc ipse Sanctus ad tertium diem coarctat. Matth. 16:21. &c. Vide & 1. Sam. 30:12. & seqq. Esth. 4:16. & 5:1. Luc 2:21. Analogice vero si sumatur, intelligi triduum illud potest, de toto illo tempore humiliationis Christi, ab extrema coena, usque ad primam vesperam, qua se discipulis vivum tot monumentis exhibuit; quod integrum adeo est triduum.
units.tr: XVIII. The difficulty they raise about the three days of Christ's death, since he was dead only about forty hours, has an easy answer. The term three days can be taken rightly, both properly and from the bare sense of the words, and by analogy. Properly, indeed, as a synecdoche, the nights are also included within those three days and their parts; this is common in the Jews and in Holy Scripture. See Genesis 1:5 and following. Hence the Holy One himself limits this number to the third day, Matthew 16:21 and following. See also 1 Samuel 30:12 and following; Esther 4:16 and 5:1; Luke 2:21. But if it is taken analogically, that three-day period can be understood of the whole time of Christ's humiliation, from the last supper to the first evening on which he showed himself alive to the disciples by so many proofs. That whole period is indeed a complete three days.

units.la: XIX. Dies quam in sepulcro exigit, fuit Sabbati; atque hactenus simi- transegit; primo autem hebdomadis die resurrexit. similis fuit omnibus mortuis, unquam resuscitatis: nunquam enim quisquam illo die excitatus legitur. Conveniebat illud utique etiam, ut ita typum Sabbati simul expleret. Dies resurrectionis fuit primus hebdomadis, qui inde in memoriam resurrectionis, ab Ecclesia primitiva Christianorum sacris conventibus dicatus & distinctus est; quare & læti & sine geniculationibus diem illum transfigere debebant. Quomodo vero simul impleti sint typi veteres, alias visum.
units.tr: XIX. The day he spent in the tomb was the Sabbath, and so far he was like all the dead who were ever raised, for no one is ever read of as raised on that day. It was fitting too that he should thus fulfil the type of the Sabbath at the same time. The day of the resurrection was the first day of the week, which the early Church of the Christians afterwards set apart and marked out for sacred assemblies in memory of the resurrection. For this reason they ought to spend that day joyfully and without kneeling. How the old types were fulfilled at the same time is a matter for another place.

units.la: XX. Tandem sequuntur hic denique advertenda resurrectionis effecta & fructus; tum Christi, tum nostrum respectu. Christum quod spectat, resurgendo declaratus est victor mortis & dux vitæ. Jesus Christus primogenitus ex mortuis & princeps Regum terræ. Apoc. 1: 5. Rursus autem quum introducit primogenitum in orbem habitabilem, dicit: & adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei. Hebr. 1: 6. regius sacerdos. Dabit ipsi Dominus Deus thronum Davidis, Patris ipsius. Luc. 1: 32. Unde & salvare ad perfectum potest accedentes per ipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro ipsis. Hebr. 7: 25. Rom. 8: 34. Nos quod attinet, per resurrectionem Christi ad nos pervenit testamenti ejus executio, quæ præstari debebat ab ipso Christo vivo. Qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4: 25. Hebr. 9: 12. atque ita fructus omnis mortis Christi in nos derivatus est.
units.tr: XX. Finally, we must now note the effects and fruits of the resurrection, both with respect to Christ and with respect to us. As regards Christ, by rising he was declared the victor over death and the prince of life. Jesus Christ, the firstborn from the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth. Rev. 1:5. And again, when he brings the firstborn into the habitable world, he says: and let all the angels of God worship him. Heb. 1:6. He is a royal priest. The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father. Luke 1:32. Wherefore he is also able to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. Heb. 7:25; Rom. 8:34. As for us, through the resurrection of Christ the execution of his covenant has come to us, which had to be performed by Christ himself while living. Who was delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification. Rom. 4:25; Heb. 9:12. And so every fruit of the death of Christ has been derived to us.

units.la: XXI. Oritur ergo hinc 1. certitudo justificationis nostræ; cum resurrectione sua absolutus sit Christus ab omni reatu nostri ergo ipsi incumbente. Rom. 4: 25. Quum Jesum Deus excitavit, solvens dolores mortis, sicut non erat possibile, ipsum ab ea teneri. Act. 2: 24. cum & hic obtineret illud Matth. 5: 26. Amen dico tibi, non exibis inde, donec dederis ultimum quadrantem. Hinc baptismus est ἐπερώτημα bona conscientiæ per resurrectionem Christi. 1 Pet. 3: 21. 2. In hac resurrectione exemplar nobis datum est & arrha nostræ resurrectionis suturæ. Ego sum resurrectio & vita, qui credit in me, etiamsi moriatur, vivet. Joh. 11: 25. Rom. 8: 11. 1. Pet. 1: 3. 1. Cor. 15: 12. Si autem Christus prædicatur quod ex mortuis excitatus sit, quomodo quidam inter vos dicunt, quod non sit resurrectio mortuorum? inde Christus dicitur primitiæ eorum qui obdormiverunt 1. Cor. 15: 20. cum tota fidelium massa in eo sit sanctificata. 3. Agnoscitur in ea deformatio resurrectionis nostræ spiritualis. Sicut surrexit Christus ex mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Rom. 6: 4. & 7: 4. Vos mortificati estis legi, per corpus Christi, ut fieretis alterius, qui ex mortuis surrexit, ut fructum feramus. XXII. Plane XXII. Plane alienum est, quod hic statuunt Socociniani, Deum per resurrectionem hanc nihil aliud intendisse, quam gloriam suam, respectu sui ipsius; respectu vero nostri confirmationem fidei nostræ, ut credamus hominem mortalem, Deo obedientem, excitari posse. Quod mirari licet, cum carnis resurrectionem negent.
units.tr: XXI. From this there arise, first, the certainty of our justification, since by his resurrection Christ was absolved from every guilt of ours that lay upon him. Rom. 4:25. Whom God raised up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. Acts 2:24. Here also holds that saying of Matthew 5:26: Verily I say to you, you shall by no means come out thence until you have paid the uttermost farthing. Hence baptism is the answer of a good conscience [ἐπερώτημα] through the resurrection of Christ. 1 Pet. 3:21. Second, in this resurrection a pattern has been given to us and a pledge of our future resurrection. I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live. John 11:25; Rom. 8:11; 1 Pet. 1:3; 1 Cor. 15:12. Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? Hence Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Cor. 15:20, since the whole mass of the faithful has been sanctified in him. Third, in it is recognised the form of our spiritual resurrection. As Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so also we should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6:4; 7:4. You have been made dead to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who was raised from the dead, that we may bear fruit. XXII. It is quite foreign to the truth what the Socinians maintain here, that God intended by this resurrection nothing other than his own glory with respect to himself, and with respect to us only the confirmation of our faith, that we may believe a mortal man, obedient to God, can be raised. One may well wonder at this, since they deny the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: De Ascensione Christi.
units.tr: On the Ascension of Christ.

units.la: I. ALter gradus exaltationis Christi est ejus ascensio, quando triumphali quasi curru ovans in cœlum sublatus est. Act. 1:11. Eph. 4:10. Qui descendit, ipse est & is qui ascendit, supra omnes cœlos, ut impleat omnia. Cujus tratio ut ordine fiat, videnda 1. ascensio ipsa. 2. ejus certitudo. 3. ad cœlos, locus. 4. tempus. 5. causa. 6. finis & fructus.
units.tr: I. The second step of Christ's exaltation is his ascension, when he was lifted up into heaven, as it were exulting in a triumphal chariot. Acts 1:11. Eph. 4:10. He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. If its treatment is to proceed in order, we must consider: 1. the ascension itself; 2. its certainty; 3. the place to the heavens; 4. the time; 5. the cause; 6. its end and fruit.

units.la: II. Ipsi Deo interdum ascensio tribuitur ἀναβαίνειν. Gen. 11:5. & 17:22. & 18:21. hic autem proprie sumitur pro translatione substantiæ corporeæ è loco inferiore ad superiorem, seu à corporum inferiorum vicinia in vicíniam corporum superiorum. Act. 1:11. Hic Jesus qui sublatus est a vobis in cœlum. &c. Marc. 16:19. Luc. 24:51. Proprie ergo convenit naturæ Christi humanæ, divinæ tantum figurate, quatenus nempe in illa manifestavit gloriam suam; & metonymice, quatenus ascensionis fuit causa; unde & de tota persona divina ascensio prædicatur. Psal. 47:6. Ascendit Deus cum clangore, Jehovah cum voce tubæ. & 68:19. Ascendisti in cœlum, egisti prædam, accepisti dona in hominibus; & ex eo Eph. 4:8,9.
units.tr: II. Ascent is sometimes attributed to God himself (Gen. 11:5; 17:22; 18:21), with the Greek [anabainein]. Here, however, it is taken properly for the transfer of a bodily substance from a lower place to a higher one, that is, from the neighbourhood of lower bodies to that of higher bodies. Acts 1:11, This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc. Mark 16:19. Luke 24:51. Properly, then, the ascension belongs to the human nature of Christ; to the divine nature only figuratively, inasmuch as in that nature he displayed his glory; and metonymically, inasmuch as the divine nature was the cause of the ascension. Hence the ascension is also predicated of the whole divine person. Ps. 47:6, God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet. And 68:19, You have ascended into heaven, you have taken captives, you have received gifts among men; and from this, Eph. 4:8, 9.

units.la: III. Certitudo constat 1. Ex vaticiniis. Psal. 68:18,19. & Psal. 110. conf. Act. 2:34. 2. Ex typis. Ita, sicut Pontifex, semel quotannis, & quidem post exordium novi anni, intrabat in Sanctum Sanctorum, non sine sanguine Lev. 16. idem Christo etiam faciendum erat, in initio temporis gratiæ & libertatis, fuso suo sanguine, ut viam in cœlum apertam nobis dedicaret. Hebr. 9:23, 24. Necesse ergo figuras quidem eorum, quæ in cœlis sunt, hisce mundari: ipsa autem cœlestia majoribus hostiis præ ipsis. Non enim in manu facta Sancta introvit Christus, verorum instar habentia, sed in ipsum cœlum, ut nunc appareat facies Dei pro nobis. rupto velo carnis suæ.
units.tr: III. The certainty of the ascension is established: 1. from prophecies, Ps. 68:18, 19 and Ps. 110, compare Acts 2:34. 2. From types. Just as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year, indeed after the beginning of the new year, and not without blood (Lev. 16), so Christ also had to do the same at the beginning of the time of grace and liberty, having poured out his own blood, in order to dedicate for us a way into heaven. Heb. 9:23, 24: It was necessary, then, that the copies of things in the heavens should be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us, the veil of his flesh having been torn.

units.la: Pars II. Hebr. 4: 16. & 10: 20. Quam initiavit nobis viam recentem & vivam, per velamen, id est, carnem suam.
units.tr: Part II. Heb. 4:16 and 10:20. Which he initiated for us as a new and living way, through the veil, that is, his flesh.

units.la: IV. Eodem spectabat Enochi & Eliae raptus, Gen. 5. 2. Reg. 2. quorum ille sub promissione, iste sub lege in coelum translati sunt; sicut Christus sub gratia; in exemplar fidelium omnium aetatum. Miraculum etiam hoc primum omnium fuit a creatione mundi, quemadmodum & ultimum futurum est, in consummatione seculi. Notandae autem hic sunt differentiae, inter hanc Christi ascensionem, & aliorum sublationes: illi nempe ascenderunt virtute aliena, Christus propria: illi vivi, Christus post mortem, quam superare & hoc modo triumphare debebat.
units.tr: IV. To the same end looked the translations of Enoch and Elijah (Gen. 5; 2 Kings 2), of whom the one was taken up into heaven under promise, the other under law, just as Christ was under grace; as an example for all the faithful of every age. This miracle was also the first of all since the creation of the world, just as the last will be at the consummation of the age. But differences between this ascension of Christ and the removals of the others must be noted here: they ascended by another's power, Christ by his own; they ascended while alive, Christ after death, which he had to overcome, and so triumph.

units.la: V. 3. Indubitate probatur ex testibus, quorum numerus sufficiens, & sanctitas supra omnem calumniam; partim Angeli; partim duodecim Apostoli, Act. 1: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 9: 1. Nonne sum Apostolus? an non liber? an non Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi?
units.tr: V. 3. The ascension is indubitably proved from witnesses, whose number is sufficient and whose holiness is beyond all calumny: partly angels, partly the twelve apostles. Acts 1:9, 10. 1 Cor. 9:1: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

units.la: VI. Turbas hic excitant Pontificii, Christo socios in ascensione adsignando; alii Patres e limbo liberatos; ex Psal. 68: 19. cum potius cogitari debeat Christus, pro more triumphantium, Diabolum cum morte, peccato & inferno, revinctis manibus in captivitatem post se traxisse. Alii ergo malunt adjunctos illi fuisse sanctos illos, qui in morte Christi resurrexerant, Matth. 27: 53. sed exigua itidem probabilitate.
units.tr: VI. The Papists stir up trouble here by assigning companions to Christ in the ascension, and others assign the Fathers freed from limbo, from Ps. 68:19; whereas rather one should think that Christ, after the manner of triumphant conquerors, dragged the devil, with death, sin and hell, bound in chains into captivity behind him. Others therefore prefer that those holy men who had risen at Christ's death (Matt. 27:53) were joined to him, but with equally slight probability.

units.la: VII. Locus in ascensione duplex considerari potest; vel unde solverit quasi; vel ubi appulerit. Prior Act. 1: 12. dicitur mons Olivveti. Luc. 24: 50. vero, Bethania. Confer. Act. 1: 12. & Joh. 11: 18. Quod ita in concordiam redigi posse videtur; ut ascenderit Christus ex monte Oliveti, eo nempe loco, quo ab urbe distabat per octo stadia (quantum est iter Sabbati Act. 1: 12.) qui ejus tractus jam inde denominabatur Bethania, a palmis ibi consitis, usque ad 15 stadia. Joh. 11: 18. sicut primus ejus tractus urbi vicinus appellabatur Bethphage, a grossis: cum generale & commune nomen horum tractuum fuerit mons Oliveti; ad quod nomen respicitur Act. 1: 12. Quae vero de vestigiis Christi, monti huic impressis scripserunt veteres, fide sua carent.
units.tr: VII. The place of the ascension can be considered in two ways: either whence he set out, as it were, or where he arrived. The former is called in Acts 1:12 the Mount of Olives, but in Luke 24:50 Bethany. Compare Acts 1:12 and John 11:18. This seems capable of being reconciled thus: that Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives, at the place which was eight stadia from the city (the distance of a Sabbath day's journey, Acts 1:12). That stretch of ground was already then called Bethany, from the palm trees planted there, extending up to fifteen stadia (John 11:18); just as its first part, near the city, was called Bethphage, from the unripe figs. Since the general and common name of these stretches was the Mount of Olives, it is to that name that Acts 1:12 refers. As for what the ancients wrote about the footprints of Christ impressed on this mountain, it lacks credibility.

units.la: VIII. Locus quo ascendit, est coelum. Ascendisti in altum. Psal. 68: 19. Hic Jesus, qui a vobis sublatus est in coelum &c. Act. 1: 11. Marc. 16: 19. 1. Petr. 3: 22. Qui est in dextra Patris, cum abiisset in coelum. Eph. 4: 10. sive coelum summum. Jesus Pontifex maximus pertransiit cælos. Heb. 4: 14. & cap. 7: 26. Altior cælis factus. Eph. 4: 10. Qui descendit, ipse est, qui ascendit supra omnes cœlos, ut impleat omnia. Pervertunt hæc Lutherani Ubiquitarii, errorem novo errore tecturi, ne pateat; cœlum etiam ubiquitarium fingentes; atque ita non loci, sed status tantum mutationem factam esse: contra ac est Joh. 6: 62. Si igitur conspiciatis Filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius. & c. 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. Phil. 3: 20. Nostra autem civitas in cœlo est, unde & Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Jesum Christum. Eph. 4: 10. 1. Thess. 4: 16. Hebr. 12: 23.
units.tr: VIII. The place to which he ascended is heaven. You have ascended on high, Ps. 68:19. This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc., Acts 1:11; Mark 16:19; 1 Pet. 3:22, who is at the right hand of the Father, having gone into heaven; Eph. 4:10, or the highest heaven. Jesus, the great high priest, passed through the heavens, Heb. 4:14; and ch. 7:26, made higher than the heavens. Eph. 4:10, He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. The Lutheran Ubiquitarians distort these passages, intending to cover one error with another so that it may not be exposed, and they feign a ubiquitous heaven as well; and so they hold that a change was made not of place but only of state. This is contrary to John 6:62, If therefore you see the Son of man ascending where he was before, and ch. 14:2, I go to prepare a place for you. Phil. 3:20, But our citizenship is in heaven, whence we also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Eph. 4:10; 1 Thess. 4:16; Heb. 12:23.

units.la: IX. Tempus ascensionis, fuit quadragesimus a resurrectione dies.
units.tr: IX. The time of the ascension was the fortieth day after the resurrection.

units.la: Act. 1: 3. qui numerus frequenter in S. Scriptura observatur, tum in Mose, Elia, aliisque, tum speciatim in Christo, secundum varios ipsius excellentiæ gradus. Luc. 2: 22. Matth. 4: 2. Act. 1: 3. Quibus & sitis se ipsum vivum, postquam passus ipse esset, per multa signa, per quadraginta dies visus ipsis, & differens ea quæ sunt regni Dei. Per quadraginta vero istos dies conversatus est cum hominibus, & loquutus cum discipulis de rebus regnum Dei spectantibus. Act. 1: 3. quando invigilans visit amicos suos, ut irrigaret animam linguentem, & omnem animam agram impleret; & somnus suus fuit suavis ipsi. Jer. 31: 25, 26. Quod Christo proprium & peculiare fuit ex omnibus iis qui e mortuis excitati sunt.
units.tr: Acts 1:3. This number is frequently observed in Holy Scripture, both in Moses, Elijah and others, and especially in Christ, according to the various degrees of his excellence. Luke 2:22. Matthew 4:2. Acts 1:3. To whom also he showed himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God. During those forty days he conversed with men and spoke with the disciples about matters concerning the kingdom of God. Acts 1:3, when he watches over his friends, to water the fainting soul and fill every hungry soul; and his sleep was sweet to him. Jeremiah 31:25, 26. This was peculiar to Christ and distinctive among all those who were raised from the dead.

units.la: X. Causa fuit quidem Pater illum assumens, Act. 1: 11. 1 Tim. 3: 16. ita tamen, ut divina sua potentia, qua se excitaverat, Joh. 10: 18. simul ascenderit, Luc. 24: 51. Joh. 20: 17. & 3: 13. Nemo ascendit in cælum, nisi qui ex cœlo descendit, filius hominis qui est in cœlo. & 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. conf. Joh. 8: 23. & 3: 31. Qui de sursum venit, supra omnes est. Eph. 4: 9. Hebr. 2: 10. Quo conferebat corporis glorificati ratio, quod spiritui subjectum, eadem facilitate sursum ac deorsum moveri poterat.
units.tr: X. The cause was indeed the Father, who took him up, Acts 1:11, 1 Timothy 3:16; yet in such a way that by his own divine power, by which he had raised himself, John 10:18, he ascended at the same time, Luke 24:51, John 20:17, and 3:13. No one has ascended into heaven, except him who came down from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven; and 14:2, I go to prepare a place for you. Compare John 8:23 and 3:31, He who comes from above is above all. Ephesians 4:9, Hebrews 2:10. To this the condition of the glorified body contributed, since, being subject to the spirit, it could be moved upward and downward with equal ease.

units.la: XI. Occurramus nunc erroribus, qui veritati huic offucias obducunt. Quibus se intricarunt homines, ad carnales suas cogitationes omnia metientes; quorum πρῶτον ψεῦδος est, Christum in S. Coena corporaliter esse præsentem; quod ut tuerentur, pervertenda quoque fuit ejus ascensio. Ante omnes Lutherani hic toto cœlo aberrant, distinguentes inter ascensionem Christi visibilem & invisibilem; illam semel, hanc variis vicibus factam esse volunt. Quos varios ascensionis invisibilis gradus, secutam fuisse visibilem seu ultimam & dispensatoriam statuunt, quam in disparitione & glorificatione corporis ejus collocant. Quamvis in hisce omnibus non omnes consentiant.
units.tr: XI. Let us now meet the errors which cast a veil over this truth. Men have entangled themselves in them, measuring all things by their carnal thoughts. Their first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος] is that Christ is present bodily in the Holy Supper; and in order to defend this, his ascension too had to be distorted. Above all the Lutherans go astray here by a whole heaven, distinguishing between Christ's visible and invisible ascension; they hold that the one was made once and the other at various times. They maintain that the various degrees of the invisible ascension were followed by a visible or final and dispensatory ascension, which they place in the disappearance and glorification of his body. Yet even among these men there is no agreement on all points.

units.la: XII. At 1. vanum est illud ascensionis discidium in visibilem & invisibilem; cum Scriptura unam tantum agnoscat. Per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in sancta, aeterna redemptione inventa. Hebr. 9: 12. Act. 1: 9. Joh. 20: 17. Ascendo ad Patrem meum. 2. Ascensio non consistit in sola glorificatione corporis. Aliud enim est ascendere, aliud glorificari. Matth 17. 2. Et transformatus est coram ipsis, & splenduit facies ejus, solis instar. 3. Neque etiam modo loquendi satisfit, cum dicitur disparuisse; quod magis etiam ab ascensione distat, quam glorificari. Vide Marc. 16. 19. Dominus igitur postquam locutus esset cum ipsis, sublatus est in coelum. Luc. 24. 51. Act. 2. 34. secus enim saepius jam ascendisset. Ipsorum autem oculi aperti sunt, & cognoverunt ipsum & ipse disparuit ab illis. Luc. 24. 31.
units.tr: XII. But first, that division of the ascension into visible and invisible is empty, since Scripture acknowledges only one. Through his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption. Hebrews 9:12. Acts 1:9. John 20:17, I ascend to my Father. Second, the ascension does not consist in the glorification of the body alone. For it is one thing to ascend, another to be glorified. Matthew 17:2, And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun. Third, nor is it enough to speak of his having disappeared, which is even further from the ascension than being glorified. See Mark 16:19, So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven. Luke 24:51, Acts 2:34; otherwise he would have ascended many times already. Their eyes were opened, and they knew him, and he vanished from them. Luke 24:31.

units.la: XIII. Liquet igitur hinc, Christum non amplius in terris degere, nempe secundum naturam humanam. Matth. 26. 11. & 28. 6. Joh. 16. 28. Rursus relinquo mundum, & proficiscor ad Patrem.
units.tr: XIII. It is clear from this that Christ no longer dwells on earth, namely according to his human nature. Matthew 26:11, 28:6, John 16:28, Again I leave the world and go to the Father.

units.la: 2 Cor. 5. 16. Si autem etiam Christum novimus secundum carnem, sed nunc non amplius cognoscimus, quamvis quoad personam suam & spiritualem efficientiam, quae ex humana natura etiam originem trahit, ubique sit semper. Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Matth. 28: 20. caeteroquin in coelos Christum se contulisse, relictis terris docetur Act. 3: 21. Quem oportet, ut coeli capiant, usque ad tempora restitutionis omnium.
units.tr: 2 Corinthians 5:16, Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way; although with respect to his person and his spiritual efficacy, which also derives from his human nature, he is always everywhere. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Matthew 28:20. Otherwise, it is taught that Christ withdrew into heaven, leaving the earth, Acts 3:21, whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things.

units.la: XIV. Ruit ergo Pontificiorum πολυτοπία, & Lutheranorum quorundam παντοπία naturae humanae Christi. Repugnant quippe illae 1. Ascensioni Christi, Act. 1. 9. Col. 3. 1. Ea quae sursum sunt, quarite, ubi Christus est, ad dextram Dei sedens. Hebr. 8. 4. 2. Plerisque Symboli capitibus. 3. Ipsius Christi praedictioni. Quando igitur dicant vobis, ecce in deserto est, ne exite; ecce in cubiculis, ne credite. Matth. 24: 26, 27. Johan. 6: 61, 62. 4. Institutioni Sanctae Coenae. 1 Corin. 11: 25, 26. 5. Naturae corporis, cui si locorum spatia & dimensiones demas, ipsum corpus tolli necesse est.
units.tr: XIV. Therefore the polytopy of the Papists and the panthopy of certain Lutherans concerning the human nature of Christ collapses. For these contradict, first, Christ's ascension, Acts 1:9, Colossians 3:1, Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Hebrews 8:4. Second, most of the articles of the Creed. Third, Christ's own prediction: If then they say to you, Behold, he is in the desert, do not go out; behold, he is in the inner rooms, do not believe it. Matthew 24:26, 27, John 6:61, 62. Fourth, the institution of the Holy Supper, 1 Corinthians 11:25, 26. Fifth, the nature of the body, from which, if you remove the spaces and dimensions of places, the body itself must be taken away.

units.la: XV. Putide contra hanc rem argutantur adversarii, Christum, ut iterhoc conficeret, plus quam quingentorum annorum intervallo opus habuisse. Qua in re quotidianus naturae usus, ut divinam Christi potentiam praetermittamus, eos arguere poteste: parilem enim motus velocitatem in motu planetarum & materiae subtilis animadvertimus; qualem agile illud corpus Christi etiam recipere potuit. Nec majoris sunt ponderis, quae obtendunt ex eo, quod ChriChristus postea in terris sit visus. Primum Stephano, Act. 7:55, 56. Verum apparuit ipsi non in terra, sed in coelo conspiciendus; tum omnino sit vero simile, visionem hanc fuisse ecstaticam; quo facit, ut alia mittamus, quod dicitur, Impletus Sp. Sancto. Secundum, visum volunt Christum esse Paulo, Act. 9:4, 17. 22:6. & 26:19. At primitus non visus est Paulo Iesus, sed auditus duntaxat. Act. 9:3,4,17. & 22:9. Deinceps conspectus quidem a Paulo est Christus, sed mota mente & visione interna. Act. 18:9. Dixit autem Dominus per visionem noctu Paulo: ne time, sed loquere, & ne tacueris. Act. 22:17,18. & 23:11. & 26:13. 1. Cor. 9:1. An non Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi? Postea Johanni etiam conspiciendum se praebuisse dicunt Christum Apoc. 1:10, 12, 13. Quam visionem emblematicam esse, locus ipse vel prima fronte docere potest.
units.tr: XV. Our opponents argue foolishly against this, claiming that Christ needed more than an interval of five hundred years to accomplish this again. In this matter, even apart from Christ's divine power, we could refute them by the everyday experience of nature: we observe an equal speed of motion in the movement of the planets and of subtle matter, and that agile body of Christ could also receive such speed. Nor are the arguments they bring from the fact that Christ was afterwards seen on earth of greater weight. First, to Stephen, Acts 7:55, 56. But he appeared to him not on earth, but to be seen in heaven; and it is entirely likely that this vision was ecstatic, which, to pass over other points, is shown by what is said, filled with the Holy Spirit. Second, they hold that Christ was seen by Paul, Acts 9:4, 17, 22:6, 26:19. But at first Jesus was not seen by Paul, but only heard. Acts 9:3, 4, 17, 22:9. Afterwards Christ was indeed seen by Paul, but with his mind moved and by inner vision. Acts 18:9, And the Lord said to Paul in a vision by night: Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent. Acts 22:17, 18, 23:11, 26:13, 1 Corinthians 9:1, Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Later, they say, Christ also presented himself to be seen by John, Revelation 1:10, 12, 13. That this vision was emblematic, the passage itself can show even at first glance.

units.la: XVI. Veritatem hujus rei etiam Socininai intervertunt.
units.tr: XVI. The Socinians also distort the truth of this matter.

units.la: XVI. Veritatem hujus rei etiam Sociniani intervertunt. Quando non solum plures una Christo tribuunt ascensiones, de quo supra actum: verum etiam, quamvis corpus Christi in ascensione demum glorificatum fuisse velint, carne & sanguine absorptis quasi, & in spiritum mutatis; aliud tamen corpus in coelum ab eo illatum volunt, gloriosum nempe, & ejusmodi quidem, ut corpus & ossa non habeat. Quae si vera sunt 1. Christus glorificatus constabit ex duobus spiritibus. 2. Nequidem ascensione prima, quam vult Socinus, Christus corpore suo in coelum potuerit ascendere. 3. Et nos in coelo corpus habere nequibimus. Cum oporteat nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi, ut quisque ferat, quae per corpus fecerit.
units.tr: XVI. The Socinians also distort the truth of this matter. They not only assign Christ several ascensions, as has been discussed above, but also, although they want his body to have been glorified only at the ascension, with flesh and blood as it were absorbed and changed into spirit, they still hold that another body was carried by him into heaven, a glorious one, which has neither flesh nor bones. If these things are true: (1) Christ glorified would consist of two spirits; (2) Christ could not have ascended into heaven in his body by that first ascension which Socinus proposes; (3) and we would not be able to have a body in heaven, since we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5:10. Contra vero 1. corpus carneum & osseum ipsi post resurrectionem adscribitur. Luc. 24:39. Videte manus meas & pedes meos: contrectate me & videte: nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me conspicitis habere. conf. Act. 1:11. 2. Et talis apparebit in futuro judicio. Et intuebuntur me cum eo, quem transfoderunt. Zach. 12:10. Apoc. 1:7. 3. Caro ejus corruptionem non sensit, aut ei unquam fuit obnoxia. Psal. 16:10. Non dabis sanctum tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Act. 2:31. 4. Non citra blasphemiam, coelum carni Christi inaccessum putant, perperam intellecto loco 1. Cor. 15:53. Caro & sanguis non possunt regnum Dei haereditare.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:10. On the contrary: (1) a body of flesh and bones is ascribed to him after the resurrection, Luke 24:39: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me to have. Compare Acts 1:11. (2) And such a body will appear at the future judgment: They will look on me whom they have pierced (Zech. 12:10; Rev. 1:7). (3) His flesh did not experience corruption, nor was it ever subject to it: Psalm 16:10, You will not give your Holy One to see corruption; Acts 2:31. (4) They do not hold without blasphemy that heaven is closed to the flesh of Christ, having misunderstood the passage 1 Cor. 15:53: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: XVII.
