Alieni ab hisce etiam non sunt Anabaptistae, fatentes quidem Christum corpore suo resurrexisse; at vero quali corpore, aut quo modo nunc dextram Patris claudat, ignorare se profitentes; quin volunt eum in coelo abdicasse naturam & proprietates corporis: sed contrarium jam evictum est. conf. Act. 1:9. Et haec dicens, ipsis videntibus, sublatus est. S 3 XVIII. Se-
units.tr: XVII. The Anabaptists are not far removed from these views either. They confess indeed that Christ rose again in his body, but they profess that they do not know in what kind of body, or how, he now holds the right hand of the Father; indeed they maintain that he has laid aside in heaven the nature and properties of a body. But the contrary has already been proved. Compare Acts 1:9: And saying these things, while they were looking on, he was lifted up. S 3 XVIII. Se-

units.la: II. Socinianorum.
units.tr: II. Of the Socinians.

units.la: III. Anabaptistarum. primus & duo posteriores ipsum etiam resurrectionis tempus præsigurarunt. Partes hic etiam suas habet Simson. Jud. 16: 3. Huc etiam pertinet caro sacrificii eucharistici, quæ ex præscripto legis ante tertium diem comedi debebat. Lev. 7: 16, 17, 18. Huc etiam spe-ctabat manipulus ille Lev. 23. qui in Paschate, postridie Sabbati, offerebatur, & agitabatur eo die, quo Christus surrexit.
units.tr: III. Of the Anabaptists. The first and the two latter also foreshadowed the very time of the resurrection. Samson has his part here too: Judges 16:3. To this also belongs the flesh of the eucharistic sacrifice, which by the law's prescription had to be eaten before the third day (Lev. 7:16, 17, 18). To this also looked that sheaf of Lev. 23, which was offered at Passover, on the day after the Sabbath, and was waved on the day on which Christ rose.

units.la: VII. Omnium vero clarissime tota hæc res conficitur ex historia Novi Test. & serie universa narrationis. Nam primo corpus idem fuit, ut ex novo monumento apparet. Luc. 23: 53. Joh. 19: 41. deinde furto ablatum non est; sive illud factum dicatur à discipulis timidissimis; seu à militibus custodiæ illius admotis; quod etiam somnus eorum evertit; seu ab hostibus, qui cadaver illius ostentassent; ut undequaque cadat hæc suspicio. Contra vero vivum fuisse Christum apertissime liquet 1. ex testimonio Angelorum, qui Angeli fuerunt lucis, quales se suo fulgore satis probabant, atque ideo mentiri non poterant. Matth. 28: 6. Non est hic, excitatus est, sicut dixit. Luc. 24: 5, 6. 2. mulierum iunocentissimarum, in quas nulla fraudis suspicio cadebat, cum Christum surrexisse ignorarent, quin & dolerent. 3. Petri & Johannis. Joh. 20: 5--8. qui sepulcrum videbant inane; & speciatim sepositum cum linteis sudarium; quod securitatem Christi resurgentis testabatur. 4. Thomæ aliorumque infidelitas maximum & gravissimum resurrectioni præbet argumentum. Joh. 20: 25, 27. 5. Ante omnia faciunt huc tot apparitiones Christi, eæque variis modis factæ, omnes efficacissime resurrectionem probantes. Apparuit quippe variis personis, vicibus, locis, modis, & diuturno sæpe tempore. Gravissimus etiam & locupletissimus hujus rei testis est universa Ecclesia, quando in memoriam resurrectionis Christi diem Dominicum dedicavit. Nec tenue est argumentum in baptismo gentium, post illam resurrectionem instituto, Judæorum non credentium judicio &c.
units.tr: VII. But most clearly of all, this whole matter is established from the history of the New Testament and the whole sequence of the narrative. For first, the body was the same, as appears from the new tomb (Luke 23:53; John 19:41). Then it was not stolen away, whether this is said to have been done by his most timid disciples, or by the soldiers set to guard it (and their sleep also refutes this), or by the enemies who had displayed the corpse; so that this suspicion falls in every way. On the other hand, that Christ was alive is most openly clear: (1) from the testimony of the angels, who were angels of light, as their brightness sufficiently showed, and therefore could not lie: Matt. 28:6, He is not here, he has risen, as he said; Luke 24:5, 6. (2) From the most innocent women, against whom no suspicion of fraud could fall, since they did not know that Christ had risen, and indeed were grieving. (3) From Peter and John, John 20:5-8, who saw the empty tomb, and in particular the cloth folded apart from the linen cloths, which bore witness to the safety of the risen Christ. (4) The unbelief of Thomas and the others gives the greatest and weightiest proof of the resurrection: John 20:25, 27. (5) Above all, so many appearances of Christ, made in various ways, all prove the resurrection most effectively. For he appeared to various persons, on various occasions, in various places, in various ways, and often over a long period of time. The whole Church is also a most weighty and abundant witness to this matter, since it dedicated the Lord's day to the memory of Christ's resurrection. Nor is the argument slight from the baptism of the Gentiles, instituted after that resurrection, in the judgment of the unbelieving Jews, and so on.

units.la: VIII. Maximi ergo momenti est hic articulus, & fidei Christianæ compendium. Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & crediderit in corde tuo quod Deus eum excitaverit ex mortuis, salvus futurus es. Rom. 10: 9. Ut præfractus sit Judæorum error, quo in hanc veritatem invictam insurgunt. Multum argentum dederunt milit ibus; dicentes: dicite quod discipuli ipsius, noctu venientes, surripuerunt ipsum &c. Matth. 28: 12.
units.tr: VIII. This article is therefore of the greatest importance, and is the summary of the Christian faith: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved (Rom. 10:9). That the error of the Jews, by which they rise up against this unconquered truth, may be broken: They gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away, etc. (Matt. 28:12).

units.la: IX. Considerandam nunc se offert resurrectionis natura & persectio. Per hanc autem animæ dotes eximia accessione fuerunt adau&tæ, æ pro natura scilicet humanæ animæ: summa lux fuit in intelle ætu, ut perceperit & noverit omnia, quæ scire potuit aut debuit humana natura; summa itidem in voluntate fuit sanctitas, gaudium &c. quæ summa caritate ejusque reciproco sensu cum Deo fuit & corpus conjuncta. Corpus vel in sepulcro, corruptioni nequaquam fuerat obnoxium; quod factum tum ob brevem in eo moram, tum præcipue omnipotente vi divinæ ejus naturæ, vivificantis illud & ab omni labe præservantis; resurrexit vero gloriosum, & depósito pulvere, in naturam cœlestium corporum transiit. Phil. 3: 21. Act. 13: 34. Rom. 6: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 15: 44, 49. Hebr. 2: 9, 14. Phil. 2: 9. Matth. 26: 29. quod & editæ ejus operationes satis demonstrant.
units.tr: IX. Now the nature and perfection of the resurrection presents itself for consideration. Through this the endowments of the soul were increased by a remarkable addition, namely in accordance with the nature of the human soul: there was the highest light in the understanding, so that he perceived and knew all that human nature could or ought to know; likewise in the will there was the highest holiness, joy, and so on, which was joined with the highest love and its mutual sense with God, and with the body. Even in the tomb the body was in no way subject to corruption; this was brought about partly by the brief delay there, but chiefly by the almighty power of his divine nature, which quickened it and preserved it from every stain. It rose indeed glorious, and, having laid aside the dust, passed into the nature of heavenly bodies (Phil. 3:21; Acts 13:34; Rom. 6:9, 10; 1 Cor. 15:44, 49; Heb. 2:9, 14; Phil. 2:9; Matt. 26:29). His works, which were later done, sufficiently demonstrate this.

units.la: X. Quod hisce obtendant, Christum edisse & bibisse post resurrectionem; frustra est. Non enim illud humanæ indigentiæ, sed benignitatis prorsus divinæ & liberæ œconomiæ, ad demonstrandam veritatem resurrectionis suæ; ideoque semel tantum factum est, Luc. 24: 41. 43. nam sæpius id contigisse ex Luc. 24: 30. Et factum est, cum ipse accumberet cum illis, accepto pane benedixit, & fracto dedit ipsis. Joh. 21: 13. Act. 10: 41. cogi non potest. Pariter solvitur, quæ de cicatricibus vulnerum ipsius nectitur difficultas. Primo enim dubitari non immerito potest, an eas semper habuerit. Joh. 20: 24, 25. an vero in illud tempus tantum, pro arbitratu suo & œconomice assumpserit, & deinceps sit assumpturus. Videbit eum omnis oculus, & qui eum transfixerunt. Apoc. 1: 7. Deinde, si vero eas habuerit, œconomicum nihilominus fuit, nec de gloriosô corporis illius statu quicquam demit.
units.tr: X. What they put forward against this, that Christ ate and drank after the resurrection, is in vain. For this was not done from human need, but from the entirely divine and free dispensation of kindness, to demonstrate the truth of his resurrection; and therefore it happened only once, Luke 24:41, 43. For that it happened more often cannot be inferred from Luke 24:30: And it came about, when he was reclining with them, that he took bread, blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to them; John 21:13; Acts 10:41. The difficulty that is tied up with the scars of his wounds is likewise resolved. For, first, it can not unreasonably be doubted whether he always had them (John 20:24, 25), or whether he assumed them only for that time, at his own pleasure and by dispensation, and was going to assume them thereafter. Every eye will see him, and those who pierced him (Rev. 1:7). Then, even if he did have them, it was nonetheless by dispensation, and it takes nothing away from the glorious state of that body.

units.la: XI. Obscurata tamen & obnubilata fuit hæc gloria quantisper in terris egit, quo conversari cum discipulis posset: quod docet analogia loci 2. Cor. 3: 7. Si autem ministerium mortis — in gloria factum fuit; adeo ut filii Israelis non possent intueri faciem Mosis, propter gloriam faciei ejus, quæ periret; quomodo non magis ministerium Spiritus erit in gloria? Vide Luc. 24: 16. Act. 22: 11. Cum vero non viderem præ, vel à gloria lucis illius, manu deductus — veni Damascum.
units.tr: XI. This glory, however, was obscured and clouded for as long as he lived on earth, so that he could converse with his disciples. The analogy of the passage 2 Cor. 3:7 teaches this: But if the ministry of death was made in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which was passing away; how will the ministry of the Spirit not rather be in glory? See Luke 24:16; Acts 22:11: But since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I was led by the hand and came to Damascus.

units.la: XII. Non ergo amplius secundum carnem cognoscendus est Christus, post resurrectionem. 2. Cor. 5: 16. id est, quoad infirmitatem & subjectionem sub lege. Manet tamen corpus illud idem numero & subsistentia; retinuit etiam essentiam & proprietates essentiales corporis; speciatim quoad locum & dimensionem. Sursum latus est in cœlum. Luc. 24: 51. Matth. 28: 6.
units.tr: XII. Therefore Christ is no longer to be known according to the flesh after the resurrection (2 Cor. 5:16), that is, as to weakness and subjection under the law. Yet that same body remains the same in number and substance; it has also retained the essence and essential properties of a body, specifically as to place and dimension. He was lifted up into heaven (Luke 24:51; Matt. 28:6).

units.la: XIII. Inepte igitur Pontificii corpus illud intra angustias hostiolæ cogunt, & sub specie panis contineri volunt, per esse sacramentale, ut vocant; cum esse illud tantopere ab essentia corporis differat, quantopere modus & significatio rei sacramentalis ab ipsa re. Nec melius Lutherani dimensionem ab hoc corpore auferunt, per commentum suum de ubiquitate, seu multipræsentia & replicatione, quæ sine multiplicatione cogitari nequit. Nec obstat quod ἀφανὴς dicatur factus. Luc. 24: 31. quod notat illum ex conspectu eorum subductum esse, sive quod discipulorum oculos perstrinxerit & præpedierit; sive quod celerrime se iis surripuerit: non quod ἀφανής aut invisibilis sit factus, sed quod iis non amplius fit visus. Ita nec clauso sepulcro resurrexit. ut liquet Matth. 28: 2. Nec per clausas januas se penetravit, Joh. 20. 18. illud enim loquendi genus vel tempus duntaxat significat, vespertinum scilicet, cum clausæ jam essent januæ; non vero modum: sin vero; non tamen clausæ manserunt; ut patet ex analogia loci Act. 5: 19. Angelus Domini noctu aperuit fores carceris. & com. 23. ministri – renuntiarunt, carcerem inveni-mus quidem clausum, cum omni certitudine. conf. c. 12: 10.
units.tr: XIII. Therefore the Papists foolishly confine that body within the narrow limits of a little door, and want it to be contained under the appearance of bread, by what they call a sacramental being. That being differs from the essence of the body as much as the mode and signification of a sacramental thing differ from the thing itself. The Lutherans do no better in removing dimension from this body by their invention of ubiquity, or multipresence and replication, which cannot be conceived without multiplication. Nor is there any obstacle in the statement that he became invisible [ἀφανὴς] (Luke 24:31). This signifies that he was withdrawn from their sight, either because he dazzled and blinded the disciples' eyes, or because he very quickly slipped away from them. It does not mean that he became invisible or unseen, but that he was no longer seen by them. So too he rose without the tomb being opened, as is clear from Matt. 28:2. Nor did he pass through closed doors, as John 20:18 might suggest. That form of speech signifies only the time, namely evening, when the doors were already shut, and not the manner. And if so, they did not remain shut, as is clear from the analogy of Acts 5:19, The angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and verse 23, we indeed found the prison shut, with all certainty. Compare chapter 12:10.

units.la: XIV. Graviter hic errant etiam Sociniani.
units.tr: XIV. The Socinians also err gravely here.

units.la: Qui primo, Christum ante resurrectionem, tempore mortis, esse desiisse volunt, seu in infernum non existentiæ detrudunt; quod ab horrenda blasphemia non abest. Permansit enim 1. Anima. Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23: 43. & corpus. Non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Psal. 16: 10. 2. Ipse erat vita. Ego sum via & veritas & vita. Joh. 14: 6. & 11: 25. habet potentiam vitæ indissolubilis. Hebr. 7: 16. 1 Cor. 15: 45. 3. Ita Christus bis ἐξ ἀναστάσεως emersisset, semel in generatione, iterum in resurrectione. Secundo iidem negant, corpus Christi, statim à resurrectione gloriosum esse factum, sed demum post ascensionem: præter quam supra vidimus.
units.tr: They first want Christ to have ceased to exist at the time of his death before the resurrection, thrusting him into hell of non-existence. This is not far from horrible blasphemy. For there remained (1) the soul, Today you will be with me in Paradise (Luke 23:43), and the body, You will not allow your holy one to see corruption (Ps. 16:10). (2) He himself was life: I am the way and the truth and the life (John 14:6; also 11:25), and he has the power of an indissoluble life (Heb. 7:16; 1 Cor. 15:45). (3) So Christ would have come forth twice, once in generation and again in resurrection [ἐξ ἀναστάσεως]. Secondly, the same people deny that Christ's body became glorious immediately upon the resurrection, but only after the ascension, apart from what we have seen above.

units.la: XV. Succedit nunc resurrectionis causa efficiens.
units.tr: XV. Now follows the efficient cause of the resurrection.

units.la: Facta quidem illa est virtute Christi propria, Joh. 2: 19. & 10: 18. 1 Cor. 15: 45. Zach. 6: 12. Joh. 5: 26. Act. 1: 3. tribuitur tamen generatim Deo. Hunc Iesum excitavit Deus, cujus nos omnes sumus testes. Act. 2: 32. Patri vero. Quam, præpollentiam virium, operatus est (Pater gloriæ. cum. 17.) in Christo, dum cum excitavit ex mortuis. Eph. 1: 20. Sp. S. Spiritus ejus qui Iesum è mortuis excitavit. Rom. 8: 10. Christus quidem mortificatus est carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu. 1 Pet. 3: 18. Speciali ratione Patri adscribitur, utpote qui in hoc negotio tanquam judex spectatur, qui Filium pro peccatis jam mortuum excitando, absolvit à culpa, qua peccatorum nomine tenebatur, & è carcere de-
units.tr: The resurrection was indeed effected by the proper power of Christ (John 2:19; 10:18; 1 Cor. 15:45; Zech. 6:12; John 5:26; Acts 1:3). It is nevertheless ascribed in general to God: This Jesus God raised up, of which we are all witnesses (Acts 2:32). It is ascribed to the Father in particular: the working of the strength of his power (the Father of glory, compare ch. 17) in Christ, when he raised him from the dead (Eph. 1:20). And to the Holy Spirit: the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead (Rom. 8:11). Christ indeed was put to death in the flesh, but made alive by the Spirit (1 Pet. 3:18). It is ascribed to the Father in a special way, since in this business he is regarded as judge, who, by raising the Son who had already died for sins, absolves him from the guilt for which he was held liable in the name of sins, and lets him out of prison.

units.la: ut & Sociniani. demisit. Qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4:25. conf. c. 6:4. & Hebr. 13:20. Caeteroquin virtus haec & operatio toti Trinitati fuit communis. Ut nulla cum specie Sociniani & Anabaptistae Filio hoc denegent, quia nempe Patri tribuitur.
units.tr: As do the Socinians too. Who was delivered up because of our offences, and raised because of our justification (Rom. 4:25; compare ch. 6:4; Heb. 13:20). Otherwise this power and operation was common to the whole Trinity. So the Socinians and Anabaptists deny this to the Son with no plausible ground, since it is ascribed to the Father.

units.la: XVI. Recte igitur hinc probatur Christi deitas & divina filiatio. Rom. 1:4. ὁρισθέντος, nempe Filius Dei ex resurrectione. Longe aliter ac Sociniani, qui illum inde Filium Dei denominatum fingunt, quo detorquent locum Psal. 2:7. Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. coll. Act. 13:32,33. & Hebr. 5:5. Col. 1:18. contra locorum istorum genium.
units.tr: XVI. Rightly, therefore, from this is proved the deity of Christ and his divine sonship: declared [ὁρισθέντος] (Rom. 1:4), namely Son of God by the resurrection. The Socinians take quite another view. They pretend that he was named Son of God from this, and so they twist Ps. 2:7, You are my son; today I have begotten you, compared with Acts 13:32–33, Heb. 5:5 and Col. 1:18, against the genius of those passages.

units.la: XVII. Negligenda circa hoc negotium minime etiam est circumstantia temporis. Fuit autem tertius dies. Et occident ipsum, & pus, tertio die excitabitur. Matth. 17:23. Luc. 24:21. Joh. 2:19. Solvite templum hoc, & tribus diebus excitabo illud. Act. 10:40, Hunc Jesum excitavit Deus tertio die. 1. Cor. 15:4. Tempus hoc Christo plane peculiare fuit; cum nec sub V. nec Novo Test. ullus tertio die excitatus legatur. Vide speciatim Joh. 11:39. Dixit ipsi Martha, Domine, jam olet, quarti enim dies est. Praefiguratum illud fuit in tribus praecipue viris Isaaco, Ezechia, Jona; Patriarcha, Rege, Propheta. Distinctissime vero typum hunc in se ipso exhibuit Jonas. Matth. 12:40. Reliquos typos supra lustravimus. Conf. Hos. 6:2. Vivificabit nos a duobus diebus: die tertio resuscitabit nos, & vivemus coram illo.
units.tr: XVII. The circumstance of time is by no means to be neglected in this matter. It was the third day: they will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised (Matt. 17:23; Luke 24:21). Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). God raised this Jesus on the third day (Acts 10:40; 1 Cor. 15:4). This time was entirely peculiar to Christ, since nowhere in the Old or New Testament is anyone read of as raised on the third day. See especially John 11:39: Martha said to him, Lord, by now he stinks, for it is the fourth day. This was prefigured especially in three men: Isaac, Hezekiah and Jonah, a patriarch, a king and a prophet. Jonah exhibited this type most distinctly in himself (Matt. 12:40). We have surveyed the other types above. Compare Hos. 6:2: He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live before him.

units.la: XVIII. Ad difficultatem quam hic nectunt de triduo mortis Christi, cum summum per quadraginta tantum horas mortuus fuerit; facilis est responsio: triduum illud recte dici posse, tam proprie & ex nudo literarum sensu; quam ex analogia. Proprie quidem, ut per Synecdochen, sub tribus hisce diebus, eorumque partibus, noctes etiam comprehendantur; quod Judaeis & S. Scripturae frequens est. Vide Gen. 1:5. &c. Unde & numerum hunc ipse Sp. Sanctus ad tertium diem coarctat. Matth. 16:21. &c. Vide & 1. Sam. 30:12. & seqq. Esth. 4:16. & 5:1. Luc 2:21. Analogice vero similiter sumatur, intelligi triduum illud potest, de toto illo tempore humiliationis Christi, ab extrema coena, usque ad primam vesperam, qua se discipulis vivum tot monumentis exhibuit; quod integrum adeo est triduum.
units.tr: XVIII. The difficulty they raise here about the three days of Christ's death, since he was dead for only about forty hours, has an easy answer. Three days can rightly be spoken of, both properly, from the bare sense of the words, and by analogy. Properly, indeed, by synecdoche: the nights are also included under these three days and their parts, which is frequent with the Jews and in Holy Scripture (see Gen. 1:5 etc.). Whence the Holy Spirit himself restricts this number to the third day (Matt. 16:21 etc.). See also 1 Sam. 30:12 ff., Esth. 4:16 and 5:1, Luke 2:21. Analogically, the same kind of reckoning may be applied: that three-day period can be understood of the whole time of Christ's humiliation, from the last supper to the first evening on which he showed himself alive to the disciples by so many proofs. That is indeed a complete three days.

units.la: XIX. Dies quam in sepulcro exigit, fuit Sabbati; atque hactenus simi- transegit; prime autem hebdomadis die resurrexit. similis fuit omnibus mortuis, unquam resuscitatis: nunquam enim quisquam illo die excitatus legitur. Conveniebat illud utique etiam, ut ita typum Sabbati simul expleret. Dies resurrectionis fuit primus hebdomadis, qui inde in memoriam resurrectionis, ab Ecclesia primitiva Christianorum sacris conventibus dicatus & distinctus est; quare & laeti & sine geniculationibus diem illum transfigere debebant. Quomodo vero simul impleti sint typi veteres, alias visum.
units.tr: XIX. The day he spent in the sepulchre was the Sabbath, and so far he passed it as all the dead do; but he rose on the first day of the week. He was like all the dead ever raised in this, for no one is ever read of as raised on that day. It was certainly fitting that he thus fulfilled the type of the Sabbath at the same time. The day of resurrection was the first day of the week, which the primitive Church of Christians afterwards dedicated and distinguished, in memory of the resurrection, to sacred assemblies. Therefore they ought to spend that day joyfully and without kneeling. How the ancient types were fulfilled at the same time has been considered elsewhere.

units.la: XX. Tandem sequuntur hic denique advertenda resurrectionis effecta & fructus; tum Christi, tum nostrum respectu. Christum quod spectat, resurgendo declaratus est victor mortis & dux vitae. Jesus Christus primogenitus ex mortuis & princeps Regum terrae. Apoc. 1: 5. Rursus autem quum introducit primogenitum in orbem habitabilem, dicit: & adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei. Hebr. 1:6. regius sacerdos. Dabit ipsi Dominus Deus thronum Davidis, Patris ipsius. Luc. 1:32. Unde & salvare ad perfectum potest accedentes per ipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro ipsis. Hebr. 7: 25. Rom. 8: 34. Nos quod attinet, per resurrectionem Christi ad nos pervenit testamenti ejus executio, quae praestari debebat ab ipso Christo vivo. Qui traditus est propter delicta nostra, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4: 25. Hebr. 9: 12. atque ita fructus omnis mortis Christi in nos derivatus est.
units.tr: XX. Finally, the effects and fruits of the resurrection are to be noted here, both with respect to Christ and with respect to us. As regards Christ, by rising he was declared victor over death and leader of life: Jesus Christ, the firstborn from the dead and prince of the kings of the earth (Rev. 1:5). And again, when he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: let all the angels of God worship him (Heb. 1:6). He is a royal priest: the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father (Luke 1:32). Whence he is also able to save completely those who come to God through him, always living to intercede for them (Heb. 7:25; Rom. 8:34). As for us, through the resurrection of Christ there reached us the execution of his testament, which had to be carried out by Christ himself while living: who was delivered up because of our offences, and raised because of our justification (Rom. 4:25; Heb. 9:12). Thus all the fruit of Christ's death has been derived to us.

units.la: XXI. Oritur ergo hinc 1. certitudo justificationis nostrae; cum resurrectione sua absolutus sit Christus ab omni reatu nostri ergo ipsi incumbente. Rom. 4: 25. Quem Jesum Deus excitavit, solvens dolores mortis, sicut non erat possibile, ipsum ab ea teneri. Act. 2: 24. cum & hic obtineret illud Matth. 5: 26. Amen dico tibi, non exibis inde, donec dederis ultimum quadrantem. Hinc baptismus est ἐπερώτημα bona conscientiae per resurrectionem Christi. 1 Pet. 3: 21. 2. In hac resurrectione exemplar nobis datum est & arrha nostrae resurrectionis suturae. Ego sum resurrectio & vita, qui credit in me, etiamsi moriatur, vivet. Joh. 11: 25. Rom. 8: 11. 1. Pet. 1: 3. 1. Cor. 15: 12. Si autem Christus praedicatur quod ex mortuis excitatus sit, quomodo quidam inter vos dicunt, quod non sit resurrectio mortuorum? inde Christus dicitur primitiae eorum qui obdormiverunt 1.Cor. 15: 20. cum tota fidelium massa in eo sit sanctificata. 3. Agnoscitur in ea deformatio resurrectionis nostrae spiritualis. Sicut surrexit Christus ex mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitae ambulemus. Rom. 6: 4. & 7: 4. Vos mortificati estis legi, per corpus Christi, ut fieretis alterius, qui ex mortuis surrexit, ut fructum feramus. XXII. Plane XXII. Plane alienum est, quod hic statuunt Socsiniani, Deum per resurrectionem hanc nihil aliud intendisse, quam gloriam suam, respectu sui ipsius, respectu vero nostri confirmationem fidei nostrae, ut credamus hominem mortalem, Deo obedientem, excitari posse. Quod mirari licet, cum carnis resurrectionem negent.
units.tr: XXI. Hence arise, first, the certainty of our justification, since by his resurrection Christ was absolved from all the guilt of ours that lay upon him (Rom. 4:25): whom God raised up, loosing the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it (Acts 2:24). Here also holds the saying of Matt. 5:26: Truly I say to you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny. Hence baptism is the appeal of a good conscience through the resurrection of Christ (1 Pet. 3:21). Second, in this resurrection an example has been given to us, and a pledge of our future resurrection: I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he dies, will live (John 11:25; Rom. 8:11; 1 Pet. 1:3; 1 Cor. 15:12). But if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? Hence Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20), since the whole mass of believers has been sanctified in him. Third, the pattern of our spiritual resurrection is recognised in it: as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:4; 7:4). You have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who was raised from the dead, that we may bear fruit. XXII. Quite foreign to the truth is what the Socinians set down here, that God intended nothing by this resurrection except his own glory with respect to himself, and, with respect to us, the confirmation of our faith, so that we might believe that a mortal man obedient to God can be raised. This may well be wondered at, since they deny the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: De Ascensione Christi.
units.tr: On the Ascension of Christ.

units.la: I. Alter gradus exaltationis Christi est ejus ascensio, quando triumphali quasi curru ovans in coelum sublatus est. Act. 1:11. Eph. 4:10. Qui descendit, ipse est et is qui ascendit, supra omnes coelos, ut impleat omnia. Cujus tratio ut ordine fiat, videnda 1. ascensio ipsa. 2. ejus certitudo. 3. ad coelos, locus. 4. tempus. 5. causa. 6. finis & fructus.
units.tr: I. The second stage of Christ's exaltation is his ascension, when he was carried up into heaven, as if in a triumphal chariot, exulting in victory. Acts 1:11. Eph. 4:10. He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. In order to treat this in an orderly way, we must consider (1) the ascension itself; (2) its certainty; (3) the place to which he ascended; (4) the time; (5) the cause; (6) the end and fruit.

units.la: II. Ipsi Deo interdum ascensio tribuitur. Gen. 11:5. & 17:22. & 18:21. hic autem proprie sumitur pro translatione substantiae corporeae e loco inferiore ad superiorem, seu a corporum inferiorum vicinia in viciniam corporum superiorum. Act. 1:11. Hic Jesus qui sublatus est a vobis in coelum. &c. Marc. 16:19. Luc. 24:51. Proprie ergo convenit naturae Christi humanae, divinae tantum figurate, quatenus nempe in illa manifestavit gloriam suam; & metonymice, quatenus ascensionis fuit causa; unde & de tota persona divina ascensio praedicatur. Psal. 47:6. Ascendit Deus cum clangore, Jehovah cum voce tubae. & 68:19. Ascendisti in coelum, egisti praedam, accepisti dona in hominibus; & ex eo Eph. 4:8, 9.
units.tr: II. Sometimes the ascension is attributed to God himself. Gen. 11:5, 17:22, 18:21. Here, however, it is taken properly for the transfer of a corporeal substance from a lower place to a higher, that is, from the neighbourhood of lower bodies to that of higher bodies. Acts 1:11: This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc. Mark 16:19. Luke 24:51. Properly, then, the ascension belongs to the human nature of Christ; it belongs to the divine nature only figuratively, in so far as he displayed his glory in that nature; and it belongs to him metonymically, in so far as he was the cause of the ascension. Hence the ascension is also predicated of the whole divine person. Psalm 47:6: God has gone up with a shout, Jehovah with the sound of a trumpet. And Psalm 68:19: You have ascended on high, you have led captives, you have received gifts among men; and from this, Eph. 4:8, 9.

units.la: III. Certitudo constat 1. Ex vaticiniis. Psal. 68:18,19. & Psal. 110. conf. Act. 2:34. 2. Ex typis. Ita, sicut Pontifex, semel quotannis, & quidem post exordium novi anni, intrabat in Sanctum Sanctorum, non sine sanguine Lev. 16. idem Christo etiam faciendum erat, in initio temporis gratiae & libertatis, fuso suo sanguine, ut viam in coelum apertam nobis dedicaret. Hebr. 9:23, 24. Necesse ergo figuras quidem eorum, quae in coelis sunt, hisce mundari: ipsa autem coelestia meliroribus hostiis praeipsis. Non enim in manu facta Sancta introivit Christus, verorum instar habentia, sed in ipsum coelum, ut nunc appareat facie Dei pro nobis. rupto velo carnis suae.
units.tr: III. The certainty of the ascension rests (1) on prophecies: Psalm 68:18, 19, and Psalm 110; compare Acts 2:34. (2) On types. Just as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year, and indeed after the beginning of the new year, not without blood (Lev. 16), so Christ too had to do at the beginning of the time of grace and liberty: having shed his own blood, he was to consecrate for us a way into heaven that lay open. Heb. 9:23, 24: It was necessary, therefore, that the copies of the things in the heavens should be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us, the veil of his flesh having been torn.

units.la: Pars II. S Hebr. 4: 16. & 10: 20. Quam initiavit nobis viam recentem & vivam, per velamen, id est, carnem suam.
units.tr: Part II. § Heb. 4:16 and 10:20: which he opened for us as a new and living way, through the veil, that is, his flesh.

units.la: IV. Eodem spectabat Enochi & Eliae raptus, Gen. 5. 2. Reg. 2. quorum ille sub promissione, iste sub lege in coelum translati sunt; sicut Christus sub gratia; in exemplar fidelium omnium aetatum. Miraculum etiam hoc primum omnium fuit a creatione mundi, quemadmodum & ultimum futurum est, in consummatione seculi. Notandae autem hic sunt differentiae, inter hanc Christi ascensionem, & aliorum sublationes: illi nempe ascenderunt virtute aliena, Christus propria: illi vivi, Christus post mortem, quam superare & hoc modo triumphare debebat.
units.tr: IV. To the same purpose were the translations of Enoch and Elijah, Gen. 5; 2 Kings 2. The former was taken up into heaven under the promise, the latter under the law, just as Christ was under grace; they are an example for all the faithful of every age. This miracle was also the first of all since the creation of the world, just as the last will be at the consummation of the age. Differences, however, must be noted here between this ascension of Christ and the raisings up of the others: those ascended by a power not their own, Christ by his own power; those were alive, Christ after death, which he had to overcome and in this way triumph.

units.la: V. 3. Indubitate probatur ex testibus, quorum numerus sufficiens, & sanctitas supra omnem calumniam; partim Angeli; partim duodecim Apostoli, Act. 1: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 9: 1. Nonne sum Apostolus? an non liber? an non Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi?
units.tr: V. Third, the ascension is proved beyond doubt by witnesses whose number is sufficient and whose holiness is above all calumny: partly angels, partly the twelve apostles. Acts 1:9, 10. 1 Cor. 9:1: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

units.la: VI. Turbas hic excitant Pontificii, Christo socios in ascensione adsignando; alii Patres e limbo liberatos; ex Psal. 68: 19. cum potius cogitari debeat Christus, pro more triumphantium, Diabolum cum morte, peccato & inferno, revinctis manibus in captivitatem post se traxisse. Alii ergo malunt adjunctos illi fuisse sanctos illos, qui in morte Christi resurrexerant, Matth. 27: 53. sed exigua itidem probabilitate.
units.tr: VI. Here the Papists stir up difficulties, assigning companions to Christ in the ascension: others say the fathers freed from limbo, citing Psalm 68:19, whereas we ought rather to think that Christ, after the manner of triumphant conquerors, led Satan away in captivity with his hands bound, together with death, sin and hell. Others prefer to think that those holy men who had risen at Christ's death (Matt. 27:53) went up with him, but this too has only slight probability.

units.la: VII. Locus in ascensione duplex considerari potest; vel unde solverit quasi; vel ubi appulerit. Prior Act. 1: 12. dicitur mons Oliveti. Luc. 24: 50. vero, Bethania. Confer. Act. 1: 12. & Joh. 11: 18. Quod ita in concordiam redigi posse videtur; ut ascenderit Christus ex monte Oliveti, eo nempe loco, quo ab urbe distabat pro octo stadia (quantum est iter Sabbati Act. 1: 12.) qui ejus tractus jam inde denominabatur Bethania, a palmis ibi consitis, usque ad 15 stadia. Joh. 11: 18. sicut primus ejus tractus urbi vicinus appellabatur Bethphage, a grossis: cum generale & commune nomen horum tractuum fuerit mons Oliveti; ad quod nomen respicitur Act. 1: 12. Quae vero de vestigiis Christi, monti huic impressis scripserunt veteres, fide sua carent.
units.tr: VII. The place of the ascension may be considered in a twofold way: either from where he seems to have set out, or where he arrived. The former is called the Mount of Olives in Acts 1:12, but Luke 24:50 calls it Bethany. Compare Acts 1:12 with John 11:18. These seem capable of being reconciled in this way: Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives, namely from the place which was about eight stadia from the city (which is the distance of a Sabbath day's journey, Acts 1:12). From there the stretch of ground, up to fifteen stadia, was then called Bethany, from the palm trees planted there (John 11:18); just as the first part of it, close to the city, was called Bethphage, from the unripe figs. The general and common name for these stretches was the Mount of Olives, and Acts 1:12 refers to that name. As for what the ancients wrote about the footprints of Christ impressed on this mount, it lacks reliable authority.

units.la: VIII. Locus quo ascendit, est coelum. Ascendisti in altum. Psal. 68: 19. Hic Jesus, qui a vobis sublatus est in coelum &c. Act. 1: 11. Marc. 16: 19. 1. Petr. 3: 22. Qui est in dextra Patris, cum abiisset in coelum. Eph. 4: 10. sive coelum summum. Jesus Pontifex maximus perpertranßiit cœles. Heb. 4: 14. & cap. 7: 26. Altior cœlis factus. Eph. 4: 10. Qui descendit, ipse est, qui ascendit supra omnes cœlos, ut impleat omnia. Pervertunt hæc Lutherani Ubiquitarii, errorem novo errore tecturi, ne pateat; cœlum etiam ubiquitarium fingentes; atque ita non loci, sed status tantum mutationem factam esse: contra ac est Joh. 6: 62. Si igitur conspiciatis Filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius. & c. 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. Phil. 3: 20. Nostra autem civitas in cœlo est, unde & Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Iesum Christum. Eph. 4: 10. 1. Thess. 4: 16. Hebr. 12: 23.
units.tr: VIII. The place to which he ascended is heaven: You ascended on high, Psalm 68:19. This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc., Acts 1:11; Mark 16:19; 1 Peter 3:22: who is at the right hand of the Father, having gone into heaven. Eph. 4:10, that is, the highest heaven. Jesus, the great high priest, has passed through the heavens, Heb. 4:14; and chapter 7:26: made higher than the heavens. Eph. 4:10: He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. The Lutheran Ubiquitarians pervert these passages, seeking to cover one error with another so that it may not be exposed, and they imagine even a ubiquitarian heaven; and so they say that only a change of state, not of place, has taken place. This is contrary to John 6:62: If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before; and John 14:2: I go to prepare a place for you. Phil. 3:20: But our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Eph. 4:10; 1 Thess. 4:16; Heb. 12:23.

units.la: IX. Tempus ascensionis, fuit quadragesimus a resurrectione dies.
units.tr: IX. The time of the ascension was the fortieth day after the resurrection.

units.la: Act. 1: 3. qui numerus frequenter in S. Scriptura observatur, tum in Mose, Elia, aliisque, tum speciatim in Christo, secundum varios ipsius excellentiæ gradus. Luc. 2: 22. Matth. 4: 2. Act. 1: 3. Quibus & sitit se ipsum vivum, postquam passus ipse esset, per multa signa, per quadraginta dies visus ipsis, & differens ea quæ sunt regni Dei. Per quadraginta vero istos dies conversatus est cum hominibus, & loquutus cum discipulis de rebus regnum Dei spectantibus. Act. 1: 3. quando invigilans visit amicos suos, ut irrigaret animam linquentem, & omnem animam agram impleret; & somnus suus fuit suavis ipsi. Jer. 31: 25, 26. Quod Christo proprium & peculiare fuit ex omnibus iis qui e mortuis excitati sunt.
units.tr: Acts 1:3. This number is frequently observed in Holy Scripture, both in Moses, Elijah and others, and especially in Christ, according to the various degrees of his excellence. Luke 2:22. Matt. 4:2. Acts 1:3. To these he also presented himself alive after his suffering, by many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the things of the kingdom of God. Indeed, during those forty days he conversed with men and spoke with the disciples about matters concerning the kingdom of God. Acts 1:3, when he watches over his friends, so that he might water the fainting soul and fill every thirsty soul; and his sleep was sweet to him. Jer. 31:25, 26. This was proper and peculiar to Christ among all those who were raised from the dead.

units.la: X. Causa fuit quidem Pater illum assumens, Act. 1: 11. 1 Tim. 3: 16. ita tamen, ut divina sua potentia, qua se excitaverat, Joh. 10: 18. simul ascenderit, Luc. 24: 51. Joh. 20: 17. & 3: 13. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui ex cœlo descendit, filius hominis qui est in cœlo. & 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. conf. Joh. 8: 23. & 3: 31. Qui de sursum venit, supra omnes est. Eph. 4: 9. Hebr. 2: 10. Quo confirmabat corporis glorificati ratio, quod spiritui subiectum, eadem facilitate sursum ac deorsum moveri poterat.
units.tr: X. The cause was indeed the Father, who took him up, Acts 1:11, 1 Tim. 3:16, yet in such a way that by his own divine power, by which he had raised himself, John 10:18, he ascended at the same time, Luke 24:51, John 20:17, and 3:13. No one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven. And 14:2. I go to prepare a place for you. Compare John 8:23 and 3:31. He who comes from above is above all. Eph. 4:9, Heb. 2:10. The reasoning about the glorified body confirmed this, since a body made subject to the spirit could be moved upward as easily as downward.

units.la: XI. Occurramus nunc erroribus, qui veritati huic offucias obducunt. Quibus se intricarunt homines, ad carnales suas cogitationes omnia metientes; quorum πρώτον ψεῦδος est, Christum in S. Coena corporaliter esse præsentem; quod ut tuentur, perverteda quoque fuit ejus ascensio. Ante omnes Lutherani hic toto cœlo aberrant, distinguentes inter ascensionem Christi visibilem & invisibilem; illam semel, hanc variis vicibus factam esse volunt. Quos varios ascensionis invisibilis gradus, secutam fuisse visibilem seu ultimam & dispensatoriam statuunt, quam in disparitione & glorificatione corporis ejus collocant. Quamvis in hisce omnibus non omnes consentiant.
units.tr: XI. Let us now meet the errors which throw a veil over this truth. Men have entangled themselves in these, measuring everything by their carnal thoughts. Their first falsehood [πρώτον ψεῦδος] is that Christ is bodily present in the Holy Supper; and in order to defend it, his ascension too had to be distorted. Above all, the Lutherans go wrong here by a whole heaven, distinguishing between Christ's visible and invisible ascension; they hold that the former happened once and the latter at various times. They lay down that after these various degrees of invisible ascension there followed a visible or final and dispensatory ascension, which they place in the disappearance and glorification of his body. Yet not all of them agree on all these points.

units.la: {a} Arriani erroris.
units.tr: {a} Of the Arian error.

units.la: {b} Pontificiorum & Lutheranorum. Christus postea in terris sit visus. Primum Stephano, Act. 7:55, 56. Verum apparuit ipsi non in terra, sed in coelo conspiciendus; tum omnino sit vero simile, visionem hanc fuisse ecstaticam; quo facit, ut alia mittamus, quod dicitur, Impletus Sp. Sancto. Secundum, visum volunt Christum esse Paulo, Act. 9:4, 17. 22:6. & 26:19. At primitus non visus est Paulo Jesus, sed auditus duntaxat. Act. 9:3,4,17. & 22:9. Deinceps conspectus quidem a Paulo est Christus, sed mota mente & visione interna. Act. 18:9. Dixit autem Dominus per visionem noctu Paulo: ne time, sed loquere, & ne tacuero. 22:17,18. & 23:11. & 26:13. 1. Cor. 9:1. An non Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi? Postea Johanni etiam conspiciendum se praebuisse dicunt Christum Apoc. 1:10, 12, 13. Quam visionem emblematicam esse, locus ipse vel prima fronte docere potest.
units.tr: {b} Of the Papists and the Lutherans. They say that Christ was afterwards seen on earth. First, to Stephen, Acts 7:55, 56. But he appeared to him not on earth but to be seen in heaven; and it is entirely probable that this vision was ecstatic, as is shown (to say nothing of other things) by the words, filled with the Holy Spirit. Second, they want Christ to have been seen by Paul, Acts 9:4, 17; 22:6; and 26:19. But at first Jesus was not seen by Paul, only heard. Acts 9:3, 4, 17; and 22:9. Afterwards Christ was indeed seen by Paul, but in a moved mind and an inner vision. Acts 18:9: The Lord said to Paul by a vision in the night: do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent. Also 22:17, 18; 23:11; 26:13; 1 Cor. 9:1: Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Later they say that Christ also presented himself to be seen by John, Rev. 1:10, 12, 13. That this vision was emblematic, the passage itself can teach even at first sight.

units.la: XVI. Veritatem hujus rei etiam Socdiniani intervertunt. Quan-do non solum plures una Christo tribuunt ascensiones, de quo supra actum: verum etiam, quamvis corpus Christi in ascensione demum glorificatum fuisse velint, carne & sanguine absorptis quasi, & in spiritum mutatis; aliud tamen corpus in coelum ab eo illatum volunt, gloriosum nempe, & ejusmodi quidem, ut corpus & ossa non habeat. Quae si vera sunt 1. Christus glorificatus constabit ex duobus spiritibus. 2. Nequidem ascensione prima, quam vult Socinus, Christus corpore suo in coelum potuerit ascendere. 3. Et nos in coelo corpus habere nequibimus. Cum oporteat nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi, ut quisque ferat, quae per corpus fecerit.
units.tr: XVI. The Socinians too distort the truth of this matter. They not only ascribe several ascensions to Christ, which was treated above; but also, although they want Christ's body to have been glorified only at the ascension, with flesh and blood as it were absorbed and changed into spirit, they still maintain that another body was carried by him into heaven, a glorious one, namely, such that it has no body and bones. If these things are true: 1. Glorified Christ will consist of two spirits. 2. Christ could not, by the first ascension which Socinus proposes, have ascended into heaven with his body. 3. And we will not be able to have a body in heaven, since we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may bear what he has done through the body. 2 Cor. 5:10. On the contrary, however: 1. A fleshly and bony body is ascribed to him after the resurrection. Luke 24:39: See my hands and my feet; handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having. Compare Acts 1:11. 2. And he will appear such in the future judgment: And they will look upon me whom they pierced. Zech. 12:10; Rev. 1:7. 3. His flesh did not experience corruption, nor was it ever subject to it. Ps. 16:10: You will not allow your holy one to see corruption. Acts 2:31. 4. They think, not without blasphemy, that heaven is closed to the flesh of Christ, misunderstanding the passage 1 Cor. 15:53: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5:10. Contra vero 1. corpus carneum & osseum ipsi post resurrectionem adscribitur. Luc. 24:39. Videte manus meas & pedes meos: contrectate me & videte: nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me conspicitis habere. conf. Act. 1:11. 2. Et talis apparebit in futuro judicio. Et intuebuntur me cum eo, quem transfoderunt. Zach. 12:10. Apoc. 1:7. 3. Caro ejus corruptionem non sensit, aut ei unquam fuit obnoxia. Psal. 16:10. Non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Act. 2:31. 4. Non citra blasphemiam, coelum carni Christi inaccessum putant, perperam intellecto loco 1. Cor. 15:53. Caro & sanguis non possunt regnum Dei haereditare.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:10. On the other hand, first, a fleshly and bony body is ascribed to him after the resurrection. Luke 24:39. See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. Cf. Acts 1:11. Second, he will appear in this form at the future judgment. And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced. Zech. 12:10. Rev. 1:7. Third, his flesh did not experience corruption, nor was it ever subject to it. Ps. 16:10. Thou wilt not leave thy holy one to see corruption. Acts 2:31. Fourth, they hold, not without blasphemy, that heaven is inaccessible to Christ's flesh, having misunderstood the passage in 1 Cor. 15:53. Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: XVII. Alieni ab hisce etiam non sunt Anabaptistae, fatentes quidem Christum corpore suo resurrexisse; at vero quali corpore, aut quo modo nunc dextram Patris claudat, ignorare se profitentes; quin volunt eum in coelo abdicasse naturam & proprietates corporis: sed contrarium jam evictum est. conf. Act. 1:9. Et haec dicens, ipsis videntibus, sublatus est. XVIII. Se
units.tr: XVII. The Anabaptists are not far removed from these views either. They admit indeed that Christ rose again in his body, but they profess that they do not know in what kind of body, or how he now sits at the right hand of the Father; indeed they hold that in heaven he has laid aside the nature and properties of a body. But this has already been refuted. Cf. Acts 1:9. And when he had said these things, while they beheld, he was taken up. XVIII. Se

units.la: Note III: Anabaptistarum. XVIII. Sequuntur denique ascensionis Finis & Effectus. Necessaria siquidem illa fuit, tum Christi ergo: Primus homo ex terra pulvereus erat; secundus homo, Dominus ex coelo. 1. Cor. 15: 47. Hebr. 9: 6. & 12: 24. tum praecipue nostri causa. 1. Ut coelum nobis referaret. Nondum manifesta erat facta via; adhuc priore tabernaculo habente statum. Hebr. 9: 8. 2. Ut pro nobis intercederet. Rom. 8: 34. Quis est, qui condemnat? Christus est is, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. 3. Ut nostro nomine coelum occuparet. Et conresuscitavit & collocavit in coelestibus in Christo Iesu. Eph. 2: 6. & locum nobis illic pararet. Joh. 14: 2. 4. Ut Spiritum suum in nos effunderet. Si vero proficiscar, mittam eum paracletum ad vos. Joh. 16: 7. cujus virtute coelestia quaereremus. Ea quae sursum sunt, quaerite, ubi Christus est, ad dextram Dei sedens. Col. 3: 1–3. Nostra autem civitas in coelo est, unde & Salvatorem exspectamus, Dominum Iesum Christum. Phil. 3: 20. 5. Ut τεκμήριον & certissimum nostrae ascensionis argumentum in promptu haberemus. Si quis mihi ministret, me sequatur, & ubi sum ego, ibi & minister meus erit. Joh. 12: 26. Assumam vos ad me, ut ubi ego sum, ibi & vos sitis. Joh. 14: 3. Phil. 3: 20, 21.
units.tr: Note III: On the Anabaptists. XVIII. Finally, there follow the ends and effects of the ascension. It was indeed necessary, both for Christ's own sake: The first man was of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. 1 Cor. 15:47. Heb. 9:6 and 12:24; and especially for our sake. (1) That he might open heaven to us. The way into the holiest was not yet made manifest, while the first tabernacle was still standing. Heb. 9:8. (2) That he might intercede for us. Rom. 8:34. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. (3) That in our name he might take possession of heaven. And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Eph. 2:6; and that he might prepare a place for us there. John 14:2. (4) That he might pour out his Spirit upon us. But if I depart, I will send him unto you, the Comforter. John 16:7; by whose power we might seek heavenly things. Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Col. 3:1–3. For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Phil. 3:20. (5) That we might have at hand a token and most certain proof of our ascension. If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be. John 12:26. I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also. John 14:3. Phil. 3:20, 21.

units.la: XIX. Pessime vero Sociniani adulterinas & fictas hasce ascensionis causas ponunt. 1. Ut per eam divino modo immortalis fieret, h. e. mori amplius nequiret. Cum videlicet idem corpus ante ascensionem Christo non fuerit, cum eo quod nunc habet, hoc per ascensionem ipsi acquirendum fuisse, supponunt. 2. Ut salutem nobis procuraret & praestaret. Qualem nempe in procuranda salute Servatorem illum pro arbitratu suo fingunt. De quibus tum proxime, tum alio loco egimus.
units.tr: XIX. But the Socinians put forward these causes of the ascension, which are spurious and invented, in the most wicked way. (1) That through it he might become immortal in a divine manner, that is, that he could no longer die. For they assume that, since the same body was not before the ascension what it now has, this was to be acquired by him through the ascension. (2) That he might procure and bestow salvation upon us. Indeed, they imagine that Saviour as they please in procuring salvation. We have dealt with these matters both just above and in another place.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: De Sessione Christi ad dextram Patris.
units.tr: On the Sitting of Christ at the Right Hand of the Father.

units.la: I. Ualis olim Regum in Oriente erat consuetudo, ut quos vellent insigni honore mactatos, & in secundum ab ipsis locum evectos, ad dextram suam collocarent; eodem etiam modo Spiritus sanctus exaltationem Christi describit, iisdemque utitur loquendi generibus: ita enarraturus supremum illum gradum gloriae Christi, in quem evectus est, dicit eum ad dextram Dei sedisse. Quae praerogativa soli Christo peculiaris est & propria. Consedit ad dextram magnitudinis in altis, Hebr. 1: 3. Eum exaltavit ex mortuis, & collocavit ad dextram suam in supercœlestibus. Eph. 1:20.
units.tr: I. As it was once the custom of kings in the East to seat at their right hand those whom they wished to honour with a distinguished dignity and raise to second place after themselves, so the Holy Spirit also describes the exaltation of Christ and uses the same forms of speech. Intending to describe that highest degree of Christ's glory to which he was raised, he says that Christ sat at the right hand of God. This privilege belongs to Christ alone, peculiarly and properly. He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, Heb. 1:3. He raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, Eph. 1:20.

units.la: II. Prædicta fuit hæc gloria. Dixit Jehovah Domino meo, sede ad dextram meam. Psal. 110: 1. Confer Matth. 22: 42, 43. non enim illud Davidi, vel ulli alii convenire potest.
units.tr: II. This glory was foretold: The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, Ps. 110:1. Compare Matt. 22:42, 43, for this cannot apply to David or to any other man.

units.la: III. Dextra Dei interdum potentiam Dei notat. Juravit Jehovah per dextram suam, & per brachium roboris sui. Esai. 62: 8. Dextra Dei exaltatus & promissione Sp. Sancti a Patre accepta, effudit hoc, quod nunc videtis & auditis. Act. 2: 33. Hic vero nobis paulo propius consideranda est phrasis, sedere ad dextram; quæ desumpta a more Regum Orientalium, qui proximos a se ad dextram collocare solebant. 1. Reg. 2: 19. Matth. 20: 21. Psal. 45: 10. Stat Augusta ad dextram tuam in auro Ophirino. 3. Esdr. 4: 29. Notatur ergo hoc loquendi genere honos a regio secundus, quin etiam quandoque pro re nata æqualis. Qui quum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam duxit esse insttar Dei. Phil. 2: 6. ubi Christus dicitur ἴσα θεῷ εἶναι, paria cum Deo facere. Ut perversissime Sociniani, ab una parte Christum hic honoratiori loco positum velint, quam ipse Pater; (quibus & assentitur Maldonatus Jesuita) ab altera parte nihilominus dignitatem hanc precario ipsi collatam, & honorem non nisi a Patre secundum ipsi obtingere.
units.tr: III. The right hand of God sometimes denotes the power of God: The LORD has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength, Isa. 62:8. Exalted therefore at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out what you now see and hear, Acts 2:33. Here, however, the phrase to sit at the right hand must be considered a little more closely. It is taken from the custom of the Eastern kings, who were accustomed to place those nearest to them at their right hand: 1 Kings 2:19; Matt. 20:21; The queen stands at your right hand in gold of Ophir, Ps. 45:10; 3 Esdras 4:29. By this manner of speaking, therefore, is denoted an honour second only to the royal one, and sometimes, as the occasion requires, even equal to it. Who, being in the form of God, did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God, Phil. 2:6, where Christ is said to be ἴσα θεῷ εἶναι [isa theō einai], to make himself equal with God. The most perverse Socinians, on the one hand, wish Christ to be placed here in a more honourable position than the Father himself (the Jesuit Maldonatus also agrees with them); on the other hand, they maintain that this dignity was conferred on him only by favour, and that he holds this honour only from the Father.

units.la: IV. Sessio hæc non externo & corporeo modo fingenda est, sed figurate, ad honoris hujus stabilitatem significandam. Vidi Dominum sedentem in throno celso & elato. Esai. 6: 1. Qui fecisti judicium & prima glo- jus mecum, consedisti in solium judex justus. Psal. 9: 5. 2. Thess. 2: 4. Apoc. 17: 1, 9. alibi etiam stare ad dextram dicitur Christus. Act. 7: 55. & ambulare. Apoc. 1: 13.
units.tr: IV. This sitting is not to be imagined in an external and bodily manner, but figuratively, to signify the stability of this honour. I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, Isa. 6:1. You have executed judgement and justice; you sat on the throne as a righteous judge, Ps. 9:5; 2 Thess. 2:4; Rev. 17:1, 9. Elsewhere Christ is also said to stand at the right hand, Acts 7:55, and to walk, Rev. 1:13.

units.la: V. Sessio igitur hæc supremam gloriam & honorem denotat. Collocavit eum ad dextram suam in supercœlestibus, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & potentiam, & dominationem, & omne nomen quod nominatur non tantum in seculo hoc, sed etiam in futuro. Eph. 1: 20, 21. Phil. 2: 9–11. Hebr. 1: 3. Consedit ad dextram magnitudinis in altis. & 2: 7, 8. & 8: 1. 1. Pet. 3: 22. Hebr. 12: 2. Luc. 22: 69. Matth. 26: 64. huic gloriæ junctæ simul est potestas & imperium. Sede ad dextram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum; virgam roboris tuam mittet Jehovah e Zione; dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Psal. 110: 1, 2. 1. Cor. 15: 25. ut universa regia potestas sessioni huic includatur.
units.tr: V. This sitting therefore denotes supreme glory and honour. He set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, Eph. 1:20, 21; Phil. 2:9–11; Heb. 1:3. He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, Heb. 2:7, 8; 8:1; 1 Pet. 3:22; Heb. 12:2; Luke 22:69; Matt. 26:64. Joined to this glory at the same time is power and rule: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool. The LORD will send the rod of your strength out of Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies, Ps. 110:1, 2; 1 Cor. 15:25. Thus all royal power is included in this sitting.

units.la: VI. De regno illo Christi ita habendum est; non esse illud naturale, læ cogunt, & sub specie panis contineri volunt, per esse sacramentale, ut vocant; cum esse illud tantopere ab essentia corporis differat, quantopere modus & significatio rei sacramentalis ab ipsa re. Nec melius Lutherani dimensionem ab hoc corpore auferunt, per commentum suum de ubiquitate, seu multipræsentia & replicatione, quæ sine multiplicatione cogitari nequit. Nec obstat quod ἀφαντος dicatur factus. Luc. 24:31. quod notat illum ex conspectu eorum subductum esse, sive quod discipulorum oculos perstrinxerit & præpedierit; sive quod celerrime se iis surripuerit: non quod ἀόρατος aut invisibilis sit factus, sed quod iis non amplius sit visus. Ita nec clauso sepulcro resurrexit, ut liquet Matth. 28: 2. Nec per clausas januas se penetravit, Joh. 20. 18. illud enim loquendi genus vel tempus duntaxat significat, vespertinum scilicet, cum clausæ jam essent januæ; non vero modum: sin vero; non tamen clausæ manserunt; ut patet ex analogia loci Act. 5:19. Angelus Domini nocte aperuit fores carceris. & com. 23. ministri — renuntiarunt, carcerem inventimus quidem clausum, cum omni certitudine. conf. c. 12: 10.
units.tr: VI. Concerning that reign of Christ the following must be held: it is not a natural reign. The Papists are forced to deny this, and they wish him to be contained under the appearance of bread through a sacramental being, as they call it, since that being differs from the substance of the body as much as the mode and signification of a sacramental thing differ from the thing itself. Nor do the Lutherans remove the dimension from this body any better, by their fiction of ubiquity, or multipresence and replication, which cannot be conceived without multiplication. Nor is it an objection that he is said to have become ἄφαντος [aphantos], vanished, Luke 24:31. This means that he was withdrawn from their sight, either because he dazzled and blinded the disciples' eyes, or because he very quickly slipped away from them. It does not mean that he became invisible, but that he was no longer seen by them. Likewise he did not rise with the tomb closed, as is clear from Matt. 28:2; nor did he penetrate through closed doors, John 20:19. For that form of speech signifies only the time, namely evening, when the doors were already shut, and not the manner. But if they did not remain shut, that is clear from the parallel passage, Acts 5:19: The angel of the Lord opened the doors of the prison by night, and v. 23: The ministers reported, We found the prison indeed shut, with all security; cf. ch. 12:10.

units.la: XIV. Graviter hic errant etiam Socinioni. Qui primo, Christum ante resurrectionem, tempore mortis, esse desiisse volunt, seu in infernum non existentiæ detrudunt; quod ab horrenda blasphemia non abest. Permansit enim 1. Anima. Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23: 43. & corpus. Non dabis pium tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Psal. 16: 10. 2. Ipse erat vita. Ego sum via & veritas & vita. Joh. 14: 6. & 11: 25. habet potentiam vitæ indissolubilis. Hebr. 7: 16. 1 Cor. 15: 45. 3. Ita Christus bis ἐξ ἀνάστασιν emersisset, semel in generatione, iterum in resurrectione. Secundo iidem negant, corpus Christi, statim à resurrectione gloriosum esse factum, sed demum post ascensionem: præter quam supra vidimus.
units.tr: XIV. The Socinians also err gravely here. They first want Christ to have ceased to exist before the resurrection, at the time of death, and thrust him into the non-existence of hell, which is not far from horrible blasphemy. For he remained: 1. as soul, Today you will be with me in Paradise, Luke 23:43; and as body, You will not let your Holy One see corruption, Ps. 16:10. 2. He himself was life, I am the way, the truth and the life, John 14:6; cf. 11:25; he has the power of an indissoluble life, Heb. 7:16; 1 Cor. 15:45. 3. Thus Christ would have risen twice out of non-existence: once at his generation, and again at the resurrection. Secondly, the same men deny that the body of Christ became glorious immediately from the resurrection, but only after the ascension, which is contrary to what we saw above.

units.la: XV. Succedit nunc resurrectionis causa efficiens. Facta quidem illa est virtute Christi propria, Joh. 2: 19. & 10: 18. 1 Cor. 15: 45. Zach. 6: 12. Joh. 5: 26. Act. 1: 3. tribuitur tamen generatim Deo. Hunc Jesum excitavit Deus, cujus nos omnes sumus testes. Act. 2: 32. Patri vero. Quam, præpollentiam virium, operatus est (Pater gloriæ, cum. 17.) in Christo, dum eum excitavit ex mortuis. Eph. 1: 20. Sp. S. Spiritus ejus qui Jesum è mortuis excitavit. Rom. 8: 10. Christus quidem mortificatus est carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu. 1 Pet. 3: 18. Speciali ratione Patri adscribitur, utpote qui in hoc negotio tanquam judex spectatur, qui Filium pro peccatis jam mortuum excitando, absolvit à culpa, qua peccatorum nomine tenebatur, & è carcere dedemisit. Qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4:25. conf. c. 6:4. & Hebr. 13:20. Caeteroquin virtus haec & operatio toti Trinitati fuit communis. Ut nulla cum specie Sociniani & Anabaptistae Filio hoc denegent, quia nempe Patri tribuitur.
units.tr: XV. Next comes the efficient cause of the resurrection. It was indeed accomplished by the proper power of Christ, John 2:19; 10:18; 1 Cor. 15:45; Zech. 6:12; John 5:26; Acts 1:3. Yet it is generally ascribed to God: This Jesus God raised up, of which we are all witnesses, Acts 2:32. It is ascribed to the Father: the working of the strength of his power, which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead, Eph. 1:19, 20 (the Father of glory, cf. 1:17). It is ascribed to the Holy Spirit: the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead, Rom. 8:11; Christ indeed was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit, 1 Pet. 3:18. It is ascribed to the Father in a special way, since in this business he is regarded as judge, who, by raising the Son who had already died for sins, absolves him from the guilt which he bore in the name of sins, and releases him from prison: who was delivered up for our offences and raised for our justification, Rom. 4:25; cf. 6:4 and Heb. 13:20. Otherwise this power and operation was common to the whole Trinity. So the Socinians and Anabaptists, with no appearance of reason, deny this to the Son, on the ground that it is ascribed to the Father.

units.la: XVI. Recte igitur hinc probatur Christi deitas & divina filiatio. Rom. 1:4. ολοστος, nempe Filius Dei ex resurrectione. Longe aliter ac Sociniani, qui illum inde Filium Dei denominatum fingunt, quo detorquent locum Psal. 2:7. Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. coll. Act. 13:32,33. & Hebr. 5:5. Col. 1:18. contra locorum istorum genium.
units.tr: XVI. Hence Christ's deity and divine sonship are rightly proved from Rom. 1:4, where he is ὁρισθέντος [horisthentos], that is, declared, Son of God by the resurrection. This is quite different from the Socinians, who pretend that he was therefore named Son of God from this, and who twist Ps. 2:7, You are my Son, today I have begotten you, comparing Acts 13:32, 33, and Heb. 5:5, Col. 1:18, against the sense of those passages.

units.la: XVII. Negligenda circa hoc negotium minime etiam est circumstantia temporis. Fuit autem tertius dies. Et occident ipsum, & pus, tertio die excitabitur. Matth. 17:23. Luc. 24:21. Joh. 2:19. Solvite templum hoc, & tribus diebus excitabo illud. Act. 10:40, Hunc Jesum excitavit Deus tertio die. 1. Cor. 15:4. Tempus hoc Christo plane peculiare fuit; cum nec sub V. nec Novo Test. ullus tertio die excitatus legatur. Vide speciatim Joh. 11:39. Dixit ipsi Martha, Domine, jam olet, quarti enim dies est. Praefiguratum illud fuit in tribus praecipue viris Isaaco, Ezechia, Jona; Patriarcha, Rege, Propheta. Distinctissime vero typum hunc in se ipso exhibuit Jonas. Matth. 12:40. Reliquos typos supra lustravimus. Conf. Hos. 6:2. Vivificabit nos a duobus diebus: die tertio resuscitabit nos, & vivemus coram illo.
units.tr: XVII. Nor is the circumstance of time to be neglected in this matter. It was the third day: They will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised, Matt. 17:23; Luke 24:21; John 2:19, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Acts 10:40: God raised him up on the third day, 1 Cor. 15:4. This time was entirely peculiar to Christ, since no one is read of as raised on the third day under either the Old or the New Testament. See especially John 11:39: Martha said to him, Lord, by now he smells, for it is the fourth day. This was prefigured chiefly in three men: Isaac, Hezekiah and Jonah, a patriarch, a king and a prophet. But Jonah exhibited this type most distinctly in himself, Matt. 12:40. We have reviewed the other types above. Compare Hos. 6:2: He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live before him.

units.la: XVIII. Ad difficultatem quam hic nectunt de triduo mortis Christi, cum summum per quadraginta tantum horas mortuus fuerit; facilis est responsio: triduum illud recte dici posse, tam proprie & ex nudo literarum sensu; quam ex analogia. Proprie quidem, ut per Synecdochen, sub tribus hisce diebus, eorumque partibus, noctes etiam comprehendantur; quod Judaeis & S. Scripturae frequens est. Vide Gen. 1:5. &c. Unde & numerum hunc ipse Sanctus ad tertium diem coarctat. Matth. 16:21. &c. Vide & 1. Sam. 30:12. & seqq. Esth. 4:16. & 5:1. Luc 2:21. Analogice vero, si sumatur, intelligi triduum illud potest, de toto illo tempore humiliationis Christi, ab extrema coena, usque ad primam vesperam, qua se discipulis vivum tot monumentis exhibuit; quod integrum adeo est triduum.
units.tr: XVIII. As for the difficulty raised here about the three days of Christ's death, when he was dead for only forty hours, the answer is easy. The phrase "three days" can rightly be used in two ways, both in the strict sense of the words and by analogy. Strictly, it is a synecdoche: the nights too are included within these three days and their parts, which is common among the Jews and in Holy Scripture. See Gen. 1:5 and following. For this reason the Lord himself limits the number to the third day: Matt. 16:21 and following. See also 1 Sam. 30:12 and following; Esth. 4:16 and 5:1; Luke 2:21. By analogy, if the phrase is taken that way, the three days can be understood as the whole period of Christ's humiliation, from his last supper to the first evening on which he showed himself alive to his disciples by so many proofs. That period is a complete three days.

units.la: XIX. Dies quam in sepulcro exigit, fuit Sabbati; atque hactenus Sabbatum in sepulcro transegit; primo autem hebdomadis die resurrexit. similis fuit omnibus mortuis, unquam resuscitatis: nunquam enim quisquam illo die excitatus legitur. Conveniebat illud utique etiam, ut ita typum Sabbati simul expleret. Dies resurrectionis fuit primus hebdomadis, qui inde in memoriam resurrectionis, ab Ecclesia primitiva Christianorum sacris conventibus dicatus & distinctus est; quare & laeti & sine geniculationibus diem illum transfigere debebant. Quomodo vero simul impleti sint typi veteres, alias visum.
units.tr: XIX. The day he spent in the tomb was the Sabbath, and so far he spent the Sabbath in the grave; but he rose on the first day of the week. In this he was like all the dead who were ever raised, for no one is ever read of as raised on that day. It was also fitting that he should thus fulfil the type of the Sabbath at the same time. The day of the resurrection was the first day of the week, which from then on was set apart and marked out by the primitive Church of Christians for their sacred assemblies in memory of the resurrection. For this reason they ought to spend that day joyfully and without kneeling. How the old types were fulfilled at the same time is a question for another occasion.

units.la: XX. Tandem sequuntur hic denique advertenda resurrectionis effecta & fructus; tum Christi, tum nostrum respectu. Christum quod spectat, resurgendo declaratus est victor mortis & dux vitae. Jesus Christus primogenitus ex mortuis & princeps Regum terrae. Apoc. 1: 5. Rursus autem quum introducit primogenitum in orbem habitabilem, dicit: & adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei. Hebr. 1: 6. regius sacerdos. Dabit ipsi Dominus Deus thronum David is, Patris ipsius. Luc. 1: 32. Unde & salvare ad perfectum potest accedentes per ipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro ipsis. Hebr. 7: 25. Rom. 8: 34. Nos quod attinet, per resurrectionem Christi ad nos pervenit testamenti ejus executio, quae praestari debebat ab ipso Christo vivo. Qui traditus est propter delictos nostros, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4: 25. Hebr. 9: 12. atque ita fructus omnis mortis Christi in nos derivatus est.
units.tr: XX. Finally, we must now note the effects and fruits of the resurrection, both with respect to Christ and with respect to us. As for Christ, by rising he was declared the victor over death and the prince of life. Jesus Christ is the firstborn from the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth. Rev. 1:5. And again, when he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: and let all the angels of God worship him. Heb. 1:6. He is a royal priest: The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father. Luke 1:32. Therefore he is able also to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. Heb. 7:25; Rom. 8:34. As for us, through the resurrection of Christ the execution of his testament has come to us, which had to be performed by Christ himself while living. Who was delivered up for our offences and raised for our justification. Rom. 4:25; Heb. 9:12. And so the whole fruit of Christ's death has flowed down to us.

units.la: XXI. Oritur ergo hinc 1. certitudo justificationis nostrae; cum resurrectione sua absolutus sit Christus ab omni reatu nostri ergo ipsi incumbente. Rom. 4: 25. Quem Jesum Deus excitavit, solvens dolores mortis, sicut non erat possibile, ipsum ab ea teneri. Act. 2: 24. cum & hic obtineret illud Matth. 5: 26. Amen dico tibi, non exibis inde, donec dederis ultimum quadrantem. Hinc baptismus est ἐπερώτημα bona conscientiae per resurrectionem Christi. 1 Pet. 3: 21. 2. In hac resurrectione exemplar nobis datum est & arrha nostrae resurrectionis suturae. Ego sum resurrectio & vita, qui credit in me, etiamsi moriatur, vivet. Joh. 11: 25. Rom. 8: 11. 1. Pet. 1: 3. 1. Cor. 15: 12. Si autem Christus praedicatur quod ex mortuis excitatus sit, quomodo quidam inter vos dicunt, quod non sit resurrectio mortuorum? inde Christus dicitur primitiae eorum qui obdormiverunt 1. Cor. 15: 20. cum tota fidelium massa in eo sit sanctificata. 3. Agnoscitur in ea deformatio resurrectionis nostrae spiritualis. Sicut surrexit Christus ex mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitae ambulemus. Rom. 6: 4. & 7: 4. Vos mortificati estis legi, per corpus Christi, ut fieretis alterius, qui ex mortuis surrexit, ut fructum feramus. XXII. Plane XXII. Plane alienum est, quod hic statuunt Socociniani, Deum per resurrectionem hanc nihil aliud intendisse, quam gloriam suam, respectu sui ipsius, respectu vero nostri confirmationem fidei nostrae, ut credamus hominem mortalem, Deo obedientem, excitari posse. Quod mirari licet, cum carnis resurrectionem negent.
units.tr: XXI. From this there arise, first, the certainty of our justification, since by his resurrection Christ was absolved from all the guilt that lay upon him on our account. Rom. 4:25. God raised up this Jesus, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. Acts 2:24. Here also that saying of Matthew 5:26 holds: Truly I say to you, you shall not get out of there until you have paid the last penny. Hence baptism is an appeal [ἐπερώτημα] of a good conscience through the resurrection of Christ. 1 Pet. 3:21. Second, in this resurrection an example has been given us and a pledge of our own future resurrection. I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live. John 11:25; Rom. 8:11; 1 Pet. 1:3; 1 Cor. 15:12. But if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? Hence Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Cor. 15:20, since the whole mass of believers has been sanctified in him. Third, the pattern of our spiritual resurrection is recognised in it. Just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6:4; and 7:4. You have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who was raised from the dead, that we may bear fruit. XXII. It is quite foreign to the truth what the Socinians state here, that God intended nothing by this resurrection except his own glory with respect to himself, and, with respect to us, the confirmation of our faith, so that we may believe that a mortal man obedient to God can be raised. One may well wonder at this, since they deny the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: De Ascensione Christi.
units.tr: On the Ascension of Christ.

units.la: I. Alter gradus exaltationis Christi est ejus ascensio, quando triumphali quasi curru ovans in coelum sublatus est. Act. 1:11. Eph. 4:10. Qui descendit, ipse est et is qui ascendit, supra omnes coelos, ut impleat omnia. Cujus tratio ut ordine fiat, videnda 1. ascensio ipsa. 2. ejus certitudo. 3. ad coelos. locus. 4. tempus. 5. causa. 6. finis & fructus.
units.tr: I. The second stage of Christ's exaltation is his ascension, when he was lifted up into heaven as if riding in a triumphal chariot. Acts 1:11. Eph. 4:10. He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. To treat this in order, we must consider (1) the ascension itself; (2) its certainty; (3) the place; (4) the time; (5) the cause; (6) the end and fruit.

units.la: II. Ipsi Deo interdum ascensio tribuitur ἀναβαίνειν. Gen. 11:5. & 17:22. & 18:21. hic autem proprie sumitur pro translatione substantiae corporeae e loco inferiore ad superiorem, seu a corporum inferiorum vicinia in viciniam corporum superiorum. Act. 1:11. Hic Jesus qui sublatus est a vobis in coelum. &c. Marc. 16:19. Luc. 24:51. Proprie ergo convenit naturae Christi humanae, divinae tantum figurate, quatenus nempe in illa manifestavit gloriam suam; & metonymice, quatenus ascensionis fuit causa; unde & de tota persona divina ascensio praedicatur. Psal. 47:6. Ascendit Deus cum clangore, Jehovah cum voce tubae. & 68:19. Ascendisti in coelum, egisti praedam, accepisti dona in hominibus; & ex eo Eph. 4:8, 9.
units.tr: II. Ascension is sometimes attributed to God himself, ἀναβαίνειν [anabainein]: Gen. 11:5; 17:22; 18:21. Here, however, it is taken properly for the transfer of a bodily substance from a lower place to a higher, that is, from the neighbourhood of lower bodies to that of higher bodies. Acts 1:11: This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc. Mark 16:19. Luke 24:51. Properly, therefore, ascension belongs to the human nature of Christ; it is ascribed to the divine nature only figuratively, insofar as he thereby displayed his glory; and metonymically, insofar as the divine nature was the cause of the ascension. Hence ascension is also predicated of the whole divine person. Ps. 47:6: God has gone up with a shout, Jehovah with the sound of a trumpet. And Ps. 68:19: You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts among men; and from this, Eph. 4:8, 9.

units.la: III. Certitudo constat 1. Ex vaticiniis. Psal. 68:18, 19. & Psal. 110. conf. Act. 2:34. 2. Ex typis.
