Ita, sicut Pontifex, semel quotannis, & quidem post exordium novi anni, intrabat in Sanctum Sanctorum, non sine sanguine Lev. 16. idem Christo etiam faciendum erat, in initio temporis gratiae & libertatis, fuso suo sanguine, ut viam in coelum apertam nobis dedicaret. Hebr. 9:23, 24. Necesse ergo figuras quidem eorum, quae in coelis sunt, hisce mundari: ipsa autem coelestia majoribus hostiis praeipsis. Non enim in manu facta Sancta introivit Christus, verorum instar habentia, sed in ipsum coelum, ut nunc appareat facie Dei pro nobis. rupto velo carnis suae. Hebr. 4: 16. & 10: 20. Quam initiavit nobis viam recentem & vivam, per velamen, id est, carnem suam.
units.tr: III. Its certainty rests (1) on prophecies: Ps. 68:18, 19, and Ps. 110; compare Acts 2:34. (2) On types. Just as the high priest once a year, and indeed after the beginning of the new year, entered the Holy of Holies, not without blood (Lev. 16), so Christ also had to do the same at the beginning of the time of grace and liberty, shedding his own blood to consecrate for us a way into heaven opened up. Heb. 9:23, 24: It was necessary, then, that the copies of heavenly things should be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us; the veil of his flesh having been torn. Heb. 4:16 and 10:20: which he inaugurated for us as a new and living way, through the veil, that is, his flesh.

units.la: IV. Eodem spectabat Enochi & Eliae raptus, Gen. 5. 2. Reg. 2. quorum ille sub promissione, iste sub lege in coelum translati sunt; sicut Christus sub gratia; in exemplar fidelium omnium aetatum. Miraculum etiam hoc primum omnium fuit a creatione mundi, quemadmodum & ultimum futurum est, in consummatione seculi. Notandae autem hic sunt differentiae, inter hanc Christi ascensionem, & aliorum sublationes: illi nempe ascenderunt virtute aliena, Christus propria: illi vivi, Christus post mortem, quam superare & hoc modo triumphare debebat.
units.tr: IV. Enoch's and Elijah's translations also looked to this end (Gen. 5; 2 Kings 2). The former was taken up into heaven under the promise, the latter under the law, just as Christ was under grace; they serve as examples for all the faithful of every age. This miracle was also the first of all since the creation of the world, just as the last will be at the consummation of the age. Here, however, differences must be noted between this ascension of Christ and the raptures of others. Those men ascended by another's power; Christ by his own. They ascended while alive; Christ after death, which he had to overcome and in this way triumph.

units.la: V. 3. Indubitate probatur ex testibus, quorum numerus sufficiens, & sanctitas supra omnem calumniam; partim Angeli; partim duodecim Apostoli, Act. 1: 9, 10. 1 Cor. 9: 1. Nonne sum Apostolus? an non liber? an non Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi?
units.tr: V. (3) It is indubitably proved from witnesses, whose number is sufficient and whose holiness is beyond all calumny: partly angels, partly the twelve apostles. Acts 1:9, 10. 1 Cor. 9:1: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

units.la: VI. Turbas hic excitant Pontificii, Christo socios in ascensione adsignando; alii Patres e limbo liberatos; ex Psal. 68: 19. cum potius cogitari debeat Christus, pro more triumphantium, Diabolum cum morte, peccato & inferno, revinctis manibus in captivitatem post se traxisse. Alii ergo malunt adjunctos illi fuisse sanctos illos, qui in morte Christi resurrexerant, Matth. 27: 53. sed exigua itidem probabilitate.
units.tr: VI. The Papists stir up difficulties here by assigning companions to Christ in the ascension; others say the fathers freed from limbo; citing Ps. 68:19, though rather one should think of Christ, in the manner of triumphant conquerors, leading captive the devil with death, sin and hell, his hands bound, behind him. Others therefore prefer that those holy men who had risen at Christ's death (Matt. 27:53) were joined with him, but with equally slight probability.

units.la: VII. Locus in ascensione duplex considerari potest; vel unde solverit quasi; vel ubi appulerit. Prior Act. 1: 12. dicitur mons Oliveti. Luc. 24: 50. vero, Bethania. Confer. Act. 1: 12. & Joh. 11: 18. Quod ita in concordiam redigi posse videtur; ut ascenderit Christus ex monte Oliveti, eo nempe loco, quo ab urbe distabat per octo stadia (quantum est iter Sabbati Act. 1: 12.) qui ejus tractus jam inde denominabatur Bethania, a palmis ibi consitis, usque ad 15 stadia. Joh. 11: 18. sicut primus ejus tractus urbi vicinus appellabatur Bethphage, a grossis: cum generale & commune nomen horum tractuum fuerit mons Oliveti; ad quod nomen respicitur Act. 1: 12. Quae vero de vestigiis Christi, monti huic impressis scripserunt veteres, fide sua carent.
units.tr: VII. The place in the ascension can be considered in two ways: either whence he seemed to depart, or where he arrived. Acts 1:12 names the Mount of Olives; Luke 24:50, however, names Bethany. Compare Acts 1:12 and John 11:18. These seem capable of being reconciled thus: Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives, at the place from which it was eight stadia from the city (the distance of a Sabbath day's journey, Acts 1:12); and the district from there onward, up to fifteen stadia, was already called Bethany from the palm trees planted there (John 11:18). Likewise its first stretch near the city was called Bethphage, from the unripe figs; but the general and common name of these districts was the Mount of Olives, and it is to this name that Acts 1:12 refers. As for what the ancients wrote about the footprints of Christ impressed on this mountain, they lack reliable warrant.

units.la: VIII. Locus quo ascendit, est coelum. Ascendisti in altum. Psal. 68: 19. Hic Jesus, qui a vobis sublatus est in coelum &c. Act. 1: 11. Marc. 16: 19. 1. Petr. 3: 22. Qui est in dextra Patris, cum abiisset in coelum. Eph. 4: 10. sive coelum summum. Jesus Pontifex maximus perpertransiit cœles. Heb. 4: 14. & cap. 7: 26. Altior cœlis factus. Eph. 4: 10. Qui descendit, ipse est, qui ascendit supra omnes cœlos, ut impleat omnia. Pervertunt hæc Lutherani Ubiquitarii, errorem novo errore tecturi, ne pateat; cœlum etiam ubiquitarium fingentes; atque ita non loci, sed status tantum mutationem factam esse: contra ac est Joh. 6: 62. Si igitur conspiciatis Filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius. & c. 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. Phil. 3: 20. Nostra autem civitas in cœlo est, unde & Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Iesum Christum. Eph. 4: 10. 1. Thess. 4: 16. Hebr. 12: 23.
units.tr: VIII. The place to which he ascended is heaven. You have ascended on high, Ps. 68:19. This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, etc., Acts 1:11; Mark 16:19; 1 Pet. 3:22: who is at the right hand of the Father, having gone into heaven. Eph. 4:10: or the highest heaven. Jesus, the great high priest, has passed through the heavens, Heb. 4:14; and chapter 7:26: made higher than the heavens. Eph. 4:10: He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. The Lutheran Ubiquitarians distort these passages, wishing to cover one error with another so that it may not be exposed; they imagine even a ubiquitous heaven, and so claim that only a change of state, not of place, took place. This is contrary to John 6:62: If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before; and John 14:2: I go to prepare a place for you. Phil. 3:20: But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Eph. 4:10; 1 Thess. 4:16; Heb. 12:23.

units.la: IX. Tempus ascensionis, fuit quadragesimus a resurrectione dies.
units.tr: IX. The time of the ascension was the fortieth day after the resurrection.

units.la: Act. 1: 3. qui numerus frequenter in S. Scriptura observatur, tum in Mose, Elia, aliisque, tum speciatim in Christo, secundum varios ipsius excellentiæ gradus. Luc. 2: 22. Matth. 4: 2. Act. 1: 3. Quibus & stitit se ipsum vivum, postquam passus ipse esset, per multa signa, per quadraginta dies visus ipsis, & differens ea quæ sunt regni Dei. Per quadraginta vero istos dies conversatus est cum hominibus, & loquutus cum discipulis de rebus regnum Dei spectantibus. Act. 1: 3. quando invigilans visit amicos suos, ut irrigaret animam linquentem, & omnem animam agram impleret; & somnus suus fuit suavis ipsi. Jer. 31: 25, 26. Quod Christo proprium & peculiare fuit ex omnibus iis qui e mortuis excitati sunt.
units.tr: Acts 1:3. This number is frequently observed in Holy Scripture, both in Moses, Elijah and others, and especially in Christ, according to the various degrees of his excellence. Luke 2:22. Matt. 4:2. Acts 1:3. To whom also he showed himself alive after his passion, by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God. During those forty days he conversed with men and spoke with the disciples about matters concerning the kingdom of God. Acts 1:3. When he watched over his friends, that he might refresh the fainting soul and fill every hungry soul; and his sleep was sweet to him. Jer. 31:25, 26. This was proper and peculiar to Christ among all those who were raised from the dead.

units.la: X. Causa fuit quidem Pater illum assumens, Act. 1: 11. 1 Tim. 3: 16. ita tamen, ut divina sua potentia, qua se excitaverat, Joh. 10: 18. simul ascenderit, Luc. 24: 51. Joh. 20: 17. & 3: 13. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui ex cœlo descendit, filius hominis qui est in cœlo. & 14: 2. Proficiscor, ut parem vobis locum. conf. Joh. 8: 23. & 3: 31. Qui de sursum venit, supra omnes est. Eph. 4: 9. Hebr. 2: 10. Quo conferebat corporis glorificati ratio, quod spiritui subjectum, eadem facilitate sursum ac deorsum moveri poterat.
units.tr: X. The Father indeed was the cause of his taking him up, Acts 1:11. 1 Tim. 3:16. Yet in such a way that by his own divine power, by which he had raised himself, John 10:18, he also ascended at the same time, Luke 24:51. John 20:17, and 3:13. No one ascends into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven. And 14:2. I go to prepare a place for you. Compare John 8:23, and 3:31. He who comes from above is above all. Eph. 4:9. Heb. 2:10. To this the nature of his glorified body contributed, which, being subject to the spirit, could be moved upward and downward with equal ease.

units.la: XI. Occurramus nunc erroribus, qui veritati huic offucias obducunt. Quibus se intricarunt homines, ad carnales suas cogitationes omnia metientes; quorum ἀρχὴν ἀυδ est, Christum in S. Cœna corporaliter esse præsentem; quod ut tuerentur, perverteneda quoque fuit ejus ascensio. Ante omnes Lutherani hic toto cœlo aberrant, distinguentes inter ascensionem Christi visibilem & invisibilem; illam semel, hanc variis vicibus factam esse volunt. Quos varios ascensionis invisibilis gradus, secutam fuisse visibilem seu ultimam & dispensatoriam statuunt, quam in disparitione & glorificatione corporis ejus collocant. Quamvis in hisce omnibus non omnes consentiant. Christus postea in terris sit visus. Primum Stephano, Act. 7:55, 56. Verum apparuit ipsi non in terra, sed in coelo conspiciendus; tum omnino sit vero simile, visionem hanc fuisse ecstaticam; quo facit, ut alia mittamus, quod dicitur, Impletus Sp. Sancto. Secundum, visum volunt Christum esse Paulo, Act. 9:4, 17. 22:6. & 26:19. At primitus non visus est Paulo Jesus, sed auditus duntaxat. Act. 9:3, 4, 17. & 22:9. Deinceps conspectus quidem a Paulo est Christus, sed mota mente & visione interna. Act. 18:9. Dixit autem Dominus per visionem noctu Paulo: ne time, sed loquere, & ne tacile. 22:17, 18. & 23:11. & 26:13. 1. Cor. 9:1. An non Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi? Postea Johanni etiam conspiciendum se praebuisse dicunt Christum Apoc. 1:10, 12, 13. Quam visionem emblematicam esse, locus ipse vel prima fronte docere potest.
units.tr: XI. Let us now meet the errors that throw a veil over this truth. Men have entangled themselves in them, measuring everything by their carnal thoughts. Their starting point is the claim that Christ is present bodily in the Holy Supper; and to defend this, his ascension too had to be distorted. Above all, the Lutherans go wrong here by a whole heaven, distinguishing between Christ's visible and invisible ascension; they hold that the invisible one happened once, and the other at various times. They maintain that, after these various degrees of the invisible ascension, there followed a visible or final and dispensational ascension, which they place in the disappearance and glorification of his body. Yet not all of them agree on all these points. Christ was afterwards seen on earth. First by Stephen, Acts 7:55, 56. But he appeared to him not on earth, but as one to be seen in heaven; and it is wholly probable that this vision was ecstatic; to which points, to say nothing of other things, what is said, filled with the Holy Spirit, agrees. Second, they hold that Christ was seen by Paul, Acts 9:4, 17; 22:6; and 26:19. But at first Jesus was not seen by Paul, but only heard. Acts 9:3, 4, 17; and 22:9. Afterwards Christ was indeed seen by Paul, but with his mind moved and by an inward vision. Acts 18:9. The Lord said to Paul in a vision by night: Do not fear, but speak, and do not be silent. Acts 22:17, 18; 23:11; 26:13. 1 Cor. 9:1. Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Afterwards they say that Christ also presented himself to be seen by John, Rev. 1:10, 12, 13. That this vision was emblematic, the passage itself can show even at first glance.

units.la: XVI. Veritatem hujus rei etiam Socinians intervertunt. Quando non solum plures una Christo tribuunt ascensiones, de quo supra actum: verum etiam, quamvis corpus Christi in ascensione demum glorificatum fuisse velint, carne & sanguine absorptis quasi, & in spiritum mutatis; aliud tamen corpus in coelum ab eo illatum volunt, gloriosum nempe, & ejusmodi quidem, ut corpus & ossa non habeat. Quae si vera sunt 1. Christus glorificatus constabit ex duobus spiritibus. 2. Nequidem ascensione prima, quam vult Socinus, Christus corpore suo in coelum potuerit ascendere. 3. Et nos in coelo corpus habere nequibimus. Cum oporteat nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi, ut quisque ferat, quae per corpus fecerit.
units.tr: XVI. The Socinians also pervert the truth of this matter. They not only ascribe several ascensions to Christ, which has been discussed above; but also, although they wish the body of Christ to have been glorified only at the ascension, with flesh and blood as it were swallowed up and changed into spirit, they nevertheless want another body to have been carried by him into heaven, namely a glorious one, and of such a kind that it has no body and bones. If these things are true: 1. Christ glorified will consist of two spirits. 2. Christ could not have ascended into heaven with his body at the first ascension, which Socinus wants. 3. And we shall not be able to have a body in heaven. Since we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5:10. Contra vero 1. corpus carneum & ossem ipsi post resurrectionem adscribitur. Luc. 24:39. Videte manus meas & pedes meos: contrectate me & videte: nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me conspicitis habere. conf. Act. 1:11. 2. Et talis apparebit in futuro judicio. Et intuebuntur me cum eo, quem transfoderunt. Zach. 12:10. Apoc. 1:7. 3. Caro ejus corruptionem non sensit, aut ei unquam fuit obnoxia. Psal. 16:10. Non dabis sanctum tuum, ut videat corruptionem. Act. 2:31. 4. Non citra blasphemiam, coelum carni Christi inaccessum putant, perperam intellecto loco 1. Cor. 15:53. Caro & sanguis non possunt regnum Dei haereditare.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:10. On the contrary: 1. A fleshly body and bones are ascribed to him after the resurrection. Luke 24:39. See my hands and my feet; handle me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having. Compare Acts 1:11. 2. And he will appear such at the future judgment. And they will look upon me, whom they have pierced. Zech. 12:10. Rev. 1:7. 3. His flesh did not experience corruption, nor was it ever subject to it. Ps. 16:10. You will not give your Holy One to see corruption. Acts 2:31. 4. They think that heaven is inaccessible to the flesh of Christ, and this is not without blasphemy, since they misunderstand the passage 1 Cor. 15:53. Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: XVII. Alieni ab hisce etiam non sunt Anabaptistae, fatentes quidem Christum corpore suo resurrexisse; at vero quali corpore, aut quo modo nunc dextram Patris claudat, ignorare se profitentes; quin volunt eum in coelo abdicasse naturam & proprietates corporis: sed contrarium jam evictum est. conf. Act. 1:9. Et haec dicens, ipsis videntibus, sublatus est. Hebr. 1:3. Eum excitavit ex mortuis, & collocavit ad dextram suam in supercoelestibus. Eph. 1:20.
units.tr: XVII. The Anabaptists are not far removed from these views either. They confess indeed that Christ rose again in his body; but they profess to be ignorant in what kind of body, or how he now holds the right hand of the Father; indeed they want him to have laid aside in heaven the nature and properties of a body. But this has already been refuted. Compare Acts 1:9. And when he had said these things, while they were looking on, he was taken up. Heb. 1:3. He raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places. Eph. 1:20.

units.la: II. Praedicta fuit haec gloria. Dixit Jehovah Domino meo, sede ad dextram meam. Psal. 110:1. Confer Matth. 22:42,43. non enim illud Davidi, vel ulli alii convenire potest.
units.tr: II. This glory was foretold. The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand. Ps. 110:1. Compare Matt. 22:42, 43, for that cannot apply to David or to any other.

units.la: III. Dextra Dei interdum potentiam Dei notat. Juravit Jehovah per dextram suam, & per brachium roboris sui. Esai. 62:8. Dextra Dei exaltatus & promissione Sp. Sancti a Patre accepta, effudit hoc, quod nunc videtis & audistis. Act. 2:33. Hic vero nobis paulo propius consideranda est phrasis, sedere ad dextram; quae desumpta a more Regum Orientalium, qui proximos a se ad dextram collocare solebant. 1. Reg. 2:19. Matth. 20:21. Psal. 45:10. Stat Augusta ad dextram tuam in auro Ophirino. 3. Esdr. 4:29. Notatur ergo hoc loquendi genere honos a regio secundus, quin etiam quandoque pro re nata aequalis. Qui quum esset in forma Dei, non rapinam duxit esse instar Dei. Phil. 2:6. ubi Christus dicitur ἴσα θεῷ εἶναι, pari cum Deo facere. Ut perversissime Sociniani, ab una parte Christum hic honoratiori loco positum velint, quam ipse Pater; (quibus & assentitur Maldonatus Jesuita) ab altera parte nihilominus dignitatem hanc precario ipsi collatam, & honorem non nisi a Patre secundum ipsi obtingere.
units.tr: III. The right hand of God sometimes signifies the power of God. The LORD has sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength. Isa. 62:8. Exalted at the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out this which you now see and hear. Acts 2:33. Here, however, the phrase "to sit at the right hand" must be considered a little more closely; it is taken from the custom of Eastern kings, who used to place those nearest to them at their right hand. 1 Kings 2:19. Matt. 20:21. Ps. 45:10. The queen stands at your right hand in gold of Ophir. 1 Esdras 4:29. By this manner of speaking, therefore, is denoted an honour second only to the king's, and indeed sometimes, as circumstances require, equal to his. Who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God. Phil. 2:6, where Christ is said to be equal to God [ἴσα θεῷ εἶναι], that is, to make himself on a par with God. The Socinians, in the most perverse way, on the one hand want Christ placed here in a more honourable position than the Father himself (and the Jesuit Maldonatus agrees with them); on the other hand they nevertheless maintain that this dignity was granted to him only on sufferance, and that he has this honour only from the Father, according to what is granted to him.

units.la: IV. Sessio haec non externo & corporeo modo fingenda est, sed figurate, ad honoris hujus stabilitatem significandam. Vidi Dominum sedentem in throno celso & elato. Esai. 6:1. Qui fecisti judicium cum gloria mecum, consedisti in solio judex justus. Psal. 9:5. 2. Thess. 2:4. Apoc. 17:1,9. alibi etiam stare ad dextram dicitur Christus. Act. 7:55. & ambulare. Apoc. 1:13.
units.tr: IV. This sitting is not to be imagined in an external and bodily manner, but figuratively, to signify the stability of this honour. I saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne. Isa. 6:1. You who have made judgment with glory on my side, sit upon the throne as a righteous judge. Ps. 9:5. 2 Thess. 2:4. Rev. 17:1, 9. Elsewhere too Christ is said to stand at the right hand, Acts 7:55, and to walk, Rev. 1:13.

units.la: V. Sessio igitur haec supremam gloriam & honorem denotat. Collocavit eum ad dextram suam in supercoelestibus, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & potentiam, & dominationem, & omne nomen quod nominatur non tantum in seculo hoc, sed etiam in futuro. Eph. 1:20, 21. Phil. 2:9–11. Hebr. 1:3. Consedit ad dextram magnitudinis in altis. & 2:7,8. & 8:1. 1. Pet. 3:22. Hebr. 12:2. Luc. 22:69. Matth. 26:64. huic gloriae juncta simul est potestas & imperium. Sede ad dextram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum; virgam roboris tuam mittet Jehovah e Zione; dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Psal. 110:1,2. 1. Cor. 15:25. ut universa regia potestas sessioni huic includatur.
units.tr: V. This sitting therefore denotes the supreme glory and honour. He set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the age to come. Eph. 1:20, 21. Phil. 2:9–11. Heb. 1:3. He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. And 2:7, 8; 8:1. 1 Pet. 3:22. Heb. 12:2. Luke 22:69. Matt. 26:64. Joined with this glory is also power and rule. Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet; the LORD will send the rod of your strength out of Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies. Ps. 110:1, 2. 1 Cor. 15:25. So that all royal power is included in this sitting.

units.la: VI. De regno illo Christi ita habendum est; non esse illud naturale, sed œconomicum; in quo tanquam caput & mediator Ecclesiæ eam gubernat, & assertam potenti manu tuetur, omniaque in bonum ejus dirigit. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Matth. 28:18. Phil. 2:7,8,9. quæ potestas non est proprietas Dei essentialis, sed œconomica, quæ finem habitura est in consummatione seculi, quando externa ejus administratione defunctus regnum illud Patri tradet. Deinde finis, quando tradet regnum Deo & Patri. 1 Cor. 15:24. & com 28. Et ipse filius subjicietur ei. ut scilicet regni illius functione œconomica abdicata, immediate regnet, & simul cum Patre omnia sit in omnibus. Vide lib. 1. cap. XXXIII. §. XVI.
units.tr: VI. We must hold the following about that kingdom of Christ: it is not natural but economical. In it, as head and mediator of the Church, he governs her, defends her with a strong hand once she is claimed, and directs all things to her good. All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Matth. 28:18. Phil. 2:7,8,9. This power is not an essential property of God but an economical one, which will have an end at the consummation of the age, when, having finished his external administration, he will hand the kingdom over to the Father. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father. 1 Cor. 15:24, and compare verse 28. And the Son himself will be subjected to him. That is, once the economical function of that kingdom has been laid down, he will reign immediately and be, together with the Father, all in all. See book 1, chapter XXXIII, §XVI.

units.la: VII. Primus actus hujus regni, unde illud auspicatus est, fuit effusio Sp. Sancti in Apostolos & Ecclesiam. Act. 2:33,35. Quod factum est in templo, seu cœnaculis & conclavibus ejus: de quibus vide 1. Paral. 28:2. Et dedit formam omnium, quod erat per Spiritum apud ipsum, de atriis domus Jehova, & de omnibus conclavibus circumquaque. Jer. 36:10. Illos autem in iis egisse, patet ex Luc. 24:53. Et erant semper in templo &c. conf. Act. 1:13. Ascenderunt in superiorem domus partem: juxta illud Psal. 2:6. Et ego unxi regem meum, in Zionem montem sanctum meum. coll. Act. 2:1, 2. &c. Effusionem hanc Sp. Sancti consecuta est concessio ministeriorum ad Ecclesiæ œdificationem necessariorum. Ipse dedit alios quidem Apostolos, alios autem Evangelistas, alios vero pastores & doctores — ad œdificationem corporis Christi. Eph. 4:10–13. Ad regiam hanc dignitatem pertinet quoque inter alia, judicium vivorum & mortuorum; regium enim illud est, & peculiariter etiam Christo soli competit.
units.tr: VII. The first act of this kingdom, with which he began it, was the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles and the Church. Acts 2:33,35. This took place in the temple, or in its upper rooms and chambers, on which see 1 Chron. 28:2. And he gave the pattern of all that he had by the Spirit, of the courts of the house of the LORD, and of all the chambers round about. Jer. 36:10. That they were engaged in these places is clear from Luke 24:53: and they were continually in the temple, etc.; compare Acts 1:13. They went up into the upper room of the house, in line with Psalm 2:6: Yet I have set my king on Zion, my holy hill; compare Acts 2:1,2, etc. This outpouring of the Holy Spirit was followed by the granting of the ministries necessary for building up the Church. He himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers ... for the building up of the body of Christ. Eph. 4:10–13. Among other things, the judgment of the living and the dead also belongs to this royal dignity; for it is a royal function, and it belongs peculiarly to Christ alone.

units.la: VIII. Cæterum regnum hoc æternum est. Venit principatus in humerum ipsius — ad amplificationem principatus, & pacem sine fine, super throno Davidis, & super regno ipsius. Esai. 9:5,6. 2.Sam. 7: 13. Psal. 45:7. Solium tuum, ô Deus, in seculum & perpetuum. Confer Hebr. 1:8. Luc. 1:33. quod enim illud Patri traditurus dicatur, 1.Cor. 15:24,28. non probat, illum regno movendum, sed adducturum solummodo Ecclesiam ad Deum, ut illam, & se in illa, Deo sistat consummandam, Vide superius l. v. c. xv. §. xx.
units.tr: VIII. Moreover, this kingdom is eternal. The government will be upon his shoulder ... for the increase of his government and of peace without end, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom. Isa. 9:5,6. 2 Sam. 7:13. Psalm 45:7: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever. Compare Heb. 1:8 and Luke 1:33. For the statement that he will hand the kingdom over to the Father (1 Cor. 15:24,28) does not prove that he will be removed from the kingdom, but only that he will bring the Church to God, so that he may present her, and himself in her, to God to be perfected. See above, book 5, chapter XV, §XX.

units.la: IX. Dignitas illa regia derivatur etiam in reliqua ejus munera: ita regiam nunc exercet prophetiam, regium item sacerdotium. Prophetiam, dum Spiritum in omnem carnem effundit, & ministris suis succurrit. Matth. 28:18-20. Marc. 16:20. Ipsi veracegressi prædicarunt ubique: Domino cooperante & verbum confirmante per signa subsubsequentia. Sacerdotium, dum non humiliter, sed gloriose, & convenienter regiae majestati, causam nostram in coelo agit. Tu es sacerdos in aeculum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeci. Psal. 110: 4. Zach. 6: 13. Hebr. 7: 25. Unde & salvare ad perfectum potest accedentes per ipsum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis. & 9: 24. & 10: 12, 13. Rom. 8: 34.
units.tr: IX. That royal dignity extends also to his other offices. Thus he now exercises the royal prophetic office and likewise the royal priesthood. He exercises the prophetic office when he pours out the Spirit upon all flesh and helps his ministers. Matth. 28:18–20. Mark 16:20. They went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. He exercises the priesthood when, not in lowliness but in glory, and in a manner fitting his royal majesty, he pleads our cause in heaven. You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek. Psalm 110:4. Zech. 6:13. Heb. 7:25. Therefore he is able to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. Compare Heb. 9:24, 10:12,13, and Rom. 8:34.

units.la: X. Adscribenda est haec gloria toti simul personae mediatoris & quoad utramque naturam, pro ratione utriusque: humanae scilicet, propriae & reapse data est. Matth. 28: 18. Phil. 2: 9. Deus ipsum superexaltavit & in gratia donavit ei nomen, quod supra omne nomen est. Hebr. 2: 9. divinae convenit quoad usum & potentiae & gloriae suae aeternae. Joh. 17. 5. Et nunc glorifica me, tu Pater, apud te, gloria quam habui prius quam mundus esset, apud te. Ut infinita & absolute summa gloria personae Christi conveniat: humanitati vero summa quidem competat, sed non nisi comparate ad creaturas, quibus omnibus major est. Collocavit eum ad dextram suam in supercoelestibus, supra omnem principatum &c. Eph. 1: 20. Joh. 5: 27. Liquet ex hisce quemadmodum in uno Christo concurrant omnes omnino praerogativae & privilegia, tam dignitatum, quam aliarum rerum miraculosarum, quaeque singulatim ulli unquam homini obtigerunt, eas in summo quoque fastigio unus tulit Christus; & quod nulli unquam datum est, solus ad dextram Dei sedet.
units.tr: X. This glory is to be ascribed to the whole person of the Mediator, in respect of both natures, each according to its own manner: to the human nature indeed it is properly and truly given. Matth. 28:18. Phil. 2:9. God highly exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name. Heb. 2:9. To the divine nature it belongs in respect of its use, its power and its eternal glory. John 17:5: And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was. So the infinite and absolutely supreme glory belongs to the person of Christ; to the humanity indeed the highest glory belongs too, but only in comparison with creatures, of all of whom it is greater. He set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every principality, etc. Eph. 1:20. John 5:27. From these things it is plain how, in Christ alone, all prerogatives and privileges meet, both of dignities and of the miraculous things which have each separately fallen to any man at any time; and these, at the highest pinnacle, one Christ has borne. And what has never been given to anyone else, he alone sits at the right hand of God.

units.la: XI. Testes etiam laudatissimos gloriae hujus fecit sibi Christus, Stephanum & Paulum; illum martyrum primum, hunc Apostolorum ultimum. Act. 7: 55, 56. 1. Cor. 9: 1. & 15: 8.
units.tr: XI. Christ has also made for himself, as witnesses of this glory, two most praiseworthy men, Stephen and Paul: the first of the martyrs and the last of the Apostles. Acts 7:55,56. 1 Cor. 9:1 and 15:8.

units.la: XII. Pellucent facile, ad hanc veritatem compositi, adversariorum errores. Ita 1. perversa est Socinianorum glossa, quando sedere ad dextram tantundem volunt notare, ac gerere vices Dei; 1. Socinus ut scilicet Pater nunc non regnet, sed filius, qui propterea aliquo modo honoratior sit ipso Deo. Quod tamen ipsi subruunt, negantes Christum esse aeternum illum Deum, imo potestatem hanc statuentes causam adorationis ejus; insuper Christum ideo facientes Dei vicarium, quod gubernet Dei Ecclesiam, eamque non suam, sed Patris. Ut potestas haec non sit dominium, sed tantum potestas volendi quod communis Dominus vult, seu consensus cum eo. Cum quibus quo pacto constare poterit, quod profitentur, Christum absolute & independenter potestatem hanc exercere? longum abit ab hisce Apostoli sententia, qui cum Christum haeredem omnium dicit, divinitatem ejus manifeste supponit, per quem scil. Deus secula fecerit. Hebr. 1: 2.
units.tr: XII. The errors of our opponents are easily seen when set against this truth. Thus (1) the Socinians have a twisted gloss, when they wish to sit at the right hand to mean no more than to act in the place of God, (1) namely, that the Father now does not reign, but the Son, who for that reason is in some way more honourable than God himself. Yet they undermine this themselves, by denying that Christ is that eternal God, and indeed by making this power the ground of his worship; moreover, by making Christ God's vicar, in that he governs God's Church, and a Church that is not his own but the Father's. So this power is not lordship, but only the power to will what the common Lord wills, or agreement with him. With such views, how will they be able to square what they profess, that Christ exercises this power absolutely and independently? The Apostle's judgment is far from these views: when he calls Christ heir of all things, he clearly presupposes his divinity, since through him God made the worlds. Heb. 1:2.

units.la: XIII. 2. Lutherani interdum quidem sedere ad dextram bene interpretantur per τὸ βασιλεύειν. Oportet enim ipsum regnare, usque dum posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedibus suis. 1 Cor. 15: 25. Plerumque tamen per eam intelligunt communicationem omnipræsentiæ & ubiquitatis factam naturæ humanæ. Verum ita 1. natura humana non erit omnipræsens vi unionis. 2. Diversum omnino est, gloriosum esse & omnipræsens; huc enim tantum abest, ut quid conferat omnipræsentia, ut gloriam humanæ naturæ tollat potius. 3. Omnipræsentia naturæ humanæ ad regnum Christi necessaria modo non est, sed & nulli cuiquam bono. Eph. 1: 20. Hebr. 1: 3. Consedit ad dextram magnitudinis in altis. & cap. 8: 1. Act. 7: 56. Vidit Stephanus gloriam Dei, & Jesum stantem a dextris Dei. Joh. 17: 24. Matth. 26: 11. Semper enim pauperes habetis vobiscum, me vero non semper habetis. Joh. 16: 28.
units.tr: XIII. (2) The Lutherans indeed sometimes interpret to sit at the right hand well, as to reign. For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. 1 Cor. 15:25. Yet for the most part they understand it to mean the communication of omnipresence and ubiquity made to the human nature. But in this way (1) the human nature will not be omnipresent by virtue of the union. (2) To be glorious and to be omnipresent are altogether different; for omnipresence contributes so little to glory that it rather takes away the glory of the human nature. (3) The omnipresence of the human nature is not necessary for the kingdom of Christ, and is of no benefit to anyone. Eph. 1:20. Heb. 1:3. He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. And Heb. 8:1. Acts 7:56: Stephen saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. John 17:24. Matth. 26:11: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me. John 16:28.

units.la: XIV. Inepte equidem hic objiciunt dextram Dei ubique esse, ergo & id quod ad dextram Dei sedet. Qua in re peccant tum in formam syllogismi, adhibentes quatuor terminos; nam omnino differunt dextra Dei, & sedere ad dextram Dei: tum in rem ipsam; sedet enim ad dextram Dei secundum naturam humanam Christus, non quatenus dextra illa ubique est, sed quatenus maxime gloriosa in cœlo est. Eph. 1: 20. Hebr. 1: 3. & 8: 1. Adde quod eadem etiam opera naturam Christi humanam æternam esse probari posset, cum dextra Dei æterna sit.
units.tr: XIV. Those who object here that the right hand of God is everywhere, and therefore also that which sits at the right hand of God, argue foolishly. They err both in the form of the syllogism, since they use four terms (for the right hand of God and sitting at the right hand of God are wholly different things), and in the matter itself: for Christ sits at the right hand of God according to his human nature, not in that this right hand is everywhere, but in that it is most glorious in heaven. Eph. 1:20. Heb. 1:3 and 8:1. Add that by the same argument it could be proved that the human nature of Christ is eternal, since the right hand of God is eternal.

units.la: XV. At pergunt errare Lutherani, cum sessionem hanc humanæ tantum Christi naturæ convenire arbitrantur: contra quam est Psal. 110: 1. 5. Dixit Deus Domino meo; sede ad dextram meam: ubi natura divina satis clare & aperte includitur. Et frustra reponunt; divinam naturam esse ipsam Dei dextram; atque ita secundum eam Christum non posse dici, ad dextram Dei sedere: ad quæ iterum regerimus; aliud notare dextram Dei; aliud, sessionem ad dextram.
units.tr: XV. But the Lutherans go on erring when they think this sitting belongs only to the human nature of Christ. Against this is Psalm 110:1, 5: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand," where the divine nature is quite clearly and plainly included. And they vainly object that the divine nature is itself the right hand of God, so that according to it Christ cannot be said "to sit at the right hand of God." To this we again reply: the right hand of God is one thing; sitting at the right hand is another.

units.la: XVI. Hisce erroribus mantissam adjiciunt illi inter eosdem, qui Christum secundum naturam humanam, ab utero matris, ad dextram Dei sedisse volunt; quod præter Scripturam non solum est, sed & contra eam, quando satis liquido docet, non nisi post exaltationem demum ad dextram Dei collocatum esse Christum. Dominus igitur postquam eum illis locum esset, sublatus est in cælum, & con-
units.tr: XVI. To these errors those same men add a further one: they hold that Christ according to his human nature sat at the right hand of God from the womb of his mother. This is not only without Scripture but against it, since it teaches quite plainly that Christ was placed at the right hand of God only after his exaltation. "So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven, and" —

units.la: 11. Lutheranorum. consedit à dextris Dei. Marc. 16:19. Luc. 24:26. Hebr. 1:3. Apoc. 3:21. Qui vincit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, quemadmodum & ego vici, & consedi cum Patre meo in throno ipsius.
units.tr: 11. of the Lutherans. "sat down at the right hand of God." Mark 16:19; Luke 24:26; Heb. 1:3; Rev. 3:21: "He who overcomes, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne."

units.la: XVII. Fructus hujus sessionis potissimum hi sunt. 1. Intercessio Christi pro nobis. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est; imo qui & suscitatus est; qui etiam est ad dextram Dei; qui etiam interpellat pro nobis, Rom. 8:34. 2. Defensio Ecclesiae militantis. Tu es Petrus, & in hac petra aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, & porta inferni non praevalebunt eam. Matth. 16:18. 3. Communio gloriae cum Christo servata capitis & membrorum proportione. Nos convivificavit cum Christo, & conresuscitavit & collocavit in coelestibus &c. Eph. 2:5,6. Apoc. 3:21.
units.tr: XVII. The chief fruits of this sitting are these. (1) The intercession of Christ for us: "Who is it that condemns? It is Christ who died, or rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us," Rom. 8:34. (2) The defence of the militant Church: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it," Matt. 16:18. (3) The sharing of glory with Christ, the proportion of head and members being preserved: "He made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places," etc., Eph. 2:5, 6; Rev. 3:21.

units.la: CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: De Euangelio.
units.tr: Of the Gospel.

units.la: I. Ublato in coelum Christo, non vasta & vidua relicta est terra, sed continuo Spiritus ejus replevit omnia; nec omnis abiit Christus, sed potius per terras undequaque in praedicatione Euangelii se ipsum exhibuit; & quo altius ascendit in coelos, eo illustrior in terris apparuit per annuntiationem harum rerum toto orbe factam, inceptam primo felicibus auspiciis, effuso scilicet in Apostolos Spiritu sancto, die Pentecostes Act. 2. & deinceps propriis suis temporibus. Qui dedit se ipsum redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, testimonium temporibus suis. 1. Tim. 2:6.
units.tr: I. When Christ was taken up into heaven, the earth was not left desolate and widowed. His Spirit at once filled all things. Nor did Christ depart altogether; rather, he made himself present everywhere on earth through the preaching of the Gospel. The higher he ascended into the heavens, the more brightly he appeared on earth, through the proclamation of these things made throughout the whole world. This began first under happy auspices, when the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2), and afterwards in their proper times. "Who gave himself a ransom for all, a testimony in its own times." 1 Tim. 2:6.

units.la: II. Euangelium Graecis notat vel laetum nuntium; vel munus dandum, laeta nuntianti, vel supplicationes & sacrificia pro re feliciter gesta. In sacris mutuata est haec vox a Graecis LXX. interpretibus, qui illa frequenter utuntur. Quam decori sunt in montibus pedes מבשר (LXX εναγγελιζομένου) nunciantis Euangelium, qui facit audiri pacem; qui nunciat bonum? Esai. 52:7. Venit autem apud S. Scriptores in significatione prima & propria pro laeto nuntio, speciatim de Messia; quamvis aliqua cum varietate, modo notet historiam Christi, Marc. 1:1. Principium Euangelii J. Christi filii Dei. modo promulgationem gratiae Christi. Abeuntes in totum mundum, praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae. Marc. 16:15. 1.
units.tr: II. In Greek, Euangelium denotes either a glad message, or a reward to be given to the one who brings glad news, or thanksgivings and sacrifices for an affair successfully accomplished. In sacred usage this word was taken over from the Greeks, that is, from the Seventy translators, who use it often. "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings [מבשר] (LXX εὐαγγελιζομένου), who proclaims the Gospel, who makes peace heard, who announces good!" Isa. 52:7. In the Sacred Writers it occurs first in its proper sense, for a glad message, especially concerning the Messiah, though with some variety. Sometimes it denotes the history of Christ: "The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Mark 1:1. Sometimes it denotes the proclamation of the grace of Christ: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature." Mark 16:15. 1.

units.la: Note at right margin: Illius significatio. Note: Exaltatio Christi infecta fuit ejus annunciatio per EVANGELIUM. Cor. 9. 14. & 15: 1. 2. Cor. 8: 18. modo doctrinam ipsam, praedicatione illa comprehensam. Spiritus Domini Jehova super me est: quia unxit Jehovah me, ad Evangelium nuntiandum mansuetis. Esai. 61: 1. Luc 2: 10. Gal. 1: 15, 16. Indolem suam produnt Judaei, quando impie vocem Euangelii detorquent in revelati- onem iniquitatis. Blasphemeitem monachi, praedicatores & Minoritae, Anno 1250. aliud Euangelium sibi & mundo cuderunt, aeternum ipsis dictum, ex abusu loci Apoc. 14: 6. Et vidi alium Angelum volantem in medio coeli, qui habebat Euangelium aeternum.
units.tr: Note in the right margin: its meaning. Note: the exaltation of Christ was completed by the announcement of him through the GOSPEL. 1 Cor. 9:14; 15:1; 2 Cor. 8:18. Sometimes it denotes the doctrine itself, comprised in that preaching: "The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me, because Jehovah has anointed me to preach the Gospel to the meek." Isa. 61:1; Luke 2:10; Gal. 1:15, 16. The Jews betray their character when they impiously twist the word of the Gospel into "the revelation of iniquity." The monks, preachers and Minorites blasphemed in the year 1250: they forged for themselves and the world another Gospel, which they called "eternal," from an abuse of the passage Rev. 14:6: "And I saw another angel flying in the midst of heaven, who had the eternal Gospel."

units.la: III. Euangelium hoc non demum cum incunabulis Christi incepit, ut mallet Socinus, sed ab ipso mundi exordio jam promulgatum fuit. Gen. 3: 15. Rom. 1: 2. & 10: 15, 16. Etenim nobis bonus nuncius allatus est, quemadmodum & illis. Hebr. 4: 2. Ad hoc enim & iis qui mortui sunt Euangelizatum est; ut judicentur quidem secundum homines carne, vivant autem secundum Deum spiritu. 1. Pet. 4: 6. quamvis tunc propriè ἐπαγγελία fuerit. Et nos vobis Euangelizamus promissionem factam ad Patres, quod Deus hanc impleverit, nobis filiis ipsorum, dum excitavit Jesum. Act. 13: 32. Populus, quem formaverò mihi, glorificationem meam narrabunt. Esai. 43: 21. Gal. 3: 18.
units.tr: III. This Gospel did not begin only with the cradle of Christ, as Socinus preferred, but was proclaimed from the very beginning of the world. Gen. 3:15; Rom. 1:2; 10:15, 16. "For good news has been brought to us, just as to them." Heb. 4:2. "For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit." 1 Pet. 4:6. Although at that time it was properly a promise [ἐπαγγελία]: "And we preach to you the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to us, their children, in raising up Jesus." Acts 13:32. "The people whom I formed for myself shall declare my glory." Isa. 43:21; Gal. 3:18.

units.la: IV. Speciatim vero & εὐαγγελικῶς Euangelium notat בשורה טובה ipsam rei bonae annuntiationem, distinctam ab ἐπαγγελία. Vivifecit cor meum verbo bono; dico ego: opera mea regi: lingua mea stilus scriba expediti. Psal. 45: 2. Qui bonum gustaverunt Dei verbum, ac virtutes futuri seculi. Hebr. 6: 5. Matth. 4: 23. Marc. 1: 15. Rom. 16: 25, 26. Summam hujus Euangelii breviter exhibet Apostolus Rom. 1: 3, 4. Qui filius extitit ex semine David secundum carnem, qui definite notatus est filius Dei in potentia, secundum Spiritum sanctitatis, ex resurrectione mortuorum. Vide & cap. 10: 15, 16. ex Esai. 52: 7. Continetur ergo in eo. 1. Veritas; quatenus nimirum per illud ostenditur, & luce meridiana clarius effulget; tum fides Dei, tum nomen ejus: Notum feci eis nomen tuum, & notum faciam, ut dilectio, qua dilexisti me, in ipsis sit, & ego in ipsis. Joh. 17: 26. id est, virtutes & attributa ejus; sigillatim, justitia & misericordia. 11. Pietas. Sine dubio, magnum est pietatis mysterium: Deus est manifestatus in carne. 1. Tim. 3: 16. Tit. 2: 11, 12.
units.tr: IV. More specifically, and in the evangelical sense, Euangelium denotes the very announcement of a good thing [בשורה טובה], distinct from the promise [ἐπαγγελία]. "My heart overflows with a good word; I say, my works are for the king; my tongue is the pen of a ready scribe." Ps. 45:2. "Who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come." Heb. 6:5; Matt. 4:23; Mark 1:15; Rom. 16:25, 26. The Apostle briefly sets out the sum of this Gospel, Rom. 1:3, 4: "who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead." See also chapter 10:15, 16, from Isa. 52:7. Therefore the following is contained in it: (1) Truth, insofar as through it there is shown, and shines more clearly than the midday light, both the faithfulness of God and his name: "I have made known to them your name, and I will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them." John 17:26. That is, his powers and attributes, especially justice and mercy. (2) Piety. "Without doubt, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh." 1 Tim. 3:16; Titus 2:11, 12.

units.la: V. Naturam illius Euangelii omnino pervertunt, qui id transfundunt in legem operum, eamque Mosaica perfectiorem; cum Euangelium proprie non sit lex, sed annuntiatio rei bonae, neque lege Mosaica quicquam perfectius dari potest, ut supra demonstratum. Lex autem vocatur Rom. 3:27. Ubi est gloriatio? exclusa est. per quam legem? operum? non; sed per legem fidei. Rom. 8: 2. Lex Spiritus vitae in Christo Jesu liberum me fecit a lege peccati & mortis. Gal. 6:2. Complete legem Christi. Jac. 1: 25. quatenus est demonftratio viae, (quam Hebraeis vox הורה significat) illius scilicet, qua per Christum peccatori Deum accedendi facultas conceditur: quod dicitur Jer. 31: 33. Do legem meam in medium ipsorum, & super corde eorum scribam eam: quare etiam ad instar legis sua mandata & promissiones habet. Marc. 1:15. Resipiscite & credite Euangelio. Rom. 1.17. Justitia Dei ex annunciatione Christi, revelatur ex fide in fidem. 1. Joh. 2. 25.
units.tr: V. Those who pour the whole nature of that Gospel into a law of works, and make it more perfect than the Mosaic law, utterly pervert it. The Gospel is not properly a law, but the announcement of a good thing, and nothing more perfect than the Mosaic law can be given, as has been shown above. But "law" is what it is called in Rom. 3:27: "Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith." Rom. 8:2: "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death." Gal. 6:2: "Fulfil the law of Christ." Jas. 1:25. It is so insofar as it is a demonstration of the way (which the Hebrew word הורה signifies), namely the way by which the sinner is granted the power to approach God through Christ. This is said in Jer. 31:33: "I will put my law in their midst, and write it on their heart." For this reason it also has, in the manner of a law, its commands and promises. Mark 1:15: "Repent and believe the Gospel." Rom. 1:17: "The righteousness of God is revealed from the announcement of Christ, from faith to faith." 1 John 2:25.

units.la: VI. Differt autem a lege hisce modis; nam 1. Lex data fuit homini integro; Euangelium miseró: 2. Illa exigebat justitiam operarum; hoc fidem. 3. Illa promittebat vitam aeternam; hoc salutem. 4. Illa nitebatur viribus hominis; hoc divina gratia. 5. Illa est ministerium mortis, & litera occidens, considerata nempe sine Euangelio & Spiritu Christi; hoc Spiritus vivificans. Litera occidit, Spiritus autem vivificat. Si vero ministerium mortis—fuit in gloria— quomodo non ministerium Spiritus? &c. 2. Cor. 3. 6, 7. quia Spiritus eo utitur; ut nos deducat ad vitam aeternam per Christum. Quare lex pædagogus noster extitit ad Christum, ut in Christo justificaremur. Gal. 3. 24. & com. 26. Omnes enim filii Dei estis, per fidem in Christo Jesu.
units.tr: VI. It differs from the law in the following ways. (1) The law was given to man in his integrity; the Gospel to man in his misery. (2) The former demanded the righteousness of works; the latter demands faith. (3) The former promised eternal life; the latter promises salvation. (4) The former relied on the strength of man; the latter on divine grace. (5) The former is the ministry of death and "the letter that kills," that is, considered apart from the Gospel and the Spirit of Christ; the latter is "the Spirit that gives life." "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. But if the ministry of death was in glory... how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory...?" 2 Cor. 3:6, 7. The Spirit uses the law to lead us to eternal life through Christ. "Therefore the law was our schoolmaster to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified in Christ." Gal. 3:24. And verse 26: "For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus."

units.la: VII. Quae tamen differitates non impediunt, quo minus lex illi tamen Euangelio subordinari possit; hac videlicet ratione, ut stupentem in peccatis hominem denuntiatione irae divinae excitet, dejiciat deinde & consternet, mox ab Euangelio erigendum. Gal. 3. 24. Rom. 10: 4. Finis legis Christus, ad justitiam omni credenti. Quare etiam Euangelium legem non tollit, sed eam stabilit potius. Rom. 3:31. Legem igitur irritam facimus per fidem? absit. imo legem stabilimus. quatenus nempe ostendit 1. Christum finem legis. Rom. 10: 4. 2. confirmat comminationes legis impletas in Christo. Deus, quum filium suum misisset in similitudine carnis peccati, & quidem pro peccato, condemnavit peccatum in carne. Rom. 8: 3. Gal. 3: 10, 13. 3. approbat justitiam legis, eamque implet, per Christum. Ut justi legis impleatur in nobis, qui secundum Spiritum ambulamus. Rom. 8: 4. 4. adoptat & exigit omnia praecepta legis. Affulsit gratia Dei — erudiens nos, ut abnegata impietate — tempe-ranter. ranter, juste & pie vivamus in hoc seculo. Tit. 2: 11, 12. 5. Vires nobis dat legem per Spiritum pro modulo implendi, cum illa per peccatum impotens facta esset, & viribus destituta. Lex Spiritus vitae in Christo Jesu, liberum me fecit a lege peccati & mortis &c. Rom. 8: 2, 4.
units.tr: VII. Yet these differences do not prevent the law from being subordinated to the Gospel, in this way: the law stirs up man, who is stupefied in his sins, by the declaration of divine wrath; then it casts him down and dismays him, soon to be raised up by the Gospel. Gal. 3:24; Rom. 10:4: "Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes." Therefore the Gospel also does not abolish the law, but rather establishes it. Rom. 3:31: "Do we then make void the law through faith? Far from it; rather we establish the law." Namely, insofar as the Gospel shows: (1) Christ as the end of the law. Rom. 10:4. (2) It confirms the threatenings of the law as fulfilled in Christ: "God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and indeed as an offering for sin, condemned sin in the flesh." Rom. 8:3; Gal. 3:10, 13. (3) It approves the righteousness of the law and fulfils it through Christ: "that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit." Rom. 8:4. (4) It adopts and requires all the precepts of the law: "The grace of God has appeared, training us, so that, denying ungodliness, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in this age." Titus 2:11, 12. (5) Through the Spirit it gives us strength to fulfil the law according to our measure, since the law had been rendered powerless through sin and deprived of strength: "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death, etc." Rom. 8:2, 4.

units.la: VIII. Male ergo Pontificii, hac in re Socinianis praeluserunt; dum Euangelium lege perfectius faciunt; inde nimirum nova illa & perfectior lex Christi nata est. Cum tamen tam exacte & diligenter lex facienda exigat, quam Euangelium credenda; tum quoque Euangelium proprie non continet leges morum, sed conscientias lege perterrefactas sedat; & unice in eo regnat gratia, ad quam reliqua omnia, quae in Euangelio sunt, conspirant & ordinantur.
units.tr: VIII. The Papists therefore err in this matter, and in doing so have anticipated the Socinians: they make the Gospel more perfect than the law, and from this, no doubt, came that new and more perfect law of Christ. Yet since the law demands to be done as exactly and diligently as the Gospel demands to be believed, the Gospel does not properly contain the laws of morals; rather it calms consciences terrified by the law. In it grace alone reigns, and all the other things that are in the Gospel agree with and are arranged toward it.

units.la: IX. Ad quaestionem quam hic ponunt Lutherani, an Euangelium sit concio poenitentiae; responderi potest: poenitentiam, ubi duntaxat dolorem ex peccato notat, legalem proprie esse; at ubi dicit veram resipiscentiam, solius fidei esse, atque ita ex Euangelio originem trahere. Act. 15: 9. Gal. 3: 5. Qui igitur vobis suppeditat Spiritum, & operatur potentias in vobis, an hoc facit ex operibus legis, an ex auditu fidei? & quicquid huc confert lex, non nisi per Sp. sancti speciale gratiam & opem praestare potest.
units.tr: IX. To the question the Lutherans raise here, whether the Gospel is a sermon of repentance, the answer can be given: where repentance denotes only sorrow for sin, it is properly legal; but where it denotes true repentance [resipiscentia], it belongs to faith alone, and so derives its origin from the Gospel. Acts 15:9. Gal. 3:5. He therefore who supplies you with the Spirit and works miracles among you, does he do this by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? And whatever the law contributes to this can only provide by special grace and help of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI

units.la: De vocatione Gentium.
units.tr: On the Calling of the Gentiles

units.la: I. Euangelii praecipuum opus fuit, Gentium ad Ecclesiae sinum collectio; quas, sylvescentibus quotidie Judaeorum ramis, Ecclesiae stipiti inseri & ad mitiorem naturam redigi oportebat. Cujus insignis adeo, ac maximi, si quodquam unquam, Dei in mundo operis, tum praedictiones & vaticinia olim edita; tum implementum; ac fructus denique & effecta consideranda sunt.
units.tr: I. The chief work of the Gospel was the gathering of the Gentiles into the bosom of the Church. As the branches of the Jews grew wild daily, these had to be grafted onto the stock of the Church and brought to a gentler nature. Of this work, remarkable and great beyond any other work of God in the world, we must consider the predictions and prophecies given long ago, then its fulfilment, and finally its fruits and effects.

units.la: II. Fatis autem monstratum illam olim Gentium felicitatem, ex universa Vet. Test. Scriptura patet. Gen. 3: 15. 9: 27. 12: 3. 17: 4, 5. 49: 10. Deut. 4: 6. 29: 24, 25, 29. 32: 43. Psal. 2: 8. 8: 2. 22: 29. 40: 10, 11. 45: 10, 13, 17. 68: 19. 72: 3, 9, 10, 11. 82: 8. 86: 9. conf. Apoc. 15: 4. & 87: 4, 5, 6. 96: 7, 8, 9, 10. 110: 2, 3. Jes. 2: 3, 5. 3,5.11:10,12. 19:18,19.&35.& 42: 1, 4.& 49:6,20. 52: 10, 15. 55: 1, 2. 56:6. Jer. 16: 19. Joël. 2: 23. conf. Act. 2: 21. Ac in Euangelio Christus quoque paulo ante id docuit: Alias etiam oves habeo, quae non sunt ex hac caula: illas quoque oportet me adducere: nam vocem meam audient: fietque unus grex, & unus Pastor, Joh. 10: 16. Ac variis parabolis illarum adventum delineavit, Matth. 20. & 21. Luc. 14. & 15.
units.tr: II. That this happiness of the Gentiles was foreshadowed long ago is clear from the whole of the Old Testament Scripture: Gen. 3:15; 9:27; 12:3; 17:4, 5; 49:10; Deut. 4:6; 29:24, 25, 29; 32:43; Ps. 2:8; 8:2; 22:29; 40:10, 11; 45:10, 13, 17; 68:19; 72:3, 9, 10, 11; 82:8; 86:9; cf. Rev. 15:4; and 87:4, 5, 6; 96:7, 8, 9, 10; 110:2, 3; Isa. 2:3, 5; 3:5; 11:10, 12; 19:18, 19, and 35; and 42:1, 4; and 49:6, 20; 52:10, 15; 55:1, 2; 56:6; Jer. 16:19; Joel 2:23; cf. Acts 2:21. Christ himself also taught this a little earlier in the Gospel: I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one Shepherd, John 10:16. And in various parables he sketched their coming: Matt. 20 and 21; Luke 14 and 15.

units.la: III. Apostolus autem, ubi adductionem earum mysterium, praecedentibus atatibus nondum patefactum, appellat, Eph. 3: 5. loquitur de mysterii illius impletione, quae ultimis demum temporibus reservabatur; deque omni ejus modo & ratione: quod videl. facilius longe modo, ac olim Judaei, sine legis ac rituum onere, sola fide salutem acciperent: gentes esse coheredes & concorpores, conservesque promissionis ejus in Christo per Euangelium, vs 6. Et nullum discrimen posuit inter nos & illos, fide purificans corda ipsorum, Act. 15: 9. Quod Judaei vel maxime indignabantur.
units.tr: III. When the apostle calls their bringing in a mystery, not made known in former ages, Eph. 3:5, he speaks of the fulfilment of that mystery, which was reserved until the last times, and of its whole manner and method: namely, that far more easily than the Jews of old, without the burden of the law and the rites, they would receive salvation by faith alone: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of the same body and partakers of his promise in Christ through the Gospel, v. 6. And he made no distinction between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith, Acts 15:9. The Jews were especially indignant at this.

units.la: IV. Consiliis autem Dei tandem se explicantibus, non pauci qui jam proselyti, ac de ingenti messe spicae nonnullae, ut olim in veteris Ecclesiae angustiis; sed totae nationes, ad Christum conversae, baptismum fidemque acceperunt. Ut Judaeorum Ecclesiam non tam, adfluente convenarum sobole, ditasse ac dilatasse; quam novam Ecclesiam novumque Christi populum condidisse videri possint; obliterata paulatim Judaici nominis gloria. Quod deinde infidelibus de gente illa mansit: dum nova illa Euangelii massa novum quoque nomen sortita, ac de Christo Christiana appellata est. Act. 11:26. Itaut ab Hierosolyma ad Illyricum impleverim annunciationem Christi. Rom. 15:19. Quod Euangelium praedicatum est in omni creatura, quae sub caelo est. Col. 1: 23. Stupor invicem contigit Israëli, donec plenitudo gentium intret. Rom. 11: 25. An parturitur terra uno die? an nascitur gens una vice? nam parturivit; simul peperit Zion filios suos. Esai. 66: 8.
units.tr: IV. When the counsels of God at last unfolded themselves, not a few proselytes, and some ears from the great harvest, as formerly in the narrow times of the early Church, but whole nations converted to Christ received baptism and faith. So that they could seem to have founded a new Church and a new people of Christ, rather than to have enriched and enlarged the Church of the Jews by the inflow of the offspring of sojourners, the glory of the Jewish name being gradually obliterated. This remained afterwards for the unbelievers of that nation, since that new mass of the Gospel, having received a new name too, was called Christian from Christ, Acts 11:26. So that from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the preaching of Christ, Rom. 15:19. The Gospel has been preached in every creature which is under heaven, Col. 1:23. Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, Rom. 11:25. Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth at once? For Zion travailed and at once brought forth her sons, Isa. 66:8.

units.la: V. Factum hoc, tum externo Euangelii praeconio: Quomodo autem credent, quem non audiverunt? Rom. 10: 14. Deo non peregrino amplius sono, ut olim; sed, uti domesticos sese factos agnoscerent, nota ac familiari lingua ipsos alloquente: Graece enim Nov. Test. mysteria tradita sunt; factusque tum Deus Judaeis barbarus est: Nam tunc vertam ad populos labium purum. Zeph. 3: 9. Cum peregrino sermone & lingua exotica allocutus sit populum istum Jehova. Jes. 28: 11. tum interno Spiritus alloquio, ac potenti vi. Quale Dei verbum est, quo vocat ea quae non sunt, tanquam sint. Rom. 4: 17. Ut accipiant promissionem hi, qui vocati sunt ad haereditatem, quae est in aeternum. Hebr. 9: 15.
units.tr: V. This came about partly by the external proclamation of the Gospel: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? Rom. 10:14. It no longer sounded as a foreign voice to God, as it had formerly, but so that they recognised themselves made members of the household, God addressing them in a known and familiar tongue. For the mysteries of the New Testament were delivered in Greek, and God then became a barbarian to the Jews. For then I will turn to the peoples a pure lip, Zeph. 3:9. For with stammering lips and another tongue the LORD has spoken to this people, Isa. 28:11. It came about partly also by the inward address of the Spirit and his powerful force. Such is the word of God by which he calls the things that are not as though they were, Rom. 4:17, so that those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance, Heb. 9:15.

units.la: VI. Compellati autem sunt non alio quam Euangelii & fidei verbo, absque legis ac rituum Mosaicorum onere, Act. 15. & in epist. ad Galat. Cum Deus non foret προσωπολήπτης, Act. 10: 35. quatis in Vet. Test. aliquo modo videri potuerat, ubi Judaeorum gentem praecipue deamabat. Qua nuda ac facili via dum Apostoli, ac praesertim Paulus, gentes adducerent, non mediocrem invidiam subiere. Fuitque ea in recenti illa Ecclesia prima litium ac disputationum materia, ut ex actis Apostolicis liquet; dum fideles ex Judaeis non sine dolore veterem istum cultum, dilectosque olim Deo ritus, antiquari viderent.
units.tr: VI. They were summoned by nothing other than the word of the Gospel and of faith, without the burden of the Mosaic law and rites, Acts 15 and in the epistle to the Galatians. God was not a respecter of persons, Acts 10:35 [προσωπολήπτης], although in the Old Testament he might in some way have seemed so, since he especially loved the Jewish nation. While the apostles, and Paul above all, were bringing the Gentiles in by this bare and easy way, they incurred no small hatred. In that early Church this became the first matter of quarrels and disputations, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles, since the believers from among the Jews saw with grief that their old worship and the rites once dear to God were being set aside.

units.la: VII. Crevit vero gentium Ecclesia praecipue ex Judaorum ruinis; qui dum frigidius ferrentur in oblatam sibi salutem, eamque aversarentur, & Euangelium odisse ac pertinaciter persequi tandem in animum inducerent; ex ista nocte, veluti vices servante Dei gratia, plenissima lux gentibus affulsit. Si vero delictum ipsorum divitiae sunt mundi, & damnum divitiae gentium &c. Rom. 11: 12. Atque ita omnes sub inobedientiam conclusi sunt, ut omnes misericordiam acciperent, vs 32. Ac, veluti Abrahami ac Judaeorum vocatio creationis, ita gentium conversio generationis imaginem habuit. Sicuti Apostolus insitionis figura utitur dum illi, a sylvestri matre avulsi, Judaico trunco inolescere jussi sunt. Advenientes radicabit Jacobus. Esai. 27: 16.
units.tr: VII. The Church of the Gentiles grew chiefly out of the ruin of the Jews. While they were carried more coldly towards the salvation offered them and turned away from it, and at last made up their minds to hate the Gospel and persecute it stubbornly, out of that night, as if the grace of God were taking turns, the fullest light shone upon the Gentiles. Now if their fall is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the Gentiles, etc., Rom. 11:12. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all, v. 32. And just as the calling of Abraham and of the Jews had the likeness of creation, so the conversion of the Gentiles had the likeness of generation. The apostle uses the figure of grafting, when the wild branches, torn from their wild mother, were ordered to grow into the Jewish trunk. Jacob shall take root as they come, Isa. 27:6.

units.la: VIII. Nec exigui operis istius in mundo fructus fuerunt:
units.tr: VIII. Nor were the fruits of this work in the world small:

units.la: 1. Dii enim Deaeque omnes, quae hactenus meliori orbis parti illuserant, facessere & in orcum remeare jussi sunt. Et idolorum quantum est, abibit. Illo die projiciet homo Deos nihili aureos suos ad talpas & ad vespertiliones Jef. 2: 18, 20. Ad te gentes venient a finibus terrae; & dicent, meram falsitatem haereditaverant patres nostri, vanitatem, & in quibus non erat utile. Jer. 16: 19. 2. Oracula, si quae fuerint, conticuerunt, vocalesque olim sylvae & quercus responsa edere cessarunt, ipseque Apollo Delphicus infans redditus est. 3. Deus vero, mundi conditor ac redemptor, publice in mundo agnitus est. 4. Lexque ejus ac coelestis doctrina, ut vera ac divina, celebrata est. 5. Innumeri denique mortales, atque integrae nationes, ferae hactenus & barbarae, Euangelio colla subdiderunt, ac mansuetum Christi sermonem acceperunt, & pulsa barbarie ad pietatem ac modestiam destiam formatæ sunt. Quod in ænigmate cecinit Jesaias cap. 11. Et, quod maximum est, Judæos, veterem Dei populum, non æquaverunt illi solum, sed rerum divinarum cognitione, morum pietate, cunctisque bonis artibus, immensum superarunt. Ut ipsi hodie Judæi legis suæ mysteria, ac linguæ intellectum, omnemque patriam eruditionem, ab iis, quos gentiles ipsi appellant, petere pene necesse habeant.
units.tr: (1) For all the gods and goddesses who had hitherto held sway over the better part of the world were ordered to depart and go back into the pit. And the idols shall utterly pass away. In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and gold, which he made for himself, to the moles and the bats, Isa. 2:18, 20. The Gentiles shall come to you from the ends of the earth and say: our fathers have inherited only falsehood, vanity, and things in which there is no profit, Jer. 16:19. (2) The oracles, if there were any, fell silent; the oaks and groves that once gave voice ceased to give answers, and Apollo of Delphi himself was reduced to an infant. (3) God, the creator and redeemer of the world, was publicly acknowledged in the world. (4) His law and heavenly doctrine were celebrated as true and divine. (5) Finally, countless mortals and whole nations, wild and barbarous until then, submitted their necks to the Gospel, received the gentle word of Christ, and, with barbarism driven out, were shaped into piety and modesty. Isaiah sang of this in a riddle in chapter 11. And, what is greatest, they not only equalled the Jews, the old people of God, but far surpassed them in the knowledge of divine things, in the piety of their morals, and in all good arts. So that today the Jews themselves are almost obliged to seek from those whom they call Gentiles the mysteries of their own law, the understanding of its language, and all their learning.

units.la: IX. Quæ omnia certe Euangelii divinitatem ac veritatem testantur. Illa enim doctrina, quæ talia ac tam magna in mundo præstitit, ac cui tam multum humanum genus debet, & vera, & sancta, & divina esse debet. Nisi Deum rebus humanis illudere, gentesque à paganismo non ad fidei Solem, sed ad aliam noctem & impietatem esse prolapsas impie dicas. Quomodo nec verum quicquam in mundo unquam fuerit, nec futurum porro unquam sit: sed quicquid hoc ævi est, in tenebris omne degendum reslabit.
units.tr: IX. All these things surely attest the divinity and truth of the Gospel. For that doctrine which has accomplished such great things in the world, and to which the human race owes so much, must be true, holy, and divine. Unless you say impiously that God mocks human affairs, and that the Gentiles fell from paganism not into the sun of faith but into another night and impiety. Then nothing true would ever have existed in the world, nor would anything ever exist in future; but whatever time remains would have to be spent wholly in darkness.

units.la: X. Sed & modus, quo mundus per Euangelii sermonem conversus, ac tantum non triumphatus est, admiratione plenus est, ac divinitati ejus non mediocrem fidem adstruit: sive 1. doctrinæ genium, 2. sive doctores, 3. sive denique docendi modum spectes.
units.tr: X. But also the manner in which the world was turned to the Gospel message, and all but conquered by it, is full of wonder and lends no small support to its divinity: whether you look at 1. the character of the doctrine, 2. the teachers, or 3. finally the manner of teaching.

units.la: XI. Ille enim doctrinæ istius genius erat, ut ab hominum sensu maxime remotus esset, ac absterrendis iis, quam alliciendis serviret. Nam qui in istam disciplinam veniebant 1. nihil prius imbuebantur, quam patrias religiones exuere, & profana omnia dicere quæ hactenus sacra habuerant. 2. Credere autem ac animo accipere, quæ incredibilia ac imperceptibilia erant: Nos autem prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Judæis quidem scandalum, Græcis autem stultitiam. 1. Cor. 1: 23. Quæstiones autem quasdam habebant—de Jesu quodam, qui mortuus est, quem Paulus dicebat vivere. Act. 25: 19. Quid? incredibile vobis videtur, quod Deus mortuos excitat? c. 26: 8. 3. Ac pietatem sequi duram ac difficilem, nec ad desidis ac marcentis mundi genium compositam; illumque vitæ morem induere, qui concessis etiam voluptatibus modum poneret: cujus formula extat Matth. 5, 6, 7. cap. & c. 16: 24. Si quis vult pone me venire, abdicet semetipsum, & attollat crucem suam, ac sequatur me. 4. ac ob disciplinam istam dura omnia ac acerba perpeti, & omnia vitæ commoda, ac vitam denique ipsam vilia habere: Et omnes vero volentes piè vivere in Christo Jesu, persecutionem patientur, 2 Tim. 3: 12. Non aliud ob pretium, quam quod immortalitatem sperarent, atque ignavum ducerent reditura parcere vitæ. Quæ mira doctrinæ ratio erat, dum sese revicturos crederent, interim mori non dubitare.
units.tr: XI. For the character of this doctrine was such that it was most remote from human feeling, and served to frighten people away rather than to attract them. For those who came into this discipline 1. were first of all instructed to cast off their ancestral religions and to call everything profane that they had hitherto held sacred. 2. They were then to believe and receive in their minds things that were incredible and beyond perception: But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness. 1 Cor. 1:23. They had certain questions against him about a certain Jesus, who had died, whom Paul said was alive. Acts 25:19. Why should it seem incredible to you that God raises the dead? Acts 26:8. 3. They were to follow a piety that was hard and difficult, not suited to the spirit of a lazy and languishing world; and to put on that manner of life which set limits even to the pleasures that were allowed; the form of which is found in Matthew chapters 5, 6, 7, and 16:24: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. 4. And on account of this discipline they were to endure all hardships and bitter things, and to hold all the comforts of life, and life itself, cheap: And indeed all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution, 2 Tim. 3:12. They had no other reward for this than the hope of immortality, and they thought it foolish to spare a life that would be given back. This was a remarkable principle of doctrine: while they believed they would live again, they did not hesitate meanwhile to die.

units.la: XII. Nec doctores ii erant, quibus mundus facile accederet. Jesus, fabri filius, ex paterna officina ipse prodiens, tandemque à gente sua necatus, quod non leve novae illi doctrinae scandalum fuit. Nos audivimus ex lege, quod Christus maneat in aeternum; & quomodo tu dicis, oportere efferri filium hominis? Joh. 12. 34. Nos autem praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Judaeis quidem scandalum, Graecis autem stultitiam. 1 Cor. 1: 23. Discipuli autem, seu Apostoli ejus, viri erant obscuri, idiotae, nulla arte, ingenio, aut eruditione celebres, iisque numero pauci, duodecim enim erant; quos mundum partitis operis, veluti Domini sui regnum, inter sese divisisse, & tam vasta ac incredibilia cogitavisse, supra fidem fuit. Non alia autem ad tam stupendum opus praesidia habebant quam doctrinae veritatem, vitae sanctitatem, ac miraculorum gloriam: quibus de mundo tandem triumpharunt, quanquam non sine sanguine; nam & ipsi operi isti immortui suo cruore salutem mundi dedicarunt.
units.tr: XII. Nor were the teachers such as would easily win over the world. Jesus, the son of a carpenter, who had come forth from his father's workshop, and was at last put to death by his own nation, was no slight scandal to that new doctrine. We have heard out of the law that Christ abides for ever; and how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? John 12:34. But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness. 1 Cor. 1:23. His disciples, or Apostles, were obscure men, uneducated, distinguished by no art, talent or learning, and few in number, for there were twelve of them; that they should divide the world among themselves, as if it were the kingdom of their Lord, with a division of labour, and should conceive such vast and incredible plans, was beyond belief. Yet they had no other resources for so astonishing a task than the truth of the doctrine, the holiness of their life, and the glory of their miracles: by these they at last triumphed over the world, though not without blood; for they too, dying in that very work, dedicated the salvation of the world with their own blood.

units.la: XIII. Denique docendi modus non erat ad florentis saeculi genium, cui ipsa veritas nisi compta ac ornata non placebat; sed simplex ac inaffectatus, procul omni cultu ac humano lenocinio, ut virilem ac robustam sapientiam, vereque Dei filiam, agnosceres; non armis denique aut ulla saeculi potentia adjutus & instructus. Ut omnia Deo ac caelesti veritati deberet, quae, ictu fulmineo potentius, celsa mundi, & quicquid Euangelio inimicum erat, pene momento prostravit. Et praedicatio mea non fuit in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in demonstratione Spiritus & potentia. 1 Cor. 2: 4. Quae & universa & singula divinam hanc doctrinam, Deumque ejus auctorem commendabant.
units.tr: XIII. Finally, the manner of teaching was not suited to the spirit of a flourishing age, which did not please the truth itself unless it was polished and adorned; it was plain and unaffected, far removed from all show and human allurement, so that you would recognise a manly and robust wisdom, truly the daughter of God; it was, in short, not aided or equipped by arms or any worldly power. So that everything was owed to God and to heavenly truth, which, more powerful than a thunderbolt, overthrew the lofty things of the world, and whatever was hostile to the Gospel, almost in a moment. And my preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. 1 Cor. 2:4. These things, both together and each one separately, commended this divine doctrine and God its author.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII.
units.tr: CAPUT XXVII.

units.la: De Judiciis Dei in Judaeos.
units.tr: On the Judgments of God against the Jews.

units.la: I. Dductionem gentium sequutum est Judaicae gentis repudium: quae hactenus Dei in terris sponsa, nunc ab eo diffidens, ac pudorem suum alienis diis substernens, in profanum scortum degeneraverat. Qua imagine Hoseas statum ejus depingit, cap. 1. ubi triplici veluti periodo cuncta ejus populi fata complectitur: 1. quando fuit Ammi, ac Dei populus. 2. quando, repudium passus, factus est Lo-ammi. 3. denidenique quando olim ad Dei fœdera rursus redibit, & ad priorem virum revertetur, ac Ruchamah erit.
units.tr: I. The rejection of the Jewish nation followed the calling of the Gentiles. That nation, until then the bride of God on earth, now distrusted by him, and having put its shame under foreign gods, had degenerated into a profane harlot. Hosea portrays its condition with this image in chapter 1, where he embraces the whole history of God's people in a threefold sequence: (1) when it was Ammi, the people of God; (2) when, having suffered repudiation, it became Lo-ammi; (3) and finally, when at last it will return to the covenants of God and go back to its former husband, and will be Ruchamah.

units.la: II. Statum populi ejus quando in Dei fœdere agebat, superiori libro, sub secundo temporum intervallo, latius vidimus. Unde & Messias non ad alios prius venire quam ad ipsos, nec aliis prius Euangelium annunciari debebat. Hæc enim fœderis istius prærogativa erat. Abite autem potius ad oves perditas domus Israëlis.
