Matth. 10: 6. Necesse erat vobis primum prædicari verbum Dei, Act. 13: 46.
units.tr: II. We have seen more fully, in the earlier book, the state of his people while they stood in God's covenant, during the second period of time. Hence the Messiah was to come first to them and not to others, and the gospel was to be announced to them before anyone else. For this was the privilege of that covenant. But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matt. 10:6. It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first, Acts 13:46.

units.la: III. Unde ipsi novæ Ecclesiæ primitiæ fuerunt. Ac prædicantequidem Christo, jam non pauci ex ipsis crediderant. Si eum, Jesum, sic omittamus, credent omnes in eum, Joh. 11: 48. coll. 7: 49. Erantque hæc ejus de gente illa spolia & manubiæ; quæ ipsi debebantur. Post mortem autem ac ascensionem ejus haud paulo majori studio ad disciplinam ejus aggregabantur: Additæ sunt Ecclesiæ die illo animæ quasi ter mille. Act. 2: 41. & 5: 14. Vides, frater, quod myriades sint Judæorum credentium. Act. 21: 20. Quin & integræ fere provinciæ ad Euangelii vexillum se erexerant: quibus ingens prætereanumerus ex Judæis exteris, inter gentes de gentibus, accedebat; ad quos pleræque Apostolorum epistolæ extant. Quæ non exigua Euangelii in gente ista primordia erant.
units.tr: III. For this reason they were the first fruits of the new Church. While Christ was preaching, not a few of them had already believed. If we let him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, John 11:48, compare 7:49. These were his spoils and trophies from that nation, which were rightly his. After his death and ascension they were added to his discipline with no less eagerness: On that day about three thousand souls were added to the Church. Acts 2:41, and 5:14. You see, brother, how many myriads of Jewish believers there are. Acts 21:20. Indeed, almost whole provinces had raised themselves under the banner of the gospel, and to these an immense number of foreign Jews was added, among the Gentiles and from the Gentiles, to whom most of the apostolic letters are addressed. These were no small beginnings of the gospel among that people.

units.la: IV. Nec hi de vulgo solum Judæi erant: sed & Sacerdotes multi ac primores Christo nomen dederunt. Et de principibus multi crediderant in ipsum, Joh. 12: 42. Et magna turba Sacerdotum obediebat fidei. Act. 6: 7. Inter quos eminent, Simeon, de quo Luc. 2. 25. Nicodemus & Josephus Arimathæensis, quorum & fasti Judaici sub variis involucris meminere. Quibus quidam, quanquam parum certo, accensent Gamalielem senem, Pauli præceptorem, cujus moderatum circa Christianæ rei exordia consilium legitur Act. 5. Ac præter hos etiam mulieres non ignobiles in Christi comitatu leguntur, Luc. 8: 3. magna fidei incrementa.
units.tr: IV. Nor were these Jews only of the common people; many priests and leading men also gave their name to Christ. And many of the rulers believed in him, John 12:42. And a great crowd of priests was obedient to the faith. Acts 6:7. Among them stand out Simeon, of whom we read in Luke 2:25, and Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, whom the Jewish annals also mention under various veils. Some, though with little certainty, count among these the aged Gamaliel, Paul's teacher, whose moderate counsel concerning the beginnings of the Christian cause is read in Acts 5. Besides these, we read that not undistinguished women also accompanied Christ, Luke 8:3, a great increase of faith.

units.la: V. Ac hæ quidem gentis istius primitiæ erant, ac flos delibatus, quem in Ecclesiæ aream cogi, istoque auspicio mundi messem conse crari interierat. Cæterum gens ipsa universa, si publicum ac communem ejus statum spectes, Euangelio rebellis permansit: unde & repudium à Deo passa, ac tandem funditus deleta est. Qui infidelitatis, repudiationis ac denique excisionis ejus gradus speciatim considerandi sunt.
units.tr: V. These, then, were the first fruits of that nation, the picked flower which was to be gathered into the threshing floor of the Church, and under whose auspices the harvest of the world was to be consecrated. But the nation as a whole, if you look at its public and common condition, remained rebellious against the gospel. For this reason it also suffered repudiation by God and was at last utterly destroyed. The stages of its unbelief, repudiation and finally its cutting off must be considered one by one.

units.la: VI. Est autem hoc admirandum valde, ac fidei præsertim grave, cum Christus Ecclesiæ Judaicæ tot sæculis promissus foret; illiusque proprium peculium ac decus existeret; quin & religionis ac fidei maximum haetenus apud illos caput faceret; tamen a gente illa sua non agnitum, sed rejectum, tandemque necatum fuisse: contraque gentes, haetenus ab Ecclesiafegregęs, cum accepisse, ac debitum Judæis Servatorem veluti intercepisse. Sed S. Scriptura dudum scandalo isti obviam ivit, rem ita olim futuram clarissimis vatum oraculis longe ante significans. Deut. 31. & 32. Psal. 2: 1, 2. & 81. & 95. & 118. 22. Esai. 6. & 43. & 53. 8. Hab. 1. 5. 2. 4. Zach. 12. 10. Malach. 2. 11. conf. Joh. 19. 37. Act. 2. 23, 36, 37.
units.tr: VI. Now this is very remarkable, and especially grievous for faith: though Christ had been promised to the Jewish Church for so many centuries, and was its own special treasure and glory, indeed the chief head of their religion and faith until then, nevertheless he was not acknowledged by that nation as its own, but rejected, and at last put to death; on the other hand the Gentiles, hitherto separated from the Church, received him and, as it were, intercepted the Saviour owed to the Jews. But Holy Scripture long ago met this scandal, clearly foretelling in the most distinct oracles of the prophets that the matter would so turn out. Deut. 31 and 32; Ps. 2:1, 2; 81; 95; 118:22; Isa. 6; 43; 53:8; Hab. 1:5; 2:4; Zech. 12:10; Mal. 2:11; compare John 19:37; Acts 2:23, 36, 37.

units.la: VII. Sed operæ pretium est causas tam prodigiosæ perfidiæ investigare; quæ, aliis latius narratæ, præcipuæ hæ erant: 1. quod terram illam, & urbem, & politiam, miro affectu deperibant. Unde pignore isto excuti æquo animo ferre non poterant. Cujus rei indicium est: Joh. 11:48, 50. Si enim Jesum omittamus sic, omnes credent in eum, & venient Romani, & tollent nostrum & locum & gentem — conducit nobis ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens pereat. Quare cum & Johannes Baptista, & Christus supremum urbis illius diem, fatumque gentis propinquare prædicarent, ac vana ista contemnere, jamque ad exitum sese comparare, juberent, ingenti offensioni erant; cum Judæi urbem illam, utpote religionum caput, æternam fore inani superstitione sibi persuaderent.
units.tr: VII. But it is worth the effort to investigate the causes of so prodigious a faithlessness. These, which have been set out more fully by others, were chiefly the following: (1) they were consumed with a remarkable attachment to that land, that city and that polity. For this reason they could not bear with equanimity to be shaken loose from that pledge. Evidence of this is John 11:48, 50: If we let him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation... It is expedient for us that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish. Hence, when John the Baptist and Christ foretold that the last day of that city and the fate of the nation were drawing near, and bade them despise these vain things and prepare themselves for the outcome, they were a great offence to them, since the Jews persuaded themselves, in empty superstition, that the city, as the head of their religion, would last forever.

units.la: VIII. 2. Cui conjunctus erat idem erga templum, omneque ejus ministerium affectus: cui plus æquo adhærescentes ipsum templi Dominum agnoscere non potuerunt, sed in externo illo cultu ac γυναικεία stupentes justitiam ac salutem suam ab eâ pendere existimabant. à quo errore profectum est, quod legem fidei agnoscere, seque ei subjicere non possent. Loci enim ac cultus illius reverentia obstabat, qua perculsi ac attoniti ad molem istam perpetuo suspirabant; nec adduci ullo modo poterant, ut Christum, qui imagines ac umbras istas evacuatum ibat, nudum ac sine choragio illo reciperent. Unde in actis sæpe Apostolos hoc crimine petitos legimus, quod contra urbem, & templum, ac instituta Mosis concionarentur.
units.tr: VIII. (2) Closely connected with this was their attachment to the temple and to its whole ministry. Clinging to it beyond measure, they could not recognise the Lord of the temple himself. Amazed at that external worship and ceremony, they thought their righteousness and salvation depended on it. From this error arose their inability to acknowledge the law of faith and to submit to it. For the reverence due to that place and worship stood in the way; struck and astonished by it, they sighed perpetually over that mass, and they could in no way be brought to receive Christ, who was about to abolish those images and shadows, as he was, bare and without that ornament. Hence we often read in the Acts that the apostles were attacked on this charge, that they preached against the city, the temple and the institutions of Moses.

units.la: IX. 3. Nimia autem hæc externorum veneratio, quæ, uti olim Ecclesiæ fidem aluerant, ita tum objecto obice morabantur, protecta erat ex perversa Scribarum Catechesi; quæ, cum verbum Dei paulatim negligeretur, contra ac ultimus prophetarum monuerat, memores estote legis Mosis, servi mei, Mal. 4. 4. præcipua religionis capita corruperat: cum nihil sani de Fœdere Dei, de Justitia peccatoris, de fide Patrum, de regno Dei, de Messia Deique filio, deque beneficiis illius sentirent.
units.tr: IX. (3) This excessive veneration of externals, which had once nourished the faith of the Church and now, with an obstacle placed in its way, kept it back, was protected by the perverse teaching of the Scribes. While the word of God was gradually neglected, contrary to what the last of the prophets had warned, remember the law of Moses, my servants, Mal. 4:4, they had corrupted the principal heads of religion, since they had no sound understanding of the covenant of God, of the righteousness of the sinner, of the faith of the fathers, of the kingdom of God, of the Messiah and Son of God, or of his benefits.

units.la: X. 4. Contraque Traditionum studium invaluerat: circa quas cum ista ætate mirum in modum insanirent, magisque quid Magistri edixissent, quam quid Deus jusserat, in promtu haberent, ista labes Ecclesiam prorsus devastaverat.
units.tr: X. (4) On the other hand, a zeal for the traditions had prevailed. Since they raved about these in a remarkable way in that age, and kept more readily at hand what the teachers had decreed than what God had commanded, this blight had utterly laid waste the Church.

units.la: XI. 5. Denique non minima culpa erat in ipso religionis apice, de Messia, corrupto: circa cujus personam ac regnum cum errarent, non mirum est, quod adventantem, nec illa quæ illi quærebant signa præferentem, recipere dedignarentur. Avulsum enim illud primarium religionis caput ab ipsa religione tum temporis erat. Cum enim illa spiritualis sit, ac salutem animæ spectet, hi Messiam expectabant, Regem, externa gloria præfulgentem, qui Judæorum rempubl. pristino nitori restitueret. Quod veræ doctrinæ stuprum, ut & cætera, Doctorum inertiæ ac impietati, de qua acerbas apud vatum postremum querelas legimus, adscribendum erat.
units.tr: XI. (5) Finally, in the very summit of religion, concerning the Messiah, there was no small fault, for the doctrine had been corrupted. Since they went astray about his person and kingdom, it is no wonder that they disdained to receive him when he came, bearing none of those signs which they were seeking. For that chief head of religion had by then been torn away from religion itself. Since religion is spiritual and concerns the salvation of the soul, they expected a Messiah, a King shining with outward glory, who would restore the Jewish commonwealth to its former splendour. This adultery against true doctrine, like the others, must be ascribed to the sloth and impiety of the teachers, about whom we read bitter complaints in the last of the prophets.

units.la: XII. Atque hæc populi infidelitas, & Messiæ rejectio, abdicat onis ipsorum propria ac unica causa erat. Cum enim alia populi illius peccata minoribus olim poenis castigata forent; atque antea idololatriam ejus Deus Babylonis exilio, ac brevi veluti divortio, vindicasset; hæc Messiæ rejectio ac cædes, quæ totalis à Dei foedere apostasia, & summa denique perfidia erat, non nisi universæ gentis repudio expiari poterat. Recte enim, qui à Fœdere Dei primi abierant, fidemque jam non læserant solum, sed prorsus exuerant, iidem à Deo abdicari, ac instar profanæ, nec Deo amplius fœderatæ gentis, haberi poterant. Quod futurum Prophetæ olim prædixerant. Omisisti populum tuum, domum Jacobi! Esai. 2:6. Et fiet ipsis verbum Domini, præceptum ad præceptum – ut cant, & lapsent retro, & confringantur, & illaqueentur. Esai. 28:13. Quomodo dabo te, Israel, ut Adamah, ponam te ut Zeboim! Hos. 11:8. Et urbem, & sanctum corrumpet populus principis advenæ. Dan. 9:26. Hos. 1. Ezech. 16.
units.tr: XII. This unbelief of the people and rejection of the Messiah was the one and only cause of their abdication. For while the other sins of that people had once been punished with lesser penalties (God had avenged their idolatry by the Babylonian exile, a kind of brief divorce), this rejection and slaying of the Messiah, which was a total apostasy from the covenant of God and the utmost faithlessness, could be atoned for only by the repudiation of the whole nation. For those who had first departed from the covenant of God, and had not merely violated the faith but utterly cast it off, could rightly be disowned by God, and regarded as a profane nation, no longer joined to God in covenant. The prophets had foretold this long before. You have forsaken your people, the house of Jacob! Isa. 2:6. And the word of the Lord shall be to them, precept upon precept... so that they go and fall backward, and are broken and snared. Isa. 28:13. How shall I give you up, Israel? How shall I make you like Admah? Hos. 11:8. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Dan. 9:26. Hos. 1; Ezek. 16.

units.la: XIII. Hoc gentis repudium denique non magno intervallo consecutum est ejus excidium, itidem à Prophetis prædictum. Num. 24:24. Lev. 26. Deut. 29:19,20,21. &31.&32. conf. Rom. 11:31. 1 Thess. 2:16. Deut. 18:19 conf. Act. 3:23. Esai. 8:14,15. Joel. 2. 30,31,32. conf. Act. 2:19,20,21. Zach. 5:1–4. &11. Mal. 2:3, 12. &4:6. Matth. 24:6. conf. Dan. 9:24–27.
units.tr: XIII. This rejection of the nation was not long followed by its destruction, which was likewise foretold by the Prophets. Num. 24:24. Lev. 26. Deut. 29:19, 20, 21, and 31, 32; cf. Rom. 11:31. 1 Thess. 2:16. Deut. 18:19; cf. Acts 3:23. Isa. 8:14, 15. Joel 2:30, 31, 32; cf. Acts 2:19, 20, 21. Zech. 5:1–4, and 11. Mal. 2:3, 12, and 4:6. Matt. 24:6; cf. Dan. 9:24–27.

units.la: XIV. Cujus ultimi tamen supplicii moras quasdam Deus indulsit,
units.tr: XIV. God nevertheless granted some delays of this final punishment,

units.la: Hinc secuta populi illius abdicatio.
units.tr: Hence followed the rejection of that people.

units.la: Cujus ejusque cidium. colligendis prius ex gente illa fidelium reliquiis. Unde per partes illud executus est, ac veluti gradibus quibusdam rempublicam, templum, ac gentem denique totam afflixit & tandem evertit. Quem judiciorum Dei ordinem observare licet, quomodo coeperit, ac per partes progressus fuerit, donec tandem consumta omni misericordia, cum nihil sancti, nihilque bonae frugis in Ecclesiae area superesset, arentes ac steriles praedii sui stipulas sanctissimo ac justissimo incendio depopulatus est.
units.tr: Whose destruction, [God first ordered] the gathering of the remnant of believers from that nation. From there he carried it out in stages, and, as it were by steps, afflicted the commonwealth, the temple and finally the whole nation, and at last overthrew them. It is permitted to observe the order of God's judgments: how it began, and how it advanced step by step, until at last, with all mercy spent and nothing holy or good fruit left on the threshing floor of the Church, he laid waste its dry and barren stubble with a most holy and most just fire.

units.la: XV. Primus judicii gradus erat, quod respublica auctoritas, per Romana arma jam antea non parum imminuta, tum prorsus languere coeperit, sublata judiciorum capitalium potestate: Dixerunt ergo ipsi, Judaei, nobis non licet occidere quemquam, Joh. 18. 31. Quod anno ante excidium 40. contigit, non necessitate aliqua, sed religione quadam ipsorum. Ac cum judicis simul intercalandi facultas diminuta, ac a praesidum nutu suspensa fuit.
units.tr: XV. The first step of judgment was that the commonwealth began to languish completely, its authority already not a little weakened by the Roman arms, once the power of capital judgment was taken away: The Jews therefore said to him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death, John 18:31. This happened in the fortieth year before the destruction, not from any necessity but from a certain religious scruple of their own. And at the same time the power of intercalating the calendar was diminished and made dependent on the nod of the governors.

units.la: XVI. Hunc reipublicae casum, accelerantibus gentis fatis, exceperunt deinde crebrae seditiones, & latrocinia; ac bellum deinde cum Romanis, saepius per arma ipsorum civilia dilatum, iterumque repetitum, ac Tito victore tandem absolutum. Quando urbis ipsius fatum maturavit. Qua, post ultimae miseriae exempla, tandem expugnata ac deleta, gens universa in metropolis suae funere concidit.
units.tr: XVI. Upon this collapse of the commonwealth, as the nation's fate quickened, there followed frequent seditions and robberies; then war with the Romans, often deferred by their own civil arms, renewed again, and at last brought to an end with Titus as victor. This brought on the fate of the city itself. After the last examples of misery, it was at last stormed and destroyed, and the whole nation fell in the funeral of its metropolis.

units.la: XVII. Ac cum urbe simul eversum est templum, eodem, quo primum templum absumtum erat, die; ubi varia numerorum myfteria ac responsus ostendi possent. Ac cum templa sacra quoque gentis illius interiore, cum extra locum illum celebrare illa nefas foret. Atque tum nova fidelium Ecclesia prorsus constituta; ac, remoto templo, quod utrisque adibatur, a reliquo infidelium Judaeorum grege separata est, juxta illud Esai. 52: 11. Recedite, recedite, exite inde, impurum ne tangite.
units.tr: XVII. And the temple was overthrown together with the city, on the same day on which the first temple had been consumed; here various mysteries and correspondences of numbers could be shown. And since it was unlawful to celebrate the sacred rites of that nation anywhere outside that place, the new Church of believers was then entirely established; and, with the temple removed, which both alike had frequented, it was separated from the rest of the unbelieving flock of Jews, according to the saying of Isa. 52:11: Depart, depart, go out from thence, touch no unclean thing.

units.la: XVIII. Cum templo defecerunt 4. Pontifices; quorum ultimus fuit Phannias, seu Phannafus, homo rudis & divinarum caerimoniarum imperitissimus. Atque ita postquam verus Sacerdos advenisset, tandem quoque externum illud sacerdotium periit.
units.tr: XVIII. With the temple there failed four high priests; the last of whom was Phannias, or Phannafus, a rude man most ignorant of the divine ceremonies. And so, after the true Priest had come, that external priesthood at last also perished.

units.la: XIX. 5. Utque omne decus suum gens illa amitteret, etiam Doctores hac aetate desierunt; quorum ultimus fuit Hillel princeps, Judae sancti nepos. Cum extra terram sanctam istum honorem capessere non liceret. Qui secuti enim sunt Doctores Babylonici, longe minoris dignitatis erant.
units.tr: XIX. And so that nation might lose all its glory, its teachers also ceased in this age; the last of whom was Hillel the prince, grandson of the holy Judah. Since it was not permitted to hold that honour outside the holy land. The teachers who followed them in Babylon were of far lesser dignity.

units.la: XX 6. Confusæ porro sunt tribus & familiæ, deperditis ac exustis cum templo genealogiarum saltis ac tabulis. Sapienti autem consilio Deus id accidere permisit, 1. ut populi, generis sui nobilitate ac sanctitate præferocis, animos paulatim accideret, oblumque in externos, ut sibi longe impares, ponere adsuesceret; sensimque discrimen illud Judæi & Græci de mundo tolleret: Omnes enim filii Dei estis per fidem, in Christo Jesu, Gal. 3: 26. 2. utque pro carnali cognatione spirituale illud genus, quod à Christo solo arcessitur, æstimare, istiusque stirpi nos inserere doceret, quæ sola in cœlis censetur, quæque unica Christianorum nobilitas est. Qui autem fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui est in cœlis, ille est frater meus, & soror, & mater. Matth. 12. 50. Flectlogenua mea ad Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ex quo tota familia in cœlis & in terra nominatur. Eph. 3: 14, 15. Unde inutilis nunc & vetita infinita illa genealogiarum scrutatio. Neque attendere — ad genealogias sine carentes, quæ quæstiones exhibent magis, quam ædificationem Dei in fide 1 Tim. 1: 4. coll. Tit. 3: 9.
units.tr: XX. Next, the tribes and families were confused, the genealogical lists and records having perished and been burned along with the temple. God allowed this to happen by a wise plan: (1) so that the minds of a people too proud of the nobility and holiness of its stock might gradually be humbled, and accustom itself to place its trust in foreigners, as far inferior to itself, and little by little remove that distinction between Jew and Greek from the world: For you are all sons of God through faith, in Christ Jesus, Gal. 3:26; (2) and so that it might teach us to value a spiritual kinship, which is drawn from Christ alone, rather than a carnal one, and to graft ourselves into that stock which alone is reckoned in heaven and which is the only true nobility of Christians: For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother, Matt. 12:50; I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom the whole family in heaven and on earth is named, Eph. 3:14, 15. Hence that endless searching into genealogies is now useless and forbidden: nor to give heed to myths and endless genealogies, which give rise to questions rather than to the edifying of God in faith, 1 Tim. 1:4; cf. Titus 3:9.

units.la: XXI. 7. Consecuta hæc fuit tandem universæ gentis captivitas & servitus; dum cœlo soloque suo extorres, ac toto orbe vagi, miserrima fata sua ubivis agitanda habent; omnium nationum ludibrium ac servi, cum nullibi gentem aut rempubl. componant, nec ullum terrarum angulum possideant. Cum qua hodierna eorum captivitate nulla præterita comparari potest. Nam diebus multis sedebunt filii Israel, sine rege, & sine principe; & sine sacrificio, & sine cippo: & sine Ephod, & sine imaginibus. Postea convertentur filii Israel, & quærent Jehovam Deum suum. Hos. 3: 4, 5.
units.tr: XXI. At last there followed upon this the captivity and slavery of the whole nation; banished from its heaven and soil and wandering through the whole world, it has its most wretched fate to be borne everywhere; the mockery and slaves of all nations, since it establishes no nation or commonwealth anywhere and possesses no corner of the earth. No past captivity can be compared with its present captivity. For the children of Israel shall abide many days without king, and without prince, and without sacrifice, and without pillar, and without ephod, and without images. Afterwards the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, Hos. 3:4, 5.

units.la: XXII. Estque miseriarum illarum colophon, quod non corpore magis quam animo servi, atque in perfidia sua obstinati redditi sunt; contra omnem Euangelii lucem animum oculosque pertinacissime obfirmantes, & clausi undique ac impervii. Sed obdurata sunt mentes ipsorum. 2 Cor. 3: 14. Nolo enim vos ignorare — quod supor invicem contigit Israeli, donec plenitudo gentium intret. Rom. 11: 25.
units.tr: XXII. And the crown of those miseries is that they have been made slaves not so much in body as in mind, and have become obstinate in their faithlessness; setting their minds and eyes most stubbornly against every light of the Gospel, and shut up and closed off on every side. But their minds were hardened, 2 Cor. 3:14. For I would not have you ignorant, brethren, of this mystery, that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, Rom. 11:25.

units.la: XXIII. Unde rari admodum ex illis, licet in longa adeo miseria, ad Ecclesiæ gremium convertuntur. Cujus rei causa est, partim justum Dei judicium, populi istius perfidiam ulcisentis: partim insitä genti pertinacia, atque hostile in alias gentes odium, quas divinæ legis cognitione; quam pro corona ac decore Israëlis solius habent, præ ipse præstare non ferunt: unde, ne Christianis concedere videantur, vanissimis exceptionibus, ac præstantissimorum locorum detorsionibus, sese adversus fidem eorum muniunt; ac nubes & inania captare adsueti insulsissimas tandem nugas & fabulas pro liquidissimis veritatibus habent: denique & oblata à Christianis scandala, sectae, haereses, mores denique, non satis ad legis illius, quam profitentur, sanctitatem castigati.
units.tr: XXIII. Hence very few of them, although in so long a misery, turn to the bosom of the Church. The cause of this is partly the just judgment of God, punishing the unbelief of that people; partly the obstinacy innate in the nation and its hostile hatred of other nations, whom they cannot bear to see equal to themselves in the knowledge of the divine law, which they hold as the crown and glory of Israel alone; whence, lest they seem to yield anything to Christians, they fortify themselves against their faith with most vain objections and twisted interpretations of the most excellent passages; and, accustomed to catching at clouds and empty things, they at last take most foolish trifles and fables for the clearest truths; and finally the offences given by Christians, their sects, heresies, and morals, not sufficiently chastened to the holiness of that law which they profess.

units.la: XXIV. Ut hinc tandem appareat quid de hodierno Judaismo censendum sit; quod videl. non fides, sed perfidia, & à Patrum doctrina apostasia, atque erga regnum Christi mera rebellio sit. Unde foecunda errorum omnium ac haeresium, quae vel hodie fidem Christianam exercent, vel mater, vel nutrix est. Quae pestilentissimae haereses, in varios ramos excuntes, universam religionem depopulantur ac penitus devastant. Omnes autem à Judaica perfidia vel ortum habent, vel incrementum, vel denique in eam desinunt; juxta illud Prophetae: Ex te exivit cogitans contra Jehovam malum, consiliarius nequitiae. Nah. 1:11.
units.tr: XXIV. From this it may at last appear what is to be judged of present-day Judaism: namely that it is not faith but faithlessness, and from the doctrine of the Fathers an apostasy, and towards the kingdom of Christ mere rebellion. Whence it is the fruitful mother, or nurse, of all the errors and heresies which even today assail the Christian faith. These most pestilent heresies, branching out into various shoots, lay waste and utterly devastate the whole religion. All of them, however, have their origin, growth, or end in Jewish faithlessness, according to the saying of the Prophet: Out of you has come forth one who devises evil against the LORD, a counsellor of wickedness, Nah. 1:11.

units.la: XXV. Ut vero Theologiae ac religionis scopo Judaei exciderint. Cum enim ille unice in Dei gloria, ac animarum salute positus sit; illi non nisi humano cultu Deum venerantur, &, pro superstitionis ingenio, levibus quibusdam praeceptis, ac hominum institutis, eum colunt; iisque figmentis, magico propemodum ritu, eum sibi devinctum ac obnoxium arbitrantur. Veram autem animarum salutem adeo non assequi possunt, ut eam ne quidem sperent aut expectent: sed, ut cultum suum potissimum externis operibus absolvunt, ac Messiam solum terrenum quendam Regem futurum putant; quod tamen fidei ac spei ipsorum primarium caput est; ita etiam vix aliam quam terrenam ac carnalem felicitatem somniant; nec magnopere de animae post mortem statu solliciti, molestas illas disputationes Rabbinis suis potius relinquunt. Ut non satis recte Socviniani, ac alii, Judaeos verum Deum colere; ac fidem habere, quae bonorum operum mater existat; quin & externo legis suae cultu Deo placere posse contendant. Et me nostis, & nostis unde sim; & à me non veni, sed est verus, qui misit me, quem vos nescitis. Joh. 7: 28. Est Pater meus qui glorificat me, quem vos dicitis Deum vestrum esse, & non cognovistis eum. Joh. 8: 54, 55. Novi operatua — & blasphemias eorum, qui dicunt Judaeos esse se, & non sunt, sed congregatio Satanae. Apoc. 2:9.
units.tr: XXV. Now as to how the Jews have fallen from the aim of theology and religion: since that aim is set solely in the glory of God and the salvation of souls, they worship God with merely human worship, and, according to the bent of superstition, honour him with certain slight precepts and human institutions; and by those fictions, almost with a magical rite, they think he is bound to them and bound to obey them. But they are so far from attaining true salvation of souls that they do not even hope for it or look for it; rather, they complete their worship chiefly by external works, and think the Messiah will be only a certain earthly King, which nevertheless is the chief head of their faith and hope; thus they dream of almost no happiness but earthly and carnal, and, not greatly concerned about the state of the soul after death, they leave those troublesome disputations to their Rabbis. Hence the Socinians and others are not quite right in saying that the Jews worship the true God and have a faith which is the mother of good works, or that they can please God by the external worship of their law. And you know me, and you know where I am from; and I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know, John 7:28. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God, and you have not known him, John 8:54, 55. I know your works, and the blasphemy of those who say they are Jews and are not, but a synagogue of Satan, Rev. 2:9.

units.la: LIBER VI.
units.tr: BOOK VI.

units.la: DE
units.tr: OF THE BENEFITS OF CHRIST.

units.la: BENEFICIIS CHRISTI.
units.tr: THE BENEFITS OF CHRIST.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS SEPTIMUS
units.tr: LOCUS THIRTY-SEVENTH

units.la: DE
units.tr: CONCERNING

units.la: Primis beneficiis Christi. CAPUT I.
units.tr: The First Benefits of Christ. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Gratia Christi.
units.tr: On the Grace of Christ.

units.la: I. POstquam Christi personam & officia, statusque varios decurrimus, salutemque ab eo impetratam vidimus, sequitur jam ejus applicatio, quæ impetrationis effectus & fructus, parisque cum eâ latitudinis est; ac tum vi meritorum Christi, tum S. Spiritus in fidelibus habitantis efficacià peragitur.
units.tr: I. Having run through the person and offices of Christ and his various states, and having seen the salvation obtained by him, we now come to its application. This is the effect and fruit of the obtaining, and it is as wide in scope. It is accomplished both by the power of Christ's merits and by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers.

units.la: II. Ac prout salus nostra vel in hac vitâ inchoatur, vel in futura vitâ absolvitur, ita beneficia Christi vel hujus, vel futuræ vitæ sunt; adeoque vel ad vitæ spiritualis initium, vel progressum, vel consummationem denique faciunt: atque hoc ordine sibi invicem succedunt. 1. Principium est efficax Christi gratia. 2. Cujus effectum est vocatio potens. 3. Sequitur regeneratio. 4. Fides. 5. Justificatio. 6. Adoptio. 7. Libertas Christiana. 8. Sanctificatio & bona opera. 9. Respiscentia. 10. Perseverantia. 11. Glorificatio. Quæ licet universæ œconomiæ gratiæ communia sint, cum tamen sub N. T. eminent, variisque controversiis sub eo involuta sint, hoc loco à nobis præcipuè tractari merentur.
units.tr: II. Our salvation is begun in this life and completed in the life to come, and so the benefits of Christ belong either to this life or to the future life. They therefore effect either the beginning, the progress, or the final completion of the spiritual life, and they follow one another in this order: (1) The beginning is the efficacious grace of Christ. (2) Its effect is effectual calling. (3) Regeneration follows. (4) Faith. (5) Justification. (6) Adoption. (7) Christian liberty. (8) Sanctification and good works. (9) Repentance. (10) Perseverance. (11) Glorification. Although all these are common to the whole economy of grace, they stand out especially under the New Testament, and since various controversies are entangled with them there, they deserve to be treated here by us in particular.

units.la: III. Primo occurrit gratia Christi, seu Dei in Christo. In Christo enim solo ea locum habet; quæ enim homini adhuc integro exhibebatur, improprie gratia appellatur, prout illa vox in Scripturis accipitur. Sub V.T. autem gratia illa non sine omni iræ mixtura erat: quando obtinebat particula ferventis, Esai. 54:8. & Lex irae.
units.tr: III. First comes the grace of Christ, or the grace of God in Christ. For that grace has its place in Christ alone. The favour shown to man while he was still unimpaired is called grace only improperly, as that word is used in the Scriptures. Under the Old Testament, however, that grace was not without some admixture of wrath, when the particle of heat held sway (Isa. 54:8), and the law of wrath (Rom. 4:15).

units.la: X iram operabatur, Rom. 4: 15. sub œconomia vero N.T. mera est gratia. Lex per Mosen data est; gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta est. Joh. 1: 17. ut nunc obtineant τὰ ὄντα Δαβὶδ τὰ πιστὰ beneficentiæ illæ Davidis firma. Act. 13: 34. conf. Esai. 53: 3.
units.tr: The law worketh wrath, Rom. 4:15. Under the economy of the New Testament, however, it is pure grace: the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, John 1:17. So that now the kindnesses of David are sure [τὰ ὄντα Δαβὶδ τὰ πιστὰ], Acts 13:34; compare Isa. 55:3.

units.la: IV. Per gratiam autem hic intelligimus amorem, seu favorem gratuitum Dei erga nos, propter Christum, cum potenti sua operatione & efficacia. Conjungenda enim illa sunt. Et consideranda est illa gratia, tum ut in Deo, tum ut in nobis est. In Deo gratuitum ejus amorem & benevolentiam dicit: quæ vel communior est; nec enim vel ipsos reprobos prorsus dedignatur Deus; vel specialis, ex Testam. vid. Dei, & ad solos electos se extendens; quæ proprie gratia gratum faciens appellari potest. Ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, in qua nos cumulavit in dilecto illo. Eph. 1: 6. Gratia illa salvati estis per fidem. c. 2: 8. Justificamur gratis, ipsius gratia per redemtionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Rom. 3: 24. In nobis dicit amoris Dei effecta ac dona; quæ itidem vel communia sunt, prout ipsi quoque reprobi aliquod ex Christo impendium habent & in tam magna luce aliqui quoque radii ad ipsos pertingunt; ac appellatur ea gratia gratuita data; vel electorum propria, quam vulgo, licet minus recte, Scholastici gratiam gratum facientem appellant.
units.tr: IV. By grace here we understand the free love or favour of God toward us, on account of Christ, together with his powerful working and efficacy, for these must be joined. That grace must be considered both as it is in God and as it is in us. In God it signifies his free love and goodwill, which is either more general, for God does not altogether disdain even the reprobate, or special, belonging to the elect alone, extending to them alone, and this may properly be called grace that makes one acceptable. To the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he has made us accepted in the Beloved, Eph. 1:6. By grace you have been saved through faith, Eph. 2:8. We are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, Rom. 3:24. In us it signifies the effects and gifts of God's love. These too are either common, since even the reprobate have some benefit from Christ, and in so great a light some rays reach them too; and this is called freely given grace; or they are proper to the elect, which the Scholastics commonly call, though less correctly, grace that makes one acceptable.

units.la: V. Cum autem gratiæ donum in electis vel habituale sit, vel actuale: quorum illud est habitus infusus, ut fides, spes, charitas; hoc, ipsa Dei operatio supranaturalis: illud instar auxilii sine quo non, absque quo nihil bene velle potest voluntas, quod in homine primo quoque locum habebat; hoc instar auxilii cum quo, per quod ipsa jam voluntas actu determinatur & vult; illud ad modum qualitatis, hoc ad modum actus animam actu afficientis & cientis se habet: de posteriori hic sermo est.
units.tr: V. The gift of grace in the elect is either habitual or actual. The former is an infused habit, such as faith, hope, and charity; the latter is God's own supernatural working. The former stands as the help without which the will can will nothing well, which in the first man held its place; the latter stands as the help with which, and through which, the will itself is actually determined and wills. The former is related to the soul in the manner of a quality, the latter in the manner of an act that actually affects and moves the soul. It is of the latter that we speak here.

units.la: VI. Aberrant autem Pontificii, qui gratiam omnem Dei commutant in donum, seu gratiam habitualem, ac qualitatem infusam, qua præditos fideles Deo gratos ac justos esse prædicant: qua tamen uti vel non uti in hominis potestate sit; imo qua suâ culpâ excidere ac carere tandem possit. Cum, uti vidimus, gratia Dei ipsius misericordiam æternumque in Christo amorem quoque involvat.
units.tr: VI. The Papists go astray, however, who change all the grace of God into a gift, that is, habitual grace and an infused quality, by which they declare that believers are made pleasing and righteous before God. Yet whether they use it or not lies in man's power; indeed, by his own fault he can lose it and finally be deprived of it. But, as we have seen, the grace of God includes his mercy and his eternal love in Christ.

units.la: VII. Naturam ac operationem hujus gratiæ quod attinet, non consistit illa in externa revelatione, cum auxilio sine quo non conjuncta; nec in morali solum suasione, cujus efficacia tantum metaphorica ac occasionalis est; nullaque proprie vires homini largitur; ac Deum denique in hominibus convertendis non multo potentiorem facit, quam diabolus est in iisdem corrumpendis: sed ipsum divinæ potentiæ robur, divinæque manus efficaciam dicit, nulla humana vi superabilem, sed ipsum cordis nostri lapidem frangere ac edomare, & ad instar udi ac mollis luti fingere ac flectere aptam. Et quæ excellens magnitudo potentiæ ejus in nos, qui credimus, secundum efficacitatem prævalentia virium ejus. Eph. 1: 19. Et faciam, ut in statutis meis ambuletis. Ezech. 36: 26. Deus enim est, qui efficit in vobis & ipsum velle, & ipsum agere, pro gratuita sui benevolentia. Phil. 2: 13. Aduna cor meum ad reverendum nomen tuum. Psal. 86: 11.
units.tr: VII. As for the nature and working of this grace, it does not consist in external revelation joined with a help without which it cannot work; nor in moral persuasion alone, whose efficacy is merely metaphorical and occasional; nor does it bestow any powers properly on man. Nor does it make God in converting men much more powerful than the devil is in corrupting them. Rather, it signifies the very strength of divine power and the efficacy of the divine hand, which no human force can overcome, which breaks and tames the very stone of our heart, and shapes and bends it, like soft and wet clay, into a fit form. And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the strength of his might, Eph. 1:19. And I will cause you to walk in my statutes, Ezek. 36:26. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure, Phil. 2:13. Unite my heart to fear your name, Ps. 86:11.

units.la: VIII. Duo autem præsertim agit illa gratia: 1. impedimenta conversionis amolitur & tollit; tum communia, ut fortia illa iguorantiæ ac concupiscentiæ vincula; tum peculiaria, pro cujusque perversa indole ac genio. 2. pulsis illis tenebris, atque universo cupiditatum agmine facessere jusso, animæ deinde statum serenat ac tranquillat; novaque eam luce perfundit, ac præsertim rerum cœlestium & justitiæ amorem ac delectationem infundit. Qui blandus ac potens affectus ipsum gratiæ regnum est; illa enim ineffabili hac suavitate cœlesti & spirituali delectatione universa absolvitur. Atque hæc est illa tractio, Joh. 6: 44. illa Dei unctio, 1 Joh. 2: 27. illa videl. divinæ dulcedinis gutta, quæ ubi primum in cor destillavit, jam illud sese amplius capere non potest, sed blanda ista vi possidetur prorsus & aufertur.
units.tr: VIII. This grace accomplishes two things in particular. (1) It removes and takes away the obstacles to conversion, both the common ones, such as the strong chains of ignorance and concupiscence, and the particular ones, according to each person's perverse disposition and temperament. (2) Having driven away those darknesses and ordered the whole host of desires to depart, it then calms and quietens the soul's state, floods it with new light, and especially infuses a love and delight in heavenly things and in righteousness. This gentle and powerful affection is the very kingdom of grace, for by this ineffable sweetness, the whole work is completed through heavenly and spiritual delight. This is that drawing, John 6:44, that divine anointing, 1 John 2:27, that drop of divine sweetness which, as soon as it has dripped into the heart, the heart can no longer contain, but is wholly possessed and carried away by that gentle force.

units.la: IX. Non enim gratia est virtus aliqua, vel motus extra voluntatem consistens, ac abea diversus, camque ab extrinseco movens & afficiens; neque etiam recte instar qualitatis extrinsecus accedentis ipsique inhærentis concipitur, sed potius ad instar creationis explicanda est. Atque uti in rebus naturalibus creatio, conservatio, concursus, non vim vel virtutem aliquam extra res ipsas dicunt, quæ ipsis de novo insinuetur; sed ipsas tantum res, quas Deus, si materiales sint, cum motu semel indito, si cogitantes, cum cogitationibus ac volitionibus earum variis, singulis momentis quasi reproducit, atque ita eas conservat, & ad actiones ipsarum concurrit: ita in operibus gratiæ, animam nostram reproducit cum talibus cogitationibus ac volitionibus, ad quas ipsa naturaliter est indonea; quæ operatio cum extraordinaria ac supranaturalis sit, inde gratiæ nomen sortitur.
units.tr: IX. For grace is not some power or motion existing outside the will and distinct from it, moving and affecting it from without. Nor is it rightly conceived as a quality coming in from outside and inhering in the soul. Rather, it must be explained after the manner of creation. Just as in natural things creation, conservation and concurrence do not signify some power or virtue outside the things themselves that is newly infused into them, but only the things themselves, which God, if they are material, reproduces at every moment, as it were, along with the motion once impressed on them, or, if they are thinking beings, along with their various thoughts and volitions, and so conserves them and concurs with their actions: so in the works of grace, he reproduces our soul with such thoughts and volitions as it is naturally fit for. Since this operation is extraordinary and supernatural, it takes the name of grace.

units.la: X. Unde pulchre gratiæ & liberi arbitrii concordia explicari potest: cum non magis gratiæ operatio, quam Dei conservatio, aut con-cordia.
units.tr: X. Hence the harmony of grace and free will can be neatly explained: the operation of grace is no more opposed to freedom of the will than God's conservation or concurrence, or any operation of his in us, is.

units.la: {y} ad instar creationis est. concursus, vel qualiscunque ejus in nobis operatio, cum libertate arbitrii pugnet: nec magis animæ interfit aut libertatem ejus lædat, reproduci cum cogitationibus spiritualibus ac cœlestibus, quam reproduci cum cogitationibus naturalibus; quorum alterum ordinariæ, alterum extraordinariæ conservationis & concursus, adeoque gratiæ est.
units.tr: {y} after the manner of creation. Concurrence, or whatever operation of his in us, does not fight with freedom of the will. Nor does it matter more to the soul, or harm its freedom, to be reproduced with spiritual and heavenly thoughts than to be reproduced with natural thoughts. Of these, the one is ordinary conservation and concurrence, the other extraordinary, and so belongs to grace.

units.la: XI. Præpostere autem, ac contra operationum Dei ordinem ac dignitatem rem capiunt, qui non liberum arbitrium à gratia duci ac dirigi, sed gratiam à voluntate pro arbitrio regi, & motus ejus vel admitti, vel excludi, atque eam vel efficacem reddi, vel secus, autumant. Quod est homini ac voluntati creatæ primas dare, Deumque ac operationes ejus ipsi obnoxias facere: qui error, sive in naturali Dei concursu, sive in supernaturali gratia locum habeat, universi Pelagianismi & fundamentum, & compendium est.
units.tr: XI. Those who take the matter backwards, and contrary to the order and dignity of God's operations, hold that the grace is not led and directed by free will, but that grace is ruled by the will at its own pleasure, and that its motions are either admitted or excluded, and that grace is made effective or otherwise according to it. This gives primacy to man and to the created will, and makes God and his operations subject to it. This error, whether it has its place in God's natural concurrence or in his supernatural grace, is both the foundation and the summary of all Pelagianism.

units.la: XII. Habet autem se voluntas humana in primo supervenientis gratiæ momento mere passive, seque ei fingendam & formandam unicè præbet: in secundo autem momento, jam altius animata, deque cœlo impulsa, & ipsa porro agere incipit; dumque divinis motibus obsequitur, ulterius se promovet, & ad cœleste brabeon aspirat. Cum timore ac tremore vestram ipsorum salutem conficite: Deus enim is est, qui efficit in vobis & ipsum velle, & ipsum agere, pro gratuita sua benevolentia. Phil. 2: 12, 13. Quæ tamen momenta non de temporis partibus proprie (mens enim nostra, cum purus actus sit, semper ipsa agit, nec unquam deses est) sed de naturæ ordine accipienda sunt.
units.tr: XII. The human will, at the first moment of grace coming upon it, is wholly passive and offers itself only to be shaped and formed by it. But at the second moment, now more deeply quickened and moved from heaven, it itself begins to act; and as it yields to divine motions, it advances further and strives toward the heavenly prize [βραβεῖον]. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling: for it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his gracious goodwill. Phil. 2: 12, 13. These moments, however, are to be understood not as proper parts of time (since our mind, being pure act, always acts and is never idle), but as belonging to the order of nature.

units.la: XIII. Atque hac brevi divinæ gratiæ ἐκ̀ ϑέσεως præmissa, jam ejus corruptelæ examinandæ sunt. Quo in genere primas ducunt Judæi, insignes divinæ veritatis mangones. Inter quos Sadducei, nullum Dei auxilio locum dantes, omnia ϑεσαιρέσεις relinquebant. Pharisæi Deum in partem venire, hominemque in bono adjutare ferebant, verum ita, ut majorem operis laudem homini, & præcipuè fatali astrorum necessitati, adscriberent. Pharisæus stans in se ipse, hac precabatur: Deus, gratias tibi ago, quod non sum, ut reliqui homines, rapaces, injusti, adulteri, aut etiam ut hic publicanus Luc. 18: 11. conf. Joseph. de bello Jud. lib. 2. cap. 7. Ad quos propemodum accedunt Judæi hodierni, qui internam cordis innovationem, secretumque illud Spiritus opus non agnoscentes, ad externa solum opera gratiam divinam adhibent; quæ auxilio ejus non quidem inchoari, hoc enim ipsius hominis esse statuunt, sed perfici & absolvi. solvi, quin & oblatis occasionibus hominem ad ea incitari & animari volunt. Quæ exilia nimis sunt, nec Deo decora, ut vidimus.
units.tr: XIII. With this brief account of divine grace set down by way of preface [ἐκ θέσεως], we must now examine its corruptions. In this class the first place is taken by the Jews, notorious hucksters of divine truth. Among them the Sadducees, allowing no place for God's help, left all matters to the sects [θεσαιρέσεις]. The Pharisees maintained that God came in to share the work and helped man in what is good, but in such a way that they ascribed the greater praise of the work to man, and above all to the fated necessity of the stars. The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus within himself: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector Luke 18: 11; compare Josephus, Jewish War, book 2, chapter 7. The modern Jews come close to these, for they do not acknowledge the inward renewal of the heart or that secret work of the Spirit, and they attribute divine grace only to outward works. They hold that these are not begun by its help (for they say this belongs to man himself) but are perfected and completed by it. They even want man to be spurred and encouraged to these works when opportunities are offered. These views are too thin and do not become God, as we have seen.

units.la: XIV. Apud Christianos autem fermentum istud Judaicum novæ Ecclesiæ massam protinus corrupit. Non solum enim Philosophorum discipuli, dum fumidâ & incertâ face religionis abdita explorant, ex Scholarum suarum spatiis liberrimas opiniones in Ecclesiam induxerunt, ac turpi adulterio castitatem ejus violarunt: sed & contrario errore in adversum connisus est Manes: quo in certamine dum in alteram partem inclinat Ecclesia, vehementiusque τὸ ἀντεξούσιον prædicarent Patres, non parum sinceritas ejus libata est. Pelagius enim, insignis corruptæ naturæ adulator & præco, atque infitiandum Ecclesiæ nomen; dum Manichæismi odium præfert, in Sadducaismum incidit, latamque stragem dedit. Hæseruntque semper vulneris istius vestigia in Ecclesiæ corpore; ac identidem tractatum, & proterva manu irritatum, sæpius recruduit. Pelagianos enim secuti Semipelagiani, discipuli non admodum degeneres: & deinde inter Pontificios Scholastici; hodieque Jesuitæ; ac tandem Remonstrantes; qui, Pelagianæ hæreseos infamia territi, aliter venenum istud miscuerunt.
units.tr: XIV. Among Christians, however, this Jewish leaven at once corrupted the mass of the new Church. For not only did the disciples of the philosophers, while searching out the hidden things of religion by a smoky and uncertain light, bring the freest opinions into the Church from the precincts of their schools and violated her purity with shameful adultery; but Manes, with the opposite error, also strove against her. In this conflict, while the Church leaned to the other side, and the Fathers asserted τὸ ἀντεξούσιον [the power to resist] more vehemently, her sincerity was not a little impaired. For Pelagius, a notorious flatterer and herald of corrupted nature, who denied the very name of the Church, while he preferred to hate Manichaeism, fell into Sadducaism and caused wide ruin. The traces of that wound have always remained on the body of the Church, and, handled again and again and irritated by a headstrong hand, it has often broken out afresh. For the Semipelagians followed the Pelagians, not very degenerate disciples; then among the Papists the Scholastics; today the Jesuits; and finally the Remonstrants, who, frightened by the infamy of the Pelagian heresy, mixed this poison in a different way.

units.la: XV. Pelagius cum inter alios errores abnegatæ gratiæ crimine maximè infamis esset, quod sibi peculium, suamque præ reliquo mundo prærogativam, eripi Ecclesiæ ægre ferebat; non uno schemate errorem illum velavit. 1. enim naturæ integritate, atque absolutissima libertate confisus, nihil ultra requirebat; hominem esse ipsò beatum, sibique sufficientem prædicans; quem ingenitis sibi motibus dare leges sufficere volebat: 2. utque aliquo colore speciosò gratiæ nomine uti posset, legis ac externæ doctrinæ auxilium naturæ superaddidit; quo videl. homo facilius omnia præstaret 3. Cum ne sic quidem satisfaceret, alterum præterea gratiam agnovit, qua condonantur peccata, ac culpis suis anima exsolvitur; quam tamen non omnibus necessariam statuebat. 4. Adjecit porro, præter legem, Euangelii doctrinam, & promissa, & præcipuè Christi exemplum. 5. Tandem, ut cum Ecclesia sentire videretur, & internam Spiritus operationem agnovit; quæ intellectum illustraret, & stupentem voluntatem excitaret. Omnem autem voluntatis determinationem, veramque gratiæ vim & potentiam prorsus negabat; & quicquid vanis hisce nominibus ponebat gratiæ, non tamen absolute necessarium statuebat; sed solummodo ad facilius operandum, nec tam ad incipienda, quam ad perficienda virtutus. opera conducere arbitrabatur. Ac revera hæc nihil aliud erant quam recoctus Ethnicismus, aut ad summum Judaismus, & turpe naturæ gratiæque adulterium.
units.tr: XV. Pelagius, among his other errors, was most notorious for denying grace, because he resented that the Church was taking from him what he regarded as his own special privilege and his advantage over the rest of the world. He veiled that error under more than one guise. (1) Trusting in the integrity of nature and in an absolute freedom, he required nothing further, declaring that man was blessed in himself and sufficient for himself, and he wanted nature's own inborn motions to suffice as laws for him. (2) So that he might use the name of grace with some specious colour, he added to nature the help of the law and of external teaching, by which, of course, man would more easily perform everything. (3) Since not even this satisfied, he further acknowledged another grace, by which sins are forgiven and the soul is freed from its guilt; yet he did not declare this necessary for all. (4) Next he added, besides the law, the doctrine of the Gospel, its promises, and above all the example of Christ. (5) Finally, as if he seemed to agree with the Church, he acknowledged an inward operation of the Spirit, which would enlighten the understanding and stir the dazed will. But he flatly denied any determination of the will and any true force and power of grace; and whatever he set down under these empty names of grace, he did not hold to be absolutely necessary, but thought it useful only for working more easily, and for perfecting rather than beginning virtuous works. Indeed these things were nothing other than reheated heathenism, or at most Judaism, and a shameful adultery of nature and grace.

units.la: XVI. Pelagio successerunt Massilienses, Semipelagiani, qui, Pelagii errores cum Ecclesiæ dogmatibus miscere annisi, contra Pelagium naturæ labem ac vulnus, in Adamo acceptum; contra Augustinum autem, amorem gratiamque Dei universalem urgebant; partimque à natura, partim à gratia omnes ad salutem sufficienter instructos statuebant: gratiam autem aliquando hominis voluntatem prævenire, aliquando sequi & adjuvare dicebant. Quæ quam perplexa quamque labantia undiquaque sint facile perspicitur.
units.tr: XVI. Pelagius was succeeded by the Massilians and Semipelagians, who, trying to mix Pelagius's errors with the doctrines of the Church, on the one hand against Pelagius urged the taint and wound of nature received in Adam, but on the other hand against Augustine urged the universal love and grace of God. Partly from nature and partly from grace they held that all were sufficiently equipped for salvation. They said that grace sometimes goes before the human will and sometimes follows and helps it. How confused and wavering these views are on every side is easily seen.

units.la: XVII. Revixit insequentibus temporibus Pelagianismus in Joh. Erigena, Scoto, &c, oppugnante Godeschalco, repressus fuit. Semipelagianismus vero, utpote speciosior, à Scholasticis adoptatus est; quorum illud solemne est, facienti homini quod in se est non deesse gratiam; quanquam Deus pro misericordia sua etiam immerentibus eam sæpe largiatur, utroque hominem stupentem, & é pristino veterno naufcantem excitet, & ad se convertat.
units.tr: XVII. In later times Pelagianism revived in John Scotus Erigena and others, and though it was checked by Godeschalk's opposition, it was not fully suppressed. Semipelagianism, being the more specious, was adopted by the Scholastics, whose familiar teaching is this: that grace is not lacking to the man who does what is in him, although God, in his mercy, often bestows it even on the undeserving, so that by both means he rouses man, who is stupefied and nauseated by his old drowsiness, and turns him to himself.

units.la: XVIII. Omne autem Pelagii venenum hausit, iterumque Ecclesiæ propinare studuit Socinus: qui in libero arbitrio exornando totus est, ac universæ salutis auspicium inde desumit; gratiæ autem nomine non nisi Euangelii promissa, de peccatorum remissione & vita æterna, quæ legis sermoni jam antiquato successerint, intelligit; quibus fidem adhibere vel abrogare in unius hominis potestate sit.
units.tr: XVIII. Socinus drank the whole poison of Pelagius and tried again to pour it out for the Church. He is entirely engaged in adorning free will, and from it he takes the beginning of all salvation. By the name of grace he understands only the promises of the Gospel concerning the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, which have succeeded the now antiquated word of the law; and it lies within a man's power to give or withdraw faith in them.

units.la: XIX. Pontificii hodie per gratiam ferè intelligunt qualitatem spiritualem, à Deo animæ infusam, quæ mentem illuminet, & suasu atque hortatu suo voluntatem stupentem excitet; unde & prævenientem ac excitantem eam nonnunquam appellant: ita tamen ut in hominis arbitrio sit, gratia ac instinctu isto uti, vel secus; à cujus consensu omnem ejus vim atque efficaciam suspendunt. Imo auxilium illud ipsis adeo generale est, ut vix ulli, loco ac tempore suo, desit. Quod revera nihil aliud est, quam vires nostras Deum nostrum facere. Hab. 1: 11.
units.tr: XIX. The Papists today by grace mostly understand a spiritual quality infused into the soul by God, which enlightens the mind and, by its persuasion and exhortation, rouses the dazed will. For this reason they sometimes call it preventing and stirring grace. Yet it lies in man's choice whether to use this grace and this impulse or not, and they make all its force and efficacy depend on his consent. Indeed that help is so general for them that it is scarcely lacking to anyone at any place or time. In truth this is nothing other than making our own strength our god. Hab. 1: 11.

units.la: XX. Ac ejusdem prorsus generis cum Jesuitica est Remonstrantium gratia. Nam & communem eam faciunt, & expositam omnibus; inque hominis potestate ponunt eam accipere vel repudiare; omneque hominum discrimen non ab interna gratiæ vi, sed ab ipsis hominibus, rectove vel pravo gratiæ usu petunt. Contra Apostolum: Ergo igitur non volentis est, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Rom. 9: 16.
units.tr: XX. The Remonstrant grace is entirely of the same kind as the Jesuit. For they make it common and offered to all, and they place in man's power whether to accept it or reject it; and they seek the whole difference among men not from any inward force of grace but from the men themselves, from the right or wrong use of grace. Against the Apostle: So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Rom. 9: 16.

units.la: XXI. Nec insidiis caret trita ipsorum distinctio gratiae in sufficientem & efficacem; quarum illa omnibus, haec fidelibus tantum communicetur.Quanquam enim gratiam aliquam suo in genere sufficientem statuamus, ex. gr. quantum ad gratiam externam, sufficit Euangelii sermo, qui tamen ad salutem nec efficax nec sufficiens est: ac in primo homine, partimque etiam nunc in regenitis, gratiam aliquam habitualem, ad multa sufficientem, nec tamen actu ipso semper pollentem ac efficacem,agnoscamus:in homine tamen lapso, de quo hic quaestio est, discrimen illud gratiae non accipimus, nullamque ad conversionem gratiam sufficientem vocandam censemus, quae non eadem sit efficax. Sufficit tibi gratia mea. Potentia enim mea in debilitate perficitur. 2 Cor. 12:9.
units.tr: XXI. Nor is the well-worn distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious free from snares. Of these, the one is granted to all, the other to believers only. For although we also allow some grace to be sufficient in its own kind, for example as regards external grace, the sermon of the Gospel is sufficient, yet it is neither effective nor sufficient for salvation. And in the first man, and partly even now in the regenerate, we acknowledge a certain habitual grace, sufficient for many things, yet not always powerful and effective in the act itself. In fallen man, however, who is the subject here, we do not accept that distinction of grace, and we judge that no grace is to be called sufficient for conversion which is not also efficacious. My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. 2 Cor. 12: 9.

units.la: XXII. Nec suasio ipsorum moralis gratiae nomen meretur, cum omnis ejus efficacia metaphorica sit, virisque non conferat, sed suppo-nat, ac denique cunctis hominibus ex aequo communis sit. Quod enim inter Jesuitas Suarezius commento isti fulciendo adjecit,electos majorem accipere gratiam quam alios, quia illis ex singulari Dei benevolentia ea gratia confertur,quae,ex administrationis congruitate, infallibilis sit efficaciae; eo Remonstrantes ne quidem ascendunt, nec omnem moralis suasionis potentiam gratiae illi suae concedunt, infallibilem gratiam aeque horrentes ac irresistibilem.
units.tr: XXII. Nor does their moral persuasion deserve the name of grace, since all its efficacy is merely metaphorical. It does not confer strength on people but presupposes it, and it is finally common to all men alike. Suarez, among the Jesuits, added to prop up this invention the claim that the elect receive a greater grace than others, because God bestows on them, out of singular benevolence, a grace which by the fitness of its administration is infallible in its efficacy. The Remonstrants do not even rise to this. They do not concede to their grace the full power of moral persuasion, shrinking from infallible grace as much as from irresistible grace.

units.la: XXIII. Neque etiam sani coloris est gratia, quam appellant, congrua. Multiplex enim venenum illa vox habet. Non enim gratiam, sed ipsum potius hominem certis temporibus ad salutarem conversionem ponunt congruum, & gratiae efficaciam ab ejus unius assensu suspendunt. Tam autem incongruum est, captatis temporum momentis, hominem in peccatis mortuum, tempestivo vid191. & congruo suasu, ad vitam coelestem velle adducere; quam mortui hominis cineres & ossa musicae quadam ope, & accommodato cantu ad vitam ciere velle. Ut nulli fundamento Dei illa praescientia, qua gratiam illam perite ac congrue dispensat, innitatur. Solius autem gratiae est, hominem ad salutem aptum compo- situmque reddere: quae, ut liberrima est, ita indignissimis saepe adest, multosque extrorsum pulchros & speciosos, & a saeculi labe, ut videtur, remotos, praeterit.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor is what they call congruous grace of sound character either. That phrase carries a great deal of poison. For they do not make grace congruous, but rather the man himself, at certain times, fit for saving conversion, and they make the efficacy of grace depend on his assent alone. It is as incongruous to want to lead a man who is dead in sins to heavenly life by seizing the right moments and offering timely and fitting persuasion as it would be to want to call the ashes and bones of a dead man back to life by some musical art and a tune suited to the occasion. And God's foreknowledge, by which he skilfully and fittingly dispenses that grace, rests on no foundation of God's own. Only grace can make a man apt and fit for salvation. Grace is most free, and so it is often present with the most unworthy, and passes by many who are outwardly fine and handsome, and who, as it seems, are far removed from the stain of the age.

units.la: XXIV. Errant praeterea, cum Deum, quae sustinet mandatque, eadem in nobis operari posse negant, quod haec a sapienti monitore absint. Cum haec potius Novi Test. natura sit, Deum ipsum foederis, quas exigit, conditiones, praestare, ac hominibus ultro largiri: Quamobrem hoc est pactum, quod pacisc ar domus Israelis post dies illos, dicit Dominus, Indam leges meas menti eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam; & ero ipsis Deus, & ipsi mihi erunt populus &c. Hebr. 8: 10, 11. conf. Ezech. 11: 19, 20. Nec ideo frustraneae sunt admonitiones, cum Deus cum creatura rationali agat, atque illis tanquam instrumentis opus suum in ea peragat. Nullo modo enim absurdum est, operationem Dei in homine eodem tempore simul esse physicam & moralem; ut in Pauli vocatione patuit; quam certe omnem Deo, potentique ejus virtuti, acceptam debere ferri satis constat; quam tamen Deus non sine externo verbo ac hortatu explicuit. Conf. Esai. 50: 5. Dominus, Jehovah aperuit mihi aurem, & ego non extiti inobediens, non retrocessi. Joh. 6: 63. Verba, quae ego loquor vobis, Spiritus sunt & vita. Act. 16: 14 Quaedam mulier nomine Lydia, nos audivit; cujus Dominus adaperuit cor, ut attenderet iis, quae dicebantur a Paulo. Hebr. 4: 12. Vivus enim est sermo Dei, & efficax & penetrantior quovis gladio ancipiti &c.
units.tr: XXIV. They err further when they deny that God can work in us the very things that he commands and requires, on the ground that these are far from a wise counsellor. Yet it is rather the nature of the New Testament that God himself grants the conditions of the covenant which he demands, and freely bestows them on men: This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind, and write them on their heart; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people, etc. Heb. 8:10, 11; compare Ezek. 11:19, 20. Nor are exhortations therefore in vain, since God deals with a rational creature and carries out his work in it through them as instruments. For there is no absurdity in saying that God's operation in a man is at the same time both physical and moral, as was plain in the calling of Paul. That calling must certainly be ascribed wholly to God and his mighty power, as is quite clear, yet God did not bring it about without the outward word and exhortation. Compare Isa. 50:5: The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not disobedient, nor did I turn back. John 6:63: The words that I speak to you are spirit and life. Acts 16:14: A certain woman named Lydia heard us, whose heart the Lord opened, so that she attended to the things that were said by Paul. Heb. 4:12: For the word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, etc.

units.la: XXV. Majorem vero difficultatem movent circa habitus infusos, quos a Deo infundi, simulque sub praeceptum posse cadere, non capiunt. Unde habitus tales a Deo infusos saepe negant; verecundius Pontificiis ex veteris orthodoxiae reliquiis eos agnoscentibus. Fidem enim Dei in nobis opus esse Scriptura clare dicit; idemque de charitate, reliquisque Spiritus operibus clamitat. Charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spir. S. Rom. 5: 5. Quem Spir. S. effudit in nos copiose. Tit. 3: 6. Quos tamen habitus esse, animamque pio assectu induere, inque ea manere, & habitare, eadem Scriptura affirmat. Si ἔχητε πίστιν haberetis fidem. Matth. 17: 20. Quae fides inhabitavit in matre tua Eunice; persuasus vero sum quod & in te habitet. 2. Tim. 1: 5. Unctio, quam accepistis ab eo, in vobis manet, 1 Joh. 2: 27. Neque ideo minus sub praeceptum cadunt; non quidem quatenus Dei infundentis actus sunt, sed quatenus hominis officium circa illa locum habet. Ne negligas donum quod est in te. 1 Tim. 4: 14. Jesus dixit ipsis, habete fidem Dei. Marc. 11: 22. coll. Jac. 2: 1.
units.tr: XXV. They raise a greater difficulty concerning infused habits, which they do not understand as infused by God and yet also capable of falling under command. So they often deny that such habits are infused by God, though the Papists, out of remnants of old orthodoxy, acknowledge them more modestly. For Scripture plainly says that faith is God's work in us, and it cries out the same about love and the other works of the Spirit: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Rom. 5:5. Whom he poured out on us abundantly through the Holy Spirit. Titus 3:6. Yet the same Scripture affirms that these are habits, which clothe the soul with a godly disposition and remain and dwell in it: If you had faith [ἔχητε πίστιν], you would have faith. Matt. 17:20. The faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that it dwells in you also. 2 Tim. 1:5. The anointing that you received from him abides in you. 1 John 2:27. And these habits are no less subject to command, not indeed insofar as they are acts of God who infuses them, but insofar as the duty of man has its place in regard to them. Do not neglect the gift that is in you. 1 Tim. 4:14. Jesus said to them, Have faith in God. Mark 11:22; compare Jas. 2:1.

units.la: XXVI. Praecipua autem nobis cum iis lis est de salutaris gratiae operandi modo, an eare sistibilis atque humana vi superabilis sit? Cum enim magnificis verbis olim gratiam praedicarent, omniaque illi tribuere viderentur, ut de tertio articulo inter Ecclesias nostras ipsofque vix quaestio superesse videretur, mox quarto articulo, ubi de gratiae illius potentia, deque modo ejus operandi agitur, illa omnia nia quæ liberaliter adeo concesserant, rursus abstulerunt; & quam male in universum de gratia sentirent, ostenderunt. Ubi prima controversia aperienda, tum Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententia tuenda & confirmanda venit.
units.tr: XXVI. The chief dispute between us and them, however, concerns the manner of the saving grace's working: is it resistible, and can it be overcome by human power? For although they once praised grace in grand words, and seemed to ascribe everything to it, so that on the third article there seemed to be scarcely any question left between our Churches and themselves, soon, in the fourth article, where the power of that grace and the manner of its working are treated, they took back all that they had so generously conceded, and showed how badly they thought of grace in general. Here the first controversy must be laid open, and then the opinion of our Churches must be defended and confirmed.

units.la: XXVII. Disputatur autem de gratiæ operatione ac potentia, an realis, an tantum moralis sit? an præter externam Euangelii sermonem, Spirit u secretâ quoque potentia in ipsam mentem voluntatemque agat? & an intellectum & affectus solum, an vero ipsam quoque voluntatem attingat, jussisque suis obtemperare faciat, ut repugnare nec quidem velit, adeoque nec possit?
units.tr: XXVII. The dispute concerns the operation and power of grace: whether it is real or only moral; whether, besides the outward preaching of the Gospel, the Spirit also acts by a secret power upon the very mind and will; and whether he touches only the intellect and affections, or also the will itself, and makes it obey his commands so that it neither wants nor is able to resist.

units.la: XXVIII. Volebant autem Remonstrantes 1. mentem quidem à Dei Spiritu illustrari, & admisso lumine tenebras ejus vinci, ac vim istam insuperabilem esse. 2. affectus quoque sanari; & hoc quoque irresistibiliter. 3. voluntatem autem immediatè attingi nolebant: quod quomodo cohæreat certe concipi non potest. Voluntatem vero solum invitari & allici, nec quicquam Deum apud ipsam posse nisi suasu & hortatu docent; cui tamen pro liberrimo suo arbitrio resistere homo, Deique opus abrumpere possit. Ut in præcipuo articulo gratiæ operationem non nisi moralem statuant.
units.tr: XXVIII. The Remonstrants wanted, first, that the mind be indeed enlightened by the Spirit of God, and that, the light being admitted, its darkness be overcome, and that this power be irresistible. Second, that the affections also be healed, and this too irresistibly. Third, they would not have the will touched immediately; how this can hang together can certainly not be conceived. They teach that the will is only invited and attracted, and that God can do nothing with it except by persuasion and exhortation, and that man, by his most free choice, can still resist this and break off God's work. Thus in the chief point they hold that the operation of grace is only moral.

units.la: XXIX. Nos quod attinet, vocabuli invidiam primum amoliendam censemus, & irresistibilis gratia vocem, à Jesuitis primum ortam, & ad odium conflictam, incommodam arbitramur; quasi voluntati nostræ vis fieret, eaque invita expugnaretur. Quantum autem ad rem ipsam, hominem peccatis suis indormientem, sua natura contra gratiæ motus se obfirmare fatemur; nec facile adduci posse, ut domitas Deo manus porrigat, imo eo in statu non aliter quam motibus ejus resistere posse concedimus: Duri cervice, & incircumcisi corde & auribus, vos semper Spiritui S. obnitimini. Act. 7: 51. Nam sensus carnis inimicitia in Deum est. Legi enim Dei non subjicitur. Nam nec potest. Rom. 8: 7. Electos autem quod attinet, ubi Deo ex æterno, quo vincti erant, sopore eos excitare, magnumque illud conversionis opus moliri placet; tam potenti vi eos adoritur, tamque blandâ & penetrabili suada permulcet & trahit, ipsamque ipsorum animam intus affatur, & voluntatem fingit ac format, ut repugnare nec velint amplius, nec possint. Deus enim is est, qui efficit in vobis, & ipsum velle, & ipsum agere, pro gratuitâ sua benevolentiâ. Phil. 2: 13. Nam ejus voluntati quis resistit? Rom. 9: 19. Quoad particulares autem gratiæ motus, ubi Deus non æque potenter semper operatur; sæpe iidem à Spiritus disciplina recedunt, nec cunctis ejus suasibus obsequuntur; quamvis interim non in totum aberrent, tandemque acriore stimulo admoniti ad salutis semitam redeant. Rom. 7. per totum.
units.tr: XXIX. As for us, we think first that the odium attached to the word must be removed. We judge the phrase irresistible grace, first put forward by the Jesuits and aimed at stirring hatred, to be inappropriate, as though force were done to our will and it were overcome against its wishes. As to the thing itself, we confess that man, sunk in his sins, by his nature sets himself against the motions of grace, and we grant that he cannot easily be brought to stretch out his hands, tamed by God; indeed, in that state he can resist its motions and no other way. You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. Acts 7:51. For the mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Rom. 8:7. As for the elect, however, when it pleases God to rouse them from the sleep in which they were bound from eternity and to undertake that great work of conversion, he assails them with so powerful a force, and soothes and draws them with so gentle and penetrating a persuasion, that he speaks within their very soul, and fashions and forms their will, so that they no longer wish to resist, nor are able to. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure. Phil. 2:13. For who resists his will? Rom. 9:19. As for the particular motions of grace, where God does not always work with equal power, the same people often fall away from the discipline of the Spirit and do not obey all his persuasions; yet meanwhile they do not wander off entirely, and at last, admonished by a sharper goad, they return to the path of salvation. Rom. 7, throughout.

units.la: XXX. Atque adeo haec Ecclesiae doctrina est, hominem, utcunque primum renitentem ac reluctantem, quin & postea, ubi jam conversus est, persaepe lapsantem, nec semper Spiritui auscultantem; tamen in magno illo ac praecipuo Dei opere, ubi potentiam suam in convertendo eo experiri placet (de hac enim re proprie quaestio est) adeo Dei opus impedire non posse, ut tandem ultro consentiat, Deumque vocantem sequatur, ipsique in aeternum adhaereat.
units.tr: XXX. This, then, is the doctrine of the Church: that a man, however at first he resists and struggles against God, and even afterwards, when he has already been converted, often slips and does not always heed the Spirit, nevertheless in that great and principal work of God, in which God is pleased to show his power in converting him (for this is properly the question), cannot so hinder God's work that he does not at last willingly consent, follow God's call, and cleave to him for ever.

units.la: XXXI. Argumenta Orthodoxorum in hac causa olim haec erant: 1. Scripturam valde efficacibus verbis hoc in negotio uti, quae corrumpi, & in tenuem ac nullum tandem sensum vanescere non oporteat. Appellat enim conversionem nostram regenerationem & vivificationem: Nisi quis genitus fit iterum, non potest videre regnum Dei, Joh. 3:3. Etiam nos, quum in offensis mortui essemus, vivificavit una cum Christo. Eph. 2:5. ut non magis homo Deo convertenti resistere, ac potentiam ejus superare possit, quam infans in materno utero fingentis naturae manibus repugnare; aut mortui hominis cineres, ubi immisso spiritu animantur, illum non accipere, Deoque ad superas auras evocanti reniti possunt. Vae litiganti cum fictore suo! An dicturum est lutum fictori suo, quid facturus es? Vae illi, qui dicit patri, quid facturus esses? & foemina, quid paritura esses? Isc. 45: 9. Appellat & tractionem Patris, quam, ne quis leviter nimis accipiat, cum suscitatione ex mortuis, quae Filio adscribitur, ex aequo componit: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit illum; & ego suscitabo illum die ultimo. Joh. 6:44. Adeo enim potens illa tractio est, ut non solum absque ea nemo accedere, sed & nemo ei obluctari possit: Quicquid dat mihi Pater, ad me venet. vs. 37. Nec credendi solum potentiam, sed ipsum credere, ac credendi actum donum Dei esse dicit. Fides donum Dei est. Eph. 2:8. Quia vobis donatum est — credere in ipsum Christum, Phil. 1:29. Si forte det eis Deus resipiscentiam, ad cognitionem veritatis. 2 Tim. 2:25. Atque huc pertinet quoque, quod Deus ipsum velle & perficere in nobis operari, Phil. 2:13. & corda nostra ad exemplum Lydiae aperire dicitur, Act. 16:14.
units.tr: XXXI. The arguments of the Orthodox in this matter were formerly these: 1. Scripture uses very forceful words in this business, which ought not to be corrupted and evaporate into a thin or no meaning at all. For it calls our conversion "regeneration" and "making alive": "Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3). "Even when we were dead in our trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ" (Eph. 2:5).
