So a man can no more resist God converting him, or overcome his power, than an infant in the mother's womb can resist the hands of the Maker who forms it; or than the ashes of a dead man, when the breath is breathed into them and they are quickened, can refuse it or struggle against God calling them up into the upper air. "Woe to him who strives with his Maker! Does the clay say to the potter, 'What are you making?' Woe to him who says to his father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'What are you bringing forth?'" (Isa. 45:9). It also calls it a drawing by the Father, which, lest anyone take it too lightly, it puts on a level with the raising from the dead ascribed to the Son: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day" (John 6:44). For that drawing is so powerful that not only can no one come without it, but no one can struggle against it: "Whatever the Father gives me will come to me" (v. 37). And it says that not only the power to believe but believing itself, and the act of believing, is a gift of God: "Faith is the gift of God" (Eph. 2:8); "Because it has been granted to you to believe in him" (Christ) (Phil. 1:29); "If perhaps God may give them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim. 2:25). To this also belongs that God "works in us both to will and to do" (Phil. 2:13), and is said to "open our hearts" as he did Lydia's (Acts 16:14).

units.la: XXXII. 2. Quae omnia tam potentia ac tam eximia cum Scriptura in conversione hominis Deo adscribat, inde & sancti conversionem tum suam, tum aliorum a Deo precibus exposcunt, Reduc
units.tr: XXXII. 2. Since Scripture ascribes all these things, so powerful and so excellent, to God in the conversion of man, the saints also ask God in prayer for their own conversion and that of others: Convert

units.la: {y} qu.e confir- matur. duc me, & revertar. Jer. 31: 18. Quod autem petere à Deo sancti, monitore Spiritu, jubentur, id certe in ejus potestate positum esse fatendum est.
units.tr: me, and I shall be converted (which is confirmed by) Jer. 31:18. Now, that the saints are commanded by the prompting of the Spirit to ask this of God must certainly be acknowledged as lying within his power.

units.la: XXXIII. 3. Unde & Deus, istis Ecclesiæ suæ precibus annuens, sese populo suo cor carneum largiturum esse promittit. Et dabo ipsis cor unum, & spiritum novum dabo in medio ipsorum, & auferam cor lapideum ex carne ipsorum, & dabo ipsis cor carneum. Ezech. 11: 19. conf. cap. 36: 27. Et faciam, ut in statutis meis ambuletis. Cujus non antecedens, sed consequens conditio erat, quod amotis sordibus ac abominationibus suis in statutis Dei ambulaturi forent.
units.tr: XXXIII. 3. Hence also God, granting these prayers of his Church, promises to give his people a heart of flesh: And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them, and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh. Ezek. 11:19; compare chap. 36:27. And I will cause you to walk in my statutes. The condition of this was not antecedent but consequent: once they had put away their filth and abominations, they would walk in the statutes of God.

units.la: XXXIV. 4. Addebant præterea Orthodoxi, nisi magna illa in conversione potentia Deo adscribatur, illam omnem in hominem recidere: quod nefas; illiusque proprium opus esse, quod sese præ aliis, quibus eadem gratia affulget, convertat; atque adeo illum sese discernere, quod Paulus generali sententia negat: Quis enim te discernit? 1 Cor. 4: 7.
units.tr: XXXIV. 4. The Orthodox also added that, unless that great power in conversion is ascribed to God, the whole of it falls back on the man: which is wicked; and that it is his own work that he distinguishes himself from others to whom the same grace shines, and so he discerns himself—which Paul denies in general terms: "For who makes you to differ?" (1 Cor. 4:7).

units.la: XXXV. 5. Urgebant præterea, si tam tenuiter Dei potentiam capiamus, non validiorem eum fore in homine convertendo, quam diabolus est in eodem seducendo; qui suasu, blanditiis, omnique isto armorum genere hominis credulitatem quoque adoriri, & incautum in exitium deducere novit.
units.tr: XXXV. 5. They further urged that if we conceive God's power so feebly, he will be no stronger in converting a man than the devil is in seducing him; who knows how, by persuasion, flattery, and every kind of that armoury, to assail even a man's credulity and lead the unwary into ruin.

units.la: XXXVI. 6. Denique, ne in causa victrice argumenta cumulemus, nisi hæc divinæ gratiæ potentia agnoscatur, jam ipsa quoque Dei consilia, & gratiæ testamentum, ac fœdus Dei cum Christo, incerta ac labantia sunt. Hæc enim cum in tempore demum, in opere Dei erga hominem, sese explicent; nisi illud potenter peragatur, omnemque corruptæ naturæ vim vincat, jam reliqua omnia vana & inania sunt. Nec illæsus jam manet iste salutis humanæ ordo ac veluti cinnus, quem Apostolus diversis ex annulis conformat Rom. 8: 30. Quos vero prædestinavit, eos etiam vocavit: & quos vocavit, eos etiam justificavit: quos autem justificavit, eos etiam glorificavit. Et voluntati denique ejus ac æterno consilio resisti potest, contra Rom. 9: 19. Nam voluntati ejus quis resistit?
units.tr: XXXVI. 6. Finally, lest we pile up arguments in a cause already won: unless this power of divine grace is acknowledged, the very counsels of God, the testament of grace, and the covenant of God with Christ are uncertain and tottering. For since these unfold themselves only in time, in God's work towards man, unless that work is carried on powerfully and overcomes all the force of corrupt nature, then all the rest is vain and empty. Nor does that order of human salvation remain unharmed, as if it were a chain which the Apostle forms from various links (Rom. 8:30): "Whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified." And so, against Rom. 9:19, "For who resists his will?", his will and his eternal counsel could be resisted.

units.la: XXXVII. Ut autem Remonstrantium exceptiones, quas pro causa sua afferebant, prætereamus, Achilles eorum est locus Act. 7: 51. ubi resistitisse Judæi dicuntur Spiritui S. Quod tamen non de Spiritu intus operante, ac hominis conversionem moliente, de quo nunc quæstio est; sed de externo ejus ministerio intelligendum est, cui illi duræ ac rigidæ cervicis homines non aliter quam resistere poterant: Quem prophetarum non persecuti sunt patres vestri? & occiderunt praeuangelizantes de aduentu Iusti. vs. 52. Eademque aliorum locorum ratio est.
units.tr: XXXVII. But to pass over the exceptions of the Remonstrants, which they brought forward for their cause: their chief passage is Acts 7:51, where the Jews are said to have resisted the Holy Spirit. Yet this must not be understood of the Spirit working inwardly and striving to effect the conversion of a man, which is now the question; it must be understood of his external ministry, to which those stiff-necked and hard-hearted men could only resist: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One" (v. 52). The same explanation holds for the other passages.

units.la: XXXVIII. Sed & ratiunculis quibusdam diuinam hanc veritatem lacessunt; ac ex hypothesi hac neminem omnino converti posse, quam qui actu convertatur; atque illum, qui Deo vocanti obstrepit, revera voluntatem ejus adimplere, obiectant: sed & hominem semper dubium manere volunt, num serio ad salutem vocetur, an vero alio fine: denique, si tam potens sit gratia, ipsum ut truncum ac inutile lignum moveri ac fingi clamitant. Quae inania sunt. Nam & non alios, quam quos Deus ista luce dignatur, converti posse, sano sensu verum est. Ac qui vocanti ipsi resistunt, quanquam fati legem implent, tamen non extra culpam esse, alibi ostensum est. Nec habent quod de voluntate Dei dubitent qui rite officium faciunt. Denique cum homo rationis ac libertatis potens sit, non aliter Deus in ipso operatur, quam ut illaesas istas facultates conservet: nec hominem ut molem aliquam inertem versat, ac cunctis formis induit (hoc enim non magis ex actione Dei in voluntatem, quam in intellectum & affectus hominis, quam tamen ipsi concedunt sequitur) sed ut lapidem vivum in domum spiritualem aedificat, 1. Pet. 2: 5. ac ea ratione ipsum trahit, ut ipse lubens accurrat, & ad Deum festinet. Trahe me, post te curremus. Cant. 1: 4. XXXIX. Ut autem ad erroris hujus cubile perveniamus, ita instituere coguntur adversarii, quia Dei consilium de certorum hominum salute negant, cunctosque ex aequo a Christo redemtos ac salutaris gratiae si velint participes, pronunciant. Unde, ducente eodem errore, gratiae quoque Dei obstrepere, ejusque vires minuere debent, quo eam thesibus suis ancillari cogant, & vulgarem ac promiscuam reddant. Si enim irresistibilis illa sit, jam paucorum hominum eam futuram, definitoque isti Dei consilio subservituram vident. Quod abnuunt. XL. Anabaptistarum vero errores cum iidem prope sint, nisi quo horridius paulo ac magis incondite sensa sua effari, vel involvere soleant, attingere non opus est; cum ex dictis facile jugulentur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. But they also assail this divine truth with certain little arguments, and they object that on this hypothesis no one at all can be converted except the one who is actually converted; and that the one who resists God calling him in fact fulfils his will. They also want man to remain always in doubt whether he is called seriously to salvation or for some other end; and finally, if grace is so powerful, they cry out that man is moved and shaped like a log of dead wood. These things are empty. For it is true in a sound sense that only those whom God deigns to illumine with that light can be converted; and that those who resist the one calling them, although they fulfil the law of fate, are nonetheless not free from blame, as has been shown elsewhere. Nor have those who discharge their duty properly any reason to doubt the will of God. Finally, since man is endowed with reason and freedom, God works in him only in such a way as to preserve those faculties unharmed; nor does he handle man as some inert mass and clothe him with all forms (for this follows no more from God's action on the will than on the intellect and affections of man, which they nonetheless concede), but he builds him up as "a living stone into a spiritual house" (1 Pet. 2:5), and draws him in such a way that he himself gladly runs and hastens to God: "Draw me, and we will run after you" (Song 1:4). XXXIX. Now, to come to the lair of this error: the adversaries are compelled to hold this position because they deny that God has a counsel concerning the salvation of certain men, and they declare that all men alike have been redeemed by Christ and are, if they wish, partakers of saving grace. Hence, led by the same error, they must also cavil at the grace of God and diminish its powers, so that they force it to serve their theses and make it common and indiscriminate. For if it were irresistible, they see that it would belong to a few men only and would serve that determined counsel of God, which they deny. XL. As for the errors of the Anabaptists, since they are nearly the same, except that they are wont to express or wrap up their views a little more harshly and confusedly, there is no need to touch on them; for they can easily be refuted from what has been said.

units.la: CAPUT II. De Vocatione ad salutem.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. On the Calling to Salvation.

units.la: Primus gratiæ effectus est divina vocatio, qua è mundo hoc, in cujus semitis cum reliquo hominum vulgo oberrabamus, ad cœlestis vitæ spem evocamur; &, Christo deducente, post longum divortium ad Deum reducimur.
units.tr: The first effect of grace is the divine calling, by which we are summoned out of this world, in whose paths we wander with the rest of the common herd, to the hope of a heavenly life; and, with Christ leading the way, we are brought back to God after a long estrangement.

units.la: II. Et cum Christus unica ad salutem via, Joh.14:6. & janua sit, quæ ad caulas ducit, c. 10: 9. peccatorum ante omnia cum ipso adunari oportet. Manete in me, & ego in vobis, Joh. 15:4. Quæ unio non localis, sed spiritualis est, qualis etiam inter absentes locum habet; ac Christi Spiritu, & mutuo animi nostri affectu & fide peragitur. Et in hoc cognoscimus, quod maneat in nobis ex Spiritu quem nobis dedit. 1. Joh. 3:24. Ut habitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. Eph. 3:17. Prodigiosa enim sunt, quæ Weigeliani & Osiandristæ de quadam hominis Deificatione; & Pontificii ac Lutherani de orali corporis Christi manducatione adferunt.
units.tr: II. Since Christ is the only way to salvation (John 14:6) and the door that leads to the sheepfolds (John 10:9), sinners must above all be united with him. Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4). This union is not local but spiritual, of the kind that takes place even between those who are absent, and it is effected by the Spirit of Christ and by the mutual affection and faith of our soul. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us (1 John 3:24). That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith (Eph. 3:17). For the claims that the Weigelians and the Osiandrists make about a certain deification of man, and that the Papists and the Lutherans make about the oral manducation of Christ's body, are monstrous.

units.la: III. Intelligitur ergo hic vocatio non ad munus aliquod, sive in Ecclesia, sive in republ. qualis alibi ejus vocis significatio est: Et non sibi quis sumit hunc honorem, sed qui vocatur à Deo, ut & Aaron. Hebr. 5:4. Ecce, vocavi nomine Bezaleelem. Exod. 31:2. sed longè sublimior ac sanctior est; ac totius hominis è mundi fæce segregationem, & ad Deum adductionem significat. Quomodo Plato philosophiam suam augusto nimium nomine, reditum ad Deum appellabat.
units.tr: III. Here, then, the calling is understood not as an appointment to some office, either in the Church or in the commonwealth, which is the meaning the word has elsewhere: and no one takes this honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was (Heb. 5:4); behold, I have called Bezalel by name (Exod. 31:2). It is far higher and holier than that, and it signifies the separation of the whole man from the dregs of the world and his bringing to God. In this way Plato too called his philosophy, rather grandly, a return to God.

units.la: IV. Atque est hæc vocatio certo respectu; licet quantum ad vocem non usque adeo proprie, vel æterna, seu decreti sive testamenti, à quo omnis vocationis hujus efficacia; quo certi quidam hæredes designati sunt, è mundo olim evocandi. Ut promissionem accipiant vocati æterna hæreditatis. Hebr.9:15. Sine pænitentia enim sunt dona gratiæ, & vocatio Dei. Rom. 11:29. vel quæ in tempore peragitur; quæ æternæ vocationi subordinata est. Estque ea rursus vel externa, vel interna: quæ non est divisio generis in species, sed integri in partes ac membra sua.
units.tr: IV. This calling is made with a certain reference to a fixed purpose. Although, strictly speaking, the term is not so properly applied to it, it is either eternal, belonging to the decree or the testament, from which all the efficacy of this calling comes, by which certain designated heirs were once to be called out of the world; that those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance (Heb. 9:15); for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Rom. 11:29). Or it is carried out in time, and this is subordinate to the eternal calling. This temporal calling is in turn either external or internal. This is not a division of a genus into species, but of a whole into its parts and members.

units.la: V. Vocatio externa nihil aliud est, quam externa peccatoris compellatio, & ad salutem capessendam invitatio. Quae cum per sese nondum salutaris, ac reprobis quoque communis sit, multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi, Matth. 20: 16. & 22: 14. distinguenda est ab illa vocatione, quae ex testamento ac κατα πρόθεσιν fit, quae nunquam inanis & absque fructu esse potest, ac interna potissimum gratia absolvitur. Unde Apostolus tales κατα πρόθεσιν κλητοὺς appellat, secundum propositum vocatos. Rom. 8: 28.
units.tr: V. The external calling is nothing other than the outward address to the sinner and the invitation to lay hold of salvation. Since this, in itself, is not yet saving, and is common even to the reprobate (for many are called, but few are chosen, Matt. 20:16; 22:14), it must be distinguished from that calling which proceeds from the testament and according to purpose [κατὰ πρόθεσιν], which can never be empty or without fruit, and which is accomplished chiefly by the internal grace. Hence the Apostle calls such people called according to purpose [κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοὺς] (Rom. 8:28).

units.la: VI. Quanquam neque externa salutis oblatio omni interna efficacia destituatur. Solet enim Deus saepe internae lucis radios etiam in reprobos spargere, ac tanto eos lumine perfundere, ut Deum de propinquo videant, Euangelii decora admirentur, ac rerum coelestium dulcedinem gustent: quae tamen, dum brevi tantum vitu ac gustu transmittunt gaudia solida ac aeterna non sunt, & inter mortalium bonorum blanditias, ad quarum memoriam subinde redeunt, cito expirare solent. Qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustaverintque donum illud coeleste, & participes facti fuerint Spir. S. gustaverintque bonum Dei verbum, ac virtutes futuri saeculi; si prolabantur &c. Hebr. 6: 4, 5, 6.
units.tr: VI. Yet the external offer of salvation is not wholly destitute of all inward efficacy. For God often pours rays of inward light even upon the reprobate, and floods them with such light that they see God from close at hand, admire the beauty of the gospel, and taste the sweetness of heavenly things. Yet while these delights are passed on only in a brief sight and taste, and are not solid and eternal, they usually fade quickly amid the flatteries of mortal goods, to whose memory they return from time to time. For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they then fall away (Heb. 6:4, 5, 6).

units.la: VII. Fit autem haec vocatio per Euangelii sermonem: Placuit Deo per stultitiam praedicationis salvare credentes, 1. Cor. 1: 21. sive per externum auditum: Fides ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei, Rom. 10: 17. Male autem Enthusiastae verbum non scriptum, & internos Spiritus sermones praeterea jactant. Cum Spiritus nihil cordi inscribat, nisi quod in sacris Scripturis jam antea exaraverit. Spiritus ille veritatis ducet vos in omnem veritatem, Joh. 16: 13. Quanquam non negamus eum immediate, absque externo sermone, hominem affari posse, atque isto pacto, ut videtur, nonnullos aliquando convertisse. Verum haec extraordinaria ejus opera ordinariam vocationem non tollunt.
units.tr: VII. This calling, moreover, takes place through the word of the gospel: it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (1 Cor. 1:21); or through outward hearing: faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God (Rom. 10:17). The Enthusiasts, however, wrongly boast of an unwritten word and of inward speeches of the Spirit besides. For the Spirit writes nothing on the heart except what he has already inscribed in the holy Scriptures: that Spirit of truth will lead you into all truth (John 16:13). Yet we do not deny that he can address a man immediately, without outward speech, and that in this way, as it seems, he has sometimes converted some people. But these extraordinary works of his do not abolish the ordinary calling.

units.la: VIII. Proprie autem externa haec vocatio ad electos pertinet: cum gratiae divinae effectus; & mortis Christi beneficium; ac deniique in sese testamentaria, & aeterni Dei testamenti ac foederis executio sit: quae certe promiscua & reprobis communia non sunt. Unde κατα πρόθεσιν eam fieri Apostolus dixit, Rom. 8. Quare ad alios pertinere non potest, nisi qui testamento illo scripti sunt heredes. Semperque efficax & salutaris est, nec magis frustra esse potest quam ipsum testamentum ac foedus Dei. Eitque ejus generis haec vocatio, ac illa qua Deus vocat ea quae non sunt, tanquam sint, Rom. 4: 17. quaque Abrahami posteritatem vocavit; cum ipse exextremâ ætate improlis, acuxor ejus effœta, & naturæ lege infœcunda foret; juxta illud quod dictum erat, in Isaaco vocabitur semen tuum. Gen. 21: 12.
units.tr: VIII. Properly speaking, however, this external calling pertains to the elect, since it is an effect of divine grace and a benefit of Christ's death, and finally is in itself the execution of the testamentary and eternal covenant of God. Certainly this is not something promiscuous and common to the reprobate. Hence the Apostle said that it takes place according to purpose [κατὰ πρόθεσιν] (Rom. 8). Therefore it cannot pertain to others, except to those who are written down as heirs in that testament. And it is always effective and saving, and can no more be in vain than the testament and covenant of God itself. This calling is of the same kind as that by which God calls those things which are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17), and by which he called the posterity of Abraham, when Abraham was childless from extreme old age and his wife was barren and, by the law of nature, unfruitful; in accordance with what had been said, in Isaac shall your seed be called (Gen. 21:12).

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: IX. Quod vero Euangelii sermo etiam ad reprobos fiat, ea quidem non est vocatio κατὰ πρόθεσιν Dei; cum ad gratiæ testamentum non pertineant. Nec adeo Dei ista appellatio & vocatio est, quam hominum; qui Euangelica legatione fungentes, nec eos, qui in testamento Dei scripti sunt, ab aliis dignoscere valentes, ad cunctos homines de salute ista verba faciunt. Estque hoc revera non contemnendum beneficium, quod universus mundus ex Christi adventu, atque ex Euangelio ejus accepit; quod, occasione electorum, omnes verbum salutis audiant; omnes ad curam ejus invitentur; ac veras de Deo, de regimine ejus, de mundi conditu ac fine, deque summo hominis bono, aliisque rebus gravissimis, sententias audiant; multique, cum non salutariter ad amorem Dei & sæculi contemtum imbuantur, saltem multas sordes exuant, & ad externam aliquam honestatem virtutesque civiles formentur; ut humanum genus sibi ipsi jam placere, ac pretiosum esse possit. Qua ratione divina hæc Christi philosophia plus mundo profuit, quam cunctæ veterum sapientum sectæ: cum nulla adeo universum mundum pervagata, tantum ei cultum ac decus addiderit. Ubicunque enim religio Christiana pervasit, paulatim barbariem exui, & reliquum quoque humanæ vitæ cultum accedere vidimus.
units.tr: IX. That the word of the Gospel is also preached to the reprobate is not a calling according to God's purpose [κατὰ πρόθεσιν], since they do not belong to the covenant of grace. Nor is this address God's so much as men's: those who discharge the Gospel embassy, and cannot distinguish those written in God's covenant from others, address this salvation to all men. And this is truly no small benefit, which the whole world has received from the coming of Christ and from his Gospel: that, for the sake of the elect, everyone hears the word of salvation, everyone is invited to care for it, and everyone hears true teaching about God, his government, the made and the end of the world, the highest good of man, and other most weighty matters. Many, though not savingly imbued with love of God and contempt of the world, at least cast off much filth and are formed to some outward decency and civic virtues, so that the human race can now take pleasure in itself and be esteemed. For this reason this divine philosophy of Christ has benefited the world more than all the sects of the ancient sages, since none of them, wandering over the whole world, has added such cultivation and grace to it. Wherever the Christian religion has spread, we have seen barbarism gradually cast off and the rest of the refinement of human life follow.

units.la: X. Ut satis pateat, non frustra, nec sine omni Dei consilio, ad reprobos salutis sermonem fieri; quanquam non ex testamento Dei, nec cum collatione salutis vocari eos videamus. Neque ideo vocatio eorum, quod objiciunt adversarii, hypocritica statuenda est. Nam & ab hominibus proprie, quanquam peculiariter dispensante, ac lucis istius tempora nunc his nunc illis mundi partibus distribuente Deo, ea peragitur. Ac mittunt illi quidem Euangelii sagenam magnum in mare, cunctique generis piscibus implent, sed ita, ut ad littus illi tandem explorandi veniant. Unde hypocriseos argui non possunt, cum pro muneræ omnibus officium facere suadent, ac obedientibus cœlestè præmium pollicentur; quæ & vera, & certa, & seria sunt.
units.tr: X. So that it may be plain that the word of salvation is addressed to the reprobate not in vain, nor without any counsel of God, although we see them called not from God's covenant nor with the offer of salvation: their calling is not therefore to be judged hypocritical, as our opponents object. For it is carried out through men, though God dispenses it in a particular way, distributing the times of this light now to these, now to those parts of the world. They indeed cast the great net of the Gospel into the sea and fill it with fish of every kind, but so that they may finally come to the shore to examine them. Hence they cannot be charged with hypocrisy, since they urge everyone to perform the duty of his office and promise a heavenly reward to the obedient; and these things are true, certain and serious.

units.la: XI. Non tamen hæc vocatio, quanquam communis sit sub N. T. atque absque illo populorum discrimine, quod olim obtinuit, cum hic non sit Græcus & Judæus, circumcisio & præputium, Barba- rus & Scytha, servus & liber, sed omnia & in omnibus Christus, Col. 3.11. 3:11. ideo & universalis est. Habet enim Dei gratia sua, & præsti-tuta tempora, 1. Tim. 2:6. & certa mensura & linea currit, ac diversis mundi partibus affulget: Sed secundum mensuram canonis, quam mensuram distribuit nobis Deus, ut veniamus etiam usque ad vos. 2:Cor. 10. 13. Sivit Deus omnes gentes ire viis suis. Act. 14:16. Atque alii populi prima, alii tertia hora, alii serius vocantur. Matth. 20.
units.tr: XI. Yet this calling, although it is common under the New Testament and without that distinction of peoples which once prevailed, where "there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all" (Col. 3:11), is therefore also universal. For God's grace has its own appointed times (1 Tim. 2:6), and a certain measure and line runs out and shines upon the different parts of the world: "But according to the measure of the rule which God has distributed to us, to reach even as far as you" (2 Cor. 10:13). "He allowed all nations to walk in their own ways" (Acts 14:16). Some peoples are called at the first hour, others at the third, others later (Matt. 20).

units.la: XII. Per naturæ vocem enim quosdam salutariter, quanquam remotius, vocari, atque ista via ad Deum ire Euangelii abnegatio est. Neque communis Christo cum omnibus hominibus natura gratiam quoque ejus communem ac promiscuam facit: nam præter illam naturæ cognationem propius cum ipso vinculum necessarium est, fidei videl. ac Spiritus. Neque etiam gratiæ hujus universalitatem mundi infidelitas & incredulitas, quæ in Scripturis sæpe adeo accusatur, coarguit, quasi ea acceptam cunctisque obviam Euangelii lucem præsupponeret; juxta illud, qui vero non credit, jam condemnatus est, Joh. 3:18. nam incredulitas hæc in plerisque negativa est, nec ullam gratiæ lucem infert, unde damnationis causa est sine qua non; aliter ac incredulitas privativa, quæ verbum Euangelii jam auditum, & protervè rejectum innuit.
units.tr: XII. For to say that some are called to salvation through the voice of nature, though more remotely, and that going to God by this road is a denial of the Gospel. Nor does the nature that Christ shares with all men make his grace common and indiscriminate too. For beyond that kinship of nature, a closer bond with him is necessary, namely of faith and of the Spirit. Nor does the unbelief and incredulity of the world, which the Scriptures so often condemn, prove the universality of this grace, as if it presupposed that the light of the Gospel had been received and was offered to all; according to that word, "he who does not believe is already condemned" (John 3:18). For this unbelief is in most cases negative, and brings in no light of grace; hence it is a cause of damnation only as a sine qua non. It is unlike privative unbelief, which implies that the word of the Gospel has already been heard and stubbornly rejected.

units.la: XIII. Sequitur vocatio interna, quæ altera & præcipua divinæ vocationis pars est, qua ad externum Euangelii sonum interior Spiritus vox & efficacia accedit, de qua 1 Cor. 1:26. Videtis vocationem vestram, quod non multi sapientes, secundum carnem. Apoc. 17:4. Vocati, electi, fideles. Joh. 6:46. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Quæ electorum ita propria est, ut nulla ex parte reprobis contingat. Est enim vocatio non hominis, sed Dei, cujus vocatio fustra esse nunquam potest; eaque facta juxta πρόθεσιν, Rom. 8:28. & ex æterno illo testamento, quo certos quosdam homines æternæ felicitatis hæredes scripsit. Quod decretum ac testamentum invalidum esse non potest.
units.tr: XIII. There follows the internal calling, which is the second and principal part of the divine calling, by which the inner voice and efficacy of the Spirit come to the external sound of the Gospel. Of this, 1 Cor. 1:26: "See your calling, that not many are wise according to the flesh." Apoc. 17:4: "Called, chosen, faithful." John 6:46: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." This calling is so proper to the elect that it never falls to the reprobate in any part. For it is the calling not of man but of God, whose calling can never be in vain; and it is made according to purpose (Rom. 8:28), and from that eternal covenant by which he named certain men heirs of eternal happiness. This decree and covenant cannot be invalid.

units.la: XIV. Unde vocatio hæc semper efficax est, & cum potentia peragitur; sicut vocare Dei per emphasin idem in Scriptura est quod actu creare & producere. vide Rom. 4:17. Qui vocat illa quæ non sunt tanquam sint. Psal. 33:9. Nam ipso dicente, est, ipse præcipiente, existit. Psal. 105:16. Quum advocans famem super terram, omnem scipinem panis fregit. Matth. 8:8. Solum modo loquere, & sanabitur puer meus. 1 Cor. 15:10. 1. Pet. 2:9. Unde vocatio hæc adscribitur verbo illi Jehovæ, quod stat in seculum, Esai. 40:8. cui regenerationem nostram, ut seminicuidam, assignat Petrus 1. Epist. c. 1:23,24,25.
units.tr: XIV. Hence this calling is always effective and is carried out with power; just as God's "calling," by emphasis, is in Scripture the same as actually creating and bringing into being. See Rom. 4:17: "who calls things that are not as though they were." Ps. 33:9: "For he spoke and it was; he commanded and it stood." Ps. 105:16: "When he called for famine upon the land, he broke every staff of bread." Matt. 8:8: "Only speak the word, and my servant will be healed." 1 Cor. 15:10; 1 Pet. 2:9. Hence this calling is ascribed to that word of Jehovah which "stands for ever" (Isa. 40:8), to which Peter assigns our regeneration as to an incorruptible seed (1 Pet. 1:23-25).

units.la: XV. Quæ ritum filii nobis donatur: ut qui vocationem hanc sentiunt, eo ipsò Spiritus signaculum ac notam in sese deprehendant, quo laetari, superque reliquos mortales in Deo gloriari possunt. Qui nos obsignavit, & dedit arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris. 2 Cor. 1: 22. Non enim ab homine vocationis hujus effectus dependet, quasi in ejus potestate foret illam prae aliis sequi. Occurrit enim mox Apostolus: Quis enim te ab aliis discernit? quid habes quod non acceperis? 1 Cor. 4: 7. Non est ejus, qui vult, neque ejus qui currit, sed ejus, qui miseretur, Dei. Rom. 9: 16. conf. Matth 24: 40. Tunc erunt duo in agro, unus accipietur, & alter relinquetur.
units.tr: XV. This calling is given to us as a token of sonship, so that those who feel it may thereby discern in themselves the seal and mark of the Spirit, by which they can rejoice and glory in God above the rest of mortals. "Who sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts" (2 Cor. 1:22). For the effect of this calling does not depend on man, as if it were in his power to follow it before others. The Apostle immediately meets this: "For who makes you to differ from others? What have you that you did not receive?" (1 Cor. 4:7). "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Rom. 9:16). Compare Matt. 24:40: "Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left."

units.la: XVI. Fit in hac vocatione receptio Christi, sicut in priori ejus parte oblatio locum habebat: quae & conversio, & regeneratio, aliisque vocabulis appellatur.
units.tr: XVI. In this calling there takes place the reception of Christ, just as in the former part the offering had its place. It is also called conversion, regeneration, and by other names.

units.la: XVII. Ad initium autem & primum ejus momentum habet sese homo tantum passive, ac aeternae lucis splendorem solum recipit: Quoniam Deus, qui dixit ut e tenebris lux splendescceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris, ad praebendum lucem notitiae gloriae Dei in facie Jesu Christi. 2. Cor. 4: 6. qua perfusus mox vocanti Deo parere, novamque illam vitam explicare, & in luce illa ambulare incipit. Quae tamen, ut superius quoque visum, non tam temporis, quam naturae momenta sunt, atque istum in modum distinguenda veniunt.
units.tr: XVII. At the beginning, however, and at its first moment, man has himself only passively and receives only the splendour of the eternal light: "For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, is he who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). Bathed in this light, he then begins to obey the calling God, to unfold that new life, and to walk in that light. These, however, as was seen above too, are not so much moments of time as of nature, and they are to be distinguished in this manner.

units.la: XVIII. Per gradus autem Deus in hoc opere procedit: variisque actibus illud tandem absolvit. Ac primo agnitionem miseriae, ejusque sensum & dolorem, ac de se ipso desperationem operatur; qui actus ejus praecedanei sunt; quos sequuntur suaviores Spiritus operationes, fides, dolor verecundo pudore mistus, qualis ex amore oriri solet, ac tandem resipiscentia & ad Deum cum fiducia reditus, quales filiorum effectus sunt.
units.tr: XVIII. God proceeds in this work by degrees, and at length completes it through various acts. First he works in him the knowledge of his misery, with its sense and grief, and despair of himself; these acts go before. They are followed by gentler operations of the Spirit: faith, sorrow mixed with reverent shame, such as usually arises from love, and at last repentance and a return to God with trust, which are the effects of sons.

units.la: XIX. Nullum autem hic locum habent dispositiones hominis praevia, quibus ille sese Deo commendare, ulterioremque gratiam ex merito aliquo sperare possit. Ita enim liberi arbitrii patroni homines, si naturalibus recte utatur, divinae vocationi congruum ponunt; unde & meritum de congruo appellant. Quod Arminius emollire nitens, ad rectum primae gratiae usum, quando homo per eam facit quodcunque in se est, uberiorem ipsi gratiam obtingere docuit. Qui dolus est, cum prima ista gratia revera a natura non differat. Atque ejusdem notae sunt quae ejus assecla statuunt, hominem adhuc irregenitum ex miseriae suae conscientia ad Christum posse con-
units.tr: XIX. Here, however, there is no place for any preparatory dispositions of man, by which he might commend himself to God and hope for further grace from some merit. For the defenders of free will hold that man, if he uses his natural powers rightly, makes himself congruous to the divine calling; whence they also call it merit of congruity. Arminius, striving to soften this, taught that a fuller grace is obtained by the right use of the first grace, when man by it does whatever is in him. This is a trick, since that first grace really does not differ from nature. Of the same mark are the things his followers hold: that unregenerate man, from consciousness of his misery, can come to Christ,

units.la: Pars II. confugere; atque istam miseriæ agnitionem, & prioris vitæ poe-nitentiam ac tædium, atque ardens liberationis desiderium, que ejus generis opera, regenerationem ac Sp. Sancti adventum præcedere; nec quenquam facile Spir. Dei accipere,. aut fidei lumine perfundi, nisi qui prius naturali quadam probitate ac cordis simplicitate Deo sese dignum effinxerit; atque alia similia partim ex Jesuitarum, partim ex impura Socini schola hausta.
units.tr: Part II. flee to Christ; and that recognition of their wretchedness, the repentance and weariness of their former life, and the burning desire for deliverance, which are works of this kind, precede regeneration and the coming of the Holy Spirit. They say that no one readily receives the Spirit of God, or is filled with the light of faith, unless he has first, by a certain natural uprightness and simplicity of heart, made himself worthy of God; and they hold other similar things, drawn partly from the Jesuits and partly from the impure school of Socinus.

units.la: XX. Quæ commenta divinæ voluntatis de hominum salute consilium, & præcipuam gratiæ potentiam e fundamento evertunt, atque experientiæ denique repugnant. 1. Omne enim hominum discrimen à divina prædestinatione, sive gratiæ consilio est. Dominus vero addebat quotidie Ecclesiam, qui salvarentur. Act. 2:47. Et crediderunt quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. c. 13:48. Quos vero prædestinavit eos etiam vocavit &c. Rom. 8:30. Unde nemo sese ipsum discernere potest. 1. Cor. 4:7. 2. Si quid autem in aliquo verè boni est, id omne divinæ prædestinationi ac gratiæ acceptum ferendum est; sine qua ne quidem de miseriis suis peccator gemere, atque ad Christum anhelare potest. Quod & de præparationibus quibusdam accidentalibus, gradibusque ad conversionem remotioribus intelligendum est, quibus Deum sæpe uti videmus. 3. Quanquam, quo manifestius divinæ gratiæ in hoc opere potentia appareat, sæpenumero eos, qui reliquis mortalibus perversiores habebantur, derepente, ac sine longiori molimine, motibusque præambulis, ad Christum conversos legimus, aliis, qui ad probitatem magis facti videbantur, præteritis, ac æternum valere jussis. conf. Act. 9:1. & 5:34.
units.tr: XX. These inventions overthrow from the foundation the counsel of God concerning the salvation of men and the chief power of grace, and in the end they contradict experience. (1) For every difference among men comes from divine predestination, or from the counsel of grace. "And the Lord added to the Church daily those who were being saved" (Acts 2:47). "And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed" (Acts 13:48). "Whom he predestined, them he also called," etc. (Rom. 8:30). Hence no one can distinguish himself (1 Cor. 4:7). (2) If anything truly good is found in anyone, all of it must be credited to divine predestination and grace; without it a sinner cannot even groan over his miseries or long for Christ. This must also be understood of certain accidental preparations and steps more remote from conversion, through which we often see God working. (3) Yet, so that the power of divine grace in this work may appear more clearly, we often read that those who were thought more perverse than other mortals were suddenly converted to Christ, without a long struggle or preliminary movements, while others who seemed more inclined to uprightness were passed over and bidden farewell forever (cf. Acts 9:1 and 5:34).

units.la: XXI. Ad objectamenta adversariorum respondemus: male atque extra scopum urgeri illud Christi, ex parabola Euangelica, habenti dabitur. Matth. 25. cum ibi de regenitis ac credentibus agatur, qui dona à Deo accepta bene collocare monentur, ut recto usu ea augeant. Non simul enim omnia electis dantur, sed per numeros gradusque suos à Deo illa dispensantur. Scriba autem ille, qui non longe à regno cælorum fuisse dicitur, Marc. 12:34. non benignioris naturæ ope præ reliquis ad illud aptus erat; sed, cum tam sapienter de vera justitia, deque sacrificiorum natura respondisset, à Messiæ agnitione non procul abesse videbatur. De qua rerum divinarum cognitione, quæ & ipsa non sine Dei gratia in ipso erat, non autem de internis ejus dispositionibus ibi agitur. Ac perversè imprimis Cornelius Act. 10. inter nondum conversos ponitur. Quanquam enim in Messiæ persona hæreret, & Jesum adhuc ignoraret, tamen salutem ejus ardenter desiderasse, atque inter eos qui regnum Dei, ac consolationem Israëlis, expectabant, quales tum plures erant inter Judæos, fuisse, ex tota ejus historia patet.
units.tr: XXI. We answer the objections of our opponents. That saying of Christ from the Gospel parable, "To him who has, more will be given" (Matt. 25), is wrongly and beside the point urged against us, since there it is a question of the regenerate and believers, who are warned to put to good use the gifts received from God, so that by right use they may increase them. For not all things are given to the elect at once; God dispenses them by their proper measures and degrees. That scribe, however, who is said not to be far from the kingdom of heaven (Mark 12:34), was not better suited to it than others by the help of a kinder nature; rather, since he had answered so wisely about true righteousness and the nature of sacrifices, he seemed not far from the recognition of the Messiah. The passage speaks of his knowledge of divine things, which was also in him not without the grace of God, and not of his inner dispositions. And Cornelius (Acts 10) is wrongly placed among those not yet converted. For that he was caught up in the idea of the Messiah and did not yet know Jesus, yet ardently desired salvation and was among those who awaited the kingdom of God and the consolation of Israel (as many Jews then were), is clear from his whole history.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De Regeneratione.
units.tr: On Regeneration.

units.la: I. Ocationis primus, ut diximus, effectus est regeneratio, quæ primum vitæ spiritualis gradum dicit, uti sanctificatio ejus progressum. Appellatur παλιγγενεσία Tit. 3: 5. quasi secundam generationem dicas. Prima enim origine homo corruptus exit, nec sancti quicquam possidet; unde incudi veluti reddi, atque Dei plastis manu refingi eum oportet, ut Deo dignus evadat. Quæ veteris novique hominis vocabulis Apostolus adumbrat; sicut & interioris ac exterioris hominis appellatio eo à plurimis Theologis (contradicentibus tamen rectius aliis) referri solet: quia vetus homo corporis ac membrorum servitio magis utitur, eaque veluti arma sua movet; interior vero pectoris sacrario sedet, atque inde in universum corpus sese exerit. Quamvis exterior noster homo corrumpatur, tamen interior indies renovatur. 2. Cor. 4: 16. Ergo igitur ipse ego mente quidem servio legi Dei, carne vero legi peccati, Rom. 7: 25. Condelector enim legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem, vs. 22. Sed occultus homo cordis &c. 1 Pet. 3:4.
units.tr: I. As we have said, regeneration is the first effect of the call, and it marks the first stage of spiritual life, just as sanctification marks its progress. It is called palingenesis [παλιγγενεσία] in Titus 3:5, as if you were to say a second generation. For man comes into being corrupt and possesses nothing holy, so he must be reshaped like metal on an anvil and refashioned by the hand of God the potter, so that he becomes worthy of God. The Apostle portrays this under the names of the old man and the new. The distinction between the inner and the outer man is also commonly referred to this by many theologians (though others rightly disagree): the old man makes more use of the body and its members, and moves them as his weapons; the inner man sits in the sanctuary of the breast and from there extends himself through the whole body. Though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day, 2 Cor. 4:16. So then I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin, Rom. 7:25. For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, v. 22. But the hidden man of the heart etc., 1 Pet. 3:4.

units.la: II. Ut male Socinus eam in antecedæ vitæ mutatione, atque ad Christi legem conformatione ponat. Quia videl. naturæ corruptionem ignorat. Unde & adultis solum illam competere existimat. Contra Scripturæ auctoritatem, quæ, prout naturæ nostræ scaturiginem vitiatam, ac fontem ipsum insincerum esse docet; ita universum hominem, mentem, voluntatem, affectus, corpus ac membra denique omnia regenerari debere docet; nec adultos solum, sed ipsos quoque infantes beneficii illius participes facit. Vide 1 Thess. 5: 23. Ipse vero Deus pacis sanctificet vos ὁλοτελεῖς integros. Eph. 4: 23. Renovari autem spiritu mentis vestræ. Gen. 8: 21. Eo quod figmentum cordis hominis sit malum à pueritia ipsius. Rom. 7: 14. Scimus enim legem esse spiritualem: at ego carnalis sum, venditus ut subjicerer peccato. Rom. 6: 12. Ne regnato igitur peccatum in mortali vefro corpore. & 19. Sicut sistitis membra vestra serva impuritati, & iniquitati, ad patrandam iniquitatem, ita nunc sistite membra vestra serva justitiæ ad sanctimoniam. Luc. 1: 15. Et Spiritu S. implebitur etiam à ventre matris suæ. & vs. 80. Ipse autem puerulus crescebat, & corroborabatur Spiritu&c.
units.tr: II. Socinus wrongly places it in a change of former life and a conforming of oneself to the law of Christ. This is because he does not know the corruption of nature, and so he thinks it belongs only to adults. This is against the authority of Scripture, which teaches that the source of our nature is tainted and the fountain itself unsound. So Scripture teaches that the whole man must be regenerated: mind, will, affections, body and limbs, all of them; and it makes not only adults but infants themselves partakers of this benefit. See 1 Thess. 5:23: And may the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly [ὁλοτελεῖς], Eph. 4:23: and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, Gen. 8:21: for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth, Rom. 7:14: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin, Rom. 6:12: Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, and v. 19: As you yielded your members as slaves to impurity and iniquity, leading to more iniquity, so now yield your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification. Luke 1:15: and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, and v. 80: And the child grew and became strong in spirit etc.

units.la: {*}III. Unde nec recte Pontificii partem tantum animæ inferiorem, quam sensualitatem vocant, regeneratione opus habere statuunt. Nam & inanis ista distinctio est, cum eadem sit anima, quæ sentit & quæ intelligit; & Scriptura illam expresse τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ, ac parti principi attribuit. Renovari vero spiritu mentis vestræ. Eph. 4: 23. conf. Matth. 6: 22.
units.tr: III. Therefore the Papists are not right in holding that only the lower part of the soul, which they call the sensual part, needs regeneration. That distinction is empty, since the soul that feels is the same soul that understands, and Scripture ascribes regeneration to the ruling part [τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ], the governing faculty: and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, Eph. 4:23; cf. Matt. 6:22.

units.la: IV .Principium regenerationis ex solo Deo est. Unde ex Deo nati dicimur, Joh. 1: 13. Quod adeo verum est, ut soli Christi sanguini ac merito ea adscribatur; nam adeo extra potestatem hominis ea res est, ut anima non nisi à Christo redempta, ac sanguine ejus abluta, istud decus acquirere possit. Quod apud Johannem est, regenerari ex aqua & Spiritu, c. 3: 5. Obedientia enim Christi aquæ purissimæ comparatur. conf. Hebr. 10: 23. Et abluto corpore munda aqua, retineamus confessionem spei. 1. Joh. 5: 6. Hic ille est, qui venit per aquam & sanguinem, Jesus Christus. Cui Spiritus potentia additur. conf. Ezech. 36: 25, 27.
units.tr: IV. The beginning of regeneration comes from God alone. That is why we are called born of God, John 1:13. This is so true that it is ascribed to the blood and merit of Christ alone. The thing is so far beyond human power that the soul, unless it has been redeemed by Christ and washed in his blood, cannot acquire this honour. In John it is to be born again of water and the Spirit, John 3:5, for the obedience of Christ is compared to the purest water; cf. Heb. 10:22–23: and having our bodies washed with pure water, let us hold fast the confession of our hope. 1 John 5:6: This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. To this the power of the Spirit is added; cf. Ezek. 36:25, 27.

units.la: V. Utitur autem ille ad istam rem verbi divini semine: Peperit nos per verbum veritatis, Jac. 1: 18. quod non aliud quam verbum Euangelii & gratiæ est. Quod, ut solum de amore Dei testatur, ita peccatorem ad amorem ejus adducere solùm potest. Agnoscendum tamen Deo solo fœcundante illud animari ac fructus edere posse. Novo enim corde & spiritu ad illud opus est, ut in novali isto justitia & veritas germinet. Animum mundum crea mihi, Deus, & Spiritum firmum renova intra me Psal. 51: 12.
units.tr: V. God uses for this purpose the seed of the divine Word: He brought us forth by the word of truth, James 1:18. This is nothing other than the word of the Gospel and of grace. As it bears witness only to the love of God, so it can lead the sinner to love him. Yet we must acknowledge that it can come alive and bear fruit only when God alone makes it fruitful. For a new heart and a new spirit are needed for this work, so that righteousness and truth may spring up in this newly tilled ground. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me, Ps. 51:10 [51:12 in the Latin numbering].

units.la: VI. Ut male Sociniani hominem suis auspiciis refingi, ac de propria fœtura filium Dei renasci posse existiment: ac præpostere Spiritum, qui ad novæ vitæ initia vel maximè necessarius est, regenitis demum dari docent. Quæ jam profligata sunt. Rursufque, ut Christo aliquam laudem servent, ac gratiam ejus agnoscere videantur, alio errore, non ante mortem ejus regenerationem datam fuisse statuunt: quæ videl. per doctrinam ejus, ac cœlestis vitæ promissa, quæ antea non obtinuerint, mundo demum contigerit. Quæ Theologiæ istius bellaria sunt, toties jam recoĉta, totiesque eliminata, quæ semper alia pompa ac apparatu reducî videmus. VII. Est
units.tr: VI. The Socinians wrongly suppose that man can be remade by his own initiative and that a son of God can be born from his own offspring. They also wrongly teach that the Spirit, who is especially necessary for the beginnings of new life, is given only to those already regenerate. These errors have been refuted already. Again, in order to leave some praise to Christ and to appear to acknowledge his grace, they hold by another error that regeneration was not given before his death; they say it came to the world only then, through his teaching and the promises of heavenly life, which the earlier ages had not possessed. These are the sweetmeats of that theology, which have been served up so often and so often rejected, and which we always see brought back with a different display and dressing.

units.la: VII. Est autem modus regenerationis in adultis plerunque valde sensibilis, dum nova ista luce perculsus, animus stupet, ac ad propriās sordes horret & æstuat, nec sine motu Spiritus S. opus suum peragit. Hoc audito compunctIi sunt corde. Act. 2: 37. In infantibus autem in Ecclesia natis, interque sanctas sanctorum preces in sinu ejus educatis, aliter se res habet. Illi enim, dum a teneris Deo dedicantur, ac in sanctam parentum disciplinam imbuuntur, magis regenitos se esse deprehendunt, quam regenerari senserunt. Ferè ut in naturali generatione fieri videmus.
units.tr: VII. The manner of regeneration in adults is usually very perceptible: struck by this new light, the mind is astonished, shudders and burns at its own filth, and the work is not carried out without the movement of the Holy Spirit. When they heard this, they were cut to the heart, Acts 2:37. In infants born in the Church and brought up in the holy prayers of its bosom, the matter is different. For these children, since from their tender years they are dedicated to God and imbued with the holy discipline of their parents, find that they are regenerate rather than feel that they have been regenerated. This is almost as we see happen in natural generation.

units.la: VIII. Ad novam autem hanc generationem homo tantum passive se habet, si primum ejus momentum spectes; quomodo & ad generationem naturalem se habet: ubi autem novæ vitæ auspicia adeptus est, & ipse agere incipit. Quod tamen non tam de temporis, quam naturæ ordine intelligendum, ut supra non semel monitum. Omnis enim regeneratio unico in momento absolvitur, cum vita spiritualis partes non admittat, non magis quam naturalis generatio, vel mortuorum vivificatio. Distinguendus autem ab ea est præviuus ille apparatus, & longa Spiritus molimina, quibus ad conversionem persæpe viam facit: quæ & in mortuorum suscitatione adhibita legimus: 2. Reg. 4: 34, 36. quæ moram aliquam plerunque admittunt. In iis autem formalis regenerationis ratio non consistit.
units.tr: VIII. Looking at the first moment, man is only passive in this new generation, just as he is in natural generation; but once he has received the beginnings of new life, he himself begins to act. This, however, must be understood as referring to the order of nature rather than of time, as has been noted more than once above. For all regeneration is completed in a single moment, since spiritual life does not admit of parts, just as natural generation or the raising of the dead does not. But that preliminary preparation must be distinguished from it, along with the long efforts of the Spirit by which he often prepares the way to conversion. We read of such efforts also in the raising of the dead, 2 Kings 4:34, 36. These usually admit some delay. The formal nature of regeneration, however, does not consist in them.

units.la: IX. Atque ita regeneratio. Quæ licet sub V. T. quoque fuerit in comparatione prioris creationis, quam per illam exuebant sancti; præcipue tamen locum habet sub N. T. Sicut cum Paulus 2. Cor. 5: 17. καινὴ κτίσις dicit, in mente maxime habuit τὰ ἀρχαῖα, quæ fuerunt ante manifestationem Christi, cum populus Dei sub lege esset. Quam novitatem in eo ponit, quod credimus in sermonem reconciliationis, atque ita sinus justitiæ in Christo. com. 18, 19, 21. Unde etiam colligit, se neminem cognoscere secundum carnem. com. 16. Quemadmodum etiam regenerari ex aqua & Spiritu, Joh. 3: 5. per verbum veritatis, Jac. 1: 18. nobis prædicatum, 1. Pet. 1: 25. in emphasi acceptum, proprium N.T. est bonum. vi & evanida luce mentem perstringit, quomodo & cæteras historias novimus; sed intima ac viva rei agnitio, quæ suavi sensu in animam descendens intimos ejus affectus ciet & permulcet: quomodo rem amatam non sine gustu quodam ac voluptatis sensu novimus, ac identidem recolimus, inque ea imagine sæpe obhæremus.
units.tr: IX. So much for regeneration. Although under the Old Testament too it took place, in comparison with the earlier creation from which the saints were then stripped, it nevertheless holds its place chiefly under the New Testament. When Paul says new creation [καινὴ κτίσις], 2 Cor. 5:17, he had in mind chiefly the old things, which were before the manifestation of Christ, when the people of God were under the law. He places this newness in our believing the word of reconciliation, and so in the bosom of righteousness in Christ, vv. 18, 19, 21. From this he also concludes that he knows no one according to the flesh, v. 16. Likewise, to be regenerated of water and the Spirit, John 3:5, by the word of truth, James 1:18, preached to us, 1 Pet. 1:25, received with emphasis, is a good peculiar to the New Testament. It does not strike the mind with a faint and fading light, as we know from other histories too; rather it is a deep and living knowledge of the thing, which, descending into the soul with a sweet sensation, stirs and soothes its innermost affections, just as we know that we savour and repeatedly recall a beloved thing with a certain relish and sense of pleasure, and often cling to that image.

units.la: VII. Flagitiose ergo Pontificii fidem, quæ in ævi hujus tenebris unica nobis ad cœlum dux est, vel cæcam prorsus faciunt, vel non nisi fumida & incerta face instruunt. Nam per ignorantiam eam melius quam per notitiam describi, quidam eorum dixere. Et fidem implicitam, quæ in Ecclesiam tota resolvitur, quam pro fidei videl. magistra & non dubio cœli interprete habent, miris laudibus deprædicant; cum tamen ipse nescias quid Ecclesia credat. Quod omnino insanire est, & perinde ac si cæcus jactet se videre illa omnia quæ luscus, quem ducem forte nactus est, videt. Quanquam etiam majus hic periculum est. Cum enim de salute nostra agitur, non aliena, sed propria fide niti, & propriis veluti manibus Christum apprehendere, proprioque ore sanguinem ejus haurire debemus, non autem aliena fide ignotam nobis salutis semitam terere, & fortuito gressu ad cœlum tendere; qua in re animum securum & lætum habere non possumus. Et revera Ecclesia, cum nil nisi humanum nomen sit, fides, quæ in illam revolvitur, pariter non nisi humana, nec omni errore tuta ac secura esse potest. Quod in Romana Ecclesia sollemne est, ubi merè humana omnia, non instituta solum pleraque & dogmata, & superba Ecclesiæ moles, ad humanæ reip. formam composita, ut partem populumque in mundo faciat, haud secus ac alia regna ejusque nosce ndæ signa; sed & fides denique ipsa; & Christiana persuasio, ac universa religio; quæ cum tam levi fundamento nitatur, altius assurgere, & fidens ac secura esse nunquam potest. Sed hoc agunt illi, objecta tam præclari nominis larvâ, ut populum à veri studio avertant, animosque eorum humiles reddant, quo melius servire, ac ab ipsis solis pendere, nec ultra quicquam sapere discant. Et faciebat omnes, parvos & magnos, divites & pauperes, & liberos & servos, ut daret ipsis signaturam in manu illorum dextra, aut in frontibus eorum. Apoc 13: 16. Ecce clivatur cujus non est rectà anima in ipso: justus in fide sua, vel illius, vivet. Hab. 2: 4.
units.tr: The Papists shamefully make faith either utterly blind or equip it only with a smoky and uncertain torch, which is the only guide we have to heaven in the darkness of this age. Some of them have said that faith is better described by ignorance than by knowledge. They also praise with extravagant admiration implicit faith, which is wholly resolved into the Church, and which they regard as the teacher of faith and the unerring interpreter of heaven, even though the believer himself does not know what the Church believes. This is simply madness, as if a blind man boasted that he sees everything that a one-eyed man, whom he happened to have as his guide, can see. Yet here the danger is even greater. When our salvation is at stake, we must rely not on another's faith but on our own, and grasp Christ with our own hands and drink his blood with our own mouth. We must not tread an unknown path of salvation by another's faith and walk towards heaven by chance; in such a matter we cannot have a secure and joyful mind. Indeed, since the Church is nothing but a human name, the faith that is referred back to it can likewise only be human, and cannot be safe and secure from every error. This is the common practice in the Roman Church, where everything is purely human: not only most of its institutions and dogmas and its proud mass, constructed on the model of a human commonwealth so as to make a party and a people in the world, no differently from other kingdoms and their marks of recognition, but also faith itself, the Christian persuasion, and the whole of religion. Since these rest on so slight a foundation, they can never rise higher or be confident and secure. But they act thus, putting forward the mask of a famous name, so as to turn the people away from the pursuit of truth and make their minds humble, so that they may learn to serve better, depend on them alone, and be wise in nothing further. "And he made all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slaves, to receive a mark in their right hand or on their foreheads." Rev. 13:16. "Behold, he who is puffed up, whose soul is not upright in him; but the just shall live by his faith." Hab. 2:4.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Ut autem fides nostra perfecta nondum est, sed quotidianos profectus habet, ita non repugnamus implicitam eam sæpe esse; tum in pueris & rudibus ad proficiendum paratis; tum etiam in provectioribus, in quibus lux ista nondum omnes tenebras vicit, semperque latet aliquid ac latebit, quod religioso affectu venerari, quam pervidere magis datur. Quod, utcunque in coelo demum nudandum, hic tamen credere, & velatum obsignatumque amplecti & possidere oportet. Sed differt illa fides immensum à perplexa Pontificiorum fide. Non enim, ut illa, Ecclesiae vel hominum coetui sese subjicit, ac pudendum in modum idolo illi, quod unicum in terris oraculum esse putat, deservit: sed, uni Deo subjecta, ejus solius verba audit; quae scrutari quidem omni studio non cessat; sed ita ut ubertatem eorum mirari, plenitudinem adorare, & reconditos ac inexhaustos sensus stupere non desinat. Quanquam in necessariis non deficiat, quae tanta luce perfudit Deus, ut vel infantes in Christo ea capere & pervidere possint.
units.tr: Since our faith is not yet perfect but makes daily progress, we do not deny that it is often implicit: in children and the untrained who are ready to advance, and also in the more advanced, in whom that light has not yet overcome all darkness, and something always lies hidden and will lie hidden, which is better venerated with religious feeling than fully seen. This must be laid bare only in heaven, yet here it must nonetheless be believed, and embraced and possessed veiled and sealed. But that faith differs immensely from the confused faith of the Papists. For it does not subject itself, as theirs does, to the Church or the assembly of men, serving that idol which they think is the only oracle on earth in a shameful manner. Rather, subject to one God alone, it hears his words alone. It does not cease to search them with all zeal, yet in such a way that it never ceases to marvel at their richness, to adore their fullness, and to be amazed at their hidden and inexhaustible senses. Yet in necessary matters it is not lacking, for God has bathed these in such a light that even infants in Christ can grasp and perceive them.

units.la: IX. Secundus fidei actus, seu potius primus essentialis, est assensus ad verbum gratiae adhibitus; tum generalis, ad omnia quae in verbo revelata sunt; tum specialis ad veritatem Euangelicam, Christum sufficientem esse Salvatorem omnibus ad se confugientibus, adeoque & mihi, si ad ipsum confugiam. Qui accepit ipsius testimonium, obsignavit quod Deus verus est, Joh. 3: 33. Fidelis est sermo, & omni receptione dignus, quod Christus venerit in mundum ad peccatores salvandum. 1. Tim. 1: 15. Assensus hic etiam in reprobos cadere potest: sed non sine aliqua divini Spiritus ope; cum mente animoque adeo corrupti, & tenebris cupiditatibusque immersi simus, ut infirmam aciem ad tam liquidam lucem obvertere, ac intellectum nostrum domitum ac subjugatum ei tradere non possimus. Ut sola naturae vi, absque Spiritu, assensum istum elicere homo nulla ratione posset. Animalis vero homo non capit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Stultitia enim illi sunt. Et non potest cognoscere, quia spiritualiter dignoscuntur. 1 Cor. 2: 14. Nullus potest dicere Christum Dominum, nisi per Spiritum S. C. 12: 3.
units.tr: IX. The second act of faith, or rather the first essential act, is assent given to the word of grace: first a general assent to all things revealed in the word, and then a special assent to the Evangelical truth that Christ is a sufficient Saviour for all who flee to him, and so for me as well, if I flee to him. "He who has received his testimony has set his seal that God is true," John 3:33. "Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ came into the world to save sinners," 1 Tim. 1:15. This assent can also fall upon the reprobate, but not without some help of the divine Spirit, since we are so corrupted in mind and soul, and so immersed in darkness and lusts, that we cannot turn our weak sight towards so clear a light, nor surrender our subdued and subjugated understanding to it. So by the power of nature alone, without the Spirit, a man could in no way elicit that assent. "But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." 1 Cor. 2:14. "No one can say that Jesus is Lord, except by the Holy Spirit," 1 Cor. 12:3.

units.la: X. Tertius fidei actus, quin potius essentialis secundus, est fiducia, quae electis solis propria est, & tum in Deum, tum in rem promissam fertur; ac duplicem actum habet, tum directum seu primum, tum reflexum seu secundum.
units.tr: X. The third act of faith, or rather the second essential act, is trust, which belongs to the elect alone, and is directed both towards God and towards the promised thing. It has a double act: the direct or first, and the reflexive or second.

units.la: XI. Ac primum quidem Deum ipsum ac Christum hic fidei actus quaerit ac intuetur; atque animam longis erroribus lassam in ejus sinum tandem componit, suaviterque recumbere ac quiescere facit. Est autem hic praecipuus ac proprie salutaris fidei actus nihil aliud, quam Deum in Christo amantis & ad eum confugientis, nisus & reclinatio, suique in manum ac gratiam Dei traditio & resignatio: Sed nitetur Jehovah sanƈto Israëlis in veritate, Esai. 10:20. Ut validam inhortationem haberemus arripiendi expositam spem, Hebr. 6:18. Appellat & Scriptura famem & sitim justitia, Matth. 5:6. receptionem Christi, sive manu, sive ore factam: istis enim similitudinibus utitur: Quotquot acceperunt eum &c. Joh. 1:12. Nisi comedatis carnem filii hominis, & bibatis ipsius sanguinem, non habetis vitam in vobis. cap. 6:53. Experiens an quoque apprehendam, cujus etiam rei causa apprehensus sui à Christo Jesu. Phil. 3:12. atque hinc arctam cum Deo unionem mutuamque communionem loquitur: Et inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. Eph. 3:17. Manete in me, & ego in vobis: sicut palmes non potest fructum ferre a semet ipso, nisi manserit in vite, ita nec vos, nisi in me manseritis &c. Joh. 15:3,4.
units.tr: XI. First, this act of faith seeks and looks upon God himself and Christ, and at last settles the soul, wearied by long errors, into his bosom, and makes it rest and be quiet there. This chief and properly saving act of faith is nothing other than the striving and leaning of one who loves God in Christ and flees to him, and the surrender and resignation of oneself into the hand and grace of God. "But Jehovah shall lean upon the Holy One of Israel in truth," Isa. 10:20. "That we might have a strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before us," Heb. 6:18. Scripture also calls it "hunger and thirst for righteousness," Matt. 5:6, and the "receiving" of Christ, done either by hand or by mouth, for it uses such images: "As many as received him," etc., John 1:12. "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you," ch. 6:53. "If I may also apprehend that for which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus," Phil. 3:12. From this it speaks of the close union with God and mutual communion: "And that Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts," Eph. 3:17. "Abide in me, and I in you: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me," etc., John 15:3,4.

units.la: XII. Hinc fiducia haec in rem promissam quoque fertur, eique ut praecipuo suo peculio indivulsè inhaeret. Postquam videt in Deum recubuit, ac tantam salutem offerri sibi videt, non potest non anima visu isto inardescere, ac pretiosa illa promissa de manu Dei accipere, eique veluti thesauro incubare: Certissimum habens, eum, quod promiserat, etiam faciendi potentiam habere. Rom. 4:21. coll. 2. Tim. 1:12. Quo pertinet fidei ὁμολογία, ac mutua cum Deo veluti consensio & aflipulatio, & spei robur, & inter ipsas saeculi labentis ruinas immota mens, & de Deo semper anima secura. Consideratè Apostolum & Pontificem affipulationis nostra (Christum Jesum, Hebr. 3:1. coll. 4:14. Teneamus adfipulationem spei indeclinabilem, c. 10:23. Parati autem semper ad defensionem omni, qui à vobis petit rationem spei, quae in vobis est. 1.Pet. 3:15. Atque hoc sensu fides à Scholasticis bene appellatur spes corroborata. Est autem fides eorum, quae sperantur, pollicitatio. Hebr. 11:1. Qui contra spem securè credidit, se factum esse patrem multarum gentium Rom. 4:18. Accessum nacti sumus, qui fide fit, & gloriamur in spe gloriae Dei. c. 5:2.
units.tr: XII. Hence this trust is also directed towards the promised thing, and clings to it inseparably as to its chief possession. After it has rested in God and sees that so great a salvation is offered to it, the soul cannot but be kindled by that sight, and receive those precious promises from the hand of God, and brood over them as over a treasure. "Being fully assured that what he had promised he was also able to perform," Rom. 4:21; compare 2 Tim. 1:12. To this belongs the confession of faith [ὁμολογία], the mutual agreement and covenanting with God, as it were, the strength of hope, a mind immovable amid the very ruins of a falling age, and a soul always secure about God. "Consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Christ Jesus," Heb. 3:1; compare 4:14. "Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering," ch. 10:23. "Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you," 1 Pet. 3:15. In this sense faith is rightly called by the Scholastics "hope strengthened." "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for," Heb. 11:1. "Who against hope believed in hope, that he would become the father of many nations," Rom. 4:18. "Through whom we have also obtained access by faith, and rejoice in the hope of the glory of God," ch. 5:2.

units.la: XIII. Atque ex priore illo actu exoritur certitudo & sensus divinae gratiae, ac animae suavis quies, & ineffabilia illa solatia: quae amoris nostri quaedam repercussio, & redeuntes ac restexi ejus radii sunt, qui de mutuo Dei amore, ac universae salutis spe nos certos reddunt. Fidei enim proprie est confugere ad Servatorem, eaque tota in illo animae recumbentis actu consistit. Quod autem illa, jam in sinu Dei posita, exultare ac laetari incipiat, ille fidei corroboratæ fructus est. Unde nemini contingit nisi qui prius Deo se tradiderit, inque eum tanquam unicum servatorem suum recubuerit: In quo habemus aditum cum fiducia, per fidem ipsius, Eph. 3: 12. Unde, cum fidem demum consequatur, abea, salvâ ejus essentiâ, abesse, & ad tempus non exeri potest. Quare ad fidei istam ἱλαροφορίαν contendere, ommisque ope niti jubemur: Et retineamus adstipulationem spei indeclinabilem. Hebr. 10:23. Huc quoque gaudium & pax conscientiæ ex illa fiducia nata, spectant.
units.tr: XIII. From that first act there arises certainty and a sense of divine grace, a sweet rest of the soul, and those unspeakable comforts. These are, as it were, a reflection of our love and the rays returning and bouncing back from it, which make us sure of God's mutual love and of the hope of all salvation. For it belongs properly to faith to flee to the Saviour, and that whole act consists in the soul resting upon him. But that the soul, now placed in the bosom of God, begins to exult and rejoice is the fruit of strengthened faith. Hence it happens to no one except the one who has first surrendered himself to God and leaned upon him as his only Saviour: In whom we have access with confidence, through his faith, Eph. 3:12. Hence, since it follows faith at last, it cannot be absent from faith, its essence remaining intact, nor can it be put forth for a time. Therefore we are bidden to strive after this cheerful assurance [ἱλαροφορίαν] of faith and to lean on every help: And let us hold fast the unwavering pledge of our hope. Heb. 10:23. The joy and peace of conscience born of that confidence also belong here.

units.la: XIV. Comitatur autem fiduciam hanc semper charitas. Tam fortis enim animæ ad Deum anhelatio, atque erga illum Deum affectus, & cum ipso unio & consensus, sine amore ac studio gloriæ ejus esse non potest. Est quippe ipsa fides quidam amoris Dei actus. In Christo valet fides per charitatem operans, Gal. 5:6. Sicuti nec verus Dei amor absque fide existere potest. Nemo enim Deum amare potest, qui non prius ipse de amore ejus securus fuerit, eique ut auctori fœderis per sinceram fidem adhaeserit & adstipulatus fuerit. Adeo hæc se mutuo consequuntur.
units.tr: XIV. Yet this confidence is always accompanied by love. For such an intense longing of the soul for God, such affection toward God, and such union and agreement with him cannot exist without love and zeal for his glory. Indeed, faith itself is a certain act of love toward God. In Christ, faith working through love avails, Gal. 5:6. Just as true love of God cannot exist apart from faith either. For no one can love God who has not first been sure of his love and clung to him, as the author of the covenant, with sincere faith and agreed with him. So closely do these follow one another.

units.la: XV. Quanquam fidem à charitate stricte dicta distingui non abnuamus. Nunc autem manet Fides, & Spes, & Charitas, hæc tria. Maximum autem horum est Charitas. 1. Cor. 13: 13. Alius enim est actus amoris; quo confugimus ad Deum, ac cum eo fœdus facimus, qui primus animæ affectus est: alius, quo, de amore ejus mutuò persuasi, ipsum attributaque ejus omnia veneramur, & amamus; ac proximum quoque nostrum, quia Deus in eo gloriosus esse potest, diligimus; quæ charitas proprie appellatur. Priori actu anima Deum quærit, ejusque particeps esse studet; altero, de Deo securà, sese ipsam ac sua omnia ei vicissim offert & donat. Qui posterior animæ motus facilior est priori.
units.tr: XV. Yet we do not deny that faith is strictly distinguished from love. But now faith, hope and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love. 1 Cor. 13:13. For there is one act of love by which we flee to God and make a covenant with him, which is the first affection of the soul; and there is another, by which, persuaded of his love in turn, we revere and love him and all his attributes, and also love our neighbour, because God can be glorified in him. This is properly called love. By the former act the soul seeks God and strives to share in him; by the latter, being secure in God, it offers and gives itself and all its possessions to him in turn. This latter movement of the soul is easier than the former.

units.la: XVI. Quæ autem de assensu illo generali, qui charitatem interdum habeat comitem, interdum non, adferunt Pontificii, quem pro fide justificante venditant, diluta nimis sunt, & frigida, ac præclaro illo Christianæ animæ affectui indigna. Quæ enim anima de salute sua laborat, inque isto fidei certamine æstuat, ac Christum sitit & anhelat, non levi professo assensu vel motu ferri, sed tota in ipsum ruere, cunctoque affectu & amore ampleti illum ac exardescere debet. Nam fides nisi viva esse non potest. Cum tota in cursu ac motu illo, atque animæ nisu consistat.
units.tr: XVI. What the Papists bring forward about that general assent, which sometimes has love as its companion and sometimes not, and which they puff up as justifying faith, is far too feeble and cold, and unworthy of that excellent affection of the Christian soul. For a soul that labours over its salvation, and burns in this struggle of faith, and thirsts and pants for Christ, must not be carried along by a light, professed assent or motion, but must rush wholly toward him, and be embraced and set ablaze with all affection and love. For faith cannot be anything but living, since it consists entirely in that movement and striving of the soul.

units.la: XVII. Atque ejusdem generis commentum illorum, nisi vocabulorum rum alio usu ludatur, defide informi est, quæ tantum convictionem de veritate Euangelii, & leve forte de eo accepto gaudium dicit; quam tamen dispositive ad justificationem facere, ut principium ac fundamentum ejus; accedente autem deinde charitate animari ac perfici, & plenè hominis justificationem absolvere statuunt. Quæ in concilio Tridentino audita sunt. Cum tamen fides talis, absque charitate & pio ullo animæ motu, non salutaris fides, sed informe fidei cadaver sit. Jac. 2: 17, 18, 20, 22, 26.
units.tr: XVII. Likewise, unless words are being played with in another sense, the same kind of invention of theirs is the unformed faith, which speaks only of conviction about the truth of the Gospel and perhaps some slight joy received from it. They hold that this faith disposes one to justification as its beginning and foundation, and that when love is added afterwards it is animated and perfected and fully completes a man's justification. These things were heard at the Council of Trent. Yet such a faith, without love and without any pious motion of the soul, is not saving faith but the lifeless corpse of faith. James 2:17, 18, 20, 22, 26.

units.la: XVIII. Non recte tamen iidem charitatem formam fidei statuunt, Nec tamen quæ ipsam ad actus suos promovcat. Habent enim singuli hi animæ actus propriam formam; &, si de operationum ordine quæratur, non charitas, sed fides prior est, quæ charitatis, ita proprie dictæ, fons est, dulcemque istum sensum fidelium pectoribus instillat. In Christo valet fides, per charitatem operans. Gal. 5: 6. Finis autem denunciationis est amor ex puro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non ficta, 1. Tim. 1: 5. Charitatem caeterum latiori sensu acceptam, ut fidei actus est, ita quoque formæ ejus partem esse, negari non debet. XIX. Nec melius Sociniani & Socinizantes fidem justificantem in obedientia præceptorum Christi constituunt, cum ea animi fiducia, quod per ea justitiam ac salutem adepturi simus. Quæ non est fides in sanguine Christi, Rom. 3: 25. sed de mercede obtinenda, post obedientiam præstitam, ex Christi promissis detumta fiducia. Estque nihil aliud quam fides legalis, quæ operibus nititur, quæ sæpe adeo damnatur in Scriptura, tanquam stirps venenata, quæ noxio suo succo omnem religionem corrumpit. Utque nec Legi quidem satisfacit illa fides, ita multo minus Euangelio, quod funditus evertit; cum pro obedientia Christi nostram obedientiam & nostra opera inducat.
