Ac tandem, dum in Christo tanquam sponsore ac vade fiduciam hanc collocant, non exigua Deum contumelia afficiunt; dum non solum in mero homine, qualem Christum habent, ad salutem confidunt, sed ne Deo quidem fidere, nisi sponsore homine, in animum inducunt. Cæteroquin, si fidem materialiter consideres, obedientiam eam, ac de Christianarum virtutum numero esse non diffitemur: Accepimus gratiam ad obedientiam fidei. Rom. 1: 5. Cum autem in justificationis negotio ea præcipue consideretur quatenus Christi justitiam apprehendit, non in obedientia fidei, sed in Christi merito omnis fiducia collocanda est. XX. Objectum fidei quod attinet, considerari illud potest pro di- versis II. Objeversis actibus ejus, & vel assensum, vel fiduciam dicit.
units.tr: XVIII. Yet these same men do not rightly make love the form of faith, nor anything that promotes faith to its acts. For each of these acts of the soul has its own form; and if the order of operations is asked about, faith, not love, comes first, and it is the fount of love properly so called, and instils that sweet sense into the hearts of the faithful. In Christ faith avails, working through love, Gal. 5:6. But the goal of the charge is love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, 1 Tim. 1:5. However, love taken in a wider sense, as an act of faith, must not be denied to be also a part of its form. XIX. Nor do the Socinians and those who lean toward Socinianism do any better when they place justifying faith in obedience to the precepts of Christ, together with that confidence of mind that through these we shall obtain righteousness and salvation. This is not faith in the blood of Christ, Rom. 3:25, but a confidence drawn from the promises of Christ about a reward to be obtained after obedience has been rendered. It is nothing other than legal faith, which rests on works, and which is so often condemned in Scripture as a poisonous root that corrupts all religion with its harmful juice. And just as that faith does not satisfy even the Law, so much less does it satisfy the Gospel, which it overturns from the foundations, since in place of the obedience of Christ it brings in our obedience and our works. Finally, while they place this confidence in Christ as surety and bondsman, they do Good no small insult, since they not only trust for salvation in a mere man, such as they consider Christ to be, but also bring into their minds that God is to be trusted only with a human surety. Otherwise, if you consider faith materially, we do not deny that this obedience is also among the Christian virtues: We have received grace for the obedience of faith, Rom. 1:5. But since in the business of justification it is chiefly considered insofar as it lays hold of the righteousness of Christ, all confidence must be placed not in the obedience of faith but in the merit of Christ. XX. As for the object of faith, it can be considered in different ways according to its different acts, and it signifies either assent or confidence.

units.la: XXI. Priori respectu, quatenus fidus assensum notat, objectum ejus iterum vel materiale, vel formale est, illud notat rem creditam, hoc rationem formalem, sub qua creditur. Illud est verbum & testimonium divinum, sive quaecunque à Deo revelata, in cuncta sua latitudine; seu omne Dei verbum, speciatim vero promissiones Euangelii. Qui accepit ipsius testimonium, obsignavit quod Deus verus est. Joh. 3:33. Quo nomine etiam illa venire possunt, quae alioquin ratione quoque innotescunt, modo eadem à Deo quoque revelata sint: Fide consideramus, aptata esse facula verbo Dei. Hebr. 11:3. Nam invisibilia ipsius à creatione mundi rebus factis animadversa conspiciuntur. Rom. 1:20. Quanquam magis occupetur in iis, quae rationem vel superant, vel lacessere, ac altercaricum ea videntur: in quibus nobilissima fidei victoria est: Qui contra spem sub spe credidit—ac minime infirmus fide non consideravit suum ipsius corpus jam emortuum &c. Rom. 4:18, 19. Hoc, est eadem Dei veracitas, qua talis. Ita ut fides, licet natura sua inevidens sit, certissima tamen esse non desinat, quia nititur principio ac teste infallibili.
units.tr: XXI. In the former respect, insofar as faith denotes assent, its object is again either material or formal: the material object is the thing believed, the formal object is the formal reason under which it is believed. The former is the word and testimony of God, that is, whatever has been revealed by God in its whole range, or the whole word of God, and specifically the promises of the Gospel. He who has received his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true, John 3:33. Under this heading may also come those things which are otherwise known by reason as well, provided they have also been revealed by God: By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, Heb. 11:3. For his invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, Rom. 1:20. Yet faith is more occupied with those things which either surpass reason or seem to provoke it and to be at odds with it, and in these lies faith's most noble victory: Who against hope believed in hope... and being not weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, now dead... Rom. 4:18, 19. This is the very truthfulness of God as such. So that faith, although by its nature it is not evident, nevertheless does not cease to be most certain, because it rests on a principle and witness that is infallible.

units.la: XXII. Nulla ergo auctoritas humana fidei principium aut fundamentum esse potest. Nec aliae Ecclesiae hic partes sunt, quam filiis suis Scripturarum campos aperire, manantesque ibi rivos ac latices ostendere, eoque veluti ad pastum deducere. Invenit Philippus Nathanaelem, & dicit ei: quem scripsit Moses & Prophetae, invenimus, Jesum filium Josephi à Nazareth, Joh. 1:46. Venite, videte hominem, qui mihi dixit omnia quaecunque feci, nunquid ipse sit Christus. c. 4:29. coll. v. 42. & mulieri dixerunt, non amplius propter tuam loquelam credimus, ipsi enim audivimus, & novimus, quod hic sit vere Salvator mundi, Christus. Non autem de ejus solius ore oracula divina accipienda sunt, nec ipsa in fidei dominam evehenda, aut Dei solio collocanda, nec piorum denique conscientiis imponenda est. Qua larva Pontificia sedes diu orbi illusit. Quod fidei imprimis grave est, quae non aliud quam Dei magisterium accipere docta, profanum istud in Ecclesia solium, impiumque ejus sessorem non agnoscit, sed despuit ac execratur.
units.tr: XXII. No human authority, therefore, can be the principle or foundation of faith. Nor does the Church have any other role here than to open to her children the fields of the Scriptures, show them the streams and springs flowing there, and so lead them as if to pasture. Philip found Nathanael and said to him: we have found him of whom Moses and the Prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph, John 1:46. Come, see a man who told me all things that I have done; is not this the Christ? John 4:29, compare verse 42. And they said to the woman: now we believe not because of your saying, for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, the Christ. Yet the divine oracles are not to be received from his mouth alone, nor is the Church to be raised up as mistress of faith, or set on the throne of God, nor finally is it to be imposed on the consciences of the pious. Under this mask the Papal see has long deceived the world. This is especially grievous for faith, which, having learned to receive nothing other than the teaching of God, does not acknowledge that profane throne in the Church or its impious occupant, but spits upon it and curses it.

units.la: XXIII. Utque solius Dei vocem fides nostra sequitur, ita ductu ejus falli & aberrare, & pro divina veritate nubes & inania prensare non potest. Hoc enim esset summam illam Christiani hominis virtutem in errorem atque animi vitium commutare, ut ne virtus quidem foret, sed reror; ror, Deumque ipsum falsum & mendacem, & promissa ejus cassa & inania reddere. Unde fidei divinæ subesse falsum nulla ratione potest. Sed quodcunque Deus revelat, & quicquid ex eo sequitur, id omne verum est: Veritatem novistis, & quod omne mendacium ex veritate non est.
units.tr: XXIII. Just as our faith follows the voice of God alone, so it cannot be led astray or wander, or grasp at clouds and empty things in place of divine truth. For that would turn the highest virtue of a Christian into an error and a fault of the mind, so that it would be no virtue at all but a delusion, and would make God himself false and deceitful and his promises empty and vain. Hence no falsehood can underlie divine faith in any way. Whatever God reveals, and whatever follows from it, is wholly true: You know the truth, and no lie is of the truth.

units.la: XXIV. Altero sensu, in quantum fides animi amorem, & fiduciam, ac reclinationem in Deum per Christum dicit, objectum ejus præcipuum est, non veritas vel axioma aliquod theologicum, sed ipse potius Deus in Christo consideratus: Creditis in Deum, etiam in me creditis. Joh. 14: 1. Peripsum Christum credimus in Deum, qui resuscitavit ipsum ex mortuis. 1. Pet. 1: 21. Non enim separandi illi duo. Nec, cum Socinianis, distinguendum ejus objectum primarium, quod sit Deus; & secundarium, quod sit Christus: cum fides objectum secundarium respuat, nec in alium quam in Deum ferri possit; qualis quoque Christus est, Patri par & æqualis: Judicium omne dedit Pater filio, ut omnes honorent filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem, Joh. 5: 22, 23. Nec, cum Remonstrantibus, Christi cognitio, ut non necessaria, à fide justificante sub Vet. Test. excludenda: Cum nemo veniat ad Patrem, nisi per Christum, Joh. 14: 6. Et per gratiam Jesu Christi credamus nos servatum iri, quemadmodum & illi. Act. 15: 11.
units.tr: XXIV. In the second sense, insofar as faith means the love of the soul, trust, and reliance on God through Christ, its chief object is not a truth or some theological axiom, but God himself, considered in Christ: You believe in God; believe also in me. Joh. 14: 1. Through him you believe in God, who raised him from the dead. 1. Pet. 1: 21. For those two cannot be separated. Nor, with the Socinians, should its primary object be distinguished as God, and its secondary object as Christ, since faith rejects any secondary object and cannot be directed to anyone other than God; and Christ is of the same nature, equal to the Father: The Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father, Joh. 5: 22, 23. Nor, with the Remonstrants, should the knowledge of Christ be excluded from justifying faith under the Old Testament as unnecessary: No one comes to the Father except through me, Joh. 14: 6. And we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are, Act. 15: 11.

units.la: XXV. Pertinent huc quoque beneficia Christi, ad quæ fides quoque spectat, quatenus fiducia est; quæ objectum ejus reale appellari possunt. Promissiones enim factas omnibus ad Christum confugientibus fides sibi applicat, atque ita misericordiam Dei specialem sibi reddit: sicuti Scripturæ illa pars, quæ pretiosa illa promissa continet, metonymice objectum fidei vocari potest. Respiscite, & credite Evangelio. Marc. 1: 15.
units.tr: XXV. The benefits of Christ also belong here, which faith regards insofar as it is trust, and which may be called its real object. For faith applies to itself the promises made to all who flee to Christ, and so makes the special mercy of God its own. In this way that part of Scripture which contains those precious promises can be called, by metonymy, the object of faith: Repent, and believe the gospel. Marc. 1: 15.

units.la: XXVI. Subjectum fidei, est tum commune, tum proprium.
units.tr: XXVI. The subject of faith is both general and particular.

units.la: XXVII. Illud sunt 1. homines viatores, exclusis angelis ac beatis: 3. Subjectum videmus enim adhuc per speculum, in ænigmate, tunc vero facie, 1. Cor. 13: 12. 2. homines peccatores. Adamo enim in primo statu fides non competebat. Utcunque enim potentiam ad illam habebat, in actum tamen eam deducere nunquam potuisset. Pariterque Christus, dum in terris ageret, quanquam omni Dei verbo, ac speciatim promissioni de præmio ac mercede sibi debita, assentiretur; fidem tamen, qualem nos habemus, istudque ex intimo miseriæ sensu ad salutis arcem confugium non habuit. 3. Iiique solum ad salutem electi: Secundum fidem electorum, Tit. 1: 1. Vocati, & electi, & fideles. Apoc. 17: 14. 4. & proprie adultis, adulti, prout fidei ex auditu est. Rom. 10:17. De infantibus enim cum Scriptura taceat, nec nos aetatis istius meminerimus, dicere supervacuum est. Quanquam Spiritu, fidei auctore, eos suo modo non carere certum sit. Alioqui liberi vestri impuri essent, sed sancti sunt. 1. Cor. 7: 14. Talium enim est regnum coelorum. Matth. 19: 14. Et Spiritu S. implebitur, etiam a ventre matris suae. Luc. 1: 15. Nimis crasse autem Lutherani fidem illorum adaugent, ex male intellecto loco Marc. 9: 42. Si quis offendiculo fuerit uni parvulorum credentium in me &c.
units.tr: XXVII. The general subject is: (1) human beings as wayfarers, the angels and the blessed being excluded: (3) For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face, 1. Cor. 13: 12. (2) Human beings as sinners. For faith did not belong to Adam in his first state. Although he had the capacity for it, he could never have brought it into act. Likewise Christ, while he was on earth, though he assented to every word of God, and especially to the promise of the reward and wages owed to him, nevertheless did not have the faith we have, nor did he take refuge in the stronghold of salvation out of a deep sense of misery. (3) Only the elect for salvation: According to the faith of God's elect, Tit. 1: 1. Called, and chosen, and faithful, Rev. 17: 14. (4) And properly, adults, since faith comes from hearing, Rom. 10: 17. As for infants, since Scripture is silent and we do not remember that age, it is superfluous to speak of them. Yet it is certain that by the Spirit, the author of faith, they are not without it in their own way: Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy, 1. Cor. 7: 14. For of such is the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 19: 14. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb, Luke 1: 15. The Lutherans, however, far too crudely increase their faith, from a badly understood passage, Marc. 9: 42: If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, etc.

units.la: XXVIII. Proprium autem ac intimum subjectum fidei est cor hominis: Dixit Philippus, sic credis ex toto corde &c. Act. 8: 37. Corde creditur ad justitiam. Rom. 10: 10. Quae vox, Scripturae usu, partem animae principem, tum intellectum, tum voluntatem, significat. Fides enim suo modo ad utrumque, aut potius ad solam voluntatem proprie pertinet. conf. quae §. 5. dicta sunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. The proper and innermost subject of faith, however, is the human heart: Philip said, If you believe with all your heart, etc., Act. 8: 37. With the heart one believes unto righteousness, Rom. 10: 10. In the usage of Scripture this word signifies the chief part of the soul, both the understanding and the will. For faith pertains to both in its own way, or rather, properly to the will alone. See what was said in §. 5.

units.la: XXIX. Causa efficiens fidei est Spiritus S. Habentes eundem Spiritum fidei. 2. Cor. 4: 13. adhibito verbi ministerio.: Euangelium potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. 1: 16. & prima Ecclesiae aetate, miraculorum subsidio, donec Christiana fides in mundo coalesceret; quae tamen moraliter & instrumentaliter tantum ad fidem ingenerandam concurrunt. Praecipuus enim ejus auctor ipse Deus est: qui non credendi solum potentiam, sed ipsum actum largitur, ut jam in potestate hominis non sit non credere: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem misit ille. Joh. 6: 29. Et quae excellens magnitudo potentia ipsius in nos qui credimus &c. Eph. 1: 19. Ut impleat opus fidei, in potentia. 2. Thess. 1: 11. Contra ac Pontificiorum Ecclesia in concilio Tridentino sensit.
units.tr: XXIX. The efficient cause of faith is the Holy Spirit, having the same spirit of faith, 2. Cor. 4: 13, using the ministry of the Word: The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1: 16; and in the first age of the Church, with the help of miracles, until the Christian faith took root in the world. These, however, contribute to the generating of faith only morally and instrumentally. For its chief author is God himself, who grants not only the power to believe but the act itself, so that it is no longer within a person's power not to believe: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent, Joh. 6: 29. And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, etc., Eph. 1: 19. That he may fulfil every work of faith by his power, 2. Thess. 1: 11. This is contrary to what the Church of the Papists thought at the Council of Trent.

units.la: XXX. Adjuncta fidei varia sunt: 1. ejus unitas, utpote cum Deus quoque sit unus, atque una ad ipsum via. Eph. 4: 5. Unde fidelium omnium idem in Deum amor, & fides ὁμοιμος, 2. Pet. 1: 1. 2. necessitas, non praecepti solum, sed & medii. Cum ablque illo animae affectu frustra Deum adire, ac salutem sperare liceat: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur. Marc. 16: 16. 3. imperfectio: Videmus enim adhuc per speculum in aenigmate, tunc vero facie ad faciem. 1. Cor. 13: 12. Quae ipsi non solum cum aliis virtutibus communis, sed speciali modo propria est; cum sit animae anhelantis, & necdum perfectam salutem possidentis, actus; semperque adhuc miseriae quendam sensum habeat; & Deum, quo nondum plene fruitur, quaerere, & absentem suspirare non desinat.
units.tr: XXX. The attributes of faith are various: (1) its unity, since God is also one, and there is one way to him. Eph. 4: 5. Hence all the faithful have the same love and faith toward God, of equal standing, 2. Pet. 1: 1. (2) Necessity, not only of precept but of means. For without that affection of the soul it is useless to approach God and to hope for salvation: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, Marc. 16: 16. (3) Imperfection: For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face. 1. Cor. 13: 12. This is not only common to faith with the other virtues, but is proper to it in a special way, since it is the act of a soul that longs and does not yet possess perfect salvation; it always has some sense of misery, and does not cease to seek God, whom it does not yet fully enjoy, and to sigh for him while he is absent.

units.la: XXXI. Huc spectant quoque fidei effecta, quae illi passim tribuuntur. Quod Christo nos uniat: Ut habitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris, Eph. 3: 17. Quod animum nostrum, in tutissimam arcem perductum, æterna pace perfrui faciat; Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus ad Deum. Rom. 5: 1. Quod per eam libero iam aditu quotidie Deum accedere, atque ad eum loqui liceat: In quo habemus fiduciam & accessum in confidentia, per fidem ipsius: Eph. 3: 12. Quod æterna & invisibilia sperare sueta, mundum ex alto despectet. Quis est qui vincit mundum, nisi credens? 1. Joh. 5: 5. Dumque sanctis cogitationibus animum pascit, carnis quoque tumultus & æstus extinguere, & adversus diabolum, ignita tela iaculantem, gradum componere, & pugnantem superare par sit: Cui (diabolo) resistite, firmi in fide: 1. Pet. 5: 9. Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt, cum passionibus & concupiscentiis, Gal. 5: 24. Denique, quod Christo salutis auctore nitens, ipsam tandem salutem ac æternam beatitudinem nobis conciliet: Ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Joh. 3: 16. Quæ omnia huc tandem pervenient, quod fidei sit peccatorem iustificare & sanctificare. Quæ est illa purificatio cordis, ab odio Dei ac sanctitatis ejus, & a peccati amore, quæ fidei tribuitur. Act. 15: 9.
units.tr: XXXI. To this belong also the effects of faith, which are attributed to it everywhere. It unites us to Christ: That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, Eph. 3: 17. It brings our mind into the most secure stronghold, so that it enjoys eternal peace: Therefore, justified by faith, we have peace with God, Rom. 5: 1. Through it we may approach God every day with free access and speak to him: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence through his faith, Eph. 3: 12. It accustoms us to hope for eternal and invisible things, and to look down upon the world from on high: Who is it that overcomes the world, but the one who believes? 1. Joh. 5: 5. While it feeds the soul with holy thoughts, it also quenches the tumult and heat of the flesh, and it is fitting to stand against the devil, who hurls fiery darts, and to overcome him in battle: Resist him, firm in the faith, 1. Pet. 5: 9. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, Gal. 5: 24. Finally, since it rests on Christ, the author of salvation, it wins for us salvation itself and eternal blessedness: That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life, Joh. 3: 16. All these effects come down to this: it is the work of faith to justify and sanctify the sinner. This is the purification of the heart from hatred of God and of his holiness, and from love of sin, which is attributed to faith. Act. 15: 9.

units.la: XXXII. Consideranda denique fidei dissentanea, & diversæ ejus species, saltem analogæ; quæ variæ sunt. Ac talis imprimis est fides, quæ historica appellatur, qua divinis dogmatibus, ut historiæ alicui non multum ad nos pertinenti, adstipulamur: quam Paulus Apostolus γνῶσιν & προφητείαν appellat, 1. Cor. 13: 2. Multi de principibus credebant in ipsum, sed propter Pharisæos non confitebantur. Joh. 12: 42. Et daemones credunt, sed horrent. Jac. 2: 19. XXXIII. Cui si accedat veritatis istius quidam gustus, & animi gaudium, inque Euangelio recipiendo ac publicè profitendo activitas, ista iam fides temporaria est: de qua Matth. 13: 20, 21. Qui sermonem audit, & statim cum gaudio ipsum accipit, non vero habet radicem in se ipso, sed pro tempore est. conf. Luc. 8: 13. Hebr. 6: 5, 6. Qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustaverintque donum illud coeleste, & participes facti fuerint Spir. S. gustaverintque bonum Dei verbum, ac virtutes suturi saeculi: si prolabantur &c. Quæ à fide iustificante non duratione solum, ut Pontificii ac Remonstrantes volunt, sed interiore essentia ac natura differt; cum radicem non habeat, nec feria ac severa cogitatione in intimum cordis sinum penetraverit, illumque impleverit; sed levi ac non duraturo gaudio luxurians quendam veluti stipularum ignem excitaverit; qui corda nostra repurgare non potest, sed ad primam tempestatem cito rursus deflagraturus, nec unquam maturos veræ fidei fructus produćturus fit.
units.tr: XXXII. Finally, the kinds of faith that fall short of saving faith, and its various species, at least those that are analogous to it, must be considered; these are many. First is the historical faith, by which we assent to the divine doctrines as to some history that does not much concern us. The Apostle Paul calls this knowledge [γνῶσιν] and prophecy [προφητείαν], 1 Cor. 13:2. Many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it. John 12:42. The demons also believe, and shudder. James 2:19. XXXIII. If some taste of this truth and joy of mind be added to it, and an activity in receiving the Gospel and professing it publicly, this is now temporary faith, concerning which Matt. 13:20, 21: He who hears the word and at once receives it with joy, yet has no root in himself, but endures for a time. Compare Luke 8:13 and Heb. 6:5, 6: Those who have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they fall away, etc. This differs from justifying faith not merely in duration, as the Papists and Remonstrants maintain, but in its inward essence and nature. It has no root, and it has not entered deeply into the inmost recesses of the heart with serious and steady thought, nor filled it; rather, with a light joy that does not last, it has kindled a sort of blazing fire of straw, which cannot cleanse our hearts, and which, at the first storm, will soon flare up and die out again, never producing the mature fruits of true faith.

units.la: XXXIV. Pertinet huc quoque fides miraculorum, ubi ex speciali promisso, in Christi nomine miracula nos patraturos confidimus, de qua 1. Cor. 13: 2. Si habeam fidem, adeo ut montes transferam &c. Estqueca tum passiva, in eo qui miraculum effećtum recipit; quanquam hæc non usque necessaria est; tum aćtiva, in eo qui illud peragit. Cum autem miraculorum gloria claruisse etiam eos constet, qui salutari fide carebant, fides illa à fide salvifica distingui debet: quin & ea minor est; atque prava,& instar grani sinapis appellatur, Matth. 17:20. Amen dico, si habeatis fidem, ut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti, transgredstor hinc illuc, & nihil impossibile vobis erit.
units.tr: XXXIV. To this also belongs the faith of miracles, where, on the basis of a special promise, we trust that we shall work miracles in the name of Christ, concerning which 1 Cor. 13:2: If I have faith so as to move mountains, etc. There is also a passive kind, in the one who receives the miracle wrought (although this is not always necessary), and an active kind, in the one who performs it. Since it is clear that even those who lacked saving faith have shone with the glory of miracles, this faith must be distinguished from saving faith. Indeed it is lesser, and it is called perverse, and like a grain of mustard seed, Matt. 17:20: Truly I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, Move from here to there, and nothing will be impossible for you.

units.la: XXXV. Præter diversas has fidei species, quarum omnium persećtiones fides salvifica comprehendit & supergreditur, magis direćtè ipsi opponitur hinc ἀπιςία seu infidelitas, inde superstitio: quæ nihil nisi degener Dei cultus est; non animæ ad Deum confugientis, sed Deum judiciumque ejus horrentis, aćtus; non ex amore, sed ex odio profećtus; qua Deum sibi trucem, & tanquam durum dominum effingit; quem nonnullo cultu propitiare, & lævientem veluti oblatâ stipe placare nititur, ut habeat quod in judicio responset, & non sine jurgio ipsi imputet. Quale superstitionis ingenium describitur in servo illo malo, & segni, qui talentum suum absconderat: Domine, noveram te hominem durum esse, qui metas ubi non sevisti, & inde cogas ubi non sparsisti, Matth. 25: 24.
units.tr: XXXV. Apart from these various species of faith, all of which saving faith comprehends and surpasses, the direct opposites of faith are, on the one side, unbelief [ἀπιστία], or infidelity, and, on the other, superstition. Superstition is nothing but a degenerate worship of God: it is the act not of a soul fleeing to God, but of one who shudders at God and his judgment; it springs not from love but from hatred. It pictures God as harsh to itself, as a hard master, whom it tries to appease with some worship, and to soothe, as it were, with an offered coin, so that it may have something to answer at judgment and not be charged with it in a quarrel. Such is the character of superstition described in that wicked and slothful servant, who had hidden his talent: Lord, I knew you to be a hard man, who reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter, Matt. 25:24.

units.la: XXXVI. Pariterque fidei inimica est ille animi ambigentis & alternantis æstus & disceptatio motusque incompositus: qualis est hominum διψύχων, Jac. 1. qui nec Deo, nec concupiscentiis suis constanter obediunt; inter utriusque motus medii & incerti, & alterno assensu varii, nunc huc, nunc illuc animum alternantes & dividentes. Quod à fidei constantia & simplicitate longe diversum est. Melior est pauper, ambulans in simplicitate sua, quam דרכים perversus, utens duabus viis, qui dives est. Prov. 28: 6.
units.tr: XXXVI. Equally hostile to faith is that restless agitation and wavering of a mind that is uncertain and divided, and that disordered turmoil of feeling, such as belongs to double-minded [διψύχων] men, James 1, who obey neither God nor their own desires steadily, but, wavering between the two impulses, uncertain and divided by alternating assent, now incline their minds this way, now that. This is far different from the constancy and simplicity of faith. Better is the poor man who walks in his simplicity than the one who is perverse in his ways [דרכים], though he is rich in using two roads. Prov. 28:6.

units.la: XXXVII. Est præter hæc ὀλιγοπιςία, seu pusilla fides, quæ non omnem promissionem, nec omnem gratiam amplećtitur, nec satis forti assensu in eam fertur; ita ut in graviori lućta de gradu cedere, ac non parum lædi cam sæpenumero contingat: Dixit ei Jesus, pusille fide cur dubitasti? Matth. 14: 31. Et statim Pater pueri clamans cum lacrymis dixit, credo Domine, succurre mea incredulitati, id est, infirmæ meæ fidei. Marc. 9:24. Cui opponitur fortis ac robusta fides, quæ nullas promissorum altitudines horrens, nullis repulsis fatigata, mundo vero majorac celsior, victricem sese ac triumphantem cœlo infert, auditque ruentes sub pedibus nimbos, & rauca tonitrua calcat: Amen dico vobis, ne in Israële quidem tantam fidem inveni. Matth. 8:10.
units.tr: XXXVII. Besides these there is little faith [ὀλιγοπιστία], or feeble faith, which does not embrace every promise nor every grace, and is not carried toward them with a sufficiently strong assent; so that it often happens that in a heavier struggle it gives ground and is not a little harmed. Jesus said to him, O you of little faith, why did you doubt? Matt. 14:31. And at once the father of the boy, crying out with tears, said, I believe, Lord; help my unbelief, that is, my weak faith. Mark 9:24. Opposed to this is strong and robust faith, which fears no heights of promises, is not wearied by any rebuffs, but, loftier than the world itself, presses forward victorious and triumphant to heaven, hears the storm clouds breaking beneath its feet, and tramples the hoarse thunders: Truly I say to you, I have not found such great faith even in Israel. Matt. 8:10.

units.la: XXXVIII. Generalem fidei considerationem excipit nunc paucis
units.tr: XXXVIII. Following the general consideration of faith, we now turn briefly to the following.

units.la: fides Novi Test. quæ non natura sua ac essentia, sed gradibus tantum à fide Veteris Test. discrepat. Siquidem unus est Dominus, una fides. Eph. 4:5. Atque unus est Deus, qui justificabit circumcisionem, quæ est ex fide, & præputium per fidem. Rom. 3:30. Hæc autem præcipua discrimina sunt. 1. Est in Novo Test. major mysteriorum cognitio, quæ cum veteri tempore maximam partem clausa & velata essent, nunc, nudante Christo, cunctisque umbras sua luce perfundente, aperta cunctisque expósita sunt: Et illuminem omnes, quæ sit communio mysterii, quod occultum fuit à saeculis in Deo. Eph. 3:9. Ut retecta facie gloriam Domini nunc contemplari liceat, 2. Cor. 3:18. 2. Quo pertinet modus ille docendi in Vet. T. qui; præter primariam promissionem patribus fidem, quæ omnis Catecheseos fundamentum erat, ænigmatibus tecta constabat, quorum clavis certis quibusdam hominibus credita erat. Luc. 11:52. nunc autem cum voces Dei palam extent, ac cunctis fidelibus eas audire datum sit, majori in luce Deum videmus, & non timide salutem speramus, cujus rationem omnem explanatam & palam expositam videmus, & non jam hominibus, sed ipsi Deo immediatè credimus.
units.tr: The faith of the New Testament differs from the faith of the Old Testament not in its nature and essence but only in degrees. For there is one Lord, one faith. Eph. 4:5. And there is one God, who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith. Rom. 3:30. These are the chief differences. (1) In the New Testament there is a fuller knowledge of the mysteries. In former times these were for the most part shut up and veiled, but now Christ has unveiled them and filled every shadow with his light, so that they are open and laid out for all: and to bring to light for all what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the ages has been hidden in God. Eph. 3:9. So that, with unveiled face, we may now be permitted to behold the glory of the Lord, 2 Cor. 3:18. (2) To this belongs that manner of teaching in the Old Testament which, besides the primary promise made to the fathers (the foundation of all catechesis), consisted of enigmas wrapped up in veils, whose key was entrusted to certain chosen men. Luke 11:52. But now that the voices of God are openly sounded, and all the faithful are allowed to hear them, we see God in a greater light and hope for salvation without timidity. We see his whole reasoning explained and openly set forth, and we believe not in men but directly in God himself.

units.la: 3. Faciebat enim etiam illud non leve Veteris Novique temporis discrimen, quod tum quidem Ecclesiæ fides non adeo liquido solo Deo niteretur, sed homines præterea interpretes & internuncios habebat: qualis ex. gr. Moses erat, de quo Exod. 14:31. Et crediderunt in Jehovam, & in Mosem servum ejus. coll. cap. 19:9. & 1. Cor. 10:2. Et omnes in Mosem baptizati sunt, in nube, & in mari. Novi autem Testamenti fides ipso Domino teste gloriatur: Nam multis vicibus multisque modis olim Deus locutus patribus in prophetis, ultimis diebus hisce locutus est nobis in filio. Hcb. 1:1. Baptizantes ipsos in nomine Patris, Filii & Spir. S. Matth. 28:19. Qui tres illi testes sunt, qui sunt in cœlo, & quorum opera in terris testantur. 1. Joh. 5:7. 4. Sed major præsertim in Nov. Test. fiducia, & lætitia, & libertas, & gaudium, & gloriatio est. Cum enim Veteris Testamenti fideles, nondum parta salute, famem sitimque perpetuo tolerarent, & longo desiderio cruciarentur, fides eorum potius spes & expectatio quædam erat, unde χρονημότες ante sperantes in Christo dicti Eph. 1:12. quam non sine luctu & certamine exercere poterant, ad singula momenta pavitantes trementeSpiritu illo servitutis, Rom 8: 15. ac mortis metu. Hebr. 2: 14, 15. Nunc autem in Novo Testam. mera est fides, Gal. 3:23,24. & de salute consummatâ gaudium, & gratiarum actio, & gloriatio, & libertas, & cuncti denique filiorum affectus. Rom. 8: 15. Gal. 3: 14. Unde consummata ea Ecclesia dicitur. Hebr. 11:40. Et palam gaudere, sibique benedicere jubetur, Esai. 65: 16. Gal. 3: 8,9. Esai. 45: 25. Quæ est illa ad sacrificium Christi ὁμολογία, Hebr. 3: 1. Quæ confessio & ipsa sacrificium est. Hos. 14: 3. Hebr. 13: 15. Post sacrificium enim Christi nihil aliud superest quam hæc sacrificii ac mortis ejus perpetua commemoratio & celebratio.
units.tr: 3. There was also this not slight difference between the Old and New Times: the faith of the Church then did not rest so clearly on God alone, but also had men as interpreters and intermediaries. Such, for example, was Moses, of whom Exod. 14:31: And they believed in Jehovah and in Moses his servant. Compare chap. 19:9, and 1 Cor. 10:2: And all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea. But the faith of the New Testament glories in the Lord's own witness: For God, who in many portions and in many ways spoke of old to the fathers by the prophets, in these last days has spoken to us by his Son. Heb. 1:1. Baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Matt. 28:19. These are the three witnesses who are in heaven, and whose testimony is borne on earth. 1 John 5:7. 4. But in the New Testament, especially, there is greater confidence, joy, freedom, gladness and glorying. For while the faithful of the Old Testament, before salvation was won, endured hunger and thirst continually and were tormented by long desire, their faith was rather a certain hope and expectation, whence they are called [προηλπικότες] "having hoped beforehand in Christ," Eph. 1:12. They could not exercise it without grief and struggle, trembling and quaking at every moment, under that spirit of bondage, Rom. 8:15, and in fear of death, Heb. 2:14–15. But now in the New Testament faith is pure, Gal. 3:23–24, and there is joy over a completed salvation, thanksgiving, glorying, freedom, and finally all the affections of sons. Rom. 8:15; Gal. 3:14. Hence that Church is called completed, Heb. 11:40, and it is commanded to rejoice openly and to bless itself, Isa. 65:16; Gal. 3:8–9; Isa. 45:25. This is that [ὁμολογία] confession of the sacrifice of Christ, Heb. 3:1, which is itself a sacrifice, Hos. 14:3; Heb. 13:15. For after the sacrifice of Christ nothing remains but the perpetual commemoration and celebration of that sacrifice and death.

units.la: 1. Joh. 2: 1,2. Atque ita fides Novi Test. verè gloriam Deo tribuit, atque obsignatio est, quod Deus sit verax. Joh. 3: 33.
units.tr: 1 John 2:1–2. And so the faith of the New Testament truly gives glory to God, and it is the seal that God is true. John 3:33.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS OCTAVUS DE Progressu beneficiorum Christi, in justificatione eique annexis beneficiis.
units.tr: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS OCTAVUS: On the Progress of Christ's Benefits in Justification and the Benefits Annexed to It.

units.la: CAP. V. De Justificatione.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On Justification.

units.la: I. D fidem sequitur justificatio, tanquam effectum ejus. Atque ita ad gravem hunc Christianæ fidei articulum pervenimus, qui universæ religionis præcipuum caput & compendium est. Cum enim religio omnis in eo versetur ut peccatorem Deo uniat, sitque instar sacri vinculi, quod Deum hominemque post longum divortium rursus veluti colliget, & conjungat, ruptumque olim cœli commercium redintegret; certe in hoc capite ea vim suam exerere debet. Hic enim vera unionis ac amicitiæ cum Deo tradenda ratio est: in quo si quis aberret, corruptæ religionis infamiam declinare non poterit. Ut hic articulus cæterorum omnium regula ac norma sit, ad quem illa exploranda ac judicanda sunt, atque ex justificatione hominis procurandâ, an sana an vero insana fuerint, facile ostenditur. Unde non aliam religionis nostræ notam malumus, quam hoc de justificatione dogma (quod Reformatis Ecclesiis veluti proprium vindicare licet) in quo si digna Deo & justitia ejus, digna Christo & sacrificio ejus, atque homini denique omnique ejus statui apta & convenientia docuerimus; certe doctrinam hanc neque in reliquis articulis labare, & Deo non indecoram, hominumque saluti non incommodam judicare licet.
units.tr: I. Justification follows faith as its effect. And so we come to this weighty article of the Christian faith, which is the chief head and summary of the whole religion. For since all religion is concerned with uniting a sinner to God, and is like a sacred bond that gathers God and man together again after a long separation and joins them, and restores the commerce of heaven that was once broken, certainly this article must exert its force here. For here the true account of union and friendship with God must be given, and whoever goes astray here cannot escape the disgrace of a corrupt religion. That this article is the rule and standard of all the others, by which they are to be tested and judged, and whether they are sound or insane according to how they bring about the justification of man, is easily shown. Hence we prefer no other mark of our religion than this doctrine of justification (which it is fair to claim as peculiar to the Reformed Churches). If we have taught that it is worthy of God and his justice, worthy of Christ and his sacrifice, and finally suited and fitting for man and his whole condition, then we may certainly judge that this doctrine does not waver in the other articles, is not unbecoming to God, and is not harmful to the salvation of men.

units.la: II. Est autem justificationis vox Ecclesiæ propria, quomodo & multa alia vocabula notare licet, è sæculo in Ecclesiam adoptata: habetque semper in Scriptura usum forensem. Vide Exod. 23: 7. Deut. 25: 1. Prov. 17: 15. Jef. 5: 23. Matth. 12: 37. Luc. 18: 14. Act. 13: 39. & præcipuè Rom. 8: 33, 34. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus est qui mortuus est, imo vero qui etiam suscitatus est &c. Notat autem justum aliquem habere, agnoscere, declarare: sive justus ipse & sanctus sit, 1. Tim. 3: 16. Deus justificatus est in Spiritu: sive peccator existat. Quæ hujus loci significatio est. Ac convenit talis justificatio vel ipsi judici, justum aliquem pronuncianti. Rom. 8: 33. Quis intentabit crimina? Deus est qui justificat: vel advocato, pro reo respondenti, & accusationis tela amolienti; quo sensu Christo peculiariter attribuitur, Jef. 53: 11. In cognitione sui justificabit justus servus meus multos: & denique improprie valdeac metonymice hominibus qui alios justitiæ viam docent, tribuitur. Et qui multos justos fecerunt, erunt ut stellæ. Dan. 12: 3.
units.tr: II. The word justification is a term proper to the Church, adopted into the Church from the world in the same way that many other words can be shown to have been. In Scripture it always has a forensic use. See Exod. 23:7; Deut. 25:1; Prov. 17:15; Isa. 5:23; Matt. 12:37; Luke 18:14; Acts 13:39, and above all Rom. 8:33, 34: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather who was also raised, and so on. It means to hold someone as just, to acknowledge, to declare: whether the person himself is just and holy, as in 1 Tim. 3:16, God was justified in the Spirit; or whether he is a sinner, which is the meaning of this passage. Such justification belongs either to the judge himself, pronouncing someone just (Rom. 8:33, Who shall bring a charge? It is God who justifies); or to an advocate, answering on behalf of the accused and warding off the darts of accusation, in which sense it is attributed peculiarly to Christ (Isa. 53:11, By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many); and finally, improperly and by metonymy, it is ascribed to men who teach others the way of righteousness (And those who turn many to righteousness shall shine like the stars, Dan. 12:3).

units.la: III. Atque hic in ipso limine offendunt Pontificii, & vocabuli sensum corrumpunt, quod ipsos deinde in re ipsa non leviter aberrare fecit. Alexander enim Alensis, justificationem liberi arbitrii rectitudinem esse dixit. Thomas non multo felicius eam esse motum ex morali & physico compositum; partimque peccatorum remissione, partim justitiæ infusione constare statuit. In Tridentino autem concilio loca apud Paulum de justificatione agentia effective tantum intelligi debere Soto contendit. Atque ita hodie Pontificii eam cum sanctificatione propemodum confundunt. In quo vocis abusu socios habent Mennonitas, qui ut justum sanctumque, ita quoque justificationem & sanctificationem pro eodem habent.
units.tr: III. Here, at the very threshold, the Papists stumble and corrupt the sense of the word, which then led them into no slight error about the thing itself. For Alexander of Hales said that justification is the rectitude of free will. Thomas, not much more happily, held that it is a motion composed of the moral and the physical, consisting partly in the remission of sins and partly in the infusion of righteousness. Soto contended that the passages in Paul about justification should be understood only as effective at the Council of Trent. And so today the Papists almost confuse it with sanctification. In this abuse of the word they have as companions the Mennonites, who, just as they hold the just and the holy to be the same, likewise hold justification and sanctification to be one and the same.

units.la: IV. Quæ contra Scripturæ usum sunt, quæ non aliam hujus vocis significationem quam moralem & relativam novit, & aperte justificationem à sanctificatione distinguit, 1. Cor. 1: 30. Illa autem velle conjungere vel confundere, eundemque motum moralem & physicum statuere, est sibi ipsi contradicere; & gradum ad relativam justificationem, imputatamque justitiam omnem abnegandam præbet. Quicquid autem de Latinæ vocis sono sit, istud leve nimis argumentum est.cum & alia ejus generis sint, quæ tamen realem mutationem non inferunt, neque illud Græcis Hebraicisque vocabulis, quibus Spiritus S. usus est, quiquam præscribat.
units.tr: IV. These views are contrary to the usage of Scripture, which knows no meaning of this word other than moral and relative, and clearly distinguishes justification from sanctification (1 Cor. 1:30). To wish to join or confuse these, and to set up one and the same motion as both moral and physical, is to contradict oneself, and it opens the way to denying the relative justification and the imputed righteousness altogether. Whatever the sound of the Latin word may be, this is far too weak an argument, since there are other words of this kind that nonetheless do not imply any real change, and the Greek and Hebrew words which the Holy Spirit used do not prescribe anything of the kind.

units.la: V. Justificatio ipsa, pro triplici hominis statu, triplicem veluti vultum habet: dum alia est hominis integri, alia peccatoris, alia denique hominis regeniti, atque in istis sanctitatis auspiciis Deo rursus placere incipientis; quibus gradibus ea à nobis considerari quoque meretur.
units.tr: V. Justification itself wears, as it were, a threefold face according to the threefold state of man: it is one thing for man in his integrity, another for the sinner, and finally another for the regenerate man, who under these first signs of holiness begins again to please God. These stages also deserve to be considered by us.

units.la: VI. In statu primo justificatus homo fuisset ex legis primævæ obedientia; quæ in corde ipsius inscripta cum lege morali eadem erat. Atque adeo legalis fuisset ibi justitia, dum homo ex operibus vitam speravisset, non quidem ex condigno, sed ex liberali Dei pacto.
units.tr: VI. In the first state, man would have been justified by the obedience of the original law, which, written in his heart, was the same as the moral law. And so there would have been a legal righteousness there, since man would have hoped for life from works, not indeed by merit of condignity, but by God's gracious covenant.

units.la: VII. Quanquam accuratè loquendo, ibi non tam proprii nominis justificatio, cum nulla ibi fuisset labes, quam obedientis hominis remuneratio, amorisque ejus acceptio, & publica operum ejus commendatio ac laudatio locum habuisset; idque non tam ex stricta lege, quam ex Dei bonitate ac liberrimi amoris ejus ingenio. Agebat enim tum homo in statu amicitiæ cum Deo; atque ad instar filii in paterna domo, si unicum de non gustandâ arbore præceptum excipias, non alia quam amoris lege tenebatur; quam ubi implevisset, Deus amori isti non respondere non poterat.
units.tr: VII. Strictly speaking, however, there would not have been justification in the proper sense of the term there, since no stain would have existed; rather what would have taken place is the rewarding of the obedient man, the acceptance of his love, and the public commendation and praise of his works. This would have followed not so much from the strict law as from the goodness of God and the nature of his most free love. For man then lived in a state of friendship with God, and, like a son in his father's house, he was bound by no other law than the law of love, except for the one command concerning the tree that was not to be tasted. When he had fulfilled that law, God could not fail to respond to such love.

units.la: VIII. Sed per peccatum universus ille status, & qualiscunque illa justitia, ac justificatio desiit; neque ex operibus salutem sperare homo amplius poterat. Non justificatur apud te ullus vivens. Psal. 143: 2. Sed in Christo solo eam quærere debet. Atque ita, pro alio hominis statu, atque alia, quam nunc quærere debet, justitia, sequitur quoque alia justificationis facies; justificatio videl. peccatoris, quæ ex sola fide sine operibus & lege peragitur, ob solum Christi meritum. In qua confidendum 1. Quæ ad eam justificationem requiratur justitia? sive quænam sit illius materia ac fundamentum. 2. Quomodo ejus participes evadamus? sive quænam illius sit forma. 3. Denique quomodo cacum justitia operum nullâ ex parte consistere queat?
units.tr: VIII. But through sin that whole state, and whatever righteousness and justification it had, came to an end, and man could no longer hope for salvation from works. No one living is justified before you (Ps. 143:2). He must seek it in Christ alone. And so, corresponding to another state of man and another righteousness, which he must now seek, there follows also another form of justification: namely the justification of the sinner, which is carried out by faith alone, without works and without the law, on account of Christ's merit alone. Concerning this we must inquire: 1. What righteousness is required for that justification? That is, what is its matter and foundation? 2. How do we come to share in it? That is, what is its form? 3. Finally, how can the righteousness of works in no way stand before God?

units.la: IX. Justitia, quæ in hac justificatione valet, non alia est, quam justitia Christi, nobis imputata. Quod facile patet. Cum enim duplex tan-tum detur justitia, vel nostra vel aliena, ac juxta eam duplex justificationis ratio, Rom. 4: 4, 5. Scriptura 1. nostram justitiam aperte removet, dum de homine peccatore ac reo esse agere profitetur: Omnes enim peccarunt, & posteriores sunt gloriâ Dei, Rom. 3:23. qui credit in eum, qui justificat impium. Rom. 4: 5. Et 2. alteram illam justitiam perpetuo urget & docet, acDei & Christi eam justitiam appellat, & gratiæ unicè attribuit: Justitia, quæ ex Deo est, ad fidem. Phil. 3:9. Feci propinquam justitiam meam, non elongabitur. Esai. 46: 13. O Jehova justitia nostra. Jer. 23:6. Qui factus est nobis justitia a Deo. 1 Cor. 1: 30.
units.tr: IX. The righteousness that is valid in this justification is nothing other than the righteousness of Christ, imputed to us. This is easily clear. For since there is only a twofold righteousness, either ours or another's, and corresponding to it a twofold way of justification (Rom. 4:4, 5), Scripture 1. clearly removes our own righteousness, since it declares that it is dealing with a man who is a sinner and guilty: For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom. 3:23), and to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). And 2. it constantly insists on and teaches that other righteousness, calls it the righteousness of God and of Christ, and attributes it solely to grace: the righteousness which is from God, based on faith (Phil. 3:9); I have brought near my righteousness, it will not be far off (Isa. 46:13); O LORD, our righteousness (Jer. 23:6); who became for us righteousness from God (1 Cor. 1:30).

units.la: 3. Cumque ea nostra nisi imputatione fieri non posset, neque alius ejus adipiscendæ modus sit, eam denique imputari nobis manifesto dicit; vocem λογίζεσθαι adhibitâ, quæ e mercatorum tabulis desumta ab Apostolo frequenter in hac materia usurpatur. Rom. 4. Atque eadem aliorum quoque locorum sententia est, præsertim Rom. 5: 15. Si enim unius lapsu multi mortui sunt, multo magis gratia Dei, & donatio in gratia, quæ est unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos abundavit. & 2. Cor. 5: 21. Fecit enim, ut qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum esset, ut nos efficeremur justitia Dei in eo.
units.tr: 3. Since our own righteousness could not be obtained except by imputation, and there is no other way of obtaining it, Scripture clearly says that it is imputed to us, using the word reckoning [λογίζεσθαι], which the Apostle, taking it from merchants' account books, frequently uses in this matter (Rom. 4). The sense of other passages is the same, especially Rom. 5:15: For if by the one man's trespass the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound to the many; and 2 Cor. 5:21: For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

units.la: X. Ut perverse Pontificii justitiam hanc imputatam negent, &, per varios olim errores ac superstitiones afflictam, in Tridentina tandem Synodo anathemate ferierint; quasi ea merum figmentum, & justitiæ simulachrum ac idolum esset. Iste enim color adferebatur, atque ita multos ex Patribus iis Protestantium sententiam cepisse constat, quasi illi hominem, utcunque introrsum turpem ac maculosum, externa illa justitiæ veste tantum obtectum, Deo satis placere docerent, nec ultra quidquam præterea requirerent. Cum tamen longe aliùs generis sit hæc justitiæ Christi imputatio; nec quid ea rei sit ignorari debuerit ab iis, qui Sanctorum merita, & indulgentiarum fumos, tam pretiosè vendere, atque in iis mercimoniis præcipuum Ecclesiæ suæ quæstum exercere non desinebant. Illâ tamen specie, ac insontis vocabuli odio, dumque præterea illi suo quæstui aliisque erroribus abundè faverent, ac internam justitiam & sanctitatem nimis admirarentur, inque eâ adeo stuperent, ut vel pro Dei tribunali eam tueri tantum non auderent, sensim justitiam Christi elabi sibi passi sunt, eamque profitentes diris suis perculerunt, anathema dicentes illis, qui nos formaliter justificari justitia Christi statuunt.
units.tr: X. How perversely the Papists deny this imputed righteousness, and, after it had been assailed for a long time by various errors and superstitions, finally struck it with an anathema at the Council of Trent, as if it were a mere fiction, an image and idol of righteousness. For this pretext was put forward, and it is established that many of the Fathers thereby adopted the opinion of the Protestants, as though they taught that a man, however inwardly foul and stained, covered only by that outward garment of righteousness, pleases God well enough, and required nothing further beyond this. Yet the imputation of Christ's righteousness is of a quite different kind, and those who sold the merits of the saints and the smoke of indulgences so dearly, and who did not cease to carry on their chief gain from such trade, ought not to have been ignorant of what it is. Nevertheless, under that pretext and from hatred of an innocent word, and while they lavishly favoured their own profit and their other errors, and admired inner righteousness and holiness too greatly, and were so astonished by it that they hardly dared to defend it even before God's tribunal, they gradually allowed the righteousness of Christ to slip away from them, and, professing it, struck at it with their own curses, pronouncing anathema on those who maintain that we are formally justified by the righteousness of Christ.

units.la: XI. Sed & collectiones quasdam scholasticas audiamus, quibus Ecclesiam pretioso hoc justitiæ Christi thesauro privare sese posse putant. Nam & incongruam, & impossibilem, & nullam denique eam esse ostendere satagunt. Ac primum quædam de qualitatibus internis ac inhærentibus cavillantur, ac cum iis justitiam hanc imputatam comparant. Quod alienum est. Non enim, ut alterius doctrina eruditus, vel albedine albus nemo dici potest, ita nec Christi justitia nos justos dici posse verum est. Nam non inhæsive nos justos justitiâ Christi prædicamus, quo allata exempla spectant; sed imputativè ac relatione quadam. Atque ex eodem fonte est, quod, si justitia Christi nostra sit, nos æque justos ac ipse Christus, & tantum non mundi Servatores fore inferunt. Illud enim rursus de inhærente justitia concludit. Nos autem, non Christi justitiam nobis inhærere, verum imputante Deo nostram fieri, idque non pro universo valore suo, sed quantum uniuscujusque nostrum necessitas flagitat, docemus. Addunt: Saltem dari in nobis justitiam ac sanctitatem aliquam internam; atque adeo ab ea potius, quam ab extrinseca Christi justitia justos nos vocari oportere: cum duabus in subjecto aliquo formis existentibus, illud non a formâ adhærente, sed inhærente denominari aquum sit. Verum hoc locum hic non habet; cum non ea nos intrinseca sanctitate polleamus, quæ coram Deo judice consistat, ut ea gloriari nosque ipsos commendare multum liceat; de qua tamen justitia unicè quæritur. Quod denique talem justitiam revera nullam, ac merum idolum esse urgent, cum ea ne quidem in Adamo extiterit, nec ab eo amissa, ac proinde a Christo neque reddita sit: id inde est: quod non aliam quam inhærentem justitiam perpetuo cogitant; hæc autem justitia nihil aliud est quam peccatorum remissio, quam in primo Adami statu obtinuisse mirum non est; & præterea beatum illum statum includit, quo Adamus, si perseverasset, pervenisset, nos autem ob labem ipsius caremus, & non nisi Christi merito rursus possidemus. Quæ nulla ac imperceptibilia esse dici non potest. Sed non sine blasphemiâ tandem desinunt, hominemque Christi merito justum cum Æthiope comparant, qui, quod toga alba indutus incedat, eo albus dicatur. Quæ sæva sunt, ac Christianæ animæ fidem ac spem in Christum irridentia. Quid enim, an pretiosus ille justitiæ Christi pannus nuditatem nostram tegere, nec purpura ista nos ornare quicquam potest? an piamenta ejus animæ nostræ sordes abluere non possunt? an ipse sanguis ejus jam vilis est? ac majori denique in pretio erunt lacerae nostrae justitiae vestes, & conquisitę undique Sanctorum laciniae, & sic Ecclesia ornata, & peregrino cultu adjuta sponso suo placere poterit? Sed quicquid hi Sophistae audeant, obliquarum mentium istae subtilitates sunt, ac praestigiosae quaedam sutelae, & infelices nodi, quibus se ipsos perdere, & maximam Euangelii partem fraudare amant; quibusque veluti armis contra magnam istam veritatis lucem se tutari opus habent. Certe vel in mediis Papatus tenebris, cum pii adhuc in carcere isto attinerentur, nondum omnes lucis istius radii extincti fuerunt, sed vel difficillimis Ecclesiae temporibus hinc inde emicuerunt. Ut ex Bernardo potissimum patet, posterioris aevi scriptore, quo nemo plenius, & ad solandas conscientias aptius, de primario hoc religionis capite scripsit.
units.tr: XI. But let us also hear certain scholastic collections, by which they think they can deprive the Church of this precious treasure of Christ's righteousness. For they strive to show that it is unsuitable, impossible, and in short no righteousness at all. And first they jeer at certain matters concerning internal and inherent qualities, and compare this imputed righteousness with them. This is beside the point. For it is not true that, just as no one can be called learned from another's teaching, or white from whiteness, so neither can we be called righteous by the righteousness of Christ. For we do not proclaim ourselves righteous by an inherence in Christ's righteousness, to which the examples adduced refer, but by imputation and a certain relation. And from the same source comes their inference that, if the righteousness of Christ is ours, we would be as righteous as Christ himself, and would almost become saviours of the world. For that again concludes concerning inherent righteousness. We, however, teach that Christ's righteousness does not inhere in us, but becomes ours by God's imputing it, and that not in its full value, but to the extent that the need of each one of us demands. They add: At least there is in us some inner righteousness and holiness; and therefore we ought to be called righteous from that rather than from the extrinsic righteousness of Christ, since, when two forms exist in some subject, it is fair that it be named from the inhering form rather than from the adhering one. But this has no place here, since we do not possess that intrinsic holiness which stands before God the judge, so that we may greatly glory in it and commend ourselves; yet it is concerning this righteousness alone that the question is asked. Finally, as to their insistence that such righteousness is really nothing and a mere idol, since it did not exist even in Adam, nor was it lost by him, and therefore was neither restored by Christ: this arises from the fact that they always think of no other righteousness than inherent righteousness; and this righteousness is nothing other than the remission of sins, which it is no wonder that Adam possessed in his first state, and it also includes that blessed state to which Adam would have attained had he persevered, whereas we, because of his fall, lack it and possess it again only through the merit of Christ. This cannot be called null and imperceptible. Yet at last they do not cease without blasphemy, and compare a man justified by Christ's merit with the Ethiopian, who, because he walks clothed in a white robe, is called white on that account. These are cruel words, mocking the faith and hope of the Christian soul in Christ. For what? Can that precious cloth of Christ's righteousness not cover our nakedness, and can that purple not adorn us? Can his expiations not wash away the filth of our soul? Is his very blood now worthless? And will our torn garments of righteousness, and the rags of the saints gathered from everywhere, be of greater worth, so that the Church, adorned and assisted by foreign dress, may please her bridegroom? But whatever these Sophists dare, they are the subtleties of perverse minds, certain deceptive patches and unhappy knots, by which they love to ruin themselves and defraud the greater part of the Gospel, and with which, as with weapons, they need to shield themselves against the great light of this truth. Certainly even in the midst of the darkness of Popery, while the pious were still held in that prison, not all the rays of this light were extinguished, but even in the most difficult times of the Church they shone forth here and there. This is clear chiefly from Bernard, a writer of a later age, than whom no one wrote more fully, or more aptly for comforting consciences, on this primary head of religion.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Justitia autem illa Christi nobis imputata bimembris quasi est. 1. injustitiae nostrae per sufficientis poenae λύτρον compensatio. 2. universalis justitiae legis praeceptis debitis exsolutio; seu universalis & perseverans erga caritatis legem ad mortem usque obedientia. Deut. 27:26. Rom. 6:23. Joh. 8:29. 17:4. Phil. 2:8. Prior cum in Christi passionibus ac morte maxime emicuerit, vulgo passiva; posteriori vero cum in vitae actionibus praecipue effulserit, activa dici solet.
units.tr: That justice of Christ imputed to us is, as it were, twofold: (1) the compensation of our injustice by a sufficient penalty as a ransom [λύτρον]; (2) the full discharge of the debts owed under the precepts of universal justice of the law, that is, a universal and persevering obedience to the law of love, even unto death. Deut. 27:26. Rom. 6:23. John 8:29; 17:4. Phil. 2:8. The former, since it shines forth chiefly in the passion and death of Christ, is commonly called passive; the latter, since it shines forth especially in the actions of his life, is usually called active.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Longius ergo abeunt, qui non solum obedientiam Christi activam & passivam quomodocunque distinguunt, & scrupulosis quibusdam tricis illa vitae haereditatem quaesitam, hac autem mortis reatum extinctum docent; verum istas unius justitiae veluti partes a se mutuo discerpunt, ac justitiam Christi tantum non violant ac lacerant. Dum eam omnem nobis adscribi vetant, & activam obedientiam Christo soli relinquendam, nobis autem passiones ac sanguinem ejus donatum tantum volunt: quam sententiam inter nostros magno olim ardore propugnavit Olevianus & Piscator. De qua re nos ita statuimus: 1. non sine aliqua vocum discordia obedientiam Christi in activam ac passivam distingui: cum ea omnis activa sit, nec alibi amor ac obedientia ejus magis emicuerit, quam mediis in passionibus; quae sine illo amoris certamine ac luctā, atque animae Dei gloriam quaerentis laboribus non illud pretium habuissent. Nunc autem vel maxime probata est ejus obedientia, ostensusque amoris ardor, quod obediens fuerit ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. 2:8. 2. male autem haec cum in finem distinguuntur, ut ea separent, alteramque obedientiae partem nobis tribuendo, abrogent alteram; ram; atque actiyam obedientiam ipsi Christo vindicantes, nobis solum ejus sanguinem, mortisque pretium relinquant. Quæ insincera sunt: cum quicquid Christus præstitit, & quicquid vivens moriensque peregit, id omne ad justitiam requisitum, nobisque debitum fuerit; atque unicum δικαίωμα, unicamque tandem justitiam effecerit, quæ peccatori ad Deum adducendo opus erat: quæ non separanda, aut aliquam partem abneganda, vel denique in hac vel illa obedientiæ parte collocanda, sed tota agnoscenda & prædicanda est, cum extota ea exurgat & absolvatur. 3. Non solâ enim morte ac passionibus ejus salus nostra procurari poterat. Præterquam enim, quod ne Christi quidem passiones, absque illibata illâ vitæ sanctitate, pretium suum habuissent, ejusque potius pars quædam ac complementum, obedientiaque istius universæ veluti compendium fuerunt: ipsa etiam illa perpetua vitæ sanctitas, & inoffensus obedientiæ tenor, ad justitiam nostram requirebatur, & suum in ea constituenda locum habuit. Cum enim non solum peccatorum remissio, sed & vitæ hæreditas acquirenda nobis foret; neque legis, cujusjustitia in agendo potissimum consistit, quæque istam formulam habet, quife- cerit ea homo, vivet in iis, jus ac postulatum ignotum foret, illa omnis à sponsore nostro adimpleri debebat, ut nos justi haberemur, atque suffragante ea beatitudinem adsequeremur. Quomodo & Scriptura Christum nobis factum dicit à Deo sapientiam, justitiam, sanctitatem & redemtionem, 1. Cor. 1: 30. cumque finem legis nominat, ad justitiam omni credenti, Rom. 10: 4. atque eum sese legi subjecisse tradit, ut nos redimeret, Gal. 4: 4. quævitæ obedientiam dicunt. Quomodo & obedientia ejus Adami inobedientiæ ab Apostolo opponitur; cujusutriusque in mundo veluti regnum ac hæreditatem describit. Rom. 5: 17, 18, 19.
units.tr: Those go too far who not only distinguish the active and passive obedience of Christ in some way, teaching with certain scrupulous subtleties that the inheritance of life was acquired by the one and the guilt of death removed by the other, but also tear these parts of the single justice away from each other, and all but violate and mangle the justice of Christ. While they forbid all of it to be ascribed to us, and want the active obedience left to Christ alone while only his sufferings and blood are given to us, a view which Olevianus and Piscator once defended with great zeal among our people. On this matter we set down as follows. 1. The obedience of Christ is distinguished into active and passive not without some discord of terms; for all of it is active, and nowhere did his love and obedience shine forth more than in the midst of his sufferings, which without that struggle of love and conflict, and without the labours of a soul seeking the glory of God, would not have had that worth. Now his obedience was especially proved and the ardour of his love displayed, in that he was obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, Phil. 2:8. 2. But it is wrong to make this distinction with the aim of separating the parts, so that by assigning one part of obedience to us they take away the other, claiming the active obedience for Christ himself and leaving us only his blood and the price of his death. These views are unsound, since whatever Christ performed, and whatever he did in living and dying, all of it was required for justice and was owed to us, and it made up the one dikaiōma [δικαίωμα], the one justice finally, which was needed for bringing the sinner to God. This justice is not to be separated, nor is any part of it to be denied, nor finally is it to be placed in this or that part of obedience, but it must be acknowledged and proclaimed whole, since it rises up and is completed from the whole of that obedience. 3. For our salvation could not be procured by his death and sufferings alone. For apart from the fact that not even the sufferings of Christ would have had their worth without that unblemished holiness of life, and were rather a part and completion of it, and a kind of summary of his whole obedience, that very perpetual holiness of life and the unbroken course of his obedience were required for our justice and had their place in establishing it. For since not only the remission of sins but also the inheritance of life was to be acquired for us, and the law, whose justice consists chiefly in doing and which has this formula, "the man who does these things shall live by them," was unknown as a rule and demand, all of that had to be fulfilled by our surety so that we might be held just, and by his support we might attain blessedness. So also Scripture says that Christ was made to us by God wisdom, justice, holiness and redemption, 1 Cor. 1:30; and it names him the end of the law unto justice for everyone who believes, Rom. 10:4; and it teaches that he subjected himself to the law in order to redeem us, Gal. 4:4; and these things they call the obedience of his life. So also his obedience is set by the Apostle against the disobedience of Adam, and he describes the kingdom and inheritance of each in the world, Rom. 5:17, 18, 19.

units.la: XIV. Quod urgent, Christum pro se ipso activam obedientiam de- buisse, eoque nobis eam cedere non posse, leve est.
units.tr: XIV. What they press, that Christ owed active obedience for himself and so could not transfer it to us, is a slight matter.

units.la: Cum rite rem æstimanti verum non sit, Christum per sese divinæ legis postulatis obnoxium fuisse, istumque obedientiæ cursum pro sese debuisse, nec aliter beatitudine potiri potuisse, quam sub lege domina & arbitra: de quo lib. 11. cap. xv. §. 9. actum. Cum sine gloriæ detrimento in terras venire, atq; humanis exuviis se convestire, palamque isto in corpore Deum fateri, rursusque sine certamine, ac longo obedientiæ cursu, ad cœlum contendere potuisset. Hominum enim viatorum iste sub lege statusac servitus est; non Dei filii, in humano corpore hospitantis, terrisque tantum sese ostendentis. 2. Quod autem nunc viatoris personam assumserit, id amoris erga genus humanum, ac ineffabilis cujusdam bonitatis fuit. Quod cum pro nobis omne præstiterit, quicquid illo in statu gessit, nostrum est. Adeoque non absurdum videri debet, cum strictissimam obedientiam isto in statu pro se se debuisse (viator enim, & pro humana gente sponsor erat) interimque eam omnem, pro nobis exhaustam, nobis quoque in bonum cessisse: nam hoc ultro ad statum illum consequitur; nec aliter sponsoris personam gerere poterat: Emisit Deus filium suum—factum legi subjectum, ut eos, qui legi erant subjecti redimeret. Gal. 4. 4, 5.
units.tr: For anyone who weighs the matter rightly, it is not true that Christ was himself bound by the demands of the divine law, and that he had to run this course of obedience for himself, and could not have obtained blessedness except under the law as mistress and judge; this was treated in book 11, chapter 15, §9. He could have come down to earth without loss of glory, clothed himself in human garments, and openly confessed God in that body, and then again, without struggle and a long course of obedience, have made his way to heaven. For that state and servitude belong to men who are wayfarers, not to the Son of God, who dwelt in a human body and showed himself on earth only. 2. But that he took on the person of a wayfarer now was an act of love toward the human race and of a certain ineffable goodness. Since he did everything for us, whatever he performed in that state is ours. Therefore it ought not to seem absurd that, while in that state he owed the strictest obedience for himself (for he was a wayfarer, and surety for the human race), all of that obedience, spent for us, also passed over to us for good; for this follows of its own accord from that state, and he could not otherwise have borne the role of surety: God sent his Son, made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were subject to the law. Gal. 4:4, 5.

units.la: XV. Quod ad cæteras ipsorum rationes attinet, illæ inanibus quibusdam cavillis niituntur, quale est, cum ita instituunt: Unum idemque esse justificationem cum peccatorum remissione; & cui peccata remissa sunt, eum hoc ipso vita æterna hæredem reddi; peccato quippe clausam olim cæli regiam, eo ablato rursus patere; remissionem autem peccatorum solo Christi sanguine obtingere, nec ad id justitia ejus activa opus esse. Quæ collectio non procedit, cum remissio peccatorum & justificatio, quanquam conjuncta, non tamen eadem sint: & remissio peccatorum justificationis pars & gradus tantum sit, præter quam præterea requiritur vitæ æternæ adjudicatio, ad quam perfecta legis obedientia opus est. Ut culpas nostras Christi sanguine elui non satis sit, atque ita impedimentum, quod nos à cœli regia arcebat, tolli, nisi ejus præterea obedientia nos justos, & cœlesti hæreditate non indignos constituat.
units.tr: XV. As for their other arguments, these rest on empty quibbles, such as when they argue thus: that justification and the remission of sins are one and the same; and whoever has had his sins remitted is by that very fact made heir of eternal life; for the heavenly kingdom, once shut by sin, is opened again when sin is taken away; but the remission of sins comes solely through the blood of Christ, and his active justice is not needed for it. This inference does not hold, since the remission of sins and justification, though joined, are not the same; and the remission of sins is only a part and step of justification, beyond which there is also required the adjudication of eternal life, for which the perfect obedience of the law is needed. It is not enough that our guilt be washed away by the blood of Christ, and so the obstacle that shut us out of the heavenly kingdom be removed, unless his obedience also makes us just and not unworthy of the heavenly inheritance.

units.la: XVI. Similis generis est & alia argutatio; qui non injustus est, jam justum esse; sublata enim privatione poni habitum, veluti sublata morte vita, ac nigredine ablata albedo ponitur. Quæ de habitu inhærente ac mutatione physica concludunt, & de sanctificatione agunt; à qua ad mutationem moralem & relativam, atque ad justificationem, non recte transitus fit: in qua multum diversa sunt, reatum auferre, & jus ad vitam æternam dare; auferre mortem, & conferre vitam; quanquam divisa nunquam sint, sed semper inter se conjuncta. Nec aptius concludit, quod de lege addunt, eam aut obedientiam aut pœnam postulare; unde solâ Christi morte illi satisfactum: cum revera utrumque à peccatore postulet; nec ad vitam æternam nisi obedienti ac justo suffragium suum præstet. Nec recte tandem nos obedientiâ legis solvi putant, si Christus pro nobis obedierit: cum aliæ obedientiæ nostræ maneant causæ; rectiusque de morte ac afflictionibus piorum id contra adversæ sententiæ patronos retorquere liceret. Verum hæc quidem missa faciamus.
units.tr: XVI. Another argument of the same sort is this: he who is not unjust is already just; for when privation is removed, the habit is put in its place, as life is put in place of death when death is removed, and whiteness in place of blackness when blackness is removed. They draw these conclusions about an inherent habit and physical change, and they deal with sanctification; but the transition from that to moral and relational change, and to justification, is not rightly made. In these there is great difference: to remove guilt and to give a right to eternal life; to remove death and to confer life; although these are never divided but always joined together. Nor does the argument that they add about the law conclude more aptly, namely that the law demands either obedience or punishment; therefore satisfaction was made for us by the death of Christ alone; for in truth the law demands both from the sinner, and it grants its support to eternal life only to one who is obedient and just. Nor do they rightly think that we are released from the obedience of the law if Christ obeyed for us; since our own obedience remains as a cause of the other obediences; and it would be more correct to turn this back against the defenders of the opposing view, with regard to the death and afflictions of the godly. But let us set these matters aside.

units.la: XVII. Forma iustificationis est universalis huius bimembris iustitiæ Christi imputatio. Rom. 4:11.5:18,19. 1. Cor. 1:30.2.Cor.5:21. quæ dupliciter peragitur, cum à parte Dei, tum nostra. Deus nempe dat, imputando illam nobis, ac si ipsi omnia fecissemus; nos vero eam accipimus fide, per quam illius participes evadimus. Ut remissionem peccatorum & sortem inter sanctificatos accipiant per fidem quæ est in me. Act. 26: 18.
units.tr: XVII. The form of justification is the universal imputation of this twofold justice of Christ. Rom. 4:11; 5:18, 19. 1 Cor. 1:30. 2 Cor. 5:21. This is carried out in two ways, both on God's side and on ours. God gives it by imputing it to us, as if we had done all things ourselves; and we receive it by faith, through which we become partakers of it. That they may receive remission of sins and a lot among those who are sanctified, through the faith that is in me. Acts 26:18.

units.la: XVIII. Consistit autem illa iustitiæ Christi imputatio in duabus partibus 1.in peccatorum remissione:2. in vitæ æternæ adjudicatione. Non enim mera hic tantum venia locum habet.
units.tr: XVIII. The imputation of Christ's righteousness consists of two parts: (1) the remission of sins, and (2) the adjudication of eternal life. For here mere pardon does not hold the place alone.

units.la: XIX. Peccatorum remissio, de qua Apostolus Rom. 4: 6. ex Psal. 32:1. duplici sub similitudine, cum transportationis peccatorum, tum eorundem obtectionis, Christi veluti paludamento ac veste factæ, agit: Beatus, cujus defectio ablata est; cujus peccatum tectum est: præcipuè à satisfactione Christi dependet, ejusque sanguini passim adscribitur: Sanguis Jesu Christi, filii ipsius, purgat nos ab omni peccato:
units.tr: XIX. The remission of sins, of which the Apostle speaks at Rom. 4:6 from Ps. 32:1, is described under a twofold image: both the transference of sins and their covering, as with a cloak or garment made of Christ. Blessed is he whose transgression is taken away, whose sin is covered. It depends chiefly on the satisfaction of Christ, and is everywhere ascribed to his blood: The blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin:

units.la: 1. Joh. 1:7. Sed sanguine pretioso, ut agni inculpati & immaculati, Christi, redemti estis. 1. Pet. 1:19. Multo igitur magis, justificati nunc in sanguine ipsius, salvabimur per ipsum ab ira. Rom. 5:9. Jus autem ad vitam æternam ex Christi justitia & δικαιώματι nascitur; quæ vitæ mortisque obedientiam comprehendit, quæ omnis nobis donatur, ut ea ratione ipsi quoque vitâ non indigni habeamur. Ut jus legis impleatur in nobis. Rom. 8: 4. Ad adducendam justitiam æternam. Dan. 9: 24. Sic enim decet nos implere omnem justitiam. Matth. 3: 15. Quanquam hæc ita non sint divellenda, ut justum inter peccatorum remissionem & novæ justitiæ imputationem, inter satisfactionem Christi & meritum, denique inter obedientiam ejus activam & passivam discrimen ponendum sit: conceptu enim solo illa separantur, reipsa autem conjuncta semper & eadem sunt.
units.tr: 1 John 1:7. But you were redeemed with precious blood, as of a lamb unblemished and spotless, Christ. 1 Pet. 1:19.
