Much more, then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from wrath. Rom. 5:9. The right to eternal life, however, arises from the righteousness and deed of righteousness [δικαιώματι] of Christ, which comprehends his obedience in life and death, and which is all given to us, so that on that account we may be counted worthy of life too. That the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. Rom. 8:4. To bring in everlasting righteousness. Dan. 9:24. For thus it becomes us to fulfil all righteousness. Matt. 3:15. Yet these things are not to be so divided that a distinction must be drawn between the remission of sins and the imputation of new righteousness, between the satisfaction of Christ and his merit, or finally between his active and passive obedience. For these are separated only in thought, but in reality they are always joined and are one and the same.

units.la: XX. Sequitur 2. examinandum, qua via justitiæ Christi participes evadamus. Quæ non alia est quam fides. Sicuti enim justificationis causa principalis est gratia Dei; meritoria, Christi redemtio; formalis, illius ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium; ita instrumentalis, cam apprehendens, unica est fides in sanguine ejus. Rom. 3:24,25. Qua veluti manu Dei gratiam amplectimur, nobisque ipsis applicamus. Quæ Veteris Ecclesiæ perpetua doctrina ad ipsa reformationis tempora duravit; quando ea nondum omni luce extincta, à duobus Belgii tum temporis luminibus, Rudolpho Agricola,& Wesselo Gansfortio, defensa legitur; à Luthero autem, in monasterio, ex sacerdotis senis ore hausta, A. 1518. in Augustinianorum Coenobio publicis thesibus expositta, quanquam ringentibus plurimis, pulcherrimum ad magnum illud Reformationis opus auspicium fecit.
units.tr: XX. Second, we must examine by what way we become partakers of the righteousness of Christ. This way is none other than faith. For just as the principal cause of justification is the grace of God, the meritorious cause is the redemption of Christ, and the formal cause is his propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον], so the instrumental cause, which apprehends it, is faith alone in his blood (Rom. 3:24, 25). By faith we embrace the grace of God as with the hand of God, and apply it to ourselves. This was the constant doctrine of the Ancient Church, and it lasted down to the very times of the Reformation. When the light of it was not yet wholly extinguished, it is read to have been defended by two luminaries of Belgium at that time, Rudolf Agricola and Wessel Gansfort. Luther drew it from the lips of an old priest in the monastery, and in 1518, in the Augustinian convent, he set it forth in public theses. Although very many were thundering against it, this gave the most beautiful beginning to that great work of the Reformation.

units.la: XXI. Fides autem hic consideranda est, non ut ipsa justitia nostra; sive ut δικαίωμα meritum, atque id quod justum facit, quodque vitae petendae causa est; vel ut illud, à parte nostra, quod Deum quomodocunque moveat ad nos justos pronunciandos; vel ut nova foederis conditio, à Deo ex placito electa, atque à nobis praestanda, ex qua, antiquata veteri lege, salutem nunc sperare liceat: illa enim aliena sunt: sed ut medium communionis cum Christo ac justitia ejus; ac ut instrumentum illud, quo donum justitiae in Christo per Euangelium oblatum accipimus. Per illam enim, ut ὁμολογίαν confessionem & assensum nostrum, Christi promissiones accipimus, imo per illam, ut primam productionem Spiritus ipsius, illi inserimur. 1. Cor. 12: 13. Unde apprehensive, instrumentaliter, objective & correlative justificare in scholis dicitur. Qui loquendi modi aliud pro justitiae causa manifesto offerunt, eoque fidem unice dirigunt. Ut inveniar in ipso, non habens meam justitiam, eam ex lege; sed eam, quae est per fidem Christi, justitiam, quae ex Deo est, ad fidem. Phil. 3: 9.
units.tr: XXI. Faith, however, is to be considered here not as our own righteousness; nor as a deed of merit [δικαίωμα], that which makes one righteous and is the ground of seeking life; nor as that which on our side somehow moves God to pronounce us righteous; nor as the new condition of the covenant, chosen by God's decree and to be performed by us, by which, the old law having been abolished, we may now hope for salvation. For these things are foreign to it. Rather, faith is to be considered as the means of communion with Christ and his righteousness, and as that instrument by which we receive the gift of righteousness in Christ offered through the Gospel. For through faith, as our confession [ὁμολογίαν] and assent, we receive the promises of Christ; indeed, through faith, as the first product of his Spirit, we are engrafted into him (1 Cor. 12:13). Hence the schools say that faith justifies apprehensively, instrumentally, objectively and correlatively. Those modes of speaking clearly offer something else as the cause of righteousness, and so direct faith alone toward it. That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith (Phil. 3:9).

units.la: XXII. Qui & loci Rom. 4: 5. sensus est, ubi fides imputari dicitur in Unde fide justitiam. Quae cum non alia fides sit, quam animae de se ipsa desperantis, ac ad arcem salutis confugientis; atque ejus, qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium; satis patet, non dignitatem fidei hic spectari, sed ejus, in quem illa recumbit: cum ipsa illa fides propriis manibus sese omnibus operibus spoliet, atque ad alium, tanquam causam salutis, respectet. Quo modo credentes, & ad Christum, tanquam unicam salutis rupem, sese recipientes, Deus aversari non potest, sed pro justis reputare debet; quod est istud, quod Apostolus dicit, fidem imputari in justitiam. Aliud autem est, justitia quae imputatur; aliud, fides quae justitiam illam accipit; quaeque aliter imputari nobis non potest, vel ad justitiam servire, quam quatenus Christi justitia nititur, eamque apprehendit. Unde, ut fidei ratio in hoc negotio pateat, justificari saepe dicimur fide, per fidem, ex fide, nunquam vero propter fidem; ista enim unius Christi meriti ac sanguinis ratio est. Atque hoc sensu fidem nos justificare ut est foederis gratiae conditio, voce hac recte intellecta, dici potest.
units.tr: XXII. This is also the sense of Rom. 4:5, where faith is said to be imputed "for righteousness." Since this faith is none other than that of a soul despairing of itself and fleeing to the citadel of salvation, and of one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, it is plain enough that the dignity of faith is not what is looked at here, but the dignity of him on whom it rests. For faith itself strips itself of all works with its own hands, and looks to another as the cause of salvation. In this way, God cannot turn away from believers who take refuge in Christ as the sole rock of salvation, but must reckon them righteous. This is what the Apostle means when he says that faith is imputed for righteousness. The righteousness which is imputed is one thing; the faith which receives that righteousness is another. Faith cannot be imputed to us, nor serve for righteousness, except insofar as it rests on the righteousness of Christ and lays hold of it. Hence, so that the reason of faith in this matter may be clear, we are often said to be justified by faith, through faith, from faith, but never on account of faith, for that expression belongs to the merit and blood of Christ alone. In this sense it can rightly be said that we are justified by faith, as faith is the condition of the covenant of grace, provided this word is rightly understood.

units.la: justificari dicimur.
units.tr: We are said to be justified.

units.la: XXIII. Atque hæc quoque ratio est, cur sola fides justificare dicatur: non quod sola inter virtutes ejus meriti ac dignitatis sit, ut pro tota atque unicâ fœderis conditione reputari debeat; sed quod solius fidei sit gratiam Dei accipere & amplecti, ut solius oculi est videre. Cum enim virtutes omnes hisce duabus continentur, fide & charitate, quæ omnem Christianæ animæ affectum exhauriunt; hujus est, Deo sese ac sua dare & offerre, illius autem, Deum sese nobis donantem vicissim accipere & amplecti. Unde sola quoque in accipienda Christi justitia locum habere potest. Cui & aliam rationem Apostolus adjungit; quod per fidem gloriatio exclusa est, quæ in salutis negotio ab homine prorsus abesse debet, Rom. 3: 26, 27, 28. Cum enim aliis virtutibus, ac præcipuè charitate, gloriari homo possit, quod in iis dare aliquid & offerre Deo videatur; sola fides excludit omnem gloriationem, omneque meritum, cum ipsius solum opus sit accipere oblatam gratiam. Qui petit autem & accipit aliquid, ac aliunde beatur, ille certe gloriari non poterit. -
units.tr: XXIII. This too is the reason why faith alone is said to justify: not because it alone among the virtues has such merit and dignity that it must be regarded as the whole and sole condition of the covenant, but because it belongs to faith alone to receive and embrace the grace of God, just as it belongs to the eye alone to see. For although all virtues are contained in these two, faith and love, which exhaust every affection of the Christian soul, it belongs to love to give and offer oneself and one's own to God, and to faith to receive and embrace in turn God giving himself to us. Hence faith alone can have a place in receiving the righteousness of Christ. The Apostle adds another reason to this: that glorying is excluded by faith, which ought to be wholly absent from man in the business of salvation (Rom. 3:26–28). For since a man can glory in other virtues, and especially in love, because in these he seems to give something and offer it to God, faith alone excludes all glorying and all merit, since its only work is to receive the grace offered. Whoever asks for and receives something, and is blessed from elsewhere, certainly cannot glory.

units.la: XXIV. Unde rectè contra Pontificios asserimus, sola nos fide justificari. Quæ ipsa Scripturæ vox est. Sic enim Apostolus Rom. 3: 28. Colligimus igitur fide justificari hominem, sine operibus legis. & Gal. 2: 16. Scientes, non justificari hominem ex operibus legis, sed per fidem Jesu Christi. Atque de fide miraculosâ ipse Christus, Marc. 5: 36. Noli timere, tantum crede. Ubi tamen fides non opponi debet vel gratiæ Dei, vel Christi merito: illæ enim justificationis præcipuæ, sed alterius generis, causæ sunt. Opponenda autem est operibus ac virtutibus quibuscunque aliis, quæ, utcunque cum fide semper conjunctæ, in justificatione tamen nullum pretium habent, nec cum fide ad illam peragendam conspirant. Sed operum potius ac fidei hic pugna est, quomodo Apostolus ex adverso ea inter se componit Rom. 3: 28. Eph. 2: 8, 9. Gratiâ enim salvati estis, per fidem—non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Itaque coexistere quidem eas cum fide concedimus (fidem enim operibus fœtam semper esse oportet) cooperari autem formaliter, ut ajunt, ad justificationem peccatoris, negamus.
units.tr: XXIV. Hence we rightly assert against the Papists that we are justified by faith alone. This is the very language of Scripture. Thus the Apostle, Rom. 3:28: We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law; and Gal. 2:16: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ. And concerning miraculous faith, Christ himself says (Mark 5:36): Do not fear, only believe. Yet faith is not here to be set against the grace of God or the merit of Christ, for these are the chief causes of justification, but of another kind. It is to be set against works and against all other virtues, which, however always joined with faith, have no value in justification and do not work together with faith to bring it about. Rather, the struggle here is between works and faith, and the Apostle sets them against each other in Rom. 3:28 and Eph. 2:8, 9: For by grace you have been saved, through faith—not of works, lest anyone should boast. So we concede that works and faith coexist (for faith must always be fruitful in works), but we deny that works cooperate formally, as they say, in the justification of a sinner.

units.la: XXV. Imo adeo operibus adversatur hac in causâ fides, ut se ipsam quoque excludat, si ut opus consideretur. Quanquam enim in se spectata opus sit, non tamen in justificatione ad istum modum, sed ut opus mere instrumentale consideratur. Ut malè quidam eam ut opus præclarum, & electam à Deo in novo pacto conditionem, verumque δικαίωμα. & & juris nostri ac salutis apud Deum causam, justificare dixerint: quod fine veteris legis probro, ac gratiæ Christi spolio dici non potest. Jultificat enim hac una tantum ratione, quod in Christum suavissime recumbit, istique salutis suæ pignori incubat, quod adspicere perpetuo ac tenerrimo affectu complecti non cessat. Unde fides, ne ut opus justificare putetur, gratia vocem, ac Christi sanguinem, adjunctum plerunque habet, quam Scriptura ut propriam justitiæ causam ostentat, quam fides amplecti tantum ac recipere debet.
units.tr: XXV. Indeed, faith in this matter is so opposed to works that it would even exclude itself if it were regarded as a work. For although, considered in itself, it is a work, it is not considered as a work in justification in that way, but as a purely instrumental one. Certain men have wrongly said that faith justifies as a noble work, a condition chosen by God in the new covenant, a true deed of right, and the cause of our right and salvation before God. This cannot be said without disgrace to the old law and robbery of the grace of Christ. For faith justifies in this one way only: that it rests most sweetly on Christ, lies upon him as the pledge of its salvation, and does not cease to look upon him and embrace him with a constant and tender affection. Hence faith, lest it be thought to justify as a work, usually has joined to it the word grace and the blood of Christ, which Scripture sets forth as the proper cause of righteousness, which faith ought only to embrace and receive.

units.la: XXVI. Ut vero amplius pateat, quâ ratione fides in hoc negotio versetur, actus ejus in salute apprehendenda, ac justificatione abfolvenda, considerare par est: qui, juxta illa quæ cap. superiori §. 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. dicta sunt, tres concipi possunt, 1. actus dispositivus vel præparatorius, est fidei assensus, cum generalis, tum specialis, quo remissionem peccatorum in Christo expositam esse omnibus credentibus, adeoque & sibi fi credat, peccator de longinquo veluti contemplatur. 2. actus juftificatorius formaliter, quo Christum cum amore recipiens, & tendens veluti manum, illum apprehendit cum omnibus ejus meritis, inque eum suaviter recumbit. Ille enim sese reclinantis ac recumbentis animæ actus proprie justificat. Quod & fides eodem illo actu directo cognoscere potest. Illum autem præcipuè excipit 3. actus consolatorius, seu reflexus & consequens, qui fidei corroboratæ fructus est; quo, intimo divinæ gratiæ sensu perfusa, de adepta justificatione ac salute gloriatur. Justificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus ad Deum. Rom. 5: 1.
units.tr: XXVI. To make clearer how faith is involved in this business, we should consider its acts in laying hold of salvation and in being absolved in justification. According to what was said in the previous chapter, §§ 9, 10, 11, 12 and 14, these can be conceived as three. (1) The dispositive or preparatory act is the assent of faith, both general and special, by which a sinner, believing that forgiveness of sins has been set forth in Christ for all believers, and so believes it for himself, looks on it as from afar. (2) The formally justificatory act is that by which he receives Christ with love, stretches out his hand as it were, grasps him with all his merits, and rests sweetly upon him. For this act of the soul leaning back and resting is what properly justifies, and faith can know this by that same direct act. Especially following it is (3) the consolatory act, or reflexive and consequent act, which is the fruit of strengthened faith. By it, bathed in the inner sense of divine grace, the believer glories in the justification and salvation obtained. Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God. Rom. 5:1.

units.la: XXVII. Hic autem universæ justificationis ordo & processus est 1. decrevit eam Deus nobis ab æterno. Scriptura prævidens, Deum ex fide juftificare gentes. Gal. 3: 8. 11. promisit post mox lapsum. Ponam inimicitiam inter te, & inter fœminam, & inter femen tuum, & femen ejus. Gen. 3: 15. 111. Impetravit eam Christus morte & resurrectione sua. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est. Rom. 8: 34. Qui resuscitatus est propter justificationem nostri. Rom. 4: 25. quem in finem Patri exhibuit in sacrario cœlesti passiones & meritum suum, eo nomine nos immunes vindicando à merito condemnationis: in qua fatisfactione præstita acquievit Pater. unde secuta fuit à parte Dei reconciliatio nostra, seu peccatorum remissio. Qui primus justificationis est actus extra nos factus. iv. Pronunciat sententiam illam Deus mox ad fidem nostram, qui recumbimus in ipsum per Christum. qui est actus fecundus justificationis, in foro conscientiæ, per quem Sp. S. nobis intimat ea quæ facta sunt à Patre & filio. Sentit autem eam ex illa Sp. S. intimatione fidei, actu non solum directo, sed & reflexo, deque gratia Dei accepta lætatur: & sic nos ipsos justificamus, pronunciando nos immunes à merito condemnationis propter justitiam Christi nobis imputatam & fide apprehensam, quæ non tam justificatio, quam peractæ justificationis perceptio & gustus est. v. Confirmatur per bona opera, ut certissima Spiritus in nobis habitantis signa: unde iterum nos pronunciamus justos & immunes à merito condemnationis. Atque ex iis etiam alterius generis justificatio oritur; de qua deinceps. vi. Publice autem ea declarabitur ac consummabitur in ultimo mundi actu, ad supremę illius sententiæ pronunciationem. Ex verbis enim tuis justificaberis. Matth. 12:37. conf. c. 25:34.
units.tr: XXVII. The order and process of the whole justification is this. (i) God decreed it for us from eternity. Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith. Gal. 3:8, 11. (ii) He promised it soon after the fall. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. Gen. 3:15. (iii) Christ obtained it by his death and resurrection. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died. Rom. 8:34. He was raised for our justification. Rom. 4:25. To this end he presented his sufferings and merit to the Father in the heavenly sanctuary, claiming us as free from the merit of condemnation; the Father was satisfied with this satisfaction rendered. From this followed, on God's part, our reconciliation, or the remission of sins. This is the first act of justification, done outside us. (iv) God pronounces that sentence at once to our faith, as we lean on him through Christ. This is the second act of justification, in the forum of conscience, by which the Holy Spirit makes known to us what has been done by the Father and the Son. We perceive it from that intimation of the Spirit by faith, by an act not only direct but also reflexive, and rejoice in the grace of God received. Thus we ourselves justify, declaring ourselves free from the merit of condemnation because of the righteousness of Christ imputed to us and apprehended by faith; this is less justification itself than the perception and taste of justification already accomplished. (v) It is confirmed by good works, as the most certain signs of the Spirit dwelling in us; and so again we pronounce ourselves just and free from the merit of condemnation. From these also arises another kind of justification, of which more later. (vi) It will be declared publicly and brought to completion in the final act of the world, at the pronouncement of the supreme sentence. For by your words you will be justified. Matt. 12:37; cf. 25:34.

units.la: XXVIII. Atque huc referri potest vulgata distinctio justificationis in actívam & passívam; quarum illa Dei est, hæc hominis. Activa peragitur, non ab æterno proprie (illud enim decretum justificandi dicit, quale Deus ante fidem nostram, imo ante Christi adventum habuit. Scriptura prævidens, Deum ex fide justificare gentes. Gal. 3:8.) sed in tempore, partim in cœlo, post absolutas passiones Christi, quando Christus advocatus noster, causam nostram agit, & Pater nos absolvit: Angelus, advocatus unus ex mille——& dicit, redime ipsum, ne descendat in foveam, inveni lytrum. Job 33:23,24. partim in conscientia nostra, simul ac credimus: estque sententiæ absolutionis veluti prolatio, &, ad fidem nostram, pronunciatio. Quos vocavit, hos & justificavit. Rom. 8:29. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus est qui justificat. com. 33. Passiva sententiæ illius pronunciatæ sensum & gustum, acde accepta absolutione gaudium dicit, ac præcipuè tertio isto fidei actu, quem. §. xxvi. vidimus, obsignante Sp. sancto, absolvitur. In quo etiam credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis sancto. Eph. 1:13.
units.tr: XXVIII. Here may be referred the common distinction of justification into active and passive. The active belongs to God, the passive to man. Active justification is carried out not properly from eternity (for that word refers to the decree to justify which God had before our faith, indeed before the coming of Christ: Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, Gal. 3:8), but in time: partly in heaven, after the sufferings of Christ are finished, when Christ our advocate pleads our cause and the Father absolves us: an angel, one advocate out of a thousand... and he says, Redeem him, that he not go down into the pit; I have found a ransom. Job 33:23, 24. And partly in our conscience, as soon as we believe; it is, as it were, the utterance of the sentence of absolution and, for our faith, its pronouncement. Those whom he called, these he also justified. Rom. 8:29. Who will bring charges against God's elect? God is the one who justifies. ibid. v. 33. Passive justification means the sense and taste of that pronounced sentence and joy at the absolution received; and it is sealed especially by that third act of faith, which we saw in § 26, the Holy Spirit setting his seal on it. In whom you also, having believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise. Eph. 1:13.

units.la: XXIX. Quando ergo activa & passiva justificatio simul existere dicitur, id non tam de animæ sensu, præcipuè autem de actu ejus reflexo seu ultimo, sed de actu fidei secundo, seu formaliter justificatorio intelligendum est. Fidem enim natura justificationem præcedere necesse est; quæque eam potius sequitur, cum frustra in Christum recumbere nemo possit. Ast longo eam sæpe intervallo demum subsequitur ille gratiæ divinæ sensus, & penetrabilis illa animæ dulcedo, ex justificatione orta.
units.tr: XXIX. When, therefore, active and passive justification are said to exist together, this must be understood not so much of the sense of the soul, and especially not of its reflexive or last act, but of the second act of faith, which is formally justificatory. For by nature faith must precede justification, and it rather follows it, since no one can lean on Christ in vain. But that sense of divine grace and that penetrating sweetness of soul, arising from justification, often follows only after a long interval.

units.la: XXX. Ex quibus jam patet, justificationem unicam & æqualem esse in omnibus fidelibus, ac semel factam manere immutabilem & irrevocabilem; cum ea nihil nisi Dei judicis sententia sit, ad Christi intercessionem lata, quæ semel pronunciari tantum potest, atque inde in æternum valet. Aliter ac Pontificii, aliqued docent: qui, cum justitiam nostram in operibus nostris ac qualitatibus inhærentibus quærant, variam eam & mutabilem, nec omnium fidelium æqualem ac parem facere coguntur. Qui & Remonstrantium ex eodem fundamento error est; qui justificationem distinguunt in semiplenam, hujus vitæ; & plenam, qualem eam in morte demum faciunt. Quæ aliena sunt, & occultam labem habent. Non enim illa nostris actibus, sed unico Dei actu peragitur, nec nostro aliquo opere, sed Christi solius merito nititur. Quare & unica, & perfecta, ac immutabilis omnium justificatio est. Quanquam sensum illius sæpe obscurari, nitoremque ejus infuscari contingit: quo sensu ea iterari & corroborari quoque dicitur; ad exemplum quasi remissionis à nobis fratribus iterato concessæ, de qua Matth. 18:21,22. Dixit Petrus, Domine, quoties in me peccabit frater meus, & remittam ipsi? usque septies? dixit ipsi Jesus, non dico, usque septies, sed usque septuagies septies &c.
units.tr: XXX. From these things it is now plain that justification is single and equal in all believers, and once made remains unchangeable and irrevocable. For it is nothing but the sentence of God the judge, pronounced at the intercession of Christ, which can be pronounced only once and thereafter holds good forever. The Papists teach otherwise, and some others as well: since they seek our righteousness in our works and inherent qualities, they are compelled to make it varied and changeable, and not equal and the same in all the faithful. The error of the Remonstrants comes from the same foundation: they divide justification into a half-complete one of this life and a full one, which they make to come only at death. These are foreign to the matter and have a hidden flaw. For justification is accomplished not by our acts but by the single act of God, and rests not on any work of ours but on the merit of Christ alone. Therefore justification of all is one, perfect and unchangeable. Although it often happens that its sense is obscured and its brightness dimmed, in which sense it is also said to be repeated and strengthened, as in the case of the forgiveness that we grant to our brothers again and again, of which Matt. 18:21, 22: Peter said, Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times? Jesus said to him, I do not say up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven, etc.

units.la: XXXI. Atque ita, verà justitiâ assertâ, veroque ejus adipiscendæ modo tradito, nunc ex adverso operum justitia, cui ex naturali præjudicio humanum genus tam impense studet, removenda est.
units.tr: XXXI. And so, with true righteousness asserted and the true way of obtaining it set out, now the righteousness of works, to which the human race by its natural prejudice is so eagerly devoted, must be removed from the opposite side.

units.la: XXXII. Operariorum dux & princeps mox à lapsu introducitur Cainus; qui externis prærogativis sese jactasse, atque frivolis quibusdam modis Dei pacem quæsiisse videtur. Cui Apostolus ex adverso Abelem opponit, ut justitiæ fidei typum, Hebr. 11:4. Atque idem duorum fratrum, Ismaelis & Isaci; ac post hos, Esavi ac Jacobi, fatum fuit: quos, fratrum utrobique primogenitos, diversam justitiæ sectam tenuisse, ac ob externam quandam prærogativam, quâ sese supra fratres efferre poterant, operariis istis præluisse, Apostolus Rom. 9. & Gal. 4. ostendit. Atque eadem carnalis Israelis labes fuit; qui cum externo quoque decore supra alias gentes effulgerent, quarum primogeniturAM videbantur possidere, id in justitiæ causam arripuerunt. Ignorantes enim justitiam Dei, & suam quærentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non subjecerunt se. Rom. 10:3. Ab Israële deinceps in novam Christianorum Ecclesiam hoc fermentum propagatum est, sub cujus initia jam quidam sinceritatem doctrinæ adulterare, & de fide ac operibus, deque Judaismo ac Christianismo, collyram facere nitebantur: contra quos Paulus acriter invehitur in epist. ad Gal. Quanquam vicit tandem ista tabes, ac alio schemate operum justitiam tandem invexit Pelagius, insignis Ecclesiæ corruptor; ac post eum Scholastici. Imo hæc falsarum omnium religionum unica radix, hoc que tetrum illud absinthium, & infelix illa herba est, quæ nitidum Ecclesiæ campum corrupit ac perdidit. Et universa præcipuè Papismi moles non alio tibicine magis nititur. Ne de reliquis sectis dicam.
units.tr: XXXII. The leader and prince of the workers is introduced at once after the fall: Cain, who seems to have boasted of external privileges and to have sought God's peace by certain frivolous means. Against him the Apostle sets Abel as the type of the righteousness of faith, Heb. 11:4. The same fate befell the two brothers Ishmael and Isaac, and after them Esau and Jacob. The Apostle shows in Rom. 9 and Gal. 4 that these, the firstborn of their respective brothers, held a different sect of righteousness and, because of some external privilege by which they could raise themselves above their brothers, went before those workers. The same fault of carnal Israel was there too: since they shone with external splendour above other nations, whose firstborn they seemed to possess, they seized on this as the ground of righteousness. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God. Rom. 10:3. From Israel this leaven was afterwards spread into the new Church of Christians; at its very beginning some were already trying to corrupt the purity of doctrine and to make a collyrium of faith and works, of Judaism and Christianity. Against them Paul inveighs sharply in the epistle to the Galatians. Yet this plague at last prevailed, and under another guise Pelagius, a notorious corrupter of the Church, at last brought in the righteousness of works, and after him the Scholastics. Indeed this is the single root of all false religions, this is that foul wormwood and unhappy herb which has corrupted and ruined the bright field of the Church. And the whole mass of Papism above all rests on no other prop. I say nothing of the other sects.

units.la: XXXIII. Præscribit autem contra operum justitiam consideratio
units.tr: XXXIII. Against the righteousness of works, consideration of the following points prescribes itself.

units.la: 1. tum peccati, quo omnis ejus spes decollavit; 2. tum gratiæ & Evangelii, quæ inanis redditur peregrina illa justitia admissa; quæque præcipuè gloriationem peccatoris ferre non potest, quam vigentibus operibus excludere impossibile: Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur, Eph. 2:9. coll. Rom. 3:27. 3. tum & legis ipsius, quæ, perfectissimam sanctitatis formulam exhibens, qualemcunque illam peccatoris obedientiam pro justitia accipere non potest; nec laudare eam, sed redarguere potius tenetur. Nam non est homo, qui non peccat. 1. Reg. 8:46. Omnes enim peccarunt, & posteriores sunt gloriâ Dei. Rom. 3:23. 4. Denique, si illam operum justitiam urgere libet, vel ea in irregenitis, vel in regenitis spectanda erit: illos quod attinet, cum fide careant, semper peccare, Rom. 14:23. Hebr. 11:6. hos vero, cum regeniti sint, justificatos jam esse; adeoque opera non præcedere justificationem, vel producere eam, sed illam sequi, patet. Ut in Abrahami exemplo apparuit: Credidit autem Abrahamus Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam ── Non scriptum autem est propter eum solum, quod hoc imputatum fuerat ei: sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est ut imputetur, iis nimirum qui credunt in eum &c. Rom. 4:3,23,24. Adeo ut opera in nullum censum venire hic possint. Quoi quomodo peculiarius observandum sit contra speciales operum formas, sub quibus eas obtrudunt adversarii, inferius videbimus.
units.tr: (1) First, of sin, by which every hope of such righteousness is cut off. (2) Second, of the grace of the Gospel, which is made empty if that foreign righteousness is admitted, and which especially cannot bear the boasting of a sinner. That boasting cannot be excluded while works remain in force: Not of works, lest anyone should boast, Eph. 2:9, compare Rom. 3:27. (3) Third, of the law itself*, which sets out the most perfect formula of holiness and cannot accept any obedience of a sinner, however it may be described, as righteousness. It is bound not to praise such obedience but rather to condemn it: For there is not a man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, Rom. 3:23. (4) Finally, if one insists on pressing that righteousness of works, it must be considered either in the unregenerate or in the regenerate. As for the unregenerate, since they lack faith, they always sin, Rom. 14:23, Heb. 11:6. As for the regenerate, since they have been regenerated, it is clear that they are already justified, and so works do not precede justification or produce it, but follow it. This appeared in the example of Abraham: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. But it was not written for his sake alone, that it was reckoned to him, but also for ours, to whom it will be reckoned, namely for those who believe in him, etc., Rom. 4:3, 23, 24. So works can come into no account here at all. How this is to be observed in particular against the special forms of works under which the adversaries thrust them forward, we shall see below.

units.la: XXXIV. Superest tandem perlustrandus tertius hominis status, ut de peccatore regenitus factus est; ac, pro illo cujus statu, diversa quædam justificationis ratio ac facies consideranda est; justificatio nimirum, non peccatoris, sed justi, quæ non tantum fide, verum etiam per opera fit: quam Apostolus Rom. 8:3. insinuat, dum omne legis δικαίωμα in nobis implere debere contendit; quod nondum ad plenum fit, quamdiu ea, in peccatorem corruptum dominatur &, ut δύναμις ἁμαρτίας, peccatum potius proritat & incitat: ut illum non solum Christi capitis justitiâ indui, ac veste illa tegi, sed propria quoque sanctitate decorum, & legi 111. Iustificatio justi. legi conformem esse, atque ea denique assentiente justum & inculpatum esse oporteat.
units.tr: XXXIV. It remains at last to survey the third state of man, when the sinner has become regenerate. For this state a different manner and face of justification must be considered: the justification not of the sinner but of the righteous man, which takes place not by faith alone but also through works. Paul hints at this in Rom. 8:3, when he maintains that the whole righteous requirement of the law must be fulfilled in us. This is not yet fully done, as long as sin, as the power of sin, rules in the corrupt person and rather stirs up and incites sin. Hence it is fitting that the person be not only clothed with the righteousness of Christ the head and covered by that garment, but also adorned with his own holiness, conformed to the law, and finally, with the law's assent, be just and blameless.

units.la: XXXV. Sicut enim duplex est hominis accusatio, aut de reatu, aut de hypocrisi; & duplex justitia, una imputata, quae priori accusationi occurrit; altera inhaerens, per quam de hypocrisi purgatur: ita duplex quoque est hominis justificatio, atque ita recte appellari potest; nihil enim attinet verbi superstitione laborare. Illa prima justificatio, haec secunda dici potest: illa justitia Christi imputata, haec inhaerente hominis sanctitate nititur: illa est impii, haec justi: illa consistit in peccatorum remissione, haec in justitiae inhaerentis, non quidem perfectae, attamen sincerae, agnitione: illa perfecta, haec imperfecta est: illa denique fide peragitur, haec ex operibus fluit. Utraque autem gratia Christi nititur; cum opera regenitorum non a lege, sed a gratia & Spiritu Christi proficiscantur, atque inde quoque habeant, quod, imperfecta licet, tamen apud Deum laudem habeant. Atque hoc sensu intelligi rectissime videntur, quaecunque de justificatione nostri ex operibus gratiae, fidei, vel Evangelii, deque eorum ad justificationem necessitate & concursu, passim in Scripturis, praecipue N. T. occurrunt.
units.tr: XXXV. For just as man's accusation* is twofold, either concerning guilt or concerning hypocrisy, and righteousness is twofold, one imputed, which meets the former accusation, and the other inherent, by which he is cleansed of hypocrisy, so too man's justification is twofold, and can rightly be called so. There is no point in labouring over a word out of superstition. The first justification may be called the former, the second the latter. The former rests on the righteousness of Christ imputed, the latter on the holiness of man inherent in him. The former is of the ungodly, the latter of the righteous. The former consists in the remission of sins, the latter in the acknowledgement of an inherent righteousness, not indeed perfect but nonetheless sincere. The former is perfect, the latter imperfect. Finally, the former is accomplished by faith, the latter flows from works. Yet both rest on the grace of Christ, since the works of the regenerate proceed not from the law but from the grace and Spirit of Christ, and therefore have this too: that, though imperfect, they have praise before God. It seems that in this sense alone can be rightly understood whatever passages in Scripture, especially in the New Testament, speak everywhere of our justification by works, grace, or the Gospel, and of the necessity and concurrence of these for justification.

units.la: XXXVI. Multum enim discrepat haec justificatio a Pontificiorum sensu, qui etiam primam & secundam justificationem loquuntur; sed quae utraque ipsis inhaerens est, gradibus & protectu solo differens; utraque denique nostro merito nititur; utraque denique nos Deo gratos, & ad remissionem peccatorum aptos facit. Nobis vero utraque nititur Christi solius merito; & prior quidem in justitia Christi imputata consistit, & remissionem peccatorum spectat; altera autem per Spiritum ejus in regeneratione nostra peragitur, nec ad remissionem peccatorum respectum habet. Cumque ea inhaerente justitia ac interna sanctitate hominem induat, ille ex justitia ista, imperfecta quidem, attamen sincera, justus quoque appellatur, juxta illud 1. Joh. 3:7. Qui justitiam facit, justus est.
units.tr: XXXVI. This justification differs greatly from the sense of the Papists, who also speak of a first and a second justification. Both of these, they say, are inherent in us, differing only in degrees and progress. Both finally rest on our merit, and both finally make us acceptable to God and fit for the remission of sins. For us, on the other hand, both rest on the merit of Christ alone. The former indeed consists in the imputed righteousness of Christ and regards the remission of sins. The latter is accomplished through his Spirit in our regeneration and has no regard to the remission of sins. Since this inherent righteousness and inward holiness clothes a man, he is also called just from that righteousness, though imperfect but sincere, according to 1 John 3:7: He who does righteousness is righteous.

units.la: XXXVII. Atque inservit haec diversae justitiae ac justificationis confideratio ad difficultates nonnullas, quae ex Scripturis nectuntur, solvendas. Ac spectat huc justitia causa, quam appellant (licet rectius justitia particularis dicatur) ejusdemque generis justificatio, cujus in Psalmis, atque aliis Scripturis frequens mentio est. Saepe enim sancti ex causa suae fiducia ad eam provocasse leguntur. Unde & Dei de Jobo testimonium: Non est similis ei in terra, vir integer, rectus, timens Deí, & recedens a malo. malo. cap. 1:8. coll. 42:8. Deque Phineazi facto: Surrexit Phineas, & judicium exercuit ; & reputatum est ei ad justitiam, in atatem & atatem, usque in saeculum. Pfal. 106:30,31. coll. Num.25:12,13 Et Paulus de ie ipso: Nullius mihi conscius sum, sed per hoc non justificatus sum. 1.Cor. 4:4.
units.tr: XXXVII. This consideration of different kinds of righteousness and justification serves to resolve some difficulties that arise from Scripture. To this belongs the righteousness of a cause, as it is called (though it might more correctly be called particular righteousness), and the justification of the same kind, which is frequently mentioned in the Psalms and in other Scriptures. For we read that the saints often appealed to it on the ground of their own confidence. Hence also God's testimony about Job: There is none like him on earth, a man blameless, upright, fearing God and turning from evil, Job 1:8, compare 42:8. And the deed of Phinehas: Phinehas stood up and executed judgement; and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever, Ps. 106:30, 31, compare Num. 25:12, 13. And Paul of himself: I am conscious of nothing against myself, but by this I am not justified, 1 Cor. 4:4.

units.la: XXXVIII. Et non alia facilior videtur Jacobum cum Paulo conciliandi ratio. Diversus enim utriusque Apostoli scopus est. Nam Paulus data opera causas remissionis peccatorum inquirit: Jacobus istam quaestionem ibi quidem non attingit, sed de fidei sinceritate agit, quam ex operibus ostendi & monstrari jubet: ille justitiam imputatam loquitur, hic sanctitatem internam ac inhaerentem praedicat; quae utraque in fidelibus suas partes habet. Ille distertis verbis de justificatione peccatoris, hic de justificatione justi agit; & in exemplum Abrahamum adduacit, cujus obedientiam in offerendo Isaaco laudat; quam longo tempore, postquam ex fide justificatus esset, expletam constat, ut non justificationi, sed fidei ejus probandae, ac sinceritati illius praedicandae, eam adduci pateat, Jas 21,23. Unde cum fidem operibus Abrahami cooperatam, atque ex illis consummatam dicit Jas 22. non justificationem ejus a peccato spectat, quam fide peractam testatur. Jas 23. sed fidem ejus non ignavam, qualis tum pseudo-Christianorum quorundam ratio erat, sed foecundam, & bonis operibus foetam, fuisse docet. Ut Abrahamus de hypocrisi, atque inani isto fidei ludibrio, quo plerique Christiano nomini illudebant, purgatus satis foret; atque ita fides ejus ex operibus perfecta fuerit. Atque ad iltum tandem modum concludit Apostolus: Videtis igitur, quod ex operibus justificetur homo, & non ex fide tantum. Jas 24.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Nor does there seem to be any easier way of reconciling James with Paul. The aim of each Apostle is different. Paul deliberately inquires into the causes of the remission of sins. James does not touch that question there, but treats of the sincerity of faith, which he bids be shown and demonstrated by works. Paul speaks of imputed righteousness, James proclaims inward and inherent holiness, and each of these has its place in believers. Paul speaks in plain words of the justification of a sinner, James of the justification of a righteous man. For an example he brings forward Abraham, whose obedience in offering Isaac he praises. It is evident that this was accomplished a long time after Abraham had been justified by faith, so that it is plain it was brought forward not for his justification but to prove and proclaim the sincerity of his faith, Jas. 2:21, 23. Hence when James says that faith was co-operating with the works of Abraham and made perfect by them, Jas. 2:22, he is not looking at Abraham's justification from sin, which he attests was accomplished by faith. Jas. 2:23. He teaches rather that Abraham's faith was not idle, as was the case with certain pseudo-Christians of that time, but fruitful and full of good works. Thus Abraham was sufficiently cleansed of hypocrisy and that empty mockery of faith with which many made a joke of the Christian name, and so his faith was made perfect by works. And the Apostle finally concludes in this manner: You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only, Jas. 2:24.

units.la: XXXIX. Atque haec fuit peccatoris per omnia saecula justificatio. Discrimen vero illius sub V. & N.T. est, quod justitia illorum perfecta, & N.T. τετελειωμένη consummata non fuit; quia nondum habuerunt jus gloriandi, quod nullum amplius a se chirographum exigi poslet. Peccatum enim erat in mundo, Rom. 5: 13 & sic aliquid operans iram, Rom. 4: 15, & maledictio, Gal. 3:10. introduci poterat. Patribus enim fides promissionis ad justitiam pariebat exspectationem futurae reconciliationis: Israelitis autem ea exspectatio & reatus nondum abolitus, occasione transgressionis eorum, advexit magnum onus & sarcinam praeceptorum carnalium, quibus chirographum ab iis exigebatur. Col 2: 14. Inde remissio peccatorum factorum, antequam Christus proponeretur ἱλαστήριον per fidem in sanguine ejus, vocatur πάρεσις, non ἄφεσις, transmissio. missio, dissimulatio, non remissio, Rom. 3:25. Nunc vero adducta justitia faculorum, Dan. 9:24. & deleto peccato, Zach. 3: 9. justificamur sine expectatione reconciliationis, ulla querimonia, aut opere servili, aut commemoratione peccati, tanquam adhuc superstitis & nondum deleti, neque quicquam amplius à nobis exigitur faciendum propter peccatum & reatum, tanquam ad ejus expiationem. Quae est illa remissio peccatorum promissa sub N. T. Jer. 31:31. Nam condonabo peccata ipsorum, & peccatorum eorum non recordabor amplius. Conf. Hebr. 8:12. 10:17. sicut Eph. 1:7. & Col. 1:14. conjungitur redemtio & remissio, quam habemus in Christo. Unde sub N. T. ita proponitur justificationis, & simul Euangelii summa, Act. 13:38, 39. Notum igitur sit vobis, fratres, annunciari vobis remissionem peccatorum per istum (Christum) & ab omnibus, quibus non potuistis per legem Mosis justificari, per hunc, credentem quemvis justificari.
units.tr: XXXIX. And this was the justification of the sinner in every age. The difference between it under the Old and the New Testament is that their righteousness was not consummated* [τετελειωμένη], as it is under the New Testament, because they did not yet have the right to boast, since no further bond could be demanded from them against themselves. For sin was in the world, Rom. 5:13, and so there could be introduced something working wrath, Rom. 4:15, and a curse, Gal. 3:10. For the promise of faith brought the Fathers to righteousness, with the expectation of a future reconciliation. But for the Israelites that expectation, and the guilt not yet abolished, brought on account of their transgressions a great burden and load of carnal precepts, by which the bond was demanded of them, Col. 2:14. Hence the remission of sins previously committed, before Christ was set forth as propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον] through faith in his blood, is called passing over [πάρεσις], not remission [ἄφεσις]: passing over, transmission, that is, overlooking, not remission, Rom. 3:25. But now, everlasting righteousness is brought in, Dan. 9:24, and sin is removed, Zech. 3:9, so that we are justified without waiting for reconciliation, without any complaint, without any servile work, without any recollection of sin as if it still survived and was not yet removed, and nothing more is demanded of us to be done on account of sin and guilt, as if for its expiation. This is that remission of sins promised under the New Testament: Jer. 31:31, For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. Compare Heb. 8:12, 10:17. Just as Eph. 1:7 and Col. 1:14 join redemption and remission, which we have in Christ. Hence under the New Testament this is set forth as the sum of justification and at the same time of the Gospel, Acts 13:38, 39: Be it known to you therefore, brethren, that through this man (Christ) remission of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.

units.la: XL. Ita tradita & asserta Ecclesiae de justificatione doctrina, nunc ex adverso spuriam illam justitiam, qua operarii omnes coram Dei tribunali miserè adeo sese jactant, variasque ejus formas ac colores, contemplemur. Quae labes cum per omnes extra Ecclesiam sectas dispersa sit, & non uno vultu sese prodat, nos in Judaeis, Pontificiis, ac Socinianis eorumque asseclis, justitiariorum sectae principibus, eam praecipuè lustrabimus.
units.tr: XL. Having set out and asserted the Church's doctrine of justification, let us now look from the opposite side at that spurious righteousness in which all workers so wretchedly boast before God's judgment seat, and at its various forms and colours. Since this stain is spread through all the sects outside the Church and does not show itself in one face, we shall examine it chiefly among the Jews, the Papists and the Socinians and their followers, the leaders of the sect of self-righteous people.

units.la: XLI. Ac Judaeos quidem in gravi hoc capite non mediocriter offendisse Apostolus testatur Rom. 9:31, 32. Israel autem prosequens legem rum. justitia, ad legem justitiae non pervenit. quamobrem? quia non ex fide, sed quasi ex operibus. Non quod sese insontes prorsus ac puros exististimarent, vel culpas suas facillimo pecudum sanguine elui putarent: sed quod ex sacrificiis, reliquoque cultu partem justitiae non exiguam facerent; & praeterDei gratiam, moralem praeterea caeremonialemque legem adcam conficiendam advocarent. Quae divinae gratiae ac propriae justitiae miscela, atque utriusque corruptio erat, ac Deum denique ex placito peccatorem justificare faciebat. Quo nihil magis naturae ac sanctitati ejus adversum: cum enim in praeceptis Dei ceremonialibus nulla sanctitatis ejus expressio, nec imago ejus sita foret; sed illa potius esset praecepta non bona, in quibus non vivitur, Ezech 20:11,12,25,27. nulla quidem dogmata ac placita justificare posse Apostolus recte urget Eph. 2:15. Legem praeceptorum, in placitis consistentem, ad nihilum redegit. coll. Col. 2:14. & Hebr. 7:18. Rescissio quidem fit precedentis mandati, propter infirmitatem tem ejus & inutilitatem. Idemque de legis moralis operibus concludit, ex communi generis humani peccato, ac superveniente salutis promisso in Christo; quae doctrinae capita, assertâ operum justitiâ, labare, in epist. ad Rom. & Gal. pluribus urget.
units.tr: XLI. The Apostle testifies that the Jews stumbled considerably at this serious point, Rom. 9:31, 32: "Israel, following after the law of righteousness, has not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because not by faith, but as it were by works." It was not that they thought themselves wholly innocent and pure, or that they supposed their sins could be washed away by the easy blood of cattle. Rather, they made no small part of their righteousness out of the sacrifices and the rest of the worship, and besides God's grace they called in the moral and ceremonial law to complete it. This mixture of divine grace with their own righteousness, and the corruption of both, made God justify the sinner by his good pleasure. Nothing is more opposed to his nature and holiness. For since no expression of his holiness, and no image of him, was set forth in God's ceremonial precepts, those were rather "statutes that are not good, in which they shall not live" (Ezek. 20:11, 12, 25, 27). The Apostle rightly insists that no doctrines or decrees can justify: "He abolished in his flesh the law of commandments, consisting in ordinances" (Eph. 2:15; compare Col. 2:14 and Heb. 7:18: "There is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before, for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof"). He draws the same conclusion about the works of the moral law, from the common sin of mankind and from the promise of salvation in Christ that supervenes. He presses this in many places in the epistles to the Romans and the Galatians, where, once the righteousness of works is asserted, these heads of doctrine totter.

units.la: XLII. Nec Judaicum fermentum satis caverunt Pontificii, sed infincero isto tumore massam quoque suam corrupti paulatim siverunt; dumque legem cum Euangelio, propriam justitiam cum justitiâ Christi, atque opera cum fide commiscuerunt, nec fidei nec operum justitiam retinuerunt.
units.tr: XLII. Nor did the Papists guard sufficiently against the Jewish leaven. Through this insincere swelling they gradually let their own mass be corrupted too. While they mingled law with Gospel, their own righteousness with Christ's righteousness, and works with faith, they retained neither the righteousness of faith nor the righteousness of works.

units.la: XLIII. Fidei enim justificationem adeo ignorant, ut in concilio Tridentino, cum de Lutheri dogmate ageretur, solâ nos fide justificari; verborum istorum sensum plerique non caperent. Ipsi autem statuerunt, fide, quo nomine generalem Christianae veritatis persuasionem intelligebant (quae tamen ad peccati agnitionem, inferni metum, spem salutis, Dei dilectionem, novae vitae propositum &c. duceret) hominem justificari dispositive & inchoative; quatenus nos aptos reddit ad justitiam internam, primumque ad rectum istum animi statum, in quo Deo placere possumus, & per quem justi sumus, aditum dat. Hanc praeparationem sequi volunt ipsam justificationem, quam non nisi gradibus quibusdam absolvunt, pro sanctitatis videlicet incremento, primam eam & secundam statuentes. Ac priorem quidem per baptismum, ex mera Dei gratia, sine operibus, contingere ajunt; & in peccatorum remissione, noviquejustitiae habitus infusione collocant; quem hominem ex malo bonum, & ex injusto inhaerenter justum reddere, saltem sanctitatis & justitiae initiis imbuere volunt. Posteriorem autem hominem ex justo justiorem, per charitatis profectum, reddere; jamque operum dignitate & merito Deo placentem, coram tribunali ejus ut justum absolvere & justificare ferè docent. Atque haec ipsis justificatio operum est.
units.tr: XLIII. For they are so ignorant of justification by faith that at the Council of Trent, when Luther's doctrine that we are justified by faith alone was under discussion, most of them could not grasp the sense of those words. They themselves decided that man is justified by faith "dispositively and inchoatively". By faith they understood the general persuasion of Christian truth, which nevertheless leads to the recognition of sin, the fear of hell, the hope of salvation, the love of God, the purpose of a new life, and so on. This faith makes us fit for internal righteousness, and gives access to that right state of mind in which we can please God and through which we are just. They want justification itself to follow this preparation, and they complete it only by certain degrees, namely as an increase of holiness, positing a first and a second justification. The first, they say, comes through baptism, from the mere grace of God and without works; they place it in the remission of sins and the infusion of a new habit of righteousness, which they wish to make man good instead of evil and inherently just instead of unjust, at least imbued with the beginnings of holiness and righteousness. The second, they nearly teach, makes man more just from being just, through progress in charity; and now pleasing God by the dignity and merit of works, he is absolved and justified before God's tribunal as one who is just. This, for them, is "justification by works".

units.la: XLIV. Quae multipliciter peccant. Nam 1. perverso illo principio nituntur, quod jam saepius retigimus, justificationem in qualitate inhaerente consistere. Unde in novo quodam animae habitu eam collocant. Quod nec juxta legem, nec juxta Euangelium consistit. Lex enim non ex habitu, sed ex operibus justificat, ut in Adamo patuit. Euangelium autem solam Christi justitiam agnoscit; & gratia illa Dei, quae tam saepe ibi praedicatur, non habitum aliquem nostrum, sed gratuitum Dei in Christo amorem significat. Qui justificantur gratis, ejus gratia, per redemtionem factam, in Christo Iesu, Rom. 3: 24. conf. 5: 15. 2. Hinc varios in justificatione actus, & gradus, & incrementa somniant, quin & decrementa, & nonnunquam interitum ejus admittunt; uti in aliis quoque qualitatibus usu venit. Cum tamen ea unicus & irrevocabilis Dei judicis actus sit, Christi sponsoris merito innitens, & à nostra parte sola fide acceptus, ac veluti obsignatus. 3. Altum autem apud ipsos justitiæ Christi, atque imputationis ejus silentium Quo pacto omnem Christi sponsionem corrumpunt; aut ad summum ejus δικαίωμα cum operibus nostris conjungunt; quod impossibile cogitatu est. 4. Sicuti & prodigiosum in modum opera & fidem in hoc negotio conjungere & contemperare norunt: quæ tamen Apostolus non distinguit solum, sed hac in causâ sibi mutuo opponit, Rom. 11:6. Gal. 2:16. Eph. 2:8. Quod adeo verum est, ut cooperari in hoc negotio nec quidem possint; cum fides justitiam extra nos, opera autem aliquid in nobis pro justitiæ fundamento quærant: quæ directâ fronte adversa sunt, nec una consistere possunt.
units.tr: XLIV. These errors are many. First, they rest on that perverse principle, which we have often touched on already, that justification consists in an inherent quality, and so they place it in some new habit of the soul. This agrees neither with the law nor with the Gospel. For the law justifies not by a habit but by works, as appeared in Adam. The Gospel, however, acknowledges only the righteousness of Christ. That grace of God, which is so often preached there, signifies not some habit of ours but God's free love in Christ: "Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 3:24; compare 5:15). Second, they dream up various acts, degrees and increases in justification, even decreases, and sometimes admit that it can be lost, as happens with other qualities too. Yet justification is a single and irrevocable act of God the judge, resting on the merit of Christ the surety, and received by us by faith alone and, as it were, sealed. Third, they keep a deep silence about the righteousness of Christ and its imputation. In this way they corrupt the whole surety-ship of Christ, or at most join his δικαίωμα [dikaiōma, righteous requirement] with our works, which is impossible to conceive. Fourth, they know how to join and blend works and faith in this business in a prodigious manner, yet the Apostle not only distinguishes them but in this very cause sets them against each other (Rom. 11:6; Gal. 2:16; Eph. 2:8). This is so true that they cannot even cooperate in this business, since faith seeks righteousness outside us, while works seek something in us as the foundation of righteousness. These are directly opposed and cannot stand together.

units.la: 5. Fidem vero, quod hinc sequi necesse est, alieno prorsus vultu ostendunt; necque eam in Christi amplexibus hærentem, iltique thesauro incubantem, atque ad unicam salutis arcem manus intendentem, ostentant: sed ut opus, alios quosdam motus, peccati dolorem, inferni metum, novæ vitæ cupidinem &c. in nobis excitans; & tantum non meritorium; dum remissionem peccatorum, sequentemque novum habitum vel prometeretur, vel peragit. 6. Sed & operum tandem merita, & condignitatem, in justificatione secundâ, plerique eorum apertis buccis crepant.
units.tr: Fifth, faith, which must follow from this, they show in a wholly alien aspect. They do not present it as clinging to Christ's embrace, resting on that treasure and stretching out its hands to the one citadel of salvation. They present it as a work, stirring up in us certain other motions: grief for sin, fear of hell, desire for a new life, and so on, and scarcely meritorious, since they either promise or bring about the remission of sins and the new habit that follows. Sixth, most of them, at last, loudly boast with open mouths of the merits and worthiness of works in the second justification.

units.la: 7. Et, quod ultimum ipsorum dedecus est, non ea vera, & digna Deo, digna homine, opera sunt, quibus favorem ejus aucupantur: sed externæ plerumque disciplinæ opera, monachatus, peregrinationes religiosæ, itata jejunia, ciliciorum durum tegmen, sponte verbera, pervigilia, aliaque talia minutæ ac ludicræ pietatis opera; quæ, pro superstitionis ingenio, Deo imputare, itaque veluti stipe cœlum emercari nituntur.
units.tr: Seventh, and this is their final disgrace, these are not the true works, worthy of God and worthy of man, by which they angle for his favour. They are mostly works of external discipline: monastic life, religious pilgrimages, repeated fasts, the rough covering of hair shirts, voluntary scourgings, vigils, and other such works of petty and ludicrous piety. According to the bent of their superstition, they try to impute these to God, and so, as it were, buy heaven with alms.

units.la: XLV. Cum autem Apostoli auctoritate urgentur, qui in epist. ad Roman. tam aperte opera in hoc negotio proscribit, idque non rationibus tantum, sed & exemplis docet, inani interpretamento, legis ceremonialis opera, atque Judaicam justitiam reprobari; vel illa tantum, quæ fidem antecedunt opera, ut necdum id dignitatis habentia, rejiciajunt.
units.tr: XLV. When they are pressed with the authority of the Apostle, who in the epistle to the Romans so plainly rejects works in this business, and teaches it not only by arguments but also by examples, they escape by an empty interpretation. They say that the works of the ceremonial law and Jewish righteousness are rejected, or that only those works which precede faith are rejected, as not yet having such dignity.

units.la: Cum expressè Apostolus Abrahamum & Davidem ut jam regenitos, atque ad illum modum eorum opera consideret, Rom. 4:1,2, 3.6,7,8,9. rum & imputari dicat justitiam absque operibus ei, in cujus spiritu non habitat dolus, Rom. 4:6, 7, 8. Psal. 32:1, 2. Atque in universum frivolum est, de eo quærere, an opera irregenitorum, ante fidem præstita, quæ merè peccata sunt, justificare possint. Quasi ea videl. quæstio foret, quam Apostolus tam anxiè trutinat: cum gloriam omnem humanam, omnemque gloriationem amovens, non nisi præstantissima opera cogitare potuerit; quæ uno videl. isto argumento hoc in negotio tollit & evertit. Ubi igitur gloriatio? exclusa est. P.r quam legem? operum? non: sed per legem fidei. Rom. 3: 27.
units.tr: When the Apostle expressly regards Abraham and David as already regenerate, and considers their works in that light (Rom. 4:1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9), and says that righteousness is imputed without works to him in whose spirit there is no guile (Rom. 4:6, 7, 8; Ps. 32:1, 2), then it is altogether futile to ask whether the works of the unregenerate, performed before faith and which are purely sins, can justify. As if that were the question the Apostle weighs so anxiously, when, removing all human glory and every boasting, he could have thought only of the most excellent works, which in this one matter he removes and overthrows: "Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? Nay: but by the law of faith" (Rom. 3:27).

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Sed paulo aliter respondent Socinians, eorumque sequaces, atque alia ab Apostolo opera excludi, alia admitti ajunt. Cum enim legis justitiam perpetuo rejiciat, contra autem fidem in Christum prædicet, à justificatione eum rejicere volunt illa opera, quæ naturâ vel lege duce fiunt, quæque ad legis amussim exacta vitam & mercedem postulent ex merito; atque ita quidem legis justitiam nullam esse. Cum autem isto pacto peccatorem justificari impossibile sit, atque ea sit legis imbecillitas, ut hominem beare nequeat; succurrere perditis rebus Christianam religionem, quæ imperfectæ etiam obedientiæ, attamen sinceræ, & ad Euangelicæ perfectionis, sive præceptorum Christi, formulam exactæ, cœleste præmium addicat, sed ex mera gratia: atque ita fide, h.e. juxta Christianæ fidei, seu religionis formulam, ejusque nova cum præcepta, tum promissa, nos justificari & salvari; ita ut sub novo fœdere Deus multum de veteri rigore remiserit, & ἐκιινεία quadam illud temperavit (revera enim hoc quoque operum fœdus est, sed fractum nonnihil & mitigatum) ac imperfectæ licet obedientiæ, ex fide Christi, h.e. doctrinæ Christianæ assensu, præstitæ præmium polliceatur.
units.tr: The Socinians and their followers answer somewhat differently. They say that some works are excluded by the Apostle and others admitted. Since Paul constantly rejects the righteousness of the law, while preaching faith in Christ, they wish to exclude from justification those works which are done by nature or with the law as guide, and which, being exact to the rule of the law, claim life and reward as their due. In this way, they say, there is no righteousness of the law. But since a sinner cannot be justified in this manner, and the law is so weak that it cannot make a man blessed, the Christian religion comes to the aid of ruined things. It grants heavenly reward, though only from pure grace, to imperfect obedience that is nonetheless sincere and conformed to the pattern of evangelical perfection, that is, of Christ's precepts. So we are justified and saved by faith, that is, according to the form of the Christian faith or religion and its new precepts and promises. Under the new covenant God has greatly relaxed the old rigour and tempered it by a certain indulgence [ἐπιεικείᾳ]. (In truth this too is a covenant of works, but somewhat broken and softened.) He promises a reward for imperfect obedience performed through faith in Christ, that is, through assent to Christian doctrine.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Quæ sutelæ undique laborant, & tum Apostolo refragantur, tum ipsos Christianæ fidei apices tangunt. Nam 1. aperte omnia opera excludit Paulus, additis magnis argumentis; restare alioquin homini de quo sese admiretur, ac verticem protollat. Rom. 3: 27. & 4: 2. quin & Christum ipsum frustra fore mortuum, si via alia salus parari potuit. Gal. 2: 21. quæ omnem operum justitiam, qualiscunque ea sit, evertunt. 2. Cum autem humana gens peccato succubuerit, nec perfecta justitia sperari ullibi possit; non adeo nugatur Apostolus, ut de eâ solâ perpetuo agat. Quanquam operum justitiam hoc ipso quoque damnet, quod ea ob peccatum nunc impossibilis sit reddita. Sed eadem opera, alio colore, quæsitisque temperamentis, reducta, multo magis in hac causa rejicit; & , cum contra Judæos agat, talia opera tangit, de quibus quæstio incidere poterat, & quæ ab illis ostentari poterant; quæ non erant opera omni numero perfecta, quæ illi nec habebant, nec venditabant; sed opera qualiacunque, quæ illi pro aliqua saltem justitiæ parte urgebant, quanquam ex gratia à Deo accipi ea debere concedebant. Quæ eadem operum justitia est, quam nunc Sociniani urgent, quamque Apostolus jam tum in Judæis profligavit. Utrorumque enim error est, Deum ἐκ δόγματος ex placito justificare, & opera nostra qualitercunque præstita accipere, atque sanctitatem suam abnegare posse. 2. Amplius, ut pateat qualia opera excludat Apostolus, Abrahami opera commemorat, eaque à justitia rejicit, Rom. 4:1. atque alibi & suum exemplum adducit, 1 Cor. 4:4. Ut pateat, ipsum opera à regenitis ex fide præstita, quanquam imperfecta, excludere. De quibus operibus sola poterat esse quæstio Sicut & Sociniani nunc eadem illa opera reducunt. De aliis enim operibus nulla animum subire poterat cogitatio. 4. Tum justitiam nostram esse in Christo docet Apostolus, non verò in nobis, 2.Cor.5:21. & ipsum Christum esse justitiam nostram, adeoq; non opus fidei nostræ, 1.Cor.1:30. & justificandus per fidem in se dicitur impius, Rom. 4:5. & per justitiam Christi dicimur justificati, ut per materiam justificationis; ergo non eodem sensu per fidem, Rom. 5:19. sicut & eadem de causa nusquam propter, sed per fidem, & ex fide dicimur justificati, Rom.3:22. Hebr. 11:7. Phil.3:9. 5. Abiurde porro & ἀθεολόγως justitiam legis & justitiam operum distinguunt, atque opera quædam concipiunt quæ non sunt legis, sed fidei & Euangelii. 6. Nec constitit, quod legis opera, si vel darentur, utcunque perfecta, justificare nunc non posse; alia autem opera, quæ imperfecta sunt, justificare in Euangelio contendunt. 7. In quo iste præterea dolus est, quasi fides nos à perfectâ legis observatione absolvat, nec tantam sanctitatem postulet. Cum tamen idem, contrario errore, Christum legislatorem Mosè perfectiorem, præceptaque ejus sublimiora ac sanctiora prædicent. Hic autem legis præcepta, ut nimis perfecta, nobisque impossibilia, à justitia excludunt, ut imperfectioribus Euangelii præceptis, ad quæ videl. humana imbecillitas conniti potest, locum cedant. 8. Gravius est, quod duplex operum fœdus fabricant, unum rigidum, alterum ἐπιεικείᾳ temperatum; atque universum Euangelium in novum operum pactum commutant. Cum, ut una ac immutabilis Dei sanctitas est, ita unicum tantum operum fœdus, ac lex, unicaque sanctitatis illius formula & expressio sit. Quam nec in Euangelio quidem solvi oportuit. Unde nec unquam abrogari potuit illa lex, ut novæ legi, aliique ex operibus δικαιώματι locum faceret. 9. Utque legem ac sanctitatem Dei isto commento polluunt, ita minute nimis de gratia loquuntur, quam in ἐτεροιώσει, conniventiam, ac prisca severitatis moderationem commutant. Cum gratia in Scripturis per misericordiam Dei in Christo Iesu ostensam, & favorem ejus omnimodum & merè gratuitum describatur: quæ majus quiddam quam ἐτεροίωσις quædam est. 10. Sed & ἐτεροίωσις talis, qualem ex humanarum legum exemplo somniant, in divina lege locum non habet; nec illa divinæ sanctitatis regula vel levissimam inclinationem patitur; ac nulla hic vel temperatio, vel dispensatio, vel exceptio, sine labe ejus, cogitari potest. 11. Sicuti neque acceptilatio, seu imperfectæ obedientiæ pro perfecta acceptio, in Deo locum habet. Non enim Deus de jure suo remittere, non magis quam de sanctitate sua concedere quicquam potest.
units.tr: These patches fall apart on every side: they both contradict the Apostle and touch the very summits of the Christian faith. For (1) Paul excludes all works plainly, adding strong arguments, since otherwise man would have something in which to glory and lift up his head (Rom. 3:27; 4:2). Indeed Christ himself would have died in vain if salvation could be obtained by another way (Gal. 2:21). These arguments overthrow all righteousness of works, of whatever kind it may be. (2) Since the human race has succumbed to sin, and perfect righteousness can be hoped for nowhere, the Apostle is not so trifling as to treat constantly of that alone. Yet he condemns the righteousness of works also on this very ground, that because of sin they have now become impossible. But he rejects the same works, brought back in another colour and with sought-for compromises, even more in this cause. And since he is arguing against the Jews, he touches on such works as could come into question and could be displayed by them: works that were not perfect in every respect, which they neither possessed nor boasted of, but works of whatever kind which they pressed as at least some part of righteousness, though they conceded that these must be received from God by grace. This is the same righteousness of works which the Socinians now press, and which the Apostle already then overthrew in the Jews. For the error of both is to hold that God can justify by decree [ἐκ δόγματος], accept our works however performed, and set aside his own holiness. (3) Further, so that it may be clear what kind of works the Apostle excludes, he mentions the works of Abraham and rejects them from righteousness (Rom. 4:1), and elsewhere he adduces his own example (1 Cor. 4:4). This makes clear that he excludes the works performed by the regenerate through faith, though imperfect. Only these works could be the subject of question, and the Socinians now bring back these same works. For no other works could come into anyone's mind. (4) The Apostle teaches that our righteousness is in Christ and not in us (2 Cor. 5:21), and that Christ himself is our righteousness, and therefore not a work of our faith (1 Cor. 1:30). The man to be justified through faith is said to be ungodly in himself (Rom. 4:5), and we are said to be justified by the righteousness of Christ as by the matter of justification. It follows that "through faith" does not have the same sense (Rom. 5:19). For the same reason we are never said to be justified "on account of" faith but "through" and "from" faith (Rom. 3:22; Heb. 11:7; Phil. 3:9). (5) Furthermore, they absurdly and ungodly [ἀθεολόγως] distinguish the righteousness of the law from the righteousness of works, and conceive certain works that belong not to the law but to faith and the gospel. (6) Nor does it hold together that the works of the law, even if they were given and were in some way perfect, cannot now justify, while other works, which are imperfect, justify in the gospel. (7) There is also this trick in their position, as if faith released us from the perfect observance of the law and did not demand such great holiness. Yet by the opposite error they hold that Christ the lawgiver is more perfect than Moses, and that his precepts are more sublime and holier. Here, however, they exclude the precepts of the law from righteousness as being too perfect and impossible for us, so that they may give way to the more imperfect precepts of the gospel, to which human weakness can strive. (8) It is more serious that they fabricate a twofold covenant of works, one rigid and the other tempered by equity [ἐπιεικείᾳ], and change the whole gospel into a new pact of works. Yet just as God's holiness is one and unchangeable, so there is only one covenant of works, one law, and one formula and expression of that holiness. This law ought not to have been dissolved even in the gospel. Hence that law could never be abrogated to make room for a new law and another righteousness by ordinance [δικαιώματι]. (9) And just as they pollute the law and holiness of God by this contrivance, so they speak too meanly of grace, changing it into alteration [ἐτεροιώσει], indulgence, and a moderation of the old severity. Yet in the Scriptures grace is described as the mercy of God shown in Christ Jesus, and his favour in every way and purely gratuitous. This is something greater than a mere alteration [ἐτεροίωσις]. (10) Moreover, such an alteration as they dream of from the example of human laws has no place in the divine law. That rule of divine holiness does not allow even the slightest inclination, and no temperament, dispensation or exception can be thought of here without a stain upon it. (11) Likewise acceptilation, that is, the acceptance of imperfect obedience as if it were perfect, has no place in God. For God cannot remit anything of his right, any more than he can concede anything of his holiness.

units.la: XLVIII. Verum alios præterea errores in hoc capite fovent Sociniani. Ut enim illud unicum religionis fundamentum & fulcrum est; quo eam universam conspirare, inque eum veluti sinum omnes suos latices corrivare videmus: ita, eo male posito, etiam reliquas doctrinæ partes labare rivulosque omnes insinceros fluere necesse est. Cujus rei hæc præterea in ipsis specimina sunt. 1. Justificationem fieri sine justitia, & in mera Dei misericordia, & culparum remissione, ad respiscentiam nostram facta, consistere. 2. Nec eam uno actu absolvi vel irrevocabilem esse; sed, pro vario hominis statu mutabilem esse, & sæpe mutari; ac peragi eam aliquando, aliquando everti, rursusque renovari; nec unquam eam plenam esse, nisi post obitum supremaque hominis fata, ubi ille à morte liberatus, peccatis omnibus solutus, in gloriam introducetur. 3. Quin & non omnium hominum eandem justificationem esse, sed pro dogmate ac placito Dei judicis illam mutari.
units.tr: XLVIII. Moreover, the Socinians also foster other errors in this chapter. For just as this single foundation and prop of religion is the thing towards which we see the whole of religion converge, pouring all its streams into it as into a bosom, so when this is wrongly laid, it is necessary that the remaining parts of doctrine totter and all their insincere little streams flow out. Of this the following are examples among them. (1) That justification takes place without righteousness, consists in mere mercy of God and remission of faults, made in response to our repentance. (2) That it is not completed by one act nor irrevocable, but changes with the varying state of the man and is often changed; that it is sometimes carried out, sometimes overturned, and then renewed again; and that it is never full until after death and the man's final fate, when he, freed from death and loosed from all sins, will be led into glory. (3) Indeed, justification is not the same for all men, but varies according to the decree and pleasure of God as judge.

units.la: XLIX. 4. Ac sub Veteri quidem Testamento olim patres sine Christo justificatos, peccataque eorum per sacrificia quoquomodo expiata ac deleta esse: hoc enim à Judæis habent. Cui addunt aliud mysterium. Cum enim legis justitia etiam olim impossibilis foret, veteres tamen per opera, sed alio quodam modo, justificatos esse asserunt; dum ob vitam sanctè & innocenter actam Dei amore non indigni forent, quo ille eos præter ac contra legem, ex liberrima voluntate ac misericordia tum dignatus est; uti in Abrahamo, aliisque, factum volunt.
units.tr: XLIX. (4) Under the Old Testament, the Fathers were justified without Christ, and their sins were somehow expiated and blotted out through sacrifices; for they have this from the Jews. To this they add another mystery. For since the righteousness of the law was impossible even in former times, they nevertheless assert that the ancients were justified through works, but in a certain other way: because by a life lived holily and innocently they were made worthy of God's love, by which he then deigned to regard them beyond and contrary to the law, out of his most free will and mercy. They want this to have happened in Abraham and others.

units.la: L. 5. Sub Novo autem Testamento Christum ad justificationem concurrere, non ut auctorem vel causam meritoriam, per satisfactionem ac sansanguinem suum, sed ut praeconem, ministrum, novaque legis, quae certissima ad justitiam & amorem Dei dux sit, latorem, statuunt: non enim opus esse satisfactione vel justitia Christi, ejusve imputatione, cum ea ex pura Dei misericordia peragatur; quam nobis solum annunciari, Christiique pro veritate ejus spondentis sanguine obsignari necesse sit.
units.tr: L. 5. They hold that under the New Testament Christ contributes to justification, not as its author or meritorious cause, through his satisfaction and his own blood, but as herald, minister, and bringer of a new law, which is the most certain guide to righteousness and to the love of God. For, they say, there is no need for the satisfaction or righteousness of Christ, or its imputation, since justification is accomplished by God's pure mercy. It is only necessary that this mercy be announced to us and sealed by the blood of Christ, who pledged it as true.

units.la: LI. 6. Utque Christi meritum ac justitiam tollunt, ita & fidei rationem immutant, quae illis non est causa instrumentalis justificationis a parte nostri, sed opus merum & nova hominis obedientia, ex fide promissorum Christi, & certa spe remunerationis, praeceptis Euangelicis praestita, ex qua nunc justificemur. Quae fides adeo non in Christum est, ut Euangelio & Christo directa fronte adversetur. Credere enim, justificare Deum hominem adhuc posse ex facto, est tum sanctitatem Dei & justitiam, tum mortis Christi necessitatem, & universum Euangelium abnegare. Nam si homo ex facto justificari potest, Christus frustra mortuus est. Praeterquam quod & inani fundamento nitatur; cum enim obedientia illa valde imperfecta sit, nec de perseverantia homo certus sit, vix tenuem salutis spem habere potest, sed damnationis potius metum & occultos terrores pati debet. Quibus ista fides ipsum exolvere non potest; quae huc tandem exit, si bene credid erimus, h. e. fecerimus, haud dubie vivemus; sin secus, haud amplius erimus.
