Egregiam vero fidem ac spem, quae, ut ab una parte coelum, ita ab altera parte infernum non-existentiae ostentat; quae eadem videl. illa salutaris fides ex aequo apprehendit, ac pari assensu in utrumque fertur; ut sub legis terrore factum fuisset: ut fidem hanc non male legalem, & qualis sub lege quoque obtinere potuit, vocemus; non vero Euangelicam, quae solo Christo ac salute ejus nititur, nec quicquam terroris habet.
units.tr: LI. 6. And just as they remove Christ's merit and righteousness, so they also alter the account of faith. For them faith is not the instrumental cause of justification on our side, but a mere work, a new obedience of man, performed in accordance with the Evangelical precepts, from faith in Christ's promises and a certain hope of reward, and by this we are now justified. This faith is so far from resting on Christ that it is directly opposed to the Gospel and to Christ himself. To believe that God can justify a man now on the basis of works is to deny God's holiness and righteousness, the necessity of Christ's death, and the whole Gospel. For if man can be justified by works, Christ died in vain. Moreover, this rests on an empty foundation. Since that obedience is very imperfect, and a man cannot be certain of perseverance, he can scarcely have any slender hope of salvation, but ought rather to suffer the fear of damnation and hidden terrors. This faith cannot free him from these, and it comes down to this: if we shall have believed well, that is, done (good works), we shall certainly live; but if otherwise, we shall no longer exist. Such a faith and hope, which sets heaven before us on one side and non-existence or hell on the other, and which this supposed saving faith grasps with equal weight and inclines to both alike, as would have happened under the terror of the law, is rightly called a legal faith, of the kind that could also hold under the law. It is not Evangelical faith, which rests on Christ alone and his salvation, and has nothing of terror in it.

units.la: LII. 7. Atque haec obedientia praeceptis Christi praestita, ex fide promissorum ac doctrinae ejus, iis vel maxime ad justificationem facit, & tantum non ejus causa est. Verum ulcera haec nudasse satis est. Quantopere enim haec justificationis ratio sanctitatem ac justitiam Dei, & veterum religionem ac spem; & Christi gloriam ac officium, & fidei naturam corrumpat & evertat; rursusque opera, sed falso schemate, introducat; & denique legis pariter ac Euangelii justitiae, omnique Dei gloria, quae alterutra illa ratione tantum parari, & humano generi monstrari potuit, adversa sit, ultro patet, ac saepius alibi in hoc opere ostendimus.
units.tr: LII. 7. And this obedience, performed to Christ's precepts from faith in his promises and teaching, contributes above all to justification, and is almost its cause. But it is enough to have uncovered these sores. For how greatly this method of justification corrupts and overturns the holiness and righteousness of God, the religion and hope of the ancients, the Christ's glory and office, and the nature of faith; how it again introduces works, though under a false appearance; and finally how it is opposed to the law and the Gospel alike, to the righteousness of both, and to all the glory of God, which could be secured and shown to mankind only by the other way, is plain on its face. We have shown this often elsewhere in this work.

units.la: LIII. Remonstrantium itidem placita sunt: fidem non justificare, quatenus Christi justitiam apprehendit, sed quatenus est opus & actus noster, ac novæ obedientiæ principium; ex quâ, utcunque imperfecta & impari, nec Deo prorsus digna, pro Dei tamen bonitate & gratia, in Euangelio promissa, justificemur, ac salutem adipiscamur. Quod ipsi dicunt, imputari fidem ad justitiam, ex Apostolo, Rom. 4: 3. cujus loci sensum supra dedimus. Ac consequenter non nisi perseverantibus, atque aliquem obedientiæ cursum perficientibus justificationem hanc peremtorie tribuendam censent. Unde & in extremo vitæ actu poenitentibus, nec idoneo tempore superviventibus, intrepidè cœlum addicere omnes non audent; quanquam eos per extraordinariam Dei gratiam, quam tamen præsumere nimis facile non liceat, servari adhuc posse statuant. Qui infelix justificationis illius ex fide, tanquam opere, fructus est; ut hominem in summo discrimine ad Christum, tanquam ad salutis arcem, fidenter ire, eumque apprehendere, deque eventu bené sperare vetet. Cum tamen Scriptura poenitentibus, atque ad Christum respicientibus, & vel in medià morte ad eum suspirantibus, quæ vera fides est, salutis portum aperiat: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis, & onerati estis, ego faciam vos requiescere. Matth. 11: 28. Venientem ad me non ejiciam foras. Joh. 6: 37. Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23: 43. Nec multum diversâ facie quoque opera in hoc negotio jactant, & justificationem cum sanctificatione, fidem cum operibus confundentes, à vera justitia semita aberrant. Quos errores jam ante, præsertim in Socino, qui reliquorum omnium compendium habet, extinximus.
units.tr: LIII. The Remonstrants' views are likewise these: faith justifies not insofar as it grasps Christ's righteousness, but insofar as it is our act and work, and the principle of new obedience. By this, however imperfect and unequal, and not wholly worthy of God, we are justified by God's goodness and grace, promised in the Gospel, and obtain salvation. When they say that faith is imputed for righteousness, they appeal to the Apostle, Rom. 4:3, whose sense we have given above. Consequently they hold that this justification is to be granted absolutely only to those who persevere and complete some course of obedience. Hence they do not dare to promise heaven boldly to those who repent at the last hour of life, or who survive without a suitable time, although they hold that such persons may still be saved by an extraordinary grace of God, which yet may not be presumed too easily. This is the unhappy fruit of that justification by faith as if it were a work: it forbids a man in deadly peril to go confidently to Christ, as to the citadel of salvation, to lay hold of him, and to hope well for the outcome. Yet Scripture opens the harbour of salvation to those who repent and look to Christ, and who, even in the midst of death, sigh for him, which is true faith: Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Matt. 11:28. The one who comes to me I will by no means cast out. John 6:37. Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise. Luke 23:43. Nor do they, in a not very different way, boast of works in this matter, and by confusing justification with sanctification and faith with works they wander from the true path of righteousness. We have already refuted these errors earlier, especially in Socinus, who holds a summary of all the others.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De Adoptione & Libertate Christiana.
units.tr: On Adoption and Christian Liberty

units.la: I. Ustificationis consequens est adoptio: quæ sublimis illa fidelium dignitas est, qua propter Christum in familiam Dei accipiuntur, domusque ejus partem faciunt, ac cœlestis denique hereditatis participes evadunt. Quo titulo ac honore non mediocriter natura humana extollitur. Quotquot autem acceperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem, ut filii Dei fierent, Joh. 1: 12. Quod si filii, etiam heredes &c. Rom. 8: 17.
units.tr: I. Adoption follows justification. It is that exalted dignity of believers by which, for Christ's sake, they are received into the family of God, become part of his household, and are at last made sharers in the heavenly inheritance. Human nature is not a little raised up by this title and honour. But to as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God (John 1:12). And if sons, then heirs (Rom. 8:17), etc.

units.la: II. Est autem ea, sententia Dei gratiosa, (filii enim adoptivi à naturali turali differunt; & non natura, sed gratiâ, ac per sententiam quandam Dei, in tanti nominis dignitatem veniunt) justificatoriæ sententiæ veluti appendix & coronis.
units.tr: II. This adoption is a gracious sentence of God (for adopted sons differ from natural ones, and they come to the dignity of so great a name not by nature but by grace and by a certain sentence of God), and it is, as it were, an appendix and crown of the sentence of justification.

units.la: III. Unde & eadem cum illâ momenta habet: vel ab æterno decreta in divina prædestinatione (definivit nos ad adoptionem filiorum per Jesum Christum. Eph. 1: 5.) vel in tempore, in Christo salutem peragente (Emisit Deus filium suum — ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Gal. 4: 4, 5.) vel denique in ipsis fidelibus, spectari potest; quibus per Spiritum ea intimatur, cum, à peccatis justificati, suavissimo filiorum affectu induuntur, Deumque, ut Patrem, compellare erudiuntur. Quia vero estis filii, emisit Deus Spiritum filii sui in corda vestra, clamantem Abba, Pater. Gal. 4: 6.
units.tr: III. For this reason it also has the same moments, and can be viewed either as decreed from eternity in divine predestination (he predestined us to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ, Eph. 1:5), or in time, when Christ accomplishes salvation (God sent forth his Son... that we might receive the adoption of sons, Gal. 4:4, 5), or finally in believers themselves, to whom it is made known through the Spirit, when, being justified from their sins, they are clothed with the sweetest affection of sons and are taught to address God as Father. Because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father (Gal. 4:6).

units.la: IV. In Christo autem solo quicquid istud gratiæ est possidemus; qui istum nobis titulum, partim ut redemtor paravit, partim, ut filius Dei primogenitus, nobisque ex humana natura frater, confert & applicat; ac denique honoris istius obses ac vinculum est. Emisit Deus filium suum — ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Gal. 4: 5. Decebat ipsum, multis filiis in gloriam introducere, principem salutis ipsorum per passiones consummare. Quippe & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno omnes. Propter quam causam non pudet fratres eos appellare. Hebr. 2: 10, 11, 12. Ut alia ratione, quam olim Adamus, non minus Dei, cujus imaginem gerebat, quam terræ filius, nomine isto gaudeamus; potiorisque illud gratiæ in nobis argumentum sit. Videte, quantum amorem nobis dedit Pater, ut filii Dei vocemur. 1. Joh. 3: 1. Sed accessistis — ad concionem primogenitorum. Heb. 12: 23.
units.tr: IV. Whatever this grace is, we possess it in Christ alone. He bestows and applies this title to us, partly as Redeemer, partly as the first-born Son of God and our brother by human nature; and finally he is the pledge and bond of that honour. God sent forth his Son... that we might receive the adoption of sons (Gal. 4:5). For it was fitting that he, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one; for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren (Heb. 2:10, 11, 12). Thus, by a different reason from that by which Adam of old, who bore the image of God, rejoiced in the name of son of the earth, we may rejoice in this name, and it may be a stronger proof of grace in us. See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called the sons of God (1 John 3:1). But you have come... to the assembly of the first-born (Heb. 12:23).

units.la: V. Gratiosi istius nominis signaculum & arrhabo est Spiritus Sanctus, qui Spiritus adoptionis appellatur Rom 8. Gal. 4. quod interiori illius ipsius commercio atque affatu animam nostram permulceat, & cum fiducia Deum ut Patrem adire faciat. Ut eum jam appellemus Pater; qua veluti ipsius naturæ voce ac sono, Patrem olim quærebant, qui alienæ familiæ accessuri erant. Unde & Christus illâ usus apud Patrem suum legitur, Marc. 14: 36. Sicuti autem apud Israëlitas nemini, nisi libero, ista compellatione vel uti fas erat; ita novæ Ecclesiæ libertatem inde recte concludit Apostolus: Non enim accepistis Spiritum servitutis, rursus ad metum; sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba, Pater! Rom. 8: 15. Ubi enim Spiritus Domini est, ibi libertas. 2. Cor. 3: 17.
units.tr: V. The seal and pledge of this gracious name is the Holy Spirit, who is called the Spirit of adoption in Rom. 8 and Gal. 4, because by his inward communion and address he soothes our soul and makes us approach God with confidence as Father, so that we now call him Father. This is, as it were, the very voice and sound of nature itself, the voice by which those who were about to enter an alien household used to seek a father. Hence Christ is also read to have used it with his own Father (Mark 14:36). But just as among the Israelites this form of address was lawful for no one except the free, so the Apostle rightly infers the liberty of the new Church from it: For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father! (Rom. 8:15). Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (2 Cor. 3:17).

units.la: VI. Quod
units.tr: VI. That

units.la: VI. Quod testimonium tamen non in singulari aliquo alloquió interno, ac peculiari veluti numinis responso, & ad animam oraculo, ponendum; atque à fide, aliisque Christianæ animæ affectibus scrupulosè nimis distinguendum est: quasi, postquam credidimus, alio Spiritus actu, atque immediato ejus affatu, nobis insinuetur: quomodo illum adoptionis Spiritum criminari adversarii,& cum inani ac fallaci quadam Echo comparare solent. Simulac enim credimus, & co ipso quod credimus, obsignamur; hæcque ipsa Spiritus nota & character; & fides unicum ejus signaculum est. In quo Christo etiam credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis sancto, qui est arrhabo hereditatis nostræ. Eph. 1: 13,14. coll. 4:30. Sunt enim illæ Spiritus primitiæ, Rom. 8:23. quas porro filiorum affectus & indoles, reliquumque Christianarum virtutum agmen comitatur; quæ cuncta ejus in nobis habitantis obsides & testimonia sunt.
units.tr: VI. This testimony, however, must not be placed in some singular inward address, or a peculiar, as it were, answer of the divinity, an oracle to the soul; nor must it be scrupulously distinguished too much from faith and the other affections of the Christian soul, as if, after we have believed, the Spirit were insinuated into us by another act and by his immediate address. This is how our opponents are accustomed to accuse the Spirit of adoption and compare him to some empty and deceptive echo. For as soon as we believe, and by the very fact that we believe, we are sealed; and this very faith is the mark and character of the Spirit, and faith is his sole seal. In whom, having believed, you also were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance (Eph. 1:13, 14; compare 4:30). For these are the first-fruits of the Spirit (Rom. 8:23), which are further accompanied by the affections and disposition of sons and the whole host of Christian virtues; all of these are pledges and testimonies of his dwelling in us.

units.la: VII. Ac patet jam discrimen inter adoptionem divinam & huma-nam. 1. inter homines enim persona prorsus alicna adscisci-tur, ad augendos patrisfamilias penates, quæ nullo jure in familiam istam venit. Nos autem, accepto à Christo jure ac per justificationem isti spei proximi, in Domum Dei accipimur, ac cœlestis hæreditatis candidati evadimus.
units.tr: VII. Now the difference between divine and human adoption is plain. 1. Among men, a person entirely alien is taken in, to increase the household gods of the head of the family, and this person comes into that family by no right. But we, having received the right from Christ and, through justification, the hope of this, are received into the house of God and become candidates for the heavenly inheritance.

units.la: 2. Ibi necessitate quadam, ad patrum orbitatem solandam, & ne fortuna domus collabatur, adoptionis simulachrum inventum est. Hic ex summa bonitate, utque homines, extra domum Dei exules & vagi, ab erroribus suis colligantur, illi potiori quam antea jure vocantur, & divinæ familiæ inferuntur. 3. Ibi adoptio externam solum dignitatem dicit, non autem ipsum naturæ vultum ac affectus dare potest. Hic filiali præterea animo imbuimur, omnesque filiorum motus ac affectus haurimus, ac cœlesti vitæ initiamur. 4. Inter homines denique hæreditas, post mortem Patris jam vacua, adiri solet. Hic vero nulla successio, sed paternæ hæreditatis plenissima possessio in æternum obtinet.
units.tr: 2. Among men, adoption was devised out of a certain necessity, to console the childlessness of fathers and so that the fortune of the house would not collapse. Among God's people, out of supreme goodness, and so that men, exiles and wanderers outside the house of God, may be gathered in from their errors, they are called by a stronger right than before and are brought into the divine family. 3. Among men, adoption can give only an external dignity, not the very countenance and affections of nature. Here, moreover, we are imbued with a filial mind, we draw in all the motions and affections of sons, and we are initiated into the heavenly life. 4. Finally, among men the inheritance is usually entered upon after the father's death, when it is already empty. Here, however, there is no succession, but the fullest possession of the paternal inheritance endures for ever.

units.la: VIII. Discrimen etiam est inter vioθεσίαν sub V. & N.T. cum enim jus filiorum & Spiritus filiationis non detur, ut dignum est Deo Patre, nisi postquam Christus glorificatus est, Joh. 7: 39. hinc sub V. T. hæres ad modum infantis pignoribus gratiæ, quæ habuerunt in terra, acceptis, sub servitute & pædagogo erat, Gal. 4:5,6. Rom. 8: 15. cum nobis datum fit jus ac potestas, ut filii Dei fiamus, Joh. 1: 12. hoc est, ut geramus nos apud Deum, quemadmodum par est ut filii se gerant apum Patrem, seu jus clamandi Abba, Pater, Joh. 1:12. Gal. 4:5,6. juxta promissio-nem. nem Jer. 3: 19. Ecce dixeram : Quomodo ponam te inter filios?
units.tr: VIII. There is also a difference between adoption [υἱοθεσία] under the Old and New Testament. For since the right of sons and the Spirit of sonship are not given, as is worthy of God the Father, until Christ has been glorified (John 7:39), therefore under the Old Testament the heir, like an infant, received the pledges of grace which he had on earth and was under servitude and a tutor (Gal. 4:5, 6; Rom. 8:15). But to us is given the right and power to become the sons of God (John 1:12), that is, to conduct ourselves before God as sons ought to conduct themselves before their father, or the right to cry Abba, Father (John 1:12; Gal. 4:5, 6), according to the promise of Jer. 3:19: Behold, I had said, How shall I put you among the sons?

units.la: IX. Fructus adoptionis sunt: 1. Libertas à peccati ac legis servitute; quæ Ecclesiæ perpetua fuit, tum sub Vet. tum sub Nov. Test. Nunc vero liberi facti a peccato, mancipati autem Deo. Rom. 6: 22. Si igitur filius vos liberos fecerit, verè liberi eritis. Joh. 8: 36. Quamvis major ejus gradus sub Nov. Test. enituerit, ut mox videbimus. 2. Hæreditas fidelium, ac dominium in omnes creaturas, quæ nobis nunc permissæ ac puræ. Omnia enim vestra sunt. 1. Cor. 3: 21, 22. Omnia pura puris. Tit. 1: 15.
units.tr: IX. The fruits of adoption are: 1. liberty from the bondage of sin and of the law; this has been perpetual for the Church, both under the Old and under the New Testament. But now, having been made free from sin and enslaved to God (Rom. 6:22). If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be truly free (John 8:36). Although, as we shall soon see, a greater degree of it shone forth under the New Testament. 2. The inheritance of believers, and dominion over all creatures, which are now permitted and pure to us. For all things are yours (1 Cor. 3:21, 22). To the pure all things are pure (Titus 1:15).

units.la: X. Minuunt autem eam Remonstrantes, dum morte Christi certis hæredibus cœlestem hæreditatem acquisitam negant. Quo pacto filios, nuntur & hæredes, omnemque adoptionem ac hæreditatem tantum non tollunt. contra Gal. 4: 4, 5, 6. Emisit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, ut eos, qui legi erant subjecti, redimeret, ut adoptionem acciperemus. Quoniam autem estis filii, emisit Deus Spiritum filii sui in corda vestra &c. Rursus, cum ea ponant, juxta quæ neminem in hac vita de adoptione sua certum & securum esse sinunt, nullam iterum firmam adoptionem in hac vita statuere debent. Illa enim tam firmum fidelium statum dicit, ut de eo securis esse liceat; cum nemo de eâ excidat, nec de familia Dei perire possit. Unde & tales filii promissionis, insigni appellatione dicuntur. Quod adversarii inani cavillo pervertunt, & non de certis promissionis hæredibus; sed de sectatoribus ac discipulis promissionis, per quam adoptio offertur, intelligunt: quasi non Dei beneficium, sed nostrum officium exprimeretur.
units.tr: X. The Remonstrants, however, diminish this, while by denying that the heavenly inheritance was acquired for certain heirs by the death of Christ, they scarcely abolish sons, heirs, and all adoption and inheritance. This is contrary to Gal. 4:4, 5, 6: God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption. And because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, etc. Again, since they hold the view by which they do not allow anyone in this life to be certain and secure of his own adoption, they ought in turn not to establish any firm adoption in this life. For that adoption makes the state of believers so firm that one may be secure concerning it, since no one falls out of it, and no one can perish from the family of God. Hence also such sons are called, by a notable appellation, sons of promise. Our opponents twist this with empty quibbling, and understand it not of the certain heirs of the promise but of the followers and disciples of the promise by which adoption is offered, as if what were expressed were our duty and not God's benefit.

units.la: XI. Ut adoptio justificationis, ita adoptionis comes est libertas; quæ cum essentialis, tum accidentalis est.
units.tr: XI. As justification is accompanied by adoption, so adoption is accompanied by liberty, which is both essential and accidental.

units.la: XII. Essentialis libertas, quæ à legis maledictione, seu condemnatione & peccati servitute est, in omni Ecclesiæ statu locum habuit. Cui sub Nov. Test. accessit major ejus gradus; quæ accidentalis libertas appellari potest: quo Ecclesia ab omni præcepto carnali, & legis, hominumque ejus custodum, dominatu libera, soli nunc Deo serva est. Lex Spiritus vitæ in Christo Jesu liberum me fecit a lege peccati & mortis. Rom. 8: 2. Peccatum enim vobis non dominabitur. Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratiâ. Rom. 6: 14. Corrumpetur jugum propter oleum. Esai. 10: 27.
units.tr: XII. Essential liberty, which consists in freedom from the curse of the law, or condemnation, and from the bondage of sin, has existed in every state of the Church. To this there was added under the New Testament a greater degree, which may be called accidental liberty: by it the Church, free from every carnal precept and from the dominion of the law, of men who are its guardians, is now the servant of God alone. The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death. Rom. 8:2. For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law but under grace. Rom. 6:14. The yoke shall be destroyed because of the oil. Isa. 10:27.

units.la: XIII. Quæ libertas in ambitu suo dicit 1. libertatem à maledictione & servitute chirographi. Christus nos emit, ut liberi essemus ab execratione legis. Gal. 3: 13. Delevit Christus subscriptionem manus adversus nos ad placita, quæ erat contraria nobis. Col. 2: 14. Hinc abdicata sunt sacrisacrificia Pf. 40: 7. 50: 8. Mich. 6:6,7. juxta prædictionem Dan. 9:27. Esai. 66: 1, 3. Hinc liberi sumus ab elementis mundi, Gal 4:3. à jugo cerimoniarum, omnisque carnali cultu. Nunc igitur quid tentatis Deum, imponendo in collum discipulorum jugum? Actor. 15: 10. 11. Hanc comitatur altera, quæ est in abrogatione principum prioris sæculi; quos Christus a se depositi, Col. 2: 15. quales erant, cum angeli, quibus non est subjectus orbis habitabilis futurus, Hebr. 2: 5. ut fideles non sint ipsorum δοῦλοι servi, sed hi horum meri conservi, Apoc. 19: 10. 22: 9. Unde & Paulus audet angelo ex cœlis anathema dicere, si quid aliud doceat, Gal. 1: 8. tum seniores: qui nunc aboliti sunt; cum quatenus erant vindices legis, illi populum subjicientes, κατὰ τὸ δοκεῖν αὐτοῖς, ut ipsis videbatur, Hebr. 12: 10. unde Dii dicti, quorum abrogatio prædicta, Psal. 82: 7. Zach. 11: 8. tum quatenus erant doctores necessarii, quibus tradita clavis cognitionis, Luc. 11: 52. cum nunc sub N. T. audito Christo, nemo alio doctore indigeat. Jer. 31: 34. 1. Joh. 2: 27. ubi omnes erudiuntur à Deo. Esai. 54: 13. prophetant & visiones vident. Joël. 2: 28. conf. l. v. c. 11. §. x, xi.
units.tr: XIII. This liberty, in its scope, includes: 1. freedom from the curse and the bondage of the handwriting. Christ redeemed us, that we might be free from the curse of the law. Gal. 3:13. Christ blotted out the handwriting against us, which was contrary to us, with its decrees. Col. 2:14. Hence the sacrifices were abolished, Ps. 40:7; 50:8; Mic. 6:6, 7, in accordance with the prediction of Dan. 9:27; Isa. 66:1, 3. Hence we are free from the elements of the world, Gal. 4:3, from the yoke of ceremonies, and from all carnal worship. Now therefore, why do you tempt God by putting a yoke on the neck of the disciples? Acts 15:10, 11. To this is joined a second liberty, which lies in the abolition of the rulers of the former age, whom Christ put off from himself, Col. 2:15, such as the angels, to whom the habitable world to come is not subject, Heb. 2:5, so that the faithful are not servants [δοῦλοι] of these, but their mere fellow servants, Rev. 19:10; 22:9. Hence Paul also dares to say that an angel from heaven should be accursed if he teaches anything else, Gal. 1:8. Also the elders, who are now abolished, since, insofar as they were the avengers of the law, they subjected the people to themselves according to what seemed good to them [κατὰ τὸ δοκεῖν αὐτοῖς], Heb. 12:10. Hence they were called gods, whose abolition was foretold, Ps. 82:7; Zech. 11:8. Also insofar as they were necessary teachers, to whom the key of knowledge was given, Luke 11:52, whereas now under the New Testament, with Christ heard, no one needs another teacher, Jer. 31:34; 1 John 2:27, where all are taught by God, Isa. 54:13, prophesy and see visions, Joel 2:28. Cf. book 5, chapter 11, sections 10 and 11.

units.la: XIV. Non autem libertas hæc infinitam licentiam dicit, vel ab omni divinarum humanarumque legum reverentia nos solvit; qui Libertinorum ac Anomorum furor est. Quorum profana opinio, corrumpendis moribus nata, omnis impietatis apicem immanitate sua constituit. Gratia enim sanctitati adversa non est: &, qui Christianus est, eo & sanctus probusque esse, & Deo & proximo suo multa debere non desinit. Exlegibus ut exlex. Non tamen exlex Deo, sed sublex Christo &c. 1. Cor. 9:21. Servus vocatus es, ne fit tibi cura. 1. Cor. 7:21. Servi obedite per omnia dominis secundum carnem. Col. 3:22.
units.tr: XIV. This liberty, however, does not mean unlimited licence, nor does it release us from all reverence for divine and human laws; that is the madness of the Libertines and the Antinomians. Their profane opinion, born to corrupt morals, has by its monstrousness set the summit of all impiety. For grace is not opposed to holiness; and whoever is a Christian does not cease to be holy and upright on that account, and to owe much both to God and to his neighbour. Free from the law, as one without law; yet not without law toward God, but under the law toward Christ, etc. 1 Cor. 9:21. You were called as a servant; let it not trouble you. 1 Cor. 7:21. Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh. Col. 3:22.

units.la: XV. Sicut neque ab altera parte Christus nos, à veteris legis nexu liberatos, ad perfectiorem legem transtulit: quasi ad alia pacta, aliasque leges nunc ventum sit; eaque nunc Ecclesiæ libertas vocanda sit, quod Ecclesia dominum mutarit; &, Sociniano sensu, cum legem olim haberet dominam, nunc Christum nacta sit dominum, novum videlicet legislatorem & Deum. Quæ propudia spe tetigimus.
units.tr: XV. Nor, on the other side, has Christ, having freed us from the bond of the old law, transferred us to a more perfect law, as if we had now come to other covenants and other laws, so that this should now be called the liberty of the Church because the Church has changed its lord, and, in the Socinian sense, because it once had the law as its master and now has gained Christ as its lord, namely a new lawgiver and God. We have touched on these foul notions with a brief remark.

units.la: XVI. Speciatim autem consideranda est Ecclesiæ libertas 1. Quoad leges humanas. 2. Cærimonias ac ritus sacros. 3. Adiaphora, seu indifferentia.
units.tr: XVI. Now the liberty of the Church is to be considered particularly: 1. as regards human laws; 2. as regards ceremonies and sacred rites; 3. as regards adiaphora, or things indifferent.

units.la: XVII. 1. Leges hominum quod attinet, cum conscientia solo Deo minor, eique uni obnoxia sit, aliena certe in isto Dei regno arbitria pati, & hominem judicem ferre non potest. Unde humanæ legesde suo nihil in eam juris obtinent; nec quod illæ jusserint,sanctum,quod vetaverint, profanum hoc ipso est: quasi illis edicentibus ac arbitrantibus aliquid virtus vitium ve foret, istoque nexu conscientia teneretur. Quanquam mediatè & indirectè conscientia etiam legum humanarum moderamini subjecta sit; sed ex superiori lege, quam Deus & natura jusserunt. Ideo necesse est subjici, non tantum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Rom. 13: 5.
units.tr: XVII. 1. As far as human laws are concerned: since conscience is subject to God alone and is bound to him alone, it certainly cannot suffer foreign wills in that kingdom of God, nor can it bear a man as judge. Hence human laws have no right over it in what is its own; nor is what they have commanded holy, or what they have forbidden profane, for that very reason, as if virtue or vice were determined by their edicts and judgments, and conscience were bound by that tie. Although conscience is also subject, indirectly and mediately, to the government of human laws, this is so by reason of a higher law, which God and nature have enjoined. Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. Rom. 13:5.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Quam imperandi auctoritatem cum soli magistratui in rebus humanis Deus concesserit, cœtuum Ecclesiasticorum placita in rebus alioquin indifferentibus, non tam legum, quam admonitionum naturam habent, soliusque ordinis ac decori causa, ne temere scandalum oboriatur, observanda sunt. Obedite dućtoribus vestris, & cedite. Hebr. 13: 17. Omnia decenter & ordine fiant. 1. Cor. 14:40. Quod præsertim sub Novo Test. locum habet: ubi, cum Ecclesia carnali amplius præcepto onerari non possit, nulla principum in Ecclesia potestas, nulli legislatorum throni, nullum humanum nomen, nulla denique servitus obtinet. Nemo vos subjiciat volens, in humilitate, & cultu Angelorum —si cum Christo mortui estis ab elementis mundi, quid, ut viventes in mundo, dogmata suscipitis? Col. 2: 18, 20. Ne sitis servi hominum.
units.tr: Since God has granted this authority to command in human affairs to the magistrate alone, the decrees of ecclesiastical assemblies concerning matters otherwise indifferent have the character not so much of laws as of admonitions, and are to be observed for the sake of order and decency alone, lest scandal arise rashly. Obey your leaders and submit to them. Heb. 13:17. Let all things be done decently and in order. 1 Cor. 14:40. This applies especially under the New Testament, where, since the Church can no longer be burdened with carnal precepts, no power of princes holds sway in the Church, no thrones of lawgivers, no human name, and in short no servitude. Let no one disqualify you, delighting in humility and the worship of angels... If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you submit to dogmas? Col. 2:18, 20. Do not become slaves of men. 1 Cor. 7:23.

units.la: 1. Cor. 7:23. Quamquam ordinem & regimen, ut in omni cœtu, ita in Ecclesia quoque locum habere par sit; iisque multum deferre oportet, qui præcipua Ecclesiæ curâ funguntur, &, fratrum consessum regentes, sacræ istius navis veluti clavum tenent.
units.tr: Yet order and government ought to have their place in the Church, as in any assembly; and due deference is to be paid to those who bear the chief care of the Church and, ruling the gathering of brothers, hold, as it were, the helm of that sacred ship.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Papæ autem thronum, legesque Capitolinas, cunctamque ejus tyrannidem abominamur ac despuimus. Nec ei hoc sensu ullum in Ecclefiâ locum, multo minus principem concedimus; cum Ecclesiæ minister non sit, sed prædo ac tyrannus, & sancti Christi thalami infessor; in cujus vindictam Christum Ecclesiæ Regem ac sponsum expectamus. Ultimæ autem impietatis sunt, quæ adulatorum ejus cohors jactat, ipsum regnantis in Ecclesia Christi vice fungi, ac supremum in terris mystarcham esse; adeoque & leges ferre, quæ piorum conscientias sub peccato mortali obligent, ac religiosos cultus, sanctosque ritus sancire posse, in quibus proprie cultus Dei situs sit; atque alia talia, de quibus inferius agendum erit.
units.tr: But we abhor and spurn the papal throne, the Capitoline laws, and all his tyranny. We grant him no place in the Church in this sense, much less a principate, since he is not a minister of the Church but a robber and tyrant, and an intruder into the holy bridal chamber of Christ; for whose vengeance we wait on Christ, the King and Bridegroom of the Church. But the crowd of his flatterers boast of the most extreme impiety: that he acts in the place of Christ as ruler of the Church and is the supreme mystarch on earth; and hence that he can enact laws binding the consciences of the pious under mortal sin, and can sanction religious worship and holy rites, in which the worship of God properly consists; and other such things, which will have to be treated below.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Nec remotâ ex Ecclesia potestate hac legislatoriâ, consequitur publica hæresium & religionum quarumcunque libertas & licentia, quam Sociniani aliique tuentur. Aliud est enim secreta conscientiæ pax, quæ lædenda non est: aliud, publicæ religionis ac cerimoniarum, quarum moderamen magistratui imcumbit. Cujus est providere, ut verus Deus publice colatur, verèque de eo sententiæ obtineant, nec nisi sancta ac casta disciplinâ populus imbuatur: eodem modo uti patrifamilias in privatâ domo hoc curare convenit.
units.tr: Nor, with this legislative power removed from the Church, does there follow the public freedom and license of heresies and religions of any kind, which the Socinians and others defend. For the secret peace of conscience is one thing, and it must not be disturbed; public religion and ceremonies, whose regulation falls to the magistrate, are another. It is his duty to see that the true God is publicly worshipped, that right opinions about him prevail, and that the people be imbued with nothing but holy and chaste discipline; in the same way, it is fitting for a father of a family to look after this in his private household.

units.la: XXI. Sequuntur ritus sacri: qui in duplici discrimine sunt, & vel à Christo, vel ab Ecclesia instituti sunt: illi divinæ, hæ humanæ auctoritatis; illi necessario observandi, hi non temere repudiandi sunt. Quamquam non aliam illi auctoritatem quam ordinis ac decori habeant; nec in iis per se efficacia quædam in ordine ad gratiæ effectus tribuenda sit. Videte, ne quis sit, qui vos prædetur, vel captivos agat, per Philosophiam, & vanam deceptionem, secundum traditionem hominum. Col. 2: 8. Irritum fecistis Dei mandatum per traditionem vestram. Matth. 15: 6. Unde ab unâ parte superstitio, quæ leves illos cultus amat, iisque mirifice delectatur, ac nimiam illis virtutem tribuit; ab alterâ, contemtus, & boni sanctique ordinis evertio vitanda est. XXII. Errant ergo Pontificii, qui non solum nimiâ eorum mole Ecclesiam obruerunt, sed mirificam præterea vim iis tribuunt; docentes, Ecclesiam ritus posse instituere, qui revera cultum Dei constituant; quique ad gratiam accipiendam, & peccatorum veniam obtinendam, & ad effectus spirituales utiles, & ad opus humanâ vi majus producendum apti sint (ut de exorcismis suis prædicant) ac denique mysterii causa observari debeant, ut divini olim ritus, in Vet. Test. instituti; quæ illi humanis suis cultibus ac multiplici superstitionum choragio applicant. XXIII. Est & de ritibus nonnulla cum Lutheranis controversia; quas Lutherus in Ecclesiis suis, tanquam ad sacrorum decus & dignitatem facientes, nimis imprudenter retinuit, istaque Romani scorti veluti spolia ac exuvias in iis spectari voluit. Quanquam nec ipsi ejus discipuli in omnibus consentiant, sed de Adiaphoris jam diu inter se pugnent. Nobis autem præcipua cum iis lis est de ritibus quibusdam in Baptismo & S. Cœna adhiberi solitis; ut & de aliis nonnullis cerimoniis Ecclesiasticis, confessione, absolutione, genuflexione, & canticis Latinis, denique de templorum ornatu per imagines & concentus musicos. Quæ tamen omnia nos non ejusdem generis ac momenti habemus: nec in unimen omnia nos non ejusdem generis ac momenti habemus: nec in unum hanc quæstionem tanti ducimus, ut Ecclesias, tam magnis diversum hanc quæstionem tanti ducimus, ut Ecclesias, tam magnis fidei dei capitibus conjunctas, quanquam in nonnullis adhuc partibus dissentientes, in perpetuum distrahere debeant. Non tamen omnes eas ceremonias adiaphoras statuimus.
units.tr: XXI. Next come the sacred rites, which are of two kinds: some were instituted by Christ, others by the Church; the former by divine authority, the latter by human authority; the former must necessarily be observed, the latter are not to be rashly rejected. Yet they have no other authority than that of order and decency, and no inherent efficacy is to be ascribed to them in relation to the effects of grace. See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and vain deceit, according to the tradition of men. Col. 2:8. You have made void the commandment of God through your tradition. Matt. 15:6. Hence, on one side, superstition must be avoided, which loves these trivial rites, delights in them wonderfully, and attributes excessive power to them; on the other side, contempt and the overthrow of a good and holy order must be avoided. XXII. The Papists therefore err, who have not only overwhelmed the Church with an excessive mass of them, but also ascribe wonderful power to them, teaching that the Church can institute rites which in fact constitute the worship of God; rites which are fit for receiving grace, obtaining the forgiveness of sins, and producing useful spiritual effects, and works greater than human power (as they boast of their exorcisms); and which, finally, ought to be observed for the sake of mystery, like the divine rites once instituted in the Old Testament. These they attach to their human worship and to a manifold dance of superstitions. XXIII. There is also some controversy over rites with the Lutherans, whom Luther retained too imprudently in his churches as contributing to the dignity and splendour of the sacred services, and whom he wished to be seen as the spoils and cast-off trappings of the Roman harlot. Yet even his own disciples do not agree on all points, but have long been quarrelling among themselves about the adiaphora. Our main dispute with them, however, concerns certain rites customarily used in Baptism and the Lord's Supper; and also some other ecclesiastical ceremonies: confession, absolution, genuflexion, Latin hymns, and finally the decoration of churches with images and musical harmonies. Yet we do not hold all these things to be of the same kind and weight; nor do we regard this question as so important that churches, so closely joined in the chief articles of the faith, though still disagreeing in some parts, ought to be torn apart forever. Nor, however, do we hold all those ceremonies to be indifferent.

units.la: XXIV. Quod denique indifferentia attinet, circa ea conscientia nullo modo ligata est; utpote quae liberrima ac rerum omnium domina sit: Scio, & persuasissimum, in Domino Iesu, nihil esse pollutum per se: nisi quod ei, qui quid pollutum censet, id pollutum est. Rom. 14: 14. Omnia mihi licent; at ego non redigar sub ullius potestatem. 1. Cor. 6: 12. Omnia vestra sunt. cap. 3: 22. Quanquam libertatem ipsam a libertatis usu distingui, illumque prudenter regi ac temperari debere concedamus. Obtinet enim hic illud Apostoli, Cavendum esse ab omni mali specie, 1. Thess. 5: 22. Quam regulam respectu infirmorum Apostolus tradit: quae tamen non ex vulgi, ac hominum imprudentium ac obstinatorum praejudicio, sed ex sapientum placitis, ac rei ipsius veritate explicanda est.
units.tr: XXIV. As for indifference itself, conscience is in no way bound in such matters, since it is most free and mistress of all things: I know and am fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; except to him who thinks something unclean, it is unclean. Rom. 14:14. All things are lawful for me; but I will not be brought under the power of anything. 1 Cor. 6:12. All things are yours. 1 Cor. 3:22. Yet we grant that liberty itself must be distinguished from the use of liberty, and that the latter must be governed and tempered prudently. For the saying of the Apostle holds here: One must abstain from every appearance of evil, 1 Thess. 5:22. The Apostle gives this rule with respect to the weak; yet it is to be explained not from the prejudice of the crowd and of imprudent and obstinate men, but from the judgments of the wise and from the truth of the matter itself.

units.la: XXV. Lex autem circa res indifferentes duplex est; tum fidei, tum charitatis. Illa nosmet ipsos, haec proximos spectat. Per fidem enim de recto rerum usu instrui ante omnia oportet, ne quidquam haesitante conscientia faciamus; quae si nobis obmurmuret & obstrepat, labem actionibus adspergit. Unusquisque in suo sensu certus sit. Rom. 14: 5. Beatus, qui se ipsum non judicat, in eo quod probat. v. 22. Fides contra libera ac sancta nobis omnia facit. Omnia pura puris. Tit. 1: 15. Omnis creatura Dei bona est — sanctificatur enim per sermonem Dei & intercessionem. 1. Tim. 4: 4, 5. Charitas autem non solum spectat quid liceat, verum etiam quid expediat: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia conducunt: 1. Cor. 10: 23. ac praecipue infirmorum sensu tangitur, quorum pietati adhuc tenerae & imbecillae non facile obicem poni patitur. Si propter cibum frater tuus contristatur, jam non secundum charitatem ambulas. Rom. 14: 15. Bonum non edere carnem — neque in quo frater tuus offendit, aut scandalizatur, aut infirmatur. v. 21. Quod tamen ad duros superstitiososque homines extendendum non est: Et assumens Timotheum, circumcidit eum, propter Iudaeos, qui erant in locis illis. Act. 16: 3. Sed neque Titus coactus fuit circumcidi, propter subreptitios falsos fratres. Gal. 2: 3, 4, 11. Quid autem leges, cum politicae, tum Ecclesiasticae, in rerum mediarum usu moderando valeant, supra visum est. Quae tamen, cessantibus causis ac circumstantiis earum, ultro cessant, ac rerum usum rursus liberum reddunt; praesertim accedente majore necessitate.
units.tr: XXV. The law concerning indifferent things is twofold: one of faith, the other of charity. The former regards ourselves, the latter our neighbours. For we must first be instructed by faith in the proper use of things, so that we do nothing with a doubting conscience; if this murmurs and clamours against us, it stains our actions. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. Rom. 14:5. Blessed is he who does not condemn himself in what he approves. v. 22. Faith, on the other hand, makes all things free and holy for us. To the pure all things are pure. Titus 1:15. Every creature of God is good, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. 1 Tim. 4:4, 5. But charity considers not only what is lawful but also what is expedient: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful. 1 Cor. 10:23. It is especially moved by the feelings of the weak, whose piety, still tender and feeble, it does not allow to be easily put in the way of a stumbling block. If your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Rom. 14:15. It is good not to eat meat... nor do anything by which your brother stumbles, or is offended, or is made weak. v. 21. This, however, is not to be extended to hard and superstitious men: And taking Timothy, he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. Acts 16:3. But neither was Titus compelled to be circumcised, because of the false brothers who had secretly crept in. Gal. 2:3, 4, 11. What both civil and ecclesiastical laws can do in regulating the use of intermediate things has been said above. Yet when their causes and circumstances cease, these laws cease of their own accord and make the use of things free again, especially when a greater necessity supervenes.

units.la: Pars II.
units.tr: Part II.

units.la: XXVI. Inordinatum hujus libertatis usum comitatur scandalum: quod est proprie, dictum factumve contra legem, quod aliis offendiculo est. De quo eleganter Tertull. de vel. virg. c. 3. scandalum, nisi fallor, non bona rei, sed mala res exemplum est, ædificans ad delictum. Bona res neminem scandalizant, nisi malam mentem. Estque vel datum, vel acceptum: quæ in genere eorum, quæ verè mala sunt, versantur. Cui & tertium genus additur, quod mixtum vocatur, seu infirmorum. Qui intempestiva quorundam libertate turbantur, & in pietatis cursu sufflaminantur, ac frigus quoddam patiuntur. Ubi ab utraque parte peccatur, & à dante, & ab accipiente: dum ille immodicè libertate utitur, & fratrem infirmum non respicit, aut propria scientia tumens etiam spernit; alter autem & ignorantia & charitatis defectu laborat, & suspicionibus nimis indulget, ac leviculâ quadam re sibi remoram injici patitur. Quod scandalum non fovendum, sed prudenter tollendum, & tum Ecclesiæ paci, tum Christianæ libertati ex æquo confulendum est.
units.tr: XXVI. An inordinate use of this liberty is accompanied by scandal, which is properly a word or deed against the law that is a stumbling block to others. On this Tertullian writes elegantly (On the Veiling of Virgins, ch. 3): Scandal, unless I am mistaken, is not the good thing itself but the bad thing made an example, which edifies towards sin. A good thing scandalizes no one, except a bad mind. Scandal is either given or taken, and these concern in general what is truly evil. To these a third kind is added, called mixed, or of the weak: those who are disturbed by the ill-timed liberty of some, and are hindered in their course of piety, and suffer a certain chill. Sin is committed on both sides here, both by the giver and by the receiver: the one uses his liberty immoderately and does not regard his weak brother, or even despises him, puffed up with his own knowledge; the other labours under both ignorance and a lack of charity, indulges too readily in suspicions, and allows himself to be held back by some trifling matter. This scandal is not to be fostered but wisely removed, and the peace of the Church and Christian liberty alike are to be consulted equally.

units.la: LOCUS TRIGESIMUS NONUS. DE Beneficiis Christi internis, sanctifica- tione, aliisque ei connexis. CAPUT VII. De Sanctificatione.
units.tr: THE THIRTY-NINTH TOPIC. Concerning the inward benefits of Christ, sanctification, and other things connected with them. CHAPTER VII. On Sanctification.

units.la: I. UM fideles, sanguine Christi abluti, Spiritu ejus porro mundari, ac pristinæ sanctitatis luci ac nitori restituti debeant; hinc ad justificationem sequitur Sanctificatio.
units.tr: I. Since the faithful, washed in the blood of Christ and further cleansed by his Spirit, must be restored to the light and lustre of their former holiness, sanctification follows upon justification.

units.la: II. Differt ea à justificatione; quod per illam à peccati reatu, per hanc ab ejus maculâ purgemur: ibi homo sese objectivè; hic subjectivè habet: illa unico actu, unâque judicis sententiâ; hæc gradibus ac momentis quibusdam absolvitur: illa denique in omnibus unimoda, hæc diversa, atque in eodem homine vel perfectior, vel imperfectior est; & cum justificatio in hac vita perfecta sit, illa non nisi supremo hominis fine, & ad extremum vitæ limitem perficitur.
units.tr: II. It differs from justification in this: by justification we are cleansed from the guilt of sin, by sanctification from its stain. In justification a person stands in an objective relation, in sanctification a subjective one. Justification is accomplished by a single act and a single sentence of the Judge, whereas sanctification is completed by certain degrees and stages. Justification is, finally, the same in all, while sanctification varies, and in the same person it is sometimes more perfect and sometimes less so. And although justification is perfect in this life, sanctification is brought to perfection only at the final end of a person and at the outermost limit of life.

units.la: III. Est autem Sanctificandi vox τολύσημος; & modo sanctitatis ac gloriæ agnitionem; ut in prece dominicâ, sanctificetur nomen tuum: modo rerum quarundam ad usum sacrum designationem; ut in decalogo, recordare diei Sabbati, ut sanctifices illum: modo ipsam redemtionem, ut Exod. 31:13. Hebr. 2:11. 10:10,14. vel denique sanctorum habituum inductionem significat, quo sensu hic sumitur. Quæ & conversio, renovatio, diversisque aliis modis appellatur.
units.tr: III. The word sanctify is polysemous [πολύσημος]. Sometimes it signifies the acknowledgement of holiness and glory, as in the Lord's Prayer, hallowed be your name; sometimes the setting apart of certain things for sacred use, as in the Decalogue, remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy; sometimes redemption itself, as in Exod. 31:13, Heb. 2:11, 10:10, 14; or, finally, it signifies the infusion of holy habits, and in this sense it is taken here. This is also called conversion and renewal, and by various other names.

units.la: IV. Forma ejus consistit in nativæ labis depulsione, & mentis, voluntatis, affectuum, actuum denique omnium emendatione ac sanctitate. In toto enim homine illa sedet. Transformamini renovatione mentis vestræ. Rom. 12:2. Sistite vos Deo, ut ex mortuis viventes, & membra vestra arma justitiæ. Rom. 6:13. Induistis novum hominem, qui innovatur ad cognitionem, juxta imaginem ejus, qui ipsum creavit. Col. 3:10. Ut perverse Sociniani, qui naturæ corruptionem negant, eam in solâ actuum emendatione collocent.
units.tr: IV. Its form consists in the removal of native corruption and in the amendment and holiness of the mind, the will, the affections and, finally, of all actions. For it resides in the whole person: Be transformed by the renewing of your mind, Rom. 12:2; Present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness, Rom. 6:13; You have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created him, Col. 3:10. The Socinians are wrong to deny the corruption of nature and to place sanctification in the amendment of actions alone.

units.la: V. Præcipuè ergo in mente, & in voluntate, reliquorum actuum fonte, sanctificatio locum habet. In voluntatem enim ea quoque immediatè pertingit. Quod perperam negavit doctissimus Camero, à solâ mentis luce reliquam porro animam illustrari & perfici, nec voluntatem ipsam immediatè affici, sed mentis lumini eam semper obsequi, dictitans. Quæ perperam ordinantur: cum iste facultatum earum ordo ac nexus, aut illa denique intellectus in voluntatem potestas ac imperium non sit, ut ad nudam facem, quam ille præfert, voluntas protinus sequatur. Quo accedit, quod corruptio gravius aliquo modo in voluntate hæserit, eamque altius infecerit, quam ipsam mentem; unde ad solam ejus lucem excitari, seque ipsam commovere non potest. Mentis enim collustrationem non sufficere vel ex ipsis reprobis quotidie patet. Requiritur enim præterea in voluntate attentio; quademum posita, sequitur ad clarum intellectus perceptionem inclinatio voluntatis. Illa autem Dei donum est, ut apparet in Lydia purpuraria. Act. 16:14.
units.tr: V. Sanctification therefore takes place chiefly in the mind and in the will, the source of all the other actions. For it also reaches the will immediately. The most learned Camero wrongly denied this, teaching that the rest of the soul is further illuminated and perfected by the light of the mind alone, and that the will itself is not affected immediately but always obeys the light of the mind. These things are wrongly ordered, since this order and connection of the faculties, or the power and rule of the intellect over the will, is not such that the will follows at once the bare torch he presents. Moreover, corruption has stuck more deeply in the will in some way and has infected it more profoundly than the mind itself, so that the will cannot be roused by that light alone or move itself. That mere illumination of the mind is not sufficient is plain every day even from the reprobate. For in the will there is also required attention; once this is given, an inclination of the will follows upon the clear perception of the intellect. But that attention is a gift of God, as appears in Lydia the seller of purple, Acts 16:14.

units.la: VI. Cum autem sanctificatio quidam quasi motus sit, duo ejus termini considerari possunt. Terminus à quo, est corruptio & labes peccati: Purificemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus, 2. Cor. 7:1. Terminus ad quem est, divinæ imaginis sanctitas & splendor; quæ peccatorum sordibus infuscata pristino nitori restituì debet: Induere novum hominem, qui secundum Deum est creatus. Eph. 4: 24. Unde duæ sequuntur sanctificationis partes, aversio à malo, & conversio ad bonum: Recede a malo, & fac bonum. Psal. 34: 15. Declinate male facere, discite bene facere. Esai. 1: 16, 17. Illa mortificatio veteris hominis, hæc vivificatio novi hominis; illa crucifixio quædam, hæc resurrectio apud sacros auctores appellatur. Illi adhæret dolor secundum Deum. 2. Cor. 7: 10. Huic, spes veniæ, cum gaudio spirituali, & oblectatione in lege divina: Nam apud te est condonatio, ut timearis. Psal. 130: 4. Beatus ille vir, cujus in lege Iehova voluptas est. Psal. 1: 2.
units.tr: VI. Since sanctification is, as it were, a kind of motion, two termini of it may be considered. The terminus from which is corruption and the stain of sin: Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, 2 Cor. 7:1. The terminus to which is the holiness and splendour of the divine image, which, darkened by the filth of sins, must be restored to its former lustre: to put on the new man, which after God is created, Eph. 4:24. Hence follow two parts of sanctification: turning away from evil and turning to good: Depart from evil, and do good, Ps. 34:15; Cease to do evil, learn to do good, Isa. 1:16, 17. The former is called by the sacred writers the mortification of the old man, the latter his quickening; the former a kind of crucifixion, the latter a resurrection. To the former is joined godly sorrow, 2 Cor. 7:10; to the latter, the hope of pardon, with spiritual joy and delight in the divine law: For with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared, Ps. 130:4; Blessed is the man whose delight is in the law of Jehovah, Ps. 1:2.

units.la: VII. Necessitas ejus ex cunctis religionis partibus elucet. Nam & electio & redemtio; & Dei sanctitas ac imago; ac Christi in nobis habitantis Spiritus; & fidei natura ac ratio; ipsa denique beatitudo æterna illam undique flagitant. Sicut elegit nos ante fundationem mundi, ut essemus sancti. Eph. 1: 4. Qui dedit semet ipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni adversus legem delicto, & purificaret sibi populum &c. Tit. 2: 14. Induere novum hominem, qui secundum Deum est creatus. Eph. 4: 24. Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est ipsius. Rom. 8: 9. Fide purificans corda ipsorum. Act. 15: 9. Persequimini sanctitatem illam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum. Hebr. 12: 14.
units.tr: VII. The necessity of sanctification shines out from every part of religion. For election and redemption, the holiness and image of God, the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us, the nature and reasoning of faith, and finally eternal blessedness itself, all demand it on every side: As he chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy, Eph. 1:4; who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every lawless deed and purify for himself a people, etc., Titus 2:14; to put on the new man, which after God is created, Eph. 4:24; If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his, Rom. 8:9; purifying their hearts by faith, Acts 15:9; Pursue that holiness, without which no one will see the Lord, Heb. 12:14.

units.la: VIII. Causa principalis, sive auctor ejus est Spir. S. male enim Socinus Spiritum non nisi sanctificatis dari vult. Nisi quis nascatur ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in regnum Dei. Joh. 3: 5. Instrumentalis est, verbum, cum legis, tum præcipuè Euangelii, accedente sacramentorum usu, & mediis quandoque extraordinariis. Exemplaris est, cum Deus ipse: Sancti sitis, quia ego sanctus sum. Lev. 19: 2. Matth. 5: 48. tum Christus: Discite a me, quod mitis sum, & humilis corde. Matth. 11: 29. Imitatores mei estote, ut & ego Christi. 1. Cor. 11: 1. Qui morte & resurrectione sua, cum spiritualis nostræ crucifixionis, tum novæ vitæ, quandam quasi imaginem exhibuit: Hoc scientes, veterem nostrum hominem unâ crucifixum esse, ut aboleatur corpus peccati. Rom. 6: 6. Si igitur cum Christo excitati estis, ea, quæ sursum sunt, quærite. Col. 3: 1,
units.tr: VIII. The principal cause, or author, of it is the Holy Spirit; for Socinus wrongly wishes the Spirit to be given only to those already sanctified. Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, John 3:5. The instrumental cause is the word, both of the law and, chiefly, of the Gospel, together with the use of the sacraments and sometimes extraordinary means. The exemplary cause is God himself: Be holy, for I am holy, Lev. 19:2; Matt. 5:48; and Christ: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, Matt. 11:29; Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:1. By his death and resurrection he displayed a kind of image both of our spiritual crucifixion and of the new life: knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, Rom. 6:6; If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, Col. 3:1,

units.la: 2. Causa denique administra, nosque ad istam Christi imaginem refingens, est fides. Una cum Christo crucifixus sum. Vivo autem non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus. Et vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem illam filii Dei &c. Gal. 2: 20.
units.tr: 2. Finally, the instrumental cause, which fashions us into this image of Christ, is faith: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, etc., Gal. 2:20.

units.la: IX. Cum vero Spiritus S. per gradus cam peragat, duæ sanctificatio-nis nis sunt periodi; cum hujus vitæ, tum futuræ. Ibi obtinebit ætas Ecclesiæ virilis & perfecta, hic ejus infantia locum habet. Donec perveniamus omnes ad virum perfectum, ad mensuram statura, quod completur à Christo. Eph. 4: 13. Videmus enim adhuc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc vero facie ad faciem. 1. Cor. 13: 12. Quanquam etiam respectu hujus Ecclesiæ ætatis, pro vario piorum profectu, alii infantes & pueri in Christo, alii adulti dicantur. Ac Novi quidem Testamenti respectu infantilis fuit omnis Ecclesiæ sub Vet. Test. ætas, pro parca cognitionis ac Spir. mensura. Qualis si quis sit in Novi Test. luce, infans habeatur. Omnis particeps lactis, imperitus est sermonis justitia; infans enim est. Hebr. 5: 13. Nunc autem illi infantes ac pueri dicuntur in Christo, qui prima tantum fidei elementa tenent, nec istum Euangelicæ perfectionis gradum obtinent, quem alii, & scientia, & virtutum habitu firmatiores, adepti sunt. Sapientiam loquimur in perfectis. 1. Cor. 2: 6. Non potui loqui vobis, ut spiritualibus, sed ut carnalibus, ut infantibus in Christo. 1. Cor. 3: 1.
units.tr: IX. Since the Holy Spirit carries this out by degrees, there are two periods of sanctification, one of this life and one of the life to come. There the Church will attain to manhood and perfection; here it has the place of infancy: until we all attain to the unity of the faith, to a mature man, to the measure of the stature which belongs to the fullness of Christ, Eph. 4:13; For now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face, 1 Cor. 13:12. Yet even with respect to this age of the Church, according to the varying progress of the godly, some are called infants and children in Christ, others adults. In comparison with the New Testament, the whole age of the Church under the Old Testament was infantile, given the scant measure of knowledge and of the Spirit. If anyone were in the light of the New Testament and still like that, he would be regarded as an infant. Everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant, Heb. 5:13. But now those are called infants and children in Christ who hold only the first elements of faith and have not attained that stage of Gospel perfection which others, firmer in knowledge and in the habit of virtue, have reached. We speak wisdom among the perfect, 1 Cor. 2:6; I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal, as to infants in Christ, 1 Cor. 3:1.

units.la: X. Cumque ita sanctificatio per partes absolvatur, & quotidiana incrementa habeat, duplex in sanctificatis principium observare licet, Carnem, & Spiritum. Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem. Gal. 5: 17. Quæ instar duplicis hominis in Scriptura considerantur: Docti estis deponere veteres hominem & induere novum hominem. Eph. 4: 21. Caro dicit naturam humanam, prout Dei Spiritu caret. Cum autem Spiritus ille, vel ut sanctificans, vel ut vificans ac immortalitate donans, consideretur; utroque modo caro illi in Scripturis opponitur, & vel humanam naturam nondum immortalitatis compotem, ut: Caro & sanguis non possunt hereditare regnum Dei: seritur corpus animale, suscitatur corpus spirituale. 1. Cor. 15: 50, 44. vel eandem sanctificatore Spiritu destitutum dicit. Qui hujus loci sensus est. Adeoque dicit illa nativam istam labem, malaque cupidines, quæ hominem ab ipso ortu occuparunt; nec inferiores solum animæ facultates, sed totum hominem infecerunt & corruperunt; in corpore autem ac in carne ejus præcipue dominantur, ac membra ejus tanquam arma sua movent & usurpant. Unde peccatum habitans in carne, & lex peccati, quæ est in membris, Rom. 7. passim appellatur. Spiritus vero notat formatorem novæ vitæ Spiritum S. ejusque dona & motus, omnemque in novo homine potentiam: Quod natum est ex Spiritu, Spiritus est. Joh. 3: 6.
units.tr: X. Since sanctification is thus carried out piece by piece and grows day by day, one may observe a twofold principle in the sanctified: the flesh and the Spirit. The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. Gal. 5: 17. Scripture treats these as a kind of double man: you were taught to put off the old man and to put on the new man. Eph. 4: 21. Flesh denotes human nature insofar as it lacks the Spirit of God. But when that Spirit is considered either as sanctifying, or as quickening and bestowing immortality, the flesh is opposed to him in Scripture in both ways: either as human nature not yet possessed of immortality, as in Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. 1 Cor. 15: 50, 44. or as denoting that same nature destitute of the sanctifying Spirit. This is the sense of the passage here. It thus denotes that native taint and evil desires which seized man from his very birth, which have infected and corrupted not only the lower faculties of the soul but the whole man, and which chiefly rule in the body and its flesh, moving and using its members as their weapons. Hence sin dwelling in the flesh, and the law of sin which is in the members, Rom. 7, is everywhere so called. Spirit, however, denotes the Holy Spirit, the former of the new life, with his gifts and motions and all the power in the new man: That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. John 3: 6.

units.la: Hinc duplex in sanctificatis principium. Caro & Spiritus. hominem, qui secundum Deum est creatus. Eph. 4: 24. Unde duæ sequuntur sanctificationis partes, aversio à malo, & conversio ad bonum: Recede à malo, & fac bonum. Psal. 34: 15. Diuiste male facere, discite bene facere. Esai. 1: 16, 17. Illa mortificatio veteris hominis, hæc vivificatio novi hominis; illa crucifixio quædam, hæc resurrectio apud sacros auctores appellatur. Illi adhæret dolor secundum Deum. 2. Cor. 7: 10. Huic, spes veniæ, cum gaudio spirituali, & oblectatione in lege divina: Nam apud te est condonatio, ut timearis. Psal. 130: 4. Beatus ille vir, cujus in lege Iehova voluptas est. Psal. 1: 2.
units.tr: Hence the twofold principle in the sanctified: flesh and Spirit. the man who is created according to God. Eph. 4: 24. From this follow the two parts of sanctification: turning away from evil, and turning toward good: Depart from evil, and do good. Ps. 34: 15. Cease to do evil, learn to do well. Isa. 1: 16, 17. The former is called in the sacred authors the mortification of the old man, the latter the quickening of the new man; the one is a kind of crucifixion, the other a resurrection. Joined to the former is godly sorrow, 2 Cor. 7: 10; to the latter, the hope of pardon, with spiritual joy and delight in the divine law: But there is forgiveness with you, that you may be feared. Ps. 130: 4. Blessed is that man whose delight is in the law of Jehovah. Ps. 1: 2.

units.la: VII. Necessitas ejus ex cunctis religionis partibus elucet. Nam & electio & redemtio; & Dei sanctitas ac imago; ac Christi in nobis habitantis Spiritus; & fidei natura ac ratio; ipsa denique beatitudo æterna illam undique flagitant. Sicut elegit nos ante fundationem mundi, ut essemus sancti. Eph. 1: 4. Qui dedit semet ipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni adversus legem delicto, & purificaret sibi populum &c. Tit. 2: 14. Induere novum hominem, qui secundum Deum est creatus. Eph. 4: 24. Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est ipsius. Rom. 8: 9. Fide purificans corda ipsorum. Act. 15: 9. Persequimini sanctitatem illam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum. Hebr. 12: 14.
units.tr: VII. The necessity of sanctification shines forth from all the parts of religion. For election and redemption, the holiness and image of God, the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us, the nature and reason of faith, and finally eternal blessedness itself all demand it on every side. As he chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy. Eph. 1: 4. Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every iniquity and purify to himself a people, etc. Tit. 2: 14. Put on the new man, who is created according to God. Eph. 4: 24. If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. Rom. 8: 9. Purifying their hearts by faith. Acts 15: 9. Pursue that holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. Heb. 12: 14.

Joh. 3: 5. Instrumentalis est, verbum, cum legis, tum præcipuè Euangelii, accedente sacramentorum usu, & mediis quandoque extraordinariis. Exemplaris est, cum Deus ipse: Sancti sitis, quia ego sanctus sum. Lev. 19: 2. Matth. 5: 48. tum Christus: Discite à me, quod mitis sum, & humilis corde. Matth. 11: 29. Una cum Christo crucifixus sum. Vivo autem non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus. Et vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem illam filii Dei &c. Gal. 2: 20.

Unless a man is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. John 3: 5. The instrumental cause is the Word, both of the law and especially of the gospel, together with the use of the sacraments and sometimes extraordinary means. The exemplary cause is God himself: Be holy, for I am holy. Lev. 19: 2. Matt. 5: 48. and Christ: Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart. Matt. 11: 29. Ac Novi quidem Testamenti respectu infantilis fuit omnis Ecclesiæ sub Vet. Test. ætas, pro parca cognitionis ac Spir. mensura. Qualis si quis sit in Novi Test. luce, infans habeatur. Omnis particeps lactis, imperitus est sermonis justitiæ; infans enim est. Hebr. 5: 13. Sapientiam loquimur in perfectis. 1. Cor. 2: 6. Non potui loqui vobis, ut spiritualibus, sed ut carnalibus, ut infantibus in Christo. 1. Cor. 3: 1.
units.tr: IX. Since the Holy Spirit carries this out by degrees, there are two periods of sanctification, one of this life and one of the future life. There the age of the Church will be mature and perfect; here it holds the place of infancy. Until we all attain to the unity of the faith and to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. Eph. 4: 13. For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face. 1 Cor. 13: 12. Yet even with respect to this age of the Church, some are called infants and children in Christ, others adults, according to the varying progress of the pious. In relation to the New Testament, the whole age of the Church under the Old Testament was infantile, given the scant measure of knowledge and of the Spirit. If anyone is in this condition in the light of the New Testament, he is to be considered an infant. Everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. Heb. 5: 13. Now, however, those are called infants and children in Christ who hold only the first elements of faith and do not attain that stage of evangelical perfection which others, more firm both in knowledge and in the habit of virtues, have reached. We speak wisdom among the perfect. 1 Cor. 2: 6. I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ. 1 Cor. 3: 1.

Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem. Gal. 5: 17. Quæ instar duplicis hominis in Scriptura consideratur: Docti estis deponere vetustum hominem — & induere novum hominem. Eph. 4: 21. Caro dicit naturam humanam, prout Dei Spiritu caret. Cum autem Spiritus ille, vel ut sanctificans, vel ut vivificans ac immortalitate donans, consideretur; utroque modo caro illi in Scripturis opponitur, & vel humanam naturam nondum immortalitatis compotem, ut: Caro & sanguis non possunt hereditare regnum Dei: seritur corpus animale, suscitatur corpus spirituale. 1. Cor. 15: 50, 44. vel eandem sanctificatore Spiritu destitutam dicit. Qui hujus loci sensus est. Adeoque dicit illa nativam istam labem, malasque cupiditates, quæ hominem ab ipso ortu occuparunt; nec inferiores solum animæ facultates, sed totum hominem infecerunt & corruperunt; in corpore autem ac in carne ejus præcipuè dominantur, ac membra ejus tanquam arma sua movent & usurpant. Unde peccatum habitans in carne, & lex peccati, quæ est in membris, Rom. 7. passim appellatur. units.tr: X. Since sanctification is thus carried out piece by piece and has daily increase, one may observe a twofold principle in the sanctified: the flesh and the Spirit. The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. Gal. 5: 17. These are regarded in Scripture as a kind of double man: You were taught to put off the old man — and to put on the new man. Eph. 4: 21. Flesh denotes human nature insofar as it lacks the Spirit of God. But when that Spirit is considered either as sanctifying, or as quickening and bestowing immortality, the flesh is opposed to him in Scripture in both ways: either as human nature not yet possessed of immortality, as in Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. 1 Cor. 15: 50, 44. or as denoting that same nature destitute of the sanctifying Spirit. This is the sense of the passage here. It thus denotes that native taint and evil lusts which seized man from his very birth, which have infected and corrupted not only the lower faculties of the soul but the whole man, and which chiefly rule in the body and its flesh, moving and using its members as their weapons. Hence sin dwelling in the flesh, and the law of sin which is in the members, Rom. 7, is everywhere so called. Spirit, however, denotes the Holy Spirit, the former of the new life, with his gifts and motions and all the power in the new man: That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. John 3: 6.

units.la: XI. Atque ex duplici hoc fonte perpetua in homine pugna ac lucta exoritur, inter duas illas partes, carnem ac Spiritum. In qua moderanda, ac carne debellanda, & cupidinum regno tollendo sanctificatio ferè consistit. Gal. 5: 17. Cujus illustre exemplum in Apostolo Paulo extat Rom. 7. qui licet Deo liberatori gratias agat, ꝓs 25. antea tamen ut carnalis, & peccato traditus ac venditus ibidem describitur; quod videl. ex naturæ suæ indole, & juxta eminentissimam legis sanctitatem, talis fuisset; quamvis deinceps per regenerationem alius factus esset. Lex Spiritus vitæ in Christo Iesu liberum me fecit a lege peccati & mortis. Rom. 8: 2. Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum passionibus & concupiscentiis. Gal. 5: 24. quod sine perpetua luctā, inter istas peccati reliquias, fieri non potest.
units.tr: XI. From this twofold source there arises a perpetual battle and struggle in man between those two parts, the flesh and the Spirit. Sanctification consists largely in moderating this struggle, subduing the flesh, and overthrowing the rule of the lusts. Gal. 5: 17. A famous example of this is in the Apostle Paul, Rom. 7, who, although he there gives thanks to God his deliverer, v. 25, nevertheless is described there, earlier, as carnal, and as sold and given over to sin; which, of course, he would have been by the nature of his disposition and according to the most eminent holiness of the law, though afterward he was made a different man through regeneration. The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death. Rom. 8: 2. Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Gal. 5: 24. This cannot happen without perpetual struggle against those remnants of sin.

units.la: XII. Differt autem multum regenitorum lucta ab intestino illo irregenitorum tumultu, & cupiditatum reliquæque in iis lucis certamine. Diversa enim illa sunt. 1. Subjectis: quæ hic sunt Spiritus & caro, ibi vero diversæ ac pugnantes cupiditates & affectus; vel ad summum ratio, utcunque illustrata, & ex adversa affectuum cohors: unde talibus cor duplex adscribitur. Psal. 12: 3. 2. Causis: illud jurgium, illeque mentis æstus ex servili affectu, & poenæ metu; hæc autem lucta ex nova natura, & filiali Dei amore, exoritur. 3. Objectis: ibi in atrociora tantum peccata, hic in omnia, & leviora quoque, pugnatur. 4. Eventu denique: cum ibi peccata quidem reprimantur nonnihil, sed quæ rupto tandem obice acrius exardescunt; hic autem Spiritus, carne potentior, tandem victor fit, omnemque istum animæ tumultum componat & extinguat.
units.tr: XII. The struggle of the regenerate differs greatly from that inner turmoil of the unregenerate, and from the conflict of desires and the rest of the light they have. For those are different in four ways. (1) In their subjects: here they are Spirit and flesh, but there they are divided and warring desires and affections, or at most reason, however enlightened, and against it the troop of opposing affections; hence such people are described as having a double heart (Ps. 12:3). (2) In their causes: that quarrel and that agitation of mind arise from a servile attitude and fear of punishment, but this struggle arises from a new nature and a filial love of God. (3) In their objects: there the fight is only against the more heinous sins, but here it is against all sins, even the lighter ones. (4) In their outcome: there sins are indeed held back to some extent, but when the barrier finally breaks they blaze up more fiercely; here, however, the Spirit, being stronger than the flesh, at last becomes victor and calms and extinguishes all that tumult of the soul.

units.la: XIII. Qualem luctam irregeniti inter mentem & membra, inter conscientiam & carnem hominis sub lege constituti & gratia Evangelica destituti, Paulus figurate & in propria quasi persona proponere videtur Rom. 7. in quo ꝓs 9. repræsentat statum Judæorum, primo quidem quales fuerint γωρὶς νόμε ante legem latam: dein vero ꝓs 10. quales facti sint ἐλθόσης τῆς ἐντολῆς, postquam lex data esset. quam personarum enallagen cum ibi auspicatus esset, nullum est indicium, illum ab ea destitisse ꝓs seqq. usque ad ꝓs 24. & 25. ubi demum de se ut regenito loqui incipit. Quod toto hoc capite agi, manifestum est, cum ex difficultate initio illius propositā de irritatione peccati & productione mortis in iis qui sub lege sunt & gratia Evangelii carent; cui incongrue respondere exhibendo seipsum in statu regenerationis, in qua non amplius sub lege est: tum ex collatione eorum quæ hîc de se ipso dicit ȳs 14,23. quæ contradicunt iis quæ de regenitis Cap. 6:18. & 8: 1,2.dicit, Confer & ea quæ hic ȳs 18, 19. de se prædicat, cum iis quæ dicit Phil. 2: 13. & 4: 13.
units.tr: XIII. The kind of struggle that the unregenerate have between mind and members, between conscience and flesh, when a man is placed under the law and lacks the Gospel grace, Paul seems to set out figuratively, as if in his own person, in Rom. 7. In this chapter, in vers. 9, he represents the condition of the Jews, first as they were χωρὶς νόμου [apart from the law] before the law was given, and then in vers. 10 as they became ἐλθούσης τῆς ἐντολῆς [when the commandment came], after the law had been given. That shift of persons, once he had begun it, shows no sign that he abandoned it through vers. 14 to 24 and 25, where at last he begins to speak of himself as a regenerate man. That this whole chapter is concerned with this is clear: first from the difficulty proposed at the start, about the stirring up of sin and the production of death in those who are under the law and lack the grace of the Gospel, to which he answers unsuitably if he shows himself in the state of regeneration, in which he is no longer under the law; and then from a comparison of what he says here about himself (vers. 14, 23), which contradicts what he says about the regenerate (ch. 6:18 and 8:1, 2). Compare also what he claims here about himself (vers. 18, 19) with what he says in Phil. 2:13 and 4:13.

units.la: XIV. Cum vero in hac vitâ nondum prorsus carne liberemur, mixtæ sunt omnes fidelium actiones,& vel rectissima eorum opera aliquam labem habent. Quanquam non ideo peccata ea dicenda sunt, ut Lutherani argutantur, sed peccato inquinata.
