units.tr: XIV. But since in this life we are not yet entirely freed from the flesh, all the actions of the faithful are mixed, and even their most upright works have some stain. Yet these works are not therefore to be called sins, as the Lutherans quibble, but are sinful, tainted by sin.

units.la: XV. Incidere etiam possunt fideles in gravissima peccata, quorum & ipsi fomitem ac fontem in se ipse retinent. Quanquam enim Spiritu ductore nunquam destituantur; ille quidem ad salutem eos certo deducit, in via autem offendere& obhærere nonnunquam finit,rursusque aberroribus reducit. Unde& contra conscientiam delinquere eos sæpe contingit, quatenus ejus monitus negligunt, ita ut eos damnet cor suum. A quo lapsu qui se integros servant, & veram fidem ac spem retinent, illi magnam παῤῥησίαν habent apud Deum, magnosque conscientiæ plausus referunt. Si nos condemnet cor nostrum, major nempe est Deus corde nostro, & novit omnia. Si cor nostrum non condemnet nos, libertatem habemus ad Deum. 1. Joh. 3:20, 21.
units.tr: XV. The faithful may also fall into the gravest sins, of which they themselves keep the tinder and the spring within themselves. For although they are never abandoned by the Spirit who leads them, he indeed surely brings them to salvation, yet on the way he sometimes allows them to stumble and become stuck, and again he brings them back from their wanderings. Hence it often happens that they sin even against conscience, insofar as they neglect its warnings, so that their own heart condemns them. Those who keep themselves whole from this lapse, and retain true faith and hope, have great παῤῥησίαν [boldness] before God, and gain great comfort of conscience: If our heart condemns us, God is surely greater than our heart, and knows all things. If our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God (1 John 3:20, 21).

units.la: XVI. Non possunt tamen voluntarie peccare, h. e. veritatem visam odisse,lucemque istam protervo pede conculcare,ac mero ejus odio peccare: Voluntarie enim peccantibus nobis non amplius pro peccato relinquitur hostia. Hebr. 10:26. Neque manu elata, ac obfirmata mente peccant, aut regnum ac imperium iterum peccati patiuntur; sed, quicquid peccant, ex ignorantia, vel humana infirmitate ac imbecillitate provenit. Quo sensu dicuntur non facere peccatum, nec posse peccare, quia semem Dei in iis manet, 1. Joh. 3:9. Semper enim sub Spiritus regimine manent, à quo peccatum non provenit. Nunquam enim ille Spiritus desinit, ut sæpius regenerari eos necesse sit: regeniti, non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili. 1. Pet. 1:23.
units.tr: XVI. Yet they cannot sin willfully, that is, hate a truth they have seen, trample that light with a bold foot, and sin out of pure hatred of it: For if we sin willfully, no sacrifice for sins remains for us any longer (Heb. 10:26). Nor do they sin with a raised hand and a hardened mind, nor do they again suffer the kingdom and rule of sin; but whatever they sin comes from ignorance, or from human frailty and weakness. In this sense they are said not to commit sin, nor to be able to sin, because the seed of God remains in them (1 John 3:9). For they always remain under the rule of the Spirit, from whom sin does not come. That Spirit never ceases, so that they must be regenerated again and again: born again, not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible (1 Pet. 1:23).

units.la: XVII. Voluit autem Deus luctam illam perpetuam esse,nec nisi in ultimo vitæ limite, ac in morte ipsa finiri; quando peccatum, quod hic per luctam minuitur, exuendo corpus peccati, deponemus: Nam qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato. Rom. 6: 7. Quis me eripiet è corpore mortis? c. 7:24. Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur, à nunc: ita, dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant à laboribus suis. Apoc. 14: 13. idque variosob fines:tum,uti inter vitæ hujus tædia,ac futuram beatitudinem, discrimen poneret: tum ut infirmitatum sensu humiles nos redderet, ac pudenti quadam pietate perfunderet; &c, admotis stimulis, ad futuræ vitæ perfectionem anhelare juberet: itemque demonstrandæ potentiæ suæ, quæ per tot lapsus, tamque salebrosa viâ, tamen in cœlum nos introducit: denique ut erga proximum nos placidos facilesque redderet; cum deceat peccatis veniam poscentem, reddere rursus.
units.tr: XVII. God, however, willed that this struggle should be perpetual, and that it should end only at the final limit of life, in death itself; when we will lay down the sin which is diminished here by the struggle, by putting off the body of sin. For he who has died has been justified from sin (Rom. 6:7). Who will deliver me from the body of this death? (Rom. 7:24). Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on; so, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours (Rev. 14:13). He did this for various ends: partly, that he might set a distinction between the weariness of this life and future blessedness; partly, that by a sense of our weaknesses he might make us humble, and suffuse us with a certain modest piety; and, by applying goads, that he might command us to strive toward the perfection of the future life; likewise, to demonstrate his power, which, despite so many falls and so rough a path, nevertheless leads us into heaven; and finally, that he might make us gentle and easy toward our neighbour, since it is fitting that one who asks pardon for his sins should in turn grant it.

units.la: XVIII. Ita ut perpetua obtineat in hac vita sanctificationis imperfectio: non quod perfectio ex sese impossibilis sit (est enim naturæ humanæ apprimè congrua, & conveniens, olimque præstanda) sed quod non tantum nunc Spiritus mensuram Deus largiatur, ut, omni labi purgandæ sufficiat. Quanquam quod sanctiores non simus, ejus rei non parva penes nos culpa resideat, quod Spiritum istum non satis petimus, nec sinum pandimus, omnemque ejus auram colligimus; nec venienti ac ferenti Spiritui obsequimur, neque motibus ejus usque quaque obsecundamus, nec omni studio eum fovemus & conservamus: Ne contristate Spir. S. Dei, quo obsignati estis ad diem redemtionis. Eph. 4: 30. Spiritum ne extinguite. 1. Thess. 5: 19.
units.tr: XVIII. So imperfection of sanctification persists throughout this life: not because perfection is impossible in itself (for it is most fitting to human nature and suited to it, and is to be attained in time), but because God does not for now grant such a measure of the Spirit as would suffice to purge us from every lapse. Yet the fact that we are not holier is due in no small part to our own fault, since we do not ask enough for this Spirit, nor open our bosom, nor gather in all his breath; nor do we obey the coming and bearing Spirit, nor follow his motions in every way, nor cherish and preserve him with all our zeal: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption (Eph. 4:30). Do not quench the Spirit (1 Thess. 5:19).

units.la: XIX. Atque cadit hic Pelagianorum impeccantia, quæ justitiæ operum soboles est: quam & Scripturæ, & omnium sanctorum exempla, & quotidiana denique experientia, refutant. Quis dicet, sincerum esse feci cor meum, purus sum a peccato meo? Prov. 20: 9. Si dicamus, quod peccatum non habemus, nosmet ipsos decipimus. 1. Joh. 1: 8. Nam homo non est justus in terra, qui agat bonum, & non peccet. Eccl. 7: 20. Et extimus, tanquam impurus, omnes nos, &, ut vestis remotionum, omnes justitiæ nostræ. Esai. 64: 6.
units.tr: XIX. And here the Pelagian doctrine of sinlessness falls, which is the offspring of the righteousness of works. Scripture, the examples of all the saints, and finally daily experience refute it. Who will say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? (Prov. 20:9). If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). For there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin (Eccl. 7:20). And we have all become like an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are like a filthy garment (Isa. 64:6).

units.la: XX. Adoptarunt eam Pontificii, dum regenitos peccato mortali, omniqué malo habitu, carere posse contendunt: ac, in Synodo Tridentina, justos in omni opere venialiter, nedum mortaliter peccare negant. Quam tamen sententiam sine manifesta hypocrisi, & divinæ legis violatione, tueri non possunt. Ipsâ enim imperfectionis suæ conscientiâ revicti, ut se perfectos jactitent, motus animi celeres, innatamque concupiscentiam, pro peccatis non habere, multaque præterea peccata actualia, quibus carere hominem non posse vident, provenialibus tantum culpis, quæ animæ integritatem non delibant, habere debent. Quæ alibi examinavimus. Hæc superbia accusatur Hos. 12: 9. Dixit Ephraim, certe quidem ditatus sum, inveni sufficientiam mihi: omnes qui laborant in me, non invenient mihi pravitatem, quæ sit peccatum.
units.tr: XX. The Papists have adopted this doctrine, while they contend that the regenerate can be free from mortal sin and from every evil habit; and at the Council of Trent they deny that the righteous sin in every work only venially, let alone mortally. Yet they cannot defend this opinion without manifest hypocrisy and violation of the divine law. For, convicted by their own consciousness of imperfection, in order to boast that they are perfect they must not count as sins the swift movements of the mind and innate concupiscence, and they must also count as mere venial faults, which do not diminish the integrity of the soul, the many actual sins which they see a man cannot be free from. We have examined these matters elsewhere. This pride is condemned in Hos. 12:9: Ephraim said, Surely I have become rich, I have found wealth for myself; all who labour against me will not find in me any iniquity that is sin.

units.la: XXI. Nec obstat; quod Deus τελειότητα perfectionem à nobis requirat; quitat; ac Christus sponsam suam integram & perfectam, in Salomonis tamen Cantico, praedicet, & quod quidam in Scriptura perhibentur Justi, τέλειοι Gen. 6:9. Luc. 1:6. Qui in omnibus Dei praeceptis ambulaverint, 1. Reg. 15:5. Luc. 1:6. vel quod Paulus Inspectorem velit esse irreprehensibilem, 1. Tim. 3:2. Seque ipsum valere omnia per Christum gloriatur, Phil. 4: 13. quomodo & Apostolus de omnibus fidelibus dicit, quod, qui ex Deo natus est, non peccet, & nec possit peccare. 1. Joh. 3:9. Unde opera iustorum Deo placere, Act. 10:35. atque in judicio ejus consistere dicuntur Psal. 7:9. ut perfecta ea esse oporteat. Haec enim eorum tela ac objectamenta sunt. Ad quae ordine paucis regerimus: 1. τελειότητα, quae in Scripturis a nobis requiritur, saepe sinceritatem & integritatem notare; cui cor duplex ac insincerum opponitur. 2. Atque ita Christus integrum castumque Ecclesiae suae amorem, nullo adultero affectu pollutum, in Cantico concelebrat. 3. Quae etiam justorum illorum in Scriptura ratio est; quorum integritas & virtutum studium, non omnimoda perfectio laudatur. 4. Quae via illae Dei sunt, in quibus ambulasse quidam leguntur; quanquam non sine cespitatione. 5. Qua in via qui sine querela coram hominibus vixit, ἀνεπίλημπτος & irreprehensibilis est; qualem Apostolus omnem Episcopum requirit: quod non angelicam perfectionem dicit, quae in hac vita sperari non potest; sed vitam ad legem castigatam, scelerisque puram. 6. Paulum vero non peccasse, inverecundum foret statuere. Quod autem concupiscentiae motibus id imputat, id ostendit ab ejus reliquiis ipsum nondum liberum fuisse. Nemo enim nisi volens concupiscit. 7. Quare non absolute, sed pro subjecta materia sese omnia valere dixit. Conf. Marc. 9:23. Omnia possibilia sunt credenti. Nec semper, nec in omnibus istud victricis animae epinicium locum habet. 8. de omnibus fidelibus autem mox respondimus, quo sensu non peccent amplius, nec peccare possint. 9. Ac placent quoque ipsorum opera Deo, sed ut Patri, non ut judici, cum eorum defectum 10. Quod enim de judicio Dei addunt, istud non de stricto ejus judicio, sed de judicio cum misericordia conjuncto accipiendum est. Nec tam de justitia personae, quam de causa sua ibi agit Propheta, contra hostes. Aliter enim, ubi ipse ad tribunal Dei accedit, judicium ejus potius deprecatur.
units.tr: XXI. Nor does it stand in the way that God requires perfection (τελειότητα) from us; or that Christ, in the Song of Solomon, describes his bride as whole and perfect; or that certain men in Scripture are called just and τέλειοι [perfect] (Gen. 6:9; Luke 1:6), who walked in all the commandments of God (1 Kings 15:5; Luke 1:6); or that Paul wants an overseer to be irreprehensible (1 Tim. 3:2); or that he boasts that he can do all things through Christ (Phil. 4:13). Likewise the Apostle says of all the faithful that whoever is born of God does not sin, and cannot sin (1 John 3:9). Hence it is said that the works of the righteous are pleasing to God (Acts 10:35) and stand in his judgment (Ps. 7:9), so that they must be perfect. For these are their weapons and objections. To these we reply briefly, in order: (1) The perfection required of us in Scripture often means sincerity and integrity, to which a double and insincere heart is opposed. (2) So Christ in the Song celebrates his Church's whole and chaste love, polluted by no adulterous affection. (3) This is also the sense of the term just in Scripture, where integrity and zeal for virtue are praised, not every kind of perfection. (4) The ways of God in which some are said to have walked are not without stumbling. (5) He who lives without blame before men in such a way is ἀνεπίλημπτος [blameless] and irreprehensible, as the Apostle requires of every bishop; this does not denote angelic perfection, which cannot be hoped for in this life, but a life chastened according to the law and pure of crime. (6) That Paul did not sin would be shameless to assert; and that he attributes to the motions of concupiscence what he imputes to them shows that he was not yet free from its remnants. For no one desires except willingly. (7) Hence he said that he could do all things, not absolutely, but with respect to the matter at hand (cf. Mark 9:23: All things are possible to him who believes). Nor does this triumph song of a victorious soul hold good always or in everything. (8) As to all the faithful, we have already answered in what sense they no longer sin nor can sin. (9) Their works also please God, but as a Father, not as a judge, since he overlooks their defect. (10) As for what they add about the judgment of God, this must be understood not of his strict judgment but of judgment joined with mercy. Nor does the Prophet there speak so much of the personal righteousness of the man as of his own cause against his enemies; for otherwise, when he approaches the tribunal of God himself, he rather begs for his judgment.

units.la: XXII. Socinciani autem ita perfectionem Christiani hominis urgent, ut
units.tr: XXII. The Socinians, however, press the perfection of the Christian man so hard that

units.la: peccata sua lugentes & deplorantes, quasi infimi adhuc ordinis Christianos, non sine convitio indigitent. Quasi non a peccato solum, sed a sensu quoque ejus & dolore suos illos Christianos abesse debere contendant: contra 1. Joh. 1:8. Si dicamus, quod peccatum non habemus, nosmet ipsos decipimus.
units.tr: they label as Christians of the lowest rank, and not without reproach, those who lament and deplore their sins. As if those Christians should be free not only from sin but also from any awareness or grief over it, they contend this against 1 John 1:8: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.

units.la: XXIII. Ita & Anabaptista, & ipsi quoque Pelagianae arboris furculus, non singulos solum Christianos peccato carere, sed & universum coetum suum ab isto piaculo purum esse posse volunt; nec peccatores tolerare norunt, ex Apostolorum praescripto, 1. Cor. 3, 8, 11, 15. Gal. 1, 3, 5. Rom. 14. Apoc. 2, 3. capp. Cum ipsi, illi candidi videlicet saepe ac columbuli, vitiis fere intercutibus laborent, & externam saepe tantum personam gerant.
units.tr: XXIV. Likewise the Remonstrants in many respects approach the perfectionists. For they seem to call the works of the faithful unclean, or they do not allow that they sin in any work whatever, and they set up certain degrees of perfection: for those beginning in piety they posit a δυνατόχρτον [possible perfection]; but to those more established, who have attained a habit of piety, they ascribe a certain perfection from what is equitable and good, which they call Evangelical; yet this can be overturned again by the sins into which a person often falls back. We do not entirely reject these degrees of perfection; but we think they are to be derived not so much from the firmness of a habit as from the grace of God and the seed of it remaining in the faithful. Nor is "perfection from what is equitable and good" a correct name, since the faithful are not esteemed and reckoned such in themselves, but are held righteous and perfect in Christ alone: and this alone is the Evangelical perfection and righteousness.

units.la: XXIV. Similiter Remonstrantes multis in partibus ad perfectiftas accedunt. Nam & opera fidelium immunda dici; vel cos quolibet in opere peccare non ferre videntur, ac perfectionis quosdam gradus statuunt; & incipientibus pietatem quidem δυνατόχρτον; confirmatioribus autem, ac pietatis habitum adeptis, perfectionem quandam ex aequo & bono adscribunt, quam Euangelicam vocant; quae tamen per peccata, in quae quis crebro relabatur, everti rursus possit. Quos quidem perfectionis gradus non prorsus rejicimus; sed illam non tam a firmitudine habitus, quam a Dei gratia, & semine ejus in fidelibus manente, derivandam putamus. Nec recta perfectionis ex aequo & bono appellatio est, cum fideles non in se se tales aestimentur ac reputentur, sed in Christo solo justi ac perfecti habeantur: quae sola perfectio ac justitia Euangelica est.
units.tr: XXIV. Similarly, the Remonstrants in many respects approach the perfectionists. For they seem to hold that the works of believers are unclean, or that they do not tolerate believers sinning in any work, and they set up certain degrees of perfection. To beginners in piety they grant a piety that is possible [δυνατόν]; but to those who are more firmly established and have attained a habit of piety, they ascribe a certain perfection from what is right and good, which they call Evangelical. Yet this perfection can again be overthrown through the sins into which a person often relapses. We do not altogether reject these degrees of perfection, but we think they must be derived not so much from the firmness of a habit as from the grace of God and the seed of God remaining in believers. Nor is the name "perfection from what is right and good" correct, since believers are not to be esteemed and reckoned such in themselves, but are held just and perfect in Christ alone. That alone is the Evangelical perfection and righteousness.

units.la: XXV. Nobis ergo in N. T. incumbit pacem prosequi cum omnibus & ILLAM sanctificationem, sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Hebr. 12:14. Quae nimirum est in sanguine & Spiritu Christi, in circumcisione cordis; quaeque opponitur purificationibus carnalibus Judaeorum, ad nihil proficuis. Et hoc typicae illius sanctificationis sub V. T. a vera, quae sub N. T. sola obtinet, sanctificatione discrimen est.
units.tr: XXV. Therefore it is incumbent on us in the New Testament to pursue peace with all men, and that holiness without which no one will see the Lord. Heb. 12:14. This holiness is indeed in the blood and Spirit of Christ, in the circumcision of the heart, and it is opposed to the carnal purifications of the Jews, which profit nothing. And there is a difference between this holiness and that typical holiness under the Old Testament, which alone obtains under the New Testament.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De bonis Operibus, eorumque necessitate ac merito.
units.tr: On good works, their necessity and their merit.

units.la: I. EX sanctificatione tanquam fonte profluunt bona opera, ita in Scripturis appellata. Ita splendeat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant vestra bona opera. Matth. 5: 16. Creati in Christo Iesu, propter bona opera. Eph. 2: 10. Virtutis enim nomen rarius occurrit. Si qua virtus, & si qua laus, haec animo versate. Phil. 4: 8. Omni studio collato suppeditate in fide vestra virtutem. 2. Pet. 1: 5. Quorum cum naturam, tum necessitatem, denique à quibusdam introducta merita considerabimus.
units.tr: I. From sanctification, as from a fountain, good works flow, so called in the Scriptures: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works. Matt. 5:16. Created in Christ Jesus for good works. Eph. 2:10. The name virtue occurs more rarely: If there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. Phil. 4:8. Add to your faith virtue, with all diligence. 2 Pet. 1:5. We shall consider their nature, then their necessity, and finally the merits that some have introduced.

units.la: II. Ratio formalis boni operis consistit in conformitate illius cum Lege Dei: sicuti peccatum est defectio à lege. 1. Joh. 3: 4. Ut perversa sit distinctio, inter opera juxta Euangelii normam, ac juxta legem, perfecta. Quasi darentur Euangelica quaedam consilia, uti appellant, majoris cujusdam sanctitatis ac perfectionis: cum nihil perfectius sit ista legis formula, diliges Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo: nec quisquam lege justior, luce splendidior, canone rectior, praecepto officiosior existere possit. Nazianz.
units.tr: II. The formal reason of a good work consists in its conformity to the Law of God, just as sin is the transgression of the law. 1 John 3:4. The distinction is therefore perverse which separates works according to the norm of the Gospel from works that are perfect according to the law, as if there were certain evangelical counsels, as they call them, of some greater holiness and perfection. Yet nothing is more perfect than this formula of the law: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart. Nor can anyone be found more just than the law, more splendid than light, more upright than the rule, more dutiful than the precept. Nazianzen.

units.la: III. Manifestum autem est, opus εὐνομον etiam νομικῶς fieri oportere; ac ex principio bono, ex puro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non fucata procedere, 1. Tim. 1: 5. & in bonum denique finem, Dei vid. gloriam, tendere debere. Omnia facite in gloriam Dei. 1. Cor. 10: 31. In quibus defecerunt omnes gentilium virtutes.
units.tr: III. It is clear, moreover, that a work must be done well-ordered [εὔνομον] and also lawfully [νομικῶς], and must proceed from a good principle, from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, 1 Tim. 1:5, and must finally aim at a good end, namely the glory of God. Do all things to the glory of God. 1 Cor. 10:31. In these respects all the virtues of the Gentiles fall short.

units.la: IV. Principium quo est, cum Spiritus S. omnis boni in nobis auctor & dux, ac perpetuus Ecclesiae rector: unde & fructus Spiritus dicuntur, Gal. 5: 22. tum fides; quae omnis boni in fidelibus initium ac instrumentum est: partim, quod per eam primum corda lustrantur, ac amore Dei imbuuntur; partim, quod illa Christo nitens, ac jugiter inhaerens, ex eo vires hauriat ad bene agendum, animamque sanctis motibus induendam. Unde ea sine bonorum operum comitatu esse non potest, atque ea artissimis nexibus sibi devincta habet. Fide purificatur cor. Act.
units.tr: IV. The principle by which good works are done is the Holy Spirit, the author and leader of all good in us and the perpetual ruler of the Church; hence they are also called the fruit of the Spirit, Gal. 5:22; and faith, which is the beginning and the instrument of all good in believers, partly because by it the hearts are first cleansed and imbued with the love of God, and partly because faith, resting on Christ and cleaving to him continually, draws strength from him to act well and clothes the soul with holy motions. Hence faith cannot exist without the company of good works, and it holds them bound to itself by the closest ties. By faith the heart is purified. Acts 15:9.

units.la: 15·9. 15:9. In Christo Iesu—valet fides, per charitatem operans. Gal. 5: 6. Sine fide impossibile est Deo grata facere. Hebr. 11: 6. Qui manet in me, & ego in ipso, hic fert fructum multum. Joh. 15: 5.
units.tr: In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love. Gal. 5:6. Without faith it is impossible to please God. Heb. 11:6. He who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit. John 15:5.

units.la: V. Principium quod, est homo regenitus. Ita omnis arbor bona fructus bonos fert. Putrida autem arbor putridos fructus fert. Matth. 7: 17. Irregenitorum enim opera, cum principio, norma ac fine bono destituantur, quantamcunque egregiam speciem praeferant, bona dici non possunt. Ut male Pontificii ea bona de congruo appellent. De quibus acriter à Theologis in concilio Tridentino disceptatum. Cum Pontificiis sentiunt quoque Sociniani, qui, cum non corda, sed actus nostros tantum corruptos velint, hominem irregenitum etiam bona opera edere posse affirmant.
units.tr: V. The principle that is subjective is the regenerate man. So every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. Matt. 7:17. For the works of the unregenerate, since they lack a good principle, a good rule and a good end, cannot be called good, however splendid an appearance they present. So the Papists wrongly call them good by congruity, a matter fiercely disputed by the theologians at the Council of Trent. The Socinians also agree with the Papists, who, although they want not hearts but only our actions to be corrupted, affirm that an unregenerate man can also produce good works.

units.la: VI. Sequitur 2. bonorum operum necessitas; 3. iisque adscriptum meritum. Ac primum de necessitate eorum.
units.tr: VI. There follows the second point, the necessity of good works, and third, the merit ascribed to them. First, concerning their necessity.

units.la: VII. Ubi nonnihil distinguendum est. Vel enim ad justificationem illa referri possunt, vel ad fidem, vel ad salutem. Ad illam nullum causae usum habent; nec proinde hactenus ad actum illius necessaria sunt. Fidei vero comites & fructus sunt. Salutis vero non quidem promerendae, sed adeundae inserviunt, ejusque sunt adjuncta antecedentia; ut fidei adjuncta consequentia.
units.tr: VII. Here some distinction must be made. These works may be referred either to justification, or to faith, or to salvation. With regard to justification they have no causal role, and therefore so far they are not necessary to its act. But they are the companions and fruits of faith. And they serve not to earn salvation but to reach it, being its antecedent accompaniments, as they are the consequent accompaniments of faith.

units.la: VIII. Rursus, cum alia sit necessitas praecepti, alia medii: utraque illa bonis operibus convenit. Minute enim nimis loquuntur, qui ea tantum pro causa sine qua non, habent: & hoc sensu causa moralis dici possent. Sunt autem media, non efficientiae: sed quatenus salutis via & semita sunt, quae certissimè ad coelum ducat. Ipsius sumus factura, creati in Christo Iesu propter bona opera, quae ante praeparavit Deus, ut in iis ambularemus. Eph. 2: 10. Ut male justitiarii omnes salutem in operibus suis ponant: Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Eph. 2: 9. Quae tamen & immunda, & imperfecta sunt, nec omnes verae justitiae numeros coram Deo implent.
units.tr: VIII. Again, since there is one kind of necessity of precept and another of means, both belong to good works. For those speak too minutely who regard them only as a cause without which something is not, and in this sense they might be called a moral cause. They are, however, means, not of efficiency, but insofar as they are the way and path of salvation, which most surely leads to heaven. We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. Eph. 2:10. So all the legalists wrongly place salvation in their works: Not of works, lest anyone should boast. Eph. 2:9. Yet these works are both unclean and imperfect, and they do not fulfil all the measures of true righteousness before God.

units.la: IX. Sunt ergo necessaria multis ex partibus. Nam & Dei gratia; & Christi redemtio ac meritum; & inhabitans in nobis Spiritus; & Christianorum spes, ac electionis confirmandae necessitas; & fides; & charitas, ac proximi aedificandi studium; & ipsa salus nostra; & suprema denique rerum omnium regula, Dei gloria, ea undique flagitant. Tit. 2: 11, 12. Affulsit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut— juste & pie vivamus in hoc saeculo. & ℣s 14. Qui nos redemit, —ut purificaret sibi populum in divitiis suis perpetuo habendum, aemulatorem bonorum operum, Rom. 8: 9. Vos autem non estis in carne, sed in Spiritu: siquidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. 1. Joh. 3: 3. Omnis, qui habet hanc spem in se ipso, purificet se ipsum, sicut ipse purus est. 2. Pet. 1: 10. Studeatis firmam reddere vocationem & electionem vestram. Gal. 5: 6. In Christo valet fides per charitatem operans. Jac. 2. passim. 1. Pet. 3: 1. Similiter uxores subjectae sint propriis viris, ut etiam, si quidam non obediant verbo, per uxorum conversationem sine verbo lucrifiant. Phil. 2: 12. Cum timore & tremore vestram salutem conficite. 1. Cor. 10: 31. Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Ut male quidam ex Lutheranis propositionem illam formident, bona opera ad salutem esse necessaria (quin & noxia & periculosa Nicolaus Amsdorfius superiori saeculo ausus fuit asserere) cum tamen multiplicem in iis necessitatem agnoscant, aeque ac nos; non quidem ad salutem promerendam, sed ad illam adeundam & possidendam.
units.tr: IX. They are therefore necessary in many respects. For the grace of God, the redemption and merit of Christ, the Spirit dwelling in us, the Christian hope and the need to confirm our election, faith and charity, and the zeal to edify our neighbour, our own salvation itself, and finally the highest rule of all things, the glory of God, demand them from every side. Titus 2:11, 12: The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in the present age. And verse 14: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every lawless deed and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works. Rom. 8:9: But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. 1 John 3:3: Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure. 2 Pet. 1:10: Be diligent to make your calling and election sure. Gal. 5:6: In Christ faith avails through love working. James 2 throughout. 1 Pet. 3:1: Likewise, wives, be submissive to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives. Phil. 2:12: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. 1 Cor. 10:31: Do all things to the glory of God. It is wrong of some Lutherans to shrink from the proposition that good works are necessary to salvation (Nicolaus Amsdorf in the last century even dared to assert that they were harmful and dangerous), since they acknowledge, just as we do, their manifold necessity, not indeed for earning salvation but for reaching and possessing it.

units.la: X. Ita tamen recedendum, tum a Pontificiorum erroribus, qui sese bonorum operum tantum non idololatras sxpereddunt; tum ab Antinomorum furoribus; ut interim non concedendum sit vulgi praejudiciis, quae etiam inter multos Reformatos tantum non obtinent, quibus, innato humanae naturae errore, ad operum justitiam identidem revolvuntur. Quale est: Christianae religionis praecipuam partem vitae probitate, ac morum doctrina, absolvi. Quod insincerum est. Cum enim salus nostra, non hominum, sed Dei opus sit; istud Dei circa humanam salutem opus recte tradere, explicare, agnoscere, & fide amplecti, verae religionis fundamentum & summam constituit, eamque ab aliis sectis & perversis religionibus distinguit. Unde non doctrina operum, sed fidei, ac gratiae Christi, salutis fundamentum, & religionis nostrae pars excellentior est; eoque & primum tradenda venit, ut doctrina morum ei tanquam basi innitatur. Quae & Scripturarum methodus est. Sicut surrexit Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in novitate vita ambulemus. Rom. 6: 4. Magna vero Ecclesiae corruptio hinc orta est, quod Christianismi substantia in bonis operibus collocata fuerit; sensimque Euangelium, & doctrina gratiae isto operum studio abolita, inque novam legem ac Philosophiam quandam commutata, tandemque propria justitia erecta fuit.
units.tr: X. Yet we must so depart both from the errors of the Papists, who make themselves almost idolaters of good works, and from the frenzies of the Antinomians, that we do not yield to the prejudices of the common people, which hold almost sway even among many of the Reformed, and to which, by the innate error of human nature, they keep returning to the righteousness of works. One such prejudice is that the chief part of the Christian religion is made up of uprightness of life and the teaching of morals. This is insincere. For since our salvation is the work not of men but of God, to rightly set forth, explain, acknowledge and embrace in faith this work of God concerning human salvation constitutes the foundation and sum of true religion, and distinguishes it from other sects and perverse religions. Hence the doctrine not of works but of faith and of the grace of Christ is the foundation of salvation and the more excellent part of our religion, and it must therefore be taught first, so that the doctrine of morals may rest upon it as its base. This is also the method of the Scriptures. As Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6:4. The great corruption of the Church arose from this, that the substance of Christianity was placed in good works; and gradually the Gospel and the doctrine of grace were abolished by this zeal for works, changed into a new law and a kind of philosophy, and at last a righteousness of one's own was set up.

units.la: XI. Huc pertinent & alii ejus generis errores: bona opera, ac praecipuè charitatem, esse primariam Ecclesiae notam, ac maximè visibilem Christianismi characterem: melius esse, habere pietatem quam fidem: ac satis fere dari in Ecclesia scientiae, modo adsit pietatis studium; & nimium propemodum istâ in parte laborari, defertis potioribus: nec enim magna quadam scientia ad salutem acquirendam opus esse: sed sufficere eam, quæ summam religionem præcipuaque ejus capita spectet: in sanctitate autem, in virtute, in bonis operibus omnem cardinem verti, atque istis solis cœli portam patere. Unde & doctrinas morales pro concione tractatas, populi auribus magis placere videas, quam enucleatam mysteriorum fidei explanationem; ex naturali videl. præjudicio, cum operum studium natura hominibus insitum sit, fidei autem dogmata, ut longè supra captum nostrum posita, rationi minus arrideant. Quæ quam perplexa sint, & quantopere fidem Christi, publicamque ejus confessionem, ac Dei gloriam, quæ ea constat, lædant; & quam turpe charitatis ac fidei divortium introducant, cuilibet ad oculum patet. Nec vexare temerarias istas sententias ultra attinet.
units.tr: XI. To this category belong other errors of the same kind: that good works, and chiefly charity, are the primary mark of the Church and the most visible character of Christianity; that it is better to have piety than faith; and that knowledge is nearly always sufficient in the Church, provided there is zeal for piety, and that people labour almost excessively in that part while neglecting the more important matters. For, they say, no great learning is needed to gain salvation, but that knowledge is enough which concerns the sum of religion and its chief heads; and that all the hinge of things turns on holiness, virtue and good works, and that heaven's gate lies open to these alone. Hence you may see that moral doctrines preached from the pulpit please the ears of the people more than a clear explanation of the mysteries of faith. This comes from a natural prejudice: since the zeal for works is implanted in human nature, while the dogmas of faith, being placed far above our grasp, are less pleasing to reason. How confused these errors are, and how greatly they harm the faith of Christ, its public confession, and the glory of God which rests upon it, and what shameful divorce of charity and faith they introduce, is plain to anyone. Nor is it worth our while to dwell any longer on these rash opinions.

units.la: XII. Succedit 3. bonorum operum meritum, de quo antequam discamus, indagandum primum est, quæ virtutis mensura sit, atque unde ejus pretium & magnitudo dependeat.
units.tr: XII. Third, comes the merit of good works. Before we learn about it, we must first inquire what the measure of virtue is, and on what its worth and magnitude depend.

units.la: XIII. Non autem illud, humano more, ex magnitudine commodi vel incommodi, quo Deus videl. afficitur, æstimandum est. Deus enim supra istam rationem est. Nec obsequia nostra ad beatitudinem ejus quicquam faciunt: cum sese solo beatus, in eodem felicitatis statigio sibi semper hæreat. Nec manibus hominum colitur, alicujus rei egens, quum ipse det omnibus vitam, & halitum, & omnia. Act. 17:26. conf. Job. 22:2, 3.
units.tr: XIII. Now this is not to be judged in human fashion, by the size of the benefit or harm by which God is, as it were, affected. For God is above such a standard. Nor do our services add anything to his blessedness, since he is blessed in himself alone and always remains in the same state of happiness. He is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life, and breath, and all things. Acts 17:25. Compare Job 22:2, 3.

units.la: XIV. Potior eorum sententia est, qui à majori vel minori animi proclivitate & zelo, ac erga virtutes studio, virtutum discrimen petunt. Adeo enim animi promtitudo & lubentia virtutem non minuit, ut eam augeat, ut in Christo & beatis patet. Atque hæc in cœlis maxima crit: unde maxima ac perfectissima ibi virtus ac obedientia locum habebunt. Meriti autem ratio cum aliunde peti debeat, in statu isto concipi nullo modo potest.
units.tr: XIV. The better opinion is that of those who derive the difference of virtues from the greater or lesser inclination and zeal of the mind, and from the eagerness for virtuous things. For readiness and willingness of mind do not diminish virtue but increase it, as is evident in Christ and the blessed. And this will be greatest in heaven; hence the greatest and most perfect virtue and obedience will have their place there. But since the reckoning of merit must be sought from elsewhere, it can in no way be conceived in this state.

units.la: XV. Alius autem viatoris status est, in quo tanquam in stadio virtutis præmium acquiri potest: Cujus ratio ac discrimen cum à cura ac sollicitudine vitandi peccatum, quo facile circumveniri possumus; tum à lucta illa ac labore, qui in isto virtutum cursu exantlatur, petendum est: quod præmii ac mercedis sperandæ unicum fundamentum est. Ac prout ille labor ac molestia (quæ in naturalium propensionum, in sese non malarum, abnegatione; inque dolore ac certamine illo consistit) atque universa animi contentio vel major est, vel minor; ita diversi virtutis gradus, diverlaque præmii ac mercedis magnitudo hinc mensurari potest. Quæ cum in gloria statu desint, & nec cura illa ac sollicitudo, nec molestia, ac sui abnegatio, ibi locum habeant; non quidem virtus, sed virtutis præmium & merces, utpote quibus jam pii gaudent, ibi ulteriorem rationem habere non potest.
units.tr: XV. There is, however, another state of the wayfarer, in which a reward can be gained as in the race-course of virtue. Its reasoning and distinction must be sought partly from the care and anxiety to avoid sin, by which we can easily be ensnared, and partly from that struggle and toil which is endured in this course of virtue; this is the sole foundation of the reward and wages to be hoped for. And according as that toil and trouble (which consists in the denial of natural inclinations, not evil in themselves, and in that pain and conflict) and the whole exertion of the mind are greater or smaller, so the different degrees of virtue and the different magnitude of the reward and wages may be measured. But since in the state of glory these things are absent, and neither that care and anxiety, nor trouble and self-denial, have any place there, then virtue itself cannot have a further reckoning there, though the reward and wages of virtue can, since the godly already enjoy them.

units.la: XVI. Atque ex hac virtutum ratione ac mensura, patet quarundam virtutum magnitudo & pretium. Ut in insigniori castitatis certamine, ac triumpho, quo ipsam naturam consecrari Tertullianus dixit; in martyrum certaminibus; ac præsertim fide heroicâ, Abrahami, aliorumque, videre est.
units.tr: XVI. From this reckoning and measure of virtues the greatness and worth of certain virtues becomes plain. One may see this in the more notable struggle and triumph of chastity, by which Tertullian said nature itself is consecrated; in the contests of martyrs; and especially in the heroic faith of Abraham and others.

units.la: Cum in iis multæ naturales inclinationes ac affectus tanto cum labore superandæ, & natura ipsa tantum non calcanda foret. Sed ipsi in nobis decretum mortis habuimus, ne consideremus in nobis ipsis, sed in Deo, qui suscitat mortuos. 2 Cor. 1: 9. Qui contra spem securè credidit, se factum esse patrem multarum gentium. Rom. 4: 18. Sicuti contra virtutes, hoc labore ac abnegatione carentes, minores sunt. Ac pertinent huc quædam opera per se magna & egregia, quæ tamen, quod illa molestiâ careant, non illum ad præmium acquirendum respectum habent.
units.tr: Since in these cases many natural inclinations and affections had to be overcome with such great labour, and nature itself was almost to be trampled underfoot. But we ourselves had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves but in God who raises the dead. 2 Cor. 1:9. Who against hope believed in hope, that he should become the father of many nations. Rom. 4:18. On the contrary, virtues lacking this labour and self-denial are lesser. Here belong certain works which are great and outstanding in themselves, yet, because they lack that trouble, they do not have regard to acquiring a reward.

units.la: XVII. Patetque similiter ex adverso peccatorum æstimatio. Quæ vel graviora vel leviora sunt, prout a naturalibus inclinationibus aut magis aut minus abeunt: & gravissima sunt illa peccata, quæ contra na- turam dicuntur, quæque ipsi naturæ pudorem incutiunt. XVIII. Cumque ita jam pateat, quænam opera in meriti ac præmii rationem venire proprie possent, nunc de ipso merito quærendum est.
units.tr: XVII. The estimate of sins likewise appears from the opposite side. Sins are graver or lighter according as they depart more or less from natural inclinations; and the gravest sins are those which are called against nature, and which strike shame into nature itself. XVIII. Since it is now clear which works could properly come into the reckoning of merit and reward, we must now inquire about merit itself.

units.la: XIX. Ac vocabulum primo quod attinet 1. illud in Scripturis nusquam reperimus: quamvis mercedis ex debito ibi mentio occurrat. Vox enim ἀξιοῦσθαι non hominum meritum ac dignitatem, sed dignationem divinam dicit. Vide Luc. 20: 35. Qui vero digni habiti sunt, ut sæculum illud & resurrectionem ex mortuis consequantur. conf. 21: 36. Pariterque ἀξιος non de merito & compensatione, ac quantitatis proportione, sed de qualitatis convenientia, usurpatur. Ut dignè ambuletis vocatione, qua vocati estis. Eph. 4: 1. Ferte igitur fructus dignos resipiscentiæ. Matth. 3: 8. Phil. 1: 27. Col. 1: 10. 1 Thess. 2: 12. 2. apud Patres autem, ac veterem Latinorum Ecclesiam, idem fere quod τυγχάνειν, consequi, & fructu non carere, sonat. 3. Sequioribus autem sæculis in perversum sensum abiit, qui nunc quoque apud plurimos Pontificios obtinet; quasi mercedem debitam, secundum justitiam commutativam, ex intrinseca operis dignitate, diceret. Quale meritum Scriptura ignorat, quam vis bonis operibus mercedem, coronam, hæreditatem, præmium, & similia attribuat.
units.tr: XIX. As to the word, first, the term in Scripture we nowhere find, although mention of wages owed occurs there. For the word ἀξιοῦσθαι [axioustai] does not denote human merit and worth, but divine favour. See Luke 20:35: But those who were counted worthy to obtain that world and the resurrection from the dead. Compare 21:36. Likewise ἄξιος [axios] is used not of merit, recompense, or proportion of quantity, but of the fitness of quality: That you walk worthy of the calling with which you were called. Eph. 4:1. Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance. Matt. 3:8; Phil. 1:27; Col. 1:10; 1 Thess. 2:12. Second, among the Fathers and the ancient Latin Church, it means nearly the same as τυγχάνειν [tynchanein], to obtain, and to not lack fruit. Third, in later centuries it passed into a perverted sense, which even now prevails among most Papists, as if it meant a wage owed according to commutative justice from the intrinsic worth of the work. Scripture knows no such merit, although it ascribes to good works reward, crown, inheritance, prize, and the like.

units.la: XX. Hæc autem Pontificiæ Ecclesiæ communior sententia est:
units.tr: XX. Now this is the more common opinion of the Papist Church:

units.la: 1. Christum ita pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, ut justitiæ quidem initia, per baptismum, aliaque sacramenta, ab ipso adipiscamur, idque ex opere operato. 2. verum reliquam ac perfectiorem justitiam in habitu animæ intrinseco, justo & sancto, consistere, ab ipso quidem per sacramentorum usum primum hausto; sed qui justum demum constituat eum, qui justa operatur. 3. Adeoque hominem, jam regeneratum, per bona opera, tum in bono perseverantiam, tum vitam æternam promereri.
units.tr: 1. Christ so satisfied for our sins that we obtain from him the beginnings of righteousness through baptism and the other sacraments, and this by the work wrought. 2. But the rest and more perfect righteousness consists in an intrinsic habit of the soul, just and holy, drawn first from him through the use of the sacraments; yet it is the doing of righteous deeds that finally makes a man righteous. 3. And so man, now regenerated, merits by good works both perseverance in good and eternal life.

units.la: XXI. Meritum autem iis præcipuè duplex est, de congruo, & de condigno. Cui & tertium quidam superaddunt, quod meritum ex pacto vocant.
units.tr: XXI. Merit is chiefly twofold: of congruity and of condignity. Some add a third, which they call merit by covenant.

units.la: XXII. Meritum de congruo appellant, cui de justitia quidem non debetur merces, sed tamen ex æquitate ac congruitate quadam: quod operibus irregenitorum, ante acceptam gratiam factis, adscribunt. Pro quo in Tridentino concilio multum litigatum, sicuti & multi inter Pontificios illud repudiant. Collocant autem illud, alii in promissione ex gratia divina; alii in aliquali operis dignitate, qua homo gratia justificationis non indignus fit.
units.tr: XXII. They call merit of congruity that to which a reward is not owed in justice, but still by a certain fairness and suitability; and they ascribe it to the works of the unregenerate done before grace is received. Much dispute about it took place at the Council of Trent, and many among the Papists reject it. Some place it in God's promise out of grace; others in a certain worth of the work, by which a man becomes not unworthy of the grace of justification.

units.la: XXIII. Meritum de condigno rationem debiti ac justitiæ habet; inque æqualitate meriti ad præmium consistit: atque illud justificatis multi eorum tribuunt, quos bonis suis operibus, & gratiæ augmentum, & vitam æternam, promereri ajunt. Quanquam in ratione ejus explicanda non satis concordes sint. In eo vero conveniunt communiter, vitam æternam operum mercedem secundum justitiam esse, ac per ea propriè acquiri; ac Deum per illa revera nobis debitorem fieri.
units.tr: XXIII. Merit of condignity has the character of debt and justice, and consists in an equality of merit to reward. Many of them attribute it to the justified, whom they say by their good works merit both an increase of grace and eternal life. Yet they are not in full agreement in explaining it. But they commonly agree that eternal life is the wage of works according to justice, and is properly acquired by them; and that by them God is truly made our debtor.

units.la: XXIV. Quæ propius examinanda sunt. Ac meritum quidem de congruo ex humanæ vitæ usu, ac liberali illo hominum inter se commercio, originem trahere videtur; apud quos alia officiorum, alia justitiæ regula est; & multa vel gratitudo, vel humanitas, vel charitas à nobis exigit, ad quæ stricta lege, & mero jure non obligamur. Parum enim est intra legum tabulas, atque ad mensuram, justum esse. Quæ, sive æquitas, sive decentia, nec à Deo removenda est. Atque ultro fatemur illum, pro bonitate ac gratia sua, non posse vel minimos hominum cultus dedignari, aut aversari, vel denique non remunerari. Non quod hominibus, sed sibi hoc debeat; nec, quid hominibus debeatur, sed quid sese deceat spectet.
units.tr: XXIV. Let us examine more closely what must be examined. Merit of congruity seems to arise from the practice of human life and from that generous intercourse of men with one another, among whom one rule governs duties and another governs justice; and our fellow men require from us much by way of gratitude, kindness, or charity, to which we are not bound by strict law and mere right. For it is not enough to be just within the tables of the laws and by measure. This equity or decency, whether we call it fairness or propriety, must not be removed from God either. And we freely confess that he, in his goodness and grace, cannot disdain or reject even the smallest worship of men, or finally fail to reward it. Yet this is owed not to men but to himself, and it regards not what is due to men but what befits himself.

units.la: XXV. In eo autem errant Pontificii: 1. quod qualemcunque illam remunerationem incongruè nimis meritum appellant. 2. atque illud operibus ante gratiam factis tribuunt. 3. quinet, Pelagio præeunte, gratiam isto merito præveniri docent. 4. Atque ita non solum hominem irregenitum, Dei inimicum, in peccatis mortuum, quales omnes ante gratiam sumus, aliquid boni, quodque Deo non indignum sit, præstare posse putant. 5. Sed & Deum reddunt προσωπολήπτην, qui opera aliqua externa, sine timore sui facta, in quibus sdam spectet, iisque veluti moveatur ac ducatur.
units.tr: XXV. But the Papists err in this: (1) they call that reward of whatever kind "merit," and that wrongly, since it is improper; (2) they attribute it to works done before grace; (3) and, following Pelagius, they teach that grace is anticipated by this merit; (4) and so they think that not only the unregenerate man, an enemy of God, dead in sins, as all of us are before grace, can perform something good and not unworthy of God; (5) but they also make God a respecter of persons, who looks upon certain external works done without fear of him, in which he sees some things, and is as it were moved and led by them.

units.la: XXVI. Objectant dictum Euangelii, habenti dabitur, Matth. 13: 12. & Apostoli, talibus hostiis promeretur Deus, Hebr. 13: 16. tum & exempla, obstetricum, Exod. 1: 20, 21. Jehu, 2. Reg. 10: 30. Cornelii, Act. 10: 2. in quibus meriti hujus vestigia deprehendere sese putant. Ad quæ resp. 1. Sententiam Christi non de operibus, ante gratiam factis, vel de recto naturalium usu: sed de regenitis, deque gratiæ primordiis, agere.
units.tr: XXVI. They object the saying of the Gospel, to him who has shall be given, Matt. 13:12; and the Apostle's, with such sacrifices God is won, Heb. 13:16; also the examples of the midwives, Exod. 1:20, 21; of Jehu, 2 Kings 10:30; and of Cornelius, Acts 10:2, in which they think they detect traces of this merit. To which we reply: (1) that the saying of Christ does not treat of works done before grace, or of the right use of natural powers, but of the regenerate and of the first beginnings of grace.

units.la: 2. Qui & Apostoli, ad Hebræos, sensus est. Nec promerendi verbum ibi occurrit, sed placendi, per Christum videl. ευαρεστῆσαι 3. Sicut & Cornelius vir sanctus ac regenitus erat, & Messiæ regnum sperans; quanquam Jesum Nazarenum adhuc ignoraret. Nec ullum ibi meriti vestigium. 4. Uti nec in obstetricum exemplo. Phrasis enim idcirco non proprie meritum, sed quodcunque genus consequentiæ notat. Præterquam quod & illæ regenitæ perhibeantur, cum Deum timuisse dicantur. Sicuti & alia ipsis merces tribuitur, quam conversionis & gratiæ primæ, quam huic merito adversarii deputant. 5. Sicuti neque Jehu illa mercès assignatur, sed aliud quid, nimirum regnum ad quartam nepotum progeniem propagandum. Quod tamen nullo merito consecutus est, sed qualicunque Dei gratia ac remuneratione, pro operâ præstitâ.
units.tr: (2) Such is also the sense of the Apostle to the Hebrews. Nor does the word "to earn" occur there, but "to please," namely through Christ, euarestēsai. (3) Just so Cornelius was a holy and regenerate man, hoping for the kingdom of the Messiah, although he did not yet know Jesus of Nazareth. Nor is there any trace of merit there. (4) Nor is there any in the example of the midwives. For the phrase because of this (idcirco) does not properly signify merit, but any kind of consequence. Besides, those women are called regenerate, since they are said to have feared God. And a reward is assigned to them other than conversion and first grace, which our opponents set down as merit. (5) Nor is that reward assigned to Jehu, but something else, namely a kingdom extended to the fourth generation of his descendants. Yet he obtained this not by any merit, but by a certain grace and remuneration of God, in return for the service rendered.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Meritum autem de condigno multo magis humanæ obedientiæ adscribere nefas est; sicut & Scholastici antiquiores agnoverunt, quod tale meritum in meram creaturam non cadat. Ut ex veri meriti conditionibus apparet. Opus enim meritorium 1. debet esse nostrum. 2. indebitum, 3. quin & commodum non exiguum conferre ei, apud quem meremur, 4. ut illum nobis constituere possit debitorem, sive ex justitia, sive ex gratitudine. 5. debet præterea præmio esse proportionatum, & ἀντίῤῥοπον. 6. adeoque, & partibus, & gradibus, & perseverantia denique, perfectum. Quæ cuncta & operibus nostris desunt, & Deo indigna sunt. Nam nec nostra ea sunt, cum à Deo, & vires, & virium usum, habeamus. Deus est qui operatur in nobis, & velle, & operari, Phil. 2: 13. 1.Cor. 4: 7. Nec indebita. Sic & vos, cum feceritis omnia, quæ edicta sunt vobis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus; nam quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Luc. 17: 10. Nec talia, ut Deo prodesse queamus, vel ille promeritis nostris capi possit. Nunquid Deo utilis est homo? nunquid voluptas est omnipotenti, quum justus fueris? & an lucrum, cum integras esse feceris vias tuas? Job. 22: 2, 3. magis vero indignum est, eum creaturæ suæ de jure debitorem fieri. Denique nec opera nostra cunctis numeris perfecta, aut denique magnæ isti mercedi respondentia sunt. Reputo enim, non esse dignas passiones temporis, quod nunc est, ad gloriam, quæ futurum est ut reveletur in nos. Rom. 8: 18.
units.tr: But to ascribe merit of condignity to human obedience is much more wrong; as even the older Schoolmen acknowledged, that such merit does not fall upon a mere creature. This appears from the conditions of true merit. For a meritorious work must (1) be our own; (2) not owed; (3) and moreover must confer some considerable benefit on him with whom we merit; (4) so that it can make him our debtor, whether from justice or from gratitude; (5) it must further be proportionate to the reward and equal to it in weight (antirropon); (6) and therefore perfect, both in its parts and degrees and finally in perseverance. All these things are lacking in our works and are unworthy of God. For they are not ours, since we have from God both the powers and the use of the powers: God is he who works in us both to will and to work, Phil. 2:13; 1 Cor. 4:7. Nor are they not owed: So you also, when you have done all that is commanded you, say, we are unprofitable servants; for we have only done what we ought to do, Luke 17:10. Nor are they such that we can profit God, or that he can be taken by our merits: Is a man useful to God? Is it pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous? Or is it gain to him that you make your ways perfect? Job 22:2, 3. Still more unworthy is it that he should become our debtor by right of his creature. Finally, our works are neither perfect in every respect, nor corresponding to that great reward: For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us, Rom. 8:18.

units.la: XXVIII. Accedunt & aliæ rationes. Quod merita talia Christi merito non parum derogarent: quod homini non parvam gloriationis materiam coram Deo darent; quod Scriptura tantopere abominatur. Ubi igitur gloriatio? exclusa est. Per quam legem? operum? non. Sed per legem fidei. Rom. 3: 27. Quod denique Scriptura, omisso meriti vocabulo, longe aliis loquendi modis utatur; & mortem quidem peccati demerito, viam æternam autem divinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ adscribat; exclusis etiam operibus. Stipendia peccati mors, gratiosa autem largitio Dei vita æterna, in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Rom. 6: 23. Non ex operibus in justitia, quæ feceramus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvavit nas. Tit. 3: 5. Nam non freti justitiis nostris nos effundimus supplicationes nostras coram te, sed freti misericordia tua magna. Dan. 9: 18. Undefine pretio & labore eam acquiri, & mero hæredum jure possideri, addit. Venite, emite, sine argento, & sine pretio, vinum & lac. Esai. 55: 1. Si autem filii, & haredes sumus. Heredes vero Dei, coheredes vero Christi. Rom. 8: 17. Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum vobis paratum à jacto mundi fundamento. Matth. 25: 34. XXIX. In solo autem Christo θεανθρώπῳ meritum de congruo locum habuit; cum ille personæ dignitate, & obedientiæ perfectione, gloriam illam quam accepit eminentissimam promeritus & consecutus fuerit. Ut alibi ostendimus. XXX. Nec felicius quidam ex Pontificiis, hac parte depulsi, meritum ex pacto, sive ex promissione, substituere laborant. Quod in statu quidem innocentiæ, ex primæva legis formula, locum aliquem invenisset; nunc autem, post peccatum, una cum legis regno abolitum est. Et revera illud sub Euangelio ac gratia urgere, foret gratiæ fœdus in novum fœdus operum commutare: & legem ipsam corrumpere, quæ non nisi perfectæ obedientiæ mercedem promittit; & invitâ eâ ac adversante,& potius condemnante, tamen justificari velle.
units.tr: XXVIII. Other reasons also come in. Such merits would greatly detract from the merit of Christ; they would give man no small matter for boasting before God, which Scripture so greatly abominates: Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith, Rom. 3:27. Further, Scripture, leaving out the word merit, uses quite different modes of speaking, and ascribes death to sin as its wages, but eternal life to the gracious giving and mercy of God, excluding works also: The wages of sin is death, but the gracious gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 6:23. Not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, Titus 3:5. For we do not present our supplications before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy, Dan. 9:18. It adds that it is acquired without price or labour and possessed by the mere right of heirs: Come, buy, without money and without price, wine and milk, Isa. 55:1. If we are sons, then we are heirs: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, Rom. 8:17. Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, Matt. 25:34. XXIX. But in Christ alone, the God-man, did merit of congruity have a place, since by the dignity of his person and the perfection of his obedience he merited and obtained that most eminent glory which he received. As we have shown elsewhere. XXX. Nor have some of the Papists, driven from this ground, labored more happily to substitute merit from covenant, or from promise. This might have found some place in the state of innocence, under the primal form of the law; but now, after sin, it has been abolished together with the kingdom of the law. And indeed to press it under the Gospel and grace would be to change the covenant of grace into a new covenant of works, and to corrupt the law itself, which promises a reward only for perfect obedience; and, while the law is unwilling and opposed to it, and rather condemns, still to wish to be justified.

units.la: XXXI. Cadit etiam Bellarminiana meriti explicatio, qui ab una parte gratiam & pactum Dei, ab altera ipsius operis dignitatem, conjunxit, & inter se miscuit. Quæ non solum in partibus laborant, sed & conjungi simul ac misceri nequeunt.
units.tr: XXXI. The Bellarminian explanation of merit also falls, which joined in one part the grace and covenant of God, and in another the dignity of the work itself, and mixed them together. These not only labour in their parts, but cannot even be joined or mixed.

units.la: XXXII. Ut nullum detur meritum. Nec de congruo, quod Deo hypocrisin & προσωπολημψίαν affingeret: nec de condigno, quod in meram creaturam non cadit: nec denique ex pacto, utpote quod solius fœderis operum est, nec cum Euangelio ac Christi merito consistere potest.
units.tr: XXXII. Thus no merit is granted: neither of congruity, which would impute hypocrisy and respect of persons to God; nor of condignity, which does not fall upon a mere creature; nor finally from covenant, since it belongs only to the covenant of works and cannot stand with the Gospel and the merit of Christ.

units.la: XXXIII. Urgere tamen illi merita sua non desinunt; & voculas quasdam ac modos loquendi Scripturæ excerpunt & pro causa suâ identidem repetunt. Uti enim Scripturam particulis causalibus, enim, ideo, & similibus, Matth. 25:21. ac unicuique secundum opera retributionem polliceri, Rom. 2:6. & justis, ac cœli candidatis, dignitatem adscribere non vereri, 2. Thess. 1:11. Apoc. 3:4. & vitam æternam appellare mercedem. Matth. 5:12. & 10:42. ac præmium ex justitia reddendum. 2. Tim. 4:8. 2. Thess. 1:6. denique bona opera nostra salutem operari addunt, ex Phil. 2:12. 2. Cor. 4:17. & 7:10. Jac. 1:25.
units.tr: XXXIII. Yet they do not cease to press their merits; and they pick out certain little particles and modes of speaking of Scripture and repeatedly bring them forward for their cause. Thus they do not hesitate to use the causal particles for, therefore and the like from Scripture, Matt. 25:21; to promise to each one a recompense according to works, Rom. 2:6; to ascribe dignity to the just and to the candidates for heaven, 2 Thess. 1:11; Rev. 3:4; to call eternal life a reward, Matt. 5:12; 10:42; and a prize to be rendered from justice, 2 Tim. 4:8; 2 Thess. 1:6; and finally they add that our good works work out salvation, from Phil. 2:12; 2 Cor. 4:17; 7:10; James 1:25.

units.la: XXXIV. Nos ad singula respondemus. 1. Particulas istas, non causales, sed rationales, sæpe esse, & quamcunque consequentiæ rationem dicere. Conf. 1. Tim. 1:13. 1. Joh. 2:12, 13. Ac loco citato aliam potius salutis causam adferri, benedictionem videl. Patris, & æternam ejus electionem. Adeste benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à jacto mundi fundamento. Matth. 25:34. 2. Aliud autem est, secundum opera; aliud, secundum merita, vel propter opera. Notat enim illud secundum, pro operum ratione disparem eventum & mercedem; & in malis quidem operibus demeritum proprie dictum, in bonis autem præmii & laboris convenientiam dicit; & de qualitate, non vero de vera proportione & æqualitate intelligendum est. Eadem enim epistola Apostolus c. 8:18. Reor enim minime pares esse præsentis temporis perpessiones gloriæ in nobis revelanda. 3. Qualis convenientia, & qualiscunque parilitas, etiam nomine ἄξιος & ἀξιόῶ in Scripturis denotatur. Ferte igitur fructum dignum paenitentiae, sed ἀξίως τῆς μετανοίας convenientem respiscentia. Matth. 3: 8. coll. Act. 26: 20. Cum autem fideles ipsi dicuntur ἄξιοι, illa dignitas, uti justitia eorum, non inhaerens, sed imputata; non in nobis, sed in Christo; non ex operibus, sed ex gratia est. conf. Act. 5: 41. Gaudentes, quod digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Jesu contumeliâ afficerentur. & Phil. 1: 20. 4. Unde merces quoque eorum non ex debito, sed ex gratia est, distinguente Apostolo Rom. 4: 4. Atque ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed est ex debito. Non enim merces semper meritum, ac debitum proprie dictum, infert. vide Gen. 30: 18. Et dixit Lea, Deus reddidit mercedem meam, postquam dedi ancillam meam viro meo. Ideoque vocavit nomen ejus Jssacarem. Psal. 127: 3. 5. Nec ex justitia commutativa ea persolvitur, sed ex promissione & gratia; quam praestare, ac in promissis constantem esse, justitiae Dei interest. Quanquam Paulus 2. Tim. 4: 8. coronam justitiae non aliam quam coronam Christi intelligat, ejus meritis partam, nobisque donatam: & 2. Thess. 1: 6. Siquidem justum est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem: vobis vero, qui affligimini, relaxationem &c. de vindicatione fidelium e manu improborum agat, quae ultimo die peragetur; quod summae justitiae est. 6. Denique κατεργάζεσθαι Phil. 2: 12. non causae meritoriae, sed instrumentalis, conservantis ac foventis, efficaciam dicit. Salutem enim operari recte dicimur, cum faciamus ea quae cum salute connexa sunt, Hebr. 6: 9. quanquam omne operis decus ac vis a solo Deo pendeat: Deus enim est, qui operatur in nobis, & velle, & operari. Phs 13. Quod autem Apostolus 2. Cor. 4: 17. dicit: Illico enim praeteriens levitas afflictionis nostra, excellenter excellentis gloriae pondus aeternum conficit nobis; cum ejusdem Apostoli loco Rom. 8: 18. comparandum est. Reor enim minime pares esse praesentis temporis perpessiones gloriae in nobis revelandae: ac ex ejusdem epistolae cap. 5: 3. Gloriamur de afflictionibus, scientes quod afflictio tolerantiam efficiat: & cap. 8: 28. Novimus autem iis, qui diligunt Deum, omnia simul adjumento esse ad bonum; explicandum est. Quod enim ad salutem quomodocunque facit, eamque promovet, eam operari dicitur. Tandem Jac. 1: 25. beatitudo ex operibus describitur, non tanquam causis efficientibus, sed ex signis adjunctis & concomitantibus: juxta Eph. 2: 10. Nam ipsius sumus opus, conditi in Jesu Christo ad bona opera, quae praeparavit Deus ut in iis ambulemus.
units.tr: XXXIV. We answer each point in turn. (1) These particles are not causal but rationale-marking, and they often signify any kind of reason for a consequence. See 1 Tim. 1:13 and 1 John 2:12, 13. In the passage cited, a different cause of salvation is rather given: namely the blessing of the Father and his eternal election. Come, you who are blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25:34). (2) The phrase according to works is one thing; according to merits or because of works is another. That word according to indicates a result and reward matched to the works: for evil works it denotes what is properly called demerit, and for good works it denotes the fitness of the wage to the labour. It must be understood of quality, not of a true proportion or equality. In the same epistle the Apostle says (8:18): For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us. (3) This kind of fitness, or any kind of equivalence, is also expressed in Scripture by the words axios [ἄξιος] and axioō [ἀξιόω]. Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3:8), but worthy of repentance [ἀξίως τῆς μετανοίας], befitting repentance; compare Acts 26:20. When the faithful themselves are called worthy, that worthiness, like their righteousness, is not inherent but imputed; it is not in us but in Christ; it comes not from works but from grace. Compare Acts 5:41: rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus, and Phil. 1:20. (4) Hence their reward too is not owed but comes from grace, as the Apostle distinguishes in Rom. 4:4: Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. For a reward does not always imply merit and debt in the proper sense. See Gen. 30:18: And Leah said, God hath given me my hire, because I have given my maiden to my husband. And she called his name Issachar. Also Ps. 127:3. (5) Nor is that reward paid out of commutative justice, but out of promise and grace; and it belongs to the justice of God to fulfil these and to remain constant in his promises. Yet Paul, in 2 Tim. 4:8, understands the crown of righteousness as nothing other than the crown of Christ, won by his merits and bestowed on us; and 2 Thess. 1:6, Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you; and to you who are troubled, rest, etc., deals with the deliverance of the faithful from the hand of the wicked, which will be carried out on the last day; and this is a matter of supreme justice. (6) Finally, katergazesthai [κατεργάζεσθαι] in Phil. 2:12 denotes not a meritorious cause but the instrumental efficacy of that which preserves and fosters. We are rightly said to work out salvation when we do the things that are joined with salvation (Heb. 6:9), although all the honour and power of a work depend on God alone: for it is God who works in you both to will and to do (Phil. 2:13). As for what the Apostle says in 2 Cor. 4:17, For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory, it must be compared with the Apostle's words in Rom. 8:18, quoted above, and with Rom. 5:3, We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and Rom. 8:28, And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God. What contributes to salvation in any way and advances it is said to work it. Finally, in Jas. 1:25 blessedness is described through works, not as efficient causes but as accompanying and concomitant signs, in line with Eph. 2:10: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.

units.la: XXXV. At-
units.tr: XXXV. At-

units.la: XXXV. Atque ita, profligato quocunque operum merito, iis,ut justitiæ causis, inniti & confidere, quin & gloriari, quæ Pontificiæ sententiæ arrogantia est, nos non posse satis patet. Et inveniar in ipso, non ha-bens meam justitiam, eam ex lege; sed eam, quæ est per fidem Iesu Christi; justitiam, quæ ex Deo est, ad fidem. Phil. 3:9. Ubi ergo gloriatio est? exclusa est. Per quam legem? operum? non. Sed per legem fidei. Rom. 3:27. Nec prosunt Bellarmini præstigiæ; aliud esse, fiduciam ex meritis nasci; aliud, eam in illis ponere: ac licere eam in meritis collocare, modo superbia caveatur &c. Quæ nec ipsi auctori satisfecerunt. Unde, pudendæ assertionis temeritatem perosus, tutissimum esse concludit, in sola Dei misericordia fiduciam ponere. Quo exitu longam illam de meritis disputationem, tanquam gemmâ quadam, obsignavit. Quam nos de luto isto tollere ac ostentare, non parum interest. Ut veritatis vocem ac vim, vel ex invito pectore erumpentem, agnoscamus. Adeo aliter sese animus habet, dum controversiarum æstu incalescit, & quotidiana lite in adversarios invehitur; aliter, dum velut ad thronum Dei accedens, atque ad ejus tribunal istam disputationem peragens, tandem arma omnia projicere, & argumenta, quibus ante confisus erat, odisse incipit; sequeque in supplicis ritum componens, misericordiâ potius Dei tegere, quam prolixa illa, quam contra adversarios explicuit, ratiunculârum acie confidere mavult. Non enim egra Deum perinde hæc argumenta valent, nec ad lucem istam vana ac personata colorem suum servare possunt: sed immotum ac constans esse oportet, quod eo judice subsistet.
units.tr: XXXV. And so, once every merit of works has been overthrown, it is plain enough that we cannot lean on them as grounds of righteousness, nor trust in them, nor even glory in them, which is the arrogance of the Papist opinion. And may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Jesus Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. Phil. 3:9. Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. Rom. 3:27. Bellarmine's sleight of hand does not help him, when he says that it is one thing for confidence to arise from merits, and another for it to be placed in them, and that it is permissible to place confidence in merits provided pride is avoided, and so on. These claims did not even satisfy the author himself. Hence, hating the rashness of a shameful assertion, he concludes that it is safest to place confidence in the mercy of God alone. With this conclusion he sealed that long disputation about merits, as with a kind of jewel. It matters not a little that we lift this gem out of the mud and display it, so that we may recognise the voice and power of truth, breaking out even from an unwilling breast. So differently is the mind disposed when it grows hot with the heat of controversy and rages against opponents in daily strife, and when, approaching as it were the throne of God, and conducting that disputation before his tribunal, it finally begins to throw down all its weapons and to hate the arguments in which it had trusted before; and, composing itself in the manner of a suppliant, prefers to cover itself with the mercy of God rather than to trust in the long line of little arguments it has marshalled against its opponents. For such arguments do not avail before God, nor can these vain and pretended colours keep their hue in that light; what must stand is what will stand before his judgment, and it must be firm and unmoved.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Quæritur tandem an cœlestis mercedis intuitu opera- ri liceat? Cujus sententiæ negativam non recte Antigono Sadducæorum Magistro adscribunt. Verius enim est, quanquam Deus solo præmii intuitu colendus non sit, tamen illius respectu ac intuitu quoque licere recta facere, ac ista præsertim spe in adversis tolerandis sese solari. Præcipue cum ipsum illud præmium à Deo diversum non sit: cum non alio quam Deo beata esse anima desideret. Ut, qui ad præmium respicit, eo à Deo se avertere, vel eum obstipem coleredici noh debeat. Quid enim? an Deus non est summum bonum? nonne talis haberi vult, ac talem sese creaturis offert? & an ad eum ex vitæ miseriis suspirare non licet? nonne Apostolus ipsum μισθαποδότην appellat, idque gloriæ ipsi adscribit? Credere enim oportet eum, qui accedit ad Deum, quod sit, & quærentibus se remunerator sit. Hebr. 11:6. Ut validam inhortationem habueremus accipiendi illam expositam spem. Hebr. 6: 18. Et quid alioquin de spe sive expectatione foret, quæ vel præcipua & cardinalis Christianorum virtus est, ac una ex triga illa Apostolica? Sicut & ipse fides definitur ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, Hebr. 11: 1. Ut Mosis, ac Christi ipsius exempla taceam; qui non alio fine adversa tulit, quam ut ista via in cœlum iret, ipsa sua cruce consecrandus, ac regno suo inaugurandus, ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης χαρᾶς. Hebr. 12: 2. Quo Apostolus etiam nos vocat. 1. Cor. 15: 58. Estote abundantes in opere Domini semper, quum sciatis laborem vestrum non esse inanem in Domino. Pauli enim Mosisque ecstases, ac amoris deliquia, Exod. 32: 32. Rom. 9: 3. cum singularis exempli fuerint, nec denique perpetua in ipsis, sed ad instar raptus & excessus cujusdam fuerint, regulam facere non possunt.
units.tr: Finally it is asked whether it is lawful to work with a view to heavenly reward. The Sadducee Antigonus, the teacher of the Sadducees, is not rightly credited with the negative of this opinion. For it is truer that, although God is not to be worshipped for the sake of reward alone, it is nonetheless lawful to do right with regard to that reward too, and especially to console oneself with this hope while enduring adversity. This is so especially since that reward is not different from God himself, since the soul desires to be blessed by no other than God. So, whoever looks to the reward should not on that account be said to turn away from God, or to worship him in a grudging way. For what? Is God not the highest good? Does he not wish to be considered such, and offer himself to creatures as such? And is it not lawful to sigh after him out of the miseries of life? Does not the Apostle call him the rewarder [μισθαποδότης] and ascribe glory to him for this? For he who comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. Heb. 11:6. That we might have a strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before us. Heb. 6:18. And what else would hope or expectation be, which is the chief and cardinal virtue of Christians and one of that apostolic triad? Faith itself is defined as the substance of things hoped for [ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων], Heb. 11:1. I say nothing of the examples of Moses and Christ himself, who endured adversity for no other end than that by this way he might go to heaven, consecrated by his own cross and inaugurated into his kingdom for the joy that was set before him [ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης χαρᾶς], Heb. 12:2. To this the Apostle also calls us, 1 Cor. 15:58: Be always abounding in the work of the Lord, since you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. For the ecstasies and swoons of love of Paul and Moses, Exod. 32:32, Rom. 9:3, since they were singular examples, and were not lasting in them but were in the manner of a certain rapture and excess, cannot make a rule.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De Resipiscentia.
units.tr: Of Repentance.

units.la: I. Sanctificationem & bona opera, cum imperfecta sint, excipit resipiscentia; quæ ex lapsibus quotidie resurgimus. Summitur enim ea vel latius, pro tota hominis conversione, & prima regeneratione; vel strictius, pro iterata ac quotidie renovata conversione à gravioribus lapsibus: pro qua sanctitatis parte eam nunc accipimus. Hebr. תשובה dicitur; item שוב & שובה, quod ἐπιστρέφειν & ἐπιστροφὴν ad Deum notat: Græcè μετάνοια & μεταμέλεια; quorum illud emendationis consilium, hoc mentis angores & supplicia, ob admissum peccatum, exprimit: Quanquam promiscuè hæ voces interdum usurpentur. vide Hebr. 12: 17. Matth. 21: 29. Latinus interpres pœnitentia voce usus est, qua animi tædium & pudorem expressit: quæ Pontificiis errandi vel causam, vel prætextum præbuit, dum pœnitentiam in externis castigationibus ac pœnis potissimum ponunt.
units.tr: I. Repentance follows sanctification and good works, which are imperfect, since we rise again every day from our falls. The word is taken either more broadly, for the whole conversion of a person and the first regeneration, or more narrowly, for the repeated and daily renewed conversion from more serious falls. It is in this narrower sense, as a part of holiness, that we now take it.
