In Hebrew it is called teshuvah [תשובה], and likewise shuv [שוב] and shuvah [שובה], which signify epistrephein [ἐπιστρέφειν] and epistrophēn [ἐπιστροφὴν] toward God. In Greek it is metanoia [μετάνοια] and metameleia [μεταμέλεια]. The former expresses a change of purpose toward amendment, the latter the anguish and torment of mind on account of sin committed, although these words are sometimes used interchangeably (see Heb. 12:17; Matt. 21:29). The Latin translator used the word paenitentia, which expresses weariness and shame of mind. This gave the Papists either the cause or the pretext for error, since they place repentance chiefly in external castigations and penalties.

units.la: II. Rem quod attinet, constistit ea partim in animi dolore, ex peccati sensu; partim in serio emendationis proposito.
units.tr: II. As to the thing itself, it consists partly in grief of mind arising from a sense of sin, and partly in a serious purpose of amendment.

units.la: III. Primus ejus actus est perculsæ ac vulneratæ animæ dolor, & peccatorum sensus, & horror, ac odium.
units.tr: III. The first act of repentance is the grief of a soul struck down and wounded, together with a sense of sins, horror, and hatred.

units.la: IV. Duplicis autem doloris meminit Scriptura, doloris mundi, & doloris loris secundum Deum. Nam quae secundum Deum est tristitia, ea re- fipiscentiam efficit ad salutem, cujus nunquam poeniteat: at mundi tristitia mortem efficit. 2. Cor. 7:10. Ille, sive de re aliqua terrena est, sive ob peccata & scelera, animum torquet, & quotidianis dirisagitat; sed absque vera in Deum fide, & sancto peccatorum odio; adeo ut sit horror merus, & animi implacidi anxietas, & aestus, & desperatio, & poenae formido, ac denique sanctitatis Dei odium & fuga. Qualis dolendi saevities ac amentia in Caino, Juda, aliisque impiis apparet. Dolor autem secundum Deum alio ex fonte manat; non ex odio, sed ex amore Dei ac sanctitatis ejus; nec ultra modum atrox ac saeviens, ad quodvis momentum stupet, omnemque numinis cogitationem exhorret, sed offensam potius ejus veretur; ac mollibus lacrymis culpam abluit; & pudenti denique quadam pietate mistus, peccare in posterum timet, solo Dei ac virtutis amore. Qualis in Sanctis apparuit. Psal. 51:19. Jer. 31:18, 19. Joël. 2: 12, 13. Act. 2:37, 38.
units.tr: IV. Scripture, however, speaks of a twofold grief: the grief of the world, and grief according to God. For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation, not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. (2 Cor. 7:10). The former, whether it concerns some earthly matter or sins and crimes, torments the mind and harasses it daily with dread, but it is without true faith in God and holy hatred of sin. Hence it is mere horror, restless anxiety, agitation, despair, fear of punishment, and finally hatred and flight from the holiness of God. Such savagery and madness of grief appears in Cain, Judas, and other wicked persons. Grief according to God, however, flows from another source: not from hatred but from love of God and of his holiness. It is not excessively fierce or savage, nor does it stupefy for any length of time, nor does it shrink from every thought of the divine majesty. Rather, it fears offending him, washes away its guilt with gentle tears, and, mingled with a modest kind of piety, fears to sin again, from love of God and virtue alone. Such grief appeared in the saints (Ps. 51:19; Jer. 31:18, 19; Joel 2:12, 13; Acts 2:37, 38).

units.la: V. Sumit autem hic dolor initium a fide.
units.tr: V. This grief takes its beginning from faith.

units.la: Cum enim cum amore Dei conjunctus sit, atque ex illo oriatur; ille autem absque fide in Christum esse nequeat; (quae primum Dei, ut peccatorem amantis, adspectum & sensum dicit; & primum veri amoris affectum nobis insinuat) absque fide illum existere impossibile est. Atque haec fides in Scriptura innuitur vocabulo Timoris Jehova, qui dicit, initium sapientia, imo summa sapientia, & sapientia est. Prov. 9:10. 1:7. Psal. 111:10. Job. 28:28.
units.tr: For since it is joined with the love of God and arises from it, and since that love cannot exist without faith in Christ (which first shows us the sight and sense of God as loving the sinner, and first instils in us the affection of true love), it is impossible for grief to exist without faith. This faith is indicated in Scripture by the term fear of Jehovah, which is said to be the beginning of wisdom, indeed the highest wisdom, and is wisdom itself (Prov. 9:10; 1:7; Ps. 111:10; Job 28:28).

units.la: VI. Ut jam quaestioni illi responderi possit: quomodo fides ad poenitentiam sese habeat? Differt enim 1. fides a poenitentia stricte dicta. Illa enim in Christum proprie, haec ad Deum fertur, ejusque voluntati sese conformat: tum resipiscentia strictius accepta tristitiam duntaxat de malo commisso dicit; latius autem sumta, pro tota hominis ad Deum conversione, fidem tanquam partem includit. 2. Ac hujus resipiscentiae partes quod attinet; quoad dolorem & peccatorum sensum, ea fide quoque prior est: praecipue quod ad animi sensum. Vix enim peccatorum remissionem nobis persuademus, quorum vulnera & aculeos nondum sensimus. Quo modo resipiscentiam fidei praemitti videmus, Marc. 1:15. Resipiscite, & credite Euangelio. conf. Act. 20:21. Quoad reliquam vero vitae emendationem illa fide posterior est. 3. Ut vero tristitia illa sancta sit & Deo grata, oportet resipiscentiam praecedat fides; utpote quae vitae spiritualis initium, ac sanctae conversionis primum gradum dicit, cum sine ea nihil boni in homine existere possit. Atque hoc gradu illa se invicem consequuntur; ut prima sit fides, quam sequitur tristitia secundum Deum; ac denique vitæ emendatio, & novæ sanctitatis studium.
units.tr: VI. Now we can answer the question: how does faith relate to repentance? First, faith differs from repentance strictly so called. Faith is directed properly to Christ, whereas repentance is directed to God and conforms itself to his will. Repentance taken more strictly signifies only sorrow for the evil committed, but taken more broadly, for the whole conversion of a person to God, it includes faith as a part. Second, as to the parts of repentance: as regards grief and the sense of sin, faith is also prior to it, especially as far as the feeling of the mind is concerned. For we can hardly persuade ourselves of the forgiveness of sins whose wounds and stings we have not yet felt. Thus we see repentance placed after faith: "Repent, and believe the gospel" (Mark 1:15; compare Acts 20:21). As for the rest of the amendment of life, however, it comes after faith. Third, for that sorrow to be holy and pleasing to God, faith must precede repentance, since faith is the beginning of spiritual life and the first step of holy conversion, and without it nothing good can exist in a person. In this order the one follows the other: first faith, which is followed by sorrow according to God, and finally amendment of life and the pursuit of new holiness.

units.la: VII. Alter ergo respipiscentiæ actus, est vitæ emendatio, vel ejus sal-tem verum propositum. In Christo Jesu —— valet nova creatio, Gal. 6: 15. Ut, sicut surrexit Christus ex mortuis, per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus, Rom 6: 4. Quam comitatur animus lætus,& exultans in viis Dei, ut peccatorum sensum comitabatur animi anxietas & tristitia. Condeletior legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem. Rom. 7:22. Beatus vir, cujus in lege Dei voluptas est. Psal. 1:1,2.
units.tr: VII. The second act of repentance, therefore, is the amendment of life, or at least a true purpose of it. "In Christ Jesus... a new creation avails" (Gal. 6:15). "That, as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also should walk in newness of life" (Rom. 6:4). This is accompanied by a mind that is glad and rejoices in the ways of God, just as the sense of sin was accompanied by anxiety and sorrow of mind. "I delight in the law of God after the inward man" (Rom. 7:22). "Blessed is the man whose delight is in the law of God" (Ps. 1:1, 2).

units.la: VIII. Quæ respipiscentiæ pars non ita à priori divellenda est, quasi tempore diversa foret. Cum hæ duæ respipiscentiæ partes ejusdem actionis ac mutationis diversi sint termini: quorum primus est, veteris hominis mortificatio; alter, novi vivificatio. Quanquam nec vetus homo mortificari sine adventu novi queat: sicuti mors non nisi insinuato spiritu ac vita, nec tenebræ sine lucis radiis fugari & tolli possunt. Est autem novæ vitæ primus gradus, veterem labem expurgare & tollere.
units.tr: VIII. This part of repentance is not to be separated from the first as if it were different in time. These two parts of repentance are different terms of one and the same action and change: the first is the mortification of the old man, the second the vivification of the new. Yet the old man cannot be mortified without the coming of the new, just as darkness cannot be driven away and removed without the rays of light, nor death without the infusion of spirit and life. The first step of the new life, however, is to cleanse and remove the old stain.

units.la: IX. Dilutius est, quod quidam vitæ emendationem pœnitentiæ partem esse negant, quod ejus fructus sit. Ferte igitur fructus dignos respiscentia. Matth. 3: 8. Pendet enim hoc à strictiori vel latiori pœnitentiæ acceptione: quæ si de animi dolore tantum sumatur, emendatio vitæ ejus fructus est; si vero universa comprehendatur, pars illius est, cum sine ea perfecta ac completa esse non possit.
units.tr: IX. It is weaker to say, as some do, that amendment of life is not a part of repentance but its fruit: "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance" (Matt. 3:8). This depends on whether repentance is taken more strictly or more broadly. If it is taken only as grief of mind, amendment of life is its fruit; but if it is taken in its whole extent, amendment is a part of it, since repentance cannot be perfect and complete without it.

units.la: X. Subjectum pœnitentiæ est, vel commune, vel proprium. Ad illud pertinent 1. omnes fideles, in peccata relabentes; contra Novatianos & Catharos, qui nimio olim rigore lapsos, ad limina Ecclesiæ redeuntes, ac pacem ejus exposcentes, excludebant. 2. & beata quoque virgo. Non autem Christus; qui, non privative, sed negative, non-pœnitens fuit.
units.tr: X. The subject of repentance is either common or proper. To the common subject belong, first, all believers who relapse into sin, against the Novatians and Cathari, who in former times, through excessive rigour, excluded from the peace of the Church those fallen ones who returned to its thresholds and sought its peace. Second, the blessed Virgin also. Christ, however, is not included, for he was not a penitent in the privative sense but in the negative sense, that is, a non-penitent.

units.la: 3. Reproborum vero fucata, ut fides, ita & pœnitentia est. Quæ, servili indole, non offensas, sed flagra exhorrens, nec universam animam perpurgans, & ad graviora tantum peccata perculsa, & origine, & modo, & objectis, à vera pœnitentia diffidet. 4. Infantibus denique, etsi non omnes motus Spiritus abrogandi sint, sanctamque eis indolem ipso ætatis initio insinuari sæpe contingat, non tamen illi pœnitentiæ actus, quos jam descripsimus, conveniunt. Qui non dignoscunt dextram suam à sinistra sua. Jon. 4: 11.
units.tr: Third, the feigned repentance of the reprobate, like their faith, is counterfeit. Being of a servile disposition, it dreads not offences but whips, does not cleanse the whole soul, and is struck down only by more serious sins. In its origin, manner, and objects it differs from true repentance. Fourth, as for infants: although not all movements of the Spirit are to be denied them, and it often happens that a holy disposition is instilled in them at the very beginning of life, the acts of repentance that we have already described do not suit them: "who cannot discern between their right hand and their left" (Jonah 4:11).

units.la: XI. Proprium autem pœnitentiæ subjectum est, non voluntas sola; quamvis illa praecipua ejus sedes sit; sed & intellectus, & memoria, & afsectus, ipsaque corporis nostri membra; quae omnia ad pristinam puritatem per poenitentiam restitui debent.
units.tr: XI. The proper subject of repentance, however, is not the will alone, although that is its chief seat, but also the understanding, the memory, the affections, and the very members of our body, all of which must be restored to their former purity through repentance.

units.la: XII. Objectum ejus sunt peccata omnia: unde μετάνοια ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων respiscentia ab operibus mortuis dicitur, Hebr. 6: 1. ex quibus resurgere jubemur; tum levioribus, cum quibus quotidianum nobis certamen est; tum praesertim gravioribus, quae altius conscientiam vulnerant. Excluditur autem ab hoc censu peccatum in Spiritum S., quod ejus generis est, ut impoenitentiam, & obdurati animi obstinationem pro perpetuo comite habeat. Tam atrox enim illud est, ut nullum bonum motum in animo relinquat. Nec qui ultimo isto peccandi gradu stetit, ullum ad meliorem mentem regressum sibi relinquit. Unde non dolor, sed desperatio, & divinae vindictae expectatio, & dirissima mentis supplicia, ac furiae illud consequuntur. Voluntarie peccantibus — non amplius pro peccato relinquitur hostia, terribilis autem quaedam expectatio judicii, & ignis ardor. Hebr. 10:26,27. Conf. 1. Joh. 5:16. Extra istum casum autem ab omni peccato per veram poenitentiam regressus datur; estque ea secunda post naufragium tabula; quam temere, ac non sine divinae gratiae labe nonnullis eripiunt Socinians, & Remonstrantium quidam; dum seris peccatoribus, in vitae exitu ad Deum se convertentibus, noxarum veniam ac Dei pacem afferre virentur. Improbus, cum convertetur ab omnibus peccatis suis — vivendo vivet, non morietur. Ezech 18:21.
units.tr: XII. Its object is all sins. Hence it is called "repentance from dead works" [μετάνοια ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων] (Heb. 6:1), from which we are commanded to rise, both the lighter sins with which we have daily conflict, and especially the graver sins that wound the conscience more deeply. The sin against the Holy Spirit is excluded from this class, because of its nature: it has impenitence and the obstinacy of a hardened mind as its constant companions. It is so atrocious that it leaves no good motion in the mind, and the one who has stood at this last step of sinning has no return left to a better mind. Hence it is followed not by grief but by despair, the expectation of divine vengeance, and the most dreadful torments of mind and furies. "For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation" (Heb. 10:26, 27; compare 1 John 5:16). Outside this case, return from every sin through true repentance is granted, and it is a second plank after shipwreck. Some of the Socinians and certain Remonstrants snatch this plank away rashly, and not without loss to divine grace, since they seem to offer forgiveness of sins and peace with God to late sinners who turn to God at the end of their lives. "But if the wicked will turn from all his sins... he shall live, he shall not die" (Ezek. 18:21).

units.la: XIII. Patet hinc resipiscentiae necessitas; quae in adultis absoluta est, non praecepti solum, sed medii, cum sine ea culpae nostrae elui non possit; sint. Respicite igitur, & convertite vos, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Act. 3: 19.
units.tr: XIII. From this it is plain how necessary repentance (resipiscentia) is. In adults it is absolute: it is required not only as a precept but as a means, since without it our guilt cannot be washed away. Repent therefore and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out. Acts 3:19.

units.la: XIV. Ut à Libertinorum furoribus Ecclesia longissime divertat: qui, ut boni malique discrimen confundunt, & ad infirmas hominum opiniones relegant, ita non aliis resipiscentiam opus esse dictitant, quam qui imbecillae mentis errore ita opinantur, quibus tum propriae stultitiae supplicium luendum sit. In altero autem gradu stant Pontificii, qui resipiscentiam non solum necessariam, sed & meritoriam ac satisfactoriam statuunt: cum ipsa potius peccati non imputati fructus, & indicium, ac perpetuus comes sit. Propterea sunt remissa peccata ipsius, quia multa erant, quia dilexit multum, Luc. 7:47. Sicuti & perverse Socíniani remissionem peccatorum poenitentiae effectum proprie dictum vocant; cum potius ex illa vera poenitentia profluat. Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc vivemus in eo? Rom. 6: 2. neque illi peccatorum remissio tribuatur, nisi quatenus fide eam apprehendit.
units.tr: XIV. The Church stands far apart from the frenzies of the Libertines, who blur the distinction between good and evil and refer it to the weak opinions of men. They keep saying that repentance is needed only by those who, through a feeble mind, think they must suffer for their own folly. The Papists stand at a second level: they hold that repentance is not only necessary but also meritorious and satisfactory, although it is rather the fruit and sign of sin that has not been imputed, and its constant companion. Her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much, Luke 7:47. In the same way the Socinians wrongly call the forgiveness of sins the proper effect of repentance, whereas forgiveness flows rather from true repentance. We who died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Romans 6:2. Nor is forgiveness of sins to be credited to repentance, except insofar as it is laid hold of by faith.

units.la: XV. Utque ea remissionis peccatorum non causa meritoria, sed comes & necessarium consequens est; ita nec ad justificationem lese meritorie habet. Ut male de contritione Pontificii docent. Sed prout variè accipitur, ita varium ad eam respectum habet. Poenitentia enim, quatenus legalis est, primosque animi terrores dicit, justificationem antecedit. Quatenus Euangelica est, & fidem involvit, cum eâ simul existit. Quatenus vero à fide distinguitur, & reliquam vitæ emendationem comprehendit, ut fidei, ita etiam justificationis consequens est.
units.tr: XV. Just as forgiveness of sins is not the meritorious cause of repentance but its companion and necessary consequence, so repentance does not stand in a meritorious relation to justification, as the Papists falsely teach about contrition. But since repentance is understood in various ways, it bears various relations to justification. Insofar as repentance is legal, and signifies the first terrors of the mind, it goes before justification. Insofar as it is evangelical, and involves faith, it exists together with faith. Insofar as it is distinguished from faith and includes the rest of the amendment of life, it follows justification just as it follows faith.

units.la: XVI. Peccata autem, per fidem & respiscentiam semel deleta, nunquam revivisc unt; nec formaliter, per eadem peccata; nec virtualiter, per ingratitudinem, quæ reliquorum omnium compendium & complementum est. Quod tamen gratiæ Dei est. Ac de actuali reatu intelligi debet. Nulla igitur condemnatio iis, qui in Christo Jesu sunt. Rom. 8: 1. Sine poenitentia sunt dona gratiæ, & vocatio Dei. c. 11: 29. Aliter enim de intrinseco peccatorum merito, ac de legis rigore statuendum foret. Omnes justitiæ, quas fecerat, non venient in mentem, in prævaricatione, qua prævaricatus fuerit; & in peccato suo, quod peccaverit, in eo moriētur. Ezech. 18: 24. Sicuti & male iidem Pontificii, ex quorum de meritis errore opinationes tales oriuntur, ab altera parte quoque meritorum, quæ per superuenientia peccata extincta erant, per renovationem refipiscentiæ revivisc entiam somniant. Quæ aliorum apud ipsos errorum propagines sunt.
units.tr: XVI. Sins once blotted out through faith and repentance never revive: neither formally, through the same sins, nor virtually, through ingratitude, which is the summary and completion of all the rest. Yet this too is a matter of God's grace. And this must be understood of present guilt. There is therefore no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1. The gifts and calling of God are without repentance, Romans 11:29. Otherwise we would have to judge concerning the intrinsic merit of sins, and concerning the rigour of the law, in another way. None of the righteousness which he has done shall be remembered; in his trespass that he has trespassed, and in his sin that he has sinned, in them he shall die, Ezekiel 18:24. The same Papists are also wrong here: from their error about merits such opinions arise, and on the other side they dream that merits, which were extinguished by later sins, revive through the renewal of repentance. These are offshoots of their other errors.

units.la: XVII. Auctor respipiscentiæ est Deus. Ergo etiam gentibus dedit Deus respiscentiam ad vitam. Act. 11: 18. 2. Tim. 2: 25. Quod non de prima sola conversione, sed & de secunda ac quotidiana ejus renovatione, intelligendum est. Omnem palmitem, qui fructum fert, purgat, ut uberiorem fructum ferat. Joh. 15: 2. In quam rem varia media, cum ordinaria, ut verbum, non Euangelii solum, sed & legis, & sacramenta, tum extraordinaria, pro sapientia sua adhibere novit.
units.tr: XVII. God is the author of repentance. Then God has also granted repentance to the Gentiles unto life, Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25. This must be understood not only of the first conversion but also of its second and daily renewal. Every branch that bears fruit he purges, that it may bring forth more fruit, John 15:2. To this end he knows how to use various means, both ordinary, such as the Word (not only the Gospel but also the law) and the sacraments, and extraordinary, as seems wise to him.

units.la: XVIII. Poenitentiæ externa signa, simulque ejus excitandæ ac fovendæ media, sunt actus externi, quibus nostram coram Deo humiliationem peccatique horrorem, præcipuè in luctu vel castigationibus, testamur: qualia apud veteres erant pulvis, cilicia, ploratus, preces, jejunia, eleemosynæ. Ita insternebant cinerem, 2. Sam. 13: 19. Esth. 4: 1. Jer. 6:
units.tr: XVIII. The external signs of repentance, and at the same time the means of stirring it up and fostering it, are outward acts by which we bear witness before God to our humiliation and our horror of sin, especially in mourning or in chastisements. Such were, among the ancients, dust, sackcloth, weeping, prayers, fasting and almsgiving. Thus they strewed ashes, 2 Samuel 13:19; Esther 4:1; Jeremiah 6:

units.la: 26. 26. Dan. 9: 3. vel eum substernebant, Esth. 4: 3. Esai. 58: 5. Jon. 3: 6. adeoque in pulvere sedebant. Ut vero illa quae ex hisce aut Orientalibus peculiaria erant, aut alio commodius referri possunt, mittamus, aliquid duntaxat de jejunio & eleemosynis, quae poenitentiae sub omni oeconomia sunt comites, dicemus.
units.tr: 26; Daniel 9:3; or they spread sackcloth under themselves, Esther 4:3; Isaiah 58:5; Jonah 3:6, and so they sat in dust. But we will leave aside those things which were peculiar to the Orientals or can be more conveniently referred to other matters, and say something only about fasting and almsgiving, which accompany repentance under every dispensation.

units.la: XIX. Jejunium hic non aliud intelligimus quam religiosum; quod in abstinentia a cibo, caeterisque vitae condimentis ac solatiis, ad carnis petulantiam edomandam, ac preces acuendas, ad tempus suscepta, consistit. Ne fraudate alter alterum, nisi ex consensu ad tempus, ut vacetis jejunio & orationi. 1. Cor. 7: 5. Sanctificate jejunium, edicite coetum cum cessatione. Joël. 1: 14.
units.tr: XIX. By fasting here we understand only the religious kind, which consists in abstaining from food and from the other comforts and seasonings of life, undertaken for a time to subdue the wantonness of the flesh and to sharpen prayer. Do not defraud one another, except by consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, 1 Corinthians 7:5. Sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, and cease from work, Joel 1:14.

units.la: XX. Estque illud vel publica auctoritate, tum Magistratus, tum Ecclesiae, ac publicis de causis, institutum: Et annunciaverunt Jehosaphato, dicendo, venit contra te turba magna & indixit jejunium super totam Judam. 2. Chron. 20: 2, 3. Jon. 3: 8, 9. 1. Reg. 21: 9. vel privata pietate sumtum. 1. Cor. 7: 5. Matth. 9: 14.
units.tr: XX. Fasting is appointed either by public authority, of the magistrate or of the Church, for public causes: And they told Jehoshaphat, saying, a great multitude comes against you; and he proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah, 2 Chronicles 20:2, 3; Jonah 3:8, 9; 1 Kings 21:9. Or it is undertaken from private piety, 1 Corinthians 7:5; Matthew 9:14.

units.la: XXI. Religiosum vero dicitur, non quasi religionis pars foret, ac quasi immitem trucemque Deum coleremus, qui istum in modum placari debeat: sed quod ejus medium ac instrumentum sit, & ad cultum Dei promovendum faciat; dum gulam compescimus, & carnem, subtracto pabulo languentem, Dei jugum pati docemus, animumque humilem jam magis & magis defaecatum, ac corporeis nebulis liberum, ad divina magis aptum reddimus. Sed subjicio corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo. 1. Cor 9: 27. Quo etiam tenuior victus ad longum tempus sumtus, & mensae sanctimonia, pertinet. Cibum gratum non comedi, & caro atque vinum non intravit in os meum, & non unxi me, donec implerentur tres septimanae justae. Dan. 10: 3.
units.tr: XXI. It is called religious, not as if it were a part of religion, as though we worshipped a harsh and savage God who must be appeased in this way, but because it is a means and instrument of religion and furthers the worship of God. When we restrain the belly and, by withdrawing its food, teach the flesh, now weakened, to bear God's yoke, we make the mind humbler and more and more purified and free from bodily clouds, and so better fitted for divine things. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, 1 Corinthians 9:27. To this also belongs a thinner diet taken for a long time, and the holiness of the table. I ate no pleasant food, neither did meat or wine enter my mouth, nor did I anoint myself, until three whole weeks were fulfilled, Daniel 10:3; 1 Timothy 5:23.

units.la: 1. Tim. 5: 23. Ut culpandi sint jejunatores hypocritae, qui ad scenam & fastum jejunia usurpant, resipiscentia omnisque interiore sanctitate carentia. Quando autem jejunatis, nolite sicut hypocritae, tetrici. Matth. 6: 16. Quae sunt in vexatione corporis, in explessionem carnis. Col. 2: 23. An tale erit jejunium, quod eligam? dies, quo debilitet homo animam suam? an curvare instar juncti caput suum, & saccum & cinerem substernere? an, inquam, hoc vocabis jejunium, & diem acceptationis Domino? Esa. 58: 3-7. Joël. 2: 12, 13.
units.tr: Hypocritical fasters, who use fasts for show and display, having no repentance and lacking all inward holiness, deserve blame. But when you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, with a gloomy face, Matthew 6:16. Which have indeed an appearance of wisdom in self-imposed worship and humility and severity to the body, but are not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh, Colossians 2:23. Is this the fast that I choose: a day when a man afflicts his soul? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord? Isaiah 58:3-7; Joel 2:12, 13.

units.la: XXII. Multo minus illud meritorium est, aut divinae justitiae satisfactofactorum; quasi duritie ista noxae nostrae expiarentur, Deusque nobis conciliaretur. Quod non solum Dei justitiae & sanctitati (cum in tali cultu Dei sanctificatio sita non sit) sed jejuniorum quoque rationi repugnat; quae publicam indignitatis nostrae professionem, omnisque meriti abnegationem continent, & nos divina potius ira justisque poenis dignos esse testantur.
units.tr: XXII. Still less is fasting meritorious, or a satisfaction to divine justice, as though by such hardship our guilt were atoned for and God were reconciled to us. This contradicts not only the justice and holiness of God (since the sanctification of God does not lie in such worship), but also the nature of fasting itself, which expresses a public confession of our unworthiness and a renunciation of all merit, and bears witness that we deserve divine wrath and just punishments.

units.la: XXIII. Peccant praeterea Pontificiorum jejunia quoad modum; quod ea in superstitioso ciborum delectu, & carnium praecipue abstinentia, collocant, de caetero vix quicquam de culinae apparatu mutantes. Ut lautitiae, omnisque dapum varietas, & luxuria, cum iis jejuniis consistere queat. Quae hypocrita superstitione plena, ac Christianae libertati adversa sunt. Ignorat enim Euangelium ciborum discrimina, nec Judaicorum rituum corruptelam patitur. Atque extant diserta in hanc rem testimonia: Non quod ingreditur in os, polluit hominem Matth. 15:11. Edentes & bibentes quae ab ipsis apposita fuerunt. Luc. 10:7. Edite quicquid in macello venditur. 1. Cor. 10:25. Novi & persuasum habeo per Dominum Iesum, nihil esse impurum per se, sed ei, qui reputat aliquid esse impurum, id ei impurum esse. Rom. 14:14. Quod Deus purificavit, tu ne pollueris. Act. 10:15. Ne tangas, ne gustes, neque contrectes, quae omnia sunt ad corruptionem, usu, secundum mandata & doctrinas hominum. Col. 2:21, 22. &c. ubi Apostolus omnes superstitionis istius fibras rimatur & excindit, sicut & daemonium imposturae istas doctrinas adscribit, 1. Tim. 4:1, 2, 3. Idemque longo tempore veteris Ecclesiae sensus fuit. Quod ab aliis ostensum est. Non enim veteres Christianos, sed Judaeos, Pythagorae sectam, ac veteres quosdam haereticos, Pontificii hac in re auctores sequuntur.
units.tr: XXIII. Moreover, the fasts of the Papists are at fault as to their manner. They place them in a superstitious choice of foods, and above all in abstaining from meat, while changing hardly anything else in the preparation of the kitchen. So that luxury, every variety of dainties and extravagance can coexist with such fasts. These are full of hypocritical superstition and opposed to Christian liberty. For the Gospel knows nothing of distinctions among foods, nor does it tolerate the corruption of Jewish rites. And there are plain testimonies on this point: What goes into the mouth does not defile a man, Matthew 15:11. Eating and drinking what is set before them, Luke 10:7. Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, 1 Corinthians 10:25. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; but to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean, Romans 14:14. What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean, Acts 10:15. Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, which all perish with the using, according to the commandments and doctrines of men, Colossians 2:21, 22, etc. Here the Apostle tears out and cuts away every root of this superstition, and he also ascribes these deceitful doctrines to demons, 1 Timothy 4:1, 2, 3. The sense of the ancient Church was the same for a long time, as others have shown. For in this matter the Papists follow as their authorities not the ancient Christians but the Jews, the sect of Pythagoras, and certain ancient heretics.

units.la: XXIV. Nec valida sunt quae pro superstitione sua firmanda adferunt. Praecepta enim quae adducunt, de arbore ex Paradiso non degustanda; de Naziraeorum instituto; & quae Apostoli primae Ecclesiae de sanguine & suffocato praescripserunt, ad jejunia revera nihil pertinent: cum nec Adamus, ab arbuscula illa abstinens; nec Nazarus, ad vitem non accedens; nec primi olim Christiani, sanguinis esum cavָentes, jejunaSSe dicendi sint. Praeterquam quod illa omnia ex divina institutione auctoritatem habuerunt, quae in Ecclesiae placitis, superstitiosisque institutis non reperiuntur. Nec magis ipsos juvant exempla, Eliae, 1. Reg. 19:4. Johannis Baptistae, Matth. 3:4. Timothei, 1. Tim. 5:23. quae ad sobrietatem, & gulae lubricitatem moderandam, non autem ad vanam ciborum religionem pertinent. Nec denique ratiuncula ipsorum concludit, quod ad sobrietatis disciplinam hoc institutum faciat; carnesque ideo potissimum vetet Ecclesia, quod copioso spiritu appulsu carnem tumere ac lascivire faciant. Quid enim balnea, vina, pretiosique pisces, & aromata, omnisque ista coquina; quam tamen toto jejunii tempore Ecclesia illa filiis suis indulget? Praeterquam quod temperantia per superstitionem non docenda sit; nec tam ciborum delectus, quam crebra eorum abstinentia eo faciat.
units.tr: XXIV. Nor are the arguments they offer to uphold their superstition any stronger. The precepts they cite, about not eating from the tree in Paradise, about the rule of the Nazirites, and what the apostles of the primitive Church prescribed concerning blood and what is strangled, have nothing really to do with fasting. Adam, abstaining from that little tree, cannot be called a faster, nor Nazarite, not approaching the vine, nor the first Christians, abstaining from eating blood. Moreover, all those things had their authority from divine institution, whereas the observances of the Church and its superstitious institutions have no such warrant. Nor do the examples help them any more: Elijah, 1 Kings 19:4; John the Baptist, Matt. 3:4; Timothy, 1 Tim. 5:23. These pertain to sobriety and to restraining the slipperiness of gluttony, not to a vain religious observance of foods. Finally, their little argument does not prove that this institution serves the discipline of sobriety, or that the Church forbids meats chiefly because they make the flesh swell and grow lustful through an abundant inflow of spirits. For what of baths, wines, costly fish and spices, and all that kitchen fare, which the Church nevertheless indulges in for her children throughout the whole time of fasting? Besides, temperance is not to be taught through superstition, and a careful choice of foods, still less frequent abstinence from them, does not accomplish it.

units.la: XXV. Ejusdem ingenii est, quod jejunia uno de die convivio circumscribunt; & in prandiorum vel coenarum abstinentia collocant; quae tamen vel pridiana ingluvie, vel largioribus prandii epulis, compensare facile norunt; interpositis etiam stomacho fulciendo collationibus. Quae non pietas, sed veri jejunii ludibrium est; quod in esuritione, ac omni cibi abstinentia Scriptura collocat. Quadraginta diebus tentatus a diabolo fuit; & nihil edit illis diebus. Luc. 4: 2. Jon. 3: 7.
units.tr: XXV. Of the same disposition is their practice of confining fasting to one meal a day, and placing it in abstaining from breakfast or dinner. Yet these they know well how to make up for, either by gorging the night before or by richer feasts at midday, with light refreshments interposed to fortify the stomach. This is not piety but a mockery of true fasting, which Scripture places in hunger and in abstinence from all food: He was tempted by the devil for forty days, and he ate nothing in those days. Luke 4:2. Jonah 3:7.

units.la: XXVI. Denique peccant, quod certa jejunandi tempora describant, ut dies veneris, Sabbati; quadragesimae jejunium; quatuor anni quae vocant tempora; tum quoque adventus, rogationum, ac vigiliarum in praecipuis festis tempora. Sicut ex adverso diebus Dominicis, ac Festis, & toto inter Pascha ac Pentecosten spatio jejunare prohibent: reliquo anni tempore cujusque arbitrio, ac privatae pietati permisso. Dequo nos sic censemus. Judaeis quidem sollemne jejunium quotannis indictum fuisse Levit. 16: 29. Mense septimo, decimo mensis, debilitabitis animas vestras, & nullum opus facietis, coll. Act. 27: 9. Quod peculiarem rationem habebat; quum peccatum nondum ablatum testari, deque eo publice lugere fideles cogeret. In ipsis commemoratio peccatorum anniversaria est. Hebr. 10: 3. Unde tale jejunium nunc non obtinet. Omniaque illa veterajejunia, aliquid prisci rigoris habentia (nam & alia Judaei ad publicas calamitates deflendas addiderant) sub Novi Test. laetitia in hilaritatem, & gaudium, & tempora bona commutanda Prophetacecinit, Zach. 8: 19. Sed habent nihilominus & Christiani sua jejunandi tempora: Venient autem dies, quando ablatus ab ipsis erit sponsus, & tunc jejunabunt. Matth. 9: 15. coll. Marc. 2: 20. Quarto ab hinc die, usque ad hanc horam eram jejunans. Act. 10: 30. Sed absque dierum ac temporum superstitione; cum Christiana Ecclesia ista religione nunc exsoluta sit. Ne quis igitur vos judicet in cibo aut in potu, aut in parte festi, aut novilunii, aut sabbatorum. Col. 2: 16. Nec Christus certos jejuniorum dies præscripserit. Unde non statos certosque, sed hos illosve, pro publica necessitate, aut singulorum pietate, assumtos dies Ecclesia celebrat. Ea enim jejunii natura est, ut non nisi tristia tempora flagitet: unde itaque ea esse non possunt, ne forte rebus lætis ac bonis inter cedant, ac præpostero ordine media inter gaudia jejunare nos cogant. Primus vero apud Christianos jejuniorum leges ac tempora descripsit Montanus hæreticus, liberamque hactenus Christianorum pietatem vinculis quibusdam adstrinxit.
units.tr: XXVI. Finally, they err in prescribing fixed times for fasting, such as Friday and Saturday, the Lenten fast, the so-called four seasons of the year, and also the times of Advent, the Rogations, and the vigils before the principal feasts. On the other hand, they forbid fasting on Sundays and feast days, and throughout the whole period between Easter and Pentecost, and leave the rest of the year to each one's judgment and private piety. On this matter we judge as follows. To the Jews indeed a solemn fast was appointed every year: In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls, and you shall do no work. Lev. 16:29, compared with Acts 27:9. This had a peculiar reason, since it compelled the faithful to bear witness that sin was not yet taken away, and to mourn publicly over it. In them there is a yearly remembrance of sins. Heb. 10:3. Hence such a fast does not now hold. And all those ancient fasts, which had something of old-fashioned rigour (for the Jews had added others to lament public calamities), the prophet Zechariah sang would be changed, under the joy of the New Testament, into cheerfulness, and gladness, and good seasons. Zech. 8:19. Nevertheless Christians too have their own times of fasting: But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. Matt. 9:15, compared with Mark 2:20. Until this hour I was fasting four days ago. Acts 10:30. But these are without superstition about days and times, since the Christian Church is now released from that religious observance. Let no one therefore judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths. Col. 2:16. Nor did Christ prescribe fixed days of fasting. Hence the Church observes not set and fixed days, but these or those days, taken up according to public necessity or the piety of individuals. For such is the nature of fasting that it calls only for sad times. Therefore fasts cannot be fixed for times that are joyful and good, lest they interrupt such times and, in a perverse order, compel us to fast in the midst of our joys. The first to prescribe laws and times of fasting among Christians was the heretic Montanus, who bound with certain chains the hitherto free piety of Christians.

units.la: XXVII. Jejunium sanctificatur eleemosyna: sed τὰ ἐνόντα pro copia, aut ea quæ penes vos sunt, date eleemosynam, & ecce omnia vobis pura erunt. Luc. 11:41. Quæ charitatis quidam fructus est, ad proximum, in angustiis constitutum, sive pecunia, sive alia qua ope sublevandum. Hebræi נִדְבָה appellant, quod justitiæ fructus sit. Quo nonnulli verba Danielis trahunt, cap. 4:27. Peccata tua per justitiam (LXX ἐν ἐ-λεημοσύναις) avelle.
units.tr: XXVII. Fasting is sanctified by almsgiving: but what is within [τὰ ἐνόντα], according to your means, or give alms of what is with you, and behold, all things will be clean to you. Luke 11:41. This is a fruit of charity, given to a neighbour in distress, to be relieved either with money or with some other help. The Hebrews call it nedabah [נִדְבָה], because it is a fruit of righteousness. Some draw the words of Daniel here, ch. 4:27: Break off your sins by righteousness (the Seventy: by almsgivings [ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις]).

units.la: XXVIII. Præceptum hoc æque necessarium est, ac de charitate præstanda. Quanquam modus ejus speciatim definitus non sit; uti nec in precibus, jejuniis, aliisque sacris exercitiis, contigit. Sufficit enim ad hanc rem ipsum charitatis ingenium, quæ, pro nostra copia, aliorumque egestate, facile modum definire, & rite justeque explicare sese novit. Ut male Pontificii eleemosynam abundantem non præcepti, sed consilii, faciant; cum quodcunque prudentia capiat consilium, à charitate ejusque præcepto præcipuè dirigendum sit, quæ vel incommodo nostro eleemosynas dare aliquando jubet. Hæc autem ex penuria sua omnia quæ habebat injecit, omnem victum suum. Marc. 12:44. Nam pro viribus (testor) etiam supra vires voluntarii fuerunt. 2. Cor. 8:2,3.
units.tr: XXVIII. This precept is as necessary as the duty of showing charity. Although its measure is not specifically defined, neither is it in prayers, fasts, and other sacred exercises. For the very nature of charity suffices for this matter. It knows how, according to our means and the need of others, to define the measure easily and to explain it rightly and justly. The Papists therefore wrongly make abundant almsgiving a matter of counsel rather than of precept. Whatever prudence takes as counsel must be directed chiefly by charity and its precept, which sometimes bids us give alms even to our own inconvenience. But she out of her want cast in all that she had, her whole living. Mark 12:44. For according to their power (I bear witness), they were willing even beyond their power. 2 Cor. 8:2, 3.

units.la: XXIX. Danda autem eleemosyna ex iis, quæ possidemus, ac pro facultate uniuscujusque. Si enim promptus animus adsit, pro eo quod quis habet, gratus est; non pro eo, quod non habet. 2. Cor. 8:12. Ne deneges bonum ab eo, cujus id est, cum fuerit in potestate manus tuæ facere. Prov 3:27. Meretricium enim stipem, turpemque omnem quæstum abominatur Dominus, nec in eleemosynam venire finit. Non feres quæstum meretricium & pretium canis ad domum Iehovæ. Deut. 23:19. Sed & supra vires aliquando largiri, ac in maxima Ecclesiæ difficultate relinquere omnia, & abnegare, inque fratrum & Ecclesiæ necessitates expendere, jubemur. Cujus generis erat illa extraordinaria primorum Christianorum caritas: Et nullus aliquid eorum, quæ ipsi erant, dicebat proprium esse, sed erant omnia ipsis communia. Act. 4: 32. Quæ tamen non mera bonorum communio erat, ut quidam somniant, cum non omne dominium excluderet. Nonne manens tibi manebat & venditum in tua potestate erat? Act. 5: 4. Nam adeo rerum proprietas peccatum non est, ut sine ea eleemosynis locus non sit; & panem proprium non edere vel ἀταξίας, vel extremæ miseriæ habeatur. Neque gratis panem edimus, —sed cum erumna & labore nocte dieque operantes, ne cui vestrum oneri essemus— Audimus enim aliquos ambulare inter vos inordinate, non operantes, sed inania agentes. 2. Thess. 3: 8, 11. Quin vel magnis divitiis incubare Christiano homini non prohibitum est, modo illæ bene partæ sint, & bene collocentur, nec in luxuriæ, aut injustitiæ aut carnalis fiduciæ pabulum degenerent. Jac. 5: 1–6. Peculiare autem ac extraordinarium præceptum erat, quod diviti illi juveni datum legimus Matth. 19: 21, 22. Si vis perfectus esse, abi vende quæ tibi suppetunt, & da pauperibus: habebis thesaurum in cœlo: & adsequere me; ad infirmum avarumque ejus animum pungendum.
units.tr: XXIX. Alms ought to be given from what we possess and according to the means of each person. For if the willing mind is there, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. 2 Cor. 8:12. Do not withhold good from the one to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. Prov. 3:27. For the Lord abominates the wages of a harlot and every shameful gain, and does not allow it to come into alms: You shall not bring the wages of a harlot, or the price of a dog, into the house of Jehovah. Deut. 23:19. But we are also commanded sometimes to give beyond our strength, and in the greatest difficulty of the Church to give up everything and renounce it, and to spend it on the needs of the brothers and the Church. Of this kind was that extraordinary charity of the first Christians: And no one said that any of the things which belonged to him was his own, but they had all things in common. Acts 4:32. Yet this was not a mere community of goods, as some dream, since it did not exclude all ownership: Did it not remain yours while it remained, and after it was sold, was it not in your power? Acts 5:4. For private property is so far from being sin that without it there would be no room for almsgiving, and not to eat one's own bread is regarded either as disorder or as extreme wretchedness. Nor did we eat bread gratis, but worked with toil and labour night and day, so as not to be a burden to any of you. For we hear that some among you walk disorderly, not working, but busy with idle things. 2 Thess. 3:8, 11. Indeed, it is not forbidden for a Christian to be engaged with great riches, provided they are honestly gained and well employed, and do not degenerate into food for luxury, injustice, or carnal confidence. Jas. 5:1–6. But a peculiar and extraordinary precept was given to that rich young man, as we read in Matt. 19:21, 22: If you want to be perfect, go, sell what belongs to you, and give to the poor; you will have treasure in heaven; and follow me. It was meant to prick his feeble and covetous soul.

units.la: XXX. Ad eleemosynam etiam pertinet mutuum, egenti gratis da- tum.
units.tr: XXX. Lending to the needy without interest also belongs to almsgiving.

units.la: Volentem mutuari ne te, ne averseris. Matth. 5: 42. Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes. Luc. 6: 35. Quod distinguendum est à mutuo, ob annuam mercedem seu usuram proximo præstito. Ubi contractus quidam est. Hic justitia, ibi misericordia locum habet. Nec male Scholastici orationem pro peccante, correptionem fraternam, disciplinam emendantem, aliaque id genus, ad eleemosynam referunt.
units.tr: Do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you. Matt. 5:42. Lend, expecting nothing in return. Luke 6:35. This must be distinguished from a loan that brings an annual payment or interest to the neighbour, which is a contract. Justice has its place there, but mercy has its place here. The Schoolmen were not wrong to count prayer for a sinner, brotherly correction, discipline that amends, and other things of that kind as almsgiving.

units.la: XXXI. Requisitum eleemosynæ necessarium est, lubentia, prompti- tudo, hilaritas, ac cordis quædam simplicitas, prudentiæ tamen ac discre- tioni mista.
units.tr: XXXI. Alms require willingness, readiness, cheerfulness, and a certain simplicity of heart, yet mixed with prudence and discretion.

units.la: Cum non profundendæ, sed distribuendæ sint eleemosynæ, nec spargere eas, sed partiri, justeque distribuere decet, servato personarum ordine & gradibus. Abesse autem debet omnis ostentatio & hypocrisis, quæ præstantissimo huic operi peregrinum quendam fucum adspergit, quo omnis ejus gratia perit. Quam erogandi modestiam ac simplicitatem Judæi monuerunt verbo illo, sinistram ignorare debere quid dextra peragit; vide Matth. 6: 1, 3. Attendite, ne eleemosynam vestram faciatis coram hominibus, ut videamini ab illis &c. Rom. 12: 8, 9. Qui miseretur, in hilaritate. Hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Gal. 6: 10. Operemur bonum adversus omnes, maxime vero adversus domesticos fidei.
units.tr: Alms are not to be poured out but distributed, and they should be shared out and given justly, not scattered, keeping the order of persons and their ranks. All show and hypocrisy must be absent, for these stain this most excellent work with a foreign colouring, and all its grace perishes because of them. The Jews taught this modesty and simplicity in giving with the saying the left hand should not know what the right hand does; see Matt. 6:1, 3. Take heed that you do not do your alms before men, to be seen by them, etc. Rom. 12:8, 9: He who shows mercy, let him do it with cheerfulness. God loves a cheerful giver. Gal. 6:10: Let us do good to all, but especially to the household of faith.

units.la: XXXII. Ampla eleemosynæ merces promittitur, sed ea omnia ex gratiâ.
units.tr: XXXII. A generous reward for almsgiving is promised, but all of it comes from grace.

units.la: Ampla eleemosynæ merces promittitur, sed ea omnia ex gratiâ. gratia & misericordia. Beati misericordes, quia ipsis misericordia tribuetur. Matth. 5: 7. conf. 25: 35. Dei misericordiam Dominus Onesiphori domui, quia saepe me recreavit. 2. Tim. 1: 16. Cum nihil de nostro erogemus, sed de iis quae Deus nobis prior dedit. Ut male Pontificii, post Judaeos, in iis justitiae suae partem collocent, & eleemosynarum merita jactent: quo nomine tamen plerunque pias, quas vocant, ac religiosas erogationes, sumtusque, vel viventium, vel morientium supremis arbitriis, ad insanas eorum substructiones factos, aliasque ejus generis prosusiones intelligunt; quo hominum istorum otium pascatur, atque illi de piorum agapis delicientur ac lasciviant.
units.tr: A generous reward for almsgiving is promised, but all of it comes from grace and mercy. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Matt. 5:7; cf. 25:35. May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me. 2 Tim. 1:16. For we give nothing of our own, but of what God has first given us. The Papists, following the Jews, wrongly place a part of their righteousness in these works and boast of their merits from alms. Yet by these alms they usually mean the so-called pious and religious donations and expenses, made by the living or by the dying in their last wills, for their mad building projects and other extravagances of that sort, so that the idleness of those men is fed and they themselves revel and wanton on the love feasts of the pious.

units.la: XXXIII. Quod vero ex Daniele adducunt, c. 4:27. Redime peccata tua justitia, id est, eleemosynis: id in fonte aliter est, ubi legitur abrumpe peccata tua p?p h. e. desiste ab illis. conf. Exod. 32: 2, 3. Et si vel redimendi sensus admittatur, ad animum regis movendum facit, quem spes erat, matura poenitentia, & qualicunque illa vitae emendatione, judicia Dei averruncaturum; ut in Ninevitis patuit. Ac similiter Christus Luc. 11: 41. Imo ea quae penes vos sunt date in eleemosynam, & omnia munda erunt vobis: non proprium earum meritum adstruit, sed rapinas ac injusta spolia insigni quadam converAione ac charitate compensare suadet; quibus rerum quae circa nos sunt munditiem acquiri docet.
units.tr: XXXIII. As for what they bring from Daniel, 4:27: Redeem your sins by righteousness, that is, by alms. In the source text this reads differently, where it says break off your sins, that is, cease from them; cf. Exod. 32:2, 3. And even if the sense of redeeming is admitted, it serves to move the king's heart, who had hope that by early repentance and some kind of amendment of life he would avert God's judgments, as became plain in the Ninevites. Likewise Christ, Luke 11:41: Rather, give alms of what you have, and everything will be clean for you. He does not establish a merit of their own in these alms, but urges them to make up for their plunder and unjust spoils by a notable kind of generosity and love. Through this he teaches that the cleanness of the things around us is obtained.

units.la: XXXIV. Explicata veritate, componendi nunc cum ea veniunt sectariorum errores. Ac Pontificii quidem praecipue illam corruperunt; &, vocabuli errore abducti, eam magnam partem 1. in poenis ac castigationibus externis, a poenitentiario impositis, constituerunt: sicuti & formalem ejus rationem poenalem statuunt. Qui error originem traxit ex veteris Ecclesiae disciplina, ac poenitentia publica, quae severa admodum fuit, & certis gradibus distincta erat. Cujus imaginem qualemcunque Pontificii retinentes, externam illam poenitentiam cum interna confuderunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. Having set out the truth, the errors of the sectaries now come up to be set alongside it. The Papists in particular have corrupted this truth, and, led astray by the ambiguity of the word, they have largely located it (1) in the external punishments and chastisements imposed by the confessor, and they likewise hold that its formal nature is penal. This error arose from the discipline of the ancient Church and its public repentance, which was very severe and divided into fixed stages. The Papists, retaining some kind of likeness of this, have confused the external penance with the internal.

units.la: XXXV. 11. Mirum autem valde est, eos ex illa nihilominus virtutem facere. Virtutis enim ratio in externa illa poena consistere non potest. Ac si internum dolorem spectes, & emendationis propositum, non tam specialis aliqua virtus, quam commune virtutis studium ea appellari debet.
units.tr: XXXV. 11. It is truly remarkable, however, that they nevertheless make this into a virtue. For the nature of a virtue cannot consist in that external punishment. If you look at inward sorrow and the purpose of amendment, it ought to be called not so much a special virtue as the common pursuit of virtue.

units.la: XXXVI. 111. Sed & Sacramentum ex ea faciunt, cujus partes, tum poenitentis, tum poenitentiarii, actibus absolvunt. De quo operae pretium est Tridentini Concilii definitiones audire, cum ec communissimas simul: adversariorum sententias continent, quæ alioquin de hoc sacro valde intricatæ sunt. Ajunt igitur 1. ut nascentibus, sive renascentibus, Christianis baptismi sacramentum institutum est; iisque jam ad sacram militiam initiandis confirmatio subservit; ac in longo illo cursu salutaris expuli fultura per intervalla porrigitur: ita, ne ullibi Ecclesiæ, fidelissimæ matris, cura deficiat, lapsantibus Christianis, atque in hoc certamine nonnunquam succumbentibus, alio quoque sacramento subveniri debere; adeoque ad peccata, post baptismum commissa, expianda, pœnitentiæ, veluti secundæ post naufragium tabulæ, auxilium dari. 2. Sacramentum autem illud à Christo institutum vaticinantur; cum Apostolis, ante discessum, potestatem peccata remittendi & retinendi dedit. 3. Partes ejus enumerant, contritionem, sacramentalem confessionem, sacerdotalem absolutionem, & satisfactionem denique per opera pœnalia, pro pœna temporali. 4. Materiam actibus pœnitentis comprehendunt, contritione, confessione, & satisfactione: formam constituunt in verbis sacerdotalibus, ego absolvo te. 5. Ministrum autem ejus non solo ministerio, quo remissionem peccatorum peccatori annuncict; sed, judiciali in solio residentem, potestate ac judicaturâ fungi ajunt. 6. Rem significatam denique ac effectum sacramenti reconciliationem cum Deo ponunt.
units.tr: XXXVI. 111. They also make it a sacrament, and absolve its parts by the acts of both the penitent and the confessor. On this it is worth hearing the definitions of the Council of Trent, since they contain the most common views of their opponents together, which are otherwise very tangled concerning this sacrament. They say, therefore: (1) that the sacrament of baptism was instituted for Christians who are being born, or born again; that confirmation serves those now to be initiated into sacred warfare; and that in the long course of this life the help of salvation is extended at intervals. Thus the care of the ever-faithful Mother, the Church, may nowhere fail, since Christians sometimes stumble and sometimes give way in this struggle, and they must be helped by another sacrament too. Hence repentance is given, as a second plank after shipwreck, to expiate sins committed after baptism. (2) They allege that this sacrament was instituted by Christ, who, before his departure, gave the Apostles the power of forgiving and retaining sins. (3) They list its parts: contrition, sacramental confession, priestly absolution, and finally satisfaction by penal works for temporal punishment. (4) They take the matter to be the acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, and satisfaction; and they make the form consist in the priestly words, I absolve you. (5) They say that its minister performs his office not only by the ministry by which he announces the forgiveness of sins to the sinner, but also by sitting on the judicial throne and exercising authority and judgment. (6) Finally, they place the thing signified and the effect of the sacrament in reconciliation with God.

units.la: XXXVII. Adquæ annotamus: 1. non posse intelligi, quomodo illud, quod virtutem ipsi appellant, & saltem virtutis studium dicit, simul sacramentum sit; cum ista toto genere differant. 2. Atque in Veteri Test. ac sub initia novi, pœnitentiam eandem viguisse; non tamen, vel fatentibus adversariis, sacramentum fuisse. 3. Neque sacramentum tale à Christo ullibi institutum esse. Verba enim Christi Matth. 16: 19. Quicquid ligaveris in terra, erit ligatum in cœlo: & quicquid solveris in terra, erit solutum in cœlo. & Joh. 20: 23. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remissa sunt eis; & si quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt: non judicandi auctoritatem, sed ministerium reconciliationis Apostolis tribuunt, & sacræ disciplinæ usum commendant; pro delicrimine videl. peccantium. 4. Imo, cum Christus non solum pœnitentium peccata remitti, sed & impœnitentium delicta retineri jubeat; si hic sacramentum instituatur, magna pars hujus sacramenti etiam erga impœnitentes exercebitur. Nec jam sola verba, ego absolvo te, ad sacramenti formam sufficient; sed & similia addenda erunt circa impœnitentes, ego ligo te. 5. Nullum vero sacrasacramenti hujus ostendunt signum & symbolum externum; absque quo sacramenti ratio non constat. 6. Uti nec recte materiam facramenti in tribus illis poenitentis actibus consistere faciunt. Nam & contritionem in iis numerant, cum materia omnis sacramenti externa debeat esse. Et satisfactionem post absolutionem sacerdotis rejiciunt; quod quid aliud est, quam materiam post formam sequi, idque longo sæpenumero interyallo? 7. Nec denique absolutio forma ejus dici potest, cum, concedentibus adversariis, peccatorum remissio a vere contrito & humiliato, abíque ea, acquiri possit. Improbus cum convertetur ab omnibus peccatis suis — vivendo vivet, non morietur. Ezech. 18: 21.
units.tr: XXXVII. To these things we note: (1) it cannot be understood how that which they call a virtue, and which at least expresses the pursuit of virtue, can at the same time be a sacrament, since these differ in their whole kind. (2) In the Old Testament, and at the beginning of the New, the same repentance flourished, yet it was not a sacrament, even by the admission of the opponents. (3) Nor has Christ instituted such a sacrament anywhere. For the words of Christ, Matt. 16:19: Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, and John 20:23: If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone's sins, they are retained, do not give the Apostles the authority of judging but the ministry of reconciliation, and they commend the use of sacred discipline, namely for the offence of sinners. (4) Indeed, since Christ orders not only the sins of penitents to be forgiven but also the offences of the impenitent to be retained, if this were instituted as a sacrament, a large part of this sacrament would also be exercised towards the impenitent. Nor would the words I absolve you alone then suffice for the form of the sacrament, but similar words would have to be added for the impenitent: I bind you. (5) They show no sacred sign or external symbol of this sacrament, and without this the nature of a sacrament does not stand. (6) Nor do they rightly make the matter of the sacrament consist in those three acts of the penitent. For they count contrition among them, though all the external matter of a sacrament ought to be external. And they reject satisfaction after the priest's absolution, which is what, other than making the matter follow the form, and that very often after a long interval? (7) Finally, absolution cannot be called its form, since, even by the admission of the opponents, forgiveness of sins can be obtained from a man who is truly contrite and humbled, even without it. When the wicked turns from all his sins... by living he shall live, and not die. Ezek. 18:21.

units.la: XXXVIII. iv. Actus poenitentiae, ut vidimus, tres numerant; contritionem, confessionem, & satisfactionem. Quanquam autem duo priores ex illis, si recte peragantur, in hoc negotio locum habere possint: satisfactio tamen merum est figmentum, infandae superbiae plenum, & Christi redemtioni adversum. Praeterquam quod hi actus omnes, prout in Papatu obtinent, atque in Jesuitarum praesertim morali Theologia explicantur, in Judae poenitentia assignari possint. Tunc Judas — poenitentia ductus, reddidit triginta aureos — dicens, peccavi — & discedens strangulavit se. Matth. 27: 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: XXXVIII. iv. As we have seen, they count three acts of repentance: contrition, confession, and satisfaction. Although the first two of these, if rightly performed, can have a place in this business, satisfaction is pure fiction, full of unspeakable pride, and opposed to Christ's redemption. Besides, all these acts, as they stand in Papacy and are explained especially in the moral theology of the Jesuits, could be assigned to the repentance of Judas. Then Judas, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver, saying, I have sinned, and going away he hanged himself. Matt. 27:3, 4, 5.

units.la: XXXIX. v. In specie, contritio ipsorum imperfecta, seu attritio potius, poenitentiae verae pars non est, cum nihil aliud sit, quam dolor & tristitia secundum mundum, absque vera Dei caritate & fide; non cuangelica, sed legalis ad summum; quae quomodo omnem peccandi voluntatem excludere, & vitam emendandi propositum continere possit, videre non possumus; cum illud charitatis tantum & fidei sit: prout autem perfecta est, & caritatem comitem habet, poenitentiae pars est; nihil autem facit ad fictitium hoc sacramentum. Atque utcunque contritionem & attritionem distinguere am ent; quorum illa charitatem habeat comitem, haec vero nihil sit nisi aversatio justitiae Dei, & horror gehennae, atque omissio peccati propter illud; tamen in discrimine isto assignando non conveniunt. Ac Jesuitae palam attritionem in sacramento poenitentiae sufficere, & cum absolutione sacerdotis justificare docent.
units.tr: XXXIX. v. Specifically, their contrition is imperfect, or rather it is attrition, and attrition is not a part of true repentance. It is nothing but sorrow and grief according to the world, without true love of God and faith. It is not evangelical but at most legal. We cannot see how it could exclude every will to sin and contain a purpose of amending life, since that belongs only to love and faith. But contrition, when it is perfect and accompanied by love, is a part of repentance, and it contributes nothing to their fictitious sacrament. However they may distinguish contrition from attrition, the former having love as its companion and the latter being nothing but aversion from God's justice and horror of hell, with the abandoning of sin on account of that horror, they do not agree in drawing this distinction. The Jesuits openly teach that attrition suffices in the sacrament of penance and justifies together with the priest's absolution.

units.la: XL. vi. Confessionem peccati quod attinet, de ea nos sic censemus: 1. probam & necessariam cam esse confessionem, quae coram Deo fit. Tibi soli peccavi, & malum in oculis tuis feci, Psal. 51: 6. Si confitemur peccata nostra, fidelis est & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata. 1. Joh. 1: 9. conf. Prov. 28: 13. Quae tamen cum corde potissimum fiat, à contritio— tione parum differt, nec distinctam ab ea poenitentiæ partem constituere debet. Quanquam & verbis, & supplici gestu, & non sine lacrymis ac jejunio, ut vidimus, eam quandoque peragi par sit. 2. Admittimus etiam ac urgemus, oborto graviori scandalo, confessionem Ecclesiasticam coram coetu; quo Deus honoretur, & Ecclesiæ de offensa satisfiat, ac peccator Ecclesiasticam pacem rite obtineat. Qui peccant, coram omnibus redargue, ut & reliqui timorem habeant. 1. Tim. 5: 20. Quo pertinebant quatuor illi poenitentiæ publicæ, apud veteres, gradus, προσκλαυσις, ακροασις, υποπτωσις, συστασις; quos excipiebat tandem μετανοια. Ex qua disciplina veterum poenitentia illa sacramentalis enata & corrupta est. 3. Laudamus quoq; confessionem privatam reciprocam, in mutuis offensis fidelium, juxta Jac. 5: 16. Confitemini alii aliis lapsus, & precamini alii pro aliis, ut sanemini. Quo modo illata injuria resarciri, ruptumque charitatis vinculum reconcinnari, & conscientiæ quies procurari optime potest. 4. Cui addi potest & alia confessionis privatæ species, sed ea libera, ac uniuscujusque arbitrio permissa; qua quis, in graviore conscientiæ lucta, coram pastore vel alio sapiente viro, ejus vulnera denudat, & medicinam ac consolationem ex verbo Dei quærit. 5. Urgent autem Pontificii præter hæc omnia confessionem quoque auricularem, quam omnibus Christianis imponunt, ad minimum semel in anno coram sacerdote peragendam, idque de omnibus peccatis mortalibus, ac præcipuis eorum circumstantiis; quam à Christo institutam, & de jure necessariam, affirmant. Canonistis rectius eam juris humani agnoscentibus, utpote gradibus quibusdam, primum in cœnobiis, tum dehinc publicè in Ecclesia, primum quidem libere ac pro singulorum arbitrio, tandem autem necessario, usurpatam, & ab Innocentio tertio, in concilio Lateranensi, A. 1215. Ecclesiastica lege stabilitam.
units.tr: XL. vi. As for the confession of sin, we judge as follows: 1. The confession made before God is good and necessary. Against you only have I sinned, and done what is evil in your eyes, Ps. 51:6. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, 1 John 1:9; cf. Prov. 28:13. Since this is done chiefly in the heart, it differs little from contrition and ought not to constitute a separate part of repentance, although, as we have seen, it is proper that it sometimes be carried out also with words, with a suppliant gesture, and not without tears and fasting. 2. We also admit and urge that, when a more serious scandal has arisen, there should be a public confession before the assembly, by which God is honoured, the offence is satisfied to the Church, and the sinner duly regains peace with the Church. Those who sin, rebuke in the sight of all, so that the rest also may have fear, 1 Tim. 5:20. To this belonged the four degrees of public repentance among the ancients: weeping [προσκλαυσις], hearing [ακροασις], prostration [υποπτωσις], standing with [συστασις]; and at last came repentance [μετανοια]. From this ancient discipline that sacramental penance arose and was corrupted. 3. We also commend private mutual confession among believers for mutual offences, according to James 5:16: Confess your faults to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. By this an injury done can best be made good, a broken bond of love mended, and peace of conscience secured. 4. To this may be added another kind of private confession, but a free one, left to each person's own judgment: when someone, in a more serious struggle of conscience, lays bare his wounds before the minister or some other wise man, and seeks medicine and consolation from the Word of God. 5. Besides all these, however, the Papists urge also auricular confession, which they impose on all Christians, to be made before a priest at least once a year, and this of all mortal sins and their principal circumstances. They affirm that it was instituted by Christ and is necessary by right. The Canonists more correctly acknowledge it as of human right, since it was introduced by degrees, first in monasteries, then publicly in the Church, first freely and at the discretion of individuals, and at last as a necessity, and was established by ecclesiastical law by Innocent III in the Lateran Council of 1215.

units.la: XLI. In qua nos culpamus: 1. necessitatem ac tyrannidem conscientiis impositam; quas remissionis peccatorum solatio privant, nisi omnes ejus sinus mortali homini nudaverint. Quasi, qui vera delictorum poenitentia ducitur, ac ad Dei solius thronum se abjicit, sine hominum suffragio ac judiciali quadam sententia veniæ compos fieri non possit. Hoc enim hac agendi ratione tuentur. 2. Unde & nimiam ac sacrilegam hominum potestatem in hoc negotio damnamus. Nam sacerdotem pro tribunali sedentem faciunt, &, non ministri, sed judicis instar peccatores absolventem, blasphemâ formulâ, ego absolvo te &c. Non aliis enim, vel minoribus verbis, uti fas est, ut sacrum judicium peragi agnoscamus. Unde & certo hominum genere, in Christiana Ecclesia, istam potestatem peculiari quodam charactere tributam somniant. 3. Adaugent autem fidelium jugum, quod peccata omnia ad numerum revocare, & fuquin universæ nonnunquam vitæ, labem unicà horulà excutere necesse fit. Quod, cum factu impossibile sit, ingentem animo carnificinam adferre debet. Aberrationes quis intelligat? ab occultis absolve me. Psal. 19:13. Lamosum est cor pra omnis, & incurabiliter egrum. Quis cognoscet illud? Jer. 17:9. qualis peccatorum commemoratio, præcipue sub N. T. post peractum sacrificium Christi, fieri, si vel posset, non debet.
units.tr: XLI. In this we find fault: 1. with the necessity and tyranny imposed on consciences, which deprive them of the comfort of forgiveness of sins unless they have laid open every recess of their hearts to a mortal man. As if one who is led to true repentance, and casts himself down at the throne of God alone, could not obtain pardon without the vote of men and a kind of judicial sentence. For this is how they defend their practice. 2. Hence we also condemn the excessive and sacrilegious power of men in this matter. For they make the priest sit on a judgment seat and absolve sinners not as a minister but as a judge, with the blasphemous formula "I absolve you" and so on. For it is not permitted to use other or lesser words, if we are to acknowledge that a sacred judgment is being carried out. Hence they also dream that this power has been granted by a peculiar character to a certain class of men in the Christian Church. 3. Moreover, they increase the yoke of the faithful, since it is necessary to recall all sins to number, and sometimes to wipe away the stain of a whole life in a single hour. Since this is impossible in fact, it must bring huge torment to the mind. "Who can understand his errors? Cleanse thou me from secret faults." Psal. 19:13. "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" Jer. 17:9. Such a recounting of sins, especially under the New Testament after the sacrifice of Christ has been completed, ought not to be made, even if it were possible.

units.la: 4. Ut de sacerdote præterea; qui, cum magnam confitentium turbam brevi spatio sæpe expiandam habeat, quomodo tot annorum peccata breviadeo auditu excipere & librare, juxtaque pœnitentibus pœnas imponere potest? 5. Omitto tandem & alia arcani hujus colloquii flagitia; sanda scelerum molimina, furtivas libidines, privatorum domuum secreta temerata, proditionum denique scholam, & summa regnorum momenta in religioso isto secessu librata & conculcata. Ut confessio ista nullo prætextu in Ecclesia servanda sit, quod Lutherani faciunt; quam eam, non ex divino jure, sed ex Ecclesiastica institutione, derivent. Nullà enim Scripturæ auctoritate, vel exemplo, quidquid hunc in finem producant, nititur, vel doctioribus adversariorum ad sentientibus.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, as to the priest: since he often has a great crowd of penitents to be cleansed in a short space, how can he hear and weigh the sins of so many years so hastily, and impose penances on the penitent in proportion to them? 5. Finally, I pass over the other disgraceful things of this secret conversation: wicked plots, hidden lusts, the secrets of private households violated, and, in short, a school of treachery, and the greatest affairs of kingdoms weighed and trampled in that religious retreat. So this confession must not be kept in the Church under any pretext, as the Lutherans do; they derive it not from divine right but from ecclesiastical institution. For it rests on no authority or example of Scripture, whatever they bring forward to this end, nor do the more learned of our opponents agree with it.

units.la: XLII. vii. Tertiam Pontificiæ pœnitentiæ partem quod spectat, illa est satisfactio.
units.tr: XLII. vii. As regards the third part of Papist repentance, that is satisfaction.

units.la: De qua ita sentiunt. 1. culpam peccatorum à Deo gratis remitti; nec humanæ satisfactioni in ea locum esse. 2. Remitti quoque à Deo pœnam æternam, eamque in temporalem commutari. 3. Quæ à peccatore ipso ex solvenda fit, tum vitæ hujus supplicis, tum post illam pœnis purgatoriis. 4. Atque huc jejunia, preces, eleemosynas, aliaque opera satisfactoria valere. 5. Sunt autem illa, opera bona, sed laboriosa; in tribus illis generibus possimum consistentia. 6. Estque ipsis satisfactio, præstatio operis æquivalentis, alias indebiti, ad puniendum peccatum. Cujus valorem varie examinant; ac Bellarminus, cumque eo alii, in expiatione pœnæ temporalis, ex condigno, potuit. 7. Distinguunt autem inter satisfactiones plenas, & semiplenas; quæ posteriores à Christi merito suppleri tandem debent. 8. Atque hic disquirere etiam amant, an satisfactio Christi & nostra duæ sint satisfactiones; an una? 9. Denique non proprias solum satisfactiones, sed & alienas admittunt: mittunt: tum privatas, prout meritorum aliquod commercium inter pios fingunt; quod in confraternitatibus ipsorum obtinet: tum publicas; quo venales Antistitum indulgentiæ pertinent. Quæ propius examinanda sunt.
units.tr: They hold the following about it: (1) that the guilt of sins is freely remitted by God, and that human satisfaction has no place in this; (2) that God also remits eternal punishment and changes it into temporal punishment; (3) that this temporal punishment is paid by the sinner himself, both in the course of this life through penal sufferings and after it through purgatorial punishments; (4) that fastings, prayers, almsgiving and other satisfactory works avail for this; (5) that these are good works but laborious, and that they chiefly consist in those three kinds; (6) that satisfaction for them is the performance of a work equivalent to, and otherwise not owed for, the punishing of sin. They examine its value in various ways, and Bellarmine, with others, held that it can be ex condigno in the expiation of temporal punishment. (7) They distinguish between full and half satisfactions, and the latter must finally be supplemented by the merit of Christ. (8) Here they also like to inquire whether the satisfaction of Christ and ours are two satisfactions or one. (9) Finally, they admit not only one's own satisfactions but also those of others: private, insofar as they imagine some exchange of merits among the pious, which holds in their confraternities; and public, to which the venal indulgences of the bishops belong. These must be examined more closely.

units.la: XLIII. Ac 1. quidem in genere improbandæ omnes hominum satisfactiones. Cum 1. inane fundamentum sit, remitti culpam, & non remitti pœnam: & rursus remitti pœnam æternam, non autem temporalem. Cum una peccatorum pœna mors sit, cujus gradus nullus expiata culpa restare proprie potest. 2. Ac omnis illa expiatio plenissime peracta est à Christo; cujus, ut agni inculpati ac incontaminati, pretioso sanguine redemti sumus. 1. Pet. 1:18. Quem vilem nimis habent, qui alium præterea sanguinem, aliasque satisfactiones quærunt: cum ille solus à Deo in propitiatorium propositus sit, per fidem in sanguinem ipsius. Rom. 3:25. 3. Nec aliter Christus nunc peccata remittit, quam olim, cum in terris degeret; quando eum sine pœnis illis expiatoriis peccatores in gratiam receptos videmus: Bono sis animo, fili mi, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Matth. 9:2. coll. Luc. 7:48. Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23: 43. 4. Quæcunque autem afflictiones & certamina piis adhuc restant, illa vel probandis iis, vel castigandis, carnisque lasciviæ edomandæ, vel denique Deo glorificando, ac quodam amoris martyrio honorando; nulla autem ad justitiæ ejus satisfaciendum inserviunt: atque omnes denique cum morte finiuntur, quæ ultima laborum meta & linea est. Quod vel de ipsis veterum afflictionibus, quæ alioquin præterea iræ speciem habebant, ac peccati notam ferebant, verum fuit. Qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Hebr. 2:15. Cum nunc omnis accusatio, condemnatio, maledictio & ira, quibus obnoxii erant sub V. T. fideles, ablatæ sint.
units.tr: XLIII. And first, in general, all human satisfactions are to be rejected. (1) For it is an empty foundation to hold that guilt is remitted but punishment is not, and again that eternal punishment is remitted but temporal punishment is not. The one punishment of sins is death, and no degree of it can properly remain once the guilt has been expiated. (2) And all that expiation was most fully accomplished by Christ, by whose precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb, we have been redeemed. 1 Pet. 1:18. They hold it too cheap who seek another blood and other satisfactions besides, since He alone was set forth by God as a propitiation, through faith in his blood. Rom. 3:25. (3) Nor does Christ now forgive sins otherwise than he did long ago, when he dwelt on earth, when we see sinners received into favour without those expiatory punishments: "Be of good cheer, son, your sins are forgiven you." Matt. 9:2, compare Luke 7:48. "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise." Luke 23:43. (4) Whatever afflictions and struggles still remain for the pious, these serve either to prove them or to chastise them, to subdue the lust of the flesh, or finally to glorify God and honour him with a kind of martyrdom of love; none of them serves to satisfy his justice. All of them end finally with death, which is the last goal and finishing line of labours. This was true even of the afflictions of the ancients, which otherwise also bore the appearance of wrath and carried the mark of sin: "who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage." Heb. 2:15. Now, since all accusation, condemnation, curse and wrath, to which the faithful under the Old Testament were subject, have been taken away.

units.la: XLIV. Frustra autem Christi gloriam tueri sese posse putant, dum ex ejus satisfactione istam operibus nostris dignitatem venire dicunt: atque hoc majori ipsi gloriæ esse: quin & istum in modum sanguinem ejus, omneque mortis pretium nobis applicari. Quemcunque enim colorem adhibeant, nostram satisfactionem cum Christi redemtione, hominumque sanguinem & cruciatus cum Servatoris sanguine miscere non possunt, nisi multum de Christi satisfactione imminuant, istoque spolio hominem exornent. Mira autem applicatio beneficii, quam per pœnam & cruciatum fieri volunt! vera autem, ac Christo homineque digna applicatio fit per Euangelii sermonem, per sacramenta, per Spiritus gratiam; quæ illi propriarum satisfactionum inquinamentis multum corruperunt.
units.tr: XLIV. They vainly think they can defend the glory of Christ while they say that this dignity comes to our works from his satisfaction, and that this redounds to his greater glory.
