Indeed, in this way his blood and the whole price of his death are applied to us. For whatever colour they use, they cannot mix our satisfaction with Christ's redemption, nor men's blood and sufferings with the Saviour's blood, unless they greatly diminish Christ's satisfaction and adorn man with that spoil. Yet what a strange application of benefit they want to make through punishment and torment! The true and worthy application, both to Christ and to man, is made through the word of the Gospel, through the sacraments, through the grace of the Spirit; these they have much corrupted with the defilements of their own satisfactions.

units.la: XLV. Mirabile vero, quod Apostolis pœnarum imponendarum potestatem datam concludant, illis verbis, quicunque ligaveris in terra &c. quasi, ligare, sit certum pœnarum canonem singulis definire; quod sacerdotes ipsorum non nisi in absolutione faciunt. Atque ita iidem simul ligabuntur & absolventur. Quæ mirifica explicatio est. Nec tandem in veteri Ecclesia plus præsidii habent, in qua pœnas canonicas, sed Ecclesiæ, non Deo, præstandas, obtinuisse fatemur. Ut satisfacere ibi nihil aliud fuerit, quam Ecclesiæ pœnitentiam suam approbare, eique de scandalo satisfacere.
units.tr: XLV. It is remarkable indeed that they conclude that the power of imposing penalties was given to the Apostles by those words, "whatever you bind on earth," etc., as if "to bind" meant to fix a definite canon of penalties for each sin, which their priests do only in absolution. And so the same men are bound and absolved at the same time. What a wonderful explanation! Nor do they have any more support in the ancient Church, in which, we admit, canonical penances were in force, but they were to be performed to the Church, not to God. So to satisfy there was nothing other than to approve one's repentance to the Church and to make satisfaction to it for the scandal.

units.la: XLVI. viii. Sed paulo prestius agendum est de eorum indulgentiis, omnique isto mercimonio, quo ne nunc quidem, in tanta Euangelii luce, abstinent; meris fucis ac mendaciis Christianum populum pascentes, ac cœlum, Deumque ipsum, isti suo commercio ac quæstui obnoxium facientes; quo uberiores prædas agant, ditibusque istis spoliis regnum suum fundent: quas fraudes tamen sacrorum involucris tegere, & vulgi oculis subducere sese posse putant.
units.tr: XLVI. viii. But we must now deal a little more carefully with their indulgences and all that trade, from which they do not abstain even now, in such a great light of the Gospel. They feed the Christian people with mere pretences and lies, and make heaven and God himself subject to their commerce and gain, so that they may make richer booty and enrich their kingdom with these spoils. Yet they think they can cover these frauds with the veils of sacred things and withdraw them from the eyes of the common people.

units.la: XLVII. Ortus earum recens est, nec ante annum 1100 aut 1095 publicus eorum usus constat. Cum enim in veteri Ecclesia, sub rigida illorum temporum disciplina, sæpe pœnarum canonicarum veniasac remissiones dari contingeret: atque, vel ingruente nova tempestate, quæ fideles omnes intra Ecclesiæ castra colligi juberet, vel in ultimo vitæ limite, vel denique ad martyrum deprecationem, lapsis nonnunquam, ante peractum pœnitentiæ tempus, Ecclesiasticæ pacis postliminium concederetur: translatum id deinde ad pœnas divinas, & à foro Ecclesiæ ad Dei judicium immanis transitus factus fuit. Primusque pœnarum istarum remissiones vel relaxationes promulgavit Urbanus secundus, iis, qui, ultra mare, ad bellum sacrum proficiscerentur, peccatorum expiatione promissa. Quo exemplo & aliis de causis istæ veniæ subinde à Pontificibus concessæ; sive ad Reges Romanæ Ecclesiæ minus obsequentes opprimendos, istoque auctoramento, seu subjectos, seu alios quoscunque in eos armandos; sive ad pecunias conficiendas, novisque prædis exhaustum rarium rursus ditandum. Quod tanta tandem rapacitate factum est, ut superiori sæculo, anno decimo septimo, prima reformandæ Ecclesiæ occasio & necessitas hinc enata sit: Zuinglio Lutheroque venales iistos indulgentiarum fumos, & Pontificias bullas, ad Euangelii lucem explorantibus; itaque auspicio & reliqua pseudo-Ecclesiæ illius ulcera, obscœnasque partes, nudantibus & universo orbi ostendentibus. Asserere nihilominus ausi sunt Patres Tridentini, potestatem tales venias largiendi à Christo Ecclesiæ concessam; & antiquissimis temporibus ab illa usurpatam; adeoque & nunc in ea agnosci debere: quod sub Anathematis poena sanciverunt.
units.tr: XLVII. Origin of these is recent, and their public use is documented no earlier than the year 1100 or 1095. For in the ancient Church, under the strict discipline of those times, it often happened that remissions and pardons of canonical penances were granted: either when a new storm was raging that bade all the faithful be gathered within the camp of the Church, or at the final limit of life, or finally at the entreaty of martyrs, the return to ecclesiastical peace was sometimes granted to the lapsed before the time of repentance was completed. Then this was transferred to divine punishments, and a vast transition was made from the forum of the Church to the judgment of God. Urban II was the first to proclaim remissions or relaxations of these penalties, with the expiation of sins promised to those who set out overseas for the holy war. By this example, and for other reasons, such pardons were from time to time granted by the Pontiffs: either to crush kings less obedient to the Roman Church, and by this authority to arm either subjects or others against them; or to raise money and enrich the treasury again, drained by new plunders. This was done with such great rapacity that in the last century, in the year 1517, the first occasion and need of reforming the Church arose from it. Zwingli and Luther examined those venal fumes of indulgences and the Papal bulls in the light of the Gospel, and with that signal they also uncovered the remaining ulcers and obscene parts of that pseudo-Church and showed them to the whole world. Nevertheless the Fathers of Trent dared to assert that the power of granting such pardons was given to the Church by Christ and was used by her from the most ancient times, and so must still be acknowledged in her; this they enacted under penalty of anathema.

units.la: XLVIII. Naturam earum definiunt, quod sint remissiones poenarum post sacramentum poenitentiæ superstitum, & à peccatore lucendarum. Quas poenas, non humanas, vel Ecclesiasticas (ut olim) sed divinas esse volunt; quatenus earum rei sumus in foro poenitentiario. Quod valde perplexum est, quomodo poena à sacerdote impositu divina dici; vel, si divina sit, ab homine temperari vel remitti possit.
units.tr: XLVIII. They define their nature as remissions of penalties which remain after the sacrament of penance, and which are to be paid by the sinner. They want these penalties to be not human or ecclesiastical (as formerly) but divine, insofar as we are debtors of them in the penitential forum. This is very confused: how can a penalty imposed by a priest be called divine? Or, if it is divine, how can it be moderated or remitted by a man?

units.la: XLIX. Materiam illarum constituunt inexhaustum Ecclesiæ fontem, ac thesaurum; qui superfluis Christi, ac Sanctorum meritis, constat. Nam vel unicam sanguinis Christi guttam mille mundis redimendis sufficere dixit Clemens VI.
units.tr: XLIX. They constitute the matter of these as an inexhaustible fountain and treasury of the Church, which consists of the superfluous merits of Christ and the saints. For Clement VI said that a single drop of Christ's blood was enough to redeem a thousand worlds.

units.la: L. Hujus autem thesauri administrationem Pontifici concedunt, & sub eo legato ejus; partimque etiam Archiepiscopis, ac Episcopis, in suâ diœcesi: non autem aliis, qui infra istum gradum sunt. Et sub rationabili causa distribui debere ajunt; quo honesto verbo avaritiam suam tegunt. Auro enim & argento vilissimæ istæ merces prostant, quibus, loco pretiosi agni sanguinis, nunc fidelium animas videl. redimunt. In recipiente autem simpliciter requirunt, ut in statu gratiæ sit; qui cum ipsis valde incertus sit, hinc omnis quoque indulgentiarum fructus pariter incertus est.
units.tr: L. They grant the administration of this treasury to the Pope, and under him to his legate; and partly also to archbishops and bishops in their own dioceses, but not to others who are below that rank. They say it ought to be distributed for a reasonable cause, a respectable word under which they hide their avarice. For these most vile wares are sold for gold and silver, by which, instead of the precious blood of the Lamb, they now redeem the souls of the faithful. In the recipient, however, they simply require that he be in a state of grace; and since this is very uncertain to them, the whole fruit of indulgences is equally uncertain.

units.la: LI. Varia autem mensura illas distribuunt. Aliæ enim perpetuæ sunt, quæ certo quodam anni tempore recurrunt; aliæ temporales, quæ semel duntaxat singulari quadam occasione erogantur. Sunt quædam plenariæ; quas in plenas, plenióres, & plenissimas, distinguunt; quibus Jubilæorum suorum auspicia consecrare solent: quædam partiales; quæ vel secundum certas peccatorum partes aut species, vel certa tempora, sive dies, quo quadragenæ ipsorum pertinent, sive annos, vel annorum denique millia, erogantur; quem calculum persequi nunc non luber.
units.tr: LI. They distribute these indulgences by various measures. Some are perpetual, recurring at a fixed time of the year; others are temporal, granted only once on a particular occasion. Some are plenary, which they divide into full, fuller and fullest, and with which they are accustomed to inaugurate their jubilees. Others are partial, granted either for certain parts or kinds of sins, or for certain times, whether days (which they reckon by forties), years, or even thousands of years. I do not wish to pursue this calculation now.

units.la: LII. Nectunt autem & ipsi varias quæstiones, & difficultates. An damnatis in inferno ulla ex parte prosint? An laborantibus in purgatorio? Et an purgatorium Romani Pontificis indulgentia evacuari aliquando possit? Ad quae respondere non aeque in promtu habent. Quae nos praetermittimus, atque Pontificiis istis bullis, & veniae codicillis, haec in genere opponimus.
units.tr: LII. They also raise various questions and difficulties. Do indulgences benefit the damned in hell in any way? Do they benefit those suffering in purgatory? Can the indulgence of the Roman Pontiff ever be rendered void in purgatory? The Papists do not have ready answers to these. We pass these by, and against those Papist bulls and pardon-slips we offer the following points in general.

units.la: LIII. 1. Falsum esse fundamentum, condonata culpa nondum poenae omni satisfactum; sed pro poena temporali fideli adhuc luendum. 2. Laborat & altera hypothesis: in Christi satisfactione esse quid superfluum, multumque de sanguine ejus superabundare; quod, ne pereat, in Ecclesiae thesaurum veniat, & a Pontifice erogetur. Manifestum enim est, pretium redemptionis nostrae infinitum esse debuisse; quod in partes divisi, atque ex eo aliquid tanquam superfluum abscindi non potest. Unde Scriptura communiter sanguini Christi redemptionem nostram tribuit; qui universus vel unico peccato expiando profundendus erat. Cum non aliter justitia ac sanctitas Dei ostendi potuerit. Et mirum cum sanguinis Christi pretium adeo extollant, non aeque illum pro poena temporali, ac aeterna, pro nobis valere. 3. Gravior error est, quod sanguinem Sanctorum sanguini Christi admiscent; quem tamen noxis hominum expiandis non sufficientem solum, sed & superabundantem modo praedicarunt. Ac mirum est, nisi & peccudum sanguine, & sacrificiorum apparatu, istum Sanctorum sanguinem significatum dicant; quod tamen veteris Ecclesiae fides ignoravit. 4. Et qua fronte sub Novo Testam. remissiones semiplenas & partiales introducunt? quo uberior ipsis quaestus sit; quasi nondum plena foret redemptio, atque adhuc ulla peccatorum accusatio, post fusum Christi sanguinem, locum habere posset, nec sanguis Jesu Christi nos redimeret ab omni peccato. 1. Joh. 1:7. 5. Ut de annorum centuriis & chiliadibus, quo venias suas extendere solent, sileam. Quae manifesto produnt, haec indulgentias non nisi corruptelas veteris Ecclesiae institutI esse; ubi istae Canonicarum poenarum mensurae pro delicti gravitate ac modo erant. Quod insulse ad poenas Deo debitas transferunt. Quasi poenae istae Canonicae rationem satisfactionum apud Deum haberent; vel a toto annorum poenis coram Deo liberaretur, qui pro illis apud homines satisfecisset.
units.tr: LIII. 1. The foundation is false: that once guilt is forgiven, not all punishment has yet been satisfied, but the faithful must still pay for temporal punishment. 2. A second hypothesis is also flawed: that there is something superfluous in Christ's satisfaction, and that his blood overflows, so that it would be wasted unless it came into the treasury of the Church and were dispensed by the Pope. For it is plain that the price of our redemption had to be infinite, and what is infinite, divided into parts, cannot have anything cut off from it as superfluous. Hence Scripture commonly ascribes our redemption to the blood of Christ, which had to be poured out in full to expiate even a single sin; otherwise the justice and holiness of God could not have been displayed. And it is strange that, while they extol the price of Christ's blood so highly, they do not equally allow that it avails for us as much for temporal punishment as for eternal. 3. A graver error is that they mingle the blood of the saints with the blood of Christ, and have declared it not merely sufficient but even superabundant for expiating men's offences. It is strange too, unless they say that this blood of the saints was signified by the blood of beasts and the apparatus of sacrifices, which the faith of the ancient Church did not know. 4. And with what effrontery do they introduce half-plenary and partial remissions under the New Testament? They do so for the sake of richer profit, as if redemption were not yet complete, and as if any accusation of sins could still have a place after the shedding of Christ's blood, and the blood of Jesus Christ does not cleanse us from all sin. 1 John 1:7. 5. I say nothing of the centuries and thousands of years by which they are accustomed to extend their pardons. These things clearly show that such indulgences are nothing but corruptions of the institution of the ancient Church, where these measures were canonical penalties, proportioned to the gravity and manner of the offence. The Papists foolishly transfer these to the penalties owed to God, as if those canonical penalties had the character of satisfactions before God, or as if someone who had satisfied for them before men were freed before God from the penalties of a whole year.

units.la: LIV. Alienae autem sunt, quae ex Scripturis pro nugis hisce adferunt. Ubi enim Apostolus se fe reliquias afflictionum Christi, pro corpore ipsius, Ecclesia, in carne sua, explere asserit, Col. 1:24. suam istam afflictionum, pro Christo ferendarum, partem intelligit; quæ omnis in Ecclesiæ bonum cederet; quam non prædicatione solum, sed & exemplo, quin & sanguine suo, cunctisque dirisac insuavibus patiendis ædificare deberet. Nihil vero ad Christi merita minuenda, quæ sanctorum nimirum supplemento opus habent, hæc faciunt. Similiter, ubi incestuoso, ne nimio luctu contabesceret, Ecclesiæ pacem à Corinthiis tribui vult, 2. Cor. 2. non illud poenarum coram Deo moderamen, sed peccatoris, qui Ecclesiæ de scandalo satisfecerat, in gratiam receptionem, significat. Denique, cum fideles omnes, ut aliorum onera ferant, monet, Gal. 6: 2. non de indulgentiis dandis, vel de mutuo meritorum commercio, aut de operibus communicandis; sed de proximi defectibus tolerandis & corrigendis agit; quo pacto impleri legem Christi dicit; quod in merita, vel indulgentias non cadit; quæ voluntaria, ac supra legem, sunt.
units.tr: LIV. The passages they bring from Scripture to support these trifles are foreign to it. Where the Apostle asserts that he fills up in his flesh the remnants of Christ's afflictions, for his body, the Church, Col. 1:24, he means his own share of afflictions borne for Christ, all of which would tend to the good of the Church, and which he ought to build up not only by preaching but also by example, indeed by his own blood, and by enduring every harsh and unpleasant thing. These words do nothing to diminish Christ's merits, which do indeed need, it seems, a supplement from the saints. Similarly, where he wishes the Corinthians to grant peace to the incestuous man, lest he be consumed by excessive grief, 2 Cor. 2, he signifies not a moderation of penalties before God, but the reception of the sinner back into favour, who had made satisfaction to the Church for the scandal. Finally, when he bids all the faithful bear one another's burdens, Gal. 6:2, he is not speaking of granting indulgences, or of a mutual commerce of merits, or of sharing works; he is speaking of bearing with and correcting a neighbour's failings. By doing this, he says, the law of Christ is fulfilled, and this does not fall under merits or indulgences, which are voluntary and go beyond the law.

units.la: LV. Multum etiam Judæi resipiscentiæ imputant, ac præcipuam peccati expiationem ei tribuunt: sed naturam ejus plerunque corrumpunt, & in externis fere castigationibus eam constituunt. Levia peccata confessione, gravia castigationibus, ac mortis denique supplicio, expiari statuentes. Quæ à legis sensu aliena sunt. Juxta quam olim resipiscentia in vera contritione, confessione, & peccatorum per sacrificia expiatione, consistebat: quæ in expiatione annua videre est: additis, in gravioribus noxis, etiam poenis externis, præcipuè flagellatione & morte. Quæ Judæi nunc confundunt.
units.tr: LV. The Jews also attribute much to repentance, and ascribe to it the chief expiation of sin, but they usually corrupt its nature and place it mostly in external chastisements. They hold that light sins are expiated by confession, grave ones by chastisements, and finally the most serious by the punishment of death. These views are foreign to the sense of the law. According to the law, repentance once consisted in true contrition, confession, and the expiation of sins by sacrifices, as can be seen in the annual atonement; in graver offences external penalties were added, especially flogging and death. The Jews now confuse these things.

units.la: LVI. Errant & Socinians; cum poenitentiam, non legis, sed Evangelii præceptum esse ajunt. Quasi sub Vet. Test. & promissione, nullus poenitentiæ ac veniæ locus, nec ulla salutis spes superfuerit. Sed & omnibus, vere poenitentibus, veniam patere negant; ac in extrema vitæ linea resipiscentibus cœlum addicere verentur. Quod ex corrupto illo de justitia nostra dogmate est; quasi illa in factis consistat; quæ ubi oftendi non possunt, nulla tum salutis spes superfit. Cum non opera nostra, sed Christus nostra justitia sit, qui nunquam peccatorem poenitentem, ab amplexu suo arcet, & vel extremo tantum halitu testatam poenitentiam accipit: cum omnis vera poenitentia ad vitam sit, nec ulla frustra esse possit. Ergo etiam gentibus Deus dedit resipiscentiam ad vitam. Act. 11: 18. Improbus cum convertetur ab omnibus peccatis suis — vivendo vivet, non morietur. Ezech. 18: 21. Beati esurientes & sitientes justitiam; quia ipsi saturabuntur. Matth. 5: 6. Nam idcirco etiam mortuis Evangelizatum est, ut damnarentur quidem secundum homines, carne; vivant autem secundum Deum, Spiritu. 1. Pet. 4:6. Dixitque Jesu, Domine, memento mei, cum veneris in regnum tuum. Tum dixit ei Jesus, Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23:42,43.
units.tr: LVI. The Socinians also err, when they say that repentance is a precept of the Gospel and not of the law, as if under the Old Testament and its promise there was no place for repentance and pardon, and no hope of salvation remained. They also deny that pardon lies open to all who truly repent, and they shrink from assigning heaven to those who repent at the very end of life. This comes from that corrupt dogma about our righteousness, as if it consisted in deeds; where deeds cannot be shown, no hope of salvation then remains. But our righteousness is not our works but Christ, who never keeps a penitent sinner from his embrace, and accepts repentance attested even by a final breath, since all true repentance is unto life and none can be in vain. So God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles. Acts 11:18. The wicked man, when he turns from all his sins... by living he shall live, he shall not die. Ezek. 18:21. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. Matt. 5:6. For this reason the gospel was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit. 1 Pet. 4:6. And Jesus said, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom." Then Jesus said to him, "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise." Luke 23:42, 43.

units.la: LVII. Aberrant denique & Remonstrantes: qui, ut hominem de statu gratiæ ïxpe relabi ajunt, ita eundem per liberum arbitrium, gratiamque sufficientem, sese semper restituere posse docent. Quod contra Apostolum est. Impossibile enim est, eos, qui semel illuminati sunt, & ceciderint; rursus renovare ad resipiscentiam. Hebr. 6:4,5,6. Voluntarie enim peccantibus nobis post acceptam cognitionem veritatis, non amplius pro peccato relinquitur hostia. Hebr. 10:26.
units.tr: LVII. Finally, the Remonstrants also go astray. While they say that a man often falls back from the state of grace, they teach that the same man can always restore himself by free will and sufficient grace. This is contrary to the Apostle: It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance. Heb. 6:4, 5, 6. For if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. Heb. 10:26.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS DE Consummatione beneficiorum Christi.
units.tr: Fortieth Head: On the Consummation of Christ's Benefits.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: Chapter X.

units.la: De Glorificatione hujus vitæ: ubi de Perseverantia sanctorum, & certitudine salutis.
units.tr: On the Glorification of this life: where the perseverance of the saints and the certainty of salvation are treated.

units.la: I. Sequitur, post sanctificationem, diversasque ejus partes, tandem ultimo loco Glorificatio: quæ hominis à miseria, omnique peccati pœna, liberationem, æternamque ejus felicitatem ac beatitudinem dicit. Quæ, respectu termini à quo, redemtio; respectu termini ad quem, beatificatio, vita æterna, gloria, regnum Domini, & Christi, & hereditas immortalis, aliisque nominibus, in Scriptura appellatur. Qui factus nobis est — redemtio.
units.tr: I. After sanctification and its several parts, glorification comes last. It denotes the deliverance of man from misery and from every penalty of sin, and his eternal happiness and blessedness. With respect to its starting point it is called redemption; with respect to its goal it is called beatification, eternal life, glory, the kingdom of the Lord and of Christ, and an imperishable inheritance, and Scripture gives it other names as well. Who was made to us … redemption.

units.la: 1. Cor. 1:30. Qui est arrhabo hereditatis nostræ, ad obtinendam redemtionem, ad laudem gloriæ ipsius. Eph. 1:14. Qui benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali, in cœlestibus, in Christo. Eph. 1:3. Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam. Joh. 3:36. Qui regeneravit nos — ad hereditatem incorruptibilem, & non contaminatam, & non marcescentem. 1. Pet. 1:4. Sic enim copiose suppeditabitur vobis introitus in æternum
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1:30. Who is the pledge of our inheritance, for obtaining the redemption, to the praise of his glory. Eph. 1:14. Who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. Eph. 1:3. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. John 3:36. Who has begotten us again … to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fades not away. 1 Pet. 1:4. For so an entrance into the eternal kingdom will be richly supplied to you.

units.la: Consummatio beneficiorum Christi est in GLORIFICATIONE num regnum Domini nostri, & Salvatoris Jesu Christi. 2. Petr. 1:11.
units.tr: The consummation of Christ's benefits lies in GLORIFICATION, the kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. 2 Pet. 1:11.

units.la: II. Est autem illa duplex; vel inchoata, hujus vitæ; vel perfecta, futuræ.
units.tr: II. This glorification is twofold: either begun, in this life, or perfected, in the life to come.

units.la: III. Ad hanc vitam pertinent, sensus amoris Dei in Christo. Charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris, per Spiritum S. Rom. 5: 5. spes gloriæ certa & secura. In qua, gratia, stamus, & gloriamur in spe gloriæ Dei. Rom. 5:2. perseverantia & salutis certitudo. Nullares poterit nos separare a dilectione Dei, quæ est in Jesu Christo, Domino nostro. Rom. 8:38, 39. atque hinc enascens consolatio, pax, gaudium ineffabile. In quem credentes, exultatis gaudio ineffabili & glorioso. 1. Petr. 1: 8. Gaudete potius, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis. Luc. 10: 20. spiritualium denique donorum copia & abundantia. Ut consolationem accipiant eorum corda, ipsis charitate compactis, & omni opulentia plene certiorata intelligentia, ad cognitionem mysterii Dei ac Patris Christi. Col. 2:2. Et quotidiana benevolentiæ divinæ experientia, ac gustus. Quas gloriæ primitias, plenæque messis spem ac obsidem, fideles jam possident. Sed & ipsi gemimus, qui primitias Spiritus habemus. Rom. 8:23. Nos de perseverantia sanctorum & salutis certitudine; quas plereque extra Ecclesiam sectæ hodie calumniantur & carpunt, speciatim agemus.
units.tr: III. To this present life belong the sense of God's love in Christ. The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Rom. 5:5. The sure and certain hope of glory. Through whom we stand in grace, and rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. Rom. 5:2. Perseverance and the certainty of salvation. Nothing shall separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Rom. 8:38, 39. And from these arise consolation, peace, and joy unspeakable. Believing in him, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 Pet. 1:8. Rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven. Luke 10:20. Finally, an abundance and fullness of spiritual gifts. That their hearts may be comforted, being knit together in love, and in all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery of God and of the Father and of Christ. Col. 2:2. And the daily experience and taste of the divine goodwill. The faithful already possess these, as the firstfruits of glory and the pledge and earnest of the full harvest. Yet we ourselves groan, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit. Rom. 8:23. We shall treat in particular of the perseverance of the saints and the certainty of salvation, which the many sects outside the Church today slander and carp at.

units.la: IV. Ut Pontificios omittam, qui Concilio Trid. Sess. 6. Can. 13. sanctio-hanc Sanctorum ipsem proscripserunt: præcipua de hoc articulo cum Remonstrantibus nobis lis est. Qui, utcunque artic. 5. de fidelium perseverantia ambigere solum, & tantum de modo ejus plenius erudiri velle videbantur; tamen cum fundamentum ejus præcipuum in homine ponerent; quem perseveraturum, modo ad certamen perpetuo paratus sit, Dei auxilium imploret, & ipse officio non defit, confitebantur; necessario incertam eam esse, hominemque, utcunque adgubernante Spiritu, prolabi tamen, & propria socordia deficere posse, dicere cogebantur. Et certe hic articulus necessario ex prioribus sequebatur; quod & ipsi deinceps viderunt adversarii. In medio tamen relinquebant, an non circa quosdam fideles perseverantia indefectibilis, ex speciali gratia, locum haberet.
units.tr: IV. Leaving aside the Papists, who in Session 6, Canon 13, of the Council of Trent themselves condemned this doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, our chief dispute on this article is with the Remonstrants. Although they seemed to doubt only article 5 concerning the perseverance of the faithful, and to wish to be more fully instructed about its manner, nevertheless, since they placed its principal foundation in man, they were compelled to say that it is necessarily uncertain: that a man who, provided he is always prepared for the struggle and implores God's help, and does not himself fail in his duty, will persevere, may nonetheless slip, and fall through his own sloth, even though the Spirit guides him. Indeed this article necessarily followed from their earlier ones, as the adversaries themselves later saw. Yet they left open the question whether indefectible perseverance might not hold good for certain of the faithful by special grace.

units.la: V. Quærebatur etiam de perseverantiæ principio & fundamento. Quod illi præcipue in homine, bonorumque; habituum firmitudine ponebant; nec recte donum Dei dici ferebant. Cum Scriptura illam ad fidem, & semen Dei in regenitis manens potius referat. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, Deo, peccatum non facit. Nam semen ejus in eo manet. Et non potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est. 1. Joh. 3: 9. Ut duplex ejus principium sit: partim externum, perpetua Dei custodia; partim internum, vitae spiritualis natura, atque immortale semen, fidelium cordibus inditum.
units.tr: V. They also disputed the principle and foundation of perseverance. They placed it chiefly in man and in the firmness of his good habits, and they did not rightly call it a gift of God, since Scripture rather traces it to faith and to the seed of God remaining in the regenerate. Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, for his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. 1 John 3:9. Its principle is therefore twofold: partly external, the constant keeping of God; partly internal, the nature of the spiritual life and the immortal seed implanted in the hearts of believers.

units.la: VI. Erroris hujus consectarium erat: quod, ut gratiam amitti posse, ita ex gravissimis lapsibus, & quolibetcunque peccato, ad gratiam reditum patere asserebant; libero arbitrio ad utrumque aeque valido. Quod cum Apostolo adversaretur; qui voluntarie peccantibus, atque mala lubidine, a gratia prolabentibus, omnem salutis aditum denegabat, Hebr. 10: 26. coll. 6: 4. illi, non de impossibilitate renovationis, sed de difficultate illud intelligebant.
units.tr: VI. A consequence of this error was that they asserted that grace can be lost, and that from the gravest falls, and from any sin whatever, a return to grace lies open, with free will equally capable of both. This is contrary to the Apostle, who denied every way of salvation to those who sin wilfully and fall away from grace through evil lust. Heb. 10:26, compared with 6:4. They understood that passage not of the impossibility of renewal but of its difficulty.

units.la: VII. Erat vero quaestio de perseverantia omnino duplex: 1. an detur fidelium apostasia totalis? 2. an etiam finalis? prius Augustinus interdum admittere videtur; ut & hodie Lutherani; qui tamen finalem negant. Nos vero & totalem finalem apostasiam negamus.
units.tr: VII. The question about perseverance is in fact twofold: 1. Is there a total apostasy of believers? 2. Is there also a final apostasy? Augustine sometimes seems to admit the first, as do the Lutherans today, though they deny the second. We deny both total and final apostasy.

units.la: VIII. Ubi praemittendum: 1. per Sanctos nos intelligere, non externum fidelium coetum & Ecclesiam; cujus apostasiam, tum in Vet. tum in Nov. T. contra Judaeos & Pontificios extra dubium ponimus; sed personas singulares. 2. eosque non quocunque modo Spiritus S. participes: sed vere sanctos, per Christum redemptos, & ad Deum conversos. 3. Quos, non quidem labi, & peccatorum blanditiis abduci, quin & graviter lapsare posse, negamus; sed in totum prolabi, omnemque Spiritus fomitem extinguere, & a divina gratia prorsus exulare posse, pernegamus.
units.tr: VIII. Here the following must be premised: 1. By the saints we mean not the external assembly of believers and the Church, whose apostasy, both in the Old and the New Testament, we place beyond doubt against the Jews and the Papists, but individual persons. 2. And these are not partakers of the Holy Spirit in any way whatever, but truly holy people, redeemed by Christ and converted to God. 3. We deny that such persons, though they may indeed slip and be led away by the allurements of sin, and may fall grievously, can fall away altogether, extinguish every spark of the Spirit, and be utterly cast out from divine grace; this we flatly deny.

units.la: IX. Quae Novi Foederis prae primigenio operum foedere praerogativa est; quod tantam gratiae vim atque copiam habeat comitem, ut fideles non solum perseverare possint, ut olim; sed per eam quoque certo perseveraturi sint. Quod nihil aliud est, quam τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως μέχρι τέλους βεβαίαν κατασχεῖν initium fiduciae usque ad finem firmum retinere. Hebr. 3: 14. Quae est ipsa perseverantiae descriptio. Haec vero, licet sub omni Foederis gratiae oeconomia obtinuerit, nunc tamen maxime sub Novo Test. locum habet; ubi novum obtinet foedus, quod ἀμεταπτωτον est; ut non sit defector populus, qualis sub Vet. Test. fuerat. Jer. 31: 31--33. Hebr. 8: 7--10.
units.tr: IX. The prerogative of the New Covenant over the original covenant of works is that it has such a measure and abundance of grace attending it that believers are not only able to persevere, as before, but by it are also certain to persevere. This is nothing other than to hold the beginning of confidence firm to the end [τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως μέχρι τέλους βεβαίαν κατασχεῖν]. Heb. 3:14. This is the very description of perseverance. Although this has held under every economy of the covenant of grace, it applies most of all under the New Testament, where the new covenant is unchangeable [ἀμεταπτωτον], so that the people do not fall away as they did under the Old Testament. Jer. 31:31–33. Heb. 8:7–10.

units.la: X. Fundamenta ac argumenta hujus perseverantiae sunt sequentia: 1. Consilii Dei immutabilitas: ex quo Apostolus per gradus ad ipsum tandem gloriae culmen ascendit. Rom. 8: 29, 30. Quos praenovit, etiam prae-
units.tr: X. The foundations and arguments of this perseverance are as follows: 1. The immutability of God's purpose, from which the Apostle ascends by steps to the very summit of glory. Rom. 8:29, 30. Whom he foreknew, he also predestined

units.la: Perseverantia sanctorum fundamenta. prædefinivit — Quos prædefinivit, eos etiam vocavit: & quos vocavit, eos etiam justificavit : quos autem justificavit, eos etiam glorificavit. 2. Fœderis gratiæ, ac pacti divini certitudo. Quo Christo certum semen, & certa hæreditas promissa est. Videbit semen, quod prolongabit dies. Esai. 53: 10 Omne, quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Joh. 6: 37. Quanto re abundantius Deus volens demonstrare hæredibus promissionis immutabilitatem consilii sui, interceßit juramento. Hebr. 6: 17. quo etiam pertinet Dei fidelitas. 1. Cor. 1: 8, 9. 3. Redemtionis, per Christum peractæ, valor ac pretium: quod, ut æternum est, ita æternam & immutabilem salutem fidelibus spondet. Amans suos, qui erant in mundo, in finem amavit eos. Joh. 13: 1. Et ipse est Salvator corporis. Eph. 5: 23. quo facit etiam fundamentum cui superstructi sunt, Matth. 16: 18. 4. Christi intercessio, & perpetua hæreditatis postulatio. Quæ preces irritæ esse non possunt. Ego oravi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Luc. 22: 32. Qui etiam pro nobis intercedit. Rom. 8: 34. Non rogo, ut tollas eos ex mundo ; sed ut serves eos a malo. Joh. 17: 15. Pater, gratias tibi ago, quod audivisti me. Ego vero sciebam quod semper me audias. Joh. 11: 41, 42. 5. Dei custodia; tum Patris: Qui custodimur potentia Dei, per fidem, ad salutem. 1. Petr. 1: 5. tum Filii: Et non peribunt oves mea in æternum, & non rapiet quis eas ex manu mea. Joh. 10: 28. tum etiam Spiritus sancti: Spiritus meus, qui est super te, & verba mea, quæ posui in ore tuo, non recedent ab ore tuo, & ab ore seminis tui. Esai. 59: 21. cujus unctionem & obsignationem Scriptura sæpe prædicat: Unctio, quam accepistis ab ipso, manet in vobis 1. Joh. 2: 27. In quo credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis sancto. Eph. 1: 13. coll. 4: 30. Qui obsignavit nos, & dedit arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: The foundations of the perseverance of the saints. predestined; and whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified. 2. The certainty of the covenant of grace and of the divine compact, in which a sure seed and a sure inheritance were promised to Christ. He shall see his seed, who shall prolong his days. Isa. 53:10. All that the Father gives me shall come to me. John 6:37. Wherein God, desiring more abundantly to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed with an oath. Heb. 6:17. To this also pertains the faithfulness of God. 1 Cor. 1:8, 9. 3. The worth and price of the redemption accomplished through Christ, which, being eternal, promises eternal and unchangeable salvation to believers. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. John 13:1. And he is the Saviour of the body. Eph. 5:23. In this he also supplies the foundation on which they are built. Matt. 16:18. 4. The intercession of Christ and his perpetual request for the inheritance. These prayers cannot be in vain. I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. Luke 22:32. Who also intercedes for us. Rom. 8:34. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil. John 17:15. Father, I thank you that you have heard me. And I knew that you always hear me. John 11:41, 42. 5. The keeping of God: of the Father: who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation. 1 Pet. 1:5. Of the Son: and my sheep shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. John 10:28. Also of the Holy Spirit: My Spirit, which is upon you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your seed. Isa. 59:21. Scripture often proclaims his anointing and sealing. The anointing which you have received from him abides in you. 1 John 2:27. In whom, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise. Eph. 1:13, compared with 4:30. Who has sealed us and given us the Spirit as a pledge in our hearts.

units.la: 2. Cor. 1: 22. 6. Ad quam custodiam divinitatis externam accedit & internum novæ vitæ principium, & perennis gratiæ fons; quem exarescere impossibile est. Fons aquæ, salientis in vitam æternam. Joh. 4: 14. Nec de fonte illo gustarunt unquam, sed contentim præterierunt, qui Jer. 2: 13. reliquisse dicuntur fontem aquæ vivæ. Ac facit huc quoque immortale illud semen, quod, cœlesti manu cordibus insitum, otiosum manere, vel computrescere non potest. Quisquis natus est ex Deo; peccato non dat operam: quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet: nec potest peccare, eo quod ex Deo natus est. 1. Joh. 3: 9. Ubi insulse excipiunt, regenitum deficere non posse, quandiu semen illud in ipso manet. Ac si dicant, non posse illum peccare, quandiu non peccat. Quod tenue valde est, & æque in irregenitos competit. Unde etiam regeniti se ipsos custodiunt. Novimus, quod omnis natus ex Deo non peccat. Sed qui natus est ex Deo, servat seipsum, & malus non ledit, vel tangit ipsum. 1. Joh. 5: 18. 7. Quibus omnibus addebant orthodoxi, & ipsos fideles quotidianis precibus perseverantiam à Deo poscere. Ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos a malo. Matth. 6: 13. Ut constet, Deum eam dare & posse,& solere, ne lusoriæ illæ preces sestimentur. Unde omnimodo fidelium patet perseverantia, atque impossibile est, eos quacunque tentatione prorsus superari, vel in totum deficere posse. Ut seducerent, si possibile esset, etiam electos. Matth. 24: 24. Electos ergo, cum divina manu sustententur, vel maximis certaminibus exercitos, excidere impossibile est; cum pulchriores longe resurgant ac enitescant. Oportet enim etiam hæreses inter vos esse, ut probi manifesti fiant in vobis. 1. Cor. 11: 19.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 1:22. 6. To this external guard of the divine nature there is added an internal principle of new life and a perpetual fountain of grace, which cannot dry up. A fountain of water springing up into eternal life. John 4:14. Those who are said to have forsaken the fountain of living water, Jer. 2:13, never tasted of that fountain but passed by to broken cisterns. The immortal seed, which, planted in hearts by a heavenly hand, cannot remain idle or rot. 1 John 3:9 also belongs here: Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, for his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. Here they foolishly object that the regenerate cannot fall away as long as that seed remains in them, as if to say that he cannot sin as long as he does not sin. This is very weak, and it applies equally to the unregenerate. Hence the regenerate also keep themselves: We know that everyone born of God does not sin, but he who was born of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not harm him or touch him. 1 John 5:18. 7. To all this the orthodox add that the believers themselves daily ask God for perseverance: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Matt. 6:13. It is thus clear that God gives and is able and accustomed to give this perseverance, so that these prayers are not regarded as idle play. Therefore the perseverance of the faithful stands firm in every way, and it is impossible that they should be wholly overcome by any temptation or fail altogether. So as to lead astray, if it were possible, even the elect. Matt. 24:24. Therefore, since the elect are upheld by the divine hand and tried by the greatest struggles, it is impossible for them to fall away, since they rise again far more beautiful and shine forth more brightly. For there must also be factions among you, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you. 1 Cor. 11:19.

units.la: XI. Superest, ut ad præcipuas quasdam difficultates & objectiones adversariorum breviter respondeamus.
units.tr: XI. It remains that we briefly answer certain principal difficulties and objections of our opponents.

units.la: Ac primum quidem exemplis nihil proficiunt: cum si qui à fide defecerunt, vel hoc solo argumento nunquam veri fideles fuisse deprehendantur. A nobis exierunt, sed non erant ex nobis. 1. Joh. 2: 19. Qui enim habet, dabitur ipsi. Qui autem non habet, etiam quod habet, tolletur ab ipso. Matth. 13: 12. conf. Luc. 8: 18. Neque 1. Tim. 1: 19. verba περὶ τὴν πίςιν ἐναυάγησαν, reddenda, fidei naufragium fecerunt, quasi fidem habuissent & perdidissent; sed circa fidem naufragium fecerunt: quia nempe ad eam non pervenerunt.
units.tr: First, they gain nothing from examples, since those who have fallen away from the faith are shown, by this very fact alone, never to have been true believers. They went out from us, but they were not of us. 1 John 2:19. For whoever has, to him more will be given; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken from him. Matt. 13:12; cf. Luke 8:18. Nor should the words of 1 Tim. 1:19, περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἐναυάγησαν, be rendered they made shipwreck of the faith, as if they had had faith and lost it; rather, they made shipwreck concerning the faith [περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἐναυάγησαν], because they never attained to it.

units.la: XII. Adducunt 2. loca quædam, ubi mentio fit deletionis e libro vita, Exod. 32: 32. Psal. 69: 29. Apoc. 22: 19. Ubi notandum, duplicem Dei librum, duplicemque in eo inscriptionem, dari. Est enim liber Ecclesiæ in terris. Est & electorum catalogus in cœlis. Et vel cœlesti manu, ac Deo auctore: vel ab hominibus, stulta persuasione, tum de se ipsis, tum de aliis, capta, in libro isto quidam scribuntur. Et hic scribet manum suam Jehova, & de nomine Israëlis se nominabit. Esai 44: 5. Ac de supernis quidem divinæ mentis tabulis ac commentariis nullus eraditur, neque illæ lituram admittunt. Nec Mosis zelus, ultra modum exuperans, & à Deo ipso castigatus ÿs 33. aliud quam insignem ejus charitatem, & divinæ gloriæ studium testabatur. Si qui autem in Ecclesia vel ab hominibus adscripti sunt, vel mentito nomine in membranas istas irrepsere, illos fidem rumpere,& Ecclesiæ semitam relinquere posse concedimus: de quibus agitur Apoc. 22: 19. Quin & integræ Ecclesiæ à Deo abdicari; atque, ob perfidiam, sueto hactenus populi Dei nomi-ne, ne, atque omni denique vitæ ipe privari possunt. Quæ illa deletio est ex viventium libro, quam Christus Psal. 69. Judæis obstinatis & incredulis interminatur.
units.tr: XII. They cite two passages where mention is made of being blotted out of the book of life, Exod. 32:32; Ps. 69:29; Rev. 22:19. Here it must be noted that there are two books of God and two kinds of entry in them. There is the book of the Church on earth, and there is the catalogue of the elect in heaven. Some are written in the one by a heavenly hand and by God as author; others are written in the other by men, captured by a foolish persuasion, both about themselves and about others. And the LORD shall write with his own hand, and shall name himself by the name of Israel. Isa. 44:5. No one is erased from the heavenly tablets and records of the divine mind, and those tablets do not admit any erasure. Nor did the zeal of Moses, which went beyond measure and was rebuked by God himself (Exod. 32:33), testify to anything other than his remarkable love and his concern for the divine glory. If some have been enrolled in the Church, whether by men or under a false name have crept into those lists, we grant that they can break faith and leave the path of the Church; of these Rev. 22:19 speaks. Indeed, whole churches can be disowned by God, and, on account of their faithlessness, they can be deprived of the name of the people of God hitherto held, and finally of every life. This is the blotting out from the book of the living with which Christ, in Ps. 69, threatens the obstinate and unbelieving Jews.

units.la: XIII. Addunt 3. Apostoli locum ad Hebr. 6: 4, 5, 6. ubi quosdam, superne illustratos, ac cœlestium participes, & non levi gratiæ gustu imbutos &c. recidere tamen posse innuit. Quem tamen locum de irregenitis agere ex Apostoli scopo patet; qui ignavis ac infructuosis Christianis hoc Dei judicium ob oculos ponit. vide ѱs 8, 9. Nec obstant præclara illa encomia, quod illuminati, ac Spir. S. participes sint; & de bono Dei verbo, ac futuri sæculi deliciis gustaverint &c. cum qualiscunque ille divinarum rerum gustus & sensus etiam in irregenitos cadat; quos aliquali lumine irradiari, & brevi gustu cœlestia delibare, ubi Christum & peccatorum remissionem audiunt; & Spiritus sancti in donis extraordinariis partipes esse; & futuri sæculi virtutes, id est, Novi Testamenti statum & gaudia, magnamque Dei potentiam, in publica mundi conversione, quodam veluti mentis visu antecapere non impossibile est. Quos ubi, post ruinam, excitari, ac denuo renovari posse, Apostolus negat. ѱs 6. non id primam eorum renovationem supponit: cum, inter alia quæ hic regeri possunt, dici queat, vocem πάλιν hic redundare. Ut alibi. vide Gal. 4: 9. πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν, quomodo convertimini iterum ad infirma & egena elementa?
units.tr: XIII. They add, third, the passage of the Apostle at Heb. 6:4–6, where he suggests that certain persons, enlightened from above and partakers of heavenly things, who have tasted the good gift and so on, can nevertheless fall away. But that this passage speaks of the unregenerate is clear from the Apostle's purpose, which sets before lazy and unfruitful Christians this judgment of God; see verses 8 and 9. Nor do those splendid commendations stand in the way, that they were enlightened, partakers of the Holy Spirit, and had tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and so on. For that kind of taste and perception of divine things also falls upon the unregenerate, who are illumined by some light and in a brief taste touch upon heavenly things, when they hear of Christ and the forgiveness of sins; and it is not impossible for them to share in the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, and to anticipate, as it were by a kind of mental vision, the powers of the age to come, that is, the state and joys of the New Testament and the great power of God in the public conversion of the world. The Apostle denies that such persons, once they have fallen, can be stirred up again and renewed again. Verse 6 does not presuppose their first renewal, since among other things which can be read here, it may be said that the word again [πάλιν] is redundant here, as elsewhere; see Gal. 4:9: How do you turn back again [πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν] to the weak and beggarly elements?

units.la: XIV. Quod porro, quarto loco, ex Propheta, Ezech. 18: 26, de justo, à justitia sua sese avertente, subjungunt, non melius concludit. Non enim de vere justis & regeneratis ibi agitur, sed de eo, qui justitias aliquas, h. e. recte dicta & facta, ob quæ laudabatur, fecerat, quique justitiis suis confidit; & Judæorum, propria justitia nitentium, tumor & hypocrisis tangitur; quamque vana ac fragilis ea sit, ostenditur. Præterquam quod locutio universa conditionalis sit; deque poenis præcipue temporalibus agat; quæ etiam in vere regenitos cadere possunt. Ita tamen, ut qualiscunque eorum declinatio vel castigatio apostasiam non arguat.
units.tr: XIV. What they further cite, in the fourth place, from the Prophet, Ezek. 18:26, concerning the righteous man who turns away from his righteousness, proves no better. For there the passage is not about those who are truly righteous and regenerate, but about one who has done certain righteous deeds, that is, things rightly said and done for which he was praised, and who trusts in his righteousness. It strikes at the pride and hypocrisy of the Jews, who relied on their own righteousness, and it shows how empty and fragile that righteousness is. Besides, the whole statement is conditional, and it deals chiefly with temporal punishments, which can also fall upon those who are truly regenerate. Yet even so, any declension or chastisement of theirs does not prove apostasy.

units.la: XV. Tandem quæstionem hanc de Sanctorum perseverantia quidam mere historicam vocant; atque eo rem deducunt, ut quærendum solum supersit, an apostasiæ Sanctorum revera exempladentur, an secus? ipsum alio quin viatoris statum non extra cadendi periculum esse. Nos autem, quanquam de viatore in se considerato non abnuimus; cum tamen Deum custodem ac ducem habet, statum ejus firmum ac indeclinabilem esse ex Scripturis adferimus. Cumque ille fideles de manu sua veluti pensiles teneat, non historiae vel experientiae, sed indubitatae certitudinis eorum perseverantia habenda est.
units.tr: XV. Finally, some call this question about the perseverance of the saints merely historical, and reduce the matter to this: the only question left is whether the apostasies of the saints really happen or not, since in any case the state of the wayfarer is not free from the danger of falling. We, however, though we do not deny that the wayfarer, considered in himself, is subject to this, nevertheless, since he has God as his guardian and leader, we show from the Scriptures that his state is firm and unchangeable. And since he holds the faithful as if suspended from his own hand, their perseverance is to be held not as a matter of history or experience, but of indubitable certainty.

units.la: XVI. 6. Quod denique ἀργὸν hunc esse λόγον, & carni adblandiri, putant; cum homini, de certaminis exitu securo, non magnopere de palma sit laborandum: id contra est; cum multa alia ad pugnandum incitamenta habeat, &, quicquid de pugnae exitu sit, non sine sudore & pulvere victoriam acquiri sciat. Ad quem ferendum nihil equidem validius est illa spe & certitudine victoriae: uti militem, qui alacri spe palmam jam praecerpsit, promtius imperatorem suum sequi videmus. Est ergo haec doctrina potius fons verae pietatis, sollicitudinis, & gratitudinis: cum media ad perseverandum ei non opponantur, sed amice cum ea socientur; ac praeterea eventus certitudo novum perseveranti stimulum adjiciat. Cum timore & tremore vestram salutem conficite. Deus enim est qui operatur in vobis & velle & operari propter beneplacitum. Phil. 2: 12, 13. Cum contraria doctrina mater sit, aut desperationis, si quis propriae imbecillitatis conscientiam habet; aut securitatis, ubi omne salutis arbitrium in potestate sua quotidie esse cernit.
units.tr: XVI. Finally, they think that this doctrine is an idle [ἀργὸν] doctrine [λόγον] and flatters the flesh, since a man who is secure about the outcome of the contest need not labour greatly for the palm. This is the opposite of the truth. He has many other incentives to fight, and he knows that, whatever the outcome of the battle, victory is won only with sweat and dust. Nothing is indeed more powerful for bearing this than that hope and certainty of victory; we see that a soldier who has already, in cheerful hope, plucked the palm follows his commander more readily. This doctrine is therefore rather a source of true piety, care, and gratitude, since the means of persevering are not set against it but are joined to it in friendship; and moreover the certainty of the outcome adds a new spur to the one who perseveres. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Phil. 2:12, 13. The contrary doctrine is the mother either of despair, if a man is aware of his own weakness, or of security, where he sees every decision about his salvation lying daily in his own power.

units.la: XVII. Certitudinem perseverantiae consequitur certitudo salutis; cum haec sine illa non detur, quoniam nemo nisi perseverans salvatur. Ut male quidam illa divellant, & salutis quidem certitudinem defendant, perseverantiae autem negent. Quod est certitudinem subjectivam asserere velle sine certitudine objectiva, ut vulgo, licet non satis recte, loquuntur; proprie enim omnis certitudo subjectiva est, cum sit attributum mentis ejusque assensus. Videndum autem 1. qualis haec salutis certitudo sit, 2. quae ejus sint fundamenta. 3. Ac denique adversariorum objectamentis est respondendum.
units.tr: XVII. Assurance of perseverance is followed by certainty of salvation, since the latter is not given without the former, for no one is saved unless he perseveres. Some people wrongly separate these, defending the certainty of salvation while denying the certainty of perseverance. That is to wish to assert subjective certainty without objective certainty, as people commonly (though not quite correctly) speak; for all certainty is properly subjective, since it is an attribute of the mind and its assent. We must consider (1) what this certainty of salvation is, (2) what its foundations are, and (3) finally, how the objections of opponents are to be answered.

units.la: XVII. Certitudinem quod attinet, illa duplex est, alia quae nititur evidenti rei perceptione vel demonstratione: quae metaphysica vulgo appellatur: alia vero quae petitur ex testimonio divino; quae fidei dicitur. Estque utraque illa rursus vel de rebus extra nos existentibus: quas nimirum vel intuitu, ubi termini sunt evidentissimi; vel scientia, ubi demonstratione opus est: vel fide, ex revelatione, cognoscimus: vel de actionibus mentis nostrae, quae experimentalis, sive conscientiae, est, nec longis argumentis opus habet.
units.tr: XVII. As for certainty, there are two kinds. One rests on the clear perception or demonstration of a thing, and is commonly called metaphysical. The other is drawn from divine testimony and is called of faith. Each of these again concerns either things existing outside us, which we know either by intuition, where the terms are most evident, or by science, where demonstration is needed, or by faith, from revelation; or it concerns the actions of our own mind, which is experimental, or of conscience, and needs no lengthy arguments.

units.la: XIX. Ac salutis certitudinem quod attinet, habent eam fideles, partim fidei; quae ex Scriptura credunt, quemcunque, qui Christo ad salutem conconfidit, remissionem peccatorum habituram; partimexperimentalem, ex proprio animi sensu & conscientia, ac impresso Spiritus arrhabone & charactere, quem intrinsecè fidelis deprehendit. Ut sicut primum subnixi divina auctoritate, per fidem credimus revelationi, ita deinceps per actum fiduciæ illam obsignamus: unde maxima tum certitudo in animum exundat. Quæ ex experimentali & fidei mista dici potest. Est autem omnis illa certitudo, ubi quis rite se exploraverit, formalis; nec falsum recipere potest.
units.tr: XIX. As for the certainty of salvation, the faithful have it partly of faith, since from Scripture they believe that whoever trusts in Christ for salvation will have the forgiveness of sins; and partly experimental, from the sense and conscience of their own mind, and from the seal and stamp of the Spirit impressed as an earnest, which the believer perceives within himself. So, just as we first, supported by divine authority, believe the revelation through faith, so afterwards we seal it through the act of trust; whence the greatest certainty overflows into the soul. This may be called a mixture of experimental and faith-certainty. Moreover, all such certainty, when a person has duly examined himself, is formal, and cannot receive what is false.

units.la: XX. Fundamenta hujus certitudinis sunt: 1. Salutis nostræ apud Deum firmitas & immutabilitas, ex fœdere ejus ac æterno gratiæ consilio. Hanc enim decreti divini firmitatem, quæ vulgo certitudo objectiva dicitur, certitudini nostræ præstrui oportet. Quos prænovit — hos etiam glorificavit. — Persuasum habeo, quod non futurum sit, quod — nos possit separare à dilectione Dei. Rom. 8:29, 30, 38, 39. 2. Fœderis gratia, promissionumque ejus natura ac stipulatio, quæ eam animi fiduciam requirunt. Noli metuere. Gen. 15:1. 3. Fidei natura, quæ assensus sui certa est. Qui credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in se ipso. 1. Joh. 5:10. conf. 2. Tim. 1:12. Unde nos ipsos explorare jubemur, an in fide simus. 2. Cor 13:5.
units.tr: XX. The foundations of this certainty are: (1) the firmness and immutability of our salvation with God, which rests on his covenant and his eternal counsel of grace. For this firmness of the divine decree, which is commonly called objective certainty, must be laid down before our certainty. Whom he foreknew, them he also glorified. I am persuaded that nothing shall separate us from the love of God. Rom. 8:29, 30, 38, 39. (2) The grace of the covenant, and the nature and stipulation of his promises, which require that trust of soul. Do not fear. Gen. 15:1. (3) The nature of faith, which is certain of its own assent. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. 1 John 5:10; compare 2 Tim. 1:12. Hence we are commanded to examine ourselves, whether we are in the faith. 2 Cor. 13:5.

units.la: XXI. Ac pertinet huc Spir. S. obsignatio, unctio, arrhabo, sigillum, character, testimonium, primitiæ. 2. Cor. 1:21, 22. Eph. 1:13, 14. 1. Cor. 2:12. Rom. 8:23. Quæ omnia, tam magnifice sonantia, inane nomen & nuda verba sunt, nisi fidelibus istam salutis certitudinem & sensum præbeant. Hæc vero omnia, vario licet respectu, fidei conveniunt. Peragitur enim hæc Spiritus obsignatio, operationibus ejus in anima, atque ipsa potissimum fide; quam dum nobis insinuat, & vivam eam ac audentem facit, isto pignore nos salutis certos reddit, atque illam à Deo restipulari jubet. Novi, cui crediderim; & persuasus sum, quod potens sit, depositum meum conservare in illam diem. 2. Tim. 1:12. Atque adeo idem est Spiritus, ac nostrum testimonium, nempe fides, nostraque super eam reflexio; quæ etiam respectu plenitudinis deinceps nobis conferendæ arrhabonis ac primitiarum nomine venit.
units.tr: XXI. To this also belong the sealing, anointing, earnest, seal, stamp, testimony, firstfruits of the Holy Spirit. 2 Cor. 1:21, 22; Eph. 1:13, 14; 1 Cor. 2:12; Rom. 8:23. All these, so grandly sounding, are an empty name and bare words unless they give the faithful this certainty and sense of salvation. Yet all of these, though in different respects, belong to faith. For this sealing of the Spirit is carried out by his operations in the soul, and above all by faith itself; and while he instils it in us and makes it living and bold, he makes us sure of salvation by this pledge, and bids us hold God to his pledge in return. I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day. 2 Tim. 1:12. And so the Spirit is in effect the same as our testimony, namely faith, and our reflection upon it; which, with respect to the fullness to be bestowed on us afterwards, comes under the name of earnest and firstfruits.

units.la: XXII. 4. Spei natura. Quæ viva appellatur; atque hominem gloriari facit. 1. Pet. 1:3. Rom. 5:2. Qualis spes cum à Deo mandata, nec ipsi indecora sit, vana & fallax esse non potest. Nisi potissimam Christianarum virtutum in vanum mentis ludibrium & somnium commutemus. Cupimus unumquemque vestrum idem præstare studium, ad plenitudinem spei, usque ad finem. Hebr. 6:11. Est autem fides eorum, quae sperantur, pollicitatio, aut repraesentatio, cap. 11:1. 5. Amoris erga Deum natura, qui sine mutui amoris sensu & certitudine esse non potest. 6. Quo spectat & unio nostra, ac communio cum Deo, quae in Scripturis saepe adeo praedicatur; sanctusque iste cum Deo consensus, & commercium, & divinae gratiae sensus, omnisque animae affectus; quae regni Dei in hominibus praecipuae partes sunt: quae, si salutis ac favoris Dei certitudo absint, vana sunt & inania; nec verus Dei amor, aut amicitia, aut communio ulla cum Deo locum habere potest. Atque ex his omnibus oritur tandem illa παῤῥησία, & πληροφορία, & καύχησις, & ἐτερέ-γνυσις, quaeque alia laetae ac exultanti conscientiae Scriptura tribuit. Eph. 3:12. Hebr. 10:22. Qualis in Abrahamo describitur, Rom. 4:20, 21. in Paulo, 2. Tim. 4:7,8. aliisque. Quae certitudo major est sub N. T. praeilla sub Veteri, cum fides nostra sit adstipulatio erga Pontificem consummatum, adeoque liberata sit ab omnibus illis timoribus & terroribus, quibus fideles sub V. T. obnoxii erant.
units.tr: XXII. (4) The nature of hope. It is called living, and makes a man rejoice. 1 Pet. 1:3; Rom. 5:2. Such hope, since it is commanded by God and is not shameful to the one who has it, cannot be vain or deceptive, unless we turn the chief of the Christian virtues into an empty mockery and dream of the mind. We desire that each of you show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the end. Heb. 6:11. Faith is, moreover, the substance of things hoped for, or their representation, ch. 11:1. (5) The nature of love towards God, which cannot exist without a sense and certainty of mutual love. (6) To this also relates our union and communion with God, which Scripture so often proclaims; and that holy agreement and dealing with God, and the sense of divine grace, and every affection of the soul, which are the principal parts of the kingdom of God among men. If the certainty of God's favour and salvation is absent, these are vain and empty, and no true love of God, nor friendship, nor any communion with God, can have a place. And from all these at last arises that boldness [παῤῥησία], and full assurance [πληροφορία], and glorying [καύχησις], and joyful acknowledgement [ἐπιγνῶσις] which Scripture ascribes to a glad and exulting conscience. Eph. 3:12; Heb. 10:22. Such certainty is described in Abraham, Rom. 4:20, 21; in Paul, 2 Tim. 4:7, 8; and in others. This certainty is greater under the New Testament than it was under the Old, since our faith is a sharing with the perfected High Priest, and so is freed from all those fears and terrors to which the faithful were subject under the Old Testament.

units.la: XXIII. Obsistunt huic certitudini, in qua tamen ipse Christianae vitae nucleus situs est, Pontificii praesertim; & in Concilio Trid. post longas Theologorum lites, tandem ambiguis verbis eam condemnarunt & proscripserunt. Bellarminus autem certitudinem moralem & conjecturalem, quae non merito Christi, sed caritate & bonis operibus nitatur, asseruit. Ac similiter Walenburgii inter fidem & fiduciam distinguunt. Illam sola Dei auctoritate niti, & dubitationem omnem excludere; hanc, partim divina promissione, partim nostra dispositione niti, ac posteriore respectu non omni formidine carere volunt. Quam distinctionem licet nos non rejiciamus (conf. §.xix.) inanis tamen est ista fidei & fiduciae, non tam distinctio, quam separatio; cum vera fides seipsam explorare possit, adeoque fiduciam habeat comitem. Nec recta est certitudinis conjecturalis appellatio; cum certitudo nulla sit, si falsum ei subesse possit. Falsum etiam, illam vel operibus, vel dispositionibus nostris uti causis inniti. Salutis enim nostrae causae in caelo, (atque inde ejus firmitas & immutabilitas) media vero & signa in terra sunt, fides videl. & opera nostra. Nos autem, quanquam certitudinem illam animi nostri dispositione, significque externis, ex parte nostra niti non refragamur; non tamen ideo illam formidinem concipere, ac identidem labascere, necesse est. Cum fidei suae propriorumque actuum anima sibi intime conscia, ac inde de donorum spiritualium perseverantia secura esse queat. XXIV. Ad- Certitudinis huic obstant. Pontificii.
units.tr: XXIII. Against this certainty, in which nevertheless the very core of the Christian life lies, the Papists in particular set themselves; and at the Council of Trent, after long quarrels among the theologians, they at last condemned and proscribed it in ambiguous words. Bellarmine asserted a moral and conjectural certainty, which rests not on the merit of Christ but on charity and good works. Likewise the Walenburgians distinguish between faith and trust. They want faith to rest on the authority of God alone and to exclude all doubt, while trust rests partly on the divine promise and partly on our disposition, and in this latter respect they wish it not to be free from all dread. Although we do not reject this distinction (see §19), this distinction of faith and trust is empty; it is less a distinction than a separation, since true faith can examine itself and so has trust as its companion. Nor is the name conjectural certainty correct, since there is no certainty if something false can lie beneath it. It is also false that this certainty rests on our works or dispositions as its causes. For the causes of our salvation are in heaven (and hence its firmness and immutability), while the means and signs are on earth, namely faith and our works. We, however, do not object to this certainty resting, on our side, on the disposition of our mind and on external signs; yet it is not therefore necessary that it should be conceived with fear and waver again and again, since the soul, inwardly conscious of its faith and of its own acts, can thus be secure concerning the perseverance of the spiritual gifts. XXIV. Objections to this certainty come from the Papists.

units.la: XXIV. Adferunt autem pro dubitatione sua: nullibi in Scriptura singularibus hominibus de peccatorum remissione spem factam: sed & contra, dubiam eam sæpe relinqui: Si forte remittetur tibi cogitatio cordis tui. Act. 8: 22. Ne quo modo ipse rejectaneus fiam. 1. Cor. 9: 27. Et amorem & odium non internoscit homo. Eccl. 9: 1. Et timorem tremoremque piis injungi Phil. 2: 12. cum omnis hæc certitudo securitatis ac licentiæ mater & nutrix sit. Ad quæ ordine respondemus: 1. in Scriptura in universum credentibus salutem promitti, nec ultra necesse esse: particularem autem fidei ac salutis certitudinem & applicationem ex sua cuique conscientia hauriendam. 2. Act. 8: 22. non de remissionis certitudine, sed de ipsa peccatorum remissione agitur: quæ, ob perversum Simonis cor, valde dubia erat. 3. Nec Paulo certitudo defuit, quam alibi summam in ipso videmus. Nec μὴ τις dubitantis, sed cavendis & attendentis est; ne, dum corpori nimis credit, ad Apostolatus ministerium minus utilis, & sacræ militiæ desertor habeatur. Non enim de æterna reprobatione hic sermo est. 4. Ecclesiastes autem, cum bonis malisque omnia ex æquo accidant, ex externo fortunæ vultu Dei vultum agnosci non posse ait. Unde non cum fortuna, sed cum Deo sentiendum, & bonæ menti ac conscientiæ studendum esse. Cum ex interno animæ statu Dei amor facile deprehendi possit. Quod de odio nec ipsi Pontificii negant. Quin potius dum hominem nec amorem, nec odium internoscere dicit Ecclesiastes, simpliciter hoc tantum vult, illum quid amet ac prosequatur, vel quid odio habeat vel fugiat, nescire. 5. Timor autem ac tremor, qui mandatur, non animum de summa salute fluctuantem ac incertum, & nimia formidine humilem ac vilem, dicit; sed veram humilitatem, ac indefessum salutis studium & sollicitudinem continet. Quæ animi lætitiæ ac certitudini adeo non adversa sunt, ut ei corroborandæ faciant. Servite Jehova in timore, & gaudete in tremore. Psal. 2: 11. Cum timore & tremore vestram salutem conficite. Phil. 2: 12. 6. Non etiam facit hæc certitudo superbos, aut inertes & securos. Quid enim superbiat, qui sese de Deo omnia sperare profitetur? & quomodo non omne studium adhibeat, qui illam precibus acquiri, bonorum operum exercitio foveri, & non sine sollicitudine vivam ac lætam conservari novit. Et erit fides temporis tui possessio salutis, sapientiæ scientiæ; cujus thesaurus, vel arca, in qua hæc omnia servantur, est timor Dei. Esai. 33: 6. Imo adeo illa certitudo bona opera non tollit, ut sine ea ne quidem consistere illa possint; ac nulla cum Deo communio, nulla familiaritas, sanctusve cum ipso consensus exerceri possit ab illo, qui de Dei gratia ac amore perpetuo diffidere debet, nec nullum ejus sensum habere potest. Ut non sine Christianæ vitæ detrimento abnegari illa possit.
units.tr: XXIV. They bring forward, in support of their doubt, the following: nowhere in Scripture is hope of the forgiveness of sins held out to particular men; on the contrary, it is often left doubtful. If perhaps the thought of your heart will be forgiven you. Acts 8:22. Lest by any means I myself become a castaway. 1 Cor. 9:27. Man knows neither love nor hatred. Eccl. 9:1. And fear and trembling are enjoined on the pious, Phil. 2:12, since all such certainty is the mother and nurse of carelessness and licence. To these we reply in order. (1) In Scripture salvation is promised in general to believers, and nothing more is necessary; but the particular certainty and application of faith and salvation is to be drawn from each person's own conscience. (2) Acts 8:22 does not speak of the certainty of forgiveness but of forgiveness itself, which, because of Simon's perverse heart, was very doubtful. (3) Nor did Paul lack certainty, which we see in him elsewhere to be supreme. The [μή τις] "lest anyone" is not the word of one doubting, but of one being cautious and attentive, lest, while he trusts too much to the body, he be regarded as less useful for the ministry of the apostleship and as a deserter of the sacred warfare. For this is not a discussion of eternal reprobation. (4) Ecclesiastes, since all things happen alike to good and bad, says that God's face cannot be recognised from the external countenance of fortune. Hence one must form one's judgement not by fortune but by God, and strive for a good mind and conscience, since love of God can easily be perceived from the inward state of the soul. The Papists themselves do not deny this about hatred. Indeed, when Ecclesiastes says that man knows neither love nor hatred, he simply means that he does not know what he loves and pursues, or what he hates and shuns. (5) The fear and trembling which is commanded does not describe a soul wavering and uncertain about its supreme salvation, humbled and made vile by excessive dread; it contains true humility and tireless zeal and care for salvation. These are so far from being opposed to joy and certainty of soul that they strengthen them. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Ps. 2:11. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. Phil. 2:12. (6) Nor does this certainty make men proud, or idle and careless. For why should one who professes that he hopes everything from God be proud? And how should he not apply all diligence who knows that it is acquired by prayer and nourished by the exercise of good works, and that it is kept alive and joyful only with care? And the fear of the LORD is his treasure; faith will be the possession of your times, salvation and wisdom and knowledge; the treasure or chest in which all these things are kept is the fear of God. Isa. 33:6. Indeed, this certainty does not so abolish good works that they could not even stand without it; and no communion with God, no familiarity, nor holy agreement with him, can be practised by one who ought to distrust God's grace and perpetual love, and who cannot have any sense of it. So without loss to the Christian life these certainties cannot be denied.

units.la: XXV. Remonstrantes ad summum, ad præsens, de salutis statu securum esse Christianum jubent: cum futura omnia incerta, & pro humanæ voluntatis, ad levia momenta mutabilis, arbitrio, pariter incerta sint.
units.tr: XXV. The Remonstrants, at most, bid the Christian to be secure about the state of his salvation for the present only, since all future things are uncertain and equally uncertain, being subject to the decision of human will, which changes with slight moments.

units.la: XXVI. Tandem & Anabaptistæ, cum Evangelium in legem commutent, & operum justitiam urgeant, salutis certitudinem ne peccatori quidem resipiscenti permittunt; nisi resipiscentiæ suæ supervivat, & bona opera edat. Quæ fundamenta jam diu subruimus. Quantum autem a vera fidei regula illa exerrent, ex his aliisque fructibus facile patet.
units.tr: XXVI. Finally, the Anabaptists, since they turn the Gospel into law and press the righteousness of works, do not even allow a repentant sinner certainty of salvation, unless his repentance survives and produces good works. These foundations we have long been overturning. How far they stray from the true rule of faith is easily evident from these and other fruits.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De Morte, & statu hominis post eam.
units.tr: On Death and the State of Man After It.

units.la: I. UM hominis consummatio ac æterna beatitudo, non detur nisi in futura vita; atque ante omnia mortis regnum cum comitatu ac satellitio suo, inter quæ est peccatum, & lucta miseriaque omnis, utpote quæ sunt effecta fœderis operum provenientia à peccato, aboleri debeat; de eo nunc videndum; & de morte, ac reliqua miseriarum cohorte, statuendum. Cui, suo deinceps loco, subjungenda erunt hominis novissima, cum fine sæculi, ac exitu civitatis Dei.
units.tr: I. Since the consummation of man and his eternal blessedness are not given except in the future life, and since above all the kingdom of death, with its retinue and attendants (among which are sin and all struggle and misery, as effects of the covenant of works arising from sin), must be abolished, we must now consider this and determine what to say about death and the rest of the troop of miseries. After this, in its own place, man's last things will be added, together with the end of the age and the outcome of the city of God.

units.la: II. Afflictiones, ac humanæ vitæ miseriæ, cum quibus perpetua nobis, ad mortem usque, lucta est (de altera enim lucta cum peccato ad Sanctificationem vidimus) per sese amaræ sunt peccati reliquiæ; ex quo aculeum ac stimulum habent, & naturæ graves ac pudendæ evaserunt. Piis vero, per Dei gratiam, non in peccatorum pœnam, neque isto cum horrore, ac legis aculeo, sed alias ob causas, inferuntur. Ubi tua, o mors, victoria? ubi tuus, o sepulchrum, aculeus? Aculeus vero mortis est peccatum. Vis autem peccati, Lex. 1.Cor. 15:56,57. Ac 1. ad vaideiav, & carnis disciplinam, quæ leveritate ista domanda est, ne à justa regula abeat. Quem enim diligit Dominus, castigat. — Hic autem cohibet ad utilitatem; ut participes fiamus sanctitatis ejus. Hebr. 12:6, 10. 2. ad δοκιμὴν & fidei experimentum; quæ isto igne explorari debet. Sed & gloriamur in afflictionibus; scientes, quod afflictio patientiam operetur: patientia vero probationem. Rom. 5:3. 3. Ad majorem Dei gloriam, cui ista fidei constantia, & intrepida spei confessione, ac amoris denique martyrio & sacrificio, non mediocriter placemus. Gaudentes profecti sunt a concilio, quod digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Jesu contumeliâ afficerentur. Act. 5:41. 4. Tandem ut isto in campo virtutes suas, quæ sine certamine ac adversario marcent, explicare fideles possint; & tum ipsi fortem in patiendo animum ostendere; tum aliorum adversis indolescere, & qua licet, levare ea ac mulcere queant. Partim quidem dum & cum convictis & cum afflictionibus in theatrum estis producti; partim vero dum socii facti estis eorum, qui sic agitantur. Hebr. 10:33, 34. Atque ab altera parte impii, dum in pios furunt, indolem suam produnt, & cunctantia alioquin fata impellunt ac maturant. Quod ipsis quidem est argumentum perditionis, vobis autem salutis. Et hoc a Deo. Quia vobis donatum est, pro Christo, non tantum credere in ipsum, sed etiam pro ipso pati. Phil. 1:28, 29. Nullum autem in iis meritum situm est. Cum, si quid bonæ frugis ex nostris afflictionibus redundat, id omne a Christi morte ac merito profluat: cujus sacrificio nostrum sanguinem, veluti libamen, affundimus, non peccatis expiandis, sed Deo laudando ac celebrando. Ego enim jam libor, & tempus discessus mei instat. 2. Tim. 4:6.
units.tr: II. Afflictions and the miseries of human life, with which we have a constant struggle until death (for we have already seen the other struggle with sin, for sanctification), are in themselves bitter remnants of sin. For this reason they have a sting and goad, and have become burdensome and shameful to our nature. For the godly, however, through the grace of God, they are sent not as punishment for sins, nor with that dread and the sting of the law, but for other reasons. "O death, where is your victory? O grave, where is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law" (1 Cor. 15:56, 57). They are also sent to train us in self-discipline [παιδείαν] and to tame the flesh by this gentle correction, so that it does not depart from the right rule: "For whom the Lord loves, he chastens... but he chastens us for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness" (Heb. 12:6, 10). Second, they serve as a test [δοκιμήν] and proof of faith, which must be tried by this fire: "And we glory in tribulations also, knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience experience" (Rom. 5:3). Third, they serve the greater glory of God, whom we greatly please by this steadfastness of faith, by the bold confession of hope, and finally by the martyrdom and sacrifice of love: "They departed from the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus" (Acts 5:41).
