Fourth, in this field the faithful can display their virtues, which wither without contest and adversary; they can show a brave spirit in suffering, and be moved by the troubles of others and ease and soothe them as far as they can: "Partly, while you were made a spectacle both by reproaches and afflictions; partly, while you became companions of those who were so treated" (Heb. 10:33, 34). On the other side, the wicked, while they rage against the godly, reveal their own nature and hasten and push on the fates that would otherwise delay: "This is a sign of perdition to them, but of salvation to you, and this from God. For to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him" (Phil. 1:28, 29). Yet no merit lies in these things. If any good fruit comes from our afflictions, all of it flows from the death and merit of Christ, to whose sacrifice we pour out our blood like a drink offering, not to expiate sins but to praise and celebrate God: "For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand" (2 Tim. 4:6).

units.la: III. Prænunciatæ sunt hæ afflictiones præcipuè sub Novo T.
units.tr: III. These afflictions were foretold especially under the New Testament.

units.la: Omnes volentes pie vivere in Jesu Christo, persecutionem experientur. 2. Tim. 3: 12. Quia propter te occidimur omni die, reputamur ut oves mactationis. Psal. 44:22. coll. Rom. 8:36 Quo tempore illæ non pudendæ, ut olim; sed gloriosæ evaserunt. In Veteri enim Test. cum Canaanæ finibus conclusa Ecclesia terrestri pignori incubaret; & longa pacis tempora, ac tranquilla vita hæreditatis illius partem facerent; omnis afflictio, præsertim si fideles morte immatura, ante legitimum tempus, pignoris illius usu deprivaret; vel à facie hostium fugere, & ob hostilem impetum terra ista exulare cogeret; (cum speciem divinæ iræ præferret, & perfidiæ, ac violati Dei fœderis notam gereret) fidei imprimis gravis, & non leve ejus tentamentum erat; ex quo non sine lucta & certamine sese erigere, liberalesque ac filiis Dei dignos spiritus sumere poterant. Ut in David, Hiskia, aliisque patuit. Quod afflictionum probrum Daniel etiam exaggerat, cap. 9:7. Tua, Domine, est justitia, & nobis convenit pudor faciei; ut in hoc die — in omnibus terris, quo populisti eos propter prevaricationem ipsorum. Nunc autem illa rerum facies mutata est, sub Novo Test. ubi nulli pignori Ecclesia servit, & nullum in afflictionibus probrum, nullum denique in morte malum est; postquam Christus suo exemplo & merito afflictiones omnes & mortem ipsam consecravit; ut nihil probrosi in iis amplius superfit, sed fidei potius nostrae gloriari in iis liceat. Gloriamur in afflictionibus. Rom. 5:3.
units.tr: "All who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution" (2 Tim. 3:12). "For your sake we are killed all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter" (Ps. 44:22; compare Rom. 8:36). At that time these afflictions were no longer shameful, as they once were, but became glorious. For under the Old Testament, when the Church, shut up within the borders of Canaan, rested on an earthly pledge, and long periods of peace and a quiet life formed part of that inheritance, every affliction, especially if it deprived the faithful of that pledge's use by an untimely death before the appointed time, or forced them to flee before the face of enemies and go into exile from that land because of hostile attack, was above all a grave trial of faith and no slight temptation. This was so because it bore the appearance of divine wrath and the mark of faithlessness and of a violated covenant with God. From it they could rise only not without struggle and conflict, and take up free spirits worthy of the sons of God. This is clear in David, Hezekiah, and others. Daniel too dwells on this shame of afflictions: "Yours, O Lord, is righteousness, but to us belongs open shame... in all the lands to which you have driven them because of their unfaithfulness" (Dan. 9:7). Now, however, the face of things has changed under the New Testament, where the Church serves under no earthly pledge, and where there is no shame in afflictions and no evil at last in death. Christ, by his own example and merit, has consecrated all afflictions and death itself, so that nothing shameful remains in them, but it is rather permitted for us to glory in them as the faith of the believers: "We glory in tribulations" (Rom. 5:3).

units.la: IV. Terminus afflictionum, omnisque illius certaminis est Mors: quae cum a peccato primum ortum duxerit, nunc per Dei gratiam, peccati quoque, quod sine illa immortale foret, mors ac remedium factum est. Propter peccatum enim, deponendum, morimur. Rom. 8:10. atque isto demum sine vetustus homo aboletur & extinguitur, qui non nisi cum corporis exuviis deponi poterat. Col.2:11.
units.tr: IV. The end of afflictions and of all that struggle is death. Although death first arose from sin, now through the grace of God it has become the remedy even for sin, which without death would be immortal. For "we die because of sin" to be laid aside (Rom. 8:10), and by this at last the old man is abolished and extinguished, who could be put off only together with the shedding of the body (Col. 2:11).

units.la: V Atque ita non solum afflictionum, sed & mortis horror nunc cessat; qui olim sub Veteris Test. statu, cum longaeva vita fidelibus promissa foret, nec Christus morte sua terrorem istum abolevisset, diu adeo, ex hac quoque inter alias, causa, obtinuerat: Et liberos redderet quotquot metu mortis per omnem vitam damnates erant servitutis. Hebr. 2:15. Unde neque sub Novo Test. fideles longam vitam petere videmus, ut olim sub Vet. T. sed contrario voto, calcatis mundi nebulis, dum caelum & astra, & aetherium mirantur limen Olympi, missionem saepe flagitare. Nunc dimittas servum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum, in pace. Luc. 2:29. Cupiditatem habeo ad discedendum, & ut sim cum Christo. Phil. 1:23. Sicuti nec in Novo Test. fidelium aetas, in terris exacta, quantum ad universum vitae alicujus calculum, annotata ullibi reperitur; quasi ea tanti non sit: cum in Vet. Testam. commentariis illud saepius occurrere videamus.
units.tr: V. And so not only the horror of afflictions but also the horror of death now ceases. Under the Old Testament state, when long life was promised to the faithful, and before Christ had abolished this terror by his death, that horror had prevailed for a long time, partly for this reason among others: "and might deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" (Heb. 2:15). Hence under the New Testament we do not see the faithful asking for a long life, as they did under the Old, but rather with the opposite wish, trampling the mists of the world, and while they admire heaven and the stars and the ethereal threshold of Olympus, they often beg for release: "Now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word" (Luke 2:29); "I have a desire to depart and be with Christ" (Phil. 1:23). Likewise, under the New Testament the years of the faithful spent on earth are nowhere recorded as a full count of a life's span, as if they were of no great worth; yet in the commentaries of the Old Testament we see this recorded quite often.

units.la: VI. Corporis exuviae, post mortem, rite condendae ac componendae sunt, in beatae resurrectionis spem. Nec probanda Pontificiorum superstitio, in cereis, hymnis, ac universo funebri sacro. Quae ut apud veteres victoriae ac triumphi erant insignia; ita a Romana Ecclesia, perverso ritu, propitiandis animabus, & a poenis liberandis, usurpantur.
units.tr: VI. After death the body's remains are to be duly laid to rest and arranged in the hope of a blessed resurrection. The superstition of the Papists, with its wax candles, hymns, and the whole funeral ritual, is not to be approved. As among the ancients these were marks of victory and triumph, so the Roman Church, by a perverse rite, uses them to propitiate souls and to free them from punishments.

units.la: VII. Atque ejusdem indolis est coemeteriorum consecratio, mortuosque in templis humandi mos. Qui ab Oratoriis, olim ad martyrum sepulchra extructis, originem trahens, tandem in superstitionem vertit, & ab idololatria denique contaminatus est: dum, regum principumque exemplo, primo nobiliores, deinde reliqua Christianorum plebs, dedicato prope aram loco, apud Sanctorum pulverem & ossa, quiescere, istoque pignore ipsorum patrocinio gaudere, etiam post fata, desiderarunt.
units.tr: VII. The consecration of cemeteries and the custom of burying the dead in churches are of the same character. This custom, taking its origin from oratories built long ago over the tombs of martyrs, at last turned into superstition and was finally tainted with idolatry. Following the example of kings and princes, first the nobles and then the rest of the Christian people desired to rest, near the altar in a consecrated place, among the dust and bones of the saints, and to enjoy their patronage, even after death, through this pledge.

units.la: VIII. Perverse quoque iidem mortuos sepelire meritorium habent: istique rei, in Ecclesia sua, hominum ordinem instituerunt; quales fere in veteri Ecclesia parabolani erant, qui ægris ministrabant. Quos si in opere isto, pestilente contage tactos, extingui contingat, etiam martyribus accenseri debere disputant. Cum in hisce nullum meritum; martyrium autem non nisi metaphoricum sit. Quæ & veterum mens est.
units.tr: VIII. The same people also wrongly regard burying the dead as meritorious, and in their Church they have established an order of men for this work, somewhat like the parabolani of the early Church, who ministered to the sick. They argue that if any of these, while doing this work and touched by a deadly contagion, should happen to die, they must also be counted among the martyrs, although in these there is no merit, and martyrdom is only metaphorical. This was also the mind of the ancients.

units.la: IX. Post mortem incipit Glorificatio: primo quoad animam; tum, recompositis partibus, quoad universum hominem. Videnda autem 1. animæ post mortem existentia: 2. status.
units.tr: IX. After death, glorification begins: first with respect to the soul, and then, once the parts are reunited, with respect to the whole person. We must consider (1) the soul's existence after death and (2) its condition.

units.la: X. Superstitem post fata animam esse, superiori tomo ex intima ejus natura probavimus. Cum enim illa à corpore longe diversa sit, nec quicquam cum ejus natura commercii habeat, utpote sola cogitatione constans, nulla equidem causa est, cur cum corpore extinguatur. Cum sine ea existere & cogitare possit. Error enim populi est, à rationali anima corpus proprie animari, & deficiente ea extingui illud ac collabi: cum alia sit vita corporis, alia animæ, atque ab ea toto genere diversa. Hæc enim sola cogitatione, illa sanguinis ac spiritum meatu absolvitur. Quo turbato, corpus, ad animæ ministeria ineptum redditum, ab inhabitante spiritu deseritur.
units.tr: X. We have shown in the previous volume, from the soul's inner nature, that the soul survives after death. Since it is wholly different from the body and has nothing in common with the body's nature, being made up solely of thought, there is indeed no reason why it should perish along with the body. It can exist and think without the body. It is a popular error to think that the body is properly animated by the rational soul and that, when the soul fails, the body is extinguished and collapses. The life of the body and the life of the soul are different, and entirely different in kind. The soul's life consists solely in thought, while the body's life depends on the flow of blood and spirits. When this is disturbed, the body becomes unfit for the soul's functions and is abandoned by the spirit that dwelt in it.

units.la: XI. An vero Deus, post corporis compagem solutam, etiam animam annihilare soleat; quanquam id in potestate ipsius situm Philosophia noverit; tamen ex immutabilitate ac sapientia Dei, qua nihil, quod condere dignatus est, annihilavit unquam, id non fieri, non improbabiliter colligit.
units.tr: XI. Whether God, after the body's framework has been dissolved, customarily also annihilates the soul, is a question. Philosophy recognises that this lies within God's power. Nevertheless, from the immutability and wisdom of God, by which he has never annihilated anything that he deigned to create, it reasonably concludes that this does not happen.

units.la: XII. Certo autem docet hoc Scriptura, quæ sola voluntatem Dei, omnemque rerum post hanc vitam statum & seriem explicat; in quo maxima sapientiæ ac regiminis Dei ratio vertitur. Vide Eccl. 12: 7. Et redeat pulvis ad terram, ut fuerat; & spiritus redeat ad Deum, qui dedit eum. Matth. 10: 28. Animam non possunt occidere. Luc. 16: 22. Factum autem est, ut mortuus sit pauper, & portatus sit in sinum Abrahami. Matth. 22: 32. Ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci, & Deus Jacobi. Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed viventium. Luc. 23: 43. Amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. 2. Cor. 5: 8. Sed gratum est nobis, potius abesse à corpore, & adesse apud Dominum. Phil. 1:23. Desiderio tendens ad dimissionem, & ut cum Christo sim. Apoc. 6:9, 10. Vidi sub altari animas eorum, qui mactati fuerant propter verbum Dei —clamabant autem voce magna, dicentes, usque quo Domine, qui sanctus es & verax, non judicas, neque vindicas sanguinem nostrum? &c. &c. 14: 13. Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur, a nunc: etiam, dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant à laboribus suis, & opera eorum sequuntur eos.
units.tr: XII. Scripture, which alone explains the will of God and the whole state and sequence of things after this life, in which the greatest part of God's wisdom and government is displayed, teaches this with certainty. See Eccl. 12:7: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return to God who gave it." Matt. 10:28: "They cannot kill the soul." Luke 16:22: "And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom." Matt. 22:32: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." Luke 23:43: "Verily I say unto thee, today shalt thou be with me in Paradise." 2 Cor. 5:8: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Phil. 1:23: "Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ." Rev. 6:9–10: "I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God... and they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?" etc. Rev. 14:13: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on; yes, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours, and their works follow them."

units.la: XIII. Quod autem alibi mortui non esse, & Deum non amplius laudare &c. Psal. 6:6. 30: 10. dicuntur; non simpliciter accipiendum est, sed de laudibus, quae Deo in Ecclesia, & in terra viventium dicuntur, intelligitur. Alioqui enim coelitum choros, ac concinentium hymnos Scriptura quoque celebrat. Apoc. 4:10. coll. 5:9, 11.
units.tr: XIII. The passages where it is said elsewhere that the dead are not, and that they no longer praise God (Ps. 6:6; Ps. 30:10), are not to be taken simply, but are to be understood of the praises that are sung to God in the Church and in the land of the living. Otherwise Scripture also celebrates the choirs of the heavenly beings and their harmonious hymns: Rev. 4:10; compare 5:9, 11.

units.la: XIV. Hanc animae immortalitatem negarunt olim Sadducaei; qui dixerunt, non esse resurrectionem, nec Angelum, nec Spiritum. Act. 23: 8. Angelos enim pro Dei veluti potentius, ac divinae auras effluviis habebant; ac similia fere de spiritibus à morte superstitibus philosophati fuisse videntur.
units.tr: XIV. The Sadducees once denied this immortality of the soul. They said that there is "no resurrection, neither angel nor spirit" (Acts 23:8). For they regarded angels as, as it were, more powerful beings of God and as emanations of the divine breath. And they seem to have reasoned in much the same way about the spirits that survive death.

units.la: XV. Ejusdem sententiae sceleratae tenentur hodie Sociniani. Quorum haec theologemata sunt: 1. animam, ex Dei creatione, naturâ sua immortalem non esse. Unde & Dei in ea imaginem, & vitae aeternae promissionem, ex lege primaeva, aperte negant. 2. Adeoque in morte eam redire ad Deum; instar auræ de coelo derivatae, quae ad fontem suum relabatur. Quomodo videl. & alia Dei dona, ad Deum auctorem redeunt.
units.tr: XV. Today the Socinians hold the same wicked opinion. Their theological positions are these: (1) that the soul, created by God, is not by its nature immortal. Hence they flatly deny both that the soul bears God's image and that the promise of eternal life is given to it by the primeval law. (2) Consequently, at death the soul returns to God, like a breath of air drawn from heaven that flows back to its source. In the same way, they say, other gifts of God also return to God their author.

units.la: 3. Atque illam in eo subsistere, & superstitem esse nugantur; quia nimirum ab eo reproduci possit. Quomodo res omnes ante creationem, ab aeterno in Deo exstiterunt. 4. Vitam autem aeternam, quam, ex Christi disciplina, piis promittunt, in eo consistere faciunt; non quod anima semper vivat; sed quod in rerum fine reproducenda sit, ac fideles sibi ipsis redonandi, novisque corporibus induendi, sint. 5. Sicuti infernum impiorum in eo constituunt, quod illi è statu isto, in quem post mortem omnes recidunt, nunquam liberandi ac resuscitandi sint. Atque huc tandem ista Theologia pervenit, cujus tot monstra passim tetigimus; quae huc tandem exeunt, ut vero ac unico religionis fine, beata animae immortalitate, hominem tandem spolient; quam videl. largiri sese, ex doctrinae suae genio, non posse hoc ipso satis confitentur. Quas autem nebulas locis Scripturae pro animarum immortalitate allatis aspergunt, nunc mittimus.
units.tr: (3) They trifle that the soul subsists in God and survives, because, of course, it can be reproduced by him, just as all things existed in God from eternity before creation. (4) The eternal life that they promise to the godly from the teaching of Christ they make to consist in this: not that the soul lives forever, but that it is to be reproduced at the end of things, and that believers are to be restored to themselves and clothed with new bodies. (5) Likewise they place the hell of the wicked in this: that they are never to be freed from that state into which all fall after death, nor to be raised again. And at last this theology, whose many monsters we have touched upon here and there, arrives at this point: it ends by stripping man of the true and sole end of religion, the blessed immortality of the soul. They themselves openly confess that, by the very genius of their doctrine, they cannot grant this. As for the mists they cast over the passages of Scripture brought forward for the immortality of souls, we now pass over them.

units.la: XVI. AC
units.tr: XVI. Ac

units.la: XVI. Asserta animarum post mortem existentia, sequitur considerandus earum status & locus.
units.tr: XVI. Having affirmed that souls exist after death, we must consider their state and place.

units.la: XVII. Ac statum quidem earum mox a funere beatum esse, ex Scri-pturis liquet. Illæ enim vitæ calamitates mortali vita finiunt, nec ultra earum regnum extendunt. Illico enim prateriens levitas afflictionis nostra — æternum pondus gloriæ operatur. 2. Cor. 4: 17. Qua in re exsultatis, ad exiguum tempus nunc (si oportet) in variis tentationibus tristitia affecti. 1. Petr. 1: 6. En justum, in terra hac rependitur ei; quanto magis impio & peccatori. Prov. 11: 31. Nam tempus est, ut incipiat judicium a domo Dei. Quod si primum incipit a nobis, quis erit finis eorum, qui non assentiuntur Evangelio Dei? 1. Pet. 4: 17. Ac mortem, quæ æternitatis veluti vestibulum ac janua est, in lucrum fidelibus deputant. Mihi enim vivere Christus, & mori lucrum. Phil. 1: 21. Qui, peracto veluti certamine, beati, mox ab abitu, cœlesti voce pronunciantur. Apoc. 14: 13. Quod omnium fidelium est, 1. Cor. 15: 18. 1. Thess. 4: 16. Ut potequibus parta jam laborum quies, operibus ipsos assecutos, & in cœlum usque comitantibus. Nec leve est, quod Deus, etiam post fata, fidelium Deus ac Pater appellari velit. Matth. 22: 32. Quod sine eorum felicitate intelligi non potest. Atqui potiorem expetunt, hoc est cœlestem civitatem: quapropter Deum non pudet eorum, & cognomi-nari Deus eorum; paraverat enim iis urbem. Hebr. 11: 16. Unde & apud Deum esse dicuntur. Phil. 1: 23. Et quanquam mortalis corporis exuvias, vilemque istum pulverem, ponant; non tamen nudari eos, sed potiore paludamento, ac cœlesti veluti tabernaculo, superindui idem Apostolus affirmat 2. Cor. 5: 2.
units.tr: XVII. That their state is blessed immediately after burial is clear from Scripture. For the troubles of this life end with mortal life and do not extend their rule beyond it. For the momentary lightness of our affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory. 2 Cor. 4:17. In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been distressed by various trials. 1 Pet. 1:6. Behold, the righteous is repaid on earth; how much more the wicked and the sinner. Prov. 11:31. For it is time for judgment to begin at the house of God. And if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God? 1 Pet. 4:17. They also count death, which is as it were the vestibule and gate of eternity, as gain for the faithful. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Phil. 1:21. Having finished their struggle, as it were, they are pronounced blessed by a heavenly voice immediately upon departure. Rev. 14:13. This belongs to all the faithful: 1 Cor. 15:18; 1 Thess. 4:16. Their labours are now rewarded with rest, as it were, their works having followed them and accompanying them even into heaven. Nor is it a small matter that God, even after their death, wishes to be called the God and Father of the faithful. Matt. 22:32. This cannot be understood without their happiness. But they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one; wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city. Heb. 11:16. Hence they are also said to be with God. Phil. 1:23. And although they lay aside the remains of the mortal body and this vile dust, the same Apostle affirms that they are not left naked, but are clothed upon with a better garment, as it were a heavenly tabernacle. 2 Cor. 5:2.

units.la: XVIII. Repugnat hisce animarum dormitio, & somnus, à veteribus Arabibus profectus, & ab Anabaptistis hodie adoptatus; qui animas, ut que ad supremi judicii diem, quiescere, h. e. perpetua nocte teneri asserunt. Quod fidelium spem, atque media in morte fiduciam, non leviter concutit; & justis injustisque eandem in fortem redactis, manifestis Scripturis; atque ipsi denique rationi atque animæ naturæ adversatur. Illa enim, cum in cogitatione consistat, sopore veluti ligata quiescere, omnique sui sensu ac conscientia destitui non potest. Licet fateamur, non illam omnes cogitandi modos, quos hic in corpore habuit per sensationem, imaginationem, passiones memoriamque corporeas, in illo statu retinere. Anabaptistis accedunt Sociniani, ubi nonnunquam animas à funere superesse fateri volunt. Remonstrantes autem quæstionem de Pars II.
units.tr: XVIII. The sleep of souls, which the ancient Arabs introduced and which the Anabaptists have adopted today, contradicts these things. They assert that souls rest, that is, are held in perpetual night, until the day of the last judgment. This greatly shakes the hope of the faithful and their confidence in the face of death. It also reduces the just and the unjust to the same lot, contrary to plain Scriptures, and finally contrary to reason itself and the nature of the soul. For the soul, since it consists in thought, cannot rest bound as if by slumber, nor be deprived of all its sense and consciousness. We grant that it does not retain in that state all the modes of thinking it had here in the body through sensation, imagination, passions and bodily memory. The Socinians join the Anabaptists, in that they sometimes wish to admit that souls survive after death. The Remonstrants, however, on the question of Pars II.

units.la: Cui re-pugnat ψυχο-ταννυ-ναι; χλιαρ anima separata propemodum Philosophicam habent,nec quicquam certi, aut quod necessario definiatur, sese habere profitentur.
units.tr: To this is opposed psychopannychy [ψυχοπαννυχία]. They hold a nearly philosophical view of the separated soul, and profess that they have nothing certain, nothing that can be necessarily defined.

units.la: XIX. Quando vero Scriptura Sanctorum dormitiones narrat;mortemque ipsam non injucunda somni imagine pingit; id ad piorum quietem, post vitæ hujus labores & certamina, figurandam pertinet. Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur, a nunc. Ναί, dicit Spiritus, ut requiescant a laboribus suis, Apoc. 14:13. Nec tam animarum, quam corporum iste somnus est, quæ in conditoriis suis composita,in novi sæculi aurora, beatam resurrectionem expectant. Seminatur corpus animale, suscitatur corpus spirituale. 1. Cor. 15:44. Mysticum autem est, quod de animabus sub altari quiescentibus divina Apocalypsis c 6. habet; & animarum ψυχαι adeo non adstruit, ut eam potius evertat. Atque alienum etiam est, quod ex Paulo urgent; qui, postquam Sanctorum catalogum texuisset,eos omnes promissione non adepta,sed eminus longinquo visu delibata,obdormiisse narrat Hebr. 11. Agit enim Apostolus de veteribus Patribus, nec non de laboribus, & jugo illo, quod tota vita Hebr. 2:15. tolerandum ipsis erat. Mors enim, ut rerum aliarum, ita & servitutis illius terminus ac finis erat: post quam Apostolus proximo capite ψs 23. eos consummatos vocat. Accessistis — ad spiritus justorum consummatorum. Res enim promissa, non cœlestis post mortem gloria; sed Christi in carnem adventus erat. Denique Ecclesiastes, non suam, sed profani hominis sententiam, aut ab externis duntaxat casibus defumtam opinionem, conf. ψs 21. protert; quando cap. 3:19. ait: Nam ut est contingens filiis hominis, ita & est contingens pecudi; & idem contingit illis — spiritus unus est utrisque.
units.tr: XIX. But when Scripture narrates the sleep of the saints, and depicts death itself in the not unpleasant image of sleep, this is meant to portray the rest of the pious after the labours and struggles of this life. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. Yes [Ναί], says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours. Rev. 14:13. Nor is this sleep so much of souls as of bodies, which, laid in their graves, await a blessed resurrection at the dawn of the new age. The natural body is sown, the spiritual body is raised. 1 Cor. 15:44. What the divine Apocalypse says in ch. 6 about souls resting under the altar is mystical, and it does not establish the sleep of souls so much as overturn it. Also alien is what they press from Paul, who, after weaving a catalogue of saints, relates that they all fell asleep, not having obtained the promise but having tasted it from afar with distant vision. Heb. 11. For the Apostle speaks of the ancient Fathers, and of the labours and the yoke which they had to bear all their life, Heb. 2:15. For death, as with other things, was also the term and end of that servitude; after it the Apostle, in the next chapter, v. 23, calls them made perfect. You have come ... to the spirits of just men made perfect. For the promised thing was not heavenly glory after death, but the coming of Christ in the flesh. Finally, Ecclesiastes sets out not his own opinion, but that of a profane man, or an opinion drawn merely from external events (cf. v. 21). For in ch. 3:19 he says: For as it happens to the sons of men, so it happens to the beast; and the same happens to both ... one spirit is in both.

units.la: XX. Non magni nomenti quæstio est, an animæ separatæ personæ dici mereantur? Scriptura certe ab appellatione ista non adeo abhorret, dum de fidelibus, post obitum eorum, tanquam personis, loquitur Matth. 22:32. Ego sum Deus Abrahami, Isaaci &c. Sunt enim substantiæ singulares,rationales,ab aliis omnibus subsantiis diversæ,ac sese ipsis sufficientes, & completæ. Non minus quam Angeli. Quod enim ad corpora rursus induenda aptitudinem servant, id de perfectione earum nihil delibat.
units.tr: XX. Whether separated souls deserve to be called persons is not a question of great moment. Scripture certainly does not shrink from that appellation, since it speaks of the faithful after their death as persons: Matt. 22:32. I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, etc. For they are singular, rational substances, different from all other substances, and self-sufficient and complete, no less than angels. That they retain the aptitude to put on bodies again takes nothing from their perfection.

units.la: XXI. Post mortem autem duo tantum animarum receptacula Scriptura commemorat, cœlum & infernum. Lata est via, quæ ducit ad interitum — & striśta est via, quæ ducit ad vitam. Matth. 7:13. cont. Matth.25:34.41. Luc. 16:22,23. Marc.16:16. Joh.3:36. Cum autem locus spiritibus non conveniat, nisi respectu operationum adextra;dum sine iis sunt, aut esse supponuntur, non tam locus, quam status animarum, iis vocabulis tunc intelligi debet. Ut inepti sint, qui locum & statum animarum non solum distinguunt, verum etiam divellunt; & piis, sub Vet. T. statum quidem beatum, non autem locum in coelo beatorum attribuunt. Quæ manifestæ Scripturæ adversantur: Spiritus redit ad Deum, qui dedit eum. Eccl. 12:7. Dico autem vobis, multos ab Oriente & Occidente venturos, & accubituros cum Abrahamo, & Isaaco, & Jacobo, in regno cœlorum: filios vero regni ejiciuntur in tenebras illas exteras &c. Matth. 8:11. Et portatus ipse est ab Angelis in sinum Abrahami. Luc. 16:22. In domo Patris mei μοναὶ πολλαὶ mansiones multæ sunt Joh. 14:2. Ubi μονὴ passive locum jam occupatum & habitatum, coelestesque mansiones denotat. conf. ℣s 23.
units.tr: XXI. After death Scripture mentions only two receptacles of souls, heaven and hell. Broad is the way that leads to destruction ... and narrow is the way that leads to life. Matt. 7:13; contrast Matt. 25:34, 41; Luke 16:22, 23; Mark 16:16; John 3:36. Since place suits spirits only with respect to their outward operations, while they are without bodies, or are supposed to be without them, it is not so much place as the state of souls that must be understood by these words. Foolish, then, are those who not only distinguish the place and state of souls but even separate them, and who attribute to the pious under the Old Testament a blessed state but not a place among the blessed in heaven. These views are opposed to plain Scripture. The spirit returns to God who gave it. Eccl. 12:7. But I tell you that many will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven; but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into those outer darkness, etc. Matt. 8:11. And he was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. Luke 16:22. In my Father's house are many mansions [μοναὶ πολλαὶ] John 14:2, where [μονή], in the passive sense, denotes a place already occupied and inhabited, namely the heavenly mansions. Cf. v. 23.

units.la: XXII. Cœlum beatorum, qui & sinus Abrahæ, & Paradisus, & terminum cœlum, in Scripturis appellatur, Luc. 16:22. & 23:43. 2. Cor. 12:2. est locus proprie dictus, extra mundi adspectabilis limitem. Frustra enim Lutherani inter cœlum Dei & cœlum beatorum distinguunt: quorum illud ubique esse ajunt, hoc autem an certo loco collocandum sit, inter se disceptant. An vero spatium illud visibiles hosce cœlos perpetuo ambitu incingat? an vero ex parte tantum? an in infinitum protendatur? an vero ulteriorem ab alio corpore patiatur terminum? nobis non constat: cum mundi terminos ignoremus.
units.tr: XXII. The heaven of the blessed, which in Scripture is called both Abraham's bosom and Paradise and the third heaven, Luke 16:22; 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:2, is a place properly so called, outside the limit of the visible world. The Lutherans vainly distinguish between the heaven of God and the heaven of the blessed. They say the former is everywhere, while they dispute among themselves whether the latter is to be placed in a definite location. But whether that space encloses these visible heavens in a perpetual circuit, or only in part, or whether it extends to infinity, or whether it has a further boundary from some other body, is not known to us, since we do not know the limits of the world.

units.la: XXIII. Atque in hoc cœlum animæ piorum statim post mortem concedunt. Qui tamen motus, ut & locus ipse, spiritibus non nisi improprie, & respectu operationis ad extra, convenit. Ut nulla difficultas sit in longo isto spatio emetiendo, inque animarum & Angelorum transitu, ac jugi illo inter cœlum terramque commeatu, quem nobis hic imaginamur. Ac perverse Grotius moram aliquam, in isto ad cœlum itinere, purgandis defæcandisque animabus, excogitavit. Contra Luc. 23: 43. Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso.
units.tr: XXIII. Into this heaven the souls of the pious go immediately after death. Yet this motion, like the place itself, belongs to spirits only improperly, and with respect to their outward operation. So there is no difficulty in traversing that long space, or in the passage of souls and angels, or in that constant traffic between heaven and earth which we here imagine. Grotius wrongly devised some delay on this journey to heaven, for the purging and cleansing of souls. Against this, Luke 23:43: Today you will be with me in Paradise.

units.la: XXIV. Impiorum vero animas, mox à morte, inferno carcere Scriptura includit, æternis pœnis cruciandas. Et in inferno attollens oculos suos. —Luc. 16:23. Etiam iis spiritibus, qui in carcere sunt, prædicavit.
units.tr: XXIV. Scripture confines the souls of the wicked, straight after death, in the prison of hell, to be tormented with eternal punishments. And in hell he lifted up his eyes. —Luke 16:23. He preached even to those spirits who are in prison.

units.la: XXV. Alia tamen animarum ratio videtur esse, quas, ad superas auras revocatas, mortale ævum rursus exegisse legimus. Quas interim, dum è corporibus exiissent, in loco quodam dispensationis degisse credibile
units.tr: XXV. There seems, however, to be another account of souls, which we read were called back to the upper air and spent a mortal life again. It is credible that, while they had gone out of their bodies, they meanwhile lived in a certain place of separation

units.la: Quid fa-
units.tr: What they did there

units.la: Alium cum animabus bis mordibile est: hoc est, eodem in statu, quo in corporibus erant, nec feliciori, nec infelicioris; nisi quod extra corpus agerent, sive operarentur.
units.tr: It is another matter with souls that are twice mortal. That is, they were in the same state in which they had been in their bodies, neither happier nor more wretched, except that they acted or worked outside the body.

units.la: XXVI. Non facile autem de defunctorum statu judicandum est. Est enim universus ille status silentium; nec praesentis mundi est, ultra saeculum suum sapere, ac in futuri aevi caliginem introspicere velle. Quo modo Scripturam quoque parce adeo de illo loqui videmus. Nam, utcunque Luc. 16. Lazari, in sinu Abrahae quiescentis, nomen exprimat; epulonis tamen, quem flammis cruciari narrat, nomen silentio transmittit. Et Act. 1:25. ubi Judae exitum describit, non tamen apertis verbis quo concesserit narrat; sed verborum involucris magis cogitandum, quam legendum ejus finem tradit. Ut in isto Scripturae silentio, ac futurorum propemodum veneratione, nostrum non sit, in arcana illa mittere pusillum nostrum ingenium; atque, ultra quam fas est, scrutari quod caliginosa nocte premit Deus.
units.tr: XXVI. We ought not to judge easily about the state of the dead. That whole state is a silence, and it is not for the present world to be wise beyond its own age or to want to peer into the darkness of the age to come. We see that Scripture too speaks of it sparingly in this way. For although in Luke 16 it names Lazarus, resting in Abraham's bosom, it passes over in silence the name of the rich man, whom it says is tormented in the flames. And in Acts 1:25, where it describes the end of Judas, it does not tell in plain words where he went; rather, it hands down his end in wrapped-up words, to be pondered more than read. So, given this silence of Scripture and the near-reverence owed to things still to come, it is not for us to send our little wits into those hidden matters and to search, beyond what is lawful, what God covers with a dark night.

units.la: XXVII. Errant circa mortuorum statum: 1. Judaei, quorum aliqui animas una cum corpore extingui docuerunt. Quae Sadducaeorum impietas erat. Hodierni vero Judaei, qui animarum immortalitatem tenent, multa tamen de earum statu post mortem fabulantur. Quidam enim toto anno, quamdiu nondum perpurgatae sunt, vagari eas circa sepulchra sua, & cinceres suos circumvolare ferunt. Alii earum μετεμψύχωσιν & in nova corpora transmigrationem credunt.
units.tr: XXVII. People err about the state of the dead: (1) The Jews, some of whom taught that souls are extinguished together with the body. This was the impiety of the Sadducees. The Jews of today, who hold that souls are immortal, nonetheless tell many fables about their state after death. For some say that for the whole year, as long as the souls are not yet fully purged, they wander about their graves and flit around their ashes. Others believe in metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσιν], transmigration into new bodies.

units.la: XXVIII. 2 Graeci, qui animas, usque ad diem judicii, coelo exulare faciunt, & ad specus quosdam subterraneos, & Lethaea flumina ablegant. Quae & veterum quorundam opinatio fuit: priorum enim saeculorum patres, animas demortuorum, nisi forte martyrum animabus exceptis, quibusdam locis velut Φυλακῇ carcere includebant, ubi de consummatione certae, beatam resurrectionem cum gaudio exspectent. Similis quoque fere hodierna Socinianorum & Anabaptistarum sententia est, si mollissime eam explices.
units.tr: XXVIII. (2) The Greeks, who make souls exiled from heaven until the day of judgment and send them away to certain subterranean caves and the rivers of Lethe. This was also the opinion of some of the ancients. For the Fathers of earlier centuries kept the souls of the dead, except perhaps the souls of the martyrs, shut up in certain places as if in a prison [φυλακῇ], where they wait with joy for the consummation and the blessed resurrection. The present view of the Socinians and Anabaptists is also much the same, if you explain it very softly.

units.la: XXIX. 3. Sed & Pontificii etiam mundos quosdam subterraneos excogitarunt; & non solum limbos campolque, pro veteris Ecclesiae patribus, ac infantibus sacro fonte nondum tinctis; sed praecipue ignem quendam purgatorium fabulis suis extruxerunt; qui, non nisi sero in Ecclesiam receptus, etiam hodie a Graecis ignoratur & rejicitur.
units.tr: XXIX. (3) The Papists have also devised certain subterranean regions, and they have built in their fables not only limbo and fields for the fathers of the old Church and for infants not yet washed in the sacred font, but above all a certain purgatorial fire. This was received into the Church only late, and even today it is unknown to and rejected by the Greeks.

units.la: XXX. Primus ignis purgantis meminit Origenes, qui ex Platone illum hauserat. Quanquam ille longe diversus erat a Pontificio igne. Sequentes eum Patres varie errorem illum auxerunt; & incertis opinationibus, non tam ignem illum Pontificiorum, quam alium, in mundi fine accendendum, docuerunt; quem mundo hominibusque purgandis destinabant. Dubitat tamen de universa re Augustinus, eamque ulteriori Ecclesiae disquisitioni permittit. Neque plus reperire licet apud ejus discipulos; usque ad Gregorii Magni tempora, celebris in Ecclesia superstitionum auctoris & patroni; qui, circa annum 600, ista animarum supplicia, pro levioribus noxis expiandis, apertius docuit, falsis quibusdam visionibus & narrationibus delusus. Quibus minuendis vivorum deinceps suffragia & sacrificia quaesita. Ac festum pro animabus, in carcere illo laborantibus, A.C. 1010 instituit Johannes decimus octavus, ad pacem Dei pro illis exposcendam. Promoverunt deinde errorem illum Scholastico-rum disputationes. Donec anno 1439 in Concilio Florentino publice res judicata, & purgatoriae flammae Ecclesiae diplomate sancitae sunt. Quod in Tridentino Concilio rursus confirmatum: ac praesertim preces pro mortuis, caeteraque Ecclesiae pro filiis suis in purgatorio laborantibus, solatia, ac fabulosum istud vivorum cum mortuis commercium, in quo Ecclesiasticorum lucrum vertebatur, intentiore cura commendata. Quae dogmatis hujus origo & progressus prudentiores ex adversariis illud non Scripturae, sed traditionibus, acceptum ferre coëgit; quanquam aliis repugnantibus, ac cum Bellarmino pro fidei dogmate illud habentibus.
units.tr: XXX. Origen first mentions purgatorial fire, having drawn it from Plato, although that was quite different from the Papist fire. The Fathers who followed him enlarged that error in various ways, and by uncertain opinions they taught not so much that fire of the Papists as another fire, to be kindled at the end of the world, which they meant for cleansing the world and men. Yet Augustine doubts the whole matter and leaves it to further inquiry in the Church. Nor is more to be found among his disciples, until the time of Gregory the Great, famous author and patron of superstitions in the Church, who around the year 600 taught these punishments of souls more openly, for the expiation of lighter offences, deluded by certain false visions and stories. To lessen these, the suffrages and sacrifices of the living were afterwards sought. John XVIII, in the year 1010, instituted a feast for souls labouring in that prison, to seek God's peace for them. Then the disputations of the Schoolmen furthered that error, until in 1439 at the Council of Florence the matter was publicly decided and the purgatorial flames were sanctioned by the Church's decree. This was confirmed again at the Council of Trent, and prayers for the dead and the other comforts the Church offers for her children labouring in purgatory, and that fabulous commerce of the living with the dead, from which the profit of the clergy came, were commended with more intense care. The origin and progress of this doctrine compelled the more prudent of our opponents to acknowledge that it comes not from Scripture but from tradition, although others resist this and, with Bellarmine, hold it to be a dogma of faith.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Ita autem illum describunt; ut infernalem carcerem esse discant, in quo animae, e corporibus excedentes, venialium culparum noxas, poenasque quasdam temporales, quibus adhuc obstrictae erant, luant; donec defecatae, ac ad amussim candidae, coeli limen calcare queant. Locum ejus infra terram collocant, ad inferni limitem; qui tamen cum prato illo floreo & virenti, in vicinia posito, in quem animas illas subinde emittunt, non convenit. Solis vero fidelibus eum destinant, quos flammis prope avernalibus cruciari & purgari ferunt: ita tamen, ut salutis certitudinem, & impeccantiam, & perfectum Dei amorem retineant.
units.tr: They describe it in such a way that they teach it to be an infernal prison, in which souls, departing from their bodies, pay the penalties for venial faults and certain temporal punishments to which they are still bound, until, purified and made spotless to the rule, they are able to tread the threshold of heaven. They place it below the earth, at the edge of hell; yet this does not agree with that flowery and green meadow, placed nearby, into which they from time to time send those souls. They assign it only to the faithful, whom they say are tormented and purged by flames almost like those of Avernus, yet in such a way that they keep the certainty of salvation, freedom from sin, and perfect love of God.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Tota autem illa fabula, partim Scripturis, partim rationibus inde petitis adversatur; ac denique falsis quibusdam hypothesibus innititur.
units.tr: That whole fable is opposed partly by Scripture and partly by arguments drawn from it, and in the end it rests on certain false hypotheses.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Primum enim Veteris T. Scripturae ignem illum prorsus ignorant. Cumque saepe adeo mortuorum funera, & apparatum funereum, omnemque illam lugendi disciplinam, praescribant; nullam tamen ignis subterranei mentionem faciunt; sed contra, mortuos ad Patres suos colligi, in funebri lectulo veluti quiescere, quin & statum eorum beatum esse praedicant. Ecce ego colligam te ad Patres tuos. 2. Reg. 22:20. Moriatur anima mea morte rectorum; & sit postremum meum, ut illius. Num. 23: 10. Ingrediuntur in pacem, requiescunt in cubilibus suis. Esai. 57: 2. nec servitus piorum sub V. T. duravit ultra hanc vitam, Hebr. 2: 15. Merum enim commentum est, quod Patriarchae olim ossa sua in Cananaeam non alio fine deportari jusserunt; quam ut defunctorum cineres sacrificiorum sanguine lustrarentur, manesque eorum isto piamento placarentur.
units.tr: First, the Old Testament Scripture knows nothing of that fire at all. Although it often prescribes funerals, the funeral furnishings and all that discipline of mourning, it makes no mention of any subterranean fire. On the contrary, it says that the dead are gathered to their fathers, rest as if on a funeral couch, and that their state is even blessed. Behold, I will gather you to your fathers. 2 Kings 22:20. Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his. Num. 23:10. They enter into peace; they rest in their beds. Isa. 57:2. Nor did the bondage of the godly under the Old Testament last beyond this life, Heb. 2:15. It is a mere invention that the patriarchs ordered their bones to be carried to Canaan for no other purpose than that the ashes of the dead might be cleansed by the blood of sacrifices and their shades appeased by that atonement.

units.la: XXXIV. Pariter in Novo Test. purgatorio repugnant loca sequentia:
units.tr: XXXIV. Likewise in the New Testament, the following passages stand against a purgatory:

units.la: Amen dico vobis: qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in condemnationem non veniet. Sed transfivit a morte in vitam. Joh. 5: 24. Factum autem est ut moreretur mendicus, & adportaretur ab Angelis in sinum Abrahami. Luc. 16:22. Dico autem vobis, multos ab Oriente & Occidente venturos, & accubituros cum Abrahamo, & Isaaco, & Jacobo, in regno coelorum. Matth. 8: 11. Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Luc. 23:43. Praestitutum tempus meae dimissionis instat. Certamen illud praeclarum decertavi, cursum peregi, fidem servavi. Quod reliquum est, repositia est mihi corona justitia. 2. Tim. 4: 6, 7, 8. Desiderio tendens ad dimissionem, & ut cum Christo sim. Phil. 1: 23. Scimus enim nos, si terrestris hujus domus nostra tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, aedificium ex Deo habituros, domicilium non manu factum, aeternum in coelis. In hoc etenim suspiramus, expetentes domicilio nostro, quod de coelo est, superindui. 2. Cor. 5: 1, 2. Si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est, propter peccatum: Spiritus autem vita est propter justitiam. Rom. 8: 10. Beati a nunc mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur: ut requiescant a laboribus suis: & opera eorum sequuntur eos. Apoc. 14: 13. Statutum est hominibus, ut semel moriantur. Postea vero judicium. Hebr. 9: 27. Omnes enim nos manifestos fieri oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unusquisque reportet quae in corpore fecerit. 2. Cor. 5: 10. Unica enim oblatione consummavit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur. Hebr. 10: 14. Nulla igitur nunc iis est condemnatio, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Rom. 8: 1. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus is est qui justificat. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est &c. vs 33, 34.
units.tr: Verily, verily, I say unto you, he that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. John 5:24. And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. Luke 16:22. And I say unto you, that many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. Matt. 8:11. Today shalt thou be with me in paradise. Luke 23:43. The time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness. 2 Tim. 4:6, 7, 8. Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ. Phil. 1:23. For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven. 2 Cor. 5:1, 2. If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin; but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. Rom. 8:10. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on, that they may rest from their labours, and their works follow them. Rev. 14:13. It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. Heb. 9:27. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body. 2 Cor. 5:10. For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. Heb. 10:14. There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. Rom. 8:1. Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, etc. vv. 33, 34.

units.la: XXXV. Obstant & rationes a misericordia & justitia Dei deductae.
units.tr: XXXV. Arguments drawn from the mercy and justice of God also stand in the way.

units.la: Quarum illa non fert tam diros fidelium cruciatus, ignemque inferis ipsis parem: hæc autem eos multo magis repudiat, cum, satisfactione à Christo præstita plenissima, satisfactione per homines non opus sit; multo minus illa, quæ in operosis quibusdam nugis, ac rebus frivolis, consistit; & per quam ne sapienti quidem in terris judici satisfieret.
units.tr: The former does not bear such dreadful torments for the faithful, a fire equal to that of hell itself; the latter rejects them far more, since, with the satisfaction made by Christ being most full, there is no need of satisfaction through men, much less of that which consists in certain laborious trifles and frivolous things, and by which not even a wise judge on earth would be satisfied.

units.la: XXXVI. Tandem, ut veritatum, ita & errorum quidam nexus est, ac teterrimum conjugium; ac figmentum hoc sine aliorum errorum subsidio subsistere non potest. Nititur enim 1. discrimine peccatorum venialium & mortalium. 2. distinctione inter reatum culpæ & pœnæ. 3. Satisfactionibus Christi semiplenis, & peccata ante baptismum potissimum expiantibus. 4. Satisfactionibus denique meritisque nostris, ad ignis istius cruciatus levandos utilibus. Ut nefaria missarum sacra, propitiandis defunctorum manibus valitura; & immensam Pontificum auctoritatem; & sacerdotum avaritiam, ac lucra, & rapinas; dum morientium metus scrutantur, ultimosque eorum gemitus observant, & in quæstum suum convertunt, præterea. Satis enim istæ mendaciorum ac fraudum patefecunt insidiæ, & Caci domus atra, abjuratæque rapinæ.
units.tr: XXXVI. Finally, just as there is a connection among truths, so there is among errors, a most hideous marriage; and this fiction cannot stand without the support of other errors. For it rests (1) on the distinction between venial and mortal sins; (2) on the distinction between the guilt of sin and the punishment; (3) on Christ's half-complete satisfactions, which chiefly atone for sins before baptism; (4) on our own satisfactions and merits, useful for lightening the torments of that fire. Such are the impious sacrifice of the Mass, supposed to avail for appeasing the shades of the dead; the immense authority of the Popes; the greed, gains and plunder of the priests, who search out the fears of the dying, watch their last groans, and turn them to their own profit. Moreover, these snares of lies and frauds reveal enough, as do the dark house of Cacus and the abjured robberies.

units.la: XXXVII. Videnda nunc paucis pseudo-Ecclesiæ illius argumenta, quibus purgatorii flammas, sacerdotum suorum culinis adeo necessarias, tutari solent. Ac 1. congerunt diversa loca, ubi ignis in Scriptura mentio fit, qualia sunt Psal. 66: 12. Esai. 4: 4. & 9: 18. Mich. 7: 8. Quæ certe male ad ignem purgatorium referuntur; cum ad præsentem vitam pleraque spectent, & vel Dei castigationes, vel Spiritus ejus vim ac efficaciam, igneam & penetrabilem, denotent. 2. Ignis autem conflatoris, Mal 3: 3. Christi officium, in exploranda Scribarum scoria, veraque doctrina expurganda & defæcanda, notat. Quo munere præsertim Matth. 5, 6. & 7 functus legitur. 3. Pariterque ignis probationis, de quo 1. Cor. 3: 12. Cujusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit; non proprie dictus ignis est, non magis quam lignum, fœnum, stipula, ibi memorata; sed figuratus: quod vocabulum tanquam innuit. Nec de animabus purgandis, sed de doctrina doctoribusque explorandis ibi agitur. Quod cum veluti igne quodam peragendum sit, ille quidem latissime accipiendus est; non quidem pro igne purgatorio (per illum enim illa purgatio non peragitur) sed pro omni eo quod ignis vim in Scriptura habet. 4. Non melius lacus, in quo non erat aqua, Zach. 9: 11. huc pertinet. Quem de carcere Babylonico alii; alii rectius de veteris Ecclesiæ siti & angustiis expli-
units.tr: XXXVII. Let us now briefly consider the arguments by which that pseudo-Church usually defends the flames of purgatory, so necessary to its priests' kitchens. First, they gather various passages where Scripture mentions fire, such as Psal. 66: 12, Esai. 4: 4 and 9: 18, and Mich. 7: 8. These are certainly wrongly referred to purgatorial fire, since most of them concern the present life and denote either God's chastisements or the fiery and penetrating force and efficacy of his Spirit. 2. The fire of the refiner, Mal. 3: 3, denotes Christ's office of testing the dross of the scribes and purging and refining true doctrine. He is read to have discharged this office especially in Matth. 5, 6 and 7. 3. Likewise the fire of testing, of which 1 Cor. 3: 12: Each man's work, of what sort it is, the fire will test. This is not properly fire, no more than the wood, hay and stubble mentioned there; it is figurative, as the word tanquam (as it were) indicates. Nor is it a question there of cleansing souls, but of testing doctrine and teachers. Since this has to be done as if by some fire, the term must be taken very broadly: not for purgatorial fire (for that cleansing is not accomplished by it), but for everything that fire signifies in Scripture. 4. No better does the pit in which there was no water, Zech. 9: 11, belong here. Some explain it of the Babylonian prison, others more rightly of the thirst and straits of the old Church.

units.la: Sublatis adversariorum objectionibus. explicant. 5. Carcer, in quo ultimus quadrans persolvendus est, Matth. 5: 25. vel de præsenti vita intelligitur, mentio enim eorum est, qui adhuc in via sunt; vel de inferno; nullo autem modo de purgatorio. 6 Neque illud ex phrasi loquendi, non remittetur ipsi, neque in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro, Matth. 12: 32. exsculpi poterit. Non enim, quod in hoc sæculo remissum non est, in altero remitti posse, ibi innuitur; ut Pontificii concludere debent: sed contra peccatum, tam atrox, quod in hoc sæculo remissum non est, neque in furuto remittendum esse docetur. Sensus autem phrasis simpliciter est, non remittetur in æternum. Marc. 3: 29. Luc. 12: 10.
units.tr: Objections of the adversaries having been removed. They explain. 5. The prison in which the last farthing must be paid, Matth. 5: 25, is understood either of the present life (for it speaks of those who are still on the way) or of hell; but in no way of purgatory. 6. Nor can that be carved out of the phrase, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come, Matth. 12: 32. For it is not implied there that what is not forgiven in this age can be forgiven in the next, as the Papists ought to conclude. Rather, it is taught that against a sin so grave that it is not forgiven in this age, it is not to be forgiven in the age to come either. The sense of the phrase is simply: it shall never be forgiven. Marc. 3: 29; Luc. 12: 10.

units.la: XXXVIII. 7. Quod ad locum obscurissimum 1. Cor. 15: 29. attinet: Quid facient, qui baptizantur, vel lavantur, propter mortuos? cum multas veterum ac recentiorum interpretationes admittat; quas hic referre nihil attinet; illæ tamen omnes fere in eo conveniunt, quod per mortuos simpliciter ac promiscue ii, qui mortui sunt, & mortuorum status, intelligiuntur. Sicuti de resurrectione ac reditu à morte eo loci Apostolus agit. Solis autem Pontificiis, ex erroris sui præjudicio, mortui, in purgatorio cruciati, in mentem venerunt: qui tamen quomodo lotionibus ac baptismis nostris juvari possint, intelligi non potest. Quod ad reliquum interpretum diffensum pertinet, ille circa lotionem potissimum est: quam alii vulgarem, circa mortuo ustitatam, in resurrectionis spem: alii sacram, per baptismatis undam; quæ resurrectionis à morte publica universæ Ecclesiæ testera & obsignatio est: alii clinicorum, ita dictorum, baptismum: alii denique cæremonialem, in Veteri Testam. ob contactum mortuorum, Num. 19: 11. conf. Syr. 34: 27. rectius intelligunt; qua is, qui tactu cadaveris impurus redditus, atque isto tempore in statu mortuorum collocatus fuerat, postquam juxta legem ablutus erat, iterum in Ecclesiæ cœtum, & statum veluti viventium, admittebatur; quæ non levis futuræ olim è mortuorum statu resurrectionis figuratio erat. illa autem omnia huc non pertinent. Nec ultra locum hunc scrutari attinet. Ex cujus tenebris, & tot interpretamentorum fumo purgatoriis ignem & flammas educere velle, insanum est. XXXIX. 8. Addunt, hominem, usque ad extremum vitæ terminum, peccati reliquias secum trahere: cum autem nihil inquinatum in civitatem cælestem introiturum sit, Apoc. 21: 27. illum, antequam cœlo recipiatur, lustrari primum oportere. Quasi non una cum morte veteris hominis exuviæ ponantur: aut peccati regnum etiam ultra vitæ hujus limitem producendum sit. Qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato Rom. 6:7. Qui ingressus est in requiem ejus, etiam ipse requievit ab operibus suis, quemadmodum à suis Deus. Hebr. 4: 10. 9. Vix serium autem est, quod sub terra quoque homines quaerunt, qui Christo regnanti genua flectant, juxta illud Phil. 2: 10. In nomine Jesu omne genu se flectat — eorum qui sub terra sunt: quos non alibi quam in purgatorio deprehendi putant. Non aliud enim ibi dicitur, quam Christum viventium ac mortuorum dominum & judicem esse, juxta alium ejusdem Apostoli locum: In hoc enim Christus & mortuus est, & resurrexit, & revixit, ut mortuorum & vivorum dominus sit — omnes enim stabimus ad tribunal Christi. Rom. 14: 9, 10, 11.
units.tr: XXXVIII. 7. As for the most obscure passage, 1 Cor. 15: 29, What will they do who are baptized for the dead? Or why are they baptized for the dead? Since it admits many interpretations, old and recent, which it is pointless to report here, almost all of them nonetheless agree that by the dead are simply and indiscriminately understood those who have died and the state of the dead, just as the Apostle is there treating of resurrection and return from death. Only the Papists, from the prejudice of their error, have thought of the dead tormented in purgatory; yet how they could be helped by our washings and baptisms cannot be understood. As for the rest of the interpreters' disagreement, it concerns chiefly the word lotion (washing). Some understand a common washing practised over the dead in hope of resurrection; others the sacred washing through the water of baptism, which is a public testimony and seal of resurrection from death for the whole Church; others the so-called baptism of the sick-bed; and finally others, more rightly, a ceremonial washing in the Old Testament on account of contact with the dead, Num. 19: 11; cf. Syr. 34: 27. By this washing, one who had been rendered unclean by touching a corpse, and at that time placed in the state of the dead, after being cleansed according to the law, was admitted again into the assembly of the Church and the state of the living; this was no slight figure of the future resurrection from the state of the dead. But none of these things pertains here, and it is not worth searching this passage any further. To wish to draw purgatorial fire and flames out of its darkness and the smoke of so many interpretations is madness. XXXIX. 8. They add that a man carries the remnants of sin with him to the last end of his life, and since nothing defiled will enter the heavenly city, Apoc. 21: 27, he must first be cleansed before he is received into heaven. As if the old man's garments were not laid aside together with death, or as if the reign of sin had to be extended beyond the limit of this life. He who has died has been justified from sin, Rom. 6: 7. He who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his, Hebr. 4: 10. 9. Scarcely more serious is what they also seek under the earth: men who bow the knee to Christ reigning, according to Phil. 2: 10, at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those who are under the earth, whom they think are to be found nowhere but in purgatory. For nothing else is said there than that Christ is Lord and judge of the living and the dead, according to another passage of the same Apostle: For to this end Christ died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord of the dead and of the living… for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Rom. 14: 9, 10, 11.

units.la: XL. 10. Ad veteris Ecclesiae auctoritatem jam respondimus, primum Origenem talis ignis meminisse; qui tamen à Pontificiorum igne valde diversus sit. Concilia autem nulla illum agnoverunt, nisi nupera, Florentinum & Tridentinum. Quanquam superstitionem circa mortuos, cultumque omnem funereum antiquum fuisse non negamus. 11. Rectius vero Philosophorum, Poetarum, ac veterisGentilismi asslensum jactant. Quem illis facile concedimus, atque Theologiam istam Platonicam ultro largimur, dummodo nobis Hierosolymam Athenis anteferre, & magis porticum Salomonis, quam Stoicorum calcare liceat. 12. Tandem & mortuorum apparitiones, animarumque responsa adducunt. Quas nos falsas, merasque fraudes ac fabulas esse non dubitamus. Sicuti in Ecclesiis reformatis illos manium occursus, & ejulatus, exilesque voces, ignoramus. Quin & ipsa Romana Ecclesia multa ejus generis rejecit. 13. Denique quod utilem istum purgatorii terrorem putant, ad mentes hominum sollicitas habendas, ne nimia socordia prolabantur: id nec pium, nec usquequaque verum est. Non enim horror iste veram pietatem operatur, sed animum potius perplexum, & nimia formidine humilem abjectumque reddit. Quanquam alii parabili adeo ac promercali venia facile subterranei illius foci horrorem exuunt, & inexorabile fatum subjiciunt pedibus, strepitumque Acherontis avari. Rectius Apostolus: Scientes igitur terrorem Domini, homines ad fidem adducimus, Deo autem manifesti sumus. 2. Cor. 5: 11.
units.tr: XL. 10. We have already answered the authority of the early Church: first, that Origen does mention such a fire, but it is quite different from the fire of the Papists. No councils recognised it except recent ones, Florence and Trent. Yet we do not deny that there was superstition about the dead and that all the ancient funeral rites existed. 11. Those who boast of the agreement of philosophers, poets and ancient paganism are speaking more correctly. We readily concede that to them, and even give up to them that Platonic theology, provided we may prefer Jerusalem to Athens and the Porch of Solomon to the Stoics' colonnade. 12. Finally, they bring forward apparitions of the dead and answers from souls. We have no doubt that these are false, mere frauds and fables. In the reformed Churches we know nothing of those meetings with ghosts, wailing and thin voices. Indeed the Roman Church itself has rejected many things of this kind. 13. Lastly, as for their claim that the terror of purgatory is useful for keeping anxious minds from sinking into excessive complacency, that is neither godly nor true in every respect. For that terror does not produce true piety but rather makes the mind perplexed and abjectly humble through excessive fear. Yet others, by a ready and bought pardon, easily shed the horror of that underground hearth, and trample under foot inexorable fate and the roaring of greedy Acheron. The Apostle speaks more correctly: Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God. 2 Cor. 5:11.

units.la: XLI. Ut error errorem trahit, ita cum purgatorio cohaerent, pro mortuis vivorum suffragia & preces; & quacunque manibus eorum placandis adhibentur. Quae sollicite adeo in Concilio Tridentino commendantur.
units.tr: XLI. Just as one error draws another, so with purgatory there go the suffrages and prayers of the living for the dead, and whatever is used to appease their shades. These things are commended with great care at the Council of Trent.

units.la: 11. Preces pro mortuis.
units.tr: 11. Prayers for the dead.

units.la: XLII. Non diffitemur autem, morem istum antiquissimis temporibus in Ecclesia obtinuisse. Ac, hausta ex Ethnicorum parentalibus superstitione, privatas primo, pro singulorum pietate; mox publicas pro defunctis preces fusas; tandemque cum sacramentorum administratione sollemnes eas recitationes in ecclesia conjunctas fuisse. Differebant autem illæ ab hodierno Pontificiorum Ecclesiæ usu, tum objecto, tum scopo ac fine. Orabant enim veteres pro omnibus, qui defuncti erant, pro piis impiisque ex æquo. Ac pro his quidem, humano affectu, ut poena eorum nonnihil levaretur. Pro illis autem, tum ut refrigerio ac quiete frucrentur, cum perfrpe dubitarent, an ante supremi judicii diem Dei visione gauderent: tum ut regni Christi in terris, quod mille annorum futurum permulti credebant, & resurrectionis illius inter primos participes fierent: tum ut misericordiam in die ultimo consequerentur, ultimique incendii flammas (quod ipsorum purgatorium erat) mitiores experirentur: vel denique, ubi de beato defunctorum statu non dubitabant, vel solius affectus testandi causa ad tumulos eorum orabant. Ac sæpe etiam emortualia hæc sacra; & ad mortuorum memorias conventus, ac publicæ nominum illorum ex tabulis diptychis ad Domini mensam recitationes, nil nisi mortuorum elogia, & hymni, & gratiarum actiones erant: quibus defunctis de peractis vitæ laboribus gratulabantur; Deoque de servis istis suis, ac preciosa eorum morte, gratias agebant; & animæ immortalitatem, ac futuræ resurrectionis fidem, testabantur; ac viventibus denique eorum exempla ob oculos ponebant, ut eos ad idem virtutum certamen incitarent. Ut ex qualibuscunque istis precibus purgatorii fides in veteri Ecclesia probari non posset. Nam alias ob causas olim oratum est. Et Græca Ecclesia etiam hodie pro mortuis orat; & purgatorium tamen ignorat.
units.tr: XLII. We do not deny that this custom prevailed in the Church in the most ancient times. Drawing on the superstition of the heathen funeral feasts, prayers for the dead were first offered privately, according to each person's devotion; soon public prayers for the departed were poured out; and finally these solemn recitations were joined to the administration of the sacraments in the church. Those prayers, however, differed from the present practice of the Papist Church, in object, aim and purpose alike. The ancients prayed for all who had died, equally for the pious and the impious. For the latter they prayed out of human feeling, that their punishment might be somewhat lightened. For the former they prayed, first, that they might enjoy refreshment and rest, since they very much doubted whether they would enjoy the vision of God before the day of the last judgment; second, that they might share in the kingdom of Christ on earth, which very many believed would last a thousand years, and be among the first partakers of that resurrection; third, that they might obtain mercy on the last day and experience the flames of the final conflagration (which was their purgatory) as milder; or finally, where they had no doubt about the blessed state of the departed, they prayed at their tombs merely as a sign of their own affection. Often too these funeral rites and gatherings at the memorials of the dead, and the public recitation of their names from the diptychs at the Lord's table, were nothing but praises of the dead, hymns and thanksgivings. In these, they congratulated the departed on the labours of their lives now finished; they gave thanks to God for these his servants and for their precious death; they bore witness to the immortality of the soul and to the faith in a future resurrection; and finally they set the examples of these men before the living, to stir them up to the same contest of virtues. So, whatever such prayers were, the faith in purgatory cannot be proved from them in the ancient Church. For they prayed for other reasons in former times. And the Greek Church even today prays for the dead, and yet knows nothing of purgatory.

units.la: XLIII. Suffragiorum autem pro mortuis nomine hæc tria nunc intelligunt Pontificii, 1. missæ sacrificium, 2. orationes, 3. opera pœnalia & satisfactoria, eleemosynas, jejunia &c. Quibus indulgentias superadduntur. Dubitant autem, an per modum suffragii, an vero potestate clavium, per absolutionem illæ dispensentur. Sed vana ac fallacia hæc omnia.
units.tr: XLIII. Under the name of suffrages for the dead, the Papists now understand these three things: 1. the sacrifice of the mass; 2. prayers; 3. penal and satisfactory works, alms, fasting and so on. Indulgences are added to these. They doubt, however, whether these are dispensed by way of suffrage or by the power of the keys, through absolution. But all of this is empty and deceptive.

units.la: XLIV. 1. Si enim indulgentiarum, à Pontifice concessarum, ea vis, tum reliquo suffragiorum genere ne quidem opus erit, cum thesaurus earum infinitus sit. Et quid rei est, cur eas non concedat plenissimas, omnemque istum carcerem animabus captivis liberet? Sed ad quaestum eas unice comparatas esse, vel coecus videat: nam & promercales sunt; nec pauperibus facile datur; & ubi singularibus de causis erogantur, nunquam simpliciter dantur; & tot laqueis ac difficultatibus impeditae sunt, ut facile constet Pontifices ex isto suo thesauro non nisi fumos dare. 2. Opera, quae vocant, poenalia & satisfactoria ne vivis quidem, qui ea praestant, in meritum cedunt: hoc enim Christi satisfactioni repugnat: multo minus mortuis. Quibus quomodo hominum vivorum satisfactiones prosint, cum Christi meritum non profuerit; & quomodo nova illis post obitum merita comparari possint; intelligi non potest; & multi ex Scholasticis quoque negant. 3. de missae sacrificio postea agetur. Quanquam, si iustud valeat; atque illud nihil aliud quam sacrificii Christi applicatio sit, tot certe missarum demurmurationibus opus non erit. Nam, sacrificio hoc vel semel oblato, ab omnibus poenis liberari animam necesse est. 4. Orationes denique nostrae quomodo mortuis prosint, quibus liberandis nec Christi quidem sanguis & intercessio valere possunt? Nam iis ipsis, qui igne illo torquentur, ad ultimum quadrantem persolvendum ajunt. Et quid iis fiet, quibus vivorum suffragia forte desunt? an illi propterea diutius in illo carcere detinebuntur, quod largioribus eleemosynis Ecclesiae preces redimere nequiverunt? Sed orant etiam Pontificiorum ritualia pro iis, qui dormiunt in somno pacis; qui certe in purgatorio non sunt. Sicuti & pro Catechumenis, & infantibus, mox a baptismo mortuis, orant, quos tamen coelo protinus adscribunt. Quin & pro damnatis in inferno, qui sunt in profundo lacu, preces fundunt. Ut ex precibus eorum pro mortuis purgatorium tamen concludi non posset. Denique nulla Scripturae auctoritate, vel exemplo hae preces niituntur.
units.tr: XLIV. 1. For if indulgences granted by the Pontiff have such force, then no other kind of suffrage will be needed at all, since their treasury is infinite. And what reason is there why he would not grant them in the fullest measure and free all those captive souls from that whole prison? But that they were devised solely for profit, even a blind man can see: they are sold for money, they are not easily given to the poor, and when they are dispensed for particular reasons they are never given simply; and they are so hampered by snares and difficulties that it is easily evident the Pontiffs give out only smoke from that treasury. 2. So-called penal and satisfactory works do not even count as merit for the living who perform them, for this runs counter to Christ's satisfaction; much less do they count for the dead. How the satisfactions of living men could benefit the dead, when Christ's merit did not avail, and how new merits could be acquired for them after death, cannot be understood; and many of the Schoolmen also deny it. 3. The sacrifice of the Mass will be discussed later. Still, even if it were valid, and were nothing other than the application of Christ's sacrifice, there would certainly be no need for so many mumblings of masses. For once this sacrifice has been offered, even once, the soul must be freed from all penalties. 4. Finally, how do our prayers benefit the dead, when neither the blood nor the intercession of Christ can avail to free them? For they say that those very people who are tormented by that fire must pay the last farthing themselves. And what will become of those for whom the suffrages of the living perhaps fail? Will they be kept longer in that prison because they could not buy off the Church's prayers with more generous alms? But the Papists' rituals also pray for those who sleep in the sleep of peace, who certainly are not in purgatory. Likewise they pray for catechumens and infants who die soon after baptism, whom nonetheless they enrol at once in heaven. Indeed they pour out prayers even for the damned in hell, who lie in the deep lake. So from their prayers for the dead, purgatory could not in any case be inferred. Lastly, these prayers rest on no authority of Scripture or example.

units.la: XLV. Unicum occurrit Christi, pro mortuo deprecantis, exemplum; non ad animae levamen, sed ad corporis resuscitationem. Joh. 11:21, 22. Quod factum, cum miraculosum sit, ad imitationem rapi non potest. Catera autem, quae adversarii adferunt in hac controversia, valde levia sunt. Non enim veterum luctus, ac planctus, lessusque funebres, tales preces ac suffragia fuerunt, quae animas eorum levarent 1. Sam. 31:13. 2. Sam. 1:12. Nec Judae Maccabaei factum, de quo 2. Macc. 12:42 divinam auctoritatem habet; aut praesenti negotio applicari potest. Quis enim illum purgatorium credidisse opinetur? Mortui autem illi erant in peccato mortali; quod Pontificiorum hypothesibus adversatur. Quod ne vivis, isto peccato contaminatis,
units.tr: XLV. There occurs only one example of Christ praying for a dead man: not for the relief of the soul, but for the raising of the body. John 11:21, 22. Since that deed was miraculous, it cannot be drawn into imitation. The other things the opponents bring forward in this controversy are very weak. For the mourning, lamentations and funeral dirges of the ancients were not such prayers and suffrages as would relieve their souls: 1 Sam. 31:13; 2 Sam. 1:12. Nor can the deed of Judas Maccabeus, concerning which 2 Macc. 12:42 has divine authority, be applied to the present matter. For who would suppose he believed in purgatory? Those dead men were in mortal sin, which is opposed to the Papists' hypotheses, lest that sin should harm the living who were contaminated by it,

units.la: Ol. in contrarium allata solvuntur. tis, noceret; utque in eo mortui expiarentur, si forte, & beata olim reͳsurrectione potirentur, Deum sibi exorandum ac placandum duxit Judas;aut ita saltem mentem ejus interpretatur scriptor iste,ut sollicita ni· mis pietate modum excesserit:hoc autem Ecclesiæ legem non facit. Cum quodcunque hoc potius contra divinam legem sit, quæ preces & sacrificia pro mortuis ignorat. Recentiorum autem Judæorum exemplum, pro parentibus mortuis Deum rogantium, longe minus sequendum est. Quis enim gentis istius fabulas, & audacissimas nugas, de mortuorum statu ignorat? Sed & Novi Testamenti auctoritatem urgent; ac præsertim dicto Christi Luc. 16: 9. nituntur: Facite vobis amicos ex mammona injusto, vel instabili, ut, quando defecerit, accipiant vos in æterna tabernacula: h. e. qui pro vobis, in purgatorii igne laborantibus, Deum exorent. Quæ valde alienæ sunt. Cum sensus simpliciter sit, eleemosynas, ut præcipuos fidei fructus, mercede sua in altera vita non carere. Et si, per amicos, fideles, nostris eleemosynis adjuti, intelligendi sunt; illi, non vivi, ut Pontificiis placet, sed mortui potius, intelligi debent; qui improprie eos, à quibus benigniter olim habiti sunt, in cœlestia templa recipiunt. Vide similes loquendi modos, Esai. 14: 9. Ezech. 32:22,23. Tandem, ad veteris Ecclesiæ exempla supra respondimus: & morem illum, quanquam antiquissimum, tamen Apostolicis temporibus posteriorem, absque Dei mandato, ex ἐθελοθρησκεία, ac supervacua animi erga mortuos religione, ortum vidimus. Prout nullibi superstitio luxuriari magis solet, quam circa mortuos; quorum memoriam amamus, omnique ratione colimus; & quorum status obscurus, ac ultra præsentis sæculi captum est. Nunquam etiam ab illis de purgatorio, cogitatum ostendimus.
units.tr: Objections brought to the contrary are answered. ...harm; and that in it the dead might be expiated, if perhaps they might also one day obtain the blessed resurrection, Judas thought God had to be entreated and appeased; or at least the writer interprets his mind thus, that through an overly anxious piety he went beyond due measure. But this does not make a law for the Church, since the divine law is rather against it, and that law knows nothing of prayers and sacrifices for the dead. The example of the more recent Jews, who ask God on behalf of their dead parents, is much less to be followed. For who does not know that nation's fables and most audacious nonsense about the state of the dead? But they also press the authority of the New Testament, and chiefly lean on the saying of Christ, Luke 16:9: Make for yourselves friends out of unrighteous mammon, or unstable mammon, so that when it fails they may receive you into the everlasting tabernacles: that is, those who, by praying to God, will help you who are labouring in the fire of purgatory. These are very far from the meaning. For the sense is simply that alms, as the chief fruit of faith, will not lack their reward in the next life.
