And if by "friends" faithful people aided by our alms are to be understood, they should be understood not as living, as the Papists like, but rather as dead, who improperly receive into the heavenly dwellings those by whom they were once kindly treated. See similar modes of speech at Isa. 14:9 and Ezek. 32:22, 23. Finally, to the examples of the ancient Church we have answered above; and we have seen that that custom, though very ancient, nonetheless arose in later times than the apostolic ones, without God's command, from will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] and a superfluous religious feeling of the mind towards the dead. Superstition is nowhere wont to run riot more than around the dead, whose memory we love and honour in every way, and whose state is obscure and beyond the grasp of this present age. Nor have we ever shown that they thought about purgatory.

units.la: XLVI. Mira autem conversione ex hoc errore contrarius etiam error natus est: ut cum primitus pro sanctis demortuis suffragia fierent, dein mutato errore, illorum suffragia pro nobis captata sint, atque hoc nomine ipsi invocati, etiamnumque à multis invocentur.
units.tr: XLVI. By a strange reversal, a contrary error has also arisen from this one: whereas at first prayers were offered for the holy dead, afterwards, when the error was changed, the suffrages of those same dead were sought on our behalf, and under this title they were invoked, and are still invoked by many.

units.la: Quod ut Origenis & Cypriani ætate, sive circa A. C. 250. particularis intercessionis nomine primitus in Ecclesiam invehi coepit; ita sequenti demum sæculo, circa A. C. 370. mortuorum invocatio illi superaddita est, præeuntibus publice illis populo, quibus cura ejus instituendi commissa erat: donec, licet inter varias contradictiones, gliscente superstitione, septimo & octavo sæculo preces ad sanctos, præcipue autem Beatam Virginem, insigniter promotæ sunt; sequentiumque sæculorum scriptoribus, præsertim
units.tr: As this began to be introduced into the Church in the age of Origen and Cyprian, that is, around the year 250 after Christ, under the name of particular intercession; so only in the following century, around the year 370, the invocation of the dead was added to it, with the public lead of those to whom the care of instructing the people had been entrusted. Then, although amid various objections, as superstition grew, prayers to the saints, and especially to the Blessed Virgin, were remarkably promoted in the seventh and eighth centuries; and among the writers of the following centuries, especially the Schoolmen, who devoted all their effort to this, superstition and idolatry at last prevailed; and in the last age this was also confirmed by the Council of Trent.

units.la: Preces ad mortuos. tim Scholasticis, omnem operam huc conferentibus, obtinuit tandem superstitio & idololatria; quæ superiori quoque sæculo à Tridentino Concilio roborata est. Quæ quum divinum honorem præcipue lædat, primumque Decalogi præceptum impetat, alio loco examinanda & confutanda erit. Sufficit hoc loco monere, præstare qualibuscunque illis circa mortuos officiis abstinere, & non nimis affectui indulgere; istudque precum ac officiorum commercium, omnemque Sanctorum communionem, juxta Scripturam, non cum fato functis, sed cum viventibus exercere; cum mortui partem inter viventes non amplius habeant, & alterius Ecclesiæ cives facti sint.
units.tr: Prayers to the dead. Since this chiefly injures the divine honour and assails the first precept of the Decalogue, it will be examined and refuted in another place. It is enough to advise at this point that we abstain from any services whatever towards the dead, and not indulge our affections too much; and that this exchange of prayers and offices, and all communion of saints, according to Scripture, be exercised not with those who have departed this life, but with the living, since the dead no longer have a part among the living and have become citizens of another Church.

units.la: LIBER VII. De Verbo & Sacramentis N. T.
units.tr: BOOK VII. On the Word and Sacraments of the New Testament

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS PRIMUS DE Revelatione & Verbo sub Oeconomia N. FOEDERIS. CAPUT I.
units.tr: LOCUS FORTY-FIRST: ON REVELATION AND THE WORD UNDER THE ECONOMY OF THE NEW COVENANT. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Verbo Dei sub N. T. hominumque circa illud laboribus.
units.tr: On the Word of God under the New Testament and men's labours concerning it.

units.la: Ostquam plerasque doctrinae Christianae partes pertractavimus, Christumque cum beneficiis suis nudavimus; sequuntur nunc tantorum beneficiorum obsides Sacramenta; quae Christi beneficiorumque ejus fidem, verbo Euangelii in nobis genitam, una cum verbo obsignant roborantque, & simul praecipuam cultus N. T. partem conficiunt. Quemadmodum enim in omni Oeconomiae foederis divini parte, hactenus tres Theologiae partes nobis occurrerunt, nimirum divina praecepta, promissa, & denique ritus; quorum illa obedientiae, ista fidei, hi vero cultus externi norma sunt: ita etiam in hac ultima divinae Oeconomiae sub N. T. parte eadem nobis se exhibent. Praecepta enim vitae omnia ab Euangelio adoptata, & humanis scoriis sordibusque defaecata, perfectissima plenitudine & latitudine, a Servatore nobis propósita, superius vidimus. Fidei vero, omnibus figuris aenigmatisque evolutae, canonem exhibuit nobis in suavissimis suis promissis Euangelium. Succedat ergo nunc ultimo loco rituum cerimoniarumque sacrarum minime operosus apparatus, in verbi, quod sub N. T. nobis revelatum est, prædicatione, sacramentorumque illi additorum administratione: quæ, una cum precum spiritualium simplicissimis ritibus, N. T. externum cultum absolvunt.
units.tr: Now that we have treated most parts of Christian doctrine and have laid bare Christ with his benefits, there follow the sacraments, the pledges of these great benefits. They seal and strengthen, together with the word, the faith in Christ and his benefits that the gospel word has begotten in us, and at the same time they make up the chief part of the worship of the New Testament. For just as in every part of the divine economy of the covenant, the three parts of theology have so far presented themselves to us, namely the divine precepts, promises, and finally rites, of which the first are the rule of obedience, the second of faith, and the third of external worship, so also in this last part of the divine economy under the New Testament, the same things show themselves to us. For we have seen above that all the precepts of life, adopted from the gospel and cleansed of human dross and filth, were set before us by the Saviour in the most perfect fullness and breadth. Of faith, unfolded from all figures and enigmas, the gospel has given us the rule in its most sweet promises. Let there now follow, in the last place, the very unburdensome apparatus of sacred rites and ceremonies: the preaching of the word revealed to us under the New Testament, and the administration of the sacraments added to it. These, together with the very simple rites of spiritual prayer, complete the external worship of the New Testament.

units.la: II. Adulta igitur œconomia Mosaica, Deus supremam manum relationi sui jam impositurus, illi operi perficiundo filium suum unigenitum, ab æterno destinatum, ab initio autem promissum, in temporis plenitudine misit. Hebr. 1: 1,2. Gal. 4:4. Unde ἀπόστολος καὶ ἀρχιερεὺς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν dicitur, Hebr. 3: 1. & ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίστεως, c. 12: 2. Inde hæc revelatio Dei, ut ultima, ita & perfectissima fuit. Ut nobis curiositate opus non sit post J. Christum, nec inquisitione post Euangelium: cum credimus, nihil desideramus ultra credere: hoc enim prius credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debemus; ut recte & eleganter Tertull. præscript. adversf. hæres.
units.tr: II. Therefore, when the Mosaic economy had come to maturity, God, about to put the final hand to his own revelation, sent his only-begotten Son, destined from eternity and promised from the beginning, in the fullness of time, to bring that work to completion (Heb. 1:1, 2; Gal. 4:4). Hence he is called "the apostle and high priest of our confession" (Heb. 3:1) and "the author and finisher of faith" (Heb. 12:2) [ἀπόστολος καὶ ἀρχιερεὺς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν; ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίστεως]. Thus this revelation of God was, as the last, so also the most perfect. So that, as Tertullian rightly and elegantly says in the Prescription against Heretics, we have no need of curiosity after Jesus Christ, nor of inquiry after the gospel: when we believe, we desire nothing further to believe, for we believe this first, that there is nothing else we ought to believe.

units.la: III. Revelationis hujus Christus Dominus, qui ejus cognitionem habebat perfectissimam, utpote filius unigenitus, qui in sinu Patris fuerat, quique eum edidisset, Joh. 1: 8. ipse in diebus carnis suæ prædicatione. Eamque partim viva voce, partim per Spiritum, quem dono à Patre post ascensionem accepit, cum discipulis suis, qui doctrinam ejus in omnes gentes propagaturi erant, in usum totius Ecclesiæ, communicavit: qui non solum viva voce, sed & verbo scripto, in libris N. T. illam nobis exhibuerunt; propheticaetiam, ut sub vetere œconomia quoque factum erat, in partes veniente. Unde fundamento Apostolorum & Prophetarum inædificati dicimur, Eph. 2:20. quos Novi Testamenti, ut Apostolos, ita Prophetas esse, apparet ex c. 3:5. & 4:11. Prohetiam nempe in N. T. copiosam fore, prædixit Joël. c. 2:28. Apostolos in prophetia excelluisse notum est: & somnia ac visiones secundum literam etiam non defuisse, historia Apostolica docet, & sanctissima Johannis Apocalypsis. Prophetæ etiam, qui demonstrant veritam Euangelii ex Scripturis, semper & in perpetuum Ecclesiæ dantur. Et cum clavem cognitionis à nullo homine aut cathedra nunc repetant filii Dei, cum lex Dei in omnium ore & cogitatione collocata sit, Jer. 31:33. ut nunc omnes Dei discipuli sint, Esai. 54:13. inde certe omnes qui credunt Euangelio, illudque cum prophetiis comparant, prophetant. Præterquam quod, cum in Euangelio & prophetiis antecedentibus contineantur quoque promissiones de rebus futuris, & de amplificatione regni Christi, & denunciationes etiam judiciorum Dei, & præmonitiones de futuris scandalis; qui eas prophetias intelligunt, credunt & inculcant, etiam hoc modo prophetant.
units.tr: III. Christ the Lord, who had the most perfect knowledge of this revelation, as "the only-begotten Son who was in the bosom of the Father and had declared him" (John 1:18), himself published it in the days of his flesh by preaching. And he imparted it, partly by the living voice and partly through the Spirit, whom he received from the Father after his ascension, to his disciples, who were to spread his teaching among all nations, for the use of the whole Church. These men set it before us not only by the living voice but also in written word, in the books of the New Testament, and also prophetically, as had happened under the old economy, when matters came to be divided. Hence we are said to be "built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets" (Eph. 2:20), and it is clear from chapters 3:5 and 4:11 that the apostles of the New Testament were prophets as well as apostles. Joel foretold that prophecy would be abundant in the New Testament (Joel 2:28). That the apostles excelled in prophecy is well known, and the Apostolic history and the most holy Apocalypse of John show that dreams and visions, in the literal sense, were not lacking either. Prophets who demonstrate the truth of the gospel from the Scriptures are also given to the Church always and for ever. And since the sons of God now seek the key of knowledge from no man or chair, since the law of God is placed in the mouth and thought of all (Jer. 31:33), so that now all are "taught of God" (Isa. 54:13), certainly all who believe the gospel and compare it with the prophecies prophesy. Moreover, since the gospel and the preceding prophecies also contain promises of future things, of the enlargement of Christ's kingdom, denunciations of God's judgements, and forewarnings of future offences, those who understand these prophecies, believe and inculcate them, also prophesy in this way.

units.la: LIBER VII. De Verbo & Sacramentis N. T.
units.tr: LIBER VII. On the Word and Sacraments of the New Testament

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS PRIMUS DE Revelatione & Verbo sub Oeconomia N. FOEDERIS. CAPUT I.
units.tr: FORTY-FIRST PLACE: ON REVELATION AND THE WORD UNDER THE ECONOMY OF THE NEW COVENANT. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Verbo Dei sub N. T. hominumque circa illud laboribus.
units.tr: On the Word of God under the New Testament and the labours of men concerning it.

units.la: I. OSTquam plerasque doctrinæ Christianæ partes pertractavimus, Christumque cum beneficiis suis nudavimus; sequuntur nunc tantorum beneficiorum obsides Sacramenta; quæ Christi beneficiorumque ejus fidem, verbo Euangelii in nobis genitam, una cum verbo obsignant roborantque, & simul præcipuam cultus N. T. partem conficiunt. Quemadmodum enim in omni Oeconomiæ fœderis divini parte, hactenus tres Theologiæ partes nobis occurrerunt, nimirum divina præcepta, promissa, & denique ritus; quorum illa obedientiæ, ista fidei, hi vero cultus externi norma sunt: ita etiam in hac ultima divinæ Oeconomiæ sub N. T. parte eædem nobis se exhibent. Præcepta enim vitæ omnia ab Euangelio adoptata, & humanis sccoriis sordibusque defæcata, perfectissima plenitudine & latitudine, à Servatore nobis proposita, superius vidimus. Fidei vero, omnibus figuris ænigmatisque evolutæ, canonem exhibuit nobis in suavissimis suis promissis Euangelium. Succedat ergo nunc ultimo loco rituum cerimoniarumque sacrarum minime operosus apparatus, in verbi, quod sub N. T. nobis revelatum est, prædicatione, sacramentorumque illi additorum administratione: quæ, una cum precum spiritualium simplicissimis ritibus, N. T. externum cultum absolvunt.
units.tr: I. Having now treated most parts of Christian doctrine and laid Christ bare with his benefits, there follow the sacraments, the pledges of these great benefits. They seal and strengthen the faith in Christ and in his benefits, which is begotten in us by the word of the Gospel, together with the word itself, and at the same time they make up the chief part of the worship of the New Testament. For just as in every part of the economy of the divine covenant we have so far met three parts of theology, namely the divine precepts, promises and finally rites, of which the first is the rule of obedience, the second of faith, and the third of external worship, so the same appear to us in this last part of the divine economy under the New Testament. We have already seen that all the precepts of life, taken over from the Gospel and cleansed of human dross and filth, were set before us by the Saviour in the most perfect fullness and breadth. The Gospel has given us the canon of faith, unfolded from all figures and enigmas, in its most sweet promises. So now, in the last place, there follows the least laborious apparatus of rites and sacred ceremonies: the preaching of the word revealed to us under the New Testament and the administration of the sacraments added to it. These, together with the simplest rites of spiritual prayers, complete the external worship of the New Testament.

units.la: II. Adulta igitur œconomia Mosaica, Deus supremam manum revelationi sui jam impositurus, illi operi perficiendo filium suum unigenitum, ab æterno destinatum, ab initio autem promissum, in temporis plenitudine misit. Hebr. 1: 1,2. Gal. 4:4. Unde ἀπόστολος καὶ ἀρχιερεὺς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν dicitur, Hebr. 3: 1. & ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίστεως, c. 12: 2. Inde hæc revelatio Dei, ut ultima, ita & perfectissima fuit. Ut nobis curiositate opus non sit post J. Christum, nec inquisitione post Evangelium: cum credimus, nihil desideramus ultra credere: hoc enim prius credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debemus; ut recte & eleganter Tertull. præscript. adverf. hæresf.
units.tr: II. Therefore, when the Mosaic economy had matured, God, about to put the final hand to his revelation, sent his only-begotten Son, destined from eternity and promised from the beginning, in the fullness of time, to bring that work to completion (Heb. 1:1, 2; Gal. 4:4). Hence he is called "the apostle and high priest of our confession" (Heb. 3:1) [ἀπόστολος καὶ ἀρχιερεὺς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν] and "the author and perfecter of faith" (ch. 12:2) [ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίστεως]. Hence this revelation of God was as final as it was most perfect. So, as Tertullian rightly and elegantly says in the Prescription against the heretics, we have no need of curiosity after Jesus Christ, nor of inquiry after the Gospel: since we believe, we want nothing further to believe, for we believe this first, that there is nothing else we ought to believe.

units.la: III. Revelationis hujus Christus Dominus, qui ejus cognitionem habebat perfectissimam, utpote filius unigenitus, qui in sinu Patris fuerat, quique eum edidit, Joh. 1: 8. ipse in diebus carnis suæ præconfuit: eamque partim viva voce, partim per Spiritum, quem dono à Patre post ascensionem accepit, cum discipulis suis, qui doctrinam ejus in omnes gentes propagaturi erant, in usum totius Ecclesiæ, communicavit: qui non solum viva voce, sed & verbo scripto, in libris N. T. illam nobis exhibuerunt; prophetica etiam, ut sub vetere œconomia quoque factum erat, in partes veniente. Unde fundamento Apostolorum & Prophetarum inædificati dicimur, Eph. 2:20. quos Novi Testamenti, ut Apostolos, ita Prophetas esse, apparet ex c. 3:5. & 4:11. Prohetiam nempe in N. T. copiosam fore, prædixit Joël. c. 2:28. Apostolos in prophetia excelluisse notum est: & somnia ac visiones secundum literam etiam non defuisse, historia Apostolica docet, & sanctissima Johannis Apocalypsis. Prophetæ etiam, qui demonstrant veritatem Evangelii ex Scripturis, semper & in perpetuum Ecclesiæ dantur. Et cum clavem cognitionis à nullo homine aut cathedra nunc repetant filii Dei, cum lex Dei in omnium ore & cogitatione collocata sit, Jer. 31:33. ut nunc omnes Dei discipuli sint, Esai. 54:13. inde certe omnes qui credunt Evangelio, illudque cum prophetiis comparant, prophetant. Præterquam quod, cum in Evangelio & prophetiis antecedentibus contineantur quoque promissiones de rebus futuris, & de amplificatione regni Christi, & denunciationes etiam judiciorum Dei, & præmonitiones de futuris scandalis; qui eas prophetias intelligunt, credunt & inculcant, etiam hoc modo prophetant. Quibus omnibus modis major & abundantior est prophetia in N. T. quam unquam fuit in V. T. modo non negligatur & contemnatur. Unde etiam visionem (quæ ante Christi adventum adhuc erat ad tempus definitum, Hab. 2:3.) & Prophetam (Christus obsignare dicitur, Dan. 9:24.
units.tr: III. Christ the Lord himself, who had the most perfect knowledge of this revelation, as the "only-begotten Son who was in the bosom of the Father and has declared him" (John 1:18), set it forth in the days of his flesh. He communicated it partly by the living voice and partly through the Spirit, whom he received from the Father after his ascension, to his disciples, who were to spread his teaching among all nations, for the use of the whole Church. They set it forth to us not only by the living voice but also in written form, in the books of the New Testament, and, as had also happened under the old economy, prophetically as the matter arose. Hence we are said to be "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets" (Eph. 2:20), and that the apostles, like the prophets, belong to the New Testament appears from ch. 3:5 and 4:11. Joel foretold that prophecy would be abundant in the New Testament (ch. 2:28). That the apostles excelled in prophecy is well known, and that dreams and visions in the literal sense were not lacking is taught by the apostolic history and by the most holy Apocalypse of John. Prophets, too, who demonstrate the truth of the Gospel from the Scriptures, are always and perpetually given to the Church. Since the sons of God now seek the key of knowledge from no man or chair, since the law of God is placed in the mouth and thought of all (Jer. 31:33), so that now all are disciples of God (Isa. 54:13), certainly all who believe the Gospel and compare it with the prophecies prophesy in this way. Besides, since the Gospel and the earlier prophecies also contain promises concerning future things and the enlargement of Christ's kingdom, and also announcements of God's judgments and warnings of future offences, those who understand these prophecies, believe and inculcate them, also prophesy in this way. In all these ways prophecy is greater and more abundant in the New Testament than it ever was in the Old, provided it is not neglected and despised. Hence also the vision (which before Christ's coming was still for an appointed time, Hab. 2:3) and the prophet (of whom it is said that Christ seals him, Dan. 9:24).

units.la: IV. Ex hisce ergo Veteris Novique Testamenti libris Verbi ac revelationis omnis completus tandem & confectus est canon: quem cum operi huic, tanquam illius fundamentum & principium, præstruxerimus, hoc tantum relictum nobis videtur, ut varios circa illum Iudæorum Christianorum que labores, qui quidem in N. T. tempora inciderunt, compendio hic edisseramus. Et utrorumque quidem labores vel in ipso verbo scripto hactenus tradito conservando ornandoque; vel ex adverso in illo per humanum verbum spuriave scripta corrumpendo occupati fuerunt.
units.tr: IV. From these books of the Old and New Testaments, then, the whole canon of the Word and revelation has at last been completed and made whole. Having set this down as the foundation and beginning of this work, there seems to remain only that we briefly set out here the various labours of Jews and Christians concerning it, which indeed fall within New Testament times. Both groups have been occupied either in preserving and adorning the written word itself, as handed down so far, or, on the other side, in corrupting it through human words or spurious writings.

units.la: V. Labores Iudæorum verbo scripto conservando ornandoque impensi, Masoræ nomine vulgo veniunt. Masora nimirum, quasi traditio & genus disciplinæ, a מסר tradidit, nihil aliud est, quam Doctrina Iudæorum critica, circa rectam lectionem S. Scripturæ; quique eam tractant, vocantur Masorethæ, qui memorabili diligentia consideraverunt omnes S. Scripturæ litteras, carumque diversas formas, & situm, & numerum in singulis libris; tum etiam vocales, ubi aliqua a communi punctorum regula deflectit; & accentus; & vocabula integra, ad eorum defectus, situm, significationes attendentes; denique & versus in singulis Scripturæ libris, & in singulis Pentateuchi sectionibus, ad calculum vocarunt, & medium quemque librorum versum annotarunt.
units.tr: V. The labours of the Jews devoted to preserving and adorning the written word are commonly known by the name Masora. Masora, namely "tradition" and a kind of discipline, from the Hebrew מסר [masar], "to hand down", is nothing other than the critical doctrine of the Jews concerning the correct reading of Holy Scripture. Those who handle it are called Masorites. With remarkable diligence they examined all the letters of Holy Scripture, their various forms, their position and their number in each book; then also the vowels, where something departs from the common rule of the points; and the accents; and whole words, attending to their defects, positions and meanings. Finally they also counted the verses in each book of Scripture and in each section of the Pentateuch, and noted the middle verse of each book.

units.la: VI. Observarunt quoque xviii. voces, quæ תקון סופרים correctio scribarum vocantur; quas quia verebantur ne depravarentur, ordinarunt ut legerentur sicut scriptæ sunt, quam vis textus cohærentia aliud requirere videretur: & alias v. voces, quæ vocantur שמור כתיב ablatio scribarum, ex quibus Vau, iis adscriptum, auferri volunt: tandem etiam circa notationem variarum lectionem Keri & Ketibh, quæ ad mille ferme recensentur, eorum diligentia & studium occupatum fuit.
units.tr: VI. They also observed eighteen words which are called תקון סופרים [tiqqun sopherim], "correction of the scribes". Because they feared these might be corrupted, they ordered that they be read as they are written, although the coherence of the text seemed to require otherwise. They also noted five words called שמור כתיב [sevir ketiv], "removal of the scribes", from which they wish the vav added to them to be removed. Lastly, their diligence and zeal were occupied with the notation of the variant readings, the Keri and Ketib, which are reckoned at nearly a thousand.

units.la: VII. Originem variarum istarum lectionum, & studii Masorethici quod attinet, antiquiores quædam ex illis videntur, quam ut omnes Tiberiensibus, ineptiores autem aliæ, quam ut Esræ tribui possint. Non errant ergo fortasse qui ab Esræ temporibus earum primordia deducunt: sequentibus vero sæculis, usque ad ætatem Tiberiensium, circa annum Christi 500. studii ejus consummatio adscribenda est. Ita ut nullus Masorethárum confessus vel Synogoga unquam fuerit, verum Doctores quidam variis sæculis & locis studio huic incubuerint.
units.tr: VII. As for the origin of these variant readings and of the Masoretic study, some of them seem too ancient to be ascribed to the Tiberians, while others are too trivial to be attributed to Ezra. It is therefore perhaps not wrong of those who trace their beginnings back to the times of Ezra. But the completion of this study must be assigned to the following centuries, down to the age of the Tiberians, about the year of Christ 500. So no Masorite ever made a confession, nor did any synagogue ever do so; rather, certain teachers in various centuries and places devoted themselves to this study.

units.la: VIII. Characterum seu literarum permutationem, Esræ à multis adscriptam, adeoque ad hanc œconomiam non pertinentem, breviter attigimus lib. IV. cap. XXXVII. §. VIII. Punctorum seu vocalium originem quod attinet (de qua obiter quoque aliquid ibi diximus) variæ sunt de illa sententiæ; cum alii ea antiqua, alii nova esse velint. Ita ad Masorethas auctores ea referent Elias Levita, superioris sæculi Rabbinus, & ante eum Aben Ezra; quibus Christiani multi astipulantur, qui punctorum novitatem defendunt; quamvis vario sensu: dum alii ea simul uno tempore à Tiberiensibus addita; alii istud studium multis etiam sæculis deinceps continuatum censent; alii rursus divino suggestu; alii humano ingenio ea adscripta volunt.
units.tr: VIII. We have briefly touched on the change of characters or letters, ascribed by many to Ezra and therefore not belonging to this economy, in Book IV, ch. XXXVII, §VIII. As to the origin of the points, or vowels (about which we also said something in passing there), opinions vary, since some want them to be ancient and others new. Thus Elias Levita, a rabbi of the last century, and before him Aben Ezra, refer them to the Masorites as authors. Many Christians agree with them and defend the novelty of the points, though in different senses: some think they were added all at once by the Tiberians, others think this study was continued for many centuries afterwards, others again hold that they were added under divine inspiration, and others that they were added by human ingenuity.

units.la: IX. De quibus licet in utramque partem probabiliter disseratur, hoc tamen statui posse videtur. 1. Linguæ Hebrææ vocales & puncta nunquam defuisse. 2. an autem nudo sono, an vero notis & figuris eas semper distinxerint, incertum esse. 3. Et punctis antiqua exemplaria caruisse plane probabile est, cum iis careant litteræ Samaritanæ, quibus multa exemplaria descripta fuisse nemo negat, & iis quoque careant Tragumim, & libri vetustiores Arabici, & Syriaci, & hodierna quoque Rabbinorum scripta. 4. linguæ notitiam & consuetudinem legendi fecisse, ut puncta vix videantur fuisse necessaria: nisi forte paucissimis in locis, privato scribarum, aut etiam puerorum usui. Unde sicut ante dispersionem non magna illorum fuit necessitas, ita neque ante illam inventa & recepta fuisse liquet. Nihil ergo absurdi erit, si sequentibus sæculis, cum in Palæstina adhuc hærerent Judæorum Scholæ, ante plenariam dispersionem, illa textui sacro addita ponamus. Saltem non adeo antiqua sunt, sed posteriorum temporum inventa: quod variis argumentis ostendi posset. 5. divina promissione nos niti posse. Deus enim voluit legem conservari in ore Judæorum, usque ad ultimos dies, Cui fini jam inservium puncta, in dispersione. Quando autem addi coeperunt, etiam agnita sunt, ut testes usitatæ lectionis. Quod ad fidei firmitatem sufficit.
units.tr: IX. Although these questions may be probably argued on either side, this much seems capable of being established. 1. The Hebrew vowels and points never failed the language. 2. Whether they always distinguished the vowels by bare sound or by signs and figures is uncertain. 3. It is quite probable that the ancient manuscripts lacked points, since the Samaritan letters, in which no one denies that many manuscripts were written, lack them, and so do the Targums, the older Arabic and Syriac books, and the present-day writings of the rabbis too. 4. Knowledge of the language and the custom of reading made the points hardly necessary, except perhaps in a very few places, for the private use of scribes or even of boys. Hence, just as their need was not great before the dispersion, so it is clear that they were not invented and received before it. Nothing absurd, then, will follow if we suppose that they were added to the sacred text in the following centuries, while the schools of the Jews still persisted in Palestine, before the full dispersion. At least they are not so ancient, but inventions of later times, which could be shown by various arguments. 5. We may rest on divine promise. For God willed the law to be preserved in the mouth of the Jews until the last days, and to this end the points served in the dispersion. But when they began to be added, they were also recognised, as witnesses of the usual reading. This is enough for the firmness of faith.

units.la: X. Divisionem commatum, seu Versuum in V. T. quod attinet, eam Elias Levita Masorethis Tiberiensibus adscribit; statuens, juxta Rabbinorum dictum, totam legem fuisse olim quasi unum versum: alii, vel ab Esra & viris Synagogæ magnæ, vel ab ipsis librorum auctoribus eam
units.tr: X. As for the division into verses (Versuum) in the Old Testament, Elias Levita ascribes it to the Tiberian Masoretes, holding, in line with the saying of the rabbis, that the whole Law was once like a single verse. Others derive it from Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue, or from the authors of the books themselves, and

units.la: Pars II. — Pp deducunt. Verius tamen longe putamus, versuum distinctionem, non à Mose aut librorum sacrorum auctoribus, sed à Masorethis itidem esse. XI. Versus autem N. Foederis praecedenti saeculo additi dicuntur; cum omnes codices ante excusi versuum distinctione careant. Et vulgo quidem R. Stephano hoc adscribitur.
units.tr: Part II. The Papists derive it. We think it far more probable, however, that the division into verses is likewise the work of the Masoretes and not of Moses or the authors of the sacred books. XI. The verses of the New Testament are said to have been added in the previous century, since all the earlier printed codices lack the division into verses. And it is commonly ascribed to Robert Estienne.

units.la: XII. Distinctionem Capitum autem quod spectat, illa necab ipsis auctoribus, nec ab Esra est, sed recentioris longe originis, quae quinque saecula non excedit: sive illa distinctio incerti auctoris sit, sive Stephano Langtono, Episcopo Cantuariensi, qui saeculo xiii. floruit, sive Hugoni Cardinali attribuenda. Quod Christianorum institutum deinceps ipsi quoque Judaei approbarunt & adoptarunt. Speciaiiores pentateuchi in varias sectiones divisiones Judaeis relinquimus.
units.tr: XII. As for the division into chapters, it is neither from the authors themselves nor from Ezra, but of much more recent origin, not older than five centuries. Whether that division is the work of an unknown author, or is to be attributed to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, who flourished in the thirteenth century, or to Hugh the Cardinal, it was adopted by the Christians, and afterwards the Jews themselves approved and adopted it. The more detailed division of the Pentateuch into various sections we leave to the Jews.

units.la: XIII. Notis etiam distinctionum & accentuum carnerunt veteres, nec in eorum libris ex inveniuntur, sed quicquid earum hodie iis inest, id omne est à recentioribus additum. Quod & ipsum praesertim in Scriptura N. T. locum habet. Non enim ab Evangelistis & Apostolis notae hae additae, sed longo post tempore, cum ea jam repertae essent, etiam sacris libris à Christianis adjectae sunt. Hinc varia adhibetur in quibusdam locis interpunctio; unde etiam magna sensus fluit varietas.
units.tr: XIII. The ancients also lacked the marks of punctuation and accents; they are not found in their books. Whatever such marks are present in them today was all added by more recent writers. This holds especially for the text of the New Testament. For these marks were not added by the Evangelists and Apostles but long afterwards, when they had already been devised, and they were added by Christians even to the sacred books. Hence a varied punctuation is used in some places, from which also arises a great variety of meaning.

units.la: XIV. Sed & laudabilis Judaeorum pariter & Christianorum opera desudavit, in communicandis sacratissimis verbis divini mysteriis cum alterius linguae vel dialecti populis, per codicis sancti in illas versiones.
units.tr: XIV. But the praiseworthy labour of both Jews and Christians has also been expended in communicating the most sacred words and the divine mysteries to peoples of other languages or dialects, through translations of the holy codex into those tongues.

units.la: XV. Quem in finem praecipuas tum V. tum N. T. versiones perlustrabimus. Et V. quidem Test. versiones praecipuae duplices sunt: factae nimirum in gratiam Judaeorum dispersorum, cum inter Chaldaeos, tum inter Graecos; unde natae sunt versiones duae, cum Chaldaica, tum Graeca.
units.tr: XV. To this end we shall survey the principal versions of both the Old and the New Testament. The chief versions of the Old Testament are indeed twofold: made, namely, for the sake of the Jews dispersed both among the Chaldeans and among the Greeks; whence two versions arose, the Chaldee and the Greek.

units.la: XVI. Chaldaica versio Targumim, seu paraphrasis Chaldaica appellatur; quae duae praecipue fuerunt; una Rabbi Jonathanis, filii Uzielis, discipuli Hillelis, qui 30 annis ante Christum floruisse à plerisque creditur, & Prophetas, cum anteriores, tum posteriores convertisse; altera Onkelosi, sive Aquilae, proselyti, qui legem vertit, anno, juxta plerosque, post Christum circiter 90. Licet utrumque hunc paraphrasten longe recentiorem esse justa non desit suspicio. Liber etiam Job Targum suum tempore Gamalielis senioris habuit. Quae autem praeterea extant Targumim in Pentateuchum, aut Hagiographa, minoris longe auctoritatis sunt.
units.tr: XVI. The Chaldee version is called the Targumim, or Chaldee paraphrase. Two were chiefly in use. One is that of Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, a disciple of Hillel, who by most accounts flourished thirty years before Christ, and who translated the Prophets, both the former and the latter. The other is that of Onkelos, or Aquila, a proselyte, who translated the Law around the year 90 after Christ, according to most. Yet there is a not unfounded suspicion that both these paraphrasts are much more recent. The book of Job also had its own Targum in the time of Gamaliel the Elder. The other Targumim that exist on the Pentateuch or the Hagiographa are of far less authority.

units.la: XVII. Extat etiam Samaritana foliis Pentateuchi versio, quae textum saepe feliciter reddit, antiquitate autem sua veneranda est; quippe quae ante Christum nata creditur. XVIII. Ex-
units.tr: XVII. There also exists a Samaritan version of the leaves of the Pentateuch, which often renders the text well, and it is to be venerated for its antiquity, since it is believed to have been produced before Christ. XVIII. Ex-

units.la: XVIII. Extat quoque Vet. Test. versio Syriaca; verum ex non a Judæis (qui illa lingua in sacris parum delectabantur) sed à Christianis composita; eaque duplex; una ex versione Græca τῶν LXX, sed qua Syri non utuntur; altera ex ipso textu Hebraeo expressa, incerti auctoris & temporis, perantiqua tamen & fidelis, idoque non contemnenda.
units.tr: XVIII. There also exists a Syriac version of the Old Testament. It was composed not by Jews (who took little pleasure in that language for sacred purposes) but by Christians. It is twofold: one made from the Greek version of the Seventy, which the Syrians do not use, and another translated from the Hebrew text itself, of unknown author and date, yet very ancient and faithful, and therefore not to be despised.

units.la: XIX. Facta quoque est V. T. versio Arabica, antiqua, in multis accurata & fida, licet non tam Græcum, quam Syrum interpretetur sequatur.
units.tr: XIX. An Old Testament Arabic version was also made, ancient, in many places accurate and faithful, although it follows the Syriac rather than the Greek.

units.la: XX. Versiones in gratiam Judæorum Ἑλληνιστῶν factæ variæ numerantur: omnium autem prima & augustissima habetur illa, quæ LXX interpretibus tribuitur: de qua, cum sub veteri œconomia facta sit, supra lib. IV. cap. XXXVII. §. XII. & seqq. vidimus.
units.tr: XX. Various versions made for the sake of the Hellenistic Jews [Ἑλληνιστῶν] are enumerated. The first and most venerable of all is held to be that which is attributed to the Seventy translators, concerning which, since it was made under the old economy, we have seen above in Book IV, chapter XXXVII, §§ XII and following.

units.la: XXI. Secunda versio Græca fuit Aquilæ Pontici, ex Gentili Christiani, & ex Christiano Judæi facti; qui vixisse creditur sub Imperatore Adriano, anno Christi 137.
units.tr: XXI. The second Greek version was that of Aquila of Pontus, a Gentile who became a Christian and then a Christian who became a Jew. He is believed to have lived under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of Christ 137.

units.la: XXII. Tertia est Theodotionis, Marcionitæ, tandemque Judæi, facta sub Commodo Imperatore, anno Christi 184. quæ tamen paulo antiquior est.
units.tr: XXII. The third is that of Theodotion, a Marcionite and finally a Jew, made under the emperor Commodus, in the year of Christ 184, though it is somewhat older.

units.la: XXIII. Quarta est Symmachi, Samaritæ vel Ebionitæ, facta sub Imperatore Severo, anno Christi 193. Atque hæ tres versiones apud Græcos, post versionem τῶν LXX, magis communes & vulgatæ fuerunt.
units.tr: XXIII. The fourth is that of Symmachus, a Samaritan or Ebionite, made under the emperor Severus, in the year of Christ 193. These three versions, after the version of the Seventy, were the most common and widespread among the Greeks.

units.la: XXIV. Quinta incerti fuit auctoris, inventa sub Caracalla, in dolio, in urbe Jericho, anno Christi 220.
units.tr: XXIV. The fifth, of unknown authorship, was discovered under Caracalla, in a jar, in the city of Jericho, in the year of Christ 220.

units.la: XXV. Similiter & sexta, incerti auctoris, in dolio inventa fuit Nicopoli, apud Actium Promontorium, sub Alexandro Mammææ, anno Christi 230.
units.tr: XXV. Likewise the sixth, of unknown authorship, was found in a jar at Nicopolis, near the promontory of Actium, under Alexander Mamaea, in the year of Christ 230.

units.la: XXVI. Successit his Origines, qui quatuor primas versiones, modo narratas, in unum volumen disposuit, & columnis distinxit; quæ erant ipsius τέτραπλα: quibus addidit deniceps duas alias columnas, continentes textum Hebræum, Hebræo & Græco charactere descriptum, atque hæc erant ejus ἕξαπλα: denique, adjectis duabus illis anonymis versionibus, dedit ὀκταπλα.
units.tr: XXVI. To these succeeded Origen, who arranged the four principal versions just described in a single volume, dividing them into columns; these were his tetrapla [τέτραπλα]. To these he afterwards added two further columns containing the Hebrew text, written in Hebrew and Greek characters, and these were his hexapla [ἕξαπλα]. Finally, with those two anonymous versions added, he produced the octapla [ὀκταπλα].

units.la: XXVII. Octava versio erat Luciani, Presbyteri Antiochenai, & Martyris, circa annum 311.
units.tr: XXVII. The eighth version was that of Lucian, presbyter of Antioch and martyr, about the year 311.

units.la: XXVIII. Nona fuit Hesychii, Ægyptiis & Alexandrinis usitata. Quæ omnes versiones (excepta ea, quæ LXX dicitur) magna ex parte perierunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. The ninth was that of Hesychius, in use among the Egyptians and the Alexandrians. All these versions, except the one called that of the Seventy, have for the most part perished.

units.la: XXIX. Ex Græcis versionibus hisce factæ sunt deinceps versiones Latinæ, pene innumeræ, omnes ex versione LXX. expressæ. Omnium autem antiquissima & præstantissima fuit, quæ Itala, vetus, & vulgata dicebatur, auctoris incerti.
units.tr: XXIX. From these Greek versions there were subsequently made numerous Latin versions, almost countless, all translated from the version of the Seventy. The most ancient and excellent of all was that called the Itala, the old, and the vulgate, of unknown author.

units.la: XXX. Excipit hanc versio Hieronymi, duplex 1. Vet. Test. è Græco τῶν LXX in Latinum versio. 2. Utriusque Test. ex Hebraeo & Græco, non tam nova versio, quam Latinæ veteris emendatio. Qui ejus labor Latinæ Ecclesiæ primo ingratus, deinceps vero probatus fuit. Ita ut duæ tum essent versiones Latinæ celeberrimæ, Itala Vetus, & Nova Hieronymiana. Cum vero ex duplici hac versione in Ecclesia rixæ orirentur, aliis hanc, aliis illam probantibus, ex utraque illa una facta est, & illa est Vulgata hodierna, quæ in Ecclesia Romana obtinet; quamvis ea lapsu temporis nunc ita immutata, variisque locis corrupta appareat, ut Hieronymi appellari amplius non posset; quod & doctiores ex adversariis confitentur, & manifestis quoque argumentis doceri posset.
units.tr: XXX. This is followed by the version of Jerome, twofold: 1. a Latin translation of the Old Testament from the Greek of the Seventy; 2. a translation of both Testaments from the Hebrew and Greek, not so much a new version as an emendation of the old Latin. His labour was at first unwelcome to the Latin Church, but afterwards it was approved. So there were then two celebrated Latin versions, the Old Itala and the New Hieronymian. But since disputes arose in the Church over this double version, some favouring this one and others that, the two were merged into one, and this is the Vulgate of today, which holds sway in the Roman Church. Yet with the passage of time it now appears so altered and corrupted in various places that it could no longer be called Jerome's; this even the more learned of our adversaries confess, and it could be shown by manifest arguments.

units.la: XXXI. Verum, cujuscunque laudabilis hæc versio auctoris sit, ac debeat, majoris momenti est, quod Romana Ecclesia in Trid. Concilio versionem hanc authenticam pronunciare non eruberit, ac palam edicere, ne quis eam quovis pratextu rejicere audeat, vel præsumat.
units.tr: XXXI. But whatever the merit of this version and whoever its author, what is of greater weight is that the Roman Church, at the Council of Trent, did not blush to declare this version authentic, and openly to decree that no one may dare or presume to reject it on any pretext whatever.

units.la: XXXII. Super cujus decreti mente laboratur ab ipsis Pontificiis: unde quidam eam absolute & simpliciter authenticam declarant, nullo in apice mutandam; alii solum catenus, quod nullum in fide & moribus errorem contineat.
units.tr: XXXII. The Papists themselves labour over the meaning of this decree. Hence some declare it absolutely and simply authentic, not to be changed in the least point; others only so far as it contains no error in faith and morals.

units.la: XXXIII. Verum innumeris absurdis laborat hic Canon. Nam 1. incerta redditur Theologia & fides omnis, cum ante hoc decretum nullum verbum Dei authenticum fuisse sequatur. 2. Cum post conditura hunc canonem vulgata versio auctoritate concilii emendata demum prodierit, quomodo concilium eam jam isto tempore authenticam pronunciare potuit? 3. Nec ipsæ illæ, quæ secutæ sunt, editiones inter se conveniunt. Quam enim Sixtus V. adscitis undique viris doctissimis, versionem correxerat, & sub anathemate recipi jusserat, emendavit post Gregorium XIV. rursus Clemens VIII. & plane aliam fecit, eamque & bullis suis communivit. Ut inter hæc Pontificum dissidia incerta Papistarum fides fluctuari necesse habeat.
units.tr: XXXIII. But this canon labours under countless absurdities. For 1. all theology and all faith become uncertain, since it follows that before this decree there was no authentic word of God. 2. Since the Vulgate, emended by the authority of the council, appeared only after this canon was drawn up, how could the council already at that time pronounce it authentic? 3. Nor do the editions that followed agree with one another. Sixtus V, having called in the most learned men from every quarter, corrected the version and ordered that it be received under anathema; but after Gregory XIV, Clement VIII again emended it, made it quite different, and fortified it with his bulls. Amid these disagreements of the Pontiffs, the uncertain faith of the Papists must inevitably waver.

units.la: XXXIV. 4. Præposterè etiam authenticam fecerunt editionem Latinam, cum jam diu Latina Ecclesia defecerit; atque etiam aliis per orbem Ecclesiis consultum oportuisset. 5. Quomodo autem authentica ea esse potest, cum originalis non sit? quod enim authenticum in se non est, nulla humana auctoritate authenticum fieri potest. 6. Et quomodo hoc intelligendum, quod nullo praetextu eam versionem rejici velint? an ne quidem originalis textus praetextu, si ei repugnare deprehendatur? an vero respectu aliarum versionum hoc tantum intelligunt? verum hoc versionem istam authenticam facere non potest; cum ita (altem textui originali subjicienda sit.
units.tr: XXXIV. 4. They have also absurdly made the Latin edition authoritative, although the Latin Church has long since failed; and they ought rather to have consulted the other Churches throughout the world. 5. But how can it be authentic when the original is not? For what is not authentic in itself can never be made authentic by any human authority. 6. And how are we to understand their claim that they want that version rejected on no pretext? Not even on the pretext of the original text, if it is found to conflict with it? Or do they mean this only with respect to the other versions? But this cannot make that version authentic, since it must in any case be subordinated to the original text.

units.la: XXXV. Falso autem praetexunt, necessarium esse in Ecclesia versionem aliquam pronunciari authenticam, cum non omnibus Hebraeos vel Graecos codices adire contingat. Illa enim ἐξοχὴ solis Scripturis θεοπνεύστος debetur: & sacrilegum est, versionem aliquam in istud auctoritatis culmen evehere, ut nullo praetextu eam rejicere liceat. Unde & ex ipsis adversariis primarii non veriti sunt, post conditum hoc decretum, innumera in ista versione vitia notare; quod Isidorus Clarius & Lucas Brugensis fecere; vel novas versiones adornare; aut ab aliis adornatas auctoritate sua approbare.
units.tr: XXXV. They falsely pretend that it is necessary for the Church to pronounce some version authentic, since not everyone can consult the Hebrew or Greek codices. For that pre-eminence [ἐξοχὴ] is owed to Scripture alone, which is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος]. It is sacrilegious to raise any version to such a height of authority that it may not be rejected on any pretext. Hence, too, the leading men among the adversaries themselves have not hesitated, since this decree was issued, to note countless faults in this version, as Isidore Clarius and Lucas of Bruges did, or to produce new versions, or to approve with their own authority those produced by others.

units.la: XXXVI. Praeter hanc vulgatam variae aliae latinae versiones editae sunt, quarum prima est inter Pontificios Santis Pagnini, Lucensis, edita A.C. 1528. auspiciis Leonis X. quae praecipuis Doctoribus Pontificiis probata fuit.
units.tr: XXXVI. Besides this Vulgate, various other Latin versions have been published. The first among the Papists is that of Santes Pagninus of Lucca, published in 1528 under the auspices of Leo X, which was approved by the leading Papist teachers.

units.la: XXXVII. 2. Eam Benedictus Arias Montanus, Hispalensis, una cum aliis Theologis Hispanis, ad id delegatis, in Biblia, quae vocantur interlinearia, transtulit, & ubi opus, licet non nimis feliciter, correxit, rejecto ad marginem Pagnini textu.
units.tr: XXXVII. 2. Benedictus Arias Montanus of Seville, together with other Spanish theologians delegated for this purpose, translated Pagninus's version into the Bibles called interlinear, and where needed corrected it, though not very happily, with Pagninus's text relegated to the margin.

units.la: XXXVIII. 3. Post hos Isidorus Clarius, Brixianus, anno 1542. aliam versionem edidit, ad Hebraicam & Graecam veritatem.
units.tr: XXXVIII. 3. After these, Isidore Clarius of Brescia published another version in 1542, made according to the Hebrew and Greek truth.

units.la: XXXIX. Inter Reformatos 1. Sebastianus Munsterus, tribus ante Pagninum annis, versionem Bibliorum edidit, nimirum A.C. 1525. quam deinceps iterato emendavit.
units.tr: XXXIX. Among the Reformed: 1. Sebastian Münster published a version of the Bible three years before Pagninus, namely in 1525, which he afterwards revised again.

units.la: XL. 2. A.C. 1535. Johannes Oecolampadius totum fere V. Test. interpretatus est.
units.tr: XL. 2. In 1535 John Oecolampadius translated almost the whole Old Testament.

units.la: XLI. 3. Secuta sunt Biblia Leonis Judae, ab ipso inchoata, a Bibliandro, Pellicano, & Cholino absoluta, A.C. 1544. quae, Tiguri cum essent edita, Tigurina dicta sunt. Hanc versionem biennio post Robertus Stephanus, non nominato ejus auctore, ad vulgatam adjecit, una cum notis Francisci Vatabli; unde Biblia Vatabli, quamvis non recte, dicta sunt.
units.tr: XLI. 3. There followed the Bibles of Leo Jud, begun by him and completed by Bibliander, Pellican and Cholin, in 1544. Since they were published at Zurich, they were called the Tigurine. Two years later Robert Stephanus added this version to the Vulgate without naming its author, together with notes by Francis Vatablus; hence it is called the Bible of Vatablus, though not rightly.

units.la: XLII. 4. A.C. 1550. Sebastianus Castellio, Basileæ Biblia publicavit, sermone latino, tersò & florido. Unde quorundam laudem, plurium autem convitia retulit. Eadem & gallice paucis post annis transtulit.
units.tr: XLII. 4. In 1550 Sebastian Castellio published the Bible at Basel in Latin, polished and flowery. Hence he won the praise of some and the abuse of many. He translated it into French a few years later.

units.la: XLIII. 5. Post hos Lucas Osiander, Theologus Tubingensis, versionem Vulgatam exhibuit, eamque varie supplevit ac correxit, sua, vel potius Lutheri Germanica versione addita.
units.tr: XLIII. 5. After these, Lucas Osiander, theologian of Tübingen, presented the Vulgate, supplementing and correcting it in various ways, with his own German version, or rather Luther's, added alongside.

units.la: XLIV. 6. Successit Tremellii & Junii versio, anno 1574, magno Ecclesiarum Reformatarum applausu excepta, deinde autem aliquoties recusa, & a Junio, quod factum quidam nollent, anno 1587. recognita & alicubi immutata.
units.tr: XLIV. 6. There followed the version of Tremellius and Junius, in 1574. It was received with great applause by the Reformed Churches, but was afterwards reprinted several times, and in 1587 Junius revised it, which some did not want, and changed it in places.

units.la: XLV. 7. Secuta sunt, inter alia, Piscatoris Biblia, quæ, Junianam versionem in plerisque sequuntur, in plurimis tamen corrigunt, magis accurata & Hebraicæ veritati consentanea, cum scholiis luculentis.
units.tr: XLV. 7. Among other things came the Piscator Bibles, which follow the Junian version in most places but correct it in very many, being more accurate and agreeable to Hebrew truth, with illuminating scholia.

units.la: XLVI. 8. Ad magnificentiam autem & usum simul prodierunt Biblia Complutensia, Regia Plantiniana & Parisiensia, Polyglotta; quibus non cedunt, sed præferenda potius sunt nupera Londinensia.
units.tr: XLVI. 8. The Complutensian, Royal Plantin and Parisian Polyglot Bibles appeared, both splendid and useful. They are not inferior to these, but the recent London ones are rather to be preferred.

units.la: XLVII. Novi T. versiones præcipuæ quatuor sunt. 1. est Syriaca, omnium antiquissima, è Græco textu expressa, incerto auctore & tempore; nisi quod ad Hadriani temporq quidam eam referant.
units.tr: XLVII. There are four principal versions of the New Testament. 1. The Syriac is the oldest of all, rendered from the Greek text, its author and date uncertain, except that some refer it to the time of Hadrian.

units.la: XLVIII. 2. N.T. versio Latina est Erasmi, Leoni X. Pontif. in-
units.tr: XLVIII. 2. The Latin version of the New Testament is that of Erasmus, dedicated to Pope Leo X ... in-

units.la: XLIX. 3. Est Bezæ, qui multis locis Erasmum castigavit: sicut cum rursus alii; inter quos excellit Ludovicus de Dieu.
units.tr: XLIX. 3. There is Beza's, who criticised Erasmus at many points, as others did in turn; among them Louis de Dieu excels.

units.la: L. 4. Benedicti Ariæ Montani, de verbo ad verbum facta, indeque multis probata. Atque hiisce accenseri quoque possunt aliæ versiones N.T. una cum Veteris translatione, superius memoratæ, factæ
units.tr: L. 4. That of Benedictus Arias Montanus, made word for word and therefore approved by many. To these may also be added the other versions of the New Testament, together with the translation of the Old mentioned above, which were made

units.la: LI. Vernaculæ Scripturæ versiones plures omni ævo fuerunt, etiam inter veteres, pro vario populorum captu & ingenio. Plurimæ autem præterito & nostro sæculo, in linguis maxime Europæis, prodierunt: speciatim Gallica, seu Genevensis; quod à Pastoribus Genevensibus elaborata sit, circa A.C. 1560. doctrinæ, judicii ac fidei laudem merita: qualis etiam est, quam deinceps Joh. Diodatus, cum doctissimis notis edidit, cum Gallicam, tum Italicam: Anglicana, quæ auspiciis serenissimi Regis Jacobi, consilio & labore præcipue Episcoporum concinnata est, A.C. 1611. eruditionis, acuminis & judicii non vulgaris; & Belgica quidem duplex: una vetus, maximam partem ex Germanica Lutheri versione traducta, à variis tamen secundum varias versiones interpolata: cujus errores innumeros detexit D. Amama: inde, post frustraneos Marnixii, Arnoldi Cornelii, & Helmichii labores, nova versio; auctoritate Celsissimorum Belgii Foederati Ordinum, & decreto Synodi Dordracenæ, a xv. viri;, A. C. 1637, cum notis edita est, postquam aliis Theologis revisa & approbata fuerat. Quæ eruditionis, fidelitatis & elegantiæ nomine cum præcipuis conferri potest. Ejus tamen notas maxime improbarunt Remonstrantes, utpote sibi minime congruas: alii vero nimium verborum adscititiorum & uncinulis inclusorum, in ipsa versione, copiam, in notis vero prolixitatem, notarunt.
units.tr: LI. There have been many vernacular versions of Scripture in every age, even among the ancients, according to the varying capacity and temperament of peoples. Very many have appeared in the past and in our own century, especially in the European languages. Notable are the French, or Genevan, produced by the Genevan pastors around 1560, deserving praise for doctrine, judgment and faith; and such also is the one which Joh. Diodatus afterwards published with very learned notes, both in French and in Italian: English, prepared under the auspices of the most serene King James, chiefly by the counsel and labour of the bishops, in 1611, of no common learning, acuteness and judgment; and the Dutch, which is twofold. One is old, for the most part translated from Luther's German version but interpolated in various places according to various versions; its countless errors were uncovered by D. Amama. Then, after the fruitless labours of Marnix, Arnold Cornelis and Helmich, came a new version, published with notes in 1637 by the authority of the most illustrious Orders of the United Netherlands and by decree of the Synod of Dort, from fifteen men, after it had been revised and approved by other theologians. In learning, fidelity and elegance it can be compared with the principal versions. Its notes, however, were especially disapproved by the Remonstrants, as wholly unsuited to themselves; others noted, in the version itself, an excess of added words enclosed in brackets, and, in the notes, prolixity.

units.la: LII. Sed & inter Pontificios quoque, paucos ante annos, Michael de Marolles, Abbas, N. T. in Gallicum transtulit: atque alius Psalmos Davidicos, non sine laude cantus vernaculi, in eandem linguam convertit. Quemadmodum etiam A. C. 1665. Doctor Sorbonicus, ex eorum numero, qui Jansenistæ vulgo audiunt, N. Fœdus secundum editionem Vulgatam, ex ipso fonte accurate emendatam, in idem idioma transtulit. Singulari sane inter Pontificios exemplo.
units.tr: LII. But also among the Papists, a few years ago, Michael de Marolles, abbot, translated the New Testament into French; and another turned the Davidic Psalms into the same language, not without praise for its vernacular song. Likewise in 1665 a Doctor of the Sorbonne, from the number of those commonly called Jansenists, translated the New Covenant into the same idiom, according to the Vulgate edition, carefully emended from its source. A singular example indeed among the Papists.

units.la: LIII. Et hæc quidem Verbo scripto conservando propagandoque hactenus operabatur diligentia. Sicut vero nunquam circa divina occupatum est humanum ingenium, quin simul suo magisterio sapiat & de suo aliquid revelatis addere conetur, & ex suo fumo lucemdare; itacorrupta jam adeo Ecclesia Judaica, nihil melius ab illa circa verbum divinum expectari poterat. Vidimus jam supra lib. iv. c. xxx. §. 11. & c. xxxv §. xi. quo pacto a fundamentis Theologiæ Mosaicæ gens illa deficere cœperit. Quæ defectio post excessum Prophetarum majora incrementa fecit.
units.tr: LIII. Thus far the diligence of men has laboured to preserve and propagate the written Word. But just as the human mind is never occupied with divine things without at the same time savouring its own teaching and trying to add something of its own to what has been revealed, and to kindle light from its own smoke, so the Jewish Church, already so corrupted, could expect nothing better from it concerning the divine word. We have already seen above, book iv, chap. xxx, §11, and chap. xxxv, §11, how that nation began to fall away from the foundations of Mosaic theology. That defection, after the passing of the Prophets, made greater progress.

units.la: LIV. Postquam enim sacer Prophetarum chorus terras reliquisset, sensim a lege Patrum discessum, & humanis commentis ac traditionibus religionis castitas contaminata fuit: præcipuo ejus rei auctore Hillele, Babylonio, cxl. circiter annis ante secundum templi excidium.
units.tr: LIV. For after the holy band of Prophets had left the earth, little by little there was a departure from the law of the Fathers, and the purity of religion was contaminated by human inventions and traditions. The chief author of this was Hillel the Babylonian, about 140 years before the second destruction of the Temple.

units.la: LV. Atque exinde, ut Judæi tum in sectas scindi cœperant, & nova facile placebant, duplex obtinuit Hierosolymis doctrina; una Scripturæ, altera traditionum: cui docendæ in singulis Synagogis; duo attributa erant auditoria. Defecit autem paulatim Scripturæ studium, ac prævaluerunt Traditiones. Quod factum anno post urbis excidium quinquagesimo. Deinde enim quæ hactenus traditionum seniorum prætextu venerant, legis oralis nomine venerunt. Tunc enim præter legem scriptam Judæi aliam à Mose legem, in monte Sinai acceptam commenti sunt; quæ, cum sublimioris sapientiæ foret, oreexcepta, eodem modo propagari debuerit; unde תורה שבעל פה appellant, uti scriptam תורה שבעל כתב. Quam Moses, ante excellum, Josuae; hic LXX Senioribus; hi Prophetis; illi autem viris Synagogae M. tradiderint. Donec tandem conscripta, & in Talmud, tanquam pandectas, relata est. Labente enim tempore, ne per Judaeorum exilia, crebrasque fugas, tam pretiosum depositum periret, Rabbi Jehuda Princeps, seu Sanctus, qui sub Antoninis floruit, anno post templum excisum cxx in unum volumen traditiones illas congessit; quod Misna, vel Sepher Mishnajoth seu Deuteroseon volumen appellatur.
units.tr: LV. From then on, as the Jews had begun to be split into sects and new things easily found favour, a twofold teaching prevailed at Jerusalem: one of Scripture, the other of traditions. For teaching the latter there were two lecture-halls assigned in each synagogue. But the study of Scripture gradually failed and the traditions prevailed. This happened in the fiftieth year after the destruction of the city. For then what had hitherto come in under the pretext of the traditions of the elders came in under the name of the oral law. Then, besides the written law, the Jews devised another law, received by Moses on Mount Sinai, which, since it was of a higher wisdom, ought to be handed down by word of mouth in the same way. Hence they call it the oral law [תורה שבעל פה], just as they call the written one the written law [תורה שבכתב]. Moses, they say, handed it on before his death to Joshua; he to the Seventy Elders; they to the Prophets; and the Prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue. At last it was written down and set in the Talmud as in a set of pandects. For as time slipped away, lest so precious a deposit perish through the exiles of the Jews and their frequent flights, Rabbi Judah the Prince, or the Holy, who flourished under the Antonines, gathered those traditions into a single volume in the year 120 after the destruction of the Temple. It is called the Mishnah, or Sepher Mishnajoth, that is, the volume of repetitions.

units.la: LVI. Hisce successerunt Doctores, qui in explicatione Misnajoth, disputationibusque circa illas, verlabantur; ex quibus altera Talmudis pars, Gemara dicta, coaluit; quae pro auctorum & scholarum discrimine rursus duplex est, Hierosolymitana & Babylonica.
units.tr: To these succeeded the teachers, who were occupied with explaining the Mishnayoth and with disputations about them; from these the second part of the Talmud, called Gemara, took shape. This is itself twofold, according to the authors and schools, Jerusalem and Babylonian.

units.la: LVII. Lex autem haec ipsorum oralis hisce tribus constat. 1. difficiliorum legis sensuum explanatione; quam Moses ex ore Dei acceperit. 2. novorum quorundam praeceptorum, instar sepimenti, ad legem additione. 3. denique Logica quadam mystica, quam ipsi Cabbalam nuncupant; cujus ope occultos legis sensus rimantur.
units.tr: LVII. This oral law of theirs consists of three parts. 1. An explanation of the more difficult senses of the law, which Moses is supposed to have received from the mouth of God. 2. The addition to the law of certain new precepts, serving as a hedge around it. 3. Finally, a kind of mystical logic, which they call the Cabbalah, by whose help they search out the hidden senses of the law.

units.la: LVIII. Nos quod attinet, etsi Mosem circa legis sensum cunctumque ejus mysterium, multa prae reliquis a Deo didicisse non diffiteamur, quae ore quoque tradiderit: atque apud Judaeos Catechesin, & παράδοσιν doctrinae Prophetarum & Seniorum obtinere debuisse; & multa, quae ritus caerimoniasque spectarent, vix aliter quam per traditiones intelligi potuisse concedamus: quin & seniores ipsos populo jugum & praecepta, disciplinae imponere potuisse, ultro fatemur. Hoc tamen negamus:
units.tr: LVIII. As for us, although we do not deny that Moses learned from God many things beyond the rest about the sense of the law and all its mystery, which he also handed on by word of mouth, and although we concede that among the Jews there ought to have been a catechesis and a tradition [παράδοσιν] of the teaching of the Prophets and the Elders, and that many matters concerning rites and ceremonies could scarcely be understood except through tradition, and we freely admit that the elders could impose yoke, precepts and discipline on the people; nevertheless we deny this:

units.la: 1. Ista legem aliam ac diversam facere. Cum omnes illae expositiones, omnisque Patrum Catechesis, ad legem Moses referenda & examinanda fuerint. 2. Mosem, praeter legem scriptam, non solum omnes ejus expositiones & sensus; sed & fabulosam illam Cabbalam, seu mysticorum sensuum clavem infallibilem; ac praeterea occulta quaedam mandata, aliamque praeterea legem oralem accepisse. 3. Ac denique illa omnia incorrupta ad Judaeos pervenisse; librosque ipsorum Talmudicos expositiones traditionesque illas veterum, & veram Cabbalam, & universa denique legis oralis praecepta plenissime continere.
units.tr: 1. That these things make another and different law. For all those expositions, and the whole catechesis of the Fathers, had to be referred to and tested against the law of Moses. 2. That Moses received, besides the written law, not only all its expositions and senses, but also that fabulous Cabbalah, the infallible key to mystical senses, and moreover certain secret commandments and another oral law. 3. And finally that all these things came down to the Jews uncorrupted, and that their Talmudic books fully contain the expositions and traditions of the ancients, the true Cabbalah, and indeed all the precepts of the oral law.

units.la: LIX. Legem enim oralem quod attinet, nulla vel minima ejus in Scripturis mentio aut indicium occurrit. Moses contra, quae a Deo acceperat, scribere omnia jussus est, & revera scripsit. Edixit Jehova Mosi, scribe tibi verba hac; quia secundum ea pango tecum fœdus. Exod. 34: 27. Moses, quum enarravisset populo verba Jehovæ, — scripsit Moses omnia verba Jehovæ. c.24: 3, 4. Unde usitata formula: Sicut scriptum in lege Mosis. Semperque ad legem scriptam ablegamur. Vide Deut. 10: 12. 13. & 28: 1, 58. & 29: 9, 19. & 30: 20. & 32: 45, 46. Illaque perfecta esse perhibetur, ut nec addi nec demi ei quicquam possit, Deut. 4: 1, 2. & 12: 32. Psal. 19: 8.
units.tr: LIX. As for the oral law, no mention or trace of it appears in the Scriptures, or hardly any. Moses, on the other hand, was commanded to write down everything that he had received from God, and indeed he did write it. Jehovah said to Moses, write these words for yourself, for according to them I make a covenant with you. Exod. 34: 27. Moses, when he had declared to the people the words of Jehovah, — Moses wrote all the words of Jehovah. c. 24: 3, 4. Hence the customary formula: As it is written in the law of Moses. And we are always sent back to the written law. See Deut. 10: 12, 13; 28: 1, 58; 29: 9, 19; 30: 20; 32: 45, 46. And that law is declared to be perfect, so that nothing can be added to it or taken from it, Deut. 4: 1, 2; 12: 32; Ps. 19: 8.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Quod excipiunt, legem obscuram, sensusque ejus dubios perfæpe esse, præcipue in abstrusis ac minutissimis cærimoniarum partibus; id multo magis in traditionibus ipsorum locum habet, quæ non dubiæ solum, & incertæ, sed sibi mutuo sæpe contrariæ sunt. Nec illud aliam legem, sed legis tantummodo expositionem, ac declarationem requireret. Lex autem ipsa, in doctrinæ ac fœderis Dei summa, clara est.
units.tr: What they object, that the law is often obscure and its senses doubtful, especially in the abstruse and minute parts of the ceremonies, applies much more to their traditions, which are not only doubtful and uncertain but often contrary to one another. Nor would that require another law, but only an exposition and explanation of the law. The law itself, however, in the sum of God's teaching and covenant, is clear.

units.la: LXI. Atque hinc & cætera cadunt. De seniorum præceptis lib. 1. c. ix. §. xxviii. & lib. iv. c. xxiv. §. iv. vidimus. Cabbalam autem quod spectat: etsi mysticum diversarum rerum, quæ in Scripturis occurrunt, intellectum, & mystica quædam legis interpretamenta concedamus (quæ tamen non vocum proprie interpretationes, aliusve eorum sensus; sed rerum vocibus contentarum ad altiora quædam denotanda relationes sunt) eaque non promiscue & vulgo cunctis patuisse, sed viris θεοπνεύστοις, & præsertim Apostolis ac Evangelistis, sacro instinctu revelata; cæteris autem accurato Scripturarum scrutinio, ac præsertim Evangelii rerumque ipsarum luce, ostensa, non refragemur: longe tamen hæc differunt à nugaci Judæorum Cabbala, delirisque illis ac putidis interpretamentis, quæ ex literulis quibusdam, earumque compositione ac resolutione varia, venantur, & tanquam mysteria venditant. Quæ, ut ut laboriosa ac difficilis, tamen persæpe inepta, vana, quin turpis & impia, magorumque secretis affinis est. Cum nihil non ista clave recludi, & tam falsa quam vera inde excidi possint. Ut indignum sit, futilis istus artis originem consecrare, & ad Deum auctorem referre velle, quin & divinæ legis partem statuere.
units.tr: LXI. From this also the rest falls away. We have seen about the precepts of the elders in book 1, chapter 9, section 28, and book 4, chapter 24, section 4. As for the Cabbalah, although we grant a mystical understanding of various things that occur in the Scriptures, and certain mystical interpretations of the law (which, however, are not properly interpretations of words or other senses of them, but relations of things contained in words to certain higher matters), and grant that these were not open promiscuously and to all the common people, but were revealed by sacred inspiration to men divinely inspired [θεοπνεύστοις], and especially to the Apostles and Evangelists, and were shown to others by careful scrutiny of the Scriptures, and especially by the light of the Gospel and of the things themselves, we do not object. Yet these differ far from the trifling Cabbalah of the Jews, and those mad and foul interpretations, which they hunt out from little letters, through various combinations and resolutions of them, and peddle as mysteries. Though laborious and difficult, these are very often silly, vain, indeed base and impious, and akin to the secrets of magicians. For nothing at all can be unlocked by that key, and things both false and true can be drawn out by it. So it is unworthy to consecrate the origin of this futile art and to wish to refer it to God as its author, or even to make it a part of the divine law.

units.la: LXII. Denique & Talmudis jam ratio patet. 1. Nulla enim datur lex oralis, ut diximus. Unde nec in Talmude ea continetur. 2. Quæ autem Deuteroseon ac Traditionum, ibi contentarum, sit certitudo, quamque incorruptæ ex permanserint, vel ex eo colligi potest, quod brevi temporis interstitio ipsam legem scriptam propè deperditam legamus, 2. Reg. 22: 8. & 2. Chron. 34: 15. Unde mirandum valde, non simile tratraditionum fatum fuisse, verum illas, per tot saeculorum seriem, non scripto saltem, sed ore conservatas, & incorrupte traditas fuisse. 3. Non autem divinas leges proprie, sed magistrorum controversias & disputationes ac resolutiones liber ille continet; ut ab humano ingenio prosectum constet. 4. Quibus fabulosa multa & impia, sibique invicem, ac divinis legibus contraria, accedunt. Ut non sine blasphemia Deo imputari possint. Licet alia multa utiliora, & ad intelligentiam Sacri Codicis apprime facientia in Talmude quoque contineri libenter fateamur, eoque nomine Christianorum manibus illud excuti nollemus.
units.tr: LXII. Finally, the nature of the Talmud is now also clear. 1. For there is no oral law, as we have said. Hence it is not contained in the Talmud either. 2. As for the certainty of the traditions and the decisions contained in it, and how uncorrupted they have remained, this can be gathered from the fact that in a short interval of time we read that the written law itself was almost lost, 2 Kings 22: 8, and 2 Chron. 34: 15. Hence it is very remarkable that the traditions did not suffer a similar fate, but that through so long a succession of centuries they were preserved, if not in writing, at least by word of mouth, and handed down uncorrupted. 3. Moreover, that book contains not properly divine laws but the controversies, disputations and resolutions of the teachers; so that it is plainly a product of human ingenuity. 4. To these are added many fabulous and impious things, contrary both to one another and to the divine laws, so that they cannot be imputed to God without blasphemy. Although we gladly admit that many other more useful things, very much conducive to understanding the Sacred Code, are also contained in the Talmud, we would not on that account wish it to be wrested from the hands of Christians.

units.la: LXIII. Atque haec traditionum ac humanarum institutionum in Ecclesia origo; quas inter Christianos etiam venditare postea coepere Pontificii, qui eas pro maximo religionis suae munimento habent. Utque olim Judaei Synedrium errare non posse, & ut ea ac explicationem legis, quam dabant, propter ipsorum nomen ac auctoritatem, recipiendam esse statuebant; similem in modum nunc illi instituunt, & Ecclesiam, ejusque justa, crepant. Atque etiam in causa suae praesidium Judaicae Ecclesiae exemplum & Cathedram Mosis, Matth. 23:2. adferunt. Quae & alibi excusa sunt.
units.tr: LXIII. Such is the origin in the Church of these traditions and human institutions, which the Papists afterwards began to peddle also among Christians, and which they regard as the greatest bulwark of their religion. And just as the Jews once held that the Sanhedrin could not err, and that its decisions and its explanation of the law were to be received on account of their name and authority, so now they set up the same thing, and they boast of the Church and its judgments. And they even bring forward, in defence of their cause, the example of the Jewish Church and the Chair of Moses, Matt. 23: 2. These matters have been discussed elsewhere too.

units.la: LXIV. Praeterea etiam Pseudepigraphis spuriisque scriptis, Apostolis virisque Apostolicis falso suppositis, illusum est Ecclesiae Christianae primitivae. Quorum catalogum hic non exhibebimus, cum illecommodius in historia Ecclesiastica recensetur. Nullus autem liber errorum feracior fuit, magisque fidem Christianam corrupit, quam ille, qui Sibyllarum nomen fert, continens Sibyllina carmina, ab otiosis hominibus confecta, & circa ultima Imp. Hadriani tempora. Ex quibus veteres religionem Christianam saepe adstruunt, & crebra testimonia contra gentiles adducunt.
units.tr: LXIV. Moreover, the early Christian Church was also deceived by pseudepigraphic and spurious writings, falsely ascribed to Apostles and men of Apostolic times. We will not set out a catalogue of these here, since they are better reviewed in ecclesiastical history. But no book has been more fruitful of errors, or corrupted the Christian faith more, than the one bearing the name of the Sibyls, containing the Sibylline oracles, composed by idle men and dating to around the last years of the Emperor Hadrian. From these the ancients often built up the Christian religion, and they adduce frequent testimonies against the Gentiles.

units.la: LXV. Verum libri hi supposititii sunt: nam, licet una istarum vatum se in arca Noe fuisse memoret, & de Mose vaticinetur, adque adeo sese eo, qui omnium consensu primus scriptor fuit, antiquiorem ferat; tamen ea oracula post Christum nata esse patet, cum mentionem faciant rerum atque opinionum postea demum ortarum: & imprimis tam clare religionis Christianae mysteria evolvant, praesertim in acrostircho, ut nullus Prophetarum eo assurgat; quod diaboli vatibus a Deo concessum fuisse nemo dixerit: & vocabulis utantur partim ineptis, partim ex S. Scriptura manifeste desumtis; & adeo accurate perpetuum atque inoffensum rei gestae ordinem perspicua oratione prosequantur: qui modus scribendi di à furiosis illis fœminis, quales illæ fuisse supponuntur, vel maxime abfuit.
units.tr: LXV. But these books are spurious. For although one of these prophetesses recalls that she was in the ark of Noah, and prophesies about Moses, and so claims to be older than him who by universal consent was the first writer, nevertheless it is plain that those oracles were produced after Christ, since they mention matters and opinions that arose only later; and above all they unfold the mysteries of the Christian religion so clearly, especially in the acrostic, that no prophet rises to it; which no one would say God allowed to the prophetesses of the devil. And they use words partly unsuitable, partly plainly taken from Holy Scripture, and they pursue the continuous and unbroken order of events in so precise and clear a style, a manner of writing that is most remote from those frenzied women, such as they are supposed to have been.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Symbolis & Confessionibus.
units.tr: On Creeds and Confessions.

units.la: I. POst verbum divinum, aliquam etiam in Ecclesia N. F. auctoritatem nacta sunt scripta Ecclesiastica; inter quæ eminent Symbola & Confessiones, Catecheses, & Liturgia.
units.tr: I. After the divine Word, the ecclesiastical writings of the Church of the New Covenant have also gained some authority. Among them stand out the Creeds and Confessions, the Catechisms, and the Liturgy.

units.la: II. Palmam inter omnia Symbola obtinet illud, quod Apostolicum dicitur; incerta nominis istius ratione. Veterum quidam sic appellatum putaverunt, quia ab Apostolis ipsis compositum sit: verum nullum ejus rei inter Acta Apostolica indicium occurrit: atque alias potius fidei Synopses & formulas Apostoli Ecclesiis tradiderunt.
units.tr: II. Among all the creeds, the one called Apostolic holds the palm, though the reason for that name is uncertain. Some of the ancients thought it was so called because it was composed by the Apostles themselves. But no trace of this appears in the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apostles rather handed down to the Churches summaries and formulas of faith of another kind.

units.la: 2. Tim. 1: 13. Hebr. 6: 1, 2. Neque etiam phrases illæ, Ecclesia Catholica, descendit ad inferos &c. Apostolorum ætatem sapiunt: unde quoque nulla apud antiquos Ecclesiæ scriptores symboli hujus mentio.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 1:13. Heb. 6:1, 2. Nor do those phrases, "the holy Catholic Church," "he descended into hell," and so on, smack of the age of the Apostles. Hence also no ancient ecclesiastical writer mentions this creed.

units.la: III. Apostolicum ergo potius dicendum est, quia ex Apostolorum scriptis haustum, summa Christianæ fidei capita continet. Videtur autem paraphrasin quandam & explicationem continere formulæ in baptismo adhibitæ, & per singula ejus capita ire, confessionem veluti edens fidei nostræ de Patre, & Filio, & Sp. S. Unde & ea, veluti à singulis Christianis usurpanda, in singulari numero effertur, credo &c.
