units.tr: III. It should therefore rather be called the Apostles' creed, because, drawn from the writings of the Apostles, it contains the chief heads of the Christian faith. It seems, moreover, to be a kind of paraphrase and explanation of the formula used in baptism, going through its individual heads and, as it were, setting out our confession of faith concerning the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. For this reason it is also expressed in the singular number, I believe, as if to be used by each Christian individually.

units.la: IV. Originem tempusque ejus assignare non adeo in proclivi est. Sunt, qui à Synodo Nicæna illud compositum volunt. Sed, cum illa Synodus proprium condiderit symbolum, verbis sententiisque ab hoc Apostolico multum discrepans, probabilius est, si non certum, conditum esse symbolum Apostolicum ab Episcopo & clero Romano: ab illa autem Ecclesia ad alias Occidentis Ecclesias derivatum est; Orientis Ecclesiis interim alia symbola usurpantibus. Non simul & semel autem ea forma, qua nunc extat, compositum est; sed paulatim variorum articulorum, adversus exorientes hæreses, adjectione auctum, & in hanc tandem formam redactum.
units.tr: IV. It is not very easy to assign its origin and time. Some hold that it was composed after the Nicene Synod. But since that Synod drew up its own creed, differing considerably in words and sense from this Apostles' creed, it is more probable, if not certain, that the Apostles' creed was put together by the bishop and clergy of Rome. From that Church it was then passed on to the other Churches of the West, while the Churches of the East used other creeds in the meantime. It was not, however, composed all at once and in the form in which it now exists; it was gradually enlarged by the addition of various articles against the heresies that arose, and was finally brought into this form.

units.la: V. Principales autem & primogenii articuli fuerunt illi de S.S. Trinitate, & de persona, officio & statu Christi. Reliqui diversis occasionibus contra hæreticos adjecti sunt. Speciatim illa verba, descendit ad inferos, ex Aquilejensi symbolo adoptata videntur; cum in veteribus, tum Romanæ, tum aliarum Ecclesiarum symbolis non occurrant. Quin & antiquissima symbola in articulo de Sp. S. desierunt.
units.tr: V. The principal and original articles were those concerning the Most Holy Trinity and the person, office and state of Christ. The rest were added on various occasions against heretics. In particular, the words he descended into hell seem to have been taken from the Creed of Aquileia; they do not occur in the ancient creeds either of the Roman Church or of other Churches. Indeed, the most ancient creeds stopped short at the article on the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VI. Deinde etiam alia symbola contra particulares hæreticos huic adjecta fuerunt, in iv. Conciliis generalibus, Niceno, Constantinopolitano, Ephesino, Chalcedonensi: quo etiam refertur symbolum Athanasio, quamvis falso, tributum.
units.tr: VI. Then also other creeds were added against particular heretics, at the four general councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon. To this category also belongs the creed attributed to Athanasius, although falsely.

units.la: VII. Auctoritas igitur hujus symboli, quantum ad verba & formam, humana tantum est, quamvis sententiæ illius sint authenticæ. Et male Pontificii ex traditione Canonicam ejus auctoritatem probant, cum nulla, ut alias visum, talis traditio fit.
units.tr: VII. The authority of this creed, as to its words and form, is therefore merely human, although its sense is authentic. And the Papists wrongly prove its canonical authority from tradition, since, as we have said elsewhere, no such tradition exists.

units.la: VIII. Est tamen illud religionis Christianæ symbolum tale, ut hæretici reipsa & in vero sensu, illud recipere nequeant. Unde Antitrinitarii omnes hoc symbolo refutantur, ut & omnes illi qui mysterium incarnationis & redemptionis nostræ negant. Pariterque Pontificii, quamvis hoc symbolum ostentent, in præcipuis tamen suis erroribus per illud ipsum refutantur: sicut in Papatu ejus auxilio multi Papismum evitarunt & salvi facti sunt olim, atque etiamnum fiunt.
units.tr: VIII. Nevertheless, this creed of the Christian religion is of such a kind that heretics cannot receive it in its true sense. Hence all the Antitrinitarians are refuted by this creed, as are all those who deny the mystery of the incarnation and of our redemption. Likewise the Papists, although they make a show of this creed, are refuted by it in their principal errors. Just as in the Papacy, with its help, many escaped Popery and were saved, as they were of old and still are being saved.

units.la: IX. Sunt autem Symbola confessiones Ecclesiæ universales: Confessiones vero Ecclesiarum particulares sunt declaratio consensus & profectus piorum in agnitione veritatis, obligantes non per se, sed vi demonstrationis ad conscientiam. Quosquot itaque perfecti sumus, hoc sentiamus. Phil. 3: 15. Ut observetis eos, qui dissensiones & scandala praeter doctrinam, quam vos didicistis, faciunt. Rom. 16: 17. Tit. 3: 10, 11, Quo etiam referendæ Catechesis, & Liturgiæ.
units.tr: IX. Creeds are the universal confessions of the Church; particular confessions of the Churches, however, are declarations of the agreement and progress of the godly in the knowledge of the truth, binding not in themselves but by the force of demonstration upon the conscience. Therefore let as many of us as are perfect be thus minded. Phil. 3:15. Mark them which cause divisions and offences, contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned. Rom. 16:17. Tit. 3:10, 11. To these also belong the Catechism and the Liturgy.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De Fundamento & articulis fundamentalibus.
units.tr: On the Foundation and the Fundamental Articles.

units.la: I. QUm Scriptura V. & N. Fœderis, & speciatim sub N. F. doctrina Jesu Christi, quam hactenus expositimus, contineat religionis fundamentum; de hoc etiam nunc agendum.
units.tr: I. Since Holy Scripture of the Old and New Covenant, and especially the doctrine of Jesus Christ under the New Covenant, which we have so far set out, contains the foundation of religion, this too must now be discussed.

units.la: II. Fundamentum vel incomplexe sumitur, estque unicum, nimirum Jesus
units.tr: II. The foundation is taken either as a whole, and is one only, namely Jesus.

units.la: Ex doctrina hactenus tradita discitur religionis fundamentum. Jesus Christus. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest statuere praeter id quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus. 1. Cor. 3: 11. 1 Petr. 2: 4. Esai. 28: 16. & 45: 22. Ut ita fundamentum idem sit, qui & lapis angularis est, Eph. 2: 20. unde & adificati in Petra dicimur, Matth. 16: 18. vel complexe, & tum notat veritatem fundamentalem, sine cujus notitia & confessio- ne nemo dici potest Deo & verbo ejus credere. Ut peritus artifex, fundamentum posui &c. 1. Cor. 3: 10. Eph. 2: 20.
units.tr: From the doctrine delivered so far we learn that the foundation of religion is Jesus Christ. No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 3:11; 1 Pet. 2:4; Isa. 28:16; 45:22). So the same foundation is also the chief cornerstone (Eph. 2:20), whence we are also said to be built upon the Rock (Matt. 16:18). Or it is taken as a complex, and then it denotes the fundamental truth, without the knowledge and confession of which no one can be said to believe God and his word: As a skilled craftsman, I have laid the foundation, etc. (1 Cor. 3:10; Eph. 2:20).

units.la: III. Quænam autem hæc veritas fundamentalis sit, ex notis ac proprietatibus ejus optime agnoscitur. Hæ autem sequentes sunt.
units.tr: III. Which truth is the fundamental one is best recognised from its marks and properties. These are the following.

units.la: IV. 1. Veritas fundamentalis est istud verbum gratiæ, quod peccatori ad salutem omnino necessarium est, Rom. 1: 16. quod rite creditum in statu gratiæ peccatorum collocat; & quod corruptum ac adulteratum fidem omnem plane tollit: quoque proinde explicite & distinctè tenerì ac credi debet, cum in eo sit ipsa adstipulatio fœderis gratiæ; quæ sine expresso assensu fieri nequit.
units.tr: IV. 1. The fundamental truth is that word of grace which is absolutely necessary to the sinner for salvation (Rom. 1:16); which, when rightly believed, places the sinner in a state of grace; and which, when corrupted and adulterated, utterly destroys all faith. It must therefore also be held and believed explicitly and distinctly, since in it lies the very ratification of the covenant of grace, which cannot take place without express assent.

units.la: V. 2. Veritas etiam hæc est axioma latissime patens; atque adeo credi debet non solum ut veritas, sed præcipue ut fundamentum aliarum fidei veritatum, & ut norma falsitatis ac mendacii. Vos unctionem habetis a sancto illo, & nostis omnia &c. 1. Joh. 2: 20, 21, 22. &c. Unde & in multa alia membra ac capita diduci potest, qui similiter articuli fundamentales appellantur.
units.tr: V. 2. This truth is also an axiom of the widest reach; and so it must be believed not only as a truth, but especially as the foundation of the other truths of faith, and as the rule by which falsehood and lies are judged. You have an anointing from that Holy One, and you know all things, etc. (1 John 2:20, 21, 22, etc.). Hence it can also be divided into many other members and heads, which are likewise called fundamental articles.

units.la: VI. 3. Atque hæc veritas clare & distinctè in Scriptura revelata est; & frequenter in ea occurrit, variisque phrasibus exprimitur & repetitur; quin & multis typis ac figuris olim adumbrata fuit; ita tamen ut hæc veritas unica semper fuerit & immutabilis.
units.tr: VI. 3. This truth is set forth clearly and distinctly in Scripture, and it frequently occurs there, being expressed and repeated in various phrases; indeed it was also long ago foreshadowed by many types and figures, yet in such a way that this truth has always been one and unchangeable.

units.la: VII. Hisce notis quidam hanc etiam accensent, quod veritas fundamentalis non cadat in controversiam. Hoc autem refutatur experientia, cum & olim & hodie de pluribus veritatibus fundamentalibus disputetur.
units.tr: VII. Some also count among these marks that the fundamental truth does not fall into controversy. But this is refuted by experience, since both in former times and today many fundamental truths are disputed.

units.la: VIII. Veritas ergo illa fundamentalis, cui omnes hæ notæ conveniunt, nulla est alia, nisi illa quæ complectitur unicum fundamentum salutis, nimirum Jesum Christum, filium Dei. Speciatim autem illius in carne manifestatio, passio & consummatio, cum necessariis appendicibus, veritatem fundamentalem N. Fœd. constituunt. Hæc est vita æterna, ut te cognoscant illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum. Joh. 17: 3. Et sine dubio magnum est pietatis mysterium: Deus est manifestatus in carne &c. 1. Tim. 3: 16.
units.tr: VIII. That fundamental truth, then, to which all these marks belong, is none other than that which comprises the one foundation of salvation, namely Jesus Christ, the Son of God. In particular, his manifestation in the flesh, his passion and his consummation, with their necessary appendages, constitute the fundamental truth of the New Covenant. This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). And without doubt great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, etc. (1 Tim. 3:16).

units.la: IX. Ita veritatem hanc proponit Scriptura, in qua & Christus, & axioma Christo fa'utem attribuens, pariter fundamentum fidei appellantur. 1. Cor. 3: 11, 12. 16:22. Col. 2: 2, 3. 1. Joh. 2:20, 21. Act. 4: 11, 12. Ita & Apostoli in communionem Ecclesiæ accipiebant eos, qui confitebantur Iesum Christum, Filium Dei, Act. 2: 37, 38. & 8: 37. & 10: 43. Atque idem fuit primitivæ Ecclesiæ, post Apostolorum tempora, sensus; quæ veritatem hanc in symbolo Apostolico summatim exposuit. Similiterque Ecclesiæ Euangelicæ idem fundamentum agnoscunt, quamvis diversis modis illud explicent, & vel paucioribus, vel pluribus articulis summam ejus comprehendant.
units.tr: IX. Scripture thus sets forth this truth, in which both Christ and the axiom attributing salvation to Christ are likewise called the foundation of faith (1 Cor. 3:11, 12; 16:22; Col. 2:2, 3; 1 John 2:20, 21; Acts 4:11, 12). So also the Apostles admitted to communion with the Church those who confessed Jesus Christ, the Son of God (Acts 2:37, 38; 8:37; 10:43). And this was the sense of the primitive Church after the time of the Apostles, which summarised this truth in the Apostles' Creed. Likewise the Evangelical Churches acknowledge the same foundation, although they explain it in different ways, and comprise its sum in fewer or more articles.

units.la: X. Estque hoc fundamentum unicum tam in Vet. quam in N. T & immutabile ac perpetuum: neque enim aliud verbum nunc expectandum habemus, cum ipsum corpus & figurarum omnium veritatem possideamus. Quæ sunt umbra rerum futurarum, at corpus est Christi. Col. 2. 17. Umbram enim habens lex futurorum bonorum &c. Hebr. 10:1.
units.tr: X. This foundation is one and the same, and enduring and perpetual, in both the Old and the New Testament; for we have no other word yet to expect, since we possess the body itself and the truth of all the figures. Which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ (Col. 2:17). For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, etc. (Heb. 10:1).

units.la: XI. Pluribus autem modis fundamentum hoc efferri, & in plu resarticulos ac membra dispesci potest; ita tamen ut omnia in hac veritate ad unitatem semper redeant.
units.tr: XI. This foundation can be set forth in many ways, and divided into several articles and members; yet in such a way that all the parts of this truth always return to unity.

units.la: XII. Gravis autem hic movetur quæstio de numero articulorum fundamentalium, quorum expressam cognitionem & professionem Deus postulat: hoc enim religionis nostræ ad Papismum Apostatæ perpetuo a nobis flagitant, ut articulos istos necessarios enumeremus. Ad quod notandum.
units.tr: XII. A weighty question arises here concerning the number of the fundamental articles, whose explicit knowledge and profession God requires. For the Papists, the apostates from our religion, constantly demand of us that we enumerate these necessary articles. On this we must note the following.

units.la: XIII. 1. Quæstionem hanc esse novam & non-necessariam, cum Scriptura nunquam hunc numerum definiverit, qui nec a nobis definiendus est, sed generalibus tolum axiomatis salutem & beatitudinem describat. vide Psal. 15. & alia loca.
units.tr: XIII. 1. This question is new and unnecessary, since Scripture has never fixed this number, nor is it for us to fix it; rather it describes salvation and blessedness only by general axioms. See Psalm 15 and other passages.

units.la: XIV. 2. Deinde & temerarium foret, ac modestiæ Christianæ contrarium, determinare velle quantitatem minimam necessariorum, quorum cognitionem Deus substernere posset suæ operationi, qua fidem salvificam infundit & salutem confert; cum hoc nullibi revelaverit: adeoque nefas esset liberrimam & absolutam Dei potestatem in salvando homine velle circumscribere. Matth. 11:26. & 20: 15. An non licet mihi quod volo facere in meis rebus? An oculus tuus malus est quia ego bonus sum?
units.tr: XIV. 2. Further, it would be rash, and contrary to Christian modesty, to wish to determine the smallest quantity of necessary things whose knowledge God might lay as the basis of his operation, by which he infuses saving faith and confers salvation; since he has nowhere revealed this. It would therefore be wicked to wish to limit the most free and absolute power of God in saving man. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own things? Or is your eye evil because I am good? (Matt. 11:26; 20:15).

units.la: XV. 3. Verum etiam determinatio hæc propemodum impossibilis est: cum enim fides diversis Dei actionibus in homine produci possit, neque ille simili in omnibus modo operetur; quis earum numerum inire, vel Deum ad illum adstringere poterit? Et manifestum quoque est hominum ac temporum descrimen. Alia enim in V.T. alia in N. cognitionis mensura fuit; alia secundis ac florentibus, alia adversis Ecclesiæ temporibus; & pro vario fidelium statu, vel læto, vel tristi ac tentationibus infesto, & pro varia eorum indole ac ingenio, vel plura vel pauciora ab illis requiruntur; quo facit similitudo seminis Matth. 13. cujus non eadem est ratio respectu omnis terræ.
units.tr: XV. 3. Indeed this determination is also almost impossible. For since faith can be produced in man by various actions of God, and he does not work in the same way in everyone, who could count their number, or bind God to it? The difference between men and times is also plain. The measure of knowledge was one thing in the Old Testament and another in the New; one thing in prosperous and flourishing times of the Church, another in adverse times; and according to the varied state of the faithful, whether joyful or sad and beset by temptations, and according to their varied disposition and temperament, more or fewer things are required of them. To this the parable of the seed (Matt. 13) points, whose reckoning is not the same with respect to all soil.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Non incumbit ergo Theologis necessitas articulos omnes fundamentales præcise enarrandi, etsi ipsi distinguant inter articulos credituneccessarios, & non-necessarios. Veritates enim fundamentales singulæ ex notis antea traditis discerni possunt, quam vis determinatus eorum numerus definiri non possit.
units.tr: There is therefore no obligation on theologians to set out precisely all the fundamental articles, although they themselves distinguish between articles that must be believed and those that are not necessary. For each of the fundamental truths can be recognised from the marks handed down earlier, even though their exact number cannot be fixed.

units.la: XVII. Neque etiam absurdum est, dicere posse, aliquem in fundamento errare, ut Pontificii; alios vero fundamentum tenere, quod de Lutheranis dicimus; etsi constitutum non habeamus quot vel qui articuli præcise fundamentales sint. Convenientia enim illa vel discrepantia ex eo facile constat, si quis fundamentum salutis, & fœderis Dei inviolatum retineat, neque alia illud evertentia superaddat, vel contra. Atque ad illud dijudicandum sufficit, scire in specie hanc vel illam veritatem fundamentalem esse; non autem opus est, quot numero fundamentales articuli sint, præcise cognitum habere.
units.tr: XVII. Nor is it absurd to say that one may err regarding the foundation, as the Papists do, while others hold the foundation, as we say of the Lutherans; even though we do not have settled how many or which articles are precisely fundamental. For that agreement or disagreement is easily established if someone keeps the foundation of salvation and of the covenant of God inviolate, and does not add other things that subvert it, or the reverse. And to judge this it is enough to know that this or that particular truth is fundamental; it is not necessary to know exactly how many fundamental articles there are.

units.la: XVIII. Necessariorum ergo ad salutem quantitatem minimam præcise determinare non est opus: at quantitatem corum maximam, quæ in eo consistit, ut non plura sint absolute necessaria, determinare posiumus; constituendo nimirum eam, in cognitione communium illarum Ecclesiæ formularum: Symboli Apostolici, Decalogi, Orationis Dominicæ, & Institutionis Baptismi ac S. Cœnæ. Ultra quæ plura ad salutem absolute necessaria non sunt. Atque ita etiam Scriptura, dum integrum fœdus Dei, sive id quod Deus in fœdere gratiæ a nobis stipulatur, ad hæc duo revocat, fiduciam nimirum in Christum Servatorem, & studium Deo obediendi, quasi digito nobis ea, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, commonstrare censenda est. Nam in Christo Jesu neque circumcisio quid valet, neque præputium, sed fides per charitatem operans. Gal. 5:6. Hoc est ejus præceptum, ut credamus nomini filii ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus alii alios, sicut præcepit nobis. 1. Joh. 3:23. XIX. Non temere ergo damnandi & aeterno exitio adjudicandi sunt, qui forte unum vel alterum symboli articulum ignorant, vel hoc aut illo in capite non sufficienter sunt instructi. Nos enim arcana judiciorum divinorum penetrare non possumus, & nescimus quae intellectus imbecillitas, vel alius invincibilis & nobis incognitus defectus, talibus obstet. Aliud autem est, si quis summa illa religionis capita, vel alia etiam dogmata revelata, malitiose & praefracte cognoscere negligat: ille enim non solum quae ad salutem necessaria sunt non tenet, sed potius viam salutis negligit, Deoque se subjicere detrectat.
units.tr: XVIII. It is therefore not necessary to determine precisely the smallest amount of what is necessary for salvation; but we can determine its greatest amount, which consists in this: that nothing more is absolutely necessary, namely by fixing it in the knowledge of those common formularies of the Church: the Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and the institution of Baptism and of the Holy Supper. Beyond these, nothing more is absolutely necessary to salvation. And so also Scripture, when it reduces the whole covenant of God, or what God requires of us as the condition of the covenant of grace, to these two things, namely trust in Christ the Saviour and zeal to obey God, ought to be regarded as having pointed out to us, as with a finger, what is necessary to salvation. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. Gal. 5:6. This is his command, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he has commanded us. 1 John 3:23. XIX. Those therefore who perhaps do not know one or another article of the creed, or are not sufficiently instructed in this or that chapter, are not to be rashly condemned and adjudged to eternal ruin. For we cannot penetrate the hidden counsels of God's judgments, and we do not know what weakness of understanding, or other invincible defect unknown to us, stands in their way. It is otherwise if someone maliciously and obstinately neglects to know the chief heads of religion, or other revealed doctrines even: for he not only does not hold what is necessary to salvation, but rather neglects the way of salvation and refuses to submit himself to God.

units.la: XX. Quod vero attinet ad illa, quae, praeter haec ad salutem necessaria, in religione porro traduntur, simplex Christianus, si post omnem adhibitam diligentiam de iis judicare non possit, judicium suum suspendet, cavebitque ne aliquam sententiam, de qua ultro citroque disputatur, sibi ex verbo Dei non satis clare perspectam, fide suscipiat: sic enim in errores non delabetur, sed simpliciter in fidei suae simplicitate, h. e. in primis fidei fundamentis, permanebit. Eam vero Ecclesiam merito habebit suspectam, quae cum non clarissime istorum, quae addit, veritatem ex verbo Dei ostendere possit, assensum tamen imperare velit. Et si ea hoc non obstante tyrannidem in conscientiam & corpus exerceat, sufficientem eam deserendi causam habebit.
units.tr: XX. As for those things which, besides these necessary to salvation, are further handed down in religion, the simple Christian, if after all diligence applied he cannot judge about them, will suspend his judgment, and will take care not to receive by faith any opinion, about which there is dispute back and forth, that is not sufficiently clearly perceived by him from the word of God: for in this way he will not fall into errors, but will simply remain in the simplicity of his faith, that is, in the first foundations of faith. That Church, however, he will rightly regard with suspicion, which, when it cannot clearly show from the word of God the truth of those things which it adds, nevertheless wishes to impose assent. And if it nonetheless exercises tyranny over conscience and body, he will have a sufficient reason for deserting it.

units.la: XXI. Sicut autem ita nec necessarium, nec possibile est, determinare veritates fundamentales; ita ex oppositio idem statuendum est de erroribus fundamentalibus. Illos enim particulatim scire non opus est; cum quisque eorum ad damnationem sufficiat: unde & Scriptura non tam ad numerum, quam ad qualitatem eorum attendit. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur, qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Marc. 16:16. Qui asperanatur me, nec recipit verba mea, habet qui condemnet ipsum. Joh. 12:48. An ignoratis, injustos non esse Dei haeredes? Ne erretis, neque fornicatores, neque idololatrae &c.
units.tr: XXI. But just as it is neither necessary nor possible to determine the fundamental truths, so by contrast the same must be held concerning fundamental errors. For it is not necessary to know them one by one, since each of them is sufficient for condemnation: whence Scripture also looks not so much to their number as to their quality. He who believes and is baptised will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned. Mark 16:16. He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who will judge him. John 12:48. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, etc.

units.la: XXII. Varii etiam errorum sunt gradus, juxta quos eorum est discrimen: alii errores leviter sunt concepti, alii altiores agunt radices: alius est error theoreticus, alius practicus: ille iterum vel conclusio tantum est, vel etiam principium, ex quo alii insuper errores deducuntur: rursus error vel separatim tenetur, vel cum aliis mixtus, & in ordinem veluti redactus. Etenim vos concinnatores mendacii, medici nihili omnes estis. Job. 13:4.
units.tr: XXII. There are also various degrees of errors, according to which they differ: some errors are lightly conceived, others strike deeper roots; one error is theoretical, another practical; again, one is merely a conclusion, another is also a principle from which further errors are deduced; moreover, an error is either held by itself or mixed with others and, as it were, arranged into an order. For you are all forgers of lies, worthless physicians. Job 13:4.

units.la: XXIII. Similiter quoque discrimen est respectu errantium; quorum alii profunditates Satanæ ignorant; alii contra quibusvis artibus fraudem tegere & tueri conantur: aliud etiam est, diserte errorem profiteri; aliud est, illud statuere, ex quo per consequentiam error sequitur, quem tamen non videas: aliud errorem premere, aliud eum propagare; aliud ita errare, ut errori nulla ex parte catur obviam, aliud, simul tenere aliam veritatem, per quam erroris periculum & venenum inhibeatur. Quæ omnia cum magnam in erroribus pariant diversitatem, clarum est, non posse errores omnes fundamentales ad certum numerum revocari. Illud in genere statui potest, errorem fundamentalem esse, qui fundamentale dogma evertit.
units.tr: XXIII. Likewise there is also a difference with respect to those who err: some are ignorant of the depths of Satan; others on the contrary try by all kinds of arts to conceal and defend their deceit. It is also one thing to profess an error openly, and another to lay down a position from which the error follows by consequence, though you do not see it; one thing to suppress an error, another to propagate it; one thing to err in such a way that no opposition is offered to the error on any side, another to hold at the same time another truth by which the danger and poison of the error is checked. Since all these things produce great diversity among errors, it is clear that not all fundamental errors can be reduced to a fixed number. This may be stated in general: an error is fundamental if it overturns a fundamental doctrine.

units.la: XXIV. In defectu autem hic peccant 1. Socinani, qui fundamentalia nulla nisi expressis verbis in Scripturis contenta, eaque non nisi praetica, admittunt, non tam ex Evangelio quam ex lege desumta, quæ ad duo capita revocant, fiduciam & obedientiam; quam vis cæteroquin circa particularem eorum numerum inter se discrepent.
units.tr: XXIV. Now the following sin by defect: 1. the Socinians, who admit no fundamentals except those contained in express words of Scripture, and those only practical, drawn not so much from the Gospel as from the law, which they reduce to two heads, trust and obedience; although in other respects they disagree among themselves about their particular number.

units.la: XXV. 2. Ita & Remonstrantes fundamentalia statuunt paucissima, quæ tribus hisce capitibus absolvunt, fide divinarum promissionum, obedientia divinorum præceptorum, & debita Scripturis reverentia: eorumque, inter alia, hoc statuunt κριτήριον, ut apud Christianos omnes in confesso sint, adeoque nec controversa sint, neque etiam controverti possint; quia tam clara sunt, ac sol meridie, cum vel totidem verbis in Scriptura extent, vel manifestissimis consequentiis, quæ omnium occulis se ostendant, ex ea eliciantur. Hinc omnes fere Christianorum cœtus in fundamentalibus istis inter se convenire statuunt, atque adeo eos inter se debere coalescere contendunt; qui ipsorum scopus, & circa hæc omnia πρῶτον ψεῦδος est.
units.tr: XXV. 2. Likewise the Remonstrants set down very few fundamentals, which they comprise under three heads, faith in the divine promises, obedience to the divine precepts, and due reverence for Scripture; and among other things they lay down this criterion: that whatever is fundamental must be agreed upon by all Christians, and so must be neither controverted nor capable of being controverted; because it is as clear as the sun at midday, since either it stands in Scripture in just so many words, or it is drawn from it by most evident consequences that show themselves to everyone's eyes. Hence they hold that almost all assemblies of Christians agree with one another about these fundamentals, and so they contend that they ought to unite with one another; which is their aim, and in all these matters a first falsehood.

units.la: XXVI. In excessu peccant 1. Veteres, qui fundamentalius sæpe accensebant leviora, & in iis dissentientes ut hæreticos traducebant. 2. Novatiani, Donatistæ, qui, nullo in fundamentalibus dissensu, temere in schismata recedebant. 3. hodieque Pontificii, fundamentale fere statuentes quicquid definiverit Ecclesia Romana: unde fœnum suum & stipulas in fundamentalium dogmatum censum reponunt, eorumque numerum plus æquo multiplicant: quam vis iterum ab alia parte fide sua implicita eum obscurent atque confundant.
units.tr: XXVI. The following sin by excess: 1. the ancients, who often counted lesser matters as fundamental and branded as heretics those who dissented on them. 2. the Novatians and Donatists, who, with no dissent on fundamentals, rashly withdrew into schisms. 3. And today the Papists, who regard almost as fundamental whatever the Roman Church has defined: whence they heap up their hay and stubble into the census of fundamental doctrines, and multiply their number beyond what is fitting; although on the other side, by their implicit faith, they again obscure and confuse it.

units.la: XXVII. Atque ex hac fundamentalium delineatione jam statui potest, quid circa Syncretismum ac tolerantiam, cum hæreticis ac schismatici. {a}cis sentiendum sit; prout nimirum illi in fundamento conveniunt, vel non. Syncretismus quidem cum nullo errore, etiam non fundamentali, instituendus est: tolerantia vero, seu consociatio potius, cum iis, qui in fundamento non errant, institui potest; ita tamen, ut eorum errores aut religionem errantem non adoptemus.
units.tr: XXVII. And from this outline of the fundamentals it may now be settled what is to be thought concerning syncretism and toleration with heretics and schismatics; namely, according as they agree in the foundation or not. Syncretism, indeed, is not to be undertaken with any error, even a non-fundamental one; but toleration, or rather association, may be undertaken with those who do not err in the foundation; provided, however, that we do not adopt their errors or their erring religion.

units.la: XXVIII. Improbandi hic ergo 1. Sociniani & Remonstrantes, hoc agentes, ut omnes tantum non cœtus Christiani in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coalescant. 2. Libertini & prophani, universalem syncretismum, cum omnium controversiarum eliminatione & contemtu molientes. 3 Cassandri, Grotii, Milleterii, aliorumque motimina, de componendo Pontificios inter & Orthodoxos dissidio, non sublato dissidii fundamento, Papisino & Papatu.
units.tr: XXVIII. Here, therefore, the following are to be condemned: 1. the Socinians and Remonstrants, who aim that almost all Christian assemblies should coalesce into one body of the Church. 2. the Libertines and profane persons, who labour toward a universal syncretism, with the elimination and contempt of all controversies. 3. the Calixtines, Grotians, Molanus and other movements, which aim at composing the dissension between Papists and Orthodox, without removing the foundation of the dissension, namely Papism and the Papacy.

units.la: XXIX. Ex adverso rejicienda 1. Anabaptistarum temeritas, mutuo se damnantium ob dissensum in adiaphoris. 2. Brownista, seu Separatista, ob levia quædam segreges cœtus facientes. 3. ac deplorandum infelicissimum scisma inter Reformatos & Evangelicos, quod levibus de causis ortum, tanto animorum dissidio etiam hodie alitur & continuatur.
units.tr: XXIX. On the other side, the following must be rejected: (1) the rashness of the Anabaptists, who condemn one another for disagreeing about things indifferent; (2) that of the Brownists, or Separatists, who form separate congregations over some trivial matters; and (3) the deplorable and most unhappy schism between the Reformed and Evangelicals, which arose from slight causes and is still fed and kept alive today by such bitter division of minds.

units.la: XXX. Fundamento vero jam cognito, nemo in eo subsistere debet, sed, cui aliqua modo suppetit occasio, debet is, pro modulo virium, donorum & vocationis, operam dare, ut fundamento illi inædificet, atque in omni sapientia, quæ tam ποlυποικιλος in mysterio nunc revelata est, porro proficiat. Sermo Christi inhabitet in vobis copiose cum omni sapientia. Col. 3: 16. Ut notificetur nunc principatibus & potestatibus, qui in supercœlestibus sunt, per Ecclesiam Dei, sapientia Dei, quæ plurimam varietatem habet. Eph. 3: 9, 10.
units.tr: XXX. Once the foundation is known, no one ought to remain upon it alone. Whoever has any opportunity at all should, according to his measure of strength, gifts and calling, labour to build upon that foundation and to advance in all wisdom, which is now revealed in the mystery in so [πολυποίκιλος] manifold a form. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom. Col. 3:16. That now to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places might be made known by the Church the manifold wisdom of God. Eph. 3:9, 10.

units.la: XXXI. Omnia vero, quæ ex verbo Dei, ultra fundamentum, discuntur, cum illo fundamento comparanda, ad illud referenda, illi adjungenda & super-imponenda sunt. Quod ipsa fundamenti appellatio, & theologicarum quoque veritatum indoles ac natura requirit; quarum cognitio nisi in aliensu fundamenti fundetur, & ex eo enascatur, non est sapientia, neque fides, & in infidelem quoque cadere potest. Divina enim sapientia confusa & indigesta non est, sed certo ordine, per meditationem principii & fundamenti, h. e. Scripturæ, & doctrinæ de justitia Dei in Christo, & per comparationem spiritualium cum spiritualibus, comparatur. Ut det vobis spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis, in cognitione ipsius &c. Eph. 1: 17, 18. Ut pertus architectus fundamentum statui. Porro quisque videat quomodo superædificet. Quod si quis superædificet anrum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, fœnum, stipulam. Cu-jusque opus manifestum fiet. &c. 1. Cor. 3: 10–13.
units.tr: XXXI. Everything that is learned from the Word of God beyond the foundation must be compared with that foundation, referred to it, joined to it and built upon it. The very name of foundation requires this, and so does the nature and character of theological truths. Unless the knowledge of these is grounded in and grows out of the foundation, it is not wisdom, nor is it faith, and it can even fall to an unbeliever. For divine wisdom is not confused and disordered, but is acquired in a fixed order, by meditating on the principle and foundation, that is, on Scripture and the doctrine of God's righteousness in Christ, and by comparing spiritual things with spiritual. That he may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, etc. Eph. 1:17, 18. As a wise master builder I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one take heed how he builds upon it. If anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one's work will become manifest, etc. 1 Cor. 3:10–13.

units.la: XXXII. Cum ergo post Apostolorum ætatem nulla nova expectanda sit revelatio; juxta illud, Non docebit quisque proximum suum &c. Jer. 31:33. Hebr. 8: 10 atque etiam verba fundamenti nunc ita in propatulo sint collocata, omniumque cogitationibus & sermonibus frequentata, ut nemo adultus sit, qui non aliquod Scripturæ dictum, quo hoc fundamentum indicetur, memoria teneat; ut difficilius videatur illud ignorare, quam scire posse: clarum est, nulli fideli aut Theologo licere, post Prophetas & Apostolos, novum fidei vel Theologiæ fundamentum jacere aut docere.
units.tr: XXXII. Since, then, after the age of the Apostles no new revelation is to be expected, in accordance with that saying, No one shall teach his neighbour, etc. Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10, and since the words of the foundation are now set out so openly and are so often on everyone's lips and in their thoughts, that there is no adult who does not keep in memory some saying of Scripture by which this foundation is indicated, so that it seems harder to be ignorant of it than to know it, it is clear that no believer or theologian may lay down or teach a new foundation of faith or theology after the Prophets and Apostles.

units.la: XXXIII. Igitur, juxta Vincentii Lirinensis commonitorium, triennio post Synodum Ephesinam contra Nestorium habitam scriptum, c 3. Magnopere curandum est, ut id teneamus, quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum: hoc enim est vere proprieque Catholicum.
units.tr: XXXIII. Accordingly, according to the Commonitory of Vincent of Lérins, written three years after the Synod of Ephesus held against Nestorius, ch. 3: We must take great care to hold that which has been believed everywhere, always and by all; for that is truly and properly Catholic.

units.la: XXXIV. Cum autem Theologia duobus absolvatur, explicatione fundamenti, & eorum quæ inde deducuntur, & satis constet in fundamento innovari non posse; videndum etiam, an in reliquis dogmatis, fundamento contradistinctis, novitas admitti possit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Since theology consists of two parts, the explanation of the foundation and of the things deduced from it, and since it is clear enough that nothing can be renewed in the foundation, we must also consider whether novelty can be admitted in the remaining doctrines, which are distinguished from the foundation.

units.la: XXXV. Et quidem ex dictis jam liquet, nihil posse esse in professu fidei & scientiæ theologicæ, quod in antiquo ejusdem fidei & Theol. principio, S. Scriptura non contineatur, quodque adeo revera antiquum non sit, quatenus in antiquorum Dei verborum virtute & valore continetur. Ut discatis, supra id quod scriptum est non sapere. 1. Cor. 4: 6. Insta tibi & doctrinæ: mane in iisdem. 1. Tim. 4: 11, 13. Unde prophetare juxta analogiam fidei, Rom. 12: 6. & per comparationem spiritualium, 1. Cor. 2: 13. jubemur.
units.tr: XXXV. Indeed, it is already clear from what has been said that nothing can be put forward in the profession of faith and theological science which is not contained in Holy Scripture, the ancient principle of the same faith and theology, and which therefore is not in fact ancient, insofar as it is contained in the force and value of God's ancient words. That you may learn not to go beyond what is written. 1 Cor. 4:6. Attend to reading, to exhortation, to teaching; continue in these things. 1 Tim. 4:11, 13. Hence we are commanded to prophesy according to the analogy of faith, Rom. 12:6, and by comparing spiritual things with spiritual, 1 Cor. 2:13.

units.la: XXXVI. Non debet ergo Theologus ex vinea Domini, quoad doctrinam, novelletum facere. Tam perfecte enim plantata est à Deo per Prophetas & Apostolos, ut qui superveniunt, potius rigent, quam plantent: unde exprobatur Judæis, quod plantarent palmitem extranei, Eai. 17: 10, 11. cum planta omnis vel plantatio, quam non plantavit Pater cœlestis, eradicanda sit. Matth. 15: 13.
units.tr: XXXVI. A theologian, then, ought not to make a new vineyard out of the Lord's vineyard as far as doctrine is concerned. For it has been planted by God through the Prophets and Apostles so perfectly that those who come afterwards should rather water it than plant it. Hence the Jews are reproached that they planted a strange vine, Isa. 17:10, 11, since every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted. Matt. 15:13.

units.la: XXXVI. Litet tamen Theologo ex vetusto principio & fundamento fidei discere & docere nova, non respectu illius principii & fundamenti, sed respectu cognitionis suæ, vel aliorum. Modo non illa affectet, contemtis veteribus, tanquam jam detritis & inutilibus. Et nemo, qui biberit vetus, statim novum... vetus vinum, si autem vult novum. dicit enim, vetus utilius est. Luc. 5: 39. & cum pruritu aurium, 2. Tim. 4: 3.
units.tr: XXXVI. Yet a theologian may learn and teach new things from the ancient principle and foundation of faith. These are new not with respect to that principle and foundation, but with respect to his own knowledge or that of others. Only let him not aim at them by despising the old as already worn out and useless. And no one who has drunk old wine immediately wants new; for he says, the old is better. Luke 5:39. Nor should he do so with itching ears, 2 Tim. 4:3.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quibus scopulis evitatis, laudabile est in Christianæ fidei Doctore, si ex Scripturis quotidie proficiat, atque ex ea identidem producat nova, tum argumenta, quæ semel traditam fidem confirment, & majori Scripturarum luce perfundant, tum inventa, quibus Christianorum prophetia & cognitio, maxime de Regni Christi statu & incrementis, adaugeatur. Ut ita sit scriba, doctus in regno cœlorum, similis patrifamilias, qui promit e thesauro suo nova & vetera, Matth. 13: 52. Sic & de sponsa, seu Ecclesia N. T. etiam seriorum temporum dicitur, quod sponso suo seponat pretiosos fructus, recentes simul & veteres. Cant. 7: 13 cum quibus convenit novum illud vinum, quod Christus in regno suo promittit suis, Matth. 26: 29. Luc. 22: 16, 18. quod dubio procul non unius tantum est temporis.
units.tr: XXXVIII. If these rocks are avoided, it is praiseworthy in a teacher of the Christian faith to make daily progress from the Scriptures, and to bring forth from them from time to time new things: both arguments which confirm the faith once delivered and bathe it in a greater light of the Scriptures, and discoveries by which the prophecy and knowledge of Christians, especially concerning the state and growth of the kingdom of Christ, may be increased. So that the scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure new things and old. Matt. 13:52. So too the bride, that is, the Church of the New Testament, even in later times, is said to store up for her beloved precious fruits, both new and old. Song 7:13. With these agrees that new wine which Christ promises to his own in his kingdom. Matt. 26:29; Luke 22:16, 18. Without doubt this is not for one age only.

units.la: XXXIX. Hæc illa est promissio Dan. 12: 4, 9. Abscondita & obsignata sunt verba illa usque ad tempus finis, quo scrutabuntur multi, & major fiet cognitio. Monstrosum enim esset, si Ecclesia in posterum quidem pergat crescere membrorum numero & ætate, non vero sapientia etiamsi omnium præteritorum sæculorum meditationibus & operâ utatur. Beatum ergo hoc Ecclesiæ tempus omni studio & voto accelerandum est: præcipue cum in Scripturarum studio tam multa nobis adhuc δυσνόητα, & prope ἄλυτα sint; cum tamen nihil in S. Codice occurrere videatur, cujus sensum Ecclesiæ aliquando aperiendum & revelandum esse sperare non liceat.
units.tr: XXXIX. This is the promise of Dan. 12:4, 9: Those words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end, when many shall search, and knowledge shall be increased. For it would be monstrous if the Church continued in future to grow in the number and age of its members, but did not grow in wisdom, even though it made use of the meditations and labours of all past centuries. This blessed time of the Church is therefore to be hastened with all zeal and prayer, especially since in the study of the Scriptures there are still so many [δυσνόητα] hard to understand and almost [ἄλυτα] unsolvable things for us; and yet nothing appears in the holy Book whose sense we may not hope will one day be opened and revealed to the Church.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS SECUNDUS. CAPUT IV.
units.tr: THE FORTY-SECOND LOCUS. CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Sacramentis in genere.
units.tr: On Sacraments in general.

units.la: I. VErbum, ut in omni, ita quoque in N. Fœderis œconomia, sequuntur Sacramenta, ceu sacra signa, & sigilla verbi; per quæ Deo placuit fœdus suum obsignare, istaque veluti tessera populum suum insignire, & a reliquo mundo distinguere. Quæ, licet dudum antea occurrerint, quia tamen sub N. F. maxime excellunt, multisque sunt involuta controversiis, quæ in veteri œconomia minus locum habuerunt; hic eorum natura primum in genere declarabimus: tum de singulis Novi Test. Sacramentis in specie agemus: & denique falsos spuriosque ritus iis superadditos examinabimus.
units.tr: I. The Word, as in everything else, so also in the economy of the New Covenant, is followed by Sacraments, as holy signs and seals of the Word. Through them God has been pleased to seal his covenant and, as it were, to mark his people with a token and set them apart from the rest of the world. Although these were already found long before, because they excel especially under the New Covenant and are wrapped in many controversies that had less place in the old economy, we shall first set out their nature in general here. Then we shall treat the individual sacraments of the New Testament in particular, and finally we shall examine the false and spurious rites added to them.

units.la: II. Sacra illa symbola Latinis Sacramenta, Græcis μυστήρια appellantur. Duo autem Sacramenti vox Latinæ linguæ auctoribus olim significavit: 1. pecuniam, sive pignus, a litigantibus, apud Pontifices, in sacro loco, depositum; quo multabatur is, qui causa cadebat. 2. Jusjurandum, sacro ritu peractum. Qua notione in re militari frequenter usurpatur. Scriptores autem Ecclesiastici quodvis mysterium, ac Christianæ religionis arcanum; & speciatim rem sacram, arcanam, symbolicam, spiritualis gratiæ significativam, adeoque quemlibet ritum sacrum, cunctasque cæremonias, quibus arcana illa vel velabantur, vel adumbrabantur, eo vocabulo denotare cœperunt. Atque ita ad fœderis symbola & sigilla denotanda adhiberi cepit. Quod a Tertulliano primum factum. Ut male Pontificii, ex latiore vocabuli usu, plura Sacramenta proprie dicta colligant. Cum & Patres, & Vulgatus Interpres, & ipsum Pontificale Romanum, res omnes, ritusque sacros, ista voce complectantur.
units.tr: II. Those holy symbols are called sacraments by the Latins and [μυστήρια] by the Greeks. Writers of the Latin tongue once used the word "sacrament" in two senses: (1) a sum of money, or a pledge, deposited by litigants before the pontiffs in a sacred place, which the losing party forfeited; (2) an oath taken with a sacred rite, a sense often used in military matters. Ecclesiastical writers, however, began to use the word to denote any mystery or secret of the Christian religion, and in particular any holy, hidden, symbolic thing that signifies spiritual grace, and so every sacred rite and all the ceremonies by which those secrets were either veiled or foreshadowed. In this way it came to be applied to the symbols and seals of the covenant. Tertullian was the first to do this. The Papists wrongly gather many things under the proper name of sacrament from the wider use of the word, since both the Fathers, the Vulgate translator, and the Roman Pontifical itself embrace all things and sacred rites under this term.

units.la: III. Atque idem vocis μυστηρίου apud Græcos usus: quo illi, partim arcana Christianæ religionis dogmata, partim etiam sacra illa signa & cæremonias expresserunt: tum, quod occulta Græcorum sacra & mysteria multiplicibus olim constabant ritibus; tum, quia externi illi ritus & signa gna arcanam significationem habent, & latente mysterio sese potissimum commendant.
units.tr: III. The Greeks use the word [μυστήριον] in the same way: they applied it partly to the hidden doctrines of the Christian religion, and partly also to those holy signs and ceremonies. This was because the secret rites and mysteries of the Greeks once consisted of many ceremonies, and because those outward rites and signs have a hidden meaning and recommend themselves chiefly by a concealed mystery.

units.la: IV. Scriptura rectius signa sacderis appellat, Gen. 9. 12, 13. & 17:11. sigilla justitiae fidei, Rom. 4: 11. & signa simpliciter, Exod. 12: 13. & ὑποδείγματα, Hebr. 8: 5. & 9: 23. & ἀντίτυπα, 1. Pet. 3: 21. Quae Spiritus sancti voces longe aptiores sunt. Quibus inhaerere praestitisset, quam peregrino vocabulo Christianae religionis caistitatem contaminare. Quanquam, vulgato jam vocabuli illius usu, & Ecclesiastici juris reddito, non ea verborum superstitione ducamur, ut signa illa Sacramenta appellare vereamur. Quae Socinianorum fraus est; qua non tam vocabulum, quam ipsam Sacramentorum naturam petunt.
units.tr: IV. Scripture more properly calls them signs of the covenant (Gen. 9:12, 13; 17:11), seals of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11), and simply signs (Exod. 12:13), and [ὑποδείγματα] (Heb. 8:5; 9:23), and [ἀντίτυπα] (1 Pet. 3:21). These words of the Holy Spirit are far more fitting, and it would have been better to keep to them than to defile the purity of the Christian religion with a foreign word. Nevertheless, since that word is now in common use and has passed into ecclesiastical law, we need not be so superstitious about words that we fear to call those signs sacraments. The Socinians' trick lies here: they attack not so much the word as the very nature of the sacraments.

units.la: V. Sunt autem Sacramenta, signa seu signacula foederis, a Deo instituta, ad divinas promissiones veluti sacro pignore nobis obsignandas; ac vicissim iis, tanquam sacratissimis obedientiae testeris, obsequium nostrum, omnemque animae affectum, ipsi deferendum, & publice testandum.
units.tr: V. Sacraments, then, are signs or seals of the covenant, instituted by God, to seal to us his divine promises, as it were, with a holy pledge; and in turn, as most sacred testimonies of our obedience, they are to be offered to him, and our devotion and every affection of the soul is to be publicly attested by them.

units.la: VI. A sacrificiis differunt: quod illa a Deo ab hominibus; haec autem homini a Deo tradantur. Figura autem Sacramento latior est. Quo in genere utrimque peccant Pontificii.
units.tr: VI. They differ from sacrifices in that sacrifices are offered by men to God, whereas sacraments are given by God to men. A figure, however, is a wider notion than a sacrament. On both points the Papists go wrong.

units.la: VII. Genus Sacramenti est signum. Non actio: ut male Lutherani. Quaecunque enim actiones hic concurrunt, non alium quam significandi usum habent. Cumque omne signum vel naturale sit, vel voluntarium: idque vel ab hominibus, vel a Deo, institutum: ad postremum genus referuntur Sacramenta, quippe a Deo, singulari consilio, instituta. Cumque rursus, ex signis voluntariis, alia sint μνημοσυνικά, sive rerum praeteritarum monumenta; alia σημαντικά, & res praesentes designantia; alia προσημαντικά, & rerum futurarum praenuncia; quas vel simpliciter adumbrant & significant, vel signaculo quodam obsignant & tradunt; denique signa alia visu, alia aliis sensibus, cum externis, tum internis, percipiantur: omnes signorum horum perfectiones comprehendunt Sacramenta. Cum non nuda signa, sed sigilla, sint; eaque visibilia: quod genus signorum praestantissimum est: res praeteritas, praesentes, & futuras non solum memorantia, & per analogiam significantia; sed & obsignantia; &, per substitutionem, dato pignore ac arrhabone, exhibentia & confirmantia.
units.tr: VII. The genus of a sacrament is sign, not action, as the Lutherans wrongly hold. For whatever actions meet here have no use other than that of signifying. And since every sign is either natural or voluntary, and the voluntary is instituted either by men or by God, sacraments belong to the last kind, being instituted by God with a singular purpose. Again, among voluntary signs, some are [μνημοσυνικά], that is, memorials of past things; some [σημαντικά], designating present things; some [προσημαντικά], foretelling future things, which either merely shadow forth and signify these, or by a certain seal confirm and deliver them. Finally, some signs are perceived by sight and others by other senses, both outward and inward. Sacraments comprise all the perfections of these signs. For they are not bare signs but seals, and visible ones, which is the most excellent kind of sign: they not only remind us of past, present and future things and signify them by analogy, but also seal them, and, by substitution, present and confirm them, given a pledge and earnest.

units.la: VIII. Quum autem Sacramenta sint signa sacra, ex instituto significantia; facile patet non alium ea instituere posse quam Deum. Ego enim accepi a Domino, quod & tradidi vobis. 1. Cor. 11:23. Sicuti ipsius foliuseft, sacramentorum vim implere; & quæcunque ea obsignant actu ipso largiri & tradere. Absque quo illa cassa signa, & inania sacra, forent. Quomodo illa sunt, quæ ab hominibus instituuntur: quæ cum gratiæ vehicula non sint, utpote quam donare homines non possunt, mera tantum picturæ & umbræ sunt, ad vacuas mentes pascendas, & puerili superstitione implendas, aptæ. Cujus generis sunt signa, quæ appellant, sacramentalia; quæ Pontificii ab Ecclesia instituti & sacrari posse autumant.
units.tr: VIII. Since sacraments are holy signs signifying by institution, it is easy to see that none but God can institute them. For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you (1 Cor. 11:23). It is his prerogative to fulfil the power of the sacraments, and to bestow and deliver in very deed whatever they seal; without this they would be empty signs and vain sacred things. Such are those which are instituted by men. Since these are not vehicles of grace, which men cannot bestow, they are mere pictures and shadows, fit only to feed empty minds and to fill them with childish superstition. Of this kind are the things which they call sacramentals, which the Papists maintain may be instituted and consecrated by the Church.

units.la: IX. Instituit vero Christus, una cum sacramentis, sacramentorum administros; qui non alii sunt, quam quibus ordinarium verbi ministerium tradidit. Ut penes eosdem sit divinarum tabularum, & sigillorum iis appensorum, custodia & dispensatio; quæ Christus mandato & institutione sua conjunxit. Profecti ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, Sp. S. docentes eos, servare omnia &c. Matth. 28: 19, 20. Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de ministris Christi, & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. 1. Cor. 4: 1. Cui ordini contrahitur Sociniani, qui, ut non multum sacri in sacramentis vident, ita usum ac administrationem eorum Christianis omnibus promiscuum faciunt. Quod Pontificii quoque de nonnullis sacramentis concedunt.
units.tr: IX. Christ, however, instituted along with the sacraments the ministers of the sacraments, who are none other than those to whom he committed the ordinary ministry of the Word. So the custody and dispensing of the divine tablets, and of the seals appended to them, rests with the same men, whom Christ joined to them by his command and institution. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; teaching them to observe all things (Matt. 28:19, 20). Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Cor. 4:1). The Socinians, who see little of what is holy in the sacraments, make their use and administration common to all Christians; the Papists too concede this for some sacraments. We reject this.

units.la: X. Cumque a Christi institutione sacramentorum vis dependeat, illa per ministri indignitatem corrumpi vel minui non potest; modo ille apostata non sit, vel de Ecclesia exeat. Quamdiu enim ipsi verbi ministerium constat, etiam sacramentorum administratio constare debet. In cathedra Moysi sedent Scriba, & Pharisæi. Omnia ergo quæ dixerint vobis ut servetis, servate & facite. Sed secundum opera eorum ne facite. Matth. 23: 2, 3. Ac nonnulli quidem per invidiam & contentionem, nonnulli vero etiam bono affectu Christum prædicant — quid igitur, attamen quo vis modo; sive in speciem, sive sincere, Christus annunciatur. Et de hoc gaudeo, atque gaudebo. Phil. 1: 15, 18. Nam neque is, qui plantat, est aliquid, neque is qui rigat; sed Deus qui dat crescendi vim.
units.tr: X. Since the power of the sacraments depends on Christ's institution, it cannot be corrupted or diminished by the unworthiness of the minister, provided he is not an apostate or has departed from the Church. For as long as the ministry of the Word itself stands, the administration of the sacraments must stand too. The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do; but do not act according to their works. Matt. 23: 2, 3. Some indeed preach Christ out of envy and strife, but some also out of good will... whatever the way, whether in pretence or in sincerity, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and will rejoice. Phil. 1: 15, 18. For neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters; but God who gives the increase. 1 Cor. 3: 7.

units.la: 1. Cor. 3: 7. Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua, ad resipiscentiam. Is vero, qui post me venit, validior est me; cujus non sum dignus qui soleas portem. Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu S. & igne. Matth. 3: 11. Quod contra Novatianos & Donatistas observandum.
units.tr: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. But he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. Matt. 3: 11. This is to be noted against the Novatians and the Donatists.

units.la: XI. Pariter nec intentio ministri ad essentiam sacramenti absolute requiritur; contra ac Concilium Florentinum, & hodierna Pontificiorum rum Ecclesia censet; de qua re anxie inter se quærunt, & disputant, mirosque conscientiis laqueos & compedes injiciunt. Ad integritatem vero ejus sufficit, si publice ea fiant, quæ Christus in Sacramenti institutione jussit. Si quid autem in occulto minister peccet, & non caste satis sacra tractet; id ipsius quidem peccatum est, non item de Sacramenti religione quicquam delibat; quod non ex ministri intentione, sed ex Dei ordinatione & mandato æstimandum est. Aliter enim errabundæ ac lapsanti hominis cogitationi amplius tribuendum erit, quam certissimo Christi mandato & institutioni: ac incerta erunt omnia, & nutantia: & quicquid consolationis adferunt sacramenta conscientiis, id omne iis eripietur; ac homo tantum non in idolum erigetur; a cujus videl. nutu, & bono malove animo, sacramenti vis & efficacia suspendenda erit; ut Ecclesiæ nihil boni Spiritus, nisi de ipsius manu, ac illo dispensante & moderante, obveniat. Quo & alia Papalis Ecclesiæ dogmata aurigantur.
units.tr: XI. Likewise, the intention of the minister is not absolutely required for the essence of the sacrament, contrary to what the Council of Florence and the present-day Church of the Papists hold. On this matter they anxiously argue and dispute among themselves, and they throw strange snares and fetters on consciences. For its integrity, however, it is enough that those things be done publicly which Christ commanded in the institution of the sacrament. If the minister sins in secret and does not handle the holy things sufficiently purely, that is indeed his own sin, and it does not in any way detract from the sanctity of the sacrament; it must be judged not by the minister's intention but by God's ordinance and command. For otherwise more weight would have to be given to the erring and faltering thought of a man than to the most certain command and institution of Christ; everything would be uncertain and wavering, and whatever comfort the sacraments bring to consciences would be snatched away; and man would be raised almost to an idol, on whose nod and good or bad disposition the power and efficacy of the sacrament would depend, so that nothing good of the Spirit would reach the Church except from his hand, and at his dispensing and governing. By this the other dogmas of the Papal Church are also steered.

units.la: XII. Cum vero sacramenta signa sint, ut plene eorum natura percipiatur, attendendum in iis est primo ad symbolum externum; secundo ad rem significatam.
units.tr: XII. Since sacraments are signs, two things must be considered in them if their nature is to be fully understood: first the external sign, and second the thing signified.

units.la: XIII. Ad illud pertinet, cum externum elementum, tum usus ejus; qui sacramento ita essentialis est, ut extra usum suum non constet, Quod contra Pontificios tenendum est.
units.tr: XIII. The first concerns both the external element and its use. The use is so essential to a sacrament that it does not exist apart from its use. This must be maintained against the Papists.

units.la: XIV. Elementum autem similitudinem quandam cum re cœlesti habere debet, ut eam figurare possit. Quanquam sola similitudo non sufficit; sed verbum institutionis, quod ex elemento sacramentum faciat, &c, pro re cœlesti, terrestrem, tanquam illius arrham & pignus, substituat, accedere præterea necesse sit. Constat autem hoc verbum mandato Christi, elementis externis recte utendi; & promissio, usum illum frustra non fore. Unde eleganter Augustinus: Detrahe verbum, & quid est aqua, nisi aqua? accedit verbum ad elementum, & fit sacramentum, etiam ipsum tanquam visibile verbum. Unde ista tanta virtus aquæ, ut corpus tangat & cor abluat, nisi faciente verbo? non quia dicitur, sed quia creditur.
units.tr: XIV. The element must bear some resemblance to the heavenly thing, so that it can represent it. Yet resemblance alone is not enough. It is also necessary that the word of institution, which makes the sacrament out of the element, etc., set the earthly thing in place of the heavenly, as its earnest and pledge. This word is joined to the command of Christ to use the external elements rightly, and to the promise that such use will not be in vain. Hence Augustine well says: Take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, as if it were itself a visible word. Whence comes such power in water, that it touches the body and cleanses the heart? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.

units.la: XV. Cum autem verbum illud Christi unicum sacræ hujus actionis fundamentum sit, identidem illud repeti, piisque precibus præsenti actioni applicari debet. In qua voluntatis Christi declaratione, ac religiosa institutionis commemoratione, faustisque precibus, reliquaque actione sacra, omnis sacramenti consecratio absolvitur; atque ea solum ratione ex elemento fit sacramentum. Cum enim Christus panem vinumque in corporis sui sacramentum consecraret, sola pignoris istius traditione; & voluntatis suae, qua illud rerum coelestium figuram & sigillum ferre volebat, declaratione usus est. Atque ita ministri quoque externa signa consecrant; non panem vinumque alloquentes; sed fideles de usu & ratione istarum rerum, deque voluntate & institutione Christi edocentes; atque institutum illud juge & perenne, ex mandato ejus, in Ecclesia vigere oportere docentes; & signis praesentibus applicantes; ac cunctam denique actionem ad exemplum Christi efformantes & absolventes. Quod verbum, sive institutionis, sive concionale appelletur; prout institutionis Christi vel stricta repetitio & applicatio, vel ejusdem uberior explicatio est, parum interest. Aliud enim verbum, quam institutionis, aut de institutione Christi, hic non agnoscimus; nec certa ac peculiari consecrationis vocabula ab eo distinguimus. Ac longe imprimis valere jubemus Pontificiorum susurros magicos, & imperiosa verba; quibus, non populum Christianum, sed ipsa elementa alloquuntur; quaeque operatoria vocant, arcanam iis vim inesse docentes; quibus consecrationes suas peragunt. Quae verborum potentia ad infanda magorum sacra pertinet. Christum certe, non panem vinumque, sed fideles accumbentes allocutum constat. Unde ad ejus exemplum, non bruta elementa affari, sed populum Christianum de voluntate ac institutione Christi, omnique sacramenti ratione docere potius convenit. Quae, cum sacro ejus usu conjuncta, tota elementi consecratio est.
units.tr: XV. Since that word of Christ is the sole foundation of this sacred action, it should be repeated again and again and applied to the present action with devout prayers. By this declaration of Christ's will, this pious recalling of the institution, and these prayers of blessing, together with the rest of the sacred action, the whole consecration of the sacrament is completed, and in this way alone the element becomes a sacrament. For when Christ consecrated bread and wine as the sacrament of his body, he used only the handing over of this pledge and the declaration of his will, by which he wished it to bear the figure and seal of heavenly things. So also the ministers consecrate the external signs. They do not address the bread and wine, but they teach the faithful about the use and purpose of these things, and about the will and institution of Christ. They teach that this institution, by his command, ought to remain continuous and perpetual in the Church, and they apply it to the signs present. Finally, they shape and complete the whole action after the example of Christ. Whether this word is called the word of institution or the word of preaching makes little difference, since it is either a strict repetition and application of Christ's institution, or a fuller explanation of it. We acknowledge no other word here than that of institution, or about the institution of Christ, and we do not distinguish from it any fixed and special formulas of consecration. Above all we bid farewell to the magical whisperings and imperious words of the Papists, by which they address not the Christian people but the elements themselves, and which they call operative, teaching that a hidden power lies in them, by which they perform their consecrations. This power of words belongs to the unspeakable rites of magicians. It is certain that Christ spoke to the faithful reclining at the table, not to bread and wine. Therefore, after his example, it is better to address not the mute elements but the Christian people, teaching them about the will and institution of Christ and about the whole nature of the sacrament. This teaching, joined to the sacred use of the elements, is the whole consecration of the element.

units.la: XVI. Res significata, sive spiritualis, quae altera sacramentorum pars est, est Christus cum omnibus meritis ac beneficiis suis: speciatim autem cum passione & morte sua. Quae etiam ratio videtur esse, cur sacramenta nunquam illustria aut splendida, sed vilia magis, aut vulgaria saltem, a Deo instituta fuerint. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi est? 1. Cor. 10: 16. Christus autem in omnibus foederis gratiae sacramentis ex aequo expressus ac delineatus fuit: quanquam, pro diversa signorum ratione, variaque eorum pictura, diverso modo, ac gradu: prout aliter in baptismo, aliter in coena, nobis exhibetur; quorum illud insitionis in Dei foedus, hoc perpetuae nutritionis sacramentum est. Et omnes eandem escam spiritualem ediderunt: & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Bibebant enim ex sequente spirituali petra. Petra vero illa erat Christus. 1. Cor. 10: 3, 4.
units.tr: XVI. The thing signified, or spiritual thing, which is the other part of the sacraments, is Christ with all his merits and benefits, and especially with his passion and death. This also seems to be the reason why God instituted sacraments that were never splendid or showy, but rather humble, or at least common. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 Cor. 10:16. Christ is set forth and portrayed equally in all the sacraments of the covenant of grace, though in different ways and degrees, according to the different character of the signs and their different pictures. He is presented to us one way in baptism and another in the Supper. The former is the sacrament of our engrafting into God's covenant, the latter the sacrament of continual nourishment. And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of that spiritual rock which followed them, and that rock was Christ. 1 Cor. 10:3, 4.

units.la: XVII. Vis autem & intima natura sacramentorum consistit in analogia & σχέσει signi terreni ad rem significatam: qua res illa externa rem coelestem, tum declarat & adumbrat, tum divinae promissionis virtute obsignat & tradit.
units.tr: XVII. The force and inner nature of the sacraments consists in the analogy and relation [σχέσει] of the earthly sign to the thing signified, by which that external thing both declares and shadows forth the heavenly thing, and by the power of divine promise seals and delivers it.

units.la: XVIII. Est autem unio illa, quae inter signum & rem signatam in sacramento intercedit, non physica; nec localis; ac nec spiritualis quidem, ut ipsis signis vis regenerandi inhaereat: sed relativa & sacramentalis; qualis in signis locum habet, quae se ipsa sensibus, rem autem signatam fidei ac intellectui exhibent. XIX. Nec ideo mudae picturae aut simulachra relinquuntur. Nam, respectu rei exhibitae, atque ob exhibitionis certitudinem, unio illa maxime realis est: cum realis rei significatae fiat communicatio, sicuti in contractu, per traditionem instrumenti, praedii vel domus fit translatio. Quod nemo nisi rerum & verborum imperitus ignoraverit. XX. Ac vi huius unionis, ob Christi ordinationem & promissionem, fit mystica signorum in res signatas conversio, & transelementatio: Graecis τροπή, μεταβολή, μετασχηματισμός, μεταβίβασις & μετενέργεια, appellata. Latini olim immoxie transubstantiationem dixere, cum substantia pro substantia hic supponatur. Quae vox tandem propudiosi erroris occasio fuit. XXI. Ex eadem unione, & sacramentali conversione est, atque ad obsignationis evidentiam & certitudinem testandam facit; quod nomina & attributa signorum, & rerum signatarum, inter se variae commutentur & reciprocentur: quodque vel signum praedicatur esse res signata; vel res signata accipit nomen signi; vel effectum signati signo attribuitur; vel proprietates denique signi de re signata usurpantur. Quae locutiones sacramentales appellantur; passimque in Scriptura extant: atque ex unione illa sacramentali oriuntur, quae signum & rem signatam, eo, quo dictum est, modo, conjungit. Quod contra Pontificios & Lutheranos, τὸ ἡητὸν urgentes, probe observandum est. XXII. Sequitur sacramentorum finis, qui est, foedus Dei obsignare, & mutuo pignore Deum hominesque unire, atque artissime devincire. Illa enim obsignatio mutua est, cum Dei promittentis, tum hominis adstipulantis, atque obedientiam testantis, respectu. Appellat enim ea Scriptura signa foederis, à Deo promissionibus adjuncta, quae ab hominibus accipi & usurpari jubet, Gen. 17: 11. Sigilla, σφραγῖδες, Rom. 4: 11. quae gratiam Dei fidelibus non solum obsignant, sed & obsignando etiam quoque tradunt & applicant; eo videl. modo, quo per signa ea tradi potest: itemque lætæ conscientiæ fulcra & ἐκμυήματα, quibus illa nixa Deum accedere, & de hæreditate interpellare audet.
units.tr: XVIII. The union that exists between the sign and the thing signified in a sacrament is neither physical, nor local, nor even spiritual, so that a power of regeneration inheres in the signs themselves. It is relative and sacramental, such as obtains in signs, which present themselves to the senses and present the thing signified to faith and understanding. XIX. Nor for this reason are they left as bare pictures or images. For with respect to the thing exhibited, and on account of the certainty of its exhibition, that union is most truly real, since a real communication of the thing signified takes place, just as in a contract a transfer of an estate or house is effected by the handing over of a deed. No one but an ignoramus in matters and words would fail to know this. XX. By the power of this union, and on account of Christ's ordinance and promise, there comes about a mystical conversion and transelementation of the signs into the things signified. The Greeks call this conversion [τροπή], change [μεταβολή], transformation [μετασχηματισμός], transference [μεταβίβασις] and transenergy [μετενέργεια]. The Latins formerly called it transubstantiation, since here substance is put in place of substance. That word at last became an occasion of shameful error. XXI. From the same union and sacramental conversion there also arises, and serves to attest the clarity and certainty of the sealing, that the names and attributes of the signs and of the things signified are variously exchanged and reciprocated with one another. Either the sign is said to be the thing signified, or the thing signified takes the name of the sign, or the effect of the thing signified is ascribed to the sign, or finally the properties of the sign are applied to the thing signified. These are called sacramental expressions, and they occur everywhere in Scripture. They arise from that sacramental union, which joins the sign and the thing signified in the manner just described. This must be carefully observed against the Papists and the Lutherans, who press the literal sense [τὸ ῥητόν]. XXII. There follows the end of the sacraments, which is to seal the covenant of God and to unite God and men by a mutual pledge, binding them most closely together. For this sealing is mutual, with respect both to God who promises and to man who assents and attests his obedience. Scripture therefore calls them signs of the covenant, attached by God to promises, which he commands men to receive and use. Gen. 17:11. Seals [σφραγῖδες], Rom. 4:11, which not only seal God's grace to the faithful but also, in sealing, deliver and apply it, in the manner in which it can be delivered through signs. They are also the props [ἐκμυήματα] of a glad conscience, on which it leans when it dares to draw near to God and to plead for the inheritance.

units.la: XXIII. Atque hæc sacramentorum & verbi inter se ratio est. Quod, cum utraque Christi merita & gratiam nobis ob oculos ponant, sacramenta ad verbum accedant tanquam sigilla. Unde verbum communiusest, sacramentis peculiarior operatio est. Quanquam enim verbum per se certissimum, ac sacramentis prius sit; cum illa verbo posteriora sint, sicuti & verbum absque sacramentis, sacramenta autem absque verbo esse non possunt: hominum tamen imbecillitas talibus adminiculis fulciri debet. Nec culpanda est Dei sapientia, quod nobis, in carne hærentibus, istas cœlestium rerum imagines indulgere voluerit; non, quo in terreno isto spectaculo defixi hæruseremus; sed ut ista in umbra rerum spiritualium qualemcunque aspectum haberemus, ad de accepto pignore lætaremur & fiduciam sumeremus.
units.tr: XXIII. Such is the relation of the sacraments and the word to one another. Since both set Christ's merits and grace before our eyes, the sacraments come to the word as seals. Hence the word is more general, and the sacraments have a more particular operation. For although the word is in itself most certain and comes before the sacraments, and the sacraments come after the word, just as the word can exist without the sacraments but the sacraments cannot exist without the word, nevertheless human weakness ought to be supported by such aids. Nor is God's wisdom to be blamed, that he has been willing to indulge us, while we still cling to flesh, with these images of heavenly things. He did not intend that we should stay fixed on this earthly spectacle, but that we should have some kind of view of spiritual things in this shadow, and that we should rejoice in the pledge received and take up confidence.

units.la: XXIV. Notandæ hic autem diversæ errorum facies. Quorum alii sacrorum signorum dignitatem minuunt, alii nimium adaugent, inque ea tanquam idola insaniunt. Medio autem loco, atque extra illa utrimque præcipitia, collocata est veritas.
units.tr: XXIV. Here we should note the different faces of error. Some diminish the dignity of the holy signs, others magnify them excessively and go mad over them as if they were idols. Truth, however, lies in the middle, set apart from the precipices on either side.

units.la: XXV. Perverse enim ab una parte sectarii in sacramentis nil præter inania signa, & mortis Christi μνημόσυνον ac picturam, & nudam rei gestæ repræsentationem, atque externa Christianæ societatis symbola & tesseras agnoscunt. Quæ Socinianorum, & Anabaptistarum, ac partim Remonstrantium, sententia est; qui, virtute omni sacramentorum exhausta, nec quicquam præter externa simulachra, ac jejuna spectacula, Christianis relinquunt. Unde omnem promissorum ac fœderis Dei obsignationem tollunt, nec quicquam Deum nobis per ista pignora largiri statuunt. Cujus erroris invidia & nos præter meritum pulsant Pontificii & Lutherani; quasi nil præter nudas imagines in sacramentis relinqueremus. Quæ quantopere a veritate absint, ex dictis patet.
units.tr: XXV. The sectarians, on the one hand, wrongly acknowledge in the sacraments nothing but empty signs, a memorial [μνημόσυνον] of Christ's death and a picture, a bare representation of the event, and the outward symbols and tokens of Christian fellowship. This is the view of the Socinians and Anabaptists, and in part of the Remonstrants, who drain the sacraments of all their power and leave Christians nothing but outward likenesses and dry spectacles. Hence they remove any sealing of God's promises and covenant, and they hold that God grants us nothing through these pledges. The Papists and Lutherans charge us with this error, though we do not deserve it, as if we left nothing in the sacraments but bare images. How far this is from the truth is clear from what has been said.

units.la: XXVI.
