Ab altera parte incedunt Pontificii, asseetantibus eos ex intervallo aliquot Lutheranis; qui sacramenta Novi Test. gratiæ justificantis causas veras & proprias, licet secundarias, statuunt. In qua sententia explicanda magnum inter ipsos opinionum certamen est. Omnes autem sacramenta gratiam continere; ejusque vehicula esse; eamque, ubi legitime administrata sunt, actu operari; & proxime, & immediate, atque ex opere operato, conferre, asserunt. Per opus autem operatum, in causas, ex opere Con-
units.tr: XXVI. On the other side, the Papists press forward, with some Lutherans following at a distance; these hold that the sacraments of the New Testament are true and proper causes of justifying grace, though secondary ones. There is great conflict among them over how this view is to be explained. All of them, however, assert that the sacraments contain grace, that they are its vehicles, that where they are lawfully administered they actually work, and that they confer grace proximately, immediately, and by the work performed. By the work performed, moreover, they understood, among the causes, from the work of the Con-

units.la: Concilio Tridentino, externam sacramentorum celebrationem intelli‑gebant; quæ non ponentibus obicem peccati mortalis, etsi aloqui fide & pietate vacuis, salutaris gratiæ causa & instrumentum sit. Lutherani, quanquam verbis Pontificiorum opus operatum negent, reipsa illud introductum eunt, dum fideles & infideles ex equo corpus Christi edere statuunt. Quod physicam sacramentorum vim & efficaciam non parum redolet. Quo & aliæ eorum theses ducunt.
units.tr: ...at the Council of Trent they understood the external celebration of the sacraments, which, even when approached by those empty of faith and piety, who place no obstacle of mortal sin in the way, is a cause and instrument of saving grace. The Lutherans, although they deny in words the work performed as the Papists state it, in fact introduce it, when they hold that believers and unbelievers alike eat the body of Christ. This smacks not a little of a physical power and efficacy in the sacraments, and their other theses lead the same way.

units.la: XXVII. Nos autem physicam istam, ac infallibilem, in omnibus qui sacramenta recipiunt, neque iis obicem ponunt, operationem illorum negamus. Nec aliam sacramentorum potentiam agnoscimus, quam moralem, qualis in signis & verbis est; ad rem non efficiendam & producendam, sed significandam & obsignandam. Unde in fidelibus tantum, iisque, qui non solum illum qualemcunque mortalis peccati obicem removerunt, sed & pios sanctosque motus habent, illa valent; & mediante Dei Spiritu, ac fide, gratiæ Dei obsides, & signacula sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. We, however, deny that physical and infallible operation of the sacraments in all who receive them and place no obstacle in their way. Nor do we acknowledge any power in the sacraments other than a moral one, such as belongs to signs and words; not to effect and produce the thing, but to signify and seal it. Hence these things avail only in believers, and in those who have not only removed whatever obstacle of mortal sin there may be, but also have pious and holy motions of heart; and by the mediation of God's Spirit and faith they are pledges and seals of the grace of God.

units.la: XXVIII. Atque hæc 1. perpetua Scripturæ sententia est: quæ sacramenta signa appellat, nec aliam quam moralem & sacramentalem operationem iis assignat; & fide ea usurpari debere docet. Ita enim baptismus nos salvat, non qui est depositio sordis carnis, sed bona conscientiæ firmamentum ad Deum. 1. Pet. 3:21. Qui & veteris Ecclesiæ sensus fuit. 2. Et vero ἀΦθάρτου nimis, ac propudiosum, est, elementa illa externa vitali inhærente impregnare; ut in animam agere possint, ad reatum tollendum, motusque spirituales producendos, eamque iustitiæ initiis imbuendam. Nulla enim externorum symbolorum ad spiritualia ista effecta proportio est. 3. Sed & iustitiariorum hac in parte dolus latet. Nam per sacramenta iustitiam nostram procurari ajunt; ea, quam diximus, ratione: prout per illa sic nobis Christi merita applicantur, ut inde donum iustitiæ in nobis emergat; quod iustitiæ nostræ causa & fundamentum sit. Qua veri falsique mixtura tandem veritas adulterata, & meritorum Christi evacuatio facta est. 5. Unde a Christo sensim abducitur Ecclesia; &, loco sponsi, tantum pictura ejus pascitur: dumque sacramentis adeo portentosa vis adscribitur, ac tantum non ipsa salus abiis suspenditur; in iis Servatoris sui signis & imaginibus hærerem ea, ac tantum non stupere, docetur. Quod in Papatu nimis luctuoso eventu comprobatum fuit: ubi major sacramentorum, quam Christi ipsius veneratio conspicitur. 6. Quin in idola illa tandem erecta sunt; dum immensa vi aucta, ac immodico populi affectu & cultu celebrata sunt. 7. Ut taceam errore hoc ipsi Christi Testamento obrogatum, ac non parum ei adjectum fuisse. Agit enim illud de ipso Christi corpore & sanguine, non de aquæ vel sacrati panis mystica quadam vi, & immensa propemodum potestate. Nec signa illa in testamento proprie scripta, sed tanquam testamenti signacula nobis tradita, eique appensa sunt. Quo loco si semper habita, ipsumque testamentum Christi perpetuo lectum & servatum fuisset; non ille pudor Ecclesiæ venisset, ut istis sanguinis Christi signis ac picturis non solum se oblectaret, sed eadem adoraret. 8. Nec satisfaciunt illi inter adversarios, qui vim quidem internam in animam agendi sacramentis abrogant; sed eadem, qualescunque tandem causæ sint, infallibiliter tamen gratiam producere statuunt: Deo videlicet, ex quadam lege, seu pacto, ad eorum præsentiam operante. Quanquam enim hi virtutem omnem Deo, non sacramentis, tribuant; tamen reliqua prioris sententiæ probra non effugiunt. Nam & Dei virtutem externis istis signis alligant, quasi ad eorum præsentiam solum operetur: quod & falsum est, cum etiam ante percepta sacramenta gratiam suam largiri Deus soleat; cujus acceptæ ea tantum signa & indicia sunt; & parum a magica signorum & verborum superstitione abhorret. Prout Scriptura hos religionis corruptores, qui externis verbis & signis in sacris tantum tribuunt, magos appellare non semel solet. Et præterea, ut priores illi, externis illis symbolis fidelium animas nimium adfigunt & obstringunt; cum sine iis gratiam Dei, ac vitam æternam vix dari autumént. Unde eadem justitiæ & salutis causas suo in ordine quoque statuunt. Quæ signorum superstitio, affectusque idololatricus, omni modo cavendus ac eliminandus est.
units.tr: XXVIII. And, first, this is the constant teaching of Scripture, which calls the sacraments signs, assigns them no other operation than a moral and sacramental one, and teaches that they ought to be used with faith. So: "Baptism saves us, not as the removal of the filth of the flesh, but as the pledge of a good conscience toward God" (1 Pet. 3:21). This was also the sense of the ancient Church. 2. Indeed, it is too much, and shameful, to imbue those external elements with a living, indwelling incorruptible [ἀφθάρτου] power, so that they could act upon the soul, remove guilt, produce spiritual movements, and imbue it with the beginnings of righteousness. For there is no proportion between external symbols and these spiritual effects. 3. But the deceit of the justifiers also lies hidden in this matter. For they say that our righteousness is procured through the sacraments, in the manner we have described: that through them the merits of Christ are so applied to us that from them a gift of righteousness springs up in us, which becomes the cause and foundation of our righteousness. By this mixture of truth and falsehood the truth has at last been adulterated and the merits of Christ emptied out. 5. Hence the Church is gradually led away from Christ, and instead of the bridegroom she feeds only on his picture; and while such a marvellous power is ascribed to the sacraments that salvation itself is all but hung upon them, she is taught to cling to and almost to marvel at the signs and images of her Saviour. This was proved by the most lamentable outcome in the Papacy, where greater veneration is seen toward the sacraments than toward Christ himself. 6. Indeed, in the end they were erected into idols, while they were celebrated with immense power and with an immoderate devotion and worship of the people. 7. I say nothing of how this error detracts from Christ's own Testament and adds not a little to it. For the Testament speaks of the body and blood of Christ himself, not of some mystical power and almost boundless potency of water or of consecrated bread. Nor are those signs written into the Testament, but were handed down to us as seals of the Testament and appended to it. If this had always been kept in view, and Christ's Testament had been read and observed constantly, that shameful thing would not have come upon the Church, that she should not only delight herself in these signs and pictures of Christ's blood, but also worship them. 8. Nor do those among our opponents satisfy, who indeed deny that the sacraments have any inner power to act upon the soul, but nonetheless hold that, whatever their causes may be, they infallibly produce grace, namely because God, by a certain law or pact, works at their presence. For although these men ascribe all power to God and not to the sacraments, they do not escape the disgraces of the former view. For they also bind God's power to these external signs, as if he worked only at their presence; which is false, since God is accustomed to bestow his grace even before the sacraments are received, of which the sacraments are only signs and indications once it has been received; and this differs little from the magical superstition of signs and words. Scripture often calls those corrupters of religion, who ascribe such power to external words and signs in holy things, magicians. Moreover, like the former, they bind and fasten the souls of the faithful too tightly to those external symbols, since they hardly think that the grace of God and eternal life can be given without them. Hence they also set up the causes of righteousness and salvation in their own order. This superstition of signs and idolatrous affection must be guarded against and removed in every way.

units.la: XXIX. Præter præcipuum hunc sacramentorum finem, accedunt ali- ii quoque fines secundarii.
units.tr: XXIX. Besides this chief end of the sacraments, there are also other, secondary ends.

units.la: 1. Quod in iis publica fidei ac spei nostræ fiat professio. 2. Quod ad contesterandos fideles, & Christianorum societatem sanciendam ea pertineant. 3. Quod Euangelii veritati demonstrandæ inserviant, ac publicum ejus in mundo sint præconium. Absque eo enim ritus illi tam universaliter, ac tam constanter, in mundo nunquam obtinuissent. Unde Christianæ religioni non exiguum fulcrum addunt. Quandiu enim illi ritus usurpantur, illa non poteit non perennare. 4. Quod denique præcipuum Christianæ fidei articulum, de morte & passione Christi, in Ecclesia semper integrum conservent, nec corrumpi prorsus sinant. Quod in maximis Ecclesiæ tenebris patuit.
units.tr: (1) That in them a public profession of our faith and hope is made. (2) That they serve to attest the faithful and to ratify the fellowship of Christians. (3) That they serve to demonstrate the truth of the Gospel and are a public proclamation of it in the world. For without them those rites could never have prevailed so universally and so constantly in the world, and so they add no small support to the Christian religion. As long as those rites are kept up, the Gospel cannot fail to endure. (4) That, finally, they preserve in the Church, always whole, the chief article of the Christian faith, concerning the death and passion of Christ, and never allow it to be wholly corrupted. This became clear in the darkest times of the Church.

units.la: XXX. Subjectum sacramentorum sunt fœderati, seu fideles. Ea aquam: quid prohibet me baptizari? Dixit vero Philippus: si credis ex toto corde, licet. Respondens autem ille dixit, credo Iesum Christum esse Filium illum Dei. Act. 8: 36, 37. Quamvis enim sacramentorum efficacia a Christi institutione dependeat; tamen ad rectum eorum usum fides requiritur. Absque qua qui ea usurpare nituntur, illa contemerant, & nuda tantum signa tractant.
units.tr: XXX. The subjects of the sacraments are the covenanted, or believers. "Look, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said: "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." Acts 8:36, 37. For although the efficacy of the sacraments depends on the institution of Christ, faith is nonetheless required for their right use. Those who strive to use them without faith profane them and handle nothing but bare signs.

units.la: XXXI. Ac patet jam eorum effectus; qui est, fœdus Dei ac bona fœderis, nobis obsignare & tradere. Cui Pontificii perperam addunt commentitium characterem: quem praeterea sacramenta quaedam animo imprimant. Quod figmentum Sacrae Scripturæ, veterique Ecclesiæ ignoratum, & inter Scholasticorum controversias varie vexatum, vel ipsa pugnantium sententiarum absurditate perimitur & confoditur. Et non omnibus, sed quibusdam tantum sacramentis vim istam animam perarandi tribuunt; ac Veteris Testamenti signis eam prorsus abrogant; quæ ista videlicet nota characteristica a Novi Testam. sacramentis distinguunt. Multaque praeterea quæstiones nugacissimas de hoc non enterunt. Ut in tenebris eos micare, &c., nulla Scriptura duce, de figmentis tantum suis dimicare, patet.
units.tr: XXXI. The effect of the sacraments is now also plain: it is to seal to us and deliver the covenant of God and the blessings of the covenant. To this the Papists wrongly add an invented character, which they say certain sacraments impress on the soul. This fiction, unknown to Holy Scripture and to the early Church, and variously troubled among the controversies of the Schoolmen, is destroyed and undermined by the very absurdity of their conflicting opinions. They also ascribe this power of stamping the soul not to all sacraments but only to some, and they deny it altogether to the signs of the Old Testament, which of course is what they use to distinguish this characteristic mark from the sacraments of the New Testament. Besides, they raise many most trifling questions about it. That they grope about in darkness, and fight over their own fictions with no guide from Scripture, is plain.

units.la: XXXII. Testimonia tamen fucando huic commento ex Scripturis conquirunt; & quanquam Vetus Testam. isto charactere caruisse velint, tamen circumcisionis notam; ac loca quaedam prophetarum, ubi signi & signaculi fit mentio, ad spurium istum characterem referunt. Quo pertinent, Ezech. 9: 4. Transi per medium civitatis &c. Esai. 66: 18, 19. Quum factorum erga hos, cogitationumque erga hos quaeque adveniet, ponam in his signum &c. Et in Novi Test. Pauli stigmata, Gal. 6: 17. & Timothei dona, ad ministerium obeundum, 1. Tim. 4: 14. in eandem rem adferunt. Ac Spiritus denique arrhabonem ac σφραγίδα, 2. Cor. 1: 21, 22. Eph. 1: 13, 14. & 4: 30. qui tamen non aliud, quam ipsa gratia & fides nostra, est, putido huic figmento commodare in animum inducunt. Quæ aliena, ac cum charactere, quem ipsi perhibent, pugnantia esse, quivis facile videt.
units.tr: XXXII. Yet to lend colour to this invention they seek out testimonies from Scripture. Although they want the Old Testament to have lacked this character, they nonetheless refer the mark of circumcision, and certain passages of the prophets where mention is made of a sign and a seal, to that spurious character. To this belong Ezek. 9:4, "Pass through the midst of the city," etc., and Isa. 66:18, 19, "Of their works and their thoughts I will come... and I will set a sign among them," etc. In the New Testament they bring in, for the same purpose, the stigmata of Paul, Gal. 6:17, and the gift of Timothy for performing the ministry, 1 Tim. 4:14. Finally they bring in the Spirit as the earnest [ἀρραβών] and seal [σφραγίς], 2 Cor. 1:21, 22; Eph. 1:13, 14; and 4:30, which is in fact nothing other than grace itself and our faith, and they are persuaded to adapt this rotten fiction to it. That these things are foreign to, and inconsistent with, the character they themselves maintain, anyone can easily see.

units.la: XXXIII. Atque ex isto sacramentorum fine & effectu facile de necessitate eorum judicari potest. Cum enim gratiam non largiantur, nec producunt; sed obsignent, ex Dei institutione & præcepto; non absolutam (quasi ipsa gratiam in se continerent ac conferrent) sed solam mandati & præcepti necessitatem habent. Utque ea non contemnenda; cum gratiæ Dei sint pignora, quæ de manu Dei accipere, deque iis lætare tenemur: ita nec superstitiose nimis signis illis salus nostra alliganda & obstringenda est. Quæ Pontificiæ Ecclesiæ labes est. Quæ mirifice signorum illorum apparatu & choragio se oblectat; & universam pene religionem externis istis ritibus occupavit. Quo pacto eam in meram scenam commutavit, & fideles, non sine fidei opprobrio, elementis quibusdam terrenis deservire rursus coègit. Unde & tantæ necessitatis ea faciunt, ut sine iis, vel earum saltem voto (ubi mitissime loquuntur) salutem patere negent. Cum non solum sine sacramentorum usu, sed & sine voto eorum multi fideles servati sint, qui istam sacramentorum necessitatem ignorabant.
units.tr: XXXIII. From this end and effect of the sacraments, their necessity can easily be judged. For since they do not bestow or produce grace, but seal it, by God's institution and command, they have not an absolute necessity (as if they themselves contained and conferred grace), but only the necessity of the command and precept. And just as they are not to be despised, since they are pledges of the grace of God, which we are bound to receive from God's hand and to rejoice in, so our salvation must not be superstitiously tied and bound to those signs. This is the blot on the Papal Church, which delights wonderfully in the display and pageantry of those signs and has taken up almost the whole of religion with these external rites. By this means it has turned religion into mere stage-play, and has once again forced the faithful, to the disgrace of faith, to serve certain earthly elements. Hence they make the sacraments of such necessity that they deny that salvation is open without them, or at least without the desire for them (where they speak most gently). Yet many faithful have been saved without the use of the sacraments, and even without the desire for them, who were ignorant of this necessity of the sacraments.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Sacramentis Veteris & Nov. Test. in genere; eorumque convenientia & discrimine.
units.tr: On the Sacraments of the Old and New Testament in general, and their agreement and difference.

units.la: I. Um sacramenta fœderis sint sigilla, pro fœderum diversitate varia ea fuerunt. Ac prout gratiæ fœdus varie administratum fuit; &, quamquam re & substantia semper idem, pro temporum diversitate, mutata veluti veste, diversum apparuit; ita signorum quoque quædam diversitas extitit.
units.tr: I. Since the sacraments are seals of the covenants, they have varied according to the diversity of the covenants. Just as the grace of the covenant has been administered in various ways, and has appeared differently as the times changed, like a garment changed, though always the same in thing and substance, so too there has been a certain diversity of signs.

units.la: II. Sub fœdere operum sacramenti rationem habuerunt, Paradisus & arbor vitæ; quæ homini integro, & in proposito certamine victori, vitam æternam in Christo ostentabant. Arbor autem scientiæ eam rationem non habuit. De quibus priore tomo egimus.
units.tr: II. Under the covenant of works they had the sacraments Paradise and the tree of life, which showed eternal life in Christ to man, who was upright and victorious in the appointed contest. The tree of knowledge, however, did not have this character. We have treated of these in the earlier volume.

units.la: III. Sub primo fœderis gratiæ curriculo, sive sub promissione sacrificia, & ad ea pertinentia sacra convivia, sacramentalia fuerunt. Quibus, Noachi tempore, diluvii, 1. Pet. 3:20, 21. & iridis, Gen. 9: 13-18. Esai. 54:9. mysteria accesserunt. Abrahamo denique data fuit circumcisio, Gen. 17. quæ fœdus Dei, fœderisque bona, familiæ ipsius, quæ Ecclesiæ mater atque hospes futura erat, addiceba t.
units.tr: III. In the first course of the covenant of grace, that is, under the promise, sacrifices and the sacred meals belonging to them were sacramental. To these, in Noah's time, were added the mystery of the flood, 1 Pet. 3:20, 21, and of the rainbow, Gen. 9:13-18, Isa. 54:9. Finally, circumcision was given to Abraham, Gen. 17, which bound the covenant of God and its blessings to his family, which was to be the mother and host of the Church.

units.la: IV. Sequens Ecclesiæ ætas variis rursus sacramentis insignis fuit. Erant enim signa extraordinaria, baptismus in nube & mari, manna cibatio; & manantes ex petra aquæ; de quibus 1. Cor. 10:1,2,3. Necessitabant ordinaria, uti sacrificia, ac sacrificales epulæ; & lotiones ac expiatio‐ nes legales, aliæque cerimoniæ, quæ Christi beneficia adumbrabant. Hebr. 9: 10, 13. Eminebant autem in ista periodo circumcisio & pascha; quorum illa initionem in fœdus, hoc confirmationem in eo obsigna‐ bat. Col. 2: 11. 1. Cor. 5: 7.
units.tr: IV. The following age of the Church was again marked by various sacraments. There were extraordinary signs: baptism in the cloud and the sea, the feeding on manna, and waters flowing from the rock, concerning which see 1 Cor. 10:1, 2, 3. There were ordinary ones, such as sacrifices and sacrificial feasts, and washings and legal purifications, and other ceremonies, which foreshadowed the benefits of Christ, Heb. 9:10, 13. In this period circumcision and the Passover stood out: the former sealed the entrance into the covenant, the latter its confirmation within it, Col. 2:11; 1 Cor. 5:7.

units.la: V. Sub Novo Testamento autem duo tantum a Christo instituta, & ab Ecclesia accepta, leguntur sacramenta, Baptismus & S. Cœna. Quo spectant Apostoli loca 1. Cor. 10: 2, 3, 4. Et omnes in Mosen baptizatos esse, nube & mari: & omnes eandem escam spiritualem edisse: & omnes eundem potum spiritualem bibisse. Bibebant enim ex sequente spirituali petra. Petra vero illa erat Christus. Et cap. 12: 13. Etenim per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, & Judæi, & Græci, & liberi, & servi, & omnes potati sumus in unum Spiritum. Hebr. 9: 10. In cibis duntaxat & potionibus, & diversis ablutionibus ac ritibus carnalibus &c. ubi solam salutaris undæ & mysticî cibi, ac potus, mentionem facit; cum‐ que iis veterum ritus comparat.
units.tr: V. Under the New Testament, only two sacraments are read of as instituted by Christ and received by the Church: Baptism and the Holy Supper. To these belong the Apostle's passages, 1 Cor. 10:2, 3, 4: And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food; and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. And that rock was Christ. And ch. 12:13: For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free; and we were all made to drink of one Spirit. Heb. 9:10: Only with foods and drinks, and various washings and carnal ordinances, etc., where he mentions only the saving water and the mystical food and drink, and compares with them the rites of the ancients.

units.la: VI. Antequam vero de singulis agamus, signorum Veteris & Novi Test. inter se convenientia, & discrimen, annotanda veniunt.
units.tr: VI. Before we deal with each sacrament separately, the agreement and difference between the signs of the Old and New Testaments must be noted.

units.la: VII. Conveniebant: 1. in generali signorum natura, & relatione ad rem significatam. 2. auctore, Deo. 3. re significata, Christo, cum beneficiis suis. 4. instrumento applicationis, quod utrobique fides erat. 5. fine denique & effectu, quod pariter fœdus Dei obsignarent, & fidem nostram confirmarent. Unde antitypa, id est, ducti ex eodem archetypo typi, eademque forma signati, & spectantes ad eundem Christum imagines, appellantur, 1. Pet. 3: 21. quod latius exequitur Paulus 1. Cor. 10. ubi eandem Patrum nobiscum fidem, & mysticam escam, & potum, eundemque utrobique Christum, loquitur.
units.tr: VII. They agreed: (1) in the general nature of signs and their relation to the thing signified; (2) in their author, God; (3) in the thing signified, Christ with his benefits; (4) in the instrument of application, which on both sides was faith; (5) finally, in purpose and effect, namely that they equally sealed God's covenant and confirmed our faith. Hence they are called antitypes, that is, types drawn from the same archetype, stamped with the same form and looking to the same Christ as images, 1 Pet. 3:21. Paul works this out more fully in 1 Cor. 10, where he speaks of the same faith of the Fathers as ours, the same mystical food and drink, and the same Christ on both sides.

units.la: VIII. Discrimen situm erat in accidentibus quibusdam & circumstant- iis.
units.tr: VIII. The difference lay in certain accidents and circumstances.

units.la: Differunt enim: 1. signis ac ritibus externis; quæ sub N. F. magis naturalia & simplicia, adeoque nunc mutabilia sunt. 2. numero. 3. utendi facilitate; quod ex baptismi & circumcisionis comparatione liquet. 4. objecti amplitudine; cum illa solos Abrahami posteros obsignarent, hæc ad omnes gentes pertineant. 5. Significationis modo, qui hic longe illustrior est: cum illa venturæ lucis umbræ & strictturæ; hæc præsentis ejusdem, ac pleno in die splendentis radii sint, Hebr. 10: 1. 6. Temporis duratione; cum enim vetera sua periodo desinerentur, nostra non nisi cum sæculo interibunt. 7. Claritate & perspicuitate; quæ in verborum sacramentalium emphasi potissimum apparet. 8. Euangelica denique suavitate. Cum illa de legis rigore multum haberent, ac nondum abolitam reatus professionem continerent, Gal. 5:2. hæc autem nihil nisi gratiam spirent: utpote in quibus τελείωσις est. Unde Augustino pauca pro multis, factu facillima, intellectu augustissima, observatione castissima recte dicuntur.
units.tr: They differ: (1) in external signs and rites, which under the New Testament are more natural and simple and therefore now changeable; (2) in number; (3) in ease of use, as is clear from comparing baptism with circumcision; (4) in breadth of object: the former sealed only the posterity of Abraham, while the latter pertain to all nations; (5) in the mode of signifying, which here is far clearer: the former were shadows and outlines of the coming light, while the latter are rays of the same light now present, shining in full day, Heb. 10:1; (6) in duration: since the old ones were to cease at their appointed period, ours will perish only with the age; (7) in clarity and perspicuity, which appears chiefly in the emphasis of the sacramental words; (8) finally, in evangelical sweetness. The former had much of the rigour of the law and contained a profession of guilt not yet abolished, Gal. 5:2, whereas the latter breathe nothing but grace, since in them there is [τελείωσις], perfection. Hence Augustine rightly says of them: few in number, most easy to perform, most august in meaning, most chaste in observance.

units.la: IX. Alia autem fingunt discrimina Pontificii; & vetera novaque sacramenta, non modo solum significandi, sed & tantum non ipsa re significata, divera statuunt: ac illa quidem nil nisi tenues umbras, vix aliquid lucis habentes, fuisse volunt; & vix quicquam supernaturale, aut spiritualis significationis vel promissionis, in iis relinquunt. Ita enim hæc distinguere amant: 1. Sacramenta Veteris Test. gratiam contulisse ex opere operantis; Novi Test. signa eandem conferre ex opere operato. 2. illa figuras & signa qualiacunque gratiæ fuisse; hæc autem ipsam gratiam continere, ut causas. 3. imo illa nostrorum potius sacramentorum figuras fuisse. 4. denique ad purificationem carnis illa solummodo fecisse, nullas autem promissiones spirituales habuisse. Quibus assertionibus partim Novi Test. sacramenta immensum, ac præter fas, adaugent; partim Veteris Test. signa, omnemque istius Ecclesiæ statum, quasi corporeis solum rebus patta fuerit, nec veram sponsi sui imaginem unquam viderit, minimum deprețiant.
units.tr: IX. The Papists, however, invent other differences. They set the old and new sacraments apart not only in their power of signifying but almost in whether they are the thing signified itself. They want the old ones to have been only thin shadows, hardly having any light, and they leave in them hardly anything supernatural, or of spiritual signification or promise. For they love to distinguish thus: (1) the sacraments of the Old Testament conferred grace ex opere operantis, while the New Testament signs confer it ex opere operato; (2) the former were figures and signs of grace of whatever kind, while the latter contain grace itself, as its causes; (3) indeed, the former were rather figures of our sacraments; (4) finally, the former did only the purification of the flesh and had no spiritual promises. By these assertions they partly magnify the sacraments of the New Testament immensely and beyond right, and partly they greatly depreciate the signs of the Old Testament and the whole state of that Church, as if it had been concerned only with corporeal things and had never seen the true image of its Bridegroom.

units.la: X. Contra, eodem efficacia genere, ac pari significandi & obsignandi vi & potestate, & hæc & illa sacramenta polluisse, ex Apostolo 1 Cor. 10: 1--4. potentissime patet; qui unicus locus controversiam hanc finire potest. Nam & veteribus escam potumque spiritualem, in manna, & mysticæ rupis imagine, exhibitum fuisse; atque utramque Ecclesiam eadem salutis testeras habuisse, docet. Atque illis eandem, quam nos gustamus, escam, eundemque potum, fuisse, diserte affirmat. Et præterea, ut paritatem ostendat, novorumac veterum sacramentorum nomina inter se commutat; & nubis umbraculum, ac maris transitum, baptismum appellat, & cœlestes cibos, quibus Ecclesia in deserto pasta est, cum sacræ Cœnæ epulo confert. Sicuti alibi veterum sacramentorum nomina ad novam Ecclesiam transfert. 1. Cor 5:7. Phil. 3:3. Col. 2:11. Quæ nominum permutatio, illa conspirantes ejusdem rei imagines & typos fuisse docet. Nec leve est, quod circumcisio fœdus Dei, Gen. 17: 7--10, 14. & justitiæ, quæ per fidem est, sigillum ab Apostolo, Rom. 4: 11. appellatur. Quæ tam excelsa sunt, ut majora de Novi Test signis prædicari nequeant.
units.tr: X. On the contrary, that both these and those sacraments were of the same efficacy, and had equal power and authority in signifying and sealing, is most powerfully clear from the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10:1-4, and this single passage can end the controversy. For he teaches that spiritual food and drink were exhibited to the ancients in the manna and in the image of the mystical rock, and that both Churches had the same pledges of salvation. He expressly affirms that the same food which we taste, and the same drink, were theirs. Moreover, to show the parity, he exchanges the names of the new and old sacraments: he calls the shade of the cloud and the passage through the sea baptism, and compares the heavenly food on which the Church was fed in the wilderness with the feast of the holy Supper. Just as elsewhere he transfers the names of the old sacraments to the new Church, 1 Cor. 5:7; Phil. 3:3; Col. 2:11. This interchange of names shows that those were converging images and types of the same thing. Nor is it a slight matter that the Apostle, Rom. 4:11, calls circumcision the seal of the righteousness that is by faith, and Gen. 17:7-10, 14 calls it the covenant of God. These things are so lofty that nothing greater can be said of the signs of the New Testament.

units.la: XI. Ad istas autem discriminum notas, quas ipsi adferunt, paucis admonamus: 1. opus operatum nullibi, & ne in Novi quidem Test. sacramentis, locum habere; opinionemque eam, uti voce, ita magis sensu, barbaram esse; cum externis signis sacrilegam potestatem attribuat; proque ipso Christo externorum rituum idola Ecclesiæ tractanda & colenda offerat. 2. Sacramenta Veteris Testam. umbras quidem & imagines fuisse, Col. 2: 17. sed quæ eandem gratiam figurarent, ac obsignarent; cumdemque Christum Ecclesiæ in manum traderent, quem Novi Test. sacramenta exhibent. Ut non illa magis, quam hæc, inania simulachra, ac fugientes umbræ, appellanda sint. Quanquam enim Christus nondum advenïsset, jam tamen spoponderat, atque ista externis tabulis signacula appendi fecerat, quæ piorum fidei pascendæ & roborandæ sufficerent. Metonymia autem est, ex arta signorum & rei significatæ unione orta, quod Novi Test. sacramenta, ac præsertim baptismi aquæ, mundare, regenerare &c. dicantur, Tit. 3: 5. Cum similes locutiones de Veteris Test. sacramentis ac cærimoniis occurrant. Nam & circumcisio dicitur ipsum fœdus; & sacrificia Levitica dicuntur expiationes peccati, Gen. 17: 10. Lev. 4:20: 3. Perversum autem est, quod Veteris Test. sacramenta Novi Testam. sacramentorum mubras & typos, agnumque ex. gr. paschalem Eucharistiæ figuram fuisse volunt; quo Apostoli locum trahunt, 1.Pet. 3:21. ubi baptismum ἀντίτυπον, indiluvio fluitantis, vocat ἀντίτυπον. Quod sacramentorum naturæ repugnat, quæ necessario ipsius fœderis firmamenta & sigilla, non autem æmulorum signorum typi & umbræ, primæque lineæ ac deformationes, existunt. Ac insulsum est, figurarum alias figuras, & imagines veluti traduces, ac sæpius reparabiles (quæ tamen ipsum Christum non exhibeant: quod cogitatu impossibile est) & signorum signa, & umbrarum umbras, velle introducere. Cum nullæ nisi corporis umbræ dentur, illudque unum depingant & exprimant; cum autem baptismus arcæ, aquis innatantis, vocatur ἀντίτυπος; duæ ejusdem rei imagines inter se componuntur, atque ad idem corpus referuntur. Notat enim ἀντίτυπον non rem signatam, aut ἀρχέτυπον (nam pro simplici typo sumitur Hebr 9: 24.) sed similem, seu parallelum ejusdem rei typum, eadem imagine percussum ac signatum: qualia & arca, & baptismus, sunt respectu obedientiæ & sanguinis Christi. 4. Atque huc tandem illa deveniunt, quod non solum veterum Ecclesiam veris Christi signis, ac fœderis signaculis, sed & re significata, spiritualibus videl. promissionibus, caruisse velint. Quæ non exigua in Deum, qui sollemni fœdere, adjectisque insuper symbolis bolis ac sigillis, sese piorum Deum testabatur, Matth. 22: 32. Act. 2:39. Rom. 4: 11. & in Ecclesiam ipsam contumelia est. Quasi illa nihil spiritualium bonorum gustaverit, nec Christum in tot imaginibus viderit, contra ac Apostolus diserte urget, 1. Cor. 10. & terrenis denique bonis pasta, instar pecudum, ignobile aevum traduxerit. Quod Pelagii ac Socini ulcus est.
units.tr: XI. As for the marks of difference which they bring forward, we briefly remark: (1) that opus operatum has no place anywhere, not even in the sacraments of the New Testament; and that this opinion is barbarous, in sense as much as in word, since it attributes a sacrilegious power to external signs and offers the idols of external rites to be handled and worshipped by the Church in place of Christ himself. (2) The sacraments of the Old Testament were indeed shadows and images, Col. 2:17, but they figured and sealed the same grace, and placed in the Church's hand the same Christ whom the sacraments of the New Testament exhibit. So they are no more to be called empty simulacra and fleeting shadows than these are. For although Christ had not yet come, he had nevertheless promised, and had caused those signs to be hung up as external tablets and seals, which were sufficient to feed and strengthen the faith of the pious. Now, it is a metonymy, arising from the close union of the sign and the thing signified, that the sacraments of the New Testament, and especially the water of baptism, are said to cleanse, to regenerate, and so on, Titus 3:5. Similar expressions occur about the sacraments and ceremonies of the Old Testament: circumcision itself is called the covenant, and the Levitical sacrifices are called expiations of sin, Gen. 17:10; Lev. 4:20; 3. It is perverse, however, to claim that the sacraments of the Old Testament were shadows and types of the sacraments of the New Testament, and that the paschal lamb, for example, was a figure of the Eucharist. They draw the Apostle's passage, 1 Pet. 3:21, into this, where he calls baptism [ἀντίτυπον], antitype, to the flood in which the ark floated. This runs against the nature of sacraments, which necessarily are the firm supports and seals of the covenant itself, and not the types and shadows, the first outlines and deformations, of rival signs. It is also silly to want to introduce figures of figures, and images that are as it were tracings, often renewable (which yet do not exhibit Christ himself, which is unthinkable), and signs of signs and shadows of shadows. Since only shadows of a body are given, and they depict and express that one thing, but baptism is called the [ἀντίτυπος] antitype of the ark floating on the waters, two images of the same thing are set side by side and referred to the same body. For [ἀντίτυπον] does not denote the thing signified, nor the [ἀρχέτυπον] archetype (for it is taken in the sense of a simple type at Heb. 9:24), but a similar or parallel type of the same thing, struck and sealed with the same image. Such are both the ark and baptism with respect to the obedience and blood of Christ. (4) And at last they come to this: that they want the ancient Church to have lacked not only the true signs of Christ and the seals of the covenant, but also the thing signified, the spiritual promises. This is no small insult to God, who by a solemn covenant, with symbols and seals added besides, declared himself the God of the pious, Matt. 22:32; Acts 2:39; Rom. 4:11, and it is an insult to the Church itself. It is as if the Church had tasted nothing of spiritual goods, nor seen Christ in so many images, contrary to what the Apostle expressly insists on, 1 Cor. 10; as if it had fed on earthly goods alone, like cattle, and passed an ignoble age. This is the ulcer of Pelagius and Socinus.

units.la: XII. Pontificiis socios sese praebent Anabaptistae; qui cum tam tenuiter de Veteris Test. statu, deque omni Dei foedere, sentiant; non mirum est, quod & foederis sigilla vi ac potestate sua spolient. Unde ea pro nudis emblematis ac spectaculis habent, quae ventura olim bona, omnemque Christi gratiam, utcunque figuraverint, ac de longinquo adumbraverint; nullum autem spirituale bonum veteri Ecclesiae tanquam proprium addixerint & confirmaverint. Quia & circumcisionem gratiae foedus veluti obtexisse, eique velum praetendisse asserunt. Quod, ex vero haustum, in malum sensum apud ipsos detorquetur.
units.tr: XII. The Anabaptists make themselves allies of the Papists; since they think so meanly of the state of the Old Testament and of every covenant of God, it is no wonder that they also strip the seals of the covenant of their force and power. Hence they regard them as mere empty emblems and spectacles, which, however they may have prefigured the good things to come and all the grace of Christ, only shadowed them from afar; but they have never ascribed to the ancient Church, as its own, any spiritual good, nor confirmed it. For they also assert that circumcision veiled the covenant of grace as it were and held a veil before it. Which, drawn from the truth, is twisted among them into a bad sense.

units.la: XIII. Nec recte etiam Lutherani negant, parem sacramentorum Vet. & Novi foederis, quod ad rem significatam attinet, rationem fuisse, quia illa tum absens erat. Nam & nostris quoque nunc sensibus absens est Christi corpus & sanguis, quae tamen fidei interiorique animae perceptioni sunt praesentia: & hac quoque ratione Christus veteribus olim fuit praesens; cujus diem Abrahamus vidit, Joh. 8: 56. quique heri & hodie idem est, & in saecula, Hebr. 13: 8. cujus etiam veteres hoc modo participes fuere; utpote qui omnes eundem escam spiritualem manducaverunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. 1. Cor. 10: 3, 4.
units.tr: XIII. Nor do the Lutherans rightly deny that, as far as the thing signified is concerned, there was a like reason for the sacraments of the Old and New Covenants, on the ground that the thing was then absent. For Christ's body and blood are absent even to our senses now, yet they are present to faith and to the perception of the inner soul; and in this way Christ was also present to the ancients of old, whose day Abraham saw, John 8:56, and who is the same yesterday, today and forever, Heb. 13:8; of whom the ancients also were partakers in this way, inasmuch as they all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink, 1 Cor. 10:3, 4.

units.la: XIV. Sacramentis autem omnibus, cum Veteris, tum Novi Test. Christum initiatum fuisse constat. Cum enim divini cultus esset obscurantissimus, religiosos istos ritus adeo non aspernatus est, ut eos summo studio consectatus legatur. Et, cum homo, ac electorum caput & sponsor foret, ista divini favoris symbola adeo ab ipso non erant aliena, ut non alio modo foederis ac promissiorum Dei veritas, tum ipsi, dum stadium illud decurreret; tum fidelibus omnibus, in ipso censitis, melius affirmari & obsignari potuerit.
units.tr: XIV. It is clear that Christ was initiated into all the sacraments, both of the Old and of the New Testament. For since the worship of God was very obscure, he did not disdain those religious rites so much that he is read to have pursued them with the greatest eagerness. And since he was man, and the head and surety of the elect, these symbols of divine favour were so far from alien to him that the truth of God's covenant and promises could be affirmed and sealed to him, while he ran that course, and to all the faithful reckoned in him, in no better way.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS TERTIUS: DE BAPTISMO. CAPUT VI.
units.tr: LOCUS FORTY-THIRD: OF BAPTISM. CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Baptismi institutione
units.tr: On the institution of baptism

units.la: I. Sacramentorum Novi Test. primum est baptismus. Cujus 1. institutionem. 2. externam administrationem. 3. internam significationem. 4. ac denique adjuncta considerationem mus.
units.tr: I. Baptism is the first of the sacraments of the New Testament. We shall consider (1) its institution, (2) its external administration, (3) its internal signification, and (4) finally the related matters.

units.la: II. Βαπτισμὸς & βάπτισμα, si etymon spectes, proprie immersionem notat. Et baptizatus Jesus, ascendit statim ex aqua. Matth. 3: 16. conf. Act. 8: 38. juxta quoidam etiam aspersionem, & quamcunque lotionem, seu ablutionem: quo sensu usurpari putant Marc. 7: 4. lotiones — lectorum: metaphorice adspectabalem Spiritus S. donorum effusionem: Ipse vos baptisabit Spir. sancto, & igne. Matth. 3: 11. Act. 1: 5. itemque aerumnas & calamitates quascunque; ipsamque mortem & martyrium denotat. Potestis poculum bibere, quod ego bibiturus sum, & baptismate, quo ego baptisor, baptisari. Matth. 20: 22, 23. Atque eadem figura sacrae doctrinae aquas, ac rorem vivificum, seu potius doctrinam baptismi, dicit. Sciens tantum baptisma Johannis. Act. 18: 25. Atque hinc vulgata illa distinctio, in baptismum fluminis, sanguinis, flaminis: cui & quartum addunt, luminis ac doctrinae. Nos de primo baptismo vocem istam accipimus.
units.tr: II. Considered by its etymology, baptismos and baptisma [βαπτισμὸς, βάπτισμα] properly denote immersion. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightaway out of the water, Matt. 3:16; cf. Acts 8:38. Some also take it to mean sprinkling and any washing or ablution, which they think is the sense in Mark 7:4: the washings of cups and pots. Metaphorically it refers to the outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit: He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire, Matt. 3:11; Acts 1:5. It also denotes any afflictions and calamities, and death itself and martyrdom: Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized? Matt. 20:22, 23. In the same figurative way, sacred doctrine is called water and life-giving dew, or rather the doctrine of baptism: knowing only the baptism of John, Acts 18:25. Hence comes the common distinction between the baptism of water, of blood and of the Spirit, to which some add a fourth, of light, that is, of doctrine. We understand the word in the first sense.

units.la: III. Est autem baptismus omnis, vel Gentilium, vel Judaeorum, vel Christianorum. Nam & Gentiles lotiones in sacris olim habuerunt: tum in peccatorum labe excipanda; quae fluminea aqua tolli, stulte, & non sine Poetarum irrisu credebant: tum in celebrioribus mysteriis peragendis. Quae eorum aquae cum divina auctoritate ac promissis carerent, atque extra Dei foedus usurparentur, inutiles ac viduae erant; ut non incleganter Tertullianus, lib. de baptism. Sed & de viduis aquis sibi mentiuntur: tur: non enim maritae, vel ulla spiritus potentia foecundae erant, nec omnino unda ista genitalis fuit.
units.tr: III. Every baptism is either that of the Gentiles, that of the Jews, or that of the Christians. For the Gentiles also had washings in their rites: some to cleanse the stain of sin, which they foolishly believed could be removed by river water, to the mockery of the poets; others in performing their more celebrated mysteries. But since those waters lacked divine authority and promises, and were used outside God's covenant, they were useless and barren. Tertullian rightly says in his book On Baptism: They also lie to themselves about "widowed waters." For they were not married, nor fruitful with any power of the Spirit, and that water was not life-giving at all.

units.la: IV. Iudaeorum baptismus duplex erat: alter pollutorum טבילה נידה qui, antequam sacrorum participes redderentur, lotionibus quibusdam ac piamentis uti debebant: alter proselytorum, מבילה גרה per quem alienigenae in Judaeorum rempubl. ac religionem initiabantur: hi enim praeter circumcisionem & sacrificium baptismo praeterea in Judaeorum sacra transibant. Nunc autem, cessantibus sacrificiis, sola circumcisione & baptismo proselytos adoptant.
units.tr: IV. Jewish baptism was of two kinds. The first was the baptism of the defiled, tevilat niddah [טבילה נידה], by which those who were unclean had to use certain washings and purifications before they could be admitted to the sacred things. The second was the baptism of proselytes, mevilat gerah [מבילה גרה], by which foreigners were initiated into the Jewish commonwealth and religion. For proselytes, besides circumcision and sacrifice, passed over into the Jewish sacred rites by baptism. Now, however, with the sacrifices having ceased, they admit proselytes only by circumcision and baptism.

units.la: V. Incertus autem est apud Judaeos baptismi illius ortus: dum quidam ad Jacobum Patriarcham, familiam suam lustrantem, Gen. 35:2. alii verosimiliter ad Mosem, in deserto, illum ritum referunt. Exod. 19: 10, 11. Et dixit Jehova Moschi, ito ad ipsum populum, ut sanctificet eos hodie & cras, & lavent vestimenta sua: ut sint parati in diem tertium. qui fuerit baptismus in nube & mari, Paulo memoratus, 1. Cor. 10:2. Hoc certum est; sive ista occasione coeperit, sive postquam Samaritae circumcisionem acceperunt; sive denique post templi excidium, aut ferius; baptismum illum, ad sacrarum lotionum, aut apud veteres, aut in templo deinceps usitatarum, exemplum, primum usurpatum fuisse.
units.tr: V. The origin of this Jewish baptism is uncertain. Some refer it to the Patriarch Jacob, who purified his household, Gen. 35:2; others probably refer the rite to Moses in the wilderness, Exod. 19:10, 11: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, so that they may be ready for the third day." Paul mentions this as the baptism in the cloud and in the sea, 1 Cor. 10:2. This much is certain: whether it began on that occasion, or after the Samaritans received circumcision, or finally after the destruction of the temple, or later, that baptism was first used as a pattern for the sacred washings that were afterwards practised either among the ancients or in the temple.

units.la: VI. Peragebatur haec lustratio statim a circumcisione, mox ubi dolores ejus intetquieverant. Praemittebatur autem examen sollemne. Dumque novus fidei candidatus abluebatur, religionis articuli praelegebantur; interimque ipse mergebatur, adstante sapientum triumviratu. Eodem ritu & liberi ejus lustrabantur, atque universa familia, etiam qui sequioris sexus erant. Et, si parentes praemortui forent, locum eorum tres isti e sapientum collegio, qui baptismis praerant, implebant; atque iis quasi testibus illi initiabantur. Et qui ita expiati erant, in Judaicae gentis nomen ac decus venibant; atque, exuta peregrinitate, & pristina consanguinitate oblitterata, novorum quasi natalium jus accipiebant, ac deinceps pro Judaeis, ac Dei domesticis, habebantur. Unde posteros eorum rursus tingi, & novo baptismo inaugurari fas non erat, cum pro veris Israelitis censerentur.
units.tr: VI. This purification was performed immediately after circumcision, as soon as the pain of the wound had subsided. A solemn examination preceded it. While the new candidate for the faith was being washed, the articles of religion were read aloud, and meanwhile he was immersed, with a triumvirate of wise men standing by. His children were purified by the same rite, and the whole family, including those of the weaker sex. And if the parents had died before, three of the learned college who presided over the baptisms took their place, and the candidates were initiated in their presence as witnesses. Those who had been cleansed in this way came into the name and honour of the Jewish nation; and, having put off their foreignness and having lost their former kinship, they received, as it were, the right of a new birth, and from then on were regarded as Jews and members of God's household. Hence it was not lawful for their descendants to be dipped again and inaugurated by a new baptism, since they were counted as true Israelites.

units.la: VII. Atque hunc Judaeorum baptismum, qui humanus ac ecclesiasticus duntaxat ritus erat, Christus, ex eorum sententia, qui jam tum illum obtinuisse censent, consecravit, &, rejecta circumcisione, novae Ecclesiae sacramentum esse jussit. Ita ut, sicuti olim per circumcisionem & baptismum, ita nunc per baptismum solum Deo liberi nascantur.
units.tr: VII. This Jewish baptism, which was merely a human and ecclesiastical rite, Christ consecrated, according to the view of those who hold that it was already in use at that time. He rejected circumcision and ordered baptism to be the sacrament of the new Church. So, just as formerly children were born free to God through circumcision and baptism, so now they are born free to God through baptism alone.

units.la: VIII. Primus illum ulurpavit Johannes, ab eo ritu Baptiftes dictus, non sine Dei auctoritate acjussu. Ne quis pro nudo ritu ac cærimonia illum habeat. Factum est verbum Domini ad Iohannem, Zachariæ filium, in deserto: venit igitur in omnem regionem circumjacentem fordani, prædicans baptismum respiscentia &c. Luc. 3:2. Sed qui misit me, ut baptisarem, ille mihi dixerat, super quem videris Spiritum descendentem &c. Joh. 1:33. Baptisma Iohannis unde erat, e cœlo, an ex hominibus? Matth. 21:25.
units.tr: VIII. John was the first to use it, and he was called the Baptist from this rite, not without the authority and command of God. No one should regard it as a bare rite or ceremony: The word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the wilderness. He came therefore into all the region round about the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance, Luke 3:2, 3. He who sent me to baptize said to me, "On whomever you see the Spirit descending…", John 1:33. The baptism of John, was it from heaven or from men? Matt. 21:25.

units.la: IX. Convenit ergo, quoad rem ipsam, baptismus ejus cum nostro, atque idem novæ Ecclesiæ sacramentum fuit. Idem enim utrobique ritus, Marc. 1:4. eadem utrobique doctrina & promissio. Joh. 1:29, 30. Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Hic est, de quo dicebam &c. conf. ꝑs 34, 36. Matth. 3:11. Ego baptiso vos aqua ad conversionem. Ille autem, qui post me venit — ipse baptizat vos Spiritu S. & igne. conf. Marc. 1:2. Act. 2:38. Ac par utriusque auctoritas fuit, Joh. 1:33. Qui misit me, ut baptizarem &c. Ubi autem & signum, & res signata, est eadem; eademque obsignandi auctoritas & efficacia; idem sacramentum quoque existere oportet: Neque quicquam refert inter eos, quos Johannes in Iordane, & quos Petrus in Tiberi tinxit. ut Tertull. Unde Christus quoque baptismum illum accepit, ac proprio in corpore consecravit, Matth. 3. Necalia unda Apostolos ejus ablutos constat. Quos omnes inani, ac prisci ævi cærimonia, in ipso novæ Ecclesiæ exordio, inaugurratos; aut Johannis aquas ejusdem cum nostris dignitatis ac efficaciæ dicere oportet. Atque hoc potius est; cum ista nascentis Ecclesiæ fuerint initia, quæ vano ac casso ritu absolvere non decet.
units.tr: IX. So, as far as the thing itself goes, his baptism agrees with ours, and it was the same sacrament of the new Church. The rite was the same on both sides, Mark 1:4, and the doctrine and promise were the same on both sides, John 1:29, 30: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. This is he of whom I said…; cf. vv. 34, 36. Matt. 3:11: I baptize you with water for repentance; but he who comes after me… will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire; cf. Mark 1:2; Acts 2:38. And the authority of both was equal, John 1:33: He who sent me to baptize, etc. Where the sign and the thing signified are the same, and the authority and efficacy of sealing are the same, the sacrament must also be the same. Tertullian: Nor does it matter whether they were dipped by John in the Jordan or by Peter in the Tiber. Hence Christ also received that baptism and consecrated it in his own body, Matt. 3. And it is clear that his apostles were washed in no other water. To say that all of these were initiated by an empty rite of ancient times, at the very beginning of the new Church, or that the waters of John were of the same dignity and efficacy as ours, is not right. Rather, since these were the beginnings of the infant Church, it is not fitting to end them with an empty and worthless rite.

units.la: X. Agnoscendum tamen quoddam circumstantiarum & graduum discrimen. Cum enim Johannes Christo præcurreret, ac adventanti populum colligeret & præpararet; Messiam non nisi venturum, aut potius venientem, Act. 19:4. prædicabat, inque fidem ejus credentes e Judæis obsignabat; Spiritu quoque, quandiu Christus nondum manifestatus erat, parcius ad baptismum ejus veniente, nec tanta donorum copia aquas ejus imprægnante. Quæ uberiora in Apostolorum Baptismo fuerunt. Ubi major & adspectabilis sæpe Spiritus S præsentia; & magna donorum copia; & clarior obsignatio; & non Judæorum tantum, quorum finibus Johannis cursus claudebatur, sed & gentium immersio, ad obedientiam fidei; cum ad eos etiam Spir. sancti rivi & aquæ permanarent. Vide Matth. 28: 19. Profecti ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos &c. Matth. 3: 11. Ego baptizo vos aqua ad resipiscentiam. Is vero, qui post me venit, vos baptizabit Spiritu S. & igne. Joh. 7: 39. Qui credit in me, flumina aqua viva ex ventre ipsius fluent. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu illo, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Nondum enim erat Spiritus S. quia Iesus nondum erat glorificatus.
units.tr: X. Yet a certain difference of circumstances and degrees must be acknowledged. For John went before Christ and gathered and prepared the people for his coming. He preached that the Messiah was only to come, or rather was coming, Acts 19:4, and he sealed those Jews who believed in him. Likewise the Spirit came more sparingly to his baptism, as long as Christ had not yet been manifested, and the water was not impregnated with such an abundance of gifts. These were fuller in the baptism of the apostles, where the presence of the Holy Spirit was often greater and more visible, the abundance of gifts was great, and the sealing was clearer. Moreover, the immersion was not only of Jews, to whose borders John's course was confined, but also of the Gentiles, unto the obedience of faith, since the streams and waters of the Holy Spirit flowed out to them as well. See Matt. 28:19: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them, etc.; Matt. 3:11: I baptize you with water unto repentance. But he who comes after me will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire; John 7:38, 39: He who believes in me, out of his heart shall flow rivers of living water. But he said this of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified.

units.la: XI. Ut perverse Pontificii Johannis baptismum minuant; nec pro Novi Test. sacramento, sed pro nudo ritu ac caerimonia; proque externa tantum corporis lotione, ac inani signo, habeant; nihilque in eo praeter externam aquam videant. Ita enim, post Scholasticos, nunc sentiunt Jesuitae, ac, cum Anabaptistis, in baptismo illo nihil Euangelicum agnoscunt; sed ritum tantum Veteris Testamenti a Johanne repetitum volunt; adeoque iterari & repeti eum oportuisse contendunt. Quae alia ex ista communione paululum mitigant; & remissionem peccatorum baptismo isti comitem fuisse, verum aliter ac in Euangelicis sacramentis, & ex opere operantis solummodo affirmant. Alii rursus baptismum illum non praecepti, sed consilii fuisse, docent. Omnes autem in eo conveniunt, quod Johannis Baptismum a nostro non gradu solo, sed specie ac substantia distinguunt. Quorum argumenta breviter excutienda sunt.
units.tr: XI. The Papists perversely diminish John's baptism. They hold that it was not a sacrament of the New Testament but a bare rite and ceremony, only an external washing of the body and an empty sign, and that there is nothing in it but external water. For after the Scholastics, so the Jesuits now think, and together with the Anabaptists, they recognise nothing evangelical in that baptism. They want it to be merely the rite of the Old Testament repeated by John, and they contend that it ought to have been repeated and done again. Others from the same communion soften this somewhat. They affirm that remission of sins accompanied that baptism, but in a different way from the evangelical sacraments, and only ex opere operantis. Others again teach that that baptism was a matter of counsel, not of precept. All agree in this, that they distinguish John's baptism from ours not merely by degree but by kind and substance. Their arguments must be briefly examined.

units.la: XII. Ac 1. contra manifestam Scripturam est, quod divinam originem ac auctoritatem Johannis Baptismo abrogant; &, non a Deo, sed a Johanne ipso institutum, indeque Johannis baptismum dictum, volunt. Disertissima enim testimonia in contrarium vidimus. Luc. 3: 2. Joh. 1: 33. Matth. 21: 25. 2. Nec dignitatem ejus minuit, quod baptismus poenitentiae appelletur. Cum poenitentia illa, ac veteris instituti, falsaque justitiae derelictio, fidem in Christum includeret; qua sancta disciplina Johannes proselytos suos imbuebat; pariterque & noster baptismus poenitentiae initiatio est; ac de nostra quoque unda, nativa sorde eluta, ad novae vitae auspicia renascimur. Consepulti sumus igitur ei per baptismum in mortem: ut, sicuti suscitatus est Christus ex mortuis in gloriam Patris, ita & nos nova vita ambulemus. Rom. 6: 4. 3. Ad discrimen illud, quo Johannes baptismum suum a Christi baptismo distinguit, Marc. 1: 8. Matth. 3: 11. dici posset, illud non minus in ordinario ministrorum baptismo locum habere; cum neque is, qui plantat, fit aliquid; neque qui rigat; sed Deus, qui dat crescendi vim. 1. Cor. 3: 7. Nam externa ablutio, externaque aquae, semper a Deo, Spirituque eas animante & fœcundante, distinguenda sunt. Sed cum Johannes hic revera non distinguat inter actionem suam externam & virtutem Christi internam, sed inter suum & Christi baptismum, libenter damus, majorem Spiritus copiam, ac Johannis baptismum comitabatur, in posterum à Christo dandam hic promitti 4. Leve autem est, quod de verborum formula contendunt; quod Johannes non legatur suos in Trinitatis fidem obsignasse; quæ Christiani baptismi ratio est, Math. 28:19. Sufficit enim, rem utrobique eandem esse. Non enim formula ista substantiam baptismi facit; cum necquidem Apostoli ea semper usi sint; ac Christus in gentium baptismo eam demum exprimat. Neque S.S. Trinitatis testimonio Johannis baptismus prorsus caret: cum Matth. 3. in illustri illo, quo baptismus ejus commendatus fuit, miraculo, referatis cœlis, tota Trinitas quodam modo ad ejus baptismum venerit, voce, Pater; natus, corpore; flamen, ave. 5. Gravius est, quod retinctos exististimant, qui jam antea à Johanne baptisati fuerant. Quod ex Act. 19: 3, 4, 5. & Act. 2:41. coll. Marc. 1:5. sese probare putant. Et verba quidem illa Act. 19:5. Qui vero illum audierunt, baptizati sunt in nomen Domini Jesu: non Lucæ narrantis, sed Pauli concionantis esse, ex particularum μὲν & δὲ nexu satis evinci multis videtur. Unde, non retinctos illos, sed eos, qui à Johanne olim abluti erant, à Paulo, impositis manibus, majore extraordinarii Spiritus copia donatos, diceretur. Quam Spiritus potentiam hactenus ignoraverant. Sed cum ille particularum nexus quandoque fallat, & alia quædam hujus loci verba, & totus verborum contextus optime admittant, hosce xii. viros Johannis baptismo olim tinctos, à Paulo de novo tinctos esse, quæ veterum fuit communis interpretatio; nihil aliud hinc sequeretur, nisi illos qui a Johanne antea in Jesum venientem baptizati erant, postea, Jesu manifestato & consummato, in expresso nomine domini Jesu, qui jam venerat, iterum tingi potuisse. Quale circumstantiarum discrimen inter baptismum Johannis & Apostolorum jam indicavimus. Nec ingens illa turba, quæ in celebri ista Christianæ Ecclesiæ pentecoste, sacro lavacro expiata est, Act. 2. omnis è Johannis discipulina venerat; nec ab eo jam ante abluta fuerat. Magnam enim partem erant Judæi exteri. Quanquam, ubi aliquot millia baptismum petebant, Apostolos curiosius inquisivisse non exstimemus, ne quis forte, à Johanne, olim ablutus, in tanta multitudine lateret. Et illorum, si retincti fuerint, eadem, quæ xi i. illorum discipulorum, fuisset ratio. Quod enim de Johanne urgent ex Marc. 1:5. Et exibat ad ad eum omnis Judaica regio, ac Hierosolymita, ac baptisabantur omnes &c: idem de Apostolis objici posset, ex Joh. 4: 1, 2. Cognovit Dominus, Pharisaos audisse, ipsum plures discipulos facere, & baptizare quam Johannem. Quanquam Jesus ipse non baptizabat, sed discipuli ejus. Ut ex Apostolorum quoque proselytis, inter tot millia, non defuisse videantur qui jam a Johanne tincti fuerant. Cui difficultati hoc modo facilius a nobis, quam ab ipsis satisfieri existimamus.
units.tr: XII. First, it is contrary to plain Scripture that they deny John's baptism its divine origin and authority, and hold that it was instituted not by God but by John himself, and so is called John's baptism. For we have seen most explicit testimonies to the contrary: Luke 3:2; John 1:33; Matt. 21:25. 2. Nor does it diminish its dignity that it is called the baptism of repentance. That repentance, together with the abandonment of the old way of life and of false righteousness, included faith in Christ, and into this holy discipline John initiated his proselytes. Likewise our baptism is an initiation into repentance, and we too are reborn in that washing, our native filth being cleansed away, to the beginnings of a new life. We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. Rom. 6:4. 3. As for the distinction by which John separates his baptism from Christ's (Mark 1:8; Matt. 3:11), it could be said that it applies no less to the ordinary baptism of ministers, since neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase. 1 Cor. 3:7. The external washing and the external water must always be distinguished from God, and from the Spirit who animates and makes them fruitful. But since John here does not really distinguish between his external action and Christ's inner power, but between his baptism and Christ's, we willingly grant that the greater abundance of the Spirit, which accompanied John's baptism, is here promised to be given later by Christ. 4. Trifling, too, is their objection about the wording of the formula: that John is not read as having sealed his disciples into faith in the Trinity, which is the pattern of Christian baptism (Matt. 28:19). For it is enough that the thing is the same in both. The formula does not make the substance of baptism, since the Apostles did not always use it, and Christ spells it out only in the baptism of the Gentiles. Nor does John's baptism lack the testimony of the Most Holy Trinity. In Matt. 3, in the famous miracle by which his baptism was commended, with the heavens opened, the whole Trinity came, in a way, to his baptism: the Father by voice, the Son in body, the Spirit as a dove. 5. More serious is their view that those who had already been baptized by John were baptized again. They think they prove this from Acts 19:3, 4, 5 and Acts 2:41, compared with Mark 1:5. Many indeed think it is shown by the connection of the particles μὲν and δὲ that the words of Acts 19:5, Those who heard him were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, belong not to Luke's narrative but to Paul's preaching. Whence it would be said that those men were not rebaptized, but that those who had long before been washed by John were, with hands laid on them by Paul, given a greater measure of extraordinary Spirit, a power of the Spirit they had hitherto not known. But since that connection of particles sometimes deceives, and other words of this passage and the whole context admit this reading well, the view that these twelve men, once baptized with John's baptism, were baptized anew by Paul (which was the common interpretation of the ancients) implies nothing more than this: that those who had earlier been baptized by John, as he was coming to Jesus, could afterwards, when Jesus had been made manifest and completed, be baptized again in the express name of the Lord Jesus, who had now come. We have already pointed out this difference of circumstances between the baptism of John and that of the Apostles. Nor was that huge crowd, cleansed by the holy washing at the famous Pentecost of the Christian Church (Acts 2), all from John's disciples, nor had it been washed by him before; for most of them were foreign Jews. Although, when some thousands asked for baptism, we do not think the Apostles inquired too closely, lest someone washed earlier by John might be hidden in so great a multitude. And if those men were rebaptized, the reasoning would be the same as for the twelve disciples. For what they urge about John from Mark 1:5, And all the Judean region and all the Jerusalemites went out to him, and all were baptized, could equally be objected about the Apostles from John 4:1, 2: The Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that he was making and baptizing more disciples than John. Yet Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples. So among the Apostles' proselytes too, among so many thousands, there seem to have been some who had already been dipped by John. We think this difficulty is answered more easily by us than by them, in this way.

units.la: XIII. Quæri autem potest: quid de baptismo Spiritus ac ignis, de quo Johannes concionabatur, Matth. 3: 11. Luc. 3: 16. censendum sit. Proprie enim, ac κατὰ ῥητὸν, quidam baptismum illum acceperunt, ac igni olim baptizarunt. Veteres quidam ignem inferni; alii ignem probationis, seu purgatorii cogitavere. Communior sententia verba illa conjungit, &c, per ἐν διὰ πυρὸς, vel Spiritum ardentem ac igneum, vel ignem spiritualem, intelligit. Ubi conferre licet similes loquendi modos. Joh. 3: 5. Act. 1: 5. & 2: 4. Sed forte non incommode ea distingui possent, & per baptismum Spiritus, Spiritus in Nov. T. promissus, ingensque ejus copia. Joh. 7: 38, 39. Act. 2: 15, 16. per baptismum ignis autem secundum literam, instans Dei in Judæos contumaces judicium, ac gentis templique per ignem excidium intelligi: de quo & Johannes in eadem concione ÿs 12. dixit: quanquam & alia, quæ per ignem in Scriptura intelligi solent conjungi posse non abnuamus. Vide 1. Pet. 4: 12. Ne, tanquam peregrini, exploratione illa per ignem, quæ fit in vobis, ad vestri experimentum, percellimini, Zach. 13: 9. Et introducam tertiam partem in ignem, & conflabo illos, ut conflatur argentum.
units.tr: XIII. But it may be asked what is to be thought of the baptism of the Spirit and of fire, of which John preached (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16). Some have taken that baptism properly and literally, as if they had once been baptized with fire. Some of the ancients thought of the fire of hell; others of the fire of trial, or purgatory. The more common view joins the words with "and," and understands by [ἐν διὰ πυρὸς] either a burning and fiery Spirit, or spiritual fire. Here one may compare similar modes of speech (John 3:5; Acts 1:5; Acts 2:4). But perhaps these might not unsuitably be distinguished, so that by the baptism of the Spirit is meant the Spirit promised in the New Testament and his abundant gift (John 7:38, 39; Acts 2:15, 16), while the baptism of fire, taken according to the letter, means the impending judgment of God on the stubborn Jews, and the destruction of the nation and temple by fire, of which John also spoke in the same sermon (verse 12). Though we do not deny that other things which are usually understood by fire in Scripture may also be joined. See 1 Pet. 4:12: Do not be startled, as if something strange were happening to you, by that fiery trial which comes upon you for your testing. And Zech. 13:9: And I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined.

units.la: XIV. Baptizatus autem a Johanne legitur Christus; non quod regeneratione indigeret, sed aliis de causis. Nam 1. istud amoris Dei pignus accipere, & tractare, a Christo homine alienum non erat. 2. Cumque Ecclesiæ dux atque caput foret, a Patre in Salvatorem mundo ostendi, atque isto ritu publice obsignari, debebat. Quo oraculum in baptismo ejus de cœlo editum spectat. 3. Sed & ad Ecclesiam de justitia per ipsum, ut sponsorem nostrum, parta, securam reddendam hoc favoris Dei testimonium pertinebat; atque eluendis, non propriis, sed nostris sordibus, ipsi imputatis, itæ aquæ serviebant. Rom. 8: 3. 4. Pertinebat etiam ad exemplum, ne quos sacros ritus Christus omitteret, sed eos omnes proprio in corpore honoraret & consecraret. 5. Cumque tam veteris, quam novæ legis sacramenta susciperet, se unum omnium illorum finem, ac fœderis fundamentum, & utriusque populi, tum veteris, tum novi,
units.tr: XIV. Christ is read as having been baptized by John, not because he needed regeneration, but for other reasons. 1. To receive this pledge of God's love and to take it upon himself was not foreign to Christ as man. 2. And since he was to be the leader and head of the Church, he had to be shown to the world by the Father as Saviour, and publicly sealed by this rite; to this the oracle uttered from heaven at his baptism looks. 3. This testimony of God's favour also pertained to making the Church secure about the righteousness won through him as our surety; and that water served to wash away filth, not his own, but ours, imputed to him. Rom. 8:3. 4. It also pertained to example: that Christ might not omit any sacred rite, but might honour and consecrate them all in his own body. 5. And since he underwent the sacraments of the old law as well as of the new, he declared himself the one end of them all, the foundation of the covenant, and the Saviour of both peoples, the old and the new,

units.la: Pars II. V v SerServatorem declaravit. 6. Tandem & Johannis doctrinæ isto pacto testimonium reddebat; cum ipse publicum ab eo testimonium accipere, ac baptismo ejus ablui non abnueret. Recepit ergo ab eo baptismum externum. Internum vero non tam accepit, quam ipse & aliis, & sibi dedit. Unde non ab aquis mundatus, sed ipsas potius aquas mundasse a veteribus dicitur. Quæ etiam causa est, quod ipse nunquam baptisasse, aut externas aquas ministrasse; sed quicquid hoc muneris erat, discipulis permisisse, legitur Joh. 4: 2. utpote cum ad eum præcipue internus per Spiritum S. baptismus pertineret. Ipse vos baptisabit Spiritu S. & igne, Matth. 3: 11.
units.tr: Pars II. V v SerServatorem declaravit. 6. Finally, he also gave testimony to John's teaching in this way: he did not refuse to receive public testimony from John, or to be washed in John's baptism. He therefore received external baptism from him. Internal baptism, however, he did not so much receive as give, both to himself and to others. Hence it is said that he was not cleansed by the waters, but rather that he cleansed the waters, as the ancients put it. This is also why he himself never baptized or administered external water. Whatever this office was, he left it to his disciples, as is read in John 4: 2, since internal baptism through the Holy Spirit pertained above all to him. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire, Matth. 3: 11.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De Baptismi administratione.
units.tr: On the administration of baptism.

units.la: I. UT ergo ad baptismi administrationem, ejusque ministros, pergamus; baptizarunt potissimum Apostoli, Christi jussu atque auctoritate. Jesus ipse non baptisabat, sed discipuli ejus. Joh. 4: 2. Profecti ergo, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, Filii, & Spiritus S. Matth. 28: 19. Act. 2: 41.
units.tr: I. So, to turn to the administration of baptism and its ministers: the Apostles chiefly baptized, by Christ's command and authority. Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples. John 4:2. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Matt. 28:19. Acts 2:41.

units.la: II. Quando enim Paulus, non ad baptismum, sed ad Evangelium ministrandum, missum se esse dicit, 1. Cor. 1: 17. præcipuam muneris sui partem exprimit: quod in Evangelio annunciando, cui non omnes idonei erant, consistebat; tingendi ministerio aliis, qui ad illam facilius sufficiebant, mandato; qui ex Apostolorum auctoritate illud administrabant. Quanquam & Paulum quoque baptisasse satis constat. conf. com. 14. Prudentiæ autem erat, in ea Ecclesia, ubi partim studia increbescebant, dum quisque illos, a quibus ad sacrum fontem perducus erat, tanquam fidei magistros sequebatur, a tingendo abstincere; ut inter diffidentes idoneus pacis auctor & sequester foret; nec quisquam ex Apostolica tinctura prærogativam supra reliquos fratres præsumeret.
units.tr: II. When Paul says he was sent not to baptize but to preach the Gospel (1 Cor. 1:17), he states the chief part of his office, which consisted in announcing the Gospel, for which not everyone was fit. The ministry of dipping he committed to others, who were more readily equal to it, and who administered it by the authority of the Apostles. Yet it is quite certain that Paul also baptized; see the commentary on chapter 14. In that church, however, where factions were increasing, while each person followed those by whom he had been brought to the sacred font as his teachers of the faith, it was a matter of prudence to abstain from baptizing, so that there might be a suitable peacemaker and mediator among those who distrusted one another, and so that no one would claim, from his Apostolic dipping, a prerogative above the other brothers.

units.la: III. Præter Apostolos, baptizarunt quoque Evangelistæ, aliique ministri, qui ipsis auctoribus hoc munus usurpabant. Quum vero crediderunt Philippo evangelizanti — baptizabantur viri & fœminæ. Act. 8: 12. Et quum surrexisset (Saulus) baptizatus est ab Anania. c. 9: 18. & 10: 40. Sicut in veteri Ecclesia ab Episcopo, vel presbytero, novi Christiani stiani lustrabantur. Atque in universum publica illa fidelium initiatio, cum non ad domesticam vel privatam disciplinam (qualis singulis Christianis incumbit) sed ad publicum officium pertineat; publicos Ecclesiæ ministros solum spectat. Atque ii solum, quibus præcipua Ecclesiæ cura, & sacrorum mysteriorum custodia commissa est, publice docere, & tingere, novosque fratres adoptare, permittuntur. Hæc enim duo conjunguntur, docete omnes gentes, baptisantes. Matth. 28: 19. Nec cuiquam privato ausu sacra sigilla tractare licet: cum & inter homines, qui injussu imperatoris publicas tabulas conficiunt, ultimi criminis rei habeantur.
units.tr: III. Besides the Apostles, evangelists also baptized, and other ministers who, with their authority, claimed this office. When they believed Philip preaching the Gospel, they were baptized, both men and women. Acts 8:12. And when (Saul) had risen, he was baptized by Ananias. Acts 9:18, and 10:40. As in the ancient Church, new Christians were washed by the bishop or the presbyter. And in general, since that public initiation of the faithful pertains not to domestic or private discipline (which falls to each individual Christian) but to public office, it concerns only the public ministers of the Church. And only those to whom the chief care of the Church and the custody of the sacred mysteries have been entrusted are permitted to teach publicly, to baptize, and to adopt new brothers. For these two are joined together: teach all nations, baptizing. Matt. 28:19. Nor is it lawful for anyone to handle the sacred seals by private daring, since even among men, those who draw up public records without the emperor's command are held guilty of the gravest crime.

units.la: IV. Invalescente autem jam olim nimia signorum religione, ac baptismi præsertim necessitate, etiam Laicis tingere permissum fuit. Atque in eam sententiam multi ex patribus eunt. Atque ulterius iverunt Pontificii, & in concilio Florentino, non Laicis solum, sed mulierculis, simo & hæreticis, & Ethnicis, urgente necessitate, baptismum largiri, concesserunt. Quod γυναικοβάπτισμα veteres adeo non probaverunt, ut ad hæreticos auctores illud referat Epiphanius; alibique id nec B. virgini indulgeat; cum alioqui ipsa potius, quam Johannes, filium suum baptizatura fuerit. Temere autem Pontificii de docendi potestate primis Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctoribus litem intendunt; cum ipsi baptisandi potestatem adeo communem & promiscuam faciant. Pontificios aliquo intervallo sequuntur Lutherani, ex eadem necessitatis præsumtione, ac nimia signorum admiratione. Nec dissentiunt, in eo vulgari reddendo, Socinians, quanquam alio ac contrario errore; utpote qui omne mysterium sacramentis abrogant.
units.tr: IV. But since long ago an excessive reverence for signs had gained strength, and especially the belief in the necessity of baptism, it was allowed for even laymen to baptize. Many of the Fathers go in that direction. The Papists went further, and at the Council of Florence conceded that baptism might be bestowed, under urgent necessity, not only by laymen but by women, even by heretics and pagans.
