After this, as the first stage of faith, we are then justified and obtain the forgiveness of our offences, which those cleansing waters chiefly signify. Baptism for those who repent, for the forgiveness of sins. (Mark 1:4) Let each of you be baptized in the name of J. Christ for the forgiveness of sins. (Acts 2:38) Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins. (Acts 22:16) Moreover, that image of washing and immersion signifies also our inborn filth and the stain of origin, and those external waters figure the Holy Spirit; and so they are also a pledge and guarantee of sanctification. Hence the phrase the washing of regeneration, in which we put off our old filth, and the baptism of repentance occurs among the sacred writers (Titus 3:5; Matt. 3:2; Luke 3:3). Finally, since all these things are very imperfect in this life, and since we are chiefly washed as an earnest of the life to come, we also possess in those waters a pledge of glorification, a declaration [ἐκφώνησιν] of a good and joyful conscience, and an earnest (1 Pet. 3:21). Nor is the mystical immersion and emergence a slight foreshadowing of the resurrection to come after death. The Apostle teaches, at Rom. 6:4, 5, that the death and resurrection of Christ, and our fellowship with them, are not lightly figured by that rite. We have therefore been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in new life. For if we have grown together with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also grow together with him in the likeness of his resurrection. Compare Col. 2:11, 12.

units.la: V. Ex quibus patet, baptismi signum, circumcisioni vicarium, eadem per omnia bona adumbrare, eandemque justitiam fidei obsignare, quam veteri Ecclesiæ circumcisio obsignabat. Nisi quod baptismus, ad novæ Ecclesiæ statum accommodatior, nullo jugo, ac nulla priscæ servitutis imagine, eam territ & premat. Quæ in circumcisionis sacramento fuerunt.
units.tr: V. From these things it is clear that the sign of baptism, the substitute for circumcision, shadows in every respect the same blessings, and seals the same righteousness of faith which circumcision sealed for the old Church. Except that baptism, better suited to the state of the new Church, does not terrify or oppress with any yoke or any image of former servitude. These things belonged to the sacrament of circumcision.

units.la: VI. Sicut autem baptismus fidem nostram confirmat, ita ab altera parte fidem requirit: absque qua inanis pompa, & scena, & vilis aquæ libatio, & magica propemodum februatio est: nuda nimirum ablutio sordium corporis, non vero firmamentum interrogationis bonæ conscientiæ ad Deum. 1. Pet. 3:21.
units.tr: Just as baptism confirms our faith, so on our side it requires faith in return. Without faith it is an empty show, a theatrical display, and a cheap sprinkling of water, almost a magical purification: nothing more than a washing away of the filth of the body, and not the pledge of a good conscience toward God. 1 Pet. 3:21.

units.la: VII. Repræsentatur autem omne baptismi mysterium in solenni ejus formula Matth. 28:19. Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Istis enim verbis partim Ecclesia in S.S. Trinitatis nomen inaugurat; istisque tanquam salutis testibus & auctoribus gloriatur; ac nomen istud Dei sui palam in mundo profitetur, tanquam populus ejus peculiaris: partim etiam Deus Ecclesiam in fidem suam accipit, eique infallibilis salutis sponsor exitit; ac fideles filiorum & filiarum loco in domo sua habet. Manifesta enim adoptionis imago est, dum pulchrum S.S. Trinitatis nomen super baptizandos invocatur. Jac. 2:7.
units.tr: VII. The whole mystery of baptism is set forth in its solemn formula, Matth. 28:19: baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. By these words the Church is partly initiated into the name of the Holy Trinity, and glories in them as witnesses and authors of salvation, and openly professes that name of her God in the world as his peculiar people. Partly also God receives the Church into his faith, and becomes for her the surety of an infallible salvation, and holds the faithful in his house in the place of sons and daughters. For it is a clear picture of adoption when the noble name of the Holy Trinity is invoked over those being baptized. Jas. 2:7.

units.la: VIII. Notandi hic adversariorum errores. Socinianî, ut solent, in defectu peccant, & tenuiter de hoc sacramento sentiunt, nec mysterii quicquam in eo relinquunt. Nudas enim aquas, nulla vi ac spirituali gratia fœtas, hic agnoscunt; nec ablui iis aut purgari nos ferunt: sed baptismum illum pro nuda Christianæ professionis testera habent, quæ nihil nobis obsignet aut tradat; solummodo, externo ritu, in Christiana sacra transfire nos testetur.
units.tr: VIII. The errors of the adversaries must be noted here. The Socinians, as usual, sin by deficiency and think meanly of this sacrament, leaving nothing of the mystery in it. For they acknowledge here only bare water, not fertile with any power or spiritual grace, and they say we are not washed or cleansed by it. They regard that baptism as a mere testimony of the Christian profession, which seals and conveys nothing to us, but only shows by an outward rite that we pass over into the Christian sacred community.

units.la: IX. In alteram partem eunt Pontificii, qui aquas illas nimia vi imprægnant; nec pro signo solum aut sigillo, sed pro causa gratiæ continente, eas habent; & regenerationis ac justificationis instrumentum certissimum, per modum operis operati, appellant. Quibus ex parte accedunt Lutherani, qui hic etiam crassius loquuntur, & baptismum causam regenerationis inchoantem esse statuunt. De quibus libri hujus cap. 1. latius egimus.
units.tr: IX. The Papists go to the other extreme, who saturate those waters with excessive power; and they hold them to be not only a sign or seal but the containing cause of grace, and they call them the most certain instrument of regeneration and justification, by way of the work done (ex opere operato). The Lutherans come close to them on this point, speaking here too more crudely, and they hold that baptism is the cause that initiates regeneration. Concerning these matters we treated more fully in chapter 1 of this book.

units.la: X. Errat pariter Romana Ecclesia circa baptismi effectum, quem nimis augent. Nam non solum peccatorum remissionem, & prisci reatus extinctionem; sed & labis originalis ac concupiscentiæ ablationem, & reliquæ maculæ abstersionem, ci adscribunt: atque in eum finem vim quandam miraculificam genitali isti undæ indunt; aut saltem eam ad sacramenti administrationem praesentem semper faciunt. Quod & contra Scripturam; & contra ipsum hominum sensum & experientiam est; & denique sacrorum signorum vim sacrilege exaltat. Nam & fidelium infantes, quanquam baptizatos, mori quotidie videmus: atque ipsi quoque fideles, post baptismi aquas, veterem labem in se adhuc persentiscunt, Rom. 7. Et Scriptura morti demum, Col. 2:11, 12. & futuro saeculo illam fidelium perfectionem transcribit: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. 1. Joh. 1:8. Nec baptismali undae, tanquam causae efficienti, vel continenti, sed Spiritui S. potentem istam gratiam assignat.
units.tr: X. The Roman Church likewise errs about the effect of baptism, which it greatly exaggerates. For it ascribes to baptism not only the remission of sins and the extinction of the former guilt, but also the removal of original stain and concupiscence and the wiping away of the remaining blemish; and to this end it invests that generative water with a certain miracle-working power, or at least always makes it present in the administration of the sacrament. This is contrary both to Scripture and to the very sense and experience of men, and finally it sacrilegiously exalts the power of the sacred signs. For we see even the infants of believers, though baptized, die every day; and believers themselves, after the waters of baptism, still feel the old stain within them, Rom. 7. And Scripture assigns that perfection of believers to death at last and to the future age, Col. 2:11, 12. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, 1 John 1:8. Nor does it assign this powerful grace to the baptismal water as an efficient or containing cause, but to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XI. Rursus baptismi efficaciam nimis extenuant iidem, quasi tolat tantum poenas aeternas, non vero temporales, eluatque tanquam noxas praeteritas, non vero eas, quas post baptismum contrahimus; quibus expiandis sacramento poenitentiae, velut altera post naufragium tabula, opus sit. Qui error, ex Novati ac Catharorum fonte haustus, multis olim causa fuit, baptismum ad ultimum vitae finem differendi. Scriptura autem simpliciter ac generalibus verbis, peccatorum remissionem sacramento isti tribuit: Praedicabat Johannes baptismum respiscentia, ad remissionem peccatorum. Matth. 1:4. Baptizetur quisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum. Act. 2:38. conf. 22: 16. Et certum est, aeque late baptismi effectum patere, ac Dei foedus & gratia & Christi Salvatoris morsa meritum, ac justitia, se extendunt. Istis enim obsignandis baptismus servit. Illa autem omnibus peccatis delendis sufficere, ipsi non diffitentur adversarii. Unde idem de baptismo tatendum: necalterum sacramentum, ad recentes animae labes purgandas, invehendum. Cum baptismi, semel suscepti, pia recordatio, ac fidei renovatio, una cum sincera resipiscentia, quotidianas peccatorum sordes abunde abluat. Quod male damnaverunt in Concilio Tridentino Pontificii.
units.tr: XI. Again, the same men diminish the efficacy of baptism too much, as if it removed only eternal punishments and not temporal ones, and washed away the sins that are past but not those we contract after baptism, for the expiation of which the sacrament of penance is needed, like a second plank after shipwreck. This error, drawn from the source of Novatus and the Cathari, was once the cause of many people postponing baptism to the very end of life. Scripture, however, in simple and general words, grants the remission of sins to this sacrament: John was preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, Matth. 1:4; Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, Acts 2:38; compare 22:16. And it is certain that the effect of baptism extends as widely as God's covenant and grace, and the merit of Christ our Saviour's death and righteousness, extend. For baptism serves to seal these things. The adversaries themselves do not deny that these are sufficient to blot out all sins. Hence the same must be said of baptism: there is no need to introduce another sacrament to cleanse the fresh stains of the soul. The pious remembrance of baptism, once received, and the renewal of faith, together with sincere repentance, abundantly wash away the daily filth of sins. The Papists wrongly condemned this at the Council of Trent.

units.la: ab altera autem nimium depriment.
units.tr: On the other side, however, they depress it too much.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De Baptismi adjunctis.
units.tr: On the Adjuncts of Baptism.

units.la: I. Equuntur denique baptismi adjuncta, necessitas ejus & irreiterabilitas.
units.tr: I. Finally, the adjuncts of baptism follow: its necessity and its unrepeatability.

units.la: II. Necessitatem baptismi elevarunt nimium, tum, inter veteres, haeretici non unius generis; tum hodie Sociniani: qui pro Ecclesiastico ritu ac caerimonia eum habent, adscicendis ad Christi fidem ex Judaismo ac Gentilismo proselytis; inter Christianos autem vix amplius eo opus esse censent.
units.tr: II. Both inside and outside the early Church, various heretics, not of one kind, have raised the necessity of baptism too high. Today the Socinians do the same: they regard it as an ecclesiastical rite and ceremony for admitting proselytes from Judaism and paganism to the faith of Christ, and they think it hardly needed at all among Christians.

units.la: III. Adstrinxerunt eam plus aequo, inter veteres, non pauci Ecclesiae Doctores. Quorum princeps fuit Ambrosius, qui absque salutari lavacro vitam aeternam patere negavit; solos martyres, accum baptismi desiderio morientes, excipiens; quos videl. fides sua, ac fusus pro Christo cruor, lavat, & petitio consecrat, ut idem de Valentiniano Caesare. Secutus est Ambrosium Augustinus, qui infantes non tinctos, tanquam victimas nil miserantis Orci, inferis transcribere non est veritus; quanquam mitioribus flammis cos ustulandos censeat. Quo ex occasione Pelagiani certaminis delapsus est. Unde, ut fieri consuevit, tanti nominis auctoritate, error ille facile proserpsit: &, cum Latina Ecclesia Augustino doctore potissimum uteretur, hoc quoque dogma inter discipulos eos propagatum, tandemque a futilissimae scholae doctoribus adoptatum, universam propemodum Ecclesiam occupavit.
units.tr: III. Among the ancients, not a few teachers of the Church bound it tighter than was fair. The chief of them was Ambrose, who denied that eternal life lies open without the saving bath, making an exception only for martyrs who die with a desire for baptism; their own faith and the blood shed for Christ, he said, washes them, and petition consecrates them, as he said of the emperor Valentinian. Augustine followed Ambrose. He did not hesitate to consign unbaptized infants to the lower world, as victims of a pitiless Orcus, though he judges that they are to be burned there with gentler flames. On this occasion he fell into the Pelagian controversy. Hence, as usually happens, that error crept in easily under the authority of so great a name; and since the Latin Church made Augustine its chief teacher, this doctrine too was spread among his disciples and at last adopted by the teachers of a most trifling school, and it has taken possession of almost the whole Church.

units.la: IV. Pontificii, quamvis ambiguis verbis in Tridentino Concilio quaestionem illam absolverint, nec doctores ipsorum per omnia consentiant, ac variis exceptionibus rigorem illum emollire nitantur; tamen communiter duplicem baptismi necessitatem statuunt, cum praecepti, tum medii; ac solis adultis, per martyrium ac poenitentiam, ejus veniam largiuntur. Caeteroquin, ubi nondum lustrati decesserint, inferni illis poenas; infantibus autem (nisi quod & hos martyrii coronam aliquando decerpere, seque ipsos sanguine suo abluere, statuant) perpetuum, in limbo aliquo, extra Paradisi spatia, exilium, sed absque dolore ac sensu ullo, decernunt. In quo ab Augustini vestigiis, quae sese premere jacitant, discedunt.
units.tr: IV. The Papists, although in ambiguous words they settled that question at the Council of Trent, and although their teachers do not agree in every point and try to soften that rigour with various qualifications, nevertheless commonly hold a twofold necessity of baptism, of precept and of means, and grant pardon for lack of it only to adults, through martyrdom and penance. Otherwise, they decree, those who die not yet washed suffer punishments of hell; but for infants (though they also hold that these sometimes gather the crown of martyrdom and wash themselves in their own blood) they decree a perpetual exile in some limbo outside the spaces of Paradise, yet without any pain or sense at all. In this they depart from the footsteps of Augustine, which they are fond of pressing.

units.la: Pars II.
units.tr: Part II.

units.la: V. Nec rigorem istum veterum satis fugiunt Lutherani: qui, cum regenerationis initia sacramento illi deputent, quod praeter Augustanam confessionem est, magnam istam externi signi necessitatem effugere non possunt. Quanquam hodie moderatius nonnulli ex ista Ecclesia sentiant.
units.tr: V. The Lutherans do not escape that ancient rigour either. Since they assign the beginnings of regeneration to that sacrament, which goes beyond the Augustana Confession, they cannot avoid this great necessity of the outward sign. Yet today some in that Church think more moderately on the matter.

units.la: VI. Orthodoxa autem Ecclesia diversos necessitatis gradus distinguit. Cumque necessitas, alia absoluta, alia hypothetica; alia medii, alia praecepti sit; non priori, sed posteriori modo baptismum necessarium facit. Ex hypothesi videl. gemina, cum efficientis, ac praecipientis Dei, Matth. 28: 19. tum finis, cum divini foederis signaculum, ac amoris ejus arrhabo sit; quem repudiare hominis Deum nec amantis, nec reverentis, foret. Adeo ut non privatio, sed contemtus baptismi damnet. Quae sententia inter Socinianorum ac Pontificiorum errores media est.
units.tr: VI. The orthodox Church, however, distinguishes different degrees of necessity. Since necessity is one thing absolute and another hypothetical, one of means and another of precept, baptism is necessary not in the former way but in the latter. Hypothetically, it is necessary twofold: on the part of God, the efficient and commanding cause (Matt. 28:19), and on the part of the end, since it is the sign of the divine covenant and the pledge of his love; to reject it would show a man to be neither loving nor reverent toward God. So it is not the lack but the contempt of baptism that condemns. This view lies midway between the errors of the Socinians and the Papists.

units.la: VII. Ac nimiam istam severitatem, & sacrorum signorum necessitatem, redarguit, cum Scripturarum auctoritas, tum rationes ex ca deductae. Nam 1. nondum baptizatis, aut divinis sacramentis initiatis, saepe divini favoris ac gratiae testimonia perhibentur: uti Jacobo, Rom. 9: 11. Puerulis Hierosolymitanis, Matth. 19: 13. Davidi, aliisque. Quos, de matre cadentes, excepit statim Deus, & benigno sinu fovit; ac vixdum naturae manu fictos divina sua manu protinus refinxit. Vide Psal. 71: 6. Tibi innitor inde ab utero; a visceribus matris mea tu abripuisti me. Jer. 1: 5. Antequam exires ex utero, sanctificavi te. Luc. 1: 15. Spiritu S. implebitur etiam a ventre matris sue. Gal. 1: 15. Qui me separavit ab utero matris mea. Nec omittendum Cornelii Centurionis exemplum, cui, ante baptismi lavacrum, pietas & sanctitas, aliaque Spiritus S. dona attribuuntur, Act. 10: 12, 15, 44, 47. De Latronc, ad Christi crucem converso, hoc certum est, non ablutum in coelum ascendisse, Luc. 23: 43. contra autem, Simonem Magum nequicquam tinctum fuisse, nec plamina ista quicquam ipsi profuisse, Act. 8: 13, 20--23. 11. Sed & sacramentorum natura consideranda est. Cum enim gratiae tantum signa, & foederis signacula sint; quid vetat gratia ipsa aliquem potiri, qui ejus signo careat, quique inevitabili aliquo casu carere eo aeternum debeat?
units.tr: VII. The Scriptures, as well as the reasons drawn from them, refute that excessive severity and the necessity of the sacred signs. For, first, testimonies of divine favour and grace are often given to people not yet baptized or initiated into the divine sacraments: as to Jacob (Rom. 9:11), to the little children of Jerusalem (Matt. 19:13), to David, and to others. God received them at once when they fell from their mother's womb and cherished them in his gentle bosom; and as soon as they were shaped by the hand of nature, he immediately re-formed them with his own hand. See Ps. 71:6: I have leaned on you from the womb; you took me out of my mother's bowels. Jer. 1:5: Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. Luke 1:15: He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. Gal. 1:15: He who set me apart from my mother's womb. Nor should we pass over the example of the centurion Cornelius, to whom piety and holiness and other gifts of the Holy Spirit are ascribed before the washing of baptism (Acts 10:2, 15, 44, 47). It is certain that the thief who turned to the cross of Christ was not washed and yet ascended into heaven (Luke 23:43); on the other hand, Simon Magus was baptized in vain, and that washing did him no good at all (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Second, the nature of the sacraments must also be considered. Since they are only signs of grace and seals of the covenant, what forbids grace itself from possessing someone who lacks its sign, and who must lack that sign for ever through some unavoidable accident?

units.la: III. Certe foedus Dei potius est externo ejus signo. Et qui foederis particeps est, quod fidelium liberis, natalium quasi jure, Apostolus tribuit, 1. Cor. 7: 14. Alioquin liberi vestri impuri essent, nunc autem sancti sunt; is, quod nondum signilla foederis adeptus, nec publice in Ecclesia obsignatus est, non ea de causa tanquam profanus haberi, bonisque foederis deris excidere meretur. iv. Et revera, si quidquam hic peccetur, non illa infantum, sed parentum potius culpa est: quam in innoxiam illam ætatem vindicari Dei misericordia non permittit. v. Ac denique iniquum est Dei gratiam externo signo alligare, ac coërcere, quasi extra illud Spir. S. non operetur; ac externæ cuiusdam cæremoniæ, quæsæpe extra nostram potestatem est, universam salutem velle affigere; atque ita rem omnium maximam de tenuissimo filo suspendere. vi. Suffragatur Veteris Testam. analogia; ubi, si quis sine circumcisionis nota de vita excederet, non ideo à Deo non agnoscebatur, aut cælo excludebatur. Ego accedo ad ipsum, & ille ad me non revertetur. 2. Sam. 12:23. Non minor autem existimanda est Novi temporis gratia, quam Veteris. vii. Ac mirum equidem, Pontificios baptismi gratiam adultis sæpe facere, modo vel sanguine suo, vel lacrymarum torrente, tanquam vicario baptismo, lustrentur; in infantes autem duros adeo esse; quos, nisi martyrii honore, ac mortis purpura, insignes sint, sine venia extra cœli spatia relegant; non aliam ob causam, quam quod, antequam salutari aqua tingi potuerint, nascentia ipsorum fata mors immatura abruperit; quique, quod unum forte diem non supervixere, æternum jam miseri esse debent. Quod crudele est. Certe de remedio aliquo cogitare deberet Ecclesia, atque liberis suis consulere. Verum hæc, aliaque, quæ in hoc argumento congeri possent, satis ostendunt, abjiciendam procul istam signorum superstitionem, ac mitigandam veterum severitatem, & immitis sententiæ horrorem, quæ sua immanitate satis sese prodit, de Ecclesia demendum. Utque Romana Ecclesia veterum errorem, in præbenda infantibus Eucharistia, jam diu correxit; ita non minori ratione & hic, qui ejusdem cum priori generis est, & absoluta sacramentorum necessitate nititur, in baptismo errore tollendus, ac procul habendus esset.
units.tr: III. Surely the covenant of God is greater than its outward sign. The one who shares in the covenant, which the Apostle attributes to the children of believers almost by a right of birth (1 Cor. 7:14: Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy), is not to be regarded as profane, nor deserves to fall from the benefits of the covenant, merely because he has not yet received the seal of the covenant and has not been publicly sealed in the Church. iv. And indeed, if any fault is committed here, it lies not with the infants but rather with the parents, whom the mercy of God does not allow to be punished in that innocent age. v. Finally, it is unjust to tie and confine the grace of God to an outward sign, as if the Holy Spirit did not work outside it, and to wish to hang the whole salvation on some outward ceremony, which is often beyond our power, and so to suspend the greatest matter of all from the finest thread. vi. The analogy of the Old Testament supports this: there, if someone died without the mark of circumcision, he was not for that reason unrecognised by God or shut out of heaven. I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Sam. 12:23). Yet the grace of the New Time must not be thought less than that of the Old. vii. It is indeed remarkable that the Papists often make the grace of baptism available to adults, who are washed either by their own blood or by a torrent of tears as if by a substitute baptism, but are so hard toward infants that, unless they are distinguished by the honour of martyrdom and the purple of death, they relegate them without pardon beyond the bounds of heaven. And this for no other reason than that an untimely death cut short their new-born lives before they could be washed with the saving water; and because they did not live even a single day, they must now be wretched for ever. This is cruel. Certainly the Church ought to think of some remedy and provide for its children. But these arguments and others that could be gathered on this subject show well enough that that superstition about signs must be cast far away, and the ancient severity softened, and the horror of that harsh opinion, which betrays itself by its own savagery, must be removed from the Church. Just as the Roman Church has long since corrected the error of the ancients in giving the Eucharist to infants, so for no lesser reason this error in baptism, which is of the same kind as the former and rests on an absolute necessity of the sacraments, ought to be removed and kept far away.

units.la: VIII. Ad objectiones respondemus. i. Locum palmarium, Joh. 3:5.
units.tr: VIII. We reply to the objections. (i) The chief passage, John 3:5.

units.la: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non poterit introire in regnum Dei, ab adversariis urgeri non posse; nisi jam ante Christi mortem eandem baptismi necessitatem statuant; ac pariter de Eucharistia sentiant, de qua ex Joh. 6:53. eadem leguntur verba, NISI ederitis carnem filii hominis, & biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Quod utrumque tamen ab iis negatur; & nec baptismus ante mortem Christi, nec in universum Eucharistia ita necessaria ab ipsis exis-timantur. Nec plane certum est omnibus, de baptismo istic loci agi; quanquam non multum de eo contendere velimus. Nam si vel baptismi aquam intelligant, necessitas ejus in communi intelligenda est, respectu ordinis in Ecclesia perpetuo servandi. Regenerationis autem, quæ baptismo obsignatur, summa est necessitas; idque docere præcipue Servator voluit. Quod multo magis sequetur, si obtineat eorum sententia, qui, sive Spiritus S. gratiam, per ἐν διὰ δυοῖν, in colloquio hoc cum Pharisæo intelligunt; quæ, allusione ad legales ablutiones & βαπτισμὸς facta; aquæ spiritualis nomine venit; qua virtute legales aquæ, & multifarii mundandi ritus, carebant; sive Christi obedientiam & meritum, quod vel præcipue animam a peccati labe emundare potest, ac sine quo ipse Spiritus regenerans non datur, hic adducunt. Conf. Hebr. 10:22,23. Ezech. 36:25. Certe externæ aquæ absoluta necessitas hic non intelligitur, nisi novam Ecclesiam aquæ, priscisque elementis, magis obnoxiam statuere velis, quam in veteri unquam Israelitarum Ecclesia factum est.
units.tr: The adversaries cannot press Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, unless they also hold that baptism was necessary before Christ's death. Likewise they should hold the same about the Eucharist, of which John 6:53 reads the same way: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. Yet they deny both: they hold that baptism was not necessary before Christ's death, and that the Eucharist is not necessary at all. It is also not entirely certain to everyone that baptism is meant in that place, though we do not wish to contend much about it. For if they understand the water of baptism, its necessity must be understood in general, with respect to the order to be kept perpetually in the Church. But the necessity of the regeneration that is sealed in baptism is supreme, and this the Saviour chiefly wished to teach. This would follow all the more if the opinion of those prevails who understand, in this conversation with the Pharisee, the grace of the Holy Spirit expressed by "through two" [ἐν διὰ δυοῖν]. This is said with allusion to the legal ablutions and the baptism [βαπτισμὸς], and it is called by the name of spiritual water, by whose power the legal waters and the many rites of cleansing were lacking. Or they bring in here the obedience and merit of Christ, which above all can cleanse the soul from the stain of sin, and without which the regenerating Spirit himself is not given. Compare Hebrews 10:22, 23 and Ezekiel 36:25. Certainly an absolute necessity of external water is not meant here, unless you wish to set up a new Church more bound to water and to the older elements than was ever the case in the old Church of the Israelites.

units.la: 11. Marci autem cap. 16:16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur. Qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur; cum de baptismo gentium agatur, adulti potissimum spectantur. Nec illa, quæ in una oratione conjunguntur, ejusdem ideo necessitatis sunt. Conf. Rom. 10:10. Corde creditur ad justitiam, fit autem ore professio ad salutem. Matth. 17:21. Hoc genus dæmoniorum non egreditur nisi per precationem & jejunium. Unumquodque enim gradu ac loco suo considerandum est. Sicuti altero commate, quod diltrictius est, non-baptizatorum mentio omittitur; solummodo autem non-credentibus Euangelio salus abrogatur: Servatore studio dictionem temperante, nec eodem, quo inceperat, pede sententiam absolvente: qui autem non crediderit, condemnabitur. 111. Denique male infantes non circumcisos orco adscribunt, ex vexata illa phrasi, exscindetur e populo suo, Gen. 17. Non unum enim istius locutionis sensum esse, atque aliud de infantibus, aliud de adultis; rursusque aliud, pro criminum diversitate, sonare, supra loco suo vidimus.
units.tr: As for Mark 16:16, He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned, since it speaks of the baptism of the Gentiles, adults are chiefly in view. Nor are those things which are joined together in one sentence for that reason of the same necessity. Compare Romans 10:10: With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Matthew 17:21: This kind of demon does not go out except by prayer and fasting. For each thing must be considered in its own rank and place. So too, in the other clause, which is more precise, mention of the unbaptized is omitted; only salvation is denied to those who do not believe the Gospel. The Saviour moderated his wording with care, and did not finish the sentence on the same footing on which he began: but he who does not believe will be condemned. (iii) Finally, they wrongly assign uncircumcised infants to hell from that troubling phrase he shall be cut off from his people, Genesis 17. For this expression does not have one sense, the one for infants and another for adults; and, as we saw above in its place, it has a different sound according to the diversity of sins.

units.la: IX. Alterum baptismi adjunctum est irreiterabilitas, ab Ecclesia constanter credita, & miraculo aliquando, ut fertur, adstructa. Cujus tamen causam diversimode reddunt. Pontificii characteri, ac notæ cuidam indelebili, quem post se baptismus relinquit, illam tribuunt; adeoque iterari baptismum posse negant. Quod æreum nugamentum libri hujus cap. 1. diffiavimus. Vera autem ejus ratio a voluntate Dei & sacramenti hujus natura & scopo repetenda est. Est enim nostræ initiationis, tionis, atque in Christum insitionis,& spiritualis nativitatis sacramentum. Quæ initia cum fustra esse nequeant, atque immortale istud semen corrumpi, nulloque fructu evanescere tandem, & extingui non possit; neque etiam solemnis illa in fœdus Dei initiatio repeti potest. Obstat enim fœderis ac amoris Dei constantia; quod, non obstante qualicunque nostra infirmitate, viget nihilominis ac permanet; cum frangi istæ tabulæ non possint, nec fractis illis aliæ spes restent. Ut, si prior baptismus nos non abluerit, ne secundus quidem, aut tertius, illud præstare possit. Obstat & mortis Christi pretium, quæ repeti iterum non potest, cum unico ipso sacrificio satis litatum sit, Hebr. 10: 14. Quod si abnegemus, spes omnis salutis redauspicandæ periit. cap. 10: 26. Et ipsius tandem regenerationis natura adversatur, quæ æterna est, nec corrumpi ac intercidi potest. Ut obtineat hic illud Joh. 13: 10. Ei, qui lotus est, non opus est nisi ut pedes laver. Sed est mundus totus. Quæ beneficia Dei cum nec deperdi prorsus, nec iterari rursus possint, nec baptismum, quo bona illa obsignantur, iterari posibile est. Denique ex comparatione spiritualis nativitatis cum naturali, Joh. 3. non magis baptismum, quam maternum uterum repeti posse patet. Quo & Veteris Test. analogia confert, ubi, qui semel circumcisus erat, iterum abscindi necesse non habebat. Unde nullum quoque iterandi hujus lavacri præceptum, qualc de S. Cœna extat, 1. Cor 11: 26 quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc &c. nullum in Scriptura exemplum; nulla denique necessitas, occurrit. Sed lapsi, post baptismum, non ad novas aquas, sed ad primæ lotionis memoriam revocantur; ne undam istam inquinare, ac flagitiosa vita profanare audeant. Et hæc eratis quidem; sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis &c. 1. Cor. 6: 11. Nam quicunque in Christum baptizati fuistis, Christum induistis. Gal. 3: 27.
units.tr: IX. The second attribute joined to baptism is irreiterability, which the Church has always held and which, as it is said, was at some point confirmed by a miracle. Yet they give different reasons for it. The Papists attribute it to a character, an indelible mark that baptism leaves behind, and so they deny that baptism can be repeated. We refuted this bronze trifle in chapter 1 of this book. The true reason, however, must be drawn from the will of God and from the nature and purpose of this sacrament. For it is the sacrament of our initiation, of our ingrafting into Christ, and of spiritual birth. Since these beginnings cannot be in vain, and that immortal seed cannot be corrupted, nor vanish without fruit, nor be extinguished, that solemn initiation into the covenant of God cannot be repeated either. The constancy of God's covenant and love stands in the way. Despite whatever weakness is ours, that covenant remains and abides nonetheless, since those tablets cannot be broken, and no other hopes remain once they are broken. So if the first baptism did not wash us, neither could a second, or a third, accomplish it. The price of Christ's death also stands in the way, which cannot be paid again, since it has been sufficiently atoned by the one sacrifice itself, Heb. 10:14. If we deny this, all hope of salvation to be begun anew has perished, Heb. 10:26. Finally, the very nature of regeneration opposes it, since it is eternal and cannot be corrupted or perish. So that holds what John 13:10 says: He who has been washed needs only to have his feet washed, but is clean all over. Since these benefits of God can neither be utterly lost nor received again, it is not possible to repeat the baptism by which those benefits are sealed. Finally, from the comparison of spiritual with natural birth, John 3, it is plain that baptism can no more be repeated than the mother's womb. The analogy of the Old Testament agrees, where one who had been circumcised once did not need to be circumcised again. Hence there is also no command to repeat this washing, such as exists for the Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 11:26, as often as you eat this bread, etc.; no example of it in Scripture; and finally no necessity for it arises. But those who have fallen after baptism are called back not to new waters but to the memory of their first washing, so that they do not dare to defile that wave and profane it by a shameful life. And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, etc., 1 Cor. 6:11. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ, Gal. 3:27.

units.la: X. Damnandus ergo Anabaptismus, cum veterum, tum recentiorum. Mota autem in ipsa Ecclesia olim controversia de rebaptisandis hæreticis: Cypriano, Episcopo Carthaginensi, post Agrippinum, (cum hæreticorum baptisma nullum, nec aquas illas sacras, ac sacro Spiritu imprægnante, efficaces, reputaret) eos rctingi, aut potius rite in Ecclesia primum tingi debere; Stephano autem Episcopo Urbico contra contendente, ac de quacunque hæresi venientes, sine ullo discrimine, illotos in Ecclesiæ sinum recipiente. Ubi hactenus recta procul dubio Cypriani sententia erat; quod, cum extra Ecclesiam nullam baptisma agnosceret, tingi primum & lustrari de novo accedentes volebat: quanquam
units.tr: X. Anabaptism, therefore, is to be condemned, both that of the ancients and that of more recent times. In the Church itself, however, there once arose a controversy about rebaptizing heretics. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, following Agrippinus (since he judged the baptism of heretics to be no baptism, nor their waters to be sacred or effective through the Holy Spirit), held that such people should be washed again, or rather that they should first be properly baptized in the Church. Stephen, bishop of Rome, contended against him and received those coming from any heresy whatever into the bosom of the Church without any distinction, and without washing them. Up to this point Cyprian's opinion was undoubtedly correct, since he, acknowledging no baptism outside the Church, wished those coming to be first dipped and cleansed anew, although

units.la: Y y in illo erraverit, quod nullum hæreseon discrimen faceret; ac ipsos quoque scismaticos, & quicunque extra Orthodoxorum numerum erant, ut profanos, nullaque in Ecclesiæ parte, haberet. Pendet enim quæstionis hujus decisio a fundamentalium articulorum retentione aut abnegatione. Ubi enim in Ecclesia aliqua verba fundamenti, licet multos inter errores, adhuc sonant; ac vera baptismi forma & essentia obtinet; baptismum illum, non obstantibus istis erroribus, verum agnoscere oportet; cum per illum liberi Christo gigni adhuc possint. Ubi vero nihil sani in cœtu aliquo occurrit, nec quicquam sacri in baptismo ejus deprehenditur; profanæ illæ aquæ, & baptismi mimus, non magis pro fœderis sacramento & signaculo habendus est, quam quælibet aquæ sparsio vel mergitatio. Atque ita Ecclesia deinceps hanc litem decidit, facta inter hæreticos distinctione, & graviore hæresi redeuntes (quales præsertim iis erant, qui non baptisabant in nomen S.S. Trinitatis; quem baptismum non purgare, sed inquinare & polluere existimabant) retingi; ab aliis vero baptizatis sola manuum impositione Ecclesiasticæ pacis postliminium tribui jussit. Novatianorum autem, & Donatistarum, reliquorumque Catharorum, Anabaptismum constanter repudiavit.
units.tr: he erred in this, that he made no distinction among heresies, and regarded schismatics too, and all who were outside the number of the orthodox, as profane and having no place in any part of the Church. For the decision of this question depends on the retention or the denial of the fundamental articles. Where in some Church the words of the foundation still sound, despite many errors, and the true form and essence of baptism obtains, that baptism must be acknowledged as true notwithstanding those errors, since through it free people can still be begotten to Christ. But where nothing sound occurs in some assembly, and nothing holy is found in its baptism, those profane waters and that mimicry of baptism are no more to be held as a sacrament and seal of the covenant than any sprinkling or immersion whatever. And so the Church thereafter settled this dispute, by making a distinction among heretics. It ordered those returning from the graver heresies (such especially were those who did not baptize in the name of the Holy Trinity, a baptism which they thought did not cleanse but defiled and polluted) to be rebaptized. But for those baptized by others, it ordered that restoration to the peace of the Church be granted by the laying on of hands alone. The Anabaptism of the Novatians, the Donatists, and the other Cathari, it constantly rejected.

units.la: XI. Errorem illorum nostro tempore imitantur, qui ex hoc capite Anabaptistæ appellantur. Solent autem illi infantes, in Ecclesia tinctos, rebaptizare; idemque erga adultos præstant, qui extra ipsorum cœtum baptizati sunt. Quin & aquis atque baptismis suis, tanquam re tralatitia, ludentes, ab una inter ipsos secta ad aliam transeuntes similiter abluere primum, ac sic in fratrum cœtum recipere solent. Quæ rei sacræ non levis profanatio est. Non enim defectus alicujus Ecclesiæ sacramentorum vim magis tollit, quam multiplex olim Israëlitica Ecclesiæ idololatria circumcisionem contaminare vel tollere potuit. Cum autem infantes, rite olim ablutos, frivolo aliquo prætextu iterum lavant; mirum quod non potius adultis hypocritis, vel gravius post baptismum lapsis, simili modo novum baptismum largiantur; cum prior baptismus peccato illo (nam fideles in universum prolabi posse putant) dudum obliteratus & deletus sit. De loco autem Act. 19: 1-5. quem in causæ præsidium adferunt, jam ante respondimus: & licet illi qui a Johanne mersi erant, a Paulo iterum baptizati fuisse ponantur; non tamen exemplum illud ipsos juvare potest; cum Johannis Baptismum toto genere diversum, nec de ista tinctura Christianum gigni potuisse putent. De quo quid sit, & quousque illud verum sit, supra vidimus. Saltem de baptismo
units.tr: XI. Those who are called Anabaptists for this reason imitate the error of those people in our time. They are accustomed to rebaptize infants who were baptized in the Church, and they do the same to adults who were baptized outside their own gathering. Moreover, playing with waters and baptisms as if they were some traditional thing, they pass from one sect among themselves to another, and similarly are accustomed first to wash people and so receive them into the assembly of the brethren. This is no slight profanation of a holy thing. For a defect in some Church does not diminish the force of the sacraments any more than the manifold idolatry of the Israelite Church once could contaminate or abolish circumcision. But since they wash again infants who were rightly washed long ago, on some flimsy pretext, it is strange that they do not rather bestow a new baptism in the same way on hypocritical adults, or on those who have fallen more gravely after baptism. For the earlier baptism has long since been blotted out and erased by that sin (they think the faithful can fall away in general). As for Acts 19:1-5, which they bring forward in support of their cause, we have already answered it above. Although those who had been immersed by John are said to have been baptized again by Paul, that example cannot help them, since they think John's baptism was entirely different in kind, and that one could not be born a Christian by that dipping. What it was, and how far that is true, we have seen above. At least our own baptism, performed in the name of the Holy Trinity, cannot in any way be said to be of that kind; hence there is also no necessity of repeating it.

units.la: tumre-centio-rum. ptismo nostro, in S.S. Trinitatis nomine peracto, illud dici nullo modo potest; unde nec eadem ejus repetendæ necessitas.
units.tr: ...our baptism, performed in the name of the Holy Trinity, can in no way be said to be of that kind; hence there is also no need to repeat it.

units.la: XII. Culpandus etiam Æthiopum mos, qui quotannis, Epiphaniæ die, baptismum renovant; in Christi quasi honorem; quem eo die olim baptizatum volunt. Qui prætextus nullus, & superstitiosus est.
units.tr: XII. The custom of the Ethiopians is also to be condemned, for every year on the day of Epiphany they renew their baptism, as though in honour of Christ, who they hold was baptized on that day. This pretext has no basis and is superstitious.

units.la: XIII. Agnoscimus autem ac servamus baptismum, cum in aliis coetibus, tum in Romana Ecclesia, in nomine S.S. Trinitatis, collatum. Cum inter hominum errores tamen baptismus vim suam ab institutione Christi retineat. Qui autem a laicis, vel mulierculis, aspersi sunt; cum baptismus ille nihil sacri sit; a nobis vero demum baptismo obsignantur. Socinianorum vero, ac Antitrinitariorum, baptismum, cum veteri Ecclesia rejicimus; cum S S. Trinitatis professione careat; ac præterea illi sanguinem Christi negent; nec vero magnam aliquam sanctitatem baptismo illi suo tribuant, sed plerunque pro nudo, nec quicquam obsignante ritu, habeant. Rursus Anabaptistarum ac similium baptismum, quamdiu publice cum damnatis illis cœtibus communionem non habent, recipimus. Universi enim cœtus fides & professio, non hujus vel illius doctoris perfidia spectanda est. Similemque in modum ad quæstionem, an baptisma in Ecclesia Orthodoxa, a ministro Antitrinitariis erroribus imbuto, collatus valeat? respondemus. Consideranda enim publica Ecclesiæ fides, in quam ille, qui baptisandus est, imbuitur: factæque ei a Christo promissiones. Quæ cum a ministro non pendeant, ille, si vel occulta hæresi laboraret, irrita illa ac vana reddere minime potest.
units.tr: XIII. We acknowledge and retain the baptism conferred both in other assemblies and in the Roman Church, in the name of the Holy Trinity. Although baptism retains its power from the institution of Christ amid the errors of men, those who have been sprinkled by laymen or old women, since that rite is nothing sacred, are sealed by us only when they receive baptism from us. We reject the baptism of the Socinians and Antitrinitarians, together with the ancient Church, since it lacks the profession of the Holy Trinity; moreover, they deny the blood of Christ, and they do not attribute any great holiness to their baptism, but generally regard it as bare water, with a rite that seals nothing. On the other hand, we accept the baptism of the Anabaptists and similar groups, so long as they have no public communion with those condemned assemblies. For the faith and profession of the whole assembly must be looked at, not the treachery of this or that teacher. In the same way we answer the question whether a baptism conferred in the Orthodox Church by a minister imbued with Antitrinitarian errors is valid. For the public faith of the Church, into which the one to be baptized is initiated, must be considered, along with the promises made to him by Christ. Since these do not depend on the minister, he cannot make them void and empty, even if he were secretly afflicted with heresy.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS QUARTUS DE S. Coena, aliisque ritibus.
units.tr: Chapter Forty-Four: On the Holy Supper and Other Rites.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De S. Coenae nominibus, personis, symbolis ritibusque externis.
units.tr: On the names, persons, symbols, and external rites of the Holy Supper.

units.la: {a}UTi priscarum mundationum ac lotionum quaedam imago erat in baptismo; ita S. Coena sacris ipsorum epulis ac conviviis respondet, ac alterum Novi Test. sacramentum constituit. Quae veteris legis instituta Apostolus conjungit, Hebr. 9:10. Cibi, & potus, & variae lotiones, & instituta carnis, usque ad tempus emendationis incumbebant. Cum autem partim re externa & terrestri, partim interna & coelesti, coena illa constet; de illa primo agemus; ac praemissa nominis theoria, personas, symbola, ritus, seu actiones, ac circumstantias ad eam spectantes, ordine percurremus.
units.tr: Just as there was a certain image of the old cleansings and washings in baptism, so the Holy Supper corresponds to their sacred feasts and banquets, and constitutes the other sacrament of the New Testament. The Apostle joins these institutions of the old law in Hebr. 9:10: "Meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation." Since that supper consists partly of an external and earthly thing and partly of an internal and heavenly one, we shall treat of the outward part first. After a preliminary account of the name, the persons, the symbols, the rites or actions, and the circumstances pertaining to it, we shall go through them in order.

units.la: II. Nomina hujus sacramenti partim ex S. Scriptura, partim ex Ecclesiasticis auctoribus, ac Ecclesiae usu, desumta sunt.
units.tr: II. The names of this sacrament are drawn partly from Holy Scripture, and partly from ecclesiastical writers and the usage of the Church.

units.la: III. Appellationes, in Scriptura obviae, sunt octo, 1. δεῖπνον κυριακόν, Coena Domini. 1. Cor. 11:20. tum quia, pro more coenae, vespere (quam temporis circumstantiam Ecclesia diu servavit) tum quia a Domino, epulum illud institutum. Quo, uti auctore, ita & fine ac scopo nititur; cum morti ejus perpetuum celebrandae inserviat. 2. εὐλογία, benedictio, propter Christum εὐλογήσαντα, dum sacra ista signa tractaret. Matth. 26:26. Marc. 14:22. 1. Cor. 10:16. Quae vox deinde ad sacrati panis particulas, quae absentibus, aliisque, Christianae communionis testandae causa missitabantur, denotandas adhibita. 3. εὐχαριστία, ab eadem Christi actione, ut & fidelium laudibus & hymnis, Deo liberatori dictis, Matth. 26:27. Luc. 22:19. 1. Cor. 11:24. 4. καινὴ διαθήκη, Luc. 22:26. Matth. 26:27, 28. Sicuti in Veteri Test. Deus circumcisionem נתיח fœdus sium appellat. Sic autem dicitur a fœdere, quod, cæsa dignissima illa victima, nobiscum sancivit. 5. τράπεζα κυρίε, mensa Domini, ubi cum Domino assidemus, 1. Cor. 10: 21. Quæ mensa, dum sacrificales dapes contineret, veteribus etiam altare dicebatur: in quod, primum nomine, deinde glisc ente superstitione, reipsa transfiit. 6. κλάσις ἄρτυ, fractio panis, 1. Cor. 10: 16. Quo a plerisque etiam refertur locus Act. 2:42. Et perseverabant in doctrina Apostolorum, & communicatione, & fractione panis, & orationibus. & 46. Frangebant domatim panem. conf. cap. 20: 7, 11. Alicna autem sunt Luc. 24: 30. & Act. 27: 30. 7. κοινωνία, communio corporis & sanguinis dominici, 1. Cor. 10: 16. 8. Denique σῶμα τῆ χριστῷ, ex verbis institutionis. Matth. 26: 26.
units.tr: III. There are eight names found in Scripture. 1. δεῖπνον κυριακόν [deipnon kyriakon], the Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 11:20; both because it was after the manner of a supper, in the evening (a circumstance of time the Church long preserved), and because this feast was instituted by the Lord. It rests upon him as its author, and equally upon its purpose and aim, since it serves to celebrate his death perpetually. 2. εὐλογία [eulogia], blessing, because Christ blessed (εὐλογήσας [eulogesas]) when he handled these holy signs, Matt. 26:26; Mark 14:22; 1 Cor. 10:16. This word was then used to denote the particles of consecrated bread which were sent to the absent and to others, to attest Christian communion. 3. εὐχαριστία [eucharistia], thanksgiving, from the same action of Christ, and also from the praises and hymns of the faithful, spoken to God the deliverer, Matt. 26:27; Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24. 4. καινὴ διαθήκη [kaine diatheke], the new covenant, Luke 22:20; Matt. 26:27, 28. Just as in the Old Testament God calls circumcision a covenant (בְּרִית [berith]), so this supper is so called from the covenant which he ratified with us, when that most worthy victim was slain. 5. τράπεζα κυρίου [trapeza kyriou], the table of the Lord, where we sit down with the Lord, 1 Cor. 10:21. Since this table held sacrificial feasts, the ancients also called it an altar; and by this name, first, and then, as superstition grew, it passed over in reality. 6. κλάσις ἄρτου [klasis artou], the breaking of bread, 1 Cor. 10:16. Many also refer to this the passage in Acts 2:42: "And they continued in the apostles' doctrine, and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers"; and verse 46: "breaking bread from house to house." Compare chapter 20:7, 11. Luke 24:30 and Acts 27:35 are of a different kind. 7. κοινωνία [koinonia], communion in the body and blood of the Lord, 1 Cor. 10:16. 8. Lastly, σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ [soma tou Christou], the body of Christ, from the words of institution, Matt. 26:26.

units.la: IV. Ecclesiastica vocabula sunt viginti quatuor.
units.tr: IV. There are twenty-four ecclesiastical terms.

units.la: 1. δοχὴ convivium. 2. τροφὴ πνευματικὴ, alimentum spirituale. 3. λειτουργία, cultus. Quæ vox alioquin latius sonat, atque universum cultum & ministerium Ecclesiasticum comprehendit. 4. λατρία, cultus. Augustinus pietatem vocat. 5. σύναξις & συνέλευσις, conventus & congregatio, præeunte Scriptura. Act. 20: 7. 1. Cor. 11: 20, 26, 27, 33. & 10: 16. 6. Latini collectam dicebant, eodem sensu. 7. μυστήριον, mysterium. voce ab occultis Ethnicorum sacris desumta. 8. Desiderata. eodem prope sensu. Illa enim etiam in Gentilium mysteriis erant; nec omnibus initiatis protinus patebant. Semper enim servabat aliquid, quod revisentibus oftenderet Eleusis. 9. χάρις, a re significata. 10. τὰ ἀγιάσματα. 11. eodemque sensu ἁγίαι μερίδες, a sacris signis. 12. μετάληψις. quod per ea ad Christi communionem admittimur. 13. δώρον donum. sive a collaticiis dapibus, ex quibus cœna illa instructabatur; sive a S. Spiritu, ad cœnam istam venientc, qui præcipuum Ecclesiæ donum est. 14. pariter τὸ ἀγαθόν; quia Christum, boni omnis fontem, exhibet. 15. ἐφόδιον, viaticum; quod de vita exeuntibus aliquando Ecclesia dabat. 16. vita, Augustino & Afris. 17. Pax; a pacis osculo, quod libabant. 18. πάσχα. Cum in ea veri agni sacrificium repræsentetur. 19. θυσία, sacrificium; propter dominici sacrificii memoriam, & laudum ac gratiarum pro peracta salute oblationem. 20. Quomodo & εὐχὴ apud Græcos appellabatur. 21. ἄιμα. synecdochice, ab altera sacramenti parte. 22. rursusque sacramentum panis, & panis simpliciter. Quem quotidie in nonnullis Ecclesiis sumebant. 23. Missa; cum a Catechumenorum, tum a fidelium, dimissione. Quæ, partim initio, partim fine, mysteriorum, ficebat. 24. ἀγάπαι. Quæ vox tamen crebrius de piorum conviviis, charitatis testandæ causa in Ecclesia olim (licet quidam aliter censeant) celebratis, quibusque annectebatur Eucharistia, usurpatur. Quæ diversæ appellationes, pro veterum pietate, frequentatæ, non tanta tamen auctoritaris sunt: ac aliquæ earum, præsertim duæ illæ, sacrificium & missa, prodigioso errori tandem occasionem & commeatum præbuerunt.
units.tr: 1. δοχή [doche], a banquet. 2. τροφὴ πνευματικὴ [trophe pneumatike], spiritual nourishment. 3. λειτουργία [leitourgia], worship; a word which otherwise has a wider sense and comprehends all worship and ecclesiastical ministry. 4. λατρεία [latreia], worship; Augustine calls it piety. 5. σύναξις and συνέλευσις [synaxis and synelevsis], assembly and gathering, as Scripture leads the way: Acts 20:7; 1 Cor. 11:20, 26, 27, 33; and 10:16. 6. The Latins called it the collect, in the same sense. 7. μυστήριον [mysterion], mystery, a word taken from the secret rites of the Gentiles. 8. Desiderata (the things desired), in nearly the same sense; for these too were found in the mysteries of the Gentiles, and were not at once open to all the initiated. For Eleusis always kept something back, which it might show to those who came again. 9. χάρις [charis], grace, from the thing signified. 10. τὰ ἁγιάσματα [ta hagiasmata], the holy things. 11. and in the same sense ἁγίαι μερίδες [hagiai meridES], holy portions, from the holy signs. 12. μετάληψις [metalepsis], participation, because through these we are admitted to communion with Christ. 13. δῶρον [doron], gift; either from the contributed dainties out of which that supper was prepared, or from the Holy Spirit, who comes to this supper and is the chief gift of the Church. 14. Likewise τὸ ἀγαθόν [to agathon], the good; because it exhibits Christ, the fountain of all good. 15. ἐφόδιον [ephodion], viaticum, provision for the journey; which the Church once gave to those departing from life. 16. Vita [life], according to Augustine and the Africans. 17. Pax [peace], from the kiss of peace, which they shared. 18. πάσχα [pascha], Passover, since in it the sacrifice of the true Lamb is represented. 19. θυσία [thysia], sacrifice; on account of the memory of the Lord's sacrifice, and the offering of praises and thanksgivings for the salvation accomplished. 20. In the same way it was called εὐχή [euche], prayer, among the Greeks. 21. αἷμα [haima], blood; by synecdoche, from the other part of the sacrament. 22. And again sacramentum panis [the sacrament of bread], and simply panis [bread], which they received daily in some churches. 23. Missa [dismissal], from the dismissal both of the catechumens and of the faithful; which, partly at the beginning and partly at the end, marked the mysteries. 24. ἀγάπαι [agapai], love-feasts. This word, however, is more often used of the banquets of the pious, celebrated in the Church of old for the sake of attesting charity (though some think otherwise), to which the Eucharist was attached. These different names, though frequently used in keeping with the piety of the ancients, did not carry such authority; and some of them, especially those two, sacrificium [sacrifice] and missa [mass], at length offered occasion and a passage to a prodigious error.

units.la: V. Succedit, post nominum considerationem, res ipsa: quam, juxta ordinem institutum, primum in externo illo ministerio, cunctisque ejus partibus ac circumstantis, videbimus. Ubi, tum de personis, tum de rebus ac signis externis, denique de ritibus ac actionibus sacris agendum nobis erit.
units.tr: V. After the consideration of the names, the thing itself follows; which, according to the order laid down, we shall first see in that external ministry and all its parts and circumstances. Here we must treat both of the persons, and of the things and external signs, and finally of the rites and sacred actions.

units.la: VI. Primo in ordine, ac loco, occurrit Dominus Iesus, sacrificalis epuli auctor & institutor. Unde Domini cœna continuo appellatur, 1. Cor. 10:20, 23, 26, 27, 29. Ac, post illum, sacramenti ministri fuerunt ejus Apostoli; ac qui illos secuti sunt Ecclesiæ rectores ac præsides.
units.tr: VI. First in order and place comes the Lord Jesus, the author and institutor of the sacrificial feast. Hence it is continually called the Lord's supper, 1 Cor. 10:20, 23, 26, 27, 29. After him, the ministers of the sacrament were his Apostles, and those who followed them, the rulers and presidents of the Church.

units.la: VII. Ut ferenda non sit Socinianorum ἀταξία, qui a privatis cœnam quoque fieri permittunt; ac, privato in epulo, a quibuslibet Christianis, sacrificii Christi memoriam rite peragi posse arbitrantur. Ita ut actio illa non amplius publica, nec sacra sit. Quibus accedit Episcopius, qui & mulierum coetui illam potestatem tribuere non veretur. Quæ contra Christi institutum, ac primam cœnæ administrationem, Ecclesiæque usum sunt. A quibus temere non discedendum. Nec mirum illos ita sentire, qui nullum mysterium in S. Cœna agnoscunt; solaque mortis ac martyrii Christi recordatione illam absolvunt. Unde nuda ista signa a quibuslibet Christianis tractari ægre non ferunt. Sed jam antea vidimus, ista præterea amoris Dei certissima pignora & symbola esse. Quæ Deus certe non aliter quam per præsidum manus erogare solet; quibus peculiarem sacrorum curam ac ministerium dedit; ne promiscuo usu contaminentur, ac inter tractantium manus paulatim evilescant. Quæ & veteris Ecclesiæ fere ratio fuit, Ecclesiastico quoque canone Synodi sextæ, Canon. 57. fancita. Licet diaconorum ministerium antiquioribus sæculis hic quoque intervenerit. Nec privatas istas cœnas Apostolus auctoritate sua firmat cum de poculo, cui benedicimus; & pane, quem frangimus, loquitur, 1. Cor. 10:16. quasi communia illa redderet, cunctisque Christianis ex æquo panis & poculi benedicendi potestatem largiretur. Universa enim Ecclesiæ facere prohibetur, quod Ecclesiæ nomine coetus præses ac minister facit. Ac habet præterea partes suas in sacro illo universa Ecclesia; cum de sacris panibus esitet (quod, non inusitata phrasi, panem frangere quoque dicitur) & hymnis laudibusque sacram hanc actionem prosequatur.
units.tr: VII. The disorder of the Socinians cannot be tolerated, who permit the supper to be held even by private persons, and think that, at a private feast, the memory of Christ's sacrifice may be duly celebrated by any Christians whatever; so that the action is no longer public or sacred. To these is added Episcopius, who does not hesitate to grant that power even to a gathering of women. These things are contrary to Christ's institution, to the first administration of the supper, and to the custom of the Church, from which we must not lightly depart. Nor is it surprising that those think so who acknowledge no mystery in the Holy Supper, and finish it with the bare remembrance of Christ's death and martyrdom. Hence they do not take it ill that these bare signs are handled by any Christians whatever. But we have seen before that these are also the most certain pledges and symbols of God's love. God certainly does not normally dispense them except through the hands of presidents, to whom he has given the special care and ministry of holy things, lest they be polluted by promiscuous use and gradually lose their value in the hands of those who handle them. This was almost the practice of the ancient Church also, and was established by the ecclesiastical canon of the Sixth Synod, Canon 57. Although in the earlier centuries the ministry of deacons also intervened here. Nor does the Apostle confirm these private suppers by his authority when he speaks of the cup of blessing which we bless, and the bread which we break, 1 Cor. 10:16; as if he made them common and gave to all Christians alike the power of blessing the bread and cup. For what the assembly's president and minister does in the name of the Church is forbidden to be done by the whole Church. Moreover, the whole Church has its own part in that sacred action, since it eats of the holy bread (which, in a not unusual phrase, is also said to be "broken") and accompanies this sacred action with hymns and praises.

units.la: VIII. Personæ communicantes ac convivantes, in prima coena, fuerunt, ad minimum, Apostoli; non exclusô, ut plane videtur ex Luc. 22: 21. conf. com. 19, 20. Juda. Ac veniunt nunc in numerum illum omnes fideles, ac veri Christiani, qui ad mensam istam rite comparati sunt, & mysteria illa didicerunt, ac vita puros integrosque se præstant. Exploret autem quisque se ipsum, & ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat. 1. Cor. 11:28.
units.tr: VIII. The persons who communicated and feasted at the first supper were, at the least, the Apostles; Judas was not plainly excluded, as is evident from Luke 22:21, compare verses 19, 20. Now there come into that number all the faithful and true Christians who have duly prepared themselves for that table, have learned those mysteries, and show themselves pure and blameless in life. "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup." 1 Cor. 11:28.

units.la: IX. Non probandus autem veterum mos, qui, per aliquot sæcula, infantibus, per ætatem nondum huic mysterio maturis, Eucharistiam instillare soliti fuerunt. Nec ab infantibus differunt furiosi & amentes, quibus sacra symbola ingerere, est ea profanare. De surdis & amentibus, cum interior Dei potentia arctari non debeat, ex elucentibus fidei indiciis, & melioribus intervallis judicandum est. Nec neganda illis symbola, in quibus præsentem Spiritum agnoscimus. Ad illam autem non invitandi sunt profani, & scelerosi, nec vera ulla virtute redemti; utcunque domesticorum nomen & titulos mentiantur. Manifestum denique est, cum S. Cœna Christianorum mysteriorum maximum sit, ad eam non admittendos, qui minoribus mysteriis initiati nondum sunt. Adeoque baptismo lustratum prius esse oportere, qui Dei conviva deinde suturus sit.
units.tr: IX. The custom of the ancients, which for several centuries was followed of dripping the Eucharist into infants, who were not yet mature enough for this mystery, is not to be approved. Madmen and the insane do not differ from infants, and to press sacred symbols upon them is to profane them. As for the deaf and the insane, since the inner power of God ought not to be restricted, judgment must be made from the evident signs of faith and from their lucid intervals. Nor should the symbols be denied to them, in which we recognise the Spirit present. Profane and wicked persons, and those not redeemed by any true virtue, are not to be invited to it, however falsely they may claim the name and titles of the household of faith. Finally, it is plain that since the Lord's Supper is the greatest of the Christian mysteries, those who have not yet been initiated into the lesser mysteries are not to be admitted to it. Thus whoever is to sit later as God's guest must first have been cleansed by baptism.

units.la: X. Apud veteres Christianos, ut eorum quoque morem lustremus, universa Ecclesia ad mensam hanc accedebat; nullis, de fratrum cœtu, qui sacris intererant, exeuntibus, nisi qui ipsius Ecclesiæ judicio adhuc erant, vel ob crimen arcebantur; Catechumenis vid. & pœnitentibus, quibus & Energumenos, si forte adessent, adjungebant. Qui Christianorum fervor, labente deinde disciplina, dum fideles socordiæ sese dedunt, & dignos sese S. Cœna facere laborem exstimant, ac sacris symbolis carere malunt, non paulum refrixit. Unde factum deinceps, ut multi qui sacris intererant, nihilominus communione abstinerent.
units.tr: X. Among the early Christians, to review their custom as well, the whole Church approached this table. No one from the assembly of the brothers who attended the sacred rites withdrew, except those whom the judgment of the Church itself still held back, or excluded on account of a crime: catechumens, that is, and penitents, to whom they also joined the energumens, if by chance any were present. This Christian fervour, however, cooled not a little afterwards, as discipline slipped, while the faithful gave themselves over to sloth and thought themselves unworthy to partake of the Lord's Supper, preferring to go without the sacred symbols. Hence it came about that many who attended the sacred rites nevertheless abstained from communion.

units.la: XI. (Catechumeni duplici in ordine erant. Audientes, qui primo in gradu consistebant; & competentes, qui, decurso isto stadio, baptismi jam candidati, præscripto tempore illum expectabant. Qui omnes, antequam sacra mensa instrueretur, post acceptam benedictionem, jussi à Diacono, exibant. Quæ Catechumenorum missa erat.
units.tr: XI. (The catechumens were in two orders. The hearers stood in the first grade; the competents, who had completed that stage and were now candidates for baptism, awaited it at the appointed time. All of these, before the sacred table was set up, were dismissed by the deacon after the blessing had been received. This was the dismissal of the catechumens.

units.la: XII. Pœ
units.tr: XII. Of repentance

units.la: XII. Poenitentium quoque varii gradus erant. προσκλαίοντες, ἀκροώμενοι, ὑποπίπτοντες, tum denique illi, qui ἐν τῇ συνάσει τῶν πιστῶν εὐχαῖς communicabant. Qui tamen & ipsi, dictis ab Episcopo precibus, & accepta benedictione, ante sacrorum mysteriorum celebrationem, discedebant. Quibusdam autem, qui gravius peccaverant, Ecclesiae venia, non longo solum annorum intervallo, sed ad vitae usque finem negabatur. Atque ista sub disciplina Ecclesia diu stetit. Solis autem fidelibus, qui actu communicarent, in sacro epulo disciplina nimis rigida, praesentibus esse licuit; caeteris ne quidem adspectare illud fas erat, cum istud maximum religionis mysterium haberent, quod ἀμυήτοις non propalandum ducebant.
units.tr: XII. There were also various grades of penitents: those weeping [προσκλαίοντες], those hearing [ἀκροώμενοι], those prostrating themselves [ὑποπίπτοντες], and finally those who communicated in the prayers of the assembly of the faithful [ἐν τῇ συνάσει τῶν πιστῶν εὐχαῖς]. Yet even these, after the prayers were said by the bishop and the blessing received, withdrew before the celebration of the sacred mysteries. Pardon of the Church was refused to some who had sinned more grievously, not merely for a long interval of years but until the end of life. And this strict discipline held in the Church for a long time. Only the faithful who were actually communicating were allowed to be present at the sacred feast under the very strict discipline; the rest were not even permitted to look on, since they held this to be the greatest mystery of religion, which they did not think should be disclosed to the uninitiated [ἀμυήτοις].

units.la: XIII. Post personas, spectandae res & signa externa. Instituit autem Servator convivium sacrum, commemorandae ultimae ac emortuali suae coenae; utque tristissimae illius noctis imago, atque universae passionis ac sacrificii ejus memoria de Ecclesia nunquam deperiret. Ac sicuti in baptismo ritum quendam Judaeorum imitatus est, quem in novae Ecclesiae sacramentum consecravit: ita haec coena, ad paschalem mensam primum coepta, cujus vel pars vel appendix erat, in N. T. sacramentum commutata est, ac nobiliorem in usum dedicata: unde deinde in paschatis locum successit, ac in Ecclesia obtinuit. Postquam enim verus agnus venisset, qui ipse in ultimo epulo praesens erat, ac lucem suam umbram illam explebat sacrificalibus agnis opus non amplius erat.
units.tr: XIII. After the persons, the things and external signs are to be considered. The Saviour instituted the sacred feast, to commemorate his last and deadly supper, so that the image of that most sorrowful night, and the memory of his whole passion and sacrifice, might never fail from the Church. And just as in baptism he imitated a certain rite of the Jews, which he consecrated as the sacrament of the new Church, so this supper, which first began at the Passover table and was either a part or an appendix of it, was changed into a sacrament of the New Testament and dedicated to a nobler use. Hence it afterwards took the place of the Passover and prevailed in the Church. For once the true Lamb had come, who was himself present at the last feast, and once he had fulfilled by his light those shadows, there was no longer any need for sacrificial lambs.

units.la: XIV. Elementum ergo, ut in convivio sacro, hic duplex est, panis, & vinum. Quanquam enim in baptismo solae aquae emundandae Ecclesiae sufficerent; tamen in coena, ut integra ea foret, & spiritualis alimoniae mysterium adimpleret, duplex requirebatur symbolum, tum cibi, tum potus; ut vitam victumque spiritualem, quem in Christo habemus, perfecte adumbraret.
units.tr: XIV. The element, therefore, as in the sacred feast, is twofold here: bread and wine. For although in baptism water alone would suffice to cleanse the Church, yet in the supper, so that it might be complete and fulfil the mystery of spiritual nourishment, a twofold symbol was required, of food and of drink, so that it might perfectly portray the spiritual life and sustenance which we have in Christ.

units.la: XV. Ubi mirari licet divinam providentiam, quae res adeo naturales, simplices, ac ubivis obvias, Ecclesiae, pro rerum coelestium pignore & arrhabone, tradidit. Cujus instituti complures rationes sunt. 1. Cum enim sacramentum hoc ad finem usque saeculi, & quibuscunque in locis ac regionibus, in usu fidelium permanere deberet, certe minutis quibusdam ac molestis ritibus constare non debebat; ne vel ubivis eorum copia non esset, vel incuria, aut fato aliquo, multiplex adeo sacrorum apparatus sensim ex usu ac memoria hominum deperiret. Quod plerisque Veteris Testamenti caeremoniis contigit. 11. Neque Deus illustrioribus symbolis, qualia in deserto aliquando exhibuit, Ecclesiam detinere voluit. Non parum enim externus ille splendor spirituali fidelium visui offecisset; qui non externo signo, sed re significata pasci jam & satiari debebant: ac Servatorem suum quotidiana in imagine adspicere potius ac amplecti, quam in illustri aliquo signo stupere, atque illo veluti idolo sese oblectare malebant. Quibus accedebat superstitionis periculum, quæ, in illustrioribus signis occupata, evitari adeo non potuisset; ut ne nunc quidem Ecclesia, in tam humilibus signis, istam labem effugerit; sed ordinariis illis ac pene quotidianis symbolis, tandem ad idololatriam abusa fuerit. III. Denique mysterio non caret, quod non animalium carnes, & cruentas, ac sanguine manantes, dapes, uti in sacris Veteris Test. epulis, ad hanc mensam instituerit; sed solis panibus ac vino onerari eam voluerit. Ea enim Novi Test. natura est, quod, post fusum Christi sanguinem, nullus amplius sanguis in sacris profundi debeat. Unde vel animalium sanguine in sacro hoc convivio abstineri voluit; & panem solum vinumque convivantibus distribuit: quæ simplices epulæ, & nutritionem nostram spiritualem, & peractum semel Christi sacrificium (cujus ex instituto Christi clarissimam memoriam perhibent) non minus adumbrant & obsignant, quam olim sacrificiorum carnes, & crassæ illæ veteris populi figuræ.
units.tr: XV. Here one may marvel at the divine providence, which delivered to the Church things so natural, simple and everywhere at hand, as the pledge and earnest of heavenly things. There are several reasons for this institution. (1) Since this sacrament was to remain in the use of the faithful until the end of the age and in whatever places and regions, it certainly ought not to depend on certain petty and burdensome rites, lest either their supply should fail in some places, or through carelessness or some chance this manifold array of sacred things should gradually perish from the practice and memory of men. This happened to most of the ceremonies of the Old Testament. (2) Nor did God wish to hold the Church to more striking symbols, such as he once displayed in the desert. For that external splendour would have greatly obstructed the spiritual sight of the faithful, who ought now to be fed and satisfied not by an external sign but by the thing signified, and who preferred to behold and embrace their Saviour in a daily image rather than to gape at some dazzling sign and delight themselves in it as if it were an idol. Added to this was the danger of superstition, which, fixed on more striking signs, could not have been so easily avoided; indeed, even now the Church has not escaped that blemish in such humble signs, but in those ordinary and almost daily symbols it has at last been abused into idolatry. (3) Finally, there is a mystery in the fact that he did not institute for this table the flesh of animals, bloody and dripping with gore, as the feasts of the sacred Old Testament had, but willed that it be furnished only with bread and wine. For it is the nature of the New Testament that, after the blood of Christ has been poured out, no more blood should be shed in sacred rites. Hence he wished that even the blood of animals be abstained from in this sacred feast, and distributed only bread and wine to those who feast. These simple foods portray and seal our spiritual nourishment and the sacrifice of Christ once accomplished (which they declare by the most clear memorial, according to Christ's institution) no less than the flesh of the old sacrifices and those gross figures of the ancient people did of old.

units.la: XVI. Panis, quo Christus in prima cœna usus est, fuit azymus.
units.tr: XVI. The bread which Christ used at the first supper was unleavened.

units.la: Quod accidentarium fuit, ex lege paschatis, quæ fermento omni abstinere reperceos dies jubebat. Unde vetus Ecclesia quotidiano ac cibario pane usa est. Plane ad sensum Christi, qui non alium panem, quam quo in communibus epulis vescimur, ad concinniorem mysterii significationem, instituit. Quo & Apostoli, tum in Judæa, tum inter gentes, postea usi sunt, Act. 2:42. Et perseverabant in fractione panis, & precibus. c. 20:7. Cum discipuli congregati essent, Troadæ, ut panem frangerent. conf. 1. Cor. 10:16, 17. & 11:20. Cum azymus ad Veteris Testam. cærimonias potius pertineret. Ut Romana Ecclesia, pertinacius in Ecclesias tyrannidis crimine, laboret. Quanquam enim non minus Græci, quam Latini, a scopo aberrent: dum illi Christum fermentato usum volunt, quod Judæorum Paschta uno die antevertere (quod factum fuisse non videtur; nec si vel factum, huc faceret, cum nunquam Pascha quocunque tempore celebraretur, cum fermentato panecedere fas esset) hi autem ex Christi exemplo, qui, ob temporis rationem, azymis usus est, eandem necessitatem Ecclesiæ per omnia sæcula imponunt: Græcorum tamen, quam Latinorum, error tolerabilior est; dum illi, infirmo quamvis fundamento, communem & usualem panem sumendum urgent; hi autem ex mera superstitione non nisi in azymis coenam rite fieri autumant.
units.tr: This was incidental, arising from the law of the Passover, which commanded abstaining from all leaven for seven days. Hence the early Church used ordinary bread for daily food. Christ, however, in instituting the rite, intended no other bread than that which we eat at common meals, so that the meaning of the mystery might be more fittingly expressed. The Apostles later used the same bread, both in Judea and among the Gentiles: Acts 2:42, "And they continued in the breaking of bread, and in prayers"; Acts 20:7, "When the disciples came together to break bread at Troas"; cf. 1 Cor. 10:16, 17, and 11:20. Unleavened bread pertained rather to the ceremonies of the Old Testament. The Roman Church labours more stubbornly under the charge of tyranny against the Churches. For although the Greeks go astray from the mark no less than the Latins, the Greeks want Christ to have used leavened bread, because the Jews' Passover fell a day earlier (which does not seem to have happened, and even if it had, it would not bear on the point, since the Passover was never celebrated at any time when it was lawful to eat leavened bread). The Latins, following the example of Christ, who on account of the time used unleavened bread, impose the same necessity on the Church in every age. Yet the error of the Greeks is more tolerable than that of the Latins: the Greeks insist, on however weak a foundation, that common and everyday bread must be taken, whereas the Latins, from sheer superstition, claim that the Supper is rightly celebrated only in unleavened bread.

units.la: XVII. Gravius est, quod ne panem quidem, sed panis quisquilias, & tenuissimum crustulum, in coena sua usurpant; eamque hostiis quibusdam orbicularibus, crucifixi imagine signatis, peragunt. Quod & contra sacramenti naturam, quod altera sui parte defraudant, & figurationem ejus tenuiorem reddunt; & contra Christi, ac universæ veteris Ecclesiæ auctoritatem, est; quorum panes Eucharisticos, ex ipso fractionis ritu ac mysterio, tum quod omnes de uno pane, unum Ecclesiæ corpus adumbrante, comederent, grandiores fuisse apparet. Nec improbabile est, istas panum minutias, cum transubstantiationis commento, dudum post millesimum a Christo nato annum, in Ecclesiam irrepsisse; cui monstro alendo non parum ancillari vitæ sunt.
units.tr: XVII. It is more serious that in their Supper they use not even bread, but the crumbs of bread and a very thin wafer; and they celebrate it with certain round hosts stamped with the image of the crucified. This is contrary both to the nature of the sacrament, since they deprive the people of one part of it and make its figure rather meagre, and to the authority of Christ and of the whole ancient Church. From the very rite and mystery of the breaking, it is clear that their Eucharistic breads ought to have been larger, since all ate of one bread, which represents the one body of the Church. Nor is it improbable that these crumbs of bread, together with the fiction of transubstantiation, crept into the Church long after the thousandth year from the birth of Christ; and these monstrous things have not a little been served by the idle life of those who were supposed to minister.
