units.la: XVIII. Alterum signum est vinum, vitis genimen, Matth. 26:29. Quanquam in regionibus, ubi vini penuria est, loco potus ex uvis expressi, illud, quod vini vicem ibi præstat, licite usurpari possit. quod de pane quoque intellectum volumus.
units.tr: XVIII. The second sign is wine, the fruit of the vine, Matt. 26:29. Yet in regions where wine is scarce, something else pressed from grapes, which takes the place of wine there, may lawfully be used in its stead. We intend this to apply to the bread as well.

units.la: XIX. Quæritur autem, an vinum Eucharisticum, admixta lympha, diluendum sit. Ac Servatorem quidem, in suprema ac parentali coena, mixto poculo usum, Pontificii, cum veterum plerisque, nec incpte, juxta ritus convivii paschalis, sentiunt. Antiquum etiam in primitiva Ecclesia illum morem fuisse, ac populi fidelis cum Christo coalitioni significandæ usurpatum, & a Latina Græcaque Ecclesia, exceptis solis Armenis, ad hæc usque tempora frequentatum, satis constat. Nos vero hoc Christi exemplum nobis non magis legem figere, quam alterum panis azymi, censemus. Ac præsertim aquam de necessitate hujus sacramenti esse, atque in ea religionem ac cultus partem poni, aut denique, Apostolicæ traditionis prætextu, a Romana Ecclesia omnibus imponi non ferimus. Quanquam corrumpi prorsus S. Coenam non putamus, si quis poculum diluat; præsertim ubi regionis mos est, in quotidiano quoque usu vina nimium generosa frangere, & admixta lympha mitescere cogere.
units.tr: XIX. It is asked whether the Eucharistic wine ought to be diluted with added water. The Papists, together with most of the ancients, hold, not without reason, that the Saviour at his last and farewell supper used a mixed cup, according to the rites of the Passover feast. It is also quite certain that this custom was ancient in the primitive Church, used to signify the union of the faithful people with Christ, and was kept up by the Latin and Greek Churches, except only the Armenians, down to our own times. We, however, judge that this example of Christ binds us no more as a law than does the example of the unleavened bread. In particular, we do not endure the claim that water is necessary to this sacrament, that a part of religion and worship is placed in it, or, finally, that it is imposed on everyone by the Roman Church under the pretext of apostolic tradition. Yet we do not think the Lord's Supper is utterly corrupted if someone dilutes the cup, especially where it is the custom of the region to break very strong wines even in daily use and to temper them by adding water.

units.la: XX. Pa
units.tr: XX. Pa

units.la: XX. Pariter intincti panis offulas, quas veteres ad ægrotos mittebant; & infantibus dabant, quod siccum panem manducare non poterant; & nonnullis in locis, pro complemento communionis, plebi Ecclesiasticæ distribuebant; admittendas non censemus: quod Christi exemplo ac scopo repugnant, qui non uno, sed duplici elemento ac symbolo, Ecclesiæ fidem alere ac sustentare voluit.
units.tr: XX. Likewise, we do not think that morsels of bread dipped in wine should be admitted. The ancients sent these to the sick, gave them to infants, who could not eat dry bread, and in some places distributed them to the ecclesiastical people as a completion of communion. Such practices run counter to the example and purpose of Christ, who willed to nourish and sustain the faith of the Church not by one element and symbol only, but by a double one.

units.la: XXI. Solebant autem, apud veteres, panis ac vini copia a fidelibus spontanea liberalitate conferri, atque ex collatitia dape S. Cœna instrui. Unde oblationis, & oblatarum, & sacrificii, nomina. Ac reprehendit Cyprianus, sermone de eleemosynis, mulierem, quæ in Dominicum sine sacrificio veniebat, ac partem ex sacrificio, quod pauper obtulerat, sumebat. Quæ vocabula sequioribus sæculis corrupta, & non de populi, sed de sacerdotis oblatione, & sacrificio, usurpata fuerunt. Addebant & alia dona, instruendo convivio; quod Agapen, seu charitatis epulum vocabant: in quo communem cibum capiebant, & post cibum sumtum, Eucharistiæ, ad exemplum Christi, participes facti fuisse credebantur. Quæ tamen convivia tandem irrepente abusu sublata sunt.
units.tr: XXI. Among the ancients, the supply of bread and wine was commonly contributed by the faithful out of spontaneous generosity, and the Supper of the Lord was furnished from this collected feast. Hence the names oblation, the things offered, and sacrifice. Cyprian, in his sermon on almsgiving, rebukes a woman who came to the Lord's table without a sacrifice and took a portion of the sacrifice which a poor man had offered. In later centuries these terms were corrupted and applied to the oblation and sacrifice of the priest, not of the people. They also added other gifts to furnish the meal, which they called the Agape, or feast of charity. At this feast they took common food, and after eating they believed that they were made partakers of the Eucharist, after the example of Christ. Yet these feasts were in time abolished, as abuse crept in.

units.la: XXII. Transmittimus autem veterum hæreticorum prodigia, ac ritus sacrilegos, quibus S. Cœnam contaminabant; quales erant Aquarii, Gnostici, Cataphryges, Artotyritæ, Semidalitæ, Marcosii &c. qui, ut de Christo prodigiose sentiebant, ita sacra corporis ac sanguinis ejus signa turpiter defœdabant. De quibus Epiphanius, Augustinus, aliique hæresium scriptores, videri possunt.
units.tr: XXII. We pass over the monstrous errors and sacrilegious rites of the ancient heretics, by which they defiled the Lord's Supper: such as the Aquarians, Gnostics, Cataphrygians, Artotyrites, Semidalites, Marcosians, and others, who, as they thought monstrous things about Christ, so they shamefully defiled the holy signs of his body and blood. On these matters Epiphanius, Augustine, and the other writers on heresies may be consulted.

units.la: XXIII. Symbolis seu elementis S. Cœnæ accedere debent ritus & actiones sacræ, absque quibus sacramentum hoc non constat. Quæ cum circa panem, tum circa vinum, observanda sunt.
units.tr: XXIII. Besides the symbols or elements of the Lord's Supper, there must be added the sacred rites and actions, without which this sacrament does not stand. These are to be observed both with regard to the bread and with regard to the wine.

units.la: XXIV. Circa panem, in prima cœna, quinque occurrunt Christi actiones: 1. ejus sumtio. 2. benedictio. 3. fractio. 4. traditio. 5. & manducatum comedendi. Matth. 26: 26. Marc. 14: 22. Luc. 22: 19.
units.tr: XXIV. Concerning the bread, in the first supper five actions of Christ occur: (1) his taking; (2) blessing; (3) breaking; (4) giving; and (5) the command to eat. Matt. 26:26; Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19.

units.la: XXV. Panem primum in manus sumsit Servator, atque isto ritu benedictionem ejus peregit. Quæ & Judæorum consuetudo erat, apud quos Paterfamilias, integrum adhuc panem manu tenens, super eum solemnibus verbis benedictionem recitabat; nec ante quicquam de eo gustare fas erat. Factum autem illud a Domino, inter cœnandum. εὐλόγησεν αὐτῶν, testibus Matthæo & Marco. quod pro ratione convivii paschalis, ad alteram panis azymi fractionem, aut ad ultima agni paschalis frustula, in fine convivii comedenda, quorum loco panem hunc dederit, referri posse videtur.
units.tr: XXV. The Saviour first took the bread into his hands, and by this action performed its blessing. This was also the custom of the Jews, among whom the head of the household, holding the whole loaf in his hand, recited the blessing over it with solemn words; and it was not lawful to taste anything of it before this. That the Lord did this during the supper is attested by Matthew and Mark, who write "he blessed" (εὐλόγησεν). It seems that this may be referred to the Passover meal, to the second breaking of the unleavened bread, or to the last morsels of the paschal lamb, which were eaten at the end of the supper, and in whose place he may have given this bread.

units.la: XXVI. Deinde benedixit. Quæ non simplex cibariorum benedictio fuisse videtur, quam & Judæi certis quibusdam precibus peragebant sed insuper externi istius elementi consecratio, & ad sacrum ac sacramentalem usum destinatio; ut deinceps non communis & vulgaris panis, sed corporis Christi symbolum ac sacramentum esset. Quæ consecratio, tum precibus, tum gratiarum actione, tum expressis verbis, quibus voluntatem suam testabatur, istudque corporis sui pignus Ecclesiæ tradebat, constitit. Scriptura, tum εὐλογίαν, benedictionem, Matth. 26:26. Marc. 14:22. tum εὐχαριστίαν, gratiarum actionem, Luc. 22:19. 1. Cor. 11:24. vocat. Eodemque modo & hodie Ecclesia symbolorum istorum sanctificationem, seu consecrationem, paragit; partim instituti ac mandati Christi commemoratione, partim fausti precibus ac gratiarum actionibus, denique universa illa actione ad Christi normam & exemplum composita.
units.tr: XXVI. Then he blessed. This does not seem to have been a simple blessing of food, such as the Jews also performed with certain set prayers, but in addition a consecration of this external element and its designation to a sacred and sacramental use, so that from then on it would be not common and ordinary bread but a symbol and sacrament of the body of Christ. This consecration consisted in prayer, in thanksgiving, and in express words by which he declared his will and handed this pledge of his body to the Church. Scripture calls it blessing (εὐλογίαν), Matt. 26:26; Mark 14:22, and thanksgiving (εὐχαριστίαν), Luke 22:19; 1 Cor. 11:24. And in the same way the Church today carries out the sanctification, or consecration, of these symbols: partly by recalling the institution and command of Christ, partly by prayers and thanksgivings for his blessing, and finally by that whole action arranged according to the rule and example of Christ.

units.la: XXVII. Non ferenda enim Pontificiorum ἐφωρίας, qui certam consecrationis formulam, ac certa verba, à Christo adhibita, & ab Ecclesia usurpanda comminiscuntur: Hoc enim est corpus meum. Quæ magico susurro super panem demurmurant, ac totidem syllabis consecrationis actum circumscribunt & absolvunt. Quæ insincera sunt. Nam certa verba & syllabarum apices numerare, & operatoria appellare, ac vim illis ἐνεργητικὴν adscribere, a Magorum mysteriis, & profana verborum potentia non longe abit. Unde & tacito susurro, non populuni, sed sacra signa affantur, atque imperiosis verbis in Christi corpus illa transmutant, & è crusto Christum faciunt. Quæ infanda sunt. Certe Christum verbis illis consecrationem peregisse, absurdum est; cum, antequam illa enuntiaret, panem benedixisse & fregisse, commemoretur; ut tum non amplius panis communis, sed sacer ac benedictus fuerit, quem proinde in corporis sui symbolum ac pignus tradebat: Hoc enim est corpus meum. Consecratio igitur Christi exemplo, precibus, hymnis, sacroque symbolorum usu, ac perpetua illa & publica, quam jussit, mortis ejus commemoratione, in Ecclesia peragitur.
units.tr: XXVII. The Papists' incantations cannot be tolerated, who devise a fixed formula of consecration, with set words used by Christ and to be used by the Church: "For this is my body." They mutter these words over the bread in a magical whisper, and by just so many syllables they enclose and complete the act of consecration. These things are insincere. For to count out fixed words and the marks of syllables, to call them operative, and to ascribe to them an active power, is not far from the mysteries of the magicians and from the profane power of words. Hence they address not the people but the sacred signs with a silent murmur, and with imperious words they transmute those things into the body of Christ, making Christ out of a crust. These things are unspeakable. Certainly, it is absurd to suppose that Christ performed the consecration with those words, since before he uttered them the record mentions that he had blessed and broken the bread, so that it was no longer common bread but sacred and blessed, which he then handed over as a symbol and pledge of his body: "For this is my body." Consecration, therefore, is carried out in the Church after the example of Christ, by prayers, hymns, the sacred use of the symbols, and by that perpetual and public remembrance of his death which he commanded.

units.la: XXVIII. Atque ita & vetus Ecclesia sacramentum hoc peregit; cujus morem, ac sacrum convivandi ritum, a Pontificiorum mysteriis, ac magico illo ministerio, longissime abfuisse satis constat. Audiebatur enim ibi primum sacra lectio; tum concio, vel sermo; inde preces concipiebantur &c. atque ita ad sacrorum mysteriorum participationem veniebant. Paratis enim precibus, post osculi collugationem, quod orationis signaculum Tertullianus vocat; & dextræ congressum, quod ipsi est pacem miscere; offerebantur præsidi a ministro vel diacono oblatarum partes. Quibus ille acceptis, postquam nomina offerentium fausta commemoratione prosecutus esset, panem & vinum, non arcano murmure, sed clara voce, audiente & acclamante populo, benedicebat. Quæ benedictio fere laudibus Deo dictis, pro parta salute, sacrisque istis donis ac symbolis, constabat; ac variis formulis, quæ in liturgiis veterum occurrunt, comprehendebatur. Circa quartum sæculum Spiritus S. invocatio, ad sacra ista signa, ut ea corpus & sanguinem Christi facerent, adhiberi cœpta est. Quam Hieronymus imprecationem, Græci ἐπίκλησιν vocant. Atque hoc veteribus est, conficere ore sacro corpus Christi, conficere corpus, quod ex virgine, conficere venerabilia sacramenta. Aug. Hieron. Quæ cuncta precibus fiebant. Omnia autem publice, & clara voce peragebantur, ut populus posset Amen ingeminare, quod apud Græcos Latinosque tum in usu. Nec ista Ecclesiæ ætate, ut hodie in Pontificiorum Eleusiniis, murmurque, humilesque susurros; & fida silentia sacris, aliaque ex Gentilium ritibus deprehendere adhuc licebat.
units.tr: XXVIII. And so the ancient Church also celebrated this sacrament; and it is well established that its custom and the sacred rite of the shared meal were far removed from the mysteries of the Papists and that magical ministry. For there, first, a sacred reading was heard; then a sermon or discourse; after that prayers were offered, and so they came to take part in the sacred mysteries. For when the prayers had been prepared, after the kiss of greeting (which Tertullian calls the seal of prayer) and the joining of right hands (which is itself to share peace), the portions of the offerings were presented to the president by the minister or deacon. He received them and, after he had recited the names of those who made the offerings with a favourable commemoration, he blessed the bread and the wine, not with a hidden murmur but in a clear voice, with the people listening and responding. This blessing consisted almost entirely of words of praise to God for the salvation obtained and for these sacred gifts and signs, and it was contained in various formulas that occur in the liturgies of the ancients. Around the fourth century the invocation of the Holy Spirit began to be used over these sacred signs, so that they might make the body and blood of Christ. Jerome calls this the imprecation, and the Greeks call it the epiclesis. Hence the expressions of the ancients: to make the body of Christ with the sacred mouth, to make the body which was born of the virgin, to make the venerable sacraments. (Augustine, Jerome.) All these things were done by prayer. Everything, moreover, was carried out publicly and in a clear voice, so that the people could add their Amen, which was then in use among both Greeks and Latins. Nor in that age was it possible, as it is today in the Papists' Eleusinian rites, to detect a muttering and low whispers, a faithful silence over the sacred things, and other features taken from the rites of the Gentiles.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Benedictionem panis excipit ejus fractio, more a cœnis Judaicis desumto, ubi paterfamilias, peracta benedictione, panes frangebat, & convivis distribuebat. Nec Christus solum, sed & Apostoli panem fregisse leguntur (unde & κλάσις τῆς ἄρτου dicitur) Act. 2: 42.
units.tr: The blessing of the bread is followed by its breaking, a practice taken over from the Jewish meals, where the head of the household, after the blessing was said, broke the loaves and distributed them to the guests. And we read that not only Christ but also the Apostles broke bread (whence it is called the breaking of bread), Acts 2:42.

units.la: 1. Cor. 10: 16. atque universa vetus Ecclesia, prioribus octo, imo duodecim sæculis. Pertinebat autem Eucharistici panis fractio, non solum ad ejus distributionem, verum etiam ad carnis Christi laceratæ, ac mysticæ fidelium de uno corpore communicationis, repræsentationem faciendam. Ut sacramenti violatio sit, ritum illum, qui ad sacramenti integritatem facit, nec sine mysterio a Christo usurpatus est, omittere. Quod Romana Ecclesia, ob transubstantiationis doctrinam (fractio enim merorum accidentium esse non potest) & Lutherani, ob consubstantiationis errorem (ne videl. Christus quasi una laceretur) instituunt: male excusantes, ritum hunc, utcunque utilem, non tamen de necessitate sacramenti, esse: nam ad integritatem ejus fractionem pertinere, & Christi exemplo, & significationis mysterio, satis patet.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 10:16; and so the whole ancient Church did for the first eight, indeed the first twelve, centuries. The breaking of the Eucharistic bread served not only for its distribution but also to represent the laceration of Christ's flesh and the mystical communion of the faithful in the one body. So to omit that rite, which contributes to the integrity of the sacrament and which Christ employed not without mystery, is a violation of the sacrament. The Roman Church omits it on account of its doctrine of transubstantiation (for the breaking of mere accidents cannot happen), and the Lutherans on account of their error of consubstantiation (lest, that is, Christ should seem to be torn in some way). They make a poor excuse, claiming that this rite, however useful, is not necessary to the sacrament; for that the breaking belongs to its integrity is sufficiently clear both from Christ's example and from the mystery of its signification.

units.la: XXX. Fractionem panis sequitur distributio. Primum autem, ex Judæorum more, de eo degustabat paterfamilias; tum convivæ cæteri. Ut male Socinus Christum symbola dispensasse, non autem de cœna illa gugustasse, velit. Obstat enim coenarum Judaicarum ratio. Ac spectare co loca Luc. 22: 15. Desiderio desideravi hoc Pascha vobiscum edere, antequam ego patiar. Matth. 26: 29. Dico autem vobis, non bibam, ab hoc tempore, ex hoc fructu vitis, usque ad diem illum, quum ipsum bibam vobiscum novum, in regno Patris mei.
units.tr: XXX. The breaking of the bread is followed by the distribution. At first, after the Jewish custom, the head of the household tasted of it, and then the other guests. So Socinus is wrong to want Christ to have distributed the signs without tasting of that supper himself. For the manner of Jewish meals stands in the way. And the passages Luke 22:15 apply here: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer." And Matthew 26:29: "But I say to you, I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father."

units.la: XXXI. Apud veteres distribuendi ritus varius fuit. Justini tempore diaconi sacras partes populo distribuebant, & ad absentes quoque deferebant. Clemens, in Alexandrina Ecclesia, ipsum populum de patina consecratas offas accepisse scribit. Tertullianus, sua aetate, non de aliorum, quam de praesidentium manu, eas sumi dixit. Non enim ubivis, aut omni tempore, uniformis coenae ritus erat. Postea autem frequentius Episcopi Presbyteris, Presbyteri Diaconis, Diaconi fere Laicis, ac reliquae Ecclesiae plebi, symbola ministrabant. Ordine autem quodam communio peragebatur; ut primum communicaret Clerus, Episcopi, Presbyteri, Diaconi &c. atque hi deinceps sanctiori Ecclesiae loco, intra ipsa altarium septa; tum extra illa populus, primo viri, dein mulieres; & hae non nisi velatae; unusquisque ordine suo. Quorum altera communio Ecclesiastica, altera laica vocabatur: ad quam nonnunquam clerici, ignominiae causa, rejiciebantur. Optimus autem procul dubio coenae ministrandae modus est, quem Christus usurpavit; ut populus de praesidis manu sacra signa accipiat. Quod de pane Eucharistico saltem factum videtur. Calicis enim non eadem ratio videtur, cum ille in orbem obambulare posset. Sed cum nec de pane id certum sit, praesidet de distributionis modo, modo fractio obtineat, non contendere. Latinorum autem novitas est, quod panem sacrum communicantibus distribuendum non solum non frangant, sed nec unum panem distribuant; verum hostiolas plures offerant; modo illas offerant seu distribuant.
units.tr: XXXI. The practice of distribution varied among the ancients. In Justin's time deacons distributed the sacred portions to the people and also carried them to those who were absent. Clement, in the Church of Alexandria, writes that the people themselves took the consecrated pieces from the paten. Tertullian, in his own day, said that they were received not from the hands of others but only from those presiding. For the form of the supper was not uniform everywhere or at all times. Later, however, more frequently bishops gave the signs to presbyters, presbyters to deacons, and deacons for the most part to the laity and the rest of the congregation. The communion, moreover, was carried out in a certain order: first the clergy communicated, bishops, presbyters, deacons and so on; and these then in the more sacred place of the Church, within the enclosure of the altar; then the people outside those enclosures, first the men and then the women, and these only veiled, each in his own order. The one was called the ecclesiastical communion, the other the lay communion; and sometimes clergy were relegated to the lay communion as a mark of disgrace. Certainly the best method of administering the supper is the one Christ used, namely that the people receive the sacred signs from the hand of the president. This seems to have been done at least with the Eucharistic bread. For the cup does not seem to have been handled in the same way, since it could go around the circle. But since even concerning the bread it is not certain whether the distribution was made in this manner or by breaking, we need not contend over the method of distribution. The novelty of the Latins, however, is that they not only do not break the sacred bread to be distributed to the communicants, but do not even distribute one loaf; instead they offer several small hosts, and they offer or distribute them in this way.

units.la: XXXII. Succedit tandem, post symbolorum distributionem, mandatum accipiendi & comedendi. Matth. 26: 26. Quod iterum ad temporum istorum morem intelligendum; quibus, juxta Judaeorum ritualia, paterfamilias fractum panem convivis vel in manus tradebat, vel ad mensam juxta ipsos collocabat. In veteri Ecclesia variatum: & primum simpliciter manibus, tum iisdem certo ritu in crucis formam compositis, dehinc adhibitis vasculis & furcillis aureis, nonnunquam etiam roundis linteolis, corpus dominicum acceptum; donec tandem, nimia elementorum veneratione, ea contrectare populo interdictum fuit. Quem morem hodie quoque sequuntur Pontificii & Lutherani, qui, ex dominicæ carnis, sub pane latitantis, religione, panem illum communicantibus non in manus, sed in os tradunt. Quod superstitiosum, & contra Christi institutum, est. Apostolos enim ore ingestas offas accepisse non legimus; nec cum accubitus eorum ratione congruit. Sed & additum a Christo mandatum comedendi; quod Pontifici aperte negligunt in missis, quas vocant, privatis, quas solus obligurit sacerdos. Quod merum cœnæ dominicæ ludibrium est. A quo tantopere abhorruit Ecclesia antiqua, ut prioribus novem a Christo nato sæculis missæ illæ solitariæ inauditæ fuerint; imo primis quatuor sæculis nemo fidelium divino officio, in quo conficiebatur Eucharistia, interesset, qui non ejus particeps fieri vellet, aut deberet.
units.tr: XXXII. After the distribution of the signs comes at last the command to take and eat (Matthew 26:26). This too must be understood in light of the customs of that time, when, according to the Jewish ritual, the head of the household either handed the broken bread to the guests in their hands or set it before them on the table. In the ancient Church this varied: first the body of the Lord was received simply with the hands, then with the same hands arranged in the form of a cross, later with golden vessels and forks, and sometimes even with clean linen cloths; until at last, because of an excessive veneration of the elements, it was forbidden for the people to handle them. The Papists and Lutherans still follow this custom today, and, out of reverence for the Lord's flesh supposedly hidden under the bread, they place that bread into the mouths of the communicants rather than into their hands. This is superstitious and contrary to Christ's institution. For we do not read that the Apostles received morsels put into their mouths, nor does this agree with the manner of their reclining at table. Moreover, Christ also added the command to eat, which the Papists openly neglect in their so-called private masses, which the priest alone tastes. This is sheer mockery of the Lord's Supper. The ancient Church so abhorred this that in the first nine centuries after Christ's birth those solitary masses were unheard of; indeed in the first four centuries no believer would attend the divine service in which the Eucharist was consecrated without wishing, or being obliged, to partake of it.

units.la: XXXIII. Circa poculum iidem fere ritus repetebantur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Concerning the cup, almost the same rites were repeated.

units.la: Usus autem est Christus in prima cœna poculo paschali; de cujus forma Judæorum ritualia consuli possunt. Incerta enim sunt, quæ veteres de illo poculo tradunt; quod ἀμφορεύς, binis ansis instructum, fuisse volunt, ac diversis in locis in thesauris Ecclesiasticis ostentant. Usa autem est antiqua Ecclesia omne genus vasis, ligneis, vitreis, argenteis, ac, crescente sacrorum pompa, aureis tandem, & gemmatis. Ut ex mera παχοζηλῶ fit, quod Pontificii Eucharistiæ vasa aurea vel argentea requirant, & Lutherani hodie non nisi in aureo calice cœnam rite fieri existimant.
units.tr: Christ used the paschal cup at the first Supper, and the Jewish ritual books can be consulted about its shape. The ancient writers' accounts of that cup are uncertain. Some claim it was an amphora fitted with two handles [ἀμφορεύς], and they display it in various places among the Church's treasures. The ancient Church used every kind of vessel: wooden, glass, silver, and, as the pomp of worship grew, finally gold and jewelled ones. This is pure excess of zeal [παχυζηλία], whence the Papists require golden or silver vessels for the Eucharist, and the Lutherans today think the Supper is not rightly celebrated unless it is in a golden chalice.

units.la: XXXIV. Poculum hoc accepit Christus, in manus nempe.
units.tr: XXXIV. Christ took this cup, namely into his hands.

units.la: Quod non sine sollemni ritu a Judæis, in cœna paschali, fieri consuevit, ut peculiarem super eo benedictionem pronunciarent.
units.tr: The Jews customarily did this at the Passover supper with a solemn rite, so that they might pronounce a special blessing over it.

units.la: XXXV. Et benedixit.
units.tr: XXXV. And he blessed.

units.la: Non enim una & eadem benedictione super pane & vino defungi, sed distinctis formulis ea consecrare solebant. Usus autem videtur Christus partim communi formula; partim eandem ad præsens institutum nonnihil accommodasse; & pro verbis, hic est fructus vitis, sanguis uvarum, verba illa, hic est sanguis meus &c. supposuisse, & circumlata illa patera sanguinem Novi Testam. dedicasse. Cum vero numerentur apud Judæos pocula paschalia quatuor, quorum tertium appellabatur poculum benedictionis post sumtum cibum, ultimum vero poculum hymni dicebatur, quo Pascha claudi solebat; Christum in Novi Test. symbolum tertium illud poculum consecrasse, probabile est. Quo pertinet Luc. 22:20. Similiter etiam poculum accepit, & dedit, postquam cœnassent.
units.tr: For they did not discharge the blessing over bread and wine with one and the same blessing, but consecrated them with separate formulas. Christ seems to have used partly the common formula, and partly adapted it somewhat to his present purpose. In place of the words, this is the fruit of the vine, the blood of grapes, he put in the words this is my blood, and by passing around that cup he dedicated the blood of the New Testament. Since the Jews count four paschal cups, of which the third was called the cup of blessing after the meal was eaten, and the last was called the cup of the hymn, with which the Passover was usually concluded, it is probable that Christ consecrated that third cup as the symbol of the New Testament. To this belongs Luke 22:20: Likewise also the cup he took and gave, after they had supped.

units.la: XXXVI. Infusionis vini in poculum, quæ panis fractioni respondet.
units.tr: XXXVI. The pouring of the wine into the cup, which corresponds to the breaking of the bread.

units.la: & sanguinis Christi effusi imaginem habet, nulla peculiaris hic mentio est; quod nulla peculiari caeremonia perageretur. In mystica tamen explicatione, ubi expresså sanguinis Christi fusi mentio est, ad eam manifesto alluditur. Ut inobservatam eam transmittere non liceat.
units.tr: It also bears the image of Christ's shed blood, but there is no special mention of it here, because it was not performed with any particular ceremony. In the mystical explanation, however, where the shed blood of Christ is expressly mentioned, it is clearly alluded to, so that it may not be passed over unnoticed.

units.la: XXXVII. Succedebat poculi traditio: cujus varia apud antiquos ratio. Saepe a Diacono illud fiebat, qui sanguinem Christi ministrare dicebatur. Atque accipiebant illum fideles primum simpliciter, ac convivantium in morem; tum venerabundi, & corpore inclinato. Dein a sacerdote poculum fidelium ori admovebatur, & sacrum vinum illi infundebatur; ad qualemcunque effusi Christi sanguinis imaginem faciendam. Augescente porro superstitione, fistulae argenteae adhibitae; ne quid calicem inter supremaque labra de Christi sanguine periret. Eodemque consilio, saeculo duodecimo, abbatiae sacerdotum barbae, ne quid de Domini corpore vel sanguine iis adhaeresceret. Quae nimia signorum reverentia, portentoso errore, dogmate transubstantionis nata, mutilatione calicis, aliisque erroribus jam tum viam parabat.
units.tr: The handing over of the cup followed. Its practice among the ancients varied. Often it was done by the deacon, who was said to administer the blood of Christ. The faithful received it first simply, in the manner of diners at a table, and then reverently, with the body bowed. Next, the priest brought the cup to the mouths of the faithful and poured the consecrated wine into them, to make some kind of image of the shed blood of Christ. As superstition grew further, silver pipes were used, so that nothing of the blood of Christ should perish from the cup between the lips. For the same reason, in the twelfth century, the beards of the abbey priests were shaved, so that nothing of the body or blood of the Lord should cling to them. This excessive reverence for the signs, born of the monstrous error of the doctrine of transubstantiation, was already preparing the way for the mutilation of the cup and other errors.

units.la: XXXVIII. Tandem jussit Christus, ut omnes de eo biberent, Matth. 26:27. Et, annotante Marc. 14:23. biberunt ex eo omnes. Atque ita quoque factum in veteri Ecclesia, per duodecim integra saecula, fatentibus Pontificiorum doctissimis. Prima ejus rei mutatio facta est in Occidente, a Concilio Constantiensi, A.C. 1415. Quod, LICET CHRISTUS sub utraque specie, panis & vini, hoc venerabile sacramentum discipulis suis administraverit — & LICET in primitiva Ecclesia idem sacramentum reciperetur sub utraque specie; TAMEN HOC NON OBSTANTE, illud a conficientibus, sub utraque, & a Laicis, tantummodo sub specie panis, suscipi debere, edixit: idque habendum pro lege, quam non licet reprobare, sub poena excommunicationis statuit, sess. 13. Cujus decreti nullas alias dant causas, nisi has, tum quia hac consuetudo ad evitandum aliqua pericula & scandala rationabiliter introducta est; tum quia integrum corpus Christi, tam sub specie panis, quam sub specie vini veraciter continetur. Eademque concilii Basiliensis sententia fuit, sess. 30. Quae tamen non sine pugna & certamine obtinuit, Christiano orbe hanc sibi injuriam fieri indignante: Bohemis praesertim, Calixtinis dictis, pro calice acriter contendentibus; ubi ea res non exiguam bellorum & tumultuum materiam praebuit; aliisque, imperatore praesertim, Gallo ac Bavaro, in Concilio Tridentino illum repetentibus. Sed inani eventu. Istud enim, non sine insigni verborum artificio, tandem decrevit, nullo divino praecepto Laicos, & Clericos non conscientes, obligari, ad Eucharistia sacramentum sub utraque specie sumendum s neque ullo pacto, salva fide, dubitari posse, quin illis alterius speciei communio ad salutem sufficiat. De expresso autem præcepto, & salutis necessitate, tantum mentionem faciunt: & fideles ad calicis usum strictè obligari negant. Studio enim asperiora verba vitabant, ne principum oratores læderent. Quod autem ibi utcunque tegebant,ac mollius explicabant, ac si videri vellent,de absoluta calicis ad salutem necessitate quæstionem solum esse;quam ipsi videl,negabant; id in Catechismo ad parochos apertius explicant; ubi non calicis necessitatem negant,aut liberum & indifferentem ejus usum permittunt; sed omnem ejus usum laicis interdicunt: Quod vero ad communicandi ritum pertinet, doceant Parochi, Sancta Ecclesia lege interdictum esse; ne quis, sine ipsius Ecclesiæ auctoritate, prater sacerdotes, corpus Domini in sacrificio conficientes, sub utraque specie sacram Eucharistiam sumat.
units.tr: XXXVIII. At last Christ commanded that all should drink of it, Matt. 26:27; and, as Mark 14:23 notes, they all drank of it. And so it was also done in the ancient Church for twelve full centuries, as the most learned of the Papists confess. The first change in this matter was made in the West by the Council of Constance, in the year A.D. 1415. Although CHRIST administered this venerable sacrament to his disciples under both kinds of bread and wine, and although in the primitive Church the same sacrament was received under both kinds, NEVERTHELESS, the council decreed that it should be received by the celebrants under both kinds, and by the laity only under the kind of bread. It established this, under penalty of excommunication, as a law which may not be rejected, Sess. 13. The council gives no other reasons for this decree except these: first, that this custom was reasonably introduced to avoid certain dangers and scandals; second, that the entire body of Christ is truly contained both under the kind of bread and under the kind of wine. The Council of Basel held the same view, Sess. 30. Yet this did not prevail without struggle and conflict, since the Christian world indignantly protested that this injury was being done to it, especially the Bohemians, who, following the Calixtines, contended fiercely for the cup. There the matter gave no small occasion for wars and disturbances. Other rulers, especially the Emperor, the Frenchman and the Bavarian, renewed the demand at the Council of Trent, but to no effect. For Trent, not without remarkable skill in words, finally decreed that by no divine precept are the laity, and the clergy who do not celebrate, obliged to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds; and that it cannot be doubted in any way, without loss of faith, that communion under one kind is sufficient for their salvation. They make mention only of an express precept and of necessity for salvation, and they deny that the faithful are strictly bound to use the cup. For they took care to avoid harsher words, lest they offend the envoys of princes. What they covered up in some way and explained more gently, as if they wished it to seem that the question was only about the absolute necessity of the cup for salvation, which they themselves denied, they explain more plainly in the Catechism for parish priests. There they do not deny the necessity of the cup, nor do they permit its free and indifferent use; rather they forbid the laity any use of it at all: As for the rite of communicating, let parish priests teach that holy Church has forbidden by law that anyone, without the authority of the Church itself, apart from the priests who consecrate the body of the Lord in the sacrifice, receive the holy Eucharist under both kinds.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Quod revera est, corrumpere Testamentum Domini,& sacratissimæ rei spolium committere, ac, non sine sacrilegio, Ecclesiam dominici sanguinis pignore privare. Manifesta enim est Christi institutio, non exemplo solum, sed & mandato ejus firmata: Accepto poculo, & gratiis actis, dedit iis; dicens, bibite ex eo omnes. Matth. 26. Luc. 22. quod factum ab iis Marcus testatur,cap. 14:23. Et quam diserte Paulus, ubi rem ex dominica institutione repetere se præfatur,injungit 1.Cor. 11:26. Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis,mortem Domini annunciate, donec venerit. & 28. Experet se ipsum homo, & sic ex pane edat, & ex poculo bibat. Atque huc quoque facit, quod, 1. Cor. 12: 13. Omnes ad unum Spiritum potatos dicit. Nec rejici ab adversariis possunt ipsius Christi verba, Joh. 6:53. Nisi comedatis carnem filii hominis, & bibatis ipsius sanguinem, non habetis vitam in vobis. Quæ de Eucharistia agere ipsi sentiunt. Saltem sanguinem suum spiritualiter hauriri debere Christus inculcat. Quod absque omni dubio nullibi efficacius, quam in sacramentorum communione peragitur; ubi a sanguine ejus fideles arceri indignum & impium est. Quod non leviter consolationem ipsorum concutit, ac si non illi quoque in testamenti tabulis hæredes scripti essent; ac verba illa, dulcissimæ consolationis plenissima, utrique symbolo a Christo addita, Quod pro vobis tradetur, qui pro vobis effundetur, non ad ipsos quoque pertinerent: sed sacrificulorum cohors, quibus obrasum caput, inunctæque manus, & ab altari quotidie tidie calentes, in Servatoris testamento prærogativam aliquam haberent. Hoc certum est, omnibus fidelibus ex æquo dici posse, & debere, Hic est sanguis Novi Test. qui pro vobis effundetur: & quid ergo causæ est, quod sanguinis istius pignore priventur, nec quoque proxime insequentia verba audiant, bibite ex eo omnes?
units.tr: This is truly to corrupt the testament of the Lord, to surrender the spoils of a most sacred thing, and, not without sacrilege, to deprive the Church of the pledge of the Lord's blood. For Christ's institution is plain, confirmed not only by his example but also by his command: Taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, saying, Drink of it, all of you. Matt. 26; Luke 22. Mark testifies that they did so, ch. 14:23. And how plainly Paul enjoins this, where he professes to repeat the matter from the Lord's institution: 1 Cor. 11:26, As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes; and v. 28, Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. To this also belongs what he says, 1 Cor. 12:13, All were made to drink of one Spirit. Nor can our opponents reject the words of Christ himself, John 6:53, Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. They themselves feel these words concern the Eucharist. At the very least, Christ insists that his blood must be drunk spiritually. Beyond all doubt, this is nowhere carried out more effectively than in the communion of the sacrament, where it is wrong and impious to keep the faithful from his blood. This shakes their consolation not lightly, as if they too were not written as heirs in the tablets of the testament, and as if those words, most full of sweetest consolation, added by Christ to both symbols, which is given for you, which is poured out for you, did not pertain to them as well; but rather a crowd of little sacrificers, whose heads are shaved, whose hands are anointed, and who warm themselves daily at the altar, would hold some prerogative in the Saviour's testament. This is certain: it can and must be said equally to all the faithful, This is the blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for you. Why then are they deprived of the pledge of that blood, and do not also hear the words that follow at once, Drink of it, all of you?

units.la: XL. Frivoli autem ac tenues nimium sunt prætextus, quibus tanta in re utuntur. Vanissimo enim concomitantiæ commento, fictisque quibusdam difficultatibus, de effusione calicis, abstemiis &c. se tuentur; & denique cœnam Emaunticam, aliasque ex Scripturis memorant, quas sacramentales fuisse volunt, in quibus nulla consecrati calicis mentio. Ad quæ respondemus: 1. non quæri, quomodo integrales corporis Christi partes inter se cohæreant; sed quo consilio, modo & fine, illæ nobis exhibeantur & figurentur. Illud autem Dei consilium est, non solum cibum, sed & potum spiritualem, in Christi corpore ostendere; istudque ut fractum, sanguinem ejus ut fusum, fidei exhibere: sine qua sanguinis effusione & illius a carne separatione, divinæ hostiæ ratio non constitisset; unde tota sacramenti ratio in una specie non absolvitur.
units.tr: XL. The pretexts they use in so great a matter are frivolous and far too thin. With the most empty invention of concomitance and certain made-up difficulties, they defend themselves regarding the spilling of the cup, the abstainers, and so on. Finally, they cite the Emmaus supper and other passages of Scripture, which they want to be sacramental, though in them there is no mention of the consecrated cup. To these we reply: (1) The question is not how the integral parts of Christ's body cohere with one another, but by what counsel, manner and end those parts are exhibited and figured to us. That counsel of God is to show in Christ's body not only food but also spiritual drink, and to present the one as broken and the other, his blood, as poured out, to faith. Without the pouring out of the blood and its separation from the flesh, the reason of the divine sacrifice would not have stood, and so the whole reason of the sacrament is not completed in one kind.

units.la: 2. Nec incommoda illa, quæ nec ipse Christus ignoravit constitutum ab eo ordinem evertere possunt. Rariissima enim illa sunt. Neque parcorum exemplum reliquis fidelibus regulam facere debet. Nec denique, si quis omnino vini usum, edoremque omnem, aversetur, ita ad elementum istud tenetur, ut non & alio potu cœnam facere possit. 3. Tandem cœna Emauntica non fuit sacrificalis. Nec, si vel maxime sacra fuisset, non ideo, quod nulla calicis isto in loco mentio est, existimandum est, cœnas illas siccas fuisse. Usitatissima enim Hebræis synecdoche est, per fractionem panis universum convivium designare.
units.tr: (2) Those inconveniences, which Christ himself did not overlook, cannot overturn the order he established. For those cases are very rare. Nor should the example of the sparing few make a rule for the other faithful. Finally, if someone altogether shuns the use of wine and every drink, he is not so bound to that element that he cannot celebrate the supper with some other drink. (3) Finally, the Emmaus supper was not sacrificial. Nor, even if it had been most holy, should it be thought that those suppers were without drink because no cup is mentioned in that place. For it is a most usual Hebrew synecdoche to designate the whole banquet by the breaking of bread.

units.la: XLI. Mittimus reliquos veterum ritus, qui sequentis Ecclesiæ erroribus non leve auspicium fecerunt. Deferebant enim sacratum panem non solum ad absentes, sed & deinceps ad infirmos; quin & vino intinctum moribundis in os ingerebant, unde commeatum, & viaticum dixere. Domum etiam persæpe secum adferebant, fervente præsertim persecutione, quo quotidie Christum gustare, atque ad certamen se præparare possent. Quem morem præpositore imitantur Pontificii, dum consecratam hostiam, in ornata cistula, in templo proponunt, non gustandum, sed adorandum. Denique & alium præterea panem habebant veteres, sacrum quidem, sed non sacramentalem; quem, communis fidei testandæ causa, Episcopi ad dioceses suas Presbyteros, vel ad alios CoëpiCoëpiscopos missitabant. Vocabant autem istas micas Eulogias. Qui tamen ritus, ac nonnulli alii, conciliorum auctoritate nonnunquam compressi leguntur, ac nimia illa signorum religio sæpe castigata & repressa. Quanquam irrito conatu, augescente superstitione, atque ad idololatricum signorum cultum gradum faciente.
units.tr: XLI. We pass over the remaining ancient rites, which gave no small beginning to the errors of the later Church. For they carried the consecrated bread not only to the absent but afterwards also to the sick; and indeed they put bread dipped in wine into the mouths of the dying, whence they called it commeatus and viaticum. They often brought it home with them, especially while persecution was raging, so that they could taste Christ every day and prepare themselves for the contest. The Papists imitate this custom to excess, when in the temple they display the consecrated host in an adorned little box, not to be tasted but to be adored. Finally, the ancients also had another bread, holy indeed but not sacramental, which the bishops sent to the presbyters of their dioceses, or to other chorepiscopi, to attest the common faith. They called these crumbs eulogiae. Yet these rites, and some others, are read to have been sometimes checked by the authority of councils, and that excessive reverence for signs was often rebuked and restrained, though with futile effort, as superstition grew and advanced toward the idolatrous worship of signs.

units.la: XLII. Clausit cœnam Dominus hymno paschali, ut ex historia Euangelica colligi videtur. Ac porro sermonibus sanctissimis extremam illam noctem in terris egit. Atque ita & veteres gratiarum actione ad extremum defungi, & data ex more pace populum dimittere solebant, sollemni formula, ite in pace. Unde, quod concio tum missa esset, missa quia abnomen; quod universo isti sacro tandem proprium factum est. Residua autem micæ in agaparum usum; quod S. Cœnæ, ut olim antecoenium, ita deinceps, mutato ordine, perdiu veluti corollarium fuit; vel, iis abolitis, Clero, aut Catechumenis, aut pueris de ludo redeuntibus, aut denique pauperibus cedebant. Fuere & qui igne concremarent. Nullibi eas primis sæculis in Ecclesia, nedum ad pompam & cultum, asservabant; qui nunc Romanæ Ecclesiæ mos est.
units.tr: XLII. The Lord closed the supper with a paschal hymn, as the Gospel history seems to gather. Then he spent that last night on earth in most holy discourses. And so the ancients too were accustomed to conclude with thanksgiving, and, giving peace according to custom, to dismiss the people with the solemn formula, Go in peace. Hence, because the sermon was then ended, the rite took its name missa (mass); this name at last became proper to that whole sacred action. The remaining crumbs were used for love-feasts (agapae). Just as the supper once had an appendix before it, so afterwards, with the order reversed, it long served as a kind of corollary to the Lord's Supper; or, when these had been abolished, they went to the clergy, or to the catechumens, or to boys returning from school, or finally to the poor. Some even burned them with fire. In the early centuries they did not keep them anywhere in the Church, let alone for display and worship, as is now the custom of the Roman Church.

units.la: XLIII. Sequuntur tandem, post symbola, ritusque sacros, considerandæ quædam hujus cœnæ circumstantiæ. Quæ præcipue hæ duæ sunt, locus, & tempus.
units.tr: XLIII. Finally, after the creeds and the sacred rites, certain circumstances of this supper must be considered. The principal ones are these two: place and time.

units.la: XLIV. Prima cœna celebrata fuit in ædibus privatis; in quibus Christus paschale epulum instrui jusserat: πρὸς τὸν δεῖπνον, Matth. 26: 18. Marc. 14: 13, 14, 15. Luc. 22: 10, 11. Festorum enim sollemnium tempore, solebant Hierosolymis etiam privatorum ædes patere Judæis advenis, qui ad sacrum confluxerant. Eratque tum sancta illa urbs communis gentis illius civitas & patria, quam universam sinu suo accipiebat. Solebant postea & Apostoli in privata domo, uti docere persæpe, ita & convivari. Frangebant domatim panem, Act. 2: 46. Templis autem erectis, privatæ istæ cœnæ Ecclesiasticis edictis abrogatæ sunt. Quanquam nunquam ita privatæ forent, quin in fratrum conventu celebrarentur, & plures simul assiderent, testanda fidei ac communionis causa. Quæ & convivii paschalis ratio erat. Cum igitur convenitis eodem loci; hoc non est dominicam cænam edere, 1. Cor. 11: 20. Ut, fratres mei, coëuntes ad edendum, alii alios expectetis. com. 33. conf. 1. Cor. 10: 16. Ut missæ Pontificiorum solitariæ merum cœnæ ludibrium sint. Nec facile adeo probandus quorundam mos ægris Eucharistiam ministrandi; qui & præter S. Cœnæ institutum, & primorum maximæ sæculorum exemplum est.
units.tr: XLIV. The first supper was celebrated in private houses, in which Christ had ordered the paschal meal to be prepared: to the supper [πρὸς τὸν δεῖπνον], Matt. 26:18; Mark 14:13–15; Luke 22:10–11. For at the time of the solemn feasts, the houses of private persons in Jerusalem also commonly stood open to Jewish strangers who had gathered for the feast. That holy city was then the common city and homeland of that whole nation, and received all of them into its bosom. Afterwards the apostles, as they often taught in private houses, so also dined there: they broke bread from house to house, Acts 2:46. But once churches were built, those private suppers were abrogated by ecclesiastical edicts. Yet they were never so private that they were not celebrated in the assembly of the brethren, with many sitting down together, for the sake of attesting faith and communion. This was also the manner of the paschal feast. When you come together in one place, it is not to eat the Lord's supper, 1 Cor. 11:20; So, my brethren, when you come together to eat, wait for one another, v. 33; compare 1 Cor. 10:16. The solitary masses of the Papists are a mere mockery of the Lord's supper. Nor is the custom of some, of administering the Eucharist to the sick, easy to approve; it is contrary both to the institution of the Supper and to the example of the greatest part of the first centuries.

units.la: XLV. Per-
units.tr: XLV. Per-

units.la: Loci: varius.
units.tr: Of the place: varied.

units.la: XLV. Peracta fuit prima cœna ad communem mensam, Matth. 26:20. 1. Cor. 10:20. Non potestis participes esse mensæ Domini, & mensæ dæmoniorum. Quæ veteribus lignea & portatilis erat, ac linteamine operiebatur. Altaria enim primæva Ecclesia ignoravit. Quanquam sacrificalem mensam nonnunquam improprie hoc nomine appellarent, uti cœnam ipsam sacrificium dicebant. Pessime vero Pontificii rursus in Ecclesia aras, & altaria proprie dicta, excitarunt. Quæ, post oblatum Christi sacrificium, reducere velle Christianismi corruptio & venenum est. Habemus altare, ex quo edendi potestatem non habent, qui tabernaculo serviunt. Hebr. 13:10. Nec sine omni fermento est, quod Lutherani adeo altarium formas deament, atque ad ea cœnam sam celebrent; cum tamen Papistarum sacrificium detestentur. Quid enim ara sine victima?
units.tr: XLV. The first supper was held at a common table, Matt. 26:20; 1 Cor. 10:20: You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. For the ancients it was wooden and portable, and was covered with a linen cloth. For the primitive Church did not know altars. Yet they sometimes improperly called the table of the supper by that name, just as they called the supper itself a sacrifice. But the Papists most wickedly set up altars and proper altars again in the Church. To want to bring these back, after the offering of Christ's sacrifice, is the corruption and poison of Christianity. We have an altar, from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat, Heb. 13:10. It is not without some leaven that the Lutherans, who so detest the forms of the altars, nevertheless celebrate the supper at them, while they abhor the sacrifice of the Papists. For what is an altar without a victim?

units.la: XLVI. Mensæ huic, pro sæculi ac regionis more, accubuit Christus, in lectulo vid. tricliniari; atque infra supraque eum reliqui discipuli. Qui convivantium habitus erat, in paschali epulo quoque observari solitus. Et ipse vobis ostendet cœnaculum magnum, stratum, &c. Marc. 14:15. Atque ita & veteres deinceps accubitu cœnam faciebant, Agapis conjunctam. Deinde stantes; nunquam autem de genibus, adorantium in morem, sacra mysteria sumebant. Qui deinceps Ecclesiæ meretricantis atque in idololatriam prolabentis, mos fuit. Quod tamen sine insectatione illorum, qui citra sacramenti adorationem, ex mera reverentia, genibus positis Eucharistiam accipere consueverunt, dictum sit.
units.tr: XLVI. Christ reclined at this table, on a couch of the kind used in the custom of that age and region, that is, a dining couch, with the other disciples lying above and below him. This was the posture of diners, and it was usually observed at the Passover feast too: "And he will show you a large upper room, furnished," etc., Mark 14:15. So the ancients also afterwards took the supper reclining, joined with the Agapes. Later they took the sacred mysteries standing, and never on their knees in the manner of worshippers. That custom came afterwards, from the Church when it had turned harlot and slipped into idolatry. Yet this should be said without censuring those who, apart from any adoration of the sacrament, and out of mere reverence, have customarily received the Eucharist kneeling.

units.la: XLVII. Tempus quod attinet, prima cœna celebrata est feria quinta, ante festum paschatis. Quem diem deinde annuatim Ecclesia vetus quoque servavit, in tristissimæ illius noctis memoriam. Cæteroquin & aliis diebus communicabant: præsertim dominico, Justino teste. Quo Apostolorum exemplum ex parte facit, Act. 20: 7. Primo autem die hebdomadis, congregatis Apostolis ad frangendum panem, differebat Paulus &c.
units.tr: XLVII. As to the time, the first supper was celebrated on Thursday, before the feast of the Passover. The ancient Church afterwards also kept that day every year, in memory of that most sorrowful night. Otherwise they also communicated on other days, especially on the Lord's day, as Justin testifies. The example of the Apostles partly agrees with this, Acts 20:7: "On the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached to them," etc.

units.la: XLVIII. Horam quod spectat, vespertino tempore Christus convivatus est; ob paschatis sollenne, quod alio diei tempore edere nefas erat: Dominus, ea nocte, qua proditus est, accepit panem. 1. Cor. 11:23. Servaruntque illud diu veteres, quorum nocturnas, & deinceps antelucanas cœnas sæpe legimus. Quanquam & aliæ cœnandi horæ ipsis postea usurpatæ fuerint. Nam ubi jejunia, vel semi-jejunia agitabant, qua hora illa solvebantur; vel ubi jejunare non licebat, matutino tempore, cœnam faciebant. Plerunque autem jejuni eam celebrabant. Unde deinceps nata Latinorum lex, qua Eucharistiam, nisi jejunantes, non sumunt.
units.tr: XLVIII. As to the hour, Christ sat at table in the evening, because of the solemnity of the Passover, which it was unlawful to eat at any other time of day: "The Lord, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread," 1 Cor. 11:23. The ancients kept this practice for a long time, and we often read of their night suppers and, later, pre-dawn suppers. Yet other hours for supper were afterwards adopted by them as well. For where they were keeping fasts or half-fasts, they took the meal at the hour when the fast ended; and where it was not permitted to fast, they made the supper in the morning. Most often, however, those who were fasting celebrated it. Whence arose later the Latin rule by which they do not receive the Eucharist unless they are fasting.

units.la: XLIX. Repetendam autem illam sæpius (aliter ac in baptismo fit, ex qua unda tantum semel renasci licet) atque ad ultimum mundi finem celebrandam; usque dum Christus ipse tamen diu vocatus adsit, ex Scripturis constat. Nulla enim, ut prisci cæremoniis contigit, mutatio, vel innovatio, in Ecclesia amplius expectanda est. Hoc facite ad mei commemorationem. Luc. 22: 19. Quotiescunque enim ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annunciate, usque quo venerit.
units.tr: XLIX. That this rite is to be repeated often (unlike baptism, in which one can be born again from that water only once), and is to be celebrated until the last end of the world, until Christ himself, though long called for, is present, is established from the Scriptures. For no change or innovation, such as happened to the ceremonies of old, is to be expected any more in the Church. "Do this in remembrance of me," Luke 22:19. "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes."

units.la: 1. Cor. 11: 24, 25, 26. Atque ita Ecclesiam Apostolicam, in doctrina Apostolorum, & communione, & fractione panis, & precibus, quotidie perseverasse, primæ Ecclesiæ Acta tradunt, Act. 2: 42, 46. Ac duravit aliquandiu hic fervor, dum Ecclesia, a Spiritu recens, de igne isto adhuc incalesceret; & magno zelo ac ardore sacra pignora amplexari & tractare non desineret. Primitus singulis dominicis Ecclesiam panem vitæ sumsisse constat: quidam etiam dominicæ adjiciebant sabbata. Deinceps, oblationum causa, quotidiana reddita est communio. Quod Cypriani, Ambrosii & Augustini, tempore obtinuit. Postmodum certis diebus, bis, vel ter, vel etiam quater sacra communio hebdomadatim peragobatur. Sed refrigiuit paulatim zelus, dum nonnulli tertia quaque dominica, alii vix bis terve, imo semel duntaxat, in anno communicarent; donec lege Ecclesiastica ad tres majores anni sollemnitates, sive festa, communio adstricta est.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:24, 25, 26. Thus the Acts of the primitive Church relate that the apostolic Church "continued daily in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread and in prayers," Acts 2:42, 46. This fervour lasted for some time, while the Church, newly moved by the Spirit, still glowed with that fire, and did not cease to embrace and handle these sacred pledges with great zeal and ardour. It is certain that at first the Church received the bread of life every Lord's day, and some also added the Sabbaths. Afterwards, for the sake of the offerings, daily communion was introduced. This prevailed in the times of Cyprian, Ambrose and Augustine. Later, on certain days, holy communion was celebrated twice, or three times, or even four times a week. But zeal gradually cooled, as some communicated every third Lord's day, others scarcely twice or three times, and some only once a year; until by ecclesiastical law communion was bound to the three greater solemnities, or festivals, of the year.

units.la: L. Cum vero Christus nulli certo tempori sacrum hocce epulum adstrinxerit; aliter ac in paschate, reliquisque veteris sæculi cæremoniis, contigit; quæ, sublata temporum religione, una desierunt; Ecclesiæ vero libera omnia reliquerit; hoc tantum, quod sæpe in cœtus convenire, ac Domini sacrificium & mortem celebrare jusserit, 1. Cor. 11: 25, 26. servandus hic, ut in rebus omnibus, modus. Non nimis frequenter ad hanc cœnam coëundum, ne temeraria gula illam polluamus, ac quotidiano usu, ut fieri consuevit, tandem cibus ille evilescat: nec etiam raro nimis carpenda illa esca; ne sacrificium Domini neglectim habere deprehendamur; quod, tanquam juge nostrum, perpetuo colendum & celebrandum est.
units.tr: L. Since Christ bound this sacred feast to no fixed time, unlike what happened with the Passover and the other ceremonies of the old age, which ceased all together once the religious observance of times was removed, but left all else to the Church's freedom, and commanded only that they assemble often to celebrate the Lord's sacrifice and death (1 Cor. 11:25, 26), the measure is to be kept here, as in all things. We should not come together too often to this supper, lest by rash gluttony we defile it, and by daily use, as usually happens, that food at last become cheap; nor again should that food be taken too rarely, lest we be found to hold the Lord's sacrifice in neglect, which, as our perpetual yoke, is to be honoured and celebrated continually.

units.la: LI. Merum itaque, frigus est, quod illustris & magnus Grotius, non semper communicandum esse per symbola, edito libello persuadere annisus est; quo videlicet libera ac soluta obtineat pietas, nec uno cœtu Christianorum, claudatur dilectio. Quae larvae sunt, & praestigiosae fraudes. Non enim vilia esse debent illa symbola, quae Dominus, tanquam amoris sui signacula & arrhabonem, Ecclesiae tradidit; quaeque dum ipse in coelo degit, ab ea interim tractari, &c, tanquam absentis pignora, coli vult; addito expresso mandato, Hoc facite ad mei commemorationem, usque dum ipse de coelo reditypus, & praesens Ecclesiam beaturus est; mortem Domini annunciare, usque dum venerit. 1. Cor. 11: 26. Certe nec religio, nec pietas, sine externo & publico cultu constat. Unde Deus omni Ecclesiae aetate, cum ante lapsum, tum post illum, per singulas ejus periodos, sacramenta quaedam visibilia instituit; quas, tanquam publicas Ecclesiae tesseras, & symbola, palam usurpari, & haberi voluit. Ut de altero Novi Test. sacramento, baptismo, taceam; quem eodem colore ut inutilem tollere liceret. Atque ita quidem, abolitis sacris signis, quae omne religionis Christianae mysterium continent, & in omne aevum eam conservant, ipsa quoque Christiana religio paulatim extingueretur & deperiret. Quae sententia istius, prima specie blandae, pericula notasse sufficit; ut patet quam male consulatur rei Christianae ab hominibus istis, insignioris charitatis specie ad omnes coetus rei paratis; atque omnes religiones, tanquam non necessaria lite certatum hactenus fuisset, conciliare nitentibus. Quae non Sanctorum Ecclesia, nec illibatus Christi thalamus, sed hara potius quaedam & stabulum foret, quod pecus & dominos communi clauderet umbra.
units.tr: LI. Therefore it is sheer nonsense, the view which the illustrious and great Grotius, by publishing a little book, strove to persuade, that one should not always communicate by the symbols, so that free and unfettered piety might prevail and love not be shut in within one assembly of Christians. These are masks and deceptive frauds. For those symbols ought not to be cheap, which the Lord gave to the Church as the seals and pledge of his love; and which, while he himself dwells in heaven, he wills her meanwhile to handle and honour, as the pledges of one absent, with the express command added, "Do this in remembrance of me," until he himself returns from heaven and, present, blesses the Church, "proclaiming the Lord's death until he comes," 1 Cor. 11:26. Certainly neither religion nor piety exists without external and public worship. Hence God, in every age of the Church, both before the fall and after it, through each of its periods, instituted certain visible sacraments, which he willed to be openly used and held as the public tokens and symbols of the Church. Not to mention the other sacrament of the New Testament, baptism, which one might on the same grounds remove as useless. And so, with the sacred signs abolished, which contain the whole mystery of the Christian religion and preserve it for all time, the Christian religion itself would gradually be extinguished and perish. It is enough to have noted the dangers of this view, which is pleasing at first sight. It is plain how badly these men serve the Christian cause, who, under the appearance of a greater charity, are ready for every assembly and strive to reconcile all religions, as though the contest hitherto had been over matters that were not necessary. This would be not the Church of the saints nor Christ's unspotted bridal chamber, but rather a sort of pigsty and stable, which would shut in the herd and their masters under one common shade.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De re significata S. Coenae.
units.tr: Concerning the thing signified by the Holy Supper.

units.la: I. Postquam quod externum & visibile est in S. Coena consideravimus, sequitur nunc ejus mysterium & significatio. Quod attentius consideranda est, quia illud non ab omnibus satis plene exhauritur; dum plerique vel circa controversias excurrunt; sicut, quod dolendum est, ipsa S. Coena maxima nunc inter Christianos facta est controversia: vel omnem coenae praxin in anxia quadam & scrupulosa pietate constituunt, de intimo ejus mysterio non adeo solliciti, nec adeo attendentes, quid Deus, quid Christus, & qua sub imagine, in sacrificali isto epulo fidelibus exhibeant, bibeant, & quam amœnam spiritualium bonorum pictuam delineent; quam quomodo fidelesad cœnam istam comparare sese debeant; in quo se multum fatigant, & levibus quibusdam præceptiunculis, quæ vix ultra alphabetum Christianismi assurgunt, illos, onerant; sponsam ipsam, quam in convivalem thalamum introducere deberent, multrum in vestibulo morantes, ac, leviculi cujusdam cultus causa, longum detinentes. Quæ absque invidia dicta sunto. Præit autem nobis Spir. S. qui, cum parcius & fere unico verbo de externis signis agat, tam clare & luculenter universum cœnæ mysterium pandit. Videbimus autem distinctè, 1. externorum S. Cœnæ symbolorum ac rituum significationem. 3. spirituale bonum ac effectum, quod ex illa cœna ad fideles resultat.
units.tr: I. Having considered what is external and visible in the Holy Supper, we now come to its mystery and signification. This deserves closer attention, because not everyone draws it out fully. Most either run off into controversies, or, which is lamentable, the Holy Supper itself has now become a very great controversy among Christians. Or else they make the whole practice of the Supper a matter of anxious and scrupulous piety, not very concerned with its inner mystery, and not attending closely to what God and Christ present, give, and drink to the faithful at this sacrificial feast, under what image, and what pleasant picture of spiritual goods they draw. They also do not consider how the faithful ought to prepare themselves for this Supper. In this they weary themselves greatly and burden the faithful with certain slight precepts, which hardly rise above the alphabet of Christianity. They keep the bride herself, whom they should lead into the banqueting chamber, lingering long in the vestibule and detaining her for the sake of some trifling worship. These things are said without ill will. The Holy Spirit goes before us, and although he speaks of the external signs sparingly and almost in a single word, he unfolds the whole mystery of the Supper so clearly and brightly. We shall consider distinctly: (1) the signification of the external symbols and rites of the Holy Supper; (3) the spiritual good and effect that results for the faithful from that Supper.

units.la: II. De pane ipse Christus dixit, Hoc est corpus meum. Solebant autem Hebræi Agnum paschalem appellare corpus paschatis. נופו של מצה / ad quorum morem, ut & alia in hac cœna, Christi verba referenda sunt: ut pro corpore agni, quod modo comederant, jam in pane illo proprium corpus offerat, quod jamjam frangendum foret. Unde pro agno, qui priscæ liberationis monumentum erat, panem jam fideles tradere jubet; quem pro corpore suo substituit, tanquam pignus & sigillum ejus certissimum. Utitur autem Euangelium voce σῶμα, quæ corpus exangue & examine significat, tanquam σῶμα. Luc. 17: 37. Ubi σῶμα cadaver, illuc congregabuntur aquilæ. v. Matth. 14: 12. Quod emphasi non caret. Exhibetur enim nobis in sacramentis Christus, non ut gloriosus, sed ut mortuus. Mortem Domini annunciate, donec venerit, 1. Cor. 11:26. Rom. 6:4. Sola enim mors ejus salutis nostræ pretium, & fidei unicum pabulum est.
units.tr: II. Concerning the bread, Christ himself said, "This is my body." The Hebrews used to call the paschal lamb "the body of the passover" [נופו של מצה], and in keeping with their custom, Christ's words, like others in this Supper, must be referred to it. So, in place of the body of the lamb, which they had just eaten, he now offers in that bread his own body, which was about to be broken. Thus, in place of the lamb, which was a memorial of the ancient deliverance, he bids the faithful take bread, which he substitutes for his body as a sure pledge and seal of it. The Gospel uses the word σῶμα [soma], which denotes a lifeless and dead body, as in Luke 17:37: "Where the body [σῶμα] is, there will the eagles be gathered together." Compare Matt. 14:12. This is not without emphasis. For in the sacraments Christ is set before us not as glorious but as dead: "You proclaim the Lord's death until he comes," 1 Cor. 11:26; Rom. 6:4. For his death alone is the price of our salvation and the only food of faith.

units.la: III. Frangitur hic panis, ad sacrificii ac mortis Christi memoriam: fractum Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis fractum est. 1. Cor. 11:24. Utque nos ipsos, qui a divina manu conteramur, dignos fateamur: denique ut concupiscentias frangere, deque passionibus Christi gultare, corpusque hoc nostrum propter Christum frangendum & lacerandum præbere non abnuamus.
units.tr: III. The bread is broken here, in remembrance of the sacrifice and death of Christ: "This is my body, which is broken for you," 1 Cor. 11:24. We also acknowledge ourselves worthy to be crushed by the divine hand; finally, we refuse not to break our lusts and to mortify our passions, and to offer this body of ours to be broken and torn for Christ's sake.

units.la: IV. Vini mysterium est in sanguine Christi. τοῦτο ἐστὶ τὸ αἷμά μου. Hic est sanguis meus, ille Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Marc. 14: 23. Matth. 26: 28. Ita enim pro nomen τοῦτο, non ad κοτήμιον, sed potius ad τὸ αἷμα, referendum. Non, hoc, sed hic est sanguis meus. Eodem modo, ut commate præcedente de pane sermo est, non ἄρτος, vid. ἄρτος, sed τοῦτο ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμά μου. Ubi auautem Luc. 22:20. 1. Cor. 11:25. de poculo dicitur, τῆτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη &c. impropria & sacramentalis locutio est, ut sigillum testamenti intelligatur. Ex poculo enim testamentum Dei, vel ejus partem, velle facere esset testamento Dei ἐνιδιατίθεσθαι; quod jam firmatum, & in solo Christi sanguine ratificatum erat. Manifestum autem est intelligi Testamentum Novum, veteris populi haereditati ac servituti oppositum. Ecce dies veniunt, ait Iehovah, & pangam cum domo Israel, & cum domo Juda foedus novum. Jer. 31:31. Quod testamentum sanguine Christi jam initiabatur, juxta Heb. 9:16. Ubi testamentum est, mortem necesse est contingere testatoris. Qui sanguis effundi dicitur; ad modum sanguinis sacrificiorum quo Vetus Testam. olim dedicatum, ac perpetuo irrigatum fuit. Et dixit Moses, ecce sanguis foederis testamenti, quod pepigit Jehova vobiscum, super omnibus hisce verbis. Exod. 24:8. Et fere in sanguine omnia mundantur, juxta legem, & sine effusione sanguinis non fit remissio. Hebr. 9:22. Pro multis. Ut Novi Testam. praerogativa agnoscatur. Non enim, ut sanguis victimarum olim unicam tantum gentem expiabat, & quarundam unius solum hominis peccatum; ita Christi sanguis tam paucos adspergit. Pro multis enim ille fusus est. Cui opposite ad veteris Ecclesiae angustias mundi nomine appellantur, Joh. 3:16. & 6:33. εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, ad remissionem peccatorum, plenissimam nempe & uberrimam, oblata jam victima Deo digna. Veteris enim Testamenti sanguis, cum vere expiare non posset, πάρεσιν utcunque & noxarum dissimulationem pariebat; quae tamen meliori sanguine expiandae adhuc restabant. Eph. 2:7. coll. Col. 1:14.
units.tr: IV. The mystery of the wine is in the blood of Christ: "This is my blood" [τοῦτο ἐστὶ τὸ αἷμά μου]. "This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many, for the remission of sins," Mark 14:23; Matt. 26:28. For the pronoun τοῦτο [touto] is to be referred not to the cup but rather to τὸ αἷμα [to haima], the blood: not "this," but "this is my blood." In the same way, since the preceding clause speaks of the bread, it is not ἄρτος [artos], but "this is my body" [τοῦτο ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμά μου]. Where, however, in Luke 22:20 and 1 Cor. 11:25 it is said of the cup, "This cup is the new covenant" [τῆτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη] etc., it is an improper and sacramental way of speaking, so that the cup is understood as the seal of the covenant. For to make the cup itself the covenant of God, or a part of it, would be to ἐνιδιατίθεσθαι [enidiatithesthai], that is, to add a new disposition to God's covenant, which had already been confirmed and ratified in the blood of Christ alone. It is clear, moreover, that the New Testament is meant, set against the inheritance and bondage of the old people: "Behold, the days come, says Jehovah, when I will make with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant," Jer. 31:31. This covenant was now being inaugurated by the blood of Christ, according to Heb. 9:16: "Where there is a testament, there must of necessity be the death of the testator." This blood is said to be poured out, after the manner of the blood of the sacrifices by which the Old Testament was once dedicated and continually sprinkled. "And Moses said, Behold the blood of the covenant, which Jehovah has made with you upon all these words," Exod. 24:8. "And almost all things are purified with blood according to the law, and without shedding of blood there is no remission," Heb. 9:22. For many: so that the prerogative of the New Testament may be acknowledged. For the blood of the victims once atoned only for one nation, and the sin of some one man only; but the blood of Christ does not sprinkle so few. For it was shed for many. In contrast to the narrowness of the old Church, the world is called "the world," John 3:16 and 6:33. Εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν [eis aphesin hamartiōn], "for the remission of sins," namely the fullest and most abundant, since the victim worthy of God has now been offered. For the blood of the Old Testament, since it could not truly atone, produced a kind of πάρεσις [paresis], a passing over and a somewhat overlooking of offences, which nevertheless still had to be expiated by a better blood. Eph. 2:7, compared with Col. 1:14.

units.la: V. Jubet autem Servator saepe haec symbola usurpare, atque idem, quod ipse tum agitabat, a nobis fieri. Hoc facite, quod non est sacrificare, sed sacrum epulum celebrare. In mei recordationem. Ut alia hic sit ἀνάμνησις quam in paschate olim; hic enim sacrificii Christi, omnimque ejus beneficiorum, perpetua saneitur commemoratio. Quam non praestant, qui in Novo Test. quotidie adhuc sacrificant, litant vero nunquam. Quid enim in sacrificiis illis, quae identidem repetuntur, nisi perpetua peccati recordatio & exprobratio est? Hebr. 10:3.
units.tr: V. The Saviour bids us use these symbols often, and to do the same thing that he himself was then doing: "Do this," which is not to sacrifice, but to celebrate a sacred feast, "in remembrance of me." Here the ἀνάμνησις [anamnēsis] is different from that of the Passover of old; for here a perpetual commemoration of Christ's sacrifice and of all his benefits is established. Those do not provide it who in the New Testament still sacrifice daily, and yet never make atonement. For what is there in those sacrifices, which are repeated again and again, but a perpetual reminder and reproach of sin? Heb. 10:3.

units.la: VI. Addit Apostolus 1. Cor. 11:26. Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annunciate, usque quo venerit. Quae Novi Testamenti Haggadah est, longe sanctior & celebrior, ac illa paschatis: de qua Exod. 12:26,27. Et erit, quando dicent vobis filii vestri, quis cultus hic vobis? & dicetis, sacrificium Paschæ illud est Iehova, qui gradum fecit prater domos filiorum Israel in Ægypto, eum percuteret Ægyptum, & domos nostras eriperet. Ad quem morem manifesta hic allusio est.
units.tr: VI. The Apostle adds, 1 Cor. 11:26: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." This is the Haggadah of the New Testament, far holier and more celebrated than that of the Passover, concerning which Exod. 12:26, 27 says: "And it shall be, when your children ask you, What is this service to you? you shall say, It is the sacrifice of the Passover to Jehovah, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians and delivered our houses." Here there is a clear allusion to that custom.

units.la: VII. Atque est hæc vera & potissima mortis Christi annunciatio; ubi anima omnem fructum ac dulcedinem ejus, intimo sensu quærens, cam haurit & gustat, ac, cœlo ipso plena, inter immortalium donorum delicias tantum non expirat. Ad quod summa virium contentione, maximoque animæ motu opus est; cui solida hæc solatia tum demum insinuantur, cum terrena fæce remota, puro in lumine Christum, cunctaque ejus beneficia contemplatur, iisque artissime inhæresci, & immoritur. Qui lætantis animi motus, & gaudia, & gratulatio, & exultatio, & acquiescentia, procul ab anxietate & terrore omni, veras S. Coenæ praxis, & fidei triumphus est. Non parum enim de animæ pace ac serenitate delibant, nec epuli hujus delicias capiunt, qui S. Coenæ praxin magna ex parte in tristitia atque horrore ob peccata constituunt; &, ad mortis Christi mentionem, aut quamlibet historiæ illius tractationem, ad luctum ac tristitiam fideles vocant; quasi ea fletu decoranda sit, atque ea demum digna mortis ejus celebratio sit. Qui error est. Cum mors Christi, ut dignissimum pro peccatis nostris sacrificium, pia gratulatione potius prosequenda sit: neque illi, tanquam tragico spectaculo, illacrymandum, sed nobiliori ac spirituali prorsus affectu ea commemoranda, & non sine sensu, perpetuo recolenda est, cum universæ salutis nostræ summam, ac fidei nostræ fastigium contineat. Unde & Christus, in carne adhuc agens, & morti proximus discipulorum lacrymas, teneriores que affectus cohibuit, Luc. 23: 28. ut multo minus in Christum glorificatum nunc illa conveniant. Christus enim, potiores animi operationem requirebat, suaque in imagine Dei sanctitatem, justitiam, amorem, bonitatem, spectari volebat. Cumque mors ejus Euangelii compendium sit, in illa animam vagam, & inquietam & de peccatis suis quærentem, quiescere tandem, & lætari atque æternum exultare convenit.
units.tr: VII. This is the true and chief proclamation of the death of Christ, where the soul, seeking every fruit and sweetness of it with an inward sense, draws it in and tastes it, and, filled with heaven itself, almost faints away among the delights of immortal gifts. For this a great effort of strength and a very great stirring of the soul are needed; to this solid comforts are then insinuated, when earthly dregs are removed and, in pure light, the soul contemplates Christ and all his benefits, and clings to them most closely and dies to itself.
