Such movements of a joyful mind, and joy, and thanksgiving, and exultation, and quiet acquiescence, far from all anxiety and terror, are the true practice of the Holy Supper and the triumph of faith. For those who mostly make the practice of the Holy Supper a matter of sadness and dread over sins, taste little of the peace and serenity of the soul, nor do they enjoy the delights of this feast. And at the mention of Christ's death, or any treatment of that history, they call the faithful to grief and sorrow, as though it were to be adorned with tears and only so a worthy celebration of his death. This is an error. Since the death of Christ, as the most worthy sacrifice for our sins, ought rather to be followed with holy thanksgiving, it is not to be wept over as a tragic spectacle, but is to be commemorated with a nobler and altogether spiritual feeling, and to be continually recalled with understanding, since it contains the sum of all our salvation and the summit of our faith. Hence Christ himself, while still in the flesh and close to death, restrained the tears and tenderer feelings of his disciples (Luke 23:28), so much the less should such feelings be fitting now toward Christ glorified. For Christ required the more excellent working of the mind, and wanted his holiness, justice, love and goodness to be seen in his image of God. And since his death is the summary of the Gospel, it is fitting that the soul, wandering, restless, and seeking for its sins, should at last rest in it, and rejoice, and exult for ever.

units.la: VIII. Atque ita fide potissimum S. Coenæ praxis absolvitur. Cujus universum opus his videre licet. Stipulatur enim eam Deus: Exploret autem quisque seipsum, & sic ex pane edat, & ex poculo bibat. 1 Cor. 11: 28. Respondet ad illam stipulationem homo, & pulcherrimam fidei confessionem ὁμολογίαν, suumque cum Deo consensum, edit. Denique, pignore isto roboratus, jam Deum accedere, deque hæreditate vi-cissim cissim interrogare, audet. Quae fidei restipulatio est. Ita omnia foederis faciem habent.
units.tr: VIII. And so the practice of the Holy Supper is chiefly completed by faith. The whole work of it may be seen in these terms. God stipulates it: "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup." 1 Cor. 11:28. Man answers that stipulation, and gives forth a most beautiful confession of faith [ὁμολογία], and his consent with God. Finally, strengthened by this pledge, he dares in turn to approach God and to ask about the inheritance. This is the restipulation of faith. Thus all things have the appearance of a covenant.

units.la: IX. Atque hinc opus est seria & severa sui ipsius exploratione, de fame nostra & siti spirituali, de fide in Christum, de sanctioris vitae proposito; ne audacI manu mysticos cibos consceleremus, ac corporis dominici rei deprehendamur. Exploret se ipsum homo, & sic ex pane edat, & ex poculo bibat. Nam qui edit, & bibit, indigne, damnationem sibi edit, & bibit, non discernens corpus Domini. 1. Cor. 11:28, 29.
units.tr: IX. Hence there is need of a serious and strict self-examination: concerning our hunger and spiritual thirst, concerning faith in Christ, concerning the purpose of a holier life; lest we rashly defile the mystical food with a guilty hand and be found guilty of the body of the Lord. "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks damnation to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." 1 Cor. 11:28, 29.

units.la: X. Ex quibus tandem patet, quis S. Coenae sit usus & fructus, quioptime exprimitur 1. Cor. 10: 16. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne est communio sanguinis Iesu Christi? panis quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi? Est enim coena illa artissimae cum Christo unionis pignus, ac mutuae quoque fidelium communionis vinculum, & fraternae charitatis coagulum: sequiturque eam fidei confirmatio, & roboratio, quae, de Deo jam secura, pignore isto coelum sperare, & tantum non praelibare, audet.
units.tr: X. From these things it finally becomes clear what the use and fruit of the Holy Supper is, which is best expressed in 1 Cor. 10:16: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Jesus Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" For that feast is a pledge of the closest union with Christ, and also a bond of the mutual communion of believers and a binding together of brotherly love. There follows from it the confirmation and strengthening of faith, which, now secure concerning God, dares to hope for heaven by this pledge and, as it were, to taste it beforehand.

units.la: XI. Ubi ab una parte rejicienda Latinorum superstitio. Qui, uti S. Coenae convivium in sacrificium converterunt, ita missis suis, tanquam amuletis, utuntur, ad bona quaelibet impetranda, & mala averruncanda; nec homines solum, sed & bruta, resque inanimes, hoc sacro expiant. Deficiunt ab altera parte Sociniani, qui nulla hic amoris Dei pignora, nullum foederis signaculum, nullam fidei obsignationem, nec quicquam denique a Deo nobis dari, aut conferri, ad hanc mensam volunt: solas autem hominis hic partes esse statuunt; qui emortuali isto epulo mortem ac martyrium Christi quotidie concelebret, ac Christianae religionis fidem, & charitatem in fratres, publice profiteatur. Qui & Anabaptistarum, ac ex parte plerorumque Remonstrantium, error est. Nisi quod de fidei confirmatione tenuiter addunt, illam, uti aliis pietatis officiis, ita isto actu non leviter roborari. Ita hi S. Coenam partem solummodo divini cultus, & merum hominis opus, agnoscunt. Cum tamen praeterea sacramentum Domini sit, & convivium, mensa, & poculum Domini, appelletur, in quo a Domino pascimur & potamur. 1. Cor. 11:20, 21. & 10:21. & 12: 13. Quorum vocabulorum vim praestare hi homines non possunt.
units.tr: XI. On the one side the superstition of the Latins is to be rejected. Just as they have turned the banquet of the Supper into a sacrifice, so they use their masses as amulets, to obtain whatever goods and to avert evils; and they cleanse not only men but also beasts and inanimate things with this sacred rite. On the other side the Socinians fall short, who in this table want no pledges of the love of God, no seal of the covenant, no confirmation of faith, and in short want nothing to be given or conferred on us by God; they hold that only the part of man is here; he, they say, celebrates daily in this funeral feast the death and martyrdom of Christ, and publicly professes the faith and charity of the Christian religion toward the brethren. This is also the error of the Anabaptists, and in part of most of the Remonstrants; except that they add weakly that faith is confirmed in this act not lightly, just as by other offices of piety. Thus they acknowledge the Holy Supper to be only a part of divine worship and a mere work of man. Yet it is moreover a sacrament of the Lord, and is called the banquet, the table, and the cup of the Lord, at which we are fed and given drink by the Lord. 1 Cor. 11:20, 21; 10:21; 12:13. These men cannot render the force of these words.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: De effectis Eucharistiae, unione cum Christo & manducatione corporis ejus.
units.tr: On the effects of the Eucharist, union with Christ, and the eating of his body.

units.la: I. SEquitur igitur, postquam symbolorum & rituum mysteria vi- dimus, ut de isto S. Coenae effectu ac fructu, quam unionem nostri cum Christo esse dicimus, paulo amplius videamus: ac 2. modum explicemus, quo ea nobis exhibetur; per manduca- tionem videl. corporis Christi, & potationem sanguinis ejus. In qua re praecipuum coenae hujus mysterium consistit.
units.tr: I. Having seen the mysteries of the symbols and rites, we should now look a little more fully at the effect and fruit of this Lord's Supper, which we say is our union with Christ, and (2) explain the manner in which it is given to us, namely by eating the body of Christ and drinking his blood. The chief mystery of this Supper consists in this matter.

units.la: II. Unio cum Christo, quae in S. Coena nobis repraesentatur & ob- signatur, intelligitur hic mystica & spiritualis: quae μονὴ manso Christi ut in nobis, Joh. 14:23. κόλλησις agglutinatio, 1. Cor. 6:17. κατοίκησις in habitatio, Eph. 3:17. συσσωμάτωσις concorporatio, Eph. 3:6. in Scripturis dicitur. Quamque variis similitudinibus, tum a natura, tum a societate civili, tum ab arte desumptis, Spiritus S. adumbrat. Quales sunt, unio membrorum & corporis, 1. Cor. 12:12, 17. Rom. 12:5. Eph. 5:30. Col. 1:18. Palmitis & vitis, Joh. 15:5. adoptivi surculi & arboris, Rom. 6:5. Cibi & corporis nostri, Joh. 6. Mariti & uxoris, Eph. 5:23. Lapidis angularis & aedificii, Eph. 2:20,21,22. Hebr. 3:6.
units.tr: II. The union with Christ, which is represented and sealed to us in the Lord's Supper, is here understood as mystical and spiritual. Scripture calls it Christ's abiding [μονή] in us (John 14:23), gluing together [κόλλησις] (1 Cor. 6:17), dwelling [κατοίκησις] (Eph. 3:17), and being joined in one body [συσσωμάτωσις] (Eph. 3:6). The Holy Spirit shadows it forth by various likenesses, drawn from nature, from civil society and from the crafts. Such are the union of the members and the body (1 Cor. 12:12, 17; Rom. 12:5; Eph. 5:30; Col. 1:18); the branch and vine (John 15:5); the grafted shoot and tree (Rom. 6:5); food and our body (John 6); husband and wife (Eph. 5:23); the cornerstone and building (Eph. 2:20, 21, 22; Heb. 3:6).

units.la: 2. Cor. 6:16. Panis, ex multis granis coacti, 1. Cor. 10:17. & vestium denique, Gal. 3:27.
units.tr: (The temple of God, 2 Cor. 6:16); bread, made up of many grains (1 Cor. 10:17); and finally garments (Gal. 3:27).

units.la: III. Praestruitur mysticae huic unioni personalis filii Dei cum natu- ra humana unio & conjugium. Prius enim Dei filius ad nos descendere debebat, quam nos ipsi misceri poteramus. Quod homo est, Christus esse volui; ut homo, quod Christus est, esse posset. inquit Cyprianus. Quanquam haec naturae cognatio non sufficit, nisi arctius praeterea vinculum accedat; a parte Christi, Spiritus; a nostra parte, fides. Quo mutuo amplexu unio haec peragitur. Et in uno Spiritu nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus. 1. Cor. 12:13. In hoc cognoscimus, quod in ipso manemus, & ipse in nobis, quia ex Spiritu suo nobis dedit. 1. Joh. 4:13. Ut habitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. Eph. 3:17. Gal. 2:20. Utex unionis hujus modo & forma spiritualem eam esse constet.
units.tr: III. The personal union and marriage of the Son of God with human nature prepares the way for this mystical union. For the Son of God had to come down to us before we could be joined to him. "What man is, Christ willed to be, so that what Christ is, man might be able to be," says Cyprian. Yet this kinship of nature is not enough unless a closer bond is added: on Christ's part, the Spirit; on our part, faith. By this mutual embrace the union is brought about. "In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body" (1 Cor. 12:13). "We know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit" (1 John 4:13). "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Eph. 3:17; Gal. 2:20). From the manner and form of this union it is clear that it is spiritual.

units.la: IV. Atque haec jam nostra cum Pontificiis controversia est: an ad beatam cum Christo communionem sufficiat hoc Spiritus & fidei vinculum: an vero praeterea corporea unione opus sit, & de carne Christi gustare, deque sanguine ejus bibere, ipsumque corpus Christi corpus nostrum intrare necesse sit, ad unionem hanc consummandam? atque illud in S. Coena demum obtineat? Quae crassa nimis adversariorum sententia est. Nos prius asserimus, nec corporeo contactu in tanto mysterio opus esse statuimus. Sufficit enim, & viva fides, & mutui Spiritus vinculum, amorisque Dei traditum & usurpatum in S. Coena symbolum, & pignus certissimum. Quae longe uberiora sunt, quam qualiscunque corporum accessus. Ut perverse Pontificiiunionem hanc cum Christo realem negent, quod corporea non sit. Cum vel inter homines spirituum actiones, & praecipue inde orta animorum concordia, carnali ac corporea operatione, & inde producta corporum unione, longe praestantior ac perfectior sit; & fructus ac effectus maxime reales edat.
units.tr: IV. This is the point at issue between us and the Papists: whether this bond of the Spirit and of faith suffices for blessed communion with Christ, or whether a bodily union is also needed, so that we must taste the flesh of Christ and drink his blood, and the very body of Christ must enter our body, in order to complete this union, and this is obtained only in the Lord's Supper. This is the adversaries' view, which is far too crude. We first assert that in so great a mystery no bodily contact is needed. For a living faith and the bond of the mutual Spirit, and the symbol and sure pledge of God's love, handed over and received in the Lord's Supper, are enough. These are far richer than any kind of bodily approach. The Papists wrongly deny that this union with Christ is real because it is not bodily, when even among men the actions of spirits, and above all the concord of minds arising from them, is far more excellent and perfect than a carnal and bodily operation and the union of bodies produced by it, and it yields the most real fruits and effects.

units.la: V. Effectum denique hujus unionis praeterea est, mutua fidelium unio, & consensus, in uno capite Christo: de cujus Spiritu omnes animantur; & pari ac iscorripta fide praediti, eodemque charitatis igne accensi, iisdem denique aquis abluti, ac cibi pasti, Deum divinaque omnia communia habent.
units.tr: V. Finally, the effect of this union is also the mutual union and agreement of the faithful in the one head, Christ, by whose Spirit all are quickened; and, endowed with the same faith received, kindled with the same fire of love, washed with the same waters, and fed with the same food, they hold all things in common, God and the divine gifts.

units.la: VI. Haec autem cum Christo unio cum in S. Coena potissimum peragatur, & manducationis imagine pingatur, de ista unionis illius modo ac medio nunc videndum. Estque illa manducatio corporis Christi duplex, cum externa & symbolica in S. Coena, tum interna & spiritualis, quae per Spiritum Christi & fidem fit, atque omnium locorum & temporum est.
units.tr: VI. Since this union with Christ is carried out chiefly in the Lord's Supper and is depicted under the image of eating, we must now consider the manner and means of that union. This eating of the body of Christ is twofold: one external and symbolic, in the Lord's Supper; the other internal and spiritual, which takes place through the Spirit of Christ and faith, and belongs to all places and times.

units.la: VII. Externa unio varia fuit, pro symbolorum, quae Deus olim exhibuit, diversitate. Caeterum sub manducationis imagine eam veteribus quoque repraesentatam fuisse, ex sacris ac miraculosis cibis, uti manna, agno paschali, sacrificalibus in templo epulis &c. satis patet. Quo etiam faciunt promissiones de cibatione & exsatiatione populi Dei factae: cui dabitur edere pinguia terrae, Psal. 22: 30. cui mensa proposita est, Psal. 23: 5. & similes. Ad quorum rationem S. Coenae institutum in Nov. Test. quoque exigendum est.
units.tr: VII. The external union varied according to the diversity of the symbols which God once exhibited. Moreover, that the ancients too were given this union under the image of eating is plain enough from the sacred and miraculous foods, such as the manna, the paschal lamb, the sacrificial feasts in the temple, and so on. The promises made about feeding and satisfying the people of God point the same way: to whom it will be given "to eat the fat things of the earth" (Ps. 22:30), for whom "a table is set" (Ps. 23:5), and similar passages. The institution of the Supper in the New Testament must also be explained in the light of these.

units.la: VIII. Non enim in S. Coena spectanda tantum qualiscunque cibi & potus cum Christi corpore & sanguine, spirituali animae nostrae cibo, analogia. Altius enim surgendum est. Est enim coena haec plane sacrificalis, atque ad eum modum praecipue consideranda, & cum veterum conviviis, quæ de victimarum carnibus in templo celebrabant, comparanda est. Quod & Apostolus facit. 1. Cor. 10: 16, 17, 18. Poculum be- nedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne est communio sangui- nis Christi? Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi? Quia unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Omnes enim unius panis participes su- mus. Videte Israëlem secundum carnem. Nonne qui edunt sacrificia, al- taris participes sunt? Quare operæ pretium est, ut nostræ cœnæ mysterium pervideamus, prius sacras veterum cœnas, & manducandi ritum, & sacrificales dapes, lustrare.
units.tr: VIII. For in the Lord's Supper we must not look only at some analogy between food and drink on the one hand and the body and blood of Christ, the spiritual food of our soul, on the other. We must rise higher. This Supper is plainly sacrificial, and must be considered chiefly in that way, and compared with the feasts of the ancients, who celebrated their meals on the flesh of the victims in the temple. The Apostle also does this: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of one bread. Look at Israel according to the flesh: do not those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar?" (1 Cor. 10:16, 17, 18). Therefore it is worth while to examine the mystery of our Supper, first by surveying the sacred meals of the ancients, the rite of eating, and the sacrificial feasts.

units.la: IX. Hoc autem veteris legis institutum erat, quod sacerdotibus, peracto sacrificio, de victimarum carnibus epulari fas esset. Quæ manducatio sacrificii pars & appendix erat: utpote quod rite factum censeri non poterat, nisi sacerdos de partibus illis degustasset. Quod tum in eucharisticis, tum in expiatoriis, locum habuit. Lev. 6: 16, 17, 18, 25, 26. & 7: 6, 7. 31-34. Cujus rei ratio editur Lev. 10: 17. quod Sacerdos ferre debebat peccatum cœtus, atque ipse aliquo modo pro eo victima fieri. Quod tum fieri censebatur, cum partes victimæ delibabat, ac in propriam substantiam convertebat. Quæ egregia Christi sacerdotis pariter, & victimæ nostræ, repræsentatio erat.
units.tr: IX. Under the old law it was an established practice that, once the sacrifice was completed, the priests were allowed to feast on the flesh of the victims. This eating was a part and appendix of the sacrifice, since the sacrifice could not be regarded as rightly performed unless the priest had first tasted of those portions. This applied both to the thank-offerings and to the sin-offerings (Lev. 6:16, 17, 18, 25, 26; 7:6, 7, 31–34). The reason for this is given in Lev. 10:17: the priest was to bear the sin of the congregation, and in some way himself become a victim for it. This was held to happen when he tasted the portions of the victim and turned them into his own substance. This was an outstanding representation of Christ, both our priest and our victim.

units.la: X. Præter sacerdotem manducabat de victimarum carnibus quoque populus. Quod in Eucharisticis tantum locum habuit. Hæc enim fundamentalis sacrificiorum lex erat, neminem de piaculari victima pro iefe oblata participare posse; ut idem simul ipsi & piamentum & cibus esset. Unde nec ipsi sacerdoti, qui de victimis, pro cœtu oblatis, epulabatur, in proprio sacrificio, aut in sacrificio pro toto cœtu, hoc licuit. Lev. 4: 3. & seqq. 13. & seqq. & 6: 30. Adeo ut caro ista, quæ non modo res sancta erat, sed & legis instituto peccatorem quoque sanctificabat, tamen ipsi interdicta & vetita esset. Quæ non levis infirmitatis sacrificiorum istorum accusatio erat, quæ nec cibum, nec verum piamentum, peccatori præstare poterant. Unde abstinere illis, aliamque victimam, aliasque epulas, quæ animam vere nutrire possent, expectare debebat. Sicuti non aliam ob rationem quoque sanguinis, uti rei sacræ, esus tum vetitus fuit. Nam anima carnis est in sanguine, & ego dedi eum vobis super altare, ad expiandum pro animabus vestris. Nam sanguis pro anima expiat. Ideo dixi filiis Israelis, nulla anima ex vobis edet sanguinem. Lev. 17: 11, 15.
units.tr: X. Besides the priest, the people also ate of the flesh of the victims. This took place only in the thank-offerings. For this was the fundamental law of the sacrifices: no one could partake of a sin-offering offered for himself, so that the same victim might be at once his atonement and his food. Hence not even the priest himself, who fed on the victims offered for the congregation, was allowed to do so in his own sacrifice, or in a sacrifice for the whole congregation (Lev. 4:3 ff., 13 ff.; 6:30). So the flesh, which was not only a holy thing but by the institution of the law also sanctified the sinner, was nevertheless forbidden and prohibited to him. This was no slight accusation of the weakness of those sacrifices, which could give the sinner neither food nor true atonement. So he had to abstain from them and wait for another victim and other feasts, which could truly nourish the soul. For a similar reason the eating of blood, as a holy thing, was forbidden at that time: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for the blood makes atonement by means of the life. Therefore I said to the children of Israel, no soul among you shall eat blood" (Lev. 17:11, 15).

units.la: XI. Atque hæc manducationis sub Vet. Test. ratio erat. Ex qua manducationis illius, quæ sub Novo Test.institura est, præstantia patescit.
units.tr: XI. This, then, was the manner of eating under the Old Testament. From the excellence of that eating which was to be instituted under the New Testament, its superiority becomes plain.

units.la: 1. Hoc enim jam satis patet,Christi carnem non simpliciter in cibum animæ proponi; in qua analogia multi subsistere amant, multaque panis & vini cum Christo similitudines,interdum parum appositas, congerunt; sed præcipue considerandam eam, ut carnem piacularis victimæ. Ut mensa hæc sacrificalis prorsus sit, 2. Cum manducare autem victimam istam jubcamur, quid hoc aliud, quam intimam nostri cum ea unionem designat, qua unum evadimus cum victima pro nobis oblata, ac si ipsi oblati ac mortui fuissemus? 3. Cum autem nulla veteribus cum victimis piacularibus permitteretur communio, solumque de eucharisticis gustare permitterentur: hic, contraria lege, de Christo, ut victima expiatoria, edere jubemur. Accipite, edite, hoc ENIM est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur. 4. Idemque circa sanguinem fit. Cujus usus, non solum populo, sed & sacerdotibus olim, strictissima lege, ablatus, quia altaribus debebatur, ad expiationem faciendam, nunc fidelibus ob eandem rationem permittitur. Bibite ex eo omnes: hic ENIM est sanguis meus, effusus pro multis, in remissionem peccatorum. Quod notatu dignum est, eandem ob rationem sanguinis communionem à Christo fidelibus dari, ob quam à Mose interdictus olim erat.
units.tr: 1. For it is now sufficiently clear that the flesh of Christ is not simply set forth as food for the soul. Many love to rest in this analogy, and they heap up many likenesses between bread and wine and Christ, sometimes not very apt ones; but the flesh must be considered chiefly as the flesh of a sin-offering, so that this table is altogether a sacrificial table. 2. Now when we are bidden to eat that victim, what does this signify but an intimate union with it, by which we become one with the victim offered for us, as if we ourselves had been offered and had died? 3. Whereas under the old law no fellowship was permitted with the atoning sacrifices, and only the eucharistic offerings might be tasted, here, by a contrary law, we are bidden to eat of Christ as the expiatory victim. Take, eat; for this is my body, which is broken for you. 4. The same holds of the blood. Its use, which of old was withheld from the people and even from the priests by the strictest law, because it was owed to the altars for the making of atonement, is now granted to believers for the same reason. Drink of it, all of you; for this is my blood, shed for many for the remission of sins. It is worth noting that Christ gives believers communion in the blood for the same reason that Moses once forbade it.

units.la: XII. Offertur autem nobis carnis ac sanguinis Christi communio, sub panis & vini symbolis. Alieno enim sanguine, post Christi sanguinem, opus non amplius est. Unde pecudum lanienæ nunc cessant; & non cæsarum ovium vel boum cruorem, vel carnes nobis gustandas Christus offert; sed sub quotidiani cibi ac potus imagine sese ipsum suamque carnem & sanguinem fidelibus exhibet. Quorum symbolorum analogia cum corpore & sanguine Christi nunc perspici potest. Non enim longe lateque panis & vini proprietates hic conquirendæ, ut quibusdam in more est; sed in sola cibi ac potus ratione, quæ una hic spectanda est, conquiescendum est.
units.tr: XII. Now the communion of Christ's flesh and blood is offered to us under the signs of bread and wine. For there is no longer any need of another's blood, since the blood of Christ has been shed. Hence the slaughter of cattle has now ceased; and Christ does not offer us to taste the blood of slaughtered sheep or oxen, or their flesh; but under the image of daily food and drink he gives himself, his flesh and blood, to the faithful. The analogy of these signs with the body and blood of Christ can now be seen. For it is not necessary to search far and wide for the properties of bread and wine, as some are wont to do; rather, we must rest in the one respect of food and drink, which alone is to be regarded here.

units.la: XIII. Atque omnis symbolorum illorum cum Christi corpore analogia, quæ quidem in Scripturis fundamentum habet, huc reduci potest. 1. Uti panis ac vinum fulciendo corpori faciunt, ita spiritualis animæ alitura in Christo adumbratur. Unde Christi corpus non simpliciter, qua tale, sed quatenus fractum, ac pro nobis datum est, hic consideratur. Qua sola ratione animæ cibus ac potus est. Ego sum panis ille vivus, qui e cœlo descendi. Si quis ederit ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum. Panis autem, quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita. Joh. 6: 51. 2. Pertinet huc quoque symbolorum diversitas, ut non carnem solum, sed & sanguinem Christi, eumque e corpore effusum, nobis porrigi intelligamus. 3. Granorum multitudo, ex quibus panis conquitur, & innumeri uvarum botri, qui in unum lacum despumant, multitudinem fidelium, eorumque in uno Christo unionem dicunt. 4 Utque de uno pane fideles gustant, atque de eodem poculo bibunt; ita unius Christi, ad universam Ecclesiam implendam, sufficientia depingitur.
units.tr: XIII. And the whole analogy of those signs with the body of Christ, which indeed has its foundation in the Scriptures, can be brought back to this. 1. Just as bread and wine sustain and strengthen the body, so the spiritual nourishment of the soul is foreshadowed in Christ. Hence the body of Christ is considered here not simply as such, but as broken and given for us; and only in this way is it food and drink for the soul. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever. And the bread that I shall give is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world. John 6:51. 2. To this also belongs the diversity of the signs, so that we understand that not only the flesh but also the blood of Christ, poured out from his body, is offered to us. 3. The multitude of grains from which bread is made, and the countless clusters of grapes which foam together into one vat, signify the multitude of the faithful and their union in the one Christ. 4. And just as the faithful partake of one bread and drink from the same cup, so the sufficiency of the one Christ to fill the whole Church is portrayed.

units.la: XIV. Ex qua signorum analogia, ac cum resignata unione, fluunt locutiones sacramentales, in Scripturis frequentatæ; in quibus signi & rei signatæ nomina inter se permutantur, sine ulla transubstantiatione & consubstantiatione.
units.tr: XIV. From this analogy of the signs, and from the union signified, there arise the sacramental expressions, frequent in the Scriptures; in which the names of the sign and of the thing signified are interchanged, without any transubstantiation or consubstantiation.

units.la: XV. Ac simul patet, quæ sit ratio unionis, inter symbola, ac Christi corpus; non substantialis, sed relativa, sive significationis & obsignationis. Ita tamen, ut aliquid præter nudam figuram hic extet, ac nobis donetur: (contra ac Pontificii calumniantur) ipsum videl. Christi corpus, quod realiter per Spir. nobis datur, & oblato præterea pignore obsignatur, & per fidem apprehenditur. Distinguenda enim hic sunt symbola & veritas: atque aliquid præter externa symbola fideles accipiunt. Sicut enim duæ sunt sacramenti res, terrestris & cœlestis: duæ personæ illud dispensantes, minister & Christus: duplex manducatio, externa & interna: ita etiam duplex est exhibitio; una rei corporeæ, omnibus accumbentibus ex æquo a ministro facta, altera rei spiritualis, solis fidelibus a Christo præstita.
units.tr: XV. And at the same time it becomes plain what kind of union there is between the signs and the body of Christ: not substantial, but relative, that is, of signification and sealing. Yet it is so, that something beyond the bare figure is present here and is given to us (contrary to what the Papists slander): namely the very body of Christ, which is really given to us through the Spirit, and is sealed by the pledge offered, and is apprehended through faith. For the signs and the reality must be distinguished here: and believers receive something beyond the outward signs. For just as there are two things of the sacrament, earthly and heavenly; two persons dispensing it, the minister and Christ; a twofold eating, outward and inward; so also there is a twofold giving: one of the bodily thing, made by the minister equally to all who sit at the table, the other of the spiritual thing, bestowed by Christ on believers alone.

units.la: XVI. Manducationem externam & symbolicam consequitur interna & spiritualis; quæ externæ medulla & scopus est, & absque ea solius Spiritus ac fidei ope peragitur. Habet autem illa cum Christo communio manducationis quandam speciem; atque ita in Scripturis appellatur; quæ ad eandem similitudinem carnem quoque ejus cum cibo, & sanguinem cum potu comparant; cum illa sola animæ nostræ vitam & alimentum præstare possint. Quæ rite intelligenda sunt. Est enim caro Christi cibus noster, non sua substantia, sed solo mortis ac satisfactionis ejus merito. Habet enim ea cum reliquis cibis hoc quoque convenientiæ, quod similiter frangi & conteri debuerit. Atque hoc carni Christi proprium fuit, divinitate pretium & valorem ad istud sacrificium conferente. Atque ut corporea esca, ut corporis sit fultura, manducari debet, ita Christi caro per fidem apprehendi, atque isto ore accipi quoque
units.tr: XVI. The outward and symbolic eating is followed by the inward and spiritual eating; which is the marrow and aim of the outward, and is carried on without it by the sole working of the Spirit and of faith. Now this communion with Christ has a certain likeness of eating; and so it is called in the Scriptures; and for the same likeness they also compare his flesh with food and his blood with drink, since only these can supply the life and nourishment of our soul. These things must be understood rightly. For the flesh of Christ is our food, not by its substance, but solely by the merit of his death and satisfaction. For it has this also in common with other foods, that it had to be similarly broken and ground. And this was peculiar to the flesh of Christ, since his divinity gave worth and value to that sacrifice. And just as bodily food must be eaten that it may be the sustenance of the body, so the flesh of Christ must be apprehended through faith and received by that mouth as well.

units.la: Ⅽ Ⅽ c 2 que debet. Atque isto demum pacto vitam nostram spiritualem, hoc est peccatorum remissionem & regenerationem (in quibus vita illa consistit) nobis & confert, & auget.
units.tr: Ⅽ Ⅽ c 2 It must be. And in this way at last it both bestows on us and increases our spiritual life, that is, the remission of sins and regeneration (in which that life consists).

units.la: XVII. Agit de interna ac spirituali illa manducatione late Servator, Joh. c. 6. ubi Judæis, corpoream escam captantibus, longe meliorem cibum offert, carnem ac sanguinem suum, per mannam olim adumbrata. Ut non sola cibi analogia hic spectetur, sed ad sacros & mysticos Veteris Testam. cibos manifesta fiat allusio. De manducatione autem sacramentali coenæ ipsum non agere patet, quod illa tum nondum instituta, nec adeo stricte ac absolute ad salutem necessaria fuerit, vel fatentibus adversariis, ac ea quæ hic refertur, Contra autem manducationem illam fide sola constare, satis claris verbis ipse Salvator innuit. com. 35. Ego sum panis vita. Qui venit ad me, non esuriet. Et qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam. conf. com. 40, 47, 48, 51. Et præterea, ut à crastino illo esu auditores averteret, carnem suam, materialiter nimirum sumtam, & ita manducatam (quæ stulta horum hominum opinio erat) non prodesse; quin in coelum tandem subvehendam, ut humani oris esca esse nequeat, aperte edicit, com. 62. Hoc vos scandalizat? si igitur conspiciatis filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius? Addens com. 63. quod Spiritus sit id quod vivificet: quod caro nihil prosit: quod verba quæ loquebatur ipsis, Spiritus sint & vita sint.
units.tr: XVII. The Saviour speaks at length of this inward and spiritual eating in John chapter 6, where, offering the Jews, who were seeking bodily food, a far better food, his flesh and blood, previously foreshadowed by the manna. So the analogy of food is not the only one considered here, but an express allusion is made to the sacred and mystical foods of the Old Testament. That he is not speaking here of the sacramental eating of the Supper is clear, since that had not yet been instituted, nor was it so strictly and absolutely necessary to salvation, as even our adversaries concede; and the eating spoken of here is different. On the other hand, that this eating consists in faith alone the Saviour himself hints in quite clear words, verse 35: I am the bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst. Cf. verses 40, 47, 48, 51. And moreover, to turn his hearers away from that eating of the next day, he plainly declares, verse 62, that his flesh, taken materially and so eaten (which was the foolish opinion of these men), would profit nothing; rather that he would at last be carried up into heaven, so that it could not be food for the human mouth: Does this scandalize you? What if then you should see the Son of man ascending where he was before? adding in verse 63 that it is the Spirit who quickens, that the flesh profits nothing, and that the words he spoke to them are spirit and life.

units.la: XVIII. Mirum vero est, eos manducationem & nutritionem carnalem & corporalem in hoc loco adeo urgere 1. cum omnes similitudines, quibus unio cum Christo exprimitur, spiritualiter intelligendæ sint: 2. cum ea sacramentorum natura sit, ut a signorum potestate non excedant 3. nec in baptismo corporalem & proprie dictam nativitatem ipsi adversarii intelligant. 4. cum denique & alibi in Scriptura famis & sitis spiritualis, ejusdemque generis cibationis ac potationis, fiat mentio. 5. Cum corporalis manducatio nec à Christo in Coena usurpata sit, nec sine manifesta contradictione usurpari potuerit, nec deinque à fidelibus usurpanda sit. 6. utpote & inutilis, nec ad salutem quicquam faciens, cujus nec signum, nec res signata, est: & flagitiosa, cum vel ipsa natura ab humanis cibis adhorreat; in quo scelere illi tamen religionis summam constituunt: & summo in Christum dedecore ac contumelia mista; indignum enim est vorare quod adores, rursusque adorare quod devores: denique impossibilis ac multis in partibus secum ipsa pugnans.
units.tr: XVIII. It is indeed strange that they press so hard on bodily and corporeal eating and nourishment in this passage: 1. since all the likenesses by which union with Christ is expressed must be understood spiritually; 2. since the nature of the sacraments is such that they do not go beyond the power of the signs; 3. nor do our adversaries themselves understand a bodily and properly so-called birth in baptism; 4. since finally mention is made elsewhere in Scripture of spiritual hunger and thirst, and of a feeding and drinking of the same kind; 5. since bodily eating was neither used by Christ in the Supper, nor could it be used without manifest contradiction, nor is it to be used by the faithful afterwards; 6. being both useless, contributing nothing to salvation, having neither sign nor thing signified; and shameful, since nature itself shrinks from human food, yet in this crime they place the chief part of religion; and mixed with the greatest dishonour and insult to Christ, for it is unworthy to devour what one adores and then again to adore what one has devoured; lastly, it is impossible and in many respects self-contradictory.

units.la: XIX. Quod objiciunt, 1. Christum carnem suam vere appellare
units.tr: XIX. Their objection, 1: that Christ calls his flesh truly his own

units.la: cibum, & sanguinem vere potum, com. 55. id non de carnali manducatione modo, sed de relationis veritate, inter Christum & cibum externum, ac omni similitudinis via pondere, intelligendum est conf. Joh. 15: 1. Ego sum vitis vera. Quod 2. de crebra & expressa adeo carnis ac sanguinis ejus mentione addunt, quae inutilis foret, si nihil de carne ejus gustare liceat; cum fides divinitatem Christi potissimum intueatur :id jam supra explicuimus, fidemque Christi carne, ut redemtionis pretio, proprie pasci, diximus: cui divinitas dignitatem & valorem tribuit.
units.tr: Food, and blood truly drink, at verse 55, is to be understood not only of carnal eating but of the true relation between Christ and the outward food, by every way of likeness and weight; cf. John 15:1, I am the true vine. As to their second point, that they add the frequent and express mention of his flesh and blood, which would be pointless if it were not lawful to taste anything of his flesh, since faith looks above all to the divinity of Christ: we have already explained this above, and we said that faith feeds properly on the flesh of Christ as on the price of redemption, to which his divinity gives dignity and worth.

units.la: XX. Ut non excusanda sit Pontificiorum stupiditas, qui ipsam carnem Christi adhuc esitandam, & saltem carnalem manducationem cum spirituali conjungendam, idque ad salutem unice facere, urgent. Quae non commenta, sed portenta sunt. Quae auget praeterea Cardinalis Perronius, qui corpus Christi, non solum passione sua & merito, sed praeterea, uti veram causam efficientem, vivifica vi praeditum esse; & in carne Christi formalem residentiam facultatis vivificae existere; atque eam denique proprie & directe vitam conferre & largiri, & immortalitatis semine corpora nostra imbuere, afferre non veretur. De Euchar. l. 2. cap. 24.
units.tr: XX. The stupidity of the Papists is not to be excused, who insist that the flesh of Christ must still be eaten, and that carnal eating, at least, must be joined with spiritual eating, and that this alone brings salvation. These are not inventions but monsters. Cardinal Perron goes further still. He does not hesitate to assert that the body of Christ is endowed with a life-giving power, not only through his passion and merit but also as the true efficient cause; that a formal residence of life-giving power exists in the flesh of Christ; and that this power, properly and directly, confers and bestows life and imbues our bodies with the seed of immortality. On the Eucharist, bk. 2, ch. 24.

units.la: XXI. Quae etiam contra Lutheranos dicta sunt: qui & oralem & Luquoque manducationem, quamquam coelesti & supernaturali ratione factam (quo & Pontificii quandoque confugiunt) tuentur; nec pios solum, sed & infideles ac hypocritas (posse sent & bruta animantia addere) ipsum Christi corpus, in pane & vino ἀδιαχάτως praesens, carpere, & contaminare asserunt. ex 1. Cor. 11:29. Qui edit & bibit indigne, judicium sibi edit & bibit, non discernens corpus Domini. Cum non nisi fide haec communio cum carne Christi constet, ac in sacramento quoque a fidelibus peragatur. Qua cum infideles careant, non corpus Christi, sed nuda ejus signa tractant & polluunt. Sicuti Apostolus eos indigne panem & poculum Domini, non autem corpus & sanguinem ejus, accipere dixit, com. 27.
units.tr: XXI. Similar things have also been said against the Lutherans, who maintain both oral eating and eating of another kind, although done in a heavenly and supernatural way (to which the Papists too sometimes resort). They claim that not only the pious but also unbelievers and hypocrites (they would even add brute animals) take hold of and defile the very body of Christ, present in the bread and wine indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως]. They cite 1 Cor. 11:29: He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Yet this communion with the flesh of Christ exists only by faith, and in the sacrament it is also carried out by believers. Since unbelievers lack this, they handle and profane not the body of Christ but only its bare signs. Just so the Apostle said they receive the bread and the cup of the Lord unworthily, not the body and blood of Christ (verse 27).

units.la: XXII. Et revera mirum est, de corporea manducatione adeo contendi; cum nec ea salutem dare, & absque ea salus quoque ipsa constare, possit. Nam & ab infidelibus eam peragi posse urgent, & fidelibus sine ea salutem non dari posse, affirmare non audent. Ut profecto meliores in hac controversia nostrae partes sint; qui spiritualem manducationem in hoc sacramento, atque extra illud, perpetuo urgemus; in qua religionis robur ac vis consistit, ac omnis nostra cum Christo communio absolvitur. Quæque adeo necessaria est, ut sola absque dubio salutem dare, atque absque ea salus dari nullo modo possit.
units.tr: XXII. And indeed it is strange that such fierce contention is raised over bodily eating, since it cannot give salvation, and salvation can exist without it. For they insist that it can be performed by unbelievers, and they do not dare to affirm that salvation cannot be given to believers without it. Our side in this controversy is surely the better, for we constantly insist on spiritual eating, both in this sacrament and outside it. In it lies the strength and power of religion, and in it all our communion with Christ is completed. It is so necessary that it alone, beyond doubt, gives salvation, and salvation can in no way be had without it.

units.la: XXIII. Sed & rejiciendi Socinian, qui nullam carnis Christi manducationem agnoscunt; sicuti nec meritum Christi norunt; & ne carnem quidem ejus post ascensionem superesse firmiter credunt. Sola autem fidei ac obedientiæ professione, quæ ista cærimonia peragatur, cœnam Christianorum fieri & absolvi dicunt. Quomodo & sub illa imagine Joh. 6. metaphorice fidem in Christi doctrinam ac martyrium docere volunt. Qui cibus ac potus nostep spiritualis debeat esse. Cum tamen Christus toto illo capite carnis & sanguinis sui: efficaciam & meritum, vimque vivificandi, & Spiritus sui robur, pluribus two prædicet; nec de nostro solum officio, sed præcipue de suo beneficio agat. Quod & comparatione mannæ, veteri populo olim præbitæ, ostendit: cui mysticum carnis ac sanguinis sui cibum longe præfert; ut in eo Deus majus aliquid humano generi de cœlo largitus fuerit. Ac longe aliud dicit communio illa carnis & sanguinis Christi, quam Apostolus prædicat; quæ non in nudo officio nostro, sed Christi potissimum beneficio consistit. Cum illi solam mortis Christi memoriam & officii nostri professionem cogitent. Quo in errore comites habent Anabaptistas.
units.tr: XXIII. The Socinians also must be rejected. They acknowledge no eating of the flesh of Christ, and, just as they do not know the merit of Christ, they do not firmly believe that his flesh remains after the ascension. They say that the Christian supper is made and completed by the mere profession of faith and obedience, which is the sole thing performed in this rite. In the same way, under that image in John 6, they wish to teach metaphorically that faith in Christ's doctrine and martyrdom is the food and drink that ought to be spiritual for us. Yet throughout that whole chapter Christ speaks at length of the flesh and blood of himself: of their efficacy, their merit, their power to give life, and the strength of his Spirit. He treats not only of our duty but above all of his own benefit. He shows this also by comparison with the manna once given to the ancient people, to which he far prefers his mystical food of flesh and blood, so that in it God has bestowed from heaven something greater on the human race. And that communion of the flesh and blood of Christ which the Apostle preaches means something quite different: it consists not in our bare duty but chiefly in the benefit of Christ. The Socinians think only of the remembrance of Christ's death and the profession of our duty. Anabaptists are their companions in this error.

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De Præsentia corporis Christi in S. Cœna.
units.tr: On the Presence of Christ's Body in the Holy Supper.

units.la: I. EXposita universa S. Cœnæ ratione, sequuntur corruptelæ ejus examinandæ & refellendæ. Per quas illud unitatis sacramentum & pacis vinculum, diaboli astu, conversum est in tesseram divisionis & litium contentionumque plus quam fraternarum seminarium. Has præsertim in Pontificiorum Ecclesia considerabimus, prout illæ ordine quodam sese mutuo consequuntur. Ac 1. de Præsentia corporis Christi in S. Cœna. 2. de modo ac medio ejus, Transsubstantiatione. 3. tandem de usu, ac fine illius, in Missa; ejusque sacrificio; & adoratione, agemus.
units.tr: I. Having set out the whole account of the Holy Supper, we must now examine and refute the corruptions of it. Through these, by the cunning of the devil, that sacrament of unity and bond of peace has been turned into a token of division and a seedbed of quarrels and disputes more than brotherly. We shall consider these chiefly in the Church of the Papists, in the order in which they follow one another: first, the presence of Christ's body in the Holy Supper; second, the manner and means of that presence, transubstantiation; third and last, we shall treat of its use and purpose in the Mass, and of its sacrifice and adoration.

units.la: II. Præsentia vocabulum relativum est; ac, pro objecti, quod dicitur esse præsens; & subjecti, cui illud est præsens, ratione intelligendum est. Atque aliter in rebus corporeis, aliter in rebus spiritualibus, spectatur. In rebus corporeis praesens est, quod externis sensibus percipi potest. Spirituales autem res praesentes sunt, cum ita intellectui offeruntur, ut ille apprehendere eas, mensque iis frui possit. Ad quam rem corporali contactu opus non est.
units.tr: II. The word presence is relative, and must be understood with reference both to the object said to be present and to the subject to which it is present. It is viewed one way in bodily things and another way in spiritual things. A thing is present in bodily matters when it can be perceived by the external senses. Spiritual things, however, are present when they are offered to the intellect in such a way that it can grasp them and the mind can enjoy them. For this no bodily contact is needed.

units.la: III. Cum autem communio nostra cum Christo spiritualis sit, nec corporeis sensibus, sed anima peragatur; non ex locorum propinquitate vel longinquitate, sed ex relatione illa, quam anima cum Christo habet, ut toto corpore frui possit, aestimanda est. Unde non praestigioso corporum contactu; sed, a nostra quidem parte, fide, a Christo autem, per Spiritum sanctum, perficitur. Ista enim faciunt, ut frui Christi corpore, & sanguine ejus ac merito pasci & saturari liceat. Ad quae in Coena accedit symbolorum praeterea praesentia, externique pignoris contrectatio & usus.
units.tr: III. Since our communion with Christ is spiritual, and is carried on not by the bodily senses but by the soul, it must be judged not by the nearness or distance of places but by the relation which the soul has with Christ, so that it may enjoy his whole body. It is therefore brought about not by any magical contact of bodies but, on our part, by faith, and on Christ's part, through the Holy Spirit. For these are the things that make it lawful for us to enjoy the body of Christ and his blood, and to feed on his merit and be satisfied. To these, in the Supper, is added the presence of the symbols and the handling and use of the outward pledge.

units.la: IV. Ita ergo Christus in S. Coena praesens est, non localiter, nec corporaliter (objectum enim spirituale, quale hic Christus ad maximam partem consideratur, corporeo sensu non magis percipi, quam spiritus in corpus converti potest) sed realiter tamen, & substantialiter; cum corpus Christi substantia sit: atque interne quidem apud animum nostrum, per fidem & Spiritum S.; externe autem per symbola & sacramenta adsit. Cui, tum internae, tum symbolicae, praesentiae male Pontificii superaddunt prodigiosum corporalis, non-localis, praesentiae modum; quo Christum praeterea corporeum in modum in coena adesse, atque externo sensu percipi ajunt. Quod praesentiae monstrum, & Scriptura, & rationi, atque ipsius denique S. Coenae mysterio adversum est.
units.tr: IV. Christ is therefore present in the Holy Supper not locally, nor bodily (for a spiritual object, such as Christ is chiefly considered here, can no more be perceived by a bodily sense than a spirit can be turned into a body), but truly and substantially, since the body of Christ is a substance; and he is present inwardly with our mind through faith and the Holy Spirit, but outwardly through the symbols and sacraments. To this inward and symbolic presence the Papists wrongly add a monstrous mode of bodily, non-local presence, by which they say that Christ is present in the Supper in a bodily manner and is perceived by the outward sense. This monstrosity of presence is contrary to Scripture, to reason, and indeed to the very mystery of the Holy Supper.

units.la: V. Attribuit enim Scriptura Christo veram humanitatem, verumque corpus, quale nostrum est. Illudque in coelum ascendisse, & coelo contineri ait, ne quis ex verbis ejus cyclopicam carnis comestionem intelligeret. Hoc vos scandalisat? Si igitur conspiciatis filium hominis ascendentem, ubi erat prius? Joh. 6:61, 62. Et non nisi visibili majestate de eo olim descensurum; non autem sacrificulorum praestigiis de eo exciri quotidie, & occulto tramite in terras venire praedicat. Quin aperte vetat, ne pseudo-prophetarum miraculis credamus, qui Christum vel in eremo ostendunt, vel ταμεῖος includunt, atque illis mendaciis Christianorum fidem pascunt. Hic Jesus, qui sursum receptus est a vobis in coelum, ita veniet, quemadmodum spectastis eum proficiscentem in coelum. Act. 1:11. Itaque, si dixerint vobis, ecce in deserto est, ne egredimini. dimini. Ecce in conclavibus, ne credite. Sicut enim fulgur erit ab Oriente, & apparet usque in Occidentem, ita etiam erit adventus filii hominis. Matth. 24: 26,27. conf. Luc. 17:22.
units.tr: V. For Scripture ascribes to Christ a true humanity and a true body, such as ours is. And it says that this body ascended into heaven and is contained in heaven, lest anyone understand from his words a Cyclopean eating of flesh. Does this scandalise you? "If then you shall see the Son of man ascending up where he was before?" John 6:61, 62. And Scripture declares that he will come down from heaven once more only in visible majesty, and not that he is summoned daily from heaven by the tricks of priests and comes to earth by a hidden path. Indeed, it expressly forbids us to believe the miracles of false prophets, who show Christ either in the desert or enclose him in an inner chamber, and feed the faith of Christians on such lies. "This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven." Acts 1:11. Therefore, "if they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert, go not forth; behold, he is in the inner chambers, believe it not. For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be." Matt. 24:26, 27. Cf. Luke 17:22.

units.la: VI. 2. Nec ratio admiserit, corpus aliquod fingere illocale & inextensum, quod in loco sit per modum spiritus & angeli: quod non in uno loco, sed in pluribus adsit; ut locus multiplicetur, & non multiplicetur locatum: &, in diversis itidem locis, diversa & contraria, uno & eodem tempore, patiatur. Quae illi in corpore Christi in S. Coena admittere debent. Quibus praeterea addunt, integrum Christi corpus sub quavis hostiae parte latere; ut non solum unum corpus ponatur in pluribus locis, sed, contrario errore, unum quoque locum pluribus corporibus communem faciant. Quae inconceptibilia ac impossibilia sunt. Nec ea vanis ac aereis suis distinctionibus, ac praestigiis conciliare in aeternum poterunt.
units.tr: VI. Second, reason does not allow us to imagine some body that is non-local and unextended, which is in a place in the manner of a spirit or an angel, which is present not in one place but in many, so that the place is multiplied while what is in the place is not multiplied; and which, likewise in different places, suffers different and contrary things at one and the same time. Yet they must admit these things in the body of Christ in the Holy Supper. Besides, they add that the whole body of Christ lies hidden under every part of the host, so that not only is one body placed in many places, but, by the opposite error, they also make one place common to many bodies. These things are inconceivable and impossible, and by their empty and airy distinctions and tricks they will never be able to reconcile them.

units.la: VII. 3. Sed & ipsum S. Coena mysterium bruto ac corporeo isto praesentiae modo tollunt. Celebratur enim S. Coena in memoriam Christi, quem absentem isto pignore possidemus ac amplectimur. Repugnat autem eadem in coena absentis Christi pignus tractare, eundemque prodigioso modo praesentem venerari. Corpus praeterea Christi ut fractum, ac sanguis ejus utfusus, in coena exhibeatur: quam mysterii partem hoc figmento abrogant. Denique, quod praecipium est, in coena communio fidelium cum Christo exercetur & obsignatur. Panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi? 1. Cor. 10: 16. ad quam carnalis illa praesentia nihil profecto facit, sed ei potius obest. Quid enim, an nulla cum Christo communio est, nisi ad corporeum istum modum? an fides non aliter Christo frui, & sanguine ejus pasci potest? certe communio nostra cum Christo, quae perpetua & aeterna est, illa communione perfici non potest, quae vix paucis momentis durat. Istud autem fidei opus est, non Christum, de coelesti solio detractum, crustulo includere, atque isto idolo sese oblectare; sed sursum potius sese ipsam erigere, seque Christo non interne, sed ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις unire; istumque in modum deliciari, interimque amoris ejus arrham & pignus in terris identidem tractare. Itaque, si resurrexistis cum Christo, superna quarite, ubi Christus est; ad dextram Dei sedens. Superna curate, non terrestria. Col. 3:1. Unaque nos suscitavit, unaque collocavit in coelis, in Christo Jesu. Eph. 2:6.
units.tr: VII. Third, they also destroy the very mystery of the Holy Supper by this crude and bodily mode of presence. For the Supper is celebrated in memory of Christ, whom, being absent, we possess and embrace by this pledge. But it is inconsistent to handle in the Supper a pledge of an absent Christ, and at the same time to worship him as present in a monstrous way. Moreover, the body of Christ is set forth in the Supper as broken, and his blood as poured out; this part of the mystery they abolish by their fiction. Finally, and this is the chief point, in the Supper the communion of believers with Christ is exercised and sealed. "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" 1 Cor. 10:16. To this communion that carnal presence contributes nothing at all, but rather hinders it. For is there no communion with Christ except in that bodily manner? Can faith not otherwise enjoy Christ and feed on his blood? Surely our communion with Christ, which is perpetual and eternal, cannot be effected by that communion which scarcely lasts a few moments. But this is the work of faith: not to shut up Christ, drawn down from his heavenly throne, in a little wafer and delight ourselves with that idol; rather, to lift ourselves up on high, and to unite ourselves to Christ not inwardly only, but in the heavenly places [ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις]; and in that way to take delight, and meanwhile to handle again and again on earth the earnest and pledge of his love. "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth." Col. 3:1. "And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus." Eph. 2:6.

units.la: VIII. Cadit ergo commentum Antichristi, de corpore Christi in Cœna præsente, quem novum Deum ab eo in Ecclesiam invehendum prophetarum oracula prædixerunt. Et Deum arcium in loculamento suo honorabit, & Deum quendam, quem non agnoverant Patres ipsius, honorabit auro & argento. Dan. 11:38. Ut & Lutheranorum error, de eodem Domini corpore, sub sacramenti signis ἀδιαςάτως præsente; & à fidelibus, atque infidelibus, promiscue manducato. Quod dogma cum apud ipsos magis speculativum sit, nec ad vitetos cultus Christianos obstringat, & spiritualis ac vera corporis Christi manducatio, obstante illo velo, nihilominus peragi possit, mitius de illis censendum est.
units.tr: VIII. Thus falls the fiction of the Antichrist concerning the body of Christ present in the Supper, the new god which the oracles of the prophets foretold would be brought into the Church from him. "But in his estate shall he honour the god of forces: and a god whom his fathers knew not shall he honour with gold, and silver." Dan. 11:38. So too falls the error of the Lutherans, that the same body of the Lord is present inseparably [ἀδιαστάτως] under the signs of the sacrament and is eaten indiscriminately by faithful and unbelievers alike. Since this dogma is more speculative among them, and does not bind them to the wicked worship of Christians, and since the spiritual and true eating of Christ's body can nevertheless be carried on despite that veil, we ought to judge them more gently.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: Chapter XIV.

units.la: De Transubstantiatione & Consubstan- tiatione.
units.tr: On Transubstantiation and Consubstantiation.

units.la: 1. Um autem Christi corpus ad sacramentum hoc venire, atque imperiosis verbis de sede sua excitum, ad sacrificulorum suorum mensas quotidie adesse Romanenses statuant; illud præterea non sine μεταμορφώσει & transfelementatione peragi ajunt; ne ulla videl. signi ac sacramenti species amplius superesset. Qui alter erroris hujus gradus est, quo illum adaugent; præter corporis Christi præsentiam, panis quoque Transubstantiationem, verborum vi ac potentia peractam, invehentes. Quæ fides, uti maxima omnium esset, si vera esset; ita nunc, cum falsa sit, omnium foedissima est & monstrosissima.
units.tr: 1. The Romanists hold that the body of Christ comes to this sacrament, and that, called down from its seat by imperious words, it is present every day at the tables of their priests. They also say this cannot happen without a metamorphosis [μεταμορφώσει] and a transelementation, so that no appearance of the sign and sacrament remains. This is the second stage of this error, by which they increase it: besides the presence of Christ's body, they also bring in the transubstantiation of the bread, effected by the force and power of the words. This belief, if it were true, would be the greatest of all; but since it is false, it is the most foul and monstrous of all.

units.la: II. Est vero dogmatis hujus origo in Ecclesia recens; nec o&to prioribus sæculis ullum apud veteres ejus occurrit vestigium. Illi enim omnes docuerunt, panis ac vini in sacramento remanere substantiam; nec aliam ibi conversionem fieri, quam sacramentalem & relativam; qua panis communis mutatur in mysticum, & ad aliud officium, & usum, finemque alium, adhibetur. Atque huc spectant voces, ipsis in hoc mysterio usurpatæ, μετασχηματισμὸς, μεταβυθμίσεως, μεταβολὴς, μετατοιήσεως, μεταβάσεως, μεθιςάνει; Latinis vero, transeundi, commutandi, convertendi, aliæque locutiones hyperbolicæ; quibus in demogoriis ad populum utebantur, ut, signorum & rerum signatarum per-
units.tr: II. The origin of this dogma is recent in the Church. In the first eight centuries no trace of it appears among the ancients. All of them taught that the substance of bread and wine remains in the sacrament, and that the only conversion there is sacramental and relative, by which common bread is changed into a mystical bread and is put to another office, use and end. To this point the words they used for this mystery look: metaschēmatismos [μετασχηματισμὸς], metarrhythmiseōs [μεταρρυθμίσεως], metabolē [μεταβολὴ], metoikeiōseōs [μετοιχειώσεως], metabaseōs [μεταβάσεως], metistēsi [μεθίστησι]; and in Latin, transeundi, commutandi, convertendi, and other hyperbolic expressions, which they used in their sermons to the people. By changing the names of the signs and of the things signified, they wished to show the analogy between the two,

units.la: Pars II. Ddd permutatis nominibus, analogiam, quæ est inter utraque,declararent; mentesque Christianorum, in augusto isto mysterio, reverenti quadam pietate inducrent, & à terrenis symbolis ad res cœlestes allevarent & attollerent. Estque hæc vel ipsorum Pontificiorum confessio: primis septem sæculis nullam de Eucharistiâ in Ecclesia auditam controversiam, hæreticis circa alias doctrinæ partes, quæ Deum Christumque spectabant, occupatis.
units.tr: and to stir the minds of Christians, with a certain reverent piety, in this august mystery, and to lift and raise them from earthly symbols to heavenly things. This is even the confession of the Papists themselves: that during the first seven centuries no controversy about the Eucharist was heard in the Church, the heretics being occupied with other parts of doctrine, which concerned God and Christ.

units.la: III. Primus, qui de dogmatis hujus sinceritate aliquid delibavit, deprehenditur fuisse Anastasius, Monachus de monte Sinai, A. 674, quam aliud agens, atque alia in quæstione cum hæreticis quibusdam congressus. Major inclinatio facta est sæculo octavo, cum Iconolatrarum tempestas Ecclesiam exerceret. Atque apud Græcos quidem Damascenus, eumque secutus Theophylactus, & A.C. 787. Iconolatricum Concilium Nicenum secundum, contra orthodoxos, qui unica Christi imagine in Ecclesia contenti erant, sacris videl. corporis ac sanguinis ejus in cœna symbolis; ea, non signa aut imaginem dominici corporis, sed ipsum Christi corpus, ipsumque; ejus sanguinem esse, asserere inceperunt.
units.tr: III. The first to hint at the unsoundness of this dogma is found to be Anastasius, a monk of Mount Sinai, in the year 674, when he was engaged in another matter and in a different dispute with certain heretics. A greater inclination toward it arose in the eighth century, when the storm of the image-worshippers was troubling the Church. Among the Greeks indeed, John Damascene, and Theophylact who followed him, and the Second Council of Nicaea of the image-worshippers in 787, against the orthodox, who were content with the one image of Christ in the Church, began to assert that the sacred symbols of his body and blood in the Supper are not signs or an image of the Lord's body, but the very body of Christ and his very blood.

units.la: IV. Apud Latinos quoque circa eadem tempora antiqua fides labare cepit. Atque, in eodem de imaginibus certamine, primum circa hoc dogma exerratum: iis, qui sub Carolo M. sese imaginibus opponebant, imprudentius mystica S. Cœnæ symbola, non Christi imaginem & picturas, sed ipsum ejus corpus & sanguinem appellantibus. Qui verbis magis, quam sensu peccabant. Factum hoc Anno C.794. Atque A.811. Paschasius Radbertus in Cœna ipsam Christi carnem & sanguinem adesse scripsit. Quod tamen potius de Consubstantiatione, quam de Transubstantiatione intellexit. Cui contradixerunt varii. Præcipue Bertramus, jussu Caroli Calvi, Gallorum Regis, hac ipsa controversia famam nomenque in Ecclesia adeptus. Magis adhuc invaluit istud dogma sequenti sæculo decimo; quod ferreum & plumbeum à scriptoribus appellatur; internitentibus tamen illis tenebris quibusdam veluti stellulis, qui nonnullam Ecclesiæ lucem faciebant. Quos inter, Berengarius, Archidiaconus Andegavensis. Qui, multa ob hanc rem passus, & non uno in concilio postulatus, aliquando & ad palinodiam redactus, semper tamen ad veritatem, quam professus erat, rediit; multosque jus discipulos & hæredes in Gallia & Italia reliquit. Quos exceperunt tandem Waldenses, vera & germana Ecclesiæ proles, qui fidem istam incorruptam ad reformationis tempora produxere.
units.tr: IV. Among the Latins too, the ancient faith began to totter about the same time. In the same controversy over images, the error first arose about this dogma: those who under Charles the Great opposed themselves to images, rather unwisely called the mystical symbols of the Holy Supper not an image and pictures of Christ, but his very body and blood. They sinned more in words than in meaning. This happened in the year 794. And in 811 Paschasius Radbertus wrote that the very flesh and blood of Christ are present in the Supper. Yet he understood this rather of consubstantiation than of transubstantiation. Various men contradicted him, above all Bertram, by the command of Charles the Bald, King of the Gauls, who gained fame and a name in the Church by this very controversy. This dogma gained even more strength in the following tenth century, which writers call iron and lead; yet in the midst of that darkness some lights, as it were little stars, shone and gave some light to the Church. Among them was Berengar, Archdeacon of Angers. Although he suffered much for this cause, and was called to account at more than one council, and at last was brought to a recantation, he always returned to the truth he had professed, and left many disciples and heirs in France and Italy. These were at length received by the Waldenses, the true and genuine offspring of the Church, who brought this faith down uncorrupted to the time of the Reformation.

units.la: V. Ut-
units.tr: V. Ut-

units.la: V. Utque non unico æstu errores in Ecclesiam allapsi sunt, illa tum maxime adhuc vigebat Consubstantiatio. Transubstantiationem demum docere coepit Stephanus, Episcopus Augustodunensis, A.C. 1130. ut, ut alii, 1160 post quem eundem loquendi modum usurpavit Innocentius Tertius, in Concilio Lateranensi, A.C. 1215. Transubstantiationem in Coena fieri dictitans, ut, ad perficiendum mysterium unitatis, accipiamus ipsi de suo, quod accepit ipse de nostro. Quæ tamen verba ita obliqua sunt, & in obscurum excuntia, ut non solum perversum, sed & bonum sensum admittere possint. Non enim de vocabulo, sed de re, ac sensu ejus, contendimus. Sicuti neque ipse canon missæ transubstantiationis dogma infert, sed multa in contrarium habet, quæ ei destruendo inservire possunt. Nec denique in Concilio Florentino, A.C. 1439. ubi de quæstione ista iterum disceptatum legitur, ea ad liquidum decisa reperitur: ut demum in Concilio Tridentino, A.C. 1551. sess. 13. præsentibus quatuor Papæ legatis, nec plus quam quinquaginta quatuor Episcopis, dogma istud omnibus numeris completum ac definitum fuerit. Quod tempus certe nimis recens est, ad condendum fidei articulum.
units.tr: Utque errors did not creep into the Church in a single wave, the consubstantiation then flourished most of all. Stephen, Bishop of Autun, first began to teach transubstantiation in 1130, as others did in 1160. After him Innocent III used the same way of speaking in the Lateran Council in 1215: asserting that transubstantiation takes place in the Supper, so that, to complete the mystery of unity, we ourselves may receive from what is ours what he himself received from what is ours. Yet these words are so oblique and run into obscurity that they can admit not only a perverse sense but also a good one. For we contend not about the word but about the thing and its meaning. Just as the canon of the Mass itself does not imply the dogma of transubstantiation, but contains many things to the contrary, which can serve to destroy it. Nor, finally, is it found to have been settled clearly at the Council of Florence in 1439, where the question is again read to have been disputed. At last, in the Council of Trent in 1551, session 13, with four legates of the Pope present and no more than fifty-four bishops, this dogma was completed and defined in every respect. That time is certainly too recent for framing an article of faith.

units.la: VI. Sed rem ipsam potius videamus. Atque hæc adversariorum ratio est: præter præsentiam Christi corporalem, quam in S. Coena statuunt, signorum quoque naturam everterc; quæ quomodocunque aboleri, & in corpus ac sanguinem Christi converti ac transubstantiari, prædicant. Lutherani autem solam corporis Christi localem præsentiam tuentur, reliqua sententiæ Pontificiæ proba ac monstra omittentes.
units.tr: VI. But let us look rather at the thing itself. This is the view of our opponents: besides the bodily presence of Christ, which they hold in the Holy Supper, they also overthrow the nature of the signs, which they declare to be changed in some way, and converted and transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ. The Lutherans, however, maintain only the local presence of Christ's body, omitting the other, Papist, opinions, which are both unproven and monstrous.

units.la: VII. De modo vero conversionis non conveniunt, sed adversis inter se sententiis digladiantur. Dum alii annihilationem panis; alii conversionem ejus in corpus Christi; manente tamen externa ejus specie; alii vero successionem panis & corporis Christi, statuerre malunt. Quas pugnas ipsis reliquimus. Bellarminus non-conservationem panis appellat (quæ revera ejus annihilatio est) inque ejus locum corpus Christi, non produci, sed de cœlo adduci, & sub speciebus panis venire, dixit.
units.tr: VII. On the manner of the conversion they do not agree, but fight with opposing views. Some prefer the annihilation of the bread; others its conversion into the body of Christ, while its outward appearance remains; others again prefer a succession of the bread and the body of Christ. These battles we leave to them. Bellarmine calls it non-conservation of the bread (which in fact is its annihilation), and said that in its place the body of Christ is not produced, but brought down from heaven and comes under the species of bread.

units.la: VIII. Nos autem, qualecunque hoc monstrum sit, ac quomodocunque istud pingant ac refingant, 1. Scripturis, ac S. Cœnæ institutioni: 2. & fidei analogia, ac præsertim corporis Christi veritati ac statuti: 3. & universa sacramentorum natura: 4. & rationi: 5. & sensibus denique omnibus repugnare, ac cunctis ex partibus laborare, contendimus.
units.tr: VIII. But we contend that this monster, whatever it is and however they paint and refashion it, is opposed, 1. to the Scriptures and the institution of the Holy Supper; 2. to the analogy of faith, and especially to the truth and the established order of Christ's body; 3. to the whole nature of the sacraments; 4. to reason; and 5. finally to all the senses, and that it labours on every side.

units.la: IX. Ac de Scripturis quidem jam ante diximus; ubi Cœnam a Christo institutam per partes examinavimus; & non modo transubstantiationis tiatiōnis nullam umbram deprehendimus, sed & universam historiam ei refragari, & signorum veritatem postulare vidimus. Perpetua enim ibi panis & vini occurrit appellatio; etiam post consecrationem Matth. 26: 29. Marc. 14: 25. Et Paulus 1. Cor. 10. & 11. multoties panem benedictionis appellat. Frivola autem exceptio est, panem appellari, quod antea panis fuerat, quodque sub externa panis specie latebat. Hæc enim sunt, de quibus jam quærimus. Et cum nulla commutationis illius mentio hic fiat, nulla quoque fingendæ talis denominationis causa est. Similiter poculum jam sacratum genimen vitis Christus dixit, Matth. 26 29. Cum autem panem corpus suum appellat, istud non minus impropriè accipi debet, quam cum eodem loco poculum dicit esse Novum Testamentum, sanguine suo jam jam dedicandum. Quod non de conversione, sed de significatione, ipsi etiam accipunt adversarii. Sed & Christus ipse relationem panis & vini ad corpus & sanguinem suum, de sacrificii sui commemoratione & ἀναμνήσει explicat, Luc. 22: 19. Nec alia est ista communio corporis & sanguinis Christi. 1. Cor. 10: 16. quam corporeo sensu intelligi non debere, ex eadem Apostolica phrasi com. 20. de idolorum conviviis usurpata, apparet.
units.tr: IX. Concerning the Scriptures we have already spoken earlier, where we examined the Supper instituted by Christ part by part. There we saw that not only is there no shadow of transubstantiation, but that the whole history opposes it and demands the truth of the signs. For the appellation of bread and wine occurs there continually, even after the consecration (Matt. 26:29; Mark 14:25); and Paul in 1 Cor. 10 and 11 many times calls it the bread of blessing. The objection that it is called bread because it had been bread before, and because it lay hidden under the outward appearance of bread, is trifling. For these are the very things we are asking about. And since no mention of such a change is made here, there is no reason to invent such a designation. Likewise Christ called the cup, already consecrated, the fruit of the vine (Matt. 26:29). And when he calls the bread his body, this must be understood no less figuratively than when in the same place he calls the cup the New Testament, which he was about to dedicate by his own blood. Even our opponents take this not as a conversion but as a signification. Christ himself also explains the relation of the bread and wine to his body and blood as a remembrance [anamnēsis, ἀνάμνησις] of his sacrifice (Luke 22:19). Nor is the communion of the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor. 10:16) anything else; and that it should not be understood in a bodily sense is clear from the same Apostolic phrase, used in verse 20 of the feasts of idols.

units.la: X. Sed & 2. Fidei analogiam, tum alibi, tum præsertim in articulo de Christo, ac natura ejus humana, hoc figmento corrumpi, ac extingui, vel ad oculum apparet. 1. Attribuit enim Scriptura Christo corpus, huic nostro simile, Hebr. 2: 14, 16, 17. Illi autem in cœna ipsi corpus affingunt inextensum, illocale, invisibile, instar speculi Marcionitici; & non unum corpus, sed in eadem cœna innumera corpuscula, ac phantasmata, in singulis hostiæ partibus latitantia, mentiuntur. 2. Credere præterea nos jubet fides Catholica in Christum, de virgine natum, passum, crucifixum, mortuum, sepultum, ac, post triumphatam inferorum potentiam, è mortis claustris in auras superas reducem, ac deinde sublimem in cœlum revectum. Quem autem illi Christum in Cœna adorant, ex farina coctum, ille nihil istorum aut egit, aut passus est, nullumque istorum articulorum implevit; sed recens, & vix unius horulæ Deus est. 3. Citius autem cœlum cum terra, quam Christi ascensionem in cœlum cum quotidiana ejus in immundis suis cœnis præsentia conciliabunt. 4. Cui cœlesti ejus gloriæ quomodo impanatio, & corpus ex farina factum, & contumeliæ adhuc patiens, ac in cœna quotidie sacrificandum, conveniat, quivis videre poterit. Ut non unum, sed omnes, de Christi corpore & statu, articulos, in hoc dogmate laborare liqueat.
units.tr: X. Moreover, the second point: the analogy of faith, both elsewhere and especially in the article concerning Christ and his human nature, is plainly corrupted and destroyed by this fiction. (1) For Scripture attributes to Christ a body like our own (Heb. 2:14, 16, 17). But in the Supper they attach to him a body that is unextended, without location, invisible, like a Marcionite mirror; and they invent not one body but countless little bodies, or phantoms, lurking in the individual parts of the host. (2) Furthermore, the Catholic faith bids us believe in Christ, who was born of a virgin, suffered, was crucified, died and was buried, and, after triumphing over the power of the underworld, was led back from the prison of death into the upper air and then carried up to heaven on high. Yet the Christ whom they adore in the Supper, baked from flour, did none of these things, suffered none of them, and fulfilled none of these articles; he is a newly made god, scarcely one hour old. (3) Heaven and earth will sooner be reconciled than Christ's ascension into heaven with his daily presence in their filthy suppers. (4) Anyone can see how the impanation, and a body made from flour, and a body still subject to indignities and to be sacrificed daily in the Supper, agree with his heavenly glory. So it is clear that in this doctrine it is not one article only, but all the articles concerning the body and state of Christ, that are put in jeopardy.

units.la: XI. 3. Sed & Sacramentum ipsum, quod augustius sese reddere putant, hoc commento tollunt. Ejus enim natura omnis in eo posita est, quod signum ac sigillum gratiæ sit, atque eo modo rem ipsam continet, & fidelibus tradat. Ut in Veteris Testamenti signaculis, circumcisione & paschate, ac in Novi Testamenti baptismo, vel ipsis latentibus adversariis, videre est. Ut de cœna hoc nullo prætextu negari possit: quam non minus obsignandis fidelibus, atque a visibilibus ad invisibilia, a sensu ad fidem, a terrenis ad cœlestia, evehendis servire, ex sacramentorum analogia patet. Quam illi in S. Cœna tollunt, dum fabulosa metamorphosei ipsum signum ex sacramento auferunt, & annihilant. Si autem signum ibi non amplius adsit, jam S. Cœna nec sacramentum est.
units.tr: XI. (3) They also destroy the sacrament itself, which they think they make more august, by this invention. For its whole nature consists in this, that it is a sign and seal of grace, and in this way contains the thing itself and conveys it to believers. This can be seen in the seals of the Old Testament, circumcision and the Passover, and in the baptism of the New Testament, even by the adversaries who lurk in hiding. The same cannot be denied on any pretext for the Supper, which, as the analogy of the sacraments shows, serves no less to seal believers and to lift them from the visible to the invisible, from sense to faith, from earthly things to heavenly ones. They destroy this in the Supper when, by their fabulous metamorphosis, they take away and annihilate the sign itself from the sacrament. But if no sign remains there, the Lord's Supper is no longer a sacrament at all.

units.la: XII. 4.
