Cum qua autem ratione conciliabunt: accidentia panis & vini existere, sine subjecto suo, cui inhæreant; & contrario prodigio, corpus & sanguinem Christi existere, sine suis accidentibus & proprietatibus essentialibus: accidentia subsistere per modum substantiarum; & corpora per modum spirituum: præsens esse, quod omnium sensus testantur esse absens; & absens, quod iidem testantur esse præsens: Christi corpus ex pane creari, & tamen antea præ-exstitisse. Corpus aliquod dari, quod non sit extensum, & dimensionibus suis careat; atque illud accedere aliquo sine motu locali; & existere sine loco; & quanquam membris omnibus conformatum, subsistere in unico puncto; & totum esse in puncto illo, ac totum extra illud; & existere denique in locis distinctis, nec tamen in spatiis intermediis. Quæ tot naturæ, non miracula, sed probrn, millies quotidie, ad vilissimi cujusque sacrificuli murmur, patrari, quis sani capitis ferat, aut credat?
units.tr: XII. (4) By what reasoning will they reconcile these claims: that the accidents of bread and wine exist without the subject in which they inhere; and by a contrary prodigy, that the body and blood of Christ exist without their accidents and essential properties; that accidents subsist after the manner of substances, and bodies after the manner of spirits; that what all the senses testify is present is absent, and what the same senses testify is absent is present; that the body of Christ is created out of bread and yet had existed before; that some body is given which is not extended and lacks its dimensions, and that this body approaches without local motion, and exists without place, and, though conformed to all its members, subsists in a single point, and is whole in that point and whole outside it, and finally exists in distinct places yet not in the intervening spaces? Who of sound mind would bear or believe these many natures, which are not miracles but monstrosities, performed a thousand times daily at the murmur of every lowly little priest?

units.la: XIII. Omittimus autem otiosas atque anxias ipsorum commentationes, ex quibus nunquam sese explicabunt: quomodo desinat esse panis conversus, an per meram annihilationem, an per actionem positivam? Quomodo fiat conversio vini, præsertim admixta aqua? Quomodo operetur hæc conversio circa corpus Christi, an mutetur illud accidentaliter, an vero substantialiter? Qua virtute verborum fiat transubstantiatio, an inhærente, an assistente? Quomodo ad S. Cœnam corpus Christi veniat, an per creationem, an per nativitatem, an per loci commutationem? Ut difficillimas quæstiones, de intentione sacerdotis, de sacerdote venefico, de vermium ex corrupta hostia prorependum materia, de luti prolapso forte pani adhærescentis subjecto, plurisque alias difficultates inextricabiles & pudendas omittam. In hos autem laqueos, & intricatissima spinosarum quaestionum senticeta, & absurditates absurdissimas sese Ecclesia Romana, ob unius voculae perversum intellectum, induit: quam tamen & aliter, & longe quidem commodius, accipi potuisse, ne ipsi ejus Ecclesiae magistri differentur.
units.tr: XIII. We pass over their idle and anxious speculations, by which they never manage to explain themselves: how the bread ceases to be, whether by mere annihilation or by a positive action? How does the conversion of wine take place, especially when water is mixed in? How does this conversion work upon the body of Christ: is it changed accidentally or substantially? By what power of the words does the transubstantiation happen, by inherence or by standing by? How does the body of Christ come to the Supper: by creation, by birth, or by change of place? I omit the very difficult questions about the intention of the priest, the priest as poisoner, the worms bred from the corrupted host, the matter to be swept away, the subject of mud that may have fallen and clung to the bread, and many other inextricable and shameful difficulties. Yet the Church of Rome has entangled itself in these snares and the most intricate thickets of thorny questions and the most absurd absurdities, on account of the perverse understanding of a single little word; which could have been understood otherwise, and far more conveniently, so that the teachers of that Church themselves would not be refuted.

units.la: XIV. 5. Tandem & sensibus convitium faciunt, quos perpetuo spectro eludi necesse est, si neque panis, neque vinum, in coena superfsit; quem tamen ex colore, sapore, odore, tactu, ibi adesse, omnium hominum recte dispositi sensus judicant. Est autem haec res, utpote externa, etiam judicii sensuum.
units.tr: XIV. (5) Finally, they also do violence to the senses, which must be continually deluded by this phantom if neither bread nor wine remains in the Supper; yet all men of sound sense judge by colour, taste, smell and touch that these are present there. This matter, being external, also falls under the judgement of the senses.

units.la: XV. Hic autem illi ad Dei omnipotentiam, atque ad miracula confugiunt; quale olim in Cana Galilaeae factum fuit. Atque hoc velo tot contradictionum & absurditatum pudenda tegunt. Ad quae resp. 1. Non agnoscere nos talem in Deo potentiam, quae ipsi veritatis & constantiae laudem adimit; &, tum aperto ipsius verbo, tum naturae, perpetuam vim facit. 2. In eucharistia miracula non fieri. Ac, juxta Augustt. de Trin. lib. 3. ista honorem habere posse, tanquam religiosa, stuporem, tanquam mira, habere non posse. 3. Cumque miracula omnia sensus afficiant, & admirationem pariant, nec quotidie, sed extra ordinem fiant; nihil autem horum in S. Coena apparet; recte quotidianum illud miraculum, quod nullius sensus ferit, rejicimus & explodimus. 4. Nec denique cum miraculo Cananitico illud conferendum est; ubi mutationem factam diserte Scriptura exprimit, & sensus ex manifestis vini proprietatibus aperte evicit. Quae hic contra sunt.
units.tr: XV. Here they take refuge in the omnipotence of God and in miracles, as once happened at the wedding in Cana of Galilee. And with this veil they cover the shameful contradictions and absurdities. To these we reply: (1) We do not acknowledge such a power in God as would take away from him the praise of truth and constancy, and would do violence to his plain word and to nature alike. (2) No miracles take place in the Eucharist. And according to Augustine, On the Trinity, book 3, these things may have honour as religious rites, but cannot have wonder as miracles. (3) Since all miracles strike the senses and produce admiration, and occur not daily but beyond the ordinary course, while none of these appears in the Lord's Supper, we rightly reject and explode this daily miracle, which strikes no sense. (4) Nor finally is it to be compared with the Cana miracle, where Scripture expressly describes the change and the senses clearly prove it from the manifest properties of wine. Here the case is the opposite.

units.la: XVI. Cum autem omne causa suae praesidium in verbis dominicis reponant, Hoc est corpus meum; quorum bytὸν adeo urgent; illa propius examinanda sunt, ut pateat, nos non minus, imo commodius longe litteralem ac directum eorum sensum urgere, quam adversarios.
units.tr: XVI. Since they place all the support of their cause in the words of the Lord, "This is my body," whose "is" they press so hard, these words must be examined more closely, so that it becomes clear that we press their literal and direct sense no less, indeed far more conveniently, than our opponents do.

units.la: XVII. Ac pronomen quidem Hoc, τὸ, ad nomen aliquod antecedens referendum est; quod non aliud est quam ἄρτος, panis. Sicuti expresse de poculo occurrit, τὸ τοῦ ποτηρίου, Luc. 22:20. Nec quicquam refert, ἄρτος & τὸ genere differre. Nihil enim communius, quam pronomen stare in genere, non rei antecedentis, sed praedicati consequentis. Vid. Matth. 7:12. Luc. 8. 14. Gal. 4:24.
units.tr: XVII. The pronoun "this" (τοῦτο) must be referred to some preceding noun, which is nothing other than bread (ἄρτος). Just as the expression "of the cup" (τὸ τοῦ ποτηρίου) occurs explicitly in Luke 22:20. Nor does it matter that ἄρτος and τὸ differ in gender. For nothing is more common than for a pronoun to agree in gender not with the antecedent thing but with the predicate that follows. See Matt. 7:12; Luke 8:14; Gal. 4:24.

units.la: XVIII. Praedicatum est, esse corpus Christi. Intelligitur autem corpus Christi naturale, quod sacramenti corpore quasi secundario repraesentatur.
units.tr: XVIII. The predicate is "to be the body of Christ." But the body of Christ is understood as his natural body, which is represented in the sacrament, as it were secondarily, by the sacramental body.

units.la: XIX. Vocula est, de qua praecipue contenditur, non de esse substantivo, sed de esse significativo, intelligenda est. Non solum enim disparatum de disparato hic praedicatur, quod nisi tropice fieri non potest: sed & aperte de signo & re signata agitur; quae cum de se mutuo praedicantur, non alia quam significationis & obsignationis ibi ratio est, vel esse potest. Quod & in altera sacramenti parte ad oculum patet; ubi poculum dicitur esse Novum Testamentum. Ut alias praedicationes in Euangelio usitatas omittam. Additur & de corpore hoc manducando, & sanguine bibendo; quae similiter impropriam locutionem confirmant; juxta verissimam Augustini regulam: quotiescunque in Scriptura verba impium quid, aut scelus, significare videntur, locutionem tum esse impropriam.
units.tr: XIX. The little word "is", over which the dispute is chiefly waged, must be understood not of substantial being but of significative being. For here a thing of one kind is predicated of a thing of another kind, which cannot happen except figuratively; and clearly the sign and the thing signified are spoken of, and when these are predicated of each other, there is and can be no other reason than signification and sealing. This is plain also in the other part of the sacrament, where the cup is said to be the New Testament. I omit other predications in use in the Gospel. And there is added the eating of this body and the drinking of the blood, which likewise confirm an improper manner of speaking, in accordance with Augustine's most true rule: whenever in Scripture words seem to signify something impious or criminal, the expression is then improper.

units.la: XX. Causa autem phraseos hujus, tum a Christo, tum a S. Scriptore, usurpatae, est 1. usus linguae, qua Christus loquebatur. Hebraei enim & Syri nomina signorum cum nominibus rerum significatarum conjungere, & de se mutuo praedicare solent. Estque hic perpetuus stilus Veteris Testam. tum in omnibus signis, tum praesertim in sacramentis, usurpatus. Vide Gen. 41:26,27. Septem illae vaccae – septem anni sunt &c. Ezechiel. 37: 11. Fili hominis, ossa haec tota domus Israel sunt. Dan. 2:38. Tu es caput aureum. & 7: 17. Haec animalia magna, quae sunt quatuor, quatuor reges, qui surgent ex terra. conf. Matth. 13: 38. Apoc. 1:20. & 17:9,10. & de circumcisione, Gen. 17: 10, 11. Hoc est foedus meum – ut circumcidatur vobis omnis mas. Circumcidetis igitur carnem praeputii vestri, ut sit signum foederis inter me, & vos. Ac de agno paschali, Exod. 12: 11. Pascha est Jehova. Sicut & Graeci interpretes ad similes phrases exprimendas verbum substantivum est, in Hebraeo omissum adhibuerunt, Gen. 17: 10. & 40: 12, 18. & 41:26. Exod. 12: 11. Quos Euangelistae procul dubio in phrasi illa secuti sunt. Atque iste etiam alibi, atque de aliis quoque sacramentis, Novi Testam. stilus est. De Baptismo, Tit. 3: 5. De Petra, 1. Cor. 10: 4. Adde Joh. 1:29. 1. Cor. 5: 7. Rom. 6: 4. ut Christus ita loquendo non aliud quam linguae, qua utebatur, indolem, & S. Scripturae stilum, tum in omni signo, tum praesertim in phrasibus sacramentalibus, abhibitum servaverit. 2. Cui accedit, quod in mystica ista coena, uti adalios ritus paschales, ita etiam ad formam loquendi paschalem, non obscure alludere voluerit: dicente patrefamilias in festo illo, Hoc est corpus paschatis &c. 3. Denique ad rei evidentiam, clarioremque inter signum & rem signatam analogiam exprimendam, hic modus loquendi pertinebat. Unde in aliis sacramentis, in Veteris Novique Testam. Scripturis adhibitum jam meminimus.
units.tr: XX. The reason for this manner of speaking, used both by Christ and by the sacred writer, is first the usage of the language Christ spoke. For the Hebrews and Syrians are accustomed to join the names of signs with the names of the things signified, and to predicate them of one another. This is the constant style of the Old Testament, used in all signs and especially in the sacraments. See Gen. 41:26, 27: "The seven cows are seven years," etc. Ezek. 37:11: "Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel." Dan. 2:38: "You are the golden head." And 7:17: "These great beasts, which are four, are four kings who will arise out of the earth." Compare Matt. 13:38; Rev. 1:20; and 17:9, 10. Concerning circumcision, Gen. 17:10, 11: "This is my covenant... that every male among you be circumcised. You shall therefore circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you." And concerning the paschal lamb, Exod. 12:11: "It is the Passover of Jehovah." Just as the Greek translators, to express similar phrases, used the substantive verb, which is omitted in the Hebrew (Gen. 17:10; 40:12, 18; 41:26; Exod. 12:11), which the Evangelists undoubtedly followed in that phrase. This style of the New Testament is also found elsewhere, and concerning the other sacraments too: concerning Baptism, Titus 3:5; concerning the Rock, 1 Cor. 10:4. Add John 1:29; 1 Cor. 5:7; Rom. 6:4. Thus Christ, in speaking so, preserved nothing other than the character of the language he used and the style of Sacred Scripture, employed in every sign, and especially in sacramental phrases. 2. To this is added that in this mystical supper, as in the other paschal rites, he wished also to allude plainly to the paschal manner of speaking, the father of the household saying at that feast, "This is the body of the Passover," etc. 3. Finally, for the sake of making the matter evident and of expressing more clearly the analogy between the sign and the thing signified, this mode of speaking was appropriate. Hence we have already noted that it is used in the other sacraments, in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments.

units.la: XXI. Ut ex hisce, contra Pontificios, pateat, nos vel maximè τὸ ῥητὸν observare, & litteralem sensum sequi. Præsertim ubi attendimus linguæ illius, qua hæc verba extant, ac rei, de qua agitur, genium & indolem. Nam & tropicus sensus litteræ sensus est; nec ille, ubi de signo & re signata sermo est, alius esse potest, quam tropicus. Signi enim natura procul dubio consistit in significando.
units.tr: XXI. From these things it is clear, against the Papists, that we especially observe the to rhêton [τὸ ῥητὸν], and follow the literal sense. Especially when we attend to the genius and character of the language in which these words stand, and of the matter under discussion. For a figurative sense is also the sense of the letter; nor can that sense, where the discourse concerns a sign and the thing signified, be other than figurative. For the nature of a sign undoubtedly consists in signifying.

units.la: XXII. Non magni vero momenti quæstio est, qualis in locutione hæc sacramentaria tropus sit, & ubi sedeat. Nos potissimum metonymiam hic esse censemus, per quam signum substituitur pro re signata. Quanquam & alio respectu metaphora & synecdoche adsit. Sedem tropi quod attinet, illam quidam in voce corpus collocant, quæ ponatur pro signo corporis; alii in copula constituunt; cum non aliud corpus intelligatur, quam corpus Christi naturale, quod per panem significetur & obsignetur. Ut esse ponatur, pro significatur.
units.tr: XXII. Yet the question of what kind of trope this sacramental manner of speaking is, and where it resides, is not of great importance. We chiefly judge it to be metonymy here, by which the sign is put for the thing signified. Although in another respect metaphor and synecdoche are also present. As for the seat of the trope, some place it in the word "body," which is taken for the sign of the body; others place it in the copula, since no other body is understood than the natural body of Christ, which is signified and sealed by the bread. That "is" is put for "is signified."

units.la: XXIII. Ipsi autem adversarii litteram, quam adeo urgent, non uno modo corruptum eunt. Unde laborare eos adeo videmus in sensu pronominis Hoc reddendo; in quo nihil habent quod consistere possit. Nam, per vocabulum istud, vel panem, vel corpus Christi, vel accidentia panis, vel denique præ desperatione vagum quiddam, & quod effari non possunt, intelligunt, & in confuso quodam conceptu latere volunt. Quæ cuncta fluida & labantia sunt. Non enim per pronomen hoc panem intelligere possunt, nisi transubstantiationem suam læ-dant. Nec etiam corpus Christi: hoc enim ad primum istud verbum nondum extat. Nec accidentia panis: nam nec illa ad primum istud verbum sola extant; & præterea absurdum foret, accidentia esse corpus Christi. Quas difficultates cum alii videant, nihil certo definiri, sed vagum quiddam, & incertum, quod sacerdos manibus teneat, quicquid illud denique sit, eo designari autumant, & in occulto illo sensu se occultant ac involvunt. Atque illum denique illorum verborum sensum edunt: Hoc est corpus meum, id est, sub accidentibus panis & vini continetur corpus meum. Quæ verborum Christi transpositio, mutatio, & corruptio est: quam tamen quomodo sine tropo efficiant, cogitari equidem non potest.
units.tr: XXIII. But the adversaries themselves do not go about the letter, which they press so hard, in one way only. Hence we see them labouring so much in rendering the sense of the pronoun "This," in which they have nothing that can stand. For by that word they understand either the bread, or the body of Christ, or the accidents of the bread, or finally, out of despair, some vague thing which they cannot name, and they wish to lie hidden in a certain confused concept. All of these are fluid and wavering. For they cannot understand the bread by the pronoun "this" unless they undermine their own transubstantiation. Nor the body of Christ either, for that does not yet exist at this first word. Nor the accidents of the bread, for those too do not exist alone at this first word; and besides, it would be absurd for the accidents to be the body of Christ. Since others see these difficulties, they assert that nothing is defined with certainty, but that "some vague thing," uncertain, which the priest holds in his hands, whatever it finally is, is designated by it, and they hide and wrap themselves in that obscure sense. And at last they put forth this sense of those words: "This is my body," that is, "my body is contained under the accidents of bread and wine." This is a transposition, change, and corruption of Christ's words; yet how they could accomplish this without a trope cannot indeed be conceived.

units.la: XXIV. Alia erroris facies est, quando pro Transubstantiatione adoptatur. (Consubstantiatio. Quæ ipsa Transubstantiatione antiquior, & à & a Johanne Damasceno, Paschasio, Ruperto Tuiticensi, olim asserta; ac, post introductam transsubstantiationem, ad incommoda ejus vitanda, per Scholasticos quosdam, imprimis Cardinalem Cameracensem, rur- sus renovata, tandem Luthero ac discipulis ejus placuit; ac triste illud Reformatarum Ecclesiarum divortium constituit. Quae, in hoc uno capite primitus, discedentes, paulatim aliis quoque articulis distingui coepere.
units.tr: XXIV. Another form of error is when Consubstantiation is adopted in place of Transubstantiation. This doctrine is older than Transubstantiation itself, and was asserted long ago by John of Damascus, Paschasius, and Rupert of Deutz; and after transubstantiation was introduced, it was renewed again by certain Schoolmen, above all the Cardinal of Cambrai, in order to avoid its inconveniences; and it finally pleased Luther and his disciples, and established that sad division of the Reformed Churches. Those who departed, at first on this one point, gradually began to be distinguished by other articles also.

units.la: XXV. Non uno autem modo hoc dogma explicant. Varius enim in hac parte fuit Lutherus. Et, cum olim panem diceret esse corpus Christi substantialiter (quod a transsubstantiatione non procul aberat) deinceps synecdochen maluit statuere: quod subjectum hoc duas res contineret conjunctas, panem & corpus Christi. Atque haec potissima ejus est sententia. Discipuli ejus paulo aliter rem explicuere: & cum omnem locutionem figuratam refugiant, per hoc duas res simul praesentes, visibilem panem, & invisibile Christi corpus, monstrari dixerunt. Hodierni Lutherani, occultae illi & invisibili duarum substantiarum coexistentiae asserendae, tres voculas addidere, in, cum, sub pane & vino. Verum hac ratione non recte Consubstantiatores appellantur hujus sententiae patroni; cum nulla hic fit ουνουσία, sive diversarum substantiarum in unum commixtio: sed διαυσία potius, vel ουνυπερξις, sive duarum substantiarum, suppositis distinctarum, coexistentia.
units.tr: XXV. They do not explain this dogma in one way, however. Luther was inconsistent on this point. And although once he said that the bread is substantially the body of Christ (which was not far from transubstantiation), afterwards he preferred to posit synecdoche, namely that the subject contained two things joined together, bread and the body of Christ. This is his principal opinion. His disciples explained the matter somewhat differently: and since they shun every figurative mode of speech, they said that through "this" two things present at once, the visible bread and the invisible body of Christ, are pointed out. Present-day Lutherans, in order to assert that hidden and invisible coexistence of two substances, added three little words: "in," "with," "under" the bread and wine. Yet in this way the advocates of this opinion are not rightly called Consubstantiators, since there is no ousiosis [οὐσίωσις], that is, no mixing of different substances into one; but rather diousia [διουσία] or ounyparxis [οὐνυπαρξις], that is, the coexistence of two substances, distinct and each subsisting.

units.la: XXVI. In qua sententia multa sunt absurda & ἀσύγκρατα. Nam corpus hoc Christi invisibile in S. Coena, variis fidei articulis, praesertim de humana Christi natura, ex Maria virgine; deque praesenti ejus statu ac gloria; & sacramentorum analogia, quae rem signatam, non substantialiter continent, sed obsignant; & prime Jesu Christi Coenae, ubi ipse visibiliter accubuit, & non corpus, sed panem, fregit, &, tradito poculo, dixit, hoc est Novum Testamentum &c. & denique ipsis Christi verbis, adversatur. Quae ipsi, ut sibi subservire faciant, non leviter immutant & corrumpunt. Nam in verbis illis, Hoc est corpus meum, per hoc intelligere debent, in hoc, vel, sub hoc, per est, continetur, & includitur: per corpus, aliquid quod nec quantum, nec visibile, nec locale est. Et haec omnia tamen sine tropo ac figuris conficere sese posse somniant.
units.tr: XXVI. In this opinion there are many absurdities and inconsistencies [ἀσύγκρατα]. For it is opposed to this invisible body of Christ in the Holy Supper, to various articles of faith, especially concerning the human nature of Christ from the Virgin Mary, and concerning his present state and glory; to the analogy of the sacraments, which do not substantially contain the thing signified but seal it; to the first Supper of Jesus Christ, where he himself reclined visibly, and broke not a body but bread, and, having handed over the cup, said, "This is the New Testament," etc.; and finally to Christ's very words. These people, so that these may serve their purpose, change and corrupt them not lightly. For in those words, "This is my body," they must understand by "this" something in this, or under this, by "is" it is contained and included, and by "body" something which is neither quantitative, nor visible, nor local. And yet they dream that they can accomplish all these things without any trope or figure.

units.la: XXVII. Omnis autem ille error ex male intellectis verbis S. Coenae ortus est; quae proprie ac simpliciter sumi debere pertendunt, ne Coena nostra prima Christi Coena, in qua ipse corpore suo praesens aderat, inferior existimetur. Sed perperam nullum tropum, nullam figuram in ultimis Christi verbis agnoscunt. Cum enim ipsa sacramenta non nisi figuræ sint, mirum non est figuratas locutiones in iis audiri. Saltem sequentia verba de poculo, Hoc est Novum Testam. in sanguine meo, quomodo sine figura intelligi possint, non liquet. Ne ipsorum interpretamenta repetam, quæ non unam figuram involvunt. Sufficit enim phrases non ignotas & claras adhiberi; figuratas eas esse nihil obstat. Denique nostra Cœna primæ Christi Cœnæ in sacramenti ratione ac natura conformis est, nec plus requiritur. Nil enim vetat, circumstantias quasdam diversas esse.
units.tr: XXVII. Now all this error arises from badly understood words of the Holy Supper; which they insist must be taken properly and simply, lest our Supper be judged inferior to the first Supper of Christ, in which he himself was present in his body. But they wrongly recognise no trope, no figure, in Christ's last words. For since the sacraments themselves are nothing but figures, it is no wonder that figurative expressions are heard in them. At least how the following words about the cup, "This is the New Testament in my blood," can be understood without a figure is not clear. Not to repeat their own interpretations, which involve more than one figure. For it is enough that phrases which are neither unknown nor obscure are used; that they are figurative is no obstacle. Finally, our Supper is conformed to the first Supper of Christ in the reason and nature of the sacrament, and nothing more is required. For nothing forbids that certain circumstances be different.

units.la: XXVIII. Atque hæc de quæstione illa, quæ, in ipso Euangelii renascentis exordio, funestum illud Ecclesiarum dissidium invexit. Quanquam res illa tanti momenti non erat, ut tantum fratrum bellum excitaret, & Ecclesias, primariis fidei apicibus conjunctas, tam longum dissociaret. Unde ab hoc capite, in quo Ecclesiæ Euangelicæ primum discedere visæ sunt, reconciliationis initia merito auspicanda sunt. Est autem in præcipua Eucharistiæ parte consensus; cum rem signatam, ac spiritualem cum ea communionem, ut sacramenti partem præcipuam, utrique ex æquo urgeamus. Nec etiam altera pars ista signi superstitione, ac cultu idololatrico, laborat, qualem in Romana Ecclesia damnavimus. Sola de signo, & non tam de re, quam de modo, controversia est: quæ scil. præsentiæ Christi in S. Cœna ratio? quique nostræ manducationis modus sit? quam illi, tum præsentiam Christi, tum nostri cum eo communionem, corporalem quoque dari existimant. Unde & ab infidelibus mandi quoque Christum volunt. Quæ, utcunque crassa & dura, cum tamen a signi adoratione longe absint; & ipsi adversarii spiritualem manducationem longe præferant; fundamentalia non sunt. Unde propter istas quæstiones non scindendæ Ecclesiæ, sed, post longum divortium, potius reuniendæ. Cujus consensus exempla, vel ab ipso Luthero, extant. Nam & Melanthonem & Lutherum olim convenisse; & in conventu Marpurgico, inter Lutherum & Swinglium concordiam ictam, A. C. 1529. & deinceps inter utriusque partes Doctores, imo Ecclesias non semel repetitam constat. Ille autem reconciliationis faciendæ modus optimus est: ut, relictis vocabulis ambiguis & novis, solæ Scripturarum, ac veteris Ecclesiæ, locutiones adhibeantur; quæ ad veras sententias infirmos & aberrantes fratres, Deo tam pio operi benedicente, tandem reducerent.
units.tr: XXVIII. These, then, are my remarks on that question which, at the very dawn of the renewed Gospel, brought in that disastrous division among the Churches. Yet the matter was not so weighty as to stir up so great a war among brothers, or to sever for so long Churches that are joined in the chief points of the faith. Therefore, from this head, on which the Evangelical Churches first seemed to part ways, the beginnings of reconciliation rightly ought to be made. Now there is agreement on the principal part of the Eucharist: we both insist equally that the thing signified, and the spiritual communion with it, is the principal part of the sacrament. Nor does the other side labour under that superstition of the sign or idolatrous worship which we have condemned in the Roman Church. The only controversy concerns the sign, and not so much the thing as the mode: namely, what is the manner of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper, and what is the manner of our eating? They think that Christ's presence, and our communion with him, is given also bodily, and so they want Christ to be eaten even by the unbelieving. However crude and harsh this may be, since they are far from adoring the sign, and the adversaries themselves greatly prefer spiritual eating, it is not a fundamental matter. Therefore, on account of these questions the Churches should not be torn apart, but rather, after a long separation, reunited. Examples of such agreement exist, even from Luther himself. For it is well established that Melanchthon and Luther once came together, and that at the Marburg conference a concord was struck between Luther and Zwingli in 1529, and afterwards was not once but repeatedly renewed between the teachers of both sides, indeed between the Churches. The best method of effecting reconciliation is this: that, with ambiguous and novel words set aside, only the expressions of Scripture and of the ancient Church be employed, which might at last lead weak and erring brethren, with God blessing so pious a work, back to the true opinions.

units.la: CAPUT XV. De MISSA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV. On the Mass.

units.la: I. SIcuti veritatum, ita & errorum, quidam nexus ac cinnus est. Quod hac in parte apud Latinos patuit. Uti illi enim præsentiam Christi corporalem in Cœna per Transubstantionem explicuere, atque errorem errore auxere; ita Christum, quem in Cœna præstigioso modo præsentem fecere, jam immolare, iterumque in ara offerre ausi sunt. Huc enim cuncta tandem redeunt. Ideoque Christus in Cœna præsens arcessitur, ut in ea tandem offeratur. Quod, non sacrificium, sed sacrilegium, quod Missam appellant, reliquorum errorum scopus & finis, atque Antichristianæ civitatis unicum Palladium est.
units.tr: I. Just as there is a bond and chain among truths, so there is one among errors. This has been plain among the Latins in this matter. For just as they explained Christ's bodily presence in the Supper through transubstantiation, and multiplied error by error, so they have dared to sacrifice Christ, whom they had made present by a trick, and to offer him again on the altar. All things finally come back to this. Hence Christ is summoned to be present in the Supper so that in the end he may be offered there. This thing, which they call the Mass, is not a sacrifice but a sacrilege. It is the goal and end of the other errors, and the one Palladium of the Antichristian city.

units.la: II. Missa nomen, ab Hebræa matre perperam a quibusdam deduetum, Deut. 16: 10. Latinæ potius originis est. Latini enim illud primo ufurparunt, & ab illa externi cultus circumstantia, tum universum cultum sacrum, tum præcipuas ejus partes, Missam appellarunt. Estque illa vox circa finem tertii sæculi primum audita. Dicebatur autem missa, quasi missio; uti remissa pro remissio; a dimissione populi: quæ duplex erat, tum Catechumenorum, ante sacramenti communionem, tum fidelium, post illam peractam; proclamante Diacono, Ite, missa est. A qua solemni voce, tum cultus universus, tum præcipue Eucharistia, & preces, ac liturgia ejus, missæ nomen acceperunt. Pontificii autem eo nomine hodie intelligunt, externum illud ac proprie dictum Ecclesiæ sacrificium expiatorium; quo ipsum Dei filium, pro expiandis vivorum ac mortuorum peccatis, aliisque rebus, vel impetrandis, vel averruncandis, Deo Patri, sub accidentibus panis & vini, per sacerdotem quotidie offerunt. Quod impurissimum sacrum, Christo contumeliosum, fidei & Scripturis adversum, Christianis pudendum, ac piis omnibus execrandum, religionis ac fidei apud illos summam constituit.
units.tr: II. The name Mass, which some have wrongly derived from the Hebrew, see Deut. 16:10, is rather of Latin origin. The Latins were the first to use the word, and from that outward circumstance of the rite they called both the whole sacred worship and its chief parts the Mass. The word was first heard near the end of the third century. It was called missa, as if from missio, just as remissa stands for remissio, from the dismissal of the people. This dismissal was twofold: that of the catechumens, before communion in the sacrament, and that of the faithful, after it was completed, when the deacon proclaimed, Go, it is the dismissal. From this solemn formula the whole worship, and especially the Eucharist with its prayers and liturgy, took the name of Mass. The Papists, however, today understand by that name the external and properly so called expiatory sacrifice of the Church, by which every day, through the priest, under the appearances of bread and wine, they offer the Son of God himself to God the Father, to expiate the sins of the living and the dead, and to obtain or avert other things. This most impure rite, insulting to Christ, opposed to faith and Scripture, shameful to Christians and detestable to all the pious, forms the sum of their religion and faith.

units.la: III. Hinc tanta apud ipsos missarum frequentia, & varietas, ac tam multæ earum species. Habent enim missas, alias ordinarias, quas in Sanctorum quoque ac B. virginis nomine peragere non verentur; alias extraordinarias, quas certis tantum occasionibus, in novi Episcopi, templi &c. consecrationibus habent. Habent missas magnas, & parvas: inferiores, & superiores: a colore paramentorum (ut vocant) insuper distinctas: item siccas, & humidas: publicas, & privatas &c.
units.tr: III. Hence the great frequency and variety of masses among them, and the many kinds of them. For they have masses that are ordinary, which they do not hesitate to celebrate even in the name of the saints and the blessed Virgin; and others that are extraordinary, which they hold only on certain occasions, such as the consecration of a new bishop, a church, and so on. They have great and small masses, higher and lower ones, further distinguished by the colour of the vestments (as they call it); also dry and wet masses, public and private ones, and so on.

units.la: IV. Hoc enim ad S. Coenæ ludibrium addunt, quod missas quoque privatas celebrent, sine signorum distributione, & nullo fidelium communicante, ac, si qui adsint, spectatorum solum officio fungentibus. Quod, contra Christi institutum, qui edere & bibere omnes jussit, Luc. 22: 19. Matth. 26: 25. contra Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ usum, Act. 2: 41, 42. & 20: 7. 1. Cor. 10. & 11. & contra primitivæ Ecclesiæ praxin; ubi adeo fideles omnes communicabant, ut primis seculis ne quidem ulli noncommunicanti ad coenæ mysterium adesse, idque aspectare, liceret: sacram denique Domini mensam in meram scenam & mimum convertit, non animæ, sed oculis pascendis idoneum. Quæ S. Coenæ illusio maxime sæculo decimo tertio, post Concilii Lateranensis institutum de communione semel saltem in anno, prævia peccatorum confessione ad genua sacerdotis, celebranda, exorta est.
units.tr: IV. For they add this mockery of the holy Supper, that they celebrate even private masses, without distribution of the signs and with no faithful person communicating, the attendants, if any are present, doing only the work of spectators. This is against Christ's institution, who bade all to eat and drink, Luke 22:19; Matt. 26:25; against the practice of the apostolic Church, Acts 2:41, 42 and 20:7; 1 Cor. 10 and 11; and against the practice of the primitive Church, where all the faithful communicated so fully that in the first centuries it was not even lawful for any non-communicant to be present at the mystery of the Supper or to look on at it. Finally, they have turned the holy table of the Lord into a mere stage and pantomime, fit to feed the eyes, not the soul. This mockery of the holy Supper arose especially in the thirteenth century, after the Lateran Council had instituted that communion be celebrated at least once a year, preceded by confession of sins kneeling before the priest.

units.la: V. Nec deest huic scenæ suum choragium. Ac missaticam omnem pompam, si quis spectare libeat, eam succincte explicat ac per partes tradit inter alios Sleydanus, Commentar. de statu relig. lib 21. Ita enim, partim Gentilitiis superstitionibus, partim Judaicis cæremoniis, hocce sacrum inquinarunt, & histrionicarum denique gesticulationum probro adspersĕrunt, ut non coenæ & convivii, sed theatri speciem spectatoribus præbeat.
units.tr: V. This stage has its own chorus-leader too. Anyone who wishes to view the whole pomp of the Mass may see it briefly explained and set out part by part by, among others, Sleidan, Commentary on the State of Religion, book 21. For they have defiled this sacred rite partly with pagan superstitions and partly with Jewish ceremonies, and have finally spattered it with the disgrace of theatrical gestures, so that it presents to the onlookers the appearance not of a supper and feast but of a theatre.

units.la: VI. Ut vel externa missæ administratione pateat, quantopere a primævo Christi instituto aberratum sit. Pro pastoribus enim & ministris Euangelii, quos Christus instituit, 1. Cor. 11. 23. hic sacerdotes unctos, & rasos, aspicias: pro mensa, altare: pro pane, hostiam: pro sacramento denique sacrificium. Pariterque fidelium communionem, in unius sacrificuli gesticulationes; sacrarum partium distributionem, in sacramenti ostentationem & circumgestationem; perceptionem, in adorationem; preces ad Deum, in magicos susurros, externo elemento incantando, & transformando, immutarunt. Nec Deum solum, sed & Sanctorum cohortem ad hoc sacrum advocant; quorum cineres, ac ossa, sub altari condita, venerantur; per hæc videl. amicorum suorum pignora ac merita Deum exoraturi. Denique lingua Latina hæc mysteria celebrant, &, modo cantu, modo religioso silentio, illa transfigunt.
units.tr: VI. The outward administration of the Mass shows how far it has strayed from Christ's original institution. In place of the ministers and ministers of the Gospel whom Christ instituted, 1 Cor. 11:23, here you will see anointed and shaven priests; for the table, an altar; for the bread, a host; and finally, for the sacrament, a sacrifice. Likewise they have changed the communion of the faithful into the gestures of a single little sacrificer; the distribution of the consecrated parts into the display and carrying round of the sacrament; the reception into adoration; and prayers to God into magical whisperings, chanting over and transforming the external element. Nor do they summon only God to this rite, but also a host of saints, whose ashes and bones they keep under the altar and venerate, plainly hoping through these pledges and merits of their friends to win God's favour. Finally, they celebrate these mysteries in the Latin tongue, and carry them through now with singing, now with religious silence.

units.la: VII. Verum, missis hisce externis, de sacrificio videamus, in quo cardo hujus disputationis versatur. Ac nos quidem sacrificium tale expiatorium, quale Romana Ecclesia quotidie celebrat, non solum nulla Scirpturae auctoritate niti, sed & directe ei contrariari, asserimus. Utpote quod 1. Cum generali sacramentorum natura. 2. Speciatim cum S. Coenae institutione. 3. Cum sacrificii ipsius natura & requisitis. 4. Ac praesertim cum vero Christi sacrificio pugnet, & manifestis Scripturis adversetur. Per haec enim argumenta nunc ire placet, quae novum illud Pontificiorum sacerdotium, & sacrificium, prorsus tollunt.
units.tr: VII. But, setting these outward matters aside, let us look at the sacrifice, on which the hinge of this dispute turns. We assert that the expiatory sacrifice which the Roman Church celebrates every day not only has no support in any authority of Scripture, but is directly contrary to it. For this sacrifice (1) conflicts with the general nature of the sacraments; (2) specifically with the institution of the Holy Supper; (3) with the nature and requirements of sacrifice itself; and (4) above all, it fights against the true sacrifice of Christ and opposes manifest Scriptures. For it is these arguments that I now wish to set out, since they utterly overthrow that new priesthood and sacrifice of the Papists.

units.la: VIII. Ac i. quidem, ut de Transubstantiatione, quae unicum erroris hujus fundamentum est, sileam; & Scripturae silentium, quod Romanensium aliquos sacrificium hoc ex traditione arcessere coegit, omittam: ipsa sacramenti, ubi id solitarium est, natura huic sacrificio adversatur. Cum dispar utriusque sit ratio. Sacrificium enim hominis, ad Deum ascendentis, cultum; sacramentum autem Dei, ad homines descendentis, gratiam dicit. Cum autem in S. Coena, quam Christus testamentum vocat, Deus haeredibus suis aliquid largiatur, & coelestedonum conferat; patet, illud non sacrificii, per quod Deo aliquid a nobis offeratur, sed sacramenti, per quod ille nobis aliquid obsignet, rationem habere.
units.tr: VIII. First, then, let me set aside transubstantiation, which is the sole foundation of this error, and let me pass over the silence of Scripture, which forced some of the Romanists to derive this sacrifice from tradition. The very nature of the sacrament, where it stands alone, is opposed to this sacrifice. For the two have different purposes. A sacrifice signifies the worship of man ascending to God, whereas a sacrament signifies the grace of God descending to men. Now in the Holy Supper, which Christ calls a testament, God bestows something on his heirs and confers heavenly gifts. It is plain, then, that the Supper has the character not of a sacrifice, by which something is offered to God by us, but of a sacrament, by which he seals something to us.

units.la: IX. 2. Sed spectanda imprimis prima S. Coenae institutio: ubi nulla sacrificii species. Non enim in Coena, sed in cruce, sese Christus obtulit. Nec Patri corpus & sanguinem suum, sed discipulis panis & vini pignora tradidit. At praeterea de calice dixit, illum esse Novum Testamen. in suo sanguine. Quod a sacrificii ratione longe abest. Addit denique, perenni isto convivio mortis suae memoriam in Ecclesia consecrandam. Rememoratio autem Christi absentis longe differt ad oblatione ejusdem praesentis.
units.tr: IX. Second, the first institution of the Holy Supper above all must be considered, and in it there is no kind of sacrifice. Christ did not offer himself in the Supper but on the cross. Nor did he give his body and blood to the Father, but gave the disciples the pledges of bread and wine. Moreover, he said of the cup that it was the New Testament in his blood, which is far from the nature of a sacrifice. Finally, he adds that by this perpetual feast the memory of his death is to be kept in the Church. But the remembrance of Christ absent is quite different from the offering of him present.

units.la: X. 3. Sed frustra sacrificii essentiam & requisita in hoc sacro quaras. 1. Nullam enim rem externam & visibilem, quae Deo offeratur, ostendere possunt. Quod in omni sacrificio necessarium est. Panem enim & vinum, in peccatorum piamentum offerri, merito dedignantur. Christi autem corpus, quae sola salutaris victima est, ibi, juxta veriorem sententiam, non est; juxta Pontificios autem, invisibiliter adest, & subpanis nebula latet. Quod ad sacrificii ritum non sufficit. 2. Sed, si vel adsit, quomodo illud, juxta sacrificii ritum, consecrari a sacerdote, dicent; cum ipse potius Christus universam Ecclesiam consecret & abluat? 3. Et qua in re, quibusque in verbis sacrificii istius essentiam constituent? Certe per verba, quibus Christus usus est, & quae Romanenses in consecrando imitantur, nihil Deo offertur. Nec fractio panis, nec manducatio, tio, ad sacrificaturam, quicquam facit. 4. Maxime autem in sacrificiis, sive victimæ suæ, destructione assignanda hærent. Istud enim in omni sacrificio necessarium est. Nullam autem realem corporis Christi destructionem ibi fieri vel ipsi confitentur. Præstigiosum vero est, quod Christi esse naturale, & sacramentale distinguant: ac, esse ejus sacramentale destrui, definentibus speciebus, affirmant. Quod & pudendum, & falsum, est. Nam hoc modo Christus in ore vel ventriculo sacerdotis demum sacrificaretur; ubi, corruptis speciebus, esse ejus sacramentale desinit. Sed & Christi corpus proprie unicum tantum esse habet, esse vid: naturale. Esse enim sacramentale nihil aliud est quam esse significativum Christi. Hoc vero sacrificium nostrum esse nequit.
units.tr: X. Third, you will look in vain for the essence and requirements of sacrifice in this rite. (1) For they cannot show any external and visible thing offered to God, which is necessary in every sacrifice. Indeed, they rightly disdain to offer bread and wine as an atonement for sins. The body of Christ, which alone is the saving victim, is not there according to the truer opinion; according to the Papists, however, it is present invisibly and lies hidden under a cloud of bread. That is not enough for the rite of sacrifice. (2) But even if it were present, how will they say that it is consecrated by the priest according to the rite of sacrifice, since Christ himself rather consecrates and cleanses the whole Church? (3) And in what thing, and in what words, will they set the essence of this sacrifice? Certainly, through the words which Christ used, and which the Romanists imitate in consecrating, nothing is offered to God. Neither the breaking of the bread nor the eating contributes anything to the sacrifice. (4) Above all, the essence of sacrifice lies in the destruction of the victim. This is necessary in every sacrifice. Yet even they themselves confess that no real destruction of Christ's body takes place there. Their distinction between the natural and the sacramental being of Christ is a trick, and they assert that his sacramental being is destroyed when the appearances cease. This is both shameful and false. For in this way Christ would be sacrificed only in the mouth or stomach of the priest, where, once the appearances are corrupted, his sacramental being ceases. Moreover, the body of Christ has properly only one being, namely the natural. For sacramental being is nothing other than the significative being of Christ. And this cannot be our sacrifice.

units.la: XI. 4. Præsertim autem sacrificio Christi quotidianum istud ipsorum sacrificium injurium & contumeliosum est, istique abrogando & delendo unice inservit. Istud enim quærere libet, an idem sit sacrificium Missæ cum Christi sacrificio, an vero diversum? Diversum quidem esse ipsi abnuunt. Tum enim, non sacrificium, sed manifestum sacrilegium, foret. Idem autem esse non potest: cum sacrificium Christi potissimum in obedientia ejus sub lege Dei, istoque amoris martyrio, confisat; ubi victima fuit ipse Christus; altare, ipsius divinitas; ac sacerdos, idem rursus Christus, æterni Spiritus voluntate sese offerens. Quæ omnia in Missa desunt: ubi nulla Christi obedientia, nullum martyrium, nulla mors, nullus sanguis, non ipse denique Christus, nec ut victima, nec ut sacerdos. Quod enim ex farina coquunt corporis Christi idolum, ad sacrificaturam hanc non pertinet.
units.tr: XI. 4. Above all, this daily sacrifice of theirs is injurious and insulting to the sacrifice of Christ, and it serves only to abrogate and destroy that sacrifice. Let us ask this: is the sacrifice of the Mass the same as the sacrifice of Christ, or is it different? They deny that it is different, for then it would be not a sacrifice but a plain sacrilege. But it cannot be the same. The sacrifice of Christ consists chiefly in his obedience under the law of God and in that martyrdom of love, where the victim was Christ himself, the altar his divinity, and the priest again Christ, offering himself by the will of the eternal Spirit. All these things are lacking in the Mass. There is no obedience of Christ there, no martyrdom, no death, no blood, and not even Christ himself, neither as victim nor as priest. What they bake from flour into an idol of Christ's body has nothing to do with this sacrificing.

units.la: XII. Sed efficacissime quotidianas istas libationes, post fusum semel Testam. sanguinem, proscribit Apostolus, Hebr. 9. & 10. ubi multis rationibus Christum semel tantum offerri potuisse evincit: 1. Quia cæteroquin pluries ab initio mundi pati & mori debuisset. cap. 9:26. 2. Quia ex divino ordine, ut homo moritur semel, & deinde judicium est, ita Christus semel mortuus est legi, & dein sine peccato conspicietur. com. 27, 28. 3. Quia in Christi obedientia est θέλημα & ἐυδοκία, voluntas & complacentia Dei. cap. 10:8, 9, 10. Aliter ac in pecudum sanguine; qui non sine labe erat, nec sacrificantes puros reddere poterat, adeoque iterum iterumque libari debebat, com. 1, 2, 3. 4. Quia post oblationem factam sedet in perpetuum ad dextram Dei, ac judicia in hostes suos exequitur. comm. 12, 13. Fabula ergo est, eum certorum verborum potentia quotidie a sacrificulis e cœlo evocari. 5. Quia unica oblatione consummavit omnes, qui sanctificantur, com. 14. Ubi emphasis est in voce unica; ut iterum offerri eum nefas sit.6. Denique, quia impetrata jam est ἀφεσις remissio; ut nulla amplius opus sit oblatione pro peccatis, com. 18.adeoque frustra sit, nova adhuc piamenta adhibere velle. Cum ultra remissionis gratiam nihil amplius fideles cogitare vel petere possint.
units.tr: XII. But the Apostle most effectively rules out these daily libations, after the blood of the covenant was shed once for all, in Hebrews 9 and 10, where by many arguments he shows that Christ could be offered only once. (1) Otherwise he would have had to suffer and die many times since the beginning of the world (ch. 9:26). (2) By divine order, as man dies once and after that comes judgment, so Christ died once for the sins of many and will appear a second time without sin (vv. 27, 28). (3) In Christ's obedience there is θέλημα and εὐδοκία [will and good pleasure], the will and delight of God (ch. 10:8, 9, 10). This is unlike the blood of animals, which was not without stain, could not make the worshippers pure, and therefore had to be poured out again and again (vv. 1, 2, 3). (4) Because after the offering was made he sits forever at the right hand of God and executes judgment on his enemies (vv. 12, 13). It is therefore a fable that he is daily called down from heaven by the power of certain words spoken by the little sacrificers. (5) Because by one offering he has perfected all who are sanctified (v. 14). The emphasis lies on the word one, so that it is wrong for him to be offered again. (6) Finally, because forgiveness [ἄφεσις, remission] has already been obtained, so that there is no further need of an offering for sins (v. 18), and it is vain to want to add new expiations. For beyond the grace of forgiveness the faithful can conceive or seek nothing more.

units.la: XIII. Atque haec quoque constans veteris Ecclesiae sententia fuit: quae, ad Augustini usque tempora, non aliud sacrificium expiatorium, quam quod Christus in cruce peregit, agnovit. Extant que illius Catecheseos reliquiae in ipso canone Missae; ubi sacerdos, non corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed panis & vini dona, a fidelibus oblata, Deus uti accepta habeat, & benedicat, orat; & dona ac sacrificia sancta & illibata appellat: quae verba de sacrificio Christi, quod unicum est, intelligi non possunt. Appellatur ibidem sacrificium laudis, rogaturque Deus, ut propitio & sereno vultu illud recipere dignetur, sicut accepta habuit munera Abelis: quae iterum in sacrificium Christi proprie dictum non conveniunt. Atque in eandem sententiam Scholasticorum quoque dicta adferri possunt; quae nunc omittimus.
units.tr: XIII. This also was the settled opinion of the ancient Church, which, down to the time of Augustine, acknowledged no expiatory sacrifice other than the one Christ accomplished on the cross. Remnants of that teaching survive in the very canon of the Mass, where the priest prays that God would deign to accept and bless the gifts of bread and wine offered by the faithful, not the body and blood of Christ, and calls them holy and unspotted gifts and sacrifices. These words cannot be understood of the sacrifice of Christ, which is unique. There the sacrifice is called a sacrifice of praise, and God is asked to receive it with a gracious and serene countenance, as he accepted the gifts of Abel. These again do not fit the sacrifice of Christ properly so called. Sayings of the Scholastics too may be cited to the same effect, but we omit them now.

units.la: XIV. Communis ad haec omnia exceptio est, per missae sacrificium Christi sacrificium nobis applicari. Quod in adversarios retorquere licet. Si enim applicatio ibi peragitur, ergo non sacrificium. Applicatio enim fit hominibus, sacrificium autem Deo offertur. Ut haec se mutuo perimant. Absurdum vero prorsus est, sacrificium velle applicare per Missae novum sacrificium. Quae non prioris sacrificii applicatio, sed ejus potius deletio & abolitio est.
units.tr: XIV. The common answer to all this is that through the sacrifice of the Mass the sacrifice of Christ is applied to us. This can be turned back on our opponents. For if application takes place there, then it is not a sacrifice. Application is made to men, whereas a sacrifice is offered to God. So these two destroy each other. It is utterly absurd to want to apply a sacrifice by means of a new sacrifice of the Mass. This is not an application of the earlier sacrifice but rather its undoing and abolition.

units.la: XV. Ruunt simul blasphemae nugationes de sacrificio Christi primario & secundario (quomodo & inter sacerdotem primarium & secundarios distinguunt) propitiatorio & commemoratorio; cruento & incruento. Scriptura enim non nisi unicum Novi Testam. sacrificium agnoscit, quod ejus dignitatis est, ut non nisi a primario sacerdote (quem nos unicum habemus) offerri possit. Estque illud vere propitiatorium. Nam sacrificium in Novo Test. comminisci, quod tantum commemoratorium sit; non sacrificii Christi memoriale, sed peccatorum potius accusatio & exprobratio foret. Qualis in Vet. Test. obtinuit, Hebr. 10: 3. Pariterque insulsum est, illud simul expiatorium vocare, ratione alterius cujusdam sacrificii, cui repraesentando inserviat. Hoc enim de qualicunque sacrificii expiatorii imagine dici non potest: cum ibi solum expiatio sit, ubi realis est oblatio. Tandem & illud non nisi cruentum est, cum incruenta oblatione peccatorum remissio impetrari non potuerit, Hebr. 9:22. Et certe Christi victimam cruentam fuisse fateri debent: cum qua si eadem sit illa hostia, quam sacrificuli ipsorum quotidie osserunt, sanguinis effusione ea carere non debet. Nisi & Christi sacrificium ἀναίμακτον fuisse statuant. Nec sacrificii incruenti vestigia ullibi deprehendas.
units.tr: XV. At the same time the blasphemous trifles about the primary and secondary sacrifice of Christ fall to the ground (just as they distinguish between the primary priest and secondary priests), the propitiatory and the commemorative, the bloody and the unbloody. Scripture acknowledges only one sacrifice of the New Testament, and by its dignity it can be offered only by the primary priest, whom we have as the one priest. That sacrifice is truly propitiatory. To invent a sacrifice in the New Testament that is merely commemorative would make it not a memorial of Christ's sacrifice but rather an accusation and reproach of sins. That was the case under the Old Testament (Heb. 10:3). Equally foolish is it to call the same thing expiatory, on account of some other sacrifice which it is meant to represent. For this cannot be said of any image of an expiatory sacrifice, since expiation exists only where there is a real offering. Finally, that sacrifice is not bloodless, since forgiveness of sins could not be obtained without an unbloody offering (Heb. 9:22). Indeed they must admit that Christ's victim was bloody. If the victim is the same as that host which their sacrificers offer daily, it ought not to lack the shedding of blood. Unless they also hold that the sacrifice of Christ was [ἀναίμακτον] bloodless. Yet nowhere can you find any trace of an unbloody sacrifice.

units.la: XVI. Errorem denique errore augent, cum nihilominus missaticum illud sacrum pro vivis & mortuis valere; &c, ad quaecunque bona impetranda, & mala averruncanda, facere praedicant. Omnis enim expiandi, favoremque Dei impetrandi, vis ad Christi unius sacrificium, in cruce oblatum, pertinent. 1. Joh. 1:7. Rom. 5:10. Quo si mortui nondum plene purgati sunt, ne millenae quidem missae prodesse illis possunt. Sacramentum autem, quod Christus instituit, vivis solum prodest, non mortuis: missae vero neutris, nisi quod sacerdotum superstitum coquinae valde necessariae sunt.
units.tr: XVI. Finally they multiply error by error, for they nonetheless proclaim that this sacred Mass avails for the living and the dead, and that it serves to obtain all kinds of good things and to avert evils. For all power to expiate and to obtain the favour of God belongs to the one sacrifice of Christ offered on the cross (1 John 1:7; Rom. 5:10). If the dead are not yet fully cleansed by that sacrifice, not even a thousand Masses can help them. The sacrament which Christ instituted profits only the living, not the dead; but Masses profit neither, except that the kitchens of the surviving priests are very much needed.

units.la: XVII. Atque uti sacrificium, ita & novum sacerdotum ordinem in N. T. instituunt adversarii; ex Melchisedeci videl. ritu: quos Christus creaverit per haec verba, in ultima coena, Hoc facite &c. Cum tamen unicum tantum Novi Testam. sit sacerdotium, solius videl. Christi; qui cum juramento constitutus est sacerdos, in aeternum; & solus dignam victimam, quam offerret, habuit; inque isto munere, nec successores, nec vicarios, ferre potest; cum sacerdotium ejus sit ἀπαράβα-τον, nec ψιλὸς ἀνθρώπως admittere possit. Psal. 110. Hebr. 7. Si quicunque in Novi Testam. Scripturis sacerdotes nominantur, ii sacerdotes spirituales sunt; atque ad universum fidelium gregem illa nomenclatura pertinet. Rogo vos, fratres, per misericordiam Dei, ut exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem, sanctam, placentem Deo, rationalem cultum vestrum. Rom. 12:1. Conf. 1. Pet. 2:5, 9.
units.tr: XVII. As they devise a sacrifice, so our opponents also institute in the New Testament a new order of priests, after the manner of Melchizedek, whom they say Christ created by these words at the last supper, Do this, etc. Yet the New Testament has only one priesthood, namely that of Christ alone, who was appointed priest with an oath forever, and alone had a worthy victim to offer. In that office he admits neither successors nor vicars, since his priesthood is [ἀπαράβατον] untransferable, and cannot admit a mere [ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος] man (Ps. 110; Heb. 7). If in the Scriptures of the New Testament anyone is named a priest, such priests are spiritual, and that title belongs to the whole flock of the faithful: I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, your reasonable service (Rom. 12:1). Compare 1 Pet. 2:5, 9.

units.la: XVIII. Perverse autem novi hi flamines, ac pseudo-mystae, ordinem suum ex Christi institutione arcessunt, Hoc facite &c. Et sacrificaturam Christi perennem ac ἀπαράβατον constare non putant, nisi ad ipsos honoris ac nominis istius successio pertinet; ac ad Melchizedeci denique institutum, qui, in Eucharistiae typum, pane & vino fecit, originem suam referunt. Nam 1. Christus, cum verba ista proloqueretur, nec sacerdotem ipse egit, nec sacerdotes alios instituit. Paulus enim, verborum dominicorum optimus interpres, de coena facienda illa interpretatur, & ad fideles omnes ex aequo refert. 1. Cor. 11:25, 26. & 10:16. 10: 16. 2. Et mirum vero est, Christum non posse esse sacerdotem æternum, nisi homines peccatores in istam quoque dignitatem admittat, qui Christi vice fungantur, atque ipsum in terris quotidie offerant: cum contra, eo quod sacrificatura ipsius perennis & ἀπαράβατος sit, successores, & ministros, & vicarios omnes excludat. Quæ Aaronicæ præfecturæ ratio erat; a qua Christi sacerdotium longe diversum est. Cum Christo non magis sacerdotes vicarii dari, quam sacrificium vicarium in Ecclesia existere possit. Nec minorum ac secundariorum sacerdotum color juvat; cum illi non minus quam secundarii mediatores & sponsores, testatores, excludantur. 3. Tandem Melchizedechum quod attinet, ipsum lagano vel placentula fecisse, mera fabula est; quam nec primores inter adversarios credunt; qui Gen. 14. in verbis ꝁ &c. non sacrificium, sed convivium, agnoscunt. Paulus certe, qui omne Melchisedeci mysterium Ecclesiæ aperuit, istam panum ac vini oblaturam ignorat. Neque enim isto modo ille typum Christi gessisset, quod tamen vel maxime urgent adversarii: cum ille non panem vel vinum, sed se ipsum in cruce obtulerit, atque ita sacerdotem ex Melchizedeci ordine egerit. Ut ipsum quoque Melchizedechum, non sine victima & sanguine, sacerdotem egisse, certum sit. Alioqui enim & Christus, in sacerdotium ejus succedens, solo panis ac vini libamine munus suum absolvisset. Unde jam patet, non sine sacrilegio Romanenses istum sacerdotii honorem sibi rapere, & reliqua Ecclesia sese sanctiores ferre; quin, si Deo placet, Deum inter, homınesque veluti medios, quandam generis humani procurationem sibi sumere; atque injussos munus istud ultro sibi arrogare. Quæ ultra Core, Dathanis, ac Abironis scelus eunt; quod tam severe olim Deus vindicavit. Qui dicunt, accede ad te (sive, contrahe te) ne tangas me, quia sanctus sum tibi: bi sunt fumus in naso meo, ignis ardens toto die. Esei. 65: 5.
units.tr: XVIII. But these new priests and pseudo-mystagogues wrongly derive their order from Christ's institution, Do this, etc. They do not think that Christ's perpetual and [ἀπαράβατον] untransferable sacrifice holds good unless the succession of this honour and title belongs to them, and they finally trace their origin to the institution of Melchizedek, who, as a type of the Eucharist, made an offering of bread and wine. For (1) when Christ spoke those words, he neither acted as a priest himself nor appointed other priests. Paul, the best interpreter of the Lord's words, explains them as referring to the making of that supper and applies them equally to all the faithful (1 Cor. 11:25, 26; 10:16). (2) And it is truly strange that Christ cannot be an eternal priest unless he admits sinful men to that dignity too, to act in his place and offer him daily on earth. On the contrary, because his sacrifice is perpetual and [ἀπαράβατος] untransferable, it excludes all successors, ministers and vicars. This was the principle of the Aaronic office, from which the priesthood of Christ is very different. There can be no vicarious priests with Christ, any more than a vicarious sacrifice can exist in the Church. Nor does the pretext of lesser and secondary priests help them, since these, no less than secondary mediators, sponsors and testators, are excluded. (3) As for Melchizedek, that he offered a little flagon or a small cake is pure fable, which not even the leading men among our opponents believe; they acknowledge in Genesis 14, in the words "he brought forth bread and wine," not a sacrifice but a feast. Paul certainly, who disclosed the whole mystery of Melchizedek to the Church, knows nothing of that offering of bread and wine. For in that way he would not have borne the type of Christ, which nonetheless our opponents press most strongly, since Melchizedek offered not bread or wine but himself on the cross, and so acted as priest after the order of Melchizedek. It is certain that Melchizedek himself also acted as priest not without victim and blood, for otherwise Christ, succeeding to his priesthood, would have discharged his office with nothing more than a libation of bread and wine. From this it is now clear that the Romanists seize this honour of the priesthood for themselves not without sacrilege, and bear themselves as holier than the rest of the Church; indeed, if it pleases God, they assume for themselves a certain procuration of the human race, standing between God and men as it were, and presume to claim that office for themselves uninvited. These men go beyond the crime of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, which God once punished so severely: Who say, Stand by yourself, come not near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire burning all day long (Isa. 65:5).

units.la: XIX. Ultro autem sequitur, si nec sacrificium externum, nec sacerdotes, in N. T. dentur, nec aras & altaria, cæterumque sacrificiorum apparatum, ibi esse. Figurata enim sunt, & de Christi solius morte ac sacrificio intelligi debent, quæ occurrunt, Hebr. 13: 10. Habemus altare, ex quo edendi potestatem non habent, qui tabernaculo serviunt. Apoc. 6: 9. Vidi sub altari animas macta-torum proter sermonem Dei, Apoc. 8: 3, 4. Alius Angelus venit, & constitit apud altare, habens thuribulum aureum &c. Improprie autem, & incaute nimis in veteri Ecclesia mensæ Eucharisticæ altaria dici, & esse paulatim, cœperunt. Conf. supra Cap. 10. §45. Tollitur quoque altaria sub N. T.
units.tr: XIX. It follows that if neither an external sacrifice nor priests are given in the New Testament, then neither altars nor altar furniture nor the rest of the sacrificial apparatus exist there either. The passages that occur are figurative and must be understood as referring to the death and sacrifice of Christ alone: Heb. 13:10, We have an altar, from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. Rev. 6:9, I saw under the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God. Rev. 8:3, 4, Another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer, etc. But in the early Church the name "altars" was applied improperly and rashly to the tables of the Eucharist, and gradually they came to be called and to be altars. See above, chap. 10, §45. Altars are also removed under the New Testament.

units.la: XX. Adferunt adversarii, pro tuendo Ecclesiae suo sacerdotio & sacrificio, tum typos Veteris T. tum vaticinia; tum loca quaedam Novi Test. ac denique Veterum auctoritates. Quae nobis breviter respondebimus; transmittemus.
units.tr: XX. To defend their priesthood and sacrifice, our opponents bring forward the types of the Old Testament, the prophecies, certain passages of the New Testament, and finally the testimonies of the Fathers. We shall answer these briefly, and pass over them lightly.

units.la: XXI. Inter typos Eucharistiae sacrificium adumbrantes, numerant Melchizedeci oblationem, Agnum paschalem, sanguinem in Vet. Test. dedicatione fusum, Exod. 24:8. tum & alia sacrificia, Lev. 1. &c. praesertim paupertinum illud, in similae oblatione, quod ipsi incruentum vocant, Lev. 5:11. Quae omnia cum & typi Eucharistiae, & simul sacrificia, fuerint; in Eucharistia quoque sacrificari debere contendunt. Quod eodem modo procedit, ac si urgerem, in precibus Christianorum quoque sacrificium proprie dictum peragi; quod veteris templi libamina, suffitus, ac odoramenta, quae in sacrificiorum numerum veniebant, illas adumbraverint. Psal. 141: 2. Apoc. 5:8. Sed nos de typis illis, quos appellant, alias respondimus. Hoc solum in genere addimus, illos non panis Eucharistici, sed sacrificii Christi, in cruce oblati, figuras extitisse. Non enim, ut ante observavimus, sacramenta Veteris Testam. typi erant sacramentorum nostrorum; sed & haec, & illa, erant antitypa, & ejusdem corporis imagines & umbrae, & radii, corpus nunc antecedentes, nunc consequentes, pro varia Ecclesiae luce, & diverso solis justitiae situ.
units.tr: XXI. Among the types foreshadowing the sacrifice of the Eucharist they count Melchizedek's offering, the paschal lamb, the blood shed at the dedication of the Old Testament, Exod. 24:8, and other sacrifices, Lev. 1, etc., especially that poor offering of fine flour, which they themselves call unbloody, Lev. 5:11. Since all these were both types of the Eucharist and sacrifices at the same time, they contend that the Eucharist too ought to be offered as a sacrifice. This argument runs in the same way as if I should press that a proper sacrifice is also performed in the prayers of Christians, because the libations, incense and perfumes of the ancient temple, which were counted among the sacrifices, foreshadowed them: Ps. 141:2; Rev. 5:8. But we have answered those so-called types elsewhere. We add only this in general: those types were figures not of the Eucharistic bread but of the sacrifice of Christ offered on the cross. For, as we noted before, the sacraments of the Old Testament were not types of our sacraments; rather both were antitypes, images and shadows of one and the same body, and rays going before the body at one time and following it at another, according to the varying light of the Church and the different position of the Sun of righteousness.

units.la: XXII. Alterum argumentum ex variis prophetarum locis contexunt: ubi altaris, & incensi, & minchae ac oblationis munda, sub Nov. Test. offerendae, fit mentio. Quo referunt Esai. 19:21. Dan. 8:11. & 12:11. ac praesertim Mal. 1:11. Cum tamen manifestum sit, in locis istis Prophetas de spirituali Dei cultu; deque fide in unicum Christi sacrificium, post Euangelii promulgationem, inter gentes omnibus locis propaganda; deque Gentium ipsarum oblatione per Apostolorum ministerium, agere: atque ista vocabulis, ex veteris temporis cultu desumtis, adumbrare; ac proinde figurate ipsorum dicta accipi debere. Praesertim cum idem alibi externa & materialia sacrificia in Novo Test. non instauranda, sed abolenda, clarissimis verbis praedicent.
units.tr: XXII. They weave a second argument from various passages of the prophets, where mention is made of an altar, incense, meat offering and pure offering to be offered under the New Testament. To this they refer Isa. 19:21, Dan. 8:11, 12:11, and especially Mal. 1:11. Yet it is plain that in these places the prophets are speaking of the spiritual worship of God, of faith in the one sacrifice of Christ to be spread in every place among the nations after the promulgation of the gospel, and of the offering of the Gentiles themselves through the ministry of the apostles; and that they shadow these things with words taken from the worship of the old time, so that their words must be understood figuratively. This is especially so since the same prophets elsewhere declare in the clearest words that external and material sacrifices are not to be restored under the New Testament but abolished.

units.la: XXIII. Nec felicius concludunt, quae ex Novo Test. adferunt. Adoratio enim in Spir. & veritate, remotis veteris templi velis ac umbris, de qua Joh 4:23. in missam certe non convenit; cum istud sacrum etiam Judaicis sacrificiis operosius sit. Magis autem in illam quadrant proxima Christi verba: vos adoratis, quod nescitis. 2. Nec Christus ipse in Coena sacri ficabat, cum corpus suum frangi, & sanguinem effundi, dicediccbat. Ista enim temporis enallage rei certitudinem indicat, cum mors ejus proxime instaret, jamque certa & decreta foret. Conf. simulem phrasin Joh. 10: 15. Animam meam pono pro ovibus, & 17: 11. Et ego non amplius sum in mundo, & hi in mundo sunt, & ego ad te venio. 3. Similiter nec Apostolos sacrificare jubebat, per verba, hoc facite; sed, Paulo interprete, sacras epulas, in emortualis istius Coenae memoriam, inire jugiter suadebat. 4. Neque procedit ratiuncula, ex 1. Cor. 10: 15 &c. ubi mensa Domini cum mensa daemoniorum comparatur: unde utrobique sacrificales dapes, & sacrificium, dari concludunt. Quod nimium est. Nam simpliciter tantum dicit Apostolus, niminem mensae dominicae, & epularum in idoleo participem esse posse. 5. Praecipue istant in loco Act. 13: 2. ubi ex voce λειτουργούντων, primos illos Ecclesiae doctores missificantes introducunt. Quod Paedagogorum ferulam meretur. Cum vox λειτουργεῖν latissime pateat, nec certum aliquod ministerium dicat. Confer Luc. 1: 23. Hebr. 9: 21. & 10: 11. & 8: 1, 2. & 1: 14. Rom. 13: 6 Phil. 2: 25, 30. Rom. 15: 27. Quaenam autem Apostolorum λειτουργεία & quodnam ministerium fuerit, ex com. 2. & 3. Illis autem jejunantibus &c. & Rom. 15: 16. Ad hoc ut sim minister Jesu Christi apud gentes: operans Euangelio Dei, ut oblatio gentium fiat accepta, sanctificata per Spir. S. apparet.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor do they conclude more happily from what they bring from the New Testament. The worship in spirit and truth, John 4:23, with the veils and shadows of the old temple removed, certainly does not fit the Mass, since that rite is even more laborious than the Jewish sacrifices. The words of Christ that come closest to it fit it better: you worship what you do not know. 2. Nor did Christ himself sacrifice at the Lord's Supper when he said that his body was to be broken and his blood poured out. That change of tense indicates the certainty of the thing, since his death was at hand and already certain and decreed. Compare the similar phrase John 10:15, I lay down my life for the sheep, and 17:11, And I am no longer in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to you. 3. Likewise he did not command the apostles to sacrifice by the words do this; rather, as Paul explains, he urged them to keep the sacred feast continually in remembrance of that death-bringing Supper. 4. Nor does the little argument from 1 Cor. 10:15 etc. hold, where the table of the Lord is compared with the table of demons; from this they conclude that on both sides there are sacrificial feasts and a sacrifice. That is going too far. For the apostle says simply that no one can be a partaker of the Lord's table and of the feasts of idols. 5. They press especially the passage Acts 13:2, where from the word ministering [λειτουργούντων] they bring in those first teachers of the Church as offering sacrifice. That deserves the rod of the schoolmasters. For the word to minister [λειτουργεῖν] has a very wide range and does not denote any one definite ministry. Compare Luke 1:23, Heb. 9:21, 10:11, 8:1, 2, 1:14, Rom. 13:6, Phil. 2:25, 30, Rom. 15:27. What the apostles' ministry [λειτουργεία] was, and what their office was, appears from verses 2 and 3, while they were fasting, etc., and from Rom. 15:16, that I should be a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles might be made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XXIV. Denique non plus in Patrum auctoritate praesidii habent: qui ut augustius de sacramentis solebant loqui, S. Coenam sacrificium appellabant; non Pontificio sensu, ac proprie, sed alias ob causas. 1. Ob praecipuum S. Coenae scopum ac finem; quia ea publica sacrificii Christi commemoratio erat; ac nihil nisi mors ac oblatio Christi in ea audiebatur, ac repraesentabatur. 2. Quia preces & hymni, quae sacrificii nomine apud sacros Scriptores veniunt, ibi offerebantur. Quod Tertulliano est, sacrificare pura prece &c. Unde incruentae oblationis appellatio; oppositae ad cruenta veterum sacra. Cyrillus ἀναιμάκτως θυσίας & δοξολογίας dixit. 3. Accedebant ad spiritualia illa sacrificia, post secundum a Christo nato saeculum, etiam dona, & oblationes externae panis & vini, & aliarum rerum; tum in sacri epuli usum, tum in pauperum alimoniam. Quae Apostolus hostia, Deo accepta, nomine dignatur. Hebr. 13: 16. Phil. 4: 18. Ex quibus oblationibus, hostiae primum nomen, deinceps vero ejus expiatoria quoque vis Eucharistiae haesit; sicut & ex recitatione nominis illius qui obtulerat id, unde parabatur Eucharistia, oblatio & valor missae pro aliis, tam vivis, quam defunctis, suborta sunt. 4. Deni-
units.tr: XXIV. Finally, they have no more support in the authority of the Fathers. When they spoke more solemnly about the sacraments, they called the holy Supper a sacrifice; but not in the Popish sense, nor properly, and for other reasons. 1. Because of the chief aim and purpose of the holy Supper, since it was a public commemoration of the sacrifice of Christ; and in it nothing but the death and offering of Christ was heard and represented. 2. Because the prayers and hymns, which the sacred writers call sacrifices, were offered there. This is what Tertullian means by to sacrifice with a pure prayer, etc. Hence the name "unbloody offering," set over against the bloody rites of the ancients. Cyril called them bloodless sacrifices and doxologies [ἀναιμάκτως θυσίας καὶ δοξολογίας]. 3. After the second century from the birth of Christ, gifts and external offerings of bread and wine and other things were also added to those spiritual sacrifices, both for the use of the sacred feast and for the feeding of the poor. The apostle honours these with the name sacrifice acceptable to God, Heb. 13:16, Phil. 4:18. From these offerings the name of victim first clung to the Eucharist, and afterwards its expiatory power as well; and in the same way, from the recitation of the name of the person who had offered the material from which the Eucharist was prepared, the offering and value of the Mass for others, both living and dead, arose. 4. Moreover, that name was given to add dignity to the Christian religion and to exalt the mystery of the holy Supper, so that the accusations of the heathens might be met, since they understood no religion without an altar and sacrifice.

units.la: ex Patri-bus. que ad Christianæ religionis decus, & S. Cœnæ mysterium extollendum, appellatio illa faciebat: ut Ethnicorum criminationibus obviam iretur, qui nullum religionem sine ara ac sacrificio intelligebant. Paulatim vero, obsolescente veritatis doctrina, hæ figuratæ locutiones errori ansam præbuerunt, & Cœna in sacrificium; Pastores, in sacerdotes; mensæ, in altaria; ac corporis Christi signa, horrenda μεταμορφώσει, in ipsum corpus Christi transierunt, omniaque ad sacrificii formam composita sunt. Quam Helenam isti Parides ut sibi lucrosam fovere, utque novos amatores alliciat, quocunque fuco linere non desinunt.
units.tr: ...from the Fathers. But gradually, as the teaching of the truth fell into disuse, these figurative expressions gave occasion to error: the Supper turned into a sacrifice, the ministers into priests, the tables into altars, and the signs of the body of Christ, through a dreadful transformation [μεταμορφώσει], into the very body of Christ; and everything was arranged to the form of a sacrifice. These Paris-like men never cease to smear Helen, as they think she is profitable to them, with whatever paint, so as to keep her and attract new lovers.

units.la: XXV. Sed non substitit hic error. Tandem enim sacramentum hoc, quod tot spoliis, & direptis ex Christi corpore exuviis auxerant, in idolum in Ecclesia erexerunt. Qui summus erroris gradus est. Ita ut panis ipsorum venenum sit; cum non manducetur solum, sed & adoretur.
units.tr: XXV. But this error did not stop here. For at last they set up as an idol in the Church this sacrament, which they had enlarged with so many spoils and with relics stripped from the body of Christ. This is the highest degree of error. So their bread becomes poison, since it is not only eaten but also adored.

units.la: XXVI. Primum autem sacerdos hostiam a se adoratam elevat, & concioni spectandam exhibet: quæ, ad id spectaculum religione percussa, prono vertice terram tangit, præscribente id Honorio 3. circa sæculum 13.
