Quanquam enim apud veteres, post plura demum à Christo nato sæcula, consecratus panis religioso ritu in altum levaretur, quod à more Judaico, in sacrificiis quibusdam usitato, haustum quidam putant, adgenicultatio tamen & adstantis coronæ religiosa inclinatio non ante Honorii tempora obtinuit.
units.tr: XXVI. First, the priest lifts up the host he has adored and displays it to the congregation to be gazed upon; and the congregation, struck with religious awe at that sight, touches the ground with bowed head, as Honorius III prescribed around the thirteenth century. For although among the ancients, only many centuries after the birth of Christ, the consecrated bread was raised on high with religious ritual, which some think was borrowed from the Jewish custom used in certain sacrifices, yet the kneeling and religious bowing of the standing crowd did not prevail until the time of Honorius.

units.la: XXVII. Elevatum, & in alto expositum, panem universa deinde concio adorat. Quod, contra Christi & Apostolorum institutum; contra veteris Ecclesiæ consuetudinem (cujus hæc sollemnis formula, sursum corda) originem suam Romanorum Pontificum superstitioni debet. Qui, post constitutum Transubstantiationis dogma, corpus illud Christi, ex farina præstigiosa metamorphosi factum, publice adorari, codemque cultu, qua S. S. Trinitatem, affici præceperunt. Atque hæc Honorii, uti diximus, qui post Innocentium tertium sedit, qui Transubstantiationem A.C. 1215. canonisavit, præcipua laus est. Cui Urbanus iv. non leve incrementum dedit, instituto sacrilego illo, quod corporis Christi vocant, festo. Qui corruptelarum circa hoc sacramentum veluti apex est: dum panis ille, quem Christus frangi, distribui, manducari præcepit; non sine pompa ostentatur, circumgestatur, & adoratur. Atque hoc videl. est Cœnam facere, & convivantium in morem accumbere, quod Christum & Apostolos fecisse legimus.
units.tr: XXVII. Once it has been lifted up and displayed on high, the whole congregation then adores the bread. This practice runs against the institution of Christ and the Apostles, and against the custom of the ancient Church, whose solemn formula was lift up your hearts. It owes its origin to the superstition of the Roman Pontiffs, who, after they had established the dogma of Transubstantiation, ordered that the body of Christ, made from flour by a deceptive metamorphosis, be adored publicly and honoured with the same worship as the Holy Trinity. This, as we have said, is the chief praise of Honorius, who sat after Innocent III and who canonised Transubstantiation in 1215. Urban IV gave it no small increase by instituting that sacrilegious feast which they call the feast of the Body of Christ. This is, as it were, the summit of the corruptions surrounding this sacrament: that bread which Christ commanded to be broken, distributed and eaten is displayed with pomp, carried about and adored. And this, namely, is to make a supper and to recline at table in the manner of those present, which we read that Christ and the Apostles did.

units.la: XXVIII. Nos autem hoc pacto sacrilegio & idololatria contaminari Ecclesiam, Deumque novum, quam Patres nostri non noverunt, invehi, vehi, Dan. 11: 38. & furfuraceum denique numen coli contendimus.
units.tr: XXVIII. But we contend that by this practice the Church is contaminated with sacrilege and idolatry, that a new God, whom our fathers did not know, is brought in and carried about (Dan. 11:38), and, in short, that a flimsy bran-stuffed deity is worshipped.

units.la: XXIX. Nec juvat color, non panem, sed Christum, qui ista specie tegatur, ab ipsis adorari: saltem in Eucharistia ipsum praesentem esse. neminem negare posse: unde quaeri ibi ac religioso cultu propitiari quoque debeat. Verum haec meri fuci, & meretricia pigmenta sunt, quibus vel crassissima idololatria obduci, & pro germano Dei cultu produci possit. Nam 1. quid vetat & Ethnicos, unctum in trivio lapidem adorantes, ita excipere: non saxum sese colere, vel statuam, sed vim divinam in ea hospitantem; Deumque ipsum in corpore isto suo (ita enim de statuis sapiebant) praesentem. 2. Sacramentum autem a Pontificiis adorari, idque honore prosequendum, publica Ecclesiae istius vox est; dum in Tridentino Concil. latriae cultum, qui vero Deo debetur, illi quoque sacramento habendum scisciunt, sess. 3. cap. 6 Sacramenti autem appellatione panis & vini accidentia comprehendi, ipsi fatentur. Unde idololatriam non effugiunt, non panem, sed panis accidentia & species adorantes. Certe populum ipsorum illud, quod corporeis oculis in sacramento usurpatur, quodque cerni & tangi potest, adorare, & palam Deum Dominumque suum vocare, nec id ab ipsis culpari, in propatulo est. 3. Et si vel Christum adorare se perhibeant, qualis videl. in sacramento illo est; ille non alius Christus est, quam ex farina coctus, non qualis de matre virgine prodiit: atque ita falsus ille Christus est, non sine sacrilegio adorandus. Adorant nempe aliquid, quod Christus non est, sed idolum. Unde, cum verum objectum cultus mutetur, formaliter hic idololatria est. Quod palpabile est. 4. Quibus accedit, quod ipsi panem, sub quo Christum praesentem credunt, post adorationem, manducant. Quae eo magis execranda est idololatria, infidelibus inaudita, ipsique maxime scandalosa. 5. Sed &, si revera praesens ibi esse Christus intelligatur, id de corpore ac cadavere ipsius intelligendum esset. De divina enim ejus natura quaestio nulla est. Corpus autem vel cadaver Christi, quod mera creatura est, per sese divino honore coli, religio non fert. 6. Christum autem corporaliter ibi praesentem esse, jam ante sustulimus. Nec errorem isto praetextu minuunt, sed augent: dum Christum non solum, verbis quibusdam, in Coena praesentem sistunt; sed & ut praesentem, quanquam abnuentibus omnibus sensibus & ratione, quam ejurare coguntur, adorant. Qui jam non simplex error, sed idololatria est, qua priorem errorem cumulant. 7. Quod autem Christus in Eucharistia peculiariter praesens sit, id rite intelligendum est. Non enim de elemento illud, vel panc vel vino, intelligendum est, quasi sub eo quaerendus Christus foret: sed de sacra illa actione, & S. Coenae usu, accipi debet. Atque ita Christum in Eucharistia adorandum, inque symbolorum istorum usu fide quaerendum & amplectendum fatemur. Quae tamen ab elementorum superstitione procul abeunt. 8. Omnibus autem istis fucis ac praestigiis opponimus sanctissimas Christi admonitiones: Mulier, crede mihi, quod veniat hora, quum neque in monte hoc, neque Hierosolymis, adorabitis Patrem. Sed venit hora, & nunc est, quum veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & veritate, Joh. 4: 21, 23. Itaque, si dixerint vobis, Ecce, in deserto est; ne egredimini: Ecce in conclavibus, ne credite. Sicut enim fulgur erit ab Oriente, & apparet usque in Occidentem, ita etiam erit adventus Filii hominis. Matth. 24:26. Quibus docetur, Ecclesiam, jam ab omni locorum religione liberam, non ad aram, vel templum, vel quemcunque locum, preces suas affundere necesse habere: caeremonialem enim ad certa loca, & signa, quae religiosum respectum habeant ad rem signatam, adorationem nunc cessare; nec Deum certo jam in loco quaeri velle, ut olim; nec memoriae suum, ac numinis veluti praesentiam, alicui loco vel symbolo affixisse: contra autem, Christum jam in coelo esse, ibi eum quaerendum; &, cum terra universa ex aequo vel sancta, vel profana, nobisque vel patria, vel hospita, sit, ad coelestem illam patriam unice suspirandum & properandum, abdicata omni cujuscunque terrae, vel terrarum angului, amore ac religione.
units.tr: XXIX. Nor does it help that they plead the colour that it is not the bread but Christ, who is hidden under that appearance, whom they adore; that at least it cannot be denied that he is present in the Eucharist, and that therefore he ought to be sought there and propitiated with religious worship. But these are mere paints and harlot's cosmetics, with which even the grossest idolatry can be covered over and presented as the genuine worship of God. For (1) what would prevent the heathen, who adore an anointed stone at a crossroads, from making the same reply: that they do not worship the stone or the statue, but the divine power dwelling in it, and God himself present in that body of his (for so they thought about statues)? (2) That the sacrament is adored by the Papists, and is to be honoured with worship, is the public voice of that Church; for at the Council of Trent they decree that the worship of latria, which is due to the true God, is to be given also to that sacrament (sess. 3, cap. 6). Yet they themselves admit that by the name sacrament the accidents of bread and wine are understood. Hence they do not escape idolatry, since they adore not the bread but the accidents and appearances of the bread. Certainly it is plain that their people adore what is used in the sacrament with bodily eyes, and what can be seen and touched, and openly call it God and their Lord, and that this is not blamed by them. (3) And even if they claim to adore Christ, namely as he is in that sacrament, that is not the Christ who was born of the virgin mother, but a Christ baked from flour; and so that Christ is false and is not to be adored without sacrilege. They adore, of course, something that is not Christ but an idol. Hence, since the true object of worship is changed, this is formally idolatry. This is palpable. (4) To which is added that they themselves eat, after adoration, the bread under which they believe Christ to be present. This idolatry is all the more detestable, unheard of among unbelievers, and most scandalous to them. (5) But also, if Christ is truly understood to be present there, this would have to be understood of his body and corpse; for there is no question about his divine nature. But the body or corpse of Christ, which is a mere creature, is not, by its own power, a thing to be worshipped with divine honour; religion does not allow it. (6) That Christ is bodily present there, we have already refuted. Nor do they lessen their error by this pretext, but increase it: for they not only set Christ present in the Supper by certain words, but also adore him as present, although all the senses and reason, which they are forced to renounce, deny it. This is no longer simple error but idolatry, by which they heap up their earlier error. (7) But that Christ is present in the Eucharist in a peculiar way is to be understood rightly. For this must not be understood of the element, whether bread or wine, as though Christ were to be sought under it; it must be understood of that sacred action and of the use of the Lord's Supper. And so we confess that Christ is to be adored in the Eucharist, and is to be sought and embraced by faith in the use of these symbols. Yet these things are far removed from the superstition of the elements. (8) Against all these paints and tricks we set the most holy admonitions of Christ: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth (John 4:21, 23). So if they say to you, "Behold, he is in the desert," do not go out; "behold, he is in the inner rooms," do not believe it. For as the lightning comes out of the east and shines even to the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be (Matt. 24:26). By these words it is taught that the Church, now free from all local religion, does not need to pour out its prayers at an altar, or a temple, or any particular place; for the ceremonial adoration tied to certain places and signs, which have a religious regard to the thing signified, has now ceased; nor does God wish to be sought in one particular place now, as formerly, nor has he attached his memory and, as it were, his presence of divinity to any place or symbol. On the contrary, since Christ is now in heaven, he is to be sought there; and since the whole earth is alike either holy or profane, and to us either a homeland or a foreign place, we must long and hasten only towards that heavenly homeland, renouncing all love and reverence for any land or corner of the lands.

units.la: XXX. Adorationem sequitur hostiae asservatio. Solent enim sacratum panem, in ornata cista, ad cultum in templis proponere; & cum religiosa pompa per vicos deferre; ac, sollemnioribus festis, theatralem in modum, circumgestare, canticis interim & Psalmis compita celebrantes. Quae & sacramenti naturae repugnant, quod in solo usu, & panis fractione, ac manducatione, consistit; extra quam nulla signi analogia, ac nullum sacramentum est, & Christi instituto, & antiquae Ecclesiae exemplo, refragantur: ac glisccnti denique idololatriae non exiguum commeatum exhibent, tandemque inexplicabilibus difficultatibus causam praebent; ut ex Scholasticorum disputationibus, de corruptis forte vel arrosis speciebus, patet.
units.tr: XXX. The adoration is followed by the reservation of the victim. For they usually set out the consecrated bread in an adorned case in the churches for worship, and carry it about the streets with religious pomp; and on the more solemn feasts they carry it around in theatrical fashion, while the crowds celebrate with songs and psalms at the crossroads. These practices are contrary both to the nature of the sacrament, which consists solely in its use, in the breaking and eating of the bread, outside of which there is no analogy of sign and no sacrament, and they go against the institution of Christ and the example of the ancient Church. They also provide no small passage to the idolatry that is growing, and finally they give rise to inexplicable difficulties, as is clear from the scholastic disputations about the species that may have been corrupted or gnawed.

units.la: XXXI. Ex hisce omnibus patet, quam vere a Catech. Heidelb. q. 80. concludatur, ipsum Missae fundamentum nihil aliud esse, quam abnegationem unici illius sacrificii & passionis Jesu Christi, & execrandam idololatriam. Specie enim sacrificii Christi, Patri quotidie offerendi, exco- gitatum hic fuit, diaboli astu, sacrificium saltum & idololatricum, unice comparatum ad abolendum verum Christi sacrificium, & exstirpandum omnem ejus vim & memoriam. Hi nempe sunt illi, Qui instruunt Turmae mensam, & implent Numero crama. Esai. 65: 11. Ut vere in illud quadret, quod de Gentilium sacrificiis ex Mose docet Paulus 1. Cor. 10: 20. Quae immolant gentes, daemoniis immolant, & non Deo: nolo autem vos consortes daemoniorum esse. Ut si ullibi, hic certe necessaria sit aurea Apostoli Johannis gnome & cautela: Filioli, custodite vos ipsos ab idolis. 1. Epist. 5: 21.
units.tr: XXXI. From all these things it is plain how truly the Heidelberg Catechism (q. 80) concludes that the very foundation of the Mass is nothing other than a denial of that unique sacrifice and passion of Jesus Christ, and a detestable idolatry. For under the appearance of a sacrifice of Christ, to be offered daily to the Father, there was devised here, by the cunning of the devil, a sacrifice that is false and idolatrous, designed solely to abolish the true sacrifice of Christ and to root out all its power and memory. These are indeed those who prepare the table for the troop and fill the cup for the number (Isa. 65:11). It fits exactly what Paul teaches from Moses about the sacrifices of the Gentiles: What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to be partners with demons (1 Cor. 10:20). And if anywhere, here surely is needed the golden maxim and caution of the Apostle John: Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: De Sacramentis supernumerariis.
units.tr: Concerning Supernumerary Sacraments.

units.la: I. ACtenus de germanis & legitimis Ecclesiae sacramentis, quae sola in Scripturis reperiuntur, & a veteri Ecclesia agnita fuerunt. Quanquam latius aliquando sacramenti nomen usurpaverint, & cuicunque mysterio, & signo, ac ritui sacro illud accommodaverint. Qua ratione innu-mera forent sacramenta.
units.tr: I. So far I have spoken of the genuine and lawful sacraments of the Church, which are found only in Scripture and were acknowledged by the early Church. Writers have sometimes used the word "sacrament" more broadly, applying it to any mystery, sign or sacred rite. On that reckoning there would be countless sacraments.

units.la: II. Ecclesia Romana septem numerat sacramenta. Qui numerus primum apud Hugonem de S. Victore occurrit, A.C. 1130. Quem secutus Lombardus, illum sequentis scholae Doctoribus tradidit. Confirmavit eum Ecclesia in Concilio Florentino. Quanquam non adeo explicate ea omnia proprie dicta esse sacramenta, nec plura reperiri, definierit. Quae Concilium Tridentinum addidit. Mittimus autem lepidas eorum probationes, & de septenario lusus.
units.tr: II. The Roman Church counts seven sacraments. This number first appears in Hugh of St Victor, in the year 1130. Lombard followed him and handed it on to the teachers of the following school. The Church confirmed it at the Council of Florence, though that council did not explain clearly that all of these are properly called sacraments, nor did it declare that no more are to be found. The Council of Trent added these. We pass over their clever proofs and their playing with the number seven.

units.la: III. Erroris occasio fuit, 1. quod ritus quoslibet sacros, & actiones, in quibus aliquid mysterii exist ere putabant, temere nimis in sacramenta commutarunt. Quae praecipua erroris causa fuit. Hinc omnium illorum ortus debetur χειροθεσία, seu manus impositioni. 2. Quod ex κακοζηλία, quae miraculose ab Apostolis patrabantur, ea perpetua in Ecclesia esse voluerint; & cum miraculum non sequeretur, mysterii nihilominus causa observari. 3. Quosdam etiam ritus, & sacramenta, ex metaphoris in Scriptura usitatis, de novo fabricarunt. Cumque mera verba, & loquendi modi, essent, in caeremonias ea tranformarunt. 4. Lapsi denique sunt in vocis Sacramentum usu; quod vulgatus interpres pro quolibet mysterio ponit.
units.tr: III. The occasion of the error was: (1) they all too rashly turned into sacraments any sacred rites and actions in which they thought some mystery existed. This was the chief cause of the error, and from it arose the origin of all those things traced to the laying on of hands [χειροθεσία], that is, the imposition of hands. (2) From a mischievous imitation [κακοζηλία], they wanted the things the Apostles performed miraculously to remain in the Church permanently; and when no miracle followed, they nevertheless observed them for the sake of a mystery. (3) They also newly fashioned some rites and sacraments out of metaphors in common use in Scripture. Since these were mere words and modes of speaking, they turned them into ceremonies. (4) Finally they slipped in their use of the word sacrament, which the Vulgate translator applies to any mystery whatever.

units.la: IV. Nos autem adoptiva ista sacramenta, quae furto in nominis illius dignitatem irrepserunt, non agnoscimus, cum omni Scripturae auctoritate careant; nec signa sacra sint, nec mandatum divinum habeant, nec foederis denique gratiae promissionem contineant. Non Ecclesiae novorum signorum cudendorum potestatem damus. Multo minus ut adulterini quidam ritus divinis sacramentis, non solum aequandi, sed & anteponendi sint, ut quibusdam eorum in Papatu contigit. Sed operae pretium erit haec Ecclesiae Romanae additamenta per partes lustrare.
units.tr: IV. We, however, do not acknowledge these adopted sacraments, which have crept in by theft into the dignity of that name. They lack all authority of Scripture: they are neither holy signs, nor have they a divine command, nor do they contain the promise of the covenant of grace. We do not grant the Church any power to coin new signs, and much less that certain counterfeit rites should be not only equated with the divine sacraments but even preferred to them, as has happened in Papacy with some of them. It will, however, be worthwhile to review these additions of the Roman Church part by part.

units.la: V. Baptismo immediate subjungunt Confirmationem. Quam Episcopus ministrare solet jam baptizatis, sed aetate provectioribus: quorum frontibus, certis verbis ac ritibus, olei vel balsami liquorem allinit; unctosque leviter alapa caedit; in Christianae militiae rudimentum. Essectum ejus dicunt, quod ita initiati novum robur, novumque Spiritus incrementum accipiant, atque ita auspicato in sacram militiam immittantur.
units.tr: V. Immediately after baptism they join Confirmation. The bishop usually administers it to those already baptized but of more mature age. On their foreheads, with certain words and rites, he smears a liquid of oil or balsam, and gently strikes the anointed person on the cheek, as the beginning of Christian soldiering. They say its effect is that those so initiated receive new strength and a new increase of the Spirit, and so are auspiciously sent into sacred warfare.

units.la: VI. Originem istius ritus vetustiores ex Scholasticis concilio Meldensi adscribunt. Alii autem Chrisma illud ad ipso Christo, vel ab Apostolis institutum ferunt. Atque huc adferunt, quae de Spiritus effusione, ac impositione manuum in Scriptura occurrunt. Luc. 24:28. Joh. 14:16. & 15:26. & 16:13. Act. 1:5. & 8:17. & 19:6. Quorum illud promissionis, hoc signi vicem habeat: mandatum autem ex ipsa Ecclesiae illius praxi colligunt. Sed vana haec sunt. Nullibi enim in istis locis vel olei, vel balsami, vel caeterorum rituum, in hoc sacro adhibitorum, vel chrismationis denique alicujus mentio fit: neque illud in Ecclesia primitiva, nisi saeculo demum secundo, eoque praecipiti, exstitit. Impositio autem manuum, quae ab Apostolis usurpata legitur, ad dona extraordinaria spectabat. Miraculum vero in sacramentum ordinarium convertere nefas est. Quicquid enim autem efficaciae illi adscribitur, baptismi spolium est; quo solo Christiani renascuntur, & divino Spiritu imbuuntur, ad bella Domini gerenda. Nec alio ad istam rem auspicio, aliove ad Christianam militiam sacramento, opus est.
units.tr: VI. The older writers ascribe the origin of this rite to the Scholastics at the Council of Meaux. Others trace this chrism to Christ himself or to the Apostles, and they bring forward what Scripture says about the outpouring of the Spirit and the laying on of hands: Luke 24:28, John 14:16, 15:26, 16:13, Acts 1:5, 8:17, 19:6. Of these, the former serves as the promise and the latter as the sign; they gather the command from the practice of that Church itself. But these arguments are empty. Nowhere in these passages is there any mention of oil, balsam, the other rites used in this sacrament, or chrismation of any kind. Nor did this rite exist in the primitive Church until the second century at the earliest, and then in a hasty form. The laying on of hands which we read was used by the Apostles pertained to extraordinary gifts, and it is wrong to turn a miracle into an ordinary sacrament. Whatever efficacy is ascribed to it belongs to the baptism it has despoiled; by baptism alone Christians are reborn and imbued with the divine Spirit to wage the Lord's wars. For this matter no other auspice, and for Christian warfare no other sacrament, is needed.

units.la: VII. Veteres quod attinet, illorum chrisma ritus erat, baptismo adjunctus; quem in peculiare sacramentum, quod multis post baptismum annis plerunque ministratur, ac diversam significationem ac effectum habet, Romana Ecclesia commutavit. Quod sensim factum est. Dum unctio illa paulatim a baptismo separari coepit: cum vel ab haeresi venientes, non novo baptismo, sed unctione, vel manuum impositione, in Ecclesiae communionem reciperentur; vel qui, urgente necessitate, a laicis, vel alioquin a Diacono aut presbytero baptizati erant, postea ab Episcopo (cui videl. soli novos Christo milites legere fas erat) vel ungerentur, vel manu simpliciter imposita confirmarentur. His enim aliisque occasionibus paulatim ille ritus a baptismo divelli, & tandem, augescente superstitione, pro singulari sacramento haberi coeptus est.
units.tr: VII. As for the ancients, their chrism was a rite attached to baptism. The Roman Church changed it into a special sacrament, usually administered many years after baptism, with a different meaning and effect. This happened gradually. That anointing little by little began to be separated from baptism: when those coming from heresy were received into communion with the Church not by a new baptism but by anointing or the laying on of hands; or when those who, under pressing necessity, had been baptized by laymen, or otherwise by a deacon or presbyter, were afterwards either anointed or simply confirmed by the laying on of hands by the bishop, to whom alone it was lawful to enlist new soldiers of Christ. By these and other occasions that rite was gradually torn away from baptism and at last, as superstition grew, came to be regarded as a separate sacrament.

units.la: VIII. Sequitur lapsorum sacramentum, quos per Poenitentiam rursus reconcinnari, & commissorum veniam adipisci ajunt: atque esse hoc alterum peccatis expiandis sacramentum: ac, sicuti per baptismum labes originalis abluitur, ita per poenitentiam quotidianos lapsus deleri. Nos poenitentiam Deo gratam, ac Ecclesiae mandatam, concedimus: sacramentum esse negamus; cum externo ac divinitus instituto symbolo, & sacramentali materia ac forma careat.
units.tr: VIII. Next comes the sacrament for the fallen, whom they say are restored again through Penance and obtain forgiveness of their sins. They say this is a second sacrament for expiating sins, and that just as original guilt is washed away by baptism, so daily lapses are blotted out through penance. We grant that repentance is pleasing to God and commanded by the Church; we deny that it is a sacrament, since it lacks an external sign instituted by God and a sacramental matter and form.

units.la: IX. Mirum vero est, illos in hac re nugantes audire. Pro materia enim, non externum ac visibile aliquod, & ne ministri quidem sacramentum ministrantis, sed ipsius poenitentis actus adferunt, uti contritionem, confessionem, satisfactionem. Formam ejus in verbis sacerdotalibus, Ego absolvo te, constituunt. Et, pro institutione Christi probanda, loca quaedam, ad morum emendationem, vel servandam in Ecclesia disciplinam, facientia adjiciunt. Matth. 3: 1. Marc. 1: 15. Matth. 16: 19. & 18: 18. Joh. 20: 22. Quae nos universa quam veritatem habeant, & quomodo ad sacramentum tale constituendum faciant, alia occasione latius excussimus, libro videl. vi.cap.ix. ut ea repetere nunc necesse non sit.
units.tr: IX. It is remarkable to hear them babbling on this point. For as matter they cite not some external and visible thing, nor even the act of the minister administering the sacrament, but the very acts of the penitent himself, such as contrition, confession and satisfaction. They fix its form in the priestly words, "I absolve you." And to prove its institution by Christ, they add certain passages that bear on the amendment of conduct or on keeping discipline in the Church: Matt. 3:1; Mark 1:15; Matt. 16:19 and 18:18; John 20:22. What truth all of these hold, and how they serve to establish such a sacrament, we have examined at greater length on another occasion, namely in book vi, chapter ix, so there is no need to repeat it now.

units.la: X. Sed & Ordines Ecclesiasticos in sacramenta convertunt. Quos septem numerant. De Episcopali enim ordine, deque tonsura simplici inter ipsos lis est. Unde certis ritibus ac symbolis eos conferunt, quos materiam hujus sacramenti nuncupant; & divina charismata accipientibus imprimere asserunt. Institutionem autem divinam, adjunctumque ritum, & symbolum probant ex locis sequentibus. Act. 13: 3. Et postquam jejunassent, & orassent, imposuerunt eis manus, & dimiserunt eos. & 20: 28. Attendite ad totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus ille S. constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei. coll. Eph. 4: 11. & Joh. 20: 21. Quemadmodum me misit Pater, & ego mitto vos. Et, hoc diIto, insufflavit in ipsos. Et dicit eis, accipite Spir. S. Act. 6: 6. Quos statuerunt in conspectu Apostolorum. Qui, precati, imposuerunt eis manus, & 14: 23. Χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς πρεσβυτέρους κατ' ἐκκλησίαν, ψυμμque precatis essent, cum jejuniis, commendarunt eos Domino, in quem crediderant. 1. Tim. 4: 14. Ne negligas donum, quod est in te, quod tibi datum est, per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum presbyterii. conf.
units.tr: X. They also turn the ecclesiastical Orders into sacraments, which they count as seven. There is dispute among them about the episcopal order and the simple tonsure. They confer the orders by certain rites and symbols, which they call the matter of this sacrament, and they assert that these imprint divine gifts on the recipients. They prove the divine institution, the attached rite and the symbol from the following passages: Acts 13:3, And after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them away. Acts 20:28, Take heed to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God; compared with Eph. 4:11, and John 20:21, As the Father sent me, so I send you. And, saying this, he breathed on them, and says to them, Receive the Holy Spirit. Acts 6:6, Whom they set before the Apostles, who, having prayed, laid their hands on them; and 14:23, Χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς πρεσβυτέρους κατ' ἐκκλησίαν, And when they had appointed elders for them in every congregation, with fasting and prayer, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed. 1 Tim. 4:14, Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the elders.
Compare 2 Tim. 1:6.

units.la: XI. Adquæ nos regerimus: 1. Agnoscere nos ministerium verbi a Christo institutum; non vero ordinem aliquem sacrum, peculiari in Ecclesia charactere fulgentem, quique cum imperio & potestate in ea agat, & super reliquos fideles peculiari sanctitate emineat. Quæ veteris temporis fuerunt. Multo minus ut novum sacerdotium, novumque sacrificium, introduci feramus. Quod Antichristi commentum paulo ante profligavimus. 2. Agnoscimus pariter, ritum impositionis manuum vetustissimæ in Ecclesia originis esse; & a Patriarchis olim, & Mose, in legendo successore, & ab Apostolis in ministris Novi Test. consecrandis adhibitum: non tamen ritum illum sacramentalem, vel novæ Ecclesiæ sacramentum esse, concedimus. Uti nec in veteri fuit. Nam & divina Christi institutione, & elemento externo, & gratiæ salutaris promissione caret. Cum non eadem beneficia vel præbeat, vel obsignet, quæ reliqua sacramenta; sed ad summum docendi auctoritatem conferat, quæ & ipsa absque ritu illo acquiri quoque potest, ac cum sacramento nihil commune habet. 3. Multo minus in sacramentorum censum venire possunt Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ ordines: qui fere idololatrici sunt, & ad missaticī sacrificii drama spectant; & tanto præterea numero fabricantur, ac tam diversis inter sese ritibus constant, ut ne unius quidem sacramenti nomine comprehendi possint. Atque ita etiam de cæremoniis, & ritibus, quibus ea ministrant, de rasura, unctione, additisque certis verbis, aliisque nugis & næniis, in quibus sacramenti hujus materiam constituunt, existimandum est. 4. De impositione autem manuum Apostolica jam diximus; atque illos Euangelii ministros ordinaše, non autem potestatem offerendi corporis dominici illis tribuisse, vidimus. 5. Denique & vetus Ecclesia illos ordines ignoravit, Presbyteris solum & Diaconis contenta.
units.tr: XI. To these we reply: (1) We acknowledge the ministry of the Word as instituted by Christ; but we do not acknowledge a sacred order, shining with a peculiar character in the Church, which exercises command and power in it and stands out above the other faithful in peculiar holiness. Such things belonged to older times. Much less would we allow a new priesthood and a new sacrifice to be introduced, which we have already overthrown as a invention of Antichrist. (2) Likewise we acknowledge that the rite of laying on of hands is of most ancient origin in the Church, and was used of old by the Patriarchs, by Moses in choosing a successor, and by the Apostles in consecrating ministers of the New Testament. Yet we do not concede that this rite is a sacramental rite or a sacrament of the new Church, nor was it so in the old. For it lacks both divine institution by Christ, an external element, and the promise of saving grace. It does not confer or seal the same benefits as the other sacraments; at most it confers the authority to teach, which can also be acquired without that rite, and it has nothing in common with a sacrament. (3) Much less can the orders of the Papist Church be counted among the sacraments. They are almost idolatrous and look toward the drama of the sacrifice of the mass; they are fabricated in such numbers and consist of such diverse rites among themselves that they cannot be comprehended under the name of even one sacrament. The same must be judged of the ceremonies and rites by which they minister them: the shaving, the anointing, the added set words, and other trifles and nonsense, in which they locate the matter of this sacrament. (4) As for the laying on of hands, we have already spoken of the Apostolic practice; and we have seen that the Apostles ordained ministers of the Gospel, but did not grant them the power of offering the Lord's body. (5) Finally, the ancient Church also knew nothing of those orders, being content with elders and deacons alone.

units.la: XII. Ut vero nullus Ecclesiæ status sacramentis careret, non solum personis sacris, ac in castitatem votis, peculiarem sanctimoniam, ac proprium sacramentum adscripserunt; sed & extra illum ordinem degentibus conjugale sacrum pro sacramento dederunt; quem statum alioqui ut non omni labe carentem criminari alibi soliti sunt.
units.tr: XII. But so that no state of the Church might lack sacraments, they not only ascribed a special holiness and a proper sacrament to sacred persons and to those bound by vows of chastity, but they also made the sacred married state a sacrament for those living outside that order. Yet they were accustomed elsewhere to accuse that same state of not being free from every stain.

units.la: XIII. Nos autem 1. in matrimonio spiritualis Christi cum Ecclesia connubii imaginem concedimus. Quod Apostolus monet Eph. 5: 31, 32. qui id mysterium appellat. Loquitur autem de Christo & Ecclesia, com. 32. non de externo matrimonio. Cum autem vulgatus interpres Graecam vocem per Sacramentum redderet, quod etiam aliis in locis facit, 1. Tim. 3: 16. Eph. 1: 9, 10. & 3: 4,5,6. Apoc. 17:5,7. id non levem errori huic causam praebuit. Et, non doctrina illa, quam tradit Apostolus de Christo & Ecclesia, pro fidei Christianae sacramento & mysterio; sed ipsum matrimonium pro externo sacramento habitum fuit. 2. Nos vero, quod sacramenti proprie dicti rationem habeat, in eo non videmus. Nam nec institutio Christi, nec externum signum, nec salutaris gratiae obsignatio, quae sola sacramentum faciunt, in eo reperiuntur. Institutum enim a Deo matrimonium, ac ab initio mundi viguisse, concedimus; in sacramentum autem a Christo sub Euangelio datum ostendi petimus. Loci enim Apostolici παρεμφυεῖαν proxime tetigimus. Pariter & signum, ac elementum externum, in eo desideramus: quod, ut aliquid dicant, personas contrahentes, vel verba consensum testantia, non sine sententiarum pugna, esse dicunt: cum verba nihil visibile, personae autem potius sacramenti subiectum recipiens sint. Denique & gratiam sacramentalem ab hoc sacramento abesse contendimus. Non sufficit enim, spiritualem Christi cum Ecclesia unionem conjugali vinculo assimilari. Alioquin quotquot in Scriptura similitudines & parabolae proponuntur, Ecclesiae sacramenta essent. Unionem autem illam, ac nostram cum Christo communionem, non minus nuptiis, quam baptismo & Eucharistia, nobis obsignari oporteret. Quod a Scripturis alienum est; nec ipsi concedent adversarii. Quod de remedio contra concupiscentiam, deque amore conjugali, addunt; illa in conjugio, ex natura ejus, ac Dei institutione, concedimus; non vero haec sacramentalis gratiae nomine veniunt; illa enim non uni tantum peccato opponitur, sed proprie in peccatorum venia, ac divini Spiritus contra omnia peccata potentia consistit. 3. Sed & ipsi adversarii in hoc capite circa omnia inter se contendunt, & insociabili lite dirimuntur. Neque etiam satis consona loquuntur, cum connubialia vota pro carnis opere habent; & selectioris sanctimoniae homines ab iis mysticis videl. taedis arcent; imo contrario religionis voto illa solvere, ac omne conjugii sacramentum tum flocci habere non verentur. Ut nos longe sanctius matrimonium habeamus, ac illi qui alioquin non sacrum illud modo, sed & sacramentum esse, statuunt.
units.tr: XIII. We, however, (1) concede in marriage an image of the spiritual union of Christ with the Church. The Apostle urges this at Eph. 5:31, 32, where he calls it a "mystery". But he speaks of Christ and the Church, verse 32, not of outward marriage. When the Vulgate translator rendered the Greek word by "sacramentum", as he also does in other places (1 Tim. 3:16; Eph. 1:9, 10; 3:4, 5, 6; Rev. 17:5, 7), this gave no small occasion for this error. The doctrine which the Apostle sets out about Christ and the Church, which is the sacrament and mystery of the Christian faith, was not what was taken as the sacrament; rather, marriage itself was regarded as an outward sacrament. (2) We, indeed, do not see in marriage the nature of a sacrament properly so called. For neither the institution of Christ, nor an outward sign, nor a seal of saving grace, which alone make a sacrament, are found in it. We concede that marriage was instituted by God and flourished from the beginning of the world; but we ask that it be shown to be a sacrament given by Christ under the Gospel. For we have already touched on the Apostle's word παρεμφυεῖαν [paremphyeian]. Likewise we find in it no sign or external element. What they say, to give it something, is that the contracting persons or the words testifying to consent are the sign, but not without fierce disagreement among themselves, since words are nothing visible and the persons are rather the recipients who are the subject of the sacrament. Finally, we contend that sacramental grace is absent from this sacrament. For it is not enough that the spiritual union of Christ with the Church is likened to the marriage bond. Otherwise, every similitude and parable proposed in Scripture would be a sacrament of the Church. That union, and our communion with Christ, would have to be sealed to us no less by marriage than by baptism and the Eucharist. This is foreign to the Scriptures, and the adversaries themselves will not grant it. As for what they add about a remedy against concupiscence and about conjugal love, we grant that these belong to marriage by its nature and by God's institution; but they do not come under the name of sacramental grace. For the remedy does not stand against one sin only, but properly consists in the forgiveness of sins and in the power of the divine Spirit against all sins. (3) Moreover, the adversaries themselves on this point quarrel among themselves over everything, and are divided by an unpeaceable strife. Nor do they speak very consistently: they hold the vows of marriage to be a work of the flesh, and keep the men of more select holiness away from those mystical torches; indeed, by a contrary vow of religion they do not hesitate to dissolve them, and to set no store by the whole sacrament of marriage. Thus we hold marriage to be far more holy than those who declare it not only sacred but also a sacrament.

units.la: XIV. Succedit tandem morientium sacramentum, sive viaticum, quo exeuntes ex hoc seculo a reliqua labe purgare solent. Quod per extremam unctionem faciunt. Solet enim Episcopus conceptis verbis oleum quoddam consecrare, quo sacrificulus instructus moribundos certis ritibus inungit, & expiat, atq; exeunti animae commeatum praebet. Quod non sacramentum, sed inquinamentum est; nec a Christo institutum; nec a veteri Ecclesia usurpatum; superstitiosis denique ritibus ac caerimoniis plenum; quibus vel in morte plebem ipsorum confidere, atque oleo isto Christi sanguinem non parum obscurari videmus.
units.tr: XIV. Last comes the sacrament of the dying, or viaticum, by which those leaving this world are accustomed to be cleansed from the remaining stain. They do this by "extreme unction". For the bishop, with set words, usually consecrates a certain oil, with which the little sacrificer, equipped for the task, anoints and purges the dying with fixed rites, and grants passage to the departing soul. This is not a sacrament but a defilement; it was not instituted by Christ, nor used by the ancient Church; finally, it is full of superstitious rites and ceremonies. By these, we see, the common people put their trust even at death, and the blood of Christ is not a little obscured by that oil.

units.la: XV. Nihil enim hic faciunt loca Marc. 6: 12, 13. Egressi igitur illi, proclamabant ut resipiscerent homines: & daemonia multa ejiciebant, unguentes oleo multos aegrotos, & sanabant. & Jac. 5: 14, 15. Infirmatur aliquis inter vos; accersat presbyteros Ecclesiae; & orent pro eo, ungentes eum oleo in nomine Domini. Et ratio fidei servabit laborantem, eriget eum Dominus: quod si peccata commiserit, remittentur ei. Vel praecipuis ex adversariis confitentibus. Agunt enim illa de ordinario istius saeculi & gentis medicamine, supervenientibusque illi miraculosis sanationibus, juxta dona illa extraordinaria; quae Ecclesiae Christianae primordia illustrabant. ἄλλῳ δὲ χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων alii autem dona sanationis per eundem Spiritum. 1. Cor. 12: 9. coll. com. 28. Quorum frequens in Novi Test. historia, mentio. Unde in omnibus morbis, non autem in ultimo demum vitae limite, & ad corporis praecipue sanationem, adhibebantur. Quod enim de peccatorum remissione Jacobus addit, id de peccatis illis, quae castigationi illi causam praebuerunt, proximae intelligendum est. διὰ τοῦτο propterea inter vos multi sunt infirmi, & valetudinarii & dormiunt multi, 1. Cor. 11: 30. Quo spectat conditionalis illa locutio, si peccata commiserit. Quae tamen, non externae unctionis sacramento, sed oratione in fide facta, delenda dicuntur. Nec alia apud veteres unctio occurrit. Apud quos miraculosae illae curationes pluribus saeculis perdurarunt. Cum autem nunc donum illud cesset, nec in Ecclesiae ministris amplius corusceat, vanum est ejus rei symbolum adhuc usurpare & profanare velle.
units.tr: XV. For the passages Mark 6:12, 13 and James 5:14, 15 do nothing for them here. Mark: "So they went out and preached that men should repent, and they cast out many devils, and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them." James: "Is anyone sick among you? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him." Nor do the chief of our opponents who confess this do anything with them. For these passages deal with the ordinary remedy of that age and nation, and with the miraculous healings that came upon it, in accordance with those extraordinary gifts which adorned the beginnings of the Christian Church. "To another the gifts of healings by the same Spirit" (1 Cor. 12:9; compare verse 28). Of these there is frequent mention in the history of the New Testament. Hence they were used for all diseases, and not only at the final limit of life, and chiefly for the healing of the body. And what James adds about the forgiveness of sins must be understood of those sins which were the immediate cause of that chastisement: "For this reason many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep" (1 Cor. 11:30). To this refers the conditional phrase "if he has committed sins". Yet these sins are said to be wiped away not by the sacrament of outward anointing, but by prayer made in faith. Nor does any other anointing occur among the ancients, among whom those miraculous cures lasted for several centuries. But since that gift has now ceased and no longer shines in the ministers of the Church, it is vain to wish still to use and profane the symbol of a thing that no longer exists.

units.la: XVI. Sed & rejicienda obiter Anabaptistarum quorundam superstitio; qui duobus primariis, uti appellant, Ecclesiae sacramentis adjecerunt duo minus principalia, matrimonium, & pedilavium; ex mera Christi Domini ϰⲁⲛⲟζⲏⲣⲁ, Joh. 13. Cum ille, exemplo suo, non istum proprie actum, sed humilitatem, & obsequium, & mutuæ charitatis officia, discipulis suis commendaverit. Ac mirum est, eos non & alias lotiones, ac unctiones, Matth. 6: 17. & osculorum libationes, 1. Pet. 5: 14. aliosque ex Apostolica Ecclesia ritus imitari. Qui non magis significatu suo caruerunt, quam hæc pedum lotio; quam dominici sanguinis aspersionem adumbrasse non diffitemur. com. 8, 10. Verum eam in perpetuum Ecclesiæ ritum datum negamus, cum regionibus istis familiaris, in convivis ac hospitibus accipiendis: conf. Luc. 7: 38, 44. 1. Tim. 5: 10. non pari honestate, alias inter gentes, aliisque terrarum oris, usurparetur.
units.tr: XVI. But the superstition of certain Anabaptists must also be briefly rejected. They added to the two chief sacraments of the Church, as they call them, two less principal ones, marriage and the washing of feet, from a mere misreading of the humbling (kenosis) of the Lord Christ in John 13. For he, by his example, commended to his disciples not that act properly speaking, but humility, obedience, and the duties of mutual charity. And it is remarkable that they do not also imitate other washings and anointings (Matt. 6:17), and the kisses of greeting (1 Pet. 5:14), and other rites of the apostolic Church. These have not lost their meaning any more than this washing of feet, which we do not deny foreshadowed the sprinkling of the Lord's blood (compare verses 8, 10). But we deny that this rite was given to the Church in perpetuity: it belongs to those regions, where it was customary in entertaining guests and strangers (compare Luke 7:38, 44; 1 Tim. 5:10), and it would not have been practised with equal decency among other peoples and in other lands.

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CAPUT XVII.

units.la: De reliquis cultus N. F. Ritibus.
units.tr: On the remaining rites of the new cult

units.la: I. SAcramentorum consideratione reliquum cultus publici ordinem subnectere, utque ille sensim immutatus sit videre, non incongruum erit.
units.tr: I. It will not be out of place to add to the account of the sacraments the remaining order of public worship, and to see how it was gradually changed.

units.la: II. Erat autem initio Christiana religio sola simplicitate veneranda ac potens; utpote quæ Deum in Spiritu & veritate colit, Joh. 4: 24. quæque gestus ac ritus significativos paucissimos habet, cosque minime affectatos & maxime naturales, sine quibus vix pia in homine poteft esse cogitatio; vel qui ab ipsa cogitatione pia procedunt, eamque fovent & excitant: quales in precibus præcipue videre est.
units.tr: II. At first the Christian religion was venerable and powerful by its simplicity alone, since it worships God in Spirit and truth, John 4:24. It has very few significant gestures and rites, and those are unaffected and most natural, the kind without which a pious thought in a person can hardly exist, or which flow from pious thought itself and foster and stir it up. These are seen above all in prayers.

units.la: III. Ac præter sacramenta, quæ simpliciter peragebantur (nam fluviali aqua lustrabantur fideles. Matth. 3: 1. & 28: 19. ac S. Cœna convivii speciem habebat, Matth. 36: 26, 27.) Sermones ad populum de bona ac sacra aliqua re lingua vulgari instituebantur. Matth. 13: 34, 35. ac precibus denique & benedictionibus absolvebantur. Matth. 26: 30. Joh. 14. & 15. & 16. & 17. Luc. 24: 30. Nec alterius cultus in historia Euangelica mentio occurrit.
units.tr: III. Apart from the sacraments, which were performed simply (for the faithful were washed in river water, Matt. 3:1 and 28:19, and the Lord's Supper had the appearance of a meal, Matt. 26:26, 27), sermons to the people about some good and holy matter were given in the vernacular, Matt. 13:34, 35, and the service was finally concluded with prayers and blessings, Matt. 26:30; John 14, 15, 16, 17; Luke 24:30. Nor is any other form of worship mentioned in the Gospel history.

units.la: IV. Idem Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ ritus erant. Legebantur enim Scriptura. Act. 13: 15. & 15: 21. & 17: 2. Neque extra eas docere quicquam fas erat. Act. 26: 22. Ad quarum illustrationem, & ex ea ædificationem, prophetiæ exercitium obtinebat. 1. Cor. 14: 3. 1. Thess. 5: 19. Nec alterius quam vernacula lingua in sacris usus. 1. Cor. 14. Eadem lingua publicas preces concipiebant. 1. Cor. 14: 16. & de re sacra mutuo disserebant. 1. Cor. 14. Psalmos quoque & hymnos Christo Deo dicebant secum invicem. Col. 3: 16. Eph. 5: 19. 1. Cor. 14: 15. Et Sacramenta, ex instituto Christi, nude ac sine pompa, ministrabant. Act. 8: 36. & 2: 41. & 16: 33. & 2: 46. & 20: 7. 1. Cor. 11: 23. Nec ullae praeterea caerimoniae in piorum coetibus illo tempore comparent.
units.tr: IV. The rites of the apostolic Church were the same. Scripture was read, Acts 13:15, 15:21, 17:2, and it was not lawful to teach anything beyond it, Acts 26:22. For its illustration, and for building up from it, the exercise of prophecy was observed, 1 Cor. 14:3; 1 Thess. 5:19. Nor was any language used in worship other than the vernacular, 1 Cor. 14. In the same language they framed public prayers, 1 Cor. 14:16, and discussed sacred matters with one another, 1 Cor. 14. They also sang psalms and hymns to Christ God among themselves, Col. 3:16; Eph. 5:19; 1 Cor. 14:15. And they administered the sacraments, as Christ had instituted them, plainly and without pomp, Acts 8:36, 2:41, 16:33, 2:46, 20:7; 1 Cor. 11:23. Nor do any other ceremonies appear at the gatherings of the pious at that time.

units.la: V. Aberat autem omnis locorum temporumque superstitio. Cultum enim precum omni in loco obibant. 1. Tim. 2: 8. Eucharistiam primitus in privatis aedibus, kat' oikov domatim celebrantes, Act. 2: 46. subsequentibus autem temporibus in oratoriis; & tandem basilicis: quae ad formam fanorum gentilium deinceps constructa, multaque superstitione labentibus saeculis foedata sunt.
units.tr: V. Yet all superstition about places and times was absent. For they performed the worship of prayer in every place, 1 Tim. 2:8. At first they celebrated the Eucharist in private houses, kat' oikon, from house to house [κατ' οἶκον], Acts 2:46; in later times in oratories, and finally in basilicas. These, built afterwards on the model of pagan temples, were in the course of the centuries defiled by much superstition.

units.la: VI. Tempus cultus, abrogatis figuris, pro libertate Euangelica observabatur ab Apostolis & primitiva Ecclesia. Col. 2: 16, 17. Rom. 14: 5, 6. Gal. 4: 10, 11. Conventus enim habebantur, seu quotidiani. Act. 2: 46. seu ex occasione Sabbati Judaici, aliave, pro gentium locorumque ratione; ut passim in Actis videre est. Kyriakē seu annuae, seu hebdomadariae, mentio a Johanne facta est, Apoc. 1: 10. ut & μιᾶς τῶν σαββάτων, qua, cum panis fractione, coetus cogebantur, a Luca, Act. 20: 7. quaque collectae ad usum egenorum seponi, particulari praecepto, jubebantur a Paulo, 1. Cor. 16: 1. Ordinariis vero fidelium conventibus illam destinatam fuisse, in Scriptura nullibi legitur: quin potius in contrarium faceret locus modo memoratus 1. Cor. 16: 1. licet admodum probabile sit, occasione collectarum a fidelibus iis eo die factarum, conventus institutos, & inde, eversa sub finem istius saeculi politia Judaica, Dominicam constanter observatam a Christianis; ut e Patrum testimoniis abunde constat: donec illa tandem principali auctoritate in legem publicam, sanctissimo & maxime observando instituto, abiit.
units.tr: VI. As to the time of worship, with the figures abolished, the apostles and the primitive Church observed it according to evangelical liberty, Col. 2:16, 17; Rom. 14:5, 6; Gal. 4:10, 11. For assemblies were held either daily, Acts 2:46, or on the occasion of the Jewish Sabbath or otherwise, according to the custom of the nations and places, as may be seen everywhere in Acts. John made mention of the Lord's [Κυριακή] day, whether annual or weekly, Rev. 1:10. Luke spoke of the first day of the week [μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων], on which, with the breaking of bread, the assembly was called together, Acts 20:7; and by a particular precept Paul ordered that the collections for the needy be set aside, 1 Cor. 16:1. But that this day was appointed for the ordinary meetings of the faithful is nowhere read in Scripture; indeed the passage just cited, 1 Cor. 16:1, points the other way. Yet it is very probable that the meetings were instituted on account of the collections made by the faithful on that day, and that afterwards, when the Jewish polity was overthrown towards the end of that age, the Lord's day was constantly observed by Christians, as is abundantly clear from the testimonies of the Fathers. At last, by principal authority, it passed into public law as a most holy institution, to be observed with the greatest care.

units.la: VII. Sed non diu placuit illa simplicitas. Cum enim ad Ecclesiam aggregarentur diversa hominum genera, tum Judaei, tum Gentiles; illi veterem ac invectam illum colendi Dei modum dedignari; patrisque caerimoniis divinum cultum instruere, ac sacris majestatem quandam circumdare, non malo, ut videbatur, consilio, coepere. Ac primi numerantur in isto studio Episcopi Romani: qui, dum liberos primum cultus in legem tandem ac necessitatem vertere, & institutis a sese Ecclesiis, quales pleraque in Europae patribus erant, obtrusere, mysterio iniquitatis inscii ipsi ac imprudentes operati sunt. Quanquam successores eorum dolum & intellexerint, & struxerint, atque istis gradibus tandem stupendum illud in omnes Ecclesias sacrorum regnum creverint.
units.tr: VII. But that simplicity did not please for long. For when diverse kinds of men were joined to the Church, both Jews and Gentiles, the former began to disdain the old and inherited manner of worshipping God, and the latter, with what seemed to be no bad intention, began to furnish divine worship with the ceremonies of their fathers and to surround the sacred rites with a certain majesty. The first to be counted in this pursuit were the Roman bishops, who, while they first forced free worship into a law and necessity, and imposed it on the churches they founded, such as most of those in the fathers' lands of Europe were, worked without knowing or foreseeing the mystery of iniquity. Yet their successors both understood the deceit and built upon it, and by these steps at last grew that amazing kingdom of sacred rites over all the churches.

units.la: VIII. Praelectio autem divini verbi in coetibus, vulgari ac nota lingua, ejusdemque explicatio, diu in Ecclesia obtinuit; ut ex veterum scriptis constat. Ac sub Gregorio M. demum, ac successoribus ejus, Caroli M. tempore defecit. Sub quo Latini passim ritus, & in sacris sermo, invaluerint: ac de Euangelii corpore direptae quaedam particulae, quae Ecclesiasticae plebi in ordinem praelegerentur. Quod, bono fine institutum, in perniciem tandem Ecclesiae vertit. Quae maligne adeo pasta, ac reliquis S. Scripturae spatiis exclusa, nec delicias ejus pleno ore haurire valens, Sabbatinarum quoque itarum lectionum taedio duci coepit; magisque fabellis, & mendacis, quae non parce tum addi coeperant, attendens, religionem tandem omnem in superstitionem convertit. Atque erat tum illud tempus, quo, tenebricantibus Ecclesiae diebus, ad barbariem, tristemque noctem, quae omnia tetra caligine inducebat, magnis passibus properabatur.
units.tr: VIII. Reading aloud of the divine Word in the assemblies, in the common and known language, together with its explanation, long held its place in the Church, as is clear from the writings of the ancients. Under Gregory the Great and his successors it finally declined, at the time of Charlemagne. Under him the Latin rites and the Latin language in worship became widespread, and certain scraps were torn from the body of the Gospel and read in order to the Church's common people. This was introduced with a good end, but in time it turned to the ruin of the Church. Fed in this wretched way, and shut out from the rest of the spaces of Holy Scripture, unable to drink in its delights with full mouth, the people began to be bored even with those Sabbath readings. Attending more to fables and lies, which by then had begun to be added without restraint, they at last turned all religion into superstition. And that was the time when, in the darkening days of the Church, men hastened with great strides towards barbarism and a sad night that brought on everything in thick darkness.

units.la: IX. Nam & concionandi studium, longo tempore in Ecclesiis frequentatum, ut ex Patrum tum Graecorum tum Latinorum homiliis patet, eodem tempore defecerat. Natique tum libri, homiliarum, passionale, legendae, aliique infelices partus, excerptis quibusdam, ex Scriptura, Patribus, ac historia Ecclesiastica, constantes; multisque fabulis ac mendaciis contaminati; quibus quisquiliis populus Christianus, loco sacrae lectionis, doctaeque ac piae Scripturarum explicationis, longo tempore passus fuit. Atque, introducto tandem Missae dramate, conciones prorsus neglectae, inque officio isto sacro, ut vocabant, divinus omnis cultus constitutus est. Nisi quod ingruenti reformationis luci hoc quoque bonum debeat ipsa pontificiorum Ecclesia, quod per eam conciones sacrae etiam inter ipsos refloruerint.
units.tr: IX. For the practice of preaching, which had been maintained in the churches for a long time, as is clear from the homilies of both the Greek and the Latin Fathers, had at the same time fallen away. Then were born books of homilies, passionals, legends and other unhappy offspring, made up of certain extracts from Scripture, the Fathers and ecclesiastical history, and contaminated by many fables and lies. With these trifles the Christian people, in place of sacred reading and learned and pious explanation of the Scriptures, was for a long time content. And at last, when the drama of the Mass was introduced, sermons were altogether neglected, and all divine worship was centred on that so-called sacred office. Yet the Papal Church owes this good, too, to the dawning light of the Reformation: that through it sermons have flourished again even among themselves.

units.la: X. Cantus etiam sacer diu in primeva simplicitate stetit; concinente tota Ecclesia, tum virorum, tum mulierum, puerisque innuptisque puellis; nec Davidicos modo numeros, sed & alios hymnos Ecclesiasticos, resonante. Quanquam non una ejus in omnibus Ecclesiis ratio erat. Alexandrini enim, auctore Athanasio, longo illo vocis tractu sermonem magis quam cantum referebant. Graecae autem Ecclesiae dulciores modulos in sacris admiserunt, ciendis affectibus. Quorum suavitate ductus Ambrosius, illos in Mediolanensi sua Ecclesia quoque instituit. stituit. Unde in reliquas Latinorum Ecclesias peruenerunt. Erat autem cantus ille simpex ac intelligibus, nec nimio artificio à templorum vsu alienus.
units.tr: X. Sacred song also remained for a long time in its primitive simplicity, the whole Church singing together, men and women, boys and unmarried girls, and resounding not only the psalm tunes of David but also other ecclesiastical hymns. Yet its manner was not one and the same in all churches. The Alexandrians, following Athanasius, delivered the words with a long drawn-out tone rather than sang them. The Greek churches admitted sweeter melodies into worship, to stir the emotions. Ambrose, moved by their sweetness, introduced these into his own church at Milan as well, and from there they reached the other Latin churches. That song, however, was simple and intelligible, and not far removed from the use of the temples through excessive artifice.

units.la: XI. Postmodum introductæ sunt antiphonæ, duobus choris simul concinentibus; quas itidem Ambrosius, à Græcis haustas, Latinis tradidisse dicitur. Quibus accesserunt responsoria; in quibus, alternis cantantes, alter alteri respondebat. Quod Latinorum inventum ajunt. Ecclesiasticum autem cantum, ita multiplicatum, ordinasse fertur GregoriusM. instituto certo tempore, horisque, quas vocant, canonicis. Cumque operosior foret hæc musica, ac latina lingua constaret, paulatim populus ab ea exclusus, atque ista etiam sacri cultus parte orbatus fuit; constitutis hominibus, quibus cantorum officium imponebatur.
units.tr: XI. Afterwards antiphons were introduced, sung by two choirs at once, which Ambrose too is said to have handed on to the Latins, having drawn them from the Greeks. To these were added responsories, in which one side sang and the other answered in turn; this is said to be a Latin invention. Gregory the Great is said to have arranged the ecclesiastical chant, thus multiplied, for a fixed time and for the so-called canonical hours. And since this music was more elaborate and the Latin language was difficult, the people were gradually shut out from it and deprived of this part of the sacred worship, with men appointed to whom the office of singers was assigned.

units.la: XII. Cum ergo cantus sacer ita adulteratus esset; & magis ad voluptatem, quam ad religionem, comparatus, theatris aptior esset, quam templis; additus denique & organorum concentus; quæ fractis numeris vel choris cantantium interludebant, vel artificiosis modulis vacua templa personabant. Quo Papa Vitaliani institutum ferunt. A.C. 657. Sed falso, cum serius illud obtinuisse constet. Displicebant autem musæa ista mele, ac voluptuariæ cantillationes in templis, plurimis viris probis. Donec Deus, inducta reformatione, templi quoque musicam ad veram ac justam rationem reduxit.
units.tr: XII. Since sacred chant had been corrupted in this way, and was composed more for pleasure than for religion, and was better suited to the theatre than to the temple, and since organ music was finally added, which broke up the rhythms or choirs of singers with interludes, or filled empty churches with artful melodies, they say that Pope Vitalian introduced this in the year 657. But this is false, since it is established that it prevailed later. Those musical and voluptuous melodies in churches, however, displeased many upright men, until God, by introducing the Reformation, also brought the music of the church back to a true and just principle.

units.la: XIII. Quo moderamine adhibito, utilem etiam in cantu publico dirigendo inflammandoque operam conferunt organa musica; ut quotidiano Ecclesiarum nostratium experimento constat. Ut nulla sit ratio, instrumenta illa è templis eliminandi, aut muta saltem relinquendi; cum longe majori ædificatione phonasci vicem inter cantus sacros præstare possent, quam demisso cœtu inanibus sonis vacua templa replere. Neque ulla potest dari ratio, curminus instrumentali, adgravitatem cultus composita, quam vocali musica Deum publice laudari liceat. Quod tantum abest ut sit ἰσϑαῖζειν, ut hoc ipsum sit analogiæ præcepti Apostolorum obsequi; qui diserte non vocalem solum, sed & instrumentalem musicam Christianis commendant atque præscribunt. 1. Cor. 14: 26. Eph 5: 18, 19. Col. 3: 16. Jac. 5: 13.
units.tr: XIII. With this moderation applied, musical instruments also make a useful contribution to directing and kindling public singing, as the daily experience of our churches shows. So there is no reason to remove those instruments from the churches, or at least to leave them silent; since they could serve as an aid to the sacred songs far better than, by dropping the congregation's voices, filling empty churches with hollow sounds. Nor can any reason be given why God may be publicly praised with vocal music but not with instrumental music, as if the latter were unsuited to the dignity of worship. Far from this being ἰσϑαῖζειν (a Judaizing practice), it is in fact to obey the analogy of the apostolic precept; for they expressly commend and prescribe to Christians not only vocal but also instrumental music. 1 Cor. 14:26. Eph. 5:18, 19. Col. 3:16. Jas. 5:13.

units.la: XIV. Idem quoque cultus temporis (ne de locis nunc dicamus) accidit. Maxime sane antiquitatis est in Ecclesia Christiana observatio diei annuæ resurrectionis Dominihebdomadali ejusdem observationi fortassis tantum non suppar, humana tamen potius consuetudine, quam Apostolico instituto, ut jactatum antiquis, introducta, & incongruo nomine Pascha dicta: ne de Parasceues sollemnibus nunc dicam. Pascha insecuta est deinceps Pentecostes prolixa celebratio. Neque hic finis, donec memoriæ quoque consecrati sunt reliqui, qui præcipua Christi beneficia referunt, dies. Natalis nimirum ipsius, Epiphaniæ, Ascensionis, tandemque ipsius Circumcisionis. Finis enim non esset, si festos dies Virginis genitrici reliquorumque martyrum & Sanctorum choro dicatos prioribus adjicere velim: qui sequioribus sæculis tanta turba invecti sunt, ut dudum mole sua displicuerint fervidissimis ipsorum patronis, aliquaque sui parte non ita pridem à sacrorum istorum rege resecari opus habuerint.
units.tr: XIV. The same thing has happened with the times of worship (to say nothing now of places). The observance of the annual day of the Lord's resurrection is certainly of very great antiquity in the Christian Church, and perhaps almost equal to the weekly observance of the same; yet it was introduced by human custom rather than by apostolic institution, as is commonly claimed by the ancients, and it was called by the incongruous name Pascha. I say nothing now of the solemnities of Good Friday. After Easter there followed the lengthy celebration of Pentecost. Nor was there an end to this, until the remaining days, which recall the principal benefits of Christ, were also consecrated to memory: namely, his Nativity, Epiphany, Ascension, and finally his Circumcision. There would be no end if I were to add the feast days dedicated to the Virgin Mother and to the company of the other martyrs and saints, who were brought in in such a crowd in later centuries that long ago they displeased even their most fervent patrons by their bulk, and in some part not long ago their King of sacred things had to cut them back.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: XV. Quæ dies ut festæ lætitiæ datæ sunt, ita ab alia parte statis diebus stationes & jejunia, antehac libera, affixa sunt; tum hebdomadalia, quibus quarta & sexta Sabbati præcipue datæ, exempta semper dominica; tum annua, quo pertinet paraskeue, & ex illa sensim, multa licet cum varietate & ambagibus, nata quadragesima. Recentioris enim sunt instituti, quæ quatuor anni temporibus, Sanctorum vigiliis, adventus rogationumque diebus addicta sunt jejunia. Cui dierum discrimini, quasi id non suffecisset, adjectum est alterum ciborum; quod lege necessitatis, & ne quid jugo deesset, cum opinione meriti, conscientiis, posterioribus sæculis, impositum est.
units.tr: XV. As these days were given over to festive joy, so on the other hand fixed days of station and fasting, previously optional, were attached; some weekly, of which the fourth and sixth days of the week were especially set aside, the Lord's day always being exempted; others annual, to which belongs the preparation day (Parasceve), and from it gradually, though with much variety and circumlocution, the Lenten fast arose. For the fasts assigned to the four seasons of the year, the vigils of the saints, and the days of Advent and the Rogations are of more recent institution. To this distinction of days, as if it were not enough, another distinction of foods was added, which was imposed in later centuries, by a rule of necessity, and so that nothing should be lacking to the yoke, with the belief in merit, and with consciences.

units.la: XVI. Quibus Latinorum novitatibus si addere vellemus reliquam rituum sacrorum apud ipsos corruptionem, novorumque sine modo ac sine introductionem, esset illud sane Methusalemi horas suputare. Præcipuos tamen illorum ritus ac cærimonias, quas paucis hisce ac simplicibus, à Christo primitus institutis, superaddidere, suis locis examinamus. Certe tantum est illud cæremoniarum choragium, tanta que sub elementis mundi, quibus mortui fumus cum Christo, subjectio, Col. 2:21. ut spiritualis ac simplex ille N. T. cultus in ψυχικὰ ... vibi exierit & degenerarit, & inter istam elementorum cærimoniarumque molem nudus & egenus Christus tantum non omni vi sua spoliatus sit. Ita nempe Diaboli astus multorum mentes corrupit a simplicitate in Christum, 2. Cor. 11:3. Ut post oculos suos & elementa mundi fornicarentur, & ornamenta meretricia, quibus se mundo prostituerent, adsciverint. Ezech. 23:42. Qui est mundus ille meretricis magnæ. Apoc. 17:4.
units.tr: XVI. If we wished to add to these novelties of the Latins the rest of the corruption of their sacred rites, and their innovations without measure or end, it would indeed be like counting the years of Methuselah. Nevertheless, we will examine in their proper places the principal rites and ceremonies which they have added to those few simple ones instituted at first by Christ. Certainly so great is that troupe of ceremonies, and so great the subjection under the elements of the world, to which we died with Christ, Col. 2:21, that the spiritual and simple worship of the New Testament has gone out into the psychical... and degenerated, and amid that mass of elements and ceremonies Christ, stripped and needy, has been almost entirely deprived of his power. Thus indeed the wiles of the Devil corrupted the minds of many from the simplicity that is in Christ, 2 Cor. 11:3, so that they committed fornication after their own eyes and the elements of the world, and took up the meretricious ornaments with which they prostituted themselves to the world. Ezek. 23:42. This is that world of the great harlot. Rev. 17:4.

units.la: XVII. Eo igitur magis nobis annitendum, ne simplicem cultus nostri paraturam simili adulterio polluamus: necum illorum ritibus, ad omnia mala ducentibus, communionem habeamus: ne illos praeter verbum multiplicemus, & ex indifferentibus faciamus necessarios, cum servitute & opinione justitiae, aut cultus, & cum subjectione: neve per ritus, quos male quidam vocant indifferentes, Ecclesiae nostrae & veritatis hostibus assimilemur, iisque conciliemur. Quibus scopulis evitatis, circa ritus externos indifferentes non adeo morosum esse decet, neque propter diversum eorum usum nemo condemnandus aut aversandus est. Cum nihil repugnet, sub diversis ritibus eandem latitare fidem; imo illa ipsa varietas rituum libertati Christianae demonstrandae ac conservandae egregie conducat: ut hoc nomine, si non laudanda, certe ferenda sit.
units.tr: XVII. Therefore we must strive all the more not to pollute the simple form of our worship with a similar adultery; nor should we have fellowship with their rites, which lead to all evils; lest we multiply them beyond the Word, and make necessary what is indifferent, with a bondage and an opinion of righteousness of worship, and with subjection; nor should we, through rites which some wrongly call indifferent, be made like the enemies of our Church and of the truth, and be won over to them. Having avoided these rocks, it is fitting not to be too fussy about external indifferent rites, and no one should be condemned or shunned on account of their differing use. Since nothing prevents the same faith from lying hidden under diverse rites, indeed that very variety of rites greatly serves to demonstrate and preserve Christian liberty, so that on this account, if it is not to be praised, it must at least be tolerated.

units.la: LIBER VIII. DE Ecclesia N.F. ejusque statu & fine.
units.tr: BOOK VIII. ON the Church (N.F.), and its state and end.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS QUINTUS DE ECCLESIA N.F. CAPUT I.
units.tr: TOPIC FORTY-FIFTH: ON THE CHURCH (N.F.), CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Ecclesiæ N.F. nomine, natura & attributis.
units.tr: On the name, nature and attributes of the Church (N.F.).

units.la: I. OStquam Messiam, ac beneficia ejus, sacrosque ritus, ac signa, quibus beneficia illa hominibus offert & obsignat, consideravimus; tandem ad Ecclesiam veniendum est. Quod salutis per Christum procuratæ subjectum; atque ultimum Theologiæ nostræ caput est. Huc enim omnia tandem veniunt; atque universæ salutis opus in homine consummatur. Cum enim religio omnis, quam nunc tradimus, hominis peccatoris sit, ac salutis adipiscendæ viam tradat (aliter ac illa, quæ in cœlis obtinebit, ubi in Dei solius cultu ac laudibus ea absolvetur) in hominis tandem atque Ecclesiæ consideratione finire eam oportet. Præsertim cum aliter vel produci ea, vel cognosci, non possit, quam Christi ac beneficiorum ejus cognitione præhabita. Quæ & Apostolici, quod appellant, symboli formula est: quod, post traditum salutis mysterium, postque absolutas divinitatis personas, Ecclesiam tandem introducit; ac, post Deum Patrem, illam quoque fidelium omnium matrem considerari ac credi jubet. Est enim Ecclesia palmarium Trinitatis opus: in qua una universa Dei sapientia
units.tr: I. After we have considered the Messiah and his benefits, and the sacred rites and signs by which he offers and seals those benefits to people, we must at last come to the Church. The Church is the subject of the salvation procured through Christ, and it is the final head of our Theology. For all things come to this at last, and the whole work of salvation is brought to completion in the human being. For since all the religion we now set out belongs to sinful man, and shows the way of obtaining salvation (unlike that religion which will prevail in heaven, where it will be completed in the worship and praises of God alone), it must at last end in the consideration of the human being and the Church. Especially since it can be neither produced nor known in any other way than by a prior knowledge of Christ and his benefits. This is also the order of what they call the Apostles' Creed: which, after setting out the mystery of salvation and after the persons of the Godhead have been named, brings in the Church at last, and bids us consider and believe her, after God the Father, to be the mother of all believers. For the Church is the chief work of the Trinity, in which the whole wisdom of God

units.la: Ecclesia, the note-line glosses above are printed in the right margin. entia & potentia, ab initio mundi, usque ad extremum ejus finem, laborat, ac per partes sese spectandam præbet.
units.tr: ...wisdom and power, from the beginning of the world to its last end, labours and shows itself to be viewed in its parts.

units.la: II. Nos in ea explicanda istum ordinem servabimus: 1. naturam ejus & constitutionem. 2. ejus regimen ac ministros. 3. corruptionem in eam introductam per Antichristum. 4. ejus liberationem ab Antichristo. 5. tandem civitatis Dei finem novissimum, considerabimus.
units.tr: II. In explaining the Church we shall keep this order: (1) her nature and constitution; (2) her government and ministers; (3) the corruption introduced into her through Antichrist; (4) her liberation from Antichrist; and (5) finally, we shall consider the last end of the city of God.

units.la: III. Nomen Ecclesia, quod Ecclesiasticum prorsus est (ut varia in religione Christiana vocabula; quæ apud sæculares auctores, aut raro, aut non isto sensu, inveniuntur) ἀπὸ τῦ καλεῖν, seu ἐκκαλεῖν, evocare, quod affine est Hebræo קהל, deductum, populi conventum, cœtum ac concionem dicit; cumque non incompositum, vel promiscue ac tumultuario coëuntem, quo modo accipitur Act. 19: 39,40. quæ cæteroquin ἀγορὰ Græcis appellatur; sed præconis voce, aliove signo evocatum. Hic autem specialius cœtum a Deo evocatum, deque mundo segregatum, significat. Atque istum in sensum vox hæc, a LXX. Interpretibus accepta, qui concionem Israëliticam isto vocabulo sæpe designant, a Novi Test. scriptoribus continuo usurpatur. Voces similes sunt προσηγυρις, Hebr. 12:23. συναγωγὴ, Jac. 2:2. ἐκκλησιαγωγὴ, Hebr. 10:25. quanquam, propinquantibus Ecclesiæ fatis, atque ea angustis, quibus hactenus clausa fuerat, finibus exire gestiente, scriptores Novi Test. Synagoga appellationem potius Judaicis cœtibus reliquerint, ac Novi Testamenti populum nobiliori Ecclesia nomine insigniverint.
units.tr: III. The name Ecclesia is wholly ecclesiastical (like various other words in the Christian religion, which are found rarely, or not in this sense, in secular authors). It comes from calling, or calling out [ἀπὸ τοῦ καλεῖν, ἐκκαλεῖν], that is, to summon, and is akin to the Hebrew qahal [קהל]. It means an assembly, gathering or meeting of the people. It is not a disorderly crowd or a tumultuous mob gathering at random, as in Acts 19:39, 40, which the Greeks call an agora [ἀγορά], but a body summoned by the voice of a herald or some other signal. Here, however, the word means more specifically a body called out by God and separated from the world. The New Testament writers constantly used this word in this sense, taking it from the Seventy, who often used it to designate the assembly of Israel. Similar words are prosēgyris [προσηγυρις] (Heb. 12:23), synagōgē [συναγωγὴ] (Jas. 2:2), and ekklēsiagōgē [ἐκκλησιαγωγὴ] (Heb. 10:25). Yet the New Testament writers, as the fate of the Church drew near, and as she was eager to break out of the narrow limits within which she had hitherto been enclosed, left the name Synagoga rather to the Jewish assemblies, and honoured the people of the New Testament with the nobler name Ecclesia.

units.la: IV. Sumitur autem ea vox, vel latius, vel angustius. Nam & promiscue omnem Christianum cœtum, qui verbi Dei ac sacramentorum testeram gerit, denotat. Quomodo ea in mundo semper conspicua & visibilis est: nec unquam ita opprimitur, ut in totum eam lux ac fama deficiat. Et specialius pro cœtu regeneratorum, qui sacrum istud depositum caste sancteque habent, & vera fide ac charitate præfulgent, sumitur. Quæ interna Ecclesiæ forma cum in sensus non incurrat, ac sola mente percipi possit, externis quidem oculis invisibilis est. Denique & partes Ecclesiæ integrantes, sive Pastores, sive oves saltem, separatim nomine Ecclesiæ veniunt. Ad præsides enim & senatum Ecclesiæ, referri solet, licet non undiquaque bene, locus Matth. 18:17. Dic Ecclesia. De reliquo grege sunt sequentia loca: Act. 15:4 Quum autem pervenissent Hierosolyma, exceptis sunt ab Ecclesia, & Apostolis, & Presbyteris. & 20:28. Attendite igitur animum ad vos ipsos, & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus ille S. constituit Episcopos, ad pascendum Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo illo proprio sanguine acquisivit. 1. Tim. 3: 5. Nam si quis propriae domui præesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiam Dei curabit? Quanquam plenius ac magis proprie, pro toto cœtu, tum pastorum, tum ovium, ea vox accipiatur, 1. Cor. 1:2. Ecclesia Dei, quae est Corinthi, sanctificatis in Christo Iesu &c. 2. Thess. 1:1. Illa præsidum enim & Rectorum Ecclesia, quam repræsentativam vocant, fermentum papisticum habet. Quorum hæc sententia est: vel unum singularem hominem, quem Ecclesiæ caput appellant, vel hominum quorundam collegium, ita Ecclesiam omnem repræsentare, ut in suo sensu ac judicio sensum & judicium totius Ecclesiæ contineant, propter auctoritatem. Quæ non exiguam labem habent.
units.tr: IV. The word is taken either more broadly or more narrowly. For it indicates, indiscriminately, every Christian gathering that bears the witness of God's Word and sacraments.
