In this sense the Church is always conspicuous and visible in the world, and is never so oppressed that her light and reputation fail altogether. More specifically, it is taken for the body of the regenerate, who keep that sacred deposit chastely and holily and shine forth with true faith and love. This inner form of the Church does not fall under the senses and can be perceived only by the mind, so it is invisible to the outward eyes. Finally, the component parts of the Church, whether the ministers or at least the sheep, are also meant separately by the name Church. For the passage Matthew 18:17, Tell it to the Church, is commonly referred to the presidents and senate of the Church, although not altogether rightly. Concerning the rest of the flock the following passages apply: Acts 15:4, When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the Church, and by the apostles, and by the elders; and Acts 20:28, Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood; and 1 Timothy 3:5, For if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the Church of God? Yet the word is taken more fully and more properly for the whole body, both of ministers and of sheep, in 1 Corinthians 1:2, the Church of God which is at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus, etc., and 2 Thessalonians 1:1. That Church of presidents and rulers, which they call representative, has a papistical leaven. Its doctrine is this: either one single man, whom they call the head of the Church, or a college of certain men, represents the whole Church in such a way that, on account of their authority, their sense and judgement contain the sense and judgement of the whole Church. These views have no small taint.

units.la: V. Sed consideranda potius est Ecclesiæ natura. Quæ in eo consistit, quod sit cœtus hominum, a Deo e reliquo mundo gratiose evocatorum, ad cœlestis gloriæ spem ac communionem. Vocatis, sanctis. Rom. 1:7. Ecclesiæ Dei — vocatis, sanctis. 1. Cor. 1:2. Vocati & electi & fideles. Apoc. 17:14. Non solum enim æterna electione, sed & temporali evocatione ad illam constituendam opus est. Estque Ecclesia Dei potissimum opus, atque ab eo vocante ac segregante unice pendet. Ut non leviter errent Socinian; qui & æternam electionem, & potentem Dei vocationem, negantes, atque in vocatorum obsequio & accessu quicquid istius est ponentes, omnem de mundo Ecclesiam reipsa tolli posse, statuere necesse habent.
units.tr: V. But we should rather consider the nature of the Church. It consists in this: that it is a body of human beings, graciously called out by God from the rest of the world, to the hope and fellowship of heavenly glory. Called, holy, Romans 1:7; the Church of God, called, holy, 1 Corinthians 1:2; called, chosen and faithful, Revelation 17:14. For the Church's constitution requires not only eternal election but also temporal calling. And the Church of God is chiefly God's work, depending solely on him who calls and separates. So the Socinians err not lightly: denying both eternal election and God's effective calling, and placing whatever of this kind there is in the obedience and approach of those who are called, they are obliged to maintain that the whole Church could in fact be taken away from the world.

units.la: VI. Cum vero vocatio hæc, non externa solum in cœtus ac concilines segregatio, sed vera de reliqua mundi fæce separatio, sit; fidem illa ac obedientiam, reliquumque Christianarum virtutum chorum, in vocatis dicit. Estque hæc fides, quatenus in pluribus vocatis est, qui exinde in unum corpus cum Christo coalescunt, interna Ecclesiæ forma; qua sublata, nihil nisi nuda Ecclesiæ umbra reliqua est, quæ tanti nominis dignitatem tueri minime potest. Dicit enim procul dubio Ecclesia respectum ad Christum, qui corporis istius caput est. Fit autem artissima illa unio solo Spiritus amplexu, ac mutuo fidei ac amoris obsequio. Unde & membrorum omnium inter sese communio oritur, & de communi Spiritu (qua tanquam magna mente magnum hoc corpus animatur) sparsi in totum corpus charitatis, reliquorumque donorum, igniculi & radii; cunctarumque partium sacrum inter sese commercium. 1. Cor. 12:4, 13, 14, 20, 25, 26, 27.
units.tr: VI. But since this calling is not merely an outward separation into a gathering or assembly, but a true separation from the remaining dregs of the world, it implies faith and obedience, and the rest of the choir of Christian virtues, in those who are called. And this faith, insofar as it is present in many who are called, and who thereupon grow together into one body with Christ, is the inner form of the Church. If this is taken away, nothing remains but the bare shadow of the Church, which can by no means maintain the dignity of so great a name. For the Church undoubtedly refers to Christ, who is the head of that body. That most intimate union arises only through the embrace of the Spirit and the mutual obedience of faith and love. Hence arises also the fellowship of all the members among themselves, and from the common Spirit (by which this great body is animated as by one great mind) sparks and rays of charity and the other gifts are poured out over the whole body, and there is a holy exchange among all the parts. 1 Corinthians 12:4, 13, 14, 20, 25, 26, 27.

units.la: VII. Partes Ecclesiæ quod spectat, ridicule Pontificii, uti olim in B. Virgine, ita nunc in solo Pontifice, consistere eam ac absoli posse nugantur. Ac si numerus in unitate consistere, vel unus civis rempubl. ac cœtum facere posset. Ex Adamo autem ac Eva, quam Deus non minus viventium, quam mortalium, matrem fecit, ea olim veluti defonte profecto, porro omnes sanctæ civitatis cives ambitu suo comprehendit.
units.tr: VII. As for the parts of the Church, the Papists ridiculously babble that, as once in the Blessed Virgin, so now in the Pope alone, the Church can consist and be complete. As if a number could consist in unity, or a single citizen could make up a commonwealth and an assembly. But from Adam and Eve, whom God made the mother not only of the living but also of the dead, it (the Church) embraces within its compass, as if from a source once flowing forth, all the citizens of the holy city.

units.la: VIII. Angeli, quanquam ad familiam Dei pertineant, & electi sint, cum tamen è mundo non evocentur, nec de veteri labe purgari necesse habeant, nec denique Christo redemtore indigeant, ad hanc considerationem non spectant. Alium enim illi fatorum ordinem sortiti sunt, aliisque sub legibus ævum agitant, ac procul a terrenæ labis contagio semoti, in cœlesti aula destinato munere perfunguntur. Dicunturque fideles, postquam suum orbem impleverint, ac perpurgati fuerint, ad societatem ipsorum olim adducendi. Accessistis ad montem Zion, & civitatem Dei vivi, Hierusalem cœlestem, & myriadas angelorum, conventum universalem, & concionem primogenitorum, qui conscripti sunt in cœlis &c. Hebr. 12:22.
units.tr: VIII. The angels, although they belong to the family of God and are chosen, are not included in this consideration. Since they are not called out of the world, have no need to be purged of the ancient stain, and finally do not need Christ the Redeemer, they do not belong here. For they have obtained a different order of destinies, live their age under other laws, are set apart far from the contagion of earthly stain, and perform their appointed office in the heavenly court. And believers are said, after they have completed their own world and been thoroughly purged, to be brought at last into fellowship with them. You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, a universal assembly, and a gathering of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, etc. Hebrews 12:22.

units.la: IX. Homines autem non omnes ad Ecclesiam pertinent, sed electi solum, ac è mundo evocati. Unde & Ecclesia sancta dicitur, utpote quæ cum sacrificio, Hebr. 1:10. tum verbo ac Spiritu Christi, sanctificata est 1. Cor. 6:11. Eph. 5:25, 26, 27. Nec in censum hunc veniunt reprobi & hypocritæ: quos licet in Ecclesiæ atrio stantes reperias, Matth. 13:25, 26, 27. non tamen sanctæ civitatis cives sunt. Ecclesia enim Christi sine Christo, sine fide, sine spe, ac charitate, cæteroque virtutum agmine, esse non potest. Ut male Pontificii, omissa essentiali Ecclesiæ forma, externam illam ac accidentalem nimis spectent; & in vero ac germano Ecclesiæ filio, nec fidem, nec charitatem, sed solum externam fidei professionem, & sacramentorum usum, sub Romani Pontificis ducatu, æstiment. Unde videas eos infideles, atheos, hæreticos occultos, quosvis denique scelerator, Pontificis dictaturam agnoscentes, Ecclesiæ suæ includere.
units.tr: Men do not all belong to the Church, but only the elect, who have been called out of the world. Hence the Church is also called holy, since it has been sanctified both by the sacrifice of Christ, Heb. 1:10, and by the word and Spirit of Christ, 1 Cor. 6:11, Eph. 5:25, 26, 27. Reprobates and hypocrites are not counted in this number. You may find them standing in the courtyard of the Church, Matt. 13:25, 26, 27, but they are not citizens of the holy city. For the Church of Christ cannot exist without Christ, without faith, without hope and love, and the rest of the host of virtues. The Papists are wrong to set aside the essential form of the Church and to look too much at its external and accidental features. They judge that the true and genuine son of the Church needs no faith or love, only an outward profession of faith and the use of the sacraments under the leadership of the Roman Pontiff. Hence you may see them including within their Church unbelievers, atheists, secret heretics, and in short any criminals whatever, provided they acknowledge the Pontiff's dictatorship.

units.la: X. Ac eodem ex fonte peccant, cum infantes non-baptizatos, Catechumenos, scismaticos, & excommunicatos quoslibet, sine ullo crimine, iis tantum septis excludunt. Infantes enim ac liberos Christianorum, ad Dei familiam quoque pertinere, & pro Ecclesiæ sobole habere debere, ex Scripturis indubium est. Nec Catechumeni, etsi nondum omnibus sacris initiati, nec in externis Ecclesiæ tabulis adscripti sunt, ideo a communii ilni illa Christianorum societate excludendi veniunt. Certe Ecclesiæ filius fuit ille in cruce pendens latro, atque in isto vitæ articulo convertsus. Nec etiam omnes, qui tempestate quadam ab Ecclesiæ alicujus corpore direpti aut separati sunt, atque extra caulas oberrant, civitatis quoque Dei exules & extorres habendi sunt. Late enim patet Christianum nomen; nec uno illud coetu clauditur. Ac vera fides, & nominis Dei confessio, Christianum cum ponunt; qui tamen non sine culpa ab hoc vel illo fratrum coetu diverterit, & de domo exiverit, aliaque forte ovilia consectatus fuerit. Non enim in unico tantum coetu Deus regnat: quanquam Ecclesia una sit. Hoc vero nihilominus certum est, partes in Ecclesia facere, aut sequi; esse, sponsæ Christi contumeliam facere, sacrumque ejus corpus lacerare, & dilaniare; quod non procul a sacrilegio abest. Denique potest quis a coetu aliquo per injustam sententiam excludi, ut tamen non ideo quoque rerum coelestium exors, cæteri autem soli eorum participes habendi sint.
units.tr: X. They go wrong from the same source when they shut out, with no charge against them, unbaptized infants, catechumens, schismatics, and any excommunicated persons, by that barrier alone. That the infants and children of Christians also belong to God's family, and should be regarded as the offspring of the Church, is beyond doubt from the Scriptures. Nor are catechumens, although not yet initiated into all the sacred rites and not enrolled in the external registers of the Church, therefore to be excluded from that common fellowship of Christians. Certainly that thief hanging on the cross was a son of the Church, converted at that last moment of his life. Nor should all those who have been carried off or separated from the body of some Church by a storm, and wander outside the folds, be regarded as exiles and outcasts from the city of God. For the Christian name is widely extended, and is not confined to one assembly. True faith and the confession of God's name are what make a Christian, even though a person who turns aside from this or that company of the brethren, and leaves the house, and perhaps follows other folds, does so not without fault. For God does not reign in one assembly only, although the Church is one. Yet this is certainly true: to form factions in the Church, or to follow them, is to bring disgrace on the bride of Christ, and to tear and rend his sacred body, which is not far from sacrilege. Finally, someone may be shut out from a certain assembly by an unjust sentence, yet not for that reason be deprived of heavenly things, while the others alone are to be considered their sharers.

units.la: XI. Sequuntur Ecclesiæ attributa. Quorum 1. est Unitas. Unica columba mea, integra mea, unica illa apud matrem suam. Cant. 6: 8.
units.tr: XI. The attributes of the Church follow. The first of these is Unity. "My dove, my undefiled, is but one; she is the only one of her mother." Cant. 6:8.

units.la: Quæ unitas, non generica, vel specifica, sed individualis est. Qualis in corporibus, ex multis membris aggregatis, consspicitur. Ita enim Ecclesia consideranda est; non uti idea Platonica, vel uti natura universalis, aut corpus æreum, quod solo intellectus obtutu comprehendi possit; sed ut unum fidelium corpus, ac sodalitas, toto orbe sparsa, eadem autem fide ac charitate conjuncta & combinata. Ut, sicuti Deus unus est, ita quoque Ecclesia, quæ ipsum in mundo colit, non nisi una esse queat.
units.tr: This unity is not generic or specific but individual, such as is seen in bodies made up of many members joined together. For the Church is to be considered in this way: not as a Platonic idea, nor as a universal nature, nor as a bronze body that can be grasped only by the gaze of the intellect, but as one body and fellowship of the faithful, scattered over the whole world, yet joined and bound together by the same faith and love. Just as God is one, so the Church, which worships him in the world, can be only one.

units.la: XII. Nec male hæc Ecclesiæ unitas Catholica titulo explicatur: qui dicit aliquid integraliter universale, sive unum. Est enim Ecclesia nunc revera universalis & una. Nulli enim loco aut populo affixa, uti olim; non in familiis Patriarcharum dedicata, non in sacra Judæorum gente collocata, non alii denique genti elocata, ac veluti in servitutem tradita; tota, qua patet, orbe jam sparsa est; manetque ipsa communis omnium fidelium mater; quos, eodem lacte nutritos, eodem sinu fovet, atque eandem in spem educatos, ejusdem civitatis cives facit; mundumque hunc tandem universum commune veluti Dei templum reddit.
units.tr: XII. This unity of the Church is also rightly explained by the title Catholic, which signifies something wholly universal, or one. For the Church is now in truth universal and one. It is no longer tied to any place or people as once it was: it is not dedicated to the families of the patriarchs, not settled in the holy nation of the Jews, not finally handed over to some other nation and as it were delivered into slavery. It is now spread through the whole world as far as it extends, and it remains the common mother of all the faithful. It nourishes those whom it has fed with the same milk, and cherishes them in the same bosom, and having brought them up to the same hope, makes them citizens of the same city; and at last it makes this whole world, as it were, a common temple of God.

units.la: XIII. Quæ cum nomenclaturæ illius ratio sit, non nisi improprie ac synecdochice Ecclesia aliqua particularis Catholicæ nomen gerere potest: nisi illud de fidei Catholicæ professione intelligas. Quomodo veteres cuivis orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ istud elogium tribuerunt. Pessime autem est, tem Romanenses istum titulum sibi solis vendicant; aliis autem omnibus Ecclesiis, ad quos tamen Catholicæ fidei hæreditas devoluta est, abrogant; ac soli ipso nomine censeri & cognosci volunt. Cum eorum Ecclesia, nec Catholica, nec Catholicæ pars sit. Nam uni loco & cathedræ affixa, Romam religionis matrem ac metropolim colit, istiqué urbi assurgere omnes jubet: quod Ecclesiæ Catholicismo vel maxime adversum est; utpote quæ nullam amplius, in terris, uti olim in Vet. Testam. angustiis, religionis sedem ac matrem novit. Quin eadem, Catholicæ præterea fidei desertrix, sacrum ac venerandum istud nomen jam diu decoxit; non sponsa Christi, sed æmula, & jam notæ libidinis scortum, & lupa, quæ, per tot sæcula adulteria sua toto orbe pervulgavit, nihilque ad ultimum dedecus reliquum fecit.
units.tr: XIII. Since this is the reason for the name, the Church in any particular place can bear the name Catholic only improperly and by synecdoche, unless you understand that name as referring to the profession of the Catholic faith. The ancients so applied this honorific to any orthodox Church. But it is very wrong that the Romanists claim this title for themselves alone, deny it to all other Churches, to whom nevertheless the inheritance of the Catholic faith has passed, and wish themselves alone to be named and recognized by the name. For their Church is neither Catholic nor a part of the Catholic Church. Fixed in one place and see, it worships Rome as the mother and metropolis of religion, and orders everyone to pay homage to that city. This is most contrary to Catholicism in the Church, since it no longer knows any seat and mother of religion on earth, as it once knew in the narrow confines of the Old Testament. Moreover, this same Church, a deserter of the Catholic faith, has long since disgraced that sacred and venerable name. It is not the bride of Christ but a rival, a harlot notorious for lust, and a she-wolf, who through so many centuries has spread her adulteries throughout the whole world, and has left nothing more to add to her final disgrace.

units.la: XIV. Complectitur autem Catholicæ vox omnes locorum, temporum, personarum, ac statuum, differentias. Atque hæc latissima ejus acceptio est, qua universam Dei familiam, sive olim, sive nunc, in terris peregrinantem, perque omnia mundi tempora ac spatia diffusam uno ambitu comprehendit: cum cæteroquin vox illa sensu magis restricto Ecclesiam pariter in terris militantem duntaxat dicat.
units.tr: XIV. The word Catholic, moreover, embraces all the differences of places, times, persons and conditions. This is its widest meaning, by which it comprehends in one compass the whole family of God, whether formerly or now wandering on earth, and spread through all the times and spaces of the world. Otherwise that word, in a more restricted sense, denotes only the Church militant on earth.

units.la: XV. Atque hinc variæ oriuntur Ecclesiæ divisiones. Dum, temporum respectu, alia Veteris, alia Novi Testam. dicitur: &, pro locorum ratione, alia Occidentalis, alia Orientalis, est; aliaque præterea nomina, pro regnorum ac regionum spatiis, sortitur. Nunquam enim Ecclesia Catholica uno loco conclusa fuit. Ut male Pontificii Concilia & canones Ecclesiæ universæ nomine venditent. Statuum autem Ecclesiæ discrimen dicit, dum alia militans, alia triumphans, appellatur; cui fabulose Pontificii tertium Ecclesiæ in purgatorio laborantis statum superaddunt.
units.tr: XV. From this arise various divisions of the Church. With respect to times, one is called the Church of the Old Testament, another of the New; and according to places, one is Western, another Eastern; and besides these it receives other names according to the extent of kingdoms and regions. For the Catholic Church was never confined to one place. The Papists wrongly pass off the councils and canons of the whole Church as their own. The difference of conditions of the Church is shown when one is called militant and another triumphant. To this the Papists fabulously add a third state of the Church, that which suffers in purgatory.

units.la: XVI. Plerasque autem Ecclesiæ partes negant Socinini, ac regnum Christi non leviter circumcidunt: dum & in Veteri Testamento Ecclesiam Christi extitisse negant; & in Novo Test. eam non semper in terris superesse ajunt; denique & Ecclesiam piorum in cœlis pro non ente habent. Quæ theses non multum de regno Dei ac Christi in mundo relinquunt. Ecclesiam autem & olim sub Vet. Test. & exinde perpetuo in terris floruisse, atque etiam nunc partim in cœlo degere, clarissima Scripturæ testimonia evincunt. Tempore illo fuistis sine Christo, alienati a republ. Israelis, hospites testamentorum promissionis &c. Eph. 2: 12. Super hanc Petram ædificabo meam Ecclesiam, & portæ inferorum non prevalebunt perabunt eam. Matth. 16: 18. Ecce, ego vobiscum sum, omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi cap. 28:20. Ego rogabo Patrem, & alium advocatum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in seculum. Joh. 14:16. Cupiditatem habeo, ad discedendum, & ut sim cum Christo, quod multis partibus melius est. Phil. 1:23. Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur, a nunc. Na, dicit Spiritus; ut requiescant a laboribus suis. Opera autem eorum consequentur eos. Apoc. 14: 13.
units.tr: XVI. The Socinians deny most parts of the Church, and cut down the kingdom of Christ not lightly: they deny that the Church of Christ existed even under the Old Testament; they say that in the New Testament it does not always survive on earth; and finally they regard the Church of the godly in heaven as non-existent. These positions leave little of the kingdom of God and of Christ in the world. But the very clear testimonies of Scripture prove that the Church flourished under the Old Testament and from then on has continually flourished on earth, and that even now part of it dwells in heaven. "At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, etc." Eph. 2:12. "Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." Matt. 16:18. "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," ch. 28:20. "I will pray the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, that he may abide with you for ever." John 14:16. "I have a desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better." Phil. 1:23. "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. Yes, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works follow them." Rev. 14:13.

units.la: XVII. Ecclesiæ universalis partes integrantes sunt Ecclesiæ particulares, quæ certis in locis colliguntur: quæ de Ecclesiæ Catholicæ natura & privilegiis participant, cum in iis illa per se exsistat.
units.tr: XVII. The particular Churches are the integral parts of the universal Church. They are gathered in certain places, and they share in the nature and privileges of the Catholic Church, since in them that Church exists in its own right.

units.la: Non nimis autem illæ arctandæ sunt: quæ Anglorum Brownistarum superstitio est; qui, cogitationum angustias patientes, singulares Ecclesias unius auditorii septo concludunt; nec majores esse permittunt, quam quæ in unum locum coire, & ab uno Presbytero singulatim obiri possint. Sicut ab altera parte Pontificii novas Ecclesiæ particularis formas cudunt; ut universi orbis Ecclesiam sub uno tandem capite, Pontifice Romano, componunt: atque, hoc fas ut doceant, nil putant esse nefas. Quas Ecclesiæ facies ac formas Scriptura ignorat.
units.tr: Yet those churches should not be confined too narrowly either, as the superstition of the English Brownists does. Troubled by the narrowness of their own thinking, they enclose each individual church within the walls of a single meeting-room, and they do not allow any congregation to be larger than can assemble in one place and be served individually by one elder. On the other side, the Papists fashion new forms of the particular church and put together the Church of the whole world under one head, the Roman Pontiff. And while they teach this, they consider nothing wrong that they think is allowed. Scripture knows nothing of these appearances and forms of the Church.

units.la: XVIII Constituitur autem Ecclesia particularis per externam Euangelii professionem; qua multi fideles inter se conjuncti, ac in eandem disciplinam aggregati, sanctam inter se communionem colunt. Estque hæc publica & externa illius forma. Interna autem, qua ea Christo conjuncta est, quæ & essentiam dat toti corpori, & cuilibet corporis membro, occultior est, & sola mente perspicitur.
units.tr: XVIII. A particular church is constituted by the outward profession of the Gospel, by which many believers, joined together and gathered into the same discipline, cultivate a holy fellowship among themselves. This is its public and external form. Its inward form, by which it is joined to Christ, which gives essence both to the whole body and to each member of the body, is more hidden and is perceived by the mind alone.

units.la: XIX. Atque ex duplici hac forma Ecclesia vel visibilis, vel invisibilis, appellatur. Invisibilis enim est, quoad interiorem suam formam. Quomodo sanctos tantum & electos continet; quos externo visu dignoscere certe impossibile est. Tota gloriosa est filia regis introrsum. Psal. 45: 14. Sed qui in occulto est Judæus — cujus laus non ex hominibus, sed ex Deo. Rom. 2: 29. Qui vicerit, dabo ei edere de manna occultato, & dabo ei calculum album, & in calculo nomen novum scriptum; quod nemo novit, nisi qui accipit. Apoc. 2: 17. Ut male Pontificii Ecclesiam invisibilem tanquam ideam Platonicam, quæ nullibi extet, irrideant. Ac si Ecclesiam prorsus nullam faceremus; aut, stulto errore, eam occultis signis non nisi a conscriis dignosci posse statueremus. Hoc enim differiteri non possunt, quanquam externus cœtus, qui Ecclesiam constituit, videripossit; illud tamen, quod illam veram Dei Ecclesiam facit, fidem vi-
units.tr: XIX. From this twofold form the Church is called either visible or invisible. It is invisible as regards its inward form, in that it contains only the saints and the elect, whom it is certainly impossible to distinguish by outward sight: The king's daughter is all glorious within. Ps. 45:14. But he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and whose praise is not from men but from God. Rom. 2:29. To him who overcomes I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except he who receives it. Rev. 2:17. So the Papists wrongly mock the invisible Church as a Platonic idea that exists nowhere. It is as if we made no Church at all, or, in foolish error, held that it could be recognised by hidden signs only by those who share it. For these things cannot be separated: although the outward assembly, which constitutes the Church, can be seen, that which makes it the true Church of God, faith in Christ and the innermost sense of piety, cannot be seen. But the same Church is also visible, as regards the outward profession of faith. Yet here too certain degrees must be noted. For it is one thing for the Church to be visible, and another for it to present itself as conspicuous and public. For it has varying times of light: according as it is illumined more or less by its Sun, it is purer or less pure. And according as the times are either wicked or more fortunate, it has the opportunity either to assemble and show itself to the world, or, scattered by the fury of tyrants, it ceases both to gather and to be seen. Yet even then, while it is hidden in the clefts of the rocks, it does not cease at least to groan and lament, and it strives to make itself not only known but illustrious in the world by its own blood and martyrdom. Finally, with respect to some weaker people, it is often said to be inconspicuous. When they see the Lord's field occupied by tares and made most foul, they complain that no good grain is left in it. Such was the appearance of the Church in the times of Elijah.

units.la: Pars II. del. in Christum, intimumque pietatis sensum, conspici non posse. Sed & visibilis eadem est, quoad externam fidei professionem. Quanquam & hic gradus quidam notandi sunt. Aliud enim est, Ecclesiam visibilem esse, aliud eam conspicuam & publicam se exhibere. Habet enim ea diversa lucis tempora; prout, a Sole suo magis minusve illustrata, purior vel impurior est; atque, pro temporum seu iniquitate, seu majore felicitate, aut in coetus coeundi, seque orbi ostendendi facultatem habet; aut, tyrannorum furore dissipata, simul & congregari, & conspici, desinit. Quanquam etiam tum, de petrarum fissuris, gemitum saltem & plangere non cessaret, & vel cruore suo ac martyrio se se in mundo non solum notam, sed & illustrem reddere gestiat. Postremo & infirmiorum quorundam respectu ea inconspicua saepe dicitur: qui, dum agrum dominicum a zizaniis occupatum, factumque inquinatissimum, vident, nihil bonae frugis in eo superesse querulantur. Qualis Elianis temporibus Ecclesiae facies erat.
units.tr: XX. Moreover, whatever happens on earth, some visible Church of Christ always remains in the world. Nor will the jaws of the devil ever so deal a deadly bite to the whole Church that it wholly passes out of the memory and recollection of men. Matt. 16:18. On the other hand, it is promised that in the various times of the New Testament it will be clear and illustrious. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Matt. 5:14. And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, etc. Isa. 2:2, 3; compare Mic. 4:1, 2.

units.la: XX. Caeterum, quicquid horum in terris accidat, semper nihilominus visibilis aliqua in mundo superest Ecclesia Christi. Nec unquam in eam universam diaboli fauces morsum adeo lethiferum sunt impacturae, ut ea de fama ac memoria hominum prorsus exeat. Matth. 16: 18. Contra autem clara ea ac illustris, diversis Novi Test. temporibus, futura permittitur. Vos estis lux mundi. Non potest occultari urbs supra montem posita. Matth. 5: 14. Et erit in extremo dierum, exaltatus erit mons domus Jehova in capite montium, & sublatus pra collibus &c. Jes. 2: 2, 3. conf. Mich. 4: 1, 2.
units.tr: XXI. Here the Anabaptists and Socinians err on one side, for they confine the Church within too narrow a limit, do not allow it to be public enough, and disdain to call by the name of Church all assemblies that have not yet been sufficiently purged of scandals. They place the godly who wander elsewhere (among whom they also count the more religious among the Gentiles, who were called by no outward word) in the invisible Church. Thus they make the Church of Christ in the world either non-existent or not visible. For they describe it by such properties that they show it to be wholly hidden and removed from public knowledge, visible only to those who, speaking in the same way, know how to recognise the participants in this fellowship.

units.la: XXI. Peccant hic ab una parte Anabaptista & Socinianii, qui nimis angusto fine Ecclesiam circumscribunt; nec satis publicam eam esse sinunt; cunctosque coetus, qui a scandalis nondum satis expurgati sunt, Ecclesiae nomine dedignantur: pios autem alibi oberrantes (inter quos etiam religiosiores ex gentibus, nullo externo verbo vocatos, numerant) in invisibili Ecclesia collocant. Quomodo vel nullam, vel non aspectabilem Christi in mundo Ecclesiam faciunt. Iis enim proprietatibus eam delineant, quae ipsam penitus occultam, & a publica cognitione dimotam, eorum solummodo visui, qui, similiter effati, sodalitatis hujus participes dignoscere norunt, ostendant.
units.tr: XXII. On the other side, the Papists do not keep due measure. They make the Church not only clear and illustrious in the world, but also liken it to the form of an earthly kingdom. They have established for it a visible seat and chair, a visible head and high priest, and finally a monarchical government, fixed by a long succession of successors, and they insist that this outward form and pomp is essential to it. This is not the kingdom of the Church but slavery, and it is not the rule of Christ but of men in sacred things. In this, they are not secretly driven on by their own visibility of the Church. The kingdom of God does not come with observation [μετὰ παρατηρήσεως]; nor will they say, Look, here! or, Look, there! For behold, the kingdom of God is within you. Luke 17:20, 21.

units.la: XXII. Ab altera parte modum non tenent Pontificii, qui Ecclesiam non claram solum & illustrem in mundo faciunt; sed & in terreni regni formam assimilant; & visibilem ei sedem ac cathedram, & caput ac mystarcham visibilem, ac regimen denique monarchicum, longa successorum serie stabilitum, instituerunt; externamque illam formam ac pompam ei essentialem esse urgent. Quod non Ecclesiæ regnum, sed servitus; & non Christi, sed hominum in sacris imperium est. Ad quod illi sua illa Ecclesiæ visibilitate non occulte aurigantur. Cum regnum Dei non veniat μετὰ παρατηρήσεως: neque dicturi sint, ecce hic, aut, ecce illic, Ecce enim regnum Dei intus in vobis est. Luc. 17: 20, 21.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor do those famous prophecies about the kingdom of Christ and the Church under the New Testament lead them there. Isa. 2:2, 3; Mic. 4:1, 2; Matt. 5:14, etc. These must be understood both in contrast to the times of the Old Testament, when God reigned in one people only, and they are fulfilled by the fact that the Church after Christ's coming has now been made public. And they look also to certain times and periods in which they foretell a greater peace and happiness for the Church, some of which have been fulfilled and some still remain to be fulfilled. For the times of harm and darkness are also foretold under the New Testament: Matt. 24:24; Luke 18:8; 1 Tim. 4:1, 2, 3; 2 Thess. 2:3, 4. Finally, the rule that they have held for so long a time in the world under the name of Christ and the Church is one thing, and the rule of Christ is another; the former is of men.

units.la: XXIII. Nec ducunt eo illustria illa de Christi ac Ecclesiæ regno sub Novo T. vaticinia. Jes. 2: 2, 3. Mich. 4: 1, 2. Matth. 5: 14. &c. Illa enim, tum opposite ad Veteris Test. tempora, ubi in uno tantum populo regnabat Deus, intelligenda sunt; atque eo, quod Ecclesia post Christi adventum jam publica reddita sit, implentur: tum certa tempora ac periodos spectant, in quibus majorem Ecclesiæ pacem ac felicitatem prænunciant; quæ partim impleta sunt, partim adhuc implenda restant. Nam & noxiis, ac tenebrarum, tempora sub Novo Test. prædicta extant. Matth 24: 24. Luc. 18: 8. 1. Tim. 4: 1, 2, 3. 2. Thess. 2: 3, 4. Denique aliud est Christi, aliud est hominum, sub Christi ac Ecclesiæ nomine, in mundo regimen, quod illi tanto jam tempore obtinent.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor do the famous prophecies about the kingdom of Christ and the Church under the New Testament lead them there. Isa. 2:2, 3. Mic. 4:1, 2. Matt. 5:14, etc. For those prophecies must be understood partly in contrast to the times of the Old Testament, when God reigned over only one people, and they are fulfilled by the fact that the Church has become public since Christ's coming. Partly they look to certain times and periods in which they foretell greater peace and happiness for the Church, some of which have been fulfilled, while others still remain to be fulfilled. For there are also times of harm and darkness foretold under the New Testament. Matt. 24:24. Luke 18:8. 1 Tim. 4:1, 2, 3. 2 Thess. 2:3, 4. Finally, it is one thing to have a government of Christ, and another to have a government of men under the name of Christ and the Church, in the world, which they have now held for so long a time.

units.la: XXIV. Sed ut nostris Ecclesiis invidiam faciant, quæstionem illam potissimum agitant Pontificii. Nam & nuperas illas, ac post quindecim sæcula demum natas, & a Zwinglio, Luthero Calvinoque demum conditas criminantur. Ac identidem quæstiunculas istas movent, ubi ante Lutherum Ecclesiæ nostræ fuerint? qua in regione, urbe, domo, quibus denique in latebris per tot sæcula hæserint? Quibus non una ratione satisfieri potest; præterquam enim quod 1. non fidei, sed historiæ ista quæstio est; & ad fidem ac conscientiæ securitatem sufficit, consensum nostræ Ecclesiæ cum Apostolica, adeoque primam ac summam ejus antiquitatem, monstrare: 2. nos & priora sæcula, utpote incorruptiora, in solidum nobis vindicamus; & Ambrosios, Hieronymos, Augustinos, Chrysostomos, & quicquid ejus ætatis Patrum est, nostræ Ecclesiæ filios fuisse asserimus. 3. Cumque post illa tempora Ecclesia paulatim exerraverit, & non amplius pura fuerit, sed necdum prorsus impura, fere instar aquæ limpidæ, quam miscere jam tempestas incipit; nondum tamen protinus Spiritus S. de Ecclesia excessit; sed in media illa Ecclesia, adeoque in medio Papatu, vera Ecclesia tanquam captiva longo tempore latuit. 4. Nam & in mediis tenebris multi viri pii & sancti, tanquam stellulæ quædam intermicabant; integrique cœtus, Deum purius colentes,
units.tr: XXIV. But in order to make our Churches odious, the Papists chiefly stir up this question. For they accuse them of being recent, born only after fifteen centuries, and founded at last by Zwingli, Luther and Calvin. And again and again they raise these little questions: where were our Churches before Luther? In what region, city or house, and in what hiding-places did they lie hidden through so many centuries? These questions can be answered in more than one way. For apart from the fact that (1) this question belongs to history, not to faith, and it is enough for faith and the security of conscience to show the agreement of our Church with the Apostolic Church, and so its first and highest antiquity; (2) we claim the earlier centuries for ourselves as well, as being more uncorrupted, and we assert that Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, and whatever Fathers there are of that age, were sons of our Church; (3) since after those times the Church gradually went astray and was no longer pure, but not yet utterly impure, much like clear water which a storm is just beginning to stir, yet the Holy Spirit did not at once depart from the Church, but in the midst of that Church, and so in the midst of the Papacy, the true Church lay hidden for a long time as a captive; (4) for even in the midst of darkness many pious and holy men shone forth like little stars, and whole congregations, worshipping God more purely,

units.la: {1} Ubi fuerit Ecclesia ante Reformationem? tes, hic ibi numerabantur; & in Alpium vallibus tota gens, melioris Ecclesiæ spes & seminium. 5. Quanquam angustias istas accusare nihil attinet; cum non solo Occidente Dei regnum conclusum fuerit, sed in Asia & Africa patentissimæ, & tum, & sequentibus porro temporibus, monstrari potuerint Ecclesiæ. 6. Post longam autem noctem tandem reducta lux est; ac superiori sæculo per Euangelii sermonem discussæ illæ nebulæ, quæ candidam Ecclesiæ faciem hactenus turpaverant. Cui Dei beneficio velle obsistere, hominum malignorum est, & tenebra magis amantium quam lucem.
units.tr: {1} Where was the Church before the Reformation? [...] here and there they were counted; and in the valleys of the Alps a whole nation, the hope and seed of a better Church. 5. Yet there is no point in complaining about these narrow limits, since God's kingdom was not shut up in the West alone. In Asia and Africa, very wide regions, Churches could be pointed out both then and in the centuries that followed. 6. After a long night the light was at last brought back, and in the last century those clouds were dispersed by the preaching of the Gospel, clouds which until then had disfigured the bright face of the Church. To resist this benefit of God is the mark of malicious men, who love darkness more than light.

units.la: XXV. Secundum Ecclesiæ attributum est Infallibilitas: quod tamen de Ecclesia, non quatenus publica est, sed quatenus electorum coetum dicit, intelligendum est. Ista enim Spiritus S. custodia est, ut illi in totum exerrare, & salutem excidere non possint. Qui virtutis Dei præsidio custodimini, per fidem, ad salutem paratam revelari præstituto ultimo tempore. 1. Pet. 1: 5. Super hanc Petram ædificabo meam Ecclesiam, & porta inferorum non superabunt eam. Matth. 16: 18. Quisquis natus est ex Deo peccato non dat operam: quoniam semen Deo in eo manet. Nec potest peccare, eo quod ex Deo natus est. 1. Joh. 3: 9.
units.tr: XXV. The second attribute of the Church is infallibility. This, however, must be understood of the Church not as it is public but as it is the assembly of the elect. For this is the custody of the Holy Spirit, so that they cannot wholly go astray and fall from salvation. You who are guarded by the power of God through faith, unto a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. 1 Pet. 1:5. Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Matt. 16:18. Whoever is born of God does not practise sin, for his seed remains in him. He cannot sin, because he is born of God. 1 John 3:9.

units.la: XXVI. Cæteroquin particulares coetus non errare solum, sed & funditus labi ac extingui possunt. Ac publice quoque per universam Ecclesiam, quacunque illa patet, errores aliquos non letales obtinere adeo non repugnat, ut id olim factum fuisse puriorum sæculorum experientia satis probet. Quæ autem pro Ecclesiæ suæ infallibilitate adferunt adversarii, vel Apostolos præcipue spectant, ut Matth. 28: 20. Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem sæculi. Joh. 14: 17. Vos autem cognoscitis eum, Spiritum veritatis, quia apud vos manet, & in vobis erit: vel præfectorum Ecclesiæ officium dicunt, non autem peculiare non errandi privilegium, ut Mal. 2: 7. Labia sacerdotis servabunt scientiam, ut legem requirant ex ore ejus. Nam Angelus Jehova Dei exercituum est. Quæ & loci 1. Tim. 3: 15. ratio est: Ut scias, quomodo oporteat in domo Dei versari, quæ est Ecclesia Dei vivi; στύλος και ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας columna & firmamentum veritatis. Nisi quod ibi Ecclesiæ elogium ejusque firmitas simul significetur. Vel denique in genere Ecclesiam Christianam, ac nomen Christianum in mundo nunquam defecturum spondent. Super hanc Petram ædificabo meam Ecclesiam, & porta inferorum non superabunt eam. Matth. 16: 18. Quod tamen non omne errandi periculum excludit.
units.tr: XXVI. Otherwise, particular assemblies can not only err but even fall utterly and be extinguished. And that some non-fatal errors should prevail publicly throughout the whole Church, wherever it extends, is by no means impossible; the experience of the purer centuries sufficiently proves that this happened in the past. As for the passages which our opponents adduce for their Church's infallibility, they chiefly refer to the Apostles, such as Matt. 28:20: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. John 14:17: But you know him, the Spirit of truth, for he dwells with you and will be in you. Or else they speak of the office of the leaders of the Church, not of any peculiar privilege of not erring, as in Mal. 2:7: The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and men shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. The reason given in 1 Tim. 3:15 is of the same kind: That you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the column and ground of the truth [στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας]. Except that there the praise of the Church and its firmness are signified together. Lastly, they promise in general that the Christian Church and the Christian name will never fail in the world: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, Matt. 16:18. Yet this does not exclude every danger of error.

units.la: XXVII. Hoc enim tertium Ecclesiæ privilegium est, quod illa nunquam in totum de mundo peritura sit; neque legitima sacra ita publice excisura; ut, victore Satana ac mundo, regnum Christi in totum extinguendum, ac nomen ejus toto orbe delendum sit.
units.tr: XXVII. For this is the third privilege of the Church: that it will never perish wholly from the world, nor will it be so publicly cut off from the legitimate sacred things that, with Satan and the world victorious, the kingdom of Christ must be utterly extinguished and his name blotted out over the whole earth.

units.la: Hoc enim contra expressa verbi divini promissa est. Quod Christum semper in mundo regnaturum, & diabolum in Ecclesiam universam nunquam dentem letalem infixurum dixit. Psal. 110: 1. Matth. 16: 18. Quin contra nomen ejus sub N. T. & clarum & illustre futurum in mundo non semel legimus. Quod tamen de Ecclesia universim considerata accipiendum est; non autem de hoc vel illo cœtu. Particulares enim Ecclesiæ quoad hypocritas deficere, quoad fideles per obitum corum desinere possunt. Nec Ecclesia Romana ullam supra reliquas prærogativam ostendere potest. Ut merx fabulæ sint, quæ parasiti ejus de illa religionis videl. metropoli, deque urbe æterna, orbi venditare studeut. Cæterum quicquid horum accidit, semper tamen alicubi Christus regnum, & semper Ecclesiam in mundo visibilem & conspicuam habet; quanquam ea purior aliquando, aliquando impurior, & semper, cum mundo collata, exigua, Matth. 7: 13, 14. Luc. 12: 32. 18: 8. Apoc. 13: 3. exstat. Quod contra Socinianos, Remonstrantes, aliosque novatores, observandum; qui cœtus & Ecclesias nuper natas, quæ, temere compositæ, nullos tot retro saeculis habuere parentes, in orbem introducere annisi sunt.
units.tr: For this is contrary to the express promises of the divine Word, which tell us that Christ will always reign in the world, and that the devil will never fix his deadly tooth into the whole Church. Ps. 110:1; Matt. 16:18. Indeed, we read more than once that under the New Testament his name will be both famous and illustrious in the world. This, however, is to be taken of the Church considered universally, not of this or that assembly. For particular Churches can fail as to the hypocrites, and as to the faithful they can cease by their death. Nor can the Roman Church show any prerogative above the rest. Let them be the stuff of fable, those parasites of hers who strive to peddle to the world that metropolis of religion, that eternal city. Yet whatever of these things happens, Christ always has a kingdom somewhere, and always has a visible and conspicuous Church in the world, though at one time purer, at another more corrupt, and always, compared with the world, small. Matt. 7:13-14; Luke 12:32; 18:8; Rev. 13:3. This must be noted against the Socinians, the Remonstrants and other innovators, who have tried to introduce into the world assemblies and Churches newly born, which, rashly put together, have had no parents for so many centuries past.

units.la: XXVIII. Prodigiose ergo auctor nuperus, proxime post Apostolorum ætatem Spiritum S. de Ecclesia excessisse; atque ab isto ævo ad hæc usque tempora eam deseruisse; omnesque exinde Ecclesias Apostaticas habendas, edito libello suadere annisus est.
units.tr: XXVIII. Accordingly the recent author has prodigiously tried to persuade us, in a published booklet, that the Holy Spirit departed from the Church immediately after the age of the Apostles, that he has abandoned it from that age down to the present times, and that all Churches since then are to be regarded as apostate.

units.la: Hoc solo argumento, quod extraordinarius sancti Spir. ductus ac flatus tum defecerit. Erigi autem dum nondum redit ad Ecclesiam Spiritus, interim Ecclesiam conniventiæ ac tolerantiæ jubet: in quo merum Dei verbum, sine hominum interpretamentis, prælegatur, ac Spiritus adventus expectetur. Quo auspicio reditura aurea illa sæcula, virosque rursus Apostolicos, Ecclesiamque Apostolicam, ac puriorem Spiritus afflatum, vaticinatur. Quæ consilia, sub conciliandarum religionum, ac componendæ rei Christianæ specie, ad merum Scepticismum, Samaritanismum, Libertinismum, merumque religionis chaos, spectant; & præsentis ac præteriti temporis Ecclesias omnes criminantur; nec de futura ejus ætate recte judicant; sed suavia Chiliastarum somnia nobis enarrant.
units.tr: He rests this on the single argument that the extraordinary guidance and breath of the Holy Spirit then failed. Meanwhile, until the Spirit returns to the Church, he bids us to raise up a Church of mere tolerance and connivance, in which the bare Word of God is read aloud without human interpretations, and the coming of the Spirit is awaited. Under this auspice he prophesies that those golden ages will return, and Apostolic men again, and an Apostolic Church, and a purer inspiration of the Spirit. These counsels, under the appearance of reconciling religions and settling Christian affairs, look toward sheer scepticism, Samaritanism, libertinism, and a chaos of religion; they accuse all the Churches of the present and the past, and they do not judge rightly about the age to come, but tell us the pleasant dreams of the Chiliasts.

units.la: XXIX. Male etiam Swenkfeldius, ex non dissimili prætextu omnes
units.tr: XXIX. Swenckfeld also errs badly, under no dissimilar pretext,

units.la: omnes nunc Ecclesias ex æquo amandas & colendas, nec ullarum communionem temere fugiendam monet. Qui dissimiles ejusdem arboris fructus, parili noxa, radicis venenum satis testantur.
units.tr: now urging that all Churches be equally loved and cultivated, and that no communion with any of them be rashly shunned. Their fruits, unlike as they are from the same tree, sufficiently bear witness, with equal harm, to the poison of the root.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De NOTIS ECCLESIÆ.
units.tr: On the MARKS OF THE CHURCH.

units.la: I. Um fideles non temere vagari, sed in cœtus coire, Christique gregem in ovilia compelli oporteat; consideranda sunt Ecclesiæ notæ, quia viam ad caulas monstrent, Christique oves ab hircorum agmine separent. Quæ notæ ac γνωρίσματα dum quæruntur, non de universali illa ac mystica electorum Ecclesia; neque etiam de externa ac aspectabili Christiani nominis Ecclesia, quæ toto orbe dispersa est, inque eo non exiguam partem facit, agitur: nam altera soli Deo cognita est, Novit enim Dominus, qui sui sunt, 2 Tim. 2:19. partimque externis virtutibus sese prodit; altera autem vel sola professione dignoscitur: sed de particularibus Christianorum coetibus ac Ecclesiis, ut iis nos adjungamus, quaeritur. Quæ cum vel puriores vel impuriores sint, eodemque nomine veram Christi sponsam, & Ecclesias meretricantes & adulteras complectantur; notis quibusdam opus est, quibus sponsam Christi ab isto luparum grege, & castum ejus thalamum a meretricum sellis & stabulis dignoscamus.
units.tr: I. Since the faithful should not wander at random but gather into assemblies, and Christ's flock be driven into the folds, the marks of the Church must be considered, because they show the way to the sheepfolds and separate Christ's sheep from the herd of goats. While these marks and distinguishing signs [γνωρίσματα] are sought, the question is not about that universal and mystical Church of the elect, nor about the external and visible Church of the Christian name, which is scattered throughout the whole world and makes up no small part of it. The former is known to God alone: The Lord knows those who are his, 2 Tim. 2:19; and it partly reveals itself by external virtues. The latter is recognised by profession alone. But it is about the particular assemblies and Churches of Christians that we are inquiring, so that we may join ourselves to them. Since these are either purer or less pure, and embrace under the same name both the true bride of Christ and Churches that play the harlot and commit adultery, we need certain marks by which we may distinguish Christ's bride from that wolfish flock, and her chaste bedchamber from the seats and stables of harlots.

units.la: II. Cum autem verbum Dei Ecclesiam ejusque puritatem proxime constituat: nam per verbum ea vocatur, coque solo fides ejus nititur; ipsaque Ecclesia nihil aliud est, quam cœtus verbum Dei amplectens: constat puram verbi divini confessionem, ejusque potentiæ per charitatem demonstrationem, notam Ecclesiæ primariam esse; ex qua ea cognosci, atque an vera an falsa sit dignosci ac probari queat. Eph. 2:20. Joh. 10:27. 13:35. A qua nota principali fluit alia secundaria; legitima nimirum sacramentorum administratio. Marc. 16:16. Eph. 5:26. Quæ notæ quo purius in Ecclesiis elucent, eo puriores illæ habendæ sunt. Ac nulli omnino coetui Ecclesiæ nomen denegandum, qui caput ac fundamentum retineat, nec divini fœderis tabulas diruperit aut abnegaverit.
units.tr: II. Since the word of God primarily constitutes the Church and its purity (for it is called through the word, and its faith rests on that alone, and the Church itself is nothing other than an assembly embracing the word of God), it is established that the pure confession of the divine word, and its demonstration in power through love, is the primary mark of the Church. From it the Church may be recognised, and it may be discerned and proved whether it is true or false: Eph. 2:20; John 10:27; 13:35. From this principal mark flows another, secondary mark, namely the lawful administration of the sacraments: Mark 16:16; Eph. 5:26. The more clearly these marks shine forth in the Churches, the purer those Churches are to be held. Nor is the name of Church to be denied to any assembly at all which retains the Head and foundation and has not broken or renounced the tablets of the divine covenant.

units.la: III. Quod Pontificii Ecclesiam Scripturis notiorem prædicant, ex solita ipsorum in Scripturas reverentia est; quas Ecclesiæ auctoritati subjici malunt, quam ut quæstio de Ecclesia ex iis terminetur. Nec pretiosius est ipsorum cavillum, omnes hæreticos Scripturas jactare, adeoque; veræ Ecclesiæ eam notam esse non posse. Non enim de hominum malesanorum somniis, aut temulento impetu, sed de rei veritate quæritur.
units.tr: III. That the Papists proclaim the Church to be better known from Scripture comes from their customary reverence for Scripture; they would rather have Scripture subjected to the authority of the Church than have the question about the Church settled from it. Nor is their quibble any more valuable, that all heretics boast of Scriptures and so this cannot be a mark of the true Church. For the question is not about the dreams of mad men or the drunken passion of anyone, but about the truth of the matter.

units.la: IV. Quæ autem ab ipsis producuntur notæ, numero quindecim, ad pseudo-Ecclesiæ suæ formam compositæ & aptatæ, partim mere humanæ rationes & suadelæ sunt, quæ conscientiæ satisfacere non possunt; partim etiam aliis coetibus ac peregrinis cultibus conveniunt; partim nec in ipsam quidem Romanam Ecclesiam cadunt; & denique si quid veri habent, istud omne ad primariam illam veræ Ecclesiæ, omnisque in religione veritatis, notam, quam nos dedimus, reducitur: Ut prætermittam aliquas ex iis ita dubias & obscuras esse, ut notarum nomen tueri nulla ratione possint.
units.tr: IV. The marks they put forward, fifteen in number, composed and fitted to the form of their pseudo-Church, are partly merely human arguments and persuasions, which cannot satisfy the conscience; partly they also belong to other assemblies and foreign cults; partly they do not even fall upon the Roman Church itself; and finally, if they contain anything true, all of it is reduced to that primary mark of the true Church, and of all truth in religion, which we have given. To say nothing of the fact that some of them are so doubtful and obscure that they cannot in any way sustain the name of marks.

units.la: V. Ac 1. quidem Catholicæ nomen quid nisi titulus est? quem & Ariani olim non minus quam orthodoxi usurparunt. Si vero de re ipsa quæras, & de doctrina Catholica, illa ex solis Scripturis examinanda est. 2. Antiquitas, si de hominibus sumatur, externaque Ecclesiæ specie ac forma, fallax nota est; & quoad Romanenses, magnam partem falsa. Dogmatum autem antiquitas ex sola Scriptura æstimari potest; adeoque si quid veri in hac nota sit, illud ad nostram referendum erit. Mirum autem est, eos pro publica Ecclesiæ nota illud adferre, quod adeo sensui expositum non est, ut vix a doctissimis per tot sæculorum caliginem investigari queat. 3. Duratio diuturna, nec interrupta, Ecclesiæ particulari promissa non est. Ecclesiæ autem universæ eam competere, fide potius ex Dei promissione agnoscimus, quam sensu percipimus.
units.tr: V. And first, what is the name Catholic but a title? which the Arians too once used no less than the orthodox. If indeed you ask about the thing itself and Catholic doctrine, that must be examined from Scripture alone. 2. Antiquity, if taken of men and of the external appearance and form of the Church, is a deceptive mark, and as far as the Romanists are concerned, largely false. But the antiquity of doctrines can be judged from Scripture alone; so if there is anything true in this mark, it must be referred to ours. It is strange, however, that they bring forward as a public mark of the Church something so far from being open to the senses that it can scarcely be investigated, through the darkness of so many centuries, even by the most learned. 3. Duration, lasting and uninterrupted, has not been promised to any particular Church. That the universal Church possesses it we acknowledge by faith from God's promise rather than perceive by the senses.

units.la: 4. Amplitudo credentium, pro temporum periodis, nunc major, nunc minor, Ecclesiæ promissa est. Sæpe etiam in angustias cogenda ea perhibetur. Adeoque perpetua ejus nota esse non potest. Sed & quinam vere credentes, & quænam vera fides sit, non aliunde quam ex Scripturis constat. 5. Successio Episcoporum, si mere personalis sit, fallax nota est: namque & rupta ac turbata pastorum serie, ab Ecclesia abesse; & tyrannus Regi, ac latrones pastoribus succedere possunt. Si vero de doctrinæ successione traduce intelligatur; illa rursus non nisi ex verbo Dei, quod traditivæ hujus fons est, examinanda est. 6. Conspiratio in doctrina cum Ecclesia antiqua ac puriori, si de doctrina a Deo tradita intelligitur, uti sas est; rursus non nisi ex convenientia ejus cum verbo Dei intelligi potest; test; quæ unica antiquissimæ doctrinæ formula est. 7. Unio membrorum inter se, & cum capite, cum hic non nisi externa intelligatur, sub Papæ regno; non veræ, sed falsæ Ecclesiæ nota, & bestiæ character est. Mystica autem fidelium inter se, & cum Christo, unio invisibilis est. 8. Sanctitas doctrinæ, cum ex divina revelatione derivetur, atque ex ea sola æstimanda sit; nota hæc a nostra non differt. 9. Atque ejusdem generis est divina doctrinæ vis, & efficacia. Cum autem & erroris quædam potentia sit, & mirifica in hominum animos vis; inter Satanæ ac divini Spiritus suadam, non melius quam verbi divini face discerni potest. 10. Sanctitas vitæ primorum religionis auctorum, cum illi dudum de Ecclesiæ statio excesserint, hodiernæ Ecclesiæ notam facere non potest. Quæ, ut priscam sanctitatem, ita & doctrinæ veritatem jam dudum decoxit. Cumque etiam hypocritæ sanctitatem mentiri possint, ac vera sanctitas occulta sit; non ex externa sanctimonia doctrinæ veritas, sed ex vera doctrina vitæ morumque sanctitas æstimari ac dijudicari debet.
units.tr: 4. The amplitude of believers, according to the periods of time, now greater, now smaller, has been promised to the Church. Often too it is said to be driven into narrow straits. So it cannot be a perpetual mark. But who are truly believers, and what is true faith, is known from nothing other than Scripture. 5. Succession of bishops, if it is merely personal, is a deceptive mark: for the Church can be absent when the line of ministers is broken and disturbed, and a tyrant can succeed a king and robbers succeed ministers. If, however, it is understood as succession in doctrine by tradition, that again can be examined only from the word of God, which is the source of this tradition. 6. Agreement in doctrine with the ancient and purer Church, if it is understood of doctrine delivered by God, as is right, can again be understood only from its agreement with the word of God, which is the one formula of the most ancient doctrine. 7. Union of members among themselves and with the head, since here only the external is meant, under the rule of the Pope, is a mark not of the true but of the false Church, and the character of the beast. The mystical union of the faithful among themselves and with Christ, however, is invisible.

units.la: 11. Miraculorum gloria cum Ecclesia non semper coruscet, & falsis quoque coetibus, ac Antichristi synagogæ eam lucem Deus nonnunquam circumdet, ordinaria ejus nota esse non potest. Sufficit, nos ex Apostolicis chartis eam tenere doctrinam, quam Apostoli tot stupendis operibus, tanquam manifuris notis, signavere; nec nova sine fine signacula, iisdem tabulis adhibenda, requirere opus. 12. Eadem luminis prophetici ratio est. Nec semper in Ecclesia ista lux est. Et quid vetat Deum extra Ecclesiam aliquando loqui? 13. Adversariorum confessio inter fortuita est. Nec ab eorum testimonio Ecclesiæ sinceritas pendet. 14. Atque infelix eorum exitus, 15. Et felicitas temporalis eorum, qui Ecclesiam defenderunt, mere externa sunt; à quibus veræ religionis judicium, & summæ reiarbitrium, suspendere insanissimum foret. Non enim ex fortuito eventu vir sapiens judicat. Certe priorum sæculorum Ecclesia, tot martyrum sanguine purpurata, ista nota caruit. Manentque, quandiu manebit Ecclesia, illæ sententiæ: Oportet per multas afflictiones nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Act. 14: 12. Et omnes volentes pie vivere in Christo Jesu, persecutionem patientur. 2. Tim. 3: 12.
units.tr: 8. Holiness of doctrine, since it is derived from divine revelation and is to be judged from it alone, does not differ from our mark. 9. Of the same kind is the power and efficacy of divine doctrine. But since there is also a certain power of error and a wondrous force over men's minds, the persuasion of Satan and that of the divine Spirit cannot be distinguished any better than by the torch of the divine word. 10. Holiness of life of the first authors of the religion, since they long ago departed from the station of the Church, cannot make a mark of the present Church. The latter, as it has lost its ancient holiness, so too has long since decayed in the truth of its doctrine. And since hypocrites can feign holiness, and true holiness is hidden, the truth of doctrine must be judged not from outward sanctimony but the holiness of life and morals from true doctrine. 11. The glory of miracles, since the Church does not always shine with it, and God sometimes surrounds even false assemblies and the synagogues of Antichrist with that light, cannot be an ordinary mark. It is enough that we hold from the apostolic writings that doctrine which the Apostles marked with so many astonishing works, as with plainly visible signs; nor is there any need to demand new seals without end, to be applied to the same tablets. 12. The same reasoning applies to the light of prophecy. Nor is that light always in the Church. And what forbids God from sometimes speaking outside the Church? 13. The confession of adversaries is among chance things. Nor does the sincerity of the Church depend on their testimony. 14. The unhappy end of those 15. and the temporal happiness of those who defended the Church are merely external; to suspend the judgment of true religion and the decision of the highest matter upon these would be the height of madness. For a wise man does not judge from a chance event. Certainly the Church of earlier centuries, purpled with the blood of so many martyrs, lacked this mark. And those sayings remain, as long as the Church remains: "We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations," Act. 14:12; "And all who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution," 2 Tim. 3:12.

units.la: VI. Atque hæ Romanæ Synagogæ notæ sunt; atque hi adulteri illi fuci; quibus rugosa meretrix, postquam ætatis lenocinium amisit, sese pingere adhuc solet; ut, si novos amatores allicere amplius non possit, veteres saltem vi consuetudinis retineat.
units.tr: VI. These are the marks of the Roman synagogue, these are those adulterous paints with which the wrinkled harlot, after she has lost the allure of youth, still customarily makes herself up, so that, if she can no longer attract new lovers, she may at least keep the old ones by force of habit.

units.la: Quanquam & evanidi hi colores sunt, meræque larvæ; cum nec in ipsa Romana Ecclesia, si propius inspiciatur, hæ notæ hæreant. Adeo, præ vetustate, emarcida & striata cute est, ut ea nulla pigmentorum ope incrustari & lævigari amplius possit. Tu autem quid facis, quod induis te dibapho, quod ornas te ornatu aureo, quod laceras fuco oculos tuos? in vanum reddis te pulchram, respuunt te amasii. Jer. 4: 30.
units.tr: Yet these colours are faded and mere masks, since these marks do not cling even to the Roman Church itself, if it is looked at more closely. Such is the withered, wrinkled skin of her great age that no aid of paints can any longer plaster it over and smooth it. And you, what are you doing, that you clothe yourself in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with golden ornaments, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain do you make yourself beautiful; your lovers despise you. Jer. 4: 30.

units.la: VII. Nec felicius Tirinus ex quatuor symboli elogiis, Una, Sancta, Catholica, Apostolica, totidem Ecclesiæ suæ notas extruere nititur. Quod non sine assertione falsi peragere potest. Hæc enim veræ Ecclesiæ insignia, non nisi proter fidem ac doctrinam veram, alicui Ecclesiæ conveniunt. Ut ea demum sola Ecclesiæ nota sit. Quantopere autem Pontificii a fide illa Una, Sancta, Catholica & Apostolica, aberrent, toto hoc opere ostendimus. Unde nec vera Ecclesia, nec veræ Ecclesiæ pars sunt. Non enim Romana Ecclesia Sancta, Catholica & Apostolica; sed Apostatica, Idololatrica, & Tyrannica est. Quos titulos, pro furtivis illis titulis, ipsi reddere æquum est. Hæ tres enim falsæ istius Ecclesiæ notæ sunt; quæ satis ostendunt quam gravibus de causis divortium ab ea secerimus: ut infra suo loco ostendetur.
units.tr: VII. Tirinus does no better when he tries to build four marks of his Church from the four epithets of the creed: One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic. He cannot do this without asserting something false. For these are the distinguishing marks of the true Church, and they belong to no church except on account of the true faith and doctrine. So this alone is the mark of the Church. How far the Papists have strayed from that faith, which is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, we have shown throughout this whole work. Hence they are neither the true Church nor a part of the true Church. For the Roman Church is not holy, catholic and apostolic, but apostate, idolatrous and tyrannical. It is only fair that they give back those titles, which they have taken for themselves by theft. These three are the false marks of that Church, and they sufficiently show for what grave reasons we have separated ourselves from her, as will be shown below in its proper place.

units.la: VIII. In defectu peccant Socinianī: qui, uti Ecclesiam sæpe ex hoc mundo, ita & Ecclesiæ notas tollunt; nec magnopere de iis laborandum putant. Generalibus autem verbis, ibi Ecclesiam esse ajunt, ubi Christus rite colitur, & sanctitatis studium viget: de fidei autem articulis altum silent. Ut Ecclesia juxta ipsos esse possit, ubi fundamentalium Christianæ fidei articulorum eversio est.
units.tr: VIII. The Socinians err by defect. Just as they remove the Church often from this world, so they also remove the marks of the Church, and they do not think much trouble should be taken over them. In general terms, however, they say that the Church is wherever Christ is duly worshipped and zeal for holiness flourishes, but about the articles of faith they keep a deep silence. So, according to them, the Church could exist where the fundamental articles of the Christian faith are overthrown.

units.la: IX. Nec felicius Anabaptistæ propriam unicamque Ecclesiæ notam in vitæ sanctimonia constituunt. Quo colore portentosissima dogmata tegunt. Eamque præterea morum tristitiam, & pietatem tam anxiam & horrentem interdum inducunt, ut non diu in aliquo cœtu nota ista hærere possit. Hinc tot apud ipsos Ecclesiæ & sectæ, quæ, crudelibus edictis inter se saevientes, sese solas rerum cœlestium participes omnes credunt. Quod, ut & reliqua fere, quæ passim de illa secta observamus, præcipue de istis inter illos, qui Socinianismum Anabaptismo jungunt, dictum volumus: esse enim inter illos longe melioris commatis cœtus, veritatique multo propiores, novimus.
units.tr: IX. The Anabaptists fare no better when they place the one and only mark of the Church in holiness of life. Under this colour they conceal their most monstrous dogmas. Moreover, they bring in such a gloomy severity of manners and such an anxious and sometimes harsh piety that this mark cannot long remain with any gathering. Hence there are so many churches and sects among them, raging against one another with cruel edicts, and each believes itself alone to share in heavenly things. We wish this to be said of them, as well as nearly all the other things we observe everywhere about that sect, especially about those among them who join Socinianism to Anabaptism. For we know that there are gatherings among them of a much better stamp, much closer to the truth.

units.la: Anabaptistæ.
units.tr: Anabaptists.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS SEXTUS DE Regimine & disciplina Ecclesiæ. CAPUT III.
units.tr: LOCUS FORTY-SIXTH: ON THE GOVERNMENT AND DISCIPLINE OF THE CHURCH. CHAPTER III.

units.la: De CAPITE ECCLESI- Æ.
units.tr: On the HEAD OF THE CHURCH.

units.la: I. Ost naturam, notasque Ecclesiæ traditas, sequitur ejus regimen sive ministerium, sub Nov. Test. ejusque ministri.
units.tr: I. Following the nature and the marks of the Church already set out, there comes its government or ministry under the New Testament, and its ministers.

units.la: II. Ecclesiam, sive electorum coetum, condidit Deus Pater, in Filio, per Spirit. S. Atque ille solus immediate illam regit & perficit. Nullaque in hac re hominis potestas, aut auctoritas, est. Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis, in communionem filii ipsius, Jesu Christi, Domini nostri. 1. Cor. 1:9. Deus, omnis gratiæ auctor, qui vocavit vos ad æternam suam gloriam in Christo Jesu, is vos paulisper afflictos perficiat, stabiliat, roboret. 1. Pet. 5:10. Quanquam, quatenus ea visibilis ac externa est, hominum ministerio indigeat. Omnis namque domus paratur ab aliquo. Qui autem omnia paravit, Deus est. Et Moses quidem fidelis in tota domo ipsius, ut famulus, in testimonium eorum, quæ postea dicenda erant. Hebr. 3:4, 5. Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de ministris Christi, & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. 1. Cor. 4:1.
units.tr: II. God the Father founded the Church, or the assembly of the elect, in the Son, through the Holy Spirit, and he alone governs and perfects it immediately. No human power or authority has any part in this. God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. 1 Cor. 1:9. God, the giver of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, will himself perfect, establish, strengthen you after you have suffered a little. 1 Pet. 5:10. Although, insofar as it is visible and external, it needs the ministry of men. For every house is prepared by someone, but he who prepared all things is God. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, as a witness to those things which were to be spoken afterwards. Heb. 3:4, 5. Let a man regard us in this way, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 1 Cor. 4:1.

units.la: III. Peculiariter in Scripturis Christus Ecclesiæ Caput dicitur. Et omnia subjecit sub pedes ejus: & eum dedit caput super omnia Ecclesiæ. Eph. 1:22. In charitate crescamus in ipsum, quoad omnia; qui est caput, Christus. Ex quo omne corpus coagmentatum, & compositum, per omnem junctuam suppeditationis, secundum operationem, in mensura unius cujusque partis, incrementum corporis facit, ad ædificationem sui in charitate. cap. 4:15, 16. Vir est caput uxoris, ut est Christus caput Ecclesiæ: & ipse est Salvator corporis. cap. 5:23. Et ipse est caput corporis Ecclesiæ, qui est principatus, primogenitus ex mortuis, ut fieret in omnibus ipse primas tenens. Col. 1:18. Et estis in ipso completi, qui est caput omnis principatus & potestatis. cap. 2: 10. Et non tenens caput, ex quo omne corpus, per junöuras & vincula, suppeditationem accipiens, & coagmentatum, crescit, incrementum Dei. com. 19.
units.tr: III. In the Scriptures Christ is specially called the Head of the Church. He has put all things under his feet, and has given him as head over all things to the Church. Eph. 1:22. Let us grow up in love into him in all things, who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, fitted and joined together through every joint of supply, according to the working in due measure of each part, makes the growth of the body, for the building up of itself in love. Eph. 4:15, 16. The husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church, and he is the Saviour of the body. Eph. 5:23. And he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he may have the first place. Col. 1:18. And you are complete in him, who is the head of all principality and power. Col. 2:10. And not holding the head, from whom the whole body, receiving supply and being joined together through joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God. Col. 2:19.

units.la: IV. Caput autem dicit id quod summum & primum est. Col. 2: 10. Unde in meram creaturam convenire non potest.
units.tr: IV. Head, however, means that which is highest and first. Col. 2:10. Hence it cannot apply to a mere creature.

units.la: V. Sed, in praesenti negotio, non solum Christi principatus, sed praesertim arctissima ejus cum Ecclesiae corpore unio, & sancti Spiritus commeatus; ac sublimis illa, qua fungitur, Ecclesiae cura, hoc emblemate pingitur.
units.tr: V. But in the present matter, the emblem portrays not only Christ's sovereignty, but especially his very close union with the body of the Church, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and that lofty care of the Church which he exercises.

units.la: VI. Notat ergo capitis appellatio. 1. ejusdem in Christo & Ecclesia nature communionem. Quia pueri communem habent carnem & sanguinem, & ipse similiter factus est particeps eorundem. Hebr. 2: 14. conf. com. 11. 2. Intimam & arctissimam utriusque unionem, ut nec filius Dei sine Ecclesia sua, nec Ecclesia sine Christo sit. Ut abnegare eam Christus; hoc est, membra sua projicere & calcare: aut Ecclesia Christo carere, simulque vitam sperare non possit. Unde frequentata ista in Novo Test. phrasis, in Christo esse, manere, stare &c. quod de homine istum in modum dici sine sacrilegio non potest. Non enim tanta in merum hominem cadunt. 3. Ex hac unione sequitur bonorum ac donorum Christi communio. Ut & Christus ea decenter communicare, & Ecclesia sine ulla legis querela, accipere possit, tanquam haereditatem Ut eos, qui sub lege erant, emtos, liberaret; ut adoptionem filiorum accipe-remus. Gal. 4: 5. conf. Eph. 1: 22. 4. Praecipue notatur sacri Spiritus in membra influxus, & commercium; corporisque universi a Christo dependentia, & vita, & regimen. Quae praecipua capitis oeconomia est. Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum a semet ipso, nisi manseritis in vite; ita nec vos, nisi in me manseritis. Joh. 15: 4. Filium suum unigenitum misit Deus in mundum, ut vivamus per eum.
units.tr: VI. The name head therefore signifies: 1. the common nature of Christ and the Church. Since the children share flesh and blood, he too likewise partook of the same. Heb. 2:14, cf. the note on the 11th point. 2. the intimate and very close union of the two, so that neither the Son of God is without his Church, nor the Church without Christ. For Christ cannot disown it, that is, cast off and trample his own members, and the Church cannot lack Christ and at the same time hope for life. Hence the phrase so frequent in the New Testament, to be, remain, or stand in Christ, etc., which cannot be said of a man in this way without sacrilege, for such things do not fall to a mere man. 3. From this union follows the communion of Christ's goods and gifts. So that Christ can fittingly impart them, and the Church can receive them without any charge of law, as an inheritance. That he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. Gal. 4:5, cf. Eph. 1:22. 4. Above all, there is noted the inflow and interchange of the Holy Spirit into the members, and the dependence of the whole body on Christ for its life and government. This is the chief economy of the head. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless you abide in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me. John 15:4. God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him.

units.la: 1. Joh. 4: 9. Et ex plenitudine ipsius nos omnes accipimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Joh. 1: 16. Qui ascendit supra omnes coelos, ut adimpleat omnia. Eph. 4: 10. Distinctiones donorum, ministeriorum & actionum sunt; sed idem Spiritus, idem Dominus, idem Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. 1. Cor. 12: 4, 5, 6. Unde universa Ecclesia Christi σῶμα dicitur, Eph. 1: 23. Conf. Eph. 3: 19. Quod latius exequitur Apostolus Eph. 4: 15, 16. ubi distincte memorat 1. membrorum per varia χαρίσματα & ἐνεργείας inter se distinctionem, perque ea corporis universi ornatum & καταρτισμόν. 2. corumque rursus ἁρμογήν, seu συναρμολόγησιν & coaptationem mu-
units.tr: 1 John 4:9. And from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace. John 1:16. He who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. Eph. 4:10. There are differences of gifts, of ministries and of activities, but the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God, who works all things in all. 1 Cor. 12:4, 5, 6. Hence the whole Church of Christ is called the body [σῶμα], Eph. 1:23, cf. Eph. 3:19. The Apostle explains this more fully in Eph. 4:15, 16, where he clearly mentions 1. the distinction of the members among themselves through various gifts [χαρίσματα] and workings [ἐνεργείαι], and through these the adornment and equipping [καταρτισμός] of the whole body; 2. their further joining [ἁρμογή], or jointing together [συναρμολόγησις] and fitting,

units.la: juxta Eph. 4: 15, 16. mutuam, ac veluti concinnationem; qua amice conjurant, ac sibi mutuo operam præbent. 3. Hincque orientem corporis & compaginationem, ac firmamentum, & corporis alioqui ruentis fulturam. 4. Porro perpetuum Spiritus , deque capite, tanquam perenni fonte, manantem veluti fluvium, uberem ac perennem, per ministerium ad ultimas mystici corporis partes propagatum. 5. denique Ecclesiæ, tam large nutritæ, deque capitis fonte inundatæ lætissimos auctus, & incrementa, , ad ædificationem sui ipsius in caritate. conf. Col. 2:19.
