units.tr: according to Eph. 4:15, 16, a mutual harmony, as it were a fitting together, by which they friendly bind together and mutually render service to one another; 3. and from this the rising of the body and its framework, and the support of a body that would otherwise collapse; 4. further, the perpetual flow of the Spirit, flowing from the head as from a perennial fountain, like a river rich and everlasting, spread through the ministry to the furthest parts of the mystical body; 5. finally, the Church, so richly nourished and flooded from the fountain of the head, grows in the most joyful increase and growth, for the building up of itself in love. Cf. Col. 2:19.

units.la: VII. Quæ omnia cum in Christum cadant, longe perfectius Ecclesiæ, tanquam comparis sibi corporis, caput est; quam naturali in corpore ducatus capiti datus est; unde, non naturali solum capitis similitudine; sed & œconomica, Sponsi, Patris, Domini; & politica, Regis; ac artificiali denique, Petræ, fundamenti, & lapidis angularis, imagine in Scripturis occurrit. Ut ita summa ipsius in Ecclesiam potestas, & regimen, & artissima ac permeabilis unio, denotetur.
units.tr: VII. Since all these things apply to Christ, the head is far more perfectly given to the Church, as to its body joined to it as a companion, than leadership is given to the head in a natural body. Hence the Scriptures present him not only under the natural likeness of the head, but also under the images of the economic (household) Bridegroom, Father, Lord; of the political King; and finally of the artificial Rock, foundation, and cornerstone. Thus his supreme power over the Church, his government, and his most close and penetrating union with it, are indicated.

units.la: VIII. Quanquam autem semper isto axiomate effulserit; tamen post peractos pro Ecclesia labores, postquam humilem in terris statum absolverat, præcipue ipsum honorem sumsit; & ad dextram Dei eve Dum collocavit eum ad dextram suam in super-cœlestibus, supra omnem principatum & potestatem — & omnia subjecit sub pedes ejus, & eum dedit caput supra omnia Ecclesiæ. Eph. 1:20,21,22. Ego dico, dii estis, & filii excelsi omnes, at certe ut plebejus homo moriturî estis. Psal. 82:6,7. vide Deut. 32:42. Gladius meus vorabit carnem; sanguinem examinati, & captivitatis, a capite cæsarierum inimici. Psal. 68:22. Deus deprimet caput inimicorum suorum, verticem pilosum, qui pergit in reatibus suis.
units.tr: VIII. Although he has always shone forth in this axiom, nevertheless, after he had finished his labours for the Church, and had completed his humble state on earth, he especially took up the honour itself, and was set at the right hand of God. When he set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power, and has put all things under his feet, and has given him as head over all things to the Church. Eph. 1:20, 21, 22. I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High, but surely you shall die like men. Ps. 82:6, 7; see Deut. 32:42. My sword shall devour flesh; of the blood of the slain and of the captive, from the head of the hairy enemies. Ps. 68:22. God shall crush the head of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who goes on in his guilt. Ps. 68:22 (as printed in the text).

units.la: 2. Thess. 2:4. Sese opponens & efferens ille supra quicquid dicitur Deus, aut numen; adeo ut in templo Dei tanquam Deus sedeat, pra se ferens se esse Deum. Hinc Ecclesia Christi sub N. F. καθ' ἐκκλησίαν Ecclesia Dei vivi dicitur 1. Tim. 3:15.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 2:4. He who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or object of worship, so that he sits in the temple of God as God, presenting himself as God. Hence the Church of Christ under the New Testament is called the church of the living God [καθ' ἐκκλησίαν] in 1 Tim. 3:15.

units.la: IX. Unde sequitur, unicum tantum esse Ecclesiæ caput, quod nominis istius vim & pondus sustinere posset. Sicut Ecclesia unum tantum est corpus, quod uno isto capite tanquam unica animandum est mente. Nec magis alterum Ecclesiæ caput, quam alter Ecclesiæ sponsus, vir, dominus, mediator denique, dari potest. Quod audent tamen magnæ meretricis amasii; qui, Romanis populis ebrii, istum suum pseudoPontificem, & sacrorum regem, veluti in cœlesti solio collocant; & Ecclesiæ caput, sponsum, quin & fundamentum, appellare non verecundantur. Quo pacto partim sublime ac sacratissimum illud nomen infamant, deque sensu ejus minuunt, partim, isto colore, quæ hominis sortem supergrediuntur, Pontifici suo tribuunt; & Ecclesiam liberam servire iterum novis dominis faciunt.
units.tr: IX. From this it follows that there is only one head of the Church, one that could sustain the force and weight of that name. Just as the Church is one body, to be animated by this one head as by a single mind. Nor can another head of the Church be given, any more than another bridegroom, husband, lord, or, finally, mediator. Yet the lovers of the great harlot dare to do so; they, drunk with the Roman peoples, set up their false pontiff, the king of sacred things, as it were, on a heavenly throne, and are not ashamed to call him the head, the bridegroom, and even the foundation of the Church. By this they partly defame that lofty and most sacred name and diminish its meaning, and partly, under that pretence, they ascribe to their Pontiff what goes beyond the lot of man, and make the free Church serve new masters again.

units.la: X. Nec quicquam valent distinctionum latebræ: dum caput aliud dirigens, aliud influens; principale & ministeriale; ut & fundamentum primarium & secundarium, jactant. Nam, & contradictoria illa sunt; & meri fuci, tegendo Ecclesiæ suæ dedecori; quæ plus quam probe hominini in Ecclesia regnanti sese subiternit; cui interiorem potestatem, legesque ad conscientiam ferendi auctoritatem, adscribunt. Nec secundaria ilta nomina rei invidiam minuunt. Non magis quam si quis secundarium in casto conjugio conjugem invehat. Quicunque enim, præter Christum, Ecclesiæ caput dici amat; non caput & sponsus Ecclesiæ, sed profanus solii Christi infestor, & castissimi ejus thalami adulter & corruptor est.
units.tr: X. Nor do the hiding-places of distinctions avail anything, when they boast of one head directing and another influencing, a principal and a ministerial head, and likewise a primary and a secondary foundation. For these are self-contradictory, and mere disguises, covering the disgrace of their Church; for they very readily subject the man who reigns in the Church to themselves, and ascribe to him an interior power and the authority of enacting laws binding the conscience. Nor do those secondary names lessen the odium of the thing: no more than if someone were to bring in a secondary spouse into a chaste marriage. For whoever, apart from Christ, loves to be called the head of the Church is not the head and bridegroom of the Church, but a profane assailant of Christ's throne and an adulterer and corrupter of his most chaste bridal chamber.

units.la: XI. Nec prosunt vanissimi prætextus: mortalem illum Christi, ab Ecclesia absentis, vice fungi: quin etiam, si Christo placet, gloriæ ejus interesse, quod in amplissimo regno suo pro-regem habeat; uti in terrenis regnis fieri consuevit: nec eo majestatem ejus minui, cum prorex ille alio respectu subjectus & Ecclesiæ membrum sit: tandem & Apostolum inter diversa Ecclesiæ membra etiam caput numerare, 1.Cor. 12: 21. Nam, contra, Christus ubique, majestate suaprælens, ipse Ecclesiæ suæ per omnes partes præ-est; nec in regno suo hominem regem vel pro-regem admittit. Nam ejus dignitatis illud munus est, atque eam in Ecclesiam potestatem etiam adversarii illi tribuunt, ut in merum hominem cadere non possit. Tam longe aliter hic sese res habet, quam inter homines; ubi Rex, summam ipse rempubl. tractans, ex purpuratis aliquos suo solio propius admovere, & principalium curarum participes facere plerunque solet. Cum illa regis conditio sit, ut rebus omnibus interesse nequeat; atque ea quoque præfecturarum istarum sit ratio, ut a subjectis commodissime geri, atque illi principalis potestatis commis-sas sas sibi partes exercere possint. Nullæ autem in Ecclesia sunt præfecturæ, nulli præsides, nec quicquam de infinita illa Christi potestate delibari potest. In honorem vero Christi istam in Ecclesiam præfecturam erigere porro velle; idem est, ac si quis erecto idolo, tanquam visibili divinæ majestatis imagine, ipse Deum honorare putaret. Tandem non facit huc Apostoli locus. Diversa enim ibi capitis consideratio est. Nam non formaliter ista vox ibi usurpatur; de quo sensu nunc disputamus, ubi vel Christo a nobis, vel Papæ ab adversariis tribuitur: sed materialiter, pro nobiliori corporis membro, præcipuis quibusdam donis prædito; cui opponuntur pedes, aliaque minoris dignationis membra.
units.tr: XI. Nor do the most empty pretexts help: that the mortal man stands in the place of Christ, who is absent from the Church; or even that it pertains to the glory of Christ, if it pleases him, that in his most ample kingdom he should have a vice-king, as is customary in earthly kingdoms; nor that his majesty is diminished by this, since that vice-king is subject in another respect and is a member of the Church; and finally that the Apostle, among the various members of the Church, also counts the head, 1 Cor. 12:21. For on the contrary, Christ, present everywhere in his majesty, himself presides over his Church in all its parts, and he admits no man as king or vice-king in his kingdom. For that office belongs to his dignity, and even our adversaries ascribe to the Church a power of such a kind that it cannot fall to a mere man. The matter stands far differently here than among men, where a king, who himself manages the highest affairs of the commonwealth, is wont to bring some of the purple-clad nobles nearer to his throne and make them sharers in his principal cares. For it is the condition of a king that he cannot take part in all things; and it is the rationale of these prefectures that they can be conducted most conveniently by subjects, while the king's principal power is exercised by those entrusted with his own part. But in the Church there are no prefectures, no presidents, and nothing can be taken away from the infinite power of Christ. To wish to erect such a prefecture in the Church in honour of Christ is the same as if someone, having set up an idol as a visible image of the divine majesty, thought he was honouring God by it. Finally, the Apostle's passage does not bear on this. For there the consideration of the head is different. For that word is not used there in its formal sense, which is what we are now disputing, where it is ascribed either to Christ by us or to the Pope by our adversaries; but materially, for the more noble member of the body, endowed with certain special gifts, over against which the feet and other members of lesser dignity are set.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Legibus Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastical Laws.

units.la: I. Tergo Christus solus Ecclesiæ Caput; ita solus Ecclesiæ Rex & Legislator est. Iehova est judex noster, Iehova legislator noster, Iehova est Rex noster: ille salvat nos, Esai. 33:22. Qui autem præter eum leges Ecclesiæ ferre, cam-que in illis quæ Christus libera relinquit, judicare, majoremque aliquam in eam potestatem usurpare nititur, iste caput non tenere dicitur. Col. 2:19.
units.tr: I. Therefore Christ alone is the Head of the Church; so he alone is the King and Lawgiver of the Church. Jehovah is our judge, Jehovah is our lawgiver, Jehovah is our King: he will save us, Isa. 33:22. Whoever tries to make laws for the Church apart from him, to judge in matters that Christ has left free, and to claim some greater power over it, is said not to hold the Head, Col. 2:19.

units.la: II. Cum autem res omnes non ejusdem generis sint; & in omnibus bonus ordo, ac decorum, servari debeat; præceptum autem illud specificationem non habeat, & pro temporum ac locorum occursu, varium esse possit: explicandum porro est, quæ sit Ecclesiæ, sive cœtus fratrum, ubi solus suas res curat, isto in rerum genere potestas ac arbitrium.
units.tr: II. Since not all things are of the same kind, and good order and decency must be kept in all things, while the precept itself does not specify particulars and may vary according to the circumstances of times and places, we must next explain what power and discretion the Church, that is, the assembly of brothers where Christ alone looks after his own affairs, has in this kind of matter.

units.la: III. Sunt autem in cultu Dei quædam adeo expressa, & certa, ac necessaria, ut nemini aliter agere vel loqui liceat. Quæ Apostolus μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς cum omni præceptione, inculcanda monet. Tit. 2:11. Atque illa quivis Christianus, nedum cœtus fratrum præsides, ab aliis exigere possunt. Sunt vero illa adeo clara, &, tum in verbo Dei, tum in cordibus fidelium, cum maximorum, tum minimorum, expressa; ut non opus habeant eo in genere ναυαγίζεσθαι, & doceri, conditaque ab aliis leges accipere: cum scripturarum ἀπόδειξις, a quolibet fratrum facta, & sacra unctio ipsos planissime de iis edoceat & persuadeat. IV. Sunt vero & alia, de quibus expressum Dei verbum non datur; quae tamen alterutram in partem fieri debent. Ubi Ecclesiae directio, & consilium & διατάξεις de recto & bono ordine, locum habent.
units.tr: III. Now in the worship of God some things are so explicit, certain and necessary that no one may act or speak otherwise. The Apostle urges that these be inculcated with all authority [μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς], Titus 2:11. Any Christian, let alone the presiding men of the assembly, may demand these things of others. Indeed these matters are so clear, both in the Word of God and in the hearts of the faithful, both of the greatest and of the least, that they have no need in this area to be shipwrecked [ναυαγίζεσθαι], taught, or to receive laws imposed by others; the proof from the Scriptures, offered by any of the brothers, and the holy anointing teach and persuade them most plainly of these things. IV. There are also other matters on which the expressed Word of God is not given; yet these must be decided one way or the other. Here the Church's direction, counsel and arrangements [διατάξεις] concerning right and good order have their place.

units.la: V. Cumque ea sint vel prorsus indifferentia & libera, ut contrahere nuptias; vel talia, ut dubium esse possit, an non aliquid de iis Dominus iusserit, & generalibus regulis nobis viam commonstraverit; qualis erat casus ille, de quo Apostolus consilium suum explicat, 1. Cor. 7: 10. &c. vel denique istius generis, ut quidem res ipsa sit mandata, modus autem ejus exequendae a Deo nulla lege determinatus; qui, cum varius esse possit, a pluribus tamen non nisi uno eodemque modo & more peragi debet; uti publici cultus ratio ac exercitia: de singulis videndum.
units.tr: V. Some of these matters are wholly indifferent and free, such as contracting marriage; others are such that it may be doubtful whether the Lord has commanded anything about them, or has shown us the way by general rules, as was the case on which the Apostle sets out his advice, 1 Cor. 7:10 etc.; and finally there are matters of a kind where the thing itself is commanded, but the manner of carrying it out is determined by no law of God. Since this manner may vary, yet it must be carried out by many in one and the same way and fashion, as with the order and exercises of public worship. Each of these must be examined on its own.

units.la: VI. Ac illa quidem, quae indifferentia sunt, per nullum Ecclesiae praeceptum possunt reddi necessaria. Nec ulla talis in Ecclesia potestas est. Hoc enim contra pretiosam illam libertatem est, quam Christus nobis sanguine suo peperit; qua Ecclesiam suam nec hominibus, nec rebus ullis, amplius servire voluit. Pretio emti estis, ne efficiamini servi hominum.
units.tr: VI. The things that are indifferent cannot be made necessary by any precept of the Church. Nor does the Church have any such power. For this would be contrary to that precious liberty which Christ won for us with his blood, by which he did not wish his Church to serve men or any things any longer. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.

units.la: 1. Cor. 7: 23. Omnia mihi licent: at ego non redigar sub ullius potestatem.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 7:23. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything.

units.la: 1. Cor. 6: 12 conf. Gal. 4: 9. Ac appellat illa Scriptura mandata hominum, ac hoc nomine infamat; cum homini in Dei vivi coetu, ac Ecclesia eorum, qui coram Deo suo sedent, Psal. 133. nullus imperandi locus sit. Unde tam severe illa e regno Dei proscribuntur. Sed frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, quae sunt mandata hominum. Matth. 15: 19. Quae rationem quidem habent sapientiae, in cultu voluntario, & submissione animi, & in eo quod corpori non parcant; nec tamen ullius sunt pretii. Col. 2: 23. ad de 1. Tim. 4: 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 6:12, compare Gal. 4:9. Scripture calls such things commandments of men and brands them with this name, since in the assembly of the living God, and in the Church of those who sit before their God, Ps. 133, a man has no place to command. Hence they are so sternly banished from the kingdom of God. But in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men, Matt. 15:9. Which indeed have a show of wisdom in self-chosen worship, humility of mind, and in not sparing the body; yet they are of no value at all, Col. 2:23; compare 1 Tim. 4:3, 4, 5.

units.la: VII. Quae dubia sunt, & ambigua; & in quibus, aut consilium, aut illatio ex verbo Dei, certisque ejus regulis, locum habet; de iis Ecclesiae vel fratrum iudicium audire per est. Qui, si quod ex Scripturis verbum habent, tradere, omnique demonstrationis vi roborare; in re autem incerta consilium, juxta charitatis ac prudentiae legem, in Domino explicare debent. Quod Apostolus facit, 1. Cor. 7: 12. Reliquis autem ego dico, non Dominus &c. Est autem omnium, fratres docentes monentesque audire, ac ad factam e Scripturis demonstrationem attendere. Quae si proba & recta sit, ac ista luce, ut ab aliis quoque videri possit; tum ille, qui convictus fuerit, ad credendum & obtemperandum obligatur. Si quis vero ἀποκλύψιν illam nondum habeat, nec de mente Dei persuasus sit; ille, modo verba fundamenti retineat, ac verborum Dei metuens deprehendatur, nec ex vana contentione aut ambitione quicquam faciat; ista in re non-judicandus, nec ullo praecepto obligandus est. Nihil enim in Ecclesia, propter auctoritatem dicentis recipiendum est; nec talis in Ecclesia potestas exstitit.
units.tr: VII. Matters that are doubtful and ambiguous, and in which counsel or inference from the Word of God and its certain rules has its place, must be settled by hearing the judgment of the Church or of the brothers. If they have any word from the Scriptures, they ought to hand it down and confirm it with the full force of demonstration; but in an uncertain matter they ought to set out their counsel in the Lord, according to the rule of love and prudence. The Apostle does this, 1 Cor. 7:12: But to the rest I say, not the Lord, and so on. It is the duty of all to hear brothers who teach and admonish, and to attend to the demonstration made from the Scriptures. If this demonstration is sound and right, and so clear that it can be seen by others also, then the one who has been convinced is bound to believe and obey. But if someone does not yet have that revelation [ἀποκλύψιν], and is not persuaded about the mind of God, provided he holds to the words of the foundation and is found to fear the words of God, and does nothing out of vain contention or ambition, he is not to be judged in this matter, nor bound by any precept. For nothing is to be received in the Church on account of the authority of the one who speaks, nor has such a power existed in the Church.

units.la: VIII. Quod attinet denique externas divini cultus circumstantias, , sine quo ille decore & cum aedificatione exerceri non potest: ille a coetu absque dubio constitui debet. Habetque ille summum in ευταξία, juxta charitatis & prudentiae leges, ordinanda arbitrium. Idque ex confoederata piorum disciplina necessarium est. Ac pertinet huc canon Apostolicus: Omnia decenter & ordine fiant. 1. Cor. 14:40. Nec cuiquam ordini isti intercedere, aut per contemptum quicquam facere, licet. Obedite ductoribus vestris & cedite. Hebr. 13:17.
units.tr: VIII. As for the external circumstances of divine worship, without which it cannot be carried on decently and for edification, these must without doubt be settled by the assembly. The decision on these, according to the laws of love and prudence, rests chiefly with the assembly's judgment about good order [εὐταξία]. This is necessary for a discipline of believers bound together by covenant. The Apostolic canon applies here: Let all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. 14:40. No one may oppose this order or act against it out of contempt. Obey your leaders and submit, Heb. 13:17.

units.la: IX. In coetu autem illo, ubi ille privatim convenit, praecipua Patrum-familias, eorumque, qui sub aliorum potestate non sunt, auctoritas est. Quibus reliqui, qui sub eorum potestate sunt, non solum boni ordinis, sed & debitae obedientiae causa, obsequium debent. Sed & Senioribus, atque viris de coetu delectis, publicam illam & communem Ecclesiae curam traderè, ac ordini ab ipsis statuto universum coetum subjicere, non iniquum est. Ita tamen ut nullus fratrum a se e abdicare possit illa officia, quae ab ipso, cum publice, tum privatim, reliquis fratribus debentur. Quae varia sunt. Atque ubi ita Ecclesia regitur, sanctusque ordo observatur, atque omnia amori ac aedificationi serviunt, nec dominatio aut tyrannis viget; ibi sedent fratres una, coram Domino, tanquam unico let gilatore & praeceptore: ac regnat Deus in Zione, & coram Senioribus ejus est gloria. Psal. 133:1. Esai. 24:23.
units.tr: IX. In that assembly, however, where people gather privately, the chief authority belongs to the heads of households, and to those who are not under the power of others. The rest, who are under their power, owe them service, both for the sake of good order and out of due obedience. It is also not unfair to entrust the public and common care of the Church to elders and to men chosen from the assembly, and to subject the whole assembly to the order established by them. Yet no one of the brothers may renounce the duties which he owes to the other brothers, both publicly and privately, and these are various. Where the Church is governed in this way, holy order is kept, and all things serve love and edification, and neither domination nor tyranny flourishes, there the brothers sit together before the Lord, as under one lawgiver and teacher, and God reigns in Zion, and his glory is before his elders, Ps. 133:1; Isa. 24:23.

units.la: X. Non pertinent autem ad boni ordinis praecepta, ea quae prorsus libera sunt; quaeque, quomodocunque fiant, ad cultum Dei nullum magnopere momentum habent. Nec quicquam hic praescribi potest. Multo minus ut illa in ritus significativos mutari facile debeant. Ut si quis candida veste, nescio cujus mysterii causa, indui malit: aut in cultu divino multifarias gesticulationes adhibeat. Non enim Ecclesia oneranda; nec quisquam in talibus judicandus; multo minus sanctitas ac religio, & cultus Dei, figio in rebus illis collocanda est. Cum pietas, & religio, & cultus Dei, figio in rebus illis collocanda est; atque illa leviculis istis astringi ab hominibus ne illis posset consistere; atque illa leviculis istis astringi ab hominibus nullo modo possit. Necalia signorum sacramentalium apud Pontificios ratio est. De quibus idem judicium fieri debet.
units.tr: X. Matters that are entirely free, and which, however they are done, have no great importance for the worship of God, do not belong to the precepts of good order. Nothing can be prescribed here. Much less should they easily be changed into significant rites: as if someone preferred to be clothed in white robes for the sake of I know not what mystery, or used many gestures in divine worship. The Church is not to be burdened with such things, nor is anyone to be judged over them; much less should holiness, religion and the worship of God be placed in such trifles. Piety, religion and the worship of God cannot stand if men bind them with such trivial things; and they cannot in any way be bound by these trivial things. The same holds for the sacramental signs of the Papists, and the same judgment should be made about them.

units.la: XI. Atque ita patet, quid de Ecclesiae potestate legislativa exstiman-dum dum sit; quod videl. ea in constituenda iurisdictione, & cultus publici ordineac modo determinando, fere tota consistat. Per quam tamen privatorum conscientiæ non ultra obligantur, quam ut offendicula vitentur, nihilque proterve, ac per contemtum Ecclesiæ, cultusve publici, peraga-tur. Qui vero ab Ecclesia conduntur Canones de fidei dogmatibus, illi ex sola Scriptura auctoritatem habent. Ac reliqui porro ministrorum sermones, traditæque ab ipsis vitæ & morum regulæ, admonitionesque potius de verbo Dei depromptæ, quam veræ leges aut iuroli habendæ sunt.
units.tr: XI. And so it is clear what is to be thought of the legislative power of the Church: that it consists almost entirely in establishing jurisdiction and in determining the order and manner of public worship. Yet private consciences are bound by these only so far as offences are avoided, and nothing is done wantonly or with contempt for the Church or public worship. The canons that the Church enacts concerning the dogmas of faith have their authority from Scripture alone. The rest of the sermons of ministers, and the rules of life and morals they hand down, and their admonitions drawn from the Word of God, are to be regarded rather as admonitions than as true laws or legal rights.

units.la: XII. Ut Pontificiæ Ecclesiæ factum mirari liceat, quæ Episcopos in dioecesibus suis, & Pontificem Romanum in Ecclesia universa, veros principes Ecclesiasticos asserit; iisque, inconsulta plebe, ac fratrum coetu, ipsisque etiam Presbyteris, pro arbitrio, leges quæ conscientias obligent, ferendi, & coram judicio Dei obligandi auctoritatem tribuit; ac tandem in inobedientes non solum edictis sævire, eosque rebus cœlestibus excludere, sed & corporalibus poenis coërcere, permittit. Quæ a vero non parum abeunt.
units.tr: XII. It is remarkable what the Papist Church has done. It asserts that the bishops in their dioceses, and the Roman Pontiff in the whole Church, are the true ecclesiastical princes. It grants them the authority to make, at their own discretion and without consulting the people, the brethren's assembly, or even the elders, laws that bind consciences and bind them before the judgment of God. And finally it permits them not only to rage with decrees against the disobedient and shut them out from heavenly things, but also to restrain them with bodily punishments. These claims depart not a little from the truth.

units.la: XIII. 1. Unus enim in Ecclesia dominus, ac unus legislator est. Iehova est iudex noster, Iehova legislator noster, Iehova est Rex noster. Ille salvat nos. Jes. 33:22. Unus est legislator, qui potest servare & perdere. Tu quis es, qui damnas alium? Jac. 4:12. 2. Nec Euangelii ministri Ecclesiæ domini, sed legis divinæ præcones, ac in regno isto Christi ministri sunt. Omni autem dominatu ipsis interdicitur. Scitis principes gentium in eas dominari, & magnates potestatem exercere in eas. Verum non ita erit inter vos. Matth. 20:25,26. Pascite gregem Dei, qui penes vos est; illius inspectioni vacantes, non coacte, sed libenter, neque ut dominantes cleri, sed ut qui sitis exemplaria gregis. 1.Pet. 5:2,3. Pretio emti estis. Ne efficte servi hominum. 1.Cor. 7:23. Non quod dominemur vestræ fidei, sed quod administri sumus gaudii vestri. 2.Cor. 1:24. 3. Cumque Ecclesia Christi regnum sit, nulla hominum mandata ibi locum habent; nec illa præstare, est cultum Deo exhibere. Sed frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, quæ sunt mandata hominum. Matth. 15:9. 4. Denique ex præhabito rerum omnium, quæ sub Ecclesiæ curam cadunt, examine, patet nullum legibus proprie dictis locum superesse. Nam quæ necessaria sunt, ea Dei lege jam comprehensa sunt: quæ libera sunt & indifferentia, illa nulla humana lege coërceri debent.
units.tr: XIII. 1. There is one Lord and one Lawgiver in the Church. Jehovah is our judge, Jehovah is our lawgiver, Jehovah is our king; he will save us. Isa. 33:22. There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. Who are you, that you judge another? James 4:12. 2. Nor are the ministers of the Gospel the lords of the Church, but heralds of the divine law, and ministers in this kingdom of Christ. All lordship is forbidden to them. You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. Matt. 20:25,26. Feed the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, not as lording it over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. 1 Pet. 5:2,3. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. 1 Cor. 7:23. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are workers with you for your joy. 2 Cor. 1:24. 3. And since the Church of Christ is a kingdom, no human commands have any place in it; and to observe them is not to render worship to God. But in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. Matt. 15:9. 4. Finally, from the examination already made of all the matters that fall under the care of the Church, it is plain that no place remains for laws properly so called. For the things that are necessary are already comprehended in the law of God; the things that are free and indifferent ought not to be constrained by any human law.

units.la: XIV. Nec recte ad Leviticorum sacerdotum exemplum provocant, de quibus Deut. 17:12. Vir autem ille, qui commiserit superbe, ut non auscultet sacerdoti, constanter ministranti ibi Jehova Deo tuo, aut summo judici, utique morietur vir ille. Quanquam enim Pædagogis illis (qui tamen non tam Ecclesiastici, quam politici hic inducuntur) privum quid in Ecclesia olim concessum fuerit, quod abrogatis eorum thronis una cum ipsis extinctum est; tamen ne ipsorum quidem mandata populum obligabant, nisi quatenus legem, a Deo traditam, docerent; cujus illi peculiariter, & non sine imperio, a Deo constituti erant custodes & vindices: Ex præstituto legis, quam docuerint te, & secundum judicium illud, quod dixerint tibi, facito &c. Ys 11. Nec plus præsidii in Apostolis reperiunt. Mittuntur enim illi, sicut missus & Christus, Joh. 20: 21. non æquali potestate, nec ad leges ferendas, sed ad Euangelium prædicandum. Nec potestas ligandi, quæ ipsis traditur Matth. 16: 19. est potestas nova onera, novaque leges imponendi, sed potestas clavium circa fideles exercenda. De qua deinceps. Denique Act. 15:28. non novam legem ferunt Apostoli, sed latam olim a Deo legem repetunt; nec ex improvisa libertate in recenti Ecclesia scandalum oriretur. Cui cavendo, ac Ecclesiæ paci servandæ, hæc διάταξις unice serviebat; neque ultra obligabat: sicuti, mutatis illis circumstantiis, tandem ultro obligare desiit. Quanquam nec omnis illa potestas, quæ Apostolis singulariter, & extra ordinem, collata est, ad ordinarios Ecclesiæ ministros pertinet.
units.tr: XIV. Nor do they rightly appeal to the example of the Levitical priests, concerning whom Deut. 17:12 says: But the man who acts presumptuously and will not listen to the priest who stands there ministering to Jehovah your God, or to the chief judge, that man shall die. For although some privilege was once granted in the Church to those pedagogues (who are here introduced as political rather than ecclesiastical figures), and it was abolished together with their thrones, nevertheless not even their commands bound the people, except insofar as they taught the law given by God, of which they were appointed by God, in a special way and not without authority, to be the guardians and avengers: According to the sentence of the law which they teach you, and according to the judgment which they declare to you, you shall do, etc. Deut. 17, v. 11. Nor do they find more support in the Apostles. For they were sent as the Father sent me, John 20:21, not with equal power, nor to enact laws, but to preach the Gospel. Nor is the power of binding, which is given to them in Matt. 16:19, a power of imposing new burdens and new laws, but the power of the keys to be exercised over the faithful; of which more presently. Finally, at Acts 15:28 the Apostles do not enact a new law, but repeat a law given long before by God; nor would a scandal have arisen from an unforeseen liberty in the young Church. To guard against this, and to preserve the peace of the Church, that [διάταξις] served solely this purpose, and did not bind beyond it; just as, once those circumstances had changed, it ceased in the end to bind of its own accord. Yet not all that power which was conferred on the Apostles in a singular way and outside the ordinary course pertains to the ordinary ministers of the Church.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Disciplina Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: On Ecclesiastical Discipline

units.la: I. Eges Ecclesiasticas excipit Judicium Ecclesiasticum, quod in Disciplina præcipue se exerit. Ecclesiæ enim mandatum est judicium, & disciplinæ custodia. Sic dicit Jehova, servare judicium, & facite justitiam: nam propinqua est salus mea, ut veniat, & justitia mea, ut reveletur. Esai 56: 1. Quæ clavium potestate in Nov. Test. exprimitur. Matth. 16. Similitudine ab œconomorum & administratorum domus, Esai. 22:22. aut a Doctorum legis, qui inter alia, clavium traditione creabantur, quo pertinet clavis cognitionis, Luc. 11:32. aut etiam a janitorum templi officio, deducta. AdAdverte cor tuum ad introitum domus, cum omnibus exitibus sanctuarii. Ezech. 44: 5. Et populum meum docebunt distinguere sanctum & commune, & internoscere inter impurum ac purum. com. 23.
units.tr: I. Ecclesiastical laws are followed by ecclesiastical judgment, which shows itself chiefly in discipline. For the Church has been entrusted with judgment and with the keeping of discipline. Thus says the LORD: keep judgment and do justice, for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. Isa. 56:1. In the New Testament this is expressed by the power of the keys (Matt. 16). It is derived from the image of the stewards and managers of a household (Isa. 22:22), or from the teachers of the law, who among other things were appointed by the handing over of keys, to which belongs the key of knowledge (Luke 11:52), or else from the office of the temple doorkeepers. Mark well the entrance of the house, with all the exits of the sanctuary. Ezek. 44:5. And they shall teach my people to distinguish the holy from the common, and to discern between the unclean and the clean. Ver. 23.

units.la: II. Dividunt eas Pontificii in claves ordinis & jurisdictionis. Quarum illas etiam Presbyteris, has solis Episcopis concedunt: quibus praeter verbi & sacramentorum potestatem, caeterarum praeterea & controversiarum cognitionem, & publicum Ecclesiae regimen deferunt. Sed Scriptura illud Presbyteri ac Episcopi discrimen ignorat.
units.tr: II. The Papists divide these into the keys of order and jurisdiction. The former they grant even to presbyters, but the latter to bishops alone, to whom they assign, besides the power of Word and sacraments, also the cognizance of other matters and disputes, and the public government of the Church. But Scripture knows nothing of that distinction between elders and bishops.

units.la: III. Nostrorum quidam aliter distinguunt, inter Clavem scientiae, & regiminis. Illius mentio occurrit Luc. 11: 52. ubi Scribis τὴν κατηχήσεως corruptio, &, metaphora quadam, clavium sibi creditarum vel adulteratio vel occultatio objicitur. Clavem regiminis rursus triplicem faciunt: Ministerii, in verbi & sacramentorum administratione; Ordinis, tum in doctrinae integritate conservanda, per communes formulas, tum in Ecclesiae οἰκονομία constituenda; & Correptionis, quae disciplina Ecclesiastica dicitur. Sed haec divisio non uno incommodo laborat.
units.tr: III. Some of our own people distinguish otherwise, between the key of knowledge and the key of government. Mention of the former occurs at Luke 11:52, where the scribes are charged, by a certain metaphor, with corrupting the instruction [τὴν κατηχήσεως], or with adulterating or hiding the keys entrusted to them. The key of government they again make threefold: of ministry, in the administration of Word and sacraments; of order, both in keeping doctrine whole through common formulas and in establishing the economy [οἰκονομία] of the Church; and of correction, which is called ecclesiastical discipline. But this division labours under more than one inconvenience.

units.la: IV. Catechesis duplicem ponit clavem, cum in Evangelii praedicatione, tum in disciplinae exercitio. Ac illa quidem magis publica est, dum credentibus, Christi nomine ac jussu, salutis praeconium perhibetur, & caelum veluti aperitur; incredulis autem, quamdiu isto in statu manent, contemtae salutis supplicia, ac diras, ac divina Nemesis, denunciantur. Sic dilexit Deus mundum, ut filium unigenitum dederit, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Non enim misit Deus filium suum in mundum, ut judicet mundum; sed ut mundus salvetur per eum. Joh. 3: 16. Qui inobediens est filio, non videbit vitam; sed ira Dei manet super eum. com. 36. Haec autem magis personalis est, ac singularibus personis caelestes istas censuras, vel venias, ac redditam Dei ac Ecclesiae pacem, annunciat. Non alia autem quam Evangelicae praedicationis auctoritate nititur: quae summa ac primaria, si non unica, ministrorum clavis est.
units.tr: IV. The catechism posits two keys: one in the preaching of the Gospel, the other in the exercise of discipline. The former is more public: to believers, in Christ's name and by his command, the proclamation of salvation is made and heaven is, as it were, opened; but to unbelievers, as long as they remain in that state, the punishments of scorned salvation and dire divine vengeance are announced. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. John 3:16. Whoever is disobedient to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. Ver. 36. The latter is more personal, and it announces those heavenly censures, or pardons, and the restored peace of God and the Church, to particular persons. It rests on no other authority than that of the preaching of the Gospel, which is the highest and primary, if not the only, key of the ministers.

units.la: V. Clavium & disciplinae sub N. F. auctor est Christus, Ecclesiae Dominus. Haec dicit sanctus & verax, qui habet clavem Davidis: qui claves he aperit, & nemo claudit; claudit, & nemo aperit. Apoc. 3: 8. Qui ilium in Ecclesia sua ordinem, ac disciplinae vigorem, instituit; &, ne sanctum limen ab impuris calcaretur, claves regni caelorum, h.e. Ecclesiae sub N. & Apostolis F. Judaeis Gentibusque credentibus aperiendae, incredulis autem claudendae,
units.tr: V. Christ, the Lord of the Church, is the author of the keys and of discipline under the New Covenant. These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David: he who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens. Rev. 3:8. He who instituted in his Church an order and a vigour of discipline; and, lest the holy threshold be trodden by the unclean, he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, of the Church, to be opened under the New Covenant by the Apostles to believing Jews and Gentiles, but to be shut against unbelievers.

units.la: {y} Quibus commisit ... prae Petro ... dendæ, Petro primum ac post eum Apostolorum collegio, singulari ac infallibili auctoritate,&c, post eorum excessum, ordinariis Ecclesiæ ministris, inclinato licet sensu, minoreque auctoritate, concredidit. Tibi dabo claves regni cœlorum: & quicquid ligaveris in terra, erit ligatum in cœlis; & quicquid solveris in terra, erit solutum in cœlis. Matth. 16: 19. Quin & discipulis omnibus privatisque, qui læsi sunt, dicit, Amen dico vobis, quæcunque ligaveritis in terra, erunt ligata in cœlo: & quæcunque solveritis in terra, erunt soluta in cœlo. cap. 18: 18. Iterumque Apostolis: Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: si quorum retineatis, retinentur. Joh. 20: 23. Profecti, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos — Ecce ego vobiscum omnibus diebus iis, quæ ad consummationem sæculi. Matth. 28: 19, 20. Convenit autem illis solum ministerium, tanquam familiæ divinæ œconomis: Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de ministris Christi, & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei, 1. Cor. 4: 1.
units.tr: {y} To whom he committed [the keys] ... before Peter ... to be given: first to Peter, and after him to the college of Apostles, with singular and infallible authority, etc.; after their departure he entrusted them, though with a weaker sense and lesser authority, to the ordinary ministers of the Church. To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. Matt. 16:19. Indeed, he also says to all the disciples and to private persons who have been wronged: Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. Matt. 18:18. And again to the Apostles: If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain those of any, they are retained. John 20:23. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them ... Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the end of the age. Matt. 28:19, 20. Only the ministry belongs to them, as stewards of the divine household: Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 1 Cor. 4:1.

units.la: VI. Hoc ut plenius intelligatur, breviter tractandæ sunt duæ nobiles quæstiones, quæ huic rei insignem lucem fœnerabuntur, quæque Ecclesiam hodie exercent. De quibus paucis arbitrari æquum est. Ac 1. quæritur, an omnino talis aliqua vel disciplina, vel judicatura in Ecclesia detur? & an juris ac institutionis divinæ, an vero Ecclesiasticæ duntaxat auctoritatis & consuetudinis sit? 2. Deinde a quibus eo exercenda sit? anne ab Ecclesiæ ministris, an vero a Magistratu politico?
units.tr: VI. So that this may be understood more fully, two noble questions must be briefly treated, which will shed remarkable light on this matter and which exercise the Church today. It is fitting to offer a few thoughts on them. First, it is asked whether any such discipline or judicial authority exists in the Church at all, and whether it is of divine right and institution, or only of ecclesiastical authority and custom. Second, by whom it is to be exercised: by the ministers of the Church, or rather by the political magistrate?

units.la: VII. Ad priorem quæstionem respondemus: 1. dubitari non posse, quin, ut omni bene ordinatæ societati ac hominum cœtui, ita etiam sociis civitatibus Ecclesiasticis potestas adsit, separandi de suo grege homines incommodos & incongruos, suisque cœtus maculas & probra. Hæc enim sive potestas, sive ordo, sive disciplina, ex mutua confœderatione necessario consequitur. Nec sine ea ullus cœtus subsistere potest. Ut Ecclesiæ nulla ratione fratrem inobedientem admonendi, corripiendi, vitandi, Ecclesiastica denique sententia percutiendi, deque grege ejiciendi, potestas & auctoritas adimi possit.
units.tr: VII. To the first question we answer: 1. There can be no doubt that, just as every well-ordered society and gathering of men has the power to separate from its flock those who are troublesome and unfit, and the blemishes and disgraces of its assembly, so ecclesiastical societies united in a civil bond also have this power. For this power, or order, or discipline, follows necessarily from mutual confederation, and without it no assembly can subsist. Thus the Church can in no way be deprived of the power and authority to admonish and rebuke a disobedient brother, to avoid him, finally to strike him with ecclesiastical sentence, and to cast him out of the flock.

units.la: VIII. 2. Neque solum naturaliter ea potestas (ita enim nunc appellare libet) Ecclesiæ, ut bene ordinato hominum cœtui, competit; sed & Christus ipse ipsum ordinem, qui in Ecclesia Judaica jam obtinebat, in Ecclesia sua quoque constituit & præscripsit, istamque judicandi auctoritatem Ecclesiæ dedit. Ita enim Matth. 16: 19. mentio fit clavium regni cœlorum, Petro traditarum, quibus illud non referatur solum, sed & claudatur, ne profanis eo aditus sit. Et Matth. 18: 17. apert jussit, Dic Die Ecclesia: & peccatorem, post correptionum gradus, ac Scripturarum ἐλεγχον, Ecclesiastico judicio denique, prout & Judæis in more erat, notatum, dehinc a læsis evitari, & pro Ethnico ac publicano, quocum nullum sacrorum commercium sit, ac privatim quoque non magnus usus intercedere debeat, haberi voluit.
units.tr: VIII. 2. That power (for so it is pleasing to call it now) belongs to the Church not only naturally, as to a well-ordered gathering of men; Christ himself also established and prescribed in his own Church that same order which already prevailed in the Jewish Church, and gave this authority of judging to the Church. For Matt. 16:19 speaks of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, entrusted to Peter, by which the kingdom is not only opened but also shut, lest there be access to the profane. And Matt. 18:17 plainly commands: Tell it to the Church. A sinner, after the steps of correction and the reproof [ἔλεγχον] of Scripture, is at last marked by ecclesiastical judgment, as was also the custom among the Jews; then he is to be avoided by those he has wronged and regarded as a Gentile and a tax collector, with whom there is no fellowship in sacred things, and with whom there ought not to be much private dealing either.

units.la: IX. 3. Post Christi Domini auctoritatem, quam frustra disciplinæ hujus contemtores sollicitant, facit huc quoque Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ usus; & ipsi Apostoli, disciplinæ hujus custodes & vindices acerrimi. Quo pertinent quæ ex epistolis Paulinis allegantur. Rom. 16:17. Precor autem vos, fratres, ut observetis dissidiorum & offendiculorum auctores, contra doctrinam, quam vos didicistis, & declinetis ab eis. 1. Cor. 5: 11. & 13. Tollite igitur ipsum improbum ex vobis ipsis. Ubi respicit procul dubio ad loquendi illum modum, in lege frequentatum, de malo e medio populi auferendo, Deut. 17:7. & 19:9. & 21:21. & 22:21. & 24:7. Quod si quis non auscultat nostroper epistolam sermoni, hunc notate: & ne commercium habete cum eo, ut erubescat.
units.tr: IX. 3. After the authority of Christ the Lord, which the despisers of this discipline try in vain to undermine, the practice of the Apostolic Church also supports it; and the Apostles themselves were its keenest guardians and champions. To this belong the passages cited from the Pauline letters. Rom. 16:17. I beg you, brothers, to mark those who cause divisions and stumbling-blocks, contrary to the doctrine you have learned, and to turn away from them. 1 Cor. 5:11 and 13. Therefore remove the wicked person from among yourselves. Here he undoubtedly refers to that manner of speaking, frequent in the law, of removing evil from the midst of the people: Deut. 17:7; 19:9; 21:21; 22:21; 24:7. But if anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that man, and do not keep company with him, so that he may be ashamed.

units.la: 2. Thess. 3: 14, 15. Hæreticum hominem, post unam & alteram admonitionem repelle. Tit. 3: 10. Ac referunt huc quoque, licet forte minus commode, quidam illud Gal. 5: 12. Utinam etiam abscindantur, qui vos inquietant! Ac succinit Johannes in epist. Catholica secunda, com. 10. Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non adfert, ne recipite eum domum, nec ave ei dicite.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 3:14, 15. Reject a heretical man after one or two admonitions. Titus 3:10. Some also refer here, though perhaps less fittingly, to Gal. 5:12: Would that those who unsettle you were cut off! And John agrees in his second catholic epistle, ver. 10: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say hail to him.

units.la: X. Quod autem Apostolus habet 1. Cor. 5: 3. de probroso quodam homine Satanæ tradendo, id proprie non de ordinaria disciplina, sed de majori quadam ac peculiari Apostoli potestate accipiendum est. Cum enim publicam censuram Ecclesiæ mandasset, com. 2. superiorem hanc potestatem sibi soli reservat. Conf. 1. Tim. 1:20. Ex quibus est Hymenæus & Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ, ut castigati discerent non blasphemare. Intelligit autem corpoream aliquam pœnam & vexationem, qua peccator ille castigatus & domitus, frenum tandem accipere, & Domino parere disceret. Quod Apostolo dicitur, ad interitum corporis, ut anima servetur in die Domini.
units.tr: X. What the Apostle says at 1 Cor. 5:3 about a certain disgraceful man to be handed over to Satan must be understood not of ordinary discipline but of a greater and peculiar power of the Apostle. For when he had committed public censure to the Church, at v. 2 he reserves this higher power to himself alone. Compare 1 Tim. 1:20: Among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn by chastisement not to blaspheme. He means some bodily punishment and affliction, by which that chastised and subdued sinner might at last take the bridle and learn to obey the Lord. This is what is meant by the words to the Apostle, for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.

units.la: XI. 4. Atque hæc quidem sufficere possent ad istam Ecclesiæ judicaturam probandam. Quæ enim ex V. T. exempla petuntur, non per omnia ejusdem generis sunt, adeoque non satis commode ad hanc rem referri possunt. Quod enim huc referunt, ab ipso mundi exordio, latum a Deo ipso in Angelos apostatas judicium: & Adami extro Paradisum exilium,
units.tr: XI. 4. These things might indeed be enough to prove this judicial power of the Church. For the examples drawn from the Old Testament are not in every respect of the same kind, and so cannot be fittingly applied to this matter. For what they bring forward here, the judgment pronounced by God himself from the very beginning of the world upon the apostate angels, and the exile of Adam out of Paradise,

units.la: LII 3 exilium, procul a mysticæ arboris aspectu aut contactu: & Caini a facie Dei fugam: hæc divini potius judicii, quam humani aut Ecclesiastici exempla sunt.
units.tr: exile far from the sight or touch of the mystical tree, and Cain's flight from the face of God: these are examples of divine judgment rather than of human or ecclesiastical judgment.

units.la: XII. Sub lege deinde incircumcisos, & legaliter immundos, templo ac cærimoniis prohibitos constat. Exod. 12:48. Ezech. 44:7,9. Lev. 13:2,3. 2.Chron. 26:20,21. Lev. 5:2, 3. 12:2. Num. 9:6–10. Demorum autem ac doctrinæ labe altum ibi silentium, nec tales sacrificiis aut tabernaculo interdicti leguntur.
units.tr: XII. Under the law, it is clear that the uncircumcised and the legally unclean were excluded from the temple and the ceremonies. Exod. 12:48. Ezek. 44:7,9. Lev. 13:2,3. 2 Chron. 26:20,21. Lev. 5:2,3. 12:2. Num. 9:6–10. But there is a deep silence there about those who were excluded for defilement of morals and of doctrine; nor are such people read of as forbidden sacrifices or the tabernacle.

units.la: XIII. Hoc certum est, labente paulatim republica & αὐτονομίᾳ sub exterorum imperio, sub templo secundo excommunicationem inter Judæos audiri cœpisse; cujus primum exemplum videtur occurrere Ezr. 10:7,8. Ita deinceps de Synagoga leguntur ejecti, qui contra sacrorum leges peccaverant. Quod in Novo Test. est, ἀποσυνάγωγοι ποιεῖν, ἀφορίζειν, ἐκβάλλειν, Joh 9:22,33,34. & 11:22. & 16:2. Unde & in templo secundo peculiaris excommunicatorum porta. Ita & sub eodem templo aliqui tres disciplinæ gradus apud eos numerant, נדוי Niddui, חרם Cherem, & שמתא Shammatha. Quorum illud aliquem male Ecclesia & promiscuo convictu arcebat: istud peccatorem, ut profanum, ac a republ. Israëlis alienum, non sine diris & maledictionibus, extra Ecclesiæ ac Reipublicæ illius pomœria relegabat; ne nemini sine crimine cum eo esse & versari, & edere ac bibere liceret; cum tanquam incircumcisus haberetur; hoc autem cum suprema tandem sententia percellebat, ac extra Ecclesiam ejectum, sine ulla impositorum venia, horrendo carmine, congestisque diris ac execrationibus, inter tubarum strepitum, Dei tandem judicio relinquebat. Rectius tamen alii extremam istam sententiam apud eos non agnoscunt. Cum Niddui & Shammatha fere alternent, nec significatu, sed gradu tantum, differant. Ita ut tantum duo excommunicationis gradus apud illos fuerint; qui in Cherem, quod ex terminationem ex Israële dicebat, terminabantur. Maranatha autem, quod cum Shammatha quidam perperam comparant & confundunt, Syriace dicit, Venit Dominus; & pro confessionis Christianæ, de qua 1.Joh. 4:2. symbolo adhiberi creditur ab Apostolo, 1.Cor. 16:22. allusione ad prophetiam Enochicam facta, de horrendo Dei judicio. De qua Jud. vs 14,15. Ecce venit Dominus, cum myriadibus sanctis suis, ad faciendum judicium de omnibus, & ad redarguendum impios eorum, de omnibus operibus impietatis sua: seu potius est pronunciatio maledictionis seu anathematis in Judæos, Christi Euangeliique ejus osores; juxta vaticinium Mal. 4. Ne veniam & percutiam terram anathemate.
units.tr: XIII. This is certain: as the commonwealth gradually declined and lost its self-government under foreign rule, excommunication began to be heard of among the Jews under the second temple. The first example of it seems to occur at Ezra 10:7,8. Thereafter people are read of as expelled from the synagogue who had sinned against the sacred laws. What the New Testament calls ἀποσυνάγωγοι ποιεῖν [to make someone put out of the synagogue], ἀφορίζειν [to separate], ἐκβάλλειν [to cast out], is found at John 9:22,33,34; 11:22; 16:2. Hence there was also a special gate of the excommunicated under the second temple. So too under the same temple some of them count three grades of discipline: Niddui [נדוי], Cherem [חרם] and Shammatha [שמתא]. The first kept a man out of the Church and from common company in an ill way; the second cut off the sinner as profane and alien from the commonwealth of Israel, not without curses and execrations, banishing him beyond the boundaries of the Church and of that commonwealth, so that no one without guilt might be with him, dwell with him, or eat and drink with him, since he was regarded as uncircumcised. The third, with the final sentence, struck him down, and having cast him out of the Church without any pardon from those who imposed it, left him to God's judgment with a dreadful chant, heaped curses and execrations, amid the blare of trumpets. Others, however, more correctly do not recognise that final sentence among them, since Niddui and Shammatha nearly alternate and differ not in meaning but only in degree. So there were only two grades of excommunication among them, and these ended in Cherem, which meant expulsion from Israel. Maranatha, which some wrongly compare and confuse with Shammatha, means in Syriac The Lord comes; and it is believed that the Apostle, at 1 Cor. 16:22, used it as a creed, a formula of Christian confession (of which 1 John 4:2 speaks), with an allusion to the prophecy of Enoch concerning the dreadful judgment of God. Concerning this, Jude vv. 14,15: Behold, the Lord comes with his holy myriads, to execute judgment on all and to convict the ungodly of all their works of ungodliness. Or rather it is a pronouncement of curse or anathema upon the Jews, the haters of Christ and of his gospel, in accordance with the prophecy of Mal. 4: lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.

units.la: XIV. Ex quibus omnibus non levis conjectura est, disciplinam istam, è Judæorum Synagogis in Christianorum Ecclesias introductam, & ad earum exemplum a Christo Apostolisque efformatam. Quod & vocabulorum similitudo suadet, ἀφορίζειν, ἐκβάλλειν, ἀναθεματίζειν, ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν. Et cum primæ Christianorum Ecclesiæ ex Synagogarum Judaicarum ruinis potissimum creverint; omnino probabile est, primos fideles, patriam istam disciplinam, qua tanquam legis & religionum sepimento, sub externis præcipue principibus, utebantur, etiam, ubi Christum induissent, in coetibus suis servasse. Ista enim tum Ecclesiæ, ab Ethnicis principibus non neglectæ solum, sed & exosæ, ac undique exagitatæ, conditio erat, ut non nisi confœderata illa disciplina magistra stare posset.
units.tr: XIV. From all these things there is no slight conjecture that this discipline was carried over from the Jewish synagogues into the Christian churches, and was shaped by Christ and the Apostles after their pattern. The similarity of the words suggests this too: ἀφορίζειν, ἐκβάλλειν, ἀναθεματίζειν, ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν. And since the first Christian churches grew mainly out of the ruins of the Jewish synagogues, it is wholly probable that the first believers kept in their assemblies that ancestral discipline, which they had used as a fence of law and religion, especially under foreign princes, even after they had embraced Christ. For such was the condition of the Church at that time, not only neglected but also hated and harassed on all sides by the heathen princes, that it could not stand except with that discipline bound up with it as its guide.

units.la: XV. Unde responsio quoque ad alteram quæstionem patet; ad quos disciplinæ hujus potestas & exercitium spectet; an ad Ecclesiam ministrosque ejus, an vero ad Magistratum? Nos enim a Christo Apostolis & Ecclesiæ traditas illas claves legimus, Matth. 16:18. & 18:17, 18. & Joh. 20:22. Christus enim, ubi de corripiendo fratre agit, reique Magistratus ordinem & disciplinam pandit, ad Ecclesiam rem omnem deferri, ab Ecclesia peccatorem admoneri, corripi & judicari denique jubet.
units.tr: XV. Hence the answer to the second question also becomes plain: to whom the power and exercise of this discipline belongs, to the Church and its ministers, or to the magistrate? For we read that those keys were handed by Christ to the Apostles and to the Church: Matt. 16:18; 18:17,18; John 20:22. For Christ, when he speaks of correcting a brother, and sets out the order and discipline of the matter, bids that the whole affair be referred to the Church, that the sinner be admonished by the Church, and finally corrected and judged.

units.la: XVI. Hoc vero ut clarius pateat, civilis ac sacri regiminis discrimen breviter præmittendum est: inde de excommunicatione propius videbimus, quæ Ecclesiæ, quæ Magistratus Christiani hic partes sint, aut esse debeant.
units.tr: XVI. So that this may be made clearer, the distinction between civil and sacred government must first be set out briefly. From this we shall see more closely what the parts of the Church and of the Christian magistrate are, or ought to be, in excommunication.

units.la: XVII. Ac primum quod attinet, distinguunt communiter Theologi duo potestatum seu regiminum genera, ecclesiasticam, sive sacram, & civilem. Atque illa, maxime ubi separata sunt, natura sua differre volunt; cum objecto, fine, forma & modo, inter se fere differant. Illius enim objectum est fidelis & Ecclesiæ; hujus, Respublicæ, civis. Illa circa res spirituales, & hominem internum; hæc circa res terrenas, & hominem externum multum versatur. Illius finis est, sancta Ecclesiæ ædificatio, & peccatoris emendatio; hujus, licet sacrum quoque finem habeat, peculiaris tamen finis est Reipublicæ securitas, & pacis conservatio; quam vindice gladio tutari, malefactos homines compescere debet. Unde diversus ubique procedendi modus, Ecclesia etiam in leviora, magistratu in graviora tantum crimina, quæ publicam pacem turbant, animadvertente. Cum que Ecclesia pœnitenti peccatori ignoscat, quin & congratuletur; civiles tamen leges ei poenas irrogare non desinunt; quin &, cum vita, nonnunquam poenitendi spatium & viam tollunt; quoniam ita publice interest; ac ignorant illae moras istas, & gradus, & molimina, quibus Ecclesia peccatorem ad sanitatem deducit. Denique & forma: civilis potestas est αὐτοκρατορικὴ, & cum imperio, ac cogendi auctoritate; cum Ecclesiae nil nisi ministerium relictum sit; nec viac coactione, sed solo verbi Dei elencho uti possit.
units.tr: XVII. First, as far as the first point is concerned, theologians commonly distinguish two kinds of power or government, the ecclesiastical or sacred, and the civil. They hold that these differ in their nature, especially where they are separated, since they differ from one another almost in object, end, form and manner. For the object of the former is the believer and the Church; of the latter, the citizen of the commonwealth. The former is concerned chiefly with spiritual things and the inner man; the latter with earthly things and the outer man. The end of the former is the holy edification of the Church and the amendment of the sinner; the latter, although it too has a sacred end, has as its own particular end the security of the commonwealth and the preservation of peace, which it must guard with the avenging sword, restraining evildoers. Hence the manner of proceeding is everywhere different: the Church takes notice only of lighter offences, the magistrate only of graver crimes which disturb the public peace. And while the Church forgives the penitent sinner, and even congratulates him, civil laws nonetheless do not cease to impose penalties on him; indeed, sometimes they even take away the space and the way of repentance, since the public interest requires it. Those laws know nothing of those delays, stages and efforts by which the Church leads the sinner back to health. Finally, there is also a difference of form: civil power is autocratic and carries command and authority to compel, whereas nothing but a ministry has been left to the Church, nor can it use coercion, but only the refutation of God's Word alone.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: De hac autem, quae sola Ecclesiae superest, potestate quidam illi controversiam movent; ac quicquid ejus generis est ad magistratum politicum pertinere contendunt. Quam de excommunicatione controversiam movit superiore saeculo Thomas Erastus, Medicus Heidelbergensis. Quem praeverat Brunerus, eadem in urbe Ecclesiae Minister. Quibus Beza respondit. Censebant enim Helvetii, jam inde a Zuinglio, sub Magistratu Christiano, excommunicationis vix aliquem magnopere usum esse: cum ille officium facere, ac sceleratos civili auctoritate compescere debeat. Verum illi ulterius tendebant: Ecclesiae nullam proprie excommunicandi potestatem a Christo datam esse: unde illam, sub magistratu Christiano, istam auctoritatem usurpare, ex mera Magistratus delegatione: cum omnis politia externa, omne regimen, omnisque minorum coetuum potestas in republica, a summa majestate derivari, inque eam refundi, debeat: unde nolunt quoque auctores illi, Magistratuum fasces Ecclesiasticorum sententiis obnoxios esse: non enim aliter quam per modum consilii ipsos audiri: quae etiam Clar. viri Riveti sententia est. Similiter a sententiis Ecclesiasticis ad magistratuum tribunalia provocationem permittunt; utpote quibus ultimum ac supremum rerum omnium in reipubl. judicium conveniat. Imo improprie Ecclesiae forum, & sententiae dictionem, attribui: cum non aliquam verbi praedicandi potestas ei conveniat, nec quisquam, nisi volens, eam audire teneatur. Ac peccatorem quidem, qui salutis suae cura ducitur, illam audire, deque scandalo satisfacere, atque Ecclesiae nonnunquam publice reconciliari debere: non tamen istud forum aliquod Ecclesiae inferre; cum ille vel minimo Christiano, quem laeserit, hoc ossicium debeat; atque in omni hominum coetu ac collegio istud locum habeat; quae in totidem fora et tribunalia in republica erigere inauditum sit.
units.tr: Some people raise objections against this power, which alone remains to the Church, and they contend that everything of this kind belongs to the civil magistrate. Thomas Erastus, a physician of Heidelberg, raised this controversy about excommunication in the last century. He was preceded by Brunerus, a minister of the Church in the same city, and Beza replied to them. For the Swiss, from Zwingli onward, held that under a Christian magistrate excommunication was scarcely used to any great extent, since the magistrate ought to do this work and restrain wrongdoers by civil authority. But those writers went further. They maintained that the Church has not been given any proper power of excommunication by Christ, and that when she exercises this authority under a Christian magistrate, she does so purely by delegation from the magistrate. For all external polity, all government, and all power of the lesser assemblies in a commonwealth must derive from the supreme majesty and be referred back to it. Hence these authors also deny that the magistrate's fasces are subject to ecclesiastical sentences; the magistrates should hear the Church only by way of advice, which is also the opinion of the distinguished Rivet. Likewise they allow appeal from ecclesiastical sentences to the tribunals of the magistrates, since the final and supreme judgment of all things belongs to the commonwealth. They even say that the Church's forum and her pronouncing of sentence are improperly attributed to her, since she has no power of proclaiming the word that binds anyone, and no one is obliged to listen to her unless he wishes. A sinner who cares for his own salvation ought indeed to hear the Church, make amends for the scandal, and sometimes be publicly reconciled to the Church; yet this does not establish any forum of the Church, since he owes this duty to the humblest Christian whom he has wronged, and it applies in every gathering and college of men. To set up so many forums and tribunals within the commonwealth would be unheard of.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Ita illi. Quibus nos brevem hanc ἐπίκρισιν subjungimus:
units.tr: Thus they. To these views we add this brief examination.

units.la: 1. Aliud in disciplina Christiana esse ligationem & solutionem per verbum; aliud, excommunicationem. Atque in ea rursus distingui debere, re, abstentionem a Coena, separationem a coetu, denique devotionem per diras. 2. Ligatio & solutio, per verbum, unicuique Christiano, qui verbum illud in ore habet, competit. Nec erga fratrem poenitentem vel impoenitentem ista fraternitatis officia omitti debent. 3. Praecipua tamen disciplinae custodia ad pastores pertinet; qui ligant & solvunt ratione muneris. Unde ipsis ovilis cura data. 4. Ad disciplinam hanc pertinet abstentio a S. Coena. Sanctissima enim Christianorum pignora profanari non debent, neque indignis & scelerum manifestis communionio Christi obsignari. Ac Ecclesiae interest, scelerosum hominem, vel qui alioquin dato scandalo fraternitatem laeserit, a communi pastu arceri. Cujus rei arbitrium ac judicium penes reliquas oves, oviumque magistros, est. 5. Eadem est ratio separationis de coetu. Quae cura, tum Christi & Apostolorum jussu, tum ex jure naturali, cuicunque hominum coetui competente, Ecclesiae committa est. Sicuti corporis est, tabida ac fluentia membra, ne ultra noceant, de communi corpore separare. 6. Atque ubi Ecclesia libera est, nec quicquam cum republica commercii habet, privo jure disciplinam istam administrat. 7. Ubi vero magistratus de aeterna subjectorum suorum felicitate sollicitus, non rempublicam solum, sed Ecclesiam quoque curat; tum sub tutela illius, ac auspiciis, Ecclesia res suas placide agit. 8. Et quanquam, ubi magistratus officium facit, in peccatis extirpandis, ulteriori Ecclesiae censura non adeo opus sit: attamen, cum nunquam ita beatae sint respublicae, ut omnes temere loquentes, vel ambulantes, coerceantur; atque ea Ecclesiae sit sanctitas, ut non sufficiat intra leges publicas probum esse; cum aliae Christi, aliae Caesaris sint leges: ac aliud Paulus noster, aliud Papinianus loquatur; ac longe plura in coelestis quam in terrenae civitatis cive requirantur: equidem recte agunt magistratus, quod accuratiorem istam disciplinae custodiam Ecclesiae relinquant. 9. Est tamen eorundem advertere, ut Ecclesia ac ministri officium faciant; ne disciplinae praetextu regnum aliquod religionis agitent, aut immitibus sententiis in gregem promiscue grassentur. 10. Quod vero excommunicationem ulteriorem attinet, qua quis ultimis diris configitur, &c, lata quasi sententia, cum potestate, de rebus coelestibus excluditur; illam non agnoscimus. Cum nulla talis in Ecclesia potestas sit. Nec aliud quam verbi ministerium hic agnoscendum est, per quod peccator poenitens, aut impoenitens, solutus aut ligatus declaratur. Estque haec Pontificiae Ecclesiae arrogantia; qui in Ecclesia tribunal, judicia, judices, forum inter-num num &c. loquuntur; atque ejusmodi potestatem mentiuntur, qua si quis Ecclesiæ sententia percussus sit, insons alioquin & innocuus, tamen hoc ipso deteriori apud Deum conditione sit quam antea. Quæ sæva & Antichristiana sunt.
units.tr: 1. In Christian discipline, binding and loosing by the word is one thing, and excommunication is another. Excommunication, in turn, must be distinguished into its parts: abstention from the Supper, separation from the assembly, and finally devotion to curses. 2. Binding and loosing by the word belong to every Christian who has that word on his lips. Toward a brother, whether penitent or impenitent, these duties of brotherly fellowship must not be omitted. 3. Yet the chief guardianship of discipline belongs to the ministers, who bind and loose by virtue of their office; hence the care of the flock has been entrusted to them. 4. To this discipline belongs abstention from the Lord's Supper. The most holy pledges of the Christians must not be profaned, nor the communion of Christ sealed to the unworthy and to those manifestly guilty of crimes. The Church has an interest in keeping from the common meal a wicked man, or one who has otherwise given scandal and wounded the brotherhood. The decision and judgment in this matter rest with the rest of the sheep and with the shepherds of the sheep. 5. The same reasoning applies to separation from the assembly. This care has been committed to the Church, both by the command of Christ and the Apostles and by natural law, which belongs to every human assembly. Just as with the body, rotting and festering limbs are cut off from the common body so that they do no further harm. 6. Where the Church is free and has no dealings with the commonwealth, she administers this discipline by her own right. 7. Where, however, the magistrate, concerned for the eternal happiness of his subjects, cares for the Church as well as for the commonwealth, the Church carries out her affairs peacefully under his protection and auspices. 8. And although, where the magistrate does his duty in rooting out sins, further censure by the Church is not very necessary, nevertheless commonwealths are never so blessed that everyone who speaks or walks rashly is restrained. The holiness of the Church is such that it is not enough to be upright within the public laws, since the laws of Christ and of Caesar are different, and our Paul speaks differently from Papinian, and far more is required of a citizen of the heavenly city than of an earthly one. Indeed the magistrates act rightly in leaving this stricter guardianship of discipline to the Church. 9. Yet it is also their business to see that the Church and the ministers do their duty, and that under the pretext of discipline they do not set up some kingdom of religion, or rage with harsh sentences against the flock indiscriminately. 10. As for the further excommunication by which someone is struck with the final curses, and is shut out from heavenly things by a pronounced sentence with power, we do not acknowledge it, since no such power exists in the Church. Here we must recognise nothing but the ministry of the word, through which a penitent or impenitent sinner is declared loosed or bound. This is the arrogance of the Papist Church, which speaks of tribunals, judgments, judges, and the internal forum in the Church, and falsely claims such a power that anyone struck by its sentence, though otherwise innocent and harmless, is thereby in a worse condition before God than before. These things are cruel and antichristian.

units.la: XX. Ecclesia autem vox, qua Christus Matth. 18: 17. utitur, respondet 1. תֹּ֣ךָ / ac totius populi cœtum notat. Hic est ὁ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ in deserto cum Angelo, Act. 7: 38. Sunt ergo in hoc negotio aliquæ totius cœtus partes. Non enim de fraternitate, nisi fratrum consensu, quisquam excludendus est. Atque omnes de redargutione, an rite facta sit, judicare debent. Nec potest Ecclesia, vel ullus fratrum, a se abdicare judicium, quod ab ipso vel privatim, vel publice, erga peccatorem contumacem exercendum est. 2. Veruntamen & hoc verum est, posse fratrum cœtum Senioribus, de corpore suo delectis, potestatem aliquam dare, ut præcipua cœtus cura fungantur, & separatim ea tractent ac curent, quæ ad universam Ecclesiam pertinent; quæque ob nimiam fratrum frequentiam, utque confusiones caveantur, coram toto cœtu agi non possunt. Atque huc spectant verba Catechesis, quæst. 85. Ecclesia indicantur, aut iis, qui ab Ecclesia ad istam curam constituti sunt. 3. Posse autem istud fieri, & in magnis quoque cœtibus fieri oportere, non solum honestas & decorum, quod in omnibus rebus observandum est, suadet: cum in popularii judicio, ubi multi ad curam istam inepti sunt, plerunque tumultu & partim studiis omnia geri videamus: Non autem est tumultus auctor Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus Ecclesiis sanctorum. Mulieres vestra in conventibus sileant &c. 1. Cor. 14: 33, 34. Sed & in Veteri olim T. sacerdotum Leviticorum ea cura erat, quorum erat inter purum & impurum discernere, Lev. 10: 9, 10. Hagg. 2: 11, 12. Ezech. 44: 23. Et in Novo Test. Christus, ubi disciplinæ ordinem instituit, ut in plerisque novæ Ecclesiæ institutis, ita etiam hic, ad Ecclesiæ Judaicæ formam illam composuit. Ibi autem judicia, non ab universa plebe sed a synedrio, selectisque viris tractabantur. conf. Luc. 22: 66. Act. 22: 5. Sicuti & in Novi Test. Ecclesia Synedriorum mentio occurrit, 1. Tim. 4: 14. dicunturque Apostoli Seniores convocasse, ut cum iis deliberarent, Act. 21: 18, 22. ac frequens Seniorum, 1. Tim. 5. πρεσβύτερων, πρεσβυτέριον, Rom. 12: 8. ...
units.tr: XX. The word Church, which Christ uses in Matt. 18:17, corresponds to the Hebrew [תֹּךָ], and denotes the assembly of the whole people. "He who was in the church in the wilderness with the Angel" (Hic est ὁ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ in deserto cum Angelo [ὁ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ]), Acts 7:38. There are therefore certain parts of the whole assembly involved in this business. For no one is to be excluded from the brotherhood except by the consent of the brothers, and all must judge whether the reproof has been rightly made. Nor can the Church, or any of the brothers, renounce the judgment that must be exercised toward a stubborn sinner, whether privately or publicly. 2. Yet it is also true that the assembly of the brothers can give some power to Elders chosen from its own body, so that they may carry out the chief care of the assembly and deal with and manage separately those matters which pertain to the whole Church and which, because of the great number of the brothers and to avoid confusion, cannot be handled before the whole assembly. To this refer the words of the Catechism, question 85: Ecclesia indicantur, aut iis, qui ab Ecclesia ad istam curam constituti sunt ("they are declared to the Church, or to those who have been appointed by the Church to this care"). 3. That this can be done, and ought to be done even in large assemblies, is recommended not only by honesty and propriety, which must be observed in all things; for we see that in popular judgment, where many are unfit for this care, everything is usually carried on with tumult and partly with partisan zeal. Non autem est tumultus auctor Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus Ecclesiis sanctorum. Mulieres vestra in conventibus sileant ("For God is not the author of confusion but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints. Let your women keep silence in the assemblies"), 1 Cor. 14:33, 34. In the Old Testament, too, this care belonged to the Levitical priests, whose task it was to distinguish between the clean and the unclean, Lev. 10:9, 10; Hag. 2:11, 12; Ezek. 44:23. And in the New Testament, Christ, when he set up the order of discipline, arranged it as he did in most institutions of the new Church, after the form of the Jewish Church. There, however, judgments were handled not by the whole common people but by the Sanhedrin and chosen men (compare Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5). So too in the Church of the New Testament the mention of Synedriorum ("presbyteries") occurs, 1 Tim. 4:14, and the Apostles are said to have summoned the Elders to deliberate with them, Acts 21:18, 22, and there is frequent mention of Elders, 1 Tim. 5; πρεσβυτέρων, πρεσβυτέριον, Rom. 12:8 ...

units.la: 1. Cor. 12: 28. & Ductorum ac Antecessorum, Hebr. 13. in Scripturis appellatio. Qui Ecclesiæ oculi appellantur, 1. Cor. 12: 14, 31. & 14: 32. & Angeli, Apoc. 2: 2, 20. Ita ut latius patet, Ecclesiæ gubernationem non esse mere democraticam. Ita enim Anabaptistarum morositas est, qui imperitæ & contentiosæ plebi, imo quidam ex iis ne fœminas quidem excipiunt, omnem hanc judicaturam deferunt. Sicuti ab altera parte Pontificii, ad solum Papam & Consistorium ejus hoc judicium referentes, Ecclesiæ regimen monarchicum faciunt. Inter quæ extrema media est sententia, quam explicuimus: quæ ita ministris hanc curam assignat, ut tamen, non nisi conscio & acquiescente coetu, ea in re arbitrentur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 12:28, and the name of Leaders and Guides, Heb. 13, is used in the Scriptures. They are called the eyes of the Church, 1 Cor. 12:14, 31 and 14:32, and Angels, Rev. 2:2, 20. So it is evident that the government of the Church is not purely democratic. The peculiar view of the Anabaptists, who hand over all this judicial power to an unskilled and quarrelsome common people, and some of whom do not even exclude women, errs in that way. On the other side, the Papists refer this judgment solely to the Pope and his consistory, and so make the government of the Church monarchical. Between these extremes lies the middle opinion that I have explained, which assigns this care to the ministers in such a way that they nevertheless deliberate in this matter only with the knowledge and assent of the assembly.

units.la: XXI. Nec morari nos debet difficultas, qualis hic intelligi debeat Ecclesia, an Judaica, an Christiana? & cujusnam judicandi in Ecclesia partes sint, an universi coetus, an primorum tantum? Et an non præcipuum quiddam Apostolis hic tribuatur? 1. Apparet enim ex loco cognato Matth. 16: 18. eam Ecclesiam intelligi, quam Christus super Petram ædificaturus erat. Proxime enim ad illam promissionem consequuntur hæc verba, Dabo tibi claves Ecclesiæ. Ut novam Christi Ecclesiam facile intelligamus.
