Quanquam & Judæorum Ecclesias ac coetus; quæ, primum conversæ, magna rei Christianæ erant incrementa; ad istud usque tempus, dum nondum publice ab iis discedere cogebantur fideles, eo nomine libenter comprehendamus. 2. Cum autem vox ἐκκλησία quæ coetum notat, ut visum, hic occurrat; apertum est, judicium hoc ad universum coetum spectare; & partes ejus aliquas a singulis tractari debere & posse. Non solum dum cuncti publico Ecclesiæ judicio subscribunt, ac peccatorem juste damnatum non amplius fraternum in modum habent: sed etiam dum & ipsi fratrem temere loquentem vel ambulantem certo in casu aut ligant, aut solvunt; aut, cessante forte Ecclesia, pro Ethnico & profano habent. 3. Singulari autem modo istud judicium peragebant Apostoli: qui non solum prædicatione verbi regnum cœlorum & introitum in illud, hominibus aperiebant; sed & nunquam fallente calculo, quos visum erat, suprema auctoritate vel absolvebant, vel damnabant; eratque quicquid illi agebant, ratum protinus & firmum in cœlo; cum clave, uti appellant, non errante universum illud ministerium peragerent. Quo pacto speciali ac excellentiori quodam modo promissæ iis cœli claves. Matth. 16. Joh. 20. Nec hæreditatis istius successio ad Pontificem Romanum, qui sese portarum cœli calves de zona pensiles habere jactat, ullo modo pertinet. Ordinaria autem disciplinæ custodia universæ Ecclesiæ, cunctisque ejus ministris, ex æquo incumbit.
units.tr: XXI. Nor should we be troubled by the question of what kind of Church is meant here: a Jewish one or a Christian one? Or who has the power to judge in the Church: the whole assembly, or only its leaders? And is nothing special given here to the Apostles? (1.) This is clear from the parallel passage, Matt. 16:18, where the Church meant is the one Christ was about to build upon the Rock. For the words that immediately follow that promise are, I will give you the keys of the Church. So we readily understand the new Church of Christ. Still, we may gladly include under that name the Jewish congregations and assemblies, which, once converted, were great increases for the Christian cause, up to the time when the faithful were not yet compelled to separate from them publicly. (2.) Since the word ἐκκλησία [ekklēsia], which means an assembly, appears here, as seems likely, it is plain that this judgment concerns the whole assembly, and that some parts of it may and should be handled by individuals. This happens not only when all subscribe to the public judgment of the Church and no longer treat the justly condemned sinner as a brother, but also when individuals themselves bind or loose a brother who speaks or lives rashly in a particular case, or, if the Church happens to be silent, regard him as a heathen and a profane person. (3.) The Apostles, however, exercised this judgment in a unique way. They not only opened the kingdom of heaven and the entrance into it to men by preaching the Word, but also, by a never-failing sentence, with supreme authority either absolved or condemned whomever they saw fit; and whatever they did was at once valid and firm in heaven, since they carried out that whole ministry with the key, as they call it, never going astray. In this special and more excellent way the keys of heaven were promised to them (Matt. 16; John 20). Nor does the succession to this inheritance belong in any way to the Roman Pontiff, who boasts that he carries the keys of the gates of heaven hanging from his belt. The ordinary guardianship of discipline, on the other hand, rests equally upon the whole Church and all its ministers.

units.la: XXII. Denique immerito in dubium vocat Erastus, an verba, Si tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, peccatorem de coetu exulem, & sacris ac caerimoniis interdictum, notent. Constat enim satis, quid Judaeiista phrasi velint; & quo in numero, ac qua in sacrorum parte Ethnicos ac Publicanos habeant. Talis autem fratri laeso erat laedens: si admonitionibus locum non daret: talesque Synagogae habebantur obstinati peccatores; adeoque ad ejus exemplum, ita praescribente Christo, eodem loco illi habendi sunt Ecclesiae Christianae.
units.tr: XXII. Finally, Erastus rashly calls in doubt whether the words, If he refuses to hear them, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector, mean a sinner who is exiled from the assembly and forbidden the sacred rites and ceremonies. For it is sufficiently established what the Jews meant by that phrase, and in what number, and in what part of the sacred rites, they counted heathens and tax collectors. Moreover, the one who injured a brother was regarded as an offender if he did not give place to admonitions; and such people were regarded in the synagogue as obstinate sinners. Therefore, following that pattern, and with Christ so prescribing, they are to be held in the same place by the Christian churches.

units.la: XXIII. Objectum disciplinae vel personale est, vel reale. Personale est frater peccans, Matth. 18: 15. 1 Cor. 5: 11. Qui enim extra Ecclesiam limen est, extra hanc curam degit; ac incustoditae instar ovis aberrat. Qui autem Ecclesiae frater censeri vult, cujuscunque dignitatis ac conditionis sit, ad hanc curatelam pertinet. Vos autem ne vocamini Rabbi. Unus est enim doctor vester Christus: omnes autem vos fratres estis. Matth. 23: 8. Simeon Petrus — Simeon Petrus — gratia. 2 Pet. 1: 1, 2. Non est servus, & liber — sed omnia in omnibus Christus. Col. 3: 11. Ut male Pontificii Papam censurae hujus immunem faciant, & a nullo judicari posse asserant. Quo ipso illum Ecclesiae civem & fratrem negant. Sed & per verse iidem disciplinam hanc nimium extendunt; & bruta animantia, mortuos, absentes, ignotos & inauditos, quin integros populos, sine discrimine, incesto addentes integrum, sententia ista percutiunt. XXIV. Objectum reale est tum vitae, tum doctrinae, labes. Si vero peccaverit in te frater tuus, ito & argue eum &c. Math. 18: 15. Ne commiseceamini, si quis, quum frater nominetur, sit scortator, aut alieni avidus, aut idololatra, aut conviciator, aut ebriosus, aut rapax: cum ejusmodi, inquam, ne edatis quidem. 1 Cor. 5: 11. Rogo vos, fratres, ut animadvertatis eos, qui dissidia & scandala, praeter doctrinam, quam vos didicistis, faciunt; & recedite ab iis. Rom. 16: 17. Quorum est Hymenaeus & Alexander; quos tradidi Satanae, ut castigati discant non blasphemare.
units.tr: XXIII. The object of discipline is either personal or real. The personal object is the brother who sins (Matt. 18:15; 1 Cor. 5:11). For whoever is outside the Church's threshold lives outside this care, and wanders like a sheep without a shepherd. But whoever wishes to be counted a brother of the Church, of whatever rank or condition he may be, belongs to this guardianship. But you are not to be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, Christ, and all of you are brothers (Matt. 23:8). Simon Peter — Simon Peter — grace (2 Pet. 1:1, 2). There is neither slave nor free — but Christ is all and in all (Col. 3:11). So the Papists wrongly make the Pope immune from this censure and assert that he cannot be judged by anyone. By this very fact they deny that he is a citizen and brother of the Church. But these same men also stretch this discipline too far, and by this sentence they strike brute animals, the dead, the absent, the unknown and the unheard of, and even whole peoples, without distinction, adding an entire incest. XXIV. The real object is the stain of life or of doctrine. But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him, etc. (Matt. 18:15). Do not associate with anyone who, though named a brother, is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber; with such a person, I say, do not even eat (1 Cor. 5:11). I beg you, brothers, to take note of those who create divisions and stumbling blocks, contrary to the teaching you have learned; and turn away from them (Rom. 16:17). Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn through punishment not to blaspheme (1 Tim. 1:20).

units.la: 1 Tim. 1: 20. conf. Tit. 3: 10, 11. 2 Joh. com. 10. Ut male Remonstrantes de haeresi dubitent, nec facile quenquam propter illam devovendum existiment. Cum tamen doctrinae corruptio & venenum a Christo nos separet, atque Christus fermentum illud vitari, & expurgari jubeat, Matth. 16: 6, 12; ipseque tandem Apostolus non vereatur talibus anathema dicere. Gal. 1: 8. XXV. Disciplinae partes sunt, Correptio fraterna, & Excommunicatio.
units.tr: See 1 Tim. 1:20; compare Titus 3:10, 11; 2 John, verse 10. The Remonstrants wrongly doubt whether heresy is a ground for discipline, and they do not readily think that anyone should be cursed on account of it. Yet the corruption of doctrine and its poison separate us from Christ, and Christ orders that this leaven be avoided and purged out (Matt. 16:6, 12); and the Apostle himself did not hesitate to pronounce such people anathema (Gal. 1:8). XXV. The parts of discipline are fraternal correction and excommunication.

units.la: XXVI. Correptio vel privata est, vel publica. Exprimuntur autem gradus ejus a Christo, Matth. 18: 15. &c Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, i. e. si te laeserit, vel quocunque crimine offenderit, redargue ipsum, inter te, & ipsum. Istud enim cujuscunque Christiani officium est; nec ulli a fraternis admonitionibus temperare licet. Prov. 27: 5, 6. Faciendae autem illae sine contumelia, sine digiti extensione. Esai. 58: 9. animo miti & placido; & cum Scripturarum demonstratione ac elegxw; ne videamus nos ipsos, ac privatae pietatis genium in fidei regulam erigere velle. Ac danda praesertim opera, ut qui opprobriis dignum latraverit, integer ipse existat, monente Christo, Matth. 7: 3, 4. Si privatum hoc charitatis officium non sufficiat, adscitcendus unus & alter de fratrum coetu; ut pudor peccatori incutiatur, atque ille repetito amoris officio concedat; saltem ut conscientiam testium illorum formidans peccare amplius desinat. Si fraternis officiis victus est, salva res est, & peccatori condonandum, nec ullus in animo rancor servandus est. Quin gratulandum nobis de ovicula ad caulam reducta. Sin secus, ac incassum labor omnis sumtus, publicandum ejus peccatum, & ad Ecclesiam reus adducendus: Quod si neglexerit eos audire, die Ecclesiae; Matth. 18: 17. Per Ecclesiam autem coetum fratrum a Christo intelligi, atque illum lectis quibusdam e suo numero judicium illud, vel partes ejus aliquas, committere posse, mox vidimus. Atque ille, post repetitas admonitiones, & Scripturarum elegxov (quae est objurgatio illa, facta a pluribus, 2. Cor. 2: 7. conf. 4: 17. & Tit. 3: 10, 11.) si contumax permaneat, & tot officiis emolliri abnuat; tum quidem habendus est pro publicano & gentili; id est, pro eo, quia fide alienus est, cui nulla fraternitatis officia praestare possumus; sed a quo recedendum potius est, uti ab impuro, & sua contagione noxio; & cui non collatandum, sed congemendum est; Deusque votis vocandus, ut pectoris istius duritiem, & robur, severiori aliqua disciplina dedolet, hominemque edomet, & acrioris verbere, si opus est, & flagello admonitum ad Ecclesiae sinum reducat. Nam istud charitatis officium, & si quae alia, ad conversionem ipsius facientia, ab Ecclesia negligi interim non debet. Vide Rom. 16: 17. Rogo vos, fratres; ut animadvertatis eos, qui dissidia & scandala, praeter doctrinam, quam vos didicistis, faciunt: & recedite ab eis. 1. Cor. 5: 11. Nunc autem scripsi vobis, ne commisceamini, si quis, quum frater nominetur, sit scortator. — cum ejusmodi inquam ne edatis quidem. Tit. 3: 10. Haereticum hominem, post unam aut alteram admonitionem rejice; sciens quod
units.tr: XXVI. Correction is either private or public. Its steps are set out by Christ (Matt. 18:15, etc.): If your brother sins against you, that is, if he has wronged you or offended you by any crime, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. For this is the duty of every Christian, and no one is permitted to refrain from brotherly admonitions (Prov. 27:5, 6). These are to be given without insult, without pointing the finger (Isa. 58:9), with a gentle and calm spirit, and with a demonstration from the Scriptures and elenchus [ἔλεγχος], so that we do not appear to set ourselves and the spirit of private piety up as the rule of faith. And special care must be taken that the one who has barked out what deserves reproach should himself be blameless, as Christ warns (Matt. 7:3, 4). If this private office of love does not suffice, one or two of the brothers of the assembly are to be taken along, so that shame may be struck into the sinner, and he may yield to a repeated office of love; or at least, fearing the conscience of those witnesses, he may cease to sin any further. If he is won over by brotherly offices, the matter is settled, and the sinner is to be forgiven, and no resentment is to be kept in the heart. Indeed, we should rejoice over the sheep brought back to the fold. But if otherwise, and all effort is spent in vain, his sin is to be made public and the offender brought before the Church: But if he refuses to hear them, tell it to the Church (Matt. 18:17). That by "the Church" Christ means the assembly of brothers, and that it can commit that judgment, or some parts of it, to chosen men from its number, we have just seen. And if he remains stubborn after repeated admonitions and the elenchus of the Scriptures (which is that rebuke given by several, 2 Cor. 2:7; compare 4:17, and Titus 3:10, 11), and refuses to be softened by so many offices, then he is to be regarded as a tax collector and a gentile; that is, as one who is a stranger to the faith, to whom we cannot render any offices of brotherhood; but from whom we should rather withdraw, as from an impure person harmful by his contagion; and with whom we are not to associate, but must not be made a companion. And God is to be called upon in prayers, so that by some severer discipline He may hew down the hardness and strength of that heart, tame the man, and bring him back, admonished by a sharper lash and a whip if need be, to the bosom of the Church. For this office of love, and any other that works toward his conversion, should not meanwhile be neglected by the Church. See Rom. 16:17: I beg you, brothers, to take note of those who create divisions and stumbling blocks, contrary to the teaching you have learned, and turn away from them. 1 Cor. 5:11: But now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who, though named a brother, is a fornicator — with such a person, I say, do not even eat. Titus 3:10: Reject a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that

units.la: {y} Corripe, ejusque gradus. quod eversus sit talis, & peccet, a se ipso damnatus. 2. Joh. com. 10. Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non adfert, ne suscipite eum domum, & ave ei ne dicite. Nam qui ipsum jubet salvere, communicat cum operibus ejus malis.
units.tr: {y} Rebuke him, and its stages: because such a man is perverted and sins, condemned by his own judgment. 2 John, verse 10: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not greet him. For whoever greets him shares in his evil works. ## XXVII.

units.la: XXVII.

XXVII. Habet autem haec excommunicatio etiam gradus suos; cum alia sit excommunicatio minor, alia major. Illa abstentio dicitur, qua ad tempus a S. Coena prohibetur peccator. Manet tamen coetus membrum, nec protinus de fratrum societate ejicitur. Cumque haec fit sententia, nec definitiva, aut absoluta, sed interlocutoria, non difficulter liberari ab ea potest. Aliter ac Anabaptistae censent. Videnturque de ea agere loca 2. Thess. 3: 14. 15. Si quis non audierit nostro per epistolam sermoni, hunc notate, & ne commisceamini cum eo, ut erubescat. Neque ut inimicum ducite, sed admonete ut fratrem, & 1. Cor. 5: 12. In majoribus autem delictis, accedente contumacia, adhibetur excommunicatio major. Qua flagitiosus peccator, de Ecclesiae corpore, ut tabidum membrum, quod pestem suam etiam partibus sinceris afflare posset, spirituali ense veluti exsecatur. Quanquam nec hic omne postliminii jus ipsi intercluditur, si quidem ad veram poenitentiam, ac peccatorum ἐξομολ. γνων, redeat; per quam semper ad coelestem civitatem reditus datur. Supremam enim in peccatorem sententiam ferre, & catholicis istis devotionibus uti, quibus peccatori omnis reditus ac veniae spes in perpetuum auferatur, ac tantummodo horrendum ac dirum Anathema ac Maranatha ingeminare, penes hominem, vel aliquem hominum in Ecclesia confessum, non est. Nec tale judicium Ecclesiae datum est. Vid. Matth. 18: 17. 1. Cor. 5: 2. 2. Cor. 7: 12, 13.
units.tr: XXVII. This excommunication also has its degrees, since one is the lesser excommunication and the other the greater. The former is called abstention, by which the sinner is kept from the Holy Supper for a time. Yet he remains a member of the congregation and is not at once cast out of the fellowship of the brethren. Since this sentence is not definitive or absolute but interlocutory, he can be freed from it without difficulty. The Anabaptists think otherwise. The passages that seem to deal with it are 2 Thess. 3:14–15: If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that man, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother; and 1 Cor. 5:12. In greater offences, however, when obstinacy is added, the greater excommunication is applied. By it the scandalous sinner is cut off, as it were, with the spiritual sword from the body of the Church, like a rotting limb that could breathe its pestilence even on the sound parts. Yet even here the right of return is not entirely shut off from him, provided he comes back to true repentance and to confession of sins [ἐξομολόγησιν]; through which a way back to the heavenly city is always open. For it is not within the power of a man, or of any men acknowledged in the Church, to pronounce the final sentence on a sinner and use those so-called "catholic" execrations by which all hope of return and of pardon is taken from the sinner forever, merely repeating the horrible and dreadful Anathema and Maranatha. Nor has the Church been given such a judgment. See Matt. 18:17; 1 Cor. 5:2; 2 Cor. 7:12, 13.

units.la: XXVIII. Cum autem peccator a fidelium consortio separatus est; fidelium officium est, illum ut incestum & maculosum vitare, nec fratrum officia cum ipso colere; quanquam quae communis charitatis sunt, quaeque tum natura, tum publica jura, & leges flagitant, ipsi deneganda non sunt. Quin eum, non ut hostem haberi, sed ut fratrem officii sui identidem admoneri, neque ullam, ut rursus Ecclesiae lucrifiat, occasionem praetermitti Apostolus jubet, 2. Thess. 3: 14, 15. 1. Cor. 5: 9, 10, 11. Canonistae: Os, orare, vale, communio, mensa, negatur.
units.tr: XXVIII. When a sinner has been separated from the fellowship of the faithful, it is the duty of the faithful to avoid him as defiled and unclean, and not to maintain the offices of brotherhood with him; yet what belongs to common charity, and what natural and public law and the statutes require, must not be denied him. Indeed, the Apostle bids us to admonish him again and again, not to regard him as an enemy but as a brother, and not to let slip any opportunity of winning him back to the Church: 2 Thess. 3:14, 15; 1 Cor. 5:9, 10, 11. The canonists say: Speech, prayer, greeting, fellowship, and table are refused.

units.la: XXIX. Atque hinc jam patet, quomodo hoc Ecclesiae judicium differat a judicio Seniorum Veteris Testamenti. Si qui enim apud illos ab institutis majorum discedebant, illi, florente olim republ. externis multis & poenis, quin & morte, coercebantur: Deut. 17: 12. Sequentibus deinde temtemporibus, non sine contumelia, ut profani, ac spei Israelis expertes, de Synagoga pellebantur. Esai. 66: 5. Ezr. 10: 8. Joh. 9: 22. Nec adeo ad emendationem, quam ad vindictam, haec disciplina faciebat, Nam interim hypocritae multi & scelesti, ac temeraria loquentes, modo adversus publicas caerimonias non peccarent, tum quod potentes nimium essent, in populo Dei versari permittebantur, nec religionibus interdicebantur. Ac tenebantur fideles cum tali hominum agmine idem templum, eadem sacra quotidie obire, isque perpetuo sese immiscere; quae non exigua luctus ac quaerimoniarum ipsis causaverat. Ezech. 44: 7, 9. Aliter ac in Novo Test. fit, ubi quis, non de externo cultu & caerimoniis pro Ecclesiae cive censetur, nec juxta δόγματα seu placita de constitutione statuitur; sed ex verbis fundamenti, ex fide in Christum, vitaque tam eximia professione digna, admittitur. Sicuti neque flagris ac multis externis in eos, qui de Ecclesiae limine sese proripiunt, saevitur; sed, ad patriae disciplinae normam, crebris admonitionibus, omnique amoris ingenio, ad extremum luctu, & supremo veluti lestu, fugitivum filium Ecclesia prosequitur.
units.tr: And from this it is already plain how this judgment of the Church differs from the judgment of the elders of the Old Testament. If anyone among them departed from the institutions of their forefathers, they were restrained, while the commonwealth still flourished, by many external penalties and even by death: Deut. 17:12. In later times, not without disgrace, they were cast out of the synagogue as profane persons, having no part in the hope of Israel: Isa. 66:5; Ezra 10:8; John 9:22. Nor did this discipline aim so much at amendment as at vengeance. For meanwhile many hypocrites and wicked men, speaking rashly, did not sin against the public ceremonies, and because they were too powerful, they were allowed to remain among the people of God and were not forbidden the religious rites. The faithful were bound to enter the same temple and perform the same sacred rites daily with this crowd of men, and to mix with them constantly, which caused them no small grief and complaint: Ezek. 44:7, 9. It is otherwise in the New Testament, where someone is counted as a citizen of the Church not by external worship and ceremonies, nor is he determined according to dogmata [δόγματα] or opinions about constitution, but he is admitted on the basis of the words of the foundation, faith in Christ, and a life worthy of so excellent a profession. Nor are those who tear themselves away from the threshold of the Church punished with whips and many external penalties; rather, by the standard of paternal discipline, with frequent admonitions and every kind of loving care, and at last with grief and, as it were, a final lament, the Church pursues the fugitive son.

units.la: XXX. Sequuntur quaestiones quaedam, quibus breviter occurren- dum est.
units.tr: XXX. Certain questions follow, to which we must briefly respond.

units.la: 1. An auditu verbi arcendi excommunicati? Quod negamus. Cum illud unicum sit medium ad illos reducendos, quo Ecclesia unice spectat. Contra ac olim certo in casu in poenitentia veterum observatum. Nec facit huc Veteris Test. exemplum; ubi, qui impuri erant, tabernaculo & templo arcebantur. Constat enim hoc actum, ne caeromoniae polluerentur. Non eadem autem auditoriorum ac coetuum nostrorum sanctitas. Cum omnis locorum religio & sanctitas nunc cessaret, Joh. 4: 21, 23.
units.tr: 1. Are the excommunicated to be kept from hearing the Word? We deny it, since this is the only means by which the Church looks to bring them back. This is unlike what was once observed in certain cases of repentance among the ancients. Nor does the example of the Old Testament bear on this, where those who were unclean were kept away from the tabernacle and the temple. For it is well established that this was done so that the ceremonies would not be defiled. But our assemblies and meeting places do not have the same holiness, since all sanctity of place has now ceased: John 4:21, 23.

units.la: XXXI. Quaeritur 2. An omne civile commercium cum ipsis prohibeatur?
units.tr: XXXI. Question 2: Is all civil intercourse with them forbidden?

units.la: Qui Anabaptistarum rigor est. Contra Christi exemplum, qui cum publicanis, quibus excommunicatos comparat, accubuisse legitur. Matth. 9: 20. Cum non latius haec disciplina pateat, quam patitur Ecclesiasticae communionis ratio. Est autem sacrum omne commercium, atque arctio cum iis familiaritas & consuetudo, interdicta. Quo spectant Apostoli loca: Recedite ab iis. Rom. 16: 17. Ne communicaeamini cum tali ne comedatis 1. Cor. 5: 11. Hunc notate, & ne commiscemini ipsi, ut verecundia afficiatur. 2. Thess. 3: 14. Ne dicite ave,
units.tr: This is the severity of the Anabaptists, and it is contrary to the example of Christ, who is read to have reclined at table with the publicans, whom he compares to excommunicated persons. Matt. 9:20. For this discipline extends no further than the rule of ecclesiastical communion allows. All sacred fellowship is forbidden, and also close familiarity and habitual association with such persons. To this point the apostolic passages look: "Withdraw from them." Rom. 16:17. "Do not associate with such a one, do not even eat with him." 1 Cor. 5:11. "Mark this man, and do not mix with him, that he may be ashamed." 2 Thess. 3:14. "Do not say to him, Hail," [2 John 10].

units.la: 2. Joh. com. 10.
units.tr: 2 John, verse 10.

units.la: XXXII. Sed ulterius tendunt quidam ex isto grege, & ipsius naturae iura,
units.tr: XXXII. But some of that flock go further, and they want the rights of nature itself,

units.la: jura, ac parentum, & liberorum, & conjugum, inter sese officia ista sententia extincta volunt. Quod revera est, legem Dei superstitione sua evacuare: Nam Deus mandavit, dicens, honora Patrem tuum, & matrem — sed vos dicitis — Matth. 15: 4, 5. acapertissimis Apostoli verbis illudere, qui sanctos esse conjugum amores, etiam ubi alteruter infidelis est, pronunciare non veretur, 1. Cor. 7: 12, 13, 16.
units.tr: the rights and duties that bind parents and children and spouses to one another, to be extinguished by their opinion. This truly is to nullify the law of God by their superstition: "For God commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother" — "but you say" — Matt. 15:4, 5. It is to mock the most open words of the Apostle, who does not hesitate to declare that the love of spouses is holy even where one of them is an unbeliever, 1 Cor. 7:12, 13, 16.

units.la: XXXIII. Ejusdem erroris surculus est, quod Ecclesiastica sententia percutiendum volunt, qui uxorem diversa sacra sectantem induxerit: Nec culpae ejus reis veniam concedunt; nisi vel nova nupta proselytam sese faciat, vel alioquin praemortua fuerit. Nos quidem in Domino nubendum, 1. Cor. 7: 39. nec facile jugum cum extraneo ducendum, 2. Cor. 6: 14. aut peregrini numinis filiam in tam arctum foedus adscisicendam, Mal. 2: 11. assentimur: nuptias tamen, cum infideli contractas, ratas; usumque earum, quod fideles spectat, sanctum, 1. Cor. 7: 12, 13. adeoque perpetuam excommunicationem minime mereri, censemus.
units.tr: XXXIII. A twig of the same error is that they want those who have married a wife following a different religion to be struck with ecclesiastical censure, and they grant no pardon to the guilty party unless the new wife makes herself a proselyte or else dies beforehand. We indeed agree that one should marry "in the Lord," 1 Cor. 7:39, and that one should not readily "be yoked with an unbeliever," 2 Cor. 6:14, or take "the daughter of a foreign god" into so close a covenant, Mal. 2:11. Yet we judge that marriages contracted with an unbeliever are valid, and that their use, insofar as it concerns the faithful, is holy, 1 Cor. 7:12, 13, and so they by no means deserve perpetual excommunication.

units.la: XXXIV. Impia autem sunt Pontificiorum fulmina, quibus reges ditionibus exuere, populos sacramento solvere, omnequa humanum commercium turbare ac extinguere praesumunt, contra doctrinam Euangelii, Rom. 13: 1. 1. Tim. 2: 1, 2. Quibus larvis, ac terricula mentis, & puerilibus prope καταγραφείς, rudioribus olim saeculis, orbem infestabant: immani scelere magistratuum jura, omnemque jurisjurandi sanctitatem, ipsum denique sacrae disciplinae usum contaminantes & conculcantes. Non enim bona temporalia, sed spiritualia ista censura spectat; nec mortalibus obruendis, ac perfundandis, sed admonendis, ac reducendis, uniceque intenta, de istorum fulminum genere est, quae percussi etiam adorant.
units.tr: XXXIV. Impious, however, are the thunderbolts of the Papists, by which they presume to strip kings of their domains, to release peoples from their oath, and to disturb and extinguish all human intercourse, contrary to the doctrine of the Gospel, Rom. 13:1; 1 Tim. 2:1, 2. With these bugbears and terrors of the mind, and almost childish "pictures," they used to harass the world in the cruder ages, contaminating and trampling underfoot the rights of magistrates with monstrous wickedness, all the sanctity of the oath, and finally the very use of sacred discipline. For this censure concerns not temporal goods but spiritual ones; it is aimed not at overwhelming and drowning mortals, but at admonishing and bringing them back, and it is of the kind of thunderbolts that even those struck by them worship.

units.la: XXXV. Ac plus impietatis habent anathemata illa, sententiaeque terribiles Vejovis Capitolini; quibus integra regna, & provincias, sine discrimine, interdicto involvere, sacrisque omnibus per aliquod tempus arcere & interdicere solet. Quod censurae genus primus usurpavit Alexander III. circa Annum 1170. secutique eum Innocentius III. A. 1200. Gregorius IX. A. 1230. Innocentius IV. A. 1245. ac Bonifacius VIII. quanquam variis temperamentis; denique patrum memoria Paulus V. contra Venetos; non sine publica Christiani orbis indignatione, scriptisque pro principe republica defensionibus doctissimis ac justissimis. Et revera injustissimum ac ferale est hoc fulminum genus, hominibus non admonendis, sed perdendis, ac, cessante cultu sacro, vastirati tati Ecclesiæ faciendæ, natum. Et, cum in tanto numero non omnes sint ex æquo fontes, non omnes contumaces, nec erga singulos omnes disciplinæ gradus ac partes observari possint; quid hoc aliud est, quam justum cum injusto perdere, Gen. 18:23. & calamum quassatum confringere, Matth. 12:20. & propter succrescentia forte zizania, universam messem perdere, Matth. 13:28. & agrum dominicum populari & devastare; denique disciplina non ad ædificationem, sed ad majorem Ecclesiæ ruinam uti; quæ ad illud sacrorum omnium interstitium, ac publicum Ecclesiæ veluti justitium, non potest non sequi.
units.tr: XXXV. Yet those anathemas and terrible sentences of the Capitoline Vejovis are even more impious, by which they are accustomed to involve whole kingdoms and provinces, without distinction, in an interdict, and to bar and forbid them from all sacred rites for some time. This kind of censure was first employed by Alexander III around the year 1170, and after him Innocent III around 1200, Gregory IX around 1230, Innocent IV around 1245, and Boniface VIII, though with various moderations; and finally, within the memory of our fathers, Paul V against the Venetians, not without the public indignation of the Christian world and the most learned and most just defences written on behalf of the republic and its prince. And indeed this kind of thunderbolt is most unjust and deadly, born not to admonish men but to destroy them, and, with sacred worship ceasing, to make the whole Church a desert. And since in so great a number not all are equally sources of offence, not all are obstinate, and the degrees and parts of discipline cannot be observed in each individual, what else is this than to destroy the righteous with the wicked, Gen. 18:23; to break the bruised reed, Matt. 12:20; and, because of tares that perhaps spring up, to destroy the whole harvest, Matt. 13:28; and to ravage and lay waste the Lord's field; in short, to use discipline not for building up but for the greater ruin of the Church. This must inevitably lead to that cessation of all sacred things and public standstill, as it were, of the Church.

units.la: XXXVI. Ad quæstionem, an, qui excommunicatur, de universa Ecclesia; an vero tantum de parte ejus quadam proscribatur? Nos respondemus: cum omnium Ecclesiarum eadem doctrina ac ratio sit, cum, qui justas ob causas, ob fidei videl. vel morum maculam, exclusus est, de Ecclesia Catholica merito exulare. Commune enim crimen est. Nec, qui talis est, pro fratre ullibi agnosci potest. Cum nullus ei in regno Christi locus sit. Atque hic diversa Ecclesia ac rerumpublicarum ratio est; in quibus, propter diversas singularum leges ac constitutiones, qui ab una civitate ejectus est, in alteram accipi & admitti sæpe potest. Ecclesia autem una est, iisdemque ubique legibus constat, & qui peccat in unam ejus partem, in eam peccat universam. Unum corpus, & unus Spiritus: quemadmodum vocati estis in una spe vocationis vestræ. Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma. Unus Deus, & Pater omnium, qui est super omnibus, & per omnes & in omnibus vobis. Eph. 4:4. 5, 6.
units.tr: XXXVI. To the question whether one who is excommunicated is cut off from the whole Church, or only from some part of it, we answer: since the teaching and principle of all churches is the same, one who has been excluded for just causes, on account of a stain of faith or of morals, rightly goes into exile from the Catholic Church. For the crime is common. Nor can such a person be acknowledged as a brother anywhere. For he has no place in the kingdom of Christ. Here the situation is different from that of states, in which, because of the diverse laws and constitutions of each, one who has been expelled from one city can often be received and admitted into another. But the Church is one, and it consists of the same laws everywhere, and whoever sins against one part of it sins against the whole. "One body and one Spirit, as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." Eph. 4:4, 5, 6.

units.la: Nec, qui talis est, pro fratre ullibi agnosci potest.
units.tr: Nor can such a person be acknowledged as a brother anywhere.

units.la: XXXVII. Excommunicatio Ecclesiæ, post multiplices ac fraternas admonitiones, totque amoris circa fratrem laborantis specimina, & formas, per Scripturarum ἐλεγχον tandem peracta, ligat; nec pro humano, sed pro divino judicio habenda est. Juxta illud, quicquid ligaveris in terra, ligatum erit in cælo. Non enim potest Deus non ratum habere, quod in nomine ipsius, ex verbo ipsius, tanta cum cura, & tam anxie, ex solo ac mero amore, erga fratrem peccantem actum est. Ut ita ab Ecclesiæ domo exclusus, merito quoque Deo cœloque exul vagetur, donec per pœnitentiam iterum ad Ecclesiæ sinum redeat. Amen dico, quæcunque ligaveritis in terra, erunt ligata in cælo; & quæcunque solveritis in terra, erunt soluta in cælo. Matth. 18:18. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: si quorum retineatis, retinentur. Joh. 20:23. Nam benedicti ejus, justi, hereditant terram, & maledicti ejus exscinduntur. Psal. 37:22.
units.tr: XXXVII. Excommunication by the Church, carried out at last after many fraternal admonitions, so many examples and forms of love toward a brother who is struggling, and by the refutation of the Scriptures, binds; and it is to be regarded not as a human but as a divine judgment. This accords with the saying, "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven." For God cannot fail to ratify what has been done in his name, from his word, with such care and such anxiety, out of pure and simple love toward a sinning brother. So that one thus shut out from the house of the Church rightly also wanders as an exile from God and heaven, until through repentance he returns again to the bosom of the Church. "Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Matt. 18:18. "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained." John 20:23. "For those blessed by him shall inherit the earth, and those cursed by him shall be cut off." Ps. 37:22.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quod etiam de eo, qui alioquin ad salutem electus est, intelligendum est; qui, ista sententia perculsus, & ecclesia externa ejectus, nec pacem animi, nec vitæ æternæ spem, ad illud tempus servare potest, cum peccati merito, Dei amicitia ac communione ultra indignus sit. Veluti in stripe palmas, vel surculus, maligne pastus, jamque exarescens, & jam jam de matre avellendus; nisi novo agricolæ studio refoveatur, vitalemque rursus succum hauriat. Est autem ipsa excommunicatio non leve remedium, ad erronem filium in cœlestis parentis domum rursus reducendum.
units.tr: XXXVIII. This must also be understood of one who is otherwise chosen to salvation, who, struck by this sentence and cast out of the external Church, cannot keep peace of mind or the hope of eternal life for that time, since by the merit of sin he is unworthy of God's friendship and communion. He is like a branch or shoot on a trunk that has been fed amiss and is already withering, and about to be torn from its mother, unless it is revived by the new care of the husbandman and draws in vital sap again. Excommunication itself is not a slight remedy for bringing the erring son back into the house of the heavenly Father.

units.la: XXXIX. Ligat autem Ecclesia solo ministerio. Eodem modo, uti Levitici sacerdotes leprosum dicebantur polluere velinundare, ubi eum aut mundum, aut immundum, declarabant. Erant autem ligandi & solvendi voces, in scholis Judæorum frequentes, in magistris creandis; notabatq; illa tantundem ac prohibere, seu prohibitum declarare, hæc vero tantundem dicebat ac permittere, seu licitum declarare: quomodo speciatim ad res, non vero ad personas referebantur. conf. Matth. 16: 19. Quo modo & Christus discipulos suos magistros gentium instituit.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Church binds, however, only by the ministry. In the same way, as the priests of Leviticus were said to pollute or cleanse a leper, when they declared him either clean or unclean. The expressions "to bind" and "to loose" were, moreover, frequent in the schools of the Jews, in the creating of teachers; "to bind" signified the same as "to prohibit," or "to declare forbidden," and "to loose" said the same as "to permit," or "to declare lawful." In this way they were referred specifically to things, not to persons. Compare Matt. 16:19. In this way also Christ appointed his disciples as teachers of the nations.

units.la: XL. Ac constat jam satis ex iis, quæ jam dicta sunt, nullam infamiam, vel pœnam externam ex Ecclesiasticis sententiis sequi; nisi crimen istiusmodi sit, ut aliquem etiam publice probrosum & intestabilem reddat; quod respectu Ecclesiæ per accidens est.
units.tr: XL. And it is now sufficiently clear from what has already been said that no infamy or external penalty follows from ecclesiastical sentences, unless the crime is of such a kind that it also makes a man publicly disgraced and incapable of giving testimony; which, with respect to the Church, is incidental.

units.la: XLI. Tantum abest, ut, vel lata sententia, vel voto, aliquem æternis pœnis adjudicet, sine provocatione ac veniæ spe. Quod supra attigimus. Ista enim disciplinæ isti repugnant; quæ non letalis, sed salutifera, peccatori sanando ac convertendo unice inservit. Nec tantæ rei arbitrium ac judicium penes homines, vel cœtum aliquem est. At Michael, Archangelus ille, cum, adversus diabolum altercans, disceptaret de corpore Mosis, non ausus est illi impingere notam maledicti; sed dixit, increpet te Dominus. Jud. com. 9. Quod si quis non auscultat nostro per epistolam sermoni, hunc notate—ut erubescat. 2. Thess. 3: 14. Ad interitum carnis, ut Spiritus salvus sit die illo Domini. 1. Cor. 5: 5. Sufficit istiusmodi homini ista increpatio à pluribus illis profecta. Ut e contrario potius vos ei condonetis, eumque consolemini, ne quo modo redundante tristitia absorbeatur. Quapropter precor vos, ut ratam faciatis in illum charitatem. 1. Cor. 2: 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: XLI. Far from it: neither by a sentence passed nor by a vow does anyone condemn another to eternal punishment without any appeal or hope of pardon. We have touched on this above. Such a claim is contrary to that discipline, which is not deadly but saving, and serves solely to heal and convert the sinner. Nor does the decision or judgment in so great a matter rest with men or with any assembly. But Michael the archangel, when disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to pass a judgment of condemnation upon him, but said: The Lord rebuke thee. Jude 9. And if anyone does not obey our word by this letter, note that man, that he may be ashamed. 2 Thess. 3:14. For the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. 1 Cor. 5:5. Sufficient for such a man is this rebuke, which was given by many. So on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love towards him. 2 Cor. 2:6, 7, 8.

units.la: XLII. Quæ autem in contrarium adferuntur ex Gal. 1: 8. Etiam si nos, aut Angelus e cælo, Evangelisët vobis præter id, quod vobis Evangeligelisaevimus, anathema sit. 1. Cor. 16: 22. Si quis non amat Dominum Iesum Christum, esto anathema, maranatha: Ecclesiae istam potestatem non tribuunt. Non enim de Ecclesiae judicatura, sed de Dei judicio ibi agitur. Et generalis doctrina traditur, quid Euangelii adulteratores, & Christi Domini hostes mereantur. Pariter Rom. 9: 3. Optarim enim ego ipse anathema esse, a Christo, pro fratribus meis: Apostolus de se ipso, in isto orationis excessu, divinam propriam sententiam respicit. Ubi autem vetat Johannes 1. epist. cap. 5: 16. Orare pro eo, qui ad mortem peccaverit, iterum, non Ecclesiae, sed Dei sententia, damnatum introducit: Ecclesiam autem sese non nimium afflictare tali in casu, nec importunis precibus divinae sententiae obstrepere & obmurmurare, sed ei potius subscribere jubet. Ne orato pro populo isto in bonum. Jer. 14: 11. Cumque ista peccata vix discerni possint, nihil hic temere agendum; nec immiti sententia aliquis facile confodiendus, aut supremis dirisunquam devovendus est. Quod ne quidem in Judaica Ecclesia unquam factum. Damnamus ergo Anabaptistarum excommunicandi libidinem, qui excommunicationibus suis, levibus interdum de causis tanquam pueri talis ludunt; &c, cum in multas sectas discedant, crudelissimis edictis inter se saepe desaeviunt; seque unos rerum coelestium participes, alios autem omnes exsortes, & Deo coeloque quasi extorres miserabiliter interdum credunt.
units.tr: XLII. As for what is brought forward on the other side from Gal. 1:8: Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed. And 1 Cor. 16:22: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed, maranatha. These passages do not grant this power to the Church. For they speak not of the judgment of the Church but of the judgment of God, and they teach in general terms what those who corrupt the gospel and enemies of Christ the Lord deserve. Likewise Rom. 9:3: For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for my brothers. The Apostle, in this excess of prayer, looks to a divine sentence and not his own. Again, where John in 1 John 5:16 forbids praying for one who has sinned unto death, he presents him as already condemned by the sentence of God, not of the Church. He bids the Church not to torment itself excessively in such a case, nor to clamour and murmur importunately against the divine sentence, but rather to acquiesce in it: Do not pray for this people for their good. Jer. 14:11. And since such sins can scarcely be discerned, nothing is to be done here rashly; no one is to be lightly pierced by a harsh sentence, nor ever cursed with the final curses. This was never done even in the Jewish Church. We therefore condemn the lust for excommunication among the Anabaptists, who sport with their excommunications like children, sometimes for slight causes; and since they split into many sects, they often rage against one another with the cruellest edicts. They sometimes wretchedly believe that they alone are partakers of heavenly things, while all others are shut out, and as exiles from God and heaven.

units.la: XLIII. Ligationem excipit solutio, sive peccatoris absolutio; quae altera sententiae hujus pars est, publice adhibenda, ubi ille resipuerit, & de errore suo ad Ecclesiae sinum redierit, ejusque rei idoneam fidem fecerit. Matth. 16. & 18. Quae & peccatorum remissio, Joh. 20: 22. & condonatio, 2. Cor. 2: 7, 10. & peccatoris consolatio, ibid. & charitatis exhibitio, com. 8. appellatur.
units.tr: XLIII. Binding is followed by loosing, that is, the absolution of the sinner. This is the other part of that sentence, to be applied publicly when he has repented, has returned from his error into the bosom of the Church, and has given a suitable proof of this. Matt. 16 and 18. It is also called the remission of sins, John 20:22, and forgiveness, 2 Cor. 2:7, 10, and the comforting of the sinner, ibid., and the showing of love, verse 8.

units.la: Quae peccatori, lub tristitiae onere fatiscenti, denegan da non est. Et publice quoque, de reducta ad caulam ove, Ecclesiae gratulandum est. Nec pietas ista Deo displicet: cum de peccatore poenitente etiam in coelo gaudium sit, Luc. 15. Unde Deus, quicquid istud est, ratum in coelo quoque habet, atque istam Ecclesiae sententiam obsignat, Matth. 16. & 18. Joh. 20: 22. Mimum autem in re religiosa agunt Pontificii, cum & mortuos, & invitos, nonnunquam Ecclesiasticis diris exsolvunt; cum istud ad poenitentes solummodo pertineat.
units.tr: This must not be refused to a sinner who is failing under the burden of sorrow. And publicly too the Church ought to rejoice over the sheep brought back to the fold. Nor does such kindness displease God, since there is joy in heaven over a repentant sinner, Luke 15. Hence God, whatever this is, also holds it valid in heaven and seals this sentence of the Church, Matt. 16 and 18, John 20:22. But the Papists act a farce in religious matters when they also release the dead and the unwilling from ecclesiastical curses, since that pertains only to the penitent.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS SEPTIMUS. DE Ministris Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti. CAPUT VI. De Ministris N. F. extraordinariis.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. Of the extraordinary ministers of the New Covenant. Locus Forty-Seven: Concerning the Ministers of the Church of the New Testament.

units.la: I. UM Christus Ecclesiam suam non regat interne tantum, verum etiam externe, varia dona & charismata in eam distribuit. Quum ascendit in sublime—dedit dona hominibus—ad compactionem Sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad ædificationem corporis Christi—Ex quo (Christo) totum corpus congruenter coagmentatum, & compactum per omnes suppeditatas commissuras, ex vi intus agente, pro mensura uniuscujusque membri, incrementum capit corpori conveniens &c. Eph. 4: 6,12,16. Ex quibus varia enascuntur ministeria & διακονίαι. Distinctiones autem donorum sunt, sed idem Spiritus. Et distinctiones ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus. 1. Cor. 12: 4, 5, 8, 9, 10.
units.tr: I. Since Christ governs his Church not only inwardly but also outwardly, he distributes various gifts and charismata among its members. When he ascended on high, he gave gifts to men; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ. From him the whole body, fitly joined and knit together through every joint that supplies, by the working of each part in due measure, makes the body increase, etc. Eph. 4:6, 12, 16. From these various ministries and services [διακονίαι] arise. There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord. 1 Cor. 12:4, 5, 8, 9, 10.

units.la: II. Est autem ministerium, functio Ecclesiastica, qua homo selectus, jure speciali, sacra mysteria dispensat. Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de ministris Christi, & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. 1. Cor. 4: 1. Quum ministerium hoc habeamus, prout misericordiam consequuti sumus, 2. Cor. 4: 1. Ut alteri sacra ista tractare non æque liceat. Cum ad istud non sufficiat potestas absoluta, sive qualiscunque aptitudo, sed præterea opus sit potestate relativa, seu juris, quæ præterea auctoritatem conciliat:
units.tr: II. A ministry is an ecclesiastical function by which a man chosen by special right dispenses the sacred mysteries. Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 1 Cor. 4:1. Since we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, 2 Cor. 4:1. Thus it is not equally permitted for others to handle these sacred things. For absolute power, or any kind of aptitude, is not sufficient for this; there is also need of relative power, that is, of right, which further confers authority.

units.la: III. Ministerium appellatur, quod, nulla propria auctoritate, & arbitrio, nullo in gregem dominatu, ex solius Christi præscripto, gerendum sit. Verum non ita erit inter vos. Sed quicunque voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, esto vester minister. Matth. 20: 26. Unde, cum mere personale sit, vicariam alterius operam non admittit. Quæ Papatus corruptela est. IV. Atque oritur hinc tertius Ecclesiæ status. Sicut enim illa per fidem statum ac perfectionem suam essentialem habet, per confœderationem mutuam, integralem, ita per varia dona ac ministeria acquirit persectionem organicam, qua sibi ipsi, membrisque suis omnibus sufficere ac præesse commode potest.
units.tr: III. It is called a ministry because it is to be carried out without any proper authority or discretion of one's own, without any lordship over the flock, solely according to the prescription of Christ. But it shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your minister. Matt. 20:26. Hence, since it is purely personal, it does not admit the vicarious labour of another. This is a corruption of the Papacy. IV. From this arises the third state of the Church. For just as she has her essential state and perfection through faith, through mutual and integral confederation, so through various gifts and ministries she acquires an organic perfection, by which she can conveniently suffice for herself and all her members and preside over them.

units.la: V. Ministeriorum horum directio, politica Ecclesiastica vocatur; ac Ecclesiæ ordinem ac regimen constituit. Quod monarchicum est, respectu Ecclesiæ Christi, capitis invisibilis; quoad externam autem formam, partim aristocraticum est, partim democraticum. Hierarchia enim, atque hominum in Ecclesia dominatus, Antichristi partus est. Reges gentium dominantur — Vos autem non ita estote: sed qui maximus est inter vos, esto ut qui minimus est; & qui ductor est, sicut qui ministrat. Luc. 22:25,26. conf. Matth. 20:26. Marc. 9:35. Presbyteros, qui inter vos sunt, precor ergo unus Presbyter — Pascite Dei gregem, qui penes vos est, illius inspectionis vacantes — Non dominantes cleri, sed ut qui fitis exemplaria gregis. 1. Pet. 5:1,2,3. De cætero externum Ecclesiæ regimen & olim magna diversitate administratum fuit, & hodie, inter ipsos etiam Reformatos, administratur, pro multiplici nempe populorum locorumque genio, & reipublicæ varia forma: cum omnis sæculorum experientia docuerit plerumque politi- cularis formam sequi quoque ecclesiasticam. Ut si reliqua in Ecclesia secus bene se habeant, non tanta contentione, maxime a privatis, hic laborandum sit, nec adeo damnandi qui alia politiæ externæ forma, ac nos, utuntur: cum sub rituum regiminisque diversitate eadem retineri possit fides ac veritas.
units.tr: V. The direction of these ministries is called ecclesiastical polity, and it establishes the order and government of the Church. In respect of Christ, the invisible head of the Church, this government is monarchical; as to its external form, it is partly aristocratic and partly democratic. For hierarchy and the dominion of men in the Church is the offspring of Antichrist. The kings of the nations lord it over them... But you are not to be so; rather, let the greatest among you be as the youngest, and the leader as the one who serves. Luke 22:25, 26; cf. Matt. 20:26; Mark 9:35. I exhort the elders who are among you, I therefore urge as a fellow elder... Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not as lords over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. 1 Pet. 5:1, 2, 3. Moreover, external government of the Church has been administered in great variety both in former times and today, even among the Reformed themselves, according to the manifold character of peoples and places and the varied form of the commonwealth. For all the experience of the ages has taught that ecclesiastical form usually follows the civil form as well. Therefore, if other matters in the Church are otherwise in good order, we should not labour here with such great contention, especially as private persons, nor should those who use a different external form of polity from ours be condemned, since the same faith and truth can be retained under a diversity of rites and government.

units.la: VI. Est autem ministerium vel extraordinarium, vel ordinarium.
units.tr: VI. A ministry is either extraordinary or ordinary.

units.la: VII. Illud, vocatione, donis, & ductu denique atque afflatu Spiritus extraordinario instructum, triplici potissimum in casu Ecclesiæ affulsit. Vel ad erigendam eam, ac primitus instituendam; vel ad eam peculiariter confirmandam; vel ad collapsam denique restituendam. Ac primo quidem in casu semper conjuncta habuit miracula: Confirmante Deo signis, & prodigiis, & variis virtutibus, & distributionibus Spiritus sancti, secundum propriam voluntatem, Hebr. 2:4. Non æque in reliquis. Ut injuria Pontificii a Reformationis ducibus miracula flagitarint.
units.tr: VII. The former, equipped by vocation, gifts, and finally by the guidance and inspiration of the Spirit in an extraordinary way, appeared in the Church chiefly in three situations: either to raise it up and establish it at the beginning, or to confirm it in a special way, or finally to restore it when it had fallen. And in the first case it always had miracles joined with it: God also bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will, Heb. 2:4. It was not equally so in the rest. Thus the Papists wrongly demanded miracles from the leaders of the Reformation.

units.la: VIII. Hoc, ab extraordinariis illis ministris institutum, continuo deinde ordine in Ecclesia servatur. Ut ministri ordinarii extraordinariorum successores sint; non quidem quoad ductum illum modumque infallibilem, sed quoad essentialia muneris. Cum, illorum sit, Ecclesiam jam constitutam ædificare, ornare, & ad auctus & incrementa ejus attendere. Cumque omnis illa institutio e verbo Dei, mediisque ordinariis petenda veniat; nec ab ordine semel constituto deflectere liceat; ordinarium illud ministerium appellatur.
units.tr: VIII. This institution, begun by those extraordinary ministers, is then continuously preserved in the Church in an ordered succession. So the ordinary ministers are the successors of the extraordinary ones; not indeed in that infallible guidance and manner, but in the essentials of the office. For it belongs to them to build up and adorn the Church already constituted, and to attend to its growth and increase. And since all that institution must be sought from the Word of God and the ordinary means, and it is not permitted to depart from the order once established, that ministry is called ordinary.

units.la: IX. Prima olim Ecclesiæ institutio penes patresfamilias erat; qui suæ familiæ, non solum quoad τὰ βωμικὰ, verum etiam ad rem divinam duces erant. Qualis Noachus, Abrahamus &c. In Ægypto præcerant populo Seniores; & sacerdotium a familiarum primogenitis præcipue tenebatur, Exod. 19:22,24. & 24:5. & 13:2. Substituti iis deinceps Levitæ. Quæ tribus sacrorum curam pro toto Israële accepit, Num. 8:16, 17. Eratque ipsorum munus, præter ea, quæ in Tabernaculo apud Deum agenda erant, etiam populum divinam legem edocere. Quum labia sacerdotis observarent scientiam, & lex requireretur ex ore ipsius: nam Angelus Jehovæ exercituum est. Mal. 2:6. Quod factum ab ipsis, tum in omnibus portis; tum præcipuis in loco, quem elegerat Dominus, Deut. 17:9, 12. Utque non nisi digni ad curam istam adhiberentur, per χειροτονίαν in magistros, ac legis vindices, & custodes, ordinabantur. Ac legebantur ex isto genere cantores, quæstores, Scribæ seu ὑπομνηματογράφοι, aliique publici ministri; quin & Judices municipales; & ex parte summi concilii Hierosolymitani assessores. Pharisæi autem, & Sadducæi, sectarum nomina erant. Act. 22:6, 7.
units.tr: IX. The first institution of the Church was formerly in the hands of the heads of families, who were leaders of their households not only in the matters of the altar but also in divine worship. Such were Noah, Abraham, and others. In Egypt the elders presided over the people, and the priesthood was held chiefly by the firstborn of the families: Exod. 19:22, 24; 24:5; 13:2. Afterwards the Levites were substituted for them. That tribe received the charge of sacred things on behalf of all Israel: Num. 8:16, 17. Their office was, besides the things to be done before God in the Tabernacle, also to teach the people the divine law: For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and men should seek the law at his mouth; for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. Mal. 2:6. This was done by them both in all the gates and especially in the place which the Lord had chosen: Deut. 17:9, 12. And so that only the worthy were admitted to that charge, they were ordained by election [χειροτονίαν] as teachers, guardians and keepers of the law. From this class were chosen singers, treasurers, scribes or recorders [ὑπομνηματογράφοι], and other public ministers; indeed also municipal judges, and, on the part of the supreme council at Jerusalem, assessors. The Pharisees and Sadducees, however, were names of sects: Acts 22:6, 7.

units.la: X. Extraordinarii autem ministri erant Prophetæ. Qui, a Deo immediate vocati, vel externa voce, vel intrinseco afflatu, vel etiam adhibitis internuntiis (quorum erat, expresso Dei jussu, personas designare. Exod. 4:14. 1. Reg. 19:19.) tum futura prædicebant, tum primariam de Messia promissionem repetebant, tum etiam Ecclesiæ necessitatibus extra ordinem consulebant. Prophetandi autem auctoritatem, non a Synedrio, aut consessu humano, sed a Deo accipiebant. Ac revelationis suæ certitudinem, & veluti signaculum, ipsi quidem in cordibus suis habebant; aliis autem eam per miracula, aut eventuum fidem, faciebant. Quæ omnia accuratius sub prima temporum œconomia executi sumus.
units.tr: X. The extraordinary ministers were the prophets. Called immediately by God, either by an external voice or by an inward inspiration, or even with intermediaries employed (whose task, by express command of God, was to designate persons: Exod. 4:14; 1 Kings 19:19), they both foretold future things, repeated the primary promise concerning the Messiah, and also gave counsel for the needs of the Church outside the ordinary course. They received the authority to prophesy not from the Sanhedrin or any human assembly, but from God. The certainty of their revelation, and as it were its seal, they indeed had in their own hearts; to others, however, they gave assurance of it through miracles or the fulfilment of events. All these things we have treated more carefully under the first economy of the times.

units.la: XI. Novum Testamentum aperuit Johannes Baptistes, pœnitentiæ præco, ac Messiæ Regis anteambulo. Cujus ministerium, quanquam sub veteris temporis fine, maximam tamen partem Euangelicum fuit, ut initio œconomiæ N. F. vidimus.
units.tr: XI. John the Baptist opened the New Testament, the herald of repentance and forerunner of the Messiah the King. His ministry, although it stood at the end of the old time, was nevertheless for the most part evangelical, as we saw at the beginning of the economy of the New Covenant.

units.la: XII. Hunc
units.tr: XII. This

units.la: XII. Hunc excepit ipse Dominus, Euangelii auctor & promulgator. Fuitque hoc tempus Ecclesiae longe beatissimum, cum ipse Dei Filius, humano in corpore, inter homines versaretur; & humano ore verba Dei, non ulli hactenus exaudita, resonaret. Deut. 18: 18. Hebr. 1: 1, 2, 3.
units.tr: XII. The Lord himself, the author and proclaimer of the gospel, received this. This was by far the most blessed time for the Church, when the Son of God himself lived among men in a human body and the words of God, which no one had heard before, sounded from a human mouth. Deut. 18: 18. Heb. 1: 1, 2, 3.

units.la: XIII. Cumque ipse, parato ministerio terras relicturus foret, duodecim legit Apostolos, novae Ecclesiae duces, amplissima potestate instructos. Ac juxta hos Prophetas, Euangelistas, Pastores & Doctores dedit, ad compactionem Sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad edificationem corporis Christi. Eph. 4: 11, 12. conf. 1. Cor. 12: 28, 29. Rom. 12: 5. Quod Apostolicum munus cum omnium excellentissimum fuerit, qua potemus brevitate, paulo accuratius delineabimus.
units.tr: XIII. When he was about to leave the earth, his ministry being now complete, he chose twelve Apostles, leaders of the new Church, endowed with the fullest authority. After them he gave Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ. Eph. 4: 11, 12. Compare 1 Cor. 12: 28, 29; Rom. 12: 5. Since this apostolic office was the most excellent of all, we shall describe it in somewhat more detail, as briefly as we can.

units.la: XIV. Apostoli ergo testes per orbem eorum erant, quae Christus defecerat, & passus erat, ac potissimum miraculosae ejus post mortem resurrectionis. Erantque hi publici mundi magistri, quem omnem Euangelio, miraculis, scriptis denique suis, in sequentis Ecclesiae usum, implere, ac plenissimam de Christo fidem facere debebant. De quibus Esai. 62: 7. Quam decori sunt in montibus pedes nuntiantis Euangelium, qui facit audiri pacem? &c.
units.tr: XIV. The Apostles, then, were witnesses throughout the world of what Christ had done and suffered, and above all of his miraculous resurrection after death. They were the public teachers of the world, which they were bound to fill with the gospel, with miracles and finally with their own writings, for the use of the Church that followed, and to give a full account of their faith in Christ. Of them Isaiah 52: 7 says: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, and so on.

units.la: XV. Illorum autem notae & praerogativae hae fuerunt: 1. quod Christum in carne viderunt, ejusque consortio ac disciplina usi sunt, ut miraculorum ac doctrinae, praecipue autem resurrectionis ipsius, essent vivi & αὐτόπται testes. Testes mihi eritis in tota Judaea, Samaria & usque ad ultimos mundi fines. Act. 1: 8. conf. com. 21, 22. c. 10: 41. 22: 15. 1. Cor. 9: 1.
units.tr: XV. The marks and privileges of the Apostles were these. (1) They saw Christ in the flesh, and enjoyed his company and instruction, so that they might be living and eyewitness testimony (autoptai) of his miracles and his teaching, and above all of his resurrection. You shall be my witnesses in all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth. Acts 1: 8. Compare Acts 10: 41; 22: 15; 1 Cor. 9: 1.

units.la: XVI. 2. Quod ab ipso immediate ad munus istud vocati ac ablegati fuerunt: Quemadmodum me misit Pater, & ego mitto vos. Joh. 20: 21. conf. c. 17: 18. Gal. 1: 1. Non enim humano suffragio in sublimi hoc ministerio locus erat. Quare & Matthias forte ostensus legitur. Act. 1: 26.
units.tr: XVI. (2) They were called and sent out to this office immediately by him: As the Father has sent me, so I send you. John 20: 21. Compare John 17: 18; Gal. 1: 1. For in this high ministry there was no room for human suffrage. Hence Matthias too is read of as having been chosen by lot. Acts 1: 26.

units.la: XVI. 3. Hinc dicuntur legati Dei, 2. Cor. 5: 20. Eph. 6: 2. Ut qui illos audiret, Christum audiret, Luc. 10: 16. Utpote quos Deus fideles judicaverat, 1 Tim. 1: 2. quique signa missionis, seu tabulas legationis habebant; quae erant signa Apostoli 2 Cor. 12: 12. Quae ordinariis ministris, nisi sensu admodum diminuto, non conveniunt.
units.tr: XVII. (3) For this reason they are called ambassadors of God, 2 Cor. 5: 20; Eph. 6: 2, so that whoever heard them heard Christ, Luke 10: 16, since God had judged them faithful, 1 Tim. 1: 12, and they had the signs of their mission, or the credentials of their commission, which were the signs of an apostle, 2 Cor. 12: 12. These things do not belong to ordinary ministers, except in a very much diminished sense.

units.la: XVIII. 4. Quod immediata Christi Spiritusque S. revelatione cognitionem Euangelii mysteriorumque divinorum hauserint. Tunc aperuit illorum mentem, ut intelligerent Scripturas. Luc. 24: 45. Quum haec dixisset, afflavit eos; & dixit eis, accipite Spiritum S. Joh. 20: 22. 20:22. Neque enim ego ab homine accepi Euangelium, sed per revelationem Iesu Christi. Gal. 1:12. Vid. Luc. 24:49. Act. 1: 4,5,8. 2:1. & seqq.
units.tr: XVIII. (4) They drew their knowledge of the gospel and of the divine mysteries from immediate revelation of Christ and the Holy Spirit. Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. Luke 24: 45. When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, Receive the Holy Spirit. John 20: 22. For I did not receive the gospel from man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. Gal. 1: 12. See also Luke 24: 49; Acts 1: 4, 5, 8; 2: 1 and following.

units.la: XIX. 5. Hanc divinam inspirationem consequebatur ἀναμάρτητοια, & in Ecclesia docenda infallibilitas, quæ ipsis non minus aderat; quam veteris Ecclesiæ doctoribus ac Prophetis. Unde eadem auctoritate cum ipsis pollebant ac loquebantur. Ille Spiritus vos docebit omnia, & faciet vos commeminisse omnium, quæ dixi vobis. Ioh. 14:26. Cum vero ille venerit Spiritus veritatis, ille vos in omnem veritatem ducet. Joh. 16:13. Qui tamen Spiritus ductus per gradus ac partes ipsis accessit, prout Ecclesiæ tempora ac diversus profectus suadebant. Unde non nisi post idoneum spatium de Gentium vocatione, ac ritum abolitione, moniti sunt. Act. 10. & 15.
units.tr: XIX. (5) This divine inspiration was accompanied by sinlessness [anamartēsia] and by infallibility in teaching the Church, which were no less present in them than in the teachers and prophets of the old Church. Hence they had the same authority as those and spoke with it. That Spirit will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you. John 14: 26. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth. John 16: 13. Yet this Spirit came to them by degrees and in parts, as the times of the Church and its varying progress required. Hence they were not instructed until a suitable interval had passed, concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the abolition of the rites. Acts 10 and 15.

units.la: XX. Utque rerum nonnullarum ignorantia & hæsitatio, de quibus idoneo postea tempore erudiendi erant, de universæ ipsorum doctrinæ fide nihil deterebat; ita nec obstabat divino illi dictui Petri Apostoli factum Gal. 2. non magis quam reliqui Apostolorum lapsus ac peccata, quæ sine Ecclesiæ noxa transfire fecit Dominus. Aliud enim erat, facere quiddam ex humana infirmitate; qualis hæc in Petro perplexitas erat; aliud, ex revelatione, quam acceperant, Ecclesiam docere: quam ubi præ se ferebant, fidem omnem indubie merebantur.
units.tr: XX. Just as their ignorance and hesitation about some matters, on which they were to be taught later at a suitable time, did not detract from the trustworthiness of their whole doctrine, so neither did the deed of the apostle Peter recorded in Gal. 2 stand in the way of that divine dictate, any more than the other lapses and sins of the Apostles, which the Lord allowed to pass without harm to the Church. For it was one thing to do something out of human weakness, as Peter's confusion was; it was another to teach the Church from the revelation they had received. When they put forward the latter, they undoubtedly deserved all faith.

units.la: XXI. Atque idem veritatis Spiritus illo tempore & reliquis Ecclesiæ doctoribus, ac Apostolorum συνέργοις, Marco, Lucæ, Stephano, aliisque adfuit; qui ad novas Ecclesias condendas, mundumque Euangelii sermone primitus imbuendum dimissi, eodem spiritu accincti fuere. Qua Ecclesiæ ætate circumacta, & constituto ac uberrime confirmato fidei canone, nec eadem amplius extraordinarii ductus necessitate extante, non sine mendacio ille jam prætexi potest; omnisque spiritus ad Scripturarum plenitudinem, & fundatissimam Euangelii veritatem, ut Augustinus loquebatur, examinandus venit. Ut non ferendum sit, Romano Pontifici illum adscribere velle, eaque larva universam Dei Ecclesiam ei obnoxiam facere. Cum ille nullo signo infallibilem istum spiritum ostendat; multisque contra rationibus illum destruat.
units.tr: XXI. The same Spirit of truth was present in that age also with the other teachers of the Church, and with the fellow-workers of the Apostles [synergois], Mark, Luke, Stephen and others, who were sent out to found new churches and first to steep the world in the word of the gospel, and who were armed with the same Spirit. But once that age of the Church had passed, the canon of faith had been established and abundantly confirmed, and the necessity of extraordinary guidance no longer existed, it can no longer be put forward without falsehood; and every spirit must come to be examined by the fullness of the Scriptures and the firmly founded truth of the gospel, as Augustine put it. It is intolerable that anyone should wish to ascribe this infallible spirit to the Roman Pontiff, and by this mask make the whole Church of God subject to him, since he shows that spirit by no sign and overthrows it by many arguments.

units.la: XXII. 6. Commissæ illis sunt claves regni cœlorum, seu Ecclesiæ Missiæ, ut Judæis Gentilibusque Euangelii prædicatione illud aperirent. Quod sicut primitus & singulari modo a Petro factum est, Act. 2:41.10: 44. 15:7. ita illi claves istæ promissæ leguntur. Matth. 16:19. quo etiam pertipertinet potestas remittendi & retinendi peccata, reliquis Apostolis concessa. Joh. 20:23. & potestas ligandi solvendique. Matth. 18:18. Quae omnia Apostolis proprio & genuino, reliquis autem Euangelii ministris inclinato duntaxat sensu conveniunt.
units.tr: XXII. (6) The keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, of the Church's mission, were entrusted to them, so that they might open it to Jews and Gentiles through the preaching of the gospel. This was first done in a special way by Peter, Acts 2: 41; 10: 44; 15: 7, and to him those keys are read of as promised. Matt. 16: 19. To this also belongs the power of remitting and retaining sins, granted to the other Apostles. John 20: 23. And the power of binding and loosing. Matt. 18: 18. All these things apply to the Apostles in their proper and genuine sense, but to the other ministers of the gospel only in a derived sense.

units.la: XXIII. 7. Quod singularibus hisce Spiritus S. donis ornati, ac ingenti ejus flumine inundati, illius latices per impositionem manuum, fusaque preces, etiam in aliis largissime derivarunt. Tunc impositerunt illis manus, & acceperunt Spir. S. Act. 8:6, 7, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19. & 19:6. Quod neque Mosi, neque ulli veterum fuit concessum.
units.tr: XXIII. (7) Adorned with these singular gifts of the Holy Spirit, and flooded with his great stream, they also poured out his waters abundantly upon others, through the laying on of hands and by prayers offered. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Acts 8: 6, 7, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19; 19: 6. This was granted neither to Moses nor to any of the ancients.

units.la: XXIV. 8. Spectabat huc quoque imprimis donum miraculorum, quibus ea Ecclesiae tempora erant celebria. Ipsi praedicabant — Domino verbum confirmante per subsequentia miracula. Marc. 16:20. conf. Hebr. 2:3,4. Rom. 15:18, 19. Joh. 14:12. quo imprimis donum sanationis aegrorum faciebat. Matth. 10:1. Marc 16:18. Ecclesiae enim infantiae ac tenellae aetati ea veluti superstructa conveniebant, quibus jam adulta ac firmior non amplius indiget.
units.tr: XXIV. (8) To this also belonged especially the gift of miracles, by which those times of the Church were renowned. They went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Mark 16: 20; compare Heb. 2: 3, 4; Rom. 15: 18, 19; John 14: 12. Especially the gift of healing the sick belonged here. Matt. 10: 1; Mark 16: 18. For these were fitting for the infancy and tender age of the Church, as a kind of scaffolding built around it, which the Church, once grown up and stronger, no longer needs.

units.la: XXV. Exerebant autem ea non solum ad hominum salutem, sed & ad terrorem nonnunquam, ad hostes ac adversarios veritatis compescendos; quanquam rarius. A. 5. & 13. Eratque ejus quoque generis virga illa Apostolica, ac traditio in manum Satanae, in ipsa Ecclesia primitus usurpata; ubi severiore disciplina opus erat, ad insana & tabentia ejus membra secanda, & acriori remedio corrigenda: quod corporis saepe noxa, immissisque morbis, ac Satanae denique vexationibus fiebat, ut anima servaretur. Unde ista potestas solis Apostolis adscribitur: Quid vultis? cum virga ad vos veniam? 1. Cor. 4:21. Ob id hoc absens scribo, ne praesens severitate utar, secundum potestatem, quam mihi dedit Dominus. 2. Cor. 13:10. com. 2. coll. cap. 10:6. Quos tradidi ego Satanae, ut castigati discant non blasphemare. 1. Tim. 1:20. Ego —judicavi — talem tradere Satanae, ad perniciem carnis, ut Spiritus servetur in die Domini Jesu. 1. Cor. 5:3, 5. Omnem autem eam facultatem, non proprio lubitu, sed ex sapientissimo Dei consilio, prout gloriae ejus ac Euangelii propagationi conduceret, explicabant.
units.tr: XXV. They exercised these gifts not only for the salvation of men, but sometimes also for terror, to restrain the enemies and adversaries of the truth, though this was rarer. Acts 5 and 13. This kind of power also belonged to that apostolic rod, and to the handing over to Satan, which was first used in the Church itself, where a severer discipline was needed to cut away its mad and festering members and to correct them by a sharper remedy. This happened often by harm to the body, the sending of sicknesses, and finally by the afflictions of Satan, so that the soul might be saved. Hence this power is ascribed to the Apostles alone: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod? 1 Cor. 4: 21. For this reason I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not use severity, according to the authority which the Lord has given me. 2 Cor. 13: 10; compare 2 Cor. 10: 6. Whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn through punishment not to blaspheme. 1 Tim. 1: 20. I have judged to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. 1 Cor. 5: 3, 5. They used all this power not at their own pleasure but according to the most wise counsel of God, as it would serve his glory and the spread of the gospel.

units.la: XXVI. 9. Apostolicae praedicationis potentia & efficacia, praesentem semper Spiritum ostendens: unde tanta primae Ecclesiae incrementa. Et Ecclesia adjuncta sunt illo die animarum tanquam tria millia, Act. 2:41.
units.tr: XXVI. 9. The power and efficacy of apostolic preaching, always showing the Spirit present: hence the great growth of the first Church. And there were added to the Church that day about three thousand souls, Acts 2:41.

units.la: XXVII. 10. Quod non uni Ecclesiae affixi, communes mundi doctores constituti erant. Euntes ad discipulatum vocate omnes gentes. Matth. 28: 19. conf. Marc. 16: 15. Praeter ea, quae extra sunt – cura omnium Ecclesiarum, 2. Cor. 11: 28. Ita ut ab Hierosolyma, & circumjacentibus, usque ad Illyricum impleverim Euangelium Christi. Rom. 15: 19. Non pugnat vero cum eo, quod certo canone, 2. Cor. 10: 13, 15, 16. partitoque veluti orbe, cum universum permensi, opus Domini absolverint. Gentibus, dico, in quantum sum gentium Apostolus. Rom. 11: 13. Videntes, mihi concreditum esse Euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis. Gal. 2: 7.
units.tr: XXVII. 10. They were not attached to one Church but were appointed common teachers of the world. Go and make disciples of all nations, Matt. 28:19; cf. Mark 16:15. Besides those things which are outside, there is the care of all the Churches, 2 Cor. 11:28. So that from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions, as far as Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel of Christ, Rom. 15:19. This does not, however, conflict with their having worked, by a fixed rule (2 Cor. 10:13, 15, 16), and with the world divided, as it were, into parts, each finishing the work of the Lord once he had gone through his share. To the Gentiles, I say, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, Rom. 11:13. Seeing that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, just as the gospel of the circumcision to Peter, Gal. 2:7.

units.la: XXVIII. 11. Cumque novae Ecclesiae proceres forent, eique condendae a Deo singulariter electi, peracto opere nullos eo in munere successores reliquerunt. Cum enim per eos lex Dei jam publicata, & in medio omnium posita sit, Jer. 31: 33. aliud post illos verbum, aliudve Euangelium, expectari non debet; nec Apostolis post Apostolos opus est. Unde nullus postea tanta donorum copia, nec tanta in Ecclesia authoritate fuit, ut nomen istud tueri posset. Quod enim Episcopi nonnunquam Apostolorum successores, vel Apostolici appellati sint, id latiori sensu intelligendum est.
units.tr: XXVIII. 11. Since they were the leaders of the new Church, chosen singularly by God to establish it, once the work was complete they left no successors in that office. For since the law of God has now been published through them and placed in the midst of all, Jer. 31:33, no other word or other gospel should be expected after them, and the Apostles have no need of apostles after them. Hence no one afterwards had such an abundance of gifts, or such authority in the Church, as to be able to claim that title. For when bishops were sometimes called successors of the Apostles or apostolic, this must be understood in a looser sense.

units.la: XXIX. 12. Ex quibus omnibus surgit Apostolici muneris, supra omnia alia excellentia; ut nullum eo in terra fuerit majus, cum omnes alias functiones sacras dignitate & eminentia sua complecteretur: quibus ideo praeponitur Eph. 4: 11. 1. Cor. 12: 28. quo etiam pertinet specialis promissio illis facta, quod ἐν τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ sedituri essent super duodecim thronis, judicantes duodecim tribus Israel. Matth. 19: 28. Luc. 22: 29, 30. Preter has autem Apostolorum omnium praereliquis Ecclesiae Doctoribus praerogativas, an Petro praeterea quidquam praereliquis Apostolis tribuendum sit, suo deinceps loco commodius videbimus.
units.tr: XXIX. 12. From all this arises the office of the Apostles, pre-eminent above all others; so that no greater office existed on earth, since it embraced in its dignity and eminence all other sacred functions. For this reason it is placed before them (Eph. 4:11; 1 Cor. 12:28). To this also belongs the special promise made to them, that in the regeneration they would sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:29, 30.
