Apart from these prerogatives of all the Apostles over the rest of the teachers of the Church, we shall see in its proper place more conveniently whether anything further should be attributed to Peter above the other Apostles.

units.la: XXX. Electus autem in eorum numerum, ac veluti posthumus sacro isti collegio adscriptus quoque fuit Paulus; antea Saulus appellatus; quod nomen Benjaminitis usitatum erat; deinde in Apostolatu Paulus dictus, Act. 13: 9. Ad quem quidam referunt vaticinium Jacobi de Benjamine, Benjamin lupus, qui rapit: mane comedet praedam, & vesperi distribuet spolia. Gen. 49: 27. Paulo vero comes, seu collega potius in Apostolatu simul adjunctus fuit Barnabas, jussu Sp. sancti, dicentis: Separate mihi Barnabam & Saulum ad opus ad quod eos vocavi. Act. 13: 2. conf. Act. 14: 13. Gal. 2: 9.
units.tr: XXX. Paul, however, was also chosen into their number and joined to that sacred college as, so to speak, a late addition. Previously he was called Saul, a name customary among the Benjamites; afterwards, in his apostolate, he was called Paul (Acts 13:9). Some refer to him Jacob's prophecy about Benjamin: Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil, Gen. 49:27. Barnabas was joined with Paul as his companion, or rather colleague, in the apostolate, by command of the Holy Spirit, who said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them, Acts 13:2; cf. Acts 14:13; Gal. 2:9.

units.la: XXXI. Coepit autem Apostolorum munus, tum ante Christi mortem, quando procursu veluti in Ecclesiae campum facto, cui deinde laborandofefe totos impenluri erant, Euangelii sermone per Judaam ac Galilaeam diffuderunt, Matth. 10:7. reliquum autem tempus, hauriendæ Christi disciplinæ, ad latus ejus assiduì ac indivulsi egerunt: tum præsertim post mortem ac ascensum ejus, quando, à fuga sua in Christi morte recollecti, proprie ἀποστολὴν ac missionem suam acceperunt; non ad Judæos solum, sed ad gentis quoque; qui Apostolatus præcipuus character erat: Dicit autem eis iterum, pax vobis: sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos. Joh. 20:21. Profecti ergo, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos &c. Matth. 28: 19.
units.tr: XXXI. The apostolic office began, first before the death of Christ, when, as if a way had been opened into the field of the Church, to which they were afterwards to devote themselves wholly in labour, they spread the word of the gospel through Judea and Galilee (Matt. 10:7). They spent the rest of the time, in drawing in the discipline of Christ, close to his side, constantly and inseparably. Then, especially after his death and ascension, when, gathered again from their flight through the death of Christ, they properly received their apostleship and mission, not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles; this was the chief character of the apostolate: Jesus said to them again, Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you, John 20:21. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them, etc., Matt. 28:19.

units.la: XXXII. Munus obierunt tum docendo, tum scribendo, prout divina providentia varias ad id occasiones suppeditabat. Omne studium adhibens, de communi salute necesse habui scribere vobis, Jud. com. 3. Tenete traditiones, quas edocti estis, sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam nostram.
units.tr: XXXII. They discharged their office both by teaching and by writing, as divine providence supplied them with various occasions for it. Making every effort, I felt it necessary to write to you about our common salvation, Jude, verse 3. Hold to the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our letter.

units.la: 2. Thess. 2: 15. Nec confuso ordine, sed unusquisque juxta canonem ac lineam Apostolatus sui, singulis à Deo dimensam. Secundum mensuram canonis, quam distribuit nobis Deus. 2. Cor. 10: 13. non in alterius canone. com. 16. XXXIII. Ac primo quidem Hierosolymis Euangelii sermo auditus est, Esai. 2. Act. 2. Inde in Samariam pervenit, Act. 8. Quod auspicio (erant enim Samaritani, ut gente, ita & religione hybridæ, nec de Judæis prorsus censeri poterant (deinceps in reliquum orbem dispersus, primo Asiam; deinde, mare ac insulas pervagatus, Europam implevit; Græciam, Illyricum, Italiam, Hispaniam, continuo ordine permensus. Moxque etiam Africæ affusus; extremis denique temporibus Indiam utramque lustravit; ultimosque Orientis recessus, & Japonum ac Serum divites insulas ac terras Christianæ fidei gustu imbuit. Quæ vero de Apostolorum sortibus, quibus Thomæ Parthi, Andreæ Scythæ, Marco Ægyptus, reliquisque Apostolis reliquæ orbis partes obvenerunt narrantur, apocrypha sunt. XXXIV. Misit autem Christus, dum adhuc in terris versaretur, non longe ante excessium suum, post institutos jam Apostolos, de comitatu suo LXX discipulos; qui, brevi itinere Judæam peragrarent, eam universam Mensis jam præsentis fama implerent, regnumque ejus appropinquare nunciarent. Luc. 9: 2. & 10: 1. XXXV. Apostolis adjunguntur Prophetæ, Eph. 2: 20. 3: 5. 4: 11.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 2:15. Nor did they work in a confused order, but each according to the canon and line of his own apostolate, measured out to each by God: according to the measure of the canon which God has apportioned to us, 2 Cor. 10:13; not in another's canon, verse 16. XXXIII. First of all, the message of the gospel was heard at Jerusalem (Isa. 2; Acts 2). From there it came to Samaria (Acts 8), which, since the Samaritans were a mixed people both in race and in religion, and could not wholly be counted among the Jews, was a beginning. Afterwards, dispersed into the rest of the world, it first filled Asia; then, passing over the sea and the islands, it filled Europe, traversing in continuous order Greece, Illyricum, Italy, and Spain. Soon it also spread over Africa; in the last times it went through both Indias and imbued the most distant recesses of the East, and the rich islands and lands of the Japanese and the Chinese with a taste of the Christian faith. But what is told about the lots of the Apostles, by which Parthia fell to Thomas, Scythia to Andrew, Egypt to Mark, and the remaining parts of the world to the other Apostles, is apocryphal. XXXIV. Christ, while he was still on earth, not long before his departure, after the Apostles had now been appointed, sent out from his company seventy disciples, who, by a short journey, would traverse Judea, fill the whole of it with the report of his presence, and announce that his kingdom was drawing near (Luke 9:2; 10:1). XXXV. To the Apostles are joined the Prophets (Eph. 2:20; 3:5; 4:11).

units.la: 1. Cor. 12: 28. Act. 13: 1. 15: 32. tales autem sub N. F. appellabantur, qui, peculiari charismate veteres Scripturas explanabant; & prophetæ, phetarum interpretes, per Dei Spiritum, divinorum operum mysteria, necdum intellecta, evolvebant. 1. Cor. 14. futuraque praedicebant. Act. 11:27,28. & 20:10,11. 1. Tim. 1:18. 4:14.
units.tr: (1 Cor. 12:28; Acts 13:1; 15:32.) Under the New Testament those were called such who, by a special charisma, explained the ancient Scriptures; and the prophets, the interpreters of the prophets, through the Spirit of God, unfolded the mysteries of divine works not yet understood (1 Cor. 14), and foretold future things (Acts 11:27, 28; 20:10, 11; 1 Tim. 1:18; 4:14).

units.la: XXXVII. Evangelista, Apostolorum comites, & συνεργοί, ipsis volentibus & jubentibus, ad plantandum ubivis Evangelium mittebantur, inconversis illud praedicantes, conversos autem baptizantes, simulque miraculorum charismate aliquando donati. De quo ordine erant Marcus, Lucas, Philippus &c.
units.tr: XXXVII. The evangelists, companions and fellow workers of the Apostles, were sent, at their wish and command, to plant the gospel everywhere, preaching it to the unconverted and baptizing the converted, and at times they were also endowed with the gift of miracles. Mark, Luke, Philip, etc., were of this order.

units.la: XXXVIII. Praeter jam dictis functiones extraordinarias recensentur ab Apostolo dona 1. Cor. 12. extraordinaria, functionesque iis correspondentes, nimirum. χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων, ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων, διάκρισις πνευμάτων dona sanationum, operationes virtutum, discretio spirituum, com. 9. γένη γλωσσῶν, ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν, genera linguarum, interpretatio linguarum, com. 10. Item δυνάμεις virtutes, χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων dona sanationum, (conf. Marc. 6:5. & 16:17,18.) ἀντιλήψεις opitulationes, κυβερνήσεις gubernationes (aut profunda solertia) γένη γλωσσῶν genera linguarum, com. 28,29. quibus adduntur διερμηνεύοντες interpretantes, com. 29. De quibus omnibus singulatim nunc non agemus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Besides the functions already mentioned, the Apostle enumerates extraordinary gifts (1 Cor. 12) and the functions corresponding to them, namely: gifts of healings [χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων], workings of powers [ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων], discerning of spirits [διάκρισις πνευμάτων], the gifts of healing, the operations of powers, the discernment of spirits (v. 9); kinds of tongues [γένη γλωσσῶν], interpretation of tongues [ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν], the kinds of tongues, the interpretation of tongues (v. 10). Likewise powers [δυνάμεις], gifts of healings [χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων] (cf. Mark 6:5; 16:17, 18), helps [ἀντιλήψεις], governments [κυβερνήσεις] (or deep skill), kinds of tongues [γένη γλωσσῶν] (vv. 28, 29); to these are added interpreters [διερμηνεύοντες] (v. 29). We shall not deal with all of these individually now.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De Ministris N. F. ordinariis.
units.tr: On the Ordinary Ministers of the New Covenant.

units.la: I. Sequuntur ordinarii Ecclesiæ N. F. ministri, Pastores, ἡγούμενοι, προεστῶτες, ἐπίσκοποι, πρεσβύτεροι, promiscue dicti; nullo nominum aut officiorum in Scripturis, ac primæva antiquitate, secundum communiorem orthodoxorum sententiam, discrimine. Vide Act. 20:17. Missis autem Mileto nuncii Ephesum, accersivit Presbyteros Ecclesiæ. com. 28. Attendite ad totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus ille sanctus constituit episcopos. 1. Tim. 3:1. Si quis ἐπισκοπῆς inspectionem desiderat, bonum opus desiderat. com. 2. Oportet igitur τὸν ἐπίσκοπον inspectorem esse irreprehensibilem. Phil. 1:1. Paulus — sanctis in Christo Jesu, qui sunt Philippis, cum episcopis & Diaconis. Tit. 1:5. Reliqui te in Creta, ut quae desunt corrigas, & constitutas oppidatim presbyteros. com. 7. oportet enim Episcopum inculculpatum esse. 1. Pet. 5: 1, 2, 3, Presbyteros, qui inter vos sunt, precor ego una — presbyter — pascite gregem, qui penes vos est, ἐπισκοπῦντες illius inspectioni vacantes, non coacte, sed libenter &c.
units.tr: The ordinary ministers of the Church of the New Covenant follow: ministers, hēgoumenoi [ἡγούμενοι], proestōtes [προεστῶτες], episkopoi [ἐπίσκοποι], presbyteroi [πρεσβύτεροι], called by these names indiscriminately, since the Scriptures and primitive antiquity make no distinction between names or offices, according to the more common opinion of the orthodox. See Acts 20:17: But sending from Miletus to Ephesus, he summoned the elders of the church. (v. 28) Take heed to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops. 1 Tim. 3:1: If anyone desires the oversight [ἐπισκοπῆς] of the office, he desires a good work. (v. 2) It is necessary, therefore, that the overseer [τὸν ἐπίσκοπον] be blameless. Phil. 1:1: Paul ... to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons. Tit. 1:5: I left you in Crete so that you might correct what is lacking and appoint elders in every town. (v. 7) For a bishop must be blameless. 1 Pet. 5:1-3: I exhort the elders who are among you, I who am a fellow elder ... feed the flock which is among you, exercising oversight [ἐπισκοπῦντες] not by compulsion but willingly, etc.

units.la: II. Pastoribus adjunguntur Eph. 4: 11. Doctores. Quos quidam existimant distinctos fuisse a Pastoribus; cumque ab Apostolis per Ecclesias constituti non legantur, ut alii ministri, Act. 13:1. 1.Cor. 12:28,29. & 14: 6,26. Rom. 12: 6. censent eos ministros extraordinarios fuisse, viros nempe extraordinariis doctrinae donis praeditos, qui alios ministros informarent & ad Ecclesiarum ministerium praepararent ac instituerent. At vero longe rectius iidem statuuntur esse cum Pastoribus; tum quia Eph. 4: 11. ab iisdem non disjunguntur; tum quia, omisso pastorum nomine 1. Cor. 12:28,29. soli exprimuntur; ut videantur iidem qui διδάσκαλοι sunt quoque ποιμένες fuisse. Hi ergo ut ab una officii parte dicebantur ποιμένες & ἐπίσκοποι, ita ab alia appellabantur διδάσκαλοι, quatenus docebant Ecclesiam Dei, non ad primam fidei plantationem (quod aliorum erat) sed ad fidei confirmationem, per νουθεσίαν, παράκλησιν, instructionem, exhortationem, quibus Ecclesias jam plantatas jugi doctrinae rore amplius irrigabant & perficiebant. Quod enim ad Doctorum aut Professorum in Scholis gradus attinet, quales nunc sunt, ii longe recentiores sunt, quam ut in scriptis Apostolicis occurrant. Licet quantum ad rem ipsam attinet, nunquam in Ecclesia, etsi vario modo, defuerint Doctores, sive καθηγηταί magistri, qui doctrinam sacram per manus tradebant, non promiscuo fidelium vulgo, sed praecipue aliis, qui & ipsi Ecclesiae pastores aut magistri futuri erant.
units.tr: II. To the ministers Eph. 4:11 adds teachers. Some think these were distinct from the ministers, and since they are not recorded as being appointed by the Apostles through the Churches as the other ministers were (Acts 13:1; 1 Cor. 12:28, 29; 14:6, 26; Rom. 12:6), they hold that the teachers were extraordinary ministers, men endowed with extraordinary gifts of teaching, who instructed other ministers and prepared and trained them for the ministry of the Churches. But it is far more correct to hold that they are the same as the ministers: first, because Eph. 4:11 does not separate them from the ministers; second, because in 1 Cor. 12:28, 29 the word ministers is omitted and only the teachers are named, so that they appear to be the same persons who were also called ministers [ποιμένες]. Thus, as they were called ministers [ποιμένες] and overseers [ἐπίσκοποι] in one part of their office, so in another part they were called teachers [διδάσκαλοι], inasmuch as they taught the Church of God, not for the first planting of faith (which was the task of others) but for the confirmation of faith, by admonition [νουθεσίαν], exhortation [παράκλησιν], instruction, and encouragement, by which they watered and perfected the Churches already planted with the constant dew of doctrine. As for the rank of teachers or professors in schools, such as exist today, these are much too recent to occur in the Apostolic writings. Yet, as far as the thing itself is concerned, there have never been lacking in the Church, though in various ways, teachers or instructors [καθηγηταί], who handed on sacred doctrine by the laying on of hands, not to the common crowd of the faithful indiscriminately, but especially to others who were themselves to become ministers or teachers of the Church.

units.la: III. Semper enim munus illud in Ecclesia viguit. In Veteri enim Testam. Prophetae, ac prophetarum filii; ac posteriores temporibus Scribae, γραμματεῖς dicti, illud exercuerunt. Qui peculiari quoque ritu creabantur. Ac convenit ipsum Doctorum nomen cum magistrorum Hebraeorum titulo Rabbi: qui iis peculiariter tribuebatur, qui, legis divinae periti, eam aliis docendi auctoritatem habebant. Quales Gamaliel, Act. 5. & Nicodemus, Joh. 3. Unde & Christo nomen istud saepe datum legimus; & a Paulo quoque assumtum, quod publicus orbis magister foret. 1. Tim. 2: 7. 2. Tim. 1:2. Celebratur autem inde a Christianismi exordio potissimum hoc nomine Ecclesia Alexandrina: ubi frequentes tales διατριβαί & Scholae; praefectique iis Catechetae, Pantaenus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origines &c. Ut omnino ab istis retro saeculis diversum hoc a Presbyteris seu Episcopis, in Ecclesia munus fuerit. Quin & tanto gravius Doctoribus incumbit onus, quanto majus est ad clerum, quam ad plebem loqui: unde pastoris partes satis recte multi explent, qui tamen doctoris muneri pares non sint. Neque repugnat locus Matth. 23: 8, 10. Vos ne vocamini Rabbi. Nam, ut alia mittamus, non ibi munus, aut titulus, sed magistrale supercilium, & fastus, aliaque paedagogorum istorum crimina, notantur.
units.tr: III. This office has always flourished in the Church. In the Old Testament the prophets and the sons of the prophets exercised it, and in later times the scribes, called scribes [γραμματεῖς], did so too; these were also installed with a special rite. The very name teachers agrees with the title Rabbi of the Hebrew masters, which was given in particular to those who, being skilled in the divine law, had authority to teach it to others. Such were Gamaliel (Acts 5) and Nicodemus (John 3). Hence we read that this title was often given to Christ, and Paul also assumed it, so that he might be a public teacher of the world (1 Tim. 2:7; 2 Tim. 1:2). From the beginning of Christianity, the Church of Alexandria was especially renowned under this name, where there were frequent lecture-halls [διατριβαί] and schools, presided over by catechists: Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others. So this office in the Church was entirely different from that of elders or bishops in those earlier centuries. Moreover, the burden on teachers is all the heavier, the more it is greater to speak to the clergy than to the common people; hence many who fulfil the duties of a minister quite well are nonetheless not equal to the office of teacher. Nor does Matt. 23:8, 10 stand in the way: Do not be called Rabbi. For, to pass over other points, that passage does not condemn the office or the title, but the schoolmasterly arrogance and pride, and the other faults of those pedagogues.

units.la: IV. Est autem munus illud pastorum & doctorum in Ecclesia ordinarium & perpetuum; contra ac Libertinorum cohors, Zwenkfeldiani, ac Enthusiastae, furunt. Hoc enim requirit Ecclesiae aedificatio; ut ne ordinario verbi ac doctrinae pastu fraudetur; vel sine rectore ac regimine, naufragae pupis instar, jactetur & fluctuet. Fides ex auditu. Auditus autem per verbum Dei Rom. 10: 17. Ipse dedit alios Apostolos, alios autem Evangelistas, alios vero pastores & doctores; ad concinnationem sanctorum; ad opus ministerii, ad aedificationem corporis Christi; donec perveniamus omnes ad unicatem fidei &c. Eph. 4: 11, 12, 13. Reliqui te in Creta, ut quae desunt corrigas, & constitues oppidatim presbyteros. Tit. 1: 5. Quumque ipsis per suffragia creassent per singulas Ecclesias presbyteros, precatique essent cum jejuniis, commendarunt eos Domino. Act. 14: 23. De loco autem Jer. 31: 34. de Spiritu, ut illi putant, doctore, absque externo ministerio, supra respondimus lib. v. cap. 11. §. 11.
units.tr: IV. This office of ministers and teachers is ordinary and perpetual in the Church, contrary to the raving of the Libertine rabble, the Schwenckfeldians, and the Enthusiasts. For the building up of the Church requires it, so that it may not be deprived of the ordinary food of the Word and doctrine, or be tossed and tossed about without a pilot or government, like a shipwrecked boat. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God (Rom. 10:17). He himself gave some as apostles, some as evangelists, and some as ministers and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith etc. (Eph. 4:11, 12, 13). I left you in Crete so that you might correct what is lacking and appoint elders in each town (Titus 1:5). When they had appointed elders for them in each Church by vote, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord (Acts 14:23). As for the passage Jer. 31:34, about the Spirit as teacher, as they suppose, without external ministry, I have answered above in Book V, chapter 11, §11.

units.la: V. Munus pastorum, tum in publico verbi, precum ac Sacramentorum, ministerio; tum in reliqua gregis cura consistit. καλὸν ἔργον Apostolus vocat, 1. Tim. 3: 1. Quod alpernantur illi magnae meretricis amasii, qui, in episcopatu non tam opus, quam opes, & dignitatem, spectantes, alii, commissos sibi populos suffraganeis & vicariis regendos tradunt; alii titulares, ac revera solo titulo episcopi sunt.
units.tr: V. The office of ministers consists both in the public ministry of the Word, prayers, and the Sacraments, and in the care of the rest of the flock. The Apostle calls it a good work [καλὸν ἔργον] (1 Tim. 3:1). Those who are lovers of the great harlot reject this, who in the episcopate look not so much to the work as to the wealth and dignity; some hand over the peoples committed to them to be governed by suffragans and vicars, others are merely titular, and in reality bishops in name only.

units.la: VI. Ac perperam quidem nonnulli primitivae Ecclesiae pastores ad regimen potissimum electos; verbi autem praedicandi potestatem promiscuam, & a cunctis, qui modo donis pollerent, exercitam ajunt. Quo referunt 1. Pet. 4: 10. Ut quisque accepit donum, ita alius in alium illud subministrantes, ut boni dispensatores variae Dei gratiae. Si quis loquitur, loquatur ut eloquia Dei. Col. 3: 16. Sermo Christi habitet in vobis copiose, in omni sapientia: docentes & monentes vos invicem. Eph. 5: 18. Et ne inebriamini vino, in quo est luxuria; sed implemini Spiritu. 1. Thess. 5: 11. Quapropter adhortamini alii alios, & edificate singuli singulos, sicut facitis. Ac praesertim Corinthiacae plebis exemplum. 1. Cor. 14. Ex Judaicarum Synagogarum instituto, ubi & in imo subsellio sedenti surgendi, ac publice bonum verbum proloquendi facultas fuerit. Act. 13: 14, 15, 16. Venerunt Antiochiam Pisidiae, & ingressi Synagogam die Sabbati, consederunt. Post lectionem autem legis & prophetarum, miserunt praefecti Synagogae ad eos, dicentes: viri fratres, si quis est in vobis sermo exhortationis ad populum, dicite. Assurgens igitur Paulus &c. conf. c. 18: 24. & 11: 20. & Luc. 4: 15. Et ipse docebat in Synagogis eorum, omnibus ipsum glorificantibus. Quod autem hodie pauci in concionem prodeant, id in majoribus coetibus servandi solum ordinis causa fieri.
units.tr: VI. Some wrongly say that the ministers of the early Church were chosen mainly for governing, and that the power of preaching the Word was shared and exercised by all who were gifted. To this they refer 1 Pet. 4:10: As each has received a gift, so use it to serve one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God. Col. 3:16: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another. Eph. 5:18: And do not get drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit. 1 Thess. 5:11: Therefore encourage one another, and build up one another, just as you are doing. They also appeal especially to the example of the Corinthian people, 1 Cor. 14, and to the custom of the Jewish synagogues, where even one sitting on the lowest bench had the right to stand up and publicly speak a good word. Acts 13:14, 15, 16: They came to Antioch in Pisidia, and entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, "Brothers, if there is any word of exhortation for the people, speak." So Paul stood up etc. See also Acts 18:24; 11:20; and Luke 4:15: He himself taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. That few come forward to preach today is done only for the sake of order in larger gatherings.

units.la: VII. Contra autem est, quod Scriptura tam saepe, & tam expresse, in episcopis & pastoribus requirit docendi donum. Oportet igitur inspectorem esse — διδακτικὸν docendi peritum, 1. Tim. 3: 2. Affixum sermoni fideli, secundum doctrinam, ut valeat & adhortari in doctrina sana, & contradicentes redarguere. Tit. 1: 9. Qui laborant in sermone, & doctrina &c. 1. Tim. 5: 17. Ut in Apostolica Ecclesia presbyteros non magis ad regendum quam ad docendum institutos pateat. Imo hoc publicum ac peculiare ipsorum munus erat, dicente Apostolo, Christum, ubi terras relinqueret, dedisse alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios vero Evangelistas, alios autem Pastores & Doctores ad concinnationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad aedificationem corporis Christi, donec perveniamus omnes ad unitatem fidei &c. Eph. 4: 11, 12, 13. Quod autem Corinthiacae Ecclesiae προφῆται spectat, illa magna ex parte extraordinaria fuit; in quantum vero ordinaria fuit, in minoribus quidem coetibus certo ordine institui, vix autem in publica frequentia ac panegyri exerceri potest. Omnia enim ex ordine & decoro peragi, Apostolus eodem capite jussit. Interest autem ut publice nemo loquatur nisi ad illud vocatus, & ab Ecclesia probatus. De Synagogis vero Judaeorum, omnique illorum disciplina, alibi respondemus.
units.tr: VII. On the contrary, Scripture so often and so expressly requires the gift of teaching in bishops and ministers: It is necessary therefore that the overseer be [διδακτικὸν] skilled in teaching (1 Tim. 3:2). Holding firmly to the faithful word as taught, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Those who labour in the word and teaching etc. (1 Tim. 5:17). So it is plain that in the Apostolic Church elders were appointed not so much for ruling as for teaching. Indeed, this was their public and special office, since the Apostle says that Christ, when he left the earth, gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as ministers and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith etc. (Eph. 4:11, 12, 13). As for the prophets of the Corinthian Church, that gift was for the most part extraordinary; but insofar as it was ordinary, it could be set in order in smaller assemblies, though it could hardly be exercised in a public and crowded assembly. For the Apostle commanded in the same chapter that everything be done in order and decency. It is also necessary that no one speak publicly unless called to it and approved by the Church. As for the synagogues of the Jews and their whole discipline, I answer elsewhere.

units.la: VIII. Ulterius tendit nuperus auctor; qui, edito libello, Ecclesias Christianas multis saeculis Apostaticas fuisse criminatur, quod verbum Dei infallibile a ministris fallibilibus Dei nomine ac auctoritate, publice exponi faciant; inque co non parvam religionis ac cultus divini partem constituant. Suadet autem ipse, dum novi orbis Doctores expectantur, novusque Apostolatus oriatur, nudum Scripturae textum, sine ulla explicatione, in coetibus proponi; idque unum pro omni catechesi haberi. Quod etiam Adolphi Venatoris, A. C. 1617. consilium erat. Quod quam latam Libertinismo, ac teterrimis haeresibus, portam aperiat, supra vidimus; ac talem Ecclesiæ noxam longe abominati sumus. Nec magnum crimen est, ab hominibus fallibilibus infallibile Dei verbum exponi. Quasi non & in Veteri Test. hoc factum: & non ipse Christus, post Apostolos, fallibiles Ecclesiæ Pastores & Doctores dederit, Eph. 4. atque omnia sapientiæ, prophetiæ, & interpretationis, dona in Ecclesia inutilia jacere debeant, quod infallibilitatis privilegio careant: nec aliter denique verbum Dei tractari, vel Ecclesia ædificari possit, quam per Doctores infallibiles. Nec peccant tandem qui in coetu loquuntur, si loquantur ὡς λόγια θεῦ 1. Pet. 4: 11. imo omnem operam ad eam rem dare debent. Debetque universus coetus coire in nomine Dei, Matth. 18:20. utque omnia, ita præsertim sacra, & verbi ac sacramentorum administrationem, in sancto ejus nomine peragere. Matth. 28: 19. Col. 3: 17. Et omne quod facitis, in sermone aut in opere, omnia facite in nomine Domini Jesu, gratias agentes Deo & Patri per ipsum. Manere ergo debet in Ecclesia publica Scripturarum scrutatio, & παραγγελία annunciatio; 1. Tim. 1: 5. Quæ ut rite fiat, in enucleandis illis quatuor illa capita, quæ Apostolus refert, præcipue attendenda sunt. Omnis Scriptura à Deo inspirata etiam utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad regendum in justitia. 2. Tim. 3: 16.
units.tr: VIII. The recent author goes further. In a small book he accuses the Christian churches of having been apostate for many centuries because they have their fallible ministers publicly expound the infallible Word of God in God's name and authority, and they make this a not small part of religion and divine worship. He himself urges that, while the teachers of the new world are awaited and a new apostolate arises, the bare text of Scripture be set before the assemblies without any explanation, and that this alone be held as the whole of catechesis. This was also the plan of Adolph Venator in 1617. We have already seen how wide a door this opens to Libertinism and the most hideous heresies, and we have utterly abhorred such harm to the Church. Nor is it a great crime for fallible men to expound the infallible Word of God. As if this was not also done in the Old Testament! As if Christ himself, after the Apostles, had not given fallible pastors and teachers to the Church (Eph. 4), and as if all the gifts of wisdom, prophecy and interpretation must lie useless in the Church because they lack the privilege of infallibility! Nor, in short, could the Word of God be handled otherwise, or the Church be built up, except through infallible teachers. Nor do those sin who speak in the assembly, if they speak "as the oracles of God" [ὡς λόγια θεοῦ] (1 Pet. 4:11); indeed they ought to devote every effort to this. And the whole congregation ought to meet in the name of God (Matt. 18:20), and to carry on all things, and especially sacred things, the administration of the Word and the sacraments, in his holy name (Matt. 28:19). "And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father through him" (Col. 3:17). Therefore public scrutiny of the Scriptures and the proclamation [παραγγελία] must remain in the Church (1 Tim. 1:5). So that this may be done rightly, special attention must be given to unfolding those four heads which the Apostle sets out: "All Scripture inspired by God is also profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness" (2 Tim. 3:16).

units.la: IX. Præter verbum, etiam Sacramenta tractare pastorum est. Conjungit enim illa Christus Matth. 28: 19,20. Profecti docete omnes gentes, baptisantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus S. docentes eos servare omnia quæ mandavi vobis. Quanquam nullum peculiarem characterem, aut potestatem, qualem Pontificii in conficiendis sacramentis sacerdotibus suis tribuunt, in illis agnoscamus. Hæc enim ad Veteris Testam. inaugurationes, & consecrationes ac cærimonialem personarum sanctitatem pertinent. Turbant autem ab alia parte ordinem illum Sociniani; qui, ut verbi, ita & sacramentorum, potestatem omnibus fidelibus ex æquo faciunt. Quod ad mulieres, sed innuptas, Episcopius ratione Cœnæ extendit. Contra Apostolum, 1. Cor. 14: 34, 35. Mulieris vestra in conventibus sileant. Nec enim permissum est eis ut loquantur, sed oportet ut subdita sint, sicut & Lex dicit. Quod si quid discere volunt, domi suos viros interrogent: Nam turpe est mulieribus in Ecclesia loqui. & 1. Tim. 2: 12. Mulieri vero docere non permitto.
units.tr: IX. Besides the Word, the handling of the sacraments also belongs to the pastors. For Christ joins them together: "Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you" (Matt. 28:19, 20). Yet we do not acknowledge in these any peculiar character or power, such as the Papists attribute to their priests in administering the sacraments. For these things pertain to the inaugurations and consecrations of the Old Testament and to the ceremonial holiness of persons. On the other hand, the Socinians disturb that order, for they make the power of the Word and of the sacraments alike for all the faithful. Episcopius extends this to unmarried women with respect to the Lord's Supper, contrary to the Apostle: "Let your women keep silence in the congregations. For it is not permitted to them to speak, but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also the Law says. And if they want to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home; for it is shameful for women to speak in the Church" (1 Cor. 14:34, 35), and 1 Tim. 2:12: "But I do not permit a woman to teach."

units.la: X. Reliqua, quæ privatim ad presbyterorum officium spectant; utque illi gregem curare & obire; & languentes oves erigere; ferroculas & petulantes coërcere; ac devias denique quærere, & ad caulas compellere debeant ; Apostolus totis ad Timotheum & Titum epistolis exequitur. Ac pertinet huc 1. Pet. 5. Ezech. 34. Joh. 10. Act. 20. 1. Cor. 9. Opera hic maxime danda, ut gregem Dei pascant illiusque inspectioni vacent, μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς, ἀλλ' ἑκουσίως, non coacte, sed libenter: non turpiter affectantes lucrum, sed prompto animo: neque ὡς κατακυριεύοντες ut dominantes cleri, sed ut facti exemplaria gregis. 1. Pet. 5:2, 3. Regimen enim Ecclesiæ ministris concessum non est coactivum, non debet enim Episcopus esse πλήκτης percussor, Tit. 1:7. sed directivum duntaxat.
units.tr: X. The remaining duties which pertain privately to the office of the elders, namely that they ought to care for and attend to the flock, raise up the weak sheep, restrain the wanton and unruly, and finally seek out the straying and bring them back to the fold, the Apostle sets out at length in his epistles to Timothy and Titus. To this belong also 1 Pet. 5, Ezek. 34, John 10, Acts 20, and 1 Cor. 9. Here the chief care must be given that they "feed the flock of God and attend to its oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, not greedily for gain but with a ready mind, not lording it over those entrusted to them [ὡς κατακυριεύοντες], as the clergy do, but being examples to the flock" (1 Pet. 5:2, 3). For the governing of the Church granted to ministers is not coercive; the bishop must not be a striker [πλήκτης] (Titus 1:7), but only directive.

units.la: XI. Necessaria ad hanc curam est pastoris præsentia, seu residentia.
units.tr: XI. The presence, or residence, of the pastor is necessary for this care.

units.la: XI. Necessaria ad hanc curam est pastoris præsentia, seu residen- tia. Quemadmodum rogavit manere Ephesi, quum profecisceretur in Macedoniam; ut denunciaret quibusdam non aliter docere. 1. Tim. 1:3. Quam mille artificiis in Concilio Tridentino eludere tentavere Episcopi Itali: connivente ad eam labem Urbico Episcopo.
units.tr: XI. The presence, or residence, of the pastor is necessary for this care. Just as Paul asked Timothy to remain at Ephesus when he set out for Macedonia, so that he might charge certain people not to teach otherwise (1 Tim. 1:3). By how many devices the Italian bishops tried to evade this at the Council of Trent, with Bishop Urbicus conniving at that disgrace!

units.la: XII. Potest tamen, sæviente persecutione, si non tam grex, quam gregis custos peratur, paulisper de Ecclesia secedere, & ad meliora tempora sese servare. Quum autem persequuntur vos in ea urbe, fugite in aliam. Matth. 10:23. 2. Cor. 11:32, 33. Quod & Cyprianum Carthagine fecisse legimus. Cæteroquin, in communi periculo, non fugere, sed pro grege animam ponere debet. Bonus pastor animam deponit pro ovibus. Mercenarius vero, quique non est pastor, cujus non sunt oves propriæ, videt lupum venientem, & omittet oves, & fugit: & lupus rapit eas, & dissipat oves. Joh. 10:11, 12. Quod & in pestilentiæ, aliorumque morborum contagie faciendum, si aliter Ecclesiæ prospici non potest; nec unquam illa Pastoris abitu desolanda.
units.tr: XII. Yet, when persecution rages, if the shepherd is sought rather than the flock's guardian, he may for a while withdraw from the Church and keep himself for better times: "When they persecute you in one city, flee to another" (Matt. 10:23; cf. 2 Cor. 11:32, 33). We read that Cyprian did this at Carthage. Otherwise, in a common danger, he ought not to flee but to lay down his life for the flock: "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. But the hired hand, who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf snatches them and scatters the sheep" (John 10:11, 12). The same must be done in the contagion of plague or of other diseases, if the Church cannot otherwise be provided for; yet the Church must never be left desolate by the departure of its pastor.

units.la: XII. Di vellunt autem sacra munia, & sacros ordines, sine causa, multiplicant Anabaptistæ; dum in coetibus suis alios Episcopos, alios Paracletos, habent. Quorum hi, nulla magnopere auctoritate in gregem pollentes, solo verbi ministerio funguntur; illi vero, præcipuam Ecclesiarum curam gerentes, sacramenta administrandi, cunctaque Ecclesias regendi ex æquo potestatem habent. Quæ contra ordinem ab Apostolis institutum sunt. Eam & presbyterorum ἰσοτιμίαν, communemque illum episcopatum, cujus singuli partem possident, tollunt, contra Act. 20:28. Attendite — ad gregem totum, in quo vos Spiritus ille S. constituit Episcopos ad pascendum Ecclesiam Dei. coll. com. 17. Missis autem Mileto nunciis Ephesum, accersivit presbyteros Ecclesiæ. & unum hominem pluribus Ecclesiis imponunt; contra Tit. 1:5.—Et con-
units.tr: XII. The Anabaptists, however, multiply sacred offices and holy orders without cause, since in their assemblies they have some bishops and others as "paracletes." Of these, the latter, having no great authority over the flock, perform only the ministry of the Word; the former, bearing the chief care of the Churches, have the power both to administer the sacraments and equally to govern the Churches. These things are contrary to the order instituted by the Apostles. They also abolish the equal honour [ἰσοτιμίαν] of the elders and that common episcopate of which each holds a part, contrary to Acts 20:28: "Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God"; compare verse 17: "And sending from Miletus to Ephesus, he called the elders of the Church." And they set one man over several Churches, contrary to Titus 1:5: "That you should appoint elders in every town"; "for a bishop must be blameless". Finally, they tear apart the administration of the sacraments and of the Word in a perverse way, and they put the latter after the former, contrary to 1 Cor. 1:17: "For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel", etc.

units.la: Ppp constituas oppidatim presbyteros — oportet autem Episcopum inculpatum esse. ac denique sacramentorum & verbi administrationem perverse nimis discerpunt; atque hanc illi postponunt. contra 1. Cor. 1: 17. Non enim misit me Christus ut baptizarem, sed ut Evangelizarem &c.
units.tr: XIV. After the office of the ministers follows the calling of the minister; the support of the one called; and the removal of the unworthy. constituas oppidatim presbyteros — oportet autem Episcopum inculpatum esse.

units.la: XIV. Post ministrorum officium, sequitur ministri vocatio; vocati sustentatio; & indigni abdicatio.
units.tr: XIV. After the office of the ministers follows the calling of the minister, the support of the one called, and the removal of the unworthy.

units.la: XV. Est enim omnino vocatio, ad hoc munus gerendum, necessaria. Et non sibi quis sumit honorem hunc, sed qui vocatur a Deo, ut & Aaron. Hebr. 5: 4. Quomodo vero predicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? quemadmodum scriptum est, quam speciosi pedes Evangelizantium pacem? Rom. 10: 15. Non misi Prophetas, & illi cucurrerunt; non locutus sum ad ipsos, & illi vaticinati sunt. Jer. 23: 2.
units.tr: XV. For a calling to bear this office is wholly necessary: "And no one takes this honour for himself, but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was" (Heb. 5:4). "How shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, how beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace" (Rom. 10:15). "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied" (Jer. 23:21).

units.la: XVI. Est autem ea tum legitima, ubi vir Dei, cum aptitudinem, tum charitatem, ad pascendum gregem, sufficientem habens, piorum desideriis ad istam curam vocatur; & universae Ecclesiae, eorumque quorum hoc est, consensu, dominico ovili praeficitur; & solemni denique ritu, inauguratur.
units.tr: XVI. A calling is lawful when a man of God, who has both the fitness and the love to feed the flock, is called to this care by the desires of the godly; is set over the Lord's fold with the consent of the whole Church and of those to whom this belongs; and is finally installed with a solemn rite.

units.la: XVII. Cum autem ministerium, seu functio, a Deo sit: hominum quidem est, personam designare; muneris autem auctoritas ac potestas omnis a solo Deo derivanda est.
units.tr: XVII. Since the ministry, or office, is from God, it is for men indeed to designate the person, but all authority and power of the office must be derived from God alone.

units.la: XVIII. Unde pendet quoque vocatio originaliter a Domino, cujus est ministros legere, inque arvum Ecclesiae immittere. Et distinctiones ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus. 1. Cor. 12: 5. Et alios quidem constituit Deus in Ecclesia, primum Apostolos, deinde Prophetas, tertio Doctores &c. com. 28. Rogate igitur Dominum messis, ut emittat operarios in messem suam. Matth. 9: 38.
units.tr: XVIII. Hence the calling also depends originally on the Lord, whose task it is to choose ministers and send them into the field of the Church. There are differences of ministries, but it is the same Lord. 1 Cor. 12:5. And God has set some in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, etc., v. 28. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest that he would send out labourers into his harvest. Matt. 9:38.

units.la: XIX. Ordinatio autem istam curam Ecclesiae mandavit; quae, divinae vocationi morem gerens, certos homines, e reliquo coetu electos, supremo in gradu, tanquam in specula, collocat, ad res Ecclesiae curandas. Ut videlicet qui Ecclesiae ministraturus est, id non nisi auctoritate ejus faciat; ac, conscia ea, ac suffragante, ministerium accipiat. Quod Apostolos, quanquam summa potestate praeditos, servasse semper legimus: qui non nisi populi auctoritate & consensu Ecclesiastica munera mandare soliti erant. Vide Act. 1: 15, 23 & 6: 2, 5, 6. & 13: 1. &c. & 14: 23. Tit. 1: 5. Ne autem in magnis coetibus seditiose quidpiam agatur, rectorum judicia reliquo populo praeire non incongruum est: cui tamen, ad concionem vocato, rogationi facta vel annuere, vel abnuere, re, integrum semper manere debet. Suntque hic etiam peculiares magistratui partes; cuius est, de vocatione facta arbitrari, eamque vel accipere vel improbare. Cuius etiam est ministris Ecclesiae in suo territorio publice docendi potestatem facere: sicuti & docentibus honoraria constituere, iisque de cibariis prospicere, debet. Quin & in variis reformati orbis partibus majus quippiam pollet, ac instar patris familias, sui fundi Ecclesiis de sacrorum ministris prospicit, doctoresque invitat: quorum vocationem eo nomine tanquam illegitimam taxare velle, hominis esset, seipsum Ecclesiaeque suae ordinem, ut mollissime dicam, nimium amantis. Ubi vero Magistratus non est Ecclesiae filius, illiusque curam abjicit, ibi ipsa Ecclesia confoederata disciplina omnia supplet, ipsumque magistratus jus exercet.
units.tr: XIX. Good order, however, has committed this care of the Church to the Church itself. In obedience to the divine calling, the Church sets certain men, chosen from the rest of the assembly, in the highest rank, as on a watchtower, to take charge of the affairs of the Church. So that whoever is to serve the Church does nothing except by its authority, and receives the ministry with its knowledge and approval. We read that the apostles, though endowed with supreme power, always observed this, since they were accustomed to entrust ecclesiastical offices only with the authority and consent of the people. See Acts 1:15, 23; 6:2, 5, 6; 13:1, etc.; 14:23; Titus 1:5. Yet, lest anything seditious be done in large assemblies, it is not out of place for the judgement of the rulers to go before the rest of the people; still, the people, called to an assembly, should always remain free in fact either to assent to or to refuse the proposal made. Here the magistrate also has his own part: it is his to judge the calling that has been made and either to accept or to reject it. It is also his to grant ministers of the Church the power of teaching publicly in his territory, and he ought to provide honoraria for teachers and food for them. Indeed, in various parts of the reformed world the magistrate carries greater weight, and like the father of a household he provides for the churches of his lands with ministers of the sacred things and invites teachers. For anyone to wish to condemn their calling as illegitimate on that ground would be the act of a man who loves himself, and the order of his own Church, far too much, to put it very mildly. But where the magistrate is not a son of the Church and casts off its care, there the Church itself, bound together by a common discipline, supplies everything, and itself exercises the right of the magistrate.

units.la: XX. De jure patronatus hic etiam quaeri solet.
units.tr: XX. On the right of patronage, which is also customarily asked about here.

units.la: Cum autem antiqua valde sit beneficiorum, in electiva & collativa distinctio; ac juri isti multae Ecclesiae reformationem suam debeant: ubi illud publice agnitum & receptum est, interim pestive nimis obstrepere ei ac obluctari velle, ac litigiis istis Ecclesiae pacem quatere, temerarium est.
units.tr: Since the distinction between elective and collative benefices is very ancient, and many Churches owe their reformation to that right, it is rash to clamour against it and to wish to fight it at the wrong time, and to shake the peace of the Church with such lawsuits, when that right has been publicly acknowledged and received.

units.la: XXI. Cum autem Ecclesia dotes necessarias ministris largiri non possit, vocationem praecedere debet vocandorum exploratio. Et hi vero probantur prius, postea ministrent, vacantes accusatione. 1. Tim. 3: 10. Qui morum ac doctrinae testimonio ornati, & muneri, ad quod vocantur, pares ac insigni quadam charitate ardentes esse debent; juxta canones Apostolicos, 1. Tim. 3. Tit. 1. Non enim temere cuiquam manus imponendae, 1. Tim. 5:22 Sicuti, ab alia parte, inviti, uti aliquando factum, ad ambonem rapiendi, & ad sacram vestem sumendam cogendi non sunt. Ad sacrorum autem opprobrium vergeret, florente ac delicato hoc saeculo, illiteratis ac ἀμυήτοις, sine discrimine, sacra munera tradere velle; quod temporum necessitate olim excusatum fuit.
units.tr: XXI. Since the Church cannot bestow the necessary endowments on ministers, the examination of those to be called must precede the calling. And let these first be tested; then let them minister, being without blame. 1 Tim. 3:10. They ought to be adorned with the testimony of their morals and teaching, and to be fit for the office to which they are called and to burn with a certain remarkable love; according to the Apostolic canons, 1 Tim. 3; Titus 1. For hands are not to be laid hastily on anyone, 1 Tim. 5:22. On the other hand, they are not to be unwilling, nor to be snatched up to the pulpit, as has sometimes been done, nor compelled to take up the sacred vestment. But it would turn to the disgrace of the sacred things, in this flourishing and fastidious age, to wish to hand over the sacred offices indiscriminately to the illiterate and the uninitiated [ἀμυήτοις]. This was once excused by the necessity of the times.

units.la: XXII. Nec digni tantum, sed dignissimi eligendi, ac ceteris praeferendi sunt. Omnisque ab Ecclesia exulare debet προσωπολημψία, Jac. 2: 1. Quae tum committitur, cum externam personam aestimantes, inque reflexibus quibusdam, quae ad rem non pertinent, haerentes, isto fuco capti, indignioribus suffragamur; aliosque, quanquam dignos, eo solo, quod istam in mundo personam non praeferant, ac inanibus illis aeque non valeant, viliores habemus. XXIII. Vitanda etiam Simonis, ac turpe in re sacra mercimonium. Quod malum ex sacerdotiorum opulentia, immensisque reditibus, olim profluxit. Quae sine pretio acquiri, in tanta captatorum turba, non poterant. Ac inventus color est, non pro officio ac cura spirituali, sed pro temporali ei annexo illam qualemcunque remunerationem dari. Sicuti in Papatu sacri ordines gratis quidem conferri; pro titulo autem & Episcopatu aliove honore collato merces persolvi solet. Quo Pallii Annatarum, aliaque exactionum nomina spectant. Nec hydra illa, utcunque saepius repressa, extirpari penitus potuit. In Tridentino enim Concilio, utcunque multus ca de re sermo, nihil serio actum.
units.tr: XXII. Not only the worthy but the most worthy are to be chosen and preferred to others. And all respect of persons [προσωπολημψία] must be banished from the Church, James 2:1. This is committed when men, valuing an outward person and clinging to certain side matters that have nothing to do with the thing itself, are captivated by this paint and give their votes to the less worthy; and we hold others, though worthy, in lower esteem only because they do not carry that personal show in the world and are not equally strong in those empty things. XXIII. The simony of Simon, and the shameful traffic in sacred things, must also be avoided. This evil once arose from the wealth of the priestly offices and their immense revenues. These could not be obtained without a price in so great a crowd of seekers. And a pretext was devised, that the reward was given not for the office and spiritual care but for the temporal benefits attached to it. Thus in the Papacy, holy orders are indeed conferred freely, but payment is usually made for the title, the episcopate, or some other honour conferred. To this belong the names of the palls, annates and other exactions. Nor could that hydra, however often checked, be wholly exterminated. For in the Council of Trent, however much was said about this matter, nothing was seriously done.

units.la: XXIV. Posuit praeter haec Romana Ecclesia ministris Coelibatus legem. De Coelibatu enim votivo, in quem Monachorum familiae jurant, alibi agimus. Est autem haec Ecclesiae Romanae lex, nemini, nisi in castimoniam voto, sacra tractare licere. Quo pacto & nuptias prohibent: cum amores conjugum, Deo ipsi probatos, incestos esse jubent: & Spiritus charismata in conjugatis coercent: ac denique, contra Judaicae, Apostolicae, & primaevae Christianorum Ecclesiae exempla, ac Apostolorum ipsorum monita praescribere, iisque omnibus legem illa sua obrogare praesumunt. Estque hoc potestatis ipsorum legislatoriae in Ecclesia immane specimen. Vide loca sequentia: Dan. 11: 37. Et non habebit rationem Deorum patrum suorum; & non habebit rationem desiderii mulierum; & non habebit rationem ullius Dei; quia supra omnia magnificabit se. 1. Tim. 4: 1, 3 Spiritus diserte dicit, attenturos quosdam spiritibus seductoribus, & doctrinis daemoniorum, videlicet vetantium uxores ducere &c. cap. 5: 14. Volo igitur juniores nubere, liberos parere, domos regere, nullam ansam dare adversario convitii causa. Matth. 19: 12. Qui potest capere, capiat. 1. Cor. 7: 2. Propter fornicationes quisque suam conjugem habeat. & com. 5, 6. Ne fraudate alter alterum, nisi si quid ex consensu ad tempus, & rursum simul conveniate, ne tentet vos Satanas, hoc autem dico ex concessione, non ex imperio. com. 25. De virginibus autem imperium non habeo. com. 37. Qui vero stabilis perstat in corde, nec adigitur necessitate, sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem, & hoc decrevit in corde suo, ut servet suam virginem, bene facit. Hebr. 13: 4. Honorata nuptia sunt in omnibus, & lectus impollutus est: fornicatores vero & adulteros judicabit Deus. Col. 2: 21. Quid ut viventes in mundo dogmata suscipitis? ne tangas (ex gr. mulierem conf. 1. Cor. 7: 1.) neque gustes, neque contrectes. 1. Tim. 3: 2. Oportet inspectorem esse irreprehensibilem, unius uxoris virum. com. 4. domui suae bene consulentem, liberos habentem in subjectione, cum omni honestate Tit. 1: 6. Si quis inculpatus, unius uxoris vir, liberos habens fideles, qui non sint obnoxii crimini luxus, aut subjicienesciì. 1.Cor. 9: 5. An non habemus facultatem, sororem uxorem circumducendi, ut & reliqui Apostoli, & fratres Domini, & Cephas?
units.tr: XXIV. Besides these things, the Roman Church has laid down a law of celibacy for ministers. We shall treat of the votive celibacy, to which the families of monks swear, elsewhere. This is the law of the Roman Church: that no one may handle sacred things unless he has bound himself by a vow of chastity. By this means they also forbid marriages, since they command the loves of spouses, which God himself has approved, to be unchaste; they restrain the gifts of the Spirit in married people; and finally, against the examples of the Jewish, Apostolic and earliest Christian Church, and against the admonitions of the apostles themselves, they presume to prescribe and to repeal by their own law all these things. And this is a monstrous example of their legislative power in the Church. See the following passages: Dan. 11:37. And he shall not regard the gods of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor any god; for he shall magnify himself above all. 1 Tim. 4:1, 3. The Spirit expressly says that some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons, namely forbidding to marry, etc. 1 Tim. 5:14. I desire therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, rule the household, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach. Matt. 19:12. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it. 1 Cor. 7:2. Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife. Vv. 5, 6. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, and come together again, lest Satan tempt you. But this I say by way of concession, not of command. V. 25. Concerning virgins I have no command. V. 37. But he who stands firm in his heart, and is not constrained by necessity but has his own will in his power, and has decided in his heart to keep his own virgin, does well. Heb. 13:4. Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled; but fornicators and adulterers God will judge. Col. 2:21. Why do you submit to decrees, as though living in the world? Do not touch (for example, a woman, see 1 Cor. 7:1), nor taste, nor handle. 1 Tim. 3:2. An overseer must be blameless, the husband of one wife. V. 4. Caring well for his own household, having children in subjection, with all honesty. Titus 1:6. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, who are not open to accusation of riot or insubordination. 1 Cor. 9:5. Have we not the right to take along a sister as a wife, as do the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?

units.la: XXV. Agnoverunt illud meliores inter Pontificios. Ac in ipso Concilio Tridentino acriter huic legi reclamatum. Ac post illud Imperator Ferdinandus, ac Bavarus, litteris ad Pium V. datis, severitatem canonum hac in parte relaxari, & conjugatos ad sacros ordines admitti, magnopere petebant. Addebaturque litteris libellus memorialis Theologorum Pontificiae communionis in Germania; in quo disserebant, negari non posse, sacram utriusque Testamenti Scripturam uxores Sacerdotibus permittere: Apostolos, paucis exceptis, uxoratos fuisse: in Ecclesia primitiva, tam Orientali, quam Occidentali, matrimonia sacerdotum fuisse libera, & licita, usque ad Papam Calixtum: propter naturae fragilitatem, & servanda continentia difficultatem, paucos reperiri, qui stimulos carnis non sentiant: Paphnutium, in concilio Niceno, dicentem, castitatem esse cum propria uxore concubitum, persuasisse concilio, ne talem de caelibatu legem sciscerent: & sextam Synodum Constantinopolitanam non prohibuisse uxoris consortium, nisi quo tempore offerendum erat sacrificium: quod si Ecclesia unquam causa fuit permittendi Clericis conjugium, hoc saeculo esse: ex quinquaginta Sacerdotibus vix unum reperiri, qui non sit scortator notorius: neque Sacerdotes tantum matrimonium expetere, sed etiam saeculares, ne illam vitam turpitudinem in Clericis videant &c. vide historiam Conc. Trid. lib. 7. & 8. Mansit tamen observatio illa lex. Et quanquam religioso praetextu castimonias istas Ecclesiasticis praescriberent, revera tamen non nisi humanis rationibus adducti in veterum canonum rigore perstabant. Unde, matrimonium presbyteris concedere, nihil aliud esse, quam Hierarchiam Ecclesiasticam destruere, & Pontificem ad Romae solius Episcopatum redigere, cati homines dissercebant. Hist. Conc. Trid.
units.tr: XXV. Better men among the Papists have acknowledged this. And at the Council of Trent itself this law was strongly protested against. After that, the Emperor Ferdinand and the Bavarian, by letters sent to Pius V, earnestly asked that the severity of the canons be relaxed in this respect and that married men be admitted to holy orders. A little memorial book of the theologians of the Papist communion in Germany was added to the letters; in it they argued that it cannot be denied that the holy Scripture of both Testaments allows priests to have wives: that the apostles, with few exceptions, were married; that in the primitive Church, both Eastern and Western, the marriages of priests were free and lawful, down to Pope Callixtus; that because of the frailty of nature and the difficulty of keeping continence, few are found who do not feel the goads of the flesh; that Paphnutius, at the Council of Nicaea, saying that chastity was intercourse with one's own wife, persuaded the council not to enact such a law about celibacy; and that the Sixth Synod of Constantinople did not forbid the company of a wife except at the time when sacrifice was to be offered. If the Church was ever a reason for permitting clergy marriage, it is so in this age: of fifty priests scarcely one is found who is not a notorious fornicator; and not only priests desire marriage, but laymen too, so that they need not see such shamefulness in the clergy, etc. See the history of the Council of Trent, books 7 and 8. Nevertheless that law of observance remained. And although they prescribed these chastities to churchmen under a religious pretext, in truth they persisted in the rigour of the ancient canons only moved by human reasons. Whence shrewd men argued that to grant marriage to presbyters is nothing other than to destroy the ecclesiastical hierarchy and to reduce the Pope to the bishopric of Rome alone. History of the Council of Trent.

units.la: XXVI. Ministrorum vocationi obtrectant Socinians, qui eam non necessariam esse asserunt: de caetero unumquemque, qui sibi aptitudinis suae conscius sit, id muneris posse sumere. Quae contra Veteris Novique Testamenti exempla; ac ministerii dignitatem & ordinem sunt; & omnem potestatem Ecclesiasticam tollunt; ac meram denique in Ecclesia confusionem invehunt. Non intercedimus autem, quin, turbatis Ecclesiae rebus, ac ordine nondum constituto; vel ubi Ecclesia aliqua Pastore orbata, ac in locis solis destituta, est; eo in casu illa de suo cœtu aptissimum eligere, & ministrum constituere, omnique potestate Ecclesiastica induere possit. Quod legitimæ vocationis est.
units.tr: XXVI. The Socinians find fault with the calling of ministers, asserting that it is not necessary, and that anyone who is conscious of his own aptitude may take up that office. This is contrary to the examples of the Old and New Testaments, and it overturns the dignity and order of the ministry and all ecclesiastical authority, and finally brings sheer confusion into the Church. We do not object, however, that when the affairs of the Church are disturbed and its order not yet established, or where some congregation has been bereft of a minister and left without one, in such a case it may choose from its own company the most suitable man, appoint him as minister, and clothe him with all ecclesiastical authority. This is what a lawful calling is.

units.la: XXVII. Errant ab altera parte Pontificii, plebi in eligendis ministris jus omne eripientes. Contra Apostolicæ ac primitivæ Ecclesiæ exemplum. Act. 14:23. De qua consuetudine est, quod ipsi adhuc hodie, in ordinandis ministris, populi suffragia, licet per histrionium, exquirant. Ac de Apostolis, qui olim peculiari jure præditi erant, supra vidimus, eos ne quidem in minoris momenti negotiis, uti in legatione aliqua Ecclesiastica mandanda, quicquam citra Ecclesiæ consensum factitasse, Act. 15:22. 2. Cor. 8:19. Veteris autem Ecclesiæ consuetudinis testes sunt, inter Pontificios, Cardinalis Cusanus, Azorius &c. ac clarius in eam rem præsertim est Cyprianus in epistolis.
units.tr: XXVII. On the other side the Papists go astray, taking away from the people every right to choose ministers. This is contrary to the example of the Apostolic and primitive Church, Acts 14:23. From this custom it is that even today they still seek the votes of the people in ordaining ministers, though only by way of a stage show. As we saw above concerning the Apostles, who once had a special right, they did nothing, not even in matters of lesser importance, such as sending someone on an ecclesiastical mission, without the consent of the Church, Acts 15:22; 2 Cor. 8:19. The witnesses to the custom of the ancient Church among the Papists are Cardinal Cusanus, Azorius and others; and more clearly on this matter, especially, is Cyprian in his letters.

units.la: XXVIII. Quod autem Apostolus Timotheo mandat, ut fidis hominibus doctrinæ depositum commendet, 2. Tim. 2:2. id ministerii honorem si spectet, illum non nisi Ecclesia arbitra & conscia mandare potuit. Sicuti Titus, a Paulo jussus Cretensibus Pastores dare, Tit. 1:5. id de fidelium consensu facere debuit; si idoneus eorum numerus esset. Alia enim res est, ubi Ecclesia demum plantanda est, ubi nulli adhuc fideles degunt: ibi enim expectari non potest consensus plebis; sed in silvescentia ac horrentia arva immitti debent gnavi operarii, qui illa subigant, & Euangelii semente mitescere tandem cogant.
units.tr: XXVIII. As for the Apostle's command to Timothy, that he should commit the deposit of doctrine to faithful men, 2 Tim. 2:2: if this refers to the honour of the ministry, Timothy could not have committed it except with the Church as judge and in its knowledge. Likewise Titus, ordered by Paul to appoint elders in Crete, Titus 1:5, ought to have done this with the consent of the faithful, if there were a suitable number of them. It is another matter where the Church is yet to be planted and no faithful are living: there the consent of the people cannot be awaited, but diligent workers must be sent into the wild and bristling fields to break them up and force them at last to grow tame under the seed of the Gospel.

units.la: XXIX. Vocationem sequitur Ordinatio, seu confirmatio; qua electus, ac probatus, per sollemnem ritum in muneris possessionem immittitur, ac Ecclesiæ mancipatur. Unde ab electione dependet. Χειροτονία autem, ac externus ille ritus, à presbytereis solis peragitur; quanquam nomine Ecclesiæ. Juxta 1. Tim. 4:14. Ne negligas donum, quod est in te, quod tibi datum est per Prophetiam, cum impositione manus presbyterii. & 5:22. Manus cito nemini simpone, neque communica cum peccatis alienis. & 2. Tim. 1:6. Propter quam causam commonefacio te, ut exsuscites donum Dei, quod est in te, per impositionem manuum mearum. adde Act. 13. Nec Doctores solum, sed & Diaconi, isto modo inaugurati leguntur, Act. 6:6. Statu vero Ecclesiæ collapso, aliunde ritus ille suppletur, vel omittur. Non enim de essentia ministerii est. Ut male Bellarm. nullo modo pro pastoribus habeat, qui per manuum impositionem ab Episcopo sacrati non sunt.
units.tr: XXIX. Calling is followed by ordination, or confirmation, by which the one chosen and approved is put into possession of the office through a solemn rite and given over to the Church. Hence it depends on the election. But the laying on of hands (cheirotonia) and that external rite are performed by the elders alone, though in the name of the Church. According to 1 Tim. 4:14: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery; and 5:22: Lay hands on no one hastily, nor share in the sins of others; and 2 Tim. 1:6: For this reason I remind you to stir up the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. Add Acts 13. Not only teachers but also deacons are read of as having been inaugurated in this way, Acts 6:6. But when the state of the Church has collapsed, that rite is supplied from elsewhere or omitted, for it is not of the essence of the ministry. Thus Bellarmine wrongly holds that by no means are those to be regarded as pastors who have not been consecrated by a bishop through the laying on of hands.

units.la: XXX. Ortus autem fuit hic ritus à Judæis, qui inter alia in Doctoribus creandis illum usurpabant. Nec aliam sanctitatem habet; quam quod ista sollenni veluti cæremonia Euangelii minister in munus introducitur; &c, ne quis privatim illud usurpare audeat, Ecclesiæ publice addicitur; ac denique faustis precibus, advocata divina benedictione, ab universa concione cumulatur & consecratur. Nulla tamen inde peculiaris consecratio aut sanctitas adhæret ministris N. F. ut olim sub V. F. Nulla enim nunc datur cultus divini pars, quæ in peculiari appropinquatione ad Deum consistat, quæque non ab unoquoque Christiano, legitime ad id vocato, administrari possit, imo debeat: omnes enim regale sacerdotium (sumus. 1. Pet. 2: 5, 9. Apoc. 1: 6. Ut nunc discrimine illo Levitico sublato, vere totus cœtus sanctus sit, Num. 16: 3. neque aliud discrimen sit inter personam quæ cultu sacro defungitur, & alias, nisi ordinis duntaxat; dum ordinis causa cultus publici administratio illis committitur, quæ cæteroquin unicuique fratrum, necessariis requisitis instructo, pariter quoque imponi poliet.
units.tr: XXX. This rite, however, arose from the Jews, who among other things used it in creating teachers. It has no other sanctity than this: that by this solemn ceremony the minister of the Gospel is introduced into his office, and, lest anyone presume to take it upon himself privately, he is publicly committed to the Church; and finally, with joyful prayers and with the divine blessing invoked, he is enriched and consecrated by the whole congregation. Yet no peculiar consecration or sanctity clings to the ministers of the New Covenant from this, as it did once under the Old Covenant. For now there is no part of divine worship that consists in a special approach to God, and that cannot be, and indeed ought to be, administered by every Christian lawfully called to it. For all are a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2:5, 9; Rev. 1:6). So now, with that Levitical distinction removed, the whole congregation truly is holy (Num. 16:3), and there is no difference between the person who performs sacred worship and others except of office alone; the administration of public worship is committed to those men for the sake of order, though otherwise it could equally be laid upon any one of the brethren who is furnished with the necessary qualifications.

units.la: XXXI. Cum ergo duobus hilce Ecclesiastica vocatio absolvatur, electione & confirmatione; cui addi potest publice loquendi libertas, ac facultas, a magistratu data: male Pontificii ad creationem Episcopi tria requirunt, electionem, ordinationem, & vocationem, seu missionem, quæ ultima ipsis propriæ jurisdictionem tribuit.
units.tr: XXXI. Since, therefore, the ecclesiastical calling is completed by these two things, election and confirmation, to which may be added public freedom of speaking and the authority given by the magistrate, the Papists wrongly require three things for the creation of a bishop: election, ordination, and vocation or mission, the last of which gives them their own jurisdiction.

units.la: Nam electio à vocatione non differt. Ac nimium etiam vocationem & ordinationem separant, dum frequentes adeo ordinationes absolutas, Chalcedonensi Concilio veritas, sine vero titulo, ac Ecclesia, celebrant. Sine grege enim nemo minister ordinari potest: quamvis grege ad tempus destitutus, honorem tamen & gradum ministerii certo modo retinere possit. Sed & ordinationem variis peregrinis ritibus contaminarunt; nec presbyteris ullas in ea partes relinquunt; sed omnia ad Episcopos, tandemque ad unum Episcopum Romanum, transtulerunt.
units.tr: For election does not differ from calling. And they also separate calling and ordination too much, since they celebrate so many absolute ordinations, without a true title and without a Church, which the Council of Chalcedon forbade. For no one can be ordained a minister without a flock, although a man who for a time has been deprived of his flock can still keep the honour and rank of the ministry in a certain way. But they have also contaminated ordination with various foreign rites, and they leave the presbyters no part in it, but have transferred everything to the bishops, and finally to the one Roman Bishop.

units.la: XXXII. Injuria autem nostræ Ecclesiæ ministerium sugillant; nostrorumque ordinationes omnes vitio factas, & irritas, calumniantur, Quod videlicet unctis Episcopis, qui sacrum ordinem propagent, careamus. Unde porro universum ministerium nostrum omni potestate ac vi exspoliant; & tandem nec ministerium, adeoque nec Ecclesiam apud nos superesse, concludunt. Quæ quam vere dicantur, ex jam dictis videre licet. Nam & munera, quæ exercemus, à Christo instituta sunt: & legitima Ecclesiæ vocatione ad istum gradum pervenimus. Ista enim sola legitimæ vocationis in Scripturis expressa ratio est; cum idonei nei homines, a tota Ecclesia lecti & probati, a presbyterio confirmantur, & fausta manuum impositione, non sine universæ concionis precibus, inaugurantur. Quæ illi de sacris istis Ecclesiæ suæ Ordinibus, Papæ, Cardinalium, Patriarcharum, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, denique immensæ illius sacrificulorum turbæ, nunquam probare poterunt. Contra Scripturas autem est, solis Episcopis presbyteros creandi potestatem dare. Ac non sine sacrilegio tandem Pontifex Rom. supremum creandorum Episcoporum omnium jus sibi soli arrogat.
units.tr: XXXII. They also slander the ministry of our Church, and calumniate all our ordinations as faulty and void, because, they say, we lack bishops anointed to transmit the sacred order. From this they go on to strip our whole ministry of all power and authority, and finally conclude that neither a ministry nor a Church survives among us. How truly these things are said may be seen from what has already been said. For both the offices we exercise were instituted by Christ, and we have come to this rank by a lawful calling of the Church. For this alone is the form of lawful calling expressed in the Scriptures: when suitable men, chosen and approved by the whole Church, are confirmed by the elders, and are inaugurated with the happy laying on of hands, not without the prayers of the whole congregation. The Papists will never be able to prove these things about the sacred orders of their Church: the Pope, the cardinals, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and finally that immense crowd of little sacrificers. It is against the Scriptures to grant to bishops alone the power of creating elders. And the Roman Pontiff, not without sacrilege, claims for himself alone the supreme right of creating all bishops.

units.la: XXXIII. Sed de Reformationis Ducibus præcipuam litem movent: quos nulla auctoritate ad opus illud instructos fuisse ajunt; atque omne illud a Monachis, a Laicis, & seditiosa denique plebecula cœptum ac peractum clamitant. Atque hic miris verborum incendiis sæviunt, & immani invidia reformatas Ecclesias pulsant. Qui tamen inanes strepitus sunt. Nam non uno modo clamoribus illis responderi potest. Ac 1. quidem plurimi ex Reformatoribus Ecclesiasticam vocationem in ipso Papatu habuerunt. Qui, abstersis sordibus, ac emaculato, quo fungebantur, munere, illo ad Dei gloriam, & Ecclesiæ ædificationem, ac Papismi ipsius destructionem, uti debuerunt: nec, ejurato licet Papismo, ulla nova vocatione opus habuerunt. II. Constitutis deinde Ecclesiis, ab iis, juxta ordinem in Scriptura institutum, lecti Pastores. Quæ vocatio profecto sanctior erat, quam quæ in Romana Ecclesia sperari poterat. III. Fuit ergo vocatio illorum ordinaria: nec enim missione extraordinaria, aut miraculis, opus erat, ad Ecclesiæ errores corrigendos, eamque pristinæ luci ac nitori restituendam, & de Babylonis denique portis educendam. Sufficiebat enim mandatum conveniendi in nomine Domini (quod ubique, & quavis occasione, fieri debet) ac verbum ejus, sine commentis humanis, publice in mundo proloquendi (quod omnibus suo modo datum est) ac præsertim auribus insonabat magnum istud Apocalypticæ meretricis judicium; & verba illa, Exite ex ea populi mi! quæ quibuivis exeundi potestatem dabant. Ministrorum autem erat tanta in re duces se se præbere, & Romani scorti turpitudinem nudare, vulgataque ejus toto orbe libidines ostendere, denique universam istam pseudo-Ecclesiam vitare, portasque exeuntibus aperire. Nec illa ab ordinario iplorum munere aliena erant. Ut frustra speciale missionem, & miracula, ab iis petant adversarii; quæ ne quidem extraordinariis Doctoribus semper adfuerunt. IV. Quæ de Laicis (ita enim Magistratus appellant) aliisque, qui sanctissi-mo mo huic operi manum admoverunt, objectant, adeo nobis non obsunt, ut merito pudorem ipsis incutere debeant. Ita enim deploratæ res erant, ut ab Ecclesiastico ordine sani nihil expectari potuerit. Frustra enim à lenonum, & luparum cinædorumque principibus, non ab ædili vel prætore, aliquis coërceri lupanaria & mereticum sellas expectet. Quod ad alios autem spectat, commune ad Christianos omnes mandatum extabat, de deserenda Babylone. Nec si quid in tanto rerum motu extra ordinem gestum est, ideo opus Dei culpari debet. Quicquid autem ista in re desiderari potuit, tandem constituto Ecclesiarum ordine recomposi-tum fuit. v. Denique quod indignantur, nos illos, qui ab ipsis sacris ordinibus initiati sunt, hodie reordinare; cum tamen collatum ab iis baptisma novis aquis non eluamus: id diversam rationem habet. Quia baptismus iterandus non est, ubi essentialia baptismi servantur. Aliter autem in ordinationibus ipsorum sese res habet; quæ nihil nisi inaugurationes ad Missæ sacerdotium sunt. Quod nos profanum ac sacrilegum habemus, & præstigiosum illum ac magicum characterem, quem mystis suis imprimunt, inducto meliori delemus.
units.tr: XXXIII. But they press a chief quarrel about the leaders of the Reformation, whom they say were not equipped for that work by any authority, and they cry out that the whole thing was begun and carried through by monks, laymen, and finally a seditious rabble. And here they rage with astonishing verbal firebrands and assail the Reformed Churches with monstrous hatred. Yet these are empty noises. For there is more than one way to answer those outcries. And first, indeed, very many of the Reformers had an ecclesiastical calling within Papacy itself. These, having wiped away the filth and cleansed the office they were performing, were to use it for the glory of God, the building up of the Church, and the destruction of Popery itself; and although they renounced Popery, they had no need of any new calling. II. Then, once the Churches had been established, pastors were chosen by them according to the order instituted in Scripture. That calling was certainly holier than any that could be hoped for in the Roman Church. III. Their calling therefore was ordinary: for there was no need of an extraordinary mission or of miracles to correct the errors of the Church, to restore it to its former light and brightness, and to lead it out at last from the gates of Babylon. For it was enough to have the command to gather in the name of the Lord (which ought to be done everywhere and on any occasion), and to proclaim his word publicly in the world without human inventions (which has been given to all in their own way); and above all the great judgment of the Apocalyptic harlot was sounding in their ears, and those words, Come out of her, my people, which gave to anyone the power to go out. It was the duty of ministers in so great a matter to present themselves as leaders, to strip bare the foulness of the Roman harlot, to show the lusts of her made public throughout the whole world, and finally to avoid that whole pseudo-Church and to open the gates to those who would go out. Nor were these things foreign to their ordinary office. So the adversaries seek in vain a special mission and miracles from them; these were not always present even for extraordinary teachers. IV. As to what they object concerning the laymen (for so they call the magistrates) and others who lent a hand to this most holy work, these objections do us no harm, but rather ought to bring shame upon those who make them. For the matters were so desperate that nothing sound could be expected from the ecclesiastical order. It is vain to expect that brothels and whorehouses should be restrained not by an aedile or praetor but by the princes of pimps, whores and catamites. As for the others, the common command to all Christians stood, to forsake Babylon. And if anything was done out of order amid such great upheaval, the work of God ought not for that reason to be blamed. Whatever might have been lacking in this matter was at last set right when the order of the Churches was established. V. Finally, as to their indignation that we re-ordain those who were initiated into those sacred orders, while we do not wash away with new water the baptism conferred by them: this has a different reason. For baptism need not be repeated where the essentials of baptism are preserved. But the case is otherwise with their ordinations, which are nothing but inaugurations into the priesthood of the Mass. These we hold to be profane and sacrilegious, and by introducing a better one we blot out that deceptive and magical character which they impress on their initiates.

units.la: XXXIV. Sequitur ministrorum constitutorum fustentatio. Quam divino jure ipsis deberi Apostolus probat, 1. Cor. 9:7-13. Quis militat propriis stipendiis unquam? quis plantat vineam, & de fructu ejus non edit aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit? — Si vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum est si nos vestra carnalia messuerimus? — an nescitis, eos, qui sacris operantur, ea qui ex sacrario sunt edere? & quae altari assident, cum altare participare. Conf. Matth. 10:10. Nam dignus est operarius alimento suo. 1. Tim. 5:17, 18. Qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore afficiuntur, maxime qui laborant in sermone & doctrina. Dicit enim Scriptura: bovem triturantem non capistrabis: & , dignus est operarius mercede sua. Quæ ministerii stipendia stata & certa esse, Sacerdotum ac Levitarum exemplo, nihil vetat; utque liberius in sacro opere versentur, ἀμεϱίμνως cos & de cibariis securos reddit. Nullus militans implicat se vita negotiis. 2. Tim. 2:4.
units.tr: XXXIV. Next comes the maintenance of the ministers who have been appointed. The Apostle proves that this is owed to them by divine right, 1 Cor. 9:7-13: "Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?
