Or who tends a flock and does not drink of the flock's milk? If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things? Do you not know that those who minister in holy things eat of the things of the temple, and that those who attend the altar share in the altar?" See also Matt. 10:10: "For the workman is worthy of his food." 1 Tim. 5:17-18: "Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, 'You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain,' and, 'The labourer is worthy of his wages.'" Nothing forbids that the stipends of the ministry be fixed and certain, after the pattern of the priests and Levites; and that they may be more free to devote themselves to the sacred work, it frees them from worry about food [ἀμερίμνως]. No soldier entangles himself in the affairs of everyday life (2 Tim. 2:4).

units.la: XXXV. Ubi ab una parte culpanda Anabaptistarum anxietas, qui illiberale ac mercenarium putant, annuas mercedes pro Ecclesiasticis laboribus ex publico accipere. Unde ditioribus ista laborum præmia non permittunt; tenuioribus autem, non annuam, sed quotidianam stipem, prout necessitas eorum flagitat, assignant. Faciunt autem hoc majoris sanctimoniæ causa. Quod & Apostolus suo tempore falsorum fratrum insti-
units.tr: XXXV. Here the anxiety of the Anabaptists must be blamed on one side. They think it illiberal and mercenary to receive an annual salary from the public treasury for ecclesiastical labours. So they do not allow such rewards for their labours to the wealthier ministers, but assign to the poorer ones not an annual stipend but a daily dole, as their need requires. They do this for the sake of greater holiness. The Apostle also pointed to this practice of false brothers in his own time.

units.la: Pars II. institutum fuisse dicit, 2. Cor. 11: 12, 13. Cum tamen ipsi aliunde rem facere, & vel sacculis charitatis, vel aliis obventionibus, ac potissimum uberi mercatura civium bona inuncare interdum noverint.
units.tr: Part II. He says so in 2 Cor. 11:12-13. Yet they themselves are known to do business elsewhere, and sometimes to heap up goods from the purses of charity, or other incomes, and especially from the rich trade of the citizens.

units.la: XXXVI. Quantopere autem Pauli exemplum ipsos non juvet, vel ex ipso illo, quem adferunt, loco, satis patet. Specialibus enim de causis Corinthiacæ Ecclesiæ Euangelium ἀδάπανον præstare volebat. Non quod nullum postulandæ mercedis jus haberet (vide 1. Cor. 9:4,5,6,12.) sed ne infirmos offenderet; & ut falsorum fratrum gloriationem minueret; quibus, nascentibus primum Ecclesiis, concedere non volebat. vide Act. 20:35.
units.tr: XXXVI. How little the example of Paul helps them is clear enough even from the very passage they cite. Paul wished to offer the gospel to the Corinthian Church free of charge [ἀδάπανον] for special reasons. Not because he had no right to demand a reward (see 1 Cor. 9:4-6, 12), but so as not to offend the weak, and to diminish the boasting of false brothers, whom he did not wish to indulge while the Churches were first being planted. See Acts 20:35.

units.la: XXXVII. Ab altera autem parte Pontificii Ecclesiasticas opes, præter fas & æquum, in immensum auxerunt: dum, per privatas publicasque largitiones, non decimas solum (quæ juxta Levitarum institutum, fovendo ministerio pendebantur) sed agros, & pecunias, & vectigalia, & Comitatus ac Principatus, religionis titulo possident; istisque firmamentis monarchiam suam Ecclesiasticam fundaverunt. Quæ res quibus gradibus, quibusve artibus ac aucupii generibus, in monachis, Episcopis, ipsoque Papa, processerit, longum foret disserere. Nede testamentorum corruptione, de legatorum spoliis aliisque artibus patriciis dicam. Exundabant autem tandem omnes hi rivi in Romanæ Ecclesiæ alveum: quæ, urbis ditionisque Romanæ possessione non contenta, mille prædationum nominibus ac formis, in reliquas orbis Ecclesias grassabatur.
units.tr: XXXVII. On the other side, the Papists have increased the ecclesiastical wealth beyond all right and reason. By private and public gifts they hold under the pretext of religion not only tithes (which, after the Levites' institution, were paid to support the ministry) but fields, money, revenues, counties and principalities; and on these supports they founded their ecclesiastical monarchy. It would be a long task to set out by what steps, and by what arts and kinds of fowling, this process advanced among the monks, the bishops, and the Pope himself. I say nothing of the corruption of wills, the plundering of legacies, and other patrician tricks. All these streams at last overflowed into the channel of the Roman Church, which, not content with possession of the city and the Roman domain, raged against the remaining Churches of the world under a thousand names and forms of plunder.

units.la: XXXVIII. Qui insani Clericorum reditus, per prædas & rapinas magnam partem congesti, nunc ab Ecclesiis reformatis vindicari non possunt. Ejectis enim, ac migrare jussis, qui auro isti incubabant, illud vacuæ manus factum, fisco-que merito addictum est. Non enim Ecclesia tanta gaza eget. Nec refodere istos thesauros, & luxus ac avaritiæ irritamenta conquirere, magnopere interest. Sicut & collegia, ad pompam, vel cultus idololatricos, instituta, ac titulo isto magnam bonorum istorum partem possidentia, pro arbitrio magistratuum, vel dissolvi, vel, ejuratis Papatus sordibus, ac inducto meliori axiomate, porro bonorum istorum curam gerere, atque inde aliquem in Repub. ordinem constituere possunt. Ante omnia autem Ecclesiæ, & Scholarum, ac pauperum necessitatibus exinde prospiciendum est. Contra ac Brownistæ & Anabaptistæ censent. Sicut isti præcipua fundatorum fuit intentio, quanquam multa superstitione corrupta, religioso fini, & Ecclesiæ, vel usui, vel splendori, donaria ista dedicare. Quicunque autem prætextus adhibeantur, à sacrorum spoliis summopere cavendum est: ne, dum collatas ad pauperum vel ad exulum levamen stipes, vel olim ad sincerum Dei cultum, & Ecclesiarum necessitates, dicatas opes invadimus, hæreditatem Dei accidere, patrimonium Christo dissipare, depeculari denique ac devastare Ecclesias deprehendamur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The mad revenues of the clergy, gathered in large part by plunder and robbery, cannot now be reclaimed by the reformed Churches. For those who sat brooding over that gold have been ejected and ordered to leave, and that wealth, left with empty hands, has rightly been adjudged to the treasury. The Church has no need of such a great treasure, nor does it matter greatly to dig up those hoards and seek out the incentives of luxury and avarice. Likewise, colleges founded for pomp or idolatrous worship, which hold a large part of those goods under that title, may, at the discretion of the magistrates, either be dissolved or, once the filth of Papacy has been renounced and a better principle introduced, continue to administer those goods, and thereby establish some order in the commonwealth. Above all, provision must be made from them for the needs of the Churches, the schools, and the poor. The Brownists and Anabaptists think otherwise. Although founders' chief intention, however corrupted by much superstition, was to dedicate those gifts to a religious end, to the use or splendour of the Church, whatever pretexts are offered, we must be most careful about plundering sacred things. Otherwise, while we invade the resources dedicated to the relief of the poor and exiles, or formerly to the sincere worship of God and the needs of the Churches, we may be found to fall upon God's inheritance, to squander Christ's patrimony, and finally to despoil and lay waste the Churches.

units.la: XXXIX. Minister, ministerio aptus & habilis, ministerio abire, & s- tationem suam deserere, non nisi gravi de causa, potest.
units.tr: XXXIX. A minister who is fit and able for the ministry may leave the ministry and abandon his post only for a grave reason.

units.la: {iv}Nemo qui manum sua admota aratro, respexerit ad ea quæ retro sunt, appositus est ad regnum Dei. Luc. 9:62. Si autem, vel doctrinæ, vel morum probro, aut scelere indignum præstet, ad tempus munere interdici, vel in totum removeri debet. Estque istius rei jus & potestas penes eos qui illum admiserunt, hoc est Ecclesiam, quæ à Deo non credendi pseudo-Prophetis, iisque contradicendi, mandatum habet.
units.tr: {iv}No one who has put his hand to the plough and looks back to what is behind is fit for the kingdom of God. Luke 9:62. But if he shows himself unworthy, by a disgrace in teaching or morals, or by a crime, he must be forbidden the office for a time, or removed altogether. The right and power of this matter rests with those who admitted him, that is, the Church, which has the command from God not to believe false prophets and to contradict them.

units.la: XL. Difficilem autem nimis reddunt indigni ministri exauctorationem Pontificii, superstitiosis ac multifariis degradationibus ritibus. Qui in veteri Ecclesia olim, ad exemplum militiæ armatæ, usurpati, ad Ecclesiasticî ordinis decus, si quis de Clero ad sæcularem statum redire vellet; quo non sine nota abire poterat; vel si alioquin ob delictum sæculari potestati tradendus erat. Postea autem illud in majoribus ordinibus tantummodo usurpatum, quando aliqui judici sæculari tradendi forent, multisque cærimoniis auctum & impeditum fuit. Quæ non alio spectabant, quam ad magnam de Ecclesiasticis opinionem populo ingenerandam, iisque inanibus juris exequutionem frustrandam.
units.tr: XL. The Papists, however, make the removal of unworthy ministers too difficult with their superstitious and manifold rites of degradation. In the ancient Church these were used once, after the pattern of armed service, to preserve the dignity of the ecclesiastical order, when someone from the clergy wished to return to the secular state, from which he could not depart without disgrace; or if for some offence he was otherwise to be handed over to the secular power. Later, this was used only for the higher orders, when certain men were to be handed over to the secular judge, and it was enlarged and encumbered with many ceremonies. These aimed at nothing else than to instil in the people a high opinion of ecclesiastical persons and to frustrate the execution of justice by these empty forms.

units.la: XLI. Presbyteris, in verbo laborantibus, adjungunt alii in verbo non-laborantes; qui regimini præsunt, in nostris Ecclesiis Seniores dicti. Quo referunt 1. Tim. 5:17. Qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore afficiuntur: maxime qui laborant in sermone & doctrina. 1. Cor. 12:28. Constituit Deus in Ecclesia — κυβερνήσεις gubernationes &c. Rom. 12:8. Qui præsit, cum diligentia. Habebant & Judæi in coetibus ac Synagogis suis tales presbyteros: unde in Ecclesiam Christianam quibusdam traducti videntur. Hoc tam discrimine, quod illi judicia, & politicum regimen quoque tractarent. In Novo autem Testam. primo Ecclesiæ presbyterorum mentio fit. Act. 11:30. Mittentes ad Seniores πρὸς τὺς πρεσβυτέρους per manum Barnabæ & Saulo. tum, c. 14:23. Quumque ipsis per suffragia creassent per singulas Ecclesias presbyteros &c. Tit. 1:5, aliisque locis.
units.tr: XLI. Some add to the elders who labour in the word others who do not labour in the word, who preside over government and who in our Churches are called Seniors. To this they refer 1 Tim. 5:17: The elders who rule well are counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching. 1 Cor. 12:28: God has set in the Church … [κυβερνήσεις] governments, etc. Rom. 12:8: He who rules, with diligence. The Jews also had such elders in their assemblies and synagogues, and seem to have been in some measure carried over from them into the Christian Church, with this difference, that the Jewish elders also dealt with judgments and with political government. In the New Testament the first mention of elders in the Church is in Acts 11:30: Sending to the elders [πρὸς τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους] by the hand of Barnabas and Saul. Then in chapter 14:23: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church by vote, etc. Titus 1:5, and in other places.

units.la: XLII. Hoc tamen merito dubitari potest: an illi Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ presbyteri, qui in verbo non laborabant, peculiarem in Ecclesia ordinem constituerint? & an, de cætero Ecclesiæ ministeric & regimini in perpetuum non addicti, de populo tantum in curarum partem allecti, ac presbyteri quidam Laici fuerint? Certe in Novi Test. Scripturis Episcopis & Presbyteris, tum docendi, tum gubernandi, potestas ex æquo tribuitur; isteque partes ipsis non semel mandantur. Vide 2. Tim. 2: 2. & 4: 3. Tit. 1: 9. Unde potius videtur, de eodem presbyterorum ordine utrosque fuisse: quod autem, regimini intenti, de docendo non laboraverint, tum aliis de causis, tum ex donorum defectu contigisse. Utcunque sit, utilem Ecclesiæ esse hunc Laicorum, uti appellant, presbyteratum; isteque, de reliquo populo lectos, seniores, pastoribus non immerito assidere, Ecclesiamque curare; tum ex veteris Ecclesiæ consuetudine, cujus testis est Ambrosius, tum hodiernæ quoque experientia patet.
units.tr: XLII. Yet it may rightly be doubted whether those elders of the apostolic Church who did not labour in the word constituted a distinct order in the Church; or whether, being not permanently committed to the ministry and government of the Church, they were merely men chosen from the people to share in the cares, and were certain lay elders. Certainly in the Scriptures of the New Testament, authority both to teach and to govern is given equally to bishops and elders, and these duties are entrusted to them more than once. See 2 Tim. 2:2; 4:3; Titus 1:9. Hence it seems more likely that both belonged to the same order of elders, and that those who, intent on governing, did not labour in teaching, did so for other reasons and from a lack of gifts. However that may be, this lay presbyterate, as they call it, is useful to the Church; and that elders chosen from the rest of the people should sit beside the pastors, not undeservedly, and take care of the Church, is shown both by the custom of the ancient Church (of which Ambrose is witness) and by the experience of our own day.

units.la: XLIII. Hi ergo Seniores laici, Pastorum veluti assessores, cum iis Senatum Ecclesiæ constituunt. Potest vero aut cœtus, aut civitas, ubi vera sacra in publicum accipit, majorem aliquam potestatem, & civilis cognitionis partem, aut particulam, Senatui isti tradere: eosque erigere in pædagogos, 1. Cor. 4: 15. thronosque & judicium iisdare. Quam tamen potestatem cum ab hominibus habeant, non a Deo; moderate ea uti, & magis patres, quam pædagogos in Christo esse ostendere debent. Quantopere autem illorum judicium & auctoritas a potestate Seniorum, in Cathedra Mosis sedentium, differat, supra vidimus.
units.tr: XLIII. These lay elders, then, as assessors to the pastors, form together with them the Senate of the Church. A congregation or civil community, where true religion is received publicly, may indeed entrust to this Senate some greater power and a part of civil jurisdiction, and may set them up as tutors (1 Cor. 4:15), and give them thrones and judgment. Yet since they hold this power from men, not from God, they ought to exercise it with moderation, and show themselves to be fathers rather than tutors in Christ. How greatly their judgment and authority differ from the authority of the elders who sit in Moses' seat, we have seen above.

units.la: XLIV. Tandem, quanquam non inutile foret, eosdem semper, de cœtu delectos, summis Ecclesiæ rebus adesse; si tamen aliter suadeat, aut temporum angustia, aut peculiaris Ecclesiæ ratio, aut tyrannidis denique metus; sine perpetuo nexu, alternis regere, ac per vices alii aliis succedere possunt. Quales Levitarum & Sacerdotum in templis vices & stationes legimus. Ut ita omnes tanquam fratres coram Domino sint, alternis stantes & confidentes, sine imperio aut dominatu ullo. Psal. 133: 1. Ecce! quam bonum & quam jucundum, habitare fratres etiam una. Esai. 23: 18. Sed sedentibus coram Jehovah cedes mercimonium ejus &c. Tales Ezech. 39: 14. τὸν ἄνθρωτοι ἐνδελεχισμῶ dicuntur.
units.tr: XLIV. Finally, although it would not be unhelpful for the same men, chosen from the congregation, always to be present at the chief affairs of the Church, yet if the narrowness of the times, the particular circumstances of the Church, or indeed the fear of tyranny should suggest otherwise, they may govern in turns without a perpetual bond, and succeed one another by rotation. Such rotations and posts of the Levites and priests in the temples we read of. Thus all are as brethren before the Lord, standing and serving in turn, without any command or dominion whatever. Ps. 133:1: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together also." Isa. 23:18: "But for those who sit before Jehovah her merchandise shall be..." etc. Such men are called in Ezek. 39:14 [ἄνθρωποι ἐνδελεχισμοῦ], men of continual employment.

units.la: XLV. Corporalium, seu τὸν βιωτικῶν, administri sunt Diaconi; qui Ecclesiæ thesauros in hospitum ac egenorum solatium curant. Institutio eorum occurrit Act. 6. Ac in epistolis Apostolorum frequens eorum. corum mentio est. Rom. 12: 7,8. 1. Cor. 12: 28. 1. Tim. 3: 8. Quin & Diaconissæ, ac ministræ, ad curam istam adhibebantur. 1. Tim. 5: 9, 10. Rom. 16: 1. Varia autem eorum curatio erat; dum alii ægris, alii senibus, alii hospitibus, alii orphanis, alii pauperibus &c. adhiberentur. Quæ omnia, in primis illis Ecclesiæ angustiis, liberali ministerio peracta, nunc, auctis Ecclesiarum rebus, eleemosynarum erogatione commode præstari possunt. In quarum cum collectione, tum distributione, munus eorum absolvitur.
units.tr: XLV. The servants of bodily, or [τῶν βιωτικῶν], matters are the deacons, who look after the Church's treasures for the relief of strangers and the needy. Their institution occurs in Acts 6, and their mention is frequent in the Apostles' letters: Rom. 12:7-8; 1 Cor. 12:28; 1 Tim. 3:8. Indeed deaconesses and female ministers were also employed in this care: 1 Tim. 5:9-10; Rom. 16:1. Their care was varied, since some were assigned to the sick, others to the aged, others to strangers, others to orphans, others to the poor, and so on. All these things, in those first straits of the Church, were performed by free ministry; now, with the Churches' resources increased, they can conveniently be provided by the distribution of alms. In the collection and distribution of these alms their office is discharged.

units.la: XLVI. Crevit autem sensim eorum dignitas: ac verbi & sacramentorum ministerium apud veteres cos obiisse, satis constat. Quo sensu in historia Ecclesiastica ordinario occurrunt. Sicuti in Papatu, in missatico dramate, adhibentur. Nam & sacrificulo ministrant; &, identidem respondentes, sic ejus verba cadentia tollunt, ut credas mimum partes tractare secundas. Quoda prima eorum origine alienum est. Impositio autem manuum, de qua Act. 6: in eorum creatione, communissimus apud veteres ritus erat, qui etiam in inferioribus muneribus mandandis adhibebatur. Quin omnes Christiani hoc ritu in baptismo olim obsignabantur.
units.tr: XLVI. Their dignity, however, grew gradually, and it is quite certain that among the ancients they also performed the ministry of the Word and sacraments. In this sense they occur ordinarily in ecclesiastical history. Just as in Papacy they are employed in the drama of the Mass: for they both minister to the little priest, and by responding again and again they take up his falling words so that you would think they played the second parts in a mime. This is far from their original character. The laying on of hands, of which we read in Acts 6 at their appointment, was the most common rite among the ancients, and it was used also in committing the lesser offices. Indeed all Christians were formerly sealed with this rite in baptism.

units.la: XLVII. Anabaptistæ vero, ut duplicem tantum Ecclesiæ ordinem agnoscunt, eos, qui verbum prædicant, & qui pauperum necessitatibus præsunt ita immerito posterioribus etiam Doctorum, Seniorum, & Rectorum nomina, in Scripturis attributa volunt. Quod contra est. Vide 1. Tim. 5: 17. Tit. 1: 5. Act. 6: 2, 3, 4. Non est æquum, nos, derelicto sermone Dei, ministrare mensis. Deligite ergo, fratres, ex vobis viros septem — quos huic usui præficiamus. Nos vero in precibus, & administratione sermonis, perdurabimus.
units.tr: XLVII. The Anabaptists, however, acknowledge only a twofold order in the Church: those who preach the Word, and those who preside over the needs of the poor. Thus, wrongly, they wish the names of Teachers, Elders and Rulers, which Scripture attributes to the latter, to be given also to the former. The contrary is the case. See 1 Tim. 5:17; Tit. 1:5; Acts 6:2-4: "It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brethren, choose from among you seven men... whom we may appoint to this business. But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word."

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De Ecclesiarum unione, earumque Conci- liis & Synodis.
units.tr: Concerning the union of churches, and their councils and synods.

units.la: I. Hactenus de ministris Ecclesiæ singulatim; nunc de communi eorum Concilio ac senatu agemus: ubi, ad communes Ecclesiæ res gerendas, in majores minoresve conventus ac Synodos congregantur. Uti enim una est Dei in terris Ecclesia, ita Ecclesiarum unio omni ope tuenda, omniaque ordine & decore in ea gerenda sunt. Ibit una gens ad aliam ducendo: Eamus eundo ad supplicandum Jehove, & ad quaerendum Jehovam. Zach. 8:21. Ita Ecclesia Hierosolymitana cum Apostolis, reliquis Ecclesiis tum praecepta Spiritus S. tum fidele suum consilium fraterne exposuit, Act. 15:27,28. miseruntque, cum illa ad Antiochenos, com. 30. tum hi ad Ecclesias, qui traderent ea observanda, com. 40. cujus communicationis fructus fuit: ut Ecclesiae constabilirentur fide. c. 16:4,5.
units.tr: I. So far I have spoken of the ministers of the Church one by one; now we shall treat of their common council and senate, where, for managing the common affairs of the Church, they gather in larger or smaller assemblies and synods. For just as there is one Church of God on earth, so the union of the churches must be protected by every means, and all things in it must be conducted in good order and with decency. One nation shall go to another, saying: Let us go to entreat the LORD, and to seek the LORD. Zech. 8:21. So the church at Jerusalem, together with the Apostles, set out to the other churches both the precepts of the Holy Spirit and its own faithful counsel in a brotherly manner, Acts 15:27,28; and they sent, the one to the Antiochenes, v. 30, and these in turn to the churches, to deliver what was to be observed, v. 40. The fruit of this fellowship was that the churches were established in the faith, Acts 16:4,5.

units.la: II. Sic autem de ista re habendum. Singulas Ecclesias de jure divino liberas, nec ulli alii obnoxias esse; & Christum solum agnoscendum dominum, nullam autem Ecclesiam dominam. Si quae autem plurium Ecclesiarum datur coadunatio, & ad communes causas, communibus consiliis gerendas, confoederatio: illa partim a magistratus auctoritate est, qui istis conventibus judicandi, & de causis Ecclesiasticis statuendi potestatem in suis terris facit; partim a mutuo Ecclesiarum pacto & disciplina confoederata; quarum interest ut in cunctis Ecclesiis una veritas sonet, nec irrepente haeresi vel scismate formosum illud corpus deturpetur aut laceretur: denique ex generali praecepto, & germano Apostolorum canone, qui omnia decenter & ordine in Ecclesia Dei fieri jubet, 1.Cor. 14:40. Quo imprimis consiliorum communicationes, & plurium Ecclesiarum in unum locum legationes spectant; tum ad commune periculum arcendum, tum ad communibus commodis providendum; tum ut parti laboranti ab universo corpore succurratur.
units.tr: II. Now this matter is to be held as follows. Each single church is free by divine right and bound to no other; and Christ alone is to be acknowledged as Lord, and no church as lord. If, however, there is any gathering of several churches, and a confederation for carrying on common causes by common counsels, this rests partly on the authority of the magistrate, who grants to such assemblies the power of judging and of deciding ecclesiastical causes within his lands; partly on the mutual compact of the churches and a confederated discipline, since it is in the interest of all the churches that one truth should sound throughout, and that that beautiful body should not be disfigured or torn by a creeping heresy or schism; and finally on the general precept and the genuine canon of the Apostles, who bids that all things be done decently and in order in the Church of God, 1 Cor. 14:40. To this chiefly belong the communications of counsels and the sending of legations of several churches to one place: partly to ward off a common danger, partly to provide for common advantages, and partly so that help may be given from the whole body to a part that is in distress.

units.la: III. Specialem autem istum conventuum ordinem, & politiam, & regimen, & potestatem, aliaque hujusmodi, Christum particulatim instituisse non legimus: cum satis foret ista, communi charitatis ac prudentiae praecepto comprehensa, Ecclesiae ipsius ordini ac prudentiae relinquere. Unde neque aliam Synodorum potestatem agnoscimus, quam aut in Ecclesiarum εὐταξία constituenda, ex mutuo illo nexu earum, ac ordine mere positivo; aut in fide ex verbo Dei explicanda, erroribusque rejiciendis; ad quod aperta Scripturarum demonstratione opus est. Quae autem Ecclesiae idem ex verbo Dei sentiunt, atque ad eandem regulam incedunt; illae in eo, ad quod pervenerunt, ambulare, seseque arcte unire, & pertinaciter dissentientes communi consilio vitare & excludere juste possunt: Tantum, ad quod pervenimus, eadem incedamus regula, idem sentiamus. Phil. 3:16.
units.tr: III. We do not read that Christ particularly instituted this special order of assemblies, or their polity, government and power, and other matters of this kind, since it was enough that these be left to the order and prudence of the Church itself, comprehended under the common precept of charity and prudence. Hence we acknowledge no other power of synods than either that of establishing good order (eutaxia) among the churches, arising from that mutual bond between them and an order that is purely positive, or that of explaining the faith from the Word of God and rejecting errors, for which an open demonstration from the Scriptures is required. Churches which hold the same things as the Word of God and walk by the same rule may justly walk in what they have attained, closely unite with one another, and by common counsel avoid and exclude those who dissent obstinately: Only, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained, let us think the same. Phil. 3:16.

units.la: IV. At-
units.tr: IV. At-

units.la: IV. Atque hac ratione ἀπάντως illis, qui vulgo Independentes sese jactant, respondemus. Illi enim homines, ubi crudius loquuntur (rectius enim sentientes inter ipsos hisce non notamus) omnem Ecclesiarum unionem ac ordinem rejiciunt; Concilia ac Synodos, ut Antichristi characterem, repudiant; ipsorum decretis audacter obnunciant; in suis autem favis ac Ecclesiolis, quæ paucissimis personis, vix denis aut duodenis, perspe constant, sese continent, omnemque Ecclesiam concludunt; nec vel cunctarum universi orbis Ecclesiarum in sese arbitrium aut judicium, nisi ad consulendum, ferunt vel admittunt; ac nullo denique modo, ab ullo mortali, ista sua alvearia ac ceras conturbari ferunt. Vocant autem Ecclesias illas congregationales; quas definito numero, nec eo adeo magno, uni pastori regendas tradunt: atque isto septo se includunt, extra omne aliarum Ecclesiarum commercium.
units.tr: IV. And in this way we answer, by all means, those who vaunt themselves as commonly called Independents. For those men, when they speak more crudely (for we do not mark them down among those who think more correctly), reject every union and order of churches; they repudiate councils and synods as the mark of Antichrist; they boldly disregard their decrees; but within their own hives and little churches, which consist of very few persons, scarcely ten or twelve, they confine themselves and shut up the whole Church; nor do they bear or admit the judgment or decision of all the churches of the whole world over themselves, except for consultation; and in no way do they allow their hives and wax cells to be disturbed by any mortal. They call those churches congregational, which they hand over to be ruled by a single minister, the number being fixed and not very large; and they shut themselves within that hedge, outside all fellowship with other churches.

units.la: V. Quæ quomodo accipienda sint, jam patet. i. Hoc enim certum est, quoad conscientiam, omnem cœtum, imo omnem hominem, soli Deo subjacere. ii. Nec eo minus certum est, & singulos homines, & Ecclesias, aliorum fratrum ἐλέγχω, & demonstrationi ex Scripturis petitæ, subesse. Atque ista quidem fratrum omnium in se mutuo potestas est; quæ ne Ecclesiis quidem erga alias Ecclesias deneganda est. Nam & ibi fraterna officia, & sacra diversorum ejusdem corporis membrorum communio vigere debet. iii. Ecclesiarum autem diversarum non quidem subordinatio, sed propior unio, & commune vinculum ac nexus, adeo divino ordini non repugnat; ut non aliter illæ melius conservari, & offendicula vitari, & doctrinæ puritas retineri, possint. iv. Si autem illa unio instituta sit; &, vel magistratuum auctoritate, vel mutuo Ecclesiarum fœdere, collegio alicui judicium delatum sit; boni ordinis est, positivo ac externo illi Ecclesiarum ordini parere: nec Ecclesiæ, quæ in fœdus venerunt, istud juste detrectare possunt.
units.tr: V. How these things are to be understood is now clear. i. For this is certain: as regards conscience, every assembly, indeed every man, is subject to God alone. ii. And no less certain is it that both individual men and churches are subject to the rebuke (elenchus) of their brethren and to demonstration drawn from the Scriptures. This is indeed a power which all brethren have over one another, and it must not be denied even to churches in relation to other churches. For brotherly duties and the holy communion of the different members of the same body ought to flourish there too. iii. Now a subordination of different churches, indeed, is not repugnant to the divine order, but a closer union, and a common bond and tie, so that these things cannot otherwise be better preserved, stumbling-blocks avoided, and the purity of doctrine retained. iv. If, however, such a union has been instituted, and a judgment has been committed to some college either by the authority of the magistrates or by the mutual covenant of the churches, it is the part of good order to obey that positive and external order of the churches, nor can the churches which have entered into the covenant justly refuse it.

units.la: VI. v. Multa autem sunt, quæ ordinem istum suadent. Non solum Veteris Test. institutum in majoribus minoribusque synedriis, Deut. 17:8,9. & seqq. 2. Chron. 19:8. Psal. 122: 1,5. & primævæ Ecclesiæ usus; ubi quæstiones, in aliis Ecclesiis exortæ, ad Hierosolymitanam matrem, ubi Apostoli diutule præsidebant, delatæ leguntur; ut in illo Apostolorum ac presbyterorum cœtu finirentur, Act. 15: 1,2,4. &c. & 16: 4. ac sequentis deinde ætatis constans ac perpetua praxis. Sed & gravissimæ rationes pro eo militant. Nam & sanctorum communio, quæ latissime coli debet; & Ecclesiæ visibilis unitas; & fidei sinceritas, ritas; & externæ disciplinæ vigor; & co nmunis Ecclesiarum causa ac salus; earumque incrementa & auctus; Euangeliique in aliis partibus promotio; ac Reipublicæ denique tranquillitas; non alio modo melius procurantur.
units.tr: VI. v. Now there are many things which recommend this order. Not only the institution of the Old Testament in greater and lesser synedria, Deut. 17:8,9 and following; 2 Chron. 19:8; Psalm 122:1,5, and the practice of the primitive Church, where we read that questions arising in other churches were referred to the mother church at Jerusalem, where the Apostles presided for a while, so that they might be settled in that assembly of Apostles and elders, Acts 15:1,2,4 etc., and 16:4; and the constant and perpetual practice of the age that followed. But also the most weighty reasons fight for it. For the communion of the saints, which ought to be cultivated as widely as possible; and the unity of the visible Church; and the sincerity and purity of the faith; and the vigour of external discipline; and the common cause and welfare of the churches, and their increase and growth; and the promotion of the gospel in other parts; and finally the tranquillity of the commonwealth: these are not better secured in any other way.

units.la: VII. vi. Nec aliud æque promtum contra sectas, & hæreses, ac lapsus quosque graviores remedium; quæ alioquin, nullo intercedente, quin aliis aspectantibus Ecclesiis, integros cœtus depascere & devastare possent. Sicuti experientia testis est, non alibi tetriores hæreses enatas, & innumera sectarum examina magis ferbuisse, quam in nidis istis, & congregationalium septis, nullo ad arcendam stragem in promtu auxilio; cum cæterarum Ecclesiarum arbitrium aut judicium non admitterent. Quod enim de consulendi auctoritate addunt, adeo leve est, ut malis istis succurre non possit. Quid enim si integræ istæ congregationes, hæretica labe infectæ, non magis consilia quam judicia aliorum ferant? & ab aliis Ecclesiis à fraternitate ejectæ, contrariis edictis sæviant; &, miserabili erorre, sese solos Dei peculium, cæterasque omnes Ecclesias Deo exsortes statuant. vii. Neque vero ab altera parte periculum est, ne Ecclesiastica illa unione singulorum cœtuum libertas pereat. Est enim Synodorum potestas, non destructiva, sed cumulativa. Nam & communia tantum in illis tractantur, quæque ad universum corpus pertinent, relicto singulis cœtibus propriarum rerum arbitrio; & ipsi illi cœtus Synodos constituunt, ac singuli dicendæ in iis sententiæ jus habent. Uti in liberis nationibus, mutuo fœdere unitis, fieri videmus. Quæ adeo libertati & auctoritati singularum Ecclesiarum non repugnant, ut eam magis firment & stabiliant. Cum alioqui verendum sit, ne, dum singuli separatim pascunt, spargatur ovile Domini, ac luporum præda fiat. Zeph. 3: 19. Esai. 25: 23.
units.tr: VII. vi. Nor is there any other remedy equally ready against sects and heresies, and against the more serious lapses of individuals; for otherwise, without any intervening help, while the other churches look on, they could devour and lay waste entire assemblies. As experience bears witness, nowhere have more foul heresies sprung up, nor have innumerable trials of sects boiled up more fiercely, than in those nests and enclosures of the congregationalists, where there is no ready help to ward off the ruin, since they do not admit the judgment or decision of the other churches. For what they add about consultation is so slight that it cannot succour these evils. For what if those entire congregations, infected with the stain of heresy, bear counsels no more than judgments of others? and, cast out of fellowship by other churches, they rage with contrary edicts, and, in a wretched error, set themselves up as alone God's own possession, and all the other churches as cut off from God. vii. Nor indeed is there any danger on the other side that the liberty of the individual assemblies would perish through that ecclesiastical union. For the power of synods is not destructive but cumulative. For only common matters are treated in them, and those which pertain to the whole body, the judgment of each assembly about its own affairs being left to it; and those very assemblies constitute the synods, and each has the right to give its opinion in them. As we see happening in free nations united by a mutual covenant. These things are so far from repugnant to the liberty and authority of the individual churches that they rather strengthen and establish it. Otherwise one must fear that, while they feed separately, the Lord's flock may be scattered and become the prey of wolves. Zeph. 3:19; Isa. 25:23.

units.la: VIII. viii. Nec leviorlabes est, quod hi homines adeo parvulos cœtus instituant; quos etiam congregationales appellant, quod unum in locum, eumque non adeo magnum, coire, omnesque cultus partes obire, atque ab uno pastore regi possint. Tam exiguis enim finibus illas suas Ecclesias circumscribunt. Frequentiores autem Ecclesias vix Ecclesiæ nomine dignantur; & turbam magis ac colluviem, quam fidelium cœtum æstimant. Quæ ipsorum præcisitas quomodo cum Apostolicarum Ecclesiarum exemplo conveniat, ex Actis, & epistolis Apostolicis, videre est. Ac Hierosolymitana quidem Ecclesia multa fidelium millia comprehendebat, Act. 1: 15. & 2: 41. & 4: 4. & 5: 14, 26. De An-
units.tr: VIII. viii. Nor is it a lighter fault that these men institute such very small assemblies, which they also call congregational, because they can gather into one place, and that not very large, perform all the parts of worship, and be ruled by one minister. For they confine their churches within such narrow limits. Yet they scarcely deign to give the name of church to more frequented congregations, and they judge them to be more a crowd and rabble than an assembly of the faithful. How this their narrowness agrees with the example of the Apostolic churches may be seen from the Acts and the Apostolic epistles. And the church at Jerusalem indeed embraced many thousands of the faithful, Acts 1:15; 2:41; 4:4; 5:14, 26. Concerning the An-

units.la: Quid faciendum sit de cœtuum multitudine.
units.tr: What is to be done about the size of congregations.

units.la: Antiochena autem, ubi ob discipulorum frequentiam Christianum nomen primum natum est, ex Act. 13: 1, 43, 44. & 14: 1. judicari potest. Nec Romanæ, Corinthiacæ, Ephesinæ, aliarumque, ad quas tum Apostolorum epistolæ extant, tum in excolendis iis laboribus in Actis referuntur, minor ratio fuit. Ut præteream, & plures Ecclesias singulare Ecclesiæ nomen in Novo Test. ferre, Act. 8: 1; 3: conf. Act. 9: 1, 2 & 12: 1, 5. 1. Cor. 15: 9. Phil. 3: 6. & Judæorum Græcorumque Ecclesiam memorari, 1. Cor. 10: 32. quin & totius orbis fideles & cœtus uno illo nomine comprehendi, 1. Cor. 12: 28. Ut tam arctis unius parœciæ finibus Ecclesiæ sub Novo Test. unitatem concludere, totidemque Ecclesias, quot cœtus in majori aliqua urbe sunt, erigere, nefas sit.
units.tr: Antioch, however, where the name Christian was first given because of the number of disciples, can be judged from Acts 13:1, 43, 44 and 14:1. Nor was the situation of the Roman, Corinthian, Ephesian and other churches any smaller. Apostolic letters to them survive, and their labours are recorded in Acts. To pass over that several churches bear the singular name "Church" in the New Testament (Acts 8:1; 3; cf. Acts 9:1, 2 and 12:1, 5; 1 Cor. 15:9; Phil. 3:6), that the church of the Jews and Greeks is mentioned (1 Cor. 10:32), and that the faithful of the whole world and all congregations are included under that one name (1 Cor. 12:28): it would be wrong to confine the unity of the churches under the New Testament within the narrow bounds of one parish, and to set up as many churches as there are congregations in some larger city.

units.la: IX. Videamus autem propius unionis hujus rationem in Synodis & Conciliis, Hebr. נועד Gr. συνέδριον, σύνοδος, dictis. Quæ, pro Ecclesiarum convenientium numero, vel provincialia, vel nationalia, vel œcumenica, dicuntur. Unius autem Ecclesiæ rectorum conventus [specialius πρεσβυτέριον] appellatur.
units.tr: IX. Let us look more closely at the nature of this union in the synods and councils, called in Hebrew [נועד] and in Greek [συνέδριον, σύνοδος]. According to the number of churches that meet, they are called provincial, national or ecumenical. The gathering of the rulers of a single church is called [more specifically πρεσβυτέριον].

units.la: X. Consideranda autem hæc quatuor. 1. Conciliorum causa veluti efficiens, & eorum convocatio. 11. Materia, sive membra, ex quibus constant. 111. Forma, quoad suffragia, ordinemque externum. 1v. Dequie effectus, eorumque judicium & auctoritas.
units.tr: X. Four things are to be considered: (1) the cause of councils, as it were their efficient cause, and their convocation; (2) their matter, or the members of which they consist; (3) their form, as regards votes and external order; (4) their effects, and their judgment and authority.

units.la: XI. Ac primæ quidem Synodis exemplum adferunt ex Ecclesia Apostolica Act. 15. Ubi conventum fuisse rectorum Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ, tum Apostolorum, ibi tunc temporis præsentium, tum Presbyterorum, ac reliquæ deinceps plebis; ac consilium ab ipsis Antiochenæ Ecclesiæ datum agnoscimus: non autem variarum Ecclesiarum, per legatos coëuntium, Synodum, singularumque suffragia, ac judicia, aliaque in Synodis observari solita, videmus. Ut Colloquium potius vocandum sit, quam Concilium. Recte enim judicabat Ecclesia Antiochena, cujus doctores ibi comparebant, non melius litem illam, quæ nascentem fidem infestabat, componi posse, quam auditis Apostolis, ac consulta Ecclesia illa, unde fidei tradux ad reliquos promanasset.
units.tr: XI. For the first synod they cite the apostolic church, Acts 15. There we recognise that the rulers of the church of Jerusalem met, both the apostles who were then present and the elders, and afterwards the rest of the people; and that the counsel was given by the Antiochene church itself. But we do not see a synod of various churches meeting through legates, nor the votes and judgments of individual churches, nor the other practices customary in synods. So it should be called a colloquy rather than a council. For the Antiochene church, whose teachers were present there, rightly judged that the dispute which was troubling the nascent faith could not be settled better than by hearing the apostles and consulting that church from which the source of the error had spread to the others.

units.la: XII. Sequentibus autem ætatibus, post Apostolorum excessum, solebant Ecclesiæ, ad obortas difficultates componendas, per legationes coire, & in medium consulere. Mittebanturque eam in rem Episcopi, & viri insigniores. Quæ Ecclesiarum unio, ob crebras persecutiones, exiguis tum finibus conclusa; post pacem a Constantino datam, immensum aucta fuit. Nec provincialia tantum, uti hactenus, sed univer-
units.tr: XII. In later ages, after the departure of the apostles, the churches used to gather by delegation to settle the difficulties that arose, and to consult in common. Bishops and leading men were sent for this purpose. This union of churches, then confined to narrow bounds because of frequent persecutions, grew immensely after peace was given by Constantine. Not only provincial councils, as hitherto, but universal ones

units.la: Unionis bujus rationem. Synodi. Conciliorum congregatio. Quæ non legitur facta. Act. 15. falsa & œcumenica, in quantum videl. Romanus patebat orbis, Concilia haberi cæpta sunt. Quod, diviso deinde imperio, aliquandiu duravit. Postea autem, divulso ac collapso, aliter ea a Græcis, aliter à Latinis instituta, & nomine illo habita sunt.
units.tr: The manner of this union. Synods. The gathering of councils, which is not read of as happening in Acts 15. As the Roman world extended, councils began to be held, both provincial and ecumenical. This continued for some time after the empire was divided. Afterwards, when it was broken apart and collapsed, the Greeks and the Latins instituted and held them in different ways, and under that name.

units.la: XIII. Conveniebant autem primis temporibus Episcopi, non alia quam charitatis ac iustitiæ lege jubente, ad subiorientes Ecclesiarum necessitates. Deinde ad unum ea res delata; qui, primæ sedis dignitate in provincia illa, Synodi convocandæ ac ei moderandæ auctoritatem habebat. Quem Metropolitanum appellabant. Auctis deinde Christianorum rebus, cum Imperatores Ecclesiarum curam sumerent, eorum auctoritate Synodi convocatæ ac habitæ sunt. Præsertim ubi ex universo imperio illæ convenire deberent. Solebantque, aut ipsi, aut per præfectos ac comites, universæ actioni moderari; relictis Episcopis solis consulendi partibus. Donec tandem, exclusis Imperatoribus ab Ecclesia, omnem illam potestatem Papa sumsit. Qui adeo sui arbitrii fecit, Concilia ex Christiano orbe convocare, eademque per legatos suos regere; ut istam necessariam Conciliorum formam faciant, atque abîque eo nullum Concilium legitimum esse, assentatores ejus tueri audeant: Imperatores vero summi beneficii nunc loco habeant, si vel Concilii larvam ac umbram longis precibus ab eo possint eblandiri. Quod non leve imperatoriæ potestatis spolium; & mera in Ecclesiam tyrannis est; ac denique veterum Conciliorum exemplis repugnat.
units.tr: XIII. In the earliest times bishops met, under no law other than the command of charity and justice, to help with the needs of the churches. Then the matter was passed to one man who, by the dignity of the first see in that province, had the authority to convene the synod and preside over it. They called him the Metropolitan. Later, as the affairs of Christians grew, and the Emperors took up the care of the churches, synods were convened and held by their authority, especially where they had to gather from the whole empire. The emperors themselves, or through prefects and counts, used to direct the whole proceeding, leaving to the bishops only the part of deliberating. Until at last, with the emperors shut out of the church, the Pope assumed all that power. He made so bold of his own will to convene councils from the Christian world and to govern them through his legates, that his flatterers dare to maintain that this is the necessary form of councils, and that without him no council is lawful. Emperors now count it the greatest favour if they can coax from him, with long prayers, a mere mask and shadow of a council. This is no small plunder of imperial power, is sheer tyranny over the Church, and finally contradicts the examples of the ancient councils.

units.la: XIV. Quod enim Bellarminus objicit, nullum unquam Concilium sine Papæ auctoritate convocatum: id, si ita intelligatur, ut Imperatores, ad Episcoporum preces & postulata, Ecclesiasæ Romana ditione convocaverint; non Papam magis, quem alios Episcopos, quorum consiliis in hac re Imperator quoque usus est, juvat. Nos autem, non de iis qui Synodos postularent, & quorum consiliis Imperatores uterentur; sed de earum auctore, ac proxima indictionis causa, quærimus.
units.tr: XIV. For what Bellarmine objects, that no council was ever convened without the authority of the Pope: if it is understood to mean that emperors convened councils in the Roman territory at the prayers and demands of the bishops, it helps the Pope no more than other bishops, whose counsel the emperor also used in this matter. But we are asking not about those who requested synods, and whose counsel emperors used, but about their author and the immediate cause of the summons.

units.la: XV. Membra Conciliorum erant personæ, cum Ecclesiastica, tum Politica. Solebant enim imperatores, vel legati eorum, veteribus Conciliis, multa cum auctoritate, interesse. Ex Ecclesiis autem conveniebant Episcopi, Presbyteri, Diaconi; quin & Laici nonnunquam. Adesse verto tenebantur omnes Provinciæ Episcopi, sub segregationis pœna. Sæpe etiam absentium sententiæ audiebantur. Invitabantur quoque, ac multo cum honore admittebantur, aliarum Provinciarum ac nationum Legati. Ac præter hos aderant Notarii, Synodorum Actis componendis. Qualium tum frequens in Ecclesia usus.
units.tr: XV. The members of councils were persons, both ecclesiastical and political. For emperors, or their legates, used to attend the ancient councils with great authority. From the churches came bishops, elders and deacons, and indeed laymen sometimes too. All the bishops of the province were bound to be present, under penalty of separation. Often too the opinions of absent men were heard. Legates of other provinces and nations were also invited and admitted with much honour. Besides these, notaries were present to draw up the acts of the synods, a practice then frequent in the church.

units.la: XVI. Coibant ordinario in templi celebrioris conclave, seu secretarium. Quanquam & in imperiali Palatio, quod Trullum vocabatur, Synodum Quini-sextam habitam legimus. Ac distinctum illud erat sedilibus ac subselliis. Primusque locum capiebat Imperator, cum suis; tum Episcopi; quos, corona veluti facta, incingebant Presbyteri. Adstabant autem Diaconi. Ac sequebantur denique Laici. In medio autem positus erat Codex Euangelicus; tum religionis causa; tum ut istam fidei regulam omnes sequerentur: ac juxta eum canonum Ecclesiasticorum liber.
units.tr: XVI. They met ordinarily in the chamber, or sacristy, of a more famous church. Yet we read that the Quinisext Synod was held in the imperial palace, called the Trullo. The place was divided by seats and benches. The emperor took the first place with his people; then the bishops, whom the elders surrounded as in a crown. Deacons stood by, and finally laymen followed. In the middle was placed the Gospel book, both for the sake of religion and so that all would follow this rule of faith; beside it lay the book of ecclesiastical canons.

units.la: XVII. Praesidem agebat, in Synodo provinciali, provinciae Metropolitanus; aut loci, in quo Synodus agebatur, Episcopus. In Conciliis autem oecumenicis duplex erat praesidentiae ratio. Politicus praeses erat Imperator, aut praefecti ejus. Ecclesiasticus vero, vel peculiari imperatoris auctoritate constituebatur; vel communi consensu ad fratrum consessum regendum eligebatur. Nullum autem Pontificis Romani, vel legatorum ejus, in antiquissimis illis conciliis praesidendi fuit jus. Ut nulla ratione gnathonces ejus pro perpetua ejus in conciliis προεδρία adeo pugnent, atque absque ea illa omni auctoritate deprivent. Nulli enim Episcopo perpetuum praesidendi jus in Ecclesia competit. Multo minus ut talis alicui potestas concedenda sit, ex qua sola omne concilii robur ac auctoritas dependeat.
units.tr: XVII. In a provincial synod the president was the metropolitan of the province, or the bishop of the place where the synod was held. In ecumenical councils there was a twofold manner of presidency. The political president was the emperor, or his prefects. The ecclesiastical president was either appointed by a special authority of the emperor, or chosen by common consent to govern the assembly of brethren. But the Roman bishop, or his legates, had no right to preside in those most ancient councils. So in no way do his flatterers fight so hard for his perpetual presidency [προεδρία] in councils, and strip them of all authority without it. For no bishop has a perpetual right of presiding in the Church, much less should such a power be granted to anyone, on which alone the whole strength and authority of a council depends.

units.la: XVIII. Sequitur suffragandi ratio, & modus, aliaque ad externum ordinem spectantia. Ac in primo quidem illo Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae Concilio, non solum Apostoli, sed & presbyteri, ac universus fratrum coetus, convenisse legitur; ac de communi omnium sententia consilium, Antiochensibus mittendum, formatum fuit; ac de omnibus usurpantur verba ista, Visum est Spiritui S. & nobis. vide Act. 15:2,4,6. 12,22,23 & 16:4. Mirum autem in modum ineptit Bellarminus, dum Apostolici aevi simplicitatem ad hodiernam Pontificiorum Concilorum formam, & typum, exigere nititur.
units.tr: XVIII. Next comes the manner and method of voting, and other things pertaining to external order. In that first council of the church of Jerusalem, we read that not only the apostles but also the elders and the whole assembly of brethren met. By the common judgment of all, a letter was formed to send to the Antiochenes, and of all of them these words are used: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. See Acts 15:2, 4, 6, 12, 22, 23 and 16:4. Bellarmine is wonderfully foolish when he strives to force the simplicity of the apostolic age into the present form and pattern of Papist councils.

units.la: XIX. Hodie autem Pontificii, ut judiciorum Ecclesiasticorum potes sint, quod non leve arcanum est, solis Episcopis de jure; Cardinalibus autem, & Abbatibus, & Generalibus Ordinum, ex privilegio & consuetudine, jus sententiae in concilio dicendae tribuunt. Cumque sola natio Italica Episcoporum numero reliquas orbis nationes facile vincat, in eo Pontifex auctoritatis suae non parvum praesidium habet. Est autem
units.tr: XIX. Today, however, the Papists, as if they were the judges of ecclesiastical judgments (which is no small secret), grant by right only to bishops the power of voting, while to cardinals, abbots and generals of orders they grant the right to pronounce an opinion in council by privilege and custom. And since the Italian nation alone easily outnumbers the other nations of the world in bishops, the Pontiff has no small support for his authority in this. It is, moreover,

units.la: Ministri, Politici, & Eccles. Praeses, ut tom. 1. hæc mera tyrannis,cum revera omnibus verbi ministris, ac doctoribus, quin & quibuslibet viris piis, & rerum intelligentibus,ab Ecclesiis missis, suffragii jus competat. Est enim religionis negotium publicum, & ad omnes ex æquo pertinens; ac nemo prohiberi potest publice de ea loqui, si cum potestate ab Ecclesiis ad rem eam missus sit. Solis autem Episcopis, ob Pontificiæ dignitatis tesseram,vel majorum insularum præsidium, istam auctoritatem dare, aliosque omnes a synodali cognitione arcere, est, religionem ac Ecclesiam paucorum hominum peculium facere; ac Spiritus S. charismata prohibere eumque & cathedræ & personis quibusdam, rursus alligare velle. Quod in Novo Test. scelus est. Et sane si per rerum humanarum infirmitatem fieri posset, consultius esset per amica colloquia & consultationes veritatem in conciliis eruere, quam sententiarum ac suffragiorum rigore omnia figere ac decidere.
units.tr: Ministers, politicians and the church president (as in vol. 1) call this sheer tyranny, since in truth every minister of the Word and teacher, and indeed any pious and knowledgeable men sent by the churches, has a right to vote. For religion is a public matter, pertaining equally to all, and no one can be prevented from speaking about it publicly if he has been sent to the business with authority from the churches. But to give this authority to bishops alone, on account of the token of Papal dignity or the presidency of the greater islands, and to keep all others away from synodal deliberation, is to make religion and the Church the private property of a few men, and to prohibit the charismata of the Holy Spirit, and to want to bind him to a chair and to certain persons. This is a crime in the New Testament. And indeed, if human frailty allowed it, it would be more advisable to bring the truth out in councils by friendly conversation and consultation than to settle and decide everything by the rigour of opinions and votes.

units.la: XX. Veterum autem Conciliorum hic ordo erat. Initium capiebatur a precibus, præmisso plerunque jejunio. Confidentibus deinde patribus, prima de fide tractatio erat; sive ea exponenda, sive vindicanda foret. Tum veterum Synodorum canones relegebantur,& disciplinam ac regimen spectantia,ultimo denique loco particulares causæ, quæ singulas Ecclesias concernebant tractabantur. Ac, si quis singulare quid exponendum haberet, in medium prodibat. Per varias autem sessiones Concilii trahebatur; ac sequenti consessu acta præterita relegebantur. Ferebanturque sententiæ, vel apertis suffragiis, vel manuum porrectione. Usitatæ etiam erant acclamationes, si quæ sententia impense placuisset. Si vero quis in contrarium disserebat,præsidis erat rem componere, atque ex isto conflictu latentem veritatem eruere. Ac conclusio denique formabatur,non ex foliusEpiscopi vel præsidis sententia,sed ex plurium vel omnium suffragatione. Quæ omnia, ad quæstionem propositam pertinentia,omnemque illud examen ac judicium, Concilii Acta dicebantur. Contra ac in Concilio Tridentino, ubi sola decreta, quæ publice edebantur, & inani meraque cærimonia constabant, Concilii Acta appellabantur. Denique apud veteres, finita Synodo, aliæ audiebantur acclamationes,& gratulationes,de asserta fide, triumphato errore; additis & votis,pro imperio & Ecclesia. Subscribebant porro omnes conditis aSynodo articulis,&anathematismis(quibus tamen plerumque rectius abstinebatur) servato eo, quem in Synodo obtinuerant, ordine. Quæ omnia tandem consequebatur confirmatio imperialis, per quam fides, a Synodo stabilita, in legem ibat. Quam ubi adepti erant litteris encyclicis seu circularibus, quae in Synodo acta erant, per Ecclesias vulgabantur, atque observanda tradebantur.
units.tr: XX. The order of the ancient councils was this. They began with prayers, usually preceded by a fast. Then, when the Fathers had gathered, the first matter of business was the faith, whether it was to be set forth or defended. Next the canons of the earlier synods were read out, and matters concerning discipline and government were treated, and finally particular cases, which concerned individual churches, were dealt with. And if anyone had something special to set forth, he came forward into the midst. The council was carried on through various sessions, and at the following assembly the acts of the previous one were read over. Opinions were delivered either by open votes or by raising of hands. Acclamations were also customary if some opinion had greatly pleased. But if anyone argued to the contrary, it was the task of the president to settle the matter and to bring out the hidden truth from that conflict. Lastly the conclusion was framed not from the opinion of the bishop or president alone, but from the assent of many or of all. All these things, pertaining to the question proposed, and all that examination and judgement, were called the Acts of the Council. This is unlike the Council of Trent, where only the decrees that were published, consisting of empty and mere ceremony, were called the Acts of the Council. Finally, among the ancients, when the synod was over, other acclamations and congratulations were heard, on the faith affirmed and error triumphed over, with prayers added for the emperor and the Church. Moreover, all subscribed to the articles agreed upon by the synod and to the anathemas (though these were usually more rightly refrained from), the order which they had held in the synod being observed. All of this was finally followed by imperial confirmation, through which the faith established by the synod became law. When they had obtained this, the acts of the synod were published abroad through the churches by encyclical or circular letters, and were handed down to be observed.

units.la: XXI. Sequitur tandem, ut de Synodorum auctoritate & judicio statuamus. Quod non praetorium & absolutum est; ac si homines alii, qui fidei domini & arbitri forent; qualem definiendi auctoritatem in conciliis politicis esse necesse est: sed ministeriale, in Scripturarum explicatione, ac demonstratione, situm. Cujus exemplum in colloquio Hierosolymitano patet; ubi ex Scripturis prophetarum, ex publico Dei testimonio, quod opere ipso gentibus perhibuerat, denique ex Spiritus, qui Apostolos ducebat, sententia, universa res determinata legitur. Unde synodalia judicia, licet quoad ordinem externum ligent, apud conscientiam non plus valent, quam rationes, quibus suffulta sunt; quae ideo plerunque decretis synodicis adduntur. Dicunt autem sententiam Ecclesiarum legati, non tanquam judices, sed tanquam suffragatores, & consiliarii; explicantes, quid ex Scriptura didicerint, & quousque una pervenerint.
units.tr: XXI. It follows at last that we should lay down the authority and judgement of synods. This is not authoritative and absolute, as if men were the lords and arbiters of the faith, which kind of power of defining must belong to political councils; rather it rests on a ministerial footing, in the explanation and demonstration of the Scriptures. An example of this is plain in the Jerusalem colloquy, where the whole matter is read as settled from the prophets' Scriptures, from the public testimony of God which he had himself given to the Gentiles by the work itself, and finally from the judgement of the Spirit who led the Apostles. Hence synodal judgements, although they bind as to external order, carry no more weight with the conscience than the reasons on which they are supported; which is why reasons are usually added to synodal decrees. Moreover, the envoys of the churches give their opinion not as judges but as voters and counsellors, explaining what they have learned from Scripture and how far they have come together.

units.la: XXII. Neque iis major aliqua auctoritas accedit ex Pontificis Romani approbatione; quam adeo impudenter urgent Jesuitae, ut sine ea Synodorum auctoritatem nullam statuant, ab eo autem approbatas demum ratas & infallibiles esse constituant. Unde illum Concilio quovis majorem statuunt; & ne volentem quidem ac assentientem, coactivae ejus potestati subdi patiuntur. Quae sacrilega sunt, & ne ipsis quidem Pontificiis per omnia probata. Nos autem, & conciliis per se, & praesertim Papae, infallibilitatem omnem abrogamus. Nam & sub Vet. Test. exerrasse concilia, patuit. Sub Novo autem Test. multo minus Spiritus S. aut collegio alicui, aut cathedrae, aut homini denique singulari, adfigi aut obstringi debet. Certe ad conciliabula illa, quae ipsi nonnunquam agitant; ubi omnia patriciis artibus plena, resque Ecclesiae tam anxie librari, & tam arcanis consiliis gubernari videmus, ut summa regnorum ac rerum publicarum momenta majori calliditate procurari non possint; quae imprimis Tridenti visa sunt; venire Spiritum S. tenebrisque istis lucem suam immittere, nescio an vel ipsi quidem credant adversarii. Quod vero de Papae confirmatione addunt, quis ferat supremam ac infallibilem decernendi potestatem ipsi soli dari, logosque ejus divinis responsis aequari? certe, si ex ejus oraculo cuncta pendeant, hoc modo non solum Concilium generale, sed & Concilium dioecesanum, imo doctor quilibet privatus infallibilis reddi possit. Imo ne quidem Concilio ullo opus erit; cum Papa tantum pectoris sui adytum consulere, atque inde veras demum voces expromere, familiarisque Spiritus ope cunctas Ecclesiæ difficultates enodare posset.
units.tr: XXII. Nor does any greater authority accrue to them from the approval of the Roman Pontiff; which the Jesuits press so shamelessly that they hold the authority of synods to be nothing without it, and they declare that synods approved by him are finally valid and infallible. Hence they make him greater than any council, and they do not allow even a willing and assenting council to be subject to his coercive power. These things are sacrilegious, and are not even approved in every respect by the Papists themselves. But we abrogate all infallibility, both from councils in themselves and especially from the Pope. For it has been made plain that councils have erred even under the Old Testament. Under the New Testament the Holy Spirit ought much less to be bound or tied to any college, or chair, or finally to any single man. Certainly as for those conciliabula which they themselves sometimes hold, where we see all things full of patrician arts, and the affairs of the Church weighed so anxiously and governed by such secret counsels that the highest interests of kingdoms and commonwealths could not be secured with greater cunning, which was especially evident at Trent: whether even the adversaries themselves believe that the Holy Spirit comes and sends his light into those shadows, I do not know. As for what they add about the confirmation by the Pope, who could bear that the supreme and infallible power of deciding is given to him alone, and his words are equated with divine responses? Surely, if everything hangs on his oracle, in this way not only a general council but also a diocesan council, indeed any private teacher whatsoever, could be made infallible. Indeed there would be no need of any council at all, since the Pope could consult only the inner shrine of his own breast, and from there at last bring forth true voices, and by the help of a familiar spirit unravel all the difficulties of the Church.

units.la: XXIII. Nec est, quod, pro conciliorum suorum infallibilitate, illam Apostolorum ac fratrum Hierosolymitanorum formulam, visum est Spiritus S. & nobis, adferant: aut alioqui universæ Ecclesiæ apostasiam vereantur, si summa concilia errare possint. Jam enim annotavimus, Hierosolymitanum conventum proprie dictum concilium non fuisse. Quanquam Apostoli, non sine fratrum consilio tantam rem tractantes, sequenti Ecclesiæ, in rebus gravibus, cocundi & in commune consulendi exemplum dederint. Male autem ab infallibili Apostolorum auctoritate ad ordinarios eorum successores concluditur. Quanquam nec ipsi Apostoli propriam auctoritatem & infallibilitatem prætexuere; sed rationibus & Scripturis egere. Ut ex conventus ejus actis constat. Unde quicquid istud erat, Spirui S. visum merito dicere poterant. Quod autem & suum nomen judicio illi subscribebant, peculiarem causam habebat; & ad consensum testandum cum eo, quod docuerat Paulus, faciebat; qui falso apud Ecclesias ab Apostolica regula discessisse accusabatur.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor is there reason for them to bring forward, in support of the infallibility of their councils, that formula of the Apostles and the Jerusalem brethren, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, or else to fear an apostasy of the whole Church if the highest councils could err. For we have already noted that the Jerusalem gathering was not properly speaking a council. Although the Apostles, handling so great a matter not without the counsel of the brethren, gave the following Church an example of meeting together and consulting in common in grave affairs. But it is wrongly concluded from the infallible authority of the Apostles to their ordinary successors. Nor indeed did the Apostles themselves put forward any authority or infallibility of their own, but argued from reasons and Scriptures, as is clear from the acts of that assembly. Hence whatever that was, they could rightly say that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. As for their also subscribing their own names to that judgement, this had a particular cause, and served to attest their agreement with what Paul had taught, who was falsely accused among the churches of having departed from the apostolic rule.

units.la: XXIV. Inanis denique metus est de Ecclesiæ universæ prolapsu & interitu; nisi proceres ac Episcopi ejus in conciliis non errandi privilegium habeant. Alii enim Ecclesiæ, alii conciliorum fines sunt. Nec si ea publice defœdetur, ac rectores ejus in graves errores consentiant, ideo de universæ Ecclesiæ fide actum erit. Habent enim nihilominus, qui vere fideles sunt, non letaliter prolabendi promissionem: quaetiam mediis in tenebris, dumque publice errores grassantur, gaudent. Ad externam autem conciliorum pompam ac lcenam, Spiritus S. flatum adstringere, & promissum Ecclesiæ Spiritum publicæ isti frequentiæ ex solido addicere velle, & Scripturæ, & experientiæ adversum est.
units.tr: XXIV. Finally, fear of the overthrow and ruin of the whole Church is empty, unless its leaders and bishops in councils have the privilege of not erring. For the Church and the councils have different limits. Nor, if the council should be publicly polluted and its rulers agree to grave errors, will it therefore be all over with the faith of the whole Church. For those who are truly faithful nevertheless have the promise that they will not fall away fatally; they rejoice in this even in the midst of darkness, while errors are rampant in public. But to bind the breath of the Holy Spirit to the outward pomp and splendour of councils, and to want to assign the promised Spirit of the Church to that public assembly as a settled thing, is contrary both to Scripture and to experience.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS OCTAVUS DE MAGISTRATU.
units.tr: THE FORTY-EIGHTH PLACE: ON THE MAGISTRATE.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De magistratu, ejusque jure & munere circa civilia.
units.tr: On the magistrate, and his right and duty in civil affairs.

units.la: I. CUm fideles, dum in terris agunt, in respublicas ac politias coire, & magistratuum curam & tutelam ambire, & non secus ac alii homines regnari quoque debeant; ad Ecclesiæ considerationem spectat quoque Magistratus politicus. Cujus tum originem, tum munus, partim in sæculo, partim in ipsa Ecclesia, sequentibus lineis describemus.
units.tr: I. Since the faithful, while they live on earth, must also gather into commonwealths and polities, seek the care and protection of magistrates, and be governed like other men, the political magistrate also falls within the consideration of the Church. We shall describe in the following lines both his origin and his office, partly in the world and partly in the Church itself.

units.la: II. Ac primum in genus humanum non leviter injurii sunt, qui coetus ac societates hominum a mutuo metu originem sumsisse scisserunt, atque ex eo fundamento cuncta hominum inter se officia, periculo nimium errore, metiuntur. Contrarium enim ex ipsa rerum experientia, mundique conditi ac ordinati historia patet. Hominem enim integrum amore Dei ac proximi plenum fuisse, dubitari non potest. Ac specimen ejus, longe pulcherrimum, in renascentis Ecclesiæ exordio patuit, Act. 4: 32. Surrepente autem peccati labe, adeo non omnes amoris illius scintillæ extinctæ sunt, ut quicquid exinde in mundo pulchri ac ordinati existit, ex illo fonte unice emituerit. Neque enim adeo humanam gentem deseruit protinus Deus, ut omne amoris ac charitatis commercium, cunctaque inde pullulantia officia, de mundo tolleret. Conjugia enim, sequentis mundi spes & seminarium, ex amore procul dubio coaluerunt. Ex conjugiis autem familiæ; ex familiis civitates, respublicæ, principatus, regna denique, orta ac formata sunt. Quæ, novo adhuc orbe, ac universo hominum genere propinquo sanguinis vinculo inter se adhuc devincto & cognato, non magis metu quam amore duce constituta sunt. Ex quo fonte quo plus retinuerunt, eo ordinatiora & beatiora fuerunt. Quanquam cito discordias, vim, ambitionem, aliaque mala, invaluisse, ac imperia majori auctoritate ac terrore circumdari paulatim coepisse non negamus.
units.tr: II. First, those are not lightly mistaken about the human race who have claimed that human communities and societies arose from mutual fear, and who measure all human duties toward one another on that foundation, with a most dangerous error. For the opposite is evident from experience itself and from the history of the world as created and ordered. It cannot be doubted that man, in his integrity, was full of love for God and his neighbour. And the most beautiful example of this appeared at the beginning of the renewed Church, Acts 4:32. But when the stain of sin crept in, the sparks of that love were not so completely extinguished that whatever is beautiful and orderly in the world since then has flowed solely from that source. God did not so abandon the human race that he took from the world all intercourse of love and all the duties that spring from it. For marriages, the hope and seedbed of the coming world, surely grew up from love. From marriages came families; from families cities, commonwealths, principalities and finally kingdoms were born and formed. These were established, while the world was still new and the whole human race still bound together by the close tie of kinship, not so much by fear as by love as their guide. The more they kept to this source, the better ordered and happier they were. Yet we do not deny that discord, violence, ambition and other evils soon grew strong, and that rulers gradually began to be surrounded with greater authority and terror.

units.la: III. Ac fuit hic civitatum ortus. Primum mundum rexit Adamus, hominum omnium parens & conditor, qui diu posteritati suæ interfuit. Docebat autem natura homines, sese parentum esse; nihilque jucundius esse amore fraterno. Unde erga communem illum generis sui parentem cultus & veneratio, & erga cognatos homines fraterna officia. Quamvis, parvis adhuc rebus humanis, amorem istum non leviter pollutum per Caini scelus legamus. Atque ex illo tempore, præ metu, urbium condendarum mitium ab eo factum; cum hactenus patresfamilias, cum liberis ac pecoribus suis, arva colerent.
units.tr: III. Such was the origin of states. At first Adam ruled the world, the parent and founder of all men, who lived for a long time among his posterity. Nature taught men that they were the children of their parents, and that nothing is more pleasant than brotherly love. Hence came the worship and reverence owed to that common parent of their kind, and brotherly duties toward related men. Yet we read that this love was not lightly defiled by the crime of Cain, while human affairs were still small. And from that time, out of fear, Cain was the first to build cities, whereas until then the heads of families had tilled their fields with their children and flocks.

units.la: IV. Post diluvium Noachus præfuit, alterius mundi princeps. Diuque homines una fuere, donec, divisi linguis, ita si quoque inter se dispergerentur, & in varias civitates ac regna coirent. Dederat autem Deus ipsi Noacho mandatum, de judiciis exercendis, ac necando homine, qui fraternum sanguinem fudisset. Ut Deo ac natura duce societates conditas, ac principatus ortos, constet.
units.tr: IV. After the flood, Noah presided as prince of the second world. For a long time men lived together, until they were divided by languages, so that they were scattered among themselves and gathered into various cities and kingdoms. God had given Noah himself a command concerning the exercise of judgment and the putting to death of the man who had shed a brother's blood. It is thus clear that societies were founded and principalities arose, with God and nature as guides.

units.la: V. Ac erat initio principalis potestas penes patres. Quos, multiplicatis familiis, sæpius lcet inter se convenisse, & vel sacra, vel profana, communi consilio peregisse, non dubium videtur. Qui & necessitate urgente, seniores ex suo numero constituerunt, ad leges constituendas, & judicia exercenda. Quorum apud Israelitas, in Ægypto degentes, cum e duodecim Patriarcharum familiis, tanquam e duodecim fontibus, proxime emersissent, mentio occurrit. Diuque postea, cum in gentem jam redacti, & in rempublicam compositi essent, istud regiminis genus apud ipsos usitatum fuit: instituto etiam sacerdotio, quod hactenus penes singulas familias fuerat: excitatisque nonnunquam extra ordinem principibus ac judicibus, qui ad bellum duces, & libertatis vindices essent. Quæ forma reipubl., per gradus e Patriarcharum familiis sese protollens, a Deo ipso institura, & naturæ convenientissima, fuit.
units.tr: V. At first the supreme power lay with the fathers of families. As the families multiplied, it seems beyond doubt that they often met together and conducted both sacred and secular affairs by common counsel. Under pressing necessity they also chose elders from their own number to make laws and exercise judgment. Mention of these occurs among the Israelites while they were living in Egypt, when they had just sprung up from the families of the twelve patriarchs, as from twelve springs. Later, when they had been formed into a nation and organised into a commonwealth, this kind of government remained in use among them. The priesthood was also instituted, which until then had belonged to individual families; and at times princes and judges were raised up outside the ordinary order, to be leaders in war and defenders of liberty. This form of commonwealth, growing up through stages from the families of the patriarchs, was instituted by God himself and was most suited to nature.

units.la: VI. Undecum populus, regiminis dominici pertæsus, regem poscere; qui θεοκρατίας ipsum regeret, ad instar reliqui orientis, qui addictius regnari amabat, valde Deo istud consilium displicuit. Cum ipse enim populi ac reipubl. illius conditor, legumque ac universi ordinis in ea auctor foret; unde politia illa θεοκρατεία merito vocabatur, sese equidem suumque regimen sperni non mediocriter indignabatur. 1. Sam. 8:7.
units.tr: VI. When the people, weary of the rule of the Lord, demanded a king to rule them, in the manner of the rest of the East, which loved to be governed more absolutely, this plan greatly displeased God. For since he himself was the founder of that people and commonwealth and the author of its laws and of the whole order within it, that polity was rightly called a theocracy [θεοκρατία]; and God was indignant that he and his rule were being despised, and not moderately so. 1 Sam. 8:7.

units.la: VII. Nc.
units.tr: VII. Nc.

units.la: VII. Neque tamen populum suum vel sic deseruit Deus; ac postulantibus regem annuit. Cujus ne infinita potestas foret, certis legibus imperium ejus circumscripsit; juxta legem regiam, quam Deus jam olim in deserto tradiderat, Deut. 17: 14-20. Ac primum quidem regem constituit Saulum, in ira sua, post hunc Davidem, virum secundum cor suum; in cujus familia imperii decus per longa saecula servare decreverat. Cum autem filii cito a paterna pietate degenerarent, regnum primo in duos principatus divisit, tandemque per captivitatem Babylonicam justulit. Postquam illa tempora rursus judices, ac seniores, ac primam illam reipublicae formam, populo reddidit. Et restituam judices tuos ut primitus: & consiliarios tuos ut initio. Post illa appellaberis urbs justitiae, civitas fidelis. Esai. 1: 26. Fueruntque res eorum tum longe florentissimae.
units.tr: VII. Yet God did not abandon his people even so; he granted their request for a king. Lest his power be unlimited, he circumscribed the kingdom by fixed laws, according to the royal law which God had already given long before in the wilderness, Deut. 17:14-20. At first he appointed Saul as king, in his anger; after him David, a man after his own heart; and he had decided to preserve the glory of the kingdom in David's family through long ages. But when the sons soon degenerated from their father's piety, he first divided the kingdom into two principalities, and at last removed it through the Babylonian captivity. After that time he restored to the people the judges, the elders, and that first form of commonwealth. "And I will restore your judges as at first, and your counsellors as at the beginning; afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city," Isa. 1:26. And their affairs were then most flourishing.

units.la: VIII. Ex quibus omnibus jam patet, quid de magistratuum, ac regum institutione dicendum sit. Et quomodo supremus ille ordo, in rebus humanis, a Deo auctore & conditore sit: juxta sacras sententias: Per me reges regnant, & dominatores decernunt justitiam. Per me principes gerunt principatum, & ingenni omnes judices terra. Prov. 8: 15, 16. Et ipse mutat opportunitates, & tempora; transfert reges, & erigit reges, dat sapientiam sapientibus, & cognitionem cognoscentibus distincte. Dan. 2: 21. Tu, Rex regum, cui Deus coelorum regnum, opes, & robur, & dignitatem dedit. com. 37.
