Ut cognoscant viventes, quod potestatem habeat altissimus in regno hominum, & cui vult det illud, & humillimum hominum constituat super eo. cap. 4: 17, 25. Edicens judicibus; videte quid facturi estis. Non enim pro homine judicaturi estis, sed pro Jehova. 2. Chron. 16: 9. Ac spectant huc vaticinia, ad Novum Testamentum pertinentia, Esai. 49:23. Et erunt reges geruli tui, & principes foemina illorum lactatrices tuae. Quibus concinunt Apostolorum praecepta, Rom. 13: 1. Omnis anima potestatibus superioribus subjiciatur. Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo. Quae autem sunt potestates, a Deo ordinatae sunt. 1. Pet. 2: 13. Proinde subjecti estote omni humanae ordinationi, propter dominum; sive regi, ut supereminenti &c. 1. Tim. 2: 2. Fiant petitiones — pro regibus, & omnibus qui in eminentia sunt; ut quietam & tranquillam vitam transigamus, in omni pietate & gravitate. conf. Tit. 3: 2 Jud. com. 8. & 2. Pet. 2: 10. δόξας δὲ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες. Ac similia apud veteres Ecclesiae doctores extant.
units.tr: VIII. From all these things it is now clear what must be said about the institution of magistrates and kings, and how that supreme order among human affairs has God as its author and founder, according to the sacred sentences: "By me kings reign, and rulers decree justice. By me princes rule, and all judges of the earth." Prov. 8:15, 16. "He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding," Dan. 2:21. "You, O king of kings, to whom God has given the kingdom, power, strength and glory," ver. 37. "That the living may know that the Most High has dominion over the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wishes, and sets over it the lowliest of men," chap. 4:17, 25. "Speaking to the judges: consider what you are about to do. For you judge not for man, but for Jehovah," 2 Chron. 19:6 [cf. 16:9]. To the same purpose point the prophecies that belong to the New Testament, Isa. 49:23: "And kings shall be your foster-fathers, and their queens your nurses." These agree with the precepts of the apostles, Rom. 13:1: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God; the powers that exist are ordained by God." 1 Pet. 2:13: "Therefore submit yourselves to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme," etc. 1 Tim. 2:2: "Supplications be made for kings and all who are in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and gravity." Compare Titus 3:2; Jude, ver. 8; and 2 Pet. 2:10, "they do not tremble to speak evil of dignities" [δόξας δὲ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες]. Similar statements are found among the ancient doctors of the Church.

units.la: Pars II.
units.tr: Part II.

units.la: IX. Neque ideo populo omnem constituendi regiminis potestatem abrogamus. Ille enim, ubi liber ac sui juris est, quamcumque principatus formam eligere, ac instituere potest. Ita tamen, ut ipsa magistratuum auctoritas a Deo sit; populi autem sit, reipubl. formam, modumque, ac denique personas eligere, & designare, quibus istam rerum molem credat.
units.tr: IX. Yet we do not therefore deny the people all power of establishing a form of government. For where the people is free and has its own right, it can choose and institute whatever form of principality it pleases. But the authority of the magistrates themselves is from God, while it belongs to the people to choose and designate the form and manner of the commonwealth, and finally the persons to whom they entrust that great burden of affairs.

units.la: X. Quin &c, peccatis populi ita promerentibus, imperia herilia & despotica a Deo quoque sunt. Quando integros saepe populos, ad scelera eorum castiganda, non regibus, sed tyrannis, in servitutem dedit. Quae imperantium irae, ac immania ingenia, eo in casu ferenda sunt; nec frenum istud admordendum, aut excutiendum; nisi Deus ipse certissimus ad libertatem dux sit. Nec alia tum populi arma sunt, quam lacrymae & preces. Ubi vero liberam rempublicam habet populus, magistratuum ac Ephororum est omni modo libertatem tueri, nec novis dominis eam servire jubere. Quod non levius foret, quam si quis hominem liberum, sine causa, ad dirissimam servitutem damnaret.
units.tr: X. Indeed, when the people have deserved it by their sins, imperious and despotic rulers also come from God. Sometimes he has handed whole peoples over into slavery, not to kings but to tyrants, in order to punish their crimes. In such a case the anger of the rulers and their monstrous characters must be endured. That yoke must not be shaken off or thrown away, unless God himself is the most certain leader to freedom. Then the people have no weapons but tears and prayers. But where the people have a free commonwealth, it is the duty of the magistrates and Ephors to defend its liberty in every way, and not to order it to serve new masters. To do so would be no less serious than to condemn a free man to the harshest slavery without cause.

units.la: XI. Non ferendi autem Pontificii monarcho-mastiges, canonistae praesertim, aliique Papalis omnipotentiae patroni: qui, dare jura leonibus ausi, non solum regnorum jura ac leges suis tabulis inclulere; sed ipsa regum diademata, ac coronas, atque omnem sceptrorum dignitatem, Archimystae sui pedibus subjecerunt: hoc usi colore, quod temporalia spiritualibus servire debeant. Cui fundamento basce porro theses inaedificarunt Pontifices; sese unos reges eligendi, ac deponendi, potestatem habere; reges non nisi precario, ac sub eorum nutu, dominari; & cuncta denique regna ipsis obnoxia, ac tantum non tributaria, esse. Quae non solum dici, sed & agi in mundo potuisse, praeterita saecula viderunt. Ac non semel ingemuit orbis, inermem illum pastorem, inter aras & altaria, terrarum dominos calcantem, conatumque truces sine vi frenare potentes. Verum ab hac labe orta cum reformatione lux reges jam absolvit. Ac immemores sunt illi mystae dictorum Christi, Joh. 18. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. conf. Luc. 22:25. Scitis principes gentium in eas dominari, & magnates potestatem exercere in eas. Verum non ita erit inter vos. adde Rom. 13:1. Omnis anima potestatibus superioribus subjectatur &c.
units.tr: XI. The Papists must not be tolerated, least of all the canonists, and the other champions of papal omnipotence, the scourges of monarchs. Having dared to give laws to lions, they have not only included the rights and laws of kingdoms in their own tables, but have also placed under the feet of their chief mystagogue the crowns and diadems of kings and all the dignity of sceptres. They have used this pretext, that temporal things ought to serve spiritual things. On this foundation the popes have further built these theses: that they alone have the power to elect and depose kings; that kings rule only by sufferance and at their nod; and finally that all kingdoms are subject to them and are almost tributary. Past centuries have seen that these things could not only be said but also be carried out in the world. And more than once the world has groaned to see that unarmed shepherd, between altars and sacred tables, trampling on the lords of the earth and attempting to restrain the fierce powerful without force. But with the Reformation, light arose from this disgrace and now frees kings. Those mystagogues have forgotten the words of Christ. John 18: My kingdom is not of this world. Compare Luke 22:25: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. Add Romans 13:1: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, etc.

units.la: XII. Peccant ab altera parte contra hunc Ordinem Anabaptistae; qui nullos in Ecclesia magistratus ferunt: & quanquam a Deo illi in mundo instituti sint, tamen Christiani hominis modestiam a munere isto abhorrere ajunt. Unde Magistratus inter eos qui extra sunt, quos Deus judicat, 1. Cor. 5: 13. numerant. Nec ullam eis in sacra potestatem concedunt. Qui perniciosus in republica error est. Cui nos breviter opponimus 1. Dei institutionem, quam mox vidimus: quamque ipsi adversarii non diffitentur. 2. Veteris Novique Testamenti auctoritates, quas modo adduximus. 3. Piorum in utraque Ecclesia exempla, Josephi, Mosis, Davidis, Nicodemi, Josephi senatoris, Cornelii Romanæ cohortis ducis, Sergii Pauli pro-consulis. Quorum humilitati iste honos adversatus non est. 4. Ipsius magistratus officium: quod cum generi humano imprimis salutare sit, ac sine multarum virtutum stipatu geri non possit, nullis melius quam Christianis credi potest. 5. Ne addam, Christianismum dominorum & servorum discrimina non tollere, juxta Eph. 6. Col. 4. Quod non minus in republica, quam privata locum habet. 7. Unde pro regibus principibusque potius preces fundere Apostolus Christianos jubet, ut vitam in terris piam pacatamque degant. 1. Tim. 2: 1.
units.tr: XII. On the other side, the Anabaptists sin against this order. They recognise no magistrates in the Church, and although these have been instituted in the world by God, they say that the modesty of a Christian man shrinks from that office. Hence they count magistrates among those who are outside, whom God judges, 1 Cor. 5:13. Nor do they grant them any power in sacred matters. This is a pernicious error in the commonwealth. We oppose it briefly: (1) by God's institution, which we have just seen, and which the adversaries themselves do not deny; (2) by the authorities of the Old and New Testaments, which we have just cited; (3) by the examples of the godly in both Churches: Joseph, Moses, David, Nicodemus, Joseph the senator, Cornelius the commander of the Roman cohort, and Sergius Paulus the proconsul. This honour did not conflict with the humility of these men; (4) by the office of the magistrate itself, which, since it is especially beneficial to the human race and cannot be carried out without the company of many virtues, can be entrusted to no one better than Christians; (5) not to mention that Christianity does not abolish the distinctions between masters and servants, according to Ephesians 6 and Colossians 4, which hold no less in the commonwealth than in private life; (6) and so the Apostle bids Christians pour out prayers for kings and princes, that they may lead a godly and peaceful life on earth, 1 Tim. 2:1.

units.la: XIII. Nec quicquam magnopere habent imperiti homines, quod contra hunc Ordinem objiciant. Non enim de omni simpliciter dominatu, Nimrodicum illum ac Titanicum supra alios insurgendi conatum esse, verum est. Nec Deum regem spernunt ac repudiant, qui Magistratus legunt. Neque huc facit locus 1. Sam. 8: 7. de quo supra respondimus. Hosea autem cap. 8: 4. Constituerunt reges, at non ex me, de Jerobeami regno, per rebellionem quæsito, agitur. Quod vero Christus in Nov. Test., & ipse magistratu abstinuerit, Luc. 12: 14. Joh. 9: 15. 18: 36. & discipulis illum interdixerit, Luc. 22: 25, 26. non illum ideo profanum reddit. Privatus enim, ac humilis in mundo, Christus vivere; nec ut aliquis de sæculo Rex, sed tanquam alterius regni dominus, agnosci debuit. Apostolis autem suis discipulatum, alteriusque generis ministerium, non dominatum, dederat; nec debitas altaribus manus sceptra condecere poterant. Nec magistratui parere Apostolus vetat, 1. Cor. 7: 23. Ne fitis servi hominum. Quod ne ipsi quidem adversarii recusant. Limitate enim loquitur, ut ex loci nexu, aliisque locis collatis patet; & cœcam hominum servitutem, & vilem servilemque animum, quibusvis dominis paratum, idque in re præsertim divina ac sacra, damnat. Contemptim denique magistratum ἀνθρωπίνην κτίσιν appellant, ex 1. Pet. 2: 13. Esse enim potestatem illam a Deo manifestis verbis Paulus asserit. Rom. 13: 1. Ut istius loci alia mens sit.
units.tr: XIII. Nor do unlearned men have much that they can object against this order. For it is not true that the attempt of Nimrod and the Titans to rise above others is a rule of every kind of lordship. Nor do those who choose magistrates spurn and reject God as king. The passage 1 Sam. 8:7, which we answered above, does not bear on this. But Hosea 8:4, They have set up kings, but not by me, speaks of the kingdom of Jeroboam, which was sought by rebellion. That Christ in the New Testament abstained from the magistracy himself, Luke 12:14, John 9:15, 18:36, and forbade his disciples to take it, Luke 22:25, 26, does not make him profane for that reason. For Christ had to live in the world as a private and humble man, and he ought to be recognised not as a king of this age, but as the lord of another kingdom. He had given his apostles discipleship and a ministry of another kind, not dominion, and hands that owe the altars could not fit sceptres. Nor does the Apostle forbid obedience to the magistrate, 1 Cor. 7:23: Do not become servants of men. Even the adversaries themselves do not deny this. For he speaks in a limited way, as is clear from the context and from other passages compared with it, and he condemns blind servitude to men, and a base, servile spirit ready for any master, especially in divine and sacred matters. Finally, they contemptuously call the magistrate a human creation [ἀνθρωπίνην κτίσιν], from 1 Peter 2:13. But Paul clearly asserts in Romans 13:1 that that power is from God, so that the meaning of that passage must be different.

units.la: XIV. Præcipue autem nituntur locis quibusdam Novi Test. male intellectis, Matth. 5: 40. Et ei, qui velit tecum contendere, ac tunicam tuam capere, dimitte illi etiam pallium. 1. Cor. 6: 4. Itaque si judicia habeatis de iis, quæ ad hujus vitæ usum pertinent, eos, qui nullo loco habentur in Ecclesia, in subselliis collocate. & Rom. 12: 19. Non vosmet ipsos vindicantes, dilecti; sed date locum iræ. Scriptum est enim, mea vindicta, ego retribuam, dicit Dominus. Querum παρεμμύνεια primus ac præcipuus errorum istorum fons est. Non enim Magistratus, aut judicia, omnemque juris ordinem, aut quamcunque vindictam de rebus humanis tollit Christus, aut Apostolus. Sed privatas ominum iras, & injurias, & odia, vetat; multaque tolerare, ac charitatis velo obtegere, nec ad quasvis injurias commoveri jubet. Ac speciatim istam litigandi scabiem compescit Apostolus, qua, levissimis de causis, ob damnum quodlibet vel contumeliam acceptam, Christiani non sine scandalo Ethnicorum tribunalia obibant. Erat enim hoc ipsis Judæis detestabile ac ab institutis eorum alienum. In rebus autem gravioribus, vindictam quam privatis hominibus eripit, non solum Deo, sed & magistratui aperte transcribit. conf. Rom. 12: 19, 20, 21. & 13: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: XIV. They rely especially on certain passages of the New Testament that are misunderstood: Matthew 5:40, And if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. 1 Cor. 6:4: So if you have judgments concerning the things that pertain to the use of this life, set those who are held in no esteem in the Church to sit as judges. And Romans 12:19: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. The misapplication of these passages is the first and chief source of these errors. For Christ and the Apostle do not abolish magistrates, or judgments, or the whole order of law, or any kind of punishment in human affairs. They forbid private anger, injuries and hatreds, and bid us to bear many things and cover them with the veil of charity, and not to be stirred by any wrongs. The Apostle in particular checks that itch for litigation by which Christians, for the slightest reasons, on account of any loss or insult received, went to the courts of the Gentiles, not without scandal. For this was hateful even to the Jews themselves and foreign to their institutions. But in more serious matters, he openly transfers to the magistrate, as well as to God, the vengeance that he takes away from private persons. Compare Romans 12:19, 20, 21, and 13:1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

units.la: XV. Stabilito Magistratus munere, videndæ muneris partes, ac magistratuum officia. Quæ sequentia sunt.
units.tr: XV. Having established the office of the magistrate, let us look at the duties of that office and the functions of magistrates. These are the following.

units.la: XVI. 1. Jus inter partes dicere, ac justitiam sancte administrare Judices, & moderatores, constitutito tibi, in singulis portis, qui judicent populum judicio justo. Deut. 16: 18. Justissimam justitiam sectare, ut vivas. com. 20. Quod, nisi Judici privatim contrarium constet, juxta leges, atque acta & probata, in judicio, fieri debet.
units.tr: XVI. 1. To declare the law between the parties and to administer justice holily, appoint for yourself judges and governors in each of your gates, who shall judge the people with just judgment. Deut. 16:18: Pursue justice most justly, that you may live. Ver. 20. This ought to be done in judgment, according to the laws, acts and approved practice, unless it is privately established that the judge holds otherwise.

units.la: XVII. Quare & civibus jura petere a Magistratu licet. Nam & institutum a Deo judiciorum ordinem, legibusque definitum, constat. Deut. 16: 18. 17: 9 19: 17, 18. 2. Chron. 19: 6. Nec abrogavit illum Christus, & Apostoli, sub Novo T., sed confirmavit potius. Vide Matth. 5: 25, 26. Esto amicus adversario tuo cito — ne quando te tradat adversarius judici, & judex te tradat ministro, & in custodiam conjiciaris. Act. 25: 11. Cæsarem appello. Rom. 13: 3, 4. Nam principes non sunt metus bonorum operum. Vis autem non timere potestatem? bonum fac, & habebis laudem ex ea. Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum. Si autem malum feceris, time. Non enim frustra gladium portat. Dei enim minister est; vindex in iram ei, qui malum agit. Adeoque necessaria illa in genere humano sunt, ut hominum societates absque illis in-mera. mera latrocinia degeneratura sint. Cuncta enim potentiorum praeda erunt; & nec pauper, nec vidua, nec pupillus jus suum tueri poterunt.
units.tr: XVII. Therefore citizens may also seek their rights from the magistrate. For it is clear that the order of judgments instituted by God and defined by laws still stands. Deut. 16:18; 17:9; 19:17, 18; 2 Chron. 19:6. Christ and the Apostles did not abolish it under the New Testament, but rather confirmed it. See Matthew 5:25, 26: Come to terms quickly with your adversary, lest at any time the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Acts 25:11: I appeal to Caesar. Romans 13:3, 4: For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil. Do you wish to have no fear of the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God's minister for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For it does not bear the sword in vain. For it is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil. These institutions are so necessary to the human race that societies of men without them would degenerate into mere robberies. For everything would become the prey of the powerful, and neither the poor, nor the widow, nor the orphan could defend their right.

units.la: XVIII. Ut scrupulose nimis Anabaptistae, Sociniani, Weigeliani iStum juris ordinem sub Novo Test. damnent; ac de rebus terrenis coram judice contendi vetent. Quae enim charitatis ac amoris officia Christus commendat Matth. 5. ea publica judicia non tollunt; cum eadem quoque sub Veteri Test. injuncta fuerint. Quod & de offensarum remissione, Matth. 6. & alibi a Salvatore mandata, respondemus. Haec enim juris ordinem non evertunt. Et 1. Cor. 6. Apostolus non quascunque lites, sed solam litigandi pruriginem ac insaniam damnat. Quae res levissimas, quae prudentiorum arbitrio componi poterant, temere in forum producit, longis ibi nexibus impediendas, ac prolixo & inutili labore vix sero ad exitum perducendas. Quem dementem foriambitum, non sine Christiani nominis infamia, apud Ethnicos quoque judices, exercitum, Apostolus merito castigat, & prohibet.
units.tr: XVIII. The Anabaptists, Socinians and Weigelians are overly scrupulous when they condemn this lawful order under the New Testament and forbid disputes over earthly matters before a judge. The duties of charity and love that Christ commends in Matt. 5 do not abolish public judgments, since the same duties were also enjoined under the Old Testament. We give the same answer regarding the forgiveness of offences, which the Saviour commands in Matt. 6 and elsewhere: these do not overturn the order of law. In 1 Cor. 6 the Apostle condemns not every lawsuit but only the itch and madness of litigation, which rashly drags very trivial matters, those that could have been settled by the judgment of wiser people, into court, where they are entangled in long proceedings and brought to an end only late, with prolonged and fruitless labour. The Apostle rightly rebukes and forbids this mad and ambitious pursuit, practised even before heathen judges, not without infamy to the Christian name.

units.la: XIX. 11. Ad Magistratus quoque spectat, judicia capitalia in sontes exercere. Quae iidem sectarii negant, & ut Christianae mansuetudini adversa traducunt. Cum isto pacto peccator non corrigatur, sed omni emendationis spatio crepto, de vita quoque aeterna periclitetur. Ac furtum imprimis morte vindicari non ferunt. Atque eandem ob rationem bella quoque, omnemque armorum disciplinam, a Christiana Republ. proscribunt.
units.tr: XIX. 11. It also belongs to the magistrates to carry out capital sentences against the guilty. These same sectarians deny this and represent it as contrary to Christian gentleness. By this method a sinner is not corrected but, with all room for amendment taken away, is also put in danger of eternal life. Above all, they do not allow theft to be punished by death. For the same reason they also banish wars and all military discipline from the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: XX. De judiciis autem capitalibus expressa Dei Lex est, Noachidis lata, in ipsa mundi ΧΑΛΙΥΓΕΝΕΣΙΑ: Qui effundit sanguinem hominis, per hominem sanguis ejus effundetur; quia in imagine Dei fecit hominem. Gen. 9: 6. Quam Mosaicam, & tanquam ad veterem disciplinam pertinentem criminari non possunt. Cum longe ante illa tempora data, atque universo humano generi, in ipsis ejus initiis, tradita fit; & communi aequitate nituntur: nisi Deo dicas placuisse, ut caedibus omnia ac latrociniis, in novo mundo, complerentur; dum una caedes alia non tam vindicatur, quam cumulatur; atque ista rursum altera: quo pacto nullus caedium finis foret.
units.tr: XX. There is an explicit law of God about capital judgments, given to the descendants of Noah at the very regeneration of the world [παλιγγενεσία]: "Whoever sheds the blood of a man, by a man shall his blood be shed, because God made man in his own image." Gen. 9:6. They cannot accuse this law of being Mosaic and belonging to the old discipline, since it was given long before those times and handed down to the whole human race at its very beginnings, and it rests on common equity. Unless you say that God was pleased for the new world to be filled with murders and robberies, since one murder is not so much avenged by another as multiplied, and that one in turn by another, so that there would be no end to killings.

units.la: XXI. De lege Mosaica constat ex Exod. 21: 12. Qui percutit quemquam ut moriatur, omnino morte plectitor. coll. Lev. 24: 17. Num. 35: 16. ubi loquendi modus idem, qui Gen. 9: 6. Est autem lex haec non juris particularis, qualia multa apud Hebraeos; sed juris publici ac communis, atque aequitate sua omnibus hominibus ex aequo sese probans.
units.tr: XXI. That the Mosaic law says the same is clear from Exod. 21:12: "Whoever strikes anyone so that he dies shall certainly be punished with death"; compare Lev. 24:17 and Num. 35:16, where the wording is the same as in Gen. 9:6. This law is not a particular law of the kind found in many places among the Hebrews, but a law of public and common right, which by its own equity commends itself equally to all men.

units.la: XXII. Cum autem à Veteris Testam. reverentia dudum recesserint adversarii, nec co scle urgeri ferant; similia ex Nov. Testa. adferre licet. Quale est, Matth. 26:26. Qui gladium accepit, gladio peribit. Quæ generalia verba non nisi ad magistratum spectant, cum Christus ad veterem legem ibi respiciat, quam de novo repetit ac sancit. Ac aperte Paulus Rom. 13:4. Magistratum gladio accingit, quem & stringi ad flagitia vindicanda jubet. Non enim frustra gladium gerit. nam Dei minister est, vindex ad iram ei, qui quod malum est fecerit. Idque omne ne quis humani instituti esse, aut alioqui vitio vel nævo non carere, calumnietur, à divina institutione derivat: non est potestas nisi a Deo: ac magistratum Dei διάκονον vocat, ad bonorum tutelam, & improborum terrorem.
units.tr: XXII. Since the opponents have long since abandoned reverence for the Old Testament and cannot bear to be pressed with it, it is permitted to bring similar passages from the New Testament. Such is Matt. 26:26: "He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword." These general words refer only to the magistrate, since Christ there looks back to the old law, which he repeats and sanctions anew. Paul also clearly says in Rom. 13:4 that the magistrate is girded with the sword, which he also commands to be drawn to punish crimes: "For he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil." He derives all of this from divine institution, lest anyone accuse it of being of human invention or otherwise not free from fault or blemish: "there is no power except from God." He calls the magistrate God's servant [διάκονος], for the protection of the good and the terror of the wicked.

units.la: XXIII. Repetunt autem adversarii hic tantum follemne suum: Ne obsistite improbo &c. Matth. 5:39,40. De qua pericopa jam respondimus. Adeo enim Christus istis præceptionibus legitimum judiciorum ordinem non evertit, ut illo eodem capite potius confirmet & stabiliat. Com. 22. tenebitur judicio — tenebitur consessu — tenebitur gehenna ignis. Neque enim legem corrigit, quæ capitalia judicia aperte probat: sed Pharisæos, perversos legum magistros, omnemque istam legulejorum turbam ac colluvium, perstringit; sordesque ipsorum, quas divinæ legi intulerant, expurgat. Quale imprimis erat vindictæ privatæ studium, quod decerptis quibusdam legis divinæ particulis tegebant. Religione autem quadam adversarii a sanguine fundendo abstinent, quasi hoc pacto, demto respiscendi tempore, reorum salus quoque æterna periclitetur. Cum tamen in judiciis capitalibus semper mora aliqua reo indulgeri, ac Christiano ritu animæ ejus ad exitum præparari, atque a maculis a flagitiis, si pote expiari soleat; quo illa judiciorum severitas non parum conducit. Qua peccator domitus, quandoque felicius in ferali pegmate, quam in lectulo, expirat. De furti autem pœna alibi agetur. Nec istam disquisitionem nunc ingredimur; an fures, carceribus ac flagris sæpe admoniti, nec ad frugem redire volentes, tandem, ob perpetua flagitia, ultimo supplicio affici, ac e republica exterminari possint: ad exemplum filii prodigi; de quo Deut. 21.
units.tr: XXIII. Here the opponents only repeat their customary refrain: "Do not resist an evil person," etc., Matt. 5:39, 40. We have already answered this passage. Christ does not overturn the lawful order of judgments by these precepts; rather, in the same chapter he confirms and establishes it: "shall be liable to judgment... shall be liable to the council... shall be liable to the fire of hell" (com. 22). He does not correct the law, which plainly approves capital judgments, but rebukes the Pharisees, the perverse teachers of the law, and that whole crowd of lawyers and rabble, and cleanses the filth they had introduced into the divine law. Chief among these was the pursuit of private revenge, which they covered with certain scraps torn from the divine law. The opponents abstain from shedding blood out of a certain religious scruple, as if, by this means, the time for repentance being taken away, the eternal salvation of the guilty would also be endangered. Yet in capital judgments some delay is always granted to the accused, and his soul is prepared for death in the Christian manner, and he is wont to be cleansed of stains and crimes, if possible; to this the severity of those judgments contributes not a little. Subdued by it, the sinner sometimes dies more happily on the scaffold than in bed. The penalty for theft will be treated elsewhere. Nor do we now enter into the question whether thieves, often warned by imprisonment and whippings and unwilling to return to an honest life, may finally, on account of perpetual crimes, be subjected to the last punishment and expelled from the commonwealth, after the example of the prodigal son, concerning whom see Deut. 21.

units.la: XXIV. III. Ad magistratum pertinet, necessitate urgente, justis de causis, & legitimo modo, ac fine, bella gerere. Quæ publica in publicos hostes vindicta est. Quam crudelem disciplinam a Christianis abesse debere, Manichæi olim, & inter veteres Tertullianus; hodie autem Weigeliani, Sociniani, & Anabaptistæ, statuunt.
units.tr: XXIV. 3. It belongs to the magistrate, when necessity urges, for just causes, in a lawful manner and for a lawful end, to wage war. This is public vengeance against public enemies. The Manichaeans long ago, and among the ancients Tertullian, held that such harsh discipline ought to be absent from Christians; today the Weigelians, Socinians and Anabaptists maintain the same.

units.la: XXV. Contra autem militant bella Jehovæ, in Veteri Testam. non probata solum, sed & jussa, & Spiritu S. impulsore suscepta. Num. 21: 14. 1. Sam. 25: 28. Jud. 3: 9, 10. & 6: 34. & 11: 31. & 15: 14, 15. Ut omne armorum studium toto genere malum non esse constet. Ac in Novo Test. Johannes militibus baptisma largitus est; nec eos arma ponere, sed mercedibus suis contentos esse jussit. Luc. 3: 14. Similiter istud vitæ genus, nec a Christo, nec ab Apostolis, improbatum est. Ac celebrantur imprimis duorum Centurionum, ob pietatem & fidem, exempla. Matth 8: 5. Act. 10: 1, 2, 35. Ac laudat etiam Paulus Hebr. 11: 32. veteris sæculi heroas ac bellatores; quos, insigni fide auctos, Deo duce & auspice bella gessisse, & regna regesque deleviße prædicat. Sed & Magistratus officium id suadet; quod Paulus in eo ponit, ut sit Dei minister, in bonorum bonum, ad iram ei qui quod malum est fecerit, Rom. 13. Quod si contra privatos pacis publicæ turbatores facere teneatur; cur non & idem contra publicos hostes liceat; quibus certe Rempubl. prodere, & creditos sibi cives in prædam exponere, non licet. Sed & natura denique ipsa jus illud belli confirmat; cum sui defensionem suadeat, ac se suaque tutari jubeat. Quæ per legem Euangelicam mutata minime sunt.
units.tr: XXV. On the contrary, the wars of Jehovah fight against them: in the Old Testament these were not only approved but also commanded, and undertaken under the impulse of the Holy Spirit. Num. 21:14; 1 Sam. 25:28; Judg. 3:9, 10; 6:34; 11:31; 15:14, 15. So it is established that the whole pursuit of arms is not evil in its entire kind. In the New Testament John gave baptism to soldiers and ordered them not to lay down their arms but to be content with their wages. Luke 3:14. Likewise that way of life was not disapproved by Christ or by the Apostles. Especially praised are the examples of two centurions, for their piety and faith: Matt. 8:5; Acts 10:1, 2, 35. Paul also praises the heroes and warriors of the old age in Heb. 11:32, whom he declares, endowed with remarkable faith, to have waged wars under God's leadership and auspices and to have destroyed kingdoms and kings. The office of the magistrate also suggests this, which Paul places in this, that he is "God's minister, for the good of the good, an avenger of wrath on him who does evil", Rom. 13. If he is bound to act thus against private disturbers of the public peace, why should it not also be lawful against public enemies? To them it is certainly not lawful to betray the commonwealth and expose to plunder the citizens entrusted to him. Indeed, nature itself confirms that right of war, since it urges self-defence and bids a man protect himself and his own. These things have by no means been changed by the Gospel law.

units.la: XXVI. Ad ratiunculas ipsorum respondemus: Israelitarum duces, quos, confecto bello Midianitico, pro animabus suis piamina obtulisse legimus, Num. 31: 50. non in suscipiendo, sed in gerendo bello peccasse; quod contra interdictum Midianitidas servasset. vide com. 14-17.
units.tr: XXVI. We answer their little arguments. We read that the leaders of Israel, when the Midianite war was over, offered atonement for their souls, Num. 31:50. They sinned not in undertaking the war but in conducting it, since they had spared the Midianite women contrary to the prohibition. See verses 14-17.

units.la: 2. Ac peculiarem causam habebat, quod non Davidi bellatori, sed Salomoni Regi pacifico, templi ædificandi provincia daretur. Typum enim ac mysterium illa habent. 3. Pax autem, quæ sub Christi regno promittitur, spiritualis est; ac veterem illam in mundo inimicitiam spectat, quam, extructa inter Judæos reliquumque mundum maceria, Moses considerat. Christus autem septum illud solvit, & pacem Gentibus dedit. Manebant tamen Ecclesiam adhuc altera bella, aliaque certamina, novique semper hostes: nec certa pax promittitur, nisi sublato Antichristo. Vide Matth. 10: 34. Ne existimate m venisse, immissurum pacem in terram: non veni immissurus pacem, sed gladium. Joh. 16: 33. Hæc locutus sum vobis, ut in me pacem habeatis. In mundo afflictionem habebitis. Sed confidite, ego vici mundum, Apoc. 20: 7, 8. Et quum finiti fuerint mille anni illi, solvetur Satanas ex custodia sua. Et exibit, ad ad seducendum gentes, in quatuor angulos terræ Gog & Magog, ut congreget eos in bellum, quorum numerus ut arenæ maris. 4. Apostolus autem 2. Cor. 10:4. arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia: alia arma cogitat. De suo enim Apostolatu agit, quem non humanis præsidiis, aut sæculari sapientia vel facundia, sed divina Euangelii virtute niti ait.
units.tr: 2. The building of the temple was given to Solomon the peaceful king, not to David the warrior, and this had a particular reason: those things carry a type and a mystery. 3. But the peace promised under Christ's kingdom is spiritual, and it looks to that ancient enmity in the world which Moses considered when the wall between the Jews and the rest of the world was built. Christ, however, broke down that barrier and gave peace to the Gentiles. Yet other wars, other conflicts, and ever new enemies remained for the Church, and a sure peace is not promised until Antichrist is removed. See Matt. 10:34: "Do not think that I have come to bring peace on the earth; I have not come to bring peace but a sword." John 16:33: "I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have affliction. But take courage; I have overcome the world." Rev. 20:7, 8: "And when those thousand years are finished, Satan will be loosed from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them into war, whose number is like the sand of the sea." 4. The Apostle, in 2 Cor. 10:4, "the weapons of our warfare are not carnal," means other weapons. For he speaks of his own apostolate, which he says relies not on human protections, or secular wisdom or eloquence, but on the divine power of the Gospel.

units.la: XXVII. Ad quæstionem: an non res solum externas, sed etiam religionem & sacra armis tutari liceat? Resp. licite id fieri, ubi legitimus modus adhibetur. Neque enim minus fas est, pro aris, quam pro focis, dimicare. Est etenim religio bonum maximum & pretiosissimum. Cujus pignoris custodia magistratui vel præcipue credita est. Ac valet hic regula Apostolica Rom. 13:4. Magistratum subjectorum bono esse: quod non de corporibus magis, & externis subjectorum fortunis, quam de animis intelligitur; quos idololatria, & teterrimis erroribus, pollui, Deique cultum contaminari, ferendum non est. Ac pertinet huc Esai. 49:23. Et erunt reges nutricii tui, & fœminæ principes eorum nutrices tuæ. Nec abludit Israëlitarum exemplum, quos sincerum Dei cultum bello, contra fraternas tribus, tutari decrevisse legimus. Jos. 22: 13. Quod vero de Christo, & Apostolis, objiciunt, illos non armis, sed Euangelii prædicatione, Christianam fidem condidisse, & propria potius morte illam firmavisse; illud alienum est: cum hic non de fide plantanda vel propaganda, sed tutanda; nec de hominibus privatis, quales in hisce Christus & Apostoli erant, sed de publica potestate, quæ sola gladio armata est, agatur. Adeo autem cum charitate hoc pugnat, quam primariam religionis notam voluit Christus, Joh. 13: 35. ut charitatis potius sit, fidem sanctis semel traditam conservare, & subjectis pignus istud illibatum tueri.
units.tr: XXVII. Does it matter whether the magistrate may defend with arms not only external goods but also religion and the sacred things? Answer: this is lawful, provided the proper method is used. For it is no less right to fight for the altars than for the hearths. Religion is the greatest and most precious good, and the guardianship of this pledge has been entrusted above all to the magistrate. The apostolic rule of Rom. 13:4 applies here, that the magistrate is for the good of his subjects. This must be understood of their souls as much as of their bodies and external fortunes; it is not to be endured that souls should be defiled by idolatry and most foul errors, and God's worship contaminated. Isa. 49:23 also bears on this: And kings shall be your nursing fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. The example of the Israelites does not differ: we read that they resolved to defend the pure worship of God by war against their brethren the tribes (Josh. 22:13). As for what they object about Christ and the Apostles, that they founded the Christian faith not by arms but by the preaching of the gospel, and confirmed it rather by their own death, this is beside the point. Here the question is not about planting or spreading the faith but about defending it; and it concerns not private persons, such as Christ and the Apostles were in these matters, but public authority, which alone is armed with the sword. Moreover, this is so far from conflicting with charity, which Christ wished to be the chief mark of religion (John 13:35), that it belongs rather to charity to keep the faith once delivered to the saints and to guard that pledge unimpaired for its subjects.

units.la: XXVIII. Ad jus belli & pacis spectat quoque fœderum faciendorum potestas. Quæ cum externis quoque ac idololatris legitime jungi possunt; modo fides extra hoc commercium sit; nec religio pactis illis lædatur, sed juvetur potius. Frustra obnitentibus, atque commune istud generis humani vinculum abrumpentibus Jesuitis. Vide Gen. 14: 13, 14. & 21: 32. 2. Sam. 5:11. 1. Reg 5:12.
units.tr: XXVIII. The power of making covenants also belongs to the law of war and peace. Such covenants may lawfully be made even with foreigners and idolaters, provided that faith is kept apart from such dealings; and religion is not harmed by those pacts but rather helped. The Jesuits struggle in vain and break this common bond of the human race. See Gen. 14:13, 14; 21:32; 2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Kings 5:12.

units.la: XXIX. v. Magistratus quoque est, ad publica onera ferenda, tributa populis imponere; & domos, agros, hominesque ipsos, reipubl. vectigales facere. Nec redituum publicorum collectores, modo prædis ac rapinis abstineant, infamia notandi sunt. Qua in re tamen summa moderatio & æquitas adhibenda est. Vide Matth. 22:21. Reddite Cæsari, quæ qua sunt Cæsaris. Rom. 13:6, 7. Reddite ergo omnibus debita: cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem: cui honorem, honorem. Mich. 3:2. Nonne vestrum est nosse judicium? odio habentes bonum, & amantes malum, deripientes pellem eorum ab ipsis, & carnem ipsorum ab ossibus ipsorum. Ezech. 34:3, 4. Adipem comedistis, lana vestimini pinguem macatis: oves non pascitis: infirmatas non roboraftis, & fractas non obligastis, & depulsas non reduxistis, & perditas non quæsivistis, sed cum vi dominati estis in eas, & cum sævitia. Amos. 6:3, 4. Qui seponunt diem mali, & admovetis sessionem violentiæ.
units.tr: XXIX. It is also the magistrate's task, in bearing public burdens, to impose taxes on the people and to make houses, fields, and men themselves liable to the commonwealth. Nor are the collectors of public revenues to be branded with infamy, provided they abstain from plunder and robbery. In this matter, however, the greatest moderation and fairness must be shown. See Matt. 22:21: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Rom. 13:6, 7: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour. Mic. 3:2: Is it not for you to know judgment? You who hate the good and love the evil, who pluck off their skin from them and their flesh from their bones. Ezek. 34:3, 4: You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you kill the fatlings; you do not feed the sheep. The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the broken you have not bound up, the driven away you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought; but with force and with cruelty you have ruled over them. Amos 6:3, 4: You who put far away the evil day, and bring near the seat of violence.

units.la: XXX. Non solum autem propter iram, sed & propter conscientiam
units.tr: XXX. Not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience

units.la: ea pendenda sunt. Lex enim de tributis non est mere pœnalis; ut subjectus legi & officio suo faciat satis, si paratus sit pœnam lege constitutam subire, nullo autem modo peccati reus sit, etsi legis præceptum non observet. Cum enim Magistratus scopus sit, tributa subjectis indicere; istamque præceptionem adjunctis in transgressores pœnis corroboret: lex illa pœnalis mixta dicenda est; atque ejus generis, ut & ad culpam, & ad pœnam simul obliget: ita ut, qui legi non satisfacit, pœnam, si qua inde redundet, subire paratus, nec legi satisfaciat, nec conscientiæ.
units.tr: Such dues are to be paid. For a law about taxes is not merely penal, so that a subject satisfies the law and his duty if he is ready to undergo the penalty fixed by law, and is in no way guilty of sin even if he does not observe the precept of the law. For since the purpose of the magistrate is to impose taxes on his subjects, and he strengthens this command by penalties attached to transgressors, that law must be called mixed, a penal law of such a kind that it binds both to guilt and to punishment at once. So he who does not satisfy the law, and is ready to bear whatever penalty follows from it, satisfies neither the law nor his conscience.

units.la: XXXI. Sed quid si tributa sint immodica, nec ex fide ærarium administretur? Resp. Non tamen idoneam recusandi causam esse. Nunquam enim querulis hominibus prætextus deerunt. In gravioribus autem exactionibus, aut pro moderatione impetranda intercedendum, aut ferendæ illæ, aut alio demigrandum; nunquam autem civibus eo obtentu turbandum aut rebellandum est. In omnibus vero agnoscenda Dei providentia, cui aliquando isto etiam pacto partas opes repetere a nobis libet. XXXII. v 1. Denique penes principem est leges jubendi auctoritas. Princeps vero ipse legibus solutus est: non divinis, aut naturalibus, Deut. 17:18, 19, 20. sed positivis duntaxat; saltem quoad vim earum cogentem. Subjectorum autem est, parere propter conscientiam. Necesse est subjici, non tantum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Rom. 13:5. Subjecti estote cuivis humanæ ordinationi propter Dominum. 1. Pet. 2:13. Non quod leges illæ per se conscientiam obstringant (conscientiæ enim imperare solius Dei est; nec alium judicem illa audit) sed quod lex divina externum hominem sub Magistratus imperio constituerit, & ad parendum conscientiam ejus obliget. Nec legibus tantum æquis ac bonis, sed & durioribus, ac de iniquo aliquid trahentibus, obtemperandum est. Servi, subjecti estote cum omni timore Dominis, non solum bonis & æquis, sed etiam pravis. 1. Pet. 2: 18. Quamvis enim acerbi illi jus-sus principem non deceant; qui rempubl., uti familiam suam, curare, mitibusque imperiis regere debet; subjectorum tamen est parere, ac principum, uti parentum, iras ferre. Nisi palam iniqua, ac cum divinis tabulis pugnantia jubeant. Quo in genere tenenda est egregia Apostolorum regula, Judicate ipsi an justum sit in conspectu Dei, vobis potius auscultare, quam Deo. Act. 4: 19. & 5: 24. Est autem magistratuum æquos mittetsque se præbere, cum & ipsi sub majore domino sint; &, adinstar famuli atriensis, in conservos imperent; imo in eos, quos Deus imagine sua decoravit; quosque, tanquam herilem familiam, benigne curare, non vero superbe & contumeliose habere debent.
units.tr: XXXI. But what if the taxes are excessive, and the treasury is not administered faithfully? Answer: even so, this is not a sufficient reason for refusal. For complainers will never lack pretexts. In heavier exactions, however, one must either intercede to obtain moderation, or endure them, or emigrate elsewhere; but citizens must never be stirred up or rebel on that pretext. In all things, however, we must acknowledge the providence of God, by which he sometimes sees fit to take back from us the wealth he has granted us in this very way. XXXII. 1. Finally, the authority to command laws rests with the prince. The prince himself is, however, bound by laws: not by divine or natural laws (Deut. 17:18, 19, 20), but by positive laws only, at least as far as their compelling force goes. It is the duty of subjects to obey for conscience' sake. It is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience (Rom. 13:5). Submit yourselves to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake (1 Pet. 2:13). Not that those laws bind conscience in themselves (for it belongs to God alone to command conscience, and such laws do not hear any other judge), but that the divine law has placed the outward man under the authority of the magistrate and binds his conscience to obey. Nor must one obey only fair and good laws, but also harsher ones, and those which draw something unjust. Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward (1 Pet. 2:18). For although harsh commands do not befit a prince, who ought to care for the commonwealth as for his own household and rule it with gentle commands, it is nevertheless the duty of subjects to obey and to bear the anger of princes as of parents. Unless they command what is plainly unjust and contrary to the divine tables. In this matter the excellent rule of the Apostles must be held: Judge for yourselves whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God (Acts 4:19; 5:29). Magistrates, moreover, ought to show themselves fair and mild, since they too are under a greater Lord, and, like the steward of a household, give orders to fellow-servants; indeed to those whom God has adorned with his image, and whom they ought to care for kindly, as a master's household, and not treat proudly and insultingly.

units.la: XXXIII. Potest tandem princeps libertatem subjectorum quibusdam in rebus circumcidere, & quædam quasi regalia sibi reservare; ut ex. gr. venandi jus: itemque monetæ, rebus promercalibus, usuris, aliisque rebus, modum & pretium statuere: res autem suo genere malas, ut promiscuam libidinem, lenonum luparumque greges, aliaque probra, permittere non potest.
units.tr: XXXIII. Finally, the prince may curtail the liberty of his subjects in certain matters and reserve for himself certain things as if they were royal, for example the right of hunting; likewise he may fix the coinage, the goods of trade, interest rates, and other matters, both measure and price. But he cannot permit things that are evil in their own kind, such as promiscuous lust, the herds of pimps and whores, and other shameful things.

units.la: XXXIV. Non magnæ difficultatis quæstio est, an apud Christianos jus Romanum, in jure dicundo, auctoritatem habere possit; quod ex nimia superstitione negant Weigeliani, & Anabaptistæ, qui, Romanas soliti contemnere leges, Judaicum ediscunt, & servant, & metuunt jus, tradidit arcano quodcunque volumine Moses. Cum autem magistratus potestatem legislatoriam habeat; non dubium est, quin vel novum jus condere, vel latas olim a viris sapientissimis leges in rempublicam accipere possit. Certe Judæos olim Ægyptiorum & Babyloniorum jura agnovisse; & veteres Christianos Romanis legibus paruisse; Paulumque Apostolum illarum beneficio non semel servatum, constat. Act. 22: 25. & 25: 10. Nec ullus Christianos scrupulus tenere debet, ubi ea cum Christiana lege non pugnant. Tum enim illæ nihil aliud sunt, quam latex aut rivulus, e communi æquitatis fonte derivatus. Ubi autem pugnare deprehenduntur, auctoribus suis relinquendæ sunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. It is not a question of great difficulty whether Roman law may have authority among Christians in administering justice. The Weigelians and Anabaptists deny this out of excessive superstition; they, who are wont to despise Roman laws, learn by heart and keep and fear Jewish law, whatever Moses handed down in his secret volume. But since the magistrate has legislative power, there is no doubt that he may either enact new law or admit into the commonwealth laws once issued by most wise men. Certainly it is established that the Jews once recognised the laws of the Egyptians and Babylonians, that the early Christians obeyed Roman laws, and that the Apostle Paul was more than once preserved by their benefit (Acts 22:25; 25:10). Nor ought any Christian to feel scruple in keeping them where they do not conflict with Christian law. For then they are nothing other than a stream or rivulet derived from the common fountain of equity. But where they are found to conflict, they must be left to their own authors.

units.la: An jus Romanum in remp. Christianam admitti possit.
units.tr: Whether Roman law can be admitted into the Christian commonwealth.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De jure & munere Magistratus circa Sacra.
units.tr: On the Right and Office of the Magistrate Concerning Sacred Things.

units.la: I. CUm autem Magistratus, quod a Deo acceperunt, imperium non in corpora solum & brutam hominis partem exercere, sed etiam de æterna subjectorum salute praecipue solliciti esse debeant; sequitur altera officii ipsorum pars, quæ sacra & religiones spectat; quas ipsi publica auctoritate constituere & curare debent.
units.tr: I. Since magistrates have received from God an authority that is to be exercised not only over bodies and the brute part of man, but who must also be especially concerned for the eternal salvation of their subjects, there follows a second part of their office, which concerns sacred matters and religion. They must establish and care for these by public authority.

units.la: II. Et hinc quidem primo loco discernendum est inter ipsam sacrorum functionem, & jurisdictionem seu imperium circa illa. Functionem quod attinet, dubia est quæstio, ac functio sacra & civilis toto genere distinctæ sunt: an vero duæ illæ administrationes, in uno homine conjungi possint? Et hoc quidem in renascentis mundi ac Ecclesiæ initiis sacrum olim esse, ex Melchisedeco & Patriarcharum historiis, liquet. Quid vero nostris temporibus fieri debeat, ac factu optimum sit, non aliunde melius, quam ex temporum serie, & instituto a Deo ipso tum in Veteri, tum in Novo Test. ordine, patet.
units.tr: II. Here, first of all, we must distinguish between the sacred function itself and the jurisdiction or authority over it. As for the function, the question is disputed, since the sacred and the civil functions are distinct in their whole kind. But can those two administrations be united in one man? That in the beginnings of the renewed world and the Church the two were once joined is clear from the history of Melchizedek and the patriarchs. What ought to be done in our own times, and what is best to do, is not better shown from anywhere else than from the sequence of the times and from the order instituted by God himself, both in the Old and in the New Testament.

units.la: III. Ac Mosen quidem, populi principem, sacerdotio quoque extra ordinem functum constat: nec hoc a munere ejus alienum erat; cum non solum Propheta, sed & legislator, & sacræ ac civilis Judæorum Reipublicæ unicus formator foret: unde cura ista ad ipsum ex æquo pertinebat. Functiones autem protinus ab eo discretas videmus. Ac, rebus constitutis, post consecratum Aaronem fratrem, nullas ille amplius sacerdotii partes attigit. Peculiarem autem sacerdotum ordinem instituit, cui cæremoniarum curam mandavit. Legimus etiam institutum ab ipso LXX senum concessum, qui de summa republica judicaret. Num. 11:16.
units.tr: III. It is certain that Moses, the prince of the people, also performed the priestly office outside the ordinary arrangement. Nor was this foreign to his task, since he was not only prophet but also lawgiver and the sole shaper of the sacred and civil commonwealth of the Jews. Hence that care pertained to him equally. We see, however, that the functions were soon separated by him. Once things were set in order, after consecrating his brother Aaron, he took no further part in the priestly duties. He instituted a distinct order of priests, to whom he entrusted the care of the ceremonies. We also read of the council of seventy elders instituted by him, which judged the highest affairs of the commonwealth (Num. 11:16).

units.la: IV. Quænam autem Synedrii hujus foret jurisdictio non æque convenit: quibus sdam omnem potestatem, tum civilem, tum ecclesiasticam, iis deferentibus. Quam causam præ reliquis operose agit Doctiff. Seldenus. Aliis autem nescio qua Synagogam magnam similesque concessus Ecclesiasticos erigentibus, quibus Pontificem M. tanquam præsidem imponunt; eoque in concessu causas omnes Ecclesiasticas examinatas volunt. Quos duos supremos concessus, & personis, & causis, & actionibus, distinctos,ex Deut. 17:8,9. ubi præter sacerdotem etiam Judicis occurrit mentio,conf. 2.Chron. 19:5,8,11. Jer. 19:1. & 26:8, 16.exsculpunt. Quod tamen probum non videtur. Nam omnino unius tantum supremi apud Judæos judicii constans in S. Scriptura, ac apud Judæos, mentio est. Quod ad ultima reipubl. illius tempora duravit, autem saltem extitit: quodque omnibus de rebus, tam sacris, quam civilibus, judicabat. Allegebantur autem in hunc Ordinem, tum Judæorum nobilissimi, tum sacerdotum præcipue primores; qui, propter patriæ legis peritiam, non raro universo collegio moderabantur; Maccabæorum præsertim temporibus: cum illud tamen natura sua, ac imperandi modo, & auctoritate, mere civile foret.
units.tr: IV. What the jurisdiction of this council was, however, is not equally agreed. Some attribute to it all power, both civil and ecclesiastical. Learned Selden works this question out at length above all others. Others, I know not on what grounds, set up a Great Synagogue and similar ecclesiastical assemblies, over which they place the High Priest as president, and they want all ecclesiastical causes examined in that assembly. These men carve out two supreme councils, distinguished by persons, causes and actions, from Deut. 17:8, 9, where, besides the priest, mention is also made of the judge; compare 2 Chron. 19:5, 8, 11; Jer. 19:1; and 26:8, 16. This, however, does not seem sound. For Scripture and the Jewish sources mention only one supreme court among the Jews altogether. It lasted, or at least existed, down to the last times of that commonwealth, and it judged all matters, sacred as well as civil. Into this order were admitted both the most noble of the Jews and especially the foremost of the priests, who, on account of their knowledge of the law of the land, not seldom presided over the whole college, especially in the times of the Maccabees. Yet that body, by its nature, its manner of commanding and its authority, was purely civil.

units.la: V. Simile quoque sacræ civilisque functionis discrimen sub Nov. Fœdere instituit, seu potius jam dudum institutum, confirmavit Dominus noster; atque illam non tam potestate & imperio, quam admonitione & disciplina quadam, sine qua nullus cœtus, & ne domus quidem ulla, consistere potest, absolvit. Cujus ordinem supra vidimus. Donec labentibus Ecclesiæ rebus, in merum imperium ac tyrannidem eam commutarunt Romani Pontifices: qui, conscientiis imperitare non contenti, sacrorum obtentu, in res omnes, reges etiam & principes, summum dominatum invasere; &, religiosi judices, ex universo orbe immanes prædas egerunt. Quæ per Reformationem mutata resque ad pristinam simplicitatem rursus reducta est. Debentque reformatæ doctrinæ luci hoc ipsi, inter Pontificios, reges & principes, quod nudatis latronum istorum foveis & cubilibus, patent jam mendaciorum & fraudium Romanarum insidiæ, & Caci domus atra, abjuratæque rapinæ; nec sceptra ipsorum amplius Ecclesiæ istius Pontificium carmen horrere, atque incermis Pastoris pedo servire necesse habeant.
units.tr: V. Our Lord instituted, or rather confirmed what had been instituted long before, a similar distinction between the sacred and civil functions under the New Covenant. He released the sacred function from power and command, and gave it instead admonition and a certain discipline, without which no assembly, and not even any household, can stand. We have seen its order above. But when the affairs of the Church declined, the Roman Pontiffs changed it into mere command and tyranny. Not content to rule consciences, they, under the pretext of sacred matters, seized supreme dominion over all things, even over kings and princes, and as religious judges they plundered the whole world savagely. This was changed by the Reformation, and affairs were brought back to their former simplicity. The light of the reformed doctrine has done this for kings and princes among the Papists: with the dens and lairs of these robbers laid bare, the snares of Roman lies and frauds are now open, and the dark house of Cacus and his abjured plunder are exposed. Nor do their sceptres need any longer to dread the Papal song of that Church, or serve the crook of the unarmed Shepherd.

units.la: VI. Ita ergo discretæ sunt hæ functiones; non tanquam sibi invicem adversæ, sed potius propter grave utriusque onus, & incommodum quod illarum consociatio secum ferret, Dei Christique jussu distinctæ. Utcunque autem munera ac functiones ipsæ distinctæ sint, ac manere debeant; de imperio tamen ac gubernatione alia ratio est. Neque enim repugnat, civili potestate etiam sacra procurari; & non corpora solum, sed & animas subjectorum religionum freno compesci & cicurari. Ac contra certissimum est, cum summum imperium non nisi unum sit, ac non nisi penes unum solummodo esse possit, etiam supremam sacrorum curam & arbitrium, ac summum in Ecclesiam & Ecclesiasticos imperium, in Republ. penes principem esse. Neque enim Christi regnum humano ordini adversatur. Joh. 18: 36. Nec a principe alienum est, etsi in Ecclesia Rex aut Princeps esse nequeat; sed potius sceptrum ac diadema ibi ponere, & pro fratre se gerere debeat (cum nullus ibi dominatus aut principatus locum habeat, aut habere possit, si interiora ejus spectes:) externum tamen ejus ordinem curare & fovere, idque summa ac principali potestate & auctoritate. Quod & Veteris Testam. reges fecisse constat; & de Christianis principibus praedictum legimus Esai. 49: 23. Et erunt reges nutricii tui, & foeminae principes eorum nutrices tuae &c.
units.tr: VI. These functions are thus distinguished, not as opposed to each other, but rather by the command of God and Christ, on account of the heavy burden of each and the inconvenience that their union would bring. However the offices and functions themselves are distinguished, and must remain so, the matter of authority and government is otherwise. For it is not inconsistent that sacred matters also be cared for by civil power, and that subjects be restrained and tamed by the bridle of religion, not only in body but also in soul. Indeed it is most certain that, since supreme authority is only one and can rest only in one, the supreme care and direction of sacred matters, and the highest authority over the Church and its ministers, also rest with the prince in the commonwealth. For the kingdom of Christ is not opposed to the human order (John 18:36). Nor is it foreign to a prince, although in the Church he cannot be king or prince, but ought rather to lay aside his sceptre and diadem there and act as a brother. (Since no lordship or principality has or can have a place there, if you look at its inner nature.) Yet he ought to take care of and foster its external order, and do so with supreme and principal power and authority. This is known to have been done also by the kings of the Old Testament, and concerning Christian princes we read the prophecy of Isaiah 49:23: And kings shall be your nursing fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers, etc.

units.la: VII. Quod ut distinctius patet, primum de jure Magistratus circa sacra in genere quaeremus; tum varias officii eorum partes in specie attingemus.
units.tr: VII. To make this clearer, we shall first inquire into the right of the magistrate concerning sacred matters in general, and then touch on the various parts of their office in particular.

units.la: VIII. Ac primo quidem, ubi Ecclesiam non solum non in publicum accipi, sed contra a principibus vexari, & continuis persecutionibus agitari, contingit; tum illa sui juris reddita, se ipsam & sacra sua curare, ac plenissimo jure constituere potest. Quod naturali quadam potestate facit, quae omnibus hominum societati competit; quae ordine suo ac regimine carere nullo modo potest. Unde in coetus conveniendi, rectores constituendi, leges ferendi, Synodos cogendi, disciplinam exercendi, cunctaque pro arbitrio gerendi ac administrandi, tum summam ipsa potestatem habet. Quin & civiles controversias, eo in casu, lectis de coetu arbitris, committi ab ea posse, Paulus auctor est 1. Cor. 6.
units.tr: VIII. First, where the Church is not only not received publicly, but on the contrary is harassed by princes and troubled by continual persecutions, it has been returned to its own right, and it can care for itself and its sacred matters and establish them by the fullest right. It does this by a certain natural power, which belongs to every human society and which cannot in any way lack its own order and government. Hence it has supreme power to gather in assemblies, appoint rulers, enact laws, convene synods, exercise discipline, and carry on and manage everything at its own discretion. Indeed, in that case, Paul also teaches that it may commit civil disputes to arbiters chosen from the assembly (1 Cor. 6).

units.la: IX. Aliter autem se res habet, ubi Magistratus Christi fidem accepit, ac Ecclesiae quoque curam ex officio suscipit. Tum enim illa illius curae ac regimini se permittere in universum debet. Habetque Magistratus potestatem summam religiones constituendi & curandi. Quam ne tum quidem, cum infidelis erat, abjecerat; quanquam in Christiana Ecclesia, quam perditum ibat, eam exercere nec volebat, nec poterat.
units.tr: IX. But the matter stands otherwise where the magistrate has received the Christian faith and takes up the care of the Church as part of his office. For then the Church ought to entrust itself wholly to his care and direction. The magistrate has the supreme power of establishing and caring for religions. He had not thrown this away even when he was an unbeliever, although while he was still an enemy of the Christian Church he neither wished nor was able to exercise it in her.

units.la: X. Constat autem hoc magistratuum jus 1. ex ipsa civilis potestatis natura. Cum enim naturaliter unusquisque se ipsum, animaeque suae statum, componendi, ac religionem, qua Deum propitiare vult, constituendi, absolutum jus habeat; illam certe cultus formam, quam tanquam optimam probat, etiam iis, qui sub ejus potestate sunt, praescribere tenetur. Cumque illud, ante constitutas civitates, patrum familias in suis domibus officium fuerit; Nam cognovi ipsum (Abrahamum) ut praecipiat filiis suis & domui suae post se, ut observent viam Jehova. Gen. 18: 17, 18, 19. certe iisdem in Rempubl. jam compositis, & multarum familiarum constitutis dominis ac patribus, idem officium incumbet.
units.tr: X. This right of magistrates rests, first, on the very nature of civil power. For since by nature each man has an absolute right to order himself and the state of his soul, and to establish the religion by which he wishes to propitiate God, he is certainly bound to prescribe to those who are under his power that form of worship which he approves as best. And since, before states were constituted, this was the duty of the heads of families in their own households (For I know him (Abraham), that he will command his children and his household after him, that they keep the way of the LORD, Gen. 18:17, 18, 19), so certainly, once commonwealths are constituted and many families have their lords and fathers, the same duty falls upon them.

units.la: 2. Sed & officii sanctitas hanc a Magistratu curam postulat. Non minus enim aeternae subjectorum felicitati, quam temporali, providere debet. Unde religiones, quas in animo suo verissimas judicat, in terris suis introducere, & publice curare debet. Illius autem rei judicium penes ipsum solum est; nisi caeca obedientia fidem suam alteri gratificari, & obstringere, ac denique aberrare velit. Quanquam prudentiorum consilia audire, seque modis omnibus de rei veritate certum reddere debet. 3. Nulli enim collegio vel consessui Deus ullibi concessit infallibilem de religione arbitrandi potestatem; a cujus oraculo mortales omnes, ipsique etiam Magistratus & Principes, in religione constituendi, dependere debeant. Pontificiorum enim Cathedram de Novi Test. Ecclesia non semel removimus. Nec satis recte alii de religione definiendi potestatem Ecclesiae datam sciscunt (suam autem unusquisque Ecclesiam & coetus cogitat;) ejusque judicium definitivum publicam apud Christianos auctoritatem habere debere urgent. Nulla enim definiendi potestas est, ubi jurisdictio nulla est. Jurisdictio autem vocanda non est, cui quis non nisi propria voluntate, & judicio, ac cognita sententiae veritate, parere cogitur. Ut haec mera vocabula sint, quibus nec veritas, nec sensus ullus subest. Et, si collegium ac confessum aliquem Deus instituisset, cui omnes, atque ipsos quoque terrarum dominos, de religione credere jussisset; illud certe quale, & ubi foret, distincte insinuasset. De eo autem nihil in divinis tabulis extat. Unde omnes coetus, omnesque Ecclesias, privilegium istud temere ad se rapere videas. Quod satis ostendit, merum illum praetextum esse. Unde consequitur, cum ad aliam aliquam potestatem non pertineat, publice cum auctoritate de religione statuere; & tamen in Republ. hoc necessarium sit; ad solum Magistratum istud pertinere; qui istam sibi curam publice sumere & potest, & debet. Quanquam & ille, adhibitis omnibus mediis, rem discernere, &, ne falsas religiones pro veris invehat, attendere summopere debet. Veritati enim, ac veritatis doctoribus, semper manus tradere, ac tanta in re morem gerere, aequum est. Quod tamen rursus collegio illi quod veritatem se tradere ac docere profitetur, nullum imperium aut jurisdictionem largitur: cum omni veritati, omnique sapienti qualiscunque sit, ille honos habendus sit. 4. Sed & confideranda tandem est ipsius Ecclesiæ natura. Illa enim cum nobilissima hominum societas, ac coetus, & permagna Reipubl.pars sit, non magis a Magistratu negligi potest, quam alia civium, Doctorum, mercatorum &c. collegia. Et cum coetus hic reliquis omnibus dignior sit, illam non curare foret pleramque Rempublicam deserere, & nec principis, nec Christiani partes implere.
units.tr: 2. But the sanctity of the office also demands this care from the magistrate. For he must provide no less for the eternal happiness of his subjects than for their temporal welfare. Hence he ought to introduce into his lands, and publicly maintain, the religions he judges to be most true. The judgment of that matter, however, rests with him alone, unless he wishes to hand over his faith to another as a favour, bind himself, and finally go astray. Yet he ought to hear the counsels of the wiser men and by every means make himself certain of the truth of the matter. 3. For God nowhere granted to any college or assembly the infallible power of judging about religion, on whose oracle all mortals, and the magistrates and princes themselves, in establishing religion, ought to depend. For we have already removed the Papists' chair from the New Testament Church, more than once. Nor do others rightly enough decree that the power of defining religion is given to the Church (yet each one thinks of his own church and congregation), and they insist that its definitive judgment should have public authority among Christians. For there is no power of defining where there is no jurisdiction. Jurisdiction, however, is not to be called that to which someone is compelled to submit only by his own will and judgment, and by recognising the truth of the opinion. Those are mere words, with neither truth nor any meaning beneath them. And if God had instituted some college and assembly, to which he had commanded all people, and even the lords of the earth, to believe concerning religion, he would certainly have indicated distinctly what it was like and where it would be. But nothing about it appears in the divine tables. Hence you may see all assemblies and all churches rashly seizing that privilege for themselves. This sufficiently shows it to be a mere pretext. It follows that, since it does not belong to any other power to decree publicly and with authority about religion, and yet this is necessary in the commonwealth, this belongs to the magistrate alone, who both can and ought to take up this care publicly. Yet he too, using all means, must discern the matter and take great care lest he bring in false religions in place of true ones. For it is fitting always to lend a hand to truth and to the teachers of truth, and to show such deference in so great a matter. Yet again, this grants no command or jurisdiction to that college which professes to hand over and teach the truth, since every truth and every wise person, of whatever kind, ought to be given honour. 4. But finally the very nature of the Church must also be considered. For since it is a most noble society of men and a very large part of the commonwealth, it cannot be neglected by the magistrate any more than the other colleges of citizens, teachers, merchants, and so on. And since this assembly is more worthy than all the rest, not to care for it would be to desert most of the commonwealth and not to fulfil the part of a prince or of a Christian.

units.la: XI. Ex quibus omnibus patet, Magistratum æque leges ferre posse de rebus Ecclesiasticis, ac politicis; & pios fidelium coetus non minus quam reliquos civium conventus & societates regere ac moderari debere. Quæ leges quanquam Ecclesiasticæ sint ratione objecti, diversa tamen ratione politicæ sunt. Nihil enim repugnat eandem legem politicam & divinam esse. Imo, Magistratu edictis suis divinas leges firmante, proque lege civitatis haberi eas jubente, ipsum præceptum divinum in jus politium ac civile commutatur. Illa enim optime conveniunt.
units.tr: XI. From all these things it is plain that the magistrate can make laws about ecclesiastical matters just as about political ones, and ought to govern and regulate the pious assemblies of the faithful no less than the other gatherings and societies of citizens. Although these laws are ecclesiastical by reason of their object, they are nevertheless political in their manner. For nothing prevents the same law from being both political and divine. Indeed, when the magistrate confirms the divine laws by his edicts and orders them to be held as the law of the state, the divine precept itself is turned into political and civil law. For these fit together very well.

units.la: XII. Occasio autem magni illius inter Ecclesiam & politiam divortii; quodque Ecclesia non pro societate politica, sed pro alterius genere cœtu, a potestate politica non dependente, haberi cœpta est, ex Gentilium Imperatorum persecutionibus profluxit. (In Ecclesia enim Vet. Test., sub piis regibus, aliter fuit.) Quando nim. pii, urgente conscientia, in publicis sacris, a principum idololatria desciscere, ac alia sacra, aliosque coetus, crigere coacti; in rebus tamen aliis fidem servaverunt. Tunc enim illi proprio arbitrio in coetus coire, Ecclesias constituere, ac sacra curare, coeperunt. Quæ societates cum a Magistratibus Ethnicis institutæ non forent, ac potius ab iis turbarentur, inde considerata sunt tanquam societates alterius naturæ, ab iis non dependentes, & cum politia commune nihil habentes. Pace deinde Ecclesiis reddita, ac emergente Antichristo; ille prætextu illo non segniter usus est; constitutumque olim in Ecclesiis, persecutionum temporibus, ordinem, lege suaque omnia, sine ulla magistratuum cura aut inspectione, privatim curandi, non solum servavit, sed & immensum amplificavit; nec quicquam principibus in Ecclesia permisit, sed ut profanos ab altari abstinere jussit, ingeminatis, ad terrorem, Dathanis, Abironis, Ussiæ, aliorumque exemplis & diris. Solummodo eos Ecclesiæ nutricios esse, h. e. de farina iis & cibariis prospicere, & otiosorum hominum luxum alere jussit. Quod injustissimum erat.
units.tr: XII. The occasion for that great divorce between the Church and the polity, and for the Church to begin to be regarded not as a political society but as a society of another kind, not dependent on political power, arose from the persecutions of the heathen emperors. (In the Church of the Old Testament, under pious kings, it was otherwise.) For when the pious, pressed by conscience, were compelled to withdraw from the idolatry of the princes in public worship and to set up other rites and other assemblies, they nevertheless kept faith in other matters. Then they began to gather into assemblies of their own accord, to establish churches, and to manage sacred things. Since these societies had not been instituted by the heathen magistrates, but were rather disturbed by them, they were considered societies of another nature, independent of them and having nothing in common with the polity. Later, when peace was given to the Churches and Antichrist arose, he made no sluggish use of that pretext. The order established long ago in the Churches in times of persecution, of privately managing everything by its own law without any care or oversight of the magistrates, he not only kept but hugely enlarged. He allowed princes nothing in the Church, but ordered the profane to keep away from the altar, repeating to terrify the examples and curses of Dathan, Abiram and Uzziah. He ordered that they should be only nursing fathers of the Church, that is, provide it with meal and food and feed the luxury of idle men. This was most unjust.

units.la: XIII. Ex
units.tr: XIII. From

units.la: XIII. Ex quibus haec duo patent. 1. nullam esse consequentiam a primae Ecclesiae regimine ad omnem ejus statum & aetates. Aliter enim sub Ethnicis, aliter sub Christiano Magistratu ea degit. Ac multa praeterea alia in externo regimine, salva Ecclesiae substantia, mutari potuisse experientia variis in rebus ostendit. Non enim Christus specialem, aut potius specialissimam regiminis formam instituit, nec minutissima quaeque circumscripsit; sed omni in re ordinem ac decorum observare jubens, multa Ecclesiae libertati permisit. 1. Cor. 14: 40. 2. Non dari proprie loquendo distinctionem veram inter jurisdictionem civilem & Ecclesiasticam. Eamque omnem a Papatu esse. Omnis enim jurisdictio, rigide sumendo, in civitate est. Nec quicquam in Republ. uti observandum ac sequendum cum auctoritate imponi potest, nisi a civili potestate. Ecclesiae autem solum est, monere, hortari, docere verbo Dei; nec quisquam ei obsequi tenetur, quam qui ipse de rerum veritate e verbo Dei persuasus est. Publice autem, atque in Republ. sententiae ac canones ejus vim legum non habent, nisi magistratuum edictis firmata & roborata. Unde omnis eorum potestas.
units.tr: XIII. From these two points are plain. (1) There is no valid inference from the government of the primitive Church to every later state and age of the Church. For it lived one way under heathen rulers and another under a Christian magistracy. Experience has also shown, in many other matters of external government, that much could be changed while the substance of the Church remained intact. Christ did not lay down a special, or rather most special, form of government, nor did he define every smallest detail. Instead, while ordering that all things be done with order and decency, he left much to the freedom of the Church. 1 Cor. 14:40. (2) Properly speaking there is no true distinction between civil and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and all of it comes from the Papacy. Strictly speaking, all jurisdiction lies in the commonwealth. Nothing can be imposed in the republic with authority to be observed and followed except by the civil power. The Church has only the task of admonishing, exhorting and teaching by the Word of God, and no one is bound to obey it except one who is himself persuaded from the Word of God of the truth of the matter. Publicly, however, in the commonwealth, its decisions and canons have no force of law unless they are confirmed and strengthened by the edicts of the magistrates. Hence all their power comes from them.

units.la: XIV. Quod quidam pro coetuum Ecclesiasticorum independentia, & divisa societatis politicae Ecclesiasticae potestate, objiciunt, non magni ponderis est. Quanquam enim Ecclesiae fides & regimen non a Magistratu, sed a Christo dependeant, non ideo omne Magistratus imperium & cura ab ea eliminanda est. Nam & conjugum, & liberorum parentumque, aliorumque hominum, erga se mutuo officia Dei lege definita sunt. Qui tamen omnes magistratuum curatelae & imperio subsunt. Ut de aliarum artium regulis taceam. Non majoris momenti est, regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo. Interiora enim regni Dei ad nostram quaestionem non pertinent; istoque in genere Ecclesiam non hominibus, sed soli Deo subjectam esse concedimus. Quatenus tamen fidelium coetus externum in Republ. ordinem constituunt, ea ratione Magistratus regimini subsunt. Nec ille, cum pro aeterna civium salute excubare quoque debeat, curam istam defugere potest. Quod addunt, Magistratum non posse Theologorum & Pastorum munia gerere, sacramenta administrare &c. cum omnis ista cura rebus civilibus intentis nimis longa & impedita sit: ita est, si de functione ac muneribus ipsis agas; illo tamen praetextu imperio ac jurisdictioni ejus illa omnia subducenda non sunt. Nam & leges circa illa ferre, utque omnis ordo officium faciat, nec quicquam praepostere agat, accurare & attendere omni ope debet.
units.tr: XIV. The objection some raise on behalf of the independence of ecclesiastical assemblies and the separate power of an ecclesiastical political society has little weight. For although the faith and government of the Church depend not on the magistrate but on Christ, it does not follow that all authority and care of the magistrate must be removed from it.
