For the mutual duties of spouses, of children and parents, and of other men towards one another are defined by the law of God, and yet all of them are subject to the oversight and authority of the magistrates, to say nothing of the rules of other arts. Equally unimportant is the point that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world. For the inner matters of the kingdom of God do not bear on our question; in that respect we concede that the Church is subject not to men but to God alone. Insofar as the assembly of the faithful forms an external order in the commonwealth, however, the magistrates are subject to its government in that respect. Nor, since he must also keep watch for the eternal salvation of the citizens, can the magistrate evade this care. As for the claim that the magistrate cannot perform the duties of theologians and ministers or administer the sacraments, since all that care would be too long and too hindering for one occupied with civil affairs: that is so if you speak of the function and offices themselves; but on that pretext all these matters must not be withdrawn from his authority and jurisdiction. For he must by every means take care and attend to enacting laws concerning them, so that every order performs its duty and nothing is done out of place.

units.la: XV. Nunc praecipuas officii eorum partes lustrabimus. Quae in hisce fere constitunt. I. Eorum est religiones & caerimonias publicas rite constituere & ordinare, ut omnia juxta verbum Dei se se habeant; institutis ad exercendas eas locis temporibusque idoneis; aliisque circumstantiis, in verbo Dei non definitis, moderandis; impedimenta autem divini cultus tollere, ac imprimis operam dare; ne nomen Dei in terris suis blasphemetur, vel publice obtineant sententiae haereticae & probrosae. II. Publicum ministerium, ministrosque curare; ut illud purum ac integrum sit, hi autem officium faciant. Etsi enim ministri in munere suo magistratuum vicarii non sunt; non magis quam paterfamilias in regenda domo; cum a Christo illud institutum sit, atque ab eo auctoritatem habeat: tamen publica ejus cura magistratui data est, nec ministri in munere exercendo inspectioni ejus subtrahendi sunt.
units.tr: XV. Now we shall survey the principal parts of his office, which mostly consist of the following. I. It is his task to establish and ordain public religion and ceremonies properly, so that everything accords with the Word of God: to appoint suitable places and times for exercising them, and to regulate other circumstances not defined in the Word of God; to remove hindrances to divine worship, and above all to take care that the name of God is not blasphemed in his lands and that heretical and disgraceful opinions do not gain public standing. II. He must care for the public ministry and its ministers, so that the ministry is pure and whole and the ministers do their duty. For although ministers are not vicars of the magistrate in their office, no more than the head of a household is in governing his house, since the ministry was instituted by Christ and has its authority from him, nevertheless its public care has been entrusted to the magistrate, and ministers must not be withdrawn from his oversight in the exercise of their office.

units.la: III. Quin & vocationibus eorum praeesse debet, & in mandandis iis muneribus prospicere, ut non nisi digni coetibus praficiantur; nec alios in territorio suo tolerare; fideles autem doctores honorare, & mercedibus de publico constitutis fovere debet. IV. Huc etiam spectat ministrum, tum ob alia crimina, tum ob doctrinae aut morum labem, exauctorandi potestas. Salomonis regis exemplo, I. Reg. 2:26,27,28,35,36. Est enim exauctoratio, & de publico munere abdicatio, jurisdictionis pars. V. Ejusdem est Synodos, ad Ecclesiasticas causas disceptandas, indicere: ac pastorum deliberationibus interesse, easdemque moderari: denique decretis eorum auctoritatem suam commodare, utque in leges publicas abeant, edictis suis firmare. VI. Quin & eorum, qui se se Ecclesiasticis sententiis laesos conqueruntur, querelas admittere, novamque causae cognitionem mandare, aliosque judices dare, potest. Tandemque, ubi quem factione opprimi viderit, ipse de tota re judicare potest, VII. Scholas quoque, & publicas bonae mentis aedes, ac Christianae doctrinae seminaria erigere, & pro viribus ornare ac tueri tenetur. Neque enim in rebuspublicis Christianis illud ad Pontificem Rom. proprie spectat. VIII. Religione autem corrupta, ac statu Ecclesiae collapso, ejusdem repurgandae ac pristino nitori restituendae cura vel praecipue ad Magistratus pertinet. Ac faciunt huc laudatorum regum sub Vet. Test. exempla. Quos pii principes, institutae praecedenti saeculo instaurationis duces, feliciter imitati sunt. IX. Cumque una Christi sponsa ac Ecclesia sit, cujus universae custodia, ac veluti episcopatus, non uni singulatim,
units.tr: III. Indeed he ought to preside over their appointments and provide, in committing these offices, that only the worthy are set over the congregations, and that he tolerate no others in his territory; he ought to honour faithful teachers and support them with stipends established from public funds. IV. To this also belongs the power to depose a minister, whether for other crimes or for a taint of doctrine or morals; see the example of King Solomon, 1 Kings 2:26, 27, 28, 35, 36. For deposition, the removal from public office, is part of jurisdiction. V. It is also his to summon synods to debate ecclesiastical causes, to take part in the deliberations of the ministers and to moderate them; and finally to lend his authority to their decrees and confirm them by his edicts so that they pass into public laws. VI. Indeed he may admit the complaints of those who complain that they have been wronged by ecclesiastical sentences, commit a fresh hearing of the case, and appoint other judges. And finally, when he sees someone oppressed by a faction, he may himself judge the whole matter. VII. He is also bound to found and to adorn and protect, as far as his resources allow, schools, public houses of good learning, and seminaries of Christian doctrine. For in Christian commonwealths this does not properly belong to the Roman Pontiff. VIII. When religion is corrupted and the state of the Church has collapsed, the care of purging it and restoring it to its former brightness belongs above all to the magistrate. The examples of the kings praised under the Old Testament support this; the pious princes, leaders of the reformation instituted in the preceding century, imitated them happily. IX. And since there is one bride of Christ, the Church, the care of the whole of which, as it were its episcopate, has been committed not to any one individual but to all and each in common, it is the duty of princes not only to provide for the Churches of their own dominions but also to help the brothers who are harassed and oppressed elsewhere with aid, counsel, intercession and other means. This was once done by Christian emperors. For the dreadful prophetic threats of Judges 5:23 and Amos 6:1–7 fall upon those pampered men who, safe on their own mountains and shores, look down unmoved on the labours of their brothers.

units.la: Pars II. gulatim, sed omnibus singulisque in commune credita est; principum est, non solum suæ ditionis Ecclesiis providere, sed vexatis oppressisque alibi fratribus ope, consilio, intercessione, aliisque modis succurrere. Utab Imperatoribus Christianis olim factum. In delicatos enim illos, qui, ipsi montibus ac littoribus suis tuti, fratrum labores immoti despectant, conveniunt dirę illę propheticæ, Jud. 5:23. Amos 6:1–7.
units.tr: Part II. individually, but to all and each together; it is the duty of princes not only to provide for the Churches of their own dominion, but to succour brothers who are harassed and oppressed elsewhere by help, counsel, intercession and other means. This was done of old by Christian emperors. For on those delicate men who, safe on their own mountains and shores, look down unmoved on their brothers' labours, those dreadful prophetic words fall: Judges 5:23 and Amos 6:1–7.

units.la: XVI. x. Tandem & erga hereticos ac hæreticos officium facere debet, tum ad sanandos illos, tum ad compescendos & coercendos, ac serpentem tabem ab Ecclesiis arcendam. Adhibenda autem cautio, ne pessimi nominis invidia ipsa veritas petatur ac proscribatur. Et distingui debet inter eos, qui lenius, & qui obstinatius errant; tum illos, qui privatim, & qui publice peccant, ac nomen sectamque sibi superstitem moliuntur. Quod genus acrius castigandum est. Quanquam invalescente factione, ac ubi sine motu aut detrimento publico res transfigi non poterit, sectarios tolerare, atque coetus & Ecclesias iis permittere nonnunquam expediat. Quod Christiani Imperatores Arianis olim concesserunt. Sunt autem illi omnes Christiana institutione ad meliores sententias adducendi; non autem vi & ferro ad fidem adigendi (sicuti nec in exteros ac infideles illa justa belli causa est) siquidem verbo, non ferro, plantatur fides. Neque innocuus error, aut diversus de nuthine sensus, capite luendus est. Quanquam gravius in eos animadvertere liceat, qui eo prætextu turbas & seditiones in Repub. movent; aut, moniti sæpius & increpiti, infandis blasphemiis cœlum terramque polluere non desinunt. In omnibus autem summa prudentia ac moderatio adhibenda.
units.tr: XVI. x. Finally, he must also discharge his duty towards heretics and those who hold heretical views, both to heal them and to restrain and check them, and to keep the creeping plague away from the Churches. Care must be taken, however, that the truth itself is not attacked and proscribed under the odium of the worst name. A distinction should be drawn between those who err more mildly and those who err more obstinately, and between those who sin privately and those who sin publicly and devise a name and sect to survive them. The latter kind must be punished more severely. Nevertheless, when a faction grows strong, and where the matter cannot be settled without disturbance or loss to the public, it is sometimes expedient to tolerate the sectarians and to permit them assemblies and churches. This the Christian emperors once granted to the Arians. All of them, however, are to be led to better opinions by Christian instruction, not forced to the faith by violence and the sword (just as an unbelieving or foreign people gives no just cause for war), since the faith is planted by the word, not by the sword. Nor is an harmless error, or a differing opinion about some trifle, to be expiated with the head. Still, it is permissible to punish more severely those who use such a pretext to stir up tumults and sedition in the commonwealth, or who, admonished and rebuked again and again, do not cease to pollute heaven and earth with unspeakable blasphemies. In all of this the greatest prudence and moderation must be used.

units.la: XVII. Errant hic ab una parte Pontificii, nimium in hæreticos sævientes: Nescientes, ut pulchre Augustinus, cum quo labore verum invenitur, & quam difficile caveantur errores: quam rarum & arduum fit, earnalia phantasmata pre mentis serenitate superare: quanta difficultate sanctur oculus interioris hominis, ut possit intueri solem suum: & quantis denique suspiriis & gemitibus fiat, ut ex quantulacunque parte possit intelligi Deus. Hæreses autem nomine infamant quicquid ad Romanæ curiæ palatum non est. Estque hoc proprium Antichristi, cruces, carceres & exilia, veritatis professoribus minari; atque hiant adhuc vulnera & cicatrices, quæ ab illo prædone inflicta etiam hodie Christi Ecclesia præfert. In Scriptura autem nullibi pœna capitalis in hærchæreticos statuta legitur. Lex enim Deut. 13. non de hæretico proprie, sed deapostata & seducŧore agit; & peculiarem in ista Republ. rationem habebat. Dispar autem aliorum populorum ac regnorum conditio est; nec Deo communes adeo cum iis rationes sunt, ac olim cum populo Israelitico. Veteres autem Christiani quantopere ab hæreticis necandis abfuerint, ex Ecclesiasticis auctoribus videre est.
units.tr: XVII. Here the Papists err on one side, raging too much against heretics: not knowing, as Augustine nicely puts it, with what labour truth is found, and how difficult it is to guard against errors; how rare and arduous it is to overcome carnal phantasms by the serenity of the mind; with what difficulty the eye of the inner man is healed so that it can look upon its sun; and finally with what sighs and groans God can be understood even in the smallest part. They defame as heresy whatever does not suit the palate of the Roman court. It is the mark of Antichrist to threaten the professors of the truth with crosses, prisons and exile; and the wounds and scars which that robber inflicted still gape, and the Church of Christ bears them even today. In Scripture, however, nowhere is capital punishment laid down for heretics. For the law in Deuteronomy 13 deals not properly with a heretic but with an apostate and seducer, and it had a peculiar purpose in that commonwealth. The condition of other peoples and kingdoms is different, and God's dealings with them are not so much the same as they once were with the people of Israel. How far the early Christians were from putting heretics to death can be seen from the ecclesiastical writers.

units.la: XVIII. Peccant ab altera parte, & nimium hæreticis indulgent Socinianï. Qui eos miseratione & venia potius dignos censent, nec quicquam gravius in illos, aut libros illorum, statui ferunt; adducta Christi auctoritate Matth. 13: 30. Sinë crescere zizania, usque ad messem. Cum & Apostolum subjungunt, 1. Cor. 11: 19. oportet hæreses esse. Denique Gamalielis consilium impense probant. Nunc itaque dico vobis, abscedite ab hominibus istis, & missos ipsos facite: quoniam si est ex hominibus consilium hoc, sive opus istud, dissolvetur. Sin ex Deo est, non poteritis illud dissolvere; & videte ne etiam cum Deo pugnare deprehendamini. Act. 5: 38, 39. Quibus Respond. Christi ac Apostoli verba prædictionem continere, quid in Ecclesia eventurum sit. Toto enim illo capite Christus Ecclesiæ fata, & diversas periodos, sub parabolarum involucris proponit. Ac Apostolus præterea causas explicat, ac Deum sapienti consilio Ecclesiam suam istum in modum exercere decet. Hæc autem cum magistratuum officio non pugnant. Solummodo moderamen adhiberi Servator suadet, ne cum malis herbis etiam bonæ eradicentur. Gamalielis autem consilium in re dubia ac perplexa laudabile est, Ne doctrina aliqua, nondum satis excussa, quæ tamen multam speciem præ se fert, temere cum auctoribus suis damnetur. Explorandum enim ante omnia est, an ea ex Deo, an vero ex hominibus sit; ne renascens forte veritas, temerariis suffragiis confossa, in ipsa herba enecetur. Nitebatur autem non obscure Gamaliel media ista sententia Apostolos, quos viros bonos & innoxios judicabat, a præsenti periculo liberare. Quod & præstitit.
units.tr: XVIII. The Socinians err on the other side and indulge heretics too much. They think heretics deserve pity and forgiveness rather than anything more severe, and they propose nothing harsher against them or their books. They cite the authority of Christ, Matt. 13:30: Suffer both to grow together until the harvest. They also add the Apostle, 1 Cor. 11:19: there must be heresies. Finally, they warmly commend the counsel of Gamaliel: And now I say to you, refrain from these men and let them alone; for if this counsel or this work is of men, it will come to nothing. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it; lest perhaps you be found even to fight against God. Acts 5:38, 39. To these we reply that the words of Christ and of the Apostle contain a prediction of what will happen in the Church. For throughout that whole chapter Christ sets forth the fortunes of the Church and its different periods under the veil of parables. The Apostle further explains the causes, and how it befits God in his wisdom to deal with his Church in this way. These things do not conflict with the office of the magistrate. The Saviour only advises that moderation be used, so that the good plants are not uprooted along with the bad weeds. Gamaliel's counsel, moreover, is commendable in a doubtful and perplexing matter: a doctrine not yet sufficiently examined, which nonetheless wears a great appearance, should not be rashly condemned along with its authors. For it must first be investigated above all whether it is from God or from men, lest truth, perhaps springing up again, be cut down by hasty votes and die in the very herb. Gamaliel plainly aimed by this middle opinion to free the Apostles, whom he judged to be good and harmless men, from the present danger. And he accomplished this.

units.la: XIX. Ad Quæst. an hæreticis a Christiano principe fides servanda sit? Negative respondent Jesuitæ. Atque ita in Concilio Constantiensi, in causa Johannis Hussi, & Hieronymi Pragensis, judicatum; ac, tegendo dedecori, hæreticis nullam servandam fidem, condito canone, sancitum fuit. Quæ quantopere jurisjurandi sanctitatem, omnemque fœderum religionem evertant, ac de rebus humanis veritatem & justitiam, ac omne humanum commercium tollant, quivis videt. Ut sine insigni probro Christiani nominis talia dogmatum portenta audiri nequeant. Nec obstat, quod fides ea data sit haereticis; iis autem, qui fidem fregerunt Deo, nullo modo ea servanda sit ab hominibus. Nam & Iosua fidem Gibeonitis idololatris datam praestitit, Ioh. 9: 18, 19, 26. & 10: 5-7. conf. 2. Sam. 21: 5. Nec eo quod haeretici sunt, humana omnia ac naturalia iura amiserunt. Nisi & quemvis, qui graviori peccato erga Deum se obstringit, isto in gradu ponas. Aliud autem est, si quis fidem datam prior frangat, nec ea, quae utrinque convenerunt, praestet: tum enim & alteram partem exsolvi, nec ad pacta teneri, certum est.
units.tr: XIX. On the question whether faith is to be kept with heretics by a Christian prince: the Jesuits answer in the negative. And so it was judged at the Council of Constance, in the case of John Hus and Jerome of Prague; and, to cover its disgrace, a canon was framed and enacted that no faith is to be kept with heretics. Everyone can see how greatly such a doctrine overturns the sanctity of oaths and all reverence for covenants, and how it removes truth and justice from human affairs and all human dealings. Such monstrous dogmas cannot be heard without a notable disgrace to the Christian name. Nor does it stand in the way that the faith was given to heretics; yet to those who have broken faith with God, that faith is in no way to be kept by men. For Joshua also kept the faith given to the idolatrous Gibeonites, Josh. 9:18, 19, 26, and 10:5-7; compare 2 Sam. 21:5. Nor have all human and natural rights been lost by the fact that they are heretics. Unless you would also place in this rank anyone who binds himself to God by a more grievous sin. It is otherwise, however, if someone first breaks the faith he has given and does not perform what was agreed on both sides; for then it is certain that the other party is released and not bound to the pacts.

units.la: XX. Atque haec principalis officii, iurisque eorum erga res sacras & Ecclesiasticas praecipuae partes sunt. Quae ad omnes supremas potestates ex aequo spectant. Nec Ethnico magistratui minus iuris est, quam Christiano & orthodoxo. Quanquam ille plerunque iure isto uti dignetur, & Ecclesias potius odio habeat, ac persequatur, ac res suas sibi habere ac curare iubeat.
units.tr: XX. These are the principal parts of the office and the right of the magistrate with respect to sacred and ecclesiastical matters. They apply equally to all supreme powers. Nor does a heathen magistrate have less right in these matters than a Christian and orthodox one, although the former generally deigns not to use this right, and rather hates and persecutes the Churches, and orders them to attend to their own affairs.

units.la: XXI. Debet autem Magistratus Christianus, in officio isto exercendo, omni moderatione uti. Est enim Ecclesia societas fratrum. Ac princeps ipse in Ecclesia, quae mundana civitas non est, non nisi fratris locum occupat. Ac sicuti ille, in privatidomum coenatum veniens, privati propemodum personam sumit, nec alienae familiae imperare praesumit: ita, ubi in Ecclesiam fasces ac diadema suum intulerit, coetus istius libertatem, & ordinem, & Seniorum auctoritatem, non tollere, sed augere & tueri debet. 2. Conducit etiam supenumero, ut non omni auctoritate, quam alioquin de iure habet, utatur. Nam & causae Ecclesiasticae plerunque melius & accuratius ab Ecclesiastico iudicio tractantur; & Ecclesiae ac rectorum ejus est, operam dare, ne magistratuum fastigium concutiant, aut alioqui temere eos offendant, vel iustos iis metus faciant. 3. Iis autem in locis, ubi vel consuetudine, vel liberali magistratuum concessione, factisque eam in rem decretis publicis, Ecclesiae plusculum libertatis ac potestatis habent, ad res suas proprio arbitrio moderandas (sicuti olim ab Imperatoribus Christianis Episcopis multa potestas data est: atque hodie Reformatae Ecclesiae sua quaedam iura, & libertates, & ordinem, in rebuspublicis multis in locis, maxime hisce, habent) eam princeps, nisi maximus abusus intercedat, revocare non potest: sed potius operam dare debet, ut Ecclesiae rectores officium faciant, ac potestate illa recte, & ad bonum Ecclesiae, utantur; ut illa, amcamotis scandalis, pura & intaminata permaneat.
units.tr: XXI. A Christian magistrate, however, ought to use all moderation in exercising this office. For the Church is a fellowship of brothers. And the prince himself, within the Church, which is not a worldly commonwealth, occupies no place other than that of a brother. Just as he, when he comes as a guest into a private home, almost assumes the person of a private man and does not presume to command another's household, so, when he has brought his rods and crown into the Church, he ought not to diminish the liberty, order and authority of the elders of that assembly, but to increase and protect them. 2. It is also expedient, in a case of this kind, that he not use all the authority which he otherwise has by right. For ecclesiastical causes are generally handled better and more accurately by ecclesiastical judgment; and it is the business of the Church and its rulers to take care that they do not shake the dignity of the magistrates, or otherwise rashly offend them, or cause them just fears. 3. In those places, however, where the Churches have, by custom, or by the liberal concession of the magistrates, or by public decrees made to that end, a somewhat greater measure of liberty and power to govern their own affairs by their own judgment (as long ago the Christian Emperors granted many powers to the bishops; and today the Reformed Churches in many commonwealths, especially in these, have certain rights, liberties and order of their own), the prince cannot revoke that power unless some very great abuse intervenes. Rather, he ought to take care that the rulers of the Church perform their duty and use that power rightly and for the good of the Church, so that, with scandals removed, it may remain pure and unstained.

units.la: XXII. Post jura magistratuum sequitur vicissim Ecclesiæ erga illos officium, & cura, ac auctoritas. Cum enim princeps Ecclesiæ pars, ac in cœtu isto frater sit, rectorum officium agnoscere, ac monitionibus eorum parere tenetur. Quæ tamen ejus subjectio, non imperii aut jurisdictionis, sed directionis & consilii duntaxat est; ac ministrorum respectu accidentalis mere est, cum omnis illa reverentia divino verbo, quod in ore gerit Ecclesia, habeatur. Aliter enim Magistratus, aliter Ecclesia, imperat. Ille, potestate & imperio; hæc suasu & hortatu, sanctisque ex verbo Dei increpationibus. Qua ratione Magistratus, qui Ecclesiasticis imperat, iisdem quoque monentibus subjicere se poterit.
units.tr: XXII. After the rights of the magistrates, there follows in turn the duty, care and authority of the Church toward them. For since the prince is a part of the Church and a brother in that assembly, he is bound to acknowledge the duty of its rulers and to obey their admonitions. Yet this subjection of his is not one of command or jurisdiction, but only of direction and counsel; and with respect to the ministers it is purely accidental, since all that reverence is paid to the divine Word, which the Church bears in its mouth. For the magistrate commands in one way, and the Church in another. The former commands by power and authority; the latter by persuasion and exhortation, and by rebukes drawn from the Word of God. By this reasoning, a magistrate who commands ecclesiastical persons will also be able to submit himself to those who admonish him.

units.la: XXIII. Est ergo ministrorum Ecclesiæ, magistratum libere & prudenter officii admonere; quin & magna in necessitate, Ecclesiasticis censuris quantum fieri potest, ad meliorem mentem revocare. Isto autem prætextu majestatem ejus imminuere aut populum Sacramento Magistratum imperio, solvere nunquam possunt.
units.tr: XXIII. It is therefore the task of the ministers of the Church to remind the magistrate of his duty freely and prudently; and even, in great necessity, to recall him to a better mind by ecclesiastical censures as far as can be done. But under this pretext they can never diminish his majesty or release the people from the oath of allegiance to the magistrate's authority.

units.la: XXIV. Atque adhibenda hac in parte maxima prudentia & moderatio. Neque crimina eorum licenter in vulgus efferenda; nec publicis invectivis sceptorum majestas facile lacessenda est. Magistratus ne exerator; & principi in populo tuo ne maledicito. Exod. 22:28. Nec temere etiam, in sermone ad populum; regnorum momenta nudanda ac libranda sunt. Habent enim illa plerunque secretum suum, quod explorare, ac audacius evolvere velle, intempestivæ cujusdam sapientiæ foret. Unde fœdera, & facta magistratuum ambigua, & dubiæ interpretationis, quæque arcanis rationibus & circumstantiis nituntur, non facile publice vexanda aut traducenda sunt. Alia enim fuit olim prophetarum ratio; quos, uti regum censores ac ephoros, in ista sua Republica Deus olim singulari cum imperio mittere solebat; iisque & res, & verba, quibus uti eos volebat, in ore ponebat. Vide Jer. 26:12. Amos 7:10. & seqq. Esai. 26:2. Num. 22:38. & 23:12. Quam prudenter autem Nathan Davidem, ac Samuel Saulem increpuerit, in utriusque regis rebus videre est. 2. Sam. 12. 1. Sam. 15. Ac Christum ipsum, Dominum, rarius objurgationibus, plerunque autem instructionibus & admonitionibus, usum legimus. Cumque Paulus senem, ut patrem, modeste & reverenter increpari jubeat, 1. Tim. 5:1. certe longe major fascibus debebitur reverentia. Ac prudentiæ est, ita rem moderari, ne facile accusationi acrimonia terrarum dominos Ecclesiæ inconciliemus.
units.tr: XXIV. In this part the greatest prudence and moderation must be applied. Their crimes are not to be spread abroad recklessly among the common people, nor is the majesty of sceptres to be easily provoked by public invectives. You shall not curse the judges, nor speak evil of a ruler among your people. Exod. 22:28. Nor are the affairs of kingdoms to be laid bare and weighed rashly even in a sermon to the people. For those affairs generally have their own secrets, and to want to probe them and unravel them too boldly would be a kind of ill-timed wisdom. Hence treaties and acts of magistrates which are ambiguous, open to doubtful interpretation, and which rest upon secret reasons and circumstances, are not to be easily assailed or dragged through the mud in public. The method of the prophets was once different: God used to send them into his commonwealth with a singular commission, as censors and ephors of the kings, and he put in their mouths both the matters and the words with which he wished them to speak. See Jer. 26:12; Amos 7:10 and following; Isa. 26:2; Num. 22:38, and 23:12. How prudently Nathan rebuked David, and Samuel Saul, may be seen in the affairs of each king: 2 Sam. 12; 1 Sam. 15. And we read that Christ himself, the Lord, used rebukes rarely, but for the most part instruction and admonition. And since Paul bids an old man to be rebuked modestly and respectfully, as a father, 1 Tim. 5:1, surely much greater reverence is owed to the rods of office. And it is a matter of prudence so to manage the affair that we do not, by the bitterness of accusation, easily make the lords of the earth hostile to the Church.

units.la: XXV. Peccant ergo Anabaptistæ; qui, uti scularem Magistratum cum Christiana professione congruere negant, ita, cum Donatistis, Imperatori nihil cum Ecclesia commune esse volunt.
units.tr: XXV. The Anabaptists therefore err. While they deny that the secular magistracy agrees with the Christian profession, they likewise, with the Donatists, want the emperor to have nothing in common with the Church.

units.la: XXVI. Ulterius tendunt Pontificii; qui, uti perperam Christianum populum in Laicos & Clericos distinguunt; quos, instar duarum civitatum, a se mutuo longe distinctarum, in Ecclesia concipiunt: ita Clerum suum magistratui jurisdictioni subtrahunt; contra expressum mandatum Apostoli Rom. 13: 1. Omnis anima potestatibus superioribus subjiciatur. nec fundos ac terras eorum Reipubl. vectigales esse sinunt. Quod uti in re ministrorum exigua, ac tenui Scholasticorum suppellectile, locum habere possit; ita ad opulentas Ecclesiasticorum possessiones, & latifundia, non sine publicæ rei detrimento, extendi potest. Falsus enim color est, bona ipsorum sacra, & Deo consecrata esse, nec sæculari usui servire oportere. Istam enim rerum externarum sanctimoniam nunc non agnoscimus. Reddite ergo omnibus debita: cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem: cui honorem, honorem. com. 7.
units.tr: XXVI. The Papists go further. Wrongly dividing the Christian people into laity and clergy, they conceive of the Church as two states far separated from each other. In this way they withdraw their clergy from the jurisdiction of the magistrate, against the express command of the Apostle, Rom. 13:1: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Nor do they allow their estates and lands to be liable to taxes for the commonwealth. Although this might hold good for the small property of ministers and the meagre furnishings of the schoolmen, it can also be extended to the wealthy possessions and great estates of churchmen, not without loss to the public good. For it is a false pretence that their goods are holy and consecrated to God, and ought not to serve secular use. We do not now acknowledge this holiness of external things. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour. (com. 7.)

units.la: XXVII. Nec denique plane probandi aliorum canones: 1. Ecclesiæ regimen & ordinem nullo modo ὑπάλληλον subordinatum esse magistratui. 2. Magistratus imperium solum incorpora, & brutam hominis partem, ac circa res externas versari; Ecclesiæ autem unius esse, divinum cultum ac felicitatem hominum æternam, procurare. 3. judicium de rebus divinis apprehensivum esse Laicorum; discretivum, Magistratuum; definitivum; Pastorum; praetorium & infallibile, Dei. Quæ perplexa sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. Finally, the canons of others are not to be approved at all: (1) that the government and order of the Church are in no way subordinate [ὑπάλληλον] to the magistrate; (2) that the power of the magistrate is only over the body and the brutish part of man, and is concerned with external things, whereas it belongs to the Church alone to procure divine worship and the eternal happiness of men; (3) that judgment about divine things is apprehensive for the laity, discretive for the magistrates, definitive for the ministers, and practorian and infallible for God. These are obscure.

units.la: LOCUS QUADRAGESIMUS NONUS DE CORRUPTA ECCLESIA N. F.
units.tr: Forty-Ninth Topic: On the Corrupted Church, N. F.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: Chapter XI.

units.la: De corrupta doctrina sub Novo Fœdere.
units.tr: On corrupted doctrine under the New Covenant.

units.la: I. ATque hic quidem fuit Ecclesiæ Novi Test. modus, & forma, ad quam describi & componi eam voluit Christus. Verum licet felix sit, suo capite, Ecclesia; quod eam tutissime tueatur & conservet; non tamen eadem est membrorum, dum in hoc mundo versantur, ratio, quibus simili cum fato, & iisdem sæpe calamitatibus, ac res omnes humanæ, colluctandum est. Indeque non mutationibus tantum, sed & vitiis non exiguis sæpe, obnoxia est Ecclesia; tam circa ipsam doctrinam, quam mores & regimen. Fideles enim, in hac terra degunt, valde infirmi sunt, imo plerique vἡπιοι, pueri. 1. Cor. 3: 1. qui cum multa ignorent, facile decipi & deduci possunt a sola & angusta veritatis semita, ad latam & celebrem errorum viam. Quod maxime usu evenit, post Apostolorum obitus, quorum magna erat etiam apud improbos, dignatio; quibus veluti tibicinibus subrutis, mox in deterius lapsa est Ecclesia, & ab ingruentibus hæresibus, & irrepente Antichristo, magna, tum in doctrinam, tum in regimen invecta est mutatio.
units.tr: I. This, then, was the form and shape of the Church of the New Testament, the one Christ wished it to be described and arranged by. Yet although the Church is happy in its head, because he guards and preserves it most surely, the condition of its members is not the same while they live in this world. They must struggle with the same fate and often the same calamities as all human affairs. For this reason the Church is subject not only to change but often to no small faults, both in doctrine itself and in morals and government. The faithful live on this earth and are very weak, indeed most of them are babes [νήπιοι], children (1 Cor. 3:1). Since they know many things poorly, they can easily be deceived and led from the narrow and single path of truth onto the broad and well-trodden road of error. This happened especially after the deaths of the Apostles, whom even the wicked held in great honour. Once these pillars had been undermined, the Church soon fell into worse things, and under the attacks of heresies and the creeping in of Antichrist, a great change was introduced both in doctrine and in government.

units.la: II. Non vero inopinatum illud aut novum Ecclesiæ fatum est; verum ab ipso Christo jam prædictum. Matth. 18: 7. Necesse est ut veniant scandala. & 14: 10. Tunc offendentur multi & multi pseudoprophetæ excitabuntur, & seducent multos. Luc. 17: 1. Impossibile est ut non veniant scandala. Ita & prædicuntur hæreses; earumque necessitas & usus, tanquam abscessuum in corpore affecto, demonstratur. 1. Cor. 11: 19. Oportet enim etiam hæreses inter vos esse, ut qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos. Speciatim illas designavit Petrus Epist. 2. cap. 2: 1. quod in ipsam Christi Deitatem involaturæ essent, negantes eam, & dominium ejus tollentes, ἀρνούμενοι δεσπότην τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτούς; qui emerat eos. De eadem abnegatione futura loquitur Judas com. 4. Quæ Judæorum primo fuit hæresis; deinde Ebionitarum, Cerinthianorum, Arianorum, Samosatenianorum, Photinianorum, & similium, quibus annumerandi Sabelliani. Iis omnibus postmodum successerunt Mufelmanni. Hinc porro subsecutæ sunt hæreles circa gratiam sanctificantem & liberum arbitrium, qualis Pelagianorum & Semipelagianorum. Magnum etiam Donatistarum & Novatianorum schisma fuit.
units.tr: II. Yet this fate of the Church was neither unexpected nor new; Christ himself had already foretold it. Matt. 18:7: It must needs be that offences come. And 24:10: Then many shall be offended, and many false prophets shall arise and shall deceive many. Luke 17:1: It is impossible but that offences will come. So heresies were also foretold, and their necessity and use were shown, like abscesses in a diseased body. 1 Cor. 11:19: For there must also be heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you. Peter in his second epistle, chapter 2 verse 1, pointed out these heresies by name: that false teachers would creep in upon the very deity of Christ, denying the Lord that bought them [ἀρνούμενοι δεσπότην τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτούς], that is, denying him who had bought them, and taking away his lordship. Jude, verse 4, speaks of the same future denial. The first of these heresies was that of the Jews; then came those of the Ebionites, Cerinthians, Arians, Samosatenes, Photinians and the like, among whom the Sabellians must be counted. After all these the Mohammedans followed. From here further heresies arose concerning sanctifying grace and free will, such as those of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians. There was also the great schism of the Donatists and Novatians.

units.la: III. Alias etiam corruptelas inducendas fore, sub emblemate illo zizaniorum docuit Christus Matth. 13: 25, 26, 38. ubi frumentum sunt filii regni, & zizania filii mali; hoc est ii, qui externa specie, similitudinem mentiebantur filiorum regni, intus tamen zizania erant, vel omni fructu cassa, vel non nisi pessimæ frugis. Quales erant filii mali, id est, gentes in Ecclesiam introductæ, vel introactæ potius, sed non regeneritæ. Hæc vero zizania cum tolerari juberentur in agro Domini, hinc fieri necesse fuit, ut, in tam læto zizaniorum proventu, & tanta multitudine, illud toti Ecclesiæ commune videretur, quod errantes dicerent ac facerent; illud vero, quod servi Dei sentirent, qui zizania deprehensa a vero frumento distinguerent, haberetur, tanquam singularis aliqua, & non nisi paucorum quorundam opinatio. Quo factum est, ut frequentissima Christianorum multitudo, pueri demum esset in Christo, cum adolere non possent, presi nimium zizaniis, qui fere omnem solidum doctrinæ succum intervertebant. Quo vero modo, & quibus speciatim gradibus, res eo devenerit, videndum nunc est nobis.
units.tr: III. Christ also taught, under the image of the tares, that other corruptions would be introduced: Matt. 13:25, 26, 38, where the wheat are the children of the kingdom and the tares are the children of the wicked one. That is, those who by outward appearance pretended to be like the children of the kingdom, but inwardly were tares, either empty of all fruit or yielding only the worst kind of crop. Such were the children of the wicked one, namely the Gentiles brought into the Church, or rather thrust in, but not regenerated. Since these tares were commanded to be tolerated in the Lord's field, it was bound to happen that, amid such a rich growth of tares and such a great multitude, what the erring said and did came to seem common to the whole Church, while what the servants of God felt, who could distinguish the tares they detected from the true wheat, was held to be some peculiar opinion of only a few. As a result, the very large multitude of Christians remained, in the end, infants in Christ, since they could not grow up, being too much choked by the tares, which overturned almost all the solid juice of doctrine. Now we must see in what manner, and through what particular stages, things came to this pass.

units.la: IV. Mutatio omnis circa doctrinam Christianam facta est; vel in ritibus illius; vel in cultu; vel in doctrina ipsa & dogmatis. Atque eo ferme ordine omnis corruptela in Ecclesiam invecta est, ut, cum ceperit in ritibus; ex iis derivata sit in cultum cumque ibi adoleverit; ipsam deinde arcem doctrinæ invasit.
units.tr: IV. Every change made in Christian doctrine concerned either its rites, or its worship, or doctrine itself and its dogmas. Almost all corruption crept into the Church in this order: it began in the rites, from them it passed into worship, and once it had grown up there, it then invaded the very citadel of doctrine.

units.la: V. In ritibus ergo, utpote unicuique obviis prima resedit mali origo, quando luxuriosi nimium florentis Ecclesiæ ritus, vel in vegrandem molem excreverunt; vel interpolati sunt pro arbitrio humano, per jejunia, peregrinationes religiosas, Monachatum, ejusque vota, aliaque similes ἐθελοθρησκείας: quæ præcipuum robur tuum acceperunt sub Gregorio Magno, qui pleraque eas cerimonias, quæ nunc in Ecclesia Romana obtinent, introduxit. Quando ciborum, dierum, & vestium discrimina habere coeperunt; & post liminio revocatum fuit quicquid olim fere, sub Veteri Test.umbrarum nomine Judæorum cervicibus imminuerat; adjectis iis, quæ Gentilium vana superstitio quondam effinxerat.
units.tr: V. Thus the first origin of evil lay in the rites, as is obvious to everyone: when the rites of the Church, which had flourished too luxuriantly, either grew into an enormous mass, or were interpolated at human discretion through fasts, religious pilgrimages, monasticism and its vows, and other similar self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας]. These received their chief strength under Gregory the Great, who introduced most of the ceremonies now prevailing in the Roman Church. Then they began to make distinctions of foods, days and garments, and whatever had once been almost wholly cast off by the Jews' necks under the name of shadows of the Old Testament was brought back again, with additions taken from the empty superstition of the Gentiles.

units.la: VI. Itum inde est ad cultus adulterationem. Quomodo Gregorius Magnus, mortuos invocari jussit; sacrificia pro iis instituit, & ossibus eorum templa dedicavit. Ita assumpta est in partem honoris divini, supra ipsum filium, Virgo mater, simulque tota cohors demortuorum, & commentitiorum sæpe, sanctorum. Donec & cadaveribus, cineribus, imaginibus, lignis, lapidibusque, cultus divinus sit præstitus. Quod præcipue invaluit, post Synodos Parisiensem & Francofurtensem, sub Carolo Magno.
units.tr: VI. From this came the adulteration of worship. Gregory the Great ordered that the dead be invoked; he instituted sacrifices for them and dedicated temples to their bones. So the Virgin Mother, together with the whole throng of the departed, and often of fabricated saints, was taken into a share of divine honour, even above the Son himself. Until divine worship was offered even to corpses, ashes, images, wood and stones. This grew especially strong after the Synods of Paris and Frankfurt, under Charlemagne.

units.la: VII. Externis hisce religionis Christianæ monumentis, & quasi tesris, vel sublatis vel adulteratis, nihil in proclivi magis erat, quam ut eadem etiam corruptelæ contagio in doctrinam & dogmata dimanaret: quæ cum magnam partem ex cerimoniis spectentur & discantur; ubi illæ turbatæ sunt, necesse est ut lutulenta etiam fluat doctrina. Fundus hujus calamitatis, & origo omnis corruptelæ in doctrina, est studium propriæ justitiæ; quod sicut omni homini naturale est, & Judæos perdiderat; ita Papismi unica & princeps est causa: hi enim cum justitiæ Christi se subjicere nollent eamque recipere, aliunde justitiam suam arcessere conati sunt. Cum vero se nulla spes, aut via ad justitiam acquirendam offerret, delapsi sunt ad ἐθελοθρησκείας, ad commenta & opera humana, quibus merita & satisfactionem asscripserunt; ut per ea defectum propriæ justitiæ resarcire & explere possent. Quare Christianismum & pietatem transformarunt in γυμνασίων σωματικήν, & pristina mundi elementa cærimonialesque revocarunt, illisque omnem fere salutis vim tra-scripserunt.
units.tr: VII. When these external monuments of the Christian religion were either removed or adulterated, like its tesserae, nothing was more likely than that the contagion of the same corruption would flow into doctrine and dogmas. Since these are for the most part learned and taught through ceremonies, once these have been disturbed, doctrine too must flow muddy. The source of this calamity, and the origin of all corruption in doctrine, is the pursuit of one's own righteousness. As this is natural to every human being, it had also ruined the Jews; so it is the sole and chief cause of Papism. For these men, unwilling to submit to the righteousness of Christ and receive it, tried to seek their righteousness elsewhere. But when no hope or way of acquiring righteousness presented itself, they slipped into self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας], into human inventions and works, to which they ascribed merits and satisfaction, so that by these they might make up for the lack of their own righteousness and fill it. Hence they turned Christianity and piety into bodily exercise [γυμνασίων σωματικήν], brought back the old elements of the world and ceremonies, and transferred to them almost the whole power of salvation.

units.la: VIII. Suffecti ita sunt Christi loco, aut saltem succenturiati, & quasi tanto oneri impar esset, adjuncti varii comites, a quibus itidem salutem suam peterent homines, Sancti nimirum & Virgo mater; quos plebs, ut advocatos suos venerari edocta est: quin ut eorum animis semper obversarentur, etiam oculis præsentes fecerunt, & imagines introductæ sunt primo; deinceps & cultæ: quem in honoris partem etiam venerunt crux, Eucharistia, aliæque res consecratæ, quæ ad salutem non parum conferre posse credebantur.
units.tr: VIII. In this way they were put in Christ's place, or at least set up as his deputies, and, as if the burden were too much for him, various companions were added, from whom men might likewise seek their salvation: namely the saints and the Virgin Mother. The common people were taught to venerate them as their advocates. Indeed, so that these might always be before their minds, they also made them present to the eyes, and images were first introduced, and afterwards worshipped. To this honour there also came the cross, the Eucharist, and other consecrated things, which were believed to contribute no little to salvation.

units.la: IX. Ex mutilata ergo doctrina de Christo, ejusque justitia, consequens fuit necessario Sacramentorum corruptio; quando iis, gratiæ infusio-
units.tr: IX. From the mutilated doctrine concerning Christ and his righteousness, the corruption of the sacraments necessarily followed, when they ascribed to them the infusion of grace—

units.la: Hinc Christi adjuncti sunt Sancti, eorumque imagines, corruptis simul gratia symbolis. fusionem ex opere operato, uti loquuntur, tribuerunt; habitaque sunt, non tanquam justitiæ signa & sigilla, quæ testandi & confirmandi usum haberent; sed tanquam organa operantia, quibus aliquam justitiæ assicientiam adscribebant, modo nullus oppessulatus esset obex pecati mortalis: ita ut hac sola cautione adhibita, sacramentorum usu & observatione absolvi omnia, merito quis credere posset; quæ tamen aliunde vana prorsus & inutilia reddunt.
units.tr: Hence the saints and their images were joined to Christ, and at the same time the symbols of grace were corrupted. They ascribed to them the infusion of grace from the work worked [ex opere operato], as they say, and these were regarded not as signs and seals of righteousness, having the use of attesting and confirming it, but as working instruments, to which they attributed some efficacy towards righteousness, provided only that no bolt stood in the way as a barrier of mortal sin. So with this one precaution taken, one might reasonably believe that everything is absolved by the use and observance of the sacraments; yet on other grounds these same things render them altogether vain and useless.

units.la: X. Ex alia enim parte, quæ insignis eorum est δυσωπεία & intemperies, bonorum operum meritis, salutem imputarunt, eamque ex illis universam suspenderunt; ut frustra fuisse prorsus videatur, quicquid de sacramentorum efficacia tanto hiatu promitterent. Eodem pertinent satisfactiones proprie: cum enim discernerent, miro, sed unice in hac rem apto acumine, inter culpam & poenam; eamque iterum in temporariam, & aeternam dispescerent; ita statuerunt, remitti posse culpam, non remissa tamen omni poena; speciatim quoque eorum peccatorum, quæ post Baptismum admittebantur, gratiam posse fieri, quoad poenam æternam, ut tamen reliquæ maneant temporales poenæ, partim in hac, partim in futura vita persolvendæ. Atque inde opus esse pœnitentia, per quam poena æterna solvatur; temporariam vero poenam redimi posse & compensari actionibus pœnariis, ut jejunio, eleemosyna, oratione &c. Quibus modis effectum est, ut pœnitentia quæ animi virtus est, conversa sit in laborem pœnalem: & cum olim satisfiderent Ecclesiæ, antequam absolveretur peccator: & ubi culpæ venia illi facta esset, pœnis ullis non amplius teneretur; hic ordine præpostero, cum culpa peccatori est remissa, tum demum adhuc poena satisfactoria exigitur.
units.tr: X. On the other hand, their notable excess and intemperance was to ascribe salvation to the merits of good works and to make it hang entirely upon them, so that whatever they promised about the efficacy of the sacraments seems to have been utterly in vain, given such a gap. To the same head belong satisfactions properly so called. For when they distinguished, with a remarkable keenness suited to this matter alone, between guilt and punishment, and again divided punishment into temporal and eternal, they held that guilt can be remitted without every punishment being remitted. Specifically, for sins committed after Baptism, grace could be granted as regards eternal punishment, while temporal punishments remain, to be paid partly in this life and partly in the next. From this they inferred that repentance is needed, through which eternal punishment is dissolved, while temporal punishment can be redeemed and compensated by penal actions, such as fasting, almsgiving, prayer, and so on. In this way it came about that repentance, which is a virtue of the mind, was turned into a penal labour. Whereas formerly sinners made satisfaction to the Church before they were absolved, and once pardon of the guilt had been granted were no longer bound to any penalties, now, in a backward order, when the guilt has been remitted to the sinner, then at last a satisfactory penalty is still demanded.

units.la: XI. In subsidium ergo vocatæ sunt, indulgentiarum quasi auxiliares copiæ, quæ à foro disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ, sinistra nimium manu repetitæ sunt. Unde conflatus est ille thesaurus Ecclesiæ, ex infinitate nempe meritorum Christi, & abundantia operum & pietatis supererogatoriæ Sanctorum: qui thesaurus sola clave Ecclesiæ recludendus, & non nisi ad dispensationem Papæ, tanquam promicondi, per indulgentias illas, in solutionem & absolutionem poenarum temporalium, effundendus venit. Quasi vero, meritum Christi, quod æternæ poenæ restinguendæ par fuerat, temporarium poenam restinguere nequiret: quod etiam ne fieret, probe cautum fuit ne omnes poenæ temporales in hac vita persolvi possent; partem earum præcipuam, futuræ vitæ exhauriendam relinquentes. Ex hoc cariolo fundamento, excitatum est insanum illud ædiœdificium purgatorii, in quod, tanquam in excelsam turrim, aureus imber quotidie decpluit, unde Ecclesia Romana inundatur.
units.tr: XI. Therefore indulgences were called up as auxiliary forces in support, drawn from the court of church discipline, which had been drawn too much from the left hand. From these was built up that treasury of the Church, made of the infinite merits of Christ and the abundance of the supererogatory works and piety of the saints. This treasury, to be unlocked by the Church's key alone and to be poured out, not except at the disposal of the Pope as a dispenser, through those indulgences, for the payment and remission of temporal punishments. As if the merit of Christ, which was sufficient to extinguish eternal punishment, could not extinguish temporal punishment! Lest this happen, they took good care that not all temporal punishments could be paid in this life, leaving the principal part of them to be exhausted in the future life. From this rickety foundation was raised that mad edifice of purgatory, into which, as into a lofty tower, a golden shower rains down every day, by which the Roman Church is flooded.

units.la: XII. Atque hæc est genuina Papismi facies & descriptio, a prima origine repetita & deducta; qui Ecclesiam omnem Christianam, tanquam dirus hydrops invasit, & in modum fœdi abscessus corpore excreti, deturpavit. Qui cum omnem solidum pietatis succum depasceretur, antiquum revocavit Pharisaismum, cum præcipua simul Judaismi parte; ut hoc adeo esset, mutare tempora & legem. Dan. 7:25. id est, tempora gratiæ & legem Christi commutare cum tempore servitutis & lege veteri. Quomodo tandem omnes explevit partes bestiæ illius, quæ fuit & non est, & tamen est. Apoc. 17:8. Unde nata est Ecclesia falsa, quæ in Scripturis appellatur Civitas magna & Babylon, quæ erat commiscenda cum civitate sancta & vera Ecclesia.
units.tr: XII. This is the genuine face and description of Papism, traced and derived from its first origin, which seized the whole Christian Church like a dreadful dropsy and disfigured it, excreted from the body like a foul abscess. When it fed upon every solid juice of piety, it revived the ancient Pharisaism together with the chief part of Judaism, so that it was in fact to change times and law (Dan. 7:25), that is, to exchange the times of grace and the law of Christ for the time of bondage and the old law. In this way at last it fulfilled all the parts of that beast which was, and is not, and yet is (Rev. 17:8). Hence arose the false Church, which in the Scriptures is called the great city and Babylon, which was to be mixed with the holy city and the true Church.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: De corrupta regiminis forma sub N. Fœdere.
units.tr: On the corrupted form of government under the New Covenant.

units.la: I. Um itaque doctrinæ veritas stuprum passa esset, violata per omne nefas domina, necesse fuit, ut idem etiam in ancilla committeretur sæculo. Corruptam igitur doctrinam, continuo comitata vel consecuta est regiminis adulteratio, & invecta est in Ecclesiam consummatissima Hierarchia, quæ onerosa pompa & phantasia hierarchiam Veteris Test. & omnem sæculi politiam; dolis & artibus regendi, omnem politicorum actum longe superat; utpote quæ ex fundamentis prudenter jactis, summa cum vafritie per varias contignationes, paulatim in supremum illud fastigium excitata est. Quam ut accuratius paulo contemplemur, ab ovo, ut ajunt, ordiendum est. Semina hujus hierarchiæ jacta sunt, 1. introducto discrimine inter Clericos & Laicos. 2. invecto Monachatu. 3. constitutis Ordinibus sacris.
units.tr: I. Since, therefore, the truth of the doctrine had suffered defilement, its mistress violated by every kind of wickedness, it was necessary that the same thing should also be done to the handmaid, the world. Accordingly, the corruption of doctrine was immediately accompanied, or followed, by the corruption of government, and into the Church was introduced the most consummate hierarchy, a burdensome pomp and fantasy which far surpasses the hierarchy of the Old Testament and every political order of the world in the arts and tricks of ruling. Built on foundations laid prudently, it was raised step by step, with great cunning, through various storeys to that supreme summit. That we may examine it a little more closely, we must begin, as they say, from the egg. The seeds of this hierarchy were sown: (1) by introducing the distinction between clergy and laity; (2) by bringing in monasticism; (3) by establishing the sacred orders.

units.la: II. Digna igitur hoc molimine & prima merito erat cura, ut novo regno de subjectis prospiceretur; quod ut fieret, & ut omnes dein subjugarentur, aliqui honoris titulo, & speciali nomine erant mancipandi. Atque hinc natum est discrimen, primo sæculo incognitum, inter Clericos & Laicos; non sine grandi in populum Dei contumelia, & injuria sub eorum Novo Test. non ferenda; quando divulsus fuit populus a ministris; ac si non ejusdem corporis membra, licet haec pluribus inservirent; aut domus lapides, essent, sed utrumque corpus & aedificium singulare constitueret; & huic Laicorum, illis Clericorum nomen daretur. Quod discrimen sicut res ipsa non patitur, ita nec verba ferunt. Nomen enim Laici cum honorificum sit per se, 1. Pet. 2: 10. hic in ignominiam convertitur, quasi populus non esset simul sors haereditatis Domini; praeter quam Petrus docet, qui 1. Ep. 5: 3. monet presbyteros, ne dominentur Cleris: aut vox illa solum convenire ministris Ecclesiae; quod confundit ibidem Petrus, cum eosdem & τῆς κλήρους & τὸ ποίμνιον vocet.
units.tr: II. Therefore, with this design in view, the first care was rightly to provide for the new kingdom from among its subjects; and in order that this might be done, and that all might afterwards be brought under subjection, some were to be marked out by the title of honour and a special name. From this arose the distinction between clergy and laity, unknown in the first century, not without great insult to the people of God and an injury not to be tolerated under their New Testament; for the people were separated from the ministers, as if they were not members of the same body, although the members serve many purposes, or as if they were not stones of the same building, but as if each body and structure were distinct, and the one were given the name of laity and the other that of clergy. As the thing itself does not allow this distinction, so neither do the words support it. For the name of layman, though honourable in itself (1 Pet. 2:10), is here turned into a disgrace, as if the people were not also the lot of the Lord's inheritance; which Peter teaches, who in 1 Pet. 5:3 warns the elders not to lord it over the clergy. Or else that word applies only to the ministers of the Church; yet Peter himself confounds this in the same place, when he calls the same men both tous kleirous and to poimnion.

units.la: III. Discriminato a Laicis Clero, accessit tertius ordo Monachorum; qui olim non inter Clericos, sed inter seculares & Laicos reputabantur; de quibus nunc agendum. Christi & Apostolorum tempore Monachos fuisse, nec vola nec vestigium ullum apparet: quin imo otiosum illud genus condemnat Scriptura, Matth. 6: 33. Quaerite primo regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, & ista omnia adjicientur vobis: omnem etiam meriti & perfectionis praesumptionem profligat, Luc. 17: 10. Ita & vos quum feceritis omnia quae edicta sunt vobis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus: nam quod debuimus facere fecimus: institutiones & regulas humanas & quicquid ἐθελοθρησκείαν sapit, procul amandat Matth. 15: 9. Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas quae sunt praecepta hominum. Col. 2: 20, 21. Quid ut viventes in mundo ritibus oneramini, Ne ederis, neque gustaris, neque attigeris?
units.tr: III. Along with the clergy separated from the laity came a third order, that of the monks, who formerly were not reckoned among the clergy but among the secular people and laity; and of these we must now speak. In the time of Christ and the Apostles there appears no trace or vestige of monks at all. Indeed, Scripture condemns that idle kind of life: Matt. 6:33, Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you; it also strikes down every presumption of merit and perfection, Luke 17:10, So you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: for we have done what we ought to have done; human institutions and rules, and whatever savours of self-chosen worship, it sends far away, Matt. 15:9, In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men. Col. 2:20, 21, Why, as if living in the world, are you burdened with ordinances: Do not handle, nor taste, nor touch?

units.la: IV. Nec huic institutofavet locus Matth. 19: 21. Si vis perfectus esse, abi, vende quae habes & da pauperibus. Nam 1. omne illud extra vitam monachalem praestari poterat. 2. Non consilium, sed praeceptum datur huic juveni, quod ad omnes etiam illos pertinet, a quibus Christus illud speciatim exiget. conf. Luc. 14: 33. Sic ergo quisquis vestrum non valedicit omnibus bonis suis, non potest meus esse discipulus. 3. Non eo animo a Christo datur, ac si vellet juveni monstrare viam ad adipiscendam perfectionem; verum ut, ostendendo rigorem & postulatum legis, suam ipsi imperfectionem exprobraret & in apricum proferret. com. 23, 24. Nec Monachus fuit Joh. Baptista, qui in deserto quidem vixit, sed celebri & ab hominibus frequentato, non solo, non inculto; quin & alibi egit, nec ubicunque erat, otiosus fuit, at baptismum praedicabat; nec tam singulari, saltem non opinione meriti, cibo aut veste utebatur, quam alii homines; nisi forte quam aulici & sacerdotes. Matth. 11: 8. Quid exiistis videre hominem mollibus vestibus amictum, qui — in domibus regum sunt: ut eo magis Prophetam, & speciatim Eliam, referret Malach. 4: 5. 2. Reg. 1: 8. conf. Matth. 3: 4. Luc. 1: 17.
units.tr: IV. Nor does the passage Matt. 19:21 favour this institution, If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor. For (1) all that is said there could be done outside the monastic life; (2) a counsel, not a precept, is given to this young man, which pertains also to all those whom Christ will specifically require of it (cf. Luke 14:33, So therefore whoever of you does not renounce all his goods cannot be my disciple); (3) Christ did not give it with the intention of showing the young man the way to attain perfection, but rather, by pointing out the rigour and demand of the law, to rebuke his imperfection and bring it into the open (cf. verses 23, 24). Nor was John the Baptist a monk, who indeed lived in the desert, but a desert that was famous and frequented by men, not solitary, not uncultivated; and he also went about elsewhere, and wherever he was he was not idle, but preached baptism; nor did he use food or clothing of such singular kind, at least not from any opinion of merit, as other men did, unless perhaps the way of the courtiers and priests. Matt. 11:8, Why did you go out to see a man clothed in soft garments? Those who wear them are in the houses of kings; so that he might the more readily be taken for the Prophet, and especially Elijah (Mal. 4:5; 2 Kings 1:8; cf. Matt. 3:4; Luke 1:17).

units.la: V. Nec ullum Monachatus indicium apparet in Ecclesia Apostolica, Act. 4: 34. quamvis insignis ibi charitas, & concordia, & beneficientia, extra omne tamen votum, eluceat: cum ibi alacritas & promptitudo praedicetur, non coacta per votum beneficentia. Et fallitur Eusebius, cum Monachorum in Ægypto, mentionem factam vult a Philone Judaeo: non enim Christianos, sed Essaeos, saltem Judaeos, describit Philo.
units.tr: V. Nor does any indication of monasticism appear in the Apostolic Church (Acts 4:34), although remarkable charity, concord and beneficence shine forth there, yet all apart from any vow; since there cheerfulness and readiness are praised, beneficence not compelled by a vow. And Eusebius is mistaken when he wishes mention of the monks in Egypt to have been made by Philo the Jew; for Philo describes not Christians but the Essenes, at least Jews.

units.la: VI. Prima igitur Monachorum (licet antiquiores fuisse Ascetas non negemus) origo referenda est ad medium saeculi tertii, & reddenda auctori suo Paulo Thebaeo, qui Eremita primum, dein Monachus in Ægypto factus est, occasione decimae persecutionis. Hujus vestigia pressit Antonius itidem in Ægypto, qui plures etiam alios ad idem vitae genus transduxit; ex quibus fuit Hilarion, quem cum multi porro insequerentur; ita hisce primum auctoribus, duo prodierunt Monachorum genera, Eremitarum & Coenobitarum.
units.tr: VI. The first origin of the monks (although we do not deny that there were earlier ascetics) is therefore to be traced to the middle of the third century, and attributed to its author Paul of Thebes, who first became a hermit and then a monk in Egypt, on the occasion of the tenth persecution. Antony likewise trod in his footsteps in Egypt, and drew many others into the same kind of life; among them was Hilarion, whom many others then followed. Thus from these first authors two kinds of monks arose, hermits and cenobites.

units.la: VII. Ex Ægypto brevi tempore propagatum est hoc Monachatus institutum, in Palaestinam, per Hilarionem: per alios item in Armeniam, Paphlagoniam, Pontum: in Graeciam translatus est ab Athanasio, qui inter Monachos Ægyptios egerat: cum secutus est Gregorius Nazianzenus, cui se adjunxit Achates ejus, Basilius Magnus, monasteriorum in Oriente strenuissimus propagator. In Occidentem serius paulo monachatus fuit introductus, annitente maxime Hieronymo, in Syriam prope Bethlehemum eo nomine se conferente. Augustinus etiam vitam hinc alicubi commendat; quamvis nec ipse Monachus fuerit, nec regulas iis tradiderit.
units.tr: VII. This monastic institution was spread in a short time from Egypt into Palestine through Hilarion, and by others also into Armenia, Paphlagonia and Pontus. It was carried into Greece by Athanasius, who had lived among the Egyptian monks; then Gregory Nazianzen followed, to whom his companion Basil the Great joined himself, the most energetic promoter of monasteries in the East. Monasticism was introduced into the West somewhat later, mainly through the efforts of Jerome, who betook himself for this purpose to Syria, near Bethlehem. Augustine too somewhere commends this way of life; although he himself was not a monk, nor did he hand down rules for them.

units.la: VIII. Nec sequior sexus, qui hisce in rebus saepe primas tenere solet, huic instituto defuit. Virginum quippe in eo statu ad finem vitae perseverantium, & illibatam virginitatem servantium, jam Tertullianus & Cyprianus meminere. Monasteria vero eorum & collegia primitus deprehenduntur sub Athanasio in Ægypto; unde ingruentibus mox Arianorum persecutionibus, ab exulibus Ægyptiis Romam institutum hoc delatum est; impellente praecipue Hieronymo Romam reverso, qui Marcellam, aliasque potentes & illustres foeminas, animo forsan non malo, sed instituto parum convenienti, in Orientem ad Monachatum secum abduxit, & scriptis insuper suis in Occidente longe lateque eundem propagavit.
units.tr: VIII. Nor was the female sex, which is often wont to take the lead in such matters, lacking to this institution. Tertullian and Cyprian already mention virgins who remained in that state until the end of life and kept their virginity unspoiled. Their monasteries and communities are first found under Athanasius in Egypt; whence, when the Arian persecutions soon broke out, this institution was carried by Egyptian exiles to Rome; chiefly through the impulse of Jerome, returning to Rome, who led Marcella and other powerful and distinguished women away with him to the East for monastic life, perhaps with no bad intention, but with a way of life little suited to them; and moreover by his writings he spread the same far and wide in the West.

units.la: IX. Longe autem alia hujus Monachatus, tum Eremitici, tum Coenobitici, tunc erat ratio, ac illius quae posteris demum temporibus invaluit. Non enim solitudo quaerebatur, nisi ut sanctitati unice operam darent; & monasteria illa alio nomine erant Scholae, in quibus omnimoda eruditio ingenti studio tradebatur; nec inerti otio diffluebant Monachi, sed manuum labore vitam tolerabant; idque citra omne votum, aut ciborum vestiumque discrimen, aut humanarum regularum κεφεργίαν & anxias dolosasque cautiones. Quare eximii etiam viri ex monasteriis illis prodierunt. Virgines quoque votis & legibus humanis non tenebantur, sed Psalmis Deum laudabant, & verbum ejus vernaculo sermone legebant.
units.tr: IX. The character of this monasticism, both hermitic and cenobitic, was then quite different from that which prevailed in later times. For solitude was sought only so that they might devote their effort wholly to holiness; and those monasteries were in another sense schools, in which every kind of learning was taught with great zeal; nor did the monks dissolve in idle leisure, but supported their life by the labour of their hands; and this without any vow, or any distinction of foods and clothing, or any scrupulous observance (kephergia) of human rules and anxious, crafty precautions. Hence distinguished men also came forth from those monasteries. The virgins too were not bound by vows or human laws, but praised God with psalms and read his Word in the vernacular tongue.

units.la: X. In Occidente Monachorum collegia primo erecta legimus a Benedicto Nursino; qui Monachorum vitam tribus etiam votis illis, ut tribus clausTris adstrinxit. Ad exemplum Nursini, foeminis & virginibus ejusdem facti dux fuit foemina, soror ejus, Scholastica nomine: quae institutio brevi tempore per totum Occidentem diminavit; ut ab hice mox temporibus, non interrupta serie, ad nonum usque seculum floruerit Benedictinorum ordo.
units.tr: X. In the West we read that the first communities of monks were established by Benedict of Nursia, who bound the life of the monks also with those three vows, as with three nails. After the example of Nursia, a woman, his sister named Scholastica, became the leader of women and virgins of the same kind; and this institution spread in a short time through the whole West, so that from this time, in unbroken succession, the Order of Benedictines flourished down to the ninth century.

units.la: XI. Qui deinceps ordo in varias familias divisus est, circa decimum admodum seculum: quibus seculo duodecimo accesserunt varii ordines equestres, ut Sanctae Crucis &c. Per quae incrementa increvit omnino & collapsa est, si qua adhuc superarat, prioris Monachatus integritas, & ex Monachis facti fabri & architecti variarum superstitionum, & falsarum opinionum de propria justitia & meritis operum; atque porro prolapsi in omnia vitia: ut monasteria degenerarint in officinas omnis impietatis, ubi otium & ignorantia regnum obtinebat.
units.tr: XI. This order was afterwards divided into various families, around the tenth century. To these, in the twelfth century, were added various knightly orders, such as the Sanctae Crucis and others. With these developments the integrity of the earlier monasticism, if any was still left, was utterly overthrown and collapsed. The monks became craftsmen and architects of various superstitions and false opinions about one's own righteousness and the merits of works, and they further fell into every kind of vice, so that the monasteries degenerated into workshops of every impiety, where idleness and ignorance held sway.

units.la: XII. Exorti ergo seculo medio duodecimo Ordines mendicantium: quorum quatuor praecipue sunt familiae; Augustinianorum, Carmelitarum, Dominicanorum seu Praedicatorum, & Franciscanorum seu Minoritarum. Qui licet ordine postremi, foecunditate primi fuerunt, & immensum in numerum excreverunt commentitia Francisci miracula, & blasphemam inter Christum & illum similitudinem, & utriusque comparationem. Nato deinceps inter Dominicanos & Franciscanos schismate, posteriores hi, in varias sectas scissi sunt, quorum tres hae principes sunt: Conventualium, fratrum de Observantia & Capucinorum. Ex hisce vero sectis, tanquam variis Hydræ capitibus, licet aliquæ magnam sæpe inter se simultatem exercerent, in id unum tamen omnes conspirarunt, ut strenuam Papæ navarent operam, præcipuoque Papilmi errores & Theologiam Scholasticam inveherent.
units.tr: XII. Then, in the middle of the twelfth century, the Orders of the mendicants arose. Four families are chief among them: the Augustinians, Carmelites, Dominicans or Preachers, and Franciscans or Minorites. Although they were last in rank, they were first in fecundity, and the fabricated miracles of Francis grew to an immense number, as did a blasphemous likeness between Christ and him and a comparison of the two. Then, when a schism arose between the Dominicans and the Franciscans, the latter were split into various sects, of which these three are the principal: the Conventuals, the Brothers of the Observance, and the Capuchins. From these sects, like the many heads of a Hydra, although some of them often waged great rivalry among themselves, all conspired toward this one end: to labour zealously for the Pope and to introduce the errors of the Papists and the Scholastic theology.

units.la: XIII. Apollyon itaque per hosce suos satellites & sacras acies late tyrannus, cum jam orbem fere totum opprimeret, non diu postquam novum illud Reformationis lumen emicuisset, ultimum tandem cicadarum genus e puteo abyssi exclusit. Apoc. 9: 3, 11. Prodiit autem illud superioris seculi, anno 35. quando Jesuitarum ordo ab Ignatio Lojola, nobili Hispano, institutus est; qui infeliciter aliquandiu militem professus, ad austerius vitæ genus se contulit, & tribus ordinariis votis, quartum de cœca & speciali erga Papam obedientia, adjecit. Qui postremi, quam dignos se undequaque præstiterint, regi suo Abaddoni, jam pridem orbis magno suo malo didicit, & quotidiana docet experientia.
units.tr: XIII. So Apollyon, a tyrant spreading far and wide through these satellites and sacred battalions, when he was already oppressing almost the whole world, not long after that new light of the Reformation had shone forth, at last released the final kind of locusts from the pit of the abyss (Apoc. 9: 3, 11). This happened in the year 35 of the last century, when the order of the Jesuits was founded by Ignatius Loyola, a Spanish nobleman. After serving unsuccessfully as a soldier for some time, he turned to a stricter way of life and added to the three ordinary vows a fourth, of blind and special obedience to the Pope. How worthy these last have shown themselves in every respect to their king Abaddon, the world has long since learned to its great harm, and daily experience teaches it.

units.la: XIV. Facile hinc conspicuum est, quanto intervallo hodiernus Monachatus ab antiquo distinguitur; ut, cum olim institutus fit, in prætextum vincendi Satanam, subigendi carnem & mundum deferendi; postea conversus sit, in aptissimum Satanæ instrumentum, quo fines imperii longe protendit, caro dominata est, & universus pene mundus a Satana infestus est.
units.tr: XIV. From this it is easy to see by how great a distance today's monasticism is separated from the ancient. Though it was originally founded for the pretext of conquering Satan, subduing the flesh, and despising the world, afterwards it was turned into the most fitting instrument of Satan, by which he extended the bounds of his empire far and wide, the flesh has held dominion, and almost the whole world is harassed by Satan.

units.la: XV. Vidimus, qui & quales huic regno dati sint milites; operæ pretium erit scire quodnam regiminis genus inter illos sit stabilitum: conveniebat utique sacris hisce ordinibus sacrum regimen & Hierarchia, dignum patella operculum. De hac vero hierarchia anxie disquisitum est in Concilio Tridentino; an in ordinibus solis; an etiam in jurisdictione consistat; an vero in utriusque commixtione, quæ vulgaris est sententia. De forma ejus laboratum quoque est. Dictum autem anathema negantibus hierarchiam in Ecclesia firmatam institutione divina, quæ constat Episcopis, Presbyteris & diaconis; cum tamen Scriptura sacra & Ecclesia primæva, nec vocem hanc, nec rem ipsam, quin imo contrarium, scilicet ἱεροδιακονίαν docent.
units.tr: XV. We have seen who and what sort of soldiers were given to this kingdom; it will be worth knowing what kind of government was established among them. Surely a sacred government and a hierarchy suited these sacred orders, a lid worthy of the dish. Concerning this hierarchy the Council of Trent debated anxiously: whether it consists in the orders alone, or also in jurisdiction, or indeed in a mixture of both, which is the common opinion. Its form was also laboured over. Anathema was pronounced on those who deny that a hierarchy, established in the Church by divine institution, exists, consisting of bishops, presbyters and deacons; yet Holy Scripture and the primitive Church teach neither this word nor the thing itself, but rather the opposite, namely hierodiaconia [ἱεροδιακονίαν].

units.la: XVI. Circa ipsos Ordines quæsitum porro fuit; num ordo sit Sacramentum, & num unum tantum, quod per varios gradus in sacerdotium ascendat: ubi alii contendebant, septem tantum esse ordines; alii duos addebant, tonsuram & episcopatum. Quæ omnia generalibus verbis in decreto istius conventus intricata fuerunt. Vulgariter ergo in Papatu functiones sacras distribuunt in ordines & dignitates. Ordines vel mi-
units.tr: XVI. Concerning the orders themselves, it was further asked whether order is a sacrament, and whether there is only one, which ascends through various grades to the priesthood. Here some contended that there are only seven orders; others added two, the tonsure and the episcopate. All these matters were entangled in general terms in the decree of that council. Commonly, therefore, in Papacy they divide sacred functions into orders and dignities. The orders or mi-

units.la: III. ORDINES
units.tr: III. ORDERS

units.la: sacri minores sunt, ut Ostiariorum, Acoluthorum, Lectorum & Exorcistarum, qui per solam tonsuram constituuntur: vel majores, quibus annexus est coelibatus, nempe Subdiaconorum, Diaconorum & Sacerdotum, horumque iterum vel ecclesiarium vel regularium. Dignitates sunt Episcoporum, Metropolitanorum, Archiepiscoporum, Patriarcharum, Cardinalium & Papæ.
units.tr: nor are the lesser sacred orders, such as those of doorkeepers, acolytes, readers and exorcists, which are conferred by the tonsure alone; or the greater, to which celibacy is attached, namely those of subdeacons, deacons and priests, and these again either of the secular clergy or of the regular. The dignities are those of bishops, metropolitans, archbishops, patriarchs, cardinals and the Pope.

units.la: XVII. Quæ insana hierarchiæ moles non ab una parte laborat. Nam 1. Tota hæc ordinum & dignitatum series in Scriptura non occurrit.
units.tr: XVII. This insane mass of hierarchy labours under more than one defect. For, first, this whole series of orders and dignities does not occur in Scripture.

units.la: 2. Eadem hæc ordinum colluvies, ad nullum alium usum spectat, quam ad firmandum sacerdotium mercenarium, quod idololatricum esse scimus. 3. Ordines minores non conferuntur in exercitium; verum in præviam saltem dispositionem, uti vocant, ad vanum & imaginarium illud sacerdotium. 4. Characterem indelebilem huic ordinis sacramento tribuunt, quem tamen qualis sit, ignorant. 5. Ordinatos omnes, vi tonsuræ, civili jurisdictioni eximunt. 6. Irregularitates (ut eorum verbis utamur) multas fictitias comminiscuntur; & ordinibus hisce majoribus, a matrimonio, institutione divina sancito, obicem & impedimentum poni, statuunt. 7. Denique, speciatim Exorcistarum ordinarium munus faciunt, quod extraordinarium est Spiritus sancti charisma. Quæ omnia verbo Dei non solum adversantur, sed & sibi invicem; adeo ut universus hic apparatus & pompa, mole sua protinus rueret, nisi vi dolisque humanis sustineretur.
units.tr: Second, this heap of orders serves no other purpose than to establish a mercenary priesthood, which we know to be idolatrous. Third, the lesser orders are not conferred for exercise, but only for what they call preliminary disposition towards that vain and imaginary priesthood. Fourth, they attribute an indelible character to this sacrament of order, though they do not know what it is. Fifth, they exempt all the ordained, by virtue of the tonsure, from civil jurisdiction. Sixth, they invent many fictitious irregularities (to use their own words), and they lay down that a barrier and impediment is placed against the greater orders by marriage, which was sanctioned by divine institution. Seventh, and finally, they make the exorcists' office an ordinary function, though it was an extraordinary charisma of the Holy Spirit. All these things are not only opposed to the Word of God, but also to one another, so that this whole apparatus and pomp would at once collapse under its own weight, unless it were propped up by human force and trickery.
