units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De Episcopis, Archiepiscopis, Patriarchis & Cardi- nalibus.
units.tr: On Bishops, Archbishops, Patriarchs and Cardinals.

units.la: I. Ictum est aliquid de Ordinibus Pontificiorum; percensemus nunc eorundem Dignitates. Inter quas primum sibi locum vendicant Episcopi. De quibus anquiritur; num ex jure divino distincti sint a Presbyteris. Cum enim Episcoporum nomen & origo in Scriptura inveniatur; non est quod in illis arguamus, præter abusum rei & vocabuli, qui nunc est spespectandus. Nos igitur contra Pontificios tenemus, eosdem Presbyteros & Episcopos esse, persuasi his argumentis.
units.tr: I. Something has been said about the orders of the Papists; we now go through their dignities. Among these, bishops first claim a place for themselves. Concerning them it is asked whether they are distinct from presbyters by divine right. For since the name and origin of bishops is found in Scripture, there is no need for us to dispute about the thing itself, apart from the abuse of the thing and of the word, which is now to be considered. We therefore hold, against the Papists, that bishops and presbyters are the same, persuaded by these arguments.

units.la: II. 1. Act. 11:29,30. eleemosynæ mittuntur ad Seniores in Judæa, seu Presbyteros, nulla Episcoporum mentione facta 2. Act.14:23. creantur in Ecclesiis singulis presbyteri, de episcopo vero tacetur. 3. Act. 15:2. mittuntur Paulus & Barnabas ad Apostolos & Presbyteros Jerosolymam. vide com. 6. nihil vero de Episcopo. conf. com. 22,23. 4. Act. 20:17. Arcescuntur Presbyteri Ephesini; qui tamen com. 28. vocantur Episcopi, & quidem plures unius Ecclesiæ. 5. Fph.4:11. enumerantur Apostoli &c. Pastores & Doctores; non autem Episcopi ab his distincti. 6. Phil. 1:1. nominantur Episcopi & Diaconi unius urbis, omissis presbyteris, eodem sensu. 7. Nec aliter 1. Tim. 3:2,8. ab Episcopis transitur ad Diaconos.
units.tr: II. (1) Acts 11:29,30: alms are sent to the elders in Judea, that is, to the presbyters, with no mention of bishops. (2) Acts 14:23: presbyters are appointed in the individual churches, and nothing is said of a bishop. (3) Acts 15:2: Paul and Barnabas are sent to the apostles and presbyters at Jerusalem; see verse 6, but nothing about a bishop; compare verses 22, 23. (4) Acts 20:17: the presbyters of Ephesus are summoned; yet in verse 28 they are called bishops, and indeed several of one church. (5) Eph. 4:11: apostles, etc., pastors and teachers are enumerated, but bishops are not distinguished from these. (6) Phil. 1:1: bishops and deacons of one city are named, with presbyters omitted, in the same sense. (7) Likewise 1 Tim. 3:2,8: the transition is from bishops to deacons.

units.la: III. 8. 1. Tim. 4:14. Presbyterium dicitur impositionem manus Timotheo; qui cum Pontificiis sit Episcopus, inextricabilis hic suboritur difficultas; quando secundum leges hodiernas Pontificiorum, Presbyteri Episcopum creare nequeant. nemo enim ibi dare potest, quod non habet. 9. 1. Tim. 5:17. Presbyteri in sermone laborantes duplici honore digni judicantur, ubi de Episcopo qui illis præcellentior, altum silentium. 10. Tit. 1:5. constituuntur oppidatim Presbyteri, qui com. 7. vocantur Episcopi. vide & com.9. 11. 1. Pet.5:1. 2. Petrus συμπρεσβύτερος alloquitur πρεσβυτέρως; quos com. 2. jubet ἐπισκοπεῖν non coacte, sed libenter. id est, episcopum agere; idcirco illi duo erant iidem. 12.2. Joh. 1. & 3. Joh. 1. Johannes se ipsum presbyterum vocat; qui etiam com. 9. Epist. 3 carpit primatum ambientem inter illos Diotrephen: ὁ φιλοπρωτεύων αὐτῶν Διοτρεφὴς οὐκ ἐπιδέχεται ἡμᾶς.
units.tr: III. (8) 1 Tim. 4:14: the laying on of hands is called the "presbytery" given to Timothy; and since, for the Papists, he is a bishop, an inextricable difficulty arises here, since according to the present laws of the Papists presbyters cannot make a bishop; for no one can give what he does not have. (9) 1 Tim. 5:17: presbyters who labour in preaching are judged worthy of double honour, while about a bishop, who is superior to them, there is complete silence. (10) Titus 1:5: presbyters are appointed town by town, who in verse 7 are called bishops; see also verse 9. (11) 1 Pet. 5:1: Peter, a fellow-presbyter (συμπρεσβύτερος), addresses presbyters (πρεσβυτέρους); whom in verse 2 he bids to exercise oversight (ἐπισκοπεῖν) not under compulsion but willingly, that is, to act as bishops; therefore those two were the same. (12) 2 John 1 and 3 John 1: John calls himself the presbyter; and in 3 John 9 he rebukes Diotrephes, who loved to have the first place among them: "Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us" [ὁ φιλοπρωτεύων αὐτῶν Διοτρεφὴς οὐκ ἐπιδέχεται ἡμᾶς].

units.la: IV. Ab altera vero parte, ne desint loca, quæ ad se trahant Pontificii, duo potissimum nobis objiciunt, & Episcopos Presbyteris majores esse inde probant; nempe quod 1. Tim. 5:19. dum dicitur, adversus presbyterum accusationem ne admittito; Timotheo tribuatur jurisdictio in presbyteros; & eidem, ut & Tito, Presbyterorum constituitio Tit. 1:5. Verum Timotheus & Titus non tam habendi sunt pro Episcopis, quales hodie; quam pro sui gradus & modi Apostolis; nimirum qui ab Apostolis ipsis missi erant ad prædicandum euangelium, & constituendas Ecclesias; quorum mentio fit Act. 19:22. Phil. 2:25. & 4:3. Hac ergo auctoritate presbyteros constituebant eosque peccantes corrigebant. Tit. 1:5.
units.tr: IV. On the other side, lest the Papists lack passages to draw to their side, they put forward chiefly two objections, and from these prove that bishops are greater than presbyters: namely, that in 1 Tim. 5:19, where it is said, "do not admit an accusation against a presbyter," jurisdiction over presbyters is given to Timothy; and that to him, as also to Titus, the appointment of presbyters is attributed (Titus 1:5). But Timothy and Titus are not to be regarded so much as bishops, such as they are today, as Apostles of their own rank and manner; that is, men sent by the Apostles themselves to preach the gospel and to establish churches, who are mentioned in Acts 19:22, Phil. 2:25 and 4:3. By this authority, then, they appointed presbyters and corrected those who sinned (Titus 1:5).

units.la: V. Nullum igitur Episcopos inter & Presbyteros discrimen in Scriptura apparet; uti nec apud antiquos: quod apertissime testantur, Hieronymus, Ambrosius, Chryfoftomus, Augustinus, & recentiores alii plurimi. Si qua tamen forte fuerit inter hosce praerogativa, summum nihil fuit, nisi primatus quidam ordinis inter presbyteros, ut primus concederetur locus presbytero, seu aetate, seu ministerio primo; quemadmodum & Synagogae Judaeorum suos προεςῶτας seu praesides habebant.
units.tr: V. Therefore no distinction between bishops and presbyters appears in Scripture, nor does one appear among the ancients; this is most clearly attested by Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, and many other more recent writers. If there was any pre-eminence between these, it was nothing more than a certain primacy of order among the presbyters, so that the first place was granted to a presbyter either by age or by earlier ministry; just as the synagogues of the Jews also had their προεστῶτες, or presidents.

units.la: VI. Exinde paulum mutata est primatus ratio; sic ut qui antea illum ordine obtinebant, deinde electione primi constituerentur; quo devenitum esse refert Ambrosius, ob reliquorum presbyterorum imperitiam: Hieronymus vero ad tollenda schismata factum esse testatur, ad Epist. ad Tit. 1. forte utrumque concurrit: quamvis remedium morbo pejus esset; hoc enim modo non obviam itum est schismatis, sed fundamenta jacta sunt Antichristianae dominationis, uno presbytero supra cateros evecto; unde tandem stultus ille pastor natus est. Zach. 11: 15. Factum id jam altero, ut videtur, post Christum saeculo.
units.tr: VI. From there the method of primacy was somewhat changed, so that those who had held it previously by order were afterwards appointed by election as first. Ambrose reports that this came about because of the inexperience of the other presbyters; Jerome, however, testifies that it was done to remove schisms (on Titus 1). Perhaps both came together, although the remedy was worse than the disease; for in this way schism was not checked, but the foundations were laid of Antichristian domination, with one presbyter raised above the rest; whence at last that "foolish shepherd" was born (Zech. 11:15). This happened, it seems, already in the second century after Christ.

units.la: VII. Ne vero Episcopus frustra & solo nomine elatus esse videretur; potestas & cura Ecclesiae, quae ante penes omnes presbyteros sterterat, illi ferme soli demandata; seu ab eo arrepta est. Praecipue ipsi peculiare factum est jus ordinationis presbyterorum, ad consilium tamen eorum & societatem, ut simul cum Episcopo, ordinarent etiam presbyteri, & in thronis sederent; teste Epiphanio. Quomodo & jus ordinationis in Scriptura etiam presbyteris tribuitur; ut vidimus ex 1. Tim. 4: 14. 2. Tim. 1: 6. Act. 13: 1, 2, 3.
units.tr: VII. Lest, however, the bishop should seem to be exalted in vain and in name only, the power and care of the Church, which had previously rested with all the presbyters, was committed almost wholly to him, or was seized by him. Especially the right of ordaining presbyters became peculiar to him, yet with the counsel and fellowship of the presbyters, so that the presbyters also ordained together with the bishop and sat on the thrones; as Epiphanius testifies. In the same way, the right of ordination is attributed in Scripture also to presbyters, as we have seen from 1 Tim. 4:14, 2 Tim. 1:6, and Acts 13:1-3.

units.la: VIII. Episcopus itaque supra collegas suos evectus, iis praestans: primo, ordine; deinde, electione; tertio, ordinandi jure & Ecclesiae gubernandae potestate, presbyteros oppressit: & quo potestatem suam fundaret & stabiliret, mutata etiam sunt reliqua Ecclesiae ministeria, & introducti, Subdiaconi, Acolythi, Exorcistae, Lectores & Ostiarii, quos supra enumeravimus: unde degeneravit Episcopatus, & pessimae tandem notae factus est. Quocirca in hodierno Episcopatu tria discernenda sunt.
units.tr: VIII. The bishop, therefore, raised above his colleagues, surpassing them first in order, then in election, and thirdly in the right of ordaining and the power of governing the Church, oppressed the presbyters; and in order to found and establish his power, the remaining ministries of the Church were also altered, and subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers and doorkeepers, whom we listed above, were introduced; whence the episcopate degenerated and at last became of the worst repute. Accordingly, three things must be distinguished in the episcopate as it is today.

units.la: 1. Aliquid divini, quod habet qua Presbyter. 2. Aliquid humani, quod habet ex praerogatis humanis. 3. Aliquid tyrannici & AntiChristiani, quod illi deinceps accessit. Itaque hodiernus Episcopatus cum primaeva illius institutione minus conveniat, & hactenus minus probandus sit; quamvis pro vario populorum genio, humanus paedagogiae alicujus usus non ubique æque incommodus sit, adeoque hac ratione inter ipsos retineri possit.
units.tr: (1) Something divine, which it has in so far as it is a presbyter. (2) Something human, which it has from human privileges. (3) Something tyrannical and Antichristian, which later attached itself to it. Hence the present episcopate agrees less with its original institution, and so far is less to be approved; although, according to the varying character of peoples, a human use of some kind of guidance is not equally inconvenient everywhere, and so in this way it may be retained among them.

units.la: IX. Tria hæc hodierno Episcopatui inesse, undequaque claret. Sic Bellarminus & Pontificii omnes Episcopatum hodie considerant, non tanquam ministerium, sed tanquam potestatem regendi in spiritualibus, & proinde imperandi & puniendi: cum omnis Episcopus merus tantum sit mandatarius, sine ullo imperio vel dominio. Idem Bellarminus Episcopum Presbyteris majorem vult, tum ordinis potestate, tum jurisdictione: sed cum ordine major non sit; ordinis etiam potestate major esse non potest: omnis enim ordinis potestas, clavium est; quæ presbyteris omnibus pari modo data est.
units.tr: IX. That these three things are present in the present episcopate is clear from every side. Thus Bellarmine and all the Papists regard the episcopate today not as a ministry, but as a power of ruling in spiritual matters, and therefore of commanding and punishing; whereas every bishop is merely a mandatary, without any command or lordship. The same Bellarmine wants the bishop to be greater than the presbyters, both in the power of order and in jurisdiction; but since he is not greater in order, he cannot be greater in the power of order either: for all power of order belongs to the keys, and this has been given equally to all presbyters.

units.la: X. Plerunque vero volunt Pontificii, Presbyteros Episcopis inferiores esse, jurisdictione tum interna conscientiæ, tum externa: per quam primam regitur populus in foro interiori conscientiæ; per alteram, in foro exteriori. Sed contra hæc facit. 1. Quod Scholastici jurisdictionem interiorem omnibus sacerdotibus immediate a Christo collatam, recte censeant. 2. Utraque hæc jurisdictio etiam ad potestatem clavium pertinet: eadem enim est potestas solvendi & ligandi, in foro pœnitentiali; quæ est in foro judiciali: & ridiculum fingere, concessam Sacerdotibus a Christo potestatem hanc privatim, in aure confitentis; non vero publice coram tota Ecclesia. Quicquid ergo ex jure divino habet Episcopus, idem habet & Presbyter.
units.tr: X. The Papists, however, generally want presbyters to be inferior to bishops in jurisdiction, both internal, of conscience, and external. By the former the people are governed in the internal forum of conscience; by the latter, in the external forum. But the following tells against this. (1) The Schoolmen rightly hold that internal jurisdiction was conferred immediately by Christ on all priests. (2) Both of these jurisdictions also pertain to the power of the keys: for the power of loosing and binding is the same in the penitential forum as in the judicial forum; and it is absurd to imagine that the power was granted by Christ to priests privately, in the ear of the penitent, but not publicly before the whole Church. Whatever, therefore, the bishop has by divine right, the presbyter has the same.

units.la: XI. Similiter in Tridentino Concilio vexatum est acerrime; an Episcopatus juris divini sit; quod ut dijudicaretur vehementissime urgebant Hispani, graviter tum Papæ imminentes: legatorum vero Papæ studio declinata & cohibita res est. Speciatim præpositus generalis Jesuitarum distinctionem fabricabatur, inter jus divinum & ordinationem divinam. Illa ex jure divino esse dicens, quæ non solum in genere; verum etiam in specie a Deo sunt: quæ vero in genere tantum a Deo sunt; in specie autem ab hominibus constituta, illa ordinationis divinæ esse volebat; & hujus divinæ ordinationis censebat esse Hierarchiam & institutionem Episcoporum. Quod distinctionis commentum, rem omnem tum composuit; licet revera per eam res eadem redeat, & ex ea æque cogi possit, Episcopos qua pastores a Deo esse; qua pastores vero majores, ab hominibus & Papa.
units.tr: XI. In the same way, at the Council of Trent the question was contested most fiercely, whether the episcopate was of divine right; and while the Spaniards urged that it be decided, pressing heavily upon the Pope, the matter was turned aside and restrained by the zeal of the papal legates. In particular, the general of the Jesuits fabricated a distinction between "divine right" and "divine ordinance." He said that those things are of divine right which are from God not only in general but also in particular; but those which are from God only in general, and in particular constituted by men, he wanted to be of "divine ordinance"; and he judged that the hierarchy and the institution of bishops were of this divine ordinance. This invented distinction composed the whole matter for the time being, although in reality the same thing comes back through it, and from it one can equally conclude that bishops are from God as pastors, but as greater pastors they are from men and the Pope.

units.la: XII. Et sane jurisdictionem externam, quam nunc usurpant Episcopi, ex hominibus tantum originem trahere, docet liquido historia Ecclesiastica cum enim olim Christiani, litium suarum judicium ad pastores tanquam arbitros maxime deferrent, occasione monitionis Pauli 1. Cor. 6: 1,4. mos hic perennavit non solum prioribus seculis, dum sub cruce gemeret Ecclesia; verum etiam deinceps ab Imperatoribus prorogatus, quinimo auctus & sollemniter stabilitus fuit. Imperio vero collapso omnem porro jurisdictionem in Clerum, sibi arrogarunt; etiam in Laicos, eo ferme praetextu; quod causa vel Ecclesiastica esset, vel Magistratus officio suo deesset. Post annum millesimum eo impudentiae processerunt, ut jus hoc Imperatorum conniventia sibi concessum, a Christo ad se profectum affirmare sustinerent. Denique anno MCCC. universum illud Episcoporum jus Papae assertum est, praetextu verborum Christi, Petro dictorum; Pasce oves meas. Cum tamen revera, quicquid unquam habuerunt jurisdictionis Episcopi, ex permissione principum acceperunt; ut nempe poenis temporalibus Clericos disciplinae gratia coercere possent; quod postea in immensam tyrannidem extenderunt. Irrepsit etiam sequioribus temporibus aliud vitium in Episcopatum; quando infantes non solum Episcopi sunt ordinati, verum & titulares seu nomine tenus; cum olim Episcopus non foret sine Ecclesia, sicut non est maritus, sine uxore: Episcopatu enim qui caret, Episcopus non est.
units.tr: XII. Indeed, that the external jurisdiction now exercised by the bishops derives its origin from men alone, is clearly taught by ecclesiastical history. For when in former times Christians chiefly referred the judgment of their lawsuits to the ministers as arbiters, following the admonition of Paul in 1 Cor. 6:1-4, this custom lasted not only in the earlier centuries, while the Church groaned under the cross, but was afterwards extended by the emperors, and indeed was increased and solemnly confirmed. But when the empire collapsed, the bishops went on to claim for themselves all jurisdiction over the clergy, and even over the laity, under almost the same pretext: that the matter was either ecclesiastical or that the magistrate was failing in his duty. After the year one thousand they went so far in their impudence that they dared to assert that this right, granted to them by the tolerance of the emperors, had come to them from Christ. Finally, in the year 1300, the whole of that episcopal right was claimed for the Pope, under the pretext of the words of Christ spoken to Peter: Feed my sheep. Yet in truth, whatever jurisdiction the bishops ever had, they received from the permission of princes, namely so that they might restrain the clergy by temporal penalties for the sake of discipline; a power which they afterwards extended into immense tyranny. In later times another vice also crept into the episcopate: bishops were ordained not only for infants, but also as titular bishops, that is, in name only; whereas formerly a bishop was not without a congregation, just as a husband is not without a wife, for he who lacks a bishopric is not a bishop.

units.la: XIII. Sicut Clerum inferiorem oppressit Episcopus; ita vicissim Episcopos alii. Nam 1. illorum jurisdictioni sequioribus saeculis maxime exempti Monachi 2. Libera etiam reddita & eadem jurisdictione soluta fuerunt Capitula plurima Ecclesiarum Cathedralium. 3. Multae causae, quae ad illos spectabant, Romam pertractae sunt, per reservationes, aliaque formulas. Hac vero ratione Romanus Pontifex jurisdictionem eorum circumcidit, sibique eos subjecit.
units.tr: XIII. Just as the bishop oppressed the inferior clergy, so in turn others oppressed the bishops. For (1) in the later centuries the monks, most of all, were exempted from their jurisdiction; (2) many chapters of cathedral churches were also made free and released from the same jurisdiction; (3) many cases which belonged to the bishops were brought to Rome, through reservations and other formulas. In this way the Roman Pontiff cut back their jurisdiction and made them subject to himself.

units.la: XIV. Non vero hic sese stetit successcens per hoc gradus Hierarchia: verum sicut antea ab Aristocratica, qua communi presbyterorum consilio regebatur Ecclesia, mutata est in Episcopalem; ita & huic aliae superaccesserre formulae. Cum enim primi Episcopi pares essent, & unum haberent Episcopatum, & a communi concilio Ecclesiae ejusdem provinciae per Synodos regerentur; dein Metropolitarum Archiepiscoporum nomina nata sunt. Erat autem Metropolitanus, Episcopus istius urbis, quae provinciae erat caput seu metropolis; cujus officium erat, Synodos provinciales convocare, iisque praesidere, & recens electos episcopos confirmare: ut primitus honore potius quam potestate reliquis Episcopis major esset. Sicuti autem Episcopos, ita & Archiepiscopos inique pressit Papa, quibus varias jurisdictionis partes surripuit.
units.tr: XIV. Nor did the hierarchy stop there, advancing step by step: rather, just as the Church was formerly governed by an aristocracy, by the common council of the elders, and was changed into an episcopal form, so other forms were added on top of this one. For since the first bishops were equals, and each had one bishopric, and were governed by the common council of the Church of the same province through synods, later the names of metropolitans and archbishops arose. The metropolitan was the bishop of that city which was the head or metropolis of the province; his office was to convene provincial synods, to preside over them, and to confirm newly elected bishops. Thus at first he was greater than the other bishops in honour rather than in power. But just as the pope oppressed bishops, so he also oppressed the archbishops, stripping them of various parts of their jurisdiction.

units.la: XV. Cum vero a Constantino plures provincias in unam diœcesin redigerentur; supra Metropolitanos constituti etiam sunt superiores Patriarchæ, seu primates, Exarchi Diœcesium dicti. Primus autem Patriarcha fuit Episcopus Alexandrinus, qui jam ante hoc nomine gaudebat; licet duntaxat, tanquam Episcopus Metropolitanus, reliquis Episcopis major esset. Cum vero posterioribus temporibus plurimi legantur Patriarchæ; primitus tantum κατ' ἐξοχὴν datum est id justribus Episcopis, Romano nempe (licet ille isthoc titulo parum delectareturaliud affectans) Alexandrino & Antiocheno; quæ præcipuæ erant imperii præfecturæ, seu diœceses. Accesserunt deinde alii duo, juxta politicæ dignitatis ordinem adsciti, Constantinopolitanus, & Hierosolymitanus. Denique etiam minorum præfecturarum, Græce ἐπαρχίαι dictarum, Episcopi, Patriarchæ dicti sunt.
units.tr: XV. When later several provinces were reduced by Constantine into one diocese, patriarchs were set up above the metropolitans, also called primates or exarchs of dioceses. The first patriarch was the bishop of Alexandria, who already before had enjoyed this name; although, as a metropolitan bishop, he was only greater than the other bishops. But when in later times many patriarchs are read of, this title was at first given in the strict sense only to the three bishops: the Roman (though he was little delighted with this title, aiming at something else), the Alexandrian, and the Antiochene, which were the chief prefectures, or dioceses, of the empire. Then two others were added, according to the order of political dignity: the Constantinopolitan and the Jerusalemite. Finally, the bishops of the lesser prefectures, called in Greek eparchies, were also called patriarchs.

units.la: XVI. Sequentibus seculis aliud natum est dignitatis genus, quod a Scriptura prorsus alienum, & antiquitati vix cognitum, aut tenui saltem notitia, & vili fere nomine; cum maxime vero splendidissimum; Cardinalium nempe munus: illi enim Episcopis & Archiepiscopis longe præminentes, olim tantum Presbyteri vel Diaconi septem regionum, seu cardinum Ecclesiæ Romanæ erant. Ut ridicule nimis Pontificii, eos a cardinibus terræ denominatos velint.
units.tr: XVI. In the following centuries another kind of dignity arose, utterly foreign to Scripture and scarcely known to antiquity, or known at least by a slight acquaintance and under a humble name, though now most splendid: the office of cardinal. For cardinals, far superior to bishops and archbishops, were formerly only presbyters or deacons of the seven regions, or hinges, of the Roman Church. How ridiculously the Papists want them named from the hinges of the earth!

units.la: XVII. Usque ad decimum, imo duodecimum seculum, Cardinales hi Episcopis minores erant, donec tandem iis se etiam præposuerint; unde & Episcopatus iis sunt dati: quare hodieque obtinet triplex Cardinalium Ordo, Episcoporum, Presbyterorum & Diaconorum. Quin & unus sæpe pluribus fungitur Episcopatibus; sed & regna gubernant, quæ Romæ nimirum protectioni & curæ eorum demandata sunt; unde & bella gerunt & ordines ducunt: quodque olim toti Senatui, Clero & populo Romano convenibat, Episcopum Romanum deligere; id labentibus annis, sibi solis vendicarunt.
units.tr: XVII. Up to the tenth, indeed the twelfth, century these cardinals were inferior to bishops, until at last they placed themselves above them too; hence bishoprics were also given to them. Therefore even today a threefold order of cardinals remains: of bishops, of presbyters and of deacons. Indeed one often holds several bishoprics at once, and they govern kingdoms, which are entrusted to their protection and care at Rome; hence they also wage wars and lead armies. And what formerly belonged to the whole senate, clergy and people of Rome, namely the choice of the Roman Bishop, they in the course of the years claimed for themselves alone.

units.la: XVIII. Hæc ab ultima origine repetita, sunt Hierarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ incunabula & incrementum: quæ ingens moles ex tenuibus valde initiis excitata est, & paulatim in illam altitudinem & honoris culmen surrexit. Mittimus nunc reliquam functionum illius farraginem, ut Archidiaconatus, Suffraganeorum, Vicariatus, Decanatus: quæ una cum jam dictis Pontificiæ tyrannidi vel facilem viam pararunt, vel promptum praeiterunt ministerium. Iter nunc properamus ad ipsum Papam, omnium horum fastigium & quasi complementum.
units.tr: XVIII. These things, traced back to their earliest origin, are the cradle and growth of the ecclesiastical hierarchy: a huge mass raised from very slender beginnings, which by degrees rose to that height and summit of honour. We now pass over the rest of that medley of functions, such as archdeaconries, suffragans, vicariates and deaneries, which, together with the aforementioned, either paved an easy way for Papal tyranny or readily furnished it with ministers. We now hasten on to the Pope himself, the summit and, as it were, the completion of all these.

units.la: LOCUS QUINQUAGESIMUS DE PAPA & ANTI-CHRISTO. CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: THE FIFTIETH HEADING, CONCERNING THE POPE AND ANTICHRIST. CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: De Papa, ejusque provectione.
units.tr: Concerning the Pope and his rise.

units.la: I. Erat adhuc Hierarchiæ, post tot ordines, sibi invicem instar montium superimpositos, culmen & fastigium; nisi accessisset Papa, dignus huic operi colophon & apex; cujus monstri historiam, nunc ab ipsa nativitate, per adolescentiam & maturam ætatem, ad hanc senectutem deducamus.
units.tr: I. The hierarchy, with its many orders piled one upon another like mountains, still lacked a summit and crown. The Pope supplied that, the fitting capstone and peak of the whole structure. Let us now trace the history of this monster, from its very birth through its youth and mature age down to this old age.

units.la: II. Primitus ergo Patriarchæ cum Papa, quo nomine nobis nunc venit Romanus Episcopus, ejusdem juris & auctoritatis erant; nullo, nisi ordinis tantum habito discrimine; ut Romanus primus, Constantinopolitanus secundus esset. Allaborarunt autem præcipue duo hi primarii Patriarchæ, & id operam dederunt, ut universales fierent Episcopi; quem titulum primus usurpavit Johannes Episcopus Constantinopolitanus, eam ipsam ob causam a Gregorio Magno Antichristi præcursor dictus.
units.tr: II. At first the Patriarchs and the Pope, by which name we now refer to the Roman bishop, had equal right and authority. The only difference was one of rank: the Roman was first and the Constantinopolitan second. The two chief Patriarchs, however, worked hard and took pains to become universal bishops. John, bishop of Constantinople, was the first to claim this title, and for that very reason Gregory the Great called him the forerunner of Antichrist.

units.la: III. Quam scelesti tituli usurpationem, quam vis tam acriter in alio argueret Gregorius, & multum diverso nomine propterea se Servum Servorum dici vellet; ipsam tamen rem per occultos cuniculos variis modis ad se pertrahere nitebatur. Qua in contentione Romanus tandem prævaluit. Bonifacius III. enim, Gregorii successor, continuis praesationibus & ambitionibus, anno admodum 606. titulum hunc impetravit; adeoque Ecclesiarum omnium Orientis & Occidentis caput constitutus fuit: postquam enim adulationibus ferventem sibi Phocæ gratiam conciliassent Gregorius & Bonifacius, a parricida illo facile, quod clam prius, demum aperte ambiebant, obtinuerunt. Et inde prærogativa haec in Synodo Lateranensi confirmata est. Universalis autem Episcopi nomen licet jam usurparet Romanus, non tamen universali consensu id adeptus est, uti factum oportuerat; sed objecerunt si magno conatu Orientales; unde perpetuum Orienti cum Occidente intercessit certamen & schisma; nec in ipso quidem Occidente omnium calculos tulit: varii enim Episcopi restiterunt, sed irrito molimine.
units.tr: III. Gregory condemned this wicked usurpation of the title very sharply, and he wished to be called by a different name, the servant of servants. Yet he himself tried in various ways, through hidden channels, to draw the thing itself to himself. In this contest the Roman at last prevailed. Boniface III, Gregory's successor, by constant solicitation and ambition obtained the title in about the year 606, and so was made head of all the churches of East and West. Gregory and Boniface had first won the favour of the fervent Phocas by flattery, and from that parricide they obtained, first secretly and then openly, what they were seeking. The privilege was then confirmed in the Lateran Synod. Although the Roman now claimed the name of universal bishop, he did not gain it by universal consent, as he should have done. The Easterners resisted with great vigour, and so a perpetual struggle and schism arose between East and West. Nor did he win the votes of all even in the West itself: several bishops opposed him, but their efforts came to nothing.

units.la: IV. Episcopis sic omnibus supereminens Papa, & supremus orbis hierarchici dominator, Imperatoris etiam jugum sensim excussit. Benedictus enim secundus, ab Imperatore Constantino circa An. 684. exoravit remissionem confirmationis imperatoriae, circa electionem Papae; unde variae deinceps turbae exortae. Nec flagrans cupido dominandi hic cessavit; quin saecularem etiam potestatem & principatum appetierit. Quam acquisivit etiam, primo, ut fertur, ab Ariperto Longobardorum rege; qui, ut maxima scelera cluerent, Papae Johanni VII. An 705. donavit Alpes Cottias: mox Anno 730. Gregorius II. Romam & universam Italiam subtraxit obedientiae Leonis III. Ita ergo Papa urbis Romae, regionisque suburbicariae, saecularis etiam dominus factus est. Atque hac ratione, quod diu jam meditati erant, plane tandem ab Imperatoribus defecerunt Papae.
units.tr: IV. The Pope, now supreme over all bishops and master of the whole hierarchical world, gradually threw off the yoke of the Emperor as well. Benedict II, about the year 684, obtained from the Emperor Constantine the remission of the imperial confirmation of papal elections, and from this many disturbances arose afterwards. Nor did this burning lust for dominion stop there; the Popes went on to seek secular power and princely rule as well. They first acquired it, as is said, from Aripert, king of the Lombards, who, to cover up his great crimes, gave the Alpes Cottiae to Pope John VII in the year 705. Soon afterwards, in 730, Gregory II withdrew Rome and all Italy from the obedience of Leo III. So the Pope became the secular lord of the city of Rome and its suburban region. In this way the Popes at last completely revolted from the Emperors, as they had long been planning to do.

units.la: V. Quo specimine exhibito, non tantum se legibus Imperatoris exsolvit, sed tanquam signo erecto, ipsis Principibus gravis imminuit. Quod auspicatus est in Hilderico Francorum Rege, quem Zacharias Papa regno movit, Pipino, ejusque posteris Carolinis ipsi substitutis. Sic & Longobardorum regnum in Italia oppressit, & ad Francos transtulit, ad quos Occidentis etiam imperium devolvisse visus est. Leo III. coronato Carolo magno; a quo fidelitatis juramentum accepit, quae deceßorum vestigia posteriores Papae strenuo pressierunt. Donec praecipue Anno 1076. a Gregorio VII. anathemate percussus, & regno abdicatus Imperator Henricus, insigne testimonium dedit toti mundo, supra omnem saecularem potestatem, & omnem dictum Deum aut quod ut Deus colitur, se evehere Papam. 2. Thess. 2:4.
units.tr: V. Having shown this sample of their power, the Popes not only freed themselves from the laws of the Emperor but, like a raised standard, became a heavy burden to the princes themselves. They began this with Childeric, king of the Franks, whom Pope Zachary deposed from his kingdom, putting in his place Pepin and his Carolingian descendants. In the same way the Pope crushed the kingdom of the Lombards in Italy and transferred it to the Franks, to whom the empire of the West also seemed to have passed. Leo III crowned Charlemagne, and from him he received an oath of fealty. Later Popes vigorously pressed on in the footsteps of these predecessors. Above all, in the year 1076 Gregory VII struck the Emperor Henry with anathema and deposed him from his kingdom. This gave a striking testimony to the whole world that the Pope exalts himself above every secular power and above every so-called God or object of worship. 2 Thess. 2:4.

units.la: VI. Hinc omnibus modis supra Principes & Magistratus, nec uno nomine se extulit. 1. Quoad regnorum translationem; quando Leo III. Imperium Constantinopolitanum Carolo donat: Zacharias, deturbato Hilderico, regnum Galliae Pipino concedit: Gregorius V. Germaniae Electores constituit: Bonifacius VIII. Carolo Valesio Orientis imperium titulo tenus dedit: Alexander VI. Indiam Occidentalem Ferdinando Aragonii liberaliter largitus est. 2. Quoad fidelitatis sacramentum; ut in verba eorum jurarent, Imperatores adegerunt; & jus coronationis, quasi citra eam Imperator esse nequiret, sibi attribuerunt. Unde Innocentius II. Lotharium Imperatorem vasallum suum, seu hominem Papae obnoxium, vocavit: & Coelestinus coronam de capite Henrici V. pedibus deturbavit.
units.tr: VI. Hence the Pope raised himself above princes and magistrates in every way, and not under one heading only. 1. As to the transfer of kingdoms: when Leo III gave the Eastern empire to Charlemagne; when Zachary, having deposed Childeric, granted the kingdom of Gaul to Pepin; when Gregory V appointed the electors of Germany; when Boniface VIII gave the empire of the East to Charles of Valois in name only; when Alexander VI generously bestowed the West Indies on Ferdinand of Aragon. 2. As to the oath of fealty: they compelled emperors to swear in their words, and they claimed for themselves the right of coronation, as if an emperor could not be one without it. Hence Innocent II called the Emperor Lothair his vassal, or one bound to the Pope as his man; and Celestine threw the crown from the head of Henry V and trampled it underfoot.

units.la: VII. 3. Spectat huc, quod nomina sua Imperatorum nominibus praeponi voluerint; atque hoc cum non observaret Fredericus Barbarosa Imperator, succensuit illi valde Adrianus IV. Quid quod & ad turpissimum ministerium in coena Papali adegerint Imperatores; & stapetem sibi porrigere, quin & ejus vice fungi jusserint, & ad pedum Papae osculum damnaverint; ad imitationem sceleratissimorum & tyrannicorum olim Imperatorum. 4. Denique, utrumque sibi gladium arrogarunt, & universi orbis imperium, sive palam & directe, sive per ambages ad se pertinere arbitrati sunt. Quamobrem & jura sua Canonica, in opprobrium & vilipendium juris civilis & Caesarei, cuderunt, & orbi obtruserunt. Ita Papa Imperatoribus subjectus, eos sibi subjecit; & qui ab illis olim constituebatur & confirmabatur, versis rerum vicibus, nunc calculo suo, & quidem ante humiliter exoratus, eos approbat, & confirmat.
units.tr: VII. 3. To this belongs the demand that their names be placed before the names of the Emperors. When Frederick Barbarossa refused to observe this, Adrian IV was greatly angered with him. Again, the Emperors were forced to perform the most shameful service at the papal banquet: they held the stirrup for the Pope, even served as his groom, and were ordered to kiss his feet, in imitation of the most wicked and tyrannical emperors of old. 4. Finally, the Popes claimed both swords for themselves and judged that the rule of the whole world belonged to them, whether openly and directly or by indirect means. Therefore they fashioned their own canon law, to the disgrace and contempt of civil and imperial law, and forced it upon the world. Thus the Pope, though subject to the Emperors, made them subject to himself. He who was once appointed and confirmed by them now, the situation being reversed, approves and confirms them by his own vote, and that only after first being humbly entreated.

units.la: VIII. Non minori artificio & successu reliqua etiam omnia sibi subjecit & pessum dedit; tum plebem, tum Doctores ejus, tum denique Ecclesiam universam. Populum barbararum gentium invasionibus & inundationibus rudem ignarumque factum, in ignorantia illa fovit; & sciendi desiderium per fidem implicitam, aliasque rationes vel suffiamin navit, vel illi prorsus excussit. Porro Scripturae infallibilem & indubium interpretem se fecit; camque populo eripuit; traditionibus & verbo ἀγράφῳ substitutis; quin & mutis imaginibus docendi officio commisso, Baalismum in Ecclesiam invexit: tum cultus omnis ignota lingua peractus est; dominicae Coenae altera pars populo surrepta; jus eligendi & constituendi pastores alio translatum, & Laicorum nomen plebi Christianae per contemptum impositum est. Accessit praeterea jugum ciborum & dierum; innumerae populi expilationes, variis praetextibus factae; per satisfactiones, dispensationes, impetrationes, taxas poenitentiarias, indulgentias, jubilaeos & similes exactiones; quibus cophonem imposuit, futurae poenae metum, ex fatuo purgatorii igne. Resistentibus denique apertam etiam vim & persecutiones acerrimas paravit, quibus a Gregorii VII. tempore per secula sequentia maxime grassati sunt. Atque ita mysterium illud iniquitatis, jam ab omni parte impleri & maturescere incipiebat; dum co jam redacta erat res; ac si ad Deum accedere, nec coelo potiri, absque sacerdotibus parariis & proxenetis non liceret populo, cujus collo tam arcte jugum illud Papatus imminebat, ut vix suspirare posset.
units.tr: VIII. With no less skill and success the Popes subjected to themselves all the rest and brought them to ruin: first the common people, then their teachers, and finally the whole Church. The people, made rude and ignorant by the invasions and floods of the barbarian nations, they kept in that ignorance. They either smothered their desire to know through implicit faith and other devices, or stripped it from them altogether. Furthermore, they made themselves the infallible and undoubted interpreters of Scripture and took it away from the people, substituting traditions and the unwritten [ἀγράφῳ] word. Indeed, after entrusting the office of teaching to dumb images, they introduced Baalism into the Church. Then all worship was performed in an unknown tongue; the one half of the Lord's Supper was snatched from the people; the right to elect and appoint ministers was transferred elsewhere; and the name of laity was contemptuously imposed on the Christian people. In addition came the yoke of foods and days, countless plunderings of the people under various pretexts, through satisfactions, dispensations, impetrations, penitential taxes, indulgences, jubilees and similar exactions. The crown of all this was the fear of future punishment, drawn from the foolish fire of purgatory. Finally they prepared open violence and most savage persecutions against those who resisted, and these raged especially from the time of Gregory VII through the following centuries. And so that mystery of iniquity, already beginning to be fulfilled and to ripen on every side, had reached such a point that the people could not approach God or obtain heaven without priestly go-betweens and brokers. Upon the neck of the people, that yoke of Papacy pressed so tightly that they could scarcely draw a breath.

units.la: IX. A plebe ad Doctores & Pastores transitum est; quos omnes in verba sua jurare & mandatis suis obedientiam praestare coegit; quamvis licentiam aliquam & libertatis speciem illis permitteret; ita tamen, ut ipse omnium esset arbiter. Quos serios magis & graviores invenit, objecta offia, ad silentium redegit. Academias Episcopis exemtas, sibi soli proxime obnoxias fecit; idemque illud multis etiam monachis & monasteriis concessit; quod beneficii loco reputabatur, cum interea loci id unum egit, ut omnes eo arctius sibi devincirent, ut licet inter ipsos saepe non bene convenirent, sibi tamen omnes strenue militarent.
units.tr: IX. Next came the move from the common people to the teachers and ministers. The Popes compelled all of them to swear to their words and to render obedience to their commands, although they allowed them some licence and a semblance of liberty, but only so that the Pope himself should be the judge of all. Those whom they found more earnest and serious, they silenced by putting obstacles in their way. The Popes made the academies exempt from the bishops and subject to themselves alone, and they granted the same privilege to many monks and monasteries, which was regarded as a benefit. Yet their real aim in all this was to bind everyone to themselves more tightly, so that, although they often did not get on well among themselves, they would all serve the Pope vigorously.

units.la: X. Injurius itaque coepit esse in Pastores & Sacerdotes, jus eorum arctando, per casus sibi reservatos, & dispensationes ab ipso solo concedendas. Nihil autem iniquius in Clerum & Pastores attentari potuit, quam impurus ille coelibatus, omnibus mera vi obtrusus.
units.tr: X. Accordingly he began to be unjust toward the ministers and priests, narrowing their rights through cases reserved to himself and dispensations that only he could grant. Nothing more unjust could be attempted against the clergy and ministers than that foul celibacy, forced upon everyone by sheer violence.

units.la: XI. Episcoporum jurisdictionem accidit, Monachos & Academias, uti jam dictum, iis subtrahendo; Ecclesias etiam commendatariis commitendo, qui ab omni Episcopi inspectione liberi, solius Papae examini & potestati subjecti erant. Causas etiam & judicia Episcoporum per reservationes & appellationes ad se devolvit; multisque aliis modis dominium in Episcopos exercuit.
units.tr: XI. He encroached upon the jurisdiction of the bishops, as already said, by withdrawing monks and academies from them. He also committed churches to commendatory holders, who, free from all episcopal oversight, were subject only to the examination and power of the Pope. He drew to himself the causes and judgments of bishops through reservations and appeals, and in many other ways exercised lordship over them.

units.la: XII. Metropolitanis etiam & Archiepiscopis non pepercit; dum illos a se confirmari contendit, & Pallium Episcopale accipere voluit; quod non nisi carissimo pretio manibus ejus extorqueri debebat: quomodo & menses Papales & Annatae introductae sunt. Jus in Synodos Provinciales ad se traxit, & Suffraganeos Archiepiscoporum jurisdictioni eximit. Omnes denique Ecclesiarum summas praerogativas, in ministros suos Datarios, Cancellarios, aliaque familiaria & domestica officia transtulit.
units.tr: XII. He did not spare the metropolitans and archbishops either. He insisted that they be confirmed by him and wished to receive the episcopal pallium, which could be extorted from his hands only at a very high price. In this way the papal months and annates were introduced. He drew to himself the right over provincial synods and exempted suffragans from the jurisdiction of the archbishops. Finally he transferred all the chief prerogatives of the churches to his own ministers, dataries, chancellors, and other household and domestic officials.

units.la: XIII. Nec deerant hisce omnibus praetextus & colores, etiam non sine splendore aliquo. Urbis ipsius magnitudo omnes percellebat, & tantam illi dignitatem sponte praebere videbatur: divitiis suis ingentibus, egenis Episcopis; & potentia sua, oppressis succurrere, sibique devincire poterat; prætexta Petri successio, ipsiusque Petri primatu, omnium oculos offulcabat: primorum presbyterorum & Episcoporum Romanorum probitas & eruditio, magnam ipsi auctoritatem conciliaverat; ut & longa sedis Romanæ orthodoxia, circa præcipua fidei capita, quæ in Oriente detorta erant; unde nomine illius libenter utebatur; illudque præ se ferebat totus Occidens. Ignorantia etiam & ignavia aliorum Episcoporum fecit, ut primo sibi obnoxios redderet, dein & subjiceret. Prudentiores & sagaciores, aut vi reprimebantur aut honoris specie ipsi conciliabantur; quando, tanquam vicarii & legati Papæ illa agebant, quæ ipsi, ex jure suo agere debuissent.
units.tr: XIII. Nor were there lacking pretexts and colours for all this, some not without a certain splendour. The greatness of the city itself overawed everyone and seemed to offer him such dignity of its own accord. By his immense riches he could help needy bishops, and by his power he could relieve the oppressed and bind them to himself. The pretended succession of Peter, and Peter's primacy itself, dazzled everyone's eyes. The integrity and learning of the first Roman presbyters and bishops had won him great authority, as had the long orthodoxy of the Roman see on the chief articles of faith, which had been twisted in the East; so he gladly used its name, and the whole West displayed it. The ignorance and sloth of the other bishops also made them first bound to him and then subject. The more prudent and shrewd were either suppressed by force or won over with a show of honour, when they did as vicars and legates of the Pope what they should have done by their own right.

units.la: XIV. Illud unum denique restabat, ut tota etiam Ecclesia, per Concilium generale ibi repræsentata, ipsi tandem subjiceretur: quod variis artibus tentatum, successit demum ultimis temporibus, contra fas & æquum, & omnem antiquitatis experientiam. Nam cum olim concilia œcumenica ex solo imperio Romano convocarentur; Romani Pontificis potestas extra illud non fuisset extensa, etiamsi vel illis conciliis major fuisset. Verum nec ulla ipsi auctoritas in concilia unquam concessa fuit; quin denegarunt ipsi eam Patres Chalcedonenses; ut a veritate omnino alienum sit, quod de hoc concilio prædicarunt Gregorius Magnus, aliique Pontifici. Chalcedonensi concilio eadem in sententia præiverat concilium Constantinopolitanum; quod utriusque decretum secutum est concilium sextum. Recentioribus temporibus, Concilium Pisanum sine Pontifice congregatum fuit, imo duos Pontifices abdicavit, & Alexandrum V. elegit. Concilium Constantiense, in quo mille Patres, diserte sancivit, concilium supra Papam esse: cujus concilii legitimam auctoritatem agnoverunt Papæ, Johannes XXIII. Gregorius XII. & Martinus V. & cujus decretum de calice Laicis neganda, Tridentinum concilium approbavit. In Concilio Basileensi definitum est, Papam concilio inferiorem esse; quod tamen confirmatum est a Papa Eugenio. Ut hactenus Papa Conciliis major non appareat.
units.tr: XIV. One thing finally remained: that the whole Church, represented there through a general council, should at last be subjected to him. This was attempted by various arts and at last succeeded in the latest times, contrary to right and justice and to all the experience of antiquity. For although formerly the ecumenical councils were convened by the Roman empire alone, the power of the Roman Pontiff was not extended beyond that, even if he had been greater than those councils themselves. Yet no authority over councils was ever granted to him; indeed the Fathers of Chalcedon denied it to him. So what Gregory the Great and other pontiffs proclaimed about this council is wholly alien to the truth. The council of Constantinople had gone before Chalcedon in the same opinion, and the sixth council followed the decree of both. In more recent times the Council of Pisa was gathered without the Pope, and it deposed two popes and elected Alexander V. The Council of Constance, in which a thousand fathers were present, expressly decreed that a council is above the Pope. The popes John XXIII, Gregory XII and Martin V acknowledged the legitimate authority of this council, and the Council of Trent approved its decree that the chalice be denied to the laity. The Council of Basel defined that the Pope is inferior to a council, though this was confirmed by Pope Eugenius. Thus far the Pope does not appear greater than the councils.

units.la: XV. Primum ergo, infinitus hic Papæ primatus stabilitus est a Leone X. in Concilio Lateranensi, paulo ante exortum Lutherum; quod concilium paucorum duntaxat erat Episcoporum, eorumque Papæ addictorum; qui tamen priorum conciliorum decreta abrogare conati sunt: tam parum vero facinus illud tuum probare potuerunt; ut a præcipuis Academiis, nominatim Parisiensi, non fuerit agnitum hoc concilium. Quare nec in Tridentino concilio quæstionem hanc patribus committerè ausi sunt Paulus III. & Pius V. sed omni modo caverunt,ne de auctoritate Pontificis quæstio institueretur. Hinc etiamnum a concilijs sibi metuit Papa, eorumque coactioni intercedit.
units.tr: XV. First, then, this boundless primacy of the Pope was established by Leo X in the Lateran Council, shortly before Luther arose. That council consisted of only a few bishops, all devoted to the Pope, and even they tried to abrogate the decrees of earlier councils. Yet they were so unable to prove their deed that the chief academies, especially Paris, did not recognise this council. For this reason Paul III and Pius V did not dare to entrust this question to the fathers at Trent, but by every means took care that no question be raised about the authority of the Pontiff. Hence even now the Pope fears councils and opposes their being convened.

units.la: XVI. Licet vero nondum universo cùm assensu, voti compos sit factus Papa,tantos tamen,per has molitiones fecit progressus;ut quæ sententia ,tempore concilij Basilien sis,teste Æneâ Sylvio, nova esset; jam Bellarmini tempore fere communis sit facta; & conciliorum convocationem, ad se pertraxerit: concilijsque præsidendi, eaque confirmandi auctoritatem usurpaverit: quo factum est, ut non solum ab ipso concilia dependeant, sed & sine eo concilium non sit, quin & per eum, cum solus errare nequeat, nullo concilio opus sit.
units.tr: XVI. Although the Pope has not yet gained his wish with universal assent, he has made such progress through these efforts that the opinion which, at the time of the Council of Basel, according to Aeneas Sylvius, was new, has now by Bellarmine's time become almost common. He has drawn to himself the convocation of councils and usurped the authority of presiding over them and confirming them. As a result, not only do councils depend on him, but there is no council without him, and since he alone cannot err, there is no need for any council at all.

units.la: XVII. Quibus fundamentis innixa est illa extremæ blasphemiæ vox,quam cruciavit Bonifacius VIII. Omni creaturæ de necessitate salutis esse, ut Romano Pontifici subsit. Quo ipso universam Ecclesiam sibi omnimodo subjecit. Huc etiam pertinet blasphema illa,quam sibi arrogat, in fidei rebus, infallibilitas: quod proprium Apostolorum privilegium fuit; illamque nunc sibi tribuere certissima est Anti-Christi nota, & verum illud blasphemia nomen. Apoc. 17: 3.
units.tr: XVII. On these foundations rests that voice of extreme blasphemy which Boniface VIII uttered: that it is necessary for the salvation of every creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff. By this very claim he subjected the whole Church to himself in every way. To this also belongs the blasphemous infallibility which he claims for himself in matters of faith. This was a peculiar privilege of the Apostles, and to claim it for himself now is a most certain mark of Antichrist, and truly "the name of blasphemy." Rev. 17: 3.

units.la: XVIII. Hac vero infallibilitate opus nequaquam esse, res ipsa evincit;satis enim est infallibilis fidei norma,quam nobis exhibet S. Scriptura; non insuper requiritur,ut ministri,ex illa judicantes,in omni judicio sint infallibiles & errare nescii: quod & œconomiæ illi, quam Deus inter homines observat,& quæ rebus humanis optime convenit, maxime repugnaret: & si Deus talcs ministros hominibus indulserit, supervacua erit hæc norma.
units.tr: XVIII. The thing itself shows that there is no need for this infallibility. Holy Scripture gives us a sufficient infallible norm of faith. It is not further required that ministers, judging by that norm, be infallible and unable to err in every judgment. That would also be greatly at odds with the economy which God observes among men, and which suits human affairs very well. And if God had granted such ministers to men, this norm would be superfluous.

units.la: XIX. Tum præcipue contrarium hujus rei clamat omnium sæculorum experientia;tam sub Veteri,quam Novo Test. Errarunt enim olim Pontifices, Aaron. Exod. 32. Urias, 1. Reg. 16. Caiaphas. Joh. 11: 50. Matth. 26: 65, 66. Imo etiam multi Pontifices Romani, ut Marcellinus, Liberius, Honorius, Ioanne XXII. Tum quoque Gregorius septimus & Bonifacius, aliique, quos vel Pontificum numero expungas oportet; vel errorum & scelerum omnium voragines, & propudia humani generis, Papas quosdam fuisse fatearis. Præterea necdum liquet, penes quos infallibilitatis hujus sit sedes penes Papam ne, an concilium. Hoc totum infallibile esse nequit, cum nulla ejus pars sit infallibilis: & si vel speciali Sp. sancti privilegio illud cœtui illi cautum esset, nunquam tamen constat, an legitime congregatum sit concilium: sicut nec de illo unquam indubitate constare potuit, an verus sit Pontifex; adeoque ejus infallibilitati nullius fides inniti potest, aut in eam resolvi.
units.tr: XIX. Above all, the experience of all ages cries out against this claim, under both the Old and New Testaments. Pontiffs have erred before: Aaron, Exod. 32; Urijah, 1 Kings 16; Caiaphas, John 11: 50; Matt. 26: 65, 66. Indeed many Roman pontiffs also erred, such as Marcellinus, Liberius, Honorius, and John XXII. Then there were Gregory VII and Boniface, and others, whom you must either strike from the number of the pontiffs or confess that some popes were whirlpools of every error and crime, and the disgrace of the human race. Moreover, it is not yet clear where this infallibility resides, whether in the Pope or in the council. The whole cannot be infallible, since no part of it is infallible. And even if that assembly had been secured this privilege by a special gift of the Holy Spirit, it is never certain whether a council has been lawfully convened. Just as it could never be indubitably established whether the Pontiff was true, no one's faith can rest upon his infallibility or be resolved into it.

units.la: XX. Regerunt hisce Pontificii, I. Largientes nobis, Pontificem cum concilio generali errare posse, in controversiis facti, non vero juris. At nos respondemus; ergo & in jure, cum jus sæpe ex facto judicandum sit; quinimo errare sic poterit circa totam ferme Theologiam, quæ maxima ex parte historica est. II. Largiuntur etiam, posse errare Pontificem in quæstione juris, ut doctorem privatum, non vero ut Papam. Verum urgemus; ergo & ut Papa, cum ille etiam privatim docere teneatur. 2. Posset sic esse hæreticus, qui privatim falsa doceat. 3. Non gaudebit tum prærogativa Apostolica, qui nec privatim docentes, falli poterant. 4. Et vanum est illud disjungere, ut aliquis qua Papa sit orthodoxus, & qua homo hæreticus; quod tantum in cerebro pingi potest.
units.tr: XX. The Papists reply to these points: I. Granting us that the Pontiff with a general council can err in matters of fact, but not of right. But we answer: then he can err in matters of right too, since right must often be judged from fact; indeed he could err in this way about almost the whole of theology, which is for the most part historical. II. They also grant that the Pontiff can err on a question of right as a private teacher, but not as Pope. But we press the point: then he can err as Pope too, since he is bound to teach privately as well. 2. He could thus be a heretic who privately teaches falsehood. 3. He would then not enjoy the apostolic prerogative, since even those teaching privately could err. 4. And it is vain to separate the matter, so that someone is orthodox as Pope and a heretic as a man; that can only be painted in the brain.

units.la: XXI. ııı. Fatentur item, Papam errare posse in moribus, non autem in fide. At non instamus item; qui errare potest in moribus, potest sallere & mentiri, hoc enim ad mores spectat, adeoque decipere populum. Nec etiam plus hac ratione Papæ tribuitur, quam Diabolo. Sed majus robur causæ suæ afferre videntur ex S. Scriptura, quando magno conata objiciunt Luc. 22: 32. ubi Petro Christus dicit: Ego oravi pro te, ne fides tua deficiat; ubi tantum promittit Christus constantiam in fide interiori; quæ licet hic speciatim Petro in memoriam revocetur, omnibus tamen fidelibus communis est; ut nihil hinc pro Papæ infallibilitate possit confici.
units.tr: XXI. III. They also admit that the Pope can err in morals, but not in faith. But we likewise press: whoever can err in morals can deceive and lie, for this pertains to morals, and so can deceive the people. Nor by this reasoning is more ascribed to the Pope than to the Devil. They seem to bring greater strength to their cause from Holy Scripture, when they eagerly object Luke 22: 32, where Christ says to Peter: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." Here Christ promises only constancy in inward faith. Although this is recalled to Peter by name, it is nevertheless common to all the faithful, so nothing can be derived from it for the Pope's infallibility.

units.la: XXII. Verum ab ipsis causæ hujus propugnatoribus subruitur totum hoc negotium. Ita cum Bellarminus non solum Pontificem Romanum in fide non posse errare contendat; sed & ab Ecclesia Romana particulari, etiam personalem errorem procul removeat, ut tota illa Ecclesia non possit fieri Apostatica; eo ipso plus tribuit illi Ecclesiæ quam Papæ; qui tantum judicialiter, ut loquuntur, non vero personaliter errare posse negatur. Præterea suo se indicio prodit pudendum hoc infallibilitatis commentum, dum tam variis limitationibus tam anxie definitur, & tot sententiarum divortiis, in diversa prorsus abeuntibus, defenditur; uti apud Bellarminum aliosque videre est.
units.tr: XXII. But the very defenders of this cause undermine this whole matter themselves. For Bellarmine not only contends that the Roman Pontiff cannot err in faith, but also takes personal error far away even from the particular Roman Church, so that the whole of that Church cannot become apostate; by this very fact he attributes more to the Church than to the Pope, who is denied the ability to err only judicially, as they say, and not personally. Moreover, this shameful invention of infallibility betrays itself by its own evidence, since it is defined with such anxious qualifications and defended with so many divergent opinions, going in quite different directions, as one may see in Bellarmine and others.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: De Regimine Ecclesiæ Monarchico.
units.tr: On the Monarchical Government of the Church.

units.la: I. Idimus eluctantem tenuibus initiis, & sensim per aliquot seculorum orbes emergentem, tandem in illud culmen elatum Papam; quo vero jure, quave injuria, id nunc vindicandum nobis restat: quod omne tribus hisce capitibus absolvemus. I. An regimen Ecclesiæ Monarchicum, quod ipse usurpat, juris divini sit. II. An illud Petro præ reliquis Apostolis commissum sit. III. An Petro Papa successerit, & prærogativæ ejus in illum devolutæ sint.
units.tr: I. We have seen the Papacy struggling up from humble beginnings and gradually rising over several cycles of centuries to that summit. By what right, or by what wrong, is what we must now vindicate, and we shall settle it under three heads. I. Whether the monarchical government which he claims is of divine right. II. Whether it was committed to Peter above the other Apostles. III. Whether the Pope succeeded Peter, and whether Peter's prerogatives passed down to him.

units.la: II. Quod ad primam quæstionem attinet, de qua nunc agendum; certo certius est, nullum aliud in Ecclesiam introduci posse regimen, quam quale ipse Christus constituit. Sicut enim gravissime peccavit Israël, & non sine contumelia in Deum peregrinam regiminis formam periit. I. Sam. 8. Ita non sine gravissima in Christum injuria, novum & alienum regiminis genus Ecclesiæ, Novi præsertim Test., obtruderetur. Cujus peccati reos se manifeste faciunt Pontificii, iisdem fere argumentis persuasi, quibus carnalis olim Israël: ut eundem in utroque spiritum agnoscas: & quemadmodum, quæ ibi, sub senioribus & judicibus fuerat Theocratia, Jud. 8:23. I. Sam. 8:7. per reges immutata est; quamvis iterum promissa Esai. 1:26. Et restituam judices tuos sicut in principio, & consiliarios tuos sicut in initio: & præstita sub Novo Test. ita & hic, loco regni cœlorum & divinæ illius œconomiæ, quam Christus per pastores & ministros instituit, revocatum est regnum mundi, quando Papa regnare incepit.
units.tr: II. As to the first question, which is now to be treated, it is most certainly true that no other government can be introduced into the Church than the one Christ himself established. For just as Israel sinned very gravely, and not without insult to God, when it perished by adopting a foreign form of government (1 Sam. 8), so a new and alien kind of government would be forced upon the Church, especially the New Testament Church, not without the gravest injury to Christ. The Papists plainly make themselves guilty of this sin, persuaded by nearly the same arguments as carnal Israel of old, so that you may recognise the same spirit in both. Just as the theocracy that had existed there under elders and judges (Judg. 8:23; 1 Sam. 8:7) was changed into kingship, although it had been promised again (Isa. 1:26): And I will restore your judges as at the beginning, and your counsellors as at the first, and as it had been established under the New Testament, so here too, in place of the kingdom of heaven and that divine economy which Christ instituted through pastors and ministers, the kingdom of the world has been recalled, now that the Pope has begun to reign.

units.la: III. Regimen hoc Monarchicum tam necessarium habent Pontificii, ut in eo summam rei Christianæ collocent. Quod tamen noluerunt olim, nec permittunt etiamnum, qui Ecclesiam Papa superiorem agnoscunt, ut sine eo integra esse queat Ecclesia; quem in finem statum quidem Ecclesiæ Monarchicum esse censent, regimen vero ejus Aristocraticum, ita ut potestas tantum ministerialis & executiva, penes Papam sit. Dominatus ille Monarchicus Papæ assertus tamen est in concilio Lateranensi, sub Leone X. Anno 1516. quam vis totum negotium valde in ambiguo sit; tum propter controversias, uti jam vidimus, de re ipsa; tum speciatim de hoc etiam concilio.
units.tr: III. The Papists consider this monarchical government so necessary that they place the whole substance of the Christian religion in it. Yet those who acknowledge the Pope as superior to the Church, so that the Church could not be complete without him, did not want this in former times and still do not permit it. To that end they indeed judge the state of the Church to be monarchical, but its government aristocratic, so that only a ministerial and executive power rests with the Pope. That monarchical lordship of the Pope was asserted, however, at the Lateran Council under Leo X in the year 1516, although the whole matter is very much in doubt, both on account of the controversies, as we have already seen, about the thing itself, and specifically about this very council.

units.la: IV. Nos quod spectat; internum Ecclesiæ regimen monarchicum esse fatemur libenter, & contendimus, propter caput ejus (Christum, Eph. 4: 15, 16. Col. 1: 19. externum vero ejus regimen democraticum item non esse contra fanaticos facile agnoscimus; cum tot in eo obtineant charismata & ministeria, de quibus videre est 1. Cor. 12: 28. Eph. 4: 11, 12. sed illud, ut aristocraticum in Scriptura describi, cum per Seniores & Pastores administretur, pertendimus; ita tamen, ut potius ministerium, quam regimen sit. Speciatim vero nullum, præpter jam dictum, certum regiminis Ecclesiastici schema, in Scriptura extat, aut exhibetur, præter certam & generalem hanc amussim 1. Cor. 14: 40. Πάντα εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν γίνεσθω.
units.tr: IV. As for us, we freely confess that the internal government of the Church is monarchical, and we contend that it is so on account of its head (Christ, Eph. 4:15, 16; Col. 1:19). We readily acknowledge, against the fanatics, that its external government is likewise not democratic, since so many gifts and ministries are found in it, as may be seen in 1 Cor. 12:28 and Eph. 4:11, 12. But we maintain that it is described in Scripture as aristocratic, since it is administered through elders and pastors; yet in such a way that it is a ministry rather than a government. Specifically, however, apart from what has already been said, there is no fixed scheme of ecclesiastical government in Scripture, or set out there, except this certain and general rule (1 Cor. 14:40): All things should be done decently and in order [Πάντα εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν γίνεσθω].

units.la: V. Aliam igitur, præter spiritualem unius Christi, monarchiam Ecclesiæ superinduere, tyrannicum non modo est, sed & Antichristianum, & Scripturæ omnimodo contrarium; quæ Christum caput nostrum affirmat, nec alterius meminit, nisi quod ad mundanum aliquod regnum pertineat, hypocritarum cervicibus imponendum, & cum Ecclesia conflictaturum; quod Bestiæ, Anti-Christi, aliisque nominibus venit. Nec ulla vel levia hujus hierarchiæ vestigia apparent in Scriptura; cum tamen, si res, ut illi volunt, comparata esset, non minori sane cura, ac sub Veteri Test. Pontifex erat descriptus, sub Novo Testamento, Papa hic, cum omnibus quæ ad eum spectant, constitui, & diligenter depingi debuerat. Imo vero, non patitur tale regnum, status Ecclesiæ Novi Test. utpote ubi solus audiendus est filius Luc. 9: 35. & in qua nullus nunc sit, qui se magistrum vocare possit. Matth. 23: 8. non enim Angelis subjecta est hæc Ecclesia. Hebr. 2: 5. nedum hominibus & Patribus carnis, Hebr. 12: 9. aut certæ cathedræ & congregationi eorum; multo minus uni alicui Episcopo, tanquam infallibili ejus doctori.
units.tr: V. To introduce another monarchy into the Church, besides the spiritual monarchy of Christ alone, is not only tyrannical but also Antichristian, and altogether contrary to Scripture. Scripture affirms that Christ is our head, and mentions no other except one that pertains to some worldly kingdom, to be imposed on the necks of hypocrites and to wage war with the Church; this is called the Beast, Antichrist, and by other names. Nor do even slight traces of this hierarchy appear in Scripture. Yet if the matter were arranged as they wish, it ought surely to have been described with no less care than the High Priest was described under the Old Testament; under the New Testament this Pope, with everything that pertains to him, ought to have been set forth and carefully portrayed. Indeed, the state of the New Testament Church does not allow such a kingdom: in it alone the Son is to be heard (Luke 9:35), and in it there is now no one who can call himself teacher (Matt. 23:8). For this Church is not subjected to angels (Heb. 2:5), much less to men and fathers of the flesh (Heb. 12:9), or to a certain chair and assembly of them, and much less to any single bishop as its infallible teacher.

units.la: VI. Præcipuum vero est ut occurramus adversariorum objectionibus, quas fabricati sunt non paucas. 1. Igitur regiminis illius splendore nos percellere conantur; quod omnium optimum & præstantissimum esse prædicant. Sed non tam facile oculos nobis perstringi patimur; cum in rebus hisce non ita generatim definiri possit, quid sit optimum. Verum, si vel optimum illud esset, non idcirco universus orbis ita regi posset, quod sicuti nunquam factum, ita nec unquam fiet. Præterea, alia prorsus est ratio Ecclesiæ, alia Politiæ; nec inter has duas ullus est nexus; nam in Ecclesia ministerium tantum est. Sic nos existimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. 1. Cor. 4: 1. nec in illa locum habet ulla vis, aut violentum regimen; nec tam æqualiter conspicua est universalis Ecclesiæ unio & societas, ut ab uno capite regi queat.
units.tr: VI. It is especially important that we meet the objections of our opponents, of which they have devised not a few. 1. They try to dazzle us with the splendour of that government, which they proclaim to be the best and most excellent of all. But we do not allow our eyes to be dazzled so easily, since in such matters it cannot be defined so generally what is best. Yet even if it were the best, the whole world could not for that reason be governed in that way, since, as it has never been done, so it never will be. Moreover, the nature of the Church is quite different from that of the state, and there is no connection between the two; for in the Church there is only ministry. Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Cor. 4:1). Nor is there any place in the Church for force or violent rule, nor is the universal union and fellowship of the Church so evident that it could be governed by one head.

units.la: VII. 2. Monarchiam hanc eliciunt ex similitudine, quam habet, cum Ecclesia Angelorum, ad quam etiam exigendam volunt: sed irrito conamine; nam de Angelorum hierarchia nihil certi; de monarchia vero eorum nihil veri perhibetur: nec Angelorum rempublicam nobis describere voluit Deus, multo minus ut normam proponere; cum nec eadem Angelorum & hominum sit ratio; in illis enim nullus potestatis suæ metuendus est abusus; sicut in hisce. 3. Nec constat similitudo, inter Ecclesiæ & humani corporis conspicuum & visibile caput, cum in corpore nostro etiam duo sint pedes & aures &c. quas, si literam urgere velint, ut eo etiam modo in Ecclesia ostendant, necesse erit. Tum quoque ex illa similitudine non consequitur monarchia, cum & in aristocratia caput sit. Accedit, quod caput illud sit Christus, qui unicus Ecclesiæ Rex, Ezech. 37:22. Et rex unus erit universis ipsis in regem: & Pastor, Joh. 10: 16. Et erit unus grex, unus Pastor. ita & unicum Ecclesiæ est caput. Eph. 4: 15. Col. 2: 19. 4. Urgent alias etiam similitudines, ut unum esse in exercitu imperatorem, in domo dominum & œconomum; atque hisce assimulari Ecclesiam: cujus quidem argumenti vim sicut facile agnoscimus quatenus per id efficitur, imperatorem & dominum Ecclesiæ solum esse Christum; ita in ipsos haud difficulter retorquemus; ut, sicut idem rex variis exercitibus, varios deligit imperatores; & in magna domo plures sunt œconomi; sic inde patet, variis Ecclesiis, varios etiam præsse Pastores, directores & œconomos.
units.tr: VII. 2. They derive this monarchy from the resemblance which the Church bears to the Church of the angels, and they wish to enforce it from that; but their effort is in vain. For there is nothing certain about a hierarchy of angels, and nothing true is reported about their monarchy; nor did God wish to describe the commonwealth of the angels to us, much less to propose it as a rule, since the reasoning for angels and men is not the same: for among the angels there is no abuse of power to be feared, as there is among men. 3. Nor does the resemblance hold between the Church and the human body with its conspicuous and visible head, since in our body there are also two feet and two ears, etc., which, if they wish to press the letter, they must also show in the Church in that way. Nor does monarchy follow from that resemblance, since even in an aristocracy there is a head. Add to this that the head is Christ, who is the sole King of the Church (Ezek. 37:22): And one king shall be king to them all; and the Pastor (John 10:16): And there shall be one flock, one Pastor; so also the Church has a single head (Eph. 4:15; Col. 2:19). 4. They also press other comparisons, such as that an army has one commander, and a house one master and steward, and that the Church is likened to these. We readily admit the force of this argument insofar as it shows that the commander and master of the Church is Christ alone. But we turn it back on them without difficulty: just as the same king chooses various commanders for various armies, and in a great house there are several stewards, so it is plain that for various Churches there are various pastors, directors and stewards.

units.la: VIII. 5. Propius aliquanto rem tangere videntur, cum in Pontifice Veteris Test. qui totius mundi synagogas gubernabat, præfiguratum esse regimen Novi Test. oggerunt. At respondemus 1. Licet varia in V. Test. acciderint, quæ futuros status Ecclesiæ, etiam in N. Test. delineaverint; non tamen Ecclesia Vet. Test. in omnibus figura fuit Novi, cum eadem sit Ecclesia: nec, si vel hoc daretur, ullus foret nexus inter Pontificem Veteris & regimen Novi Test. cum & in aliis Pontifex a ministris N. T. discrepet. 2. Alia longe est ratio universi orbis, alia unius populi. 3. Nec Pontifex fuit figura Papæ, sed Christi, & quidem quoad munus ejus, non regium, sed sacerdotale. 4. Pontifex non fuit monarcha, suberat enim concilio magno. Adde quod nulla fit necessitas argumenti, ab illis temporibus ad Novum Teft.
units.tr: VIII. 5. They seem to touch the matter somewhat more closely when they argue that the government of the New Testament was prefigured in the High Priest of the Old Testament, who governed the synagogues of the whole world. But we reply: 1. Although various things happened in the Old Testament which also outlined future states of the Church in the New Testament, the Church of the Old Testament was not in all respects a figure of the New, since it is the same Church. Nor, even if this were granted, would there be any connection between the High Priest of the Old Testament and the government of the New Testament, since in other respects too the High Priest differs from the ministers of the New Testament. 2. The situation of the whole world is one thing, that of one people another. 3. Nor was the High Priest a figure of the Pope, but of Christ, and indeed as to his office, which was not kingly but priestly. 4. The High Priest was not a monarch, for he was subject to the great council. Add that there is no necessity for the argument to move from those times to the New Testament.

units.la: IX. 6. Pergunt; Christum dum in terra degeret, visibile fuisse Ecclesiae caput; ergo etiamnum tale esse oportet. Quod dum magna contentione urgent, non vident se intricatos magna difficultati; nimirum cum Ecclesia Christiana demum ceperit post ascensionem Christi, & hactenus Ecclesia Judaica obtinuerit, toto tempore vitae Christi, duo fuisse visibilia Ecclesiae capita necesse est, Christum & Pontificem Judaicum. Sed Christus, verum & unum illud caput, dum hic egit, non conspicuum majestate & gloria monarcham, sed contemptum prae vilitate servum se gessit.
units.tr: IX. 6. They go on: while he lived on earth, Christ was the visible head of the Church; therefore he must still be such. In pressing this with great vehemence, they do not see that they entangle themselves in a great difficulty. For since the Christian Church only began after Christ's ascension, and until then the Jewish Church had held sway, it follows that throughout the whole of Christ's life there must have been two visible heads of the Church, Christ and the Jewish High Priest. But Christ, the true and only head, while he was here, did not conduct himself as a monarch conspicuous for majesty and glory, but as a servant, despised for his lowliness.

units.la: X. Urgent 7. non posse Ecclesiam cateroquin propagari, nisi universalis sit Episcopus, qui totius orbis curam gerat. Sed liberant illos hac sollicitudine Apostoli, qui tales Episcopi non fuerunt, & Ecclesiam tamen tam longe lateque propagarunt: propagari potest Euangelium a quovis Christiano & ministro, quoties occasio datur illud praedicandi inter infideles. Instant autem, neminem praedicare posse nisi mittatur. Rom. 10: 15. quod verum est, a Deo nimirum, non ab hominibus. Supplicate ergo domino messis, ut emittat operarios in messem suam. Matth. 9: 38. & missio illa proprie spectabat ad Apostolos; qui mitti non poterant, nisi a Christo capite Ecclesiae; aliis vero ordinariis ministris vocandis non desunt plurimi, etiam absque vicario.
units.tr: X. They press further (7) that otherwise the Church could not be propagated unless there were a universal bishop who bore care for the whole world. But the Apostles relieve them of this anxiety: they were not such bishops, and yet they propagated the Church so far and wide. The gospel can be propagated by any Christian and minister whenever an opportunity is given to preach it among unbelievers. They insist, however, that no one can preach unless he is sent (Rom. 10:15), which is true, namely sent by God, not by men. "Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth labourers into his harvest" (Matt. 9:38). And that sending properly applied to the Apostles, who could not be sent except by Christ, the head of the Church; but for calling other ordinary ministers there is no lack of many, even without a vicar.

units.la: XI. 8. Ultimum eorum telum restat hebetandum. Summo hoc judice opus esse clamant, ut concordia haberi & dissensus tolli queant. At, quis illos docuit dissensus omnes tollendos esse, & nullas circa fidem futuras esse contentiones? deinde, sublatane sunt inter Pontificios certamina ab hoc judice? cum acerrima, etiam circa ipsum hunc judicem, ardeant & ab illis gerantur. Verum nihil impedit, quin sub multis etiam rectoribus, unitas servari possit, ut in aristocratica regiminis forma claret.
units.tr: XI. (8) Their last weapon remains to be blunted. They cry out that a supreme judge is needed, so that agreement may be kept and dissent removed. But who taught them that all dissents must be removed, and that there will be no contentions about the faith at all? Moreover, have controversies among the Papists been removed by this judge?
