When the fiercest ones, even about this very judge, rage and are waged among them. Yet nothing prevents unity from being preserved under many rulers as well, as is clear in the aristocratic form of government.

units.la: CAPUT XV- I.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.- I.

units.la: De monarchia & vicariatu Christi Petro Apostolo commissis.
units.tr: On the monarchy and vicariate committed by Christ to the Apostle Peter.

units.la: I. EMinus quasi hactenus congressi sumus: propius nunc accedendum & pugnandum cominus est; quamvis si quis rem recte putet, pugna hac facile supersedere liceret: cum enim & Scripturæ & rationi & historiæ adversari hanc monarchiam viderimus; quo colore nihilominus eam Petro collatam esse, audeat quis contendere? Cum tamen multum præsidii in hac historia sibi situm putent adversarii, hunc etiam prætextum illis suppeditamus; & videamus an tale regimen monarchicum committum sit Petro Apostolo, tanquam unico Christi Vicario.
units.tr: I. We have so far fought, as it were, at a distance; now we must come closer and fight hand to hand. Yet if anyone judged the matter rightly, he could easily forgo this fight. For since we have seen this monarchy opposed to Scripture, to reason and to history, who could dare to maintain that it was nonetheless conferred on Peter? Still, since our opponents think they have much support in this history, we also furnish them with this pretext, and let us see whether such a monarchical government was committed to the Apostle Peter as the one and only Vicar of Christ.

units.la: II. Nihil autem magis absonum est, quam Christo vicarium dari, cum regno suo non absit, ejusque negotiis præesse simul & tur & refu- possit & velit, illudque intus Spiritu suo regat & foveat, sicut tatur. Deus in regno naturæ aliquo, qui vicariam illi operam præstet, non eget. Nec corporea Christi præsentia opus est, cum spirituali & interna præsentia omnia præstet; secundum discipulorum promissionem Matth. 28:20. Ecce, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Quare & in illo solo uni sumus, non in quodam ejus vicario. Eph. 4:3-6. Studentes servare unitatem Spiritus in vinculo pacis. Unum corpus & unus Spiritus.---Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma. Unus Deus & Pater omnium. huc etiam pertinet elogium sponsi Ecclesiæ, Christo tributum, quod omnem vicarium excludit. Præterquam vero, quod Papa se vicarium Petri interdum appellans, vicarius Christi esse nequeat. Quod autem hic recoquunt; quandoquidem Christus in terris degens, visibilis fuit Ecclesiæ rector, eo etiamnum opus esse, illi præcedenti cap. satisfactum est; nam cum Christus se submisserit ordini Judaico, liquido testatus est, nec se visibilem & conspicuum esse monarcham, nec Pontificem vicarium suum, cum nullus monarcha suo se subjiciat vicario. Porro, cum Pontificii velint Christo Petrum & deinceps Papam succedisse; an non eo ipso Christum regno & munere suo plane abdicant?
units.tr: II. Nothing is more absurd than to give Christ a vicar. He is not absent from his kingdom; he is able and willing to preside over its affairs at once, and to rule and cherish it inwardly by his own Spirit, just as God, who needs no one to perform a vicarious service for him, rules the kingdom of nature. Nor is any bodily presence of Christ needed, since by his spiritual and inward presence he does all things, according to the promise to the disciples, Matt. 28:20: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world. Therefore we are united to him alone, not to some vicar of his. Eph. 4:3-6: Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit... One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all. To this also belongs the title bridegroom of the Church, given to Christ, which excludes every vicar. Besides, the Pope, who sometimes calls himself the vicar of Peter, cannot be the vicar of Christ. As for their repeated claim that, since Christ on earth was the visible ruler of the Church, there is still need of such a ruler, this was answered in the preceding chapter. For when Christ submitted himself to the Jewish order, he clearly testified that he was neither a visible and conspicuous monarch nor a Pontiff who needed a vicar, since no monarch submits himself to his own vicar. Moreover, since the Papists want Peter, and after him the Pope, to have succeeded Christ, do they not by that very claim plainly deprive Christ of his kingdom and his office?

units.la: III. Vicarius igitur Christo, siquidem dari non potuerit, Petrus etiam datus non fuit; de quo, ut & de primatu ejus, acturi, notamus 1 Non omnem primatum esse imperii, cum & primatus quidam sit ordinis. Sic primus appellatur inter Apostolos Petrus. Matth. 10:2. 2. Est etiam primatus auctoritatis; non quoad jurisdictionem, sed existimationem; quem sibi conciliarat Gamaliel. Act. 5:34. Hic primatus Petro quoque convenit, quamvis cum illo etiam aliis, ut Paulo 2 Cor. 11:5. Puto enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse summis Apostolis. & 2 Cor. 12:11. Jacobo ac Johanni. Gal. 2.9. 3. Datur & primatus honoris, ex praecedentibus conflatus; nec hic Petro denegandus est, qui hoc respectu antiquis dicitur Apostolorum princeps, id est primus vel praecipuus; & Apostolorum coryphaeus, & vertex Apostolici ordinis.
units.tr: III. Therefore, if a vicar could not be given to Christ, Peter was not given as a vicar either. In treating of him and of his primacy, we note the following. (1) Not every primacy is one of government, for there is also a primacy of order. Thus Peter is called first among the Apostles, Matt. 10:2. (2) There is also a primacy of authority, not in respect of jurisdiction but of esteem, which Gamaliel won for himself, Acts 5:34. This primacy belongs to Peter too, although other men shared it with him, as Paul did, 2 Cor. 11:5: For I think I was not a whit behind the chiefest Apostles, and 2 Cor. 12:11, and also James and John, Gal. 2:9. (3) There is also a primacy of honour, made up from what has been said before; nor is this to be denied to Peter, who in this respect is called by the ancients the prince of the Apostles, that is, the first or chief among them, the coryphaeus and the summit of the apostolic order.

units.la: IV. Ex quibus liquet, omnem Petri primatum huc redire. 1. quod primo loco recenseatur, & primus vocetur, jure πρωτοκλησίας. Matth. 10:2. Marc. 3:13,14,15,16. Luc. 6:13,14. quamvis interdum etiam alio loco compareat. 2. quod Apostolorum fuerit πρωτόγονος, seu qui verba faceret & advocatus quasi; quae praerogativa fervori ejus, praeter alia, ab antiquis adscribitur. 3. quod follenniter primum jecerit lapidem in fundamento Ecclesiae, inter Judaeos. Act. 2:41. & gentes c. 10:44.
units.tr: IV. From these points it is clear that all Peter's primacy comes back to this: (1) that he is named first and called first, by the right of first calling [πρωτοκλησία], Matt. 10:2; Mark 3:13-16; Luke 6:13-14, although at times he also appears in another place; (2) that he was the first-born of the Apostles [πρωτόγονος], that is, the one who spoke and as it were acted as their spokesman, a prerogative which the ancients ascribe to his fervour, among other things; (3) that he solemnly laid the first stone in the foundation of the Church, among the Jews, Acts 2:41, and among the Gentiles, Acts 10:44.

units.la: V. Quicquid praeterea a Pontificiis Petro tribuitur, spurium est & falsum; quod patet, tum generatim, quia pares erant omnes Apostoli; tum speciatim, quia Petro nihil peculiare prae reliquis tribuitur. Apostolos omnes pares fuisse, liquet: utpote qui pariter in regeneratione sederunt super duodecim thronis, Matth. 19:28. pariter ad docendum missi. Matth. 28:19,20. Marc. 16:15. pariter a Christo missi, cum potestate peccata remittendi aut retinendi. Joh. 20:21,23. quorum nomina duodecim fundamentis novae Hierosolymae pariter inscripta sunt. Apoc. 21:14. unde fieri nequit, ut unus aliquis instar monarchae iis praepositus fuerit. Excipit Bellarminus, summam potestatem omnes habuisse, tanquam legatos; Petrum vero tanquam pastorem ordinarium, deinde & ita summam, ut nihilominus dependerent a Petro tanquam capite. Quod posterius se ipsum tollit, ut quis & summam & tamen alicui obnoxiam habeat potestatem. Priori vero ratione deprimitur Petrus infra reliquos: ministerium quippe extraordinarium majora habuit dona, quam ordinarium: tum si ille ordinarius, quid opus reliquis extraordinariis?
units.tr: V. Whatever else the Papists attribute to Peter is spurious and false. This is evident both in general, because all the Apostles were equals, and in particular, because nothing peculiar is ascribed to Peter above the rest. That the Apostles were all equals is clear: they alike sat on twelve thrones in the regeneration, Matt. 19:28; they were alike sent to teach, Matt. 28:19-20; Mark 16:15; they were alike sent by Christ with the power of remitting or retaining sins, John 20:21, 23; and their names were alike inscribed on the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem, Rev. 21:14. Hence it cannot be that one of them was set over the others like a monarch. Bellarmine makes an exception: he says that all of them had supreme power as legates, but that Peter had it as ordinary pastor, and that the others were nonetheless so supreme that they depended on Peter as their head. The latter claim destroys itself, for it would mean that a man could have supreme power and yet be subject to someone else. By the former reasoning Peter is actually lowered beneath the rest, for an extraordinary ministry had greater gifts than an ordinary one. Moreover, if he was the ordinary one, what need was there of the others as extraordinary?

units.la: VI. Subterfugit porro Bellarminus hoc modo, ordinarium fuisse Petrum, quia in illius locum alii succedere debeant, non vero in aliorum loca, qui hoc respectu delegati tantum erant. Atqui sic omnis praerogativa Petri in eo tantum consistet, quod illi soli successor futurus sit; qua ut frueretur, ante moriendum ipsi fuit, & faciendus locus; vivo enim & videnti illius nullus erat usus. Praeterquam, quod nec in illius, nec in ullius Apostoli locum quisquam successerit. Urget Bellarminus, Petrus principatum tenuit; quod vel falsum, vel nihil huc facit; si nempe principatus ille cum Apostolatu idem sit: sin; potestas dabitur Apostolica major; quae tamen summa est.
units.tr: VI. Bellarmine further escapes by this route: Peter was the ordinary one because others ought to succeed in his place, whereas they did not succeed in the places of others, who in this respect were merely delegates. But then all Peter's prerogative would consist only in this, that he alone was to have a successor. To enjoy this, he had to die first and make room; for while he was living and seeing, there was no use for it. Besides, no one succeeded either to his place or to the place of any other Apostle. Bellarmine presses the point that Peter held the principate; but this is either false or irrelevant, if that principate is the same thing as the apostolate. If not, a greater apostolic power would have to be granted, and that power too would be supreme.

units.la: VII. Stapletonus triplex statuit inter Apostolos discrimen. 1. Quod caeteri Petro inferiores sint, respectu episcopalis & extraordinariae potestatis. Contra quod facit, quod Apostoli proprie unius alicujus civitati Episcopi non fuerint. 2. Quod Apostolorum auctoritas aequalis sit, respectu reliquorum Christianorum, non vero respectu eorum ad se invicem; cum Petrus reliquorum esset caput: quod plane negamus. Nec etiam omne caput, dicit monarchiam. 3. Quod Petro fuerit data potestas regiminis, id est, praeceptiva; Apostolis vero gubernationis, id est, executiva. Quod aeque absurdum foret, ac si Petrus diceretur Rex, qui imperaret; Apostoli vero subjecti, qui imperata exequerentur: cumque successores Petri, ex illorum sententia, eandem habeant potestatem, majores illi fuissent, & imperare potuissent Johanni, reliquisque Apostolis, Petro superstitibus.
units.tr: VII. Stapleton lays down a threefold distinction among the Apostles. (1) That the others are inferior to Peter in respect of episcopal and extraordinary power. Against this is the fact that the Apostles were not properly bishops of any one city. (2) That the authority of the Apostles is equal with respect to the rest of Christians, but not with respect to one another, since Peter was the head of the rest. This we flatly deny; nor does every headship imply a monarchy. (3) That Peter was given the power of government, that is, of command, while the Apostles had the power of administration, that is, of execution. This is just as absurd as if Peter were called a king who gave orders, while the Apostles were subjects who carried out the orders. And since, by their own judgment, Peter's successors hold the same power, they would be greater than the Apostles and could have commanded John and the other Apostles while Peter was still alive.

units.la: VIII. Asserta itaque est Apostolorum paritas. Speciatim vero Petro talem potestatem nec convenire, nec datam esse, apparet ex toto Nov. Test. Nam. 1. non alio munere, nimirum piscatorum hominum, Christus cum, ac reliquos dignatus est. Matth. 4: 18, 19. Joh. 1: 3941. 11. Pariter inter duodecim Apostolos missus & Sp. Sancto ornatus est. Matt. 10: 2-5. Joh. 20: 21, 22. 111. Omnes inde erant ἐμοϑηγοι. Matth. 19: 28. & fundamenta Ecclesiae. Eph. 2: 20. Apoc. 21: 14. 1v. Apostolicus gradus erat summus; utpote qui primo loco recensetur 1 Cor. 12: 28. Eph. 4: 11.
units.tr: VIII. The equality of the Apostles has therefore been established. That such a power neither belonged to Peter in particular nor was given to him appears from the whole of the New Testament. For (1) Christ did not honour him with any other office than that of the others, namely, that of fishers of men, Matt. 4:18-19; John 1:39-41. (2) He was likewise sent among the twelve Apostles and endowed with the Holy Spirit, Matt. 10:2-5; John 20:21-22. (3) All were therefore disciples [μαθηταί], Matt. 19:28, and the foundations of the Church, Eph. 2:20; Rev. 21:14. (4) The apostolic rank was the highest, since Peter is listed in the first place as an Apostle, 1 Cor. 12:28; Eph. 4:11.

units.la: IX. V Matth. 20. & Lucae 22. altercantur Apostoli de primatu: nulla vero Petri ibi agnoscitur praerogativa, sed omnes pariter a Christo increpantur, & ad humilitatem admonentur, iis verbis, quibus omnis monarchiae & primatus affectatio ex cordibus evellitur. Quare contra haec verba argutantur adversarii: 1. καταχυριεύειν Matth. 20: 25. notare dominatum tyrannicum, atque illum tantum vetari a Christo. Verum latiot est hujus vocis significatus: alioquin
units.tr: IX. In Matt. 20 and Luke 22 the Apostles dispute about primacy, yet no prerogative of Peter is recognised there; instead all of them alike are rebuked by Christ and admonished to humility, in words by which every affectation of monarchy and primacy is torn out of their hearts. Therefore our opponents quibble against these words. (1) They argue that katakyrieuein [καταχυριεύειν], Matt. 20:25, means to exercise tyrannical dominion, and that only this is forbidden by Christ. But the meaning of this word is broader; otherwise it would follow that all the kings of the Gentiles are tyrants, whereas Christ says, Luke 22:25: The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them [κυριεύουσιν].

units.la: {*} Euan- gelii. quin enim efficeretur, reges omnes gentilium esse tyrannos; cum Christus dicat Luc. 22:25. Reges gentium κυριεύουσιν dominantur eis.
units.tr: For otherwise it would follow that all the kings of the Gentiles are tyrants, since Christ says (Luke 22:25): The kings of the nations lord it over them [κυριεύουσιν].

units.la: X. 2. Cavillantur; Christum cum dicit, Vos autem non sic, non omnem monarchatum ab Ecclesia amandare, sed talem tantum, qualis est civilis. Respondemus vero: 1. Christum non de modo & forma dominii disputare, sed de ipsa re, de qua contendebant Apostoli; caeteroquin eadem haesisset quaestio, de modo dominii concesso aut prohibito. 2. Papae dominatus tam civilis est, quam Ecclesiasticus. 3. Particulae ὑχ ὑτως totam rem sine ulla cautione negant: ut patet ex Psal. 147: 19, 20. Annuncians sua verba Jacobo: statuta sua & judicia sua Israeli. Non fecit sic omni genti Matth. 19:8. Ab initio autem non fuit sic. 3. Pergunt captare verba Christi; & ex illis, quod quaerunt pulchre sibi extorquere videntur; cum dicunt, Christum agnoscere, esse aliquem inter eos, qui sit ὁ μείζων, & ὁ ἡγούμενος. Luc. 22:26. Sed qui maximus est inter vos &c. Sed dispellit hanc argutiam Matthaeus, quando explicat quis sit ὁ μείζων, non qui revera major sit, sed qui volet esse major; ut malam ambitionem eorum in honestam & laude dignam vertere voluerit Christus. Tum quoque non idem ἡγούμενος, qui ἡγεμών & ἀέχων: illud nomen etiam ministris Ecclesiae datur. Act. 15: 22. Hebr. 13:16, 17. hoc ducibus belli adscribitur.
units.tr: X. 2. They cavil that when Christ says But you are not so, he is not banning all monarchy from the Church, only the civil kind. We reply: 1. Christ is not disputing the mode and form of lordship, but the thing itself, over which the Apostles were contending. Otherwise the same question would remain, about a mode of lordship either granted or forbidden. 2. The lordship of the Pope is as civil as it is ecclesiastical. 3. The particles οὐχ οὕτως [not so] deny the whole matter without any qualification, as is clear from Ps. 147:19, 20: He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so for any other nation. Matt. 19:8: But from the beginning it was not so. 3. They go on snatching at Christ's words, and from them they seem to extract neatly what they are looking for. They say that Christ acknowledges that there is someone among them who is ὁ μείζων [the greater] and ὁ ἡγούμενος [the leader]. Luke 22:26: But let the greatest among you, and so on. But Matthew dispels this quibble when he explains who ὁ μείζων is: not one who is really greater, but one who wishes to be greater. Christ wanted to turn their bad ambition into something honourable and worthy of praise. Nor is ἡγούμενος the same as ἡγεμών [commander] and ἄρχων [ruler]. That name is also given to ministers of the Church (Acts 15:22; Heb. 13:16, 17), whereas the others are applied to commanders in war.

units.la: XI. vi. Pergimus statuminare sententiam nostram ex loco Matth. 18:17. ubi discipulis omnibus edicit Christus, Dic Ecclesiae. eorum vero unus erat Petrus; ergo & Petrus etiam Ecclesiae se subjicere debuit. VII. Nec in Apostolorum commentariis & actibus quicquam occurrit, quod primatui Petri faveat. Act. 1:15. Primus quidem prae zelo surgit Petrus, sed designationem Apostoli, ut & Act. 6. electionem Diaconi Ecclesiae totam committit. VIII. Petrus cum Johanne ab Apostolis mittitur Samariam, ad Euangelium praedicandum. Act. 8:14. curae igitur & prudentiae Apostolorum suberat Petrus; non vero eos ipse dirigebat. IX. Facti sui rationem Ecclesiae reddit Petrus, Act. 11:2. & seqq. quod, qua erat Apostolica auctoritate, recusare facile potuisset; at bonum scilicet exemplum successoribus suis exhibere voluit. X. Nec conventui Apostolico praesidet Petrus Act. 15. uti nec ullus alius, cum omnes, sallem Apostoli, pari auctoritate suffragia conferrent.
units.tr: XI. vi. We go on to confirm our view from Matt. 18:17, where Christ bids all the disciples: Tell it to the Church. Peter was one of them; therefore Peter too ought to have submitted himself to the Church. VII. Nor does anything occur in the records and the Acts of the Apostles that favours Peter's primacy. Acts 1:15: Peter indeed rises first, out of zeal, but he leaves the choice of an Apostle to others, and in Acts 6 he entrusts the whole election of deacons to the Church. VIII. Peter is sent with John by the Apostles to Samaria to preach the Gospel (Acts 8:14). Peter was therefore under the care and judgment of the Apostles; he did not direct them. IX. Peter gives the Church an account of his action (Acts 11:2 ff.). He could easily have refused this, by his Apostolic authority, but he wished to set a good example for his successors. X. Nor does Peter preside over the Apostolic council in Acts 15, nor does anyone else, since all of them, at least the Apostles, cast their votes with equal authority.

units.la: XII. xi. Idem probant Corinthiorum schismata 1 Cor. 1:12; 13. quando alius Pauli, alius Apollo, alius Cephae &c. se esse dicebat; quae locum non habuissent, si quidem Petrum Ecclesiae caput agnovissent. Nec juvat illud Baronii subterfugium; quosdam se Christi & Cephae esse professos, non studio contentionis, sed ut totum negotium ad principium suum revocarent, Christum nempe & Petrum: nam primo gratis illud dicitur; deinde si verum illud esset, concordes hi fuissent; jam vero reprehenduntur, tanquam schismatici. Conf. cap. 3: 21, 22.
units.tr: XII. xi. The schisms of the Corinthians prove the same thing (1 Cor. 1:12, 13), when one said he was of Paul, another of Apollos, another of Cephas, and so on. These would not have arisen if they had acknowledged Peter as the head of the Church. Nor does that subterfuge of Baronius help, that some professed themselves to be of Christ and Cephas not out of a desire for strife, but so as to refer the whole matter to its source, namely Christ and Peter. For, first, that is said without any evidence; second, if it were true, these people would have been in agreement; but as it is, they are rebuked as schismatics. Compare chap. 3:21, 22.

units.la: XIII. xii. Gal. 2: 7, 8, 9.
units.tr: XIII. xii. Gal. 2:7, 8, 9.

units.la: Jacobus, Cephas & Johannes appellantur uno omnes elogio; oi δοκοῦντες, σύτοι εἶναι qui habiti sunt columnae; & Paulo pariter dextram societatis porrigunt; & partito agunt, ut Petrus versetur inter circumcisos; Paulus inter gentes: ubi autem societas, ibi nulla subjectio; atque ubi operis distributio, ibi etiam paritas. Regerunt & hic adversarii, socios quidem fuisse in officio praedicandi, non vero in officio gubernandi. Sed hoc scopo Pauli adversatur, probantis hinc dignitatem Apostolatus sui, ejusdem juris paritate. Deinde gubernavit & Paulus gentes, quibus praedicabat, non aliter ac Petrus Judaeos; dicitur enim, versu 7. Mihi concreditum Euangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis.
units.tr: James, Cephas and John are all called by one title: those who seemed to be pillars [οἱ δοκοῦντες στύλοι εἶναι]. They give Paul the right hand of fellowship, and they divide the work, so that Peter labours among the circumcised and Paul among the Gentiles. Where there is fellowship there is no subjection, and where there is a division of work there is also equality. Here too the opponents retort that they were companions in the office of preaching, but not in the office of governing. But that runs against Paul's purpose, since he proves from this the dignity of his Apostleship by the equality of the same right. Moreover Paul too governed the Gentiles to whom he preached, no differently from the way Peter governed the Jews. For it is said in verse 7: The gospel of the uncircumcision has been committed to me, just as the gospel of the circumcision was to Peter.

units.la: XIV xiii. Idem evincitur ex comparatione Petri & aliorum Apostolorum, qui illo non minores, saepe etiam aliquibus in rebus praestitisse leguntur. Hinc veteres, Jacobum Petro non solum aequiparabant, sed & praeferebant. Hujus etiam in conventu Hierosolymitano potiores quam Petri partes fuisse videri possent. Ita & Johannes in quibusdam Petro major fuit; qui nempe in sinum Domini recubuit, & dilectus ille discipulus fuit, Joh. 21: 20. qui canonem Novi Test. clausit, & Apostolorum maxime longaevus fuit, ideoque adventum Domini vidit &c. XV. Nec Paulus ulla in re minor fuit, Apostolorum maximis.
units.tr: XIV. xiii. The same is proved by comparing Peter with the other Apostles, who were no less than he, and are often read to have excelled him in some matters. For this reason the ancients not only placed James on a par with Peter, but even put him before him. In the council at Jerusalem, James's part may seem to have been more influential than Peter's. So too John was in some respects greater than Peter: he reclined in the bosom of the Lord, and he was that disciple whom Jesus loved (John 21:20). He closed the canon of the New Testament, and of the Apostles he lived longest, and so he saw the coming of the Lord, and so on. XV. Nor was Paul in any respect less than the greatest of the Apostles.

units.la: 2 Cor. 11: 5. & 12: 11. plus, quam omnes laboravit 1 Cor. 15: 10. omnium Ecclesiarum curam sustinuit. 2. Cor. 11: 28. A nullo homine Apostolatum aut Euangelium, aut praedicationis suae ductum accepit Gal. 1: 1, 12, 17. At Petrum quidem Hierosolymae invisit, com. 18. non auctoritatis aut doctrinae accipiendae causa; comm. 8: 11, 12. sed propter falsos & irreptitios Apostolos, ut concordiam cum illo & reliquis Apostolis testaretur. Vide Gal. 2: 1, 2, 6. Praecipue, Petri non recte incedentis infirmitatem reprehendit, illique in os restitit Paulus. Gal. 2: 11. quae non simulate acta sunt, aut pro humanitate, sed pro muneris auctoritate. Atque hisce de causis aut Paul. ... (marginal note, partly legible) veteres omnes Paulum Petro æquarunt. xiv. Denique, nunquam ipse Petrus reliquis Apostolis ullo modo, ubi de jure & auctoritate agitur, se majorem, vel gerit, vel agnoscit, vel agnosci patitur; sed Apostolum, presbyterum, imo συνπρεσβύτερον le indigitat. 1 Pet. 1:1. & 5:1. aliorumque Apostolorum præcepta fidelibus inculcat. 2 Pet. 3:2. Ut memores suis doctrina nostra; qui summus Apostoli Domini & Servatoris. & com. 15. Sicut & dilectus noster frater Paulus secundum sibi datam sapientiam scripsit vobis.
units.tr: (2 Cor. 11:5; 12:11) He laboured more than all (1 Cor. 15:10); he bore the care of all the Churches (2 Cor. 11:28). He received his Apostleship and his Gospel, and the teaching of his preaching, from no man (Gal. 1:1, 12, 17). Indeed he visited Peter at Jerusalem (v. 18), not to receive authority or doctrine, but on account of false and smuggled-in Apostles (vv. 8, 11, 12), so that he might bear witness to his agreement with Peter and the other Apostles. See Gal. 2:1, 2, 6. Above all, he rebuked Peter's weakness when Peter was not walking straight, and Paul withstood him to his face (Gal. 2:11). That was not done in pretence, nor out of courtesy, but by the authority of his office. And for these reasons ... all the ancients made Paul equal to Peter. XIV. Finally, Peter himself never, in any matter touching right and authority, either assumes, acknowledges, or allows himself to be acknowledged as greater than the other Apostles. Instead he styles himself an Apostle, an elder, and indeed fellow-elder [συνπρεσβύτερος] (1 Pet. 1:1; 5:1). He also impresses on the faithful the precepts of the other Apostles (2 Pet. 3:2): That you may be mindful of our teaching, the commandment of your Apostles of the Lord and Saviour. And verse 15: Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him.

units.la: XVI. Copias nostras lustravimus; videamus nunc adversam Pontificiorum aciem; & contraria argumenta, ex quibus Petri suprematum extundunt & stabiliunt. Producunt igitur 1. Matth. 10:2. ubi primus vocatur; quomodo respectu ordinis tantum dici, jam respondimus. 2 Primo loco semper nominatur; unde primo nihil probatur; & tum falsum est; vide Gal. 2:9. 1 Cor. 1:12. & 3:22. & 9:5. 3. Primus verba facit; illud zelo & fervori ejus, aliisque causis, de quibus jam dictum, non vero potestati ejus adsignandum est. 4. Christus nomen ejus mutavit; non mutatum ei nomen, sed novum adjectum fuit. Matth. 17:25. & 2 Pet. 1:1. Tum nova hæc nominis impositio, aliis etiam Apostolis communis est. Marc. 3:17. Ubi Jacobo & Johanni fratribus, nomen Boanerges indidit Christus.
units.tr: XVI. We have reviewed our own forces; now let us look at the opposing battle line of the Papists, and at the counter-arguments by which they hammer out and establish Peter's supremacy. They bring forward first Matt. 10:2, where he is called first; we have already replied how this is said only with respect to order. 2. He is always named first; from this nothing is proved at first, and then it is false; see Gal. 2:9, 1 Cor. 1:12, 3:22, and 9:5. 3. He speaks first; this must be ascribed to his zeal and fervour and the other causes already mentioned, not to any power of his. 4. Christ changed his name; his name was not changed for him, but a new one was added (Matt. 17:25; 2 Pet. 1:1). Moreover this new imposition of a name is common to other Apostles too: Mark 3:17, where Christ gave the name Boanerges to the brothers James and John.

units.la: XVII. 5. Pro eo solo Christus didrachma solvit. Matth. 17:24. & seqq. Ratio erat, quod solus Christus cum Petro ibi habitaret; ubi autem quis commoratur, ibi etiam vectigal solvit. 6. Solus item cum Christo piscabatur. Luc. 5:4, 5, 6. Quod falsum est: uti & multa alia, quæ ipsi tribuuntur.
units.tr: XVII. 5. Christ paid the didrachma for him alone (Matt. 17:24 ff.). The reason was that Christ alone was living there with Peter; and where someone resides, there he also pays the tax. 6. He alone likewise fished with Christ (Luke 5:4, 5, 6). This is false, as are many other things that are attributed to him.

units.la: XVIII. 7. Præcipuum robur sententiæ illorum est, in duobus locis Matth. 16. & Joh. 21. quorum priori primatus Petro videtur promissus; posteriori collatus. De hisce igitur ordine plenius & accuratius tractandum est. Quod ergo priorem locum attinet, duplex in eo est metaphora; primo, fundamenti ac ædificii; tum clavium: qui locus tam figuratus, alio clariori indiget; quo tamen destituuntur. Sic autem ex illo ratiocinantur. 1. Solus Petrus Christum confessus est; & quid tum? an ergo & solus Petrus erit Apostolus & Christi confessor? quod inde æque facile efficietur, quam solum Petrum esse primum: præterquam, quod non suo tantum, sed communi omnium Apostolorum nomine, illa prolocutus sit; uti patet ex aliorum etiam Apostolorum de Christo confessionibus. Joh. 1:45, 50. Matth. 14:33. Joh. 6:68, 69.
units.tr: XVIII. 7. The main strength of their case lies in two passages, Matt. 16 and John 21. In the former, primacy seems to be promised to Peter; in the latter, it seems to be conferred on him. These must therefore be treated more fully and accurately in order. As for the former passage, it contains a double metaphor: first that of foundation and building, then that of keys. Such a figurative passage needs another, clearer one to explain it, yet they lack one. They reason from it as follows. 1. Peter alone confessed Christ. And so what? Will Peter alone then be the Apostle and confessor of Christ? That would follow just as easily as that Peter alone is first; besides, he spoke those words not only in his own name but in the common name of all the Apostles, as is clear from the other Apostles' confessions about Christ too (John 1:45, 50; Matt. 14:33; John 6:68, 69).

units.la: XIX. 1. Soli Petro dicitur, quod beatus sit. com. 17. Beatus es Simon
units.tr: XIX. 1. Peter alone is told that he is blessed, com. 17. Blessed art thou, Simon.

units.la: Pracipue 1. ex Matt. 16:16.& seqq. quo modo Christum fuerit, fusus fuerit, qui locus tam figuratus... Simon Bar Jona &c. Quemadmodum vero etiam alii Apostoli Christum, uti nunc dictum, confessi erant, ita etiam ad ipsos illud extendendum est; uti & Matth. 11:25,27.
units.tr: Chiefly 1. from Matt. 16:16 and following, on how he confessed Christ, and the passage is so figurative... Simon Bar Jona, etc. But just as the other Apostles also confessed Christ, as has just been said, so this must be extended to them as well, as also in Matt. 11:25, 27.

units.la: XX. III. Illi soli dicitur quod esset Petrus. com. 18. & quidni? cum nomen illud ipsi singulare fuerit, res tamen communis fuit reliquis Apostolis; quin imo omnibus fidelibus, qui etiam vivi dicuntur lapides. 1 Pet. 2:5. Apoc. 21:14. Et murus civitatis habens fundamenta duodecim, & in ipsis duodecim nomina duodecim Apostolorum Agni. conf. Esa. 54:11. Ecce ego colloco in carbunculo lapides tuos, & fundabo te in Sapphiris. Et ponam margaritas fenestras tuas, & portas tuas ex lapidibus carbunculis.
units.tr: XX. III. It is said of him alone that he was called Peter. com. 18. And why not? Though that name was peculiar to him, the thing it signifies was common to the other Apostles, indeed to all the faithful, who are also called living stones. 1 Pet. 2:5. Rev. 21:14: And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the twelve names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb. Compare Isa. 54:11: Behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles.

units.la: XXI. IV. Illi soli dicitur, quod sit petra, cui inædificaturus esset Ecclesiam Christus. ibidem. Petro hæc quidem dicuntur, non vero de Petro; cum ab eo distinguatur hæc Petra; quæ est, vel Petri confessio, vel ipse Christus, quem confessus erat. 1 Cor. 3:11. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus. & 10:4. At Petra erat Christus. Jud. com. 20. Sanctissima nostra fide superædificantes vosmet ipsos, in Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: XXI. IV. It is said of him alone that he is the rock on which Christ would build the Church. Ibid. These things are indeed said to Peter, but not about Peter, since this Rock is distinguished from him. It is either Peter's confession or Christ himself, whom he had confessed. 1 Cor. 3:11: For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. And 10:4: And that Rock was Christ. Jude, v. 20: Building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost.

units.la: XXII. Habent vero hisce etiam quæ opponant. 1 Petrum esse petram; cum Cephas nomen Petri, Syriace notet petram. Aliam interpretationem dat Johannes c. 1:43. Tu vocaberis Cephas, quod veritur Petrus. 2. Objiciunt. Vox Syriaca Κηφᾶς notat & Πέτρον & πέτραν, quod utrumque lapidem significat, ita ut Petrus, etiam petra, seu lapis, appellari possit. Verum aliter docuit Sp. sanctus, qui vocem Syriacam, Græce non expressit per πέτραν, sed per Πέτρον; ut Petrum a petra aperte distinguat, qui ab illa tantum denominatur. Cephas ergo appellatur denominative a Cepha petra; eodem modo, ut a Christo, lapide vivo, fideles vivos lapides nominat ipse Petrus. 1 Pet. 2:4,5.
units.tr: XXII. They also have objections to these points. 1. Peter is the rock, since Cephas, the name of Peter, in Syriac means rock. John gives another interpretation, 1:43: Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone [Petrus]. 2. They object that the Syriac word Κηφᾶς signifies both Πέτρον and πέτραν, which both mean a stone, so that Peter could also be called a rock or stone. But the Holy Spirit taught otherwise: he did not render the Syriac word in Greek by πέτραν, but by Πέτρον, so as clearly to distinguish Peter from the rock, from which he is named only derivatively. Cephas, therefore, is so called from Cepha, rock, in the same way as Peter himself calls living believers living stones after Christ, the living stone. 1 Pet. 2:4, 5.

units.la: XXIII. Non ergo super Petro, sed petra ædificanda est Ecclesia; quamvis & Petrus tanquam Apostolus μετονυμικῶς Ecclesiæ possit ex parte dici petra, quia tanquam Ecclesiæ architectus, per doctrinam suam huic petræ Ecclesiam superstruxit. Eph. 2:20. Inædificati in fundamento Apostolorum & Prophetarum, ipsa est summus lapis idem Jesu Christus. Suo etiam sensu, Ecclesia, aliquo modo ædificata dici posset in Petro, tanquam duce & primi piloeorum qui in Christo ædificati sunt: sicut olim fideles in Abrahamo benedicebantur. Gen. 12:3. In te benedicentur omnes gentes terræ.
units.tr: XXIII. The Church is therefore to be built not upon Peter but upon the rock, although Peter too, as an Apostle, may be called, metonymically [μετονυμικῶς], in part a rock of the Church, since as the architect of the Church he built the Church upon this rock through his teaching. Eph. 2:20: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone. In a sense of his own, the Church could also be said to have been built, in some way, on Peter, as its leader and first of those who were built in Christ, just as believers of old were blessed in Abraham. Gen. 12:3: In thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed.

units.la: XXIV. Male igitur Pontificii quidam petram hanc, non solumde Christo, verum etiam de Petro, Christi vicario, intelligunt, detorquentes huc loca Esai. 28: 16. Ecce ego fundo in Zion lapidem, lapidem munitionis, anguli, pretiosum, fundamenti fundati. Sed aliter docet ipse Petrus 1 Ep. 2: 6. Propter quem (J. Christum) continetur in Scriptura: Ecce pono in Sion lapidem summum angularem &c. Conf. Psal. 18: 32. Quis petra praeter Deum nostrum? & 95: 1. Jubilemus petrae salutis nostrae. & 118: 22. Lapidem reprobaverunt aedificantes, fuit in caput anguli.
units.tr: XXIV. The Papists therefore wrongly understand this rock not only of Christ but also of Peter, the vicar of Christ, twisting to this purpose the passage Isa. 28:16: Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation. But Peter himself teaches otherwise, 1 Pet. 2:6: Wherefore also it is contained in the Scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone (namely Jesus Christ), etc. Compare Ps. 18:31: For who is a rock save our God? and 95:1: Let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. And 118:22: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

units.la: XXV. Verum non ita absolvimus eos, quin obtundant porro; 1. Pronomen hanc necessario evincere, ipsum intelligi Petrum; illud enim demonstrat eandem personam de qua egerat Christus. Verum pronomen hanc, non est relativum ejus, quod proxime praecessit, sed demonstrativum, quo Christus demonstrat se ipsum; cujus rei exempla videre est. Joh. 2: 19. Solvite templum hoc τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, et in tribus diebus excitabo illud ἀυτόν. Job. 19: 26. Et postquam cutis mea distrinxerint hoc. 1 Cor. 15: 53. Oportet enim corruptibile hoc τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο induere immortalitatem: et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. hic autem eo magis illud locum habet, quod Petrum non omni ex parte excludamus; hoc enim sensu Christi verba accipimus, ac si dixisset Christus: Tu es Petrus, & super eandem petram, a qua tu denominaris (quae ego sum) aedificabo Ecclesiam meam.
units.tr: XXV. But we do not so dismiss them that they do not press further. 1. They argue that the pronoun this necessarily proves that Peter himself is meant, since it points to the same person of whom Christ had spoken. But the pronoun this is not relative to what immediately precedes it; it is demonstrative, by which Christ points to himself. Examples of this may be seen: John 2:19: Destroy this temple [τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον], and in three days I will raise it up [ἀυτόν]. Job 19:26: And though after my skin worms destroy this body. 1 Cor. 15:53: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality [τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ... τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο]. Here, however, this holds all the more, since we do not exclude Peter altogether; for we take Christ's words in this sense, as if Christ had said: "Thou art Peter, and upon this same rock, from which thou takest thy name (which I am), I will build my Church."

units.la: XXVI. 2. Objiciunt. Christus erat fundamentum principale & proximum; Petrus vero ministeriale & mediatum. Quod vanum & falsum est; cum praeter Christum nullo nos opus habeamus fundamento, & illum omnes fideles contingant, non per pararium Petrum & Apostolos, sed proxime, per propriam fidem. 3. Futurum illud tempus nobis objiciunt; non enim Christus, ut ajunt, dici poterat, aedificaturus Ecclesiam, cum jam Apostolos & discipulos in se aedificasset: referendum igitur est ad Petrum, quem nondum jecerat Ecclesiae fundamentum. Fundamentum equidem Ecclesiae fuit semper; aedificaturus tamen Ecclesiam erat Christus, non respectu Petri, sed respectu Ecclesiae Christianae, quam ex Judaeis & gentibus super se excitaturus erat Christus, atque ita regnum caelorum aperiturus, uti vocatur com. 19. Et haec est Ecclesia Christi, non Petri.
units.tr: XXVI. 2. They object that Christ was the principal and immediate foundation, but Peter a ministerial and mediate one. This is vain and false, since we need no foundation apart from Christ, and all the faithful reach him not through Peter and the Apostles as intermediaries, but immediately, through their own faith. 3. They object to us the future tense: for Christ, they say, could not be spoken of as going to build the Church, since he had already built the Apostles and disciples into himself. It must therefore be referred to Peter, who had not yet laid the foundation of the Church. Christ was indeed always the foundation of the Church; yet Christ was to build the Church not with respect to Peter, but with respect to the Christian Church, which he was to raise up for himself from Jews and Gentiles, and so to open the kingdom of heaven, as it is called in v. 19. And this is the Church of Christ, not of Peter.

units.la: XXVII. v. Soli Petro promissio fit de Ecclesiae aedificandae firmitate contra portas inferni. Illud vero de Petri persona intelligi nequit, aliud enim testatur historia vitæ ejus: ut eodem hoc capite. comm. 22, 23. & cap. 26: 34. Luc. 22: 31, 34. Gal. 2: 11. sed de Christo, quem Petrus confessus erat: huic uni & certissimo fundamento innixa Ecclesia, ut immota rupes, prævalet adversus portas inferni, seu regnum illud Antichristianum, quod nomine Ecclesiæ Petro superædificatæ se jactat. Videsis 1 Cor. 3: 11.
units.tr: XXVII. 5. The promise of the firmness of the Church to be built against the gates of hell is made to Peter alone. But this cannot be understood of Peter's person, for the history of his life testifies otherwise, as in this same chapter, vv. 22, 23; and chap. 26:34; Luke 22:31, 34; Gal. 2:11. It must rather be understood of Christ, whom Peter had confessed. The Church, resting on this one and most certain foundation, like an immovable rock, prevails against the gates of hell, that is, against that Antichristian kingdom which boasts, under the name of the Church, of being built upon Peter. See 1 Cor. 3:11.

units.la: XXVIII. Quando vero contra Pontificios ita disputamus, non eo id fit animo, ac si omnis omnino prærogativa Petro foret denegranda, quam non pœnitendam libenter ipsi tribuimus; quod scilicet peculiari ratione hujus ædificii primus fundamenta jecerit, tum inter Judæos, iucomparabili illa concione Act. 2. tum inter gentes, tam illustri visione excitus, & transinissus quasi in libertatem Novi Test. Act. 10: 10. & seqq. quam insecuta fuit Cornelii conversio, com. 44: 5. sicut & egregia apologia portam Euangelii, tam libere & sollemniter primus illis aperuit, Act. 15: 7. Vos scitis quoniam a diebus antiquis Deus in nobis elegit, per os meum audire gentes verbum Euangelii, & credere. Inde tamen nulla perpetua Petri prærogativa, multo minus hæreditaria, & quæ in successores transmittatur, mitto primatum, confici potest. XXIX. Hactenus explicatam dedimus & ab impetu adversariorum liberavimus priorem similitudinem; sequitur nunc altera, quæ est de promissione clavium regni cælorum Matth. 16: 19. Et dabo tibi claves regni cælorum &c. ubi expediendum 1. Quid per claves intelligatur. 2. Cui illæ promissæ sint. 1. Per claves illas intelligit Bellarminus, summam, eamque infallibilem, in omni Ecclesia, judicii ultimi potestatem: quam bene, alias vidimus. 2. Promittuntur hæ claves Petro, non vero illi soli, sed cum illo, suo ordine, omnibus quoque Apostolis: uti iis omnibus claves has vendicat Johannes, c. 20: 21, 22, 23. XXX. Inepte igitur Bellarminus censet Apostolos sacerdotes factos in ultima cœna, clavem jurisdictionis accepisse Joh. 20: 21. Dixit igitur ipsis Jesus iterum, pax vobis. Quemadmodum me misit Pater & ego mitto vos: clavem autem ordinis, verbis proxime sequentibus, comm. 22, 23. Et hoc dicto insufflavit in ipsos, & dicit eis, accipite Spiritum sanctum. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: si quorum retineatis, retinentur. Sic enim sacerdotes fuissent sine clavibus, & sacerdotium ac jurisdictionem habuissent, cum nondum haberent ordinem; quæ secundum ipsos ἀσύγατα sunt. XXXI. Sicut vero in priori parte, ita nec hic omnem Petri præPars II. rogativam tollimus; qui nempe claves hasce primus tractaverit, tam inter Judaeos, quam Gentiles, uti superius visum: unde speciatim illi promissae claves regni coelorum, id est, Ecclesiae Christianae ex Judaeis & gentibus colligendae; quibus regnum coelorum, hactenus sub V. T. clausum, primus aperturus erat. Non ac si illi propriae & perpetuae essent futurae; nedum ut ulla hinc Petri monarchia, multo minus successio in posteros, efficiatur. Praeterquam quod scelestè sibi soli has claves arrogat Papa; quas prudentiores Pontificii originaliter (quatenus illae adhuc superstunt) tribuunt Ecclesiae; ministerialiter vero & quoad executionem Episcopis.
units.tr: XXVIII. When we dispute thus against the Papists, we do not do so as if every prerogative whatever were to be denied to Peter, which we gladly grant him, and have no reason to regret: namely, that in a peculiar way he first laid the foundations of this building, both among the Jews, in that unparalleled sermon of Acts 2, and among the Gentiles, when he was roused by that remarkable vision, and led out, as it were, into the liberty of the New Testament, Acts 10:10 and following, which was followed by the conversion of Cornelius, com. 44, 45; just as by his excellent defence he first opened the door of the Gospel to them so freely and solemnly, Acts 15:7: Ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe. Yet from this no lasting prerogative of Peter can be established, still less a hereditary one, passing on to successors, not to mention a primacy. XXIX. We have so far explained the first comparison and freed it from the assaults of our opponents; now follows the second, which concerns the promise of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 16:19: And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc. Here two things must be settled: 1. What is meant by the keys. 2. To whom they were promised. 1. Bellarmine understands by those keys the supreme and, moreover, infallible power of final judgment in every Church, which we have seen elsewhere how well he proves. 2. These keys were promised to Peter, not to him alone, but with him, in his own rank, to all the Apostles as well; as John also assigns these keys to them all, ch. 20:21, 22, 23. XXX. Bellarmine therefore foolishly holds that the Apostles, made priests at the Last Supper, received the key of jurisdiction, John 20:21: Then said Jesus to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you. But the key of order they received in the words that immediately follow, vv. 22, 23: And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained. For in that case the priests would have been without keys, and would have had priesthood and jurisdiction before they had order; which, by their own account, are impossible things. XXXI. But just as in the earlier part, so here too we do not remove every prerogative of Peter: he was the first to use these keys, both among the Jews and among the Gentiles, as was seen above. Hence the keys of the kingdom of heaven were especially promised to him, that is, of the Christian Church to be gathered from Jews and Gentiles, by which he was to be the first to open the kingdom of heaven, which had hitherto been closed under the Old Testament. Not, however, as if these keys were to belong to him in a personal and perpetual way; much less that any monarchy of Peter, still less any succession to posterity, could be established from this. Besides, the Pope shamelessly arrogates these keys to himself alone, which the more prudent Papists attribute originally (insofar as they still survive) to the Church, and ministerially, and as to their exercise, to the bishops.

units.la: XXXII. Alter tandem ille locus sequitur, in quo primarium sibi praesidium collocare diximus Pontificios; quod in hoc, uti in superiore, nunc expugnandum restat. Locus est Joh. 21:15,16,17. Quum igitur prandissent, dicit Simoni Petro Jesus: Simon Jona, amas me magis, quam hi? dicit ipsi, ne, Domine: tu nosti quod amem te. Dicit ipsi, pasce agnos meos. Dicit ipsi denuo &c. ubi primatum reipsa Petro collatum, hisce ferme argumentis concludunt. 1. Solus Petrus ter interrogatur, an Christum amet, & quidem an magis, quam reliqui Apostoli. Sed 1. non extollendo, sed deprimendo Petro illud inserviit, ad notandam priorem ejus confidentiam, Matth. 26: 35. quare non gaudet Petrus tanquam collato beneficio, sed angitur & moeret. com. 17. Contristatus est Petrus, quod ipsi dixisset tertio, diligis me? 2. Nec monarchia inde ipsi constat; sed major tantum ab eo requiritur dilectio, quod longe major culpa quam reliquis ipsi condonata esset; ad exemplum illius foeminae Luc. 7: 47. 3. Trina confirmatione ita, ex mera Christi gratia, muneri suo restituitur; ex quo trina abnegatione merito exciderat. Quamquam & quaestio haec de amore Christi, ad omnes ministros & fideles pertineat. Ita Paulus 2 Cor. 5: 14. Charitas enim illa Christi constringit nos. & 1 Cor. 16: 22. Si quis non amat Dominum Jesum Christum, sit anathema maranatha.
units.tr: XXXII. The last of those passages follows, the one in which, as we said, the Papists place their chief defence. As with the previous one, it now remains to be overthrown. The passage is John 21:15, 16, 17. When therefore they had dined, Jesus says to Simon Peter: Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these? He says to him: Yes, Lord; you know that I love you. He says to him: Feed my lambs. He says to him again, etc. From this they conclude, with roughly these arguments, that a primacy was actually conferred on Peter. (1) Peter alone is asked three times whether he loves Christ, and indeed whether he loves him more than the other Apostles. But first, this serves not to exalt Peter but to humble him, to mark his earlier overconfidence (Matt. 26:35). That is why Peter does not rejoice as though a benefit had been conferred on him; he is distressed and grieved (v. 17): "Peter was grieved because he had said to him a third time, Do you love me?" (2) Nor does a monarchy follow from this. Only a greater love is required of him, because his fault was far greater than that of the others and had been forgiven him, like the woman's in Luke 7:47. (3) By a threefold confirmation he is restored to his office, by Christ's sheer grace, from which he had rightly fallen through his threefold denial. Yet this question about the love of Christ also concerns all ministers and believers. So Paul says (2 Cor. 5:14): For the love of Christ constrains us. And (1 Cor. 16:22): If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Maranatha.

units.la: XXXIII. 11. Dicitur ipsi soli, ter; Pasce oves meas; comm. 15,16,17. Resp. 1. Hortatio haec est, non novi muneris institutio: non aliter ac Paulus Timotheo 2 Tim. 4:2. Praedica sermonem &c. 2. Quamvis hic sermo singulariter ad Petrum dirigatur, propter singularem occasionem; res tamen ipsa, & mandatum hoc ad omnes pertinet Apostolos & Ecclesiae ministros: secundum ipsius Christi regulam Marc. 13:37. Quae autem dico vobis, omnibus dico.
units.tr: XXXIII. (2) He is told this alone, three times: "Feed my sheep" (vv. 15, 16, 17). Reply: (1) This is an exhortation, not the institution of a new office, just as Paul says to Timothy (2 Tim. 4:2): "Preach the word," etc. (2) Although this speech is addressed to Peter in particular, because of the particular occasion, the matter itself and this command pertain to all the Apostles and ministers of the Church, according to Christ's own rule (Mark 13:37): What I say to you, I say to all.

units.la: XXXIV. 111. Vox pascendi, ita pergunt adversarii, notat regiam potestatem. Sic Psal. 2:9. Reges (vel confringes) eos virga ferrea. LXX vertunt Ποιμανεῖς pascec. Et nihil frequentius est, quam Reges pastores nominari, apud profanos non solum, sed & sacros auctores; ut Esai. 44:28. Mich. 5:2. Matth. 2:6. Apoc. 2:27. & 19:15. At vero, licet reges aliquando pastores vocitentur, quemadmodum & patres, aliisque nominibus; vox tamen pascendi non est regia; sed per illam potius reges manstuetudinis & curae pastoralis monentur: ut nihil tam absonum sit, quam ex hac voce regnum probare, cum illa regibus appositā dominationem eorum mitiget, & ad pastorale munus quasi revocet. Quid quod ipse Petrus & ποιμαίνειν illud longe aliter interpretetur, opponens τὰ κατακυριεύειν dominari 1 Pet. 5:2,3. Ποιμάνατε τὸ ποίμνιον &c. μηδ' ὡς κατακυριεύοντες. Ita pastores dicuntur Eph. 4:11. Nec, si vel maxime haec ita intelligenda essent, ad Pontifices Romanos spectarent, qui non pascunt oves Christi, cum praedicationem verbi, tanquam vile nimis ministerium, contemnant & aliis demandent.
units.tr: XXXIV. (3) The opponents continue: the word "feed" signifies royal power. So Psalm 2:9: You shall break them with a rod of iron; the Septuagint render it "you shall feed them" [ποιμανεῖς]. Nothing is more common than for kings to be called shepherds, not only among profane authors but also among sacred ones, as in Isaiah 44:28, Micah 5:2, Matthew 2:6, Revelation 2:27 and 19:15. But although kings are sometimes called shepherds, as fathers are too, and by other names, the word "feed" is not a royal word. Rather, through it kings are reminded of gentleness and pastoral care. So nothing is as incongruous as proving a kingdom from this word, since the word applied to kings tempers their lordship and, as it were, calls them back to the pastoral office. Indeed Peter himself interprets "to shepherd" [ποιμαίνειν] quite differently, setting against it "to lord it over" [κατακυριεύειν] in 1 Peter 5:2, 3: Shepherd the flock of God [Ποιμάνατε τὸ ποίμνιον], not as lording it over [μηδ' ὡς κατακυριεύοντες] those in your charge. So too pastors are named in Ephesians 4:11. Nor, even if these words had to be understood in that way, would they apply to the Roman Pontiffs, who do not feed Christ's sheers. They despise the preaching of the Word as too mean a ministry and hand it over to others.

units.la: XXXV. iv. Oves suas Petro commendat Christus, atqui hae sunt omnes Christiani; ergo hi omnes Petro traduntur. An ergo & omnes Apostoli, Petri ejusque successorum oves sunt? at vero, cum Christus oves illas suas vocet, an non aperte docet, pascere non idem esse quod imperare? alienas enim oves pascere, servi est, non Domini. Sed nec omnes Christi oves pavit Petrus; cum pari pede operas inter sedivisserint Apostoli, & partito cum iis egerit Petrus: uti jam vidimus ex Gal. 2:7. nec Petro universus Christi grex magis commissus fuit, quam caeteris Apostolis; aut Apostoli ipsi Petro, quam Petrus illis; cum & Paulus Petrum corripuerit. Censemus itaque, quamvis aliqua fuerit Petri praerogativa, jam semel iterumque indicata; ex hisce omnibus tamen nullam ejus exsculpi posse monarchiam; cum contrarium docuerit evidentissime, & hodiernum Papae imperium efficacissime, ex ipsis hisce ultimis Christi verbis, profligaverit ipse Petrus. 1 Epist. 5:1,2,3,4.
units.tr: XXXV. (4) Christ commends "his sheep" to Peter. But these are all Christians; therefore all of them are handed over to Peter. Then are all the Apostles also the sheep of Peter and his successors? Yet when Christ calls them "his sheep," does he not plainly teach that to feed is not the same as to command? For to feed another's sheep is the part of a servant, not of a master. Nor did Peter feed all of Christ's sheep, since the Apostles divided the labours between themselves on equal terms, and Peter shared them out with the others, as we have already seen from Galatians 2:7. Nor was the whole flock of Christ committed to Peter more than to the other Apostles, nor were the Apostles committed to Peter more than Peter to them, since Paul also rebuked Peter. We judge, therefore, that although there was some pre-eminence of Peter, already indicated once and again, yet no monarchy can be carved out of all these things. The contrary is taught most clearly, and Peter himself, from these very last words of Christ, has most effectively overthrown the present-day empire of the Pope (1 Pet. 5:1, 2, 3, 4).

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De successione Pontificum Romanorum in monarchiam PETRI.
units.tr: On the succession of the Roman Pontiffs to the monarchy of Peter.

units.la: I. Onfecimus prius illud de monarchia Petri commentum & monstrum cerebrinum. Debellandum nunc est altera ejusdem farinæ; de cathedra Petri, ejusque successione transfinita ad Papam Romanum; in cujus gratiam fabulata sunt hæc omnia. Quod ut rite peragamus, duplicem hanc pone musquæstionem 1. An Petro successores sint dati. 2. An Papa Romanus Petri successor sit; an potius subsessor.
units.tr: I. I have already dispatched that invention and brain-born monster, the monarchy of Peter. Now we must beat down another of the same kind: the chair of Peter and its succession, carried over to the Roman Pontiff, for whose sake all these things have been fabricated. To carry this out properly, let us put the following double question: 1. Were successors given to Peter? 2. Is the Roman Pontiff Peter's successor, or rather his under-successor?

units.la: II. Si vel daremus, legitimum constare Petro hunc suum principatum; non tamen illico successio constabit: cum plurima sint munera, quæ illam respuant, qualia sunt Prophetarum, duodecim Patriarcharum, quibus Apostoli conferuntur. Successores datos esse Apostolis, non negamus, quoad episcopale munus, prædicandi verbum, Sacramenta administrandi, disciplinam exercendi, pastores ordinandi: at vero, quatenus Apostoli erant, & quoad singularem & Apostolicum illum characterem, alios & sequentes iis successisse, pernegamus: cum munus illud iis proprium & mere personale fuerit. Priore modo antiqui omnes Episcopos, æque ac Romanos, Apostolorum successores dixerunt; quam dignitatem, non nisi per summum nefas, solus Papa nunc sibi vendicat; cum enim pares Apostolos fuisse supra viderimus, omnibus successores datos fuisse oportet, aut nullli.
units.tr: II. Even if we granted that Peter's principate was legitimately his, the succession would not follow at once, since there are many offices that reject it, such as those of the Prophets and the twelve Patriarchs, to whom the Apostles are compared. We do not deny that successors were given to the Apostles as regards the episcopal office: preaching the Word, administering the Sacraments, exercising discipline, and ordaining ministers. But insofar as they were Apostles, and as regards that singular and apostolic character, we flatly deny that others followed them as successors, since that office was proper to them and purely personal. In the former sense, all the ancient writers called bishops, no less than the Romans, successors of the Apostles; this dignity the Pontiff alone now claims for himself, and that is nothing less than the greatest wickedness. For since we have seen above that the Apostles were equals, successors must have been given either to all of them or to none.

units.la: III. Tum quoque, si vel clare pateret, uni Petro collatum fuisse successionis privilegium, non idcirco uni Petro, unum tantum Episcopum succedere liqueret; quod si enim universæ Ecclesiæ moles in humeris Petri bene sedisset; quis dicat parem fore huic oneri unum Pontificem Romanum, & tanto Atlante dignum Herculem futurum? Tam ægre quis hinc vel unam micam de Petri successore, nedum uno illo, extorquere possit.
units.tr: III. Furthermore, even if it were clearly evident that the privilege of succession had been conferred on Peter alone, it would not follow from this that only one bishop succeeds Peter alone. For if the whole weight of the Church had rested well on Peter's shoulders, who would say that one Roman Pontiff would be equal to this burden, and that Hercules would be a worthy successor to so great an Atlas? With such difficulty could anyone extract from this a single crumb about Peter's successor, let alone that one man.

units.la: IV. Conturbemus etiam ea, quibus hæc sua dogmata aliis persuadere conantur, argumenta. Quæ inter alia generatim 1. instituunt, ex convenientia Veteris & Novi Test. Fuit, inquiunt, in Veteri Testamento summorum Pontificum successio; injuria ergo foret, eam denegare sedi Petri, summi Christianorum Pontificis. Sed 1. fuerunt & multa alia, quæ frustra nunc in Pontificibus hodiernis quæras; ut argumentum de successione utriusque infirmum valde sit. 2. Nec monarcha fuit Pontifex Judæus; nec figura hujus Pontificis, qui reapse nullus est; sed unici sacerdotis Christi; uti jam dictum. 3. Successionem Pontificatus Judaici ipse Deus instituit, in S. Scriptura; tale vero nil quicquam in N. Test. legitur.
units.tr: IV. Let us also overturn the arguments by which they try to persuade others of these their doctrines. Among others, they generally set up: 1. an analogy between the Old and New Testaments. There was, they say, a succession of high priests in the Old Testament; it would therefore be an injustice to deny such a succession to the see of Peter, the highest Pontiff of the Christians. But 1. there were also many other things which you would look for in vain among present-day Pontiffs, so that the argument from succession, on either side, is very weak. 2. The Jewish Pontiff was neither a monarch, nor a figure of this Pontiff, who in reality does not exist, but of the one priest of Christ, as has already been said. 3. God himself instituted the succession of the Jewish priesthood in Holy Scripture; yet nothing of the kind is read anywhere in the New Testament.

units.la: V. 11. Ex unitate Ecclesiæ, unam Ecclesiastici regiminis formam, unumque ejus rectorem arguunt, quem Apostolorum etiam tempore fuisse ajunt. Verum, Apostolorum tempore, non fuisse visibilem Ecclesiæ doctorem jam probavimus; ergo nec hodie talis esse debet. Nec eadem semper est Ecclesiastici regiminis forma; nunc enim, ut olim non præsunt Apostoli.
units.tr: V. 11. From the unity of the Church they argue for one form of ecclesiastical government and one ruler of it, whom they say existed even in the time of the Apostles. But we have already proved that in the time of the Apostles there was no visible teacher of the Church; therefore neither should there be such a one today. Nor is the form of ecclesiastical government always the same; for just as the Apostles do not now preside, so they did not then.

units.la: VI. 111. Visibilem decet esse judicem, ac communem cathedram, ubi lites solvantur & decidantur; illud vero omnibus temporibus necessarium est; ergo necessaria eorum judicum successio. Verum, præter ea quæ jam in superioribus diximus, advertendum est contra hæc; ne quidem Mosi in cathedra ejus aliquem successisse, cum filii ejus nullam publicam auctoritatem habuerint, sed privati fuerint: ut patet ex 1 Chron. 23: 14. Sola ergo mansit successio doctrinæ Mosaicæ. Quare cathedra Mosis penes Scribas & Pharisæos erat, tempore Christi. Matth. 23: 2, 3. Personarum vero nulla fuit; ergo nec ulla nunc est sub Novo Test.
units.tr: VI. 111. A visible judge ought to exist, and a common chair where disputes are settled and decided; but this is necessary at all times; therefore a succession of such judges is necessary. Yet, besides what we have said above, it must be noted against this: not even did anyone succeed Moses in his chair, since his sons had no public authority but were private persons, as is clear from 1 Chron. 23:14. Only the succession of the Mosaic doctrine therefore remained. Hence the chair of Moses was in the hands of the scribes and Pharisees at the time of Christ (Matt. 23:2, 3). But there was no succession of persons; therefore there is none now under the New Testament.

units.la: VII. Ita Petrum successorem habuisse probari nequit; quin contrarium jam patuit: ostendamus nunc etiam multo minus illud Papæ competere; neque de jure, ut loquuntur, neque de facto. Prius apparet. 1. Quod præter curam & sapientiam Christi fuisset, successorem talem constituere, & nullum unquam verbum cum Apostolis vel discipulis ea de re commutasse. aut leviter monuisse, illi negotio Papam designatum esse; cum in Veteri Fœd. tam diserta mentio facta fuerit Pontificis Judaici. 11. Si Petro quærendus suisset dignus successor, qui tanta pondera molis sustineat; fuisset ille citra omne dubium Johannes Apostolus, Christo tam tenere dilectus, & Petro triginta ferme annis superstes; cui illud sane multo majori jure debebatur, quam Episcopo Romano.
units.tr: VII. Thus it cannot be proved that Peter had a successor; indeed the contrary has already become clear. Let us now show that this is much less applicable to the Pope, neither by right, as they say, nor in fact. The first point is evident. 1. It would have been beyond the care and wisdom of Christ to appoint such a successor, and never to have said a word about this matter to the Apostles or disciples, or to have lightly warned them that the Pope had been designated for that business, since the Jewish Pontiff is mentioned so clearly in the Old Covenant. 2. If a worthy successor had to be sought for Peter, one who could bear such great weights of burden, then beyond all doubt it would have been John the Apostle, held so dear by Christ and surviving Peter by about thirty years. To him that office was certainly owed by a much greater right than to the Roman bishop.

units.la: VIII. 111. Quo jure successionem Petri sibi arrogabit; cum munera Petri, qualia sunt, pascere oves Christi. Joh. 31. & verbo docere Ecclesiam. Matth. 28: 19. aliaque non præstet Papa. Quod vero praetexant 1. Justis eum impedimentis detineri, ineptum est; nam, si quae sunt impedimenta, quae ab hoc munere eum avocare possint; ea non erunt perpetua; vel si sint, justa non erunt: prout aquam non est eos, relicto sermone Dei, ministrare mensis. Act. 6: 2.
units.tr: VIII. 111. By what right does he claim Peter's succession for himself, since he does not perform the functions of Peter, such as feeding the sheep of Christ (John 21) and teaching the Church by the word (Matt. 28:19), and others? As for their pretext, 1. that he is held back by just hindrances, this is absurd; for if there are any impediments that can call him away from this office, they will not be permanent, or if they are permanent, they will not be just, according to the saying: it is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables (Acts 6:2).

units.la: 2. Papam illud per alios praestare. Petrus vero & Apostoli hoc ipsi agebant, posthabitis aliis negotiis; quod patet ex axiomate illo mox laudato, & Apostolorum historia. Nec mandatarius munus suum in alium transferre potest. 3. Incumbere haec quidem, ajunt, Episcopis gregariis; non autem vicario Christi. Imo vero vicarius Christi dici non potest, qui vices Christi in praedicando Euangelio sibi commissas esse, vel negat, vel iis non satisfacit. Tum quoque praedicarunt ipsi olim non solum Episcopi vulgares, sed & Romani. Quin inauditum olim fuit, Episcopum esse, qui munus praedicandi non obiret. In reliquis porro muneris Episcopalis partibus, ita degeneravit Papa, praecipue quoad doctrinam, ut non tam Apostolatus Petri, quam abnegationis ejus successor factus videatur.
units.tr: 2. That the Pope performs that office through others. But Peter and the Apostles themselves did this work, setting aside other business; this is clear from that axiom just cited and from the history of the Apostles. Nor can a mandatary transfer his office to another. 3. They say these tasks fall to ordinary bishops, not to the vicar of Christ. But indeed, one cannot be called the vicar of Christ who either denies that the duties of Christ entrusted to him in preaching the Gospel are his, or does not fulfil them. Moreover, in the past not only ordinary bishops preached, but also the Roman ones. Indeed it was unheard of in former times for someone to be a bishop and not to carry out the office of preaching. In the remaining parts of the episcopal office, the Pope has so degenerated, especially in doctrine, that he seems to be the successor not so much of Peter's apostleship as of his denial.

units.la: IX. De jure vidimus; de facto etiam Petro Papam in commentitia hac monarchia non successisse facile evincitur. Nam 1. Nihil liquidius est, quam Episcopos Romanos olim delectos fuisse suffragiis plebis & Cleri Romani: quaenam vero haec est plebis Romanae potestas, quod jus, ut Ecclesiae totius orbis de capite prospexerit? II. De monarchiarum & imperiorum initiis & successione constare debet, ut sciatur qui veri sint Principes; at vero prima Episcoporum Romanorum successione nihil incertius & minus planum. Cum alii Petro subjungant Linum, dein Clementem; alii contra Clementem praeponant: alii vero a Lino proximum faciant Cletum, tum Clementem; alii iterum pro cleto Anacletum substituant; alii potius ex hisce duobus unum cudant; alii denique, vivo etiam & videnteP etro Linum sedisse affirment. Quae varietas facile arguit, subtestae fidei esse, quicquid de hac re crepant, & nullum horum in tam illustri Episcopatu Petri fuisse successorem.
units.tr: IX. We have seen the matter of right; that the Pope did not succeed Peter in this fabricated monarchy in fact is also easily proved. For 1. nothing is clearer than that the Roman bishops were formerly chosen by the votes of the people and the Roman clergy. What, then, is this power of the Roman people, and what right has it to provide for the head of the whole Church? II. The beginnings and succession of monarchies and empires must be known, so that it may be known who are the true princes; yet nothing is more uncertain and less clear than the first succession of the Roman bishops. Some place Linus after Peter, then Clement; others, on the contrary, put Clement before him; others make Cletus the next after Linus, then Clement; others again substitute Anacletus for Cletus; others rather forge one man out of these two; finally others assert that Linus held the see while Peter was still living and seeing. This variety easily shows that whatever they boast about this matter is a fabrication, and that none of these had been Peter's successor in so illustrious an episcopate.

units.la: X. III. Per aliquot proxima a Christo secula, nullum usquam apparet vestigium, vel actus, vel lex genuina, vel judicium non adulterinum; ex quo vel leviter suspicari possis, eos universales Episcopos fuisse: quin nec ipse pseudo-Dionysius, in hierarchia sua, Pontificiis recepta, mentionem hujus hierarchiae facit. v. Certum est, veteres Romanos Episcopos habitos fuisse Petri successores; in Episcopatu scilicet urbis Romae; uti opinabantur, nequaquam vero in primatu universalis Ecclesiae.
units.tr: X. III. For some of the next centuries after Christ, no trace, act, genuine law, or non-spurious judgment appears anywhere; from which you could slightly suspect that they were universal bishops. Indeed not even the pseudo-Dionysius, in his hierarchy, received by the Papists, makes mention of this hierarchy. V. It is certain that the ancient Roman bishops were regarded as successors of Peter, in the episcopate of the city of Rome, as they supposed, but by no means in the primacy of the universal Church.

units.la: XI. Breviter nunc etiam, fundamenta, quibus hanc Papæ successionem superstruunt Pontificii, subruamus. 1. Maxima est inter ipsos difficultas, & digladiantur inter se; an Dominus, perpetuum non solum, sed & Papam speciatim dederit successorem Petri; ut jure divino privilegium hoc ipsi proprium sit; an vero Ecclesiastico jure duntaxat successionem illam possideat Episcopus Romanus; quomodo successio illa ab ea auferri & in alios derivari posset. Ad quam rem acriter inter se disputant præcipui Pontificiorum Doctores, ut in ambiguo hæreat; an successio illa juris divini, adeoque perennatura sit in Ecclesia Romana. Cum itaque dubium sit, an successio hæc a Christo sit instituta; ad ipsius Petri factum tanquam ad sacram anchoram confugiunt: eum enim in finem Petrum Romam migrasse audacter affirmant, ibique sedem fixisse. At vero non illud intendebat Petrus; si verum sit, quod narrant, Petro, ante mortem Roma migrare volenti, apparuisse Christum, eumque revocasse & supplicium crucis Romæ obeundum ipsi nunciasse: unde planum erit, non eo animo, vel ante Romam ivisse, vel postea reversum esse, ut ibi thronum dominationis suæ erigeret, sed ut ipse, tanquam opprobrium mundi, ibi in crucem ageretur.
units.tr: XI. Now briefly let us also overthrow the foundations on which the Papists build this succession of the Pope. 1. The greatest difficulty among them is that they dispute fiercely among themselves whether the Lord gave a perpetual successor to Peter, and specifically to the Pope, so that this privilege would belong to him by divine right; or whether the Roman bishop possesses that succession by ecclesiastical right alone, and how that succession could be taken away from him and transferred to others. The leading teachers of the Papists argue sharply among themselves on this point, so that it remains uncertain whether that succession is of divine right and therefore destined to last perpetually in the Roman Church. Since it is therefore doubtful whether this succession was instituted by Christ, they take refuge in the deed of Peter himself as in a sacred anchor: they boldly affirm that Peter migrated to Rome for this purpose and fixed his seat there. Yet Peter did not intend this. If what they relate is true, when Peter wished to leave Rome before his death, Christ appeared to him, called him back, and announced to him that he was to undergo the punishment of the cross at Rome. Whence it will be plain that he went to Rome, or returned afterwards, not with the intention of raising there a throne of his dominion, but so that he himself, as the offscouring of the world, should be led to the cross there.

units.la: VII. Ipse etiam Bellarminus hac in re sibi non constat, dum ab una parte Episcopum Romanum, quatenus est successor Petri, jure divino esse caput Ecclesiæ, pronunciat; ab altera vero parte, non itidem certum affirmare audet, Pontificem Romanum, qua talem, Petro succedere in præfectura universali Ecclesiæ; sed tantum illud ex traditione Petri repetit. Addens, si Petrus nullam sedem particularem sibi delegisset, illum Petro successurum fuisse, quem sibi designasset Ecclesia. Verum enim vero non potuisset universalem Episcopum, Ecclesia particularis eligere; nec semper universalis Ecclesia, præcipue sub illa persecutionum diritate cogi poterat, quæ universalem sibi Episcopum distingueret. Nec magis inter se congruit, quod idem fingit, ex institutione Christi dignitatem Pontificalem fuisse personalem; ex Petri autem facto, reddita esse localem; quod enim personale est, ad successores transmitti non potest, nec illud facto suo Petrus successivum facere potuit.
units.tr: VII. Bellarmine himself is inconsistent on this point. On the one hand he declares that the Bishop of Rome, insofar as he is Peter's successor, is head of the Church by divine right. On the other hand, he does not dare to affirm with the same certainty that the Roman Pontiff, as such, succeeds Peter in the universal governance of the Church. He derives that only from a tradition about Peter, adding that if Peter had not assigned himself a particular see, the Church would have chosen as his successor whomever he had designated. But a particular church could not have elected a universal bishop, and the universal Church, especially under that harsh persecution which would have distinguished a universal bishop for itself, could not always be gathered. Nor does he agree with himself when he pretends that the Pontifical dignity was personal by the institution of Christ, but was made local by Peter's act. For what is personal cannot be transmitted to successors, and Peter could not make by his own act what was personal into something successive.

units.la: XIII. Cum autem totius controversiæ cardo in eo versetur, num Romæ fuerit Petrus, ibidemque sedem fixerit, paulo accuratius hanc rem putemus: si enim Romæ non fuerit, corruit totus Papæ principatus; quamvis, si fuerit, non ideo stabiliatur. Aliud enim est Romæ fuisse Petrum; aliud, regimen monarchicum ibi erexisse: tum porro aliud est, Papam ipsi in eo succesisse; quæ omnia laborant, & uno ictu tolluntur, si quidem Petrus Romæ non fuerit; quod ex sequenti calculo patere poterit.
units.tr: XIII. Since the whole controversy turns on the question whether Peter was at Rome and fixed his see there, let us consider this matter a little more carefully. For if Peter was not at Rome, the entire papal primacy falls. Yet if he was there, the primacy is not thereby established. For it is one thing for Peter to have been at Rome, another for him to have set up a monarchical government there, and again another for the Pope to have succeeded him in that. All these things collapse and are overthrown at a single blow if Peter was not at Rome, as can be seen from the following reckoning.

units.la: XIV. Anno Christi 34. Tiberii 19. Petrus & Johannes Hierosolyma in Samariam miserunt. Act. 8: 14. Anno 35. Saulus miraculose convertitur. Act. 9: 3. &c. uti quidam existimant; abiens inde in Arabiam. Gal. 1: 17. dein Damasci ad triennium subsistit. Anno 36. pax fuit per totam Judæam & vicinas regiones. Act. 9: 31. Unde Petrus oras illas visitavit. ibid. com. 32. Anno 37. assignatur Petro initium sedis Antiochenæ, quam per septennium tenuerit, ex communi calculo; qui a veritate alienus est, cum Paulus hoc anno Damasco Jerosolymam veniens, Petrum ibi invenit. Gal. 1: 17, 18. Actor. 9: 23, 24. 2 Cor. 11: 32. Anno 41. Caligulæ 3. Petrus Cæsarea redit Jerosolymam, & ibi absolvitur violatæ legis, propter communionem cum gentibus. Act. 11: 2. Anno 42. Paulus & Barnabas Antiochiæ multos reddunt Christianos, Christianorumque nomen ibi primo auditur. Act. 11: 25, 26. Nulla Petri mentione facta. Anno 44. Claudii 2. Petrus Romam venisse dicitur a Baronio. At potius secundum alios carceri & custodiæ mandatur Jerosolymis, Act. 12: 3, 4. Ex qua liberatus, profectus est in alium locum, Act. 12: 17. non Romam, sed in alias regiones & diversas partes, ut & deinceps apparebit. Ut frustra eum Romam excurrisse, Pontificii hinc concludant.
units.tr: XIV. In the year of Christ 34, the 19th of Tiberius, Peter and John sent [men] from Jerusalem into Samaria (Acts 8:14). In the year 35, Saul was miraculously converted (Acts 9:3, etc.), as some suppose; he then went away into Arabia (Gal. 1:17), and afterwards remained at Damascus for three years. In the year 36 there was peace throughout all Judea and the neighbouring regions (Acts 9:31), whence Peter visited those parts (ibid., v. 32). In the year 37 the beginning of Peter's see of Antioch is assigned to him, which he is said to have held for seven years, according to the common reckoning; but that reckoning is alien to the truth, since in this year Paul, coming from Damascus to Jerusalem, found Peter there (Gal. 1:17, 18; Acts 9:23, 24; 2 Cor. 11:32). In the year 41, the 3rd of Caligula, Peter returned from Caesarea to Jerusalem, and there was absolved of having violated the law by his fellowship with the Gentiles (Acts 11:2).
