Answer: Let them then cease boasting of their inquisitions and their zeal in persecuting heretics; for among those heretics we shall find the very men whom they slander as having lately emerged. Partly, therefore, the Church was held captive within the Papacy itself, just as in the times of Elijah; for although the Church appeared there too, it was at least hidden in Israel, as ours is in the Papacy. Partly it was preserved outside it in other regions of the world; just as the Church, lying hidden in Israel, appeared in Judea, outside Israel; so also in the East it was both present and flourishing. But why take such a roundabout path here? Since they will not deny that the true Church cannot fail, and since we rightly claim this title for ours, it will be sufficiently established that, even if we could not prove it from the records of history, the Church has always existed from the Word of God, even if it has not always been reformed.

units.la: XV. ix. Legitimam non esse, imo nullam Reformatorum vocationem: sed huic criminationi jam ante satisfecimus; addimus tamen; Reformatorum duo fuisse genera: quidam enim in ipsa RoRomana Ecclesia ministerio jam ante functierant; quidam non item. Postremi hi, ex communi omnium Christianorum vocatione, errantibus veram commonstrabant viam, & post multorum conversionem, ab illis ipsis docendi accipiebant auctoritatem; quæ res nec jure, nec exemplo caret, in primorum etiam temporum fidelibus. Act. 8:4. & 11:19,20. Priores vero non alia opus habuerunt vocatione, sed vi prioris suæ vocationis in ipsa Ecclesia Romana acceptæ, corruptelas ejus emendarunt, præter scopum quidem ordinantis & vocantis, non tamen ordinationis & vocationis. Sed Papam, pergunt adversarii, non agnoscitis à Christo esse, vocatio ergo ejus legitima non fuit. Resp. Suprematum ejus detestamur; Episcopatum vero, quatenus bonus est, à Christo esse fatemur; nec Episcopum eum negamus; licet illo munere pessime fungatur.
units.tr: XV. ix. That the Reformers' calling was not lawful, indeed that it was no calling at all: but we have already answered this charge; we add, however, that there were two kinds of Reformers. Some had already exercised the ministry in the Roman Church itself; others had not. These latter, on the common calling of all Christians, showed the erring the true way, and after the conversion of many they received from those very people the authority to teach; a course that lacks neither right nor precedent, even among the faithful of the earliest times. Acts 8:4; 11:19, 20. The former, however, needed no other calling, but by virtue of the prior calling they had received in the Roman Church itself, they amended its corruptions, indeed beyond the aim of those who had ordained and called them, though not beyond the ordination and calling themselves. But, the opponents go on, you do not acknowledge the Pope to be from Christ; therefore his calling was not lawful. Reply: we detest his supremacy; but his episcopate, insofar as it is good, we confess to be from Christ, nor do we deny that he is a bishop, although he discharges that office very badly.

units.la: XVI x. Defecistis vos, ajunt, ab Ecclesia nostra, nos vero à nulla. Verum 1. Nos non defecimus ab Ecclesia, sed meretrici res suas habere jussimus, & ab ea laudabili exemplo recessimus. 2. Ab Ecclesia Apostolica defecerunt Pontificii. x1. Deniqueogganniunt: sessurus in Ecclesia est Antichristus; cum vero in Pontificia Ecclesia illum sedere nos contendamus; Ecclesiam illam etiam veram esse fateamur, oportet. Sed 1. uti supra vidimus, effici inde tantum potest, Ecclesiam eorum veram fuisse, quod non negamus.
units.tr: XVI. x. You have departed, they say, from our Church, but we from none. But first, we did not depart from the Church; we merely bade the harlot keep her own goods, and withdrew from her in a praiseworthy manner. Second, it is the Papists who have departed from the Apostolic Church. xi. Finally they object: Antichrist is to sit in the Church; but since we maintain that he sits in the Papist Church, we must admit that that Church is also true. But, first, as we saw above, it can be inferred from this only that their Church was true, which we do not deny.

units.la: 2. Eodem modo lessurus est in Ecclesia, quomodo sub finem sæculi, Antichristum in Ecclesia sessurum, ipsi statuunt Pontificii; nimirum in ea, ut idolum in templo; quod inde deturbandum; & ut fur in domo patrisfamilias, qui inde, digne multatus, exigendus & capite foras protrudendus est.
units.tr: Second, he is to sit in the Church in the same way as the Papists themselves hold that Antichrist, toward the end of the age, will sit in the Church: namely, in it as an idol in a temple, which must be cast down from there; and as a thief in the house of the head of the household, who, once justly punished, must be driven out and thrust out of doors by the head.

units.la: XVII. Hæc fuit Ecclesiæ ab Antichristi jugo liberatio: quæ non tam prospera & læta fuit, uti ex hominum quidem voto conciperetur; ut non aliquo modo fuerit interrupta, & quorundam, cum canibus ad vomitum recurrentium, turpi deditione obscurata: sicut enim humanis in rebus; ita in Ecclesia, nihil est ab omni parte beatum. Nec inopinatum illud accidit; siquidem per Prophetas jam olim prædictum fuit, non omnes hujus gratiæ participes, ea fe dignos gesturos; quod multiplici nimis experientia confirmatum est in Ecclesiis reformatis. Unde Tyrus mystica, per 70 annos oblivioni tradita, fine 70 annorum ad meretricium earmen canendum rediit. Esai. 23:25,16. & abominabile stupens vel stupentis posfitum fuit. Dan. 12:11. atque ita prodierunt laxatis quatuor angelis, myriades illæ. Apoc. 9: 13, 14, 15, 16. Et Gogi exercitus corona cinxit castra sanctorum civitatem dilectam. Apoc. 20:8,9. Quæ nostris temporibus quotidie, cum maxime proh dolor! implentur. Attamen ex supra memoratis aliisque vaticiniis sperare licet, Deum non passurum, ut Ecclesia Euangelica redeat ad communionem civitatis Antichristianæ; quin potius reliquias civitatis illius humanæque auctoritatis in Ecclesiâ extirpaturum, ut solus in ea per verbum & Spiritum suum regnet.
units.tr: XVII. This was the Church's liberation from the yoke of Antichrist; it was not so prosperous and joyful as might be conceived from men's wishes, so that it was not in some way interrupted and, through the shameful surrender of some who, like dogs, return to their vomit, obscured. For as in human affairs, so in the Church, nothing is blessed in every respect. Nor did this happen unexpectedly; for it was foretold long ago through the Prophets that not all who share in this grace would prove themselves worthy of it, which has been confirmed by far too much experience in the Reformed Churches. Hence mystical Tyre, forgotten for 70 years, after the end of 70 years returned to sing the harlot's song. Isa. 23:15, 16. And the abomination that causes desolation or the desolating abomination arose. Dan. 12:11. And so those myriads came forth when the four angels were loosed. Rev. 9:13, 14, 15, 16. And the army of Gog surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Rev. 20:8, 9. These things are fulfilled daily in our times, alas, to the greatest degree! Yet from the aforementioned and other prophecies we may hope that God will not allow the Evangelical Church to return to communion with the Antichristian city; rather, he will root out from the Church the remnants of that city and of human authority, so that he alone may reign in it through his Word and his Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: De regno Ecclesiæ, & ultimis temporibus.
units.tr: On the kingdom of the Church, and the last times.

units.la: I. Andem, post finita certamina, promissum videtur Ecclesiæ Regnum. Quod utriusque instrumenti Scripturæ mira verborum pompa prædicant. Vid. Dan. 7:13, 14. Et ecce cum nubibus cœli tanquam filius hominis veniebat. Et illi datus est dominatus & dignitas & regnum. conf. com. 27. Et regnum, & dominatus, & majestas regnorum sub omni cœlo data est populo sanctorum Altissimorum, cujus regnum, regnum sæculi. ac præsertim sancta Apocalypsi id suse describit.
units.tr: I. At last, after the struggles are over, the Kingdom seems promised to the Church. Both Testaments proclaim it in wonderful richness of language. See Dan. 7:13, 14: And behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven. And there was given him dominion and glory and a kingdom. Compare the commentary on verse 27: And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven, was given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Above all, the holy Apocalypse describes it at length.

units.la: II. Appellantur ea tempora pacis. Matth. 24:37,38,39. Esai. 2:4. Mich. 4:4. & Refrigerii, Act. 3:13. Ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων, repræsentationis omnium. com. 21. Ac novum tum cœlum, & nova terra, h. e. nova & pulchrior longe Ecclesiæ ac mundi facies exoritura prædicatur. Esai. 65. Apoc. 21. Erit enim hoc tempus Ecclesiæ ultimum, τὸ ἐσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν, 2 Pet. 3:3. proxime antecedens finem rerum, & Christi Domini adventum; qui ultima ista tuba (diversa enim Ecclesiæ tempora ac periodi, magnificis quibusdam Dei operibus, veluti totidem tubis insigniri & promulgari in Scripturis solent) clarissime annunciabitur. 1. Cor. 15:52. Unde, apud Zachariam cap. 14. egregio emblemate, festum tabernaculorum (quod sacri temporis olim ultimum erat, ac fine anni celebrabatur) ab omnibus populis tunc agitandum narratur.
units.tr: II. These times are called times of peace (Matt. 24:37, 38, 39; Isa. 2:4; Mic. 4:4), and of refreshing (Acts 3:13), of the restoration of all things [ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων], that is, the restoration of all things (see ch. 21). Then also a new heaven and a new earth is proclaimed, that is, a new and far more beautiful face of the Church and of the world is to arise (Isa. 65; Rev. 21). For this will be the last time of the Church, the last of the days [τὸ ἐσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν] (2 Pet. 3:3), immediately preceding the end of things and the coming of Christ the Lord. He will be announced most clearly by that last trumpet (for the different times and periods of the Church are usually marked and proclaimed in Scripture by certain magnificent works of God, as by so many trumpets) (1 Cor. 15:52). Hence in Zechariah 14, by a striking emblem, the feast of tabernacles, which was once the last of the sacred seasons and was celebrated at the end of the year, is said to be observed then by all peoples.

units.la: III. An vero longo, an brevi spatio ista Ecclesiæ periodus finienda sit, adhuc in superæ mentis actis ac membranis latet. Quas scrutari nemini concessum est. Ut vana sint, quæ Judæi de mundi ætate,
units.tr: III. Whether this period of the Church is to be finished after a long or a short span still lies hidden in the acts and records of the higher mind, which no one is permitted to search. So vain are the things the Jews prophesy about the age of the world,

units.la: Tom. II. Gggg & sexies mille annorum duratione, ex inspecta ejus videl. genesi, vaticinantur. Quæ domus Elianæ traditio erat. Nec pluris sunt formosa nimium Chiliastarum somnia; qui nimis audaci calculo divinos numeros, Pythagoricis longe obscuriores, tentant & digitis veluti metiuntur. Quanquam nihil obstare putemus, aliquanto tempore istam Ecclesiæ felicitatem durare, & aliquo usque Christi ac Sanctorum in terris regnum extendi; istudque Dei opus longe pulcherrimum non nimis exiguo fine concludi. Cum, ut reliqua Dei opera, ita & istud, quod reliquorum omnium coronis & complementum futurum est, suum procul dubio spatium requirat; quo mundi fata lætissimo tandem exitu absolvantur & coronentur.
units.tr: and its duration of six thousand years, drawn from an inspection of its genesis. This was the tradition of the house of Elijah. Nor are the pretty dreams of the Chiliasts any more worth having, who with too bold a calculation attempt divine numbers, far more obscure than the Pythagorean ones, and as it were measure them with their fingers. Yet we think nothing prevents this happiness of the Church from lasting for some time, and the reign of Christ and of the saints on earth from being extended to some point; and that this most beautiful work of God should not be concluded with too small an end. For, like the other works of God, so this one, which is to be the crown and completion of all the rest, undoubtedly requires its own span, in which the fates of the world may at last be completed and crowned with a most joyful outcome.

units.la: IV. Beatissimi istius temporis characteres sunt: 1. Magna divinæ ac humanæ sapientiæ in terris abundantia; ac Euangelii, toto fulgore coruscantis, publica de mundo victoria & triumphus. Lux solis erit septupla. Esai. 30: 26. Inquirent multi, & augebitur cognitio. Dan. 12: 4. Plena erit terra cognitione Jehova, ut aquis maris operientibus. Jes. 11: 9. 2. Hinc Judæorum, veluti confessio jam ac publicato tot sæculorum errore, ad Ecclesiæ tabernacula accessus. Rom. 11.
units.tr: IV. The marks of this most blessed time are these: (1) a great abundance of divine and human wisdom on earth, and a public victory and triumph of the Gospel, shining in full splendour throughout the world. The light of the sun will be sevenfold (Isa. 30:26). Many will search, and knowledge will be increased (Dan. 12:4). The earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea (Isa. 11:9). (2) Hence the Jews, as if confessing their error of so many centuries now at last acknowledged and made public, will come to the tents of the Church (Rom. 11).

units.la: 3. Et gentium quoque remotissimarum isto exemplo excita sedibus suis turba, & ad idem Ecclesiæ limen concursus. Nam si abjectio illorum est reconciliatio mundi, quæ erit assumtio, nisi vita ex mortuis? Rom. 11: 15. Facta sunt regna mundi Domini nostri & Christi ejus. Apoc. 11: 15. Omnes gentes venient & adorabunt coram te. c. 15: 4. Sub quarum gentium ambitu specialem quoque Turcarum conversionis sub Assyriorum emblemate, spem in prophetiis fieri, quorundam non absurda conjectura est. 4. Inter ipsos autem Christianos cessabunt tot hæresium ac sectarum probra; mutuæque fratrum iræ ac odia, alterno sanguine funesta. Esai. 2: & 11. Ac præsertim Babyloniæ meretricis nudabuntur obscenæ partes, evertetur profanum Antichristi solium, regnumque in regno Dei b. ... gestum. Et tunc revelabitur sceleratus ille, quem Dominus interficit Spiritu oris sui, & illustri adventu suo abolebit. 2 Thess. 2: 8. Apoc. 18: 21. Omnes autem populi in eodem templo, h. e. in unitate fidei, quoad humana tert infirmitas, Deo servatori cantabunt gloriam; iisdemque in tentoriis lætissimum agitabunt festum. Zach. 14. 5. Reliqui autem mundi facies, cessantibus undiquaque bellis, ac mundo quoque Ecclesiæ otia sua præstante, secura atque alta, uti quidem videtur, in pace deget: Destructis destructoribus terræ. Apoc. 11: 18. Cum autem dicent, pax & securitas, tunc rerepentinum ipsis imminet exitium. 1. Thess. 5: 3. atque prioris mundi tempora reducet, eosdemque cum temporibus homines: Et prout factum est in diebus Noë, ita erit etiam diebus filii hominis: edebant, bibebant &c. Luc. 17: 26, 27. modo illa huc pertineant. 6. Nam nec irrisores aut ἐμπαίκτας defuturos, qui ista in pace, ac rerum omnium affluentia, mundi æternitatem optabunt ac somniabunt, dicentes, ubi est pollicitatio adventus ejus, nam ex quo die patres obdormierunt, omnia ita permanent ab initio creationis &c. S. Petrus jam olim prædixit; ac monstra ista producto creationis mundi per solum Dei verbum: ejusdemque justo judicio aquis olim inundati, exemplo, eodem in loco potentissime elisit: Illud enim volentes ipsos fugit, cælos jam olim extitisse per Dei sermonem, & terram ex aqua & in aqua consistentem. Quamobrem is, qui tum erat mundus, aqua inundatus periit. Qui vero nunc sunt cœli ac terra, eodem sermone reconditi, asservantur igni &c. 2. Pet. 3: 4, 5, 6, 7. Ipsa autem D. Petri verba, non sine magna impietate, expressisse videtur Manilius, ex profanis videl. philosophorum placitis; ubi de mundo: Idem semper erit, quoniam semper fuit idem: Non alium videre patres, aliumve nepotes aspicient. lib. 1.
units.tr: (3) And the nations also, even the most remote, roused from their dwelling places by this example, will flock to the same threshold of the Church. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be, but life from the dead? (Rom. 11:15). The kingdoms of the world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ (Rev. 11:15). All nations will come and worship before you (Rev. 15:4). Some have reasonably conjectured that, among these nations, a special hope of the conversion of the Turks is also set out in the prophecies under the emblem of the Assyrians. (4) Among the Christians themselves, the many reproaches of heresies and sects will cease, and the mutual anger and hatred of brothers, deadly through alternating bloodshed, will end (Isa. 2 and 11). Especially the obscene parts of the Babylonian harlot will be laid bare, the profane throne of Antichrist will be overthrown, and a kingdom will be established in the kingdom of God. And then that wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord will destroy with the breath of his mouth, and will abolish by his glorious coming (2 Thess. 2:8; Rev. 18:21). Moreover, all peoples, in the same temple, that is, in unity of faith, so far as human weakness allows, will sing glory to God the Saviour, and in the same tents will keep a most joyful feast (Zech. 14). (5) The rest of the world, with wars ceasing everywhere, and the world itself granting leisure to the Church, will live secure and, as it seems, lofty in peace: The destroyers of the earth being destroyed (Rev. 11:18). When they say, peace and security, then sudden destruction hangs over them (1 Thess. 5:3). It will also bring back the times of the former world, and men along with those times: And as it was in the days of Noah, so it will be also in the days of the Son of man: they were eating and drinking, etc. (Luke 17:26, 27), if those things belong here. (6) For there will also be scoffers, or [ἐμπαίκτας] mockers, who, in this peace and abundance of all things, will wish for and dream of the eternity of the world, saying, where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation, etc. St. Peter foretold this long ago, and in the same place he most powerfully refuted these monsters by the creation of the world through God's word alone, and by the example of its just judgment when once it was flooded with waters: For this they willingly forget, that the heavens existed long ago by the word of God, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water. Therefore the world that then was, being flooded with water, perished. But the present heavens and earth, by the same word, are stored up, reserved for fire, etc. (2 Pet. 3:4–7). Moreover, Manilius seems to have expressed St. Peter's own words, though not without great impiety, from the profane opinions of the philosophers, where he speaks of the world: It will always be the same, since it has always been the same. The fathers have not seen another, nor will their grandchildren see another. Book 1.

units.la: V. Sed non injucundum erit, omnem istam mundi ac Ecclesiæ veluti scenam latius explicare; atque in Apocalypsi depictam ac pulcherrime exornatam conspicere. Ita autem eam sacer scriptor ultimis capitibus exponit.
units.tr: V. It will not be unpleasing, however, to unfold more fully this whole scene of the world and of the Church, as it were, and to behold it painted in the Apocalypse and most beautifully adorned. The sacred writer sets it out in this way in the final chapters.

units.la: VI. Capite 20: 7. post mille annos (qui à reddita Ecclesiæ per Constantinum pace, erectisque in Ecclesia thronis, com. 4. numerandi videntur, adeoque in Ludovicum Bavarum desinunt;) dicitur solvendus Sathanas. Qui, è tam longo carcere furens ac saeviens, ad seducendum gentes, in quatuor angulis terræ, & cienda bella Magogica, quo vocabuli ænigmate Antichristum notari ex Ezechiele constat, egreditur. Post illa enim tempora Antichristi seductio, ac falsæ Ecclesiæ meretricium & pellacia, ἀκμὴν suam habuit. Nec dogmatum solum mendacio, sed & aperta vi ac cædibus bellum ista gravissima est. Et castra sanctorum, ac Dei civitatem cinxit. com. 9. Hæc nempe ejus temporis sunt, quo Ecclesia, è civitate magna egressa, & castra, & civitatem propriam habet: & ad sacra illa Antichristi bella, hoc ipso sæculo, in Europa gesta, aut gerenda, non obscure spectant. Ut Ecclesia non parva certaminum parte sese defunctam non sine causa sperare, seque ad reliquum discrimen majori animo comparare queat. Mox enim liliberatio ejus subjungitur, per ignem, è cælo missum, devorantem hostes ejus. com. 9.
units.tr: VI. Chapter 20:7. After a thousand years (which, from the restoration of peace to the Church through Constantine, and the thrones erected in the Church, seem to be counted from the commentary on verse 4, and so end under Louis of Bavaria), Satan is said to be loosed. Raging and fierce from so long a prison, he goes out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth, and to stir up the Magogian wars. It is clear from Ezekiel that this enigmatic name marks the Antichrist. For after those times the deception of Antichrist and the harlotry and seduction of the false Church reached their peak. And this most grievous war is waged not only by the lie of doctrines, but also by open violence and slaughter. And it surrounded the camp of the saints and the city of God (see verse 9). These, indeed, belong to the time when the Church, having gone out of the great city, has both a camp and a city of its own; and they clearly look to those sacred wars of Antichrist waged, or still to be waged, in Europe in this very century. So that the Church may not without reason hope that it has got through no small part of its struggles, and may prepare itself with greater courage for the remaining peril. For soon its deliverance is added, through fire sent from heaven, devouring its enemies (see verse 9).

units.la: VII. Dehinc, Diabolo conjecto in lacum ignis & sulphuris, com. 10. & graffatione ejus in terris cohibita, quod supremum ipsi tormentum est: apparet throni candidi. com. 11. Christi videlicet sine vicario in Ecclesia regnantis solium. A cujus facie fugit cælum: Præsulum nempe in Ecclesia cœlestis prope auctoritas; & regimen, ad veteris cœli imaginem effictum: & terra, h.e. subjecta & serviens ipsis turba, non alios, quam cœli illius maleficio vitiatos, lucis radios accipiens.
units.tr: VII. Then, with the Devil cast into the lake of fire and sulphur (verse 10), and his raging on earth restrained, which is the greatest torment for him, there appears a white throne (verse 11). That is, clearly, the throne of Christ reigning in the Church without a vicar. From whose face heaven fled: that is, the near-heavenly authority of the prelates in the Church, and their rule, fashioned on the image of the old heaven; and the earth, that is, the crowd subject to and serving them, receiving the rays of light from that heaven, though they are only corrupted by its wickedness.

units.la: VIII. Inde mortui stant coram Deo, com. 12. non, fato functi. Hæc enim in terris adhuc geruntur, ut picturæ feries ostendit. Nec supremus ac decretorius mundi dies adhuc venit. Sed mortui dicuntur, quibus mors & infernus, Antichristi satellites, dominati hactenus erant; erroribus vitiisque omnibus immersi & inundati, nec ullo virtutis aut veri studio à nativa labe redemti. Stant autem illi coram Deo, judicandi: Prolatis Scripturarum libris, qui in Antichristi regno diu neglecti, ac multa fuligine oppleti, jam plena in luce collocandi erant. Haud dubie enim una cum Ecclesiæ renovatione clarior, & illustrior Scripturarum cognitio affulsura erat. Atque ex iis judicium & ἐλεγχῶ de miscellanea ista Ecclesiæ turba faciendus erat. Quod istum eventum habiturum erat, ut multi, de mortuorum grege, lumine isto percussi, in novam spem reficturi forent. Illi videlicet, qui in libro vitæ agni adscripti erant. Nam & iste liber hic profertur. Reliqua autem Antichristi turba, quæ, ad lucem istam deles, de mortis regno exire pigrabatur, tanquam emortui prorsus ac deplorati, secundum opera sua, & judicati, & damnati sunt.
units.tr: VIII. Then the dead stand before God, v. 12: not those who have died. For these things are still going on in the world, as the sequence of the picture shows. Nor has the last and decisive day of the world yet come. The dead are so called because death and hell, the satellites of Antichrist, have hitherto held dominion over them. They were immersed and drowned in all errors and vices, and no zeal for virtue or truth had redeemed them from their native corruption. They stand before God to be judged, the books of Scripture having been brought forth, which had been long neglected in Antichrist's kingdom and smothered in much soot, and which were now to be set in full light. For without doubt, along with the renewal of the Church, a clearer and more illustrious knowledge of the Scriptures was about to shine forth. From them the judgment and refutation of that motley crowd of the Church was to be made. The outcome would be that many from the flock of the dead, struck by that light, would be restored to a new hope; namely those who were enrolled in the book of life of the Lamb. For that book too is produced here. The rest of Antichrist's crowd, who, blotted out by that light, were reluctant to leave the realm of death, were judged and condemned as utterly dead and given up, according to their works.

units.la: IX. Quo judicio in Ecclesia peracto, jam nova ac pulchrior ejus facies exurgit; quam idem Apostolus, egregius quippe Christi ac fidei ejus domesticus (ut Augustini phrasim mutuemur) toto capite penultimo mirifice pingere ac illustrare non cessat. Videt enim cælum novum, & terram novam. Ut novam, ac novissimam rerum faciem intelligamus: in qua nihil de veteri labe reliquum futurum erat. Et primum cælum, & prima terra, præterierunt. Additur: & mare non erit amplius. Omnia enim tum erunt grex unus, & ovile unum, & unus Christi populus mundi concordia nullo elementorum dissidio turbata.
units.tr: IX. With this judgment carried out in the Church, a new and more beautiful face of it now rises up, which the same Apostle, being a distinguished intimate of Christ and of his faith (to borrow Augustine's phrase), never ceases to paint and illuminate wonderfully throughout the next-to-last chapter. For he sees a new heaven and a new earth, so that we may understand the new and final aspect of things, in which nothing of the old corruption would remain. And the first heaven and the first earth have passed away. It is added: and there shall be no more sea. For then all will be one flock and one fold, and the one people of Christ will be undisturbed by any discord of the elements, in harmony with the world.

units.la: X. Isto autem rerum statu, ubi reditura in aurum tempora priscum, novam quoque progeniem cœlo demitti videt. Ita enim pergit com. 2. Et ego Johannes vidi sanctam illam civitatem Jerusalem novam, de descendentem à Deo, de cœlo paratam, tanquam sponsam ornatam n viro suo. Qui est ultimus Ecclesiæ status, quo illa, si unquam in hoc sæculo plenissime exornata conspicietur; tanquam sponsa jam parata, & jam jam in nuptialem thalamum introducenda. Quod autem ad instar civitatis, quæ, in monte condita, perpetuo jugo leniter decurrit: ita Ecclesiam de cœlo in terram videt porrigi; ut commune sit cœlestium terrestriumque habitaculum: id ad divinam illam ἀναχεφαλαίωσιν spectat, quam Paulus deprædicat Eph. 1: 10. Col. 1: 10. qua cœlitum ac fidelium in terris populus unam Ecclesiam, unamque Dei civitatem facit; vix alio quam loci discrimine relicto; dum status utrorumque in uno Christo consummatus est. Hebr. 11: ult.
units.tr: X. In that state of things, when the times are to return to the golden age of old, he sees a new offspring also let down from heaven. For he continues thus, v. 2: And I, John, saw that holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. This is the last state of the Church, in which she will be seen most fully adorned, if ever in this age; as a bride now ready, and about to be led into the nuptial chamber at any moment. As for the fact that the Church is seen stretching from heaven to earth, like a city built on a mountain that gently slopes down on a continuous ridge, so that the dwelling place of the heavenly and earthly becomes common, this refers to that divine recapitulation which Paul proclaims, Eph. 1:10, Col. 1:10, by which the people of the heavenly ones and of the faithful on earth make one Church and one city of God, with scarcely any difference left except that of place, since the state of both is brought to completion in the one Christ. Heb. 11, last verse.

units.la: XI. Simili imagine Tabernaculum Dei jam cum hominibus esse, & Deus cum ipsis habitare dicitur, com. 3. Ut Ecclesia jam unius Dei civitas intelligatur. Deleto omni hominum in Ecclesia imperio, omnibus servitutis reliquiis extinctis.
units.tr: XI. By a similar image, the Tabernacle of God is said to be now with men, and God to dwell with them, v. 3, so that the Church may now be understood as the one city of God, with every dominion of men in the Church abolished and all remnants of servitude extinguished.

units.la: XII. Describitur deinde hæc nova civitas: ac murus cjus, & portæ, & fundamenta, duodecim Christianæ Ecclesiæ ducum nominibus inscripta, recensentur. com. 12. & seqq. Templo autem carere dicitur, quod universa Dei templum sit, nec certum ad locum, certamque ad aram accedere necesse habeat. Eamque omnem, & Deus, & Agnus, plurimo sole implent. Nec enim adscititio lumine indiget; aut diei ac noctis vices amplius patitur. Cum autem non gentes solum in luce ista ambulent; sed & Reges & Principes opes gloriamque suam in Ecclesiam inferant. com. 24. satis apparet hujus sæculi statum describi.
units.tr: XII. Next this new city is described, and its wall, its gates and its foundations, inscribed with the names of the twelve leaders of the Christian Church, are listed, v. 12 and following. It is said to lack a temple, because the whole of it is the temple of God, and it has no need to approach a fixed place or a fixed altar. God and the Lamb fill all of it with abundant light. For it does not need borrowed light, nor does it suffer the alternation of day and night any longer. Since not only the nations walk in that light, but also the kings and princes bring their wealth and glory into the Church, v. 24, it is quite clear that the state of this age is being described.

units.la: XIII. Nec Spiritus, donorumque spiritualium ubertatem præterit vates, quem fluvio aquæ vivæ, largissimis rivis in media civitate exundanti, comparat. Nullum autem anathema, seu devotum ibi amplius erit, c. 22: 1. &c. Ut regnum & Ecclesiam sanctorum cogitemus, cessantibus magna ex parte scandalis; atque illis, qui civitatis hujus domestici erant, nulli amplius terrori aut execrationi obnoxiis. Non erit Cananæis amplius in domo Jehovæ Dei exercitium in die isto. Zach. 14: 21. Alieni non transibunt per eam amplius. Joël. 3: 17. Omnis populus tuus justi, Esai. 60: 21. Tandem ut perennis illa felicitas futura significetur, nullus in Ecclesia illa thronus, præter Dei & agni thronum, conspicitur, com. 4. Soliusque Dei faciem fideles vident; sine velo & tegmine, quale vicaria hominum potestas Deo regnanti veluti præpandebat. Et denique in sæcula sæculorum isto in statu regnatuři perhibentur, com. 5. Cui Ecclesiæ regno nihil magis
units.tr: XIII. Nor does the prophet pass over the Spirit and the abundance of spiritual gifts, which he compares to a river of living water overflowing in rich streams through the middle of the city. Nor shall there be any further anathema, that is, anything devoted to destruction there any more, Apoc. 22:1 and following. We are to think of the kingdom and Church of the saints, with scandals largely ceased, and with those who were household members of this city no longer subject to any terror or curse. There shall no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day. Zech. 14:21. Strangers shall no longer pass through it. Joel 3:17. Your people shall all be righteous, Isa. 60:21. Finally, so that this perpetual happiness may be signified, no throne is seen in that Church except the throne of God and of the Lamb, v. 4. And the faithful see the face of God alone, without veil or covering, such as human vicarious power used to spread out before God as he reigned. And finally they are said to reign for ever and ever in that state, v. 5. Nothing is more opposed to this kingdom of the Church than any servitude of men, which is said to be banished here forever. And in these words there is the close both of the prophecy and of the times of the Church, after which it is wrong to expect other fates and other times on earth.

units.la: Donorum-tualium in ta ubertat. Apoc. 22: 1. & seqq. magis adversum est, quam quæcunque hominum servitus; quæ hic in perpetuum exulatura dicitur. Atque in hisce verbis & prophetiæ, & temporum Ecclesiæ, clausula est; post quæ alia in terris fata, atque alia tempora expectare nefas est.
units.tr: Nothing is more opposed to this abundance of gifts than any servitude of men, which is said to be banished here forever (Apoc. 22:1 and following). And in these words the prophecy and the times of the Church come to a close, after which it is wrong to expect other fates and other ages on earth.

units.la: XIV. Atque hæc ultimæ illius ætatis apertissima descriptio est. Cujus nos summa tantum fastigia tetigimus; atque emicantes ultro & corusçantes undique radios non difficulter collegimus. In quibus clarissimam illius Ecclesiæ imaginem videmus. Qua luce nos contenti, ipsam fatorum jam properantium seriem, dum Deus umbras ac lineas illas rerum ipsarum lumine impletum ibit, non languida spe expectamus. Cætera autem audacius scrutari, & quæ nec scire datum, nec explorare concessum, stuprare velle, nec pium, nec religiosum est.
units.tr: XIV. And this is the most manifest description of that last age. We have touched only the highest peaks of it, and we have not found it difficult to gather together the rays shining out and flashing on every side. In them we see the clearest image of that Church. Content with this light, we await with no weary hope the series of fates now hastening on, while God will go on filling those shadows and outlines of things with the light of the things themselves. But to pry more boldly into the rest, and to wish to violate what has been given neither to know nor to explore, is neither pious nor religious.

units.la: LOCUS QUINQUAGESIMUS SECUNDUS DE NOVISSIMIS. CAPUT XXII. De Resurrectione mortuorum.
units.tr: LOCUS QUINQUAGESIMUS SECUNDUS DE NOVISSIMIS. CAPUT XXII. De Resurrectione mortuorum.

units.la: I. Unc civitatis Dei, in terris exulantis, cursum & ordinem, excipit ejus exitus, & consummatio, & suprema ac æterna ejus fata; in mortuorum Resurrectione; ac sequente eam Judicio, ac mundo die decretorio; & Consummatione sæculi; & Ecclesiæ denique Glorificatione æterna.
units.tr: I. After the course and order of the City of God, which sojourns on earth, comes its departure, its consummation, and its final and eternal destiny: the Resurrection of the dead, the Judgment that follows it, the decisive day of the world, the Consummation of the age, and at last the eternal Glorification of the Church.

units.la: II. Resurrectionis, qui magnus ille fidei ac spei articulus est, de cujus fide olim adeo probata fuit Abrahami obedientia, consideranda: bimus 1. Veritatem. 2. Subjectum. 3. Causam. 4. Circumstantias.
units.tr: II. The Resurrection, that great article of faith and hope, by whose faith Abraham's obedience was once so well proved, must be considered under four heads: 1. its Truth; 2. its Subject; 3. its Cause; 4. its Circumstances.

units.la: III. Est autem alia resurrectio figurate dicta; quæ de anima, de peccatis labe resurgente, Rom. 6: 4, 5. aut de mundo, per Euangelii prædicationem, veluti renascente, intelligitur. Quo ænigmata Apocalyptica de prima & secunda resurrectione spectant; opoppolite ad primam & secundam mortem. Apoc. 20. 5,6. Quarum illa post Christi adventum, & primam Euangelii promulgationem: hæc post Antichristi casum, & promulgatum Euangelium æternum, peracta est. Hic autem proprie intelligitur, de corporis, quod cecidit, è vago pulvere collectione, ac veluti reconeinnatione. Quod enim Sociniani, de suo sensu, quoque resurrectionem non corporis, sed hominis, crepant, merum vocabuli, & Christiani dogmatis, stuprum est.
units.tr: III. There is, however, another resurrection, called so figuratively, which is understood of the soul rising from the stain of sin (Rom. 6:4, 5), or of the world being, as it were, born again through the preaching of the Gospel. To this belong the Apocalyptic enigmas of the first and second resurrection, which are set over against the first and second death (Rev. 20:5, 6). The former was accomplished after Christ's coming and the first promulgation of the Gospel; the latter, after the fall of Antichrist and the proclamation of the everlasting Gospel. But properly speaking, the resurrection is understood here as the gathering of the body, which fell, out of the scattered dust, and as it were its renewal. For when the Socinians, in their own sense, also prate about a resurrection not of the body but of the man, they do nothing but violate the meaning of the word and the Christian doctrine.

units.la: IV. Nec magis admittenda præcox Chiliastarum resurrectio, martyrum & sanctorum; qui ous in his terris mille annorum triumphum, ante ultimum aliud est, quam medio in ce ... triumphum ... e; & debitam cœlo lauream intemperi in terris præcurrere; & in exilio ipso patriæ bona & commoda præcautare velle. Certum vero est, & sanctos non sine Christo ad plenum regnaturos; & Christum ipsum non nisi ad judicandum universum orbem, ultimo rerum fine, descensurum. Si igitur dixerint vobis; ecce in deserto est, ne egredimini: ecce, in conclavibus, ne credite — Tunc apparebit signum filii hominis in cælo, & tunc omnes terra plangent, & videbunt filium hominis venientem in nubibus cæli, — De die autem illo, & hora nemo scit; ne Angeli quidem cælorum; sed Pater meus solus. Matth. 24:26, 30, 36. Conf. Act. 3:21.
units.tr: IV. Nor is the premature resurrection of the Chiliasts, of martyrs and saints, to be admitted any more readily. They imagine that before the last day, on this earth, there will be a thousand years of triumph, and that the saints will run ahead on earth to the crown due in heaven, and want to enjoy in exile the goods and advantages of their homeland in advance. It is certain, however, that the saints will not reign fully without Christ, and that Christ himself will not come down except to judge the whole world at the final end of things. If therefore they shall say to you, Behold, he is in the desert, go not forth; behold, he is in the secret chambers, believe it not. Then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven. But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only. (Matt. 24:26, 30, 36.) Cf. Acts 3:21.

units.la: V. Similis Judæorum fabella est, de resurrectionis primitiis in terra Israëlis; quam Messiæ sui diebus imputant. Atque ista resurgentium veluti libamina, dum reliquus pulvis nondum animatur, sanctæ terræ deputant. Quod ex vero corruptum est. Nec melius Pontificii, non Christi, sed Antichristi tempori, quem videlicet adhuc expectant, Enochum & Eliam conjungunt: quos, post cædem, redivivos, novo miraculo Ecclesiæ hostes territaturos putant. Qui error ex loci Prophetici Apoc. 11. πασεμφύσεις ortus est.
units.tr: V. Similar is the Jewish fable about the firstfruits of the resurrection in the land of Israel, which they attribute to the days of their Messiah. They assign these first rising ones, as it were offerings, to the holy land while the rest of the dust is not yet quickened. This is a corruption of the truth. Nor do the Papists do better: they join Enoch and Elijah to the time not of Christ but of Antichrist, whom they still expect, supposing that these two, after their slaying and return to life, will terrify the enemies of the Church by a new miracle. This error arose from the Prophetic passage in Rev. 11, πασεμφύσεις [πασεμφύσεις].

units.la: VI. Fuit autem sanctissimum hoc dogma perridiculum Philosophis; qui Christianorum spem incessere, & posthumam, uti calumniabantur, immortalitatem, novamque e cineribus & favillis vitam novis modis traducere non desinebant. Vide Act. 17. Ipsi autem ad summum, aut animas post fata superstites docebant, aut eas novis corporibus indutas, per quandam μετεμψύχωσιν, in mundum rursus producebant. Quæ interpolatæ veritatis imitatio quædam erat. Sed & inter Judæos Sadducæi eam subsannabant. Act. 23:6. Et ipsa denique Ecclesiæ Christianæ primordia non leviter in hoc capite perturbata sunt. Dum alii eam aperte negant, 1. Cor. 15: 12. alii, spiritualem intellectum praeferentes, jam factam eam in mundo pertendunt. 2. Tim. 2: 18. Quas profanas sententias de Ecclesia exulare jubet Apostolus, & duplici sigillo resurrectionis fidem munit & obsignat. Firmum fundamentum Dei stat, habens signaculum hoc, novit Dominus qui sui sunt: & abstistat ab injustitia omnis nominans nomen Christi. 2 Tim. 2: 19.
units.tr: VI. This most holy doctrine was, however, most ridiculous to the philosophers, who attacked the hope of the Christians and did not cease to present, in novel ways, what they slanderously called a posthumous immortality and a new life out of ashes and embers. See Acts 17. The philosophers themselves, at most, taught either that souls survive after death, or that they are clothed in new bodies and brought back into the world through a kind of metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσιν]. This was a certain counterfeit imitation of the truth. Among the Jews the Sadducees mocked it (Acts 23:6). And even the beginnings of the Christian Church were not lightly disturbed on this point: some openly denied it (1 Cor. 15:12), while others, preferring a spiritual interpretation, asserted that it had already taken place in the world (2 Tim. 2:18). The Apostle bids such profane opinions be banished from the Church, and he confirms and seals faith in the resurrection with a twofold seal: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: the Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity (2 Tim. 2:19).

units.la: VII. Ac natura quidem mysterium hoc non docet. Quae enim de animae, vagae vid. ac errantis, desiderio, ac perpetua ad corpus suum αισθησις & inclinatione docent; incerta ac levia, nec animae ac corporis substantiis ac naturae, quae nihil admodum ad sese commercii habent, satis congrua sunt. Hoc tamen vel invita fateri debet ratio, possibilem eam esse, nec Deo indecoram: cum longe facilius sit, de generis humani pulvere, novam gentem condere, ac luteam illam progeniem veluti reformare, quam eandem primum condere. Nec Deo, mundi artifici ac plasti, negari debet, quod Prometheo, quem vulgi fictilis auctorem celebrant, poetarum fabulae adscribunt.
units.tr: VII. Now nature does not teach this mystery. For what is taught of the soul's desire, wandering and straying, and its constant sense [αἴσθησις] and inclination toward its own body, is uncertain and slight, and not sufficiently fitting to the substances and natures of soul and body, which have very little dealings with each other. Yet reason itself must, even against its will, admit that this is possible and not unworthy of God, since it is far easier to found a new race from the dust of mankind, and as it were to reform that earthen progeny, than it was to create it in the first place. Nor should it be denied to God, the artificer and former of the world, what the fables of the poets ascribe to Prometheus, whom the common people celebrate as the maker of clay figures.

units.la: VIII. Proprium autem Scripturarum ac fidei hoc dogma est. Pertinentque huc oracula: in Veteri Testam. Psal. 90: 3, 5. ubi, ad vocem imperiumque Domini, mortem, tanquam somnum, excutere homo jubetur. Redigis hominem ad minimum, & dicis: redite filii hominis — Imbre perfundis ipsos, soporantur: mane, ut gramen, recreatur. Deut. 32: 39. Videte — me morte afficere, & vita restituere, frangere me & sanare, nec esse qui e manu mea rapiat. Ubi ita spiritualis resurrectio insinuatur, ut etiam corporalis confirmetur. Quae loci quoque Ezech. 37: 11—14. ratio est: Sic dixit Dominus Jehovah: ecce ego aperio sepulchra vestra, & faciam vos ascendere ex sepulchris vestris, populemi. Adde Job 19: 26, 27. Dan. 12: 2. Esai. 26: 19. & 25: 8. Hos. 13: 14. col. 1. Cor. 15: 54, 55, 56, 57. Psal. 17: 15. & 49: 16. Spectabatque huc quoque veterum apparatus funebris, & mortuos humandi mos; spretis pyris, & rogis, & ignium sepulturis, quae apud gentes extra Ecclesiam frequentabantur.
units.tr: VIII. This doctrine, however, is peculiar to the Scriptures and to faith. To it belong the oracles in the Old Testament: Psalm 90:3, 5, where at the voice and command of the Lord man is bidden to shake off death as if it were sleep. You reduce man to dust, and say, Return, you sons of men. You sweep them away like a flood, they sleep; in the morning they are renewed like the grass (Ps. 90:3, 5). Deut. 32:39: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand. Here spiritual resurrection is so suggested that bodily resurrection is also confirmed. The same is the purpose of Ezek. 37:11–14: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, O my people. Add Job 19:26, 27; Dan. 12:2; Isa. 26:19 and 25:8; Hos. 13:14; 1 Cor. 15:54, 55, 56, 57; Ps. 17:15 and 49:16. To this also points the funeral practice of the ancients and their custom of burying the dead, rejecting the funeral pyres and burnings and the cremation of ashes that were common among the nations outside the Church.

units.la: IX. Clariora autem sunt Novi Testamenti testimonia. Matth. 25: 32. Joh. 5: 21, 28, 29. & 6: 39, 40, 44. & 11: 24. Act. 4: 2. & 17: 18. & 23: 6. & 24: 15. 1 Cor. 15. toto capite.
units.tr: IX. The testimonies of the New Testament are, however, clearer: Matt. 25:32; John 5:21, 28, 29; 6:39, 40, 44; 11:24; Acts 4:2; 17:18; 23:6; 24:15; 1 Cor. 15, the whole chapter.

units.la: X. Accedunt rationes gravissimae, e Scripturis haustae: 1. a primavi promissione, Gen. 3: 15. Conterei tibi caput. Quae, in solatium mortalitatis, tunc primum in mundum ingressae, facta, sine omnimoda mortis destructione, vigorem suum neutiquam habet; utpote quae non aliunde, quam de colubri veneno, primum profluxit. Conf. Hebr. 2: 14. Ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui imperium habebat mortis, h. e. diabolum. 1. Cor. 15: 26. Ultimus autem hostis aboletur, mors. com. 54. Quando autem mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet, quod scriptum est absorpta est mors ad victoriam. 1. Joh. 3: 8. Rom. 6: 23.
units.tr: X. There are added most weighty arguments, drawn from the Scriptures. 1. From the first promise, Gen. 3:15: He shall bruise your head. This promise, which entered the world for the first time as a comfort for mortality, cannot in any way retain its force if the destruction of death is not complete; for it came forth from nothing other than the serpent's poison. Cf. Heb. 2:14: That through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil. 1 Cor. 15:26: The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Verse 54: When this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass what is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. 1 John 3:8; Rom. 6:23.

units.la: XI. 2. A Fœdere Dei: quod cum de vita sit, omnimodam eam ac integram & perfectam intelligere, ex foederis natura, fas est. Cum qua nulla mortis portiuncula, aut suspicio, consistere potest. Qui credit in me, etiamsi moriatur, vivet. Joh. 11: 25. Ac docet hoc imprimis praeclare ipsa foederis feriundi formula: Ego sum Deus tuus. Quae verba tam magnifica & sonantia sunt, ut non aliis Christus ad Sadducaeorum impietatem obturandam uti maluerit, Matth. 22: 32. De resurrectione vero mortuorum, non legistis quod vobis dictum est a Deo, dicente: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci, & Deus Jacobi. Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed vivorum. Nec de animae solum, sed & de corporis vita, ista verba concludunt, cum Deus confoederatam sibi, & foederis sui nota inustam carnem, uti vilem pulverem, negligere; & tamen Deus ejus appellari non possit.
units.tr: XI. 2. From the covenant of God. Since this covenant concerns life, it is right, from the nature of the covenant, to understand that life as complete, whole and perfect; no small portion of death, or even any suspicion of it, can stand alongside it. He who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live (John 11:25). This is taught most clearly by the very formula by which the covenant is struck: I am your God. These words are so weighty and resounding that Christ preferred to use no others to stop the mouths of the Sadducees' impiety (Matt. 22:32): But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. These words conclude not only concerning the life of the soul but also concerning the life of the body, since God would not neglect flesh bound to him in covenant and marked with the sign of his covenant, as if it were worthless dust; and yet God could not be called its God.

units.la: XII. 3. A Christo,& redemptionis opere. Nam & corporis redemtor, uti & dominus, est. Nam emti estis pretio. Glorificate ergo Deum in corpore vestro, & in Spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei. 1 Cor. 6: 20. Et caro quoque ad ἀπολύτρωσιν ejus spectat: Nos ipsi, inquam, apud nos ipsos suspiramus, adoptionem expectantes, id est, redemtionem corporis nostri. Rom. 8: 23. Et mors inter hostes ejus numeratur. 1. Cor. 15: 26. Sicuti & ipse, exemplo suo, corporum resurrectionem dedicavit; deque monumento exiens, primus carcerem istum fregit, & horrentem specum, atque immane cadaverum stabulum, repurgavit. 1. Cor. 15: 20. Nunc vero, Christus excitatus est ex mortuis. Primitiae eorum, qui obdormierunt, facti sunt.
units.tr: XII. 3. From Christ and the work of redemption. For he is also the redeemer of the body, as he is its Lord. For you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's. 1 Cor. 6:20. The flesh also looks to his redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν]: we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, that is, the redemption of our body. Rom. 8:23. And death is numbered among his enemies. 1 Cor. 15:26. Just so, by his example, he consecrated the resurrection of bodies; coming out of the tomb first, he broke that prison, and cleansed that horrid cave and that vast stable of corpses. 1 Cor. 15:20. But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

units.la: XIII. 4. A justitia Dei: quae bonis praemia, & malis supplicia, etiam in corpore persolvi jubet. Quod cum in hac vita non fiat, ubi bonorum malorumque fata confusa sunt, post hanc vitam reanimato corpore, fieri aequum est. Siquidem justum est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem: vobis vero, qui affligimini, relaxationem vobiscum, in revelatione Domini Jesu, de caelo, cum Angelis suis potentibus, Cum igne flammante &c. 2. Thess. 1: 6, 7.
units.tr: XIII. 4. From the justice of God, which commands that rewards be paid to the good and punishments to the wicked, even in the body. Since this does not happen in this life, where the fates of good and bad are confused, it is fitting that it happen after this life, with the body brought back to life. For it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give relief to you who are afflicted, along with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven, with his mighty angels, in flaming fire, etc. 2 Thess. 1:6, 7.

units.la: XIV. v. Tandem & ipsa corpora nostra templa appellantur Spiritus S. 1. Cor. 6. unde & ossa, & reliquiæ eorum venerandæ; pulvisque ille, qui Deo olim servivit, etiam post fata pretiosius est. Nec, instar sordidorum cinerum, volucres in auras spargi, ac disperire potest. Ut de signis ac Sacramentis taceam: quorum usu corpora nostra consecrantur, & futuræ resurrectioni inaugurantur. Et consepulti per baptismum: per quem etiam cum eo suscitati estis, per fidem efficacis illius virtutis Dei, qui suscitavit eum ex mortuis. Col. 2: 12. Consepulti sumus ipsi per baptismum, in mortem —— si coaliti facti sumus similitudine mortis ipsius, non tantum, sed etiam resurrectionis erimus, Rom. 6: 4. 5. Poculum gratiarum actionis, cui benedicimus, nonne est communio sanguinis Christi, & panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio est corporis Christi? 1. Cor. 10: 16. Confer 1. Cor. 15: 29. Quid etiam lavantur propter mortuos? de quo loco supra egimus: atque Apostolum, de veteris legis cærimonia, ac baptismo eorum, qui cadaverum tactu polluti erant (βαπτιζομένοις ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, lotos a mortuo Syracides cap. 34: 27. dixit; quod Apostolus dicit, ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, Talmudica brevitate, טבול כח vel (על מח) mortuorum resurrectionem non inconcinne probare ostendimus.
units.tr: XIV. v. Finally, our bodies themselves are called temples of the Holy Spirit. 1 Cor. 6. Hence also their bones and remains are to be venerated; and that dust which once served God is more precious even after death. Nor can it be scattered into the air like filthy ashes and perish. Not to mention the signs and sacraments, by whose use our bodies are consecrated and initiated into the future resurrection. And you were buried with him in baptism, in whom you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. Col. 2:12. We were buried with him by baptism into death; if we have been joined with him in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection. Rom. 6:4, 5. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 Cor. 10:16. Compare 1 Cor. 15:29: Why are people even baptized for the dead? On which passage we have treated above; and we have shown that the Apostle, speaking of the ceremony of the old law and of the washing of those who were made unclean by touching corpses (βαπτιζομένοις ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, washed from the dead, Ecclesiasticus [Syracides] 34:27), with Talmudic brevity, said ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, which proves the resurrection of the dead not unsuitably: [טבול כח vel (על מח)].

units.la: XV. Denique confirmant hunc fidei articulum mortuorum, ad vitam reductorum exempla: quæ, tum in Veteri, tum in Novo Test. occurrunt. In quibus admiranda quadam proportione, divina sapientia lusit; ut nullum mortuorum genus extra imperium ejus degere sciremus. Ut ethnicorum, apud Minucium, sarcasmum non metuamus: Quis unus ullus ab inferis, vel Protesilai forte remeavit, horarum saltem permisso commeatu, vel ut exemplo credepemus?
units.tr: XV. Finally, the examples of the dead brought back to life confirm this article of faith, and they occur in both the Old and the New Testament. In these, the divine wisdom played with a certain wonderful proportion, so that we might know that no kind of dead person lies outside its power. Let us not fear the sneer of the pagans, which Minucius records: Has anyone ever returned from the dead, even Protesilaus, if only for a permitted leave of a few hours, so that we might believe by example?

units.la: XVI. Subjectum resurrectionis in scholis duplici modo consideratur. Estque vel subjectum quod, vel subjectum quo.
units.tr: XVI. The subject of the resurrection is considered in the schools in a twofold way. It is either the subject which or the subject in which.

units.la: XVII. Subjectum quod sunt omnes, quotquot unquam vitalem auram carpserunt, homines. Et congregabuntur coram facie ejus omnes gentes. Matth. 25: 32. Omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus Joh. 5: 28. Resurrectio mortuorum futura est, & justorum, & impiorum. Act. 24: 15. 2. Cor. 5: 10. Illi autem, quos supremus mundi dies vivos deprehendet, in isto universæ naturæ labore, mirum in modum afficientur & transformabuntur. Ecce dico vobis mysterium: Non omnes quidem obdormiemus, sed omnes transmutabimur. 1. Cor. 15: 51. Quod ipsis pro casu corporis erit. Quale & Enochi & Eliæ fatum fuit. Quos non nisi purgatos & mutatos in cœlum iisse constat.
units.tr: XVII. The subject which is all men, as many as have ever drawn the breath of life. And all nations shall be gathered before him. Matt. 25:32. All who are in the tombs will hear his voice. John 5:28. There will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust. Acts 24:15. 2 Cor. 5:10. Those, however, whom the last day of the world finds alive will be changed and transformed in a wonderful manner in this travail of all nature. Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. 1 Cor. 15:51. This will be for them in place of the fall of the body. Such was the fate of Enoch and Elijah, who are known to have gone up into heaven only after being purged and changed.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: XVIII. Nec fœtus abortivi, & monstrosi partus, aliique à natura male ficti, aut inconcinno membrorum commensu deformes, modo in hominum communitate tuerint, à resurrectionis beneficio excludendi. Hæc enim non aliud erit, quam universi humani generis de recidivatu suo recorporatio & reproductio.
units.tr: XVIII. Nor are aborted fetuses, monstrous births, and others who were badly formed by nature, or deformed by an unbalanced proportion of limbs, to be excluded from the benefit of the resurrection, provided they lived within the human community. For this will be nothing other than the re-embodiment and reproduction of the whole human race from its own remnants.

units.la: XIX. Intercedunt hic Judæi, futilissimi nugarum institutores: qui, uti materiam hanc miserandum in modum inaniis suis oppleverunt; ita non leviter in eo errant, quod ad Israëlitas solos resurrectionis beneficium restringunt, pauculis tantum exceptis Apostatis videl. Epicureis &c. Cujus tamen sententiæ impietatem tegere recentiores laborant; de Gentium quoque, qui Noachica præcepta servarunt, resurrectione; & impiorum cruciatibus, nonnihil admittentes.
units.tr: XIX. Here the Jews intervene, the most frivolous founders of trifles; who, just as they have miserably crammed this matter with their emptiness, so they err not lightly in restricting the benefit of the resurrection to the Israelites alone, with only a few apostates, namely the Epicureans, excepted. Yet more recent writers labor to cover up the impiety of this opinion, admitting somewhat a resurrection also for the Gentiles who kept the Noachic precepts, and the torments of the wicked.

units.la: XX. Judæos imitantur Socinianī, qui universalem omnium hominum resurrectionem albis dentibus ridebt. Et ad solos fideles; quos præstigiosa distinctione in justos & injustos (ita de mundi semita ad veræ pietatis regulam conversos, non sine contumelia, appellant) discerpunt; illam dignitatem referunt. Impios autem & infideles, ac nulla virtute a communi generis humani labe redemtos, ubi ipsis semel occidit brevis lux, æterna in nocte dormire & quiescere sinunt. Inferos enim, & subterranea regna; atque una transfire vadum tot millia cymba, aniles fabulas, & puerilia terriculamenta, putant.
units.tr: XX. The Socinians imitate the Jews: they laugh at the universal resurrection of all men with white teeth. And, with a deceitful distinction, they tear apart the faithful into the just and the unjust (so they call those who have turned from the way of the world to the rule of true piety, not without insult), and they assign the resurrection only to the first group. The impious and unbelieving, and those redeemed by no virtue from the common stain of the human race, they allow, once their brief light has set for them, to sleep and rest in eternal night. For they think that the underworld and the subterranean realms, and that so many thousands cross the river in one boat, are old wives' tales and childish bugbears.

units.la: XXI. Quæ impia ac feralis opinio, de atheismi ac paganismi seminio pullulans, & corrumpendis bonis moribus nata, contra omnem Scripturæ auctoritatem est. Oportet enim nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi. 2 Cor. 5: 10. Omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus & prodibunt. Joh. 5: 28, 29. Et cogentur coram eo omnes gentes, & separabit eos, alteros ab alteris &c. Matth. 25: 32. Quæ loca inepte ad homines, qui ultimo die vivi deprehendentur, restringuntur. Quid enim hoc ad terrendos præcedentium ætatum homines? Et manifesta apud Johannem sepulchrorum mentio est. Nec idonea ratio est, cur impii, qui ultima mundi ætate vivent, magis divino judicio sistendi sint, quam reliqui, qui jam fato functi sunt. Sed & Sodomæorum, & Gomorrhæorum, & Tyri ac Sidonis, & reginæ Austri, & Ninevitarum, in judiciali isto die mentio habetur, Matth. 10: 15. & 11: 21, 23. Luc. 11: 31, 32. Quæ illi, pro solito acumine, ita explicant, ac si de Judææ per Titum excidio agatur; quod Sodomæ regionis incendio longe gravius ac luctuosius suturum sit. Sed nihil hæc ad reginam Austri, & Ninevitas, vel Tyrios, ac Sidonios, qui iisdem in locis memorantur. Et aperte Christi verba de judicio Sodomæorum futuro agunt, tolerabile erit, &c, in die isto &c. unde & præsentis temporis homines affatur: quos non tam venturo olim Judææ excidio, quod isti forte non visuri erant, quam communi generis humani judicio, ac impiorum excidio terreri, æquum erat. Denique aperte Apostolus futuram resurrectionem mortuorum, justorum & impiorum, coram concilio profitetur. Act. 24: 15. Admodum autem insulsum, & contumeliosum, est, per impios, fideles conversos intelligere. Nam Scriptura pios & impios, fideles & infideles, ex æquo inter se opponere & comparare; non autem fideles in justos & injustos discriminare, solet.
units.tr: XXI. This impious and deadly opinion, sprouting from the seed of atheism and paganism, and born to corrupt good morals, is contrary to all the authority of Scripture. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ. 2 Cor. 5:10. All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth. John 5:28, 29. And all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them, one from another, etc. Matt. 25:32. These passages are foolishly restricted to the people who will be found alive on the last day. For what does this have to do with frightening the people of earlier ages? And John clearly mentions tombs. Nor is there a sound reason why the wicked who will live in the last age of the world should be brought before the divine judgment more than the rest, who have already died. But also the Sodomites and the Gomorrhites, and Tyre and Sidon, and the queen of the South, and the Ninevites, are mentioned in that day of judgment. Matt. 10:15; 11:21, 23; Luke 11:31, 32. These men, with their usual sharpness, explain these as if they referred to the destruction of Judea by Titus, which would be far more grievous and lamentable than the burning of the land of Sodom. But these words have nothing to do with the queen of the South, the Ninevites, or the Tyrians and Sidonians, who are mentioned in the same passages. And Christ's words clearly concern the future judgment of Sodom: it will be more tolerable, etc., in that day, etc.; hence he also addresses the men of the present time, who ought to be frightened not so much by the destruction of Judea, which perhaps they would not see, as by the common judgment of the human race and the destruction of the wicked. Finally, the Apostle plainly professes before the council the future resurrection of the dead, of the just and of the unjust. Acts 24:15. But it is quite foolish and insulting to understand by the impious the faithful who have been converted. For Scripture is accustomed to set the pious and the impious, the faithful and the unbelieving, over against one another and compare them on equal terms, and not to divide the faithful into the just and the unjust.

units.la: XXII. Resurgent autem pii ad beatitudinem; impii ad exitium, & supplicia æterna. Dan. 12: 2. Quo extremo fine, sicuti & causis, uti mox videbimus, piorum & impiorum resurrectio discreta est.
units.tr: XXII. The pious will rise to blessedness, and the impious to destruction and eternal punishment. Dan. 12: 2. By this final end, as well as by its causes, which we shall see presently, the resurrection of the pious is distinguished from that of the impious.

units.la: XXIII. Subjectum quo resurrectionis, est corpus humanum: quod per peccatum caducum factum, de casu isto suo suscitabitur & restituetur. Unde ejusdem corporis resurrectionem Ecclesia in symbolo suo profitetur plane ex Scripturæ sensu: ubi divinè, ab antiquissima Ecclesiæ memoria, Jobus, quasi cutem ipsam manu tenens: Et postquam cutis mea distrinxerint HOC, etiam & carne mea videbo Deum. Quem ego videbo mihi. Et oculi mei videbunt, & non alius. Job. 19: 26, 27. Atque in eundem modum, eademque emphasi, Apostolus, quasi tristes illas exuvias, quas gerebat, digito monstraret: Oportet enim corruptibile HOC (notandum provocabulum HOC) induere incorruptibilitatem; & mortale HOC induere immortalitatem. 1. Cor. 15: 53. Seritur corpus animale, suscitatur corpus spirituale. com. 43. Omnes enim nos manifestos fieri oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unus quisque reportet quæ in corpore fecerit, congruentur ad id, quod fecerit, sive bonum, sive malum. 2. Cor. 5: 10. Nos ipsi intra nos gemimus, adoptionem expectantes, redemptionem corporis. Rom. 8: 23. Quolibet tempore mortificationem Domini Jesu in corpore circumferentes, ut etiam vita illa Jesu in corpore nostro manifesta fiat. Semper enim nos, qui vivimus, morti tradimur propter Jesum, ut etiam vita Jesu manifesta fiat in corpore nostro mortali. 2. Cor. 4: 10, 11. Ne timete vobis ab iis, qui trucidant corpus, animam autem non possunt trucidare, sed timete potius eum, qui potest & animam, & corpus, perdere in gehenna. Matth. 10: 28. Qui transfigurabit corpus nostrum humile, ut conforme fiat ejus corpori glorioso, fo, provi illa efficace, quapotest etiam subjicere sibi omnia. Phil.3:21.
units.tr: XXIII. The subject of the resurrection, the thing that rises, is the human body. Through sin it has fallen into decay, and it will be raised up and restored from that fall. So the Church, in its creed, plainly professes the resurrection of this same body, and it does so on the sense of Scripture. Job, from the earliest memory of the Church, speaks of it divinely, as if holding the skin itself in his hand: And after my skin has been destroyed in THIS way, yet in my flesh I shall see God. Whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another. Job 19: 26, 27. In the same way, and with the same emphasis, the Apostle, as if pointing with his finger at the sorry remains he was carrying, says: For this corruptible THIS (note the word THIS) must put on incorruption, and this mortal THIS must put on immortality. 1 Cor. 15: 53. The animal body is sown, the spiritual body is raised. ver. 43. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things done in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. 2 Cor. 5: 10. We ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of the body. Rom. 8: 23. At all times bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our body. For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our mortal body. 2 Cor. 4: 10, 11. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Matt. 10: 28. He will transform our lowly body, that it may be conformed to his glorious body, by that working by which he is able also to subject all things to himself. Phil. 3: 21.

units.la: XXIV. Nec turbare nos debet corporei pulveris, quaquaversum dissipati, collectio: aut ejusdem corporis de cineribus suis exfuscitatio, & reconcinnatio: aut denique difficultas illa, quam ab humanis aut inhumanis ἀνθρωποφάγων cibis, & foeda gula, movent; qua integrae nationes caesorum hominum reliquias turpi in alvo condere & digerere solent. 1. Haec omnia enim infinita Dei sapientia & potentia facile expedit. Nihil enim in nihilum evanescit: semperque saltem exiguus cinis, qui novi corporis seminium continet, remanet. Quem, quocunque terrarum sparsum & jactatum, natura saltem gremio ac sinu suo tenet, ac repetenti Deo reddit. Egregie Tertullianus: Non sola anima seponitur. Habet & care suos sinus, in aquis, in ignibus, in alitibus, in bestiis. Cam in hac dissolvi videtur, velut in vasa transfunditur. Si etiam ipsa vasa defecerint, cum de illis quoque effluxerit, in suam matricem terram quasi per ambages resorbetur, ut rursus ex illa repraesentetur.
units.tr: XXIV. Nor should the gathering of bodily dust, scattered in every direction, trouble us, nor the raising and reassembling of the same body out of its ashes. Nor should that difficulty stop us, which people raise about food taken from men or from inhuman man-eaters [ἀνθρωποφάγων] and their foul gluttony, by which whole nations are accustomed to hide and digest the remains of slaughtered men in their filthy bellies. 1. For the infinite wisdom and power of God easily settles all these matters. Nothing is reduced to nothing; at least a tiny ash, which contains the seed of the new body, always remains. Wherever it has been scattered and tossed about on the earth, nature keeps it at least in her bosom and lap, and returns it to God when he calls it back. Tertullian says it well: Not the soul alone is set apart. The flesh too has its own bosoms: in waters, in fires, in birds, in beasts. When it seems to be dissolved in this, it is as if poured into vessels. If even the vessels fail, when it has flowed out of them too, it is reabsorbed, as if by a roundabout route, into its mother earth, so that it may be presented again from her.

units.la: 2. Nec ad ejusdem corporis essentiam necesse est, ut omnes ejus pulvisculi numerentur, & in reformatione ejus reconcinnentur. Sufficit, praecipuas & solidiores partes, de naturae thecis, novo homini re-exhiberi. Nam & quotidie partes alias aut particulas de corpore deperire, accedere alias, & eundem tamen manere hominem, videmus. 3. Nec de ἀνθρωποφάγοις major difficultas est. Cum divina providentia perpetuo pro humana gente excubet; & facile cavere possit, ne de inhumana ista sagina ferorum hominum caro admodum augescat: exiguum enim est, quod de alimentis in substantiam nostram transit: vel additas auctasque, de cibo illo, partes auferre, priorique domino refundere ac redhibere, sine injuria; damnumque illud aliunde resarcire commode potest. In universum autem nasutis illis & sciolis, Salvatoris verbis respondendum est: Erratis, neque Scripturas scientes, neque potentiam Dei. Matth.22:29.
units.tr: 2. Nor is it necessary for the essence of the same body that all its little particles be counted and reassembled at its re-formation. It is enough that its chief and more solid parts be restored to the new man from the sheaths of nature. For we see every day that other parts or particles fall away from the body and others are added, and yet the man remains the same. 3. Nor is there greater difficulty about the man-eaters [ἀνθρωποφάγοις]. Since divine providence keeps constant watch over the human race, it can easily take care that the flesh of men does not greatly increase from the fattening of those savage men. For what passes from food into our substance is a small amount; and the parts added and grown from that food can be removed without harm and given back to their former owner, and that loss can be conveniently made good from elsewhere. In general, however, those keen-nosed and superficial people should be answered with the Savior's words: You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. Matt. 22: 29.

units.la: XXV. Nec audiendae hic Judaeorum sollemnissimae nugationes: idem corpus de officiculo quodam, Luz dicto, renasci; quod incorruptibile ferunt, in novi videl. corporis rudimentum. Sed & novis hominibus, non idem solum corpus, sed eadem corporis deturpati notas, cicatrices, strumas, caecitudinem &c. tribuunt. Ex oraculo videl. Jer. 31:8. Esai. 35:6. Nec vestes omittunt, suetumque cultum. Animas autem corporis demum reconcinnato, & de sepulchro progressio, reddendas ajunt.
units.tr: XXV. Nor should we listen here to the Jews' most solemn trifling: that the same body is reborn from a little bone called Luz, which they say is indestructible, as the beginning of the new body. They say that it is indestructible, as the rudiment of the new body. They also attribute to the new men not only the same body but also the marks of the same deformed body: scars, cicatrices, goiters, blindness, and so on. They appeal, of course, to the oracle of Jer. 31: 8 and Isa. 35: 6. Nor do they leave out clothes and their accustomed dress. They say that souls are returned only when the body has been reassembled and has come forth from the sepulchre.

units.la: Hhhh 3
units.tr: Hhhh 3

units.la: XXVI. Sociniani contra nova hominibus corpora, coelestia plane & spiritualia, post resurrectionem tribuunt. Quomodo & Christum, positis terrenis exuviis, gloriosiori corpore indutum ferunt. Eundemque in modum vivos, in adventu Christi, homines, momento reformandos, & exuta carnea mole pretiosius revestiendos statuunt. Quos errores Apostolica auctoritate jam jugulavimus: Quando autem mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet quod scriptum est, absorpta est mors ad victoriam. 1 Cor. 15: 54. Seritur corpus cum corruptione, excitatur cum incorruptione: seritur corpus animale, suscitatur corpus spirituale. comm. 43, 44. Quae corporum latio, non de generatione naturali (ac si in mundi regeneratione & παλιγγενεσία aliud corpus, quod incorruptibile erit, formandum nobis sit) sed de morte ipsa, & sepulchro, ab Apostolo intelligitur: quod videl., dum cineres & ossa nostra custodit, novi corporis seminium continet, olim Spiritu Dei animandum & vegetandum. Nec tueri illi possunt communem Christianorum fidem, qui in symbolo suo σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν, carnis resurrectionem, profitentur. Pudenda enim detorsio est, carnem appellari, quod caro olim fuit: cum nunc animo & corpore alii homines sint. Ipsa autem caro resurget. Est autem resurrectio, ejus, quod cecidit, de ruina sua reparatio.
units.tr: XXVI. The Socinians, on the other hand, ascribe to men after the resurrection new bodies that are wholly heavenly and spiritual. In the same way they say that Christ, having laid aside his earthly garments, was clothed in a more glorious body. And in the same way they hold that living men, at the coming of Christ, will be changed in a moment, and that, with their fleshly mass cast off, they will be clothed again in something more precious. We have already overthrown these errors by apostolic authority: But when this mortal THIS has put on immortality, then shall come to pass what is written: death is swallowed up in victory. 1 Cor. 15: 54. The body is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption: the animal body is sown, the spiritual body is raised. vers. 43, 44. This change of bodies the Apostle understands not as a natural generation (as if in the regeneration of the world and regeneration [παλιγγενεσία] another body, which will be incorruptible, were to be formed for us), but as coming from death itself and the sepulchre: namely, that while it guards our ashes and bones, it holds the seed of the new body, which is one day to be quickened and enlivened by the Spirit of God. Nor can those who profess in their creed the resurrection of the flesh [σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν], the common faith of Christians, defend those men. For it is a shameful twisting of words to call it flesh because it once was flesh, when now men are other men in both soul and body. But the flesh itself will rise. Resurrection, however, is the restoration of what has fallen from its ruin.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Nec bene obtendunt errori suo verba Apostolica, Caro & sanguis non hareditabunt regnum Dei. 1. Cor. 15: 50. Explicat enim ea Apostolus proximis verbis, neque corruptibile hereditabit incorruptibilitatem. Ut non de carnis substantia ac mole, sed de vita hac animali & fugaci agatur; quae sanguinis ac spirituum meatu absolvitur; quae ubi leves in auras exhalarunt, etiam corpus hoc in vagum pulverem fatiscit. Quae mortalis corporis conditio mutanda dicitur, carni hac nostra gloriosiorem in modum reformata, & a Dei Spiritu animata, ac immortali vigore praedita. Qualis corporum status etiam in statu innocentiae ex parte obtinuisset. Nisi quod nunc etiam & venter, & esca, abolebuntur. 1 Cor. 6: 13. Non quod non extitura sint: nam corpora nostra, & membra (christi), etiam post resurrectionem, appellantur, com. 14, 15. verum quod non ad fragilem istum usum, sed ad corporum decus & integritatem solum supererunt. Quales & hodie videmus virili in corpore mammas, quae tamen lacteum rorem non fundunt. Atque ita filii resurrectionis ἰσάγγελοι à Christo appellantur. Luc. 20: 36. Non quod corporum molem iis abroget, sed quod vitae terrestris conditionem & officia, ac praepræsertim conjugii usum tum cessaturum velit: cum in cœlo non sit Angelus & Angela, ut non nemo veterum. Unde & sanguinis ac spirityum anomalos cursus, & temulentos istos impetus, quæ cupiditatum ardorem, aut procupidinem saltem ciere solent, castigandos ac cohibendos admodum probabile est.
units.tr: Nor do the words of the Apostle, "Flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God" (1 Cor. 15:50), serve well as a cover for their error. For the Apostle explains them in the words that follow, "neither does the corruptible inherit incorruption." So the passage is not about the substance and bulk of the flesh, but about this animal and fleeting life, which is sustained by the flow of blood and the spirits, and which, once it has breathed out into the thin air, leaves this body to crumble into wandering dust. This mortal condition is said to be changed, the flesh being reformed in a far more glorious manner, animated by the Spirit of God and endowed with immortal vigour. Such would have been the state of bodies, in part, even in the state of innocence, except that now even the belly and food will be abolished (1 Cor. 6:13). Not that they will cease to exist, for our "bodies" and "members" (of Christ) are still called so after the resurrection (vv. 14, 15). Rather, they will survive not for that fragile use but only for the beauty and integrity of the bodies. We see something similar today in a man's body, where the breasts do not pour out milk. And so the sons of the resurrection are called "equal to the angels" (ἰσάγγελοι) by Christ (Luke 20:36).
