Not that he takes away the bulk of their bodies, but that he means the condition and duties of earthly life, and especially the use of marriage, will then cease, since in heaven there is neither angel nor angeless, as one of the ancients said. Hence it is quite probable that the irregular courses of the blood and spirits, and those intoxicated impulses which are wont to stir up the heat of desire or at least lust, should be restrained and curbed.

units.la: XXVIII. Paria cum Socinianis errant Anabaptistæ, qui etiam corpus gloriosum de corporeo naturæ, ac proprietatum, abdicatione intelligunt. Ad exemplum videl. Christi. Quod fundamentum falsum est. Cum ille post mortem non corpus solum idem, sed & eadem corporis notas & cicatrices, ostenderit. Nec alio in corpore triumphum suum in cœlis auspicatus fuerit. Unde & eodem in corpore rursus mortalibus videbitur. Act. 21 1: Sic Jesus revertetur, quemadmodum ipsum vidistis abeuntem in cœlum.
units.tr: XXVIII. The Anabaptists err on the same lines as the Socinians, for they also understand the glorious body to mean the renunciation of the bodily nature and its properties, taking the example of Christ as their basis. That foundation is false, since after his death he showed not only the same body but also the same marks and scars of the body. Nor did he begin his triumph in heaven in any other body. Hence in the same body he will be seen again by mortals: "Jesus will return in the same way as you saw him going into heaven" (Acts 1:11).

units.la: XXIX. Nec multum abludunt Remonstrantes: qui ita quæstionem hanc elevant, & inter curiosas referunt, ut tamen non obscure in Apologia involutam animi sui notionem explicent, dum in futura vita corpus non admodum necessarium fore statuunt.
units.tr: XXIX. The Remonstrants do not differ much either. They so lift up this question and count it among the curious matters, yet in their Apology they explain plainly enough the notion of their mind, which they have wrapped up, when they hold that in the future life the body will not be very necessary.

units.la: XXX. Etsi autem corpus nostrum substantia idem, gloria tamen diversum erit. Quod Apostolus aperte docet. 1.Cor. 15: 42, 43,44. Seritur corpus cum corruptione, excitatur cum incorruptione, seritur cum ignominia, excitatur cum gloria: seritur cum infirmitate, excitatur cum potentia: seritur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale. Spirituale autem appellat, non quoad substantiam, vel quod, aerei instar corporis, non visui aut tactui humano amplius patebit. Sed quod, nullo terreno pondere degravatum ac depressum, Spiritum S. rectorem habebit, certissimum immortalitatis ducem (qua in parte ad famulantium Deo mentium naturam proxime accedet) & ductui ejus per omnia subjicietur, extincto quicquid hactenus in sanguine ac spiritibus turbidum ac incompositum. Hæc enim Spiritui S. adscribuntur. Vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per spiritum suum in vobis habitantem. Rom. 8: 11. Ut perperam Socinian, Anabaptistæ, & Weigeliani, corpora spiritualia de corporibus carne & sanguine carentibus, in futuro sæculo, intelligant. Quibus Ubiquitistæ & Scholastici præterea affingunt, illa quoque dimensionibus & spatio caritura. Quomodo ne corpora quidem erunt. Quæ somnia ex Origenistarum schola primum prodierunt.
units.tr: XXX. Although our body will be the same in substance, it will nonetheless be different in glory, as the Apostle plainly teaches: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Cor. 15:42–44). He calls it spiritual not with respect to its substance, nor because, like a body of air, it will no longer be open to human sight or touch, but because, weighed down and pressed by no earthly load, it will have the Holy Spirit as its guide, the most certain leader to immortality (in which respect it will come very near to the nature of minds that serve God), and it will be subject to his leading in all things, with whatever has hitherto been turbid and disordered in blood and spirits extinguished. For these things are ascribed to the Holy Spirit: "He will also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit dwelling in you" (Rom. 8:11). So the Socinians, Anabaptists and Weigelians wrongly understand spiritual bodies to be bodies lacking flesh and blood in the age to come. To these the Ubiquitarians and the Schoolmen add further that such bodies will also lack dimensions and space, which would mean they will not even be bodies. These dreams first came out of the school of the Origenists.

units.la: XXXI. Ad quæstionem de sexus discrimine, de quo sibi metuebant veterum nonnulli; ne iterum de Paradisi possessione hominem mulier detur baret: nos eum ad corporum decus & integritatem pertinere judicamus. Sicut & Christus, occasione alioquin oblata, non negavit jum, sed astruxit potius. Non enim affectionem ipsam, sed sexus usum tantum sustulit; cum non alia hominum, quam Angelorum tum respubl. futura sit. In resurrectione enim, neque uxores ducunt neque nuptum dantur, sed sunt ut Angeli Dei in coelo. Matth. 22: 30.
units.tr: XXXI. As to the question of the distinction of sex, which some of the ancients feared might once again lead a woman to deceive man about possession of Paradise, we judge that it pertains to the beauty and integrity of the bodies. So too Christ, when the occasion was offered, did not deny it but rather confirmed it. For he took away not the affection itself but only the use of sex, since the future state of men will be no different from that of the angels: "In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven" (Matt. 22:30).

units.la: XXXII. Corporis mensuram & modum male quidam ad dominici corporis staturam exigunt, eamque omnibus aequalem statuunt. Ex loci Paulini πλήρωμα. Eph. 4: 13. Nos justum & decorum, qualis perfectae aetatis est, quamvis non aequalem omnibus, corporis habitum statuimus. Qualis & Adamo ante lapsum contigit.
units.tr: XXXII. Some wrongly fit the measure and size of the body to the stature of the Lord's body, and make it equal for all, from Paul's word "fullness" (πλήρωμα, Eph. 4:13). We hold that the body will have a proper and fitting condition, such as belongs to a perfect age, though not equal for all, as also happened to Adam before the fall.

units.la: XXXIII. Causa resurrectionis est solus Deus: Qui suscitavit Dominum Jesum, nos quoque per Jesum suscitabit, & sistet vobiscum.
units.tr: XXXIII. The sole cause of the resurrection is God: "He who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also by Jesus, and will present us with you" (2 Cor. 4:14).

units.la: 2. Cor. 4: 14. Ac speciatim Jesus Christus: Dixit ipse Jesus, ego sum resurrectio, & vita. Joh. 11: 25. Cui, non omnipotentiae solum, sed & meriti ratione, divinum illud opus tribuitur. Nam ad mediationis officium illud necessario pertinet. Unde electos de mortis specu liberabit, tanquam vindex, & redemtor eorum: Sane ego novi, quod vindex meus vivit, & postremus super pulverem stabit. Job. 19: 25. Sicut enim omnes in Adamo moriuntur, ita & omnes in Christo vivificabuntur.
units.tr: And specifically Jesus Christ: "Jesus himself said, I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). To him that divine work is attributed, not only by reason of his omnipotence but also by reason of his merit, for it necessarily belongs to the office of mediation. Hence he will free the elect from the cave of death, as their avenger and redeemer: "For I know that my avenger lives, and he will stand last upon the dust" (Job 19:25). "For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Cor. 15:22). This resurrection is life, the chief benefit of the Mediator: "All who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life" (John 5:28, 29). "The last Adam became a life-giving Spirit" (1 Cor. 15:45). As a just judge, he will drag the reprobate from their hiding places and lead them back to life for punishment.

units.la: 1. Cor. 15: 22. Quae resurrectio vitae est, praecipuum mediatoris beneficium: Omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus; & prodibunt, qui bona fecerint, in resurrectionem vitae. Joh. 5: 28, 29. Posterior Adam factus est in Spiritum vivificantem. 1. Cor. 15: 45. Reprobos auten, ut justus judex, de latibulis suis eruet, & redivivos ad supplicium producet.
units.tr: XXXIV. In this respect the resurrection of the godly and of the ungodly is distinguished, not only by the different end and outcome of each, but also by the very kind of resurrection and its causes. For the godly will not rise by the power and auspices of Christ our head, for that resurrection is only saving and pertains to the elect alone. Rather, the ungodly will be dragged to the tribunal of Christ the judge, summoned there.

units.la: XXXIV. Quo in genere piorum & impiorum resurrectio discreta est: non solum diverso utriusque fine & exitu; sed & ipso genere, ac causis suis. Nec enim illi Christi capitis nostri virtute ac auspicio resurgent. Illa enim non nisi salutaris est; & ad solos electos pertinet. Sed a Christo judice invitati ad ejus tribunal rapientur.
units.tr: XXXV. In Christ, however, each of his natures must be considered here. By his divine nature, with an omnipotent word and command, he will gather the scattered ashes and the decayed dust from the bosom of nature and restore them to life by infusing the spirit, "by his power, by which he subjects all things to himself" (Phil. 3:21). By his human nature he has become not only the pattern and sample of the resurrection for mortals, but also, as Lord of the Church and of the world, he will appear in a circle of air, supported and adorned by a heavenly retinue.

units.la: XXXV. In Christo autem utraque ejus natura hic spectanda est. Qua Deus, omnipotente voce ac jussu sparsos cineres, & lopitum pulverem, de naturae sinu recolliget, & infuso spiritu redanimabit; Per omnipotentiam suam, qua sibi omnia subjecit. Phil. 3: 21. Qua homo autem, non solum ipse resurrectionis exemplar & specimen mortalibus factus est; verum etiam, ut Ecclesiae ac mundi Dominus, aerio in gyro apapparebit, cœlesti satellitio suffultus & exornatus.
units.tr: XXXV. In Christ, however, both of his natures must be considered here. As God, by his almighty voice and command, he will gather the scattered ashes and the dust laid to sleep from the bosom of nature, and will restore them to life by breathing in the spirit: By his power, by which he subjects all things to himself. Phil. 3: 21. As man, he has not only been made himself the pattern and specimen of resurrection for mortals, but also, as Lord of the Church and of the world, he will appear in the air, attended and adorned by a heavenly retinue.

units.la: XXXVI. Instrumentalis causa recreationis hujus dari non magis potest, quam primæva creationis: nisi quod in iis, quæ resurrectionem antecedent & consequentur, Angelorum ministerium locum habebit. Et mittet angelos suos — congregabunt electos ejus, à quatuor ventis. Matth. 24: 31.
units.tr: XXXVI. The instrumental cause of this re-creation can be no more given than that of the first creation, except that in the things which precede and follow the resurrection, the ministry of the angels will have a place. And he shall send his angels ... and they shall gather his elect from the four winds. Matth. 24: 31.

units.la: XXXVII. Locus, ubi generis humani reliquiæ reparandæ erunt, non erit peculiaris aliqua in terris regio. Uti de Palæstina Judæi fabulantur, cui hoc decus asserunt, in isto terrarum angulo gentem humanam, uti primum fictam, ita, labentibus sæculis, denuo refictam iri. Atque hanc rationem dant, cur Patriarchæ olim tanto desiderio in felici ista gleba humari desiderarunt. Quod tamen alias causas habuit. Reliquos autem Israelitas, quibus istam Corinthum, sive Hierosolymam, adire non contigit, per cæcos terræ meatus & cavernas, non sine dolore, eò devolvendos statuunt. Quas tamen fabulas hodierni Judæi verecundantur; & communem per universum orbem, quanquam non universalem, nec omnium hominum, resurrectionem statuunt. Nos, uti universum genus humanum de ruina sua suscitatum iri credimus; ita toto, qua patet, orbe, de monumentis suis mortuos prodituros; & mare, tellurem cunctaque elementa, quibus cineris nostri custodia credita est, fidem servatura, deque thecis suis generis humani pulverem redditura, affirmamus. Et mittet angelos suos — & congregabunt electos ejus à quatuor ventis. Matth. 24: 31. conf. Apoc. 20: 13.
units.tr: XXXVII. The place where the remnants of the human race are to be restored will not be any particular region on earth. The Jews fable about Palestine, which they claim has this honour, that in that corner of the earth the human race, first fashioned, will again be fashioned anew as the ages slip by. And they give this as the reason why the patriarchs long ago so earnestly desired to be buried in that happy soil, though they had other reasons too. The remaining Israelites, who have not been able to go to that Corinth, or Jerusalem, they claim will be carried down there through blind passages and caverns of the earth, not without pain. Yet today's Jews are ashamed of these fables, and they hold to a resurrection common to the whole world, though not universal, nor of all men. We, however, believe that the entire human race will be raised from its ruin, and we affirm that, throughout the whole extent of the world, the dead will come forth from their tombs; and that the sea, the earth, and all the elements, to whose keeping our ashes have been entrusted, will keep faith and return the dust of the human race from their repositories. And he shall send his angels ... and they shall gather his elect from the four winds. Matth. 24: 31. Compare Apoc. 20: 13.

units.la: XXXVIII. Tempus resurrectionis indicare, non est nostrum. Cum Christus affirmet, de die autem illo & hora nemo scit: ne Angeli quidem cœlorum. Sed Pater meus solus. Matth. 24: 36. Hoc tamen certum est, uno eodemque tempore eam peractum iri, ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῆ ὀφθαλμοῦ, momentaneo quasi oculi motu, 1 Cor. 15: 52. unoquoque tamen in suo τάγματι, ac statione quasi, constituto. Qui mortui fuerint in Christo, resurgent primum. Deinde nos vivi, qui reliqui erimus, rapiemur simul cum iis in nubes, in occursum Domini in aëra. 1 Thess. 4: 16, 17
units.tr: XXXVIII. It is not for us to determine the time of the resurrection. Since Christ affirms, "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only" (Matt. 24:36), it is nevertheless certain that it will be accomplished at one and the same time, ἐν ἀτόμῳ [in an atom, that is, in an indivisible moment], ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ [in the twinkling of an eye], by a movement, as it were, momentary as the eye (1 Cor. 15:52); yet each will be placed in his own order [τάγμα] and, as it were, his own station. "The dead in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thess. 4:16, 17).

units.la: XXXIX. Ut perperam Chiliastæ duplicem fingant resurrectionem, quarum prior mille annis præcessura sit alteram. Quod ex perverso Johannæ phrasis, in sacra Apocalypsi, intellectu ortum duxit. Apoc. 20: 6. de quo supra.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Chiliasts wrongly imagine a twofold resurrection, of which the first is to precede the other by a thousand years. This arose from a mistaken understanding of John's phrasing in the sacred Apocalypse (Rev. 20:6), concerning which see above.

units.la: XL. Judæi quoque veteres duplicem confingebant resurrectionem; particularem, quæ temporibus Messiæ continget, & universa-lem, lem, in fine mundi. A qua traditione recentiores magistri, nimia Messiae sui mora decepti, nunc abeunt; omniaque, & ipsum quoque Messiae adventum, prae desperatione, ad finem mundi rejiciunt, & confundunt. Justo equidem Dei judicio Messiam ad judicium exercendum tantum expectantes, quem ad salvandum venientem amplecti olim noluerunt.
units.tr: XL. The ancient Jews also devised a twofold resurrection: a particular one, which would occur in the times of the Messiah, and a universal one at the end of the world. The more recent teachers, deceived by the long delay of their Messiah, now abandon this tradition; and, out of despair, they push everything, including the very coming of the Messiah, back to the end of the world and confuse it all. Rightly, by the just judgment of God, they expect the Messiah only to exercise judgment, whom they refused to embrace when he came to save.

units.la: XLI. Nos, missis fabulis, quas audacius hoc in argumento, utpote, de re futura, tanquam in tenebris conisicantes, pronunt hi homines, mortuorum resurrectionem pro praecipuo Christianae fidei capite ac fulcimento habemus: itaque spe corpus hoc nostrum, quod tantae claritudinis particeps olim futurum est, sancte & reverenter habemus; & membra nostra, quae membra Christi appellat Apostolus, pro armis & instrumento justitiae offerenda novimus. Glorificate Deum in corpore vestro, & spiritu vestro. Quae sunt Dei. 1 Cor. 6: 20. Rom. 6: 13. Morbos autem, & cruciatus, ac mortem ipsam, hoc pignore contemnere jubemur: cum ignavum sit, redituræ parcere vitae; ac martyrum potius imitanda sit constantia, quibus follemne erat tormenta spernere praesentia, ne incurrerent in futura; & dum mori post mortem timebant, interim mori non timere. Ut est apud Minucium. Defunctorum autem jacturam moderate, & Christianum in modum, ferre docemur. Cum, post crudam hanc hyemem, expectandum quoque corporum ver sit; quo in beatam vitam reflorescent, qui nunc, caduci ad instar floris, emarcuerunt. Nolim autem vos ignorantia versari, fratres, quod ad eos attinet, qui obdormierunt, ut ne contristemini, sicut & reliqui, qui spem non habent. Nam si credimus, Jesum mortuum esse, & resurrexisse, ita et iam Deus eos, qui obdormierunt in Jesu, adducet cum eo. 1. Thess. 4: 13, 14.
units.tr: XLI. We, setting aside the fables which these men, more boldly in this matter because it concerns a future thing, devise as if groping in the dark, hold the resurrection of the dead as the chief article and mainstay of the Christian faith. Therefore, in hope, we hold this body of ours, which is one day to share in such great glory, as holy and to be reverenced; and we know that our members, which the Apostle calls the members of Christ, are to be offered as weapons and instruments of righteousness. "Glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's" (1 Cor. 6:20; Rom. 6:13). By this pledge we are commanded to despise diseases, torments and death itself, since it would be cowardly to spare a life that is to be restored; and rather the constancy of the martyrs is to be imitated, who customarily scorned present torments so as not to fall into future ones, and, while they feared to die after death, meanwhile did not fear to die. So it is in Minucius. We are taught to bear the loss of the dead with moderation and in a Christian manner: since, after this harsh winter, the spring of the bodies must also be awaited, in which those who now have withered, like fallen flowers, will bloom again into blessed life. "But I would not have you ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, that you should not grieve, as the others do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus" (1 Thess. 4:13, 14).

units.la: CAPUT XXIII
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII

units.la: De JUDICIO EXTREMO.
units.tr: On the LAST JUDGMENT.

units.la: I. Ortuorum resurrectionem excipit judicium extremum. De cujus tum veritate ac certitudine, tum forma ac modo, denique circumstantiis, agemus.
units.tr: I. The resurrection of the dead is followed by the last judgment. We shall treat of its truth and certainty, then of its form and manner, and finally of its circumstances.

units.la: II. Descendet autem Christus, ad censuram generis humani agendam, cum celeusmate, & voce Archangeli. Illa tuba vivorum, haec mortuorum auribus insonabit, omnesque mortales ad tribunal ejus congregabit. 1. Theff. 4: 16. Quemadmodum nunquam in Scriptura descendisse Deus, nisi ad judicandos homines, legitur.
units.tr: II. Christ will come down to hold the judgment of the human race with a shout and the voice of the archangel. That trumpet will sound in the ears of the living and of the dead, and will gather all mortals before his tribunal (1 Thess. 4:16). In Scripture it is read that God never came down except to judge men.

units.la: III. Locus, unde descensurus exspectatur, est coelum (quod contra Ubiquitarios servandum) ex quo iterum in terras redux, summa cum majestate ac gloria, universum mundum judicabit. In quo secundus ejus adventus à primo differt. Ille enim humilis, hic gloriosus erit: in illo hominem, hic Deum fatebitur: in illo, falsus reus, ab hominibus judicatus est, hic ipse homines omnes judicabit. Quem duplicem adventum dum Judæi distinguere non norunt, atque unum tantum Messiæ adventum credunt, in potestate & gloria, à Messia suo aberrarunt. Vide Phil. 3: 20. Nostra autem civitas in cœlis est; unde & Salvatorem expectamus Dominum Christum, 2 Thess. 1: 7.— In revelatione Domini Jesu, à cœlo, cum Angelis potentia sua. Matth. 24: 26, 27. Si dixerint vobis, ecce in deserto est, ne egredimini: ecce in cubiculo, ne credite. Sicut enim fulgur exit ab Oriente, & lucet usque ad Occidentem, sic etiam erit adventus filii hominis. Act. 1: 11. Hic Jesus revertetur, quemadmodum ipsum vidistis abeuntem in cœlum. Apoc. 1: 7. Ecce venit cum nubibus, & videbit eum omnis oculus, & qui eum transfixerunt.
units.tr: III. The place from which he is expected to descend is heaven (which must be maintained against the Ubiquitarians). From there he will return to earth and judge the whole world with great majesty and glory. In this his second coming differs from the first. The first was humble, the second will be glorious: in the first he was judged by men, falsely accused; in the second he will judge all men himself. The Jews, not knowing how to distinguish these two comings, and believing in only one coming of the Messiah, in power and glory, went astray from their Messiah. See Phil. 3:20: Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Saviour, the Lord Christ (2 Thess. 1:7). At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven, with his mighty angels (Matt. 24:26, 27): If they say to you, Behold, he is in the desert, do not go out; behold, he is in the inner room, do not believe it. For as the lightning comes out of the east and shines to the west, so also will the coming of the Son of Man be. (Acts 1:11): This Jesus will come again in the same way as you saw him go into heaven. (Rev. 1:7): Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him, and those who pierced him.

units.la: IX. Erit autem judicium hoc non particulare, aut occultum; quomodo facto veluti præjudicio, nonnunquam in terris sese re-gnare ostendit, fulminisque sui strictuum gentes territat; sed publicum ac universale totius generis humani. Unde Judicium æternum dicitur. Hebr. 6: 2.
units.tr: IX. This judgment will not be particular or hidden, as that judgment which, like a kind of foretaste, sometimes shows itself to reign on earth and terrifies the nations with the stroke of its lightning. It will be public and universal for the whole human race. Hence it is called the eternal judgment (Heb. 6:2).

units.la: V. Cumque tria istius generis judicia legamus. Primum, in Paradiso in generis humani parentes; alterum in mundum ante-diluvianum; tertium in societatem humanam, ad Babylonicum scelus, in campis Sinear, congregatum, editum: hocce erit quartum & ultimum. Idque non in vivos solum, ut priora illa, sed etiam in mortuos, adeoque universalissimum.
units.tr: V. We read of three judgments of this kind: the first in Paradise, upon the parents of the human race; the second upon the world before the Flood; the third upon the human society gathered in the plains of Shinar for the Babylonian crime and scattered abroad. This will be the fourth and last. And it will be directed not only at the living, as those earlier ones were, but also at the dead, and so it will be the most universal of all.

units.la: VI. Judicialis ac decretorii istius diei certitudinem probant: 1. Scripturarum oracula. Eo quod statuit diem, quo judicaturus est habitabilem in justitia. Act. 17: 31. Quodcunque verbum otiosum locuti fuerint homines, de eo reddituri sunt rationem in die judicii. Matth. 12: 36. Adde Matth. 13: 41, 42, 43. & 25: 31. & seq. 1 Cor. 4: 5. & 1: 8. 2 Cor. 5: 10. Hebr. 9: 27. 2. Pet. 3: 12. Jud. com. 6. 14, 15. Apoc. 1: 7. Eccl. 12: 1, 16. Psal. 50. aliaque loca.
units.tr: VI. They prove the certainty of this judicial and decisive day: 1. By the oracles of the Scriptures: "because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the inhabited world in righteousness" (Acts 17:31); "for every careless word that men speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment" (Matt. 12:36). Add Matt. 13:41, 42, 43; 25:31ff.; 1 Cor. 4:5; 1:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Heb. 9:27; 2 Pet. 3:12; Jude 14, 15; Rev. 1:7; Eccl. 12:1, 16; Ps. 50, and other passages.

units.la: VII. 2. Ratio, à providentia, ac justitia Dei deducta; quæ vel sanioribus Ethnicis hoc persuasit, & divinam Nemesim expectare coëgit. Cum enim in terris bonorum malorumque fata commixta, & rerum vices confusæ sint; & pii sere sint calamitosissimi, impii autem læti ac florentes; equidem tempus olim venire necesse est, quo Deus piorum impiorumque delectum agat, & res humanas emendet, seque ipsum & providentiam suam absolvat. Si quidem iustum est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem.
units.tr: VII. 2. By an argument drawn from the providence and justice of God. This convinced even the wiser heathens and made them look for a divine Nemesis. For since the fortunes of good and evil are mixed together on earth and the course of events is confused, and since the godly are for the most part most miserable while the wicked are happy and flourishing, it must surely be that a time will come when God will separate the pious from the impious, set human affairs right, and vindicate himself and his providence. For it is indeed just before God to repay affliction to those who afflict you (2 Thess. 1:6).

units.la: 2 Thess. 1: 6. Dixit autem Abrahamus: Fili, memento, te bona tua recepisse in vita tua, & Lazarum similiter mala. Nunc autem hic solamen recipit; tu vero cruciaris. Luc. 16: 23. Eccles. 11: 12, 13.
units.tr: But Abraham said, "Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted here, and you are tormented" (Luke 16:23). See Eccl. 11:12, 13.

units.la: VIII. 3. Accedit & mundi ratio. Si enim nec domus ulla, nec cœtus, nec civitas, sine judiciis ac disciplina stare potest: multo minus hæc rerum universitas, & generis humani multitudo; quæ Deum, uti rectorem, ita & judicem, habet.
units.tr: VIII. 3. Add an argument from the order of the world. If no house, no assembly, and no city can stand without judgments and discipline, much less can this whole universe of things and the multitude of the human race stand, which has God as its ruler and therefore as its judge.

units.la: IX. 4. Denique & conscientia uniuscujusque huic judicio suffragatur: quæ, dum Christus abest, & mundi fata cunctantur, vicario in homines judicio perfungitur. Qui ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, contestificante ipsorum conscientia, & inter se invicem cogitationibus accusantibus, vel etiam defendentibus. Rom. 2: 14, 15. Hinc & Gentilium, non poëtarum solum carminibus, sed & in philosophorum libris, celebratæ sententiæ; quæ vel de prisco Patriarcharum dogmate adumbratæ, vel de naturæ luce redacensæ, veritatem de invitis pectoribus erumpentem testatæ sunt. Quo majori impietate Epicurei & ἐμπαίκται, Christi judicis reditum secure contemnunt & irrident. Effer te, judex terra; redde, quod meriti sunt superbi — Animadvertite obrutissimi in populo; & stultissimi, quando intelligentes eritis? an plantator auris non audiat? aut formator oculi an non intueatur? An castigator gentium, an non reprehendat? qui docet homines scientiam an non agnoscerct? Psal. 94: 2. &c. 2 Petr. 3: 4.
units.tr: IX. 4. Finally, the conscience of each person also supports this judgment. While Christ is absent and the fates of the world are delayed, conscience carries out a judgment on men by proxy. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another (Rom. 2:14, 15). Hence also the sayings of the Gentiles, celebrated not only in the songs of poets but also in the books of philosophers, which either were foreshadowed by the ancient doctrine of the patriarchs or were drawn from the light of nature, bear witness to a truth that breaks out from unwilling hearts. The more impiously the Epicureans and the mockers [ἐμπαίκται] carelessly scorn and deride the return of Christ the judge. Lift yourself up, judge of the earth; render to the proud what they deserve. Consider, you most senseless among the people, and you fools, when will you understand? Shall he who planted the ear not hear? Or he who formed the eye not see? Shall he who chastises the nations not rebuke? He who teaches men knowledge, does he not know? (Ps. 94:2, etc.; 2 Pet. 3:4).

units.la: X. Judex erit universa Trinitas, auctoritate ac potestate; speciatim autem Christus, visibili judicatura ac imperio. Quod ipsi judicium à Patre traditum dicitur. Matth. 28: 18. Act. 10: 42. & 17: 31. Joh. 5: 22, 27. utpote Ecclesiæ Regi; & electorum suorum vindici; ac impiorum & refractariorum ultori severissimo. Quorum hoc gratiæ est, illud potentiæ. Utrumque autem ad mediationis munus pertinet.
units.tr: X. The judge will be the whole Trinity in authority and power; but Christ in particular will judge visibly and rule. It is said that this judgment has been handed over to him by the Father (Matt. 28:18; Acts 10:42; 17:31; John 5:22, 27), as King of the Church, the avenger of his elect, and the most severe punisher of the wicked and the rebellious. The one belongs to grace, the other to power. Both pertain to the office of mediation.

units.la: XI. Atque ille quidem secundùm utramque naturam actu illo perfungetur. Qua homo, visibili majestate, in nubibus, tanquam in tribunali, conspicuus. Et potestatem dedit ipsi etiam judicium faciendi, quia filius hominis est. Joh. 5:27. Sic Jesus revertetur, quemadmodum ipsum vidistis abeuntem in coelum. Act. 1:11. Apoc. 1:7. Qua Deus, coelesti auctoritate, ac imperio, & sapientia, ad cordium secreta & tenebras perrimandas; sententiamque de genere humano pronunciandam; eamque sine ulla provocatione exequendam.
units.tr: XI. He will exercise this function indeed according to both natures. As man, he will be seen in visible majesty, in the clouds, as if on a tribunal: And he has given him authority also to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27). This Jesus will come again in the same way as you saw him go into heaven (Acts 1:11; Rev. 1:7). As God, by heavenly authority, rule, and wisdom, he will search out the secrets and darkness of hearts, pronounce sentence on the human race, and carry it out without any appeal.

units.la: XII. Blasphemant enim Sociniani, & supremum ejus judicium negant; eum enim pro judice delegato tantum habent, qui instar tabellionis ac interpretis, ex auctoritate Patris, de mundo sententiam laturus sit. Quo perperam adducunt Joh. 5:22,23. Neque enim Pater judicat quenquam, sed judicium omne dedit filio, ut omnes honorent filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem, & com. 30. Non possum ego a me ipso facere quicquam: prout audio, judico: & judicium meum justum est; quia non quaero voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me, id est, Patris. Ea enim loca contrarium potius probant: & de summa ac individua ejus cum Patre unitate, & supremae judicaturae honore, ab hominibus ipsis agnoscendo, agunt.
units.tr: XII. The Socinians blaspheme and deny this supreme judgment of his. They regard him only as a judge delegated, who, like a notary or interpreter, will pronounce sentence on the world by the authority of the Father. In doing so they wrongly cite John 5:22, 23: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father; and verse 30: I can do nothing of my own accord; as I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me, that is, the Father. Those passages prove rather the opposite, and deal with his supreme and undivided unity with the Father, and with the honour of supreme judgeship, which men themselves must acknowledge.

units.la: XIII. Neque minus idem, in eodem judicio, fidelium, ac electi gregis, advocatum; & impiorum, ac reprobae gentis, accusatorem, ac adversarium severissimum aget. Nec ulla illi excusatione adversus eum tueri sese poterunt. Vide Matth. 25, Job. 19:25. Equidem novi redemtorem meum vivere; & posteriorem super pulverem resurrecturum. & 33:23. Si propinqua sit fovea animae ejus, & vita ejus lethalibus malis: & adsit einuncius, interpres, unus ex mille — & dicet, redime eum, ne descendat in foveam, expiationem inveni. Rom. 8:34. Qui etiam interpellat pro nobis.
units.tr: XIII. Likewise, in the same judgment, he will act as advocate for the faithful and the elect flock, and as the most severe accuser and adversary of the impious and the rebellious race. And they will be unable to defend themselves against him with any excuse. See Matt. 25; Job 19:25: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he will rise last upon the dust; and Job 33:23, 24: If there be near his soul a pit, and his life to deadly evils, and there is with him a messenger, an interpreter, one of a thousand, and he says, "Redeem him, that he may not go down into the pit, I have found a ransom"; Rom. 8:34: who also intercedes for us.

units.la: XIV. Judicii satellites ac apparitores erunt Angeli: quorum judiciiministri opera utetur Dominus, tum in congregandis hominibus, tum in illidem segregandis. Et mittet angelos suos — & congregabunt electos Angeli suos a quatuor ventis. Matth. 24:31. Ita erit in consummatione saeculi. Prodibunt Angeli, & separabunt improbos e medio justorum. Matth. 13:49. 1 Thess. 4:16.
units.tr: XIV. The angels will be the attendants and officers of the judgment; the Lord will use the service of these ministers of judgment both in gathering men together and in separating them. "And he shall send his angels, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds." Matt. 24:31. "So shall it be at the end of the world. The angels shall come forth and separate the wicked from the midst of the just." Matt. 13:49. 1 Thess. 4:16.

units.la: XV. Adsessores aliqua ex parte creduntur futuri Apostoli, & sancti homines. Verum duodecim illi Apostolorum throni, atque illa duodecim tribuum judicatura, quae ipsis tribuitur, Matth. 19:28. Luc. 22:30. potius figurate de doctrina illorum accipi debet; per quam illi, postascensionem Christi, terram Israelis veluti Apostolis anathemate percusserunt. Sancti autem impropriè mundum judicaturi creduntur, 1 Cor. 6:2,3. tum quatenus Christi Judicis membra sunt, cum eo ut cum capite suo coadunata: tum assensu suo, & sententiæ à Christo latæ suffragio: tum fidei ac charitatis, in terris præstitæ, exemplo; ac facto in improbos veluti præjudicio: denique uti sententia Christi ultima palam absolvendi; quæ revera reliqui orbis, qui ipsis hactenus insultavit, erit condemnatio. Sed cum revera nullibi Christo assessuri, sed omnes coram tribunali ipsius staturi in Scriptura legamur, tam oves, quam hirci, Matt. 25:31–33. 2 Cor. 5:10. rectius forte hæc accipiuntur non de judicio extremo, sed de judicio & imperio populo sanctorum Altissimorum in hoc sæculo promisso: de quo Dan. 7:18, 27. & com. 10. Judicium consedit. Quod & ad scopum Apostoli proxime facit.
units.tr: XV. In some respect the saints are believed to be future assessors, as are the apostles. But those twelve thrones of the apostles, and that judgment of the twelve tribes which is attributed to them, Matt. 19:28; Luc. 22:30, ought rather to be understood figuratively, of their teaching, through which, after Christ's ascension, they struck the land of Israel as with a curse, as it were. The saints, however, are believed to judge the world improperly, 1 Cor. 6:2,3: partly insofar as they are members of Christ the Judge, united with him as with their head; partly by their assent and their approval of the sentence pronounced by Christ; partly as an example, in the faith and love they showed on earth, and as a kind of prior judgment upon the wicked by their deeds; and finally, as the final sentence of Christ openly acquitting them, which in truth will be the condemnation of the rest of the world that has hitherto insulted them. But since we read in Scripture that all, both sheep and goats, will stand before his tribunal, and not that they will sit with Christ, Matt. 25:31–33; 2 Cor. 5:10, these words are perhaps more rightly taken not of the final judgment but of the judgment and rule of the people of the Most High promised in this age, concerning which see Dan. 7:18, 27, and the commentary on verse 10, "the judgment was set." This also bears most directly on the apostle's purpose.

units.la: XVI. Ad judicium autem spectant omnes, cum persona, tum causa.
units.tr: XVI. All, however, both persons and causes, belong to the judgment.

units.la: Ad personas pertinent etiam Angeli mali, è custodia sua tum producendi, & publice, inspectante genere humano, cui tam diu illuserunt, condemnandi. Nam si Deus Angelis, qui peccaverant, non pepercit; sed in tartarum detrusos catenis caliginis traditi servatos ad judicium. 2 Pet. 2:4. Angelos – ad judicium magnæ diei, vinculis æternis sub caligine servavit. Jud. com. 6. Matth. 25:41. Loci 1 Cor. 6:3. paulo alia ratio esse videtur.
units.tr: The persons include also the evil angels, who are to be brought out of their prison and condemned publicly, with the human race looking on, whom they have so long deceived. "For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down into hell and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment." 2 Pet. 2:4. "The angels ... he has kept in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day." Jude, verse 6. Matt. 25:41. The passage 1 Cor. 6:3 seems to have a somewhat different reasoning.

units.la: XVII. Homines autem judicandi stabunt omnes, & boni, & mali.
units.tr: XVII. Men, however, all of them, both good and bad, will stand to be judged.

units.la: Oportet enim nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi. 1. Cor. 5:10. Mandavit nobis, ut prædicemus populo, ac testificemur, eum esse, qui definitus sit à Deo judex vivorum & mortuorum. Act. 10:42. Ut hic sollemnissimus futurus sit generis humani conventus, & universalia veluti comitia, Christo præside ac judice, agenda.
units.tr: "For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ." 1 Cor. 5:10. "He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead." Acts 10:42. So that this will be the most solemn assembly of the human race, and a kind of universal assembly to be held with Christ presiding and judging.

units.la: XVIII. Causæ eo adducentur omnes; omnesque hominum actus, cum boni, tum mali. Qui ibi de secreto suo producentur & nudabuntur. Omne opus Deus vocabit in judicium super omni occulto habendum, sive bonum an malum. Eccl. 12:14. Quodcunque verbum otiosum locuti fuerint homines, de eo reddituri sunt rationem in die judicii. Matth. 12:36. Quod tamen non tam de publico examine, quam de conscientiæ luce, & perniciosissimo mentis, sese vel accusantis, vel excusantis, volatu, intelligendum videtur. Ut nulla difficultas restet de piorum peccatis: quæ cum per justificationem tecta sint, quæ sententia in judicio hoc non retractanda, sed publice ac sollemniter confirmanda est; non iterum, aut saltem non ad pudorem eorum, illa vulgabuntur; sed ita memorabuntur, conscientiæque mentes ferient, ut de adepta venia, ac publica absolutionis sententia, immensum laetaturi sint.
units.tr: XVIII. All causes will be brought there, and all human deeds, both good and bad. In that place men's secrets will be brought forth and laid bare. "God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil." Eccl. 12:14. "Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account of it in the day of judgment." Matt. 12:36. This, however, seems to be understood less of a public examination than of the light of conscience and the most destructive flight of the mind, either accusing or excusing itself. So that no difficulty remains concerning the sins of the godly: since these have been covered by justification, and this sentence is not to be reopened in that judgment but publicly and solemnly confirmed, they will not again be made known, or at least not to their shame; rather they will be remembered in such a way, and strike their consciences, that they will rejoice immensely over the pardon obtained and the public sentence of absolution.

units.la: XIX. Fiet autem universi generis humani in duas partes, ac magnas societates, separatio. Ut duas illas civitates, quae in mundo hactenus vigent, & confusae inter se immixtaeque vagantur, agnosscamus. Quod non leve futuri judicii praejudicium erit. Ovium haedorumque nomine ac imagine eos Christus signat, ac secernit, Matt. 25. Quod ex Ezechielis emblemate desumptum videtur. Ez. 34: 17. Ac collocabuntur illi quidem ad dextram, hi ad sinistram: sive ex judiciorum Hebraeorum more: sive usurpati olim moris, in lustranda, ac Deo sollemniter obliganda gente Judaea, inpronunciandis benedictionibus ac maledictionibus legis, haec imitatio est.
units.tr: XIX. There will then be a separation of the whole human race into two parts and two great societies, so that we may recognize those two cities which hitherto flourish in the world, wandering confused and mixed together. This will be no slight foretaste of the future judgment. Christ marks and separates them by the names and image of sheep and goats, Matt. 25, which seems to be taken from the emblem in Ezekiel, Ez. 34:17. And the former will be placed indeed on the right, the latter on the left: either in accordance with the Hebrew manner of judging, or, if it was an old custom, in the solemn purification and binding of the Jewish nation to God, when the blessings and curses of the law were pronounced, this is an imitation of it.

units.la: XX. Forma ipsius judicii consistit, in causae cognitione; sententiae pronunciatione; & executione.
units.tr: XX. The form of the judgment itself consists in the examination of the cause, the pronouncement of the sentence, and its execution.

units.la: XXI. Cognitio causae non admodum operosa erit: tum propter judicis omniscientiam, qui observator ac speculator omnium, occultissimis etiam cogitationibus intererrat: Non opus habebat, ut quis testaretur de homine, ipse enim noverat, quid esset in homine. Joh. 2: 25. Omnia nuda, & resupinata oculis ipsius. Hebr. 4: 13. Tum propter conscientiae lumen, quod nullum nobis secretum esse patietur, & veteres labes nudabit ac refricabit. Qua ratione occultorum manifestatio in judicio illo potissimum intelligenda. 1 Cor. 4: 5.
units.tr: XXI. The examination of the cause will not be very laborious: partly because of the omniscience of the judge, who is the observer and watcher of all and is present even in the most hidden thoughts: "He had no need that anyone should testify of man, for he himself knew what was in man." John 2:25. "All things are naked and laid open to his eyes." Heb. 4:13. And partly because of the light of conscience, which will not allow any secret to remain hidden from us and will lay bare and reopen old stains. In this way "the manifestation of hidden things" is to be understood chiefly in that judgment. 1 Cor. 4:5.

units.la: XXII. Atque uti Scriptura judicium hoc de consuetudine humana pingere fere solet: ita librorum quoque hic mentio fit, qui aperiendi, juxtaque sententiam eorum de hominibus pronunciandum erit. Qui libri a Theologis quatuor numerantur. 1. Liber praedestinationis, qui & vitae appellatur. 2. Liber omniscientiae, sive providentiae divinae. Quae divinae mentis tabularia, ac membranas Scriptura saepe depraedicat. Et libri aperti sunt, & liber alius apertus est, qui est vitae: & judicati sunt mortui ex scriptis in libris, secundum opera sua. Apoc. 20: 12. licet isto in loco caeteroquin de judicio extremo directe non agatur. Factationem meam numerasti tu ipse. Pone lacrymas meas in utre tuo; imo in rationibus tuis. Psal. 56: 9. Mal. 3: 16. 3. Liber Scriptura, legis nimir. & Euangelii: In die, cum judicabit Deus occulta hominum, secundum Euangelium meum, per Jesum Christum. Rom. 2: 16. Apoc. 20: 12. 4. Liber denique conscientiae. Qui ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, comesificante ipsorum conscientia, & inter se invicem cogitationibus accusantibus, vel etiam defendentibus. Rom. 2: 15.
units.tr: XXII. And just as Scripture usually depicts this judgment after human custom, so here mention is made of books, which will be opened, and according to whose contents men are to be judged. Theologians count four such books. (1) The book of predestination, which is also called the book of life. (2) The book of divine omniscience or providence, of which Scripture often speaks as the archive and parchments of the divine mind: "And the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged out of the things written in the books, according to their works." Rev. 20:12, although in that place the final judgment is not otherwise directly treated. "You yourself have counted my wanderings; put my tears into your bottle; yes, into your account." Ps. 56:8. Mal. 3:16. (3) The book of Scripture, namely of the law and the gospel: "On the day when God will judge the secrets of men, according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ." Rom. 2:16. Rev. 20:12. (4) Lastly, the book of conscience. "Who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts between themselves accusing or else excusing one another." Rom. 2:15.

units.la: XXIII. At-
units.tr: XXIII. And-

units.la: XXIII. Atque ex istis libris deinde sententia feretur. Quod palam, ac sermone, videtur peragendum. De operibus autem ea potissimum constabit: cum in visibili judicio visibilia requirantur testimonia; quae non de interna fide, sed de externis charitatis operibus, desumenda sunt. Atque ita Deus unicuique reddet secundum opera sua. Rom. 2:6.
units.tr: XXIII. And from these books the sentence will then be pronounced. This will seem to be done openly and by spoken word. Concerning works, the following will chiefly be established: since in a visible judgment visible evidence is required, and this must be drawn not from inner faith but from the external works of charity. And so God will render to each according to his works. Rom. 2:6.

units.la: XXIV. Quod autem maxime operum charitatis ac misericordiae in eo judicio futura sit mentio; quae a piis in tenebris ac silentio reposita, tunc in publica mundi luce splendebunt; cum judicii illius ratione vel praecipue congruit. Cum enim mortales omnes misericordiam judicis ex aequo imploraturi sint; justissimum erit judicium, quod secundum misericordiam ab ipsis factam, vel neglectam, exercebitur. Nam condemnatio absque misericordia erit ei, qui non praestiterit misericordiam. Et gloriatur misericordia adversus judicium. Jac. 2: 13. 2 Tim. 1:16.
units.tr: XXIV. Mention will be made especially of works of charity and mercy in that judgment. These, laid up by the pious in darkness and silence, will then shine in the public light of the world, since they most fittingly belong to the reason of that judgment. For since all mortals will alike implore the mercy of the Judge, the judgment will be most just, because it will be exercised according to the mercy that they themselves showed or neglected. For judgment without mercy will be shown to him who has not shown mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment. Jas. 2:13. 2 Tim. 1:16.

units.la: XXV. Ac calculis quidem utraque ex parte positis, impiorum facta, nulla amoris scintilla coruscantia, diraeque illaetabilis sententiae erunt causa promeritoria: piorum autem opera absolventis ac salutaris vocis non causae proprie, sed indicia sunt, de veris causis testificantia. Cum genuinus ille amor certissima divinae gratiae sit tessera ac symbolum. Piis enim coelestis illa gloria, ut hereditas, ex amore ac electione Dei aeterna, obventura promittitur. Venite, benedicti Patris mei, ut haereditatem possidete regnum, praeparatum vobis a jactu mundi fundamento. Matth. 25: 34. Spectatque huc Scripturae phrasis, quo judicandi dicimur secundum opera. Rom. 2:6. 2 Cor. 5:10.
units.tr: XXV. When the reckoning has been set out on both sides, the deeds of the wicked, which glitter with no spark of love, will be the meritorious cause of their dreadful and joyless sentence; but the works of the pious are not the proper causes of their absolving and saving word, but signs that witness to the true causes. For that genuine love is the most certain token and symbol of divine grace. Indeed, that heavenly glory is promised to the pious as an inheritance that comes to them from the eternal love and election of God. Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Matt. 25:34. To this point also refers the phrase of Scripture by which we are said to be judged according to works. Rom. 2:6. 2 Cor. 5:10.

units.la: XXVI. Ut valde errent Pontificii, operum meritum etiam coram tribunali ac districto Dei judicio tueri audentes. Quae Judaicae quoque fidei corruptela est: qui praesentem futuramque hominis felicitatem bonis ejus operibus adscribunt. Quanquam & gratiae mentionem suis operibus admiscent. Gentes autem, coram judicii throno relictas, affirmant.
units.tr: XXVI. The Papists greatly err in daring to defend the merit of works even before the tribunal and strict judgment of God. This is also a corruption of the Jewish faith, which ascribes both the present and the future happiness of a man to his good works, although they also mix in some mention of grace with their works. The Gentiles, however, they say, are left before the throne of judgment.

units.la: XXVII. Perlata autem sententia, atque ubi splendida Deus de genere humano fecerit arbitria, sine mora eam, per mentes sibi famulantes exequetur. Ac veluti in dicenda sententia a piis faciet initium, quos coram universo mundo absolvet, non sine multo verborum honore, ad majorem impiorum ignominiam: ita in ea exequenda ab impiis incipiet, ad uberiorem piorum consolationem. Laetabitur justus, cum viderit ultionem. Psal. 58: 11. Aut potius impiis prius loquitur, quia proxime de iis antecesserat.
units.tr: XXVII. When the sentence has been pronounced, and God has made his splendid decisions concerning the human race, he will carry it out without delay through the minds that serve him. And just as, in pronouncing the sentence, he will begin with the pious, whom he will absolve before the whole world, with much honour in words and to the greater shame of the wicked, so in carrying it out he will begin with the wicked, for the fuller comfort of the pious. The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance. Ps. 58:11. Or rather, he speaks to the wicked first because he had just spoken of them.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: XXVIII. Circumstantia hujus judicii maxime versantur in loco, & tempore.
units.tr: XXVIII. The circumstances of this judgment chiefly concern place and time.

units.la: XXIX. Locus communiter designatur per aërem & nubes. Ecce venit cum nubibus, & videbit eum omnis oculus. Apoc. 1: 7. Rapiemur simul cum iis in nubes, in occursum Domini in aëra. 1 Thess. 4: 16, 17. Quod ita interpretantur, ac si aërio in spatio, tanquam in amplissimo amphitheatro, quale videl. sola rerum natura possit effingere, inspectante universo mundo, judicium peragendum sit. Nisi potius in terra illud futurum placet; ac raptum illum aëreum judicio posteriorem dicamus, deque piis solum intelligamus.
units.tr: XXIX. The place is commonly indicated by air and clouds. Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him. Rev. 1:7. We shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air. 1 Thess. 4:16, 17. They interpret this as though the judgment were to be held in the aerial space, as in a vast amphitheatre, such as nature alone could fashion, with the whole world looking on. Or rather, we may prefer to hold that the judgment will take place on earth, and say that the rapture into the air comes after the judgment, and understand it only of the pious.

units.la: XXX: De quo quicquid sit, particularis ejus locus ignoratur. Nec admittendum Pontificiorum commentum de valle Josaphat, ex Joël. 3: 12. Quae acceptae à Judaeis fabulae imitatio ac interpolatio est. Non enim unica vallis, eaque non adeo magna, generis humani conventum capere potest. Neque agit prophetia ista de ultimo rerum humanarum actu, ac judicio; cum multa praeterea in mundo consecutura narret; sed de judicio quodam Dei particulari agit; quod sub ultima Novi Test. tempora in eos, qui Ecclesiae Reformatae limitem invaserunt, exercendum erit. Quod similis judicii, sub Josaphato Rege, comparatione exponitur & confirmatur. de quo 2 Chron. 20: 16, 26. Quid quod & vallis Josaphat appellatio aenigma habet, atque ipso nomine Deum Judicem indicat. Conserendum autem Joelis vaticinium, atque exponendum ex loco Apocalyptico, cap. 16: 16.
units.tr: XXX. Whatever the case, its particular place is unknown. Nor is the Papists' fiction about the valley of Jehoshaphat, drawn from Joel 3:12, to be admitted. It is an imitation and an interpolation of fables received from the Jews. For one valley, and not a very large one, cannot hold the assembly of the human race. Nor does that prophecy deal with the last act of human affairs and the judgment, since it narrates many other things that will follow in the world; it deals with a certain particular judgment of God, which is to be exercised near the end of the New Testament times against those who have invaded the boundary of the Reformed Church. This is set out and confirmed by a comparison with a similar judgment under King Jehoshaphat, concerning which see 2 Chron. 20:16, 26. Moreover, the name Jehoshaphat for the valley has an enigmatic character, and by its very name indicates God the Judge. Joel's prophecy should be compared, however, and explained from the apocalyptic passage, Rev. 16:16.

units.la: XXXI. Tempus judicii, Deo certum ac notum, Act. 17: 3. nulli praeterea creaturae aut homini revelatum est. De die autem illo & hora, nemo scit, ne Angels quidem coelorum, sed Pater meus solus. Matth. 24: 36. Cum enim Deus complura alia, tum opera sua, tum judicia, longe ante Ecclesiae revelaverit; tum spei piorum sustentandae, cujus est res futuras praelibare ac veluti praecerpere; tum fidei confirmandae; ac infidelibus denique potentissime confundendis & convincendis: supremum vero judicium ultimus sit rerum humanarum actus, post quem nullus fidei aut infidelitati locus erit; contraque praecisa temporis hujus explicatio securitatem potius ac ignaviam alere nata fuisset; sapientissime Deus mundi exitum caliginosa nocte premere, atque humanis visibus abscondere voluit.
units.tr: XXXI. The time of the judgment is certain and known to God, Acts 17:3, and has not been revealed to any other creature or man. But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father alone. Matt. 24:36. For although God has revealed many other things long beforehand to the Church, both his works and his judgments, partly to sustain the hope of the pious, whose office it is to foretaste future things, as it were to pluck them in advance, partly to confirm faith, and finally to confound and convince unbelievers most powerfully; yet the supreme judgment is the last act of human affairs, after which there will be no place either for faith or for unbelief. Whereas, on the contrary, a precise explanation of this time would have been born to nourish security and sloth rather than anything else. Therefore God most wisely willed to press the end of the world in a murky night and to hide it from human eyes.

units.la: XXXII. Acuendae tamen piorum industriae, & ne fides scrutari Dei opera cessaret, signa quaedam temporum in Scripturis expressit; & interjectum inter primum ac secundum Christi adventum spatium quibusdam spatiis & periodis distinxit, totidemque tubis insignivit; ac praesertim ultimi temporis statum & conditionem accuratissimis lineis describit. Vide Matth. 24. Luc. 21. Apocalypsin Johannis. conf. 1. Cor. 15:52. ad ultimam tubam; cui implementum omnium prophetiarum tribuitur. Apoc. 10:7.
units.tr: XXXII. Yet, to sharpen the diligence of the pious, and so that faith might not cease to search out the works of God, he set out in the Scriptures certain signs of the times; and he divided the space lying between the first and second coming of Christ into certain spans and periods, and marked them with as many trumpets; and above all he describes the state and condition of the last time with the most exact lines. See Matt. 24, Luke 21, and the Apocalypse of John. Compare 1 Cor. 15:52, at the last trumpet, to which the fulfilment of all prophecies is ascribed. Rev. 10:7.

units.la: XXXIII. Speciatim 1. in Ecclesia magna quaedam & illustris praedicta est rerum mutatio; & publica gentium nationumque integrarum apostasia; & falsa quaedam Ecclesia, non exiguum nomen decusque in mundo ferens: rursusque Ecclesiae a labe ista purgatio & reformatio, non nisi totali Antichristi interitu finienda.
units.tr: XXXIII. Specifically: (1) in the Church a great and conspicuous change is foretold, and a public apostasy of peoples and of whole nations, and a certain false Church bearing no small name and honour in the world; and again, the purging and reformation of the Church from this stain will not be finished except by the total destruction of Antichrist.

units.la: 2. Deinde Judaeorum conversio, itidem publica ac magna; non hominum singularium, sed gentis ac populi. Cujus tamen universa ratio cum non aeque in explicato sit, nihil temere hic definiendum, necā nostris hariolationibus divini operis exitus suspendendus. Incertum enim admodum est, quod eos in Cananaeam reducendos, ac avita in sceptra reponendos, quidam decernunt. 3. Gentium populorumque conversio, major forte & illustrior, quam hactenus visa est: & Euangelii toto orbe coruscantis insignis splendor. 4. Publica mundi pax, & quies, cum rerum omnium affluentia & ubertate. Unde multis oritur securitas, & Christi adhuc cunctantis contemptus, & quietorum irrisio ac sannae. Quae ultimi temporis peculiaris nota est. Unde insperantibus ac ineompositis superventurus Christus dicitur. Cum enim dicent, pax & securitas! tunc repentinum ipsis imminet malum. 1. Thess. 5:3. 2. Pet. 3:3,4.
units.tr: (2) Next, the conversion of the Jews, likewise public and great, not of single individuals but of the nation and people. Since, however, the whole plan of this is not equally clear, nothing is to be defined rashly here, nor is the outcome of the divine work to be made to depend on our guesswork. For it is quite uncertain that they are to be brought back into Canaan and restored to their ancestral sceptres, as some decree. (3) The conversion of the Gentiles and peoples, perhaps greater and more illustrious than has so far been seen, and a remarkable splendour of the Gospel shining through the whole world. (4) Public peace and quiet in the world, with an abundance and plenty of all things. From this arises security for many, and contempt for Christ who is still delaying, and mockery and scorn of the quiet. This is a peculiar mark of the last time. Hence Christ is said to be coming unexpectedly and at a time when men are unprepared. For when they say, Peace and security! then sudden destruction is upon them. 1 Thess. 5:3. 2 Pet. 3:3, 4.

units.la: XXXIV. Signa autem in coelo, in sole, & luna, quae Scriptura memorat, non de rerum natura intelligenda sunt, quam non facile movet Deus, sed prophetico more de Ecclesiae coelo, deque astris ejus, & sideribus, sive vero, sive falso jubare splendentibus, explicari debent. Ut nunc Ecclesiae ipsius obscuratio, noxque horrenda & terribilis, amoto videlicet sole ejus, Apoc. 9:2. 12:4. nunc falsorum siderum, maligne coruscantium, occasus indicetur. Quae videl. amovebit aliquando Deus, & toto facessere coelo jubebit, ut soli in regno suo integer locus sit. Apoc. 6:13,14.
units.tr: XXXIV. The signs that Scripture mentions, in heaven, in the sun, and the moon, are not to be understood of the nature of things, which God does not easily disturb, but must be explained, in prophetic manner, of the heaven of the Church and of its stars and constellations, whether shining with true or false light. Thus sometimes the darkening of the Church itself, and a dreadful and terrible night, namely with its sun removed, Rev. 9:2, 12:4, and sometimes the setting of false stars shining malignantly, is indicated. God will one day remove these, and will command them to depart from the whole heaven, so that there may be a whole place for the sun in his kingdom. Rev. 6:13, 14.

units.la: XXXV. Porro signum filii hominis, quod cum adventu ejus in coelo fulsurum dicitur, Matth. 24:30. non ad ferale crucis signum, aut ad ignem quo mundi machina conflagrabit, sed ad ipsum potius Christum in nubibus apparentem referendum est. Cum ipse videl. derepente in signum mortalibus apparebit. conf. Jes. 11:10. & quantum ad loquendi modum Rom. 4: 11. Matth. 12: 39. Nisi intelligere malimus insignia Christi opera in terris, ex quibus in coelo esse cognoscetur.
units.tr: XXXV. Further, the sign of the Son of Man, which is said to shine in heaven at his coming, Matt. 24:30, is to be referred not to the dreadful sign of the cross, nor to the fire by which the machinery of the world will be burned up, but rather to Christ himself appearing in the clouds. For he will then suddenly appear to mortals as a sign. Compare Isa. 11:10, and as to the manner of speaking, Rom. 4:11, Matt. 12:39. Unless we would rather understand by the sign the works of Christ on earth, by which he will be known to be in heaven.

units.la: XXXVI. Unde, cum adventus Christi tempus suis quidem coloribus descriptum videamus, ipsum autem ejus aut annum, aut saeculum, nullis certis notis augurari possimus; nostrum non est futura, quae Deus in manu sua posuit, invadere, & latens illud arcanum de Dei thesauris educere. Sed omni potius studio adventus Domini maturandus; &, depósito rerum terrenarum studio, quicquid adhuc superest temporis futilis ac caduci, rebus seriis impendendum; ne otiantibus Dominus superveniat. Cum igitur haec omnia dissolvenda sint, quales oportet vos esse in sanctis conversationibus, et pietatis officiis, expectantes & accelerantes adventum diei Dei. 2. Pet. 3: 11, 12. Quem Ecclesiae affectum pulcherrime depinxit Zacharias, c. 14: 16. dum fideles, quasi in clausura saeculi, jam exitum molientes, atque ad coeleste πολίτευμα paratos, tabernaculorum festum celebrantes faciè. Praepostera enim erat veterum sapientia, pro mora finis orantium, dum Antichristi adventum, & futura Ecclesiae certamina nimium reformidant: cum aliam precem dictarit ipse Dominus: Adveniat regnum tuum; & Domini Spiritus: Ne, veni, Domine Jesu. Apoc. 22: 20.
units.tr: XXXVI. Hence, although we see the time of Christ's coming described in its own colours, we cannot foretell from any certain marks either its year or its age. It is not for us to intrude upon what God has placed in his own hand, or to bring out of God's treasuries that hidden secret. Rather, we must hasten the coming of the Lord with all zeal: having set aside our earthly concerns, we should devote whatever remains of this futile and fading time to serious matters, lest the Lord come upon us while we are idle. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conduct and acts of godliness, looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God. 2 Pet. 3:11, 12. Zechariah depicted this feeling of the Church most beautifully, ch. 14:16, when the faithful, as if at the close of the age, already preparing their departure and ready for their heavenly citizenship, celebrate the feast of tabernacles. For it was a backward wisdom of the ancients to dread so greatly the coming of Antichrist and the future conflicts of the Church that they wished for a delay of the end. The Lord himself dictated a different prayer: Thy kingdom come; and the Spirit of the Lord says: Come, Lord Jesus. Rev. 22:20.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: De Consummatione saeculi.
units.tr: On the Consummation of the Age.

units.la: I. Udicium ultimum consequitur piorum in beatas sedes introductio; impiorum autem ad parata supplicia relegatio. Rursus venio, ut assumam vos ad me. Joh. 14: 1. Rapiemur in nubes, in occursum Domino. 1. Thess. 4: 17. Qui piorum raptus ut primum in mundo miraculum fuit, ita quoque postremum erit; utpote miraculorum omnium maximum, eorumque & finis & scopus. Sicuti in statu integritatis hoc unicum ac perpetuum videtur obtenturum fuisse miraculum.
units.tr: I. The last judgment is followed by the introduction of the pious into blessed seats, and by the consignment of the impious to the punishments prepared for them. Again I will come and take you to myself. John 14:1. We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord. 1 Thess. 4:17. The rapture of the pious, which was the first miracle in the world, will also be the last, as the greatest of all miracles and both its end and its aim. Just as, in the state of integrity, this one perpetual miracle would seem to have been going to obtain.

units.la: II. Ac consummato ita regno, peractisque Ecclesiae fatis, tradet Filius regnum Patri. 1. Cor. 15: 24. pacatum videl. deque mundo assertum; atque ab ipso jam plenissime beandum ac implendum, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus. com. 28. Ipse autem, cum Ecclesia, atque
units.tr: II. When the kingdom has thus been consummated and the fates of the Church accomplished, the Son will deliver up the kingdom to the Father. 1 Cor. 15:24. The kingdom will have been pacified and asserted in the world, and will then be fully blessed and filled by him, so that God may be all in all. Ver. 28. He himself, however, with the Church, and

units.la: Kkkk 2 atque isto veluti in corpore suo, Patri subjectus erit. Quod quomodo sine majestatis Christi imminutione, ac regni ejus labe, intelligendum sit, supra, ubi de Christi Deitate ac regno ejus aeterno, abunde expositum, ac Socinianorum blasphemiis respondimus. Ac tunc erit finis. com. 24. & saeculi clausura ac terminus, alteriusque longe beatissimi saeculi exordium.
units.tr: in it, as it were, his own body, will be subject to the Father. How this is to be understood without diminishing the majesty of Christ or staining his kingdom has been fully explained above, where we treated of Christ's Deity and his eternal kingdom and answered the blasphemies of the Socinians. Then there will be the end, ver. 24, and the close and boundary of this age, and the beginning of another, far more blessed age.

units.la: III. Praesentium rerum consummationem exprimit Scriptura per commotionem coeli & terrae, Hebr. 12:26. Hagg. 2:6. per mutationem illorum, Psal. 102:26, 27, 28. Hebr. 2:10, 11, 12. Quod tamen mora & tractu aliquo peragetur. Partim enim metaphorica haec sunt, & casum Antichristi, falsorumque in Ecclesia Deorum adumbrant. Et stellae coeli ceciderunt in terram. Apoc. 6:13. coll. Matth. 24:29. partim etiam proprie implebuntur, supremo mundi tempore; quo mare, quo tellus, correptaque regia coeli ardebit, atque mundi moles operosa laborabit. Ut purgato ac renovato mundo succedat tabernaculum aeternum, & domus aeterna, aeternaque in ea agitanda gaudia. Facite vobis amicos ex mammona iniquitatis, ut, cum defeceritis, recipiant vos in aeterna tabernacula. Luc. 16:9. Aedificium ex Deo habemus, domicilium non manu factum, aeternum in coelis. 2 Cor. 5:1.
units.tr: III. Scripture expresses the consummation of present things by the shaking of heaven and earth, Heb. 12:26; Hag. 2:6, and by their change, Psal. 102:26, 27, 28; Heb. 2:10, 11, 12. This will be accomplished, however, with some delay and duration. For partly these expressions are metaphorical and foreshadow the fall of Antichrist and of the false gods in the Church: and the stars of heaven fell to the earth, Rev. 6:13, compare Matt. 24:29. Partly they will also be fulfilled literally, at the final time of the world, when the sea, the earth, and the seized regions of heaven will burn, and the laboured mass of the world will groan. Then, the world having been purged and renewed, there will succeed an eternal tabernacle and an eternal house, and eternal joys to be lived in it. Make for yourselves friends by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail they may receive you into eternal tabernacles. Luke 16:9. We have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. 2 Cor. 5:1.

units.la: IV. Estque haec illa mundi conflagratio, non solum in Scripturis, sed & apud exteros scriptores celebrata. Quos de incendio mundi disputantes apud Senecam, aliosque e Stoica disciplina, videre est, ubi Deo videlicet in ista rerum omnium παλιγγενεσία visum fuerit ordiri meliora, vetera finire. Quibus vero ex locis tanta ignis copia suppeditanda sit, quaerere supervacuum ac curiosum est: cum non minus ignium, quam aquarum, fontes in stellis planetarumque sinubus hic mundus possideat; quos inde producere, terrisque immittere, Deo proclive erit. Quamobrem is, qui tum erat mundus, aqua inundatus periit. Qui vero nunc sunt coeli, ac terra eodem sermone reconditi, asservantur igni, in diem damnationis & exitii impiorum hominum. Unum autem hoc nevos fugiat, dilecti, unum diem apud Dominum perinde esse ut mille anni, & mille annos ut diem unum. Non tardat Dominus promissionem (ut nonnulli tarditatem hanc esse ducunt) sed patiente est animo erga nos, nolens illos perire, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam tendere. Veniet autem, sicut fur in nocte dies ille Domini, quo coeli cum stridore praeteribunt, elementa vero aestuantia solventur; terraque, & quae in ea sunt opera, exurentur. Quum igitur haec omnia dissolvenda sint, quales oportet esse vos in sanctis conversationibus, & pietatis officiis? Expectantes & properantes ad adventum diei Dei, in quo cæli conflagrantes solventur, & elementa æstuantia liquescent. 2 Petr. 3:7–13.
units.tr: IV. This is that conflagration of the world, celebrated not only in the Scriptures but also among outside writers. One may see them disputing about it in Seneca and others of the Stoic school, where it seemed good to God, in this palingenesis of all things, to begin better things and to end the old. From what sources so great a supply of fire is to be provided, it is superfluous and idle to inquire, since this world holds no fewer fountains of fire than of water in the bosoms of the stars and planets, which it will be easy for God to bring forth and send down upon the earth. Wherefore the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens and the earth that now are, by the same word are stored up, reserved for fire, against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men. But this one thing, beloved, must not escape you: that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promise (as some count slowness), but is patient toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance. But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the elements, burning, will be dissolved; and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Since therefore all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conduct and acts of godliness? Looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God, in which the heavens, being on fire, will be dissolved, and the burning elements will melt. 2 Pet. 3:7–13.

units.la: V. Cum autem ignis hic judicium ultimum non antecedat, sed consequatur, fabulosò purgatorii igni tollendo ac devorando imprimis facit. Quod cum post ultimum mundi diem non superfuturum, nec ultimis mundi hominibus purgandis serviturum sit, vel ipsis fatentibus adversariis; ne anterioris quidem ætatis homines eo lustrari opus habent.
units.tr: V. But since this fire does not precede the last judgment but follows it, it above all does away with the fabled fire of purgatory, which it would consume and devour. Since that fire will not survive the last day of the world, nor serve to purge the last men of the world, even the adversaries themselves admit this. Neither, then, do men of earlier ages have any need to be cleansed by it.

units.la: VI. Serviet autem hic ignis non abolendo prorsus mundo (quod certe per ignem fieri non potest) sed purgando, ac renovando, & de vanitate sua liberando. Præterit enim figura hujus mundi. 1 Cor. 7:31. Et quæ in eo sunt, comburentur. 2 Petr. 3:10. Vanitati enim creatura subjecta est. Rom. 8:20. Unde non solum cœlum beatorum, & infernus, sed & ipse hic mundus aspectabilis, igni illi superstes suturus videtur; sed de igne videl. renatus, meliorique auspicio fictus & fabricatus. Quod præsertim de majoribus mundi partibus, cæterarumque creaturarum materia saltem, elementisque, statuendum est. Annihilationis enim imaginem ac ideam concipere difficulter possumus. Nec ullum ejus exemplum est. Ac cum immutabilitate Dei pugnare ea videtur; qui mundum conditurus non fuisse videtur, si eum unquam, tanquam operis pertæsus, abolere in animo habuisset. Certe partem mundi aboleri, non substituta alia, ac reliquis interim mundi partibus permanentibus, cum extensi ac mundi imagine, quam homo à Deo insitam habet, vel maxime pugnat. Obtinetque hic idem quod de pugnante vacui conceptu Physici tradunt. Scriptura autem, cum ignis materialis meminit, quo veluti instrumento mundus hic reformabitur. 2 Petr. 3. cum post mundi ruinam, novum cœlum, & novam terram memorat. 2 Pet. 3:13. cum tempus restitutionis omnium expectari jubet. Act. 3:21. ad quam creatura universa tanquam fessa anhelet. Rom. 8. cum mundi scenam & χρῆμα convolvi veluti ac transfire facit. 1 Cor. 7. cum denique hominem, in cujus gratiam hæc inferiora condita sunt, post ignem illum superesse, tumque demum beatitudinem exordiri docet: quin & eundem, non in cœlo tantum, sed in terra, quam justitia h. e. homines justi inhabitabunt, 2 Petr. 3. collocat; quam videl. ex intervallo calcabit (nisi potius hæc novæ Ecclesiæ, rerumque ultimis temporibus in terris gerendarum imago sit) iis omnibus loquendi modis, non mundi aspectabilis interitum & annihilationem,
units.tr: VI. This fire, however, will serve not to abolish the world altogether (which certainly cannot be done by fire) but to purge and renew it and to free it from its vanity. For the fashion of this world passes away. 1 Cor. 7:31. And the works that are in it will be burned up. 2 Pet. 3:10. For the creature was made subject to vanity. Rom. 8:20. Hence it seems that not only the heaven of the blessed and hell, but this visible world itself, will survive that fire, yet born again from the fire and formed and fashioned under a better auspice. This must be held especially of the greater parts of the world, and at least of the matter of the other creatures and of the elements. For we can conceive the image and idea of annihilation only with difficulty, and there is no example of it. It also seems to conflict with the immutability of God, who would not seem to have been going to create the world at all, if he had ever intended, as if weary of his work, to abolish it. Certainly to abolish a part of the world, with nothing substituted and the remaining parts of the world abiding, most strongly conflicts with the extension and the image of the world which man has implanted from God. The same holds as the physicists say about the concept of a vacuum, which contradicts itself. Scripture, however, when it speaks of material fire, makes it the instrument by which this world will be reformed. In 2 Peter 3, after the ruin of the world, it speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, 2 Pet. 3:13; when it bids us expect the times of the restoration of all things, Acts 3:21, for which the whole creation groans as if weary, Rom. 8; when it makes the fashion and form of the world, as it were, be rolled up and pass away, 1 Cor. 7; and finally, when it teaches that man*, for whose sake these lower things were made, survives that fire, and only then does blessedness begin. Indeed it places the same man not only in heaven but on earth, which righteousness, that is, righteous men, will inhabit, 2 Pet. 3; which man, it says, will tread upon from a distance (unless rather this is a picture of the new Church and of the things to be done on earth in the last times). By all these modes of speaking it hands down not the destruction and annihilation of the visible world,

units.la: {1} Cor. 7:31. sed renovationem potius& παλιγγενεσίαν tradit. Conf. Psal. 102:26. Esai. 51:6. 65:17. Apoc. 21:1.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 7:31, but rather its renewal and palingenesis [παλιγγενεσία]. Compare Psal. 102:26; Isa. 51:6; 65:17; Rev. 21:1.

units.la: {a}VII. Ut male Sociniani universo mundo, & coelo ipsi, & astris, interitum denuntient; coelo tantum beatorum, quod & immortale & increatum fingunt, cum incolis suis excepto. Qui dolus eo spectat, ut & infernum, & destinatum daemonibus ac impiis hominibus carcerem, de rerum natura tollant. Cui errori non nimis temere universali illa rerum annihilatione subserviendum. Absurde etiam Lutherani praeterea corporeum quoque spatium in glorificatis tollunt. Quod αφιλόσοφον est.
units.tr: VII. The Socinians wrongly announce destruction to the whole world, to heaven itself and to the stars, excepting only the heaven of the blessed, which they also imagine to be both immortal and uncreated, along with its inhabitants. This trick aims to remove from the nature of things both hell and the prison destined for demons and impious men. Nor should one too rashly yield to that error through a universal annihilation of things. The Lutherans also absurdly remove corporeal space in the glorified. This is unphilosophical [ἀφιλόσοφον].

units.la: VIII. Post praesentis saeculi abolitionem, & mundi repurgationem, sequetur caelum novum, & terra nova. 2.Pet. 3:13. Esai. 65:17. quam inhabitatura est justitia, id est, piorum concilia & coetus. Qui tamen loci, cum terram hanc mundumque inferiorem, a piis calcandum & habitandum pronuncient, jam ante mundi finem impleri incipient, in celebri illa Ecclesiae renovatione. Vidi caelum novum & terram novam. Apoc. 21:1. complementum autem ac perfectionem habebunt in saeculo futuro. Quo ipso tempore, an pii quoque terras, habitatasque olim sedes revisuri, novamque rerum faciem miraturi sint, praesentis saeculi non est dijudicare.
units.tr: VIII.
