After the abolition of the present age and the purging of the world, there will follow a new heaven and a new earth, 2 Pet. 3:13; Isa. 65:17, which righteousness will inhabit, that is, the assemblies and gatherings of the pious. Yet since these places declare that this lower earth and world are to be trodden and inhabited by the pious, they will begin to be fulfilled even before the end of the world, in that famous renewal of the Church. I saw a new heaven and a new earth. Rev. 21:1. They will, however, receive their completion and perfection in the future age. Whether the pious will also at that very time revisit the lands and seats once inhabited, and marvel at the new face of things, it is not for the present age to determine.

units.la: IX. Corrumpunt rursus Socinian verborum horum sensum, cum novi coeli, ac novae terrae, appellatione coelum increatum intelligunt; cujus videl. pii tunc novi erunt incolae & hospites. Quae varie impingunt. Nam & coelum aliquod increatum & aeternum singunt, contra creationis fidem. Tu fecisti coelos, coelos coelorum, & omnem exercitum ipsorum. Neh. 9:6. Et coelum illud, quod modo aeternum ajunt, novum appellitant. Et coelum tandem in terram commutant; cum non coelum solum novum, sed & terram novam Scriptura depraedicet.
units.tr: IX. The Socinians again corrupt the sense of these words. By "new heaven and new earth" they understand an uncreated heaven, in which the godly will then be new inhabitants and guests. This leads them into various errors. For they invent an uncreated and eternal heaven, contrary to the faith in creation: "Thou hast made the heavens, the heaven of heavens, and all their host." Neh. 9:6. And the heaven which they now call eternal, they also call new. Finally, they change heaven into earth, whereas Scripture proclaims not only a new heaven but also a new earth.

units.la: X. Atque hoc erit saeculum illud, quod Judaeis venturum, & futurum dicitur; quod saeculo praesenti opponunt, & modo de tempore Messiae, modo de animarum mundo ac saeculo, modo de statu rerum post resurrectionem, intelligunt; aliquando etiam cuncta illa inter se confundunt.
units.tr: X. This is the age which is called "the coming and future" age by the Jews. They set it against the present age, and they understand it sometimes of the time of the Messiah, sometimes of the world of souls and the age to come, sometimes of the state of things after the resurrection. Sometimes they confuse all of these with one another.

units.la: XI. Mire autem de quocunque isto rerum statu fabulantur. In eo conveniunt; quod, paucis exceptis, qui ex Aristotele mundi aeternitatem adoptarunt, mundum hunc olim in melius commutatum iri consentiant. Quod non semel, sed saepius, post impletum sex mille annorum curriculum fieri, millenario autem quinquagesimo, quasi mundi jubilæo, omnia in nihilum redactum iri, superstite solum animarum mundo, Cabbalistæ nugantur. Illud vero indignandum æquè, ac dolendum, quod Messiæ tempora & regnum, demum post sæculi præsentis finem & resurrectionem mortuorum, auspicentur: atque illum demum mundum futurum, quem Prophetæ prænunciarunt, appellent. Quo tempore Hierosolyma quoque, & templum, & vitæ animalis statum, parilesque hominum actiones, quanquam sine noxa ac peccato, cogitant. Ita primarium hunc fidei articulum corruperunt; nec quicquam Deo homineve dignum in Messia reliquerunt; sed carnalia quædam, & terrena, de eo somniant: quæ cum in his terris sese adepturos desperent, in alterum quoque sæculum tales cogitationes producunt; ac futurum mundum, in quo pietas & justitia habitabit, in externarum quoque rerum affluentia & ubertate, quali Protoplasti in Paradiso fruebantur, sub Messia Rege constituunt & absolvunt. Rursusque, post longam ætatem ac Mathusalemi annos, morti in co statu locum faciunt, ex Jes. 65: 20. ubi puer centum annos natus moriatur; peccator autem centum annos natus maledictus futurus: ut secundæ etiam corporum resurrectioni locus sit. Nisi quod alii justos in Paradisum deinceps traducendos; aut, post positas terrestres exuvias, in animarum loco æternum quieturos somnient. Incerta enim ac pugnantia nonnunquam differunt. Nec minus ad beati illius statuS opprobrium facit, quod & morbis, aliisque calamitatibus, & peccato, quidam eorum in ipso locum faciant; juxta illud Esai. 33: 24 Non dicit decumbens ægroto; populus habitans in illa, habet condonatam pravitatem: quia videl. liberum arbitrium in homine remanebit, quod sine peccandi libertate concipere non possunt Doctores in Israële.
units.tr: XI. They talk wildly about whatever state of things that is. In this they agree: with few exceptions, those who adopted the eternity of the world from Aristotle, they all hold that this world will one day be changed for the better. The Cabbalists trifle that this happens not once but several times: after six thousand years have run their course, and then in the fiftieth millennium, as it were the jubilee of the world, all things will be reduced to nothing, with only the world of souls surviving. But it is equally outrageous and grievous that they begin the times and kingdom of the Messiah only after the end of the present age and the resurrection of the dead, and that they call the future world, which the prophets foretold, by that name. At that time they also imagine Jerusalem, the temple, the state of animal life, and similar human actions, though without harm or sin. Thus they have corrupted this primary article of faith. They have left nothing in the Messiah worthy of God or man, but dream of him as something carnal and earthly. Since they despair of attaining such things in this world, they carry the same thoughts into the other age as well. They set up and complete a future world in which piety and justice will dwell, in an abundance of external things such as the first man enjoyed in Paradise, under the Messiah as King. Again, after a long life and the years of Methuselah, they make room for death in that state, from Jes. 65:20, where "the child dies at a hundred years old, and the sinner who is a hundred years old shall be accursed," so that there may be room for a second resurrection of bodies. Others, however, dream that the righteous will afterwards be transferred to Paradise, or, after laying aside their earthly remains, will rest eternally in the place of souls. They differ among themselves with uncertain and conflicting views. Nor does it bring less disgrace on that blessed state that some of them make room in it for diseases, other calamities, and sin, in line with Esai. 33:24: "The inhabitant shall not say, I am sick; the people who dwell in it have their iniquity forgiven." They do this because free will will remain in man, and the teachers in Israel cannot conceive of it without the freedom to sin.

units.la: XII. Erroris fons est, perversus ille de regno Messiæ concepptus. Cum enim in terra illum regnaturum, & Hierosolymis, ac in Cananæa, apparituram, ex Prophetis certissimum sit: illi, præ desperatione, adventum Messiæ usque in futurum sæculum prærogantes; regnumque ejus non nisi terrenum & carnale cogitantes; hinc proserpente errore, futurum etiam sæculum, non in cœlis, sed in terra, constituerunt; felicitatemque illam in corporeo quodam statu, ac externis potissimum bonis, absolverunt. Quæ terrestris cœlestisque status mera confusio, & Messiæ bonorumque ejus corruptio, & abnegatio est.
units.tr: XII. The source of the error is that perverse notion of the kingdom of the Messiah. For it is most certain from the prophets that he will reign on earth and appear in Jerusalem and in Canaan. But out of despair they postpone the coming of the Messiah until the age to come, and, thinking of his kingdom only as earthly and carnal, they let the error spread. From this they also place the age to come not in heaven but on earth, and they complete that happiness in a certain bodily state, chiefly in external goods. This mixing of earthly and heavenly states is pure confusion, and it is a corruption and denial of the Messiah and his blessings.

units.la: CAPUT XXV. De vita & morte æterna.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. On eternal life and death.

units.la: I. LIter autem Scriptura futurum sæculum depingit: atque illi statui æternam hominis beatitudinem, plenissimam animi corporisque glorificationem, omniumque bonorum fastigium ac summam assignat. Ac finem & complementum habebunt tum omnia Christi beneficia; redemtio, Luc.21:28. Vocatio, 1 Pet.5:10. Justificatio, Matth.25: 34. Adoptio, Rom. 8:23. Sanctificatio, Eph.5:27. solaque obtinebit glorificatio, Rom.8: 30. quæ reliquorum bonorum finis & coronis est.
units.tr: I. Scripture describes the future age in plain terms. It assigns to that state the eternal blessedness of man, the fullest glorification of soul and body, and the crown and sum of all good things. All of Christ's benefits will reach their end and completion there: redemption (Luke 21:28), calling (1 Pet. 5:10), justification (Matt. 25:34), adoption (Rom. 8:23), sanctification (Eph. 5:27). Glorification alone (Rom. 8:30) will remain, as the end and crown of the other goods.

units.la: II. Appellat autem Scriptura illum statum hominis vitam æternam, cum Deo suavissime agendam: in cujus non oculis modo, sed & sinu Ecclesia tum aget; Deo suo plena, & tantum non impleta ac satiata, utpote quem non proximum solum sibi, sed insusum propemodo sentiet. Erit omnia in omnibus. 1 Cor.15:28.
units.tr: II. Scripture calls that state of man eternal life, to be spent most sweetly with God. In it the Church will dwell, not only before God's eyes but in his bosom, full of her God, and almost satisfied and sated with him, since she will feel him not merely as near to her but almost as poured into her. God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

units.la: III. Beatitudinem aliquam hominis dari, testatur immortale illud beatitudinis desiderium: quod, cum res bona sit, à Deo conditore naturæ integræ inditum fuit, nec frustra esse potest. Atque ex isto animi tormento est, quod Philosophi in summo bono quærendo adeo sese fatigarunt. Nec procul aberrant, qui in recto ac temperato rationis & liberi arbitrii usu illud posuerunt. Hoc enim summum est, quod natura dare potest. Cumque in omni statu homini adesse possit; semper eum, quoad natura pertingit, facere potest, & servare beatum. Et ne Theologia quidem illam beatitudinis vel causam vel comitem abnuit, si nebulosæ rationis lumen sublucтre & malignum fidei splendore ac jubare excitetur & adjuvetur.
units.tr: III. That some blessedness is given to man is attested by that immortal desire for blessedness, which God the Creator, while nature was still whole, implanted in us, since it is a good thing and cannot be in vain. From this inner torment came the great labour that the philosophers spent in seeking the chief good. Nor are those far wrong who placed it in the right and moderate use of reason and free will, for this is the highest that nature can give. Since it can be present to a man in every state, it can always make him blessed, and keep him so, as far as nature reaches. Nor does theology itself deny that this blessedness has a cause or a companion in that natural good, provided the light of clouded reason is lifted up and aided by the bright radiance of faith.

units.la: IV. Ut autem distinctius hanc rem expediamus, solet beatitudo hominis, vel in objecto suo, vel in forma propria, considerari.
units.tr: IV. To set out this matter more clearly, the blessedness of man is usually considered either in its object or in its proper form.

units.la: V. Illud est Deus, bonum summum & increatum animæ beandæ, perpetuumque mulcendæ, appprime conveniens & solus sufficiens: cum cæteroquin desiderium animæ nostræ longe ultra intellectum nostrum pateat, & quasi in infinitum se porrigat. Ego sum clypeus tuus, & merces magna valde. Gen.15:1. Tecum est fons vita: te lucente, videmus lucem. Psal.36:10. & 16:5. In qua confideratione procul dubio etiam Christus mediator includitur. Hæc est vita æterna, ut te cognoscant, illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum. Joh. 17: 3.
units.tr: V. The object is God, the highest and uncreated good, which is most fitting to delight the soul, and to satisfy it forever, and alone is sufficient. For the desire of our soul otherwise stretches far beyond our understanding and, as it were, extends itself to infinity. I am your shield, and your exceedingly great reward (Gen. 15:1). With you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light (Ps. 36:10; cf. 16:5). Without doubt Christ the Mediator is included in this consideration. This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3).

units.la: VI. Forma ejus, non infinitum quiddam & increatum est; nec in actione Dei consistit, qua ille videl. sese nobis infinita quadam ratione præberet, ac veluti infunderet; quæ Scholasticorum quorundam speciosa cogitatio fuisse dicitur. Respuit enim illud finita animæ natura. Sed in actione ac cogitatione ipsius animæ consistit; & in dulcedine ac beatitudine quadam creata; qua illa in perpetuo Dei conspectu & amore inhærens, ineffabili modo proluitur & inundatur.
units.tr: VI. The form of blessedness is not something infinite and uncreated, nor does it consist in an action of God by which he would present himself to us, or pour himself into us, in some infinite manner, as a certain showy notion of some of the Scholastics is said to have been. For a finite nature of the soul rejects that. Rather, it consists in the action and thought of the soul itself, and in a certain created sweetness and blessedness, by which the soul, cleaving to the perpetual sight and love of God, is bathed and flooded in an ineffable way.

units.la: VII. Quæ operatio beatifica non transiens est: nec enim Dei, ut summum bonum considerati, nec beatitudinis ratio hoc admiserit: sed animæ immanens & inhærens, penitamque ejus vim & essentiam dulcissime afficiens. Quæ, supernaturali licet robore adjuta, è propriis tamen facultatibus eam producit. Ut male Scholasticorum quidam à Deo solo eam proficisci dixerint.
units.tr: VII. This blessed operation is not transitive. Neither the notion of God as the highest good nor the nature of blessedness allows it to be so. It is immanent in the soul and cleaves to it, most sweetly affecting its innermost power and essence. Although it is aided by a supernatural strength, it nevertheless produces it from the soul's own faculties. So some of the Scholastics were wrong to say that it comes from God alone.

units.la: VIII. Facile autem patet, sensus externos infinitum istum beatitudinis fontem delibare, aut summam omnino beatitudinem capere non posse. Unde parte animæ ratiocinante, intellectu videl. ac voluntate, quibus solis Deum adimus, ea perficitur. Cumque illa animæ actio, qua beatitudinem haurimus, & appetitum, & desiderium comitem habeat; & prono impetu ad Deum, beatitudinis fontem, decurrat; eique æterno amore inhæreat, ac tantum non immoriatur; satis patet voluntatis primas hic esse partes; quæ facultas animæ est nobilissima, qua ad Deum proxime accedimus, eique uniri, & ita eo frui, & beari unice possumus. Desiderium enim, atque ille animæ procantis veluti, ac Deo conjungi gestientis, ambitus, & amor, & inde profluens gaudium, voluntatis sunt. Intellectus autem nudas rerum imagines percipit, nec ultra pertendit. Quæ ad felicitatem non sufficiunt.
units.tr: VIII. It is easy to see that our external senses cannot taste this infinite fountain of blessedness, nor grasp the supreme blessedness at all. Therefore it is perfected in the reasoning part of the soul, namely in the intellect and the will, the only faculties by which we approach God. And since that action of the soul by which we drink in blessedness has desire and longing as its companions, and runs with eager impulse toward God, the fountain of blessedness, and cleaves to him with eternal love, almost dying in him, it is plain that the will has the first place here. It is the noblest faculty of the soul, by which we draw nearest to God, and by which alone we can be united with him, and so enjoy him and be blessed. For desire, and that longing of the soul which, as it were, strains to be joined to God, and the love, and the joy that flows from them, belong to the will. The intellect, however, perceives only bare images of things and goes no further, and these do not suffice for happiness.

units.la: IX. Ut ergo summam rei complectamur, beatitudo, quæ aggregatum quiddam dicit, nec uno animæ actu absolvi potest, hæc tria dicit, beatificam Dei visionem, amorem, gaudium. Præcedit visio, lætusque numinis conspectus, qua homini Deum adire fas est; quæ beatitudinem, & ciet, & promovet; quæque ex stylo Scripturæ metonymice consequentes quoque voluntatis operationes connotat. Consistit ea proprie in animæ, Deo jam potentis, cupedine ac amore perfectissimo & jucundissimo. Consequitur autem penitum ejus gaudium, ac ovantis animæ quidam quasi triumphus, sine ulla lassitudine, aut torpore, qualis mortalia gaudia excipere, & foedare nonnunquam solet: cum nullus itius luminis recessus, nec vel levissima obumbratio timenda sit. Succedunt denique corporea bona. Ut corpore animoque homo sit integerrimus, & perfectissimus, planeque Deo dignus. Ut ad tria hæc redeat beatitudinis ístius summa. 1 Perfectam sapientiam, seu visionem Dei. 2. Sanctitatem. 3. Gloriam. Hoc est, ad lucem & vitam. Psal. 36:10. Quæ omnia per partes lustrare æquum est.
units.tr: IX. So, to grasp the sum of the matter, blessedness, which denotes a composite thing and cannot be completed by a single act of the soul, comprises these three: the blessed vision of God, love, and joy. Vision comes first, the joyful sight of the divine majesty by which it is lawful for man to approach God. This vision both kindles and advances blessedness, and by the usage of Scripture, through metonymy, it also implies the consequent operations of the will. Properly it consists in the soul's most perfect and most joyful desire and love for God, now possessed. Then follows its inmost joy, a kind of triumph of the exulting soul, without any weariness or dullness, such as earthly joys usually encounter and sometimes defile, since no withdrawal from that light, nor even the slightest shadow, is to be feared. Finally the bodily goods follow, so that man may be most whole and most perfect in body and soul, and altogether worthy of God. Thus the sum of this blessedness returns to three things: (1) the perfect wisdom, or vision of God; (2) holiness; (3) glory. That is, to light and life (Ps. 36:10). It is right to examine all of these part by part.

units.la: X. Erit ergo in intellectu visio Dei. Quæ phrasis Scripturæ nota & familiaris est, conspectumque numinis familiarem & proximum dicit; qualem nempe sese in intimo sacrario ostendit, qualisque videri cœlicolis, quantusque solet. Beati qui sunt mundo corde, nam ipsi Deum videbunt. Matth. 5:8. Satiabor, cum evigilavero, specie tua. Psal. 17:15. Nosse me facies iter vitæ, satietatis lætitiarum apud faciem tuam; amœnorum, quæ sunt in dextra tua perpetuo. Psal. 16:11.
units.tr: X. There will therefore be the vision of God in the intellect. This phrase is familiar and well known in Scripture, and it denotes a close and familiar sight of the divine majesty, such as he shows himself in his innermost sanctuary, and such as he is usually seen by the heavenly beings. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God (Matt. 5:8). I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with your likeness (Ps. 17:15). You will make known to me the path of life; in your presence is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forever (Ps. 16:11).

units.la: XI. Brutum autem est, visus humanos, oculosque corporeos, hic cogitare. Deus enim, cum spiritus sit immensus & infinitus, hoc pacto attingi nequit. Nec felicitatem hominum aspectus ille absolvere potest. Vitio vero hæc est, qualis & in Angelos cadit: Angeli ipsorum in cœlis semper vident faciem Patris mei, qui est in cœlis. Matth. 18:10. & cognitionem perfectissimam dicit. Videmus enim adhuc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem de facie ad faciem. Nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cognoscam, ut & sum cognitus. 1 Cor. 13:12. Videbimus ipsum, ut est. 1 Joh. 3:2. Ut propudiofo errore Sociniani Deum Patrem in futura vita, in cœlo illo increato, oculis corporeis conspicuum fingant. Quomodo &, singulari privilegio, à Christo in fictitio illo raptu, in mortali corpore visus fuerit. Quem tamen, ut in æternum beato illo aspectu frueretur, post mortem, glorioso corpore, quod à carnea ac terrena hac mole longe diversum sit, indutum ferunt. Ad cujus exemplum etiam fideles, post resurrectionem, novis ac lucidis exuviis revestiendos affabulantur. Quanquam alioquin & mortalibus hisce oculis Deum videri posse, & nonnunquam visum esse, non abnuant. Quod revera est, Deum ipsum corporeum effingere, & in Anthropomorphitarum castra succedere. Quæ labes quam non occulte apud homines hosce hæreat, ex Smalcio videre est, qui Christum, in glorificato corpore, naturam divinam, aut divinæ persimilem & proximam, sortitum asserit. At Deus est Spiritus. Joh. 4:24. Ecce cœli, & cœli cœlorum, non capiunt.
units.tr: XI. It is foolish, however, to think here of human sight and bodily eyes. For God, since he is an immense and infinite spirit, cannot be attained in that way, nor can that sight complete human happiness. Rather, the vision is of the kind that falls even to the angels: Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18:10). It denotes the most perfect knowledge: For now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know, even as I am known (1 Cor. 13:12). We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The Socinians, in their shameful error, imagine God the Father, in the future life, visible to bodily eyes in that uncreated heaven. In the same way they fable that Christ, by a singular privilege, was seen in a mortal body in that imagined rapture. Yet, so that he might enjoy that blessed sight forever after death, they say he was clothed in a glorious body, quite different from this fleshly and earthly mass. And on his example they also fable that the faithful, after the resurrection, will be clothed in new and bright garments. Although otherwise they do not deny that God can be seen even with these mortal eyes, and sometimes has been. This truly amounts to fashioning God as bodily, and going over to the camp of the Anthropomorphites. How deeply this stain clings to these men may be seen from Smalcius, who asserts that Christ, in his glorified body, received a divine nature, or one very like and close to the divine. But God is Spirit (John 4:24). Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him (1 Kings 8:27).

units.la: {y} Visio Dei, seu perfecta cognitio. capiunt te; multo minus domus hæc, quam condidi. 1 Reg. 8:27. Non poteris videre faciem meam, nam non videbit me homo, & vivet. Exod. 33:20. 1 Tim. 6:16.
units.tr: The vision of God, or perfect knowledge. The heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you; how much less this house which I have built. 1 Kings 8:27. You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live. Exod. 33:20. 1 Tim. 6:16.

units.la: XII. Nec juvant illos loca 1 Joh. 3:2. Videbimus ipsum, ut est. Apoc. 22:4. Et videbunt faciem ipsius. quæ de Christo homine expressè agunt. Cui Apoc. 22:3. Deus quidem adjungitur; sed ita, ut alia visione, & solo mentis oculo, attingendus sit. Exod. autem cap. 33:19. ex quo, peculiari Dei misericordia, id fieri posse concludunt, de specie tantum humano agitur, in qua Deus Mosi apparuit. Cujus ille tamen posteriora tantum, ac discedentis Dei veluti umbram & vestigia adoravit. Anteriora enim Dei videri non posse, eodem loco additur. Quanquam & misericordia Dei ad longe alia eo in loco referatur.
units.tr: XII. Nor do the passages which speak expressly of Christ as man help them: 1 John 3:2, "We shall see him as he is"; Rev. 22:4, "and they shall see his face." God is indeed joined to him in Rev. 22:3, but in such a way that he is to be reached by a different kind of vision, by the eye of the mind alone. Exod. 33:19, from which they conclude that this can happen through a special mercy of God, speaks only of the human form in which God appeared to Moses. Yet Moses worshipped only the hinder parts, the shadow and footprints of the departing God, for in the same place it is added that the face of God cannot be seen. And the mercy of God is referred in that place to something quite different.

units.la: XIII. Nec modum tenent Pontificii. Qui, cum Deus, aut in operibus, Rom. 1:20 aut in assumto corpore, Gen. 32. Exod. 33. Esai. 6. aut clarius adhuc in Christo incarnato, 1 Tim. 3:16. aut per fidem, 1 Cor. 13:12. aut denique majore in gloriæ lumine. ibid. videri tantum possit (hos enim modos Scriptura solum tradit) illi præterea superaddunt ulteriorem Deum videndi modum, immediatum nempe, & intuitivum; qua Deus videtur sicuti est, ac per essentiam suam; eamque, aut per se ipsam, aut per speciem intelligibilem haustam. Quæ audacia sunt, ac asserendi temeritate modestiam omnem corrumpentia, nec Deo plane decora; qui solus invisibilis, & intellectui creato inaccessus, perhibetur. 1 Tim. 1:17. Non enim de oculis incorporeis, quibus & alia; præter Deum, inconspicua sunt, ista accipere sufficit. Confer Joh. 1:18. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Unigenitus filius, qui est in gremio Patris, ille edisserit. 1 Tim. 6:16. Qui solus habet immortalitatem, lucem habitans inaccessam; quem vidit nemo hominum, neque videre potest. Rom. 1:21. Ipsius enim invisibilia, jam inde à condito mundo, ex iis quæ fecit, mente perpensa videntur. Atque uterque ille modus, quo essentiam divinam attingi asserunt, cogitatu plane imperceptibilis; atque omnino impossibilis est. Nec enim ipsa Dei essentia intellectum nostrum informare, &, ad modum lucis adventitiæ, ad intelligendum provehere potest: neque etiam speciem de se fundere, quo veluti æternæ lucis radio infinitam Dei essentiam comprehendamus; cum, quod æternum ac infinitum est, repræsentari nulla specie ac simulachro perfecte possit.
units.tr: XIII. Nor do the Papists keep due measure. Although God can be seen only in his works (Rom. 1:20), or in an assumed body (Gen. 32; Exod. 33; Isa. 6), or more clearly still in Christ incarnate (1 Tim. 3:16), or through faith (1 Cor. 13:12), or finally in the greater light of glory (ibid.), for Scripture transmits only these modes, they add to them a further mode of seeing God, namely an immediate and intuitive one, by which God is seen as he is and through his own essence. They claim this either through the essence itself or through an intelligible species drawn in. These are audacious claims which corrupt all modesty by their rash assertions, and are not fitting for God, who is said to be the only invisible one, inaccessible to the created intellect (1 Tim. 1:17). For it is enough to understand these words not of bodily eyes, by which other things too, apart from God, are unseen. Compare John 1:18: "No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him." And 1 Tim. 6:16: "who alone has immortality, dwelling in light inaccessible, whom no man has seen nor can see." Rom. 1:21: "For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Both of those modes by which they claim the divine essence is attained are plainly beyond thought and altogether impossible. For the divine essence itself cannot inform our intellect and raise it to understanding, in the manner of an external light, nor can it pour out from itself a species by which we might, as by a ray of eternal light, comprehend the infinite essence of God. What is eternal and infinite cannot be perfectly represented by any species or image.

units.la: XIV. Visio autem, quam Apostolus de facie ad faciem appellat, appellat,
units.tr: XIV. The vision which the Apostle calls "face to face" denotes only a clearer mode of knowing God.

units.la: 1 Cor. 13:12. clariorem tantum cognitionis divinæ modum dicit. Qualis in cælis obtinebit; ubi, quæ in hac vita tenui ac longinquo, veluti auditu percepimus, clarius, ipsisque veluti oculis subjecta, lustrabimus. Qui cognitionis modus clarior est, cum certior oculorum quam aurium fides sit. Vide Exod. 33:11. Alloquebatur autem Jehova Moscen facie ad faciem, quemadmodum alloqui solet amicus amicum. Qualiscunque vero illa Dei visio, per ideam Dei in nobis, sed clariorem ac lucidiorem, novoque lumine auctam, peragetur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13:12. Such knowledge will hold in heaven, where we shall see clearly and, as it were, with our own eyes what we have perceived in this thin and distant life as if by hearing. This mode of knowledge is clearer, since the certainty of the eyes is greater than that of the ears. See Exod. 33:11: "Jehovah spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend." However that vision of God is achieved, it will come through the idea of God in us, but clearer and brighter, increased by a new light.

units.la: XV. Sed & comprehendi Deum in futura vita, ac comprehensive intelligi, iidem nimis superbe asserunt. Qua locutionis insolentia perfectam & adæquatam cognitionem rei, secundum omnem ejus entitatem & modum, intelligunt. Ac sic beatos Deum intelligere ajunt, & essentiam ejus, & attributa, & personas, & decreta, quoad realem eorum entitatem, per visionem, ut appellant; quoad liberam autem eorum terminationem, & relationem ad hanc vel illam creaturam, per revelationem percipere; ut nihil iis de Deo lateat, atqui ille, quantaque luce circumfusus, totus, omnique ex parte, iis pervius sit. Quæ inverecunda sunt, atque ultra non hominum solum, sed & Angelorum perspicacissimas mentes eunt.
units.tr: XV. But the same men also assert too arrogantly that God is grasped in the future life and understood "comprehensively." By this unusual expression they mean a perfect and adequate knowledge of a thing according to its whole being and manner. Thus they say that the blessed understand God, and his essence, attributes, persons and decrees, as to their real being, through what they call vision, and as to their free determination and relation to this or that creature, through revelation; so that nothing about God is hidden from them, and he lies wholly open to them, in every respect, bathed in whatever light. These claims are shameless, and go beyond the most penetrating minds not only of men but of angels.

units.la: XVI. Serviunt autem hæc alii ipsorum errori, ut videlicet conficiant, Sanctos in cœlo videre quæ geruntur in terris. Quem in finem mirabile ac præstigiosum in cœlo speculum fabricant, in quo rerum omnium imagines videant. Quod inane fabulamentum est. Trinitatis enim istud fictitium speculum a beatifica visione longe diversum est. Cum in Deo non alia videant beati, quam quæ ad beatitudinem eorum consummandam pertinent; & longe admodum differant, Dei, & rerum, quæ in terris geruntur, visio. Nec ullum inter ista commercium est. Sed de die illo, ac hora, nemo scit, neque angeli quidem qui in cœlo sunt, neque ipse filius, sed Pater. Marc. 13:32. Ut putre sit fundamentum invocationis Sanctorum, cultusque, ac amoris eorum adulteri. Qui inter cultus Latinorum præcipuus est.
units.tr: XVI. These notions also serve another of their errors, namely to establish that the saints in heaven see what happens on earth. To this end they fabricate a wonderful and marvellous mirror in heaven, in which they see images of all things. This is an empty fable. For that fictitious mirror of the Church triumphant is far different from the beatific vision. The blessed see in God nothing but what pertains to the completion of their blessedness, and the vision of God is very far different from the vision of what happens on earth. Nor is there any communication between the two. "But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son himself, but the Father" (Mark 13:32). So the foundation of the invocation of saints is rotten, and so is their adulterous worship and love, which is the chief of the Latins' cults.

units.la: XVII. Sed & exempla quorundam adferunt, qui ista visione jam in terra fruiti sunt, atque ipsam Dei essentiam viderunt, Moisem vid. & Paulum, & Christum. Quæ parum librata ac perpensa sunt. Nam Christus humano intellectu ipsam Dei essentiam nec attigit, nec attingere potuit. Luc. 2:52. Nec Moses item essentiam Dei, sed nonnullas tantum gloriæ strictuias, vidit; & augustissimam forte numinis speciem, & formam corpoream, in monte lustravit. Exod. 33: 20,23. Et Paulus, in raptu illo admirabili, non visa, sed audita sibi refert, 2 Cor. 13: 4. ac postea etiam quum gloriam illam gustaverat, expressis nihilominus verbis Deum lucem habitare inaccessam docet, quem nemo hominum vidit, nec videre potest. 1 Tim. 6: 16. Ut flagitiosum ac pudendum sit, monachos quosdam, in claustris ac latibulis suis, hoc sibi vendicare; Deique majestatem familiariter in nidis istis obambulantem, ac gregalibus suis sese ostentantem, praedicare. Qui non ferendus est ἐνθουσιασμὸς hominum, Deum ipsum in os vultumque suspicere, idque ipsum publice jactare, non verecundantium. Ac collimant eodem Beginarum, Begardorum, aliorumque furores, quales ipsis tribuuntur.
units.tr: XVII. They also cite the examples of certain people who already enjoyed that vision on earth and saw the very essence of God: Moses, Paul and Christ. These are poorly weighed and considered. For Christ with his human intellect neither touched nor could touch the essence of God (Luke 2:52). Nor did Moses see the essence of God, but only some flashes of glory; on the mountain he perhaps beheld the most august appearance of the deity and a bodily form (Exod. 33:20, 23). And Paul, in that wonderful rapture, reports that he had not seen but heard (2 Cor. 13:4); and afterwards, even after he had tasted that glory, he nonetheless teaches in express words that God "dwells in light inaccessible, whom no man has seen nor can see" (1 Tim. 6:16). It is therefore shameful and disgraceful that certain monks claim this for themselves in their cloisters and hiding places, and preach that the majesty of God walks familiarly in those nests and shows himself to their companions. This enthusiasm [ἐνθουσιασμὸς] of men, who look up at God himself face to face and boast of it publicly without shame, is not to be tolerated. The frenzies of the Beguines and Beghards, of which they are accused, aim at the same thing.

units.la: XVIII. Visionem Dei comitabitur tam ampla scientiae ac intel- ligentiae copia, quanta ad creaturae beatitudinem requiritur.
units.tr: XVIII. The vision of God will be accompanied by as full a measure of knowledge and understanding as the creature's blessedness requires.

units.la: Unde perfectio isti statui adscribitur, qualis virorum est. Eph 4: 13. Et, non fides, sed praesentis quasi numinis aspectus, ac amplissima divinarum rerum cognitio ibi locum habebit: cum hic tantum Deum, tenui in imagine, uti luscios solem in undarum speculo, videamus. 2 Cor. 5: 7. 1 Cor. 13: 9–13. Quare & media cognitionis cessabunt, quibus in hac mundi schola assuevimus: & quae in naturae ludo hic didicimus, quae in verbi auditorio perfectius hausimus, in coelesti illa Academia, Deo ipso tradente, sine labore ullo, pervidebimus. Qualis autem ac quam perfecta illa cognitio ac visio futura sit, non hujus temporis ac saeculi est edisserere.
units.tr: Hence that state is credited with a perfection such as befits a man (Eph. 4:13). There, faith will give way to the very sight of the present God, and to the fullest knowledge of divine things, since here we see God only dimly, as in a mirror of water one sees the sun with weak eyes (2 Cor. 5:7; 1 Cor. 13:9–13). Therefore the means of knowing to which we are accustomed in this school of the world will also cease. What we learned here in the game of nature, and what we drew more fully in the hearing room of the Word, we shall see through completely, without any toil, in that heavenly Academy, with God himself as teacher. But to set out what that knowledge and vision will be, and how perfect, does not belong to this time and age.

units.la: XIX. Ad quaestionem, an rerum hominumque, in hoc saeculo, memoria ac cognitio permansura sit?
units.tr: XIX. Whether the memory and knowledge of things and men will endure in this age.

units.la: Resp. Rerum, ad temporalem vitam spectantium, aliarumque artium ac studiorum, inanium & futilium, facilem jacturam fore. Quomodo in hac vita homines, ad maturam aetatem perducti pueriliim deliramentorum animo obliviscuntur; &, quae juvenes didicere, senes perdunt, da fatentur. Eademque hominum personarumque, in vitae hujus stadio relictorum, ratio erit; quorum carnali desiderio beati non affligentur. Licet caeteroquin nulla appareat ratio, cur memoria rerum hominumque qui in hisce terris fuerunt, quatenus illa sine omni tristitia esse poterit, & ad Deum laudandum & glorificandum unice comparata, abolenda sit. Spiritualium autem maxime rerum notitia non peribit, sed multiplici luce augebitur, & consummabitur. Adeo nullum studii iis recte impensi, laborumque exhaustorum damnum patiemur. Quod si quis superaedificet, super fundamentum hoc, aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, foenum, stipulam,
units.tr: Answer: the loss of things that pertain to temporal life, and of other arts and studies that are empty and trivial, will be easy. Just as in this life men who have grown to mature age forget the childish nonsense of their minds, and old men admit that they lose what they learned as young men, so it will be with the persons and people left behind in the stage of this life, and the blessed will not be troubled by carnal longing for them. Otherwise there is no apparent reason why the memory of those who lived on this earth should be abolished, since it can exist without any sadness and is made solely for praising and glorifying God. But the knowledge of spiritual things above all will not perish; it will be increased and brought to completion by a manifold light. So we shall suffer no loss of the study rightly spent on them or of the labours we have spent: "If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw,"

units.la: Vitionis illi ... (marginal notes, right margin: "Visionis illius", "gaudium, & comitantur", "perfectio", "Ad rerum hominumque", "memoria ac cognitio", "perduraturae fiet?") Cujusque opus manifestum fiet — Si cujus opus manserit, quod superadificaverit, mercedem accipiet. Si cujus opus exustum fuerit, damnum faciet: ipse vero servabitur: ita tamen, ut per ignem. 1 Cor. 3: 12,13,14. Nec Ecclesiæ quoque, in his terris peregrinantis, status ejus universi, oblivio nos capiet; sed pugnas & certamina ejus etiam in cœlo recogitabimus. Quod tamen de Ecclesia universa, non de personis ac rebus singularibus intelligendum est. Et clamabant voce magna, dicentes: quousque, o quies Dominus sanctus & verax, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum ab iis, qui habitant in terra? Apoc. 6: 10.
units.tr: (Marginal notes in the right margin: "Of that vision", "joy, and accompanies", "perfection", "Of the memory and knowledge of things and men", "will it endure?") "each man's work shall be made manifest. If anyone's work remains which he built upon it, he shall receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned, he shall suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire" (1 Cor. 3:12, 13, 14). Nor will the condition of the whole Church, while it wanders in this earth, slip from our memory; we shall call to mind its battles and conflicts even in heaven. This, however, must be understood of the Church as a whole, not of individual persons and affairs. "And they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" (Rev. 6:10).

units.la: XX. Ad alteram quæstionem, an beati in vita futura se invicem agnituri sint? Similis est responsio. Hoc enim certum videtur, carnales & terrenos affectus, in cœli municipibus locum non habituros. Nec enim cognatum affinemve sanguinem ibi inani studio requiremus; aut præcipuo quodam præ reliquis cœlitibus amore, ac honore dignabimur; aut denique de amicis relictis, ac tanta felicitate fraudatis, nos multum fatigabimus. Absorbebit enim illos affectus unius Dei amor, ac studium; in quo solo deliciabimur, inque summo ejus beneplacito suavissime, sine ulla querela, recumbemus. Propterea sunt coram throno Dei, & serviunt ei die & nocte, in templo suo; &, qui sedet in throno, habitabit super eis Apoc. 7: 15. Omnes autem cœlicolas, omnes supera alta tenentes, ac universum illum beatorum chorum, ex æquo colemus & amabimus. Itaut, remoto illo terrestri, quem diximus, affectu, notos olim, ac in Ecclesia Dei cognitos, præsertim majoris dignationis viros, Apostolos, martyres, aliosque Ecclesiæ duces; quin & parentes propinquos, aliosque ibi cognituri simus. Hoc enim ad gaudii illius complementum facit; & ad cœlestem societatem requiri videtur. Vide Hebr. 12: 22,23. Sed accessistis ad panegyrin & concionem primogenitorum, qui in cœlo conscripti sunt. Luc. 13:28. Quando videbitis Abrahamum, & Isaacum, & Jacobum, & omnes Prophetas, in regno Dei. Nec abludunt, quæ de Adamo in Paradiso, Gen. 2: 23. Et dixit Adam: hæc vice hæc est os de ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea: de Apostolis, Matth. 17: 3. Et ecce, videbantur ab ipsis Moses & Elias, cum eo colloquentes: tandemque etiam in parabola Euangelica, de Epulone, Luc. 16: 23. legimus.
units.tr: XX. On the other question, whether the blessed will know one another in the future life. The answer is similar. For it seems certain that carnal and earthly affections will have no place among the citizens of heaven. We shall not seek in vain our kin or relatives there by any empty effort, nor shall we be honoured with any special love and esteem above the other inhabitants of heaven, nor finally shall we greatly trouble ourselves over friends left behind and deprived of such great happiness. For the love and zeal of the one God will absorb those affections; in him alone we shall delight, and we shall rest most sweetly in his supreme good pleasure, without any complaint. "Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will dwell among them" (Rev. 7:15). We shall honour and love equally all the dwellers in heaven, all who hold the high places above, and that whole company of the blessed. So, with that earthly affection set aside, as we have said, we shall also come to know those we once knew and who were known in the Church of God, especially men of greater dignity, the Apostles, the martyrs and the other leaders of the Church; and indeed our kindred parents and others. For this adds to the completion of that joy and seems required for heavenly fellowship. See Heb. 12:22, 23: "But you have come to the assembly and church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven." Luke 13:28: "When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God." Nor do those things disagree which we read of Adam in Paradise (Gen. 2:23): "And Adam said: This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh"; of the Apostles (Matt. 17:3): "And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him"; and finally in the Gospel parable of Dives (Luke 16:23).

units.la: XXI. Hanc intellectus perfectionem excipiet non minor voluntatis consummatio. Quæ in renovatione, ac plenissima ejus ad voluntatem divinam conformatione & obsequio consistit. Obtinebitque in illo statu, non tam sanctificatio, quam vera ac plena sanctitas. Nos autem omnes, detecta facie gloriam Domini, quasi in speculo intuentes, secundum eandem imaginem transformamur, ex gloria in gloriam, sicut à Spiritu Domini. 2 Cor. 3:18. Beati puri corde, quia ipsi Deum videbunt. Matth. 5:8. 2 Pet. 3:13.
units.tr: XXI. This perfection of the intellect will be followed by no less a completion of the will. It consists in its renewal and in its most full conformity to and obedience toward the divine will. In that state there will be obtained not so much sanctification as true and full holiness. "But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Cor. 3:18). "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8; 2 Pet. 3:13).

units.la: XXII. Consistet vero ea in purissima ac præfectissima charitate, ex immenso illo lumine, ac cœlesti intuitu, oriunda. Charitas numquam excidit. Sed & prophetiæ evanescent, & linguæ cessabunt, & cognitio evanescet. 1 Cor. 13:8. Quæ charitas, atque amor delicatissimus, nihil peregrini aut fucati habens, pro lege in isto statu erit; ac sine ullo tædio, indeclinabili cursu Deo adhærescet. Ita ut non solum nullum peccatum, sed ne minimum quidem amoris deliquium ibi locum habiturum sit. Unde etiam immutabilis erit ille status, propter confirmationem in bono & indeclinabilem complacentiam justitiæ ad non peccandum: quæ vera hominis est libertas. Adeoque sibi placebunt pii, ut nulla conditione, nullove mortalium respectu, præsentem statum mutari laturi sint. Longe aliter, ac de Christiana Pontificiorum fabellis est. Male autem Socinian, non nisi alio in corpore, atque abolita hac carne, tam plenam sanctitatem locum habere posse confidunt. Quod supra excussimus. XXIII. Magna etiam potestate, & gloria beati insignes erunt. Qui vincit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo; quemadmodum & ego vici, & consedi cum Patre meo, in throno ipsius. Apoc. 3:21. Quod tamen eo usque extendendum non est, ac si illi, mediatoriæ quoque potestatis participes, generis humani advocatione in cœlis fungerentur: aut hominum, cœtuum, urbiumque ac regionum patrocinia ac præfecturas gererent. Ita enim universum mundum, ac Ecclesiam, inter eos distribuerunt Pontificii; ac vix Deo in regno suo locum reliquerunt; &, sacrilega demum adulatione, cœlitum quoque σωτήρων moliti, religiosis eos cultibus propitiare, favoremque eorum eblandiri non desinunt. Quæ exoletæ Gentilium idololatriæ imitatio, & in Deum sanctosque non exigua contumelia est. Non adorandi enim sunt sancti propter religionem sed honorandi duntaxat propter imitationem. Alio etiam spectant loca, quæ adferunt. Apoc. 2:26. Qui vincit, & tenet usque ad finem opera mea, dabo ei potestatem in gentes. Luc. 19:17. Bene est, serve probe! quia in minimo fuisti fidelis, habeas potestatem in decem urbes. conf. Matth. 25:21. XXIV. Gloria corporis consistet 1. in omnis miseriæ, omnisque etiam cor- labis, ac cujuscunque demum infirmitatis, remotione; non solum poris. illius, quæ ex peccato ortum duxit; sed qualis etiam ex vitæ animalis conditione in statu innocentiæ obtinuisset: cum corpus ibispirituale futurum sit. 1 Cor. 15: 44. Et abstergeт Deus omnem lacrymam ab oculis ipsorum, & mors non erit amplius, neque luctus; aut clamor, aut labor non erit amplius, quia priora abierunt. Apoc. 21:4. Non esurient amplius, neque sitient amplius, neque cadet super eos Sol, neque æstus ullus. cap. 7: 16. Sed sunt ut Angeli Dei in cœlo. Matth. 22:30 Esca ventri destinatæ sunt, & venter escis: Deus autem, & hunc, & eas, abolebit. 1 Cor. 6:13. Ita tamen ut isto prætextu carnis ratio destruenda minime sit; aut alvi gurges, & intestinorum perplex volumina, ac uberum fontes, & conceptuum sinus ac receptacula, de glorioso corpore removenda. Nam ad corporis, alioquin vacaturi, integritatem & decus illa nihilominus pertinent. 2. tum in collatione immortalitatis, omnisque ornatus ac decoris; cujus corpus glorificatum capax erit. Quod Apostolus latius exsequitur 1 Cor. 15. & grani similitudine egregie depingit; quam nonnemo veterum ita explicat: Seritur granum sine folliculi veste, sine fundamento spica, sine munimento arista, sine superbia culmi. Exsurgit autem copia fœneratum, compagine ædificatum, ordine struetum, cultum, munitum, & usquequaque vestitum. Hæc sunt ei corpus à Deo aliud, in quod non abolitione, sed ampliatione mutatur.
units.tr: XXII. This state will consist in the purest and most perfect love, springing from that immense light and heavenly intuition. "Love never fails. But prophecies will fade away, tongues will cease, and knowledge will pass away" (1 Cor. 13:8). This love, most delicate and having nothing foreign or false in it, will be the rule in that state, and it will cleave to God with an unwearied and unswerving course. So not only will no sin have a place there, but not even the smallest failure of love. Hence also that state will be unchangeable, on account of the confirmation in good and the unswerving pleasure in righteousness, so that man does not sin, which is true human freedom. The godly will so delight in themselves that they will suffer the present state to be changed on no condition and by no regard for mortals. This is quite different from the Papists' Christian fables. The Socinians, however, wrongly trust that so full a holiness can exist only in another body, once this flesh has been abolished. "Which we have examined above." XXIII. The blessed will also be distinguished by great power and glory. "He who overcomes, I will give him to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne" (Rev. 3:21). This, however, must not be extended so far as if they, sharing also in the mediatorial power, performed the office of advocates for the human race in heaven, or held the patronages and governorships of men, assemblies, cities and regions. For in this way the Papists have distributed the whole world and the Church among the saints, and have scarcely left a place for God in his own kingdom; and at last, with sacrilegious flattery, they have contrived also saviours [σωτήρων] among the heavenly beings, and they do not cease to propitiate them with religious worship and to coax their favour. This is an imitation of the obsolete idolatries of the Gentiles and no small insult to God and the saints. For the saints are not to be adored for religion's sake, but only to be honoured for the sake of imitation. The passages they bring also point elsewhere. Rev. 2:26: "He who overcomes and keeps my works to the end, I will give him authority over the nations." Luke 19:17: "Well done, good servant! Because you were faithful in a very little, have authority over ten cities." Compare Matt. 25:21. XXIV. The glory of the body will consist, first, in the removal of all misery, every stain, and every infirmity whatever: not only of that which arose from sin, but also of that which would have belonged to the animal condition of life in the state of innocence, since the body will then be spiritual (1 Cor. 15:44). "And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away" (Rev. 21:4). "They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more, nor shall the sun fall on them, nor any heat" (Rev. 7:16). "But they are like the angels of God in heaven" (Matt. 22:30). "Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them" (1 Cor. 6:13). Yet on this pretext the reason of the flesh must by no means be destroyed, nor the gullet of the belly and the twisted coils of the intestines, nor the fountains of the breasts, nor the wombs and receptacles of conception, to be removed from the glorious body. For those things nonetheless belong to the integrity and comeliness of the body, which otherwise would be idle. Second, in the bestowal of immortality and of every ornament and beauty, of which the glorified body will be capable. The Apostle explains this more fully in 1 Cor. 15 and paints it admirably with the likeness of a grain, which one of the ancients explains thus: "The grain is sown without the covering of its husk, without the foundation of the ear, without the protection of the awn, without the pride of the stalk. But it rises up abundant in increase, built up in structure, arranged in order, cultivated, fortified, and clothed on every side. These are a different body given to it by God, into which it is changed not by abolition but by enlargement."

units.la: XXV. Ex hisce exsurget in toto beatis homine gaudium gaudiosissimum: Quod tamen in solo Deo erit: quitum demum erit omnia in omnibus, 1 Cor. 15: 28. seque penitus & intime fidelibus tractandum, gustandum ac fruendum dabit.
units.tr: XXV. From these things there will arise in the blessed a most joyful joy, which, however, will be in God alone, when at last God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), and will give himself to the faithful to be handled, tasted and enjoyed inwardly and wholly.

units.la: Quod status ejus erit consequens & complementum perfectissimum. Uti omnis bonæ actionis comes est voluptas, animique beata tranquillitas. Quæ hic summa erit. Scriptura gaudium illud ineffabile dicit. 1 Cor. 2:9. Psal. 31: 20. & multiplici rerum corporalium figura adumbrat. Nam & Paradisi deliciis, Luc. 23:43. & nuptiarum solemnibus, Apoc. 19: 9. & convivali lætitiæ, Matth. 8: 11. illud assimilat: & esum ac potum, Apoc. 2: 7. & citharæ cantum, Apoc. 5: 8, 9. omniumque deliciarum cumulum notat. Psal. 36: 9. & vide etiam Matth. 5: 4. & 12. Luc. 16: 25. 10: 20. Joh. 16: 22.
units.tr: This joy will be the consequence and most perfect completion of their state, just as pleasure accompanies every good action, and a blessed tranquillity accompanies the soul. Here it will be at its height. Scripture calls that joy ineffable (1 Cor. 2:9; Ps. 31:20), and it shadows it with many figures drawn from bodily things. For it likens it to the delights of Paradise (Luke 23:43), to the solemnities of a wedding (Rev. 19:9), and to the mirth of a banquet (Matt. 8:11); it denotes it by eating and drinking (Rev. 2:7) and by the singing of the harp (Rev. 5:8, 9), and by the heaping up of every delight (Ps. 36:9). See also Matt. 5:4 and 12; Luke 16:25; 10:20; John 16:22.

units.la: XXVI. Quæ tamen rite intelligenda. Nec brutæ Turcarum voluptates; aut Judæorum Cœnæ de fabuloso quodam bove, ac piscæ, & ave, ductique nectaris haustus, nescio e qua cella depromti, in statu illo admittendi. Cujus erroris fontem supra detexímus. Quo male torquent Esai. 65:21. & 66:10. cum prophetiæ omnes præsentis vitæ statu absolvantur, nec futurum sæculum admodum describant.
units.tr: XXVI. These things must, however, be rightly understood. In that state the brutish pleasures of the Turks are not to be admitted, nor the Jewish feasts of the fabulous ox and fish and bird, and the draughts of nectar drawn I know not from what cellar. We have uncovered the source of this error above. Those who twist Isaiah 65:21 and 66:10 in this way do so wrongly, since all the prophecies are fulfilled in the present state of life and do not describe the age to come at all.

units.la: XXVII. Quanquam vero ibi vitæ hujus operationes cessabunt; nec præsentis sæculi pietatem ac opera fideles exercebunt: unde nec fidei, nec spei, nec ejus charitatis, qualis hic obtinet, operibus ibi locus erit; non tamen omnes corporis functiones cessabunt. Nam & illud Deo dignum erit; & tanta gloria perfusum, gaudium quoque maximum animo suppeditabit. Quo etiam spectat quod externo sermone & cultu, Deum venerabitur, & piorum coetibus jugiter intererit. Qualis autem futuri sæculi sermo futurus sit; an Hebræus, quem Angelici nomine quidam decoratum, licet parum solide, volunt, 1Cor. 13:1. quique, de Dei magisterio homini integro traditus, mundo nascenti vernaculus fuisse multis creditur, dijudicare incertum, ac dicere incautum est. Conf. Matth. 17:3. Videbantur ab ipsis Moses, & Elias, cum ipso colloquentes. &
units.tr: XXVII. Although indeed the activities of this life will cease there, and the faithful will not exercise in that age the piety and works of the present age; hence there will be no place there for the works of faith, hope, or that charity such as obtains here. Yet not all the functions of the body will cease. For that too will be worthy of God, and the soul, filled with so great a glory, will also be supplied with the greatest joy. To this also belongs the fact that they will worship God with outward speech and worship, and will constantly take part in the assemblies of the pious. But what the speech of the coming age will be, whether Hebrew, which some, though not very soundly, honour with the name "angelic" (1 Cor. 13:1), and which, delivered to whole man by God's own teaching, is believed by many to have been the native tongue of the newborn world, it is uncertain to determine and rash to say. Compare Matt. 17:3: Moses and Elijah were seen by them, talking with him.

units.la: 1 Cor. 13:8. Sive prophetiæ abolebuntur: sive linguæ, cessabunt.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13:8: Whether there are prophecies, they will be abolished; whether there are tongues, they will cease.

units.la: XXVIII. Nec leve momentum ad beatitudinem adferet ipse locus. Qui Paradisus appellatur; veteris horti similitudine. 2 Cor. 12. Luc. 23. Quem tamen crasse nimis Judæi & Pontificii describunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. The place itself will also contribute no small weight to their blessedness. It is called Paradise, by likeness to the old garden (2 Cor. 12; Luke 23). Yet the Jews and Papists describe it far too crudely.

units.la: XXIX. Ac consummabit istum statum interminabilis æternitas, nulla cogitatione dimetienda, aut finienda. Ut secura omnimodo, ac sine ullo amittendi ejus metu, ac vel levissima suspicione, futura sit tanti boni possessio. Aliter ac in primo hominis statu obtinuit. 1 Pet. 1:4. & 5:4. Luc. 12:33. Hebr. 10:34. Apoc. 3:12. Luc. 16:9. 2 Cor. 5:1. Apoc. 21:4. 1 Cor. 15:26. Apoc. 22:5. 2 Cor. 4:17. Matth. 25:46. Joh. 3:16. & 6:27.
units.tr: XXIX. And this state will be completed by endless eternity, which cannot be measured or bounded by any thought, so that the possession of so great a good will be entirely secure, without any fear of losing it or even the slightest suspicion of it; unlike the state in which man first stood (1 Pet. 1:4; 5:4; Luke 12:33; Heb. 10:34; Rev. 3:12; Luke 16:9; 2 Cor. 5:1; Rev. 21:4; 1 Cor. 15:26; Rev. 22:5; 2 Cor. 4:17; Matt. 25:46; John 3:16; 6:27).

units.la: XXX. Movetur autem hic quæstio inter orthodoxos, de gloriæ gradibus: an nulla cujus disparitas aut differitas inter beatos lo-cum habitura sit? de qua nos sic censemus: removendum imprimis esse fastuosum Pontificiorum errorem, qui quamcunque illam diversitatem meritorum inæqualitati imputant; atque hinc diversam piorum gloriam metiuntur; & nonnullis quoque, qui, simplici merito non contenti, supererogatoria opera fecerunt, aureolas & coronulas, supra reliquam beatorum sortem, adjudicant. Quam jactantiam alibi compressimus. De cætero, qui charismatum discrimina ad decus ac incrementa Ecclesiæ in hoc stadio potissimum, necessaria esse, itamque rationem, ubi ea ad metam pervenerit, à Deo ipso jam implenda & consummanda, magenam partem cessare existimemus: tamen non facilè negandum censemus, pro charismatum diversitate & fructuum, quos quisque in hac vita tulit, copia ac varietate, etiam sæculi futuri meslem fore; Deumque ipsum dona sua in piis vario fine ac modo coronaturum. Ita tamen ut in beatis mentibus nulla invidia, aut æmulatio, aut luctus denique, locum habitura; omnium autem desideria ad plenum explenda sint.
units.tr: XXX. Among the orthodox there is a question here about degrees of glory: whether there will be no inequality or difference at all among the blessed? On this we judge as follows. The proud error of the Papists must first be removed, who ascribe every such difference to inequality of merits, and from this measure the differing glory of the pious; and who also award crowns and little golden crowns above the rest of the blessed's lot to some who, not content with simple merit, have performed works of supererogation. We have checked this arrogance elsewhere. For the rest, although we think that the differences of gifts, which are needed chiefly in this stage for the adornment and growth of the Church, and that such an order, once it has reached its goal, will for the most part cease, being now to be fulfilled and completed by God himself, yet we do not think it easy to deny that, according to the diversity of gifts and the abundance and variety of the fruits which each has borne in this life, there will also be a harvest in the age to come, and that God himself will crown his gifts in the pious with varied end and manner. Yet in such a way that no envy, no rivalry, and finally no grief will have a place in the blessed minds, and all their desires will be fully satisfied.

units.la: XXXI. Ac probant istam diversitatem 1. generalia quædam Scripturæ effata. Reddet unicuique secundum opera ipsius. Rom. 2:6. Ut quisque ferat, quæ per corpus factafunt, secundum quæ fecerit. 2 Cor. 5:10. Qui serit parce, parce etiam metet; qui autem serit cum benedictione, cum benedictione & metet. 2 Cor. 9:6. De futuræ autem vitæ semente agi, ex collatione alterius loci, ad Gal. 6:8. constat: qui seminat in carnem suam, ex carne metet corruptionem; qui vero seminat in spiritum, ex spiritu metet vitam æternam.
units.tr: XXXI. And the following general sayings of Scripture prove this diversity: (1) He will render to each according to his works (Rom. 2:6); that each may receive what has been done through the body, according to what he has done (2 Cor. 5:10); He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; but he who sows with blessing will also reap with blessing (2 Cor. 9:6). That the sowing here concerns the seed of the future life is clear from the comparison with another place, Gal. 6:8: he who sows into his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows into the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

units.la: XXXII. 2. Ex locis quibusdam specialioribus. Nam & Christus, ubi ad judicandum redibit, servis suis, utcunque fidis, pro majore tamen vel minore diligentia præstita, diversam mercedem assignat. Luc. 19:12. & Paulus diversis Ecclesiæ ministris diversam ac inæqualem in cœlis mercedem fore aperte dicit, 1 Cor. 3:14, 15. Si cujus opus, quod ædificavit, manserit, mercedem accipiet: si cujus opus exustum fuerit, damnum faciet; ipse vero servabitur, ita tamen, ut per ignem. Atque eodem fecit com. 8. Plantans autem, & irrigans, idem sunt. Quisque vero suam mercedem accipiet, secundum suum laborem. Atque ad eundem modum de resurrectione disputat 1 Cor. cap. 15. præsertim cum. 41:42. Alia est gloria Solis, & alia Lunæ & alia gloria stellarum. Stella enim stella gloria præstat. Aliam enim ibi diversitatem innui, quam quæ est inter corpus in morte depositum, & in resurrectione reassumtum, ex universo discursu patet.
units.tr: XXXII. (2) From certain more particular passages. For Christ, when he returns to judge, assigns a different reward to his servants, however faithful they are, according to the greater or lesser diligence they have shown (Luke 19:12). And Paul plainly says that there will be a different and unequal reward in heaven for different ministers of the Church (1 Cor. 3:14, 15): If anyone's work which he has built remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. And in the same way he says in verse 8: Now he who plants and he who waters are one; yet each will receive his own reward according to his own labour. In the same manner Paul also disputes about the resurrection in 1 Cor. 15, especially where he says (v. 41, 42): One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. That a different diversity is intended there, namely that between the body laid down in death and the body taken up again in resurrection, is clear from the whole course of the argument.

units.la: XXXIII. 3. Saltem hoc nullo colore negari potest, Veteris Novæque Ecclesiæ ducibus ac heroibus, majorem aliquam gloriam fore: & Patriarchas, Prophetas, Apostolos, Martyres, ac Principes, qui multum ad Christi gloriam contulerunt, doctores &c. præcipuo in loco, in cœlesti gloria, refulsuros. Pertinentque huc quæ de Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo, legimus Matth. 8:11. & Luc. 16:22. de Mose & Elia, Matth. 17. Hebr. 3. ac de Apostolis, Matth. 19:28. Sedebitis vos etiam in duodecim thronis judicantes duodecim tribus Israël. Quos thronos ut in terris ab ipsis jam occupatos non dissitemur; cum doctrina ipsorum increbresceret, ac perfidam Judæorum gentem jacto veluti anathemate percelleret: ita iisdem, in cœlis ac in triumphante Ecclesia, ubi vera demum laborum merces, decessuros non probabile est. Similis est ratio loci Apocalyptici, Apoc. 21:14. Murus habebat fundamenta duodecim, & in illis erant nomina duodecim Apostolorum agni. Certe Paulus fundatæ Thessalonicensium Ecclesiæ præcipuam sibi gloriam, in adventu Domini, non temere auguratur: Quae est nostra spes, aut gaudium, aut corona gloriationis? an non & vos in conspectu Domini nostri Jesu Christi in ejus adventu? 1 Thess. 2:19. Ac Daniel cap. 12:3. in universum doctoribus omnibus, præ discipulis, fulgorem quendam ac peculiarem splendorem promittit. Quanquam enim in alia beatitudinis parte, auditor, utpote sanctior forte, eminere possit; peculiaris tamen ac conspicua quædam, ratione muneris gesti, videtur futura piorum doctorum gloria.
units.tr: XXXIII. (3) At the very least, it cannot be denied on any ground that the leaders and heroes of the Old and New Church will have some greater glory, and that the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, and princes who contributed much to the glory of Christ, and the teachers, etc., will shine in a special place in heavenly glory. To this belong what we read of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt. 8:11; Luke 16:22), of Moses and Elijah (Matt. 17; Heb. 3), and of the Apostles (Matt. 19:28): You also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. We do not deny that these thrones were already occupied by them on earth, when their doctrine was spreading and striking down the faithless Jewish nation as if by a cast anathema; but it is not probable that they will cease to hold them in heaven and in the triumphant Church, where at last is the true reward of their labours. The Apocalyptic passage is of similar sense: Rev. 21:14: The wall had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the Apostles of the Lamb. Certainly Paul did not rashly predict for the Thessalonian Church he had founded a special glory at the coming of the Lord: For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Is it not you also, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? (1 Thess. 2:19). And Daniel 12:3 promises in general to all teachers, above the disciples, a certain brightness and peculiar splendour. For although the hearer, being perhaps more holy, may stand out in another part of blessedness, yet a peculiar and conspicuous glory of the pious teachers, by reason of the office they have discharged, seems likely to be theirs.

units.la: XXXIV. Non æque fortia sunt, quæ pro adversa sententia proserunt. Adducunt autem 1 Scripturas quaedam 2. tum rationes Theologicas. 3 denique ex similitudinibus, quibus futuræ vitæ status adumbratur, parilem piorum omnium gloriam concludunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. The arguments they put forward for the opposing view are not equally strong. They adduce (1) certain passages of Scripture, (2) theological reasons, and (3) finally, from the likenesses by which the state of the future life is foreshadowed, they conclude that the glory of all the godly is equal.

units.la: Opposita sententia argumenta examinantur.
units.tr: The arguments of the opposing view are examined.

units.la: XXXV. Ac 1. Scripturas quod attinet. Matth. 1 3:43. Justis quidem omnibus splendor solis ex æquo adscribitur. Sed ille, licet ad minora sidera sine controversia maximus sit; absolute tamen considéra-tus, præsertim in allegoria hac, gradus admittit. Et erit lux luna, ut lux solis; & lux solis erit septupla, tanquam lux septem dierum. Esai. 30:26. Matthæi autem cap. 20:9, 10. ubi omnibus operariis eadem merces adsignatur; non de solis piis; nec de futuræ, sed de præsentis vitæ conditione agitur; & hypocritarum ac operariorum ingenium depingitur. conf. c. 11. & 15. Denique quanquam Deus, in cœlesti gloria, erit omnia in omnibus, 1 Cor. 15:28. non tamen pari gloria cunctos illustrabit. Cæteroquin & in hac vita esse donorum ac charismatum æqualitas. Distinctiones operationum sunt, sed idem est Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus 1 Cor. 12:6.
units.tr: XXXV. First, as far as Scripture is concerned: Matt. 13:43. Indeed, the splendour of the sun is ascribed equally to all the righteous. But that splendour, although without dispute it is greatest compared with the lesser stars, admits of degrees when considered in itself, especially in this allegory. And the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days. Isa. 30:26. But Matt. 20:9, 10, where the same wage is assigned to all the workers, does not concern only the godly, nor the future life, but the condition of the present life, and it depicts the character of hypocrites and workers. Cf. chs. 11 and 15. Finally, although God in heavenly glory will be all in all, 1 Cor. 15:28, he will not illumine all with equal glory. Moreover, there is equality of gifts and charisms even in this life. There are varieties of operations, but it is the same God who works all in all, 1 Cor. 12:6.

units.la: XXXVI. Nec plus rationes ipsorum concludunt; quas à justificationis æqualitate, & sanguinis Christi pretio, æqualiter videl. pro omnibus effuso, desumunt. Ex ista enim æqualitate non minus sanctificationis æqualitatem in omnibus concludere possis; quod tamen contra est. Pro hujus autem diversa in piis ratione ac gradu, sese habebit futuræ vitæ glorificatio. Intercedet autem sanguinis Christi pretium; qui æqualiter peccata omnium expiabit; iis autem, quibus divina gratia majorem sanctitatis copiam, ac plus sanctæ frugis in terris dedit, majorem quoque gloriæ gradum largictur. Nec procedit, quia in cœlo omnes æque sanéti futuri simus, ideo & omnes æque beatos existimandos. Nam gloria cœlestis ex præsentis, non ex futuræ vitæ sanctitate metienda est. Latetque præterea in ista argutatiuncula petitio principii. Rursus, quod Deum omnes videbimus, sicuti est, 1 Joh. 3: 2. æqualem gloriam non dicit; nisi essentiam Dei, atque omne quod in Deo est, ab omnibus pervideri statuas. Quod supra elisimus. Erit autem dispar piorum, uti gloria, ita visio. Quanquam omnes, vel Deum, vel Christum videbunt uti est.
units.tr: XXXVI. Nor do their arguments prove more, which they draw from the equality of justification and from the price of Christ's blood, poured out equally for all. For from this same equality one could no less conclude an equality of sanctification in all, which however is contrary to fact. The glorification of the future life will stand in proportion to the diverse measure and degree of sanctification in the godly. The price of Christ's blood intervenes, indeed, and expiates the sins of all equally; but to those to whom divine grace has given a greater measure of holiness and more holy fruit on earth, it will also grant a greater degree of glory. Nor does it follow that, because we shall all be equally holy in heaven, we should therefore all be thought equally blessed. For heavenly glory is to be measured by the holiness of the present life, not of the future. Moreover, a petitio principii lies hidden in this little subtle argument. Again, that we shall all see God as he is, 1 John 3:2, does not state an equal glory, unless you assume that the essence of God, and everything that is in God, is fully seen by all. We refuted this above. But the vision of the godly will be unequal, just as their glory is, although all will see God, or Christ, as he is.

units.la: XXXVII. Quod denique addunt, omnes fideles in futura vita filiorum loco fore, Hebr. 12: 23. adeoque æquis partibus hæreditatem adituros, juxta Rom. 8: 17. omnesque ex æquo appellari Reges, Apoc. 1: 6. & ex æquo ad Christum pertinere, cum Ecclesia universa & sponsa, & corpus Christi, futura fit: non admodum ipsos juvat. Nam & in hac vita fideles, & filii, & sponsa, & corpus Christi appellantur. Ubi tamen maxima donorum disparitas conspicitur. Manetque etiam inter filios diversitas, in hæreditate adeunda; & primogenitis jus quoddam prærogativum est. Quo nomine veteris Ecclesiæ duces veniunt. Heb. 12: 23. Nec omnium regum eadem majestas & dignatio est. Psal. 89: 28. Dan. 2: 37. Sponsa autem Christi ornatus multiplex est, & vestis variegata. Psal. 45. Nec omnia mystici corporis membra eodem honore gaudent. Quod egregie exequitur Paulus 1 Cor. 12.
units.tr: XXXVII. As for what they add last, that all believers in the future life will be in the place of sons, Heb. 12:23, and so will take up the inheritance in equal shares, according to Rom. 8:17, and that all will be called kings alike, Rev. 1:6, and belong equally to Christ, since the whole Church is to be both his bride and his body: this does not greatly help them. For in this life too believers are called sons, bride and body of Christ; yet there the greatest disparity of gifts is seen. Diversity also remains among the sons in taking up the inheritance, and the firstborn have a certain prerogative right. It is under this heading that the leaders of the old Church belong, Heb. 12:23. Nor do all kings have the same majesty and dignity, Ps. 89:28; Dan. 2:37. The bride of Christ, however, has manifold adornment and a variegated garment, Ps. 45. Nor do all the members of the mystical body enjoy the same honour, as Paul admirably explains in 1 Cor. 12.

units.la: XXXVIII. Gravius errant Sociniani: qui, ut Christo in cœlo novam divinitatem tribuunt; ita & in partem ejus fideles vocant: in quibus videl. inhabitatura quoque fit divinitas, quæ antea in Christo solo habitabat. Christo autem majorem solum communis gloriæ, ac divinitatis gradum largiuntur: nullum autem ejus in reliquos dominium ac principatum agnoscunt. Adeo à deitate ejus agnoscenda absunt, ut eum in cœlo vix amplius dominum fateantur. Quæ propudia suis locis tetigimus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The Socinians err more gravely. Just as they attribute a new divinity to Christ in heaven, so they also call the faithful into a share of it, into whom, namely, the divinity that formerly dwelt in Christ alone will also come to dwell. To Christ, however, they grant only a greater degree of common glory and divinity, and they acknowledge no dominion or sovereignty of his over the rest. So far are they from acknowledging his deity that they scarcely confess him any longer to be Lord in heaven. We have touched on these shameful errors in their proper places.

units.la: XXXIX. Vitæ æternæ opponitur mors æterna. Lurida nempe, squalida, tetrica, ac terribilis nox, impiisolim, ubi ad supplicia sua reparati erunt, in infernis claustris, exantlanda. Et abibunt isti ad supplicium æternum. Matth 25: 46.
units.tr: XXXIX. Opposed to eternal life is eternal death: namely a gloomy, squalid, dismal and terrible night, to be endured by the wicked alone, where they will be restored to their punishments in the prisons of hell. And these shall go away into everlasting punishment. Matt. 25:46.

units.la: XL. Consistit illa in luctuosa eorum rejectione ac separatione, à facie Dei, ac salutari ejus visu. Quæ hic inchoata, ac prægustata, per pecpeccatum, sævumque ejus sensum, in futuro demum sæculo consummabitur; tum quoad animam, tum quoad corpus.
units.tr: XL. It consists in their sorrowful rejection and separation from the face of God and from his saving sight. This, begun here and tasted beforehand through sin and its cruel sense, will be consummated at last in the future age, both as to the soul and as to the body.

units.la: XLI. Dicitque ea, poenam tum damni, tum sensus. De illa est, Matth.7:23. Nunquam novi vos, discedite à me, operantes iniquitatem.
units.tr: XLI. It is said to be both a punishment of loss and a punishment of sense. Of the former is Matt. 7:23: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.

units.la: 2 Thess.1:9. Qui poenam luent, aeternum exitium, à facie Domini, & à gloria roboris ejus. De hac, Marc.9:44. Ubi vermis ipsorum non interit & ignis non extinguitur. Matth.8:12. Filii autem regni ejicientur in tenebras exteriores; illic erit fletus & stridor dentium. Ineptum enim est, poenam damni comminisci, sine poena sensus. Quod in quibusdam faciunt Pontificii. Procul dubio enim creatura rationalis damni sui conscia est, adeoque ejus sensum habet. Atque ille amarus, & illætabilis animi torpor, & ægritudo, & tædium non leve profecto creaturæ, ad tantam dignitatem creatæ, tormentum est. Sed accidet præterea sævissimus judicii divini sensus & æstuantis conscientiæ horror, & rabies, & laniatus intolerabiles; cum perpetuo in sanctitatem ejus jurgio, acodio acerbissimo, quod non minimam supplicii infernalis partem faciet.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 1:9: They shall pay the penalty, everlasting destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power. Of the latter, Mark 9:44: where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. Matt. 8:12: But the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. For it is absurd to invent a punishment of loss without a punishment of sense, which some Papists do. Undoubtedly a rational creature is conscious of its loss and so has a sense of it. That bitter, joyless torpor of mind, that sickness and no slight weariness, is surely a torment to a creature made for such dignity. But there will also come the most cruel sense of divine judgment, the horror of a seething conscience, rage, and intolerable lacerations, with a perpetual quarrel against his holiness and a most bitter hatred, which will form no small part of the infernal punishment.

units.la: XLII. An præterea materialis ac elementaris ibi futurus sit ignis, disquiritur. Quod de animabus separatis dubium est: cum illæ materiali igne torqueri non possint. Nisi Deus novum inter ignem illum ac animam illorum nexum creet. Unde allegorice potius ignis ille accipiendus. Sicut & aliæ corporearum rerum imagines; utpote tenebrarum, vermis, stridoris dentium, catenarum, caliginis, stagni sulphurei &c. quibus futura supplicia adumbrantur: quæ alioquin nec cum animæ nostræ conditione, nec inter se admodum conveniunt. Omnes autem tristissimam ac acerbissimam impiorum conditionem exprimunt. Quemadmodum cœlestia gaudia blandissimarum rerum typis depinguntur. Peracta autem resurrectione, ac reparatis impiorum corporibus, corporales quoque poenas & cruciatus iis infligi nihil, quantum ad animæ conditionem attinet, repugnat. Cum igne flammante infligens ultionem iis, qui Deum non noverunt. 2 Thess.1:8.conf. Hebr. 10:27. Quamvis an vel tunc etiam ignis, ut loquuntur, materialis sit futurus; an vero potius acutissimi illius dolores imago & symbolum sint ineffabilium tormentorum, quæ impii animâ & corpore in sæculo futuro patientur, anceps valde sit.
units.tr: XLII. Further, it is debated whether there will be material and elemental fire there. This is doubtful concerning separated souls, since they cannot be tormented by material fire, unless God creates some new bond between that fire and their souls. Hence that fire is to be understood allegorically rather, as are other images taken from bodily things, namely darkness, worm, gnashing of teeth, chains, mist, a sulphurous lake, etc., by which the future punishments are foreshadowed.
