These otherwise agree neither well with the condition of our soul nor well with one another, yet all express the most sorrowful and bitter condition of the wicked, just as the heavenly joys are depicted by images of the most delightful things. But once the resurrection is accomplished and the bodies of the wicked restored, it is not contrary to the condition of the soul that bodily penalties and torments should also be inflicted on them: with a flaming fire inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God, 2 Thess. 1:8; cf. Heb. 10:27. Yet whether even then the fire, as they call it, will be material, or whether rather that most acute pain is an image and symbol of the ineffable torments which the impious will suffer in soul and body in the future age, is quite uncertain.

units.la: XLIII. Locus, ubi impiorum caterva justitiæ divinæ poenas pendent, infernus dicitur, Luc. 16:23. Matth. 10:28. & gehenna ignis, Matth. 5:22. à valle Hinnon, ubi nefaria Molochi sacra peragebantur. Et locus tormentorum, Luc. 16: 28. & carcer, 1 Pet. 3: 19. & abyssus, Luc. 8: 31. ut satis constet locum specialem designari; qui deinceps erit respectu corporum damnatorum; sicut nunc status miseriae animarum damnatarum ista voce exprimitur. Ille autem locus ubi terrarum futurus sit, quaerere vanum ac curiosum est. Erunt saltem aliquibi improbi, in semetipsis habentes ignem inextinguibilem. Ubicunque autem erunt, is erit ipsorum ἀδης.
units.tr: XLIII. The place where the host of the wicked pay the penalties of divine justice is called hell, Luke 16:23; Matt. 10:28, and fiery Gehenna, Matt. 5:22, from the valley of Hinnom, where the impious rites of Molech were performed. It is also called place of torments, Luke 16:28, prison, 1 Pet. 3:19, and abyss, Luke 8:31, so that it is sufficiently clear that a special place is designated, which hereafter will be the place of the damned bodies, just as the state of misery of the damned souls is now expressed by that word. But to inquire where that place will be on earth is vain and idle curiosity. There will at least be some wicked somewhere, having within themselves an unquenchable fire. Wherever they are, that will be their Hades [ἅδης].

units.la: XLIV. Errant vero Anabaptistae; qui, ex perversa de animae separatae conditione hypothesi, nullum infernum ante judicii diem agnoscunt: supremo vero orbis igne terram hanc immutandam, ac in igneam abyssum convertendam hariolantur. Qui si de loco corporum loquerentur, minus culpari possent: at de statu animarum damnatarum ita sentientes, errant. Scriptura enim de inferno, tanquam jam existente, loquitur, tum alibi, tum Luc. 16: 23. Quod enim illum tanquam futurum indigitari arguunt, ex Matth. 8: 12. Filii autem regni ejicientur in tenebras extimas; illic erit fletus & stridor dentium: infirmum est. Voluit enim Christus poenarum illarum aeternitatem exprimere, & viventibus loquitur, quorum respectu cruciatus illi demum futuri erant. Nec denique abnuimus, poenas illas post resurrectionem demum consummatissimas fore.
units.tr: The Anabaptists err, who, from a mistaken hypothesis about the condition of the separated soul, acknowledge no hell before the day of judgment, and guess that this earth will be changed by the final fire of the world and turned into a fiery abyss. If they were speaking of the place of the bodies, they could be blamed less. But in holding this view about the state of the damned souls, they are wrong. For Scripture speaks of hell as already existing, both elsewhere and in Luke 16:23. As for their argument that it is still future, drawn from Matthew 8:12, But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, it is weak. For Christ meant to express the eternity of those punishments, and he speaks to the living, in relation to whom those torments were yet to come. Nor do we deny at last that those punishments will be fully completed only after the resurrection.

units.la: XLV. Adjuncta infernalis poenae sunt: 1. Cacodaemonum societas, Matth. 25: 48. 2. Supplicitorum inaequalitas, pro varia delictorum ratione. Amen dico vobis, tolerabilius erit terra Sodomorum, & Gomorrhaeorum, in die judicii, quam urbi illi. Matth. 10: 15. & 11: 22, 24. Ille autem servus, qui novit voluntatem Domini, & non paratus est, neque facit secundum voluntatem ipsius, cædetur multis plagis: qui autem non novit, facit vero digna plagis, cædetur paucis. Luc. 12: 47, 48.
units.tr: XLV. The following are attached to the punishment of hell: (1) the fellowship of evil spirits, Matthew 25:48; (2) the unequal degrees of punishment, according to the varying nature of the offences. Verily I say unto you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city, Matthew 10:15; 11:22, 24. And that servant which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few, Luke 12:47, 48.

units.la: 3. Poenarum aeternitas, & mortis ipsius quaedam immortalitas. Abibunt illi ad supplicium aeternum. Matth. 25: 46. Qui poenam luent, aeternum exitium a facie Domini, & a gloria roboris ipsius. 2 Thess. 1: 9. Semper enim manebit culpae reatus, nec ullo piaculo extinguetur, quia nec poenitentiae ibi locus erit; cum perpetuo judicis odio peccator flagraturus, eique mediis in flammis maledicturus sit. Quod amarum odium, & invidiae morsus & saeva indignatio, & in malo obduratio, aliaeque malae curae, quae inquietum animum exercebunt, simul & peccati, & poenae, rationem habebunt. Erunt ergo, ut peccata, ita & poenae istae duratione infinitae: sicut & respectu damni, ac ratione amissi boni, quaedam supplicium infinitas erit: quanquam respectu sensus nulla poena infinita in creaturam finitam cadere possit. 4. Quæ consequetur desperatio, & furor. Cum ex carcere illo nullus detur exitus, Luc. 16:26. Psal. 49: 9. Nam pretiosum est lytron animarum ipsorum, & deficiet in sæculum.
units.tr: (3) The eternity of the punishments, and a certain immortality of death itself. These shall go away into everlasting punishment, Matthew 25:46. Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power, 2 Thessalonians 1:9. For the guilt of sin will always remain, and will never be extinguished by any expiation, because there will be no place for repentance there; the sinner will burn with the perpetual hatred of the judge and will curse him in the midst of the flames. This bitter hatred, the gnawing of envy, savage indignation, hardness in evil, and other evil cares, which will torment the restless soul, will at once take account of both the sin and the punishment. Therefore these punishments, like the sins, will be infinite in duration; just as, with respect to the loss and the good that has been lost, there will be a certain infinite punishment, although with respect to feeling no punishment can fall infinitely on a finite creature. (4) Despair will follow, and rage, since no way out is given from that prison, Luke 16:26; Psalm 49:9. For the redemption of their souls is costly, and it shall fail for ever.

units.la: XLVI. Cadit ergo Pythagorica & Judaica μετεμψύχωσις, animæque per multa corpora errantis peregrinatio. Qua tanquam pœna lustrari ac purgari eam volunt. Ut & Origenistarum somnia, qui diabolo ac impiis, certum pœnarum terminum statuunt; quem ubi impleverint, ad superos eos redire, novaque fata, sine cessatione alternantia, exordiri, docuerunt. Sed contrarium testatur Scriptura, Matth. 25:41. Apoc. 14: 11.
units.tr: XLVI. Therefore the Pythagorean and Jewish metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις], the wandering of souls through many bodies, falls away. They wish souls to be purified and cleansed by this as a punishment. So too are the dreams of the Origenists, who set a fixed term of punishments for the devil and the wicked, and taught that once they had completed it they would return to the upper regions and begin new destinies, alternating without end. But Scripture bears witness to the contrary, Matthew 25:41; Revelation 14:11.

units.la: XLVII. Judæorum, præterquam quod de gehenna, septemque ejus cubiculis subterraneis multum fabulentur, de damnatis non una sententia est. In tres enim ordines humanum genus dispescunt (contra ac à summo judice fiet Matt. 25.) &, præter bonos malosque, intermedii generis turbam statuunt. Illis æterna gaudia; istis cruciatus æternos; his autem purgatorias quasdam flammas destinant: quibus ad tempus in inferno expiati (non enim, more Pontificio, purgatorium ab inferno distinctum habent) ad supera gaudia rursus evolent. In inferno autem nullos collocant Israelitici generis, nisi qui forte à patria religione desciverunt. Sed ne illas quidem pœnas æternas ajunt; sed, post duodecim mensium cruciatus, fontes animas & interire & annihilari ferunt.
units.tr: XLVII. Among the Jews, apart from the fact that they tell many fables about Gehenna and its seven underground chambers, there is no single opinion about the damned. For they divide the human race into three orders (contrary to what will happen at the hands of the supreme judge, Matthew 25), and besides the good and the wicked they posit a crowd of an intermediate kind. For the first there are eternal joys; for the second, eternal torments; and for the third they appoint certain purgatorial flames, in which, cleansed for a time in hell (for they do not, as the Papists do, have a purgatory distinct from hell), they fly up again to the heavenly joys. They place no one of Israelite stock in hell, except those who perhaps have fallen away from their ancestral religion. But they do not even say that those punishments are eternal; rather, after twelve months of torment, they say that the souls both perish and are annihilated.

units.la: XLVIII. His magistris Sociniani omnes impiorum pœnas in annihilatione constituunt: quam protinus à morte auspicantur: per quam pios impiosque ex æquo in infernum non existentiæ descendere faciunt. Hoc tamen discrimine, quod pios redanimandos & recorporandos tradant; sed alio ac gloriosiori corpore. Impios autem in inferno isto æterno perpetuo detinent: atque eos solummodo, quos vivos dies Domini deprehendet, coram judicio ejus sistunt. Quo ubi defuncti fuerunt, ac, in ultimo orbis incendio, quæ illis gehenna est, ephemera pœna torti; & impios, & diabolos, & ignem denique avernalem, annihilari & interire, nihilque præter sedes mentesque beatas superesse faciunt. Addunt & cavillum: ignem illum æternum dici, quia ex annihilatione illa nullus unquam reditus dabitur. Cætera autem, quæ de infernali carcere narrantur, fabulas putant, quas nec pueri credunt, nisi qui nondum ære lavantur.
units.tr: XLVIII. Following these teachers, all the Socinians place the punishment of the wicked in annihilation, which they begin at once from death. By this they make both the pious and the impious descend alike into hell of non-existence. Yet they make this distinction: they teach that the pious will be called back to life and given bodies again, but bodies of a different and more glorious kind. The impious, however, they keep perpetually in that eternal hell, and only those whom the day of the Lord finds alive they bring before his judgment. Once these have died, and in the final conflagration of the world, which is their gehenna, have been tormented with a short-lived punishment, they hold that the impious, the devils, and finally the infernal fire itself are annihilated and perish, and that nothing remains except the blessed seats and minds. They also add a jibe: that fire is called eternal because after that annihilation there will be no return at all. As for the rest that is told about the infernal prison, they think these are fables, which not even children believe, except those who have not yet been washed in bronze.

units.la: XLIX. Re-
units.tr: XLIX. Re-

units.la: LIB. VIII. CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: Book VIII, Chapter XXV.

units.la: XLIX. Remonstrantes, uti hominibus his palpum facere, & Sarmaticis portentis adblandiri solent; ita ne ipsi quidem satis à sententiæ huius impietate absunt. Adamo certè, poiterisque ejus, quibus nulla vitæ æternæ promissio facta sit, nec æternas in morte pœnas timendas: iis autem solis, quibus Euangelii prædconium factum est, uti vitæ, itæ mortis quoque æternæ, spemque metumque esse, affirmant. Episcopius pœnam damni æternam admittit; pœnam autem sensus, partim dum ignis ille urit, partim, igne illo extincto, in æterna scelerum conscientia ac desperatione ponit. Camphuisius autem apertius albis dentibus fabulam istam avernalem, uti putat, irridet, & cum Poëtarum ac Papistarum figmentis comparat.
units.tr: XLIX. The Remonstrants, as is their habit, flatter these men and court them with Sarmatian monstrosities; yet they themselves do not stand far enough from the impiety of this opinion. They affirm that Adam, and his posterity, to whom no promise of eternal life was made and who had no eternal punishments in death to fear, have not; but that only those to whom the proclamation of the Gospel has been made have both the hope and the fear of eternal life and eternal death. Episcopius admits an eternal punishment of loss; but he places the punishment of sense partly in the fire's burning, while that fire lasts, and partly, once the fire is extinguished, in an eternal consciousness of sins and despair. Camphuysen, however, more openly, with white teeth, laughs at that infernal fable, as he calls it, and compares it with the fictions of the poets and the Papists.

units.la: L. Quæ omnia pessimi sunt commatis. Nam 1. non alios, quam qui supremo die victuri sunt, divini judicii flammis adducere, manifestis Scripturis adversatur; quæ omnium sæculorum homines isto igne terrent. Sui enim temporis homines procul dubio isto terrore compellere Apostolus volebat; cum ita scribit Rom. 2:6. & secundum duritiem tuam, & corrigi pietatis nescium, thesaurices tibi iram; quæ erit in die iræ, & revelationis justi judicationis Dei. Adde 2 Pet. 2:9. Matth. 3:7. 2 Thess. 1:9. 1 Cor. 15:32. 2 Thess. 6:7,8. 2 Cor. 5:10,11. 2 Nec solam pœnam damni Scriptura dicit: cujus tamen damni impiis, utpote annihilatis, nulla erit conscientia: sed sensum acerbissimum pœnasque animo & corpore luendas, prædicit; & conjectionem in ignem, vermem æternum, ploratus, stridorem, omnemque dolendi sævitiem, emphaticis verbis exprimit. Certe, ubi ait, tali homini melius fore, si non natus esset, Matth. 26:24. aperte docet, eum annihilandum non esse. Ille enim non-natorum status erit. 3. Profanus autem sarcasmus est, mortem & ignem æternum appellitare, non sui, sed effectus ratione; quod nempe hominem in statum illum redigat, unde negant redire quenquam. Nam sic non hominibus solum, sed & bestiis mors æterna comminanda erit. Expresse autem Scriptura istum ignem à temporali quocunque cruciatu distinguit, & nunquam finiendum expressissimis verbis affirmat, Marc. 9:43,44,45,46,48. additque igni isti vermem, morsuque animi æternos. Si autem liberatio ex isto igne non datur, uti ajunt, certe permanere ac persistere oportet eum, qui non liberatur. Annihilatio enim vel maxima miseri hominis est liberatio.
units.tr: L. All of these are of the worst sort. For (1) to bring to the flames of divine judgment only those who are going to be alive on the last day is contrary to the plain Scriptures, which frighten the men of all ages with that fire. For the Apostle undoubtedly wished to drive the men of his own time with this terror, when he writes thus, Rom. 2:6: but according to your hardness, and your heart that knows not how to be corrected, you store up for yourself wrath, which will be in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. Add 2 Pet. 2:9; Matt. 3:7; 2 Thess. 1:9; 1 Cor. 15:32; 2 Thess. 1:7,8; 2 Cor. 5:10,11. (2) Nor does Scripture speak only of the punishment of loss, of which the wicked, as annihilated, will have no consciousness; but it foretells bitter sense and punishments to be paid in soul and body, and it expresses in emphatic words being cast into the fire, the eternal worm, weeping, gnashing of teeth, and every cruelty of pain. Certainly, where it says it would have been better for that man if he had not been born, Matt. 26:24, it clearly teaches that he is not to be annihilated. For that would be the state of the unborn. (3) It is a profane sarcasm to call death and the eternal fire by names drawn from their effect, namely, that it reduces a man to that state from which they deny that anyone returns. For in this way eternal death would have to be threatened not only to men but also to beasts. Scripture, however, expressly distinguishes that fire from any temporal torment, and affirms in the plainest words that it is never to be quenched, Mark 9:43,44,45,46,48, adding to that fire the worm and the eternal gnawing of the mind. If, however, there is no deliverance from that fire, as they say, then surely he who is not delivered must remain and persist. For annihilation would be the greatest deliverance of a wretched man.

units.la: LI. Sed ulterius ignem hunc scrurari ac fodicare, à sobrietate alienum est. Cujus conspectum Deus nulli unquam in terris indulsit: sicuti æternæ gloriæ quasdam corruscationes & strictûras nonnullis concessit, Act. 7: 55, 56. 2 Cor. 12: 2, 4. Uti enim illa futuri gaudii prælibatio ad pios animandos permultum facere poterat: ita orci fauces pandere, & averni specum viventibus aperire nihil attinebat. Non enim pios id solari, nec improbos admodum ad veram conversionem perducere poterat. Si enim Mosen & Prophetas non audiant, neque quidem, si quis ex mortuis resurgat, persuadebuntur. Luc. 16: 31. Unde non temere in abyssum istam irrumpendum, vel Dei urna movenda, & de mortuis dijudicandum: quod non sine præjudicio fieri potest. Præsertim cum Scriptura ipsa tam sobrie, & velo quasi oppanso, de mortuorum statu, ac de ipsis damnatis loquatur. Ut abiret Judas ad locum suum. Act. 1: 35. In quo spiritu etiam iis, qui in carcere sunt, spiritibus, abiens, prædicavit. 1 Pet. 3: 19. Unde patet, quantopere cavendum nobis sit, ne quem, absque judicis suffragio, ad istum ignem facile prædamnemus. Potius autem danda opera, ut matura resipiscentia & sancta conversatione ignem illum evitemus; & jugi pietatis studio nosmet ipsos Deo dignos fingamus; quo ad sancta piorum concilia, ac beatorum cœtus, nobis quoque aditus pateat: ubi Ecclesia, finitis omnibus certaminibus, ac decursis spatiis suis, in æternum consummanda, & Deo Christoque implenda, & beanda crit. AMEN.
units.tr: LI. But to probe and dig further into this fire is foreign to sobriety. God never granted anyone on earth a sight of it, just as he granted some glimpses and flashes of eternal glory, Acts 7:55,56; 2 Cor. 12:2,4. For while that foretaste of future joy could greatly help to encourage the godly, there was no point in opening the jaws of hell and laying bare the pit of Avernus to the living. For this could not console the godly, nor bring the wicked very far to true conversion. For if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded, even if someone rises from the dead. Luke 16:31. Hence we must not rashly rush into that abyss, nor move God's urn, nor pass judgment on the dead, which cannot be done without prejudice. Especially since Scripture itself speaks of the state of the dead, and of the damned themselves, so soberly and, as it were, with a veil drawn over: that Judas might go to his own place, Acts 1:25; in which spirit he also went and preached to the spirits that are in prison, 1 Pet. 3:19. Hence it is plain how carefully we must guard against condemning anyone lightly to that fire without the vote of the Judge. Rather we should take pains to avoid that fire by timely repentance and holy conduct, and by a constant zeal for piety to shape ourselves worthy of God; so that the way may be open for us also to the holy assemblies of the godly and the companies of the blessed: where the Church, when all struggles are finished and her course run, is to be brought to completion for eternity, and filled with God and Christ, and blessed. AMEN.

units.la: STUDIO THEOLOGICO
units.tr: THE THEOLOGICAL STUDY

units.la: feliciter instituendo.
units.tr: to be undertaken happily.

units.la: CONSILIUM DE STUDIO THEOLOGICO feliciter instituendo.
units.tr: Counsel on Undertaking the Study of Theology Happily.

units.la: CAPUT I. De apparatu ad studium Theologicum.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On the preparation for the study of Theology.

units.la: I. QUod in aliis plerunque usu venire solet, ut laudentur, quas quisque velit venales extrudere merces, illud obesse magis, quam in rem nostram praesentem quicquam facere, agnoscent libenter, qui quid Theologia sit, eique operam dare, perspectum habent.
units.tr: It usually happens with other things that people praise whatever wares they wish to push off for sale. Those who know what theology is, and have studied it closely, will readily admit that this does more harm than good to our present purpose.

units.la: Ea est hujus studii summa & propria laus, ut laude aliena non solum, sed ne sua quidem indigeat: nam quanta est omnibus hominibus immortalitatis innata cupido, tanta etiam hujus studii necessitas, utilitas & excellentia animis hominum obversatur semper; utpote quae una est ad immortalitatem via.
units.tr: This is the chief and proper praise of this study: it needs no praise from outside, nor even its own. For as strong as the innate human desire for immortality is in all people, so constantly before men's minds is the necessity, usefulness and excellence of this study, since it is the one way to immortality.

units.la: Quamobrem missis iis, quae approbando huic studio comportari solent; quod vehementissime & frequentissime exigebatur, & unum hac in re, etiam a nobis, jure desiderari videbatur, consilium nostrum de opera utiliter in hoc studio collocanda, privatis in scholis antehac properavimus; idemque illud, cum maxime, postulationibus amicorum aliorumque satisfacturi, & auditoribus nostris gratificaturi, eadem brevitate & fidelitate publicae luci exponimus. Absque quo fuisset, supervacuum judicassemus, post tot praestantissimorum hominum in hoc genere labores, & nuperius quoque Doctiss. & Clariss. Antonii Perizonii & Stephani Gaussseni de ratione studii Theologici limatissima scripta, ulterioribus libellis a nobis mundum onerari. Omne vero quod hic moneri expedit, circa tria potissimum versatur capita.
units.tr: Therefore, setting aside the commendations usually offered for this study, and the one thing that was most vehemently and frequently demanded, and which seemed rightly to be wanted from us in this matter too, we have hastened to set out in private lectures our counsel on directing effort usefully in this study. Now, chiefly to meet the requests of friends and others and to oblige our hearers, we publish the same in the same brief and faithful manner. Without this, we would have thought it superfluous, after so many labours of the most outstanding men in this field, and especially after the most learned and distinguished Antonius Perizonius and Stephanus Gaussenius, whose polished writings on the method of theological study have appeared, to burden the world with further little books from us. Indeed, everything that is worth advising here turns on three main heads.

units.la: Primum est de iis, quae spectant ad studii hujus προπαιδείαν & apparatum
units.tr: The first concerns the matters that pertain to the preliminary education [προπαιδεία] and the equipment [apparatus] for this study.

units.la: CONSILIUM DE STUDIO THEOLOGICO feliciter instituendo. CAPUT I. De apparatu ad studium Theologicum.
units.tr: A PLAN FOR BEGINNING THE STUDY OF THEOLOGY SUCCESSFULLY. CHAPTER I. On the preparation for the study of Theology.

units.la: I. Quod in aliis plerunque usu venire solet, ut laudentur, quas quisque velit venales extrudere merces, illud obesse magis, quam in rem nostram præsentem quicquam facere, agnoscent libenter, qui quid Theologia sit, eique operam dare, perspectum habent. Ea est hujus studii summa & propria laus, ut laude aliena non solum, sed ne sua quidem indigeat: nam quanta est omnibus hominibus immortalitatis innata cupido, tanta etiam hujus studii necessitas, utilitas & excellentia animis hominum obversatur semper; utpote quæ una est ad immortalitatem via. Quamobrem missis iis, quæ approbando huic studio comportari solent; quod vehementissime & frequentissime exigebatur, & unum hac in re, etiam à nobis, jure desiderari videbatur, consilium nostrum de opera utiliter in hoc studio collocanda, privatis in scholis antehac properavimus; idemque illud, cum maxime, postulationibus amicorum aliorumque satisfacturi, & auditoribus nostris gratificaturi, eadem brevitate & fidelitate publicæ luci exponimus. Absque quo fuisset, supervacuum judicassemus, post tot præstantissimorum hominum in hoc genere labores, & nuperius quoque Doctiss. & Clariss. Antonii Perizonii & Stephani Gansseni de ratione studii Theologici limatissima scripta, ulterioribus libellis à nobis mundum onerari. Omne vero quod hic moneri expedit, circa tria potissimum versatur capita. Primum est de iis, quæ spectant ad studii hujus προπαιδεῖαν & apparatum tum. Alterum, de iis quæ studium ipsum concernunt. Tertium, quæ ad vsum & praxin ejus pertinent.
units.tr: I. Those who know what theology is and have given it their attention will readily agree that the usual practice in other fields, where each man praises the wares he wants to sell off, does more harm than good to our present purpose. This is the chief and proper praise of this study: it needs no praise from others, nor even from itself. For just as the longing for immortality is innate in all men, so the necessity, usefulness and excellence of this study always present themselves to men's minds, since it alone is the way to immortality. Therefore, setting aside the arguments usually brought forward to commend this study, I have hastened to deliver in my private lectures earlier my plan for spending effort usefully on this study. This was the thing most vehemently and frequently demanded, and it seemed rightly to be the one thing wanted in this matter, even from me. Now, especially, to satisfy the requests of friends and others and to please my hearers, I set the same plan before the public light with the same brevity and faithfulness. Without these requests I would have judged it superfluous to burden the world with further booklets of my own, after so many labours of the most eminent men in this field, and especially after the most recent and polished writings on the method of theological study by the most learned and distinguished Antonius Perizonius and Stephanus Ganssenius. Everything that is worth advising here turns mainly on three heads. The first concerns what pertains to the preliminary training [προπαιδεία] and equipment of this study. The second concerns the study itself. The third concerns its use and practice.

units.la: II. Quam olim prudentiam in admittendis ad suas sapientiæ auditiones discipulis, adhibuerit Plato, testabatur, foribus inscripta sententia; Ἀγεωμέτρητος εἰσίτω: ne quis philosophiæ, bona- rumque artium (earum enim rudimenta apud veteres erant Musica & Geometria) rudis intret. Varias item regulas exigebat ab auditore Ethices suæ Aristoteles, ut nimirum non esset juvenis, nec affectibus deditus. Multo potiori jure igitur maxima habenda erit cautio in admittendis ad sacrum hoc veræ sapientiæ studium discipulis, ne illotis, quod ajunt, manibus sacra hæc tractent; & cruda studia ex scholis, vix primis linguarum rudimentis imbuti, propellentes, in hæc adyta temere involent; ad quæ non nisi probe lustratis & bonarum artium succo rite prolutis, accedere fas est. Singularem igitur & diligentem tum morum, tum ingenii πρoπαιδείαν, studium hoc requirit.
units.tr: II. The prudence with which Plato once admitted pupils to his lectures on wisdom is attested by the sentence inscribed over his door: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter" [Ἀγεωμέτρητος εἰσίτω], so that no one unskilled in philosophy and the liberal arts (for among the ancients these rudiments were music and geometry) might come in. Aristotle likewise required various qualifications of the hearers of his Ethics, namely that they should not be young and should not be given over to the passions. Much more rightly, then, the greatest caution must be taken in admitting pupils to this sacred study of true wisdom. They must not handle these holy things with unwashed hands, as the saying goes, nor rush rashly into these sanctuaries, having only just been steeped in the first rudiments of languages and driving crude studies out of the schools. It is right to approach these shrines only when one has been properly cleansed and duly bathed in the juice of the liberal arts. This study therefore requires a singular and diligent preparation, both of character and of intellect.

units.la: III. Quoad mores in idoneo Theologiæ studioso, desiderantur præcipuè hæc tria: 1. Pietas. 2. Docilitas. 3. Sedulitas. 1. Ante omnia pium esse oportere Theologiæ consecraneum, docet pietatis natura, quæ primum hujus studii fundamentum non solum est, sed & ultimum complementum; ut in hoc studio inde ordiri conveniat, in quo desinendum est postremum. Timor Domini principium scientiæ & sapientiæ. Prov.1:7. & 9:10. tale nimirum principium, quod rem non tantum incipit, sed & perficit, & in omni sapientia utramque quasi paginam facit; quare & ipsa etiam sapientia vocatur Job.28:28. Quæ aurea sententia oculis & animis omnium huic studio se mancipantium semper observari debebat. Hinc חוד / secretum seu familiare commercium Domini, est timentibus ipsum & fœdus ejus, ut eos gnaros faciat Psal.25:14. Adde Joh.7:17.&8:47.&14:21. 1Cor.2:14. Unde & magistri: Non habitat prophetia nisi apud sapientem, fortem ac divitem: fortem nempe ac divitem in concupiscentia conculcanda divitiisque contemnendis. Huc etiam requiritur ardens studium gloriæ Dei & salutis hominum; amor Euangelii & Christi, quo quis ministerium appetat; non commodi, honoris aut lucri causa quod mercenarii est; sed ad solius Dei gloriam, & proximi salutem. Quare ab ipsa jam juventute devotus, Deoque traditus esse debet; ne vel ipsa etiam juvenilia vitia, in sacrum illud munus apportentur, vel anteactæ vitæ probra Ecclesiæ scandalo, & ipsi ministerio dedecori esse queant: sicut ęo nomine venerandus Beza, quamvis non ex æquo, ab adversariis vapulavit. A prima ergo ætate studendum bonæ conscientiæ. 1 Tim. 1: 19. quæ fidei quasi custos & arca est. Addendæ preces ardentissimæ, sine quibus nihil auguratum, nil felix fausturnque erit; & per quas omnia à Deo Patre luminum exorari possunt. Jac. 1: 5, 17. Unde & tria hæc Theologum perficere statuebat B. Lutherus, Orationem, Meditationem, Tentationem. Orationum formulas in limine hoc studii Theologici adhibendas, sufficit abunde Augustinus in consessionibus; ut certi sint de auxilio divino, & persuasi non vanum fore illorum laborem in Domino; experturi aliquando veritatem proverbii illius: studiorum radicem amarum, fructus autem esse dulces. Cum cæteroquin sapientia hæc sacra profanis & impiis non detur.
units.tr: III. As for character, three things above all are required in a suitable student of theology: (1) Piety. (2) Docility. (3) Diligence. (1) Above all, the nature of piety teaches that one dedicated to theology ought to be pious. Piety is not only the first foundation of this study but also its final completion, so that one should begin this study where one must end. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge and wisdom (Prov. 1:7; 9:10). This is such a beginning as not only starts the matter but also perfects it, and it makes both pages of all wisdom. For this reason wisdom itself is also called wisdom (Job 28:28). This golden saying should always have been kept before the eyes and minds of all who give themselves to this study. Hence the secret, or intimate fellowship of the Lord, is with those who fear him, and his covenant, so that he makes them know it (Ps. 25:14). Add John 7:17; 8:47; 14:21; 1 Cor. 2:14. Hence the masters also say: "Prophecy dwells only with the wise, the strong and the rich", meaning, of course, the strong and rich in trampling down desire and despising riches. Here is also required an ardent zeal for the glory of God and the salvation of men, and a love of the Gospel and of Christ, by which a man seeks the ministry, not for the sake of convenience, honour or gain, which is the mark of a hireling, but for the glory of God alone and the salvation of his neighbour. Therefore one must be devoted and given over to God already from youth, lest either youthful vices be brought into that sacred office, or the disgraces of a past life become a scandal to the Church and a dishonour to the ministry itself. For this reason the venerable Beza, though not on the same footing, was roughly handled by his opponents. So one must study from the earliest age to keep a good conscience (1 Tim. 1:19), which is, as it were, the guardian and chest of faith. Most fervent prayers must be added, without which nothing will be auspicious, nothing happy or prosperous; and through them all things can be obtained from God the Father of lights (James 1:5, 17). For this reason the blessed Luther also laid down that three things make a theologian: prayer, meditation and trial (tentatio). Augustine's Confessions amply suffice as a model of the prayers to be used on the threshold of this theological study, so that men may be certain of divine help and persuaded that their labour in the Lord will not be in vain, and will one day experience the truth of that proverb: that the root of studies is bitter, but their fruits are sweet. For otherwise this sacred wisdom is not given to the profane and the impious.

units.la: IV. Altera virtus est docilitas; ut quis ingenio animoque sit ad discendum idoneo. Adeoque liber primo sit ab affectibus, perverso amore, odio, spe, metu, ira, gaudio, voluptate, tristitia &c. qui omnes pessimi sunt, in negotio religionis, consiliarii & magistri, uti in Judæis aliisque olim apparuit, atque etiamnum apparet. Excunda etiam & repudianda penitus sunt præjudicia, quæ ubi animum occuparunt, judicium voluntatemque occæcant, & intellectum conturbant, ut quid verum falsumque sit discernere nequeat; quod clarissime liquet in Pontificiis, qui mordicus præjudiciis suis de Ecclesiæ infallibilitate & antiquitate, Conciliorum generalium, Patrum & Papæ auctoritate, similibusque adhærent & innituntur. Et utinam non plerorumque hominum religio, ex anticipata opinione magis arrepta & à majoribus tradita esset, quam ex sincero & solido examine recepta. Deponenda igitur sunt præjudicia, & quæcunque in rebus Theologicis leguntur, animo præjudiciis vacuo contemplanda sunt, & non aliter quam illa quæ nondum recepimus, examinanda, ut non per præconceptas opiniones, sed solius veritatis, se oculis nostris ingerentis, evidentiam admittantur. Denique abjicienda procul est omnis malitia, quæ pessulum quasi obdit & validum ponit obicem sacro huic studio, & occlusis foribus lumen Spiritus non admittit. Joh. 8: 41. 1 Pet. 2: 1,2.
units.tr: IV. The second virtue is docility: that a man be fitted, in intellect and disposition, for learning. Accordingly he should be free first of all from the passions: from perverse love, hatred, hope, fear, anger, joy, pleasure, sadness, and the like. All of these are very bad counsellors and teachers in matters of religion, as was once seen among the Jews and others, and is still seen today. Prejudices, too, must be shaken off and utterly rejected. When they have taken possession of the mind, they blind judgement and will, and confuse the understanding, so that it cannot discern what is true and what is false. This is most clearly seen in the Papists, who stubbornly cling to and rest upon their prejudices about the infallibility and antiquity of the Church, the authority of general councils, of the Fathers and of the Pope, and the like. Would that the religion of most men were not received from preconceived opinion and handed down from their forebears, rather than received from sincere and solid examination! Prejudices must therefore be laid aside, and whatever is read in theological matters must be considered with a mind empty of prejudice, and examined no differently from those things we have not yet accepted, so that it is admitted not through preconceived opinions but through the evident force of truth alone presenting itself to our eyes. Finally, all malice must be put far away. Malice, like a bolt, shuts the door and sets a strong barrier against this sacred study, and with the doors closed it does not admit the light of the Spirit (John 8:41; 1 Pet. 2:1, 2).

units.la: V. Tertium quod in nostro Theologiæ studioso requiritur, est; sedulitas, seu diligentia; cum, juxta vulgatum Judæorum vembum, Prophetia non habitet neque inter tristitiam, neque inter pigritiam Unde & veterum est dictum, Di laboribus omnia vendunt; & labor omnia vincit improbus. Quare nunquam desperandum est de successu, etsi primi prima statim fronte se non offerat veritas, nec ex voto labor succedat: neque pertinaciter nimis supra vires tum instandum est aut urgendum, sed remittendum aliquantulum & mora interponenda, cum dies diem doceat, & aliàs sæpe temere eveniant, quæ nunc summa opera non assequaris. Nec multa legere sufficit, (non enim helluones laudamus) sed præcipue ea quæ legimus in succum & sanguinem vertenda sint, & diligenti meditatione ruminanda, & in unam quasi massam subigenda; eodem modo ac ex thymo & floribus apes mel conficiunt, quod tamen ita digerunt, ut nec thymum nec flores redoleat, & alia prorsus videatur materia.
units.tr: V. The third thing required in our student of theology is diligence, or industry. According to the common saying of the Jews, prophecy does not dwell amid sadness, nor amid sloth. Hence also the saying of the ancients: "The gods sell all things for toil," and unrelenting labour conquers all things. Therefore one must never despair of success, even if the truth does not at once present itself at the first glance, and labour does not succeed as one wished. Nor should one insist or press too stubbornly beyond one's strength, but must relax a little and interpose delay, since day teaches day, and often things that you cannot achieve with great effort now happen by chance at another time. Nor is it enough to read much (for we do not praise gluttons), but what we read must above all be turned into blood and sap, chewed over by diligent meditation, and kneaded into one mass, in the same way that bees make honey from thyme and flowers. Yet they so digest it that it smells neither of thyme nor of flowers, but appears to be an entirely different substance.

units.la: VI. Hisce moribus & hac virtute instructus studiosus noster, ad ipsam tandem bonæ mentis culturam, per liberales artes & scientias accedat, iisque animum polire & inscitiæ rubigine exuere allaboret. Cum autem in adolescentibus, quales plerunque studiis destinantur, magis vigeat memoria, quam judicium, ab illa auspicandum est; ita tamen, ut ad judicium dirigendum & firmandum præcipue attendatur; quamobrem non oneranda nec premenda est immani apparatu memoria, quem judicium digerere nequeat; ne similes fiant voracibus, illis qui stomacho valentes ciborum ingentem perdunt copiam, & corpore tamen vesco rancidoque manent. Usus vero memoriæ primarius est in addiscendis linguis; quare hæ in hac ætate hauriendæ sunt; non tamen tam linguarum, quam rerum ipsarum, quarum vehicula sunt verba, discendarum & inveniendarum causa: cum ex solorum verborum cura, sola sæpe rerum dependeat intelligentia, quare etiam verborum neglectum certa semper insecuta est rerum barbaries: ut diligenter admodum discendæ sint linguæ; quæ quo accuratius teneantur, eo faciliores & majores in rerum, maxime Theologicarum, cognitione fient progressus. Hæ enim Theologiæ quasi anlæ sunt.
units.tr: VI. Once our student is equipped with these habits and this virtue, let him come at last to the cultivation of a good mind through the liberal arts and sciences, and take pains to polish his mind and rub off the rust of ignorance. Since in young people, who are usually destined for study, memory is stronger than judgment, one should begin with memory, but with the aim of directing and strengthening judgment above all. For that reason the memory should not be burdened and weighed down with such a huge store that judgment cannot digest it. Otherwise he will become like those gluttons whose stomachs are strong enough to take in huge quantities of food, yet who remain flabby and sickly in body. The main use of memory, however, is in learning languages. These should therefore be absorbed at this age, but not so much for the sake of the languages as for the sake of learning and discovering the things themselves, whose vehicles are words. Understanding of things often depends on attention to words alone, and neglect of words has always been followed by a barbarism of things. So languages must be learned with great diligence, and the more exactly they are mastered, the easier and greater will be our progress in the knowledge of things, especially theological ones. For languages are, as it were, the lifeblood of theology.

units.la: VII. Inter linguas prima occurit Latina, in Scholis inferioribus jam hausta; quæ in Academia excolenda est, utpote quæ magnum huic studio præsidium & ornamentum adferat: non quasi in concionibus ad naseam usque Latinorum sententiæ tantum non plus quam ipsius S. Scripturæ, inani pompa imperitæ plebi sint propinandæ; sed tum ad communem mentis cultum, qui ex hac lingua omnium maxime peti potest; tum ad antiquorum scriptorum, præcipue vero plurimorum Patrum, ut & recentiorum Theologorum ferme omnium, intellectum; adde vulgarem inter eruditos usum: ut hujus ignorantia Theologiæ studiosis sit pudenda; cum tamen hodie nimis quam familiaris sit. Incumbendum igitur est auctoribus Latinis vulgo frequentatis; praesertim illis, qui integris virorum doctissimorum notis illustrati prodierunt & etiamnum prodeunt. Plurimùm verò conducet, ex iis scriptoribus qui solutaoratione scripserunt prae caeteris familiarem sibi reddere Ciceronem, magnum illum & facunditae & omnis sapientiae magistrum, maximo Calvino adeo tritum: multum etiam ad elegantiam & interiorem linguae notitiam conferent, Scioppii scripta de re Grammatica; Vossii Etymologicon, de Arte Grammatica, Vitiis sermonis, aliaque ejus generis.
units.tr: VII. Among the languages, Latin comes first. It has already been absorbed in the lower schools and must be cultivated at the university, since it brings great support and ornament to this study. This is not so that Latin maxims, almost more than Holy Scripture itself, are poured out in sermons to the point of nausea, to the ignorant crowd as empty show. Rather, it is for the sake of general cultivation of the mind, which can be sought from this language more than from any other, and for understanding the ancient writers, above all most of the Fathers, and almost all the more recent theologians. Add the common use of it among scholars, so that ignorance of it should be a shame to students of theology, though today it is all too familiar. Students should therefore devote themselves to the Latin authors commonly read, especially those who have appeared, and still appear, with the complete notes of the most learned men. It will be especially helpful to make Cicero, that great master both of eloquence and of all wisdom, very familiar, among those writers who wrote in prose, a writer Calvin knew thoroughly. Scioppius's works On Grammar will also contribute much to elegance and to inner knowledge of the language, as will Vossius's Etymologicon, On the Art of Grammar, On the Faults of Speech, and other works of that kind.

units.la: VIII. Nec minori opera excolenda est lingua Graeca; tum quia ab iis universam ferme sapientiam hauserunt Romani: tum ob Veteris Test. versionem Graecam; tum in primis propter authenticas Novi Test. tabulas Graece exaratas. Ne memorem Doctores sacros, ad quorum, ut & totius antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae, penitiorem intelligentiam nemo sine hujus clavis auxilio, sese penetraverit unquam. Praeter alios in illa lingua auctores, ex quibus elegantia ejus addisci possit, studiosus noster insigni cum fructu in moralibus & sacris legET Ethica, Politica & Rhetorica Aristotelis, Epicteti Enchiridion cum Arriani & Simplicii Commentariis; Theophrasti characteres, Diogenem Laertium de Vitis Philosophorum, propter exquisitam eloquentiae studium, Demosthenem: ut & Patrum Graecorum trigam, etiam ob rerum Theologicarum cognitionem, Chrysostomum, Nazianzenum, Basilium. Praecipuus vero labor sit in Novo Test. quod diligentissime evolvat. Conferunt huc, praeter trita passim Lexica & laudatissimum Stephani thesaurum, Veteres Lexicographi; Hesychium, Suidas, Etymologicum magnum, Glossaria Ptiloxeni, aliorumque.
units.tr: VIII. Greek must be cultivated with no less effort, first because the Romans drew almost all their learning from it, second because of the Greek version of the Old Testament, and above all because of the authentic writings of the New Testament, which were written in Greek. Not to mention the holy teachers, for no one can ever penetrate to a deeper understanding of them, or of all ancient Church antiquity, without the help of this key. Besides other authors in that language, from whom its elegance can be learned, our student will read with notable profit, in moral and sacred matters, Aristotle's Ethics, Politics and Rhetoric, Epictetus's Handbook with the commentaries of Arrian and Simplicius, and Theophrastus's Characters, and Diogenes Laertius's On the Lives of the Philosophers. For the exquisite study of eloquence he will read Demosthenes, and he should also read the triad of Greek Fathers, Chrysostom, Nazianzen and Basil, partly for the knowledge of theological matters. His chief labour, however, should be in the New Testament, which he should read through most diligently. To this end, apart from the common lexicons and the most praiseworthy Thesaurus of Stephanus, the ancient lexicographers contribute: Hesychius, Suidas, Etymologicum Magnum, the Glossaries of Ptoloxenus, and others.

units.la: IX. Transeundum simul est ad linguam Hebraeam; tum propter codices Veteris Test. & divina eloquia, hac lingua consignata, quorum sensum proprio quisque marte novisse & percipere debet; nec in alieno, ut ajunt, cerebro habitare convenit. Tum etiam, quod ab Hebraeis & Orientalibus omnis cognitio rerum Theologicarum derivata sit: ut ex fundamento & prima origine Christianismus intelligi nequeat, nisi perspecto penitus Judaismo; quandoquidem ipse Christianismus nihil aliud est, quam impletus Judaismus; sicut & genuinus Judaismus nihil est, nisi typicus Christianismus: praeterquam, quod loquendi genera, Phraseologiae & idiotismi, typi & emblemata Veteris T. in Novo utramque faciunt paginam. Hebraicæ linguæ fundamenta compendiosissimè & felicissimè disci poterunt, ex viri magni Lud. de Dieu compendiolo Grammatica Hebrææ, cui radices istius linguæ, brevi labore ediscendæ adjectæ sunt; unde, si lubeat, ad Buxtorfium aliosque Grammaticos transfire licebit: præcipue ad Cl. Jac. Altingii Grammaticam, quæ ex linguæ interiori genio petita est regularumque rationes suggerit. Quibus utiliter addi possunt, quæ de ratione punctationis Hebraicæ Cl. Diestii & de Raadt scripsere. Si cui etiam vacet & genius permittat, adjungat linguas, non solum Chaldaam & Syriacam; verum etiam Arabicam & Æthiopicam; in quibus affinibus linguis multæ sæpe radices & verba & vocum significationes occurrunt, quas deperditas, frustra domi & in Hebræa lingua quæras; & quarum linguarum beneficio viri præstantissimi plurimis & desperatissimis Scripturæ locis lucem ingentem affuderunt. Utilissimam hic operam navarunt Buxtorfius & Schindlerus in Lexicis; itemque beatis nunc ascriptus, celeberrimus Coccejus, Lexico singulari & ipsis rebus ita accommodato, ut non minus rerum quam verborum locuples thesaurus sit. Quibus adde in Arabicis Cl. Golii Lexicon.
units.tr: IX. At the same time one must move on to the Hebrew language, both because of the codices of the Old Testament and the divine oracles recorded in this language, whose sense each person ought to know and grasp by his own effort, and it is not fitting for it to dwell in someone else's brain, as they say. Also, because all knowledge of theological matters is derived from the Hebrews and the Orientals, so that Christianity cannot be understood from its foundation and first origin unless Judaism has been thoroughly examined. For Christianity itself is nothing other than fulfilled Judaism, just as genuine Judaism is nothing but typical Christianity. Besides, the ways of speaking, phraseology and idioms, the types and emblems of the Old Testament make up both pages of the New. The foundations of the Hebrew language can be learned most briefly and most happily from the short Hebrew Grammar of the great man Ludovicus de Dieu, to which are added the roots of this language, which can be learned with little effort. From there, if one wishes, one may pass to Buxtorf and the other grammarians, especially to the grammar of the distinguished Jacob Altingius, which is drawn from the inner genius of the language and suggests the reasons for its rules. To these can usefully be added what Diestius and de Raadt, both distinguished men, wrote on the system of Hebrew pointing. If someone has leisure and his natural ability allows, let him also add the languages, not only Chaldean and Syriac, but also Arabic and Ethiopic. In these related languages many roots, words and meanings of words often occur, which you would look for in vain at home and in Hebrew, since they have been lost there, and by the help of these languages the most distinguished men have shed great light on very many passages of Scripture that seemed hopeless. Buxtorf and Schindler have done the most useful work here in their Lexicons. Likewise the now blessed and most famous Coccejus, with his unique lexicon so well suited to the things themselves that it is a treasury rich in things as well as in words. To these add, in Arabic, Golius's Lexicon.

units.la: X. Linguarum Orientalium studio conjungenda est, antiquitatis Judaicæ non proletaria cognitio, quæ immensam dabit utilitatem, quippe unde magna ex parte Scripturarum dependet intelligentia: ideoque fundamenta hujus studii in Academia & jacienda & cum studio Theologico pari opera conjungenda sunt, & deinceps per omnem vitam excitanda. Auctores, ex quibus studium hoc hauriri potest, præcipui sunt, ex Judæis Philo, & qui inter illos solus ineptire desiit, Maimonides, cujus more Nevochim seu Doctor perplexorum liber est lectu dignissimus; cui addi potest ejusdem porta Mosis, cui Miscellaneas notas doctissimas adjecit Eduardus Pocockius: ejusdem Maimonidis fundamenta legis cum notis Guilielmi Vorstii. Tractatus Pirke Avoth seu Capitula Patrum, cum notis Fagii. Quibus addi potest nuperus Judæorum doctor, Menasse Ben Israel. Ex Christianis excellunt hic Scaliger in Elencho trihæresii; Wilh. Schickardus in variis tractatibus; Drusius multis itidem libris; Buxtorfius utraque; ut & Cappellus; Seldeni doctissima etiam scripta, & Cocceji tractatus duo Thalmudici; Constantini l'Empereur varia item opera, juxtaque Hottingeri, speciatim thesaurus ejus Philologicus; Fulleri Miscellanea, Sam. Petitus, Stelling flietus, & quæ ex tractatibus Talmudicis ab Ulmanno, Smido, aliisque in latinam linguam versa sunt. Utilis hic etiam est liber Anglicus Goodwini, sub titulo Mosis & Aaronis. MaMagnum autem harum rerum compendium aliquod & thesaurus est in ingentis operis & frugis Lexico Thalmudico seu Rabbinico Buxtorfii, & Philologico Matthiae Martinii.
units.tr: X. With the study of Oriental languages must be joined a not superficial knowledge of Jewish antiquity, which will give immense benefit, since a great part of the understanding of the Scriptures depends on it. Therefore the foundations of this study must be laid at the university, and it must be pursued with equal effort alongside theological study, and afterwards kept alive throughout life. The chief authors from whom this study can be drawn are, among the Jews, Philo, and Maimonides, who alone among them ceased to rave, whose book The Guide of the Perplexed, or Moreh Nevukhim, is most worth reading. To it can be added Maimonides's Gate of Moses, to which Edward Pococke added most learned Miscellaneous Notes, and Maimonides's Foundations of the Law, with notes by Willem Vorst. There is the tractate Pirke Avot, or Chapters of the Fathers, with notes by Fagius. To these can be added the recent Jewish teacher, Menasseh ben Israel. Among Christians, Scaliger excels here in his Elenchus of the Three Heresies; Wilhelm Schickard in various treatises; Drusius in many books likewise; Buxtorf in both of his works; and also Cappellus; Selden's very learned writings also, and Coccejus's Two Talmudic Treatises; Constantin l'Empereur's various works likewise; and, next to them, Hottinger's, especially his Philological Thesaurus; Fuller's Miscellanies; Samuel Petit and Stellingfleet; and those works translated into Latin from the Talmudic tractates by Ulmann, Schmid and others. The English book of Goodwin, under the title of Moses and Aaron, is also useful here. A great summary and treasury of these matters is found in Buxtorf's great and fruitful Talmudic or Rabbinic Lexicon, and in Matthias Martini's Philological work.

units.la: XI. Accedit linguarum notitiae historiarum quoque studium, & primo quidem Romanarum, quae in Academiis etiam tractari solent; quandoquidem à Romanis omnis ferme Occidentalium sapientia profluxit; utpote qui non solum rempublicam in idea delinearunt, quae Platonis & Aristotelis laus est; sed reapse illam exhibuerunt, & in illa omnes belli pacisque artes; unde eorum res & antiquitates singulari etiam studio hauriendae sunt: quem in finem legendi eorum historici auctoresque classici, cum notis virorum doctissimorum Gronovii & Graevii, sive publice editis, sive privatos intra parietes dictatis. Hic praetereundi non sunt rei literariae principes Scaliger, Casaubonus, Salmasius, Lipsius, ex cujus operibus excerptus est singularis libellus, sub titulo, Fax Romana historia, in quo rerum Romanarum breve quoddam est compendium. Ex quarum rerum & antiquitatum interiori notitia, non exigua saepe lux rebus sacris affulget. Graeca historiae gustum dare potest Ubbo Emmius & Salmasii tractatus de lingua Hellenistica, nisi quis utili non minus & laudabili opera ad ipsos Graecorum historicos diverti velit. Hebraicam historiam praecipue tradit Flavius Josephus, longe utilissimus liber, & post sacra Biblia summo in pretio habendus. Quo faciet etiam Hottingeri historia Orientalis, Pocockii historia Dynastiarum & specimen historia Arabica. Plures qui desiderat, addere poterit Gentii histor. Judaicam; R. Davidis Ganz Tzemach David, à Vorstio versum & illustratum.
units.tr: XI. To the knowledge of languages is added the study of history, and first of all of Roman history, which is also customarily taught in the universities. For almost all the wisdom of the West has flowed from the Romans, who not only sketched out a commonwealth in theory, which is the praise of Plato and Aristotle, but actually exhibited it, and in it all the arts of war and peace. Therefore their affairs and antiquities must be absorbed with special zeal. To this end one should read their historians and classical authors, with the notes of the most learned men, Gronovius and Graevius, whether published publicly or dictated privately within walls. Here the leaders of literary scholarship, Scaliger, Casaubon, Salmasius, Lipsius, must not be passed over. From the works of Lipsius a single excellent little book has been excerpted, under the title A Torch of Roman History, which is a short compendium of Roman affairs. From an inner knowledge of these affairs and antiquities, no small light often shines upon sacred matters. Ubbo Emmius and Salmasius's treatise on Hellenistic Greek can give a taste of Greek history, unless someone wishes to turn with equal profit and praise to the Greek historians themselves. Flavius Josephus chiefly presents Hebrew history, a far most useful book, and to be held in the highest esteem after the holy Bible. Hottinger's Oriental History, Pococke's History of the Dynasties and Specimen of Arabic History will also serve this purpose. Whoever wants more can add Gentius's Jewish History, and R. David Ganz's Tzemach David [The Branch of David], translated and illustrated by Vorst.

units.la: XII. Insigniter etiam utilis hic est labor orbem veterum, historiae omnis theatrum, cognoscere & ex mappis Geographicis perspectum habere; quod dabunt Ptolemaei tabula, Strabo, Pomponius Mela Vossii, & Cluverii Geographia. Sacram vero Geographiam sibi unice necessariam, studiosus noster discat ex Adrichomio & variis Lightfoti operis Chorographiae terrae Israelitiae felicissime impensis: adjiciat etiam Benjamini Tudelensis itinerarium, cum notis Cl. l'Empereur, in quo etiam libello tyrocinia lectionis Hebraicae sine punctis deponi possunt. Provectioribus vero studiis hisce addere licebit, magni Bochartii libros Geographiae sacrae, sub titulo Phaleg & Canaan.
units.tr: XII. This labour is also remarkably useful: to get to know the ancient world, the whole theatre of history, and to have it clearly before the eyes from geographical maps. Ptolemy's tables, Strabo, Pomponius Mela (Vossius's edition), and Cluverius's Geography will provide this. Our student should learn sacred geography, which is his alone to need, from Adrichomius and from the very well-spent labours of Lightfoot's work, Chorographia of the Land of Israel. He should also add Benjamin of Tudela's Itinerary, with the notes of the distinguished l'Empereur, in which little book the beginnings of Hebrew reading may be pursued without vowel points. For more advanced studies it will be permissible to add the great books of Bochart on sacred geography, under the title Phaleg and Canaan.

units.la: XIII. Idea etiam historiae universalis animo haurienda est; eaque tam saecularis, quam Ecclesiasticae; quae deinceps post acceptam vocationem perficienda est & uberius excolenda. Ad eam igitur manu ducere possunt Jonstoni Sceleton historiae universalis; Sleidanus de quatuor summis Imperiis, Sulpitius Severus cum notis Drusii, Hornii, Joh. Versfiii; Cluverii epitome historiae totius mundi, & Bebelii antiquitates. Ad Chronologiam recte hauriendam faciunt Vossii Isagoge Chronologiae sacrae, & Beveregii institutiones Chronologicae. Inde progrediendum ad Guhberlethi Chronologiam, quae synchronismos historiae sacrae & exoticae exhibet; licet circa historiam exoticam V. Test. minus saepe accuratus sit; ad Langium de Annis Christi, Petavii Rationarium temporum; Cappelli historiam sacram & exoticam, Genebrardi, & Baillii Chronologiam, Usserii annales; & ex quo omnes fere aliorum rivuli deducti sunt, Scaligerum de emendatione temporum: quem secutus est Setus Calvisius, uti hunc Helvicus.
units.tr: XIII. The idea of universal history too must be taken into the mind, both secular and ecclesiastical, which is to be completed and cultivated more fully afterwards, once the calling has been received. For this purpose the following may lead by the hand: Jonston's Skeleton of Universal History; Sleidan's On the Four Great Empires, Sulpicius Severus with the notes of Drusius, Horn, and John Versfeld; Cluverius's Epitome of the history of the whole world, and Bebel's Antiquities. For drawing chronology correctly, Vossius's Introduction to Sacred Chronology and Beveridge's Chronological Institutes are helpful. From there one should proceed to Guhberleth's Chronology, which sets out the synchronisms of sacred and foreign history, although in the foreign history of the Old Testament it is less often accurate; to Lang on the Years of Christ and Petavius's Rationarium temporum; to Cappel's Sacred and Foreign History, Genebrard, and Baillie's Chronology, Ussher's Annals; and to Scaliger on the Emendation of Times, from which almost all the streams of the others have been drawn. Seth Calvisius followed him, and Helvicus followed Calvisius.

units.la: XIV. Novi Test. historiae sceleton molimur in scholis privatis: illius compendium tradunt Latus & Hornius; & praeter auctores laudatos prolixius Boxhornius in historia universali; Hottingerus in historia Ecclesiastica, qui cum cura res Judaeorum persequitur; Cappellus; Eutychius Patriarcha in annalibus Alexandrinis; Usserius de successione Ecclesiarum in Occidente. Conducunt etiam Montacutii Origines Ecclesiasticae, Blondelli summi historici omnia; & laudatissimae Institutiones historico-Theologicae Forbesii. Inter adversarios adiri possunt Gualtherius in tabulis, Cabassutius in notitia Concil. orum Ecclesiae; licet multo cum judicio legendi. Praecipue vero ad ipsos fontes ascendendum est, historicos nimirum veteres, Eusebium, Socratem &c ubi omnium instar erunt Scaliger in Eusebium, & in eundem, reliquosque historicos Ecclesiasticos, Valesius praestantissimus plane scriptor; nec non suo tempore annalium Pater Baronius, cum exercitationibus Casauboni, & notis doctissimi Blondelli, brevi, ut spes est, prodituris.
units.tr: XIV. We build the skeleton of New Testament history in private schools. Its compendium is given by Lat and Horn; and, besides the authors already named, more fully Boxhorn in his Universal History; Hottinger in his Ecclesiastical History, who pursues the affairs of the Jews with care; Cappel; Eutychius, the patriarch, in the Alexandrian Annals; and Ussher on the Succession of Churches in the West. Montagu's Ecclesiastical Origins and Blondel, the greatest historian in everything, are also useful, as is the most highly praised Historico-Theological Institutes of Forbes. Among the adversaries, Gualtherus in his tables and Cabassut in his notice of the councils of the Church may be consulted, though they must be read with much judgement. Above all, however, one must ascend to the sources themselves, that is, the ancient historians, Eusebius, Socrates, etc., for which Scaliger on Eusebius will stand in place of all; and on the same author and the other ecclesiastical historians, Valesius, a most outstanding writer. Likewise Baronius, the father of annals in his own time, with the exercises of Casaubon and the notes of the most learned Blondel, which, it is hoped, will appear shortly.

units.la: XV. Accuratiorem Reformationis historiam dabit Sculteius in Annalibus Reformationis; copiose satis eam etiam, qua Belgium spectat, exhibet scriptum vernaculum, Brandt Derthaal van de Hefomatie in Nederland. Boxhorns eerste deel der Nederlandsche Historie: multum etiam huc conferunt Erasmi, Melanchthonis, aliorumque virorum doctorum Epistolae, Sleidani commentarius de statu religionis, Thuani historia, & eximius liber, Pauli Veneti historia Concilii Tridentini; Camerarii vita Melanchthonis eleganter & accurate scripta; Melchior Adamus de vitis Theologorum, tum Germanorum, tum exterorum. Quibus, si lubet, adjiciendus deinde est Flacii Illyrici Catalogus testium veritatis, similesque scriptores.
units.tr: XV. Sculteius in his Annals of the Reformation will give a more accurate history of the Reformation. A vernacular work, Brandt's History of the Reformation in the Netherlands, sets it out quite fully as far as it concerns Belgium. Boxhorn's first part of the Dutch History. The Letters of Erasmus, Melanchthon, and other learned men contribute much here, as do Sleidan's Commentary on the State of Religion, Thuanus's History, and the outstanding book, Paolo Sarpi's History of the Council of Trent; Camerarius's Life of Melanchthon, written elegantly and accurately; and Melchior Adam's Lives of Theologians, both German and foreign. To these, if one wishes, Flacius Illyricus's Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth and similar writers should then be added.

units.la: XVI. Patria nostræ historiam, ne domi peregrinus sit, sciat etiam oportet noster; quare evolvat Reidani & Meterani historias vernaculas; ut & Hoofdii, viri incomparabilis fidei, & Belgicæ nostræ Taciti, monumenta, qui rerum non solum, sed & verborum luculentus est magister, quamvis prudenter imitandus, ne quis ex illo ampullas & scenicum insolitorum verborum apparatum in suggestum apportet. Hug. Grotii Annales & historia de rebus Belgicis. Ecclesiastica patriæ gesta præter jam dictos, exhibent Triglandius & Utenbogardus. Queis adjungi possunt Martyrologia, tum nostra tum Anglica & præcipue Belgicis altera parte locupletiora Gallica. Statum Ecclesiæ Judaicæ hodiernæ exhibet Fechius, Æthiopicæ Wildius, Græcanicæ Vejelius, Allatius; quique eum emendarunt.
units.tr: XVI. Our student ought also to know the history of his fatherland, lest he be a stranger in his own home. Therefore let him read through the vernacular histories of Reidanus and Meteren, as well as the monuments of Hooft, a man of incomparable fidelity and the Tacitus of our Belgium, who is a splendid master not only of matters but also of words, though he is to be imitated prudently, lest anyone bring from him the bombast and theatrical display of unusual words into the pulpit. Hugo Grotius's Annals and History of the Affairs of the Netherlands. The ecclesiastical deeds of the fatherland, besides those already mentioned, are set out by Triglandius and Uytenbogaert. To these may be joined the Martyrologies, both our own and the English, and the French, which is richer than the Belgian in its second part. The present state of the Jewish Church is set out by Fechius, that of the Ethiopian by Wildius, and that of the Greek by Vejelius and Allatius, and those who have corrected them.

units.la: XVII. Atque ita ornata memoria, linguarum, historiarum & antiquitatum utilissima supellectile, partim ante studium Theologicum, partim una cum ipso comparanda; præcipua cura sit, ut ante omnia excolatur ratio & judicium: longe enim præstat acri & polito valere judicio, quam suffarcinata ingenti thesauro memoria. Propitia igitur sibi reddenda est ratio, & illis contradictionibus liberanda, quæ fidei ingenerandæ maxime inimicæ sunt, antequam interiori illius & Theologica cognitione imbuatur animus; ne corrupta ratio præjudiciis suis irreparabile rebus Theologicis adferat detrimentum; quod in Socinianis usu venit, qui cum falsæ rationi suæ unicè litent, fidem omnem emasculant. Quinimo adultera hæc ratio & Philosophia, unica fere errorum causa est, & Philosophi, ex antiquorum dicto, hæreticorum sunt Patriarchæ: ut nisi probe exculta sit ratio, vix res ulla clare & distinctè percipi possit; quod in idiotis apparet, qui rerum omnium sibi cognitarum, confusas plerunque cogitationes habent. Cum recta Philosophia, supposita revelatione, multa ex penu sua depromat, quorum auxilio claros & distinctos conceptus de revelatis formare discimus. Hæc ergo maxime vires intendendæ, ut per sanam Philosophiam distincti conceptus de rebus naturalibus & corporalibus, imprimis etiam de moralibus, divinis & spiritualibus formentur, & mens quasi edoceatur: cui usui idoneam non satis esse Philosophiam Peripateticam, multorum seculorum experientia docuit; & instrumentum ejus Logicam, (quæ, ut Tertullianus ait, Dialecticum format Christianismum) valere magis ad differendum de rebus jam cognitis, quam ad inveniendum ignota, & judicium rectè formandum. Meliori itaque Philosophiæ incumbendum est; qua, singulari felicitate, fæculum ornavit Nobilif. Renatus Cartefius; qui raro & inaudito hactenus exemplo, exuto præjudiciis animo, in vacuum posuit vestigia princeps, & non sensibus, sed menti, insitisque illi principiis, simplicissimis & generalissimis, superstruens solidiorem Philosophiam, continuo filo ita primis extrema coaptavit, ut integram microcosmi & macrocosmi naturam inde reseraverit. Quæ Philosophandi methodus præterquam quod rationem unice expoliat, præjudiciisque mentem liberet, Theologo insuper summopere utilis est; cum nulla alia mentis corporisque discrimen, divini numinis extantiam & interiorem notitiam, hominis ab eo dependentiam, libertatisque ipsius cum divina gratia conciliationem subtilius perrimata sit & fortius asseruerit. Ut supra omnes alias, Atheismum, corporeitatisque brutum conceptum, sæculi pestes & pernicies, ab intima fibra revellat, omnibusque gratiæ adversariis, Pelagianis, Jesuitis eorumque sequacibus irreconciliabile bellum indicat eosque funditus prosternat. Ut non gloriosiorem potuerit veritas triumphum agere, quam ore illius, e communione Papistica, qui eam maxime oppugnaturus, hoc elogio eam condecoravit, Philosophia Cartesii non potest teneri a Viro Catholico, h.e. Pontificio. Hæc ergo Philosophia imbibenda & præter ipsius Philosophi scripta, inter alios qui ipsius vestigiis insistunt, legendus, qui hominis seu mentis anatomiam intime recludit & aperit, tractatus de mente humana Ludovici de la Forge. Ad recte vero dirigendas cogitationes utilis esse potest libellus de arte bene cogitandi, e Gallico translatus; cui addi debet, Cl. Claubergii Logica, nec non Cl. Wittichii, amici mei charissimi, Consensus veritatis revelata cum Philosophia; amborumque reliqua scripta, in quibus hujus Philosophiæ usum ad cogitationes Theologicas expoliendas & perficiendas ostendunt.
units.tr: XVII. Thus, with memory adorned and with the most useful furniture of languages, histories and antiquities, to be acquired partly before the study of theology and partly alongside it, the chief care should be that reason and judgement are cultivated above all else. For it is far better to be strong in keen and polished judgement than in a memory crammed with a huge treasury. Reason must therefore be made favourable to us and freed from those contradictions which are most hostile to the generating of faith, before the mind is steeped in its inner and theological knowledge; lest a corrupted reason, by its own prejudices, bring irreparable harm to theological matters. This happens among the Socinians, who, since they offer sacrifice only to their false reason, emasculate all faith. Indeed, this adulterated reason and philosophy is almost the only cause of errors, and philosophers, according to the saying of the ancients, are the patriarchs of heretics. So unless reason has been properly cultivated, hardly anything can be perceived clearly and distinctly; this is apparent in the unlearned, who for the most part have confused thoughts about all the things they know. Yet sound philosophy, once revelation is presupposed, draws many things from its own store, with whose help we learn to form clear and distinct concepts of revealed matters. Therefore the chief efforts must be directed to this end: that through a sound philosophy distinct concepts of natural and bodily things, and above all of moral, divine and spiritual things, may be formed, and the mind may, as it were, be taught. Long experience of many centuries has shown that Peripatetic philosophy is not adequate for this use; and its instrument, logic (which, as Tertullian says, forms the Christian into a dialectician), is more useful for disputing about things already known than for discovering unknown things and forming judgement correctly. Therefore one must devote oneself to a better philosophy, with which the most noble René Descartes adorned the age with singular felicity. With a rare and hitherto unheard-of example, his mind freed from prejudices, he, as a prince, set his steps on an empty ground; and, building not on the senses but on the mind and on the principles implanted in it, the simplest and most general, he so joined the first things to the last with a continuous thread that he unlocked from them the whole nature of the microcosm and the macrocosm. This method of philosophizing, besides refining reason alone and freeing the mind from prejudices, is also greatly useful to the theologian, since no other has more subtly investigated and more strongly asserted the distinction between mind and body, the existence of the divine power and inner knowledge of it, the dependence of man upon it, and the reconciliation of his freedom with divine grace. Above all others, it tears up from its inmost root atheism, the crude concept of corporeality, the plagues and destruction of the age, and it declares irreconcilable war upon all adversaries of grace, the Pelagians, the Jesuits and their followers, and overthrows them to the foundations. Truth could not have won a more glorious triumph than from the mouth of one of the communion of the Papists, who, intending to attack it most strongly, honoured it with this commendation: The philosophy of Descartes cannot be held by a Catholic man, that is, by a Papist. This philosophy, therefore, is to be imbibed; and, besides the writings of the philosopher himself, among others who follow in his footsteps, is to be read the treatise On the Human Mind by Louis de la Forge, which intimately opens and reveals the anatomy of man or of the mind. To direct thoughts rightly, the little book On the Art of Thinking Well, translated from the French, may be useful; to it should be added the distinguished Clauberg's Logic, and also the distinguished Wittich's Consensus of Revealed Truth with Philosophy, my most dear friend's; and the remaining writings of both, in which they show the use of this philosophy for refining and perfecting theological thoughts.

units.la: XVIII. Si quis etiam ad Mathematica propendeat, utilissimum crit his studiis animum imbuere; illa enim, si quicquam, judicium acuunt & dirigunt, præcipitantiam tollunt, & verum a falso discernere docent. Qui vero non ejusmodi est ingenii, alio se vertat, qua parte maxime se valiturum putet; quisque enim se ipsum probe explorare debet, & animum ad ea applicare studia, ad quæ sive vires, sive animi propensio, sive temporum ratio ipsum rapiunt.
units.tr: XVIII. If anyone is also inclined to mathematics, it will be most useful to steep his mind in these studies, for these, if anything, sharpen and direct judgement, remove rashness, and teach us to distinguish the true from the false. But whoever is not of such a disposition of mind should turn to another field in which he thinks he will be most capable; for each person ought to examine himself well and apply his mind to those studies to which either his abilities, or the inclination of his mind, or the circumstances of the times draw him.

units.la: XIX. Magnum etiam ad res tum Philosophicas, tum Theologicas funditus percipiendas præsidium adferet, Medicinam delibasse. Quare legendi, ex veterum scriptis, accurate sunt Hippocratis aphorismi, & ubi tempus permittit, plures ipsius tractatus, adjecto Cornelio Celso. Ex recentioribus perlustranda praecipuè sunt praeclara anatomicorum inventa: & ut brevem œconomiæ animalis conspectum habeatis, legendus de eâ Hogelandius, & ipse Cartesius, licet imperfecto, tamen praestantissimo tractatu de Homine.
units.tr: XIX. This will also be a great aid to grasping thoroughly both philosophical and theological matters, to have tasted medicine. Therefore the aphorisms of Hippocrates should be read carefully from the writings of the ancients, and, when time allows, more of his treatises, with Cornelius Celsus added. Among recent writers, the notable discoveries of the anatomists should above all be surveyed; and so that you may have a brief view of the economy of the animal body, read on this Hogelandius, and Descartes himself, in his treatise On Man, admittedly unfinished but most excellent.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De ipso studio Theologico.
units.tr: On the Theological Study Itself.

units.la: I. Hisce omnibus pro cujusque genio, captu & tempore praemissis, quin & cum studio sacro conjunctis, suspenso & tardo gradu accedendum est ad ipsum Theologici studii sanctuarium; quod subire non decet nisi quodam cum tremore & summa cum veneratione: serió interim accingendus est animus, sive harum rerum cognitio consideretur in Theologia dogmatica; sive in earum usu & praxi.
units.tr: I. Once all these things have been premised, according to each person's talent, capacity and time, and joined with sacred study too, one must approach the very sanctuary of theological study with a hesitant and slow step. One ought not to enter it except with a certain trembling and the greatest reverence. Meanwhile the mind must be seriously girded, whether the knowledge of these matters is considered in dogmatic theology, or in their use and practice.

units.la: II. Cardo omnis studii hujus Theologici versatur in lectione, tum sacrae Scripturae; tum Scholarum, sive Systematum & locorum communium inde derivatorum. Fons primus, totusque fundus quaerendus in S. Scriptura, in qua omnes sapientiae divinae thesauri sunt reclusi: quare optima & sola eo nomine digna est theologia, quae biblica est & inde repetita. Sicut ergo ex Scriptura res ipsae sunt petendae, ita secundùm eam, rerum etiam series & ordo adornandus & componendus est. Ideoque Biblia sacra sine ulla intermissione legenda & à prima juventute imbibenda sunt, ut eorum phraseologia & vis in succum quasi & sanguinem nostrum convertatur: cum & solius fere Biblici studii cultura, tantos & tot excellentes viros dederit, ut Piscatorem, Lud. de Dieu, Coccejum aliosque. Praecipuè autem familiare reddendum est Novum Test. & in eo epistolae Paulinae, quae in textu authentico jugi lectione & vel per otium & deambulando in juventute ita familiares reddendae sunt, ut vel memoriter discantur.
units.tr: II. The hinge of all this theological study turns on reading, both of Holy Scripture and of the schools, that is, of the systems and commonplaces derived from it. The first and entire foundation is to be sought in the Holy Scripture, in which all the treasures of divine wisdom are enclosed. Hence the best and only theology worthy of the name is that which is biblical and drawn from Scripture. Just as the things themselves are to be sought from Scripture, so the sequence and order of things is to be arranged and composed according to it. Therefore the holy Bible is to be read without any interruption and imbibed from earliest youth, so that its phraseology and force are turned into our very juice and blood. For the cultivation of the study of the Bible alone has produced so many excellent men, such as Piscator, Lud. de Dieu, Coccejus and others. Above all, the New Testament is to be made especially familiar, and in it the Pauline epistles, which in the authentic text, by constant reading, and at leisure and while walking, in youth are to be made so familiar that they are learned even by heart.

units.la: III. Bibliorum lectionem velim hic institui duplicem; unam solius textus vernaculi; alteram ejusdem textus, sed ita; ut idem caput lectum Graece aut Hebraice relegatur, & Phraseologia sacra cum vernacula contendatur; adhibitis notis & analysibus; cui bono hic praescripsero Analysin & scholia Piscatoris in utrumque Test. cum notis Junii & Tremellii in Vetus, & Bezæ in Novum Test. adjunctis & collatis Interpretum Belgicorum notis. Hunc etiam in usum, singulorum sacrorum librorum & capitum tituli in adversariis designari possunt, in quos, brevissimis signis, referatur, quicquid ad intelligentiam librorum sacrorum observatur, sive in commentatoribus inferius laudandis, sive aliis quibusvis auctoribus, ut locorum illorum usus ad primum statim conspectum nobis suppetat; & omni modo familiaris reddatur nobis sacræ Scripturæ intelligentia; in qua, ut egregie Chrysostomus, totius sacerdotii nostri est substantia.
units.tr: III.
