I would have the reading of the Bible instituted here in two ways: one of the vernacular text alone; the other of the same text, but in such a way that the same chapter is read again in Greek or Hebrew, and the sacred phraseology is compared with the vernacular, with notes and analyses employed. For this purpose I have here prescribed Piscator's Analysis and Scholia on both Testaments, with the notes of Junius and Tremellius added on the Old Testament, and of Beza on the New, and compared with the notes of the Belgic interpreters. For this use too, the titles of individual sacred books and chapters may be marked in your notebooks, and by very brief signs there may be referred to them whatever is observed for the understanding of the sacred books, whether in the commentators cited below or in any other authors. Thus the use of those passages will be at hand at the first glance, and the understanding of Holy Scripture will become familiar to us in every way. In it, as Chrysostom admirably says, lies the whole substance of our priesthood.

units.la: IV. Ipsa sacra Biblia sequuntur Systemata ex iis deducta, quæ ut ad S. Scripturas examinanda, ita ex iis complenda & augenda sunt. Quorum omnibus aliis ego quidem præstulero, qui Theologiam disponunt secundum ordinem naturalem, œconomiam foederum Dei & administrationem salutis humanæ; juxta eam ipsam methodum & historiæ & dogmatum, quam Deus ipse in Scriptura, à sæculorum initio, usque ad finem eorum, observavit: qui ordo in locis communibus omnibus non ita conspicuus est, sed sæpe turbatus, & præter naturalem methodum plures loci extra sedem suam, in angulum vel alienum locum subinde detorti. Quem ad scopum manuductionem aliquam fortasse dabit iis, quibus eam terere lubet, Synopsis nostra Theologiæ & Oeconomiæ fœderum Dei. In qua maxime necessaria duntaxat breviter, in usum scholæ privatæ, delineavimus; multo pluribus, iisque sæpe melioribus, studio omissis: quorum tamen bonam partem in scholis nostris publicis domesticisque exhibemus. Illi superaddi potest Cloppenburgii Syntagma & Disputationes; Joh. Oweni Ecclogunomena, & præcipue Celeb. Cocceji Summa doctrinæ de Fœdere, ut & Summa Theologiæ: quæ scripta maxima cura & meditatione evolvenda & eo usque ruminanda, donec cerebrum illius viri perspectæ & pertractatæ habeantur, ne rejiciatur, quod non intelligitur; & terminorum Scripturæ, qui in illis soli, citra mixturam humanorum apparent, sensus, vis & efficacia, unoque verbo totius Theologiæ harmonia & analogia, inde discatur, & memoriæ fideliter imprimatur; quibus addas deinde reliquos ipsius viri tractatus, ubi variæ Theologiæ partes latius deducuntur aut vindicantur; hac ratione ut cum singulis œconomiæ divinæ capitibus, ad pleniorem eorum intelligentiam, conferantur. Hoc in aliis itidem auctoribus facere licebit; seu descriptione locorum observandorum, si breviora sint, seu annotatione sola si longiora; ut eorum usus, ubi opus est, praesto esse possit: quod vel per collectanea in adversariis, vel per chartas Synopsi nostrae, aut alii libro ad id selecto, insertas fieri poterit; ita tamen ut trita & vulgaria non adscribantur, quod rhapsodis quibusdam in more est, sed duntaxat ubi singulare quid & a paucissimis observatum, aut novum plane in auctoribus reperitur; quomodo ingenti labore scribendi levabimini, & res ipsas memoriae, magis, quam chartis commendabitis & tradetis.
units.tr: IV. The sacred Bible itself is followed by the systems deduced from it, which are to be used both for examining the Holy Scriptures and for completing and enlarging them. Of all these, I for my part would prefer those which arrange theology according to the natural order: the economy of God's covenants and the administration of human salvation, following that very method of both history and doctrines which God himself observed in Scripture, from the beginning of the ages to their end. This order is not so conspicuous in all the commonplaces, but is often disturbed, and, apart from the natural method, several topics are at times twisted out of their proper place into a corner or an alien location. For the purpose of guiding those who wish to tread this path, our Synopsis of Theology and of the Economy of God's Covenants may perhaps provide some guidance. In it we have sketched briefly only the most necessary matters, for use in a private school; much more, and often better, has been omitted by design, though we set out a good part of it in our public and domestic schools. To this may be added Cloppenburg's Syntagma and Disputations; John Owen's Ecclogunomena, and especially the celebrated Cocceius's Summa of the doctrine of the Covenant, as well as his Summa of Theology. These writings are to be unrolled with the greatest care and meditation, and chewed over until that man's mind is grasped and thoroughly handled, so that one does not reject what one does not understand. From them one should learn the meaning, force and efficacy of the terms of Scripture that appear in those works alone, without admixture of human things, and in a word the harmony and analogy of all theology, and faithfully impress it on the memory. To these you should then add the remaining treatises of the same man, where the various parts of theology are more fully developed or defended, in such a way that they are compared with the individual heads of the divine economy for a fuller understanding of them. This may equally be done with other authors: either by describing the observable passages, if they are shorter, or by annotation alone if they are longer, so that their use may be at hand where needed. This can be done through collections in your notebooks, or through slips inserted into our Synopsis or into another book chosen for the purpose. Yet trite and commonplace matters should not be copied out, as some scribblers are wont to do, but only where something singular, observed by very few, or entirely new, is found in the authors. In this way you will be relieved of the great labour of writing, and you will commit the things themselves more to memory than to paper.

units.la: V. Ad singularia Theologiae & Oeconomiae illius capita consuli & adiri possunt, sequentes auctores: nimirum ex iis, qui de Theologiae principio & S. Scriptura agunt; Mestrezatus de S. Scriptura. Cocceius de potentia Scripturae. Clauberg & Hundius Disputationes. Vossius de LXX Interpretum versione, & qui cum eo congressi sunt.
units.tr: V. For the individual topics of that theology and economy, the following authors may be consulted and approached. Among those who treat of the principle of theology and of Holy Scripture: Mestrezat on Holy Scripture; Cocceius on the power of Scripture; Clauberg and Hundius, Disputations; Vossius on the Septuagint version, and those who have contended with him.

units.la: VI. De Foedere Dei consulantur auctores memorati. De speciali vero foederis administratione, sub promissione & Patriarchis, agunt viri doctissimi & amicissimi, Heideggerus in Exercitationibus suis de historia Patriarcharum ante & post diluvium. Jacobus Alting. in libro, cui titulus Schilo, & Dissertationibus Academicis.
units.tr: VI. On the Covenant of God, the authors already mentioned should be consulted. On the particular administration of the covenant under the promise and the Patriarchs, the very learned and very friendly men Heidegger, in his Exercitations on the history of the Patriarchs before and after the flood, and James Alting, in the book entitled Shiloh, and in his Academic Dissertations, write.

units.la: VII. De oeconomia legali, tum cerimoniali, tum morali, tum forensi, spissum satis volumen edidit Theod. Beza. Speciatim de lege morali adeatur Rivetus, D'Espagne, Danhauwerus, ut & Amesius in secunda parte Medulla & Casibus conscientia & Episcopius in c. v. Matthai. De Origine & progressu idololatriae scripsit eximium opus Joh. Gerhardus Vossius. Consuli quoque potest Seldenus de Diis Syris. De Imaginibus Pet. Picherellus, Joh. Dallaeus, & Joh. Hoornbeekius. De foenore & usura tractant, Salmasius, & scripta quaedam vernacula, sub titulis; Res judicata & judicanda. de sorte Gatakerus.
units.tr: VII. On the legal economy, ceremonial, moral and judicial alike, Theodore Beza published a rather thick volume. Especially on the moral law, one should consult Rivet, D'Espagne, Danhauer, and also Amesius in the second part of his Medulla, and Cases of Conscience, and Episcopius on chapter 5 of Matthew. On the origin and progress of idolatry, John Gerhard Vossius wrote an outstanding work. One may also consult Selden, On the Gods of the Syrians. On images, Peter Picherel, John Dallaeus, and John Hoornbeeck. On interest and usury, Salmasius treats of it, and certain writings in the vernacular, under the titles: Matter Judged and to Be Judged; on the question of the principal, Gataker.

units.la: VIII. De rebus cerimonialibus, praeter varios auctores circa antiquitates Judaicas laudatos, egerunt, inter veteres Rob. Grotius de cessatione legalium; inter hodiernos, Frantzius & Cloppenburgius in Schola sacrificiorum, Stuckius de sacrificiis gentilium. Heideggerus de esu sanguinis & suffocati. Codex Joma Roberti Sheringhamii. Const. l'Empereur in codicem Middoth. Heylini historia Sabbati; in quam arenam nos quoque descendere necesse habuimus. Utilis etiam circa res Judaicas est Episcopius in Institutionibus Theologicis.
units.tr: VIII. On ceremonial matters, besides the various authors praised on Jewish antiquities, among the ancients Hugo Grotius, on the cessation of the legal rites, wrote; among the moderns, Frantzius and Cloppenburg in the School of Sacrifices, Stuckius on the sacrifices of the Gentiles, Heidegger on the eating of blood and of what is strangled, Sheringham's Codex Joma, Constantin l'Empereur on the Mishnaic tractate Middoth, Heylin's history of the Sabbath; into which arena we too have found it necessary to descend. Episcopius in his Theological Institutes is also useful on Jewish matters.

units.la: IX. De lege forensi & politia Judaica singulari cum fructu legi possunt, Hebraorum leges ab Hottingero editae. Schickardus de jure regio Hebraorum. Canaus & Bertramus de Republ. Judaorum, & hic quidem cum notis l'Empereur; qui & videndus est in tractatu suo de legibus forensibus. Eminet hic caeteris Seldenus de jure naturali & gentium, secundum leges Hebraeorum; de Synedriis; Successionibus; Uxore Hebraica. Quo etiam facit Zepperus de legibus Mosaicis. Propter casus autem matrimoniales in praxi occurrentes, negligendus non est Beza de divortiis, repudiis & polygamia. Carpzovius, & in subacti judicii scripto de Jure connubiorum Henricus Brouwer, affinis honorandus.
units.tr: IX. On the forensic law and the peculiar Jewish polity, the following may be read with profit: The Laws of the Hebrews, edited by Hottinger. Schickard, On the royal law of the Hebrews. Canaan and Bertram, On the Jewish Commonwealth, and this one indeed with notes by l'Empereur; who also must be seen in his treatise on forensic laws. Above the rest stands Selden, On the natural law and the law of nations according to the laws of the Hebrews; on the Sanhedrins; on successions; on the Hebrew wife. Zepper, On the Mosaic laws also serves this purpose. But on account of the matrimonial cases occurring in practice, Beza, On divorces, repudiations and polygamy should not be neglected. Carpzov, and in his writing on the Law of Marriages, written with a mature judgement, Henry Brouwer, a kindred man, deserves to be honoured.

units.la: X. Circa oeconomiam sub Novo Test. de Christi persona, beneficiis & officiis, praeter usitatos vulgo auctores, consulendus Ger. Joh. Vossius de Christi genealogia, passione, morte, resurrectione & ascensione. De justificatione egregius extat libellus Anglicus W. Bradshaw.
units.tr: X. On the economy of the New Testament concerning the person, benefits and offices of Christ, apart from the authors commonly in use, one should consult Gerhard John Vossius, on the genealogy, passion, death, resurrection and ascension of Christ. On justification there is an excellent little book in English by W. Bradshaw.

units.la: XI. De sacramentis Novi Test. videri possunt quae Vossius de Baptismo, Aubertinus, Mestrezatus, Blondellus, Dallaeus, Salmasius, Claudius, Larrogius, & ex adversariis Petrus de Marca, de Eucharistia annexisque argumentis scripserunt.
units.tr: XI. On the sacraments of the New Testament one may consult what Vossius on Baptism, Aubertinus, Mestrezatus, Blondellus, Dallaeus, Salmasius, Claudius, Larrogius, and, among the opponents, Pierre de Marca, have written about the Eucharist and the questions connected with it.

units.la: XII. De Ecclesia Novi Test. ejusque statu, regimine & adulteratione tractarunt Mestrezatus, Salmasius de primatu Papae, ut & de Episcopis & Presbyteris. Blondellus de la primaute en l'Eglise. Idem de Johanna Papissa, nec non de Episcopis & Presbyteris; & de eisdem Hammondus & Hoornbeekius. De Hierarchia Ecclesiastica Petavius. Marcus Antonius de Dominis. Parkerus. Didoclavii Altare Damascenum. De paenitentia & clavibus Petrus & Ludovicus Molinaeus in Paraenesi, una cum corollario. De templis, festis & monachis &c. Hospinianus. De Veteris & Nova Ecclesiae ritibus, Casalius: de iis & antiquitate reliqua Ecclesiastica, Justellus, Salmasius, Dallaeus, Jac. Gothofredus, Albaspineus, Hugo Menardus, Goar, Sirmondus, Petavius, Morinus, alii.
units.tr: XII. On the Church of the New Testament, its state, government and corruption, Mestrezatus, Salmasius on the primacy of the Pope, have written, and likewise on bishops and presbyters. Blondellus on the primacy in the Church (la primauté en l'Église). The same has written on Pope Joan, and also on bishops and presbyters; and on these same subjects Hammond and Hoornbeek. On the ecclesiastical hierarchy Petavius. Marcus Antonius de Dominis. Parker. Didoclavius's Damascene Altar. On penance and the keys, Pierre and Louis Molinaeus in their Paraenesis, together with its corollary. On temples, feasts and monks etc. Hospinianus. On the rites of the Old and New Church, Casalius: on these and the rest of ecclesiastical antiquity, Justellus, Salmasius, Dallaeus, Jacob Godefroy, Albaspinaeus, Hugo Menardus, Goar, Sirmond, Petavius, Morinus, and others.

units.la: XIII. Si quis vero, praeter filum hoc oeconomiae Foederum Dei sequi delectetur Locos communes ita dictos, prae omnibus aliis suasero vel Medullam Amesianam, vel Systema Cl. Marefii, adjunctis Synopsi Professorum Leydensium, aut Gomari, & Altingii didactica, ut & Catechesi Ursini, & praecipue Calvini Institutionibus, quae satis laudari nequeunt, quibusque merito tribuitur elogium illud: Praeter Apostolicas, post Christi tempora, chartas Huic peperere libro, secula nulla parem.
units.tr: XIII. If anyone, besides this thread of the economy of God's covenants, is pleased to follow the so-called Common Places, I would above all others recommend either the Medulla of Ames, or the System of the distinguished Maresius, together with the Synopsis of the Leiden Professors, or Gomarus, and the Didactics of Alting, as well as the Catechism of Ursinus, and above all Calvin's Institutes, which can never be praised enough, and to which that tribute is rightly given: Apart from the Apostolic writings, no age since the time of Christ has produced a book equal to this one.

units.la: XIV. Eruditae etiam sunt Ger. Joh. Vossii Disputationes Theologicae. Disputationes Salmurienses & Sedanenses, in quibus posterioribus maxime ximè eminent doctissimi Rambertii theses. Ad hunc censum etiam pertinent Cameronis, Gomari, Belgarum doctissimi, aliorumque opera: ne variarum gentium Theologos longo ordine hic recenseam. De materiis selectis legi possunt Clar. & Doctiss. Voetii Disputationes.
units.tr: XIV. Also learned are Gerhard John Vossius's Theological Disputations, the Disputations of Saumur and Sedan, among which the most learned theses of Rambert especially stand out in the latter. To this list belong also the works of Cameron, Gomarus, the most learned of the Dutch, and others; I will not list the theologians of the various nations here in a long series. On selected topics the distinguished and most learned Voetius's Disputations may be read.

units.la: XV. Inter veteres, seu Reformatores, post Calvinum palmam tenent Musculus & Martyr. Ex iis qui extra Ecclesiam nostram sunt, inter Lutheranos, ingeniosissimus est ipse Lutherus; inter cujus tra-ctatus varios compendium quoddam ipsius cogitationum familiarium, tum theoreticarum, tum practicarum, continent Sermones ejus convivales, Germanice Tischreden, ad seriem locorum communium dispositi. Inter sequaces ejus laboriosissimus est Joh. Gerhardus in locis communibus, seu Confessione Catholica. Viri maximi in illa communione sunt Chemnitius & Calixtus. Inter Remonstrantes, omnium fere instar est eorum primipilus Episcopius, qui adversus Judæos & Pontificios laudabilem operam contulit; in reliquis maximo cum judicio & sale legendus. Summam aliquam cognitionum ejus exhibent conciones in Joh. 17. com. 3. Inter Pontificios, & quidem Lojolitas, doctissimus & candidus satis pro ratione istius societatis est. Petavius.
units.tr: XV. Among the older writers, or Reformers, after Calvin, Musculus and Martyr hold the palm. Of those who are outside our Church, among the Lutherans the most gifted is Luther himself; among his various treatises, his Table Talks (convivales sermones, in German Tischreden), arranged in the order of the common places, contain a kind of summary of his thoughts, both theoretical and practical, as they came up in everyday conversation. Among his followers the most laborious is John Gerhard in his Loci communes, or Confessio catholica. The greatest men in that communion are Chemnitz and Calixtus. Among the Remonstrants, their chief man, Episcopius, stands almost alone; he did a commendable work against the Jews and the Papists. In the rest he is to be read with the greatest judgement and discernment. A certain summary of his teaching is given in his sermons on John 17, verse 3. Among the Papists, and indeed among the Jesuits, Petavius is learned and fair enough for that society's standards.

units.la: XVI. Hausta & cognita sic veritate, falsitatis & mendaciorum in veritatem injuriorum gnarum etiam esse oportet candidatum nostrum, & noscendæ controversiæ; quarum studium cæteroquin non nisi ex accidente necessarium est, cum non, quid sit, sed tantum quid non sit veritas, docent, & veritate bene perspecta, & Scripturis sacris intellectis facilè componi possint pleræque controversiæ. In hisce utilissimus erit Joh. Hoornbeekii liber, dictus Summa Controversiarum. Ex veteribus Catalogi hæresium Augustini & Epiphanii; ut & Anonymi à Sirmondo editi; qui laudandus in multis, in multis item vituperandus est; præsertim facinus illud ipsius Sirmondi, qui in illo Hæresin prædestinatianam, nunquam alibi cognitam, teste Auræo, Doctore Sorbonico, suppositit.
units.tr: XVI. Once truth has been drawn in and known, our candidate must also be aware of the falsehoods and lies that do injury to the truth, and must know the controversies. Otherwise the study of these is needed only by chance, since they teach not what truth is but only what it is not; and once the truth is well grasped and the Holy Scriptures understood, most controversies can easily be settled. In this area the most useful book will be John Hoornbeek's work called the Summa Controversiarum. Among the ancients, the Catalogues of Heresies of Augustine and Epiphanius, and likewise the anonymous catalogue published by Sirmond, which deserves praise in many respects but also criticism in many; especially that deed of Sirmond himself, who in it invented a predestinarian heresy, never known elsewhere, as Aurach, a Sorbonne doctor, testifies.

units.la: XVII. Controversias & res Judaicas pertractarunt, Hoornbeekius de conversione Judæorum. Hulsius de Messia. Coccejus in responsionibus ad quæstiones Judaicas. Buxtorfius in Synagoga Judaica. Episcopius in Institutionibus Theologicis, aliique supra nominati.
units.tr: XVII. Hoornbeek on the conversion of the Jews, Hulsius on the Messiah, Cocceius in his responses to Jewish questions, Buxtorf in the Jewish Synagogue, Episcopius in his Theological Institutes, and others named above have treated controversies and Jewish matters.

units.la: XVIII Papismus non tam ex doctoribus singularibus, quam ex Canonibus Concilii Tridentini, & quæ juxta illius decretum editus est à Pio V. P.P. Catechismo, hauriendes est. Cujus concilii & simul Papismi pismi interiora complexus est Paulus Venetus in historia Concilii Tridentini; vir, praeter vestem ex monachatu nihil habuit. Cui conjungendum Chemnitii examen Concilii Tridentini. De caetero Pontificiis oppositus est Amesii Bellarminus enervatus, Riveti Catholicus Orthodoxus, quamvis hic ex adversariorum scriptis Bailii Catechesin refutet, quod ad hominem argumentari vocant. Lansmanni Itoomfchie afval. Aldegondii, Ɔpchozf. splendida etiam quaedam habet Molinaeus in Clypeo fidei; Anatomia & Missa Novitate Papismi. Omnium instar autem in hac arena est, Chamieri Panstratia Catholica, nisi quod prolixior aliquantum; semper saltem status controversiae accurate definitus inde peti poterit. Quem etiam magna dexteritate & moderatione nuperius examinavit & fixit D. Ludovicus le Blanc, in disputationibus suis. Caeteroquin omnium loco, suffecerint Calvini Institutiones diligenter lectae. Ex adversariis legi possunt Thomas Aquinas & Bellarminus; quorum ille genuinum; hic alteratum & incrustatum Papismum exhibet. Quo in genere defudarunt quoque hisce annis Valerianus Magnus & Walenburgii fratres. Minoris molis est Becani manuale, ejusque compendium.
units.tr: XVIII. Papism should be drawn not so much from particular teachers as from the Canons of the Council of Trent, and from the Catechism published by Pope Pius V in accordance with that council's decree. Paolo Sarpi (Paulus Venetus), in his History of the Council of Trent, embraced the inner workings of both that council and Papism at the same time; he had nothing of a monk about him apart from his habit. To be joined with him is Chemnitz's Examination of the Council of Trent. Otherwise, against the Papists have been set Ames's Bellarminus Enervatus, Rivet's Catholicus Orthodoxus, although this last refutes Bailly's Catechism from the writings of the adversaries, which they call arguing ad hominem. Lansmann's Roman Apostasy, and Aldegonde's work (its title garbled in the scan), also have some splendid points, as does Molinaeus in his Shield of Faith, and Anatomy and the Mass of the Novelty of Papism. But the chief of all in this arena is Chamier's Panstratia Catholica, except that it is rather lengthy; at any rate, an accurately defined statement of the question of the controversy can always be drawn from it. The same was examined and settled recently with great skill and moderation by Dr. Louis le Blanc, in his disputations. Otherwise, in place of all others, Calvin's Institutes read carefully will suffice. From the adversaries one may read Thomas Aquinas and Bellarmine; the former presents genuine Papism, the latter Papism altered and encrusted. In this kind of work the brothers Valerianus Magnus and the Walenburgh brothers also toiled in recent years. Becanus's Manual and its summary are of smaller bulk.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Socinianis strenuo obviam eunt, Junius contra Praelectiones Socini: idem contra Socinum adversus Wieckum. Cloppenburgius in Compendiolo Socinianismi refutati; idem contra Smalcium de divinitate Christi & contra Bidellum de Deitate Sp. Sancti. Bisfeldius de Deo, contra Crellium. Cl. Viri, Hoornbeekius in Socinianismo refutato, & Ejsenius in triumpho crucis. Matth. Wren in confutatione Catechismi Racoviani; aliique.
units.tr: They vigorously oppose the Socinians: Junius against the Praelectiones of Socinus; the same author against Socinus, against Wiecke. Cloppenburgius in his Compendiolum Socinianismi refutati; the same author against Smalcius on the divinity of Christ and against Bidellus on the Deity of the Holy Spirit. Bisfeldius, On God, against Crellius. Among the distinguished men: Hoornbeek in Socinianismus refutatus, and Eisenius in Triumphus crucis. Matthaeus Wren in his refutation of the Racovian Catechism; and others.

units.la: XX. Anabaptistarum argutiis opponenda est Cloppenburgii Gangrena Anabaptistica. Item vernacule Bontemps & Austro Sylvius contra Anabaptistas; ut & liber accuratus Marci Boerhaven, subtitulo, Doodige Ortrueerunge des menfchen.
units.tr: XX. Against the subtleties of the Anabaptists should be set Cloppenburgius, Gangrena Anabaptistica. Likewise in the vernacular, Bontemps and Austro Sylvius against the Anabaptists; and also the careful book of Marcus Boerhaven, with the subtitle Doodige Ortrueerunge des menfchen.

units.la: XXI. Remonstrantium controversiae hoc ordine hauriri possunt, ut primo legatur Collatio Hagiensis, cum Coronide Amesii; tum utriusque partis scripta Synodalia; cum ejusdem Amesii animadversionibus; denique Catechesis Remonstrantium; cum examine venerandi Soceri, Heidani; Episcopii responso, & quam huic reposuit Heidanus, Causa Dei. Quibus superaddere licebit Twissii Vindicias, aliaque ejus scripta; & si ulterius ire lubet, Bradwardinum de Causa Dei. Historia horum errorum peti poterit ex luculenta praefatione ante Synodum Dordracenam. Veterum Pelagianorum sententias explicatas & detectas dederunt Vossius & Latius in historia Pelagiana. na; & Jansenius in praeclaro opere, Augustino.
units.tr: XXI. The controversies with the Remonstrants may be drawn from the sources in this order: first read the Conference at The Hague, with Amesius's Coronis; then the synodal writings of each side, with Amesius's own animadversions; finally the Catechism of the Remonstrants, with the examination of my revered father-in-law, Heidanus; Episcopius's reply, and the rejoinder Heidanus made to it, Causa Dei. To these it will be permissible to add Twisse's Vindiciae and his other writings; and if one wishes to go further, Bradwardine, De causa Dei. The history of these errors may be sought in the excellent preface before the Synod of Dort. Vossius and Latius, in their Pelagian history, set out and expose the opinions of the ancient Pelagians; and Jansenius in his excellent work, the Augustinus.

units.la: XXII. Contra Lutherahos adhiberi potest, Admonitio Neoftadiana. Attingii exegesis Confessionis Augustanae. Wendelini loci Communes, & Exercitationes, in quibus haec controversiae potissimum tractantur. Conducit etiam adjungere scripta irenica de tolerantia inter nos & Lutheranos, Hottonis, Marefii, Hoornbeekii, Durai. Ex Lutheranorum scriptis in hanc rem legi potest, Ekhardi fasciculus controversiarum.
units.tr: XXII. Against the Lutherans may be used the Admonitio Neostadiana, Attingius's exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Wendelin's Loci communes and Exercitationes, in which these controversies are chiefly treated. It is also useful to add the irenic writings on toleration between us and the Lutherans, by Hotton, Marefius, Hoornbeek and Durie. From the writings of the Lutherans on this matter, Ekhard's Fasciculus controversiarum may be read.

units.la: XXIII. Ad reliquas controversias, quae nobis cum infidelibus etiam intercedunt, cognoscendas legere expedit Mornaum & Grotium de veritate religionis Christianae; & ea quae inter nostros Abrah. Rogerius de Braminum & nuperius Phil. Baldaeus de Indorum religione vernacule scripserunt; Alstedii Thelogiam Polemicam, ex aliis quidem consarcinatam, sed non contemnendam. Inter veteres Lactantium & Minutii Felicis Octavium evolvisse operae pretium erit.
units.tr: XXIII. For the remaining controversies which we also have with unbelievers, it is advisable to read Mornay and Grotius on the truth of the Christian religion; and what our countrymen Abraham Roger on the religion of the Brahmins, and more recently Philip Baldaeus on the religion of the Indians, have written in the vernacular; Alsted's Theologia polemica, patched together from other sources, but not to be despised. Among the ancients, it will be worth the labour to go through Lactantius and Minucius Felix's Octavius.

units.la: XXIV. Observari hic debet, studium illud controversiarum divellendum non esse a studio & cognitione veritatis; ut separatim tradantur, vel discantur: quo pacto caeteroquin aeternae forent lites, & vix unquam quicquam tam firmum & solidum diceretur, quod non argumento, aut saltem sophismate aliquo elidi aut eludi posset. Conjungendum igitur semper mendacium est veritati, ut transluceat ex utriusque contentione; atque ita ex fundamento percipientur controversiae; atque veritate probe cognita, adversariorum omnium errores & sophismata dissilari ultro & dilui poterunt. Petendae insuper sunt controversiae non ex alienis citationibus, sed ex ipsis fontibus, scriptisque adversariorum authenticis, & quantum fieri potest, publicis. Attendendum est in iis ad causae arcem & πρῶτον ψεῦδος, ut loquuntur, ex quo totum erroris pondus illiusque consecutiones pendent. Videndum etiam quousque utriusque partis argumenta producta sint, & quousque ulterius produci possent: qua ratione sperare liceret, finem aliquando controversiae, quam tractamus, imponi eamque terminari, posse. Non inutile etiam in hisce est exercitium disputationum Academicarum publicarum; quarum sobrius & modicus usus παῤῥησίαν conciliat, firmat memoriam, excitat studium & curiositatem, solidat judicium, & adversariorum denique congressibus nos parat. Quo in excercitio a respondente specimen eruditionis suae, sicut ab opponente ingenii & dexteritatis exhibetur.
units.tr: XXIV. It must be observed here that the study of controversies must not be separated from the study and knowledge of the truth, so that they are taught or learned apart from each other. Otherwise quarrels would be endless, and scarcely anything so firm and solid could be stated that it could not be overturned or evaded by some argument, or at least some sophism. Therefore falsehood must always be joined to truth, so that the one shines through the contention of the other; and in this way controversies will be understood from their foundation, and once the truth is well known, the errors and sophisms of all opponents can readily be dissolved and refuted. Moreover, controversies are to be sought not from other men's citations but from the sources themselves, from the authentic writings of the opponents, and, as far as possible, from public ones. In these one must attend to the citadel of the cause and to the first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος], as they say, on which the whole weight of the error and its consequences depends. One must also see how far the arguments of each side have been pressed, and how far they could be pressed further; by this method one might hope that an end could at some time be put to the controversy we are treating and that it could be brought to a close. The exercise of public academic disputations is also not without use in these matters; a sober and moderate use of them wins boldness of speech [παῤῥησίαν], strengthens the memory, arouses study and curiosity, firms up judgement, and finally prepares us for encounters with opponents. In this exercise the respondent displays a sample of his learning, as the opponent does of his cleverness and skill.

units.la: XXV. Studium casuum conscientiæ quod attinet, idem etiam quod de controversiis observavimus, de eo tenerí debet, nimirum, ab ipsa Theologia positiva, locisque communibus non averruncandum esse; quin imo periculosum est, casus ullos, uti vocant, determinare, citra non solum, sed & seorsim à positivis veritatibus Theologicis, ex quibus fluunt; unde infelix divortium natum est Theologiæ theoreticæ & practicæ: minime omnium ferendum in popularibus concionibus, ut de suggestu, praxis separatim à Theologia positiva tractetur; unde tum oritur neglectus veritatis, veraeque ejus intelligentiæ, animique hominum infinitis casibus & scrupulis inquietantur; omnisque pietatis prora & puppis in exercitiis & monumentis externis, casibusque non necessariis, iisque saepe non bene decisis, aut vix unquam bene decidendis, collocatur. Praestaret sane infirmorum conscientiam non adeo operosis, sed paucis simplicibusque regulis, ad exemplum Pauli Apostoli, dirigi & expediri. Ex nostris hic potissimum adhiberi solet Amesius; ex Lutheranis Balduinus; quorum ope adhibita, praecipue prudentia ex monitis sapientum & usu rerum acquisita, & judicio animi recte firmato, ex sana veritatis cognitione solida ab inanibus discerni possunt & perplexa omnia resolvi.
units.tr: XXV. As regards the study of cases of conscience, the same must be observed as we have said about controversies: namely, that it must not be warded off from positive theology and the common topics. Indeed, it is dangerous to determine any cases, as they are called, without, and moreover apart from, the positive theological truths from which they flow. From this arose the unhappy divorce between theoretical and practical theology. It is least of all to be tolerated in popular sermons that practice should be treated from the pulpit separately from positive theology; from this follows a neglect of the truth and of its true understanding, and men's souls are troubled by endless cases and scruples, and the whole prow and stern of piety is placed in outward exercises and external observances, in unnecessary cases, which are often badly decided or scarcely ever capable of being well decided. It would certainly be better to guide and resolve the consciences of the weak not by very laborious rules, but by a few simple ones, after the example of the Apostle Paul. Among our own writers Amesius is usually employed here; among the Lutherans Baldwin. With their help, and above all with prudence gained from the counsels of the wise and from experience of affairs, and with a judgement of mind rightly strengthened, the empty can be distinguished from the solid from a sound knowledge of the truth, and all perplexities resolved.

units.la: XXVI. Scholastica Theologia non nimium inhaerendum est, nec illa animo haurienda, nisi singulari cum judicio cassa omnia & inutilia, qualia plurima sunt, secernantur, delectis iis, quæ usui esse possunt. Cui rei abunde sufficiet Magister Sententiarum, Thomae Summa, idemque contra gentes; & ex commentatoribus Cajetanus, Estius & Bannez; nisi quis in alios etiam se diffundere gestiat. Ex nostris adeundus, qui bene de hac Theologia meritus est, P. Ferrius.
units.tr: XXVI. One should not cling too closely to scholastic theology, nor take it into the mind, unless, with particular judgement, everything empty and useless, of which there is a great deal, is sifted out, and only those things that can be of use are selected. For this purpose the Master of the Sentences, Thomas's Summa, and his Summa against the Gentiles will be quite sufficient; and among the commentators Cajetan, Estius and Bañez, unless someone is eager to spread himself among others also. Among our own, the one to consult, who has deserved well of this theology, is P. Ferrius.

units.la: XXVII. Patrum etiam gustus aliquis in Academia hauriendus est; in quo nihil utilius praestari potest, quam si legatur, Aureolus Augustini libellus de doctrina Christiana, separatim excusus; ut & ejus Enchiridion ad Laurentium & Confessiones; nec non libri ejus auro contra cari de Civitate Dei; in quibus universæ civitatis Dei seu Ecclesiæ, exortum, excursum & debitos fines cernere licet. Augustinum ipsum, ejusque sententias felicissime expressit Jansenius in Augustino suo. Solus autem hic vir, omnibus simul Scholasticis subtilior & praestantior est, qui etiam vitula ipsius arant, & quaecunque frugis bonae habent, ex illo ferme omnia transcripserunt; utpote cujus stupendum ingenium nihil unquam inepte molitur: vir inimitabilis, cujusque pene solius patrocinio, causa Dei adversus Pelagianos invicta stetit, & in ipsis Papismi tenebris per tot secula servata est. Hic quidem in controversiis, & Chrysostomus in exegeticis Patrum praecipui sunt; quos etiam duos Calvinus omnium maxime sectatus est, ex iisque tantus vir evasit. Adjungi potest propter multivariam eruditionem Clemens Alexandrinus; & propter stylum Hieronymus in Epistolis; & Latinorum doctissimus ac disertissimus, Tertullianus ex editione & cum notis Rigaltii. Si quis insuper decantatas Origenis opiniones delibare delectetur, habet ille quo sitim restinguat in doctissimo & luculentissimo opere Huetii, quod Origenem & Origeniana complectitur. Reliquos Patres recensere nihil attinet, cum studium illud maturioribus duntaxat annis plenius tractari soleat. Utilissima caeteroquin Photii Bibliotheca, in qua plurimarum antiquarum rerum penus quaedam est. Ex recentioribus viam huc sternunt Rivetus in Critica sacra; Polani Symphonia; Dallaeus de usu Patrum; idemque de Dionysii Areopagitae & Ignatii Antiocheni scriptis spuriis. Lectu dignissimus etiam est Vincentii Lirinensis de Praescriptione libellus, cum doctissima praesatione G. Calixti. Adde his Gronovii observata in Scriptores Ecclesiasticos.
units.tr: XXVII. Some taste of the Fathers too should be drawn in the academy; in this nothing more useful can be provided than reading Augustine's little golden book On Christian Doctrine, printed separately; likewise his Enchiridion to Laurentius and his Confessions; and also his book, dearer than gold, On the City of God; in these one may discern the rise, course and due ends of the City of God, that is, of the Church. Augustine himself, and his opinions, Jansenius expressed most happily in his Augustinus. This man alone, more subtle and more excellent than all the Schoolmen together, is the one whose heifer they all plough with, and almost all of them have copied from him whatever good grain they have; for his stupendous genius never undertakes anything foolishly. He is an inimitable man, by whose patronage almost alone the cause of God stood unconquered against the Pelagians, and it has been preserved through so many centuries even in the very darkness of Popery. Among the Fathers, he and Chrysostom in exegesis are the chief ones in controversies; and these two above all Calvin followed, and from them that great man became what he was. Clement of Alexandria may be added on account of his many-sided learning; and Jerome in his Epistles for his style; and the most learned and eloquent of the Latins, Tertullian, in the edition with the notes of Rigaltius. If anyone further enjoys tasting the much-discussed opinions of Origen, he has something to quench his thirst in the most learned and most splendid work of Huet, which embraces Origen and the Origenian matters. There is no point in reviewing the remaining Fathers, since that study is usually pursued more fully only in riper years. Otherwise Photius's Bibliotheca is most useful, being a kind of storehouse of very many ancient things. Among more recent works, the following pave the way: Rivet, Critica sacra; Polanus's Symphonia; Daillé, On the use of the Fathers; and the same author on the spurious writings of Dionysius the Areopagite and Ignatius of Antioch. The little book of Vincent of Lérins, On Prescription, with the most learned preface of G. Calixtus, is also most worthy of being read. Add to these Gronovius's Observata on the Ecclesiastical Writers.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De studii Theologici usu & exercitio.
units.tr: On the use and practice of theological study.

units.la: I. Equitur nunc studii Theologici praxis & exercitium; tum in Oratoria sacra; tum in reliquo ministerio sacro. Proximus quidem studii hujus usus est in Oratoria sacra, seu concionibus. Quo in negotio primā cura versatur circa methodum concionandi: altera circa auctores hic adhibendos.
units.tr: I. Now follows the practice and exercise of theological study: first in sacred oratory, then in the rest of the sacred ministry. The closest use of this study is in sacred oratory, that is, in sermons. In this business, the first concern is with the method of preaching; the second is with the authors to be consulted here.

units.la: II. Ad conciones privatim, multo minus publice habendas accedendum non est, nisi Bibliis sacris serio & diligenter lectis, & locis communibus seu universa potius Theologia, quantum licet, accurate cognitis. Ut autem judicium hic ante informetur, non levis opera danda est Rhetoricae, speciatim Ecclesiasticae. Quo conducit inter veteres Quintilianus, qui praecepta tradit; praeclarus etiam est Cicero in iis quae de Oratoria scripsit. Praestantissimus etiam inter veteres Graecos dicendi magister est Demosthenes. Inter recentiores hic insignis Talaei Rhetorica, & Rami Logica quae maxime tractat & docet loca inventionis, quorum frequentissimus usus in tractandis thematibus simplicibus; quae loca quamvis à plerisque in Rhetoricis ad. tractentur, ad Logicam tamen spectant, uti Ramus observavit. Eximia etiam est Aristotelis Rhetorica, in qua de affectibus agit movendis, doctrina Oratori in primis pernoscenda; & in qua artifex singularis fuit Cicero. Utilissimus & hic est Erasmi Ecclesiastes, sive de modo concionandi, proficuus itemque libellus Hyperii de formandis concionibus; necnon Rhetorica Ecclesiastica Keckermanni. Recentiorum Theologorum regulas de arte concionandi, tum generales, tum speciales collegit Petrus Magerus. Elegantissimum quoque libellum de ratione concionandi edidit Cl. Stephanus Gaussenus. Singulari etiam artificio & judicio Oratoriam sacram tractavit Cl. Wolzogen; ut unus omnium aliorum instar esse possit.
units.tr: II. One should not approach preparing sermons privately, and much less delivering them publicly, unless the sacred Scriptures have been read seriously and diligently, and the common places, or rather the whole of theology, have been accurately known as far as possible. So that judgment may first be formed in this matter, no slight effort should be given to rhetoric, especially ecclesiastical rhetoric. Among the ancients, Quintilian is helpful, since he delivers the precepts; Cicero is also outstanding in those works he wrote on oratory. Demosthenes is also the most excellent teacher of speaking among the ancient Greeks. Among the more recent writers, Talaeus's Rhetoric is notable here, and Ramus's Logic, which especially treats and teaches the topics of invention; their most frequent use lies in handling simple themes. Although most writers treat these topics in their rhetorics, they nevertheless belong to logic, as Ramus observed. Aristotle's Rhetoric is also excellent, in which he deals with arousing the emotions, a doctrine the orator must above all know thoroughly; and in which Cicero was a singular craftsman. Erasmus's Ecclesiastes, or on the manner of preaching, is also most useful, likewise the helpful little book of Hyperius on forming sermons, and Keckermann's Ecclesiastical Rhetoric. Petrus Magerus gathered the rules of preaching from recent theologians, both general and special. The distinguished Stephanus Gaussen also published a most elegant little book on the method of preaching. The distinguished Wolzogen also treated sacred oratory with singular skill and judgment, so that he alone can stand in place of all the others.

units.la: III. Non aliis autem regulis hic opus est, quam Rhetorices, & iis prudenter usurpatis: omnis enim artis mater est prudentia. Quamvis enim exacte quis calleat omnia praecepta Logica, Medica, Juridica, uti iis non poterit, nisi adsit prudentia; quae rebus omnibus, ut magistra, praedominatur. Speciatim vero maximus methodi praeceptor est Divus Paulus, ex cujus scriptis vera & justa rerum tractatio abunde peti potest; & utinam illa multis in exemplum essent, missa tot anxiarum regularum operosa supellectile; cum unica & vera methodus ea sit, quae simplicissima est; ut a cognito ad ignotum pergatur, & ordine formentur promoveanturque cogitationes (praecipue ubi argumentum propositum deductione aliqua eget) prout natura docet res se invicem consequi, & ut nihil dicatur & proponatur credendum vel faciendum, nisi quod clare ex Scriptura aut ratione fuerit demonstratum. Hoc ipsum quoque plurimum conferet ad memoriam, non puerilem, sed cum intelligentia conjunctam. Hinc etiam multis enumerationibus & subdivisionibus non est opus, sed rem dividere sufficit, qua parte se ipsam secat. Sicut arbor dividi debet, eo modo quo ex stirpe in ramos se diffundit, & sponte se partitur. Praestat ergo magis per demonstrationes, quam similitudines incedere. Humana sapientia sponte intervenire poterit, non vero ostentanda est, ne studio propriae gloriae, quod Oratori sacro maxime obest, ideoque maxime illi fugiendum est, duci videatur. Virtutis quo jue est, nec nimis esse methodicum, nec minus; sed uti in omnibus ita & hic mediocritas servanda: cum & artis saepe sit, in loco artem negligere. Nec concionamur nos, quod Partibus saepe in more erat mere Oratorie, & sine speciali textu sacro; verum textibus nos alligamus, qui ideo sequendi sunt; ita tamen, ut aliquo modo conjungantur cum tractione textus, loci communes, & quaedam fiat mixtura oratoriæ & textualis tractationis. Quare nec in locum communem totus transire debet concionator; nec, more Albutii Rhetoris, omnia quæ dici possunt, in explicatione sacræ <bl>θεολογίας</bl>, seu, ut vulgo loquuntur, textus, dicere; sed quæ dicenda necessario sunt. In omni igitur concione præ oculis habendus est scopus textus, & ad illum assequendum, auditorique inculcandum, omnia, quæ pro concione tractantur, referenda sunt. Investigandus autem ille est fida & accurata analysis; quæ tamen domi potius privata meditatione conficienda est, quam pro concione publice ostentanda. Quibus observatis methodo jam dicta progrediendum est.
units.tr: III. Here, however, no rules other than those of rhetoric are needed, and these used with prudence; for prudence is the mother of every art. For although someone may know all the precepts of logic, medicine, or law exactly, he will not be able to use them unless prudence is present, which, as mistress, governs all things. In particular, the greatest teacher of method is the divine Paul, from whose writings a true and sound handling of matters may be drawn in abundance. Would that many took him as their example, setting aside the laborious clutter of so many anxious rules; for the only true method is the simplest one: to proceed from the known to the unknown, and to form and advance thoughts in order (especially where the proposed subject needs some deduction), as nature teaches that things follow one another, and that nothing be said or proposed as to be believed or done unless it has been clearly demonstrated from Scripture or reason. This will also contribute greatly to memory, not a childish memory but one joined with understanding. Hence there is no need for many enumerations and subdivisions; it is enough to divide the matter by the part in which it divides itself. Just as a tree ought to be divided in the way it spreads from the trunk into branches and divides itself naturally. It is therefore better to proceed by demonstrations than by similitudes. Human wisdom may come in of its own accord, but it must not be displayed, lest it appear to be led by a desire for one's own glory, which harms the sacred orator most and which he must therefore most of all avoid. It is the virtue of the matter neither to be too methodical nor less so; but, as in all things, so here moderation must be observed, since it is often the art, in a given place, to neglect art. Nor do we preach, as was often the custom of the Papists, purely in the manner of an orator and without a specific sacred text; rather we bind ourselves to texts, which therefore must be followed; yet in such a way that they are somehow joined with the treatment of the text, common places, and a certain mixture of oratorical and textual treatment is produced. Therefore the preacher must not pass wholly into a common place, nor, after the manner of the rhetorician Albutius, say everything that can be said in the explanation of the sacred theology, or, as people commonly put it, of the text; but only what must necessarily be said. In every sermon, then, the aim of the text must be kept before the eyes, and everything that is handled for the sermon must be referred to attaining it and impressing it on the hearer. That faithful and accurate analysis must indeed be investigated, though it is to be completed at home by private meditation rather than displayed publicly before the congregation. With these points observed, one must proceed by the method already described.

units.la: IV. Exordium quod attinet, commodius illud invenitur concione jam absoluta, ubi major cogitationum suppetit copia, ex quibus facili opera exordium paretur; cæteroquin enim si tanta cura comptum prodeat exordium, plerunque tantæ accurationi & ornatui finis non respondet; quare ferme fieri solet, ut qui tanta cum pompa se proferant primo, & uno quasi ictu tela sua emittant; postea imbelles sint, & orationem vix ægre trahant. Auditoris animum excitare eumque ad textum ducere debet exordium, nec tamen ei nimis affine esse, aut nimis ab eo remotum. Paucis etiam constet oportet periodis, & quoad ejus fieri potest, petendum est ex natura rei; ut per illud quasi a priori ad rem præsentem auditor deducatur.
units.tr: IV. As for the exordium, it is more conveniently devised once the sermon is finished, when there is a greater supply of thoughts from which an exordium can be readily prepared. Otherwise, if an exordium comes forth adorned with such great care, it usually does not match the end of such great precision and ornament; so it generally happens that those who present themselves with such pomp at first, and as if with one blow launch their weapons, afterwards become feeble and can scarcely drag on their speech. The exordium ought to arouse the hearer's mind and lead him to the text, yet it should be neither too closely related to it nor too far removed from it. It should also consist of only a few periods, and, as far as possible, be sought from the nature of the matter, so that through it the hearer is led, as it were a priori, to the present subject.

units.la: V. Divisio textus similiter petenda est ex natura rei, ut non violenta manu in textum inseratur, sed ex illo sponte profluere videatur. Nec putandum est semper divisione opus esse, cum interdum occurrant textus, qui instar atomorum, partes non habeant quas dispertiri queas: nisi rerum ipsarum, quas occasione istiusmodi textuum tractare decrevisti, summa capita proponas. Aliæ enim rerum, aliæ verborum divisiones sunt.
units.tr: V. The division of the text likewise should be taken from the nature of the matter, so that it is not forced into the text by a violent hand, but seems to flow from it of its own accord. Nor should one think that division is always needed, since sometimes there occur texts which, like atoms, have no parts that you could separate; unless you set forth the main heads of the things which you have decided to treat on the occasion of such texts. For there are divisions of things and others of words.

units.la: VI. Quantum vero ad rem ipsam spectat, in tractatione textus, non satis est grammaticam verborum explicationem dare, sed ipsius rei natura & historia est exhibenda, eaque eo ordine deducenda, quo facillime & distinctissime proponi possit; quod quomodo in specie faciendum sit, mox videbimus.
units.tr: VI. As far as the matter itself is concerned, in the treatment of the text it is not enough to give a grammatical explanation of the words; rather the nature and history of the thing itself must be set out, and this must be developed in the order by which it can most easily and most distinctly be presented. How this is to be done in particular we shall see shortly.

units.la: VII. Enarrata hoc modo rei natura & confirmata textus veritate, <bl>πορίσματα</bl> inde deduci possunt, quorum ea præstantissima sunt, quæ proxime ex textu fluunt, & primæ, quasi sunt emanationes: eodem modo ac vinum illud suavissimum est, quod levi pressione ex uvis exprimitur, id vero quod torcular redolet, acinos etiam sapit.
units.tr: VII. Once the nature of the thing has been thus narrated and the truth of the text confirmed, <bl>πορίσματα</bl> [corollaries] can be drawn from it, of which those are the most excellent which flow most directly from the text and are, as it were, its first emanations: just as that wine is the sweetest which is pressed out of the grapes by light pressure, while that which smells of the winepress also tastes of the skins.

units.la: VIII. Exinde subjungenda est textus applicatio, qua auditoribus sinsingulatim accommodatur, & ad usum convertitur; tum adhortationis ad virtutem; tum correptionis & increpationis in vitia invehendo; tum consolationis, & cujuscunque tandem modi, qui pro Oratoris prudentia eliciendus est. In hac applicatione, quia plerunque παθος seu affectus aliquis ibi movendus est, laudanda est θερμότης aliqua; & insignem quoque usum ibi habent argumenta, quae ab honesto, utili, jucundo &c. desumuntur, eaque pro natura rei delectas ut non omnia ubique adhibeantur; verum ubi, verbi gratia, longius a jucundo petitur argumentum, ab honesto petatur oportet. Nec tamen opus quovis loco omnes istos usus, quos Paulus 2 Tim. 3: 16. commendat, urgere; sufficit uni vel alteri primario, qui sponte se offerunt & ad scopum Sp. S. maxime faciunt, insistere. Multo minus necessum est expressis verbis auditorem in concione semper monere, hanc doctrinam, hunc usum esse: more illorum pictorum qui bovem vel equum idonee pingere nequeunt, nisi illum bovem vel equum esse appingant. Rite modo doceatur, moneatur, corripiatur, & ultro satis patebit doctrinam & usum esse.
units.tr: VIII. Next must be added the application of the text, by which it is fitted to the hearers individually and turned to use: whether by exhortation to virtue, or by rebuke and reproof in attacking vices, or by consolation, or in whatever manner finally is to be drawn out according to the prudence of the orator. In this application, since usually some emotion πάθος must be stirred there, a certain warmth θερμότης is to be commended; and arguments drawn from the honourable, the useful, the pleasant, and so on, have a remarkable use there, and they are to be chosen according to the nature of the matter, so that not all are used everywhere; but where, for example, an argument is drawn rather far from what is pleasant, it ought to be drawn from what is honourable. Nor is it necessary to press at every place all those uses which Paul commends in 2 Tim. 3:16; it is enough to insist on one or another primary use, which present themselves of their own accord and most serve the purpose of the Holy Spirit. Much less is it necessary to tell the hearer in the sermon in express words at every point that this is the doctrine and this the use: like those painters who cannot paint an ox or a horse suitably unless they write beneath it that it is an ox or a horse. If the matter is properly taught, urged, and rebuked, the doctrine and the use will of themselves be quite plain.

units.la: IX. Refutationem quod spectat, per illam si intelligatur liberatio textus a cavillis & sophismatibus adversariorum, non ad applicationem, sed ad explicationem potius referenda est, cum sit confirmatio ab opposito, uti dicitur; si vero tantundem sit ac doctrina ex textu elicita, aut argumentum quod adhiberi potest ad refutandum aliquem adversariorum errorem; sic ad ἀπὸ textu deducta pertinebit; & ad usus Scripturae sacrae, quibus utilis est ad elenchum; adeoque omnium commodissime ante doctrinam & usus practicos tractari poterit.
units.tr: IX. As for the refutation, if by that is meant freeing the text from the quibbles and sophisms of opponents, it belongs less to application than to explanation, since it is confirmation from the opposite, as the saying goes. But if it amounts to the doctrine drawn out of the text, or to an argument that can be used to refute one of the opponents' errors, then it will belong to the things deduced from the text [ἀπὸ], and to the uses of Holy Scripture by which it serves for refutation. For that reason it can most conveniently be treated before the doctrine and the practical uses.

units.la: X. Textuum vero diversitatem quod attinet, thema simplex ita tractandum est, ut circa illud consulantur affectiones Logicae, seu loci inventionis, ut vulgo appellantur, non aperte monendo auditorem, hanc esse causam, illud effectum; sed decore & venuste quodam cum artificio loca connectendo & ex se invicem deducendo; siut ea, quae opportuna sunt maxime, seligantur; quod prudentiae esse jam diximus. Hac ratione ergo tractaturus thema simplex, ex. gr. fidem, percurrantur loca inventionis, scilicet, de fidei partibus, causis, effectis, subjecto, adjunctis, consentaneis, dissentaneis, oppositis &c. quod magnam cogitationum suppeditat copiam, & pulcherrimum format concionis corpus: quomodo omnia themata simplicia, sive dogmata, tum catechetica, tum moralia & practica, ut statim dicetur, enarrari possunt.
units.tr: X. As for the variety of texts, a simple theme is to be handled by consulting the logical affections, or what are commonly called the places of invention, without openly warning the hearer that this is the cause and that the effect. Rather, the places should be connected and derived from one another with a certain graceful artistry, so that the most suitable are chosen, which, as we have already said, belongs to prudence. So, if one is to treat a simple theme such as faith in this way, one runs through the places of invention: the parts of faith, its causes, effects, subject, accompaniments, consequences, contraries, opposites, and so on. This supplies a great abundance of thoughts and forms a beautiful body of sermon. In this way all simple themes, whether doctrines, whether catechetical, moral or practical, can be expounded, as will be said shortly.

units.la: XI. Thema
units.tr: XI. Compound Theme

units.la: XI. Thema complexum ita tractandum est: ut 1. Subjectum illius.
units.tr: XI. A compound theme is to be handled thus: (1) its subject is to be shown and explained;

units.la: 2. Prædicatum, ostendatur & explicetur; tum autem ante omnia complexio seu connexio utriusque demonstretur; & in id opera præcipua intendatur, ut argumenta quæ ad veritatem connexionis probandam comportantur, a prædicato maximam partem petantur.
units.tr: (2) its predicate is to be shown and explained; then, above all, the complex or connection of the two is to be demonstrated. Special effort should be directed to making most of the arguments gathered to prove the truth of the connection come from the predicate.

units.la: XII. Utriusque quasi thematis tractatio concurrit in themate doctrinali, seu dogmatico: ipsum enim fidei caput & dogma quod tradendum est, ad instar thematis simplicis: illius vero confirmatio per argumenta ad modum complexi instituenda est. Utrumque vero ita tractandum, ut quafieri possit, brevitate & perspicuitate ipsum dogma ex fundamento repetatur, & ea dicantur, quæ ad textum præsentem illiusque scopum maxime faciunt. Nec plane in locum commune excurratur, sed tantum medulla exhibeatur istius dogmatis seu controversiæ, cum refutatione falsitatis; præcipue si dogma controversum sit, uti omnia ferme talia. Maxime tamen insistendum argumentis quæ faciunt ad veritatem probandam, licet non semper mentio fiat oppositi erroris.
units.tr: XII. The treatment of both, as it were, of the theme, comes together in a doctrinal or dogmatic theme. For the article of faith itself and the doctrine to be taught is like a simple theme, while its confirmation by arguments is to be carried out in the manner of a compound theme. Each is to be handled so that, as far as possible, with brevity and clarity, the doctrine itself is traced back to its foundation, and those things are said which bear most upon the present text and its purpose. Nor should one wander into a common place at all, but only the marrow of that doctrine or controversy be set forth, together with a refutation of the falsehood, especially if the doctrine is disputed, as nearly all such are. Yet the greatest stress should be laid on the arguments that serve to prove the truth, although mention of the opposing error is not always made.

units.la: XIII. In thematibus moralibus ita versandum est, ut si agant de virtutibus & vitiis, vivo colore exhibendi & delineandi sint eorum characteres; præterquam quod in aliis quoque argumentis plurimum juvent auditorum intelligentiam & memoriam ὑποτυπώσεις seu delineationes ad vivum, quando ita res cum præcipuis suis circumstantiis exhibetur, ut quasi coram oculis depicta cernatur. Tum addenda, quæ ad naturam virtutum aut vitiorum eorum cognoscendum pertinent, & quæ mediorum aut remediorum vices præstare poterunt: qua in re præferenda sunt ea argumenta, quæ ab honesto, utili & jucundo petuntur; eaque exaggeranda; qui modus agendi singulare aliquod πάθημα in auditore excitat; ideoque illud semper, præsertim in illis argumentis, faciendum est, ut affectus aliquis moveatur, qui concionis est finis: ea tamen adhibita cautione, ut non crasse argumenta enumerentur, sed industrie & ornate exhibeantur.
units.tr: XIII. In moral themes one should proceed so that, if they deal with virtues and vices, their characters are to be displayed and outlined in a lively colour. Apart from this, in other arguments too, outlines or vivid delineations [ὑποτυπώσεις] greatly aid the hearers' understanding and memory, when a matter is set forth with its principal circumstances in such a way that it is seen as if painted before the eyes. Then there should be added what pertains to knowing the nature of the virtues or vices, and what can take the place of means or remedies. In this matter, arguments drawn from what is honourable, useful and pleasant are to be preferred, and they are to be amplified. A manner of handling that stirs some particular emotion [πάθημα] in the hearer is to be used; therefore it must always be done, especially in such arguments, so that some affection is moved, which is the purpose of the sermon. Yet this must be done with such caution that the arguments are not listed crudely, but are presented skilfully and elegantly.

units.la: XIV. In <bl>historiis</bl> enumerari debent omnia, quæ ad historiæ quam tractamus cognitionem faciunt. Applicatio autem ita debet institui, ut si partes historiæ sint heterogeneæ, & aliquo modo divelli possint; tum explicationi cujusque partis, particularis etiam applicatio, sed brevis, & quasi per diverticulum, subjungatur, per modum porismatis: ubi observandum est, circa finem concionis, sive in applicatione generali, non tantum ultimam historiæ partem applicandam esse, uti multis in more est; verum ex totius textus scopo. Si vero partes hihistoriæ homogeneæ sint, & omnes eodem tendant, tum breviter explicandæ sunt; una autem omnium applicatio in fine concionis facienda est. Ita in historia tentationis Christi, singulæ partes singulatim etiam applicari debent, quia heterogeneæ; turbaret enim & interrumperet concionem, si tot heterogeneæ applicationes simul instituerentur; quare singulæ suis locis faciendæ sunt.
units.tr: XIV. In <bl>histories</bl> all the things that contribute to knowledge of the history we are treating ought to be enumerated. Application, however, ought to be arranged so that if the parts of the history are heterogeneous and can be separated in some way, then, after the explanation of each part, a particular application, though brief and by way of digression as a corollary, is added. Here it should be observed that near the end of the sermon, or in the general application, not only the last part of the history is to be applied, as is customary with many, but the application is to be drawn from the purpose of the whole text. If, however, the parts of the history are homogeneous and all tend to the same end, then they are to be explained briefly, and one application of all of them is to be made at the end of the sermon. Thus in the history of Christ's temptation, the individual parts ought to be applied singly, because they are heterogeneous; for it would disturb and interrupt the sermon if so many heterogeneous applications were made at once. Therefore each is to be made in its own place.

units.la: XV. Historia parabolica seu parabola nunquam sola sive divisim tractanda est, ut à multis fieri solet; verum, in eadem quoque concione, præmissa & explicata παραβολή, etiam adjungi debet ἀπόδοσις, & similitudini applicanda est; cum enim unum aliud explicet & eodem referantur, in eadem quoque concione conjungenda sunt.
units.tr: XV. A parabolic history, or parable, should never be treated alone or separately, as is often done by many. Rather, in the same sermon, after the parable [παραβολή] has been set forth and explained, the application [ἀπόδοσις] must also be added and applied to the likeness. For since the one explains the other and they refer to the same thing, they ought to be joined in the same sermon.

units.la: Attendendum vero semper est ad similitudinis scopum, & quæ eo faciunt, sola adducenda, omissis ἀπροσδιονύσοις. Verbi gratia; ubi regnum cœlorum gemmæ aut semini assimilatur Matth. 13. enarranda tantum venit gemmæ pretiositas & varius seminis succesßus pro ratione terræ: reliqua vero quæ ad sementis naturam spectant, & quæ circa eam ab agricolis fieri solent, ibi operosè enarrare velle, putidum esset; ex quo aliqui singularem gloriam aucupantur; qui non tam rei ipsius, quam similitudinis tractationem suscepisse videntur, & ad eam rem obtorto quasi collo rapere. Ita nec equuleo imponenda est parabola, ut ea, quæ extra scopum ejus sunt, rei significatæ applicentur. Quod de omnibus typis seu allegoriis Veteris Fœd. tenendum est.
units.tr: One must always attend to the purpose of the likeness, and bring forward only those things that serve it, leaving out irrelevant details [ἀπροσδιονύσοις]. For example, where the kingdom of heaven is compared to a pearl or to seed (Matt. 13.), only the preciousness of the pearl and the varied success of the seed according to the nature of the soil are to be expounded. To labour to explain there the other things that pertain to the nature of seed and that farmers customarily do with it would be tasteless. Some men hunt for a singular glory in this, who seem to have undertaken the handling not so much of the thing itself as of the likeness, and to drag it there, as it were, by the neck. Thus a parable must not be put on the rack, so that things that lie outside its purpose are applied to the thing signified. This must be held of all the types or allegories of the Old Testament.

units.la: XVI. Hisce methodi cum generalibus, tum specialibus regulis observatis supervacuum erit rerum pondera in multas frangere particulas, & infinitis divisionibus & subdivisionibus minutatim conscindere, prolixisque enumerationibus auditores fatigare; idque eo modo, ac si non corpus, sed sceleton quoddam orationis exhiberent: qui pædagogicus est concionandi modus, Prophetis, Apostolis, Patribus, primis Reformatoribus, sapientioribus etiam Germanis, Belgis, Galliæ, imo etiam Angliæ concionatoribus incognitus & inusitatus; à D. Perkinsio vero primum in scenam productus, & ex Anglia cum aliis ejusdem indolis rebus in Belgium transmissus; ibique à quibusdam adoptatus, licet non tam vero fructu, qui, ut in contusis nimium aromatibus, hoc modo sæpe intervertitur, quam specie aliqua se commendet; & artificio suo operosisque regulis illustris videatur adinstar vestis multas in partes sectæ, & artificiosè consutæ, quæ magis ad elegantiam facit, quam ad usum aut ca-
units.tr: XVI. With these general and special rules of method observed, it will be superfluous to break the weights of things into many small pieces, to cut them up bit by bit with endless divisions and subdivisions, and to weary the hearers with lengthy enumerations. This is the case even if they present not the body of a speech but a kind of skeleton of discourse. This pedagogical manner of preaching was unknown and unused by the Prophets, the Apostles, the Fathers, the first Reformers, and also by the wiser preachers of Germany, the Netherlands, France, and even England. It was first brought onto the stage by Dr. Perkins, and transmitted from England to the Netherlands along with other things of the same kind. There some adopted it, though not with much true profit, which, as with spices crushed too much, is often lost in this manner. It recommends itself by appearance, and seems illustrious through its artifice and laborious rules, like a garment cut into many pieces and cleverly sewn together, which adds more to elegance than to use or

units.la: Parabola.
units.tr: Parable.

units.la: Culpanda in concione. calorem. Ipsis etiam Oratoribus antiquis displicuit ambagiosa hæc methodus, quæ per tot præcepta, divisiones & regulas procedit. Plebs enim videns tanto cum molimine rem agi, putat insidias sibi strui, & hoc oratorem agere in fraudem & dolo se; ideoque simplicior illis placuit oratio; quæque auditores, rebus clare, distincte atque ordine propositis ultro secum rapiat. Neque etiam ex abrupto aut crasse transeundum est, sed, si fieri possit, res ita deducenda, ut ultro ad partem aliam per connexionem conceptuum oratorem ducere videatur.
units.tr: Faults to be avoided in preaching: warmth. Even the ancient orators disliked this roundabout method, which proceeds through so many precepts, divisions and rules. For the common people, seeing a matter handled with so much effort, think that snares are being laid for them, and that the speaker is acting to deceive and trick them. Therefore a simpler style pleased them better, one that carries the hearers along of its own accord when things are set forth clearly, distinctly and in order. Nor should one pass on abruptly or crudely, but, if possible, the matter should be so developed that, through the connection of ideas, the speaker appears to lead the hearer of his own accord to the other part.

units.la: XVII. Culpanda hic quædam speciatim restant. 1. Quod rei ipsius tractatione & deductione valere jussa, grammatica plerunque tractatio supponatur, & verba magis, quam res ipsa ostendantur; ut primaria rei explicatio, non alia sit, quam Lexicographa aut paraphrastica, magis inanibus verborum repetitionibus, quam rerum deductionibus, constans. 11. Vitium est quod doctrina, quæ post textus explicationem proponitur, ipse textus sit, quin & ipsius sæpe textus verbis proponatur; cum doctrina semper ex textu debeat esse derivata, in modum porisinatis. 111. Nec convenit loco deductioris & plenioris tractationis ipsius veritatis & rei, quæ in textu continetur, ad locos communes & integros tractatus digredi, & ad unam concionem nullo habito delectu convocare omnia, etiam quæ ad rhombum nihil faciunt: cum discursus simplex & nervosus, ex ipsa textus natura petitus, & rebus magis fœcundus quam verbis, longe sit efficacior ad illuminandam mentem & flectendum animum, quam ingens ille apparatus, majori labore quam judicio congestus.
units.tr: XVII. Certain specific faults remain to be noted here. (1) Because the treatment and development of the thing itself is set aside, a grammatical treatment is usually presupposed, and words rather than the thing itself are displayed. So the primary explanation of the matter is nothing but lexical or paraphrastic, consisting more of empty repetitions of words than of derivations of things. (2) It is a fault when the doctrine proposed after the explanation of the text is the text itself, and often even given in the words of the text, since the doctrine should always be derived from the text, by way of corollary. (3) Nor is it fitting, in place of a fuller and more developed treatment of the truth and the matter contained in the text, to wander off into common places and whole treatises, and to gather everything into one sermon without any selection, even things that have nothing to do with the point. A simple and forceful line of reasoning, drawn from the nature of the text itself and richer in things than in words, is far more effective for illuminating the mind and bending the heart than that huge apparatus, heaped together with more labour than judgment.

units.la: XVIII. iv. In vitio item ponendum est, quod ad omne argumenti genus, distincta signa, media & motiva adhiberi soleant; cum illa tunc duntaxat sint tradenda, ubi res id exigit, vel permittit; & tum ex intima ipsius rei natura petenda sunt; non autem continuo ad generalia illa excurrendum est; de verbo Dei; Spiritu Sancto, precibus earumque usu; quorum mediorum omnia fere centies recurrunt, & ad nauseam usque crambe illa recoquitur, & omnibus argumentis obtruditur; quod utile non est, & ingratum nimis, secundum illud tritum: Ridetur chorda, qui semper oberrat eadem. v. Ejusdem etiam genii est; quod ubi ad finem ejusmodi doctrinæ perventum est & delassatus auditor, qui concionis finem & exitum jam opperitur; nova sæpe doctrina ususque eodem modo proponitur, & auditor à meta ad carceres revocatur; quod magis ad fastidium dium, quam excitationem facit. Atque tantum est, quod de hisce monendum breviter duximus: Pergendum nunc est.
units.tr: XVIII. iv. Among the faults, one must also count the habit of using distinct signs, means and motives for every kind of argument. These should be delivered only when the subject requires it or allows it, and then they should be drawn from the inner nature of the matter itself. One should not rush at once to those general topics: the Word of God, the Holy Spirit, prayer and its use. Almost all of these means come back a hundred times, that stale cabbage is reheated until it makes people sick, and it is forced onto every argument. This is neither useful nor very welcome, according to the familiar saying: The lyre is laughed at that always strays on the same string. v. Of the same kind is this fault: when the preacher has reached the end of such a doctrine and the listener is worn out and already waits for the close and exit of the sermon, a new doctrine and use is often proposed in the same way, and the listener is called back from the goal to the starting-gate. This produces more weariness than stirring of the mind. We have thought it enough to give this warning briefly. Now we must go on.

units.la: XIX. Vox flexanima sit oportet. Cum enim triplex sit concionatoris virtus, docendi, delectandi & movendi; summa & praecipua est movendi facultas, quae divini aliquid habet; ad quam plurimum facit, prudens vocis usus & regimen. Si quid alperum habeat; aut ingratum, exercitiis privatis lectionis verbi Dei, & praecipue Prophetarum, corrigenda, & inter legendum rebus ipsis accommodanda est.
units.tr: XIX. The voice ought to be able to move the soul. Since the preacher's skill is threefold, to teach, to delight and to move, the chief and most important is the power to move, which has something of the divine in it. Much contributes to this, a prudent use and management of the voice. If the voice has anything harsh or unpleasant, it must be corrected by private exercises in reading the Word of God, especially the Prophets, and while reading it should be adapted to the subject matter itself.

units.la: XX. Actio oratoria & gestus naturales sint & decori; non autem affectati aut nimii, nec adeo opera danda est, ut externis hisce capiatur populus, quam ut ipsis rebus doceatur & moveatur. In laudandis & allegandis sacrae Scripturae locis, commata & versus designandi non sunt; praeterquam enim quod memoriae illud molestum fit, flumenque orationis interrumpat, inutilis etiam est labor populo, qui ex integra concione vix unius ejusmodi citationis meminisse poterit: praeter inanem igitur memoriae ostentationem nil quicquam praeferet; tum quoque adimit dicenti facultatem, si quis inter dicendum incidat locus, citandi; quia plerunque comma non occurrit; quae tamen subitanea citationes plerunque sunt maxime appositae. Hanc ergo argutam nimis diligentiam negligere praestat, sufficitque capitum citatione uti, neque ea quoque nisi ubi opus est; non vero uti illi agunt, qui vix Scripturae verbo utuntur, vel per modum phraseologiae, quin capita & commata adjiciant, qui tamen inter plurimas citationes, nullas ferme afferunt, secundum emphasin suam & ex scopo Sp. Sancti; saltem vix uni loco integra concione allucent; quod ubi fit, praecipuum concionis ornamentum est. Precum vero consuetis formulis te alliges, an vero de pectore eas concipias, res utrimque est indifferens, & utrimque utilis esse potest: unde consultum non videtur alterutri ita se alligare, ut alterum negligas. Maxime vero conducere videtur, ut preces quae ante concionem recitantur, ex formulis, quas habemus sane selectissimas, dicantur; cum auditor eas cogitatione sua commodissime assequi possit: quod difficilius fit quando nova adhibetur formula. Ordinarias enim precandi liturgias, omni aevo Ecclesiae usitatas, studio omittere velle, quasi per illas staret ne Spiritu monitore oraretur, Enthusiasta sane, quam Ecclesiasta dignius esset.
units.tr: XX. Oratorical delivery and gestures should be natural and becoming, not affected or excessive. Nor should one work so hard to catch the people by these outward things as to teach and move them by the matters themselves. In quoting and citing the places of holy Scripture, one should not mark out clauses and verses. Apart from the fact that this is a burden to the memory and breaks the flow of speech, it is also a useless labour for the people, who can hardly remember one such citation from a whole sermon. So apart from an empty display of memory, it gains nothing. It also takes away the speaker's ability to cite a passage that happens to come up in the course of speaking, because the clause is often not at hand; yet such impromptu citations are usually most fitting. It is better, then, to neglect this overly subtle precision, and it is enough to use citation by chapter, and that not even except where needed. We should not follow those who hardly use the words of Scripture, or only in the manner of a phrase, yet add chapter and clause numbers; these men, though they cite very many passages, bring almost none out according to their emphasis and the purpose of the Holy Spirit, and scarcely let one passage shine through a whole sermon. When that happens, it is the chief ornament of the sermon. As for prayers, whether you bind yourself to the customary forms or conceive them from your own heart is a matter of indifference on either side, and either can be useful. So it does not seem wise to bind yourself so strictly to one that you neglect the other. It seems most advisable that the prayers recited before the sermon be taken from the forms which we have, and which are certainly most carefully chosen, since the hearer can follow them most easily in his thoughts. This is harder when a new form is used. To wish deliberately to drop the ordinary liturgies of prayer, used in the Church in every age, as if the Spirit could not be prayed to without them, is indeed the mark of a fanatic rather than of a churchman.

units.la: XXI. Stylus sit gravis, simplex, purus & tersus, nulla verborum barbarie conspurcatus, ex sacris literis quantum fieri potest desumptus.
units.tr: XXI. The style should be grave, simple, pure and polished, free from any barbarism of words, and taken as far as possible from the holy writings.

units.la: Diligenter igitur se abstineat orator noster à verbis exoticis, aut etiam novis, etiamsi vernaculis, iisque quæ usu nondum frequentata sunt, qualia in scriptoribus quibusdam hodiernis leguntur, nisi additis forte vulgatioribus.
