Multo magis cavendum à trivialibus & in circulis usitatis verbis, putidisque loquendi modis, ut multis in more est, qui verborum exilitate rerum deterunt majestatem, quin & sibi ipsis inde majores videntur, quoties migrant in obscuras humiliésque sermone tabernas. Cæterum loquendum semper est, ut vulgus ædificetur, neque mellitis verborum globulis, sesamo & papavere sparsis, persuadendus est auditor; sed spirituali verbi divini potentia, eaque oratione, quæ demonstrationes habeat pro nectare, quæque non tam ingenium, quam conscientiam compellet. Usu testimoniorum humanorum, historiarum profanarum, atque etiam sententiarum Latinarum, Patrum, aliorumque, nisi singularem habeant emphasin, plane abstinendum est; aut si fieri illud necesse sit, non nisi rarissime usurpentur; aliter, ac quidam, qui flosculos hosce tam inepte depereunt, ut iis non aspergant solum concionem, sed totam pertexant; quod sæpenumero ab iis etiam fieri videas non sine risu, qui farraginem illam alienæ fidei debent, & ipsos auctores legere vel nolint vel nequeant; quos tamen si audias, non Ecclesiasticos de suggestu tractatores, sed umbraticos de cathedra doctores dicas. Utilissimum hic est primis ministerii annis elegantibus vernaculis verbis conciones exarare, quo facunditas vernaculæ assuefiat concionator, donec verborum copia suppetat & levioribus cogitationum notis contentus esse queat. Styli vero elegantiam, ex scriptoribus Belgicis accuratioribus prudentes lectis, præsertim theologis, ut Vener. Socero Heidano de causa Dei similibusque arcessat: quorum scripta idcirco cum cura legenda sunt & imitanda.
units.tr: Our orator, therefore, should carefully abstain from foreign words, or even new ones, though in the vernacular, and those not yet in common use, such as are read in some modern writers, unless perhaps they are rather familiar. Much more must he beware of trivial words and phrases in common use in social circles, and of vulgar modes of speaking, as many are accustomed to do, who by the meagreness of their words lower the dignity of the matter, and who even seem greater to themselves whenever they wander into the obscure and humble taverns of speech. Otherwise, one must always speak so that the common people are built up, and the hearer should not be persuaded by honeyed balls of words, sprinkled with sesame and poppy, but by the spiritual power of the divine Word, and by that kind of discourse which has demonstrations for its nectar, and which moves the conscience more than the wit. The use of human testimonies, of profane histories, and also of Latin sayings of the Fathers and others, should be entirely avoided unless they have some special emphasis. If it is necessary to do so, they should be used only very rarely. It is otherwise with some who so foolishly dote on these little flowers that they not only sprinkle the sermon with them but weave the whole sermon out of them. You may often see this done, not without laughter, by men who owe that hodgepodge to the trust of others and either will not or cannot read the authors themselves. If you listen to them, you would call them not churchmen preaching from the pulpit but shady teachers from the chair. Here it is most useful in the first years of the ministry to draft sermons in elegant vernacular words, so that the preacher becomes accustomed to fluency in his own tongue until he has a supply of words and can be content with lighter notes of thought. As for the elegance of style, let him seek it from the more careful Dutch writers, especially theologians, whom the prudent have read, such as my venerable father-in-law Heidanus in De causa Dei and others like him. Their writings, therefore, must be read with care and imitated.

units.la: XXII. Ipsam oratoris facunditam quod spectat, non sit loquens, sed eloquens; cum enim Episcopum oporteat esse διδακτικόν, idoneus simul etiam debet esse ad docendum res excellentissimas, easque tractandum proprie & potenter: qui enim eloquenter & aliqua cum venustate & gratia loqui non potest, indignus est ut loquatur publice in Ecclesia; sicut ait ille: Ludere qui nescit, campestribus abstinet armis.
units.tr: XXII. As for the preacher's eloquence itself, let him be not merely a speaker but an eloquent one. For since a bishop must be able to teach, he must at the same time be fit to teach the most excellent matters, and to handle them properly and powerfully. Whoever cannot speak eloquently and with some charm and grace is unworthy to speak publicly in the Church. As the saying goes: He who does not know how to play abstains from the weapons of the field.

units.la: Vera autem eloquentia non consistit in tornandis figuris & adscititio verborum ornatu; qui enim istiusmodi modis auditorem movere fatagit, nihil aliud in ipso excitat, nisi flammulam e paleis deductam, quæ ardet, dum sermo auditur; deinceps vero mox evanescit; & fultum stultum est movere affectus, quamdiu non perfusus est luce sufficienti intellectus: illud enim repugnat naturali ordini, quem Deus constituit inter facultates animae, quemque observat Sp. Sanctus in sanctificatione nostra; ut nempe instruatur primo rationibus intellectus, unde tum ex magno lumine in intellectu, magna sequitur in voluntate propensio. Vera ergo eloquentia consistit in inventione & materiarum praestantissimarum selectu, iisque simpliciter, clare, copiose atque ordine profundis: ex simplicitate enim & ordine ultro perspicuitas nascitur; & ita si quis instituat etiam barbara Scytharum lingua eloquenter loquetur; multo magis, si rebus verbisque Spiritui sancto usitatis. Atque haec quidem eloquentia insigne est Sp. Sancti donum, & ipsi omnium maxime usitatum; quam qui culpat, ipsi Spiritui sancto convicium dicit: & plerumque qui hac in parte deficiunt, carpere solent in aliis, quod recte posse praestare optarent ipsi. De caetero naturae obsequatur quisque suae, illamque dicendi & persuadendi ac flectendi viam observet, quam ipsi natura signavit. Irata enim venatur Delia, qui personam suam exuit, nturaeque vim adfert. Qualem ergo in conversatione quemque natura fingit, talem quoque in concione, quae & ipsa ἐμιλία est, quam potest decentissime, se exhibeat. Certus hanc esse optimam concionem, quam perspicue propositam memoriae facillime impresserit auditor: ut non melior orationis sacrae character sit, quam si illa repletus, eam vel, si opus redditurus, auditor domum reversus fuerit.
units.tr: True eloquence, however, does not consist in twisting figures and in borrowed ornament of words. For whoever strives to move the hearer by such means produces in him nothing but a little flame drawn from straw, which burns only while the speech is heard and soon afterwards goes out. Moreover, it is foolish to stir the affections before the understanding has been filled with sufficient light. For this is against the natural order which God has set among the powers of the soul, and which the Holy Spirit observes in our sanctification: namely, that the mind is first instructed by the reasons of the understanding, and that from the great light in the understanding there follows a great inclination in the will. True eloquence therefore consists in the invention and choice of the most excellent matters, and in setting them out simply, clearly, copiously and in a deep order. For clarity arises of its own accord from simplicity and order. So if someone should undertake to speak in the barbarous language of the Scythians, he will speak eloquently; much more so if he uses matters and words familiar to the Holy Spirit. This eloquence indeed is a notable gift of the Holy Spirit, and the most commonly used of all his gifts. Whoever finds fault with it reproaches the Holy Spirit himself. And those who are deficient in this respect are generally in the habit of carping at others for what they themselves would wish to be able to do well. For the rest, let each follow his own nature and observe that way of speaking, persuading and moving which nature has marked out for him. For Delia hunts in anger who strips off her own character and does violence to nature. Therefore, let each present himself in the sermon, which is itself a discourse [ὁμιλία], as becomingly as he can, just as nature shapes him in ordinary conversation. I am convinced that that is the best sermon which the listener grasps clearly, so that he most easily fixes it in his memory, and that there is no better character of sacred discourse than when the listener returns home full of it and able to repeat it, if need be.

units.la: XXIII. His omnibus gravissimum pondus addet, atque efficacissima erit concionatoris eloquentia, si amet ipse, quod aliosdocet, & sibi ipsi prius jam persuaserit, quae persuadere conatur aliis, ut non in labiis verba ipsi nascantur, sed ex intimo cordis affectu ebulliant. Unde & pie in capitulis Patrum dicit senex Simeon, qui Servatorem ulnis excepit: Eruditus sermo non est praecipuum, sed praxis, seu opus. Necessarium hac in re est, veram concionandi methodum ex auditorum genio, moribus, virtutibus & vitiis, infirmitatibus & tentationibus ordinare, eumque in finem familiariter cum illis agere, statum animarum recte observare & in hominum sinus influere. Auditorum quoque instituendus est delectus, & ita temperanda res ut & idiotae, quorum major semper est pars, pascantur, & tamen aspergantur talia, quibus doctiores quoque excitentur.
units.tr: XXIII. All of this will carry great weight, and the preacher's eloquence will be most effective if he loves what he teaches others and has first persuaded himself of what he tries to persuade them of, so that the words do not merely arise on his lips but well up from the inmost feeling of his heart. Hence the old man Simeon, who held the Saviour in his arms, rightly says in the sayings of the Fathers: Learned speech is not the chief thing, but practice, or work. In this matter it is necessary to shape the true method of preaching to suit the disposition, morals, virtues and vices, weaknesses and temptations of the hearers. To that end one must deal familiarly with them, observe the state of their souls carefully, and flow into the bosoms of men. The hearers must also be chosen with care, and the matter so tempered that the untutored, who always make up the greater part, are fed, and yet such things are sprinkled in as also stir up the more learned.

units.la: XXIV. Auctores, ex quibus instruendus est orator noster, nunc tandem etiam designemus. Biblia sacra cum ante, assidua & diligenti lectione revolvenda esse, monuerimus; restat nunc ut Commentatores & Interpretes maxime idoneos recenseamus. Insignem vero præ reliquis hic usum habent Biblia, sive bibliorum commentaria, Critica, ab Anglis edita, in quibus variorum Commentatorum Philologicorum, qui utilissimi sunt, syntagma est. Horum vero multorumque aliorum Synopsin indefatigabili labore ac rique judicio molitur, & ex parte jam dedit, vir Rever. & Doctiss. Matth. Polus; cujus opus ut multis aliis operibus interitumve dabit, ita vel ipsum solum in hoc scriptorum genere sufficere poterit. Si quis tamen plures vel nosse, vel superaddere velit, laudandus est inter alios interpretes maximopere, à D. Polo certis de causis omissus, Calvinus, quo vix alius est judiciosior. Inter Pontificios palmam tenet, quamvis admodum prolixus, Toftatus, seu Abulensis; nec contemnenda est Lyra glossa ordinaria. Proficuam quoque in Sacra Scriptura navavit operam P. Brugensis. At multorum commentatorum farragine opus non est ei, qui Sacra Biblia & Oeconomiam universæ theologiæ accurate legerit.
units.tr: XXIV. Now at last we shall also name the authors from whom our orator should be trained. Since we have advised that the holy Bible be read again and again, with constant and diligent reading, it remains to list the most suitable commentators and interpreters. Among these the Bible, or the commentaries on the Bible, Critica, published by the English, has a remarkable use above the rest, being a collection of the various philological commentators, which are most useful. Of these, and of many others, Matth. Polus, a reverend and most learned man, has produced a synopsis with tireless labour and sharp judgement, and has already published part of it. His work will put an end to many other works, and it alone may suffice in this kind of writing. If anyone nevertheless wishes to know or add more, the interpreter most to be praised among the others, and omitted by Dr Poli for certain reasons, is Calvin, than whom hardly any is more judicious. Among the Papists the palm is held by Toftatus, or Abulensis, though he is very prolix; nor is the Lyra glossa ordinaria to be despised. Father Brugensis has also laboured profitably on Holy Scripture. But there is no need of a crowd of commentators for one who has read the Holy Bible and the economy of all theology carefully.

units.la: XXV. In Vetus Testamentum, & speciatim in Pentateuchum, optime commentati sunt Munsterus, Fagius, Ainsworthus, similesque. Pentateucho etiam lucem aliquam pro tyronibus fœnerati videmur, in vernacula nostra ad illum commentatione. In Josuam egregie scripsit Masius. In libros Judicum, Samuelis & Regum, Martyr. In Jobum, Mercerus, & in historiam Jobi, Cl. Spanhemius. In Psalmos, Gejerus, & qui Rabbinorum sententias enarrat Viccars in Decaplis. In Proverbia, Mercerus, Cartwrightus, & vernacule Joh. de Brune. In eadem, ut & Ecclesiasten, Gejerus & Cartwrightus. In Canticum, quoad sensum literalem, in brevissimo libello vernaculo, idem Joh. de Brune. Ad Prophetas manuductionis vicem præstare poterit Molinai vates; commentariorum vero, quæ à Cl. Coccejo scripta in eos & reliquos Vet. Novique instrumenti libros, maxima ex parte elaborata sunt. Aliquem etiam fortasse tyronibus usum dabunt, quæ super historias & prophetias Vet. Test. in privatis scholis cum auditoribus calamo communicamus. XXVI. Ad Novum Test. præcipui sunt Calvinus, Erasmus, Beza, Lud. de Dieu, Cappellus, Hammondus. In Euangelia utilis est Walai confarcinatio ex præstantissimis Philologis. Addendæ sunt Ligtfooti Horæ Hebraicæ & Thalmudicæ; & Spanhemii Dubia Euangelica. Inter adversarios acerrimus est Maldonatus. In Acta, præter alios jam dictos commentatus est Strefo; & in epistolas habent hic inde quæ tolli possunt, sunt, Thomas Aquinas & Cajetanus. De Phraseologia vero universi Novi Fœd. consulendus est Joh. Vorstius de Hebraismis, & de Adagiis Novi Testi. In utramque vero Fœd. tum quoad Phraseologiam; tum quoad res ipsas laudandi sunt Glassius, Launæus, Grotius, cujus etiam errores docti sunt, itidemque Bochartus in Hierozoico, sive de animalibus sacris. Insignem quoque usum ad intelligentiam Novi Fœderis habet versionis LXX seniorum cum eo collatio: quæ cum linguæ Græcæ, tum Scripturæ sacræ studiosò commendatissima esse debet.
units.tr: XXV. On the Old Testament, and especially on the Pentateuch, Munsterus, Fagius, Ainsworthus and such like have commented excellently. I seem also to have offered some light to beginners on the Pentateuch in my commentary on it in our vernacular. On Joshua Masius has written outstandingly. On the books of Judges, Samuel and Kings, Martyr. On Job, Mercerus, and on the history of Job, the distinguished Spanheim. On the Psalms, Gejerus; and Viccars in Decaplis, who expounds the opinions of the rabbis. On the Proverbs, Mercerus and Cartwright, and in our vernacular Joh. de Brune. On the same book, as also on Ecclesiastes, Gejerus and Cartwright. On the Canticles, as to the literal sense, in a very short vernacular booklet, the same Joh. de Brune. For the Prophets the Molinaei vates can serve as a guide; but as to commentaries, those written by the distinguished Cocceius on them and on the other books of the Old and New Testament, are for the most part carefully worked out. The lectures on the histories and prophecies of the Old Testament, which I pass on with pen to my hearers in private schools, may perhaps also be of some use to beginners. XXVI. For the New Testament the chief are Calvin, Erasmus, Beza, Lud. de Dieu, Cappellus, Hammond. On the Gospels the patchwork of Walaeus, drawn from the most eminent philologists, is useful. The Hebrew and Talmudic Horae of Lightfoot should be added, and Spanheim's Dubia Evangelica. Among the opponents the most fierce is Maldonatus. On the Acts, besides the others already named, Strefo has commented; and on the epistles there are things here and there which can be left out in Thomas Aquinas and Cajetan. On the phraseology of the whole New Covenant, Joh. Vorstius on Hebraisms and on the proverbs of the New Testament should be consulted. For both covenants, both as to phraseology and as to the matters themselves, Glassius, Launaeus, Grotius are to be praised, though his errors too are instructive; likewise Bochart in his Hierozoicon, or on sacred animals. The version of the Seventy elders with comparison to it also has a remarkable use for understanding the New Testament; and it ought to be most strongly recommended to a student both of the Greek language and of Holy Scripture.

units.la: XXVII. Scriptores alios varii generis quod attinet; illi vel sunt veteres, vel recentiores. Inter Patres Græcos, concionatori utiles, eminet maxime Chrysostomus; inter Latinos, Augustinus, cujus commentaria seu sermones in verba Domini & Apostoli, in Psalmos, similiaque scripta, plurimum optimæ frugis continent. Laudem hic etiam merentur Salvianus, Raimundus Jordanus in Bibliotheca Patrum, Idiota nomine; nunc autem separatim editus. Leonis etiam & Gregorii, Magnorum homiliæ merito laudandæ sunt.
units.tr: XXVII. As for other writers of various kinds, they are either ancient or more recent. Among the Greek Fathers, useful to the preacher, Chrysostom stands out above all; among the Latins, Augustine, whose commentaries or sermons on the words of the Lord and the Apostle, on the Psalms, and similar writings contain a great deal of excellent fruit. Salvian, Raymund Jordan in the Bibliotheca Patrum, under the name Idiota, though now published separately, also deserve praise here. The homilies of Leo and of Gregory, the Great, are rightly to be praised.

units.la: XXVIII. Inter recentiores ex Scholasticis summopere utilis est Summa Thomæ, in prima & secunda secundæ, ut vulgo ajunt, in quibus partibus moralia habet, quæ à barbaris illis terminis separata & rhetorico stylo exornata, bono usui esse possunt, cum egregias sufficiant cogitationes. Ex reliquis Pontificiis laudari solent, Kempis de imitatione Christi, Drexelius & Bellarminus in opusculis; & ad πάθη movenda Granatensis, in omnibus quæ scripsit; & Stella de vanitate mundi, aliisque quæ edidit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Among the more recent scholastics the Summa of Thomas is very useful, in the first and second part of the second part, as people commonly say, in which parts it has the moral matter; separated from those barbarous terms and adorned with rhetorical style, it can be of good use, since it supplies excellent thoughts. Among the other Papists, Kempis, On the Imitation of Christ, Drexelius and Bellarmine in their smaller works are commonly praised; and for stirring the emotions [πάθη], Granatensis in all that he wrote; and Stella, On the Vanity of the World, and the other things he published.

units.la: XXIX. Ex Reformatis, omnium coryphæus est Calvinus, in omnibus suis scriptis: nominatim, in institutionibus lib. III. à capite VI. usque ad X. quibus quinque capitibus, solidiora & præstantiora habet ad praxin pietatis & vitæ regulas facientia; quam in diffusissimis & innumeris practicorum, uti vulgò ajunt, tractatibus conscribillata sunt. Conducunt huc maxime opuscula Erasmi, & Rivius Athenodorensis in operibus suis Theologicis, quæ pathetica sunt. Ex Lutheranis, legi possunt Joh. Gerhardi Meditationes & exercitia pietatis quotidiana; & Joh. Arents scripta Germanica practica. Ex Remonstrantibus Episcopius in Matth. 5. & Joh. 17. quamvis adhibita singulari cautione.
units.tr: XXIX. Among the Reformed, Calvin is the foremost of all, in all his writings; especially in the Institutes, book III, from chapter VI to X. In these five chapters he has the more solid and excellent matter that serves the practice of piety and the rules of life; which is scribbled over in the most diffuse and countless treatises of what are commonly called practical writers. The little works of Erasmus, and Rivius Athenodorensis in his theological works, which are emotionally moving, are very helpful here. Among the Lutherans, Johann Gerhard's Meditations and Daily Exercises of Piety may be read, and Johann Arndt's practical writings in German. Among the Remonstrants, Episcopius on Matthew 5 and John 17, though with singular caution.

units.la: XXX. Inter Belgas commendantur ab hac laude Taffinus, Teellingius, præcipuè in libris, De Noordsche der Godsalicheid/en noodwendig Vertoog: ut & Hoornbeekius in Theologia & tractatibus vernaculis practicis; {a}ticis; item Sprankhufius & Stermontius. De Dieu in tractatu de avaritia. Joh. de Brune in scriptis practicis. Cl. Voëtius in ascetica; & alii passim obvii. Inter Gallos excellunt ex Pontificiorum numero Espinaeus. Ex nostris Molinaeus, ab elegantiis & similitudinibus laudandus; sicut à facundia Dallaeus, à soliditate Mestrezatus, à subtilitate Amyraldus; qui moralia quoque tractat. Inter Anglos, qui plurimos hujus generis auctores habent, laudandus praecipue est Perkinsius, qui ad praxin maximè est idoneus. Ex nuperis eminent Dykii tractatus; varia opuscula Goodwini; ut & Hallii & Christoph. Love, aliiq; plurimi hic non memorandi. Circumspecte autem in iis scriptoribus versandum, qui subinde & perplexioribus regulis ac decisionibus pietatem adstringunt, & magno rigore conscientias valde percellunt, ut vix appareat interdum unde gratiam divinam fideles sibi asserant: unde non semel factum novi, vere pios homines ex lectis iisdem modi tractatibus nimium perturbatos fuisse. Caeterum haec aliaque ejus generis scripta plurima in linguam nostram vernaculam conversa plus quam satis ex suggestu audiuntur; unde saepe loco inventionis & meditationis propriae, iis modi tractatus fuse populo propinantur.
units.tr: XXX. Among the Dutch, Taffin and Teellinck are commended for this praise, especially in the books De Noordsche der Godsalicheid/en noodwendig Vertoog; as also Hoornbeek in his Theology and in his practical vernacular tracts; likewise Sprankhuizen and Stermont. De Dieu in his treatise on avarice. Joh. de Brune in his practical writings. Cl. Voetius in ascetic theology; and others met with everywhere. Among the French, Espinaeus excels from the number of the Papists. From our side Molinaeus is to be praised for his elegance and similes; Dallaeus for his eloquence, Mestrezat for his solidity, Amyraut for his subtlety, who also treats moral matters. Among the English, who have very many authors of this kind, Perkins is to be praised above all, as he is most suited to practice. Among the recent writers the treatises of Dyke stand out; the various little works of Goodwin; as also Hall and Christopher Love, and very many others not to be mentioned here. One must, however, deal cautiously with those writers who now and then bind piety with over-perplexing rules and decisions, and greatly unsettle consciences with severe rigour, so that it sometimes hardly appears on what ground the faithful may claim the grace of God for themselves. I have more than once seen truly pious people greatly disturbed by reading treatises of this sort. Moreover, many such writings, and others of this kind, translated into our vernacular, are heard from the pulpit more than enough; so that these treatises are often served up to the people in place of one's own discovery and meditation.

units.la: XXXI. Magno hic etiam cum fructu legentur auctores, qui de rebus moralibus, licet forte professione non sint Theologi, scripserunt; quales inter multos alios sunt Verulamius. Petrarcha de remediis utriusque fortunae. Charron de la Sagesse. Moulin la paix de l'ame. Aristotelis scripta ethica. Ciceronis officia. Antoninus de seipso. Epicteti Enchiridion. Theophrasti Characteres. Senault l'usage des passions; & de iisdem Cartesius, qui plurima docet non solum utilia Theologo, sed & necessaria. XXXII. Auctores vero illos novus concionator tractare non debet qui integras ediderunt conciones; quales, inter plures, Sibelius, Rudolphus Petri & similes. Propriis potius meditationibus ei incumbendum est; & si quandoque uti illis debeat, scienter & parce faciendum est, sic ut propria iis addat inventa; non vero eos exscribendo totos compilet, aut quasi pontibus asinorum, uti dicitur, abutatur. Utiliorem longe usum hic praestant Concordantiae; ex quibus verborum Scripturae vis optime deprehenditur, & Synonyma atque exempla inde suppeditantur. Inter quas in V. F. ad textum Hebraicum perfectiores sunt illae Buxtorfii; utilissimae quoque sunt ad versionem LXX seniorum illae Conr. Kircheri. Graecae N. Test. probantur quae ab Henrico Stephano & Schmidio sunt editae. Latinae utriusque Fœderis Rob. Stephani extant. Cui vero plurima hic comportare lubeat, conficienda sunt adversaria, seu tituli practici, juxta seriem alphabeticam, seu pro cujusque arbitrio, eodem modo, ut supra visum de theoreticis, in quas eclogas prudenter conjici possunt, quaecunque melioris notae apud auctores deprehenduntur, & usum aliquando in practicis sunt habitura.
units.tr: XXXI. Authors who wrote on moral matters, though perhaps not professed theologians, will also be read here with great profit; such as, among many others, Verulam; Petrarch, On the Remedies for Either Fortune; Charron, On Wisdom; Moulin, The Peace of the Soul; Aristotle's Ethics; Cicero's Duties; Antoninus, To Himself; Epictetus's Handbook; Theophrastus's Characters; Senault, On the Use of the Passions; and Descartes on the same subjects, who teaches much that is not only useful but necessary for a theologian. XXXII. A new preacher ought not to make use of those authors who have published whole sermons, such as, among many, Sibelius, Rudolph Peter and the like. He should rather apply himself to his own meditations; and if at times he must use those authors, he should do so knowingly and sparingly, so as to add his own discoveries to theirs, and not compile them whole by copying them out, or abuse them as "bridges for asses", as the saying goes. Concordances offer a far greater use here, from which the force of the words of Scripture is best grasped, and synonyms and examples are supplied. Among these for the Old Testament, the more complete ones on the Hebrew text are those of Buxtorf; those of Conrad Kircher are also most useful for the version of the Seventy elders. For the Greek New Testament, those published by Henry Stephanus and Schmid are approved. For the Latin of both covenants, Robert Stephanus is available. But whoever is pleased to collect a great deal here should compile notebooks, or practical headings, in alphabetical order, or in whatever order each prefers, in the same way as was suggested above for theoretical matters; into these he may prudently gather whatever selections of better note are found in the authors, and these will sometimes have a use in practical work.

units.la: XXXIII. Explicandae Catechesi utiles erunt Festi Hommii tabula, & D. de Witte in eam explicationes, praemisso tractatu Hoornbeekii de Catechizatione. Plurima etiam egregia congessit in explicatione Catecheseos Gallicae Jac. Crucius. In Orationem Dominicam commentati sunt Arnoldus Cornelii & Richardus Baker. Luculentas etiam nuper in Catechesin scholas nobis reliquit ὁ μακαρίτης Coccejus. Sed nec multis hic commentariis opus est: quas enim ex recenti locorum communium lectione accepit quis cogitationes, huc transferre expedit. Praestat enim illud Theologiae caput, quod in singulis Dominicis traditur, methodo in dogmaticis supra à nobis praescripta tractare; quam operose, analysi verborum Catecheseos inhaerere, iisque anxie se adstringere. Ante omnia cavendum est, ne dogmata catechetica tractentur practice, ut quidam loqui amant, id est dogmatibus ipsis omissis, lusus quidam allegorici similesque ad praxin relati substituantur; quo instituto non aliud brevius compendium est ad excoecandum populum, & sub schemate praxeos notitiam Theologicam, quae unicum praxeos fundamentum est, suffocandam.
units.tr: XXXIII. For explaining the Catechism, Festus Hommius's tables will be useful, and D. de Witte's explanations of them, with Hoornbeek's treatise on catechizing prefixed. Jacob Cruciger has also gathered many excellent things in his explanation of the French Catechism. On the Lord's Prayer, Arnold Cornelii and Richard Baxter have written commentaries. The late Coccejus also left us brilliant lectures on the Catechism. But there is no need for many commentaries here. It is worth transferring to this place the thoughts one has gathered from a recent reading of the commonplaces. It is better to treat the head of theology that is taught on each Lord's Day by the method we prescribed above for dogmatics, than to labour over an analysis of the words of the Catechism and bind oneself anxiously to them. Above all, one must take care not to handle catechetical doctrines "practically," as some like to say, that is, with the doctrines themselves left out and allegorical games and similar things put in their place as applied to practice. This method is the shortest route to blinding the people, and to smothering under the appearance of practice the theological knowledge, which is the sole foundation of practice.

units.la: XXXIV. In passionem sacram, praeter Euangeliorum interpretes, legendi sunt Beza, Joh. Martinius, Joh. Gerhardus, Merillus. Ex Pontificiis hisce addi posset Stella.
units.tr: XXXIV. For the sacred passion, besides the interpreters of the Gospels, one should read Beza, John Martinius, John Gerhard, Merrill. From among the Papists, Stella could be added.

units.la: XXXV. In typos Veteris Fæd. commentatus est Daniel Sachsius. Nos quoque eos qui in Pentateucho occurrunt, prosecuti sumus. In Dominicalia extant Sculteti Idea. Matthias Martinius. Chemnitius. Geldenhaurius & commentatores alii qui harmoniam Euangelicam enarrarunt. Textus autem illi, quantum fieri potest, singuli absolvendi, ne divellantur aut extrahantur; discidium enim illud vix permittit scopus textuum.
units.tr: XXXV. On the types of the Old Testament, Daniel Sachsius has written a commentary. We too have pursued those which occur in the Pentateuch. On the Sunday texts there are Scultetus's Idea, Matthias Martinius, Chemnitz, Geldenhauer, and other commentators who have expounded the Gospel harmony. These texts should each be treated in full, as far as possible, so that they are not torn apart or dragged out; for the scope of the texts hardly permits that division.

units.la: XXXVI. Commodum hic non exiguum dabit, si quis primis ministerii annis, textus Cathecheticos, una cum Dominicalibus tractare susceperit, ut iis absolutis leviores deinceps accidant labores cum Catecheticae conciones annuatim recurrant; Dominicales autem post aliquot annorum intervallum subinde repeti possint; nonnunquam quoque in subitaneis & inopinatis casibus, temporisque defectu. Cae-teteroquin pericopæ hæ non quovis anno in orbem repetendæ sunt; quod & concionatori & auditoribus nocivum esset. Prudentiæ etiam fuerit, hisce textibus pertractatis, singularum virtutum & vitiorum icones, modo quis iis maturus sit, ex auctoribus supra memoratis aliisque deformare; quod magni circa moralia & praxin usus est, & late admodum se diffundit, & singulare in ministerii concionumque laboribus exantlandis adjumentum præstat. Hisce vero ubi quis defunctus fuerit, ad particulares textus libros aut epistolas sacræ scripturæ progrediendum est.
units.tr: XXXVI. It will be of no small advantage if someone, in the first years of his ministry, undertakes to handle the catechetical texts together with the Sunday texts. Once these are finished, the later labours will be lighter, since the catechetical sermons recur every year. The Sunday texts may be repeated from time to time after an interval of some years, and sometimes also in sudden and unexpected cases, or when time is short. Otherwise these pericopes should not be repeated in rotation every year; that would harm both the preacher and the hearers. It will also be prudent, once these texts have been treated, to portray the images of the individual virtues and vices, provided one is mature enough for it, drawing on the authors mentioned above and others. This is of great use for morals and practice, reaches very widely, and gives a singular aid in bearing the labours of the ministry and of preaching. When one has finished with these, one should go on to the particular books or epistles of Holy Scripture.

units.la: XXXVII. Cæteroquin ad ministerii praxin & prudentiam Ecclesiasticam, quanta ex libris illa hauriri potest, ne quis plane rudis accedat, in antecessum legendus erit Wilh. Zepperi tractatus de Politia Ecclesiastica. Sandis Relatio de statu Ecclesiæ. Acontius de Stratagematis Satanæ, quamvis non nisi judicio probe allato. Ministris etiam omnibus utilis erit Gregorius Magnus de cura Pastorali, & Oliveris Bowles Pastor Euangelicus. Iisque, quibus in Belgio ministerium obtingit, assuescendum est præterea Actis & post-actis Synodi Nationalis Dordracena, Canonibus Ecclesiasticis; sub titulo, De Kerken-order van Nederlandt, cui, propter casus mixtos adjungi debent Statuta Politica, vulgo dicta, De Politijte Ordonnantien. Quin & ad plenioreim Theologiæ, & regiminis Ecclesiastici cognitionem & peritiam multum conferret, Jurisprudentia aliquem haurire gustum: quem in finem evolvendum est, tum jus publicum, de quo Grotius in præclaro opere de Jure belli & pacis; tum jus Romanum civile, in Institutionibus Juris, cum Pacii aut brevioribus Vinnii Notis; & in ipso corpore Juris, titulis illis qui de rebus Ecclesiasticis agunt; tum jus Canonicum, cujus compendium dedit Corvinus. Ante omnia huc pertinent varii Canones Ecclesiastici Veteris Ecclesiæ, de quibus videndus Justellus, aliique. XXXVIII. Usum studii theologici in ministerio sacro quod concernit, tenendum ante omnia, ne occasione ministerii à studiis divortium fiat; ut multis in more est, quibus eo usque studia utcunque cordi sunt, donec eorum subsidio examinum rigorem sustinuerunt & in ministrorum censum relati sunt. Quo voto potiti mox ad alia deflectunt; hi ad rem familiarem curandam; alii ad res agendas; alii ad pejora; libris longum valere jussis. Robustiore vero affectu studia sacra complectitur genuinus Theologiæ consecraneus. Qui per omnem vitam castissimo cœlestis hujus virginis amore ducitur, sibi ipsi semper instans, mentemque suâ ulterius excolere satagens; quin & sacram hanc sapientiam ita semper ante oculos & in deliciis habens, ut nihil uspiam legat aut observet, quod non ad studii hujus incrementum ac ornamentum confestim referat; eo intentius talentorum sibi concreditorum augmentum urgens, quo uberioribus fœnoris hujus proventibus se ditatum onustumque quotidie deprehendit.
units.tr: XXXVII. Otherwise, for the practice of the ministry and ecclesiastical prudence, so far as it can be drawn from books, and so that no one comes to it entirely unskilled, the following should be read in advance: Wilhelm Zepper's treatise on Church Polity; Sandys's Relation on the state of the Church; Acontius on Satan's Stratagems, though only with sound judgment applied. Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care and Oliver Bowles's Evangelical Pastor will also be useful to all ministers. Those to whom the ministry falls in Belgium should further become familiar with the Acts and post-Acts of the National Synod of Dort and the Church Canons, under the title De Kerken-order van Nederlandt, to which, because of mixed cases, the political statutes commonly called De Politijke Ordonnantien should be added. Indeed, for fuller knowledge and skill in theology and church government, it would also greatly help to acquire some taste for jurisprudence. To that end one should work through the public law, on which Grotius wrote in his excellent work On the Law of War and Peace; the Roman civil law, in the Institutes of Law, with Pacius or the shorter Notes of Vinnius; and in the body of the law itself, those titles which deal with ecclesiastical affairs; and the canon law, of which Corvinus gave a compendium. Above all, the various Canons of the Ancient Church belong here, on which see Justellus and others. XXXVIII. As far as the use of theological study in the sacred ministry is concerned, it must be held above all that the ministry should not bring about a divorce from study, as happens with many, who care for their studies only so far as they have withstood the rigour of the examinations and been counted among the ministers. Once they have obtained this wish, they soon turn aside to other things: some to looking after family affairs, others to business, others to worse things, having bidden books a long farewell. The genuine devotee of theology, however, embraces ssacred studies with a more robust affection. He is led through his whole life by a most chaste love for this heavenly maiden, always pressing on himself and striving to cultivate his mind further. Indeed, he keeps this sacred wisdom always before his eyes and among his delights, so that he reads or observes nothing anywhere that he does not at once refer to the growth and adornment of this study. He presses the increase of the talents committed to him all the more eagerly, the more he finds himself daily enriched and laden with the abundant returns of this interest.

units.la: XXXIX. Qualem se porro in ipso ministerio exhibere debeat, vivis coloribus delineavit Apostolus in sanctis ad Timotheum & Titum Epistolis; ex quibus optandum esset ut veri ministri Euangelii typum imbibant omnes, qui sacro isti muneri se consecravere.
units.tr: XXXIX. How he ought to conduct himself in the ministry itself the Apostle has portrayed in lively colours in his holy Epistles to Timothy and Titus. From these, it is to be wished that all who have dedicated themselves to this sacred office should imbibe the pattern of the true minister of the Gospel.

units.la: Præcipuè vero in ipso ministerio agendum est pie, prudenter & modestè. Pie obeundum est ministerium, ex amore nimirum Christi supremi Pastoris; juxta illud Domini ad Petrum: Simon Jona fili amasne me? Pasce oves meas. Joh. 21. Quare fideliter explenda sunt omnia ministerii officia, nocte & interdiu hominum animabus invigilando, monendo, carpendo, consolando omnes, præcipue ægros, viduas, orphanos, infirmos, absque majorum adulatione & minimorum ullo contemptu. Necessarium enim est animarum Pastori, ut sit ἐυσπλαγχνος & συμπαθὴς, gregisque sui onera mutua συμπαθείᾳ in se suscipiat. Juxta illud quod de Ambrosio fertur: Facere cum putes cum jacentibus, lachrymari cum lachrymantibus, gemere cum gementibus: vir clementissimus in omnem formam se transformavit, ut homines Diaboli faucibus ereptos Christo lucrifaceret. In pietate vero non captanda est externa illius facies, neque ea collocanda in γυμνασίᾳ σωματικῇ corporali exercitio; neque anxie intra ambitum multarum regularum cogenda est. Vera enim pietatis praxis est amor Dei & proximi, quem totum absolvit studium Dei glorificandi in omnibus; cum bona quandoque cogitatio, optima pietas sit; nec eam tot ambagibus regulisque tradiderunt Prophetæ & Apostoli, sed simpliciter & efficaciter, in fide & charitate, opereque ipso exhibuerunt: ut simplex illa & innocua pietatis praxis, non tot cautis callidisque canonibus sit circumscribenda, nec collocanda in artificiosa methodo, ordine, anxiis divisionibus & definitionibus, novis conscientiæ casibus, infinita signorum, motivorum & mediorum supellectile, curiosa assignatione operum pietatis in singulas hebdomadas, dies, & tantum non horas, ut Pontificiorum casuistas post se longo intervallo relinquere fere videantur. Qui, ut habet alicubi Greg. Nazianzenus, τεχνολογεῖ verius, quam θεολογεῖ, quique pietatem in artem convertunt, similemque reddunt arbori, foliorum magis, quam fructuum feraci; utpote à quibus aliquan-do
units.tr: Above all, in the ministry itself one must act piously, prudently and modestly. Piously the ministry must be discharged, out of love for Christ the supreme Shepherd, namely; according to the Lord's word to Peter: "Simon, son of Jonas, do you love me? Feed my sheep." John 21. Therefore all the duties of the ministry must be faithfully fulfilled, watching over men's souls night and day, admonishing, rebuking, and comforting all, especially the sick, widows, orphans and the infirm, without flattering the great and without contempt for the least. For it is necessary for the shepherd of souls to be compassionate and sympathetic, and to take upon himself the burdens of his flock by mutual sympathy. As is related of Ambrose: "To think yourself one with those who lie low, to weep with those who weep, to groan with those who groan: that most merciful man transformed himself into every shape, so that he might win for Christ men snatched from the jaws of the Devil." In piety, however, its outward face is not to be sought, nor is it to be placed in bodily exercise, nor anxiously forced within the bounds of many rules. For the true practice of piety is the love of God and neighbour, which is wholly accomplished by the zeal to glorify God in all things; a good thought is sometimes the best piety. Nor did the Prophets and Apostles hand it down with so many circumlocutions and rules, but presented it simply and effectively, in faith and love, and in the deed itself. So this simple and harmless practice of piety should not be hemmed in by so many cautious and crafty canons, nor placed in an artificial method, in order, anxious divisions and definitions, novel cases of conscience, an infinite stock of signs, motives and means, and a curious assignment of works of piety to each week, each day, and almost each hour. In this way they seem to leave the casuists of the Papists far behind. These men, as Gregory Nazianzen says somewhere, practise technology rather than theology [τεχνολογεῖ rather than θεολογεῖ], and turn piety into an art, making it like a tree more fertile in leaves than in fruit, since from them sometimes

units.la: {y} in quo ag-gendum, pie, do pietatis prora & puppis fere magis collocatur in eo, quod multum de pietate loquantur, disputent, scribant, magnumque ejus zelum præ se ferant, aliosque infra se contemnant, quam quod reapse & ipso facto illam exprimant, fructusque illos Spiritus sancti Gal. 5:22. recensitos, oslendant.
units.tr: The prow and stern of piety is placed, in this, that people talk much about piety, dispute about it, write about it, show off great zeal for it, and despise others beneath them, rather than actually expressing it in deed and showing forth those fruits of the Holy Spirit listed in Gal. 5:22.

units.la: XL. Prudentia quoque in ministro Euangelii maxime requiritur, ut inter solida & inania; pretiosum & vile; veritatem & speciem; τὰ βαρύτερα ᾗ νόμου, Matth. 23:23. & leviora rite discernat; ut sine conviciis, affectibus, aliisque carnis consiliariis, tanquam Dei nomine omnia agat; ut virtutem recte inculcet, vitia graviter, serio & efficaciter reprehendat; canis sit nec mutus nec mordax, & à nimia carpendi licentia abstineat, quam plerunque superbia aliqua comitatur: quare ne multi fimus magistri. Jac. 3:1. Et divinus sæpe videtur zelus, qui tamen revera sæpe nihil aliud est quam acrioris sanguinis ebullitio, & magisterii usurpatio; cui malo si quis obnoxius est, dicta sua omnia habet pro oraculis, omnesque motus & impetus suos pro dictamine juris divini; & primum aliis, deinde etiam sibi ipsi persuadet, vera esse, quæ pro captu suo dicit, nihilque illi pronius est quam dissentientes tanquam carnales, irregenitos, Spiritu carentes, profanos, imo Atheos notare. Longe vero latius & efficacius est, argumentis ex fundamento & ipsa rei veritate deductis, virtutem persuadere, atque ejus ideam auditori delineare, amoremque illius ipsi conciliare; quam acerrimis invectivis, criminationibus & conviciis, peccati horrorem & metum, quin sæpe dicentis odium, alicui ingerere: unde etiam Servator rarissimis increpationibus usus est, nedum conviciis, nisi quando detestandam Pharisæorum hypocrisin acrius perstringeret; cæteroquin virtutis amorem invictis potius rationibus inculcavit, & se ipsum præcipue in exemplum proposuit.
units.tr: XL. Prudence is also especially required in a minister of the Gospel, so that he rightly distinguishes between solid and empty things, the precious and the worthless, truth and show, and the weightier matters of the law [τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου] and the lighter ones (Matt. 23:23). He should act in all things without reproaches, passions, and other counsellors of the flesh, as if in God's name. He should urge virtue rightly and rebuke vices gravely, seriously, and effectively. He should be a watchdog, neither mute nor biting, and refrain from an excessive license to find fault, which is usually accompanied by some pride. Hence: Not many of you should become teachers (Jas. 3:1). Zeal often seems divine, yet in truth it is often nothing but the boiling over of hotter blood and the usurpation of the teacher's office. If someone is prone to this evil, he regards all his own sayings as oracles and all his impulses as the dictates of divine law. He persuades first others and then himself that whatever he says according to his own understanding is true, and nothing comes more readily to him than to brand dissenters as carnal, unregenerate, lacking the Spirit, profane, or even atheists. Far more widely and effectively, however, is virtue persuaded, and its idea outlined for the hearer, and love for it won over, by arguments drawn from the foundation and from the very truth of the matter, than by forcing upon someone a horror and fear of sin, or even often hatred of the speaker, through the bitterest invectives, accusations, and abuse. Hence the Saviour too used very rare rebukes, let alone abuse, except when he sharply exposed the detestable hypocrisy of the Pharisees. Otherwise he inculcated the love of virtue by unanswerable arguments, and he set himself forward above all as an example.

units.la: XLI. Caute cum primis versandum est circa res Politicas, quæque ad Magistratus civiles pertinent. Circa quas hæc observanda est regula quod negotia omnia humana, adeoque etiam Politica, considerari possint singula vel in se ipsis, secundum regulas suæ artis vel secundum nexum suum & dependentiam à lege divina, quæ omnis conscientiæ regula est. Priori respectu ad Theologiam non spectant, & extra sphæram ejus versantur, uti ajunt. Sic in navigatione major fides habenda nauclero quam Paulo, nisi quatenus illi revelatio aliqua fuerit facta. Act. 27. Excessuum vero & defectuum, qui in variis hisce rebus committuntur, quantum in præjudicium Dei ejusque legis tendunt, cognitio ad Theologum pertinet; atque eatenus illis occurrere ne eveniant, & si evenerint carpere, officium Theologi est. Sic ponderum, mensurarum, usurae constitutio ad Magistratus pertinet; si vero de earum iniquitate omnibus constet, & res manifesta sit; admonendi & carpendi sunt Magistratus. Sic enim scopus & lances judicii Dei sunt. Prov. 16:11. Haud facile vero in rebus Politicis quicquam iniquum judicandum est, cum arcana plerunque sit earum ratio; quam ut alii sciant, saepe nec expedit, nec necesse est; & actionum civilium natura in plurimis dependeat a circumstantiis quibusdam vulgo non cognitis; quare species externa & prima frons in hisce facile fallit; adeoque nisi de rei veritate probe & publice constet, publice etiam magistratuum actiones perstringendae non sunt; & si magnopere id fieri res flagitet, circumspecte omnique cum cura & reverentia, in illo negotio versandum est; ut neque conscientiae, neque pietati, neque etiam aedificationi Ecclesiae intercedatur, aut detrimentum aliquod reipublicae inferatur, populoque occasio detur in Magistratum insurgendi; cum ille natura sua proclivis sit ad infectandum vitia superiorum potius, quam sua. Reipublicae ergo gubernatio Magistratui in solidum relinquenda est, & quantum fieri potest privatim potius reprehendendus est, quam publice: nisi quod publice semper generatim monendus veniat, ne quid committat quod cum detrimento gloriae Dei & salutis reipublicae ac Ecclesiae conjunctum sit. Omnium exemplorum instar nobis esse potest Leicestriana in patria nostra factio superioris seculi, cujus externa tantaque pietate larvata species plurimis, isque primiceriis, Theologis imposuit, isque in legitimos Magistratus concitatis, deinceps, fraude detecta, damno & exitio fuit.
units.tr: XLI. Above all one must deal cautiously with political matters, and whatever pertains to the civil magistrates. In regard to these the following rule is to be observed: all human affairs, and therefore also political ones, can be considered either singly in themselves, according to the rules of their own art, or in their connection and dependence on the divine law, which is the rule of every conscience. In the former respect they do not belong to theology and lie outside its sphere, as people say. Thus in navigation greater trust is to be placed in the pilot than in Paul, unless some revelation had been made to him (Acts 27). But the knowledge of the excesses and defects committed in these various matters, insofar as they tend to the prejudice of God and his law, belongs to the theologian; and it is the theologian's duty to meet these so that they do not occur, and, if they do occur, to censure them. Thus the fixing of weights, measures, and interest belongs to the magistrate; but if it is clear to all that they are unjust and the matter is manifest, the magistrates are to be admonished and censured. For the balances and scales of judgment are of the Lord (Prov. 16:11). Yet in political matters nothing should readily be judged unjust, since the reason for them is usually hidden; and it is often neither expedient nor necessary that others know it. Moreover, the nature of civil actions in most cases depends on certain circumstances not commonly known, so the outward appearance and first impression easily deceive in these matters. Therefore, unless the truth of the matter is established thoroughly and openly, the actions of magistrates must not be publicly assailed. And if the matter urgently requires it, one must proceed circumspectly and with all care and reverence, so that neither conscience, nor piety, nor even the edification of the Church is harmed, nor any detriment is done to the commonwealth, nor an occasion given to the people to rise against the magistrate, since the people by nature are more inclined to attack the vices of their superiors than their own. The government of the commonwealth, therefore, is to be left wholly to the magistrate, and, as far as possible, he is to be rebuked privately rather than publicly; except that he should always be warned publicly in general terms not to commit anything connected with detriment to the glory of God and the salvation of the commonwealth and the Church. As an example of all such cases, the Leicestrian faction in our country in the last century can serve us: its outward and great show of piety deceived many, and those chief ones among the theologians, and, once stirred up against the lawful magistrates, afterwards, when the fraud was detected, it became a loss and a ruin.

units.la: XLII. Cerimonia & externum Ecclesiae regimen, non habenda sunt pro essentialibus, quatenus scilicet in verbo Dei determinata non sunt; adeoque in cerimoniarum varietate una tamen fides esse potest; quapropter moribus & statutis singularum Ecclesiarum obsequendum est; neque condemnandi facile alii, qui in talibus a nobis discrepant. Aurea hic erat Ambrosii regula, quam Monicae, Augustini matri, de jejunio quod Romae die Sabbati, Mediolani non item observabatur, consulenti, praescribebat hisce verbis: Se nihil docere posse, nisi quod ipse faceret, quia si melius nosset, id potius observaret. addebat; Romam ubi veneris, morem ejus serva, si cuiquam non vis scandalo esse, nec quenquam tibi. Quam sententiam etiam atque etiam cogitans Augustinus, ita semper habuit, tanquam eam caelesti oraculo susceperit. Quomodo circa indifferentes? susceperit.Factiones ergo nunquam faciat aut foveat noster, sed paci & togæ potius consilia sua societ, quàm bello aut sago; quin potius quàm res in nervum erumpat & Ecclesia in partes scindatur subeat martyrium pacis. Partibus jam diffidentibus ubi supervenit, si quidem salva veritate & conscientia possit, neutri parti se addicat, neque illarum litibus se immisceat, sed ιφηνευτικῶς & arbitrum utrimque se præstet: ita enim & valebit maximè apud utrosque, & desideratum pacis fructum consequetur citius.
units.tr: XLII. Ceremonies and the external government of the Church are not to be held as essentials, insofar as they are not determined in the Word of God. Hence, amid the variety of ceremonies, there can nevertheless be one faith; therefore one must comply with the customs and statutes of the individual Churches, and others who differ from us in such matters are not to be easily condemned. The golden rule here was that of Ambrose, who, when Monica, the mother of Augustine, consulted him about fasting, which was observed at Rome on Saturday but not at Milan, prescribed in these words: he could teach nothing except what he himself did, because if he knew something better, he would rather observe that. He added: When you come to Rome, keep its custom, if you do not wish to be a scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you. Augustine, thinking on this saying again and again, always held it as if he had received it from a heavenly oracle. How is this to apply to indifferent matters? he had received it. Therefore let ours never make or foster factions, but rather associate his counsels with peace and the gown rather than with war or the soldier's cloak; indeed, rather than let matters break out into a crisis and the Church be split into parties, let him undergo a martyrdom of peace. When he comes upon parties already distrustful of each other, if he can do so with truth and conscience preserved, let him attach himself to neither side, nor mix himself in their quarrels, but show himself an arbiter [ιφηνευτικῶς] to both. For in this way he will be most influential with both, and will more quickly attain the desired fruit of peace.

units.la: XLIII. Agendum denique modeste, sine omni typho & fastu, nec appetendo cathedras majores; quæ multorum juniorum ministrorum sive impatientia, sive ambitio est: nedum illas malis artibus & prensationibus ambiendo; cum quisque suo se modulo suoque pede metiri debeat, & suo loco contentus esse, reputando secum summam esse dignitatem, satisque honoris servum esse Christi; de magnis autem gregibus & villicationibus, magnam etiam reddendam esse rationem; præsertim cum fidelem esse in minimo, tantundem sit coram Domino, ac fidelem esse in magno: adeoque nullus proprio suffragio alius Ecclesiæ Episcopum se delignare debet; sed laborandum est in angulo vineæ Domini, in quem singulos extrudere ipsi placuerit.
units.tr: XLIII. Finally, one must act modestly, without any conceit or arrogance, and without seeking higher chairs, which is the impatience or ambition of many younger ministers; still less should one court them by bad arts and canvassing. Each person must measure himself by his own measure and his own foot, and be content with his own place, reckoning with himself that the highest dignity and enough honour is to be a servant of Christ. Yet for great flocks and stewardships a great account will also have to be rendered; especially since to be faithful in the least is just as much before the Lord as to be faithful in the great. Therefore no one should by his own vote designate himself as bishop of another Church; rather he must labour in the corner of the Lord's vineyard into which it has pleased him to thrust each one.

units.la: XLIV. Paucis itaque hisce consilium nostrum de studiis Theologicis, tum Theoreticis, tum Practicis rudi penicillo delineavimus; quod colophonis loco paucis regulis concludemus. I. Ut quisque naturæ suæ, geniique ductum & femina sequatur, in his aut illis studii hujus partibus majori opera excolendis, quia non omnia possumus omnes. II. Ut credat libris paucissimis opus esse ad bonam mentem, neque in multos se diffundat, præcipue in studio Academico. Nec nos tam frequenti numero eos enumeravimus, ac si omnibus semper opus esset. Absit. Sed ut dignoscì queant; cum in bonorum librorum usu & discretione, aliqua etiam eruditionis pars sita sit. Præstantissimos & maximè necessarios, suisque quoque elogiis subinde insignivimus, & ab aliis discrevimus; à pluribus vero, usu nobis compertis, citandis, quod facillimo negotio potueramus, data opera abstinuimus, cum usus reliquos suppeditaturus sit; quin & unus auctor alium sæpe indicet.
units.tr: XLIV. Thus, in these few words, we have sketched with a rough brush our plan concerning theological studies, both theoretical and practical; and by way of a colophon we will conclude with a few rules. I. Each person should follow the bent and the bias of his own nature and talent, devoting greater effort to cultivating this or that part of this study, since we cannot all do everything. II. Let him believe that very few books are needed for a good mind, and let him not spread himself across many, especially in academic study. We have not listed so many of them as if there were always need of all of them. Far be it. But so that they may be distinguished, since part of learning consists in the use and discernment of good books, we have singled out the most excellent and most necessary ones, and marked them with their own commendations, and set them apart from others. Of the rest, which we know from experience, we have deliberately refrained from citing, though we could easily have done so; the remaining ones will be supplied by use, and indeed one author often points to another.

units.la: XLV. III. Si libri non sint nimium prolixi, horum præstantiores legendi sunt integri, ut rerum connexio & plena intelligentia eo rectius percipiatur: alii autem sive minus necessarii, sive nimis prolixi, per capita & titulos consuli possunt; ex indicibus vero sapiendum non est. IV. Nec multa legenda sunt, sed multum; repetendique sunt subinde auctores praestantiores, antehac lecti. Praecipue vero cum lectione diligens conjungenda est ruminatio & prudens meditatio, ne in infinitum divagetur lectio, & plura legantur, quàm digeri possint. Praestat enim ingenium excolere, quàm memoriam. Prae omnibus, meditationibus incumbant illi, quibus satis foecundum est proprium ingenium. Caeteris magis secundae sunt reliquae sapientiae partes, qui alienos adoptare foetus, & ex aliis magistris sapere necesse habeant.
units.tr: XLV. III. If the books are not too lengthy, the more excellent of them should be read entire, so that the connection of the matters and full understanding may be grasped more rightly. Others, either less necessary or too lengthy, may be consulted by chapters and titles, but one should not rely on indexes. IV. One should read not many things, but much, and the more excellent authors already read should be repeated from time to time. Especially with diligent reading must be joined rumination and prudent meditation, so that reading does not wander endlessly and more is read than can be digested. For it is better to cultivate the understanding than the memory. Above all, let those devote themselves to meditations who have a sufficiently fruitful natural talent of their own. For the rest, the remaining parts of wisdom are more suitable, for those who must adopt other people's offspring and be wise through other teachers.

units.la: XLVI. v. Assiduitate magis utendum, quam vehementia, aut immodicis laboribus, quippe qui corpori animoque simul nocent. vi. Cavendum à praecipitantia, nec non à desultoriis studiis. Ordine studendum est, qui mater est memoriae & judicii, secundùm illud:
units.tr: XLVI. (v.) We should rely on steady application rather than on vehemence or excessive labour, which harm body and mind alike. (vi.) We must beware of haste, and likewise of scattered, restless studies. We must study in an orderly way, which is the mother of memory and judgment, according to the saying:

units.la: Ordine fac studeas, & bene doctus eris.
units.tr: Study in an orderly way, and you will be well taught.

units.la: Horis alligari velle, servile quiddam sapit, nisi in quibusdam forte ingeniis, quae regulis ita se adstringi patiuntur; cum alia plerunque sint liberiora, quibus noceas, si intra tempus aut certam ejusmodi methodum ea cogere velis. vii. Praecipue vero captanda sunt doctorum virorum colloquia, sermones, & recitationes publicae, quae magis elaboratae sunt quam privatae ipsorum scholae, & ex quibus una saepe hora plus profeceris, & de pluribus utilius monearis, quàm domi magno & irrito saepenumero conatu, multoque tempore vix acquisiveris.
units.tr: To wish to be bound to fixed hours savours of slavery, except perhaps in certain minds that allow themselves to be confined by such rules; for other minds are for the most part freer, and you would harm them if you tried to force them into a set time or some such method. (vii.) Above all, we should seek out the conversations, lectures and public recitations of learned men, which are more carefully prepared than their private lessons, and from which one hour often profits you more, and gives you more useful counsel on many matters, than you would gain with great and often fruitless effort at home, and with much time spent to scarcely any purpose.

units.la: XLVII. Summa igitur omnium huc redit: ingenium commodum, judicium non ineptum, methodus prudens, diligentia cauta, & bonus magister, perfectum discipulum, magnumque saepe virum facere possunt; praesertim si in tanta librorum multitudine & vitae brevitate, propter quam per omnia ire non licet, delectus rerum & librorum habeatur, ut optima tantum legantur, & per inutilia falsaque, quae ubique occurrent, ita transeatur, ut ex falso in verum emergatur; cum plerunque non veniamus ad veritatem, nisi per errores ex quibus ipsis in veritate proficiendum est. Longe tamen majus & praestantius est omni doctrina & eruditione, pium honestumque esse virum, nec tam ingenio valere, quam eo bene uti & bonae menti semper litare.
units.tr: XLVII. The sum of everything, then, comes to this: a good natural ability, a sound judgment, a prudent method, careful diligence, and a good teacher can often make a perfect student and a great man. This holds especially if, given the great multitude of books and the brevity of life, which does not permit us to go through everything, a selection of subjects and books is made, so that only the best are read, and one passes over the useless and false things that will meet us everywhere in such a way that one rises from error to truth; for we generally do not reach the truth except through errors, from which we must make progress toward the truth. Yet far greater and more excellent than all learning and erudition is to be a pious and honourable man, not so much to be strong in talent as to use it well and always to offer sacrifice to a good mind.

units.la: XLVIII. Consilium suggestimus, quod sequi vel rejicere vestri est arbitrii; ego ex affectu prompsi, quo vos & studia vestra prosequor; ut vel hac ratione ea, in isto multorum torpore & frigore, excitarem: quae si hinc promoveri sentiatis, Deo, cui omnis debetur honos & gratiarum actio, gratias agite.
units.tr: XLVIII. I have put forward this counsel, which it is for you to follow or reject as you judge; I have offered it out of the affection with which I regard you and your studies, so that by this means at least I might stir them up, in the midst of so much torpor and coldness among many. If you perceive that they are advanced by this, give thanks to God, to whom all honour and thanksgiving is due.
